hed: Libbie Mugrabi’s Hamptons mansion speeds to rare court-ordered auction after failing to sell for $25M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
If at first you don’t succeed, try, try — and try again.
SocialiteLibbie Mugrabi’s East End mansionis scheduled to be auctioned off on the steps of Southampton Town Hall next month following failed Hail Mary attempts to sell it through a conventional listing — and in the kind of public spectacle the haute classes of the Hamptons really hate.
The court-ordered sale, with bidding starting at $11 million, is set for Aug. 28. It traces its origin to lawsuits stemming from a $3.5 million loan Mugrabi took out on her 486 Middle Line Highway compound and admittedly never paid.
The auction of the 7-acre Bridgehampton compound follows Mugrabi’s failed attempts to get back the loan amount, and much more, by selling the estate for its original May list price of $25 million. Not long after that, the asking price lowered to $19 million after two quick price cuts.
Bidders on the property must pay in cash, take the property as-is and put down at least $2 million as a deposit, according to the auction’s marketing materials.
Mugrabi gotthe 10,687-square-foot Bridgehampton spread as part ofher $100 million divorce settlementwith billionaire art collectorDavid Mugrabifive years ago. The split, called one of the nastiest ever in New York, featured an array of accusations, including the pair physically fighting over a $500,000 Keith Haring sculpture.
Mugrabi’s lender agreed to go the auction route rather than seize the property as long as it sold by Aug. 25, with a chunk of the proceeds going to pay off the loan and associated penalties. The accord came after Mugrabi and her attorney vehemently protested the lender buying the property last year for $500 at a Zoom auction, at which it was the only bidder.
With the sale deadline approaching and no buyers in sight, the lender, affiliated with REO Assets of America, Great Neck, N.Y., is preparing to pull the trigger on the auction — and on Friday put in place the legal machination to do so in the form of the court-ordered sale. This followed obtaining the court’s authorization to conduct the sale, enforcing many legal conditions Mugrabi agreed to try and sell the home herself, and reinforcing barriers that prevent her from further litigation and refusing to leave the home.
The prospective buyers will make their offers “right on the steps” of town hall, said Daniel Russo, a former Suffolk County assistant district attorney who is now a personal injury lawyer. Russo is the auction’s court appointed “referee,” a term for the person who oversees auctions of this type.
The auction would show a rarely seen side of the privacy-obsessed Hamptons, with prospective bidders trundling into the heart of the village for a bidding session where, if tradition holds, Russo will call out the terms of the sale to the prospective buyers, and they will respond with their offers. All this just a stone’s throw from the well-heeled residents and summer visitors who are dining or shopping on Main Street.
Indeed, a public auction for a luxury address is extremely uncommon in the Hamptons, where properties, if they do have to be disposed of, generally go through private services that use discreet invite-only approaches to heavily vetted buyers, often at the properties themselves.
Daniel Gale Sotheby’s International Realty holds the home sale listing.
While Russo serves as auctioneer, lenders also typically hire a service to manage the voluminous administrative work that goes on behind the scenes. Auction.com will handle those tasks as a webservice that also does public, court ordered sales in New York. Daniel Gale realtor Orit Ofir, who holds the original sale listing, is now doing double duty as Auction.com’s point of contact, the site’s marketing materials indicate.
Who gets the lion’s share of auction’s proceeds is not clear. Mugrabi’s attorney, Claude Castro of Castro Law Group, told The Post last month that Mugrabi is holding the deed until a sale is complete. The court order for the auction came through the lender’s attorney, Vallely Mitola Ryan, case filings show.
Castro, who told the court in May 2025 the property was worth “between $10 million and $12 million,” did not return The Post’s request for comment on the auction. Mugrabi, as well as listing agents at Daniel Gale Sotheby’s International, also did not respond.
The Bridgehampton estate was still listed for sale at $19 million as of Sunday evening. It is very unlikely that a buyer will step in at that amount with the property coming to auction for almost 50% less.
“Historically, a court-ordered auction throws a major wrench into someone getting more equity out of the sale,” said attorney Steven Wallace of Wallace Law, who isn’t involved in this proceeding, and whose real estate practice has focused on foreclosures and distressed assets in New York for the past 26 years.

hed: Restored 1678 New England estate offers an ‘authentic’ glimpse into the past
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An “irreplaceable opportunity” to buy a historical First Period estate with its own ell and an antique barn has been brought to themarket in Massachusetts, where it is offering an “authentic glimpse into earlyNew England life,” as well as the chance to take on stewardship of one of the country’s oldest surviving homes.
The Gloucester, MA, residence, which has been listed for $1.25 million, was originally built in 1678—however, additional structures have been added to the 2.4-acre parcel in the years since.
Still, the meticulously preserved four-bedroom abode, which is known as theWilliam Haskell House, is still full of charm and character.
“The original house was built in the late 1600s and has stood the test of time over the years,” says listing agent Michael Selbst of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty. “It’s still standing as it were when it was built nearly 350 years ago.”
The property is named after its original owner, who harvested salt hay from the nearby tidal marshes more than three centuries ago.
Selbst says the sellers have primarily used the residence as a summer home andrented it outduring the months when they were not living there. However, he noted that it would work just as well as a primary home for anyone who is looking to relocate more permanently.
“It could do well as either a primary or secondary residence,” he said. “I could see empty nesters wanting a primary bedroom on the first floor with guest accommodations upstairs.”
“A lot of people who have looked at it have been young families. It’s located in a safe and sequestered neighborhood where you can set your kids free.”
Buyers can also rest easy in the knowledge that they aren’t going to be dealing with centuries-old plumbing; though the home appears very much as it did when it was first constructed, behind that façade lie much more modern upgrades.
While the interior has been thoughtfully protected as it existed back in the day, the home’s systems, including new wiring, plumbing, and geothermal heating, have been updated to modern standards.
“It has been fully stabilized with new electric and plumbing and new HVAC, so it’s essentially a current home wrapped in an original envelope.”
That historical wrapping does extend throughout the dwelling as well; despite undergoing multiple upgrades to its various infrastructural systems, many of the original period details that were added to the home when it was first built still remain today.
Found throughout the 3,000-square-foot interior are wide-plank floors, wood ceilings, exposed beams, wood-clad walls, and five fireplaces.
Even the more modern additions, like the cupboards in the kitchen, have been given a rustic look to ensure that they don’t mar the overall look and feel of the charming home.
The property also boasts a 1920s ell and an antique barn with an entertaining room and covered porch that overlooks the marshes.
“The barn is especially nice,” Selbst said. “It was refitted in the 1920s and has a wonderful addition off of it that is used for entertaining. This home has a sense of nostalgia that pulls you back in time.”
It is also situated near the charming town of Essex.
“The previous owners bought the home and spent love, labor, and fortune to restore the property,” Selbst added.
“They repointed the foundation, custom milled walls, and rebuilt windows. Everything was done to original standards, and not much else needs to be done. They touched every surface really beautifully.”

hed: Where the American dream is still alive for first-time buyers—and where it’s slipping away
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Budget buyers seeking entry into homeownership are finally getting some relief as the national supply of starter homes is beginning to improve. But like most aspects of the housing market, the recovery remains sluggish and starkly divided by region.
A starter home is defined by Realtor.com® economists as any listings priced below $350,000 nationally, or below 80% of a local market’s median list price. For example, in Phoenix, where the median asking price sits at $489,500 as of June, the starter home threshold is roughly $391,200.
Typically smaller and more modest than their pricier counterparts, starter homes serve as the first step on the property ladder for first-time homebuyers without the benefit of existing home equity.
No-frills, low-cost starter homes have been in short supply for years. According to a new Realtor.com report released Monday, the inventory crunch peaked in 2022, when frenzied pandemic-era demand drove up real estate prices to record highs and left entry-level buyers with fewer options than at any point in recent history.
Today, there are 220,000 more starter homes for sale than there were four years ago, and prices are down 4.2%, but Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones points out that this crucial market segment is still facing an uphill battle.
There are still approximately 300,000 fewer low-cost listings now than there were in 2019, and the typical starter home comes with a nearly $90,000 premium.
When mortgage rates are factored in, qualifying for a starter home now requires a household income of around $78,000, up from just $43,000 seven years ago.
What’s more, the starter home market looks drastically different depending on the region, with the well-supplied South presenting the rosiest picture. Thanks to an accelerated pace of new construction, builders in the area have been able to meet demand.
Since 2022, the Southern starter home price threshold dropped 3.5%, moving from $323,000 to $311,000.
Meanwhile, the share of listings below $350,000 increased from below 40% in mid-2023 to 43.6% today, translating into nearly 170,000 more affordable options than at the height off the housing crunch.
“Sun Belt builders ramped up supply during the boom years, and that inventory has reached the market just as demand has moderated,” says Jones. “The result is a region where buyers have more options and more negotiating leverage than anywhere else in the country.”
In the West, the narrative surrounding starter homes is not as clear-cut. As a whole, the region saw its starter home threshold drop 7.3% between 2022 and 2026 to $480,000, yet it is still well above the 2019 benchmark of $368,000.
Looking at Western inventory of affordable homes, just 16.7% of listings are currently priced below $350,000, or 23,000 more units than there were in 2022.
This market shift reflects meaningful progress toward affordability in several major regional markets including Denver and Phoenix, where first-time buyers are finally getting a leg up after being effectively sidelined just a few years earlier.
“The biggest factor boosting affordability in that segment right now is supply, which has ballooned to nearly five months of inventory,” Michelle Schwinghammer, an agent with West + Main Homes in Denver, tells Realtor.com. “That’s significantly higher than recent years and is putting meaningful downward pressure on prices.”
According to Schinghammer, the other major factor easing the financial burden is seller concessions.
“More than half of Denver sellers are actively conceding at closing, with buyers winning five- and even six-figure seller credits,” she says. “Those credits can help cover closing costs but are increasingly being used to fund interest rate buydowns, an especially common incentive in new construction.”
Heather O’Leary, an agent at eXp in Denver, argues that construction alone won’t solve the affordability problem that first-time buyers face.
“The key to improving starter-home affordability is not just building more homes,” she tells Realtor.com. “It is expanding the types of homes buyers are willing to consider and taking advantage of the increased inventory, softer pricing, and stronger negotiating position within the attached-home market.”
On the other side of the starter home spectrum, the chronically undersupplied Northeast and Midwest are facing even steeper hurdles.
As Jones explains, the Midwest finds itself in a tough spot. With a starter home threshold of just $263,920, the region remains the most affordable in the U.S. in absolute terms, yet for budget buyers the window of opportunity may be narrowing, because the price has increased 10% since 2022 and more than 37% since 2019.
A look at the inventory of low-priced homes drives this point home, as the share of starter listings has shrunk from roughly 70% in 2019 down to 55% in the spring of 2026.
“While the Midwest is still more affordable than much of the country, buyers are definitely feeling the pressure here too,” Erica Collica Swink, associate broker at Max Broock Realtors in Detroit, tells Realtor.com.
Among the four regions, the Northeast is in the worst shape when it comes to housing affordability, and entry-level buyers are bearing the brunt of a restrictive, inventory-starved market.
The Northeastern starter home threshold surged to $443,600 this year, up nearly 50% compared to 2019 and nearly 13% above the 2022 level.
At that price point, entry-level homeownership in the region’s major metros is increasingly reserved for buyers with significant generational wealth, or exceptionally high incomes, undercutting the very purpose of a starter home.
“The structural reasons are well-established: dense, built-out markets with limited developable land; restrictive zoning that constrains new construction; and strong, persistent demand from high-income households concentrated in major metro areas,” says Jones.
Andy Oei, real estate agent at Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Fox & Roach Realtors in Philadelphia, says finding budget-friendly homes in desirable neighborhoods remains a key stumbling block.

hed: Panic and confusion as NYC renters learn of Legionnaires’ at their building — but not from management
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Residents at the Upper East Side mega-complex Normandie Court are fuming after learning Legionella DNA was detected at their building — not from management, but through other news sources.
Despite blasting out routine emails for weather updates, angry tenants allege management for the behemoth complex stayed mum for over a week after the city’s Department of Health and Mental Hygiene collected samples on July 6.
“I first learned about the outbreak … through two different sources, neither of which was management, which is kinda annoying,” resident Pooja Shah, 33, claimed to The Post. “It’s disappointing that our building didn’t even send us an email to reassure us that our plumbing was safe, or best practices … I had no idea how airborne it is.”
Shah noted that clear communication is crucial given the high-risk population of elderly people and children in the four-building, 1,476-unit complex, which spans an entire city block between Second and Third avenues on East 95th Street.
Normandie Court was one of 31 buildings with cooling towers that tested positive for the presence of Legionella bacteria during an initial PCR (polymerase chain reaction) screening, DOH announced on July 10.
Management finally broke its silence on July 14 with a letter to tenants.
“As part of our regularly scheduled water testing protocol conducted by Metro Group, our certified water management company, the routine Legionella culture test performed on June 23 returned with no Legionella detected,” management wrote in a letter for residents and viewed by The Post. “However, we were notified today by the Department of Health that samples collected on July 6 as part of the enhanced testing initiative produced a preliminary positive PCR result.
“It is important to note that a PCR-positive result indicates the presence of Legionella DNA but does not necessarily confirm the presence of viable bacteria.”
For anxious renters, the notice was too little, too late.
Why did management wait to share about the July 6 collection until July 14, residents questioned.
“It makes me wonder,” Shah said, “if the test was negative would they have even told us at all?”
“An eight-day delay in getting a result seems a little long,” said a second resident, a lawyer who pays $5,200 to live with a roommate in a two-bedroom pad. “I think it would have been nice if they could say …  these are the precautions we’re taking. Give me some information … I pay a lot of money to live there.”
And so do many others. Amenities at the complex, where rents begin at $3,940 for a 419-square-foot studio, include a glass-enclosed swimming pool, a penthouse-level health club that spans two stories and two outdoor decks for sunbathing.
Normandie’s management said in its July 14 note to residents Metro Group “performed a full hyperhalogenation and disinfection of the cooling tower today, and the tower will then be retested pursuant to Department of Health guidelines.”
However, unanswered questions have left residents feeling uneasy.
“The gist for me is that this disease, including how it spreads and how it is treated, is confusing and not clear, and I don’t think anyone is being communicative,” a third resident alleged on the condition of anonymity. “I personally feel like this is chaotic and not well managed. But I can’t get a sense of who is to blame.”
A spokesperson for the DOH confirmed to The Post that all 76 buildings that were “ordered to clean and disinfect their cooling towers have completed remediation,” though culture test results remain pending on whether the bacteria was live.
Legionella bacteria is not spread from person to person. The cooling towers dispense the bacteria into airborne water droplets that people accidentally inhale.
The Upper East Side scare is part of a broader outbreak across Carnegie Hill and Yorkville that has sickened 74 people, hospitalized 59 andleft three dead. It is a deadly type of pneumonia that can be treated with antibiotics if caught early.
This year’s outbreak follows citations of over250 cooling towers around the Big Appleor Legionella testing failures since last year — more than half of them in Manhattan alone.
New York City sees about 200 to 700 cases of Legionnaires’ disease every year, per the DOH.
In 2025, there was an outbreak of the disease in Harlem that sickened 114 andleft five dead.
Normandie’s management didn’t respond to a request for comment.

hed: Buyers scramble to live in a Florida community home to the largest swimming pool in America
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Buyers can’t get enough of the largestswimming poolin America — and it’s turning Florida’s newest master-planned communities into hot commodities.
And we’re not talking any pool. Mirada, a sprawling development in San Antonio, Florida, located north of Tampa, boasts a 15-acre man-made Crystal Lagoon, now the biggest of its kind in the country.
For comparison, 15 acres equates to approximately 150 NBA basketball courts.
The title once belonged to Beachwalk Club’s Crystal Lagoon in St. Johns, FL., which features over 14 acres. And coming in third is the nearby Epperson, the original lagoon community built by the same developer, Metro Development Group, which spans a comparably modest 7.5 acres.
Though the sizes vary, what they hold in common is the sense of an oasis. With expanses of turquoise waters, beach areas and lounge seating, they give the impression of a luxury resort amenity in Dubai — where entertainment options never run dry.
That being said, the lagoon craze has translated directly into sales. Epperson is now 94% occupied, while Mirada, still filling out its newer sections, sits at 75%.
Homes in Mirada run from townhomes that start at $350,000 to two- to three-bedroom single-family homes from $649,000.
Currently Mirada holds 2,873 households including renters, with plans of developing up to 5,000 homes (what it is currently zoned for).
Homeowners in both communities get discounted access to the lagoons and their water activities, a perk developers say has become one of the single biggest draws for prospective buyers touring the properties.
And for those who want a slice of paradise but are not homeowners or renters in the community, they can access a day pass for $50 depending on availability.
“The lagoon is one of the biggest drivers of interest we see from buyers exploring communities like Epperson and Mirada,” Lisa Gibbings, vice president of corporate affairs for Metro Development Group, told The Post. “It creates an immediate sense of excitement because it’s something people can’t find in a traditional neighborhood.”
Beyond the water itself, Gibbings said the appeal comes from the sheer range of things to do without ever leaving the neighborhood, from paddleboarding and kayaking to a floating water obstacle course and a swim-up bar for adults.
The company also runs a program called the Social Hub, which hosts more than 300 events a year for residents.
“What makes the lagoon unique is that it has something for everyone,” Gibbings said. “No matter where you’re moving from, the Social Hub makes it easy to find your future neighbors and friends and feel at home from day one.”
Metro Development Group has been betting on the lagoon lifestyle for nearly 10 years. The company first introduced the concept at Epperson, then went bigger with Mirada.
“Metro pioneered lagoon living nearly a decade ago with a bold idea: bring the best of the coastal lifestyle inland,” Gibbings said. “Since opening Epperson, we’ve continued to innovate and push the concept forward, including building the nation’s largest lagoon at Mirada. Today, the momentum is undeniable. People want the water, the energy and the sense of escape that comes with coastal living, right outside their front door.”
Gibbings said the developer is bringing its lagoon concept to even more Florida communities, including a project at Sandal Key in Hernando County that will pair a lagoon with the company’s first lazy river.
“The lagoon concept continues to evolve,” Gibbings said. “The excitement around these communities shows that people are looking for the complete package — a beautiful home in a thriving community.”
For Gibbings, the appeal isn’t justthe water itself,but what it represents for buyers seeking something beyond a standard subdivision.
“Epperson and Mirada have proven that buyers are hungry for a different kind of community,” she said. “The lagoon is the centerpiece that creates excitement, brings people together and gives residents an experience they can’t find anywhere else.”

hed: Seven small towns that are booming in California — bucking the exodus trend
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Lured by cheaper homes and good schools, more Californians are embracing small-town life.
Seven rural and suburban towns across the state are bucking California’s population loss — each growing more than 25% population-wise over the past 15 years, according to a new analysis by theSan Francisco Chronicle.
The communities have a few things in common, such as affordable real estate and amenities for families. And they’re far from California’s ultra-expensive coastal citieslike Los Angeles, which suffered a massive exodus last year, losing roughly 54,000 residents between July 2024 and July 2025, according to the California Department of Finance.
The leafySacramentosuburb has boomed since the Covid pandemic, when countless people living in cramped city quarters decided to flee to the burbs.
The town’s population has grown by 15% to 165,455 since 2020, the Chronicle reported, and boasts much more affordable homes than in much of the Bay Area. Median home prices hover at around $650,000, making it a popular destination for young families.
Formerly rural Manteca, located in San Joaquin County, bills itself as “The Family City” and has welcomed new development over the past few decades. Its population has more than doubled since the early 1990s, transforming Manteca from a quiet farming community to a family-friendly suburb of Stockton.
Its popular amenities include Great Wolf Lodge, a recreational complex that includes a water park and hotel, and Big League Dreams, which features six baseball fields, the Chronicle reported.
Chico, home to Chico State University, has long been known as a college town. But it is increasingly a home for individuals in search of affordability, a friendly community and breathtaking natural beauty of rural Butte County.
Chico’s population has exploded 15% over 15 to 108,000 in 2026 — a 25% increase — partly due to the catastrophic fire in nearby Paradise, when some former residents resettled. The burgeoning city also added 2,306 residences over the past 10 years to accommodate the new residents, the Chronicle reported.“Chico is kind of magical,” one 22-year-old resident told the paper.
The master-planned Orange County suburb has been branded “cookie cutter,” but that hasn’t deterred new residents attracted by the town’s high-paying jobs in tech and finance and ample space.
The city of 318,000 has added 100,000 residents since 2010, per population data, and its home prices have also spiked alongside its growth. Its median home price sits at more than $1.5 million and top perks include Great Park, which includes extensive soccer fields and helium balloon rides.
The burb is also one ofAmerica’s fittest cities, according to a recent survey.
Menifee, located in the Inland Empire, is home to increasing numbers of young familes and retirees who have fled larger urban centers like Los Angeles and San Diego. Accordingly, its population has grown to 118,000 this year, an increase of roughly 40,000 people over the last 15 years.
Its boosters include Instagram personalityMenifee Mom, who regularly posts about the town’s cute bakeries, wineries, community events and other local events that make the growing enclave a popular spot for families.
Clovis’ 35% population growth over 15 years makes it one of the fastest-growing cities in California, and its excellent schools are an important reason why.
The town of 130,000, near Fresno, has added a brand-new shopping center and new housing developments over the last several years and has an average home price of $520,000. Residents rave about its highly-rated school district, the Chronicle reported.
“Clovis is one of the last places in California where you can buy an affordable house in a really great neighborhood with great schools,” local realtor  Bryan Souza told the paper.
The once-sleepy Tri-Valley town of Dublin is hailed as a safe and affordable community with good schools and more spacious homes than elsewhere in the Bay Area. Its population more than doubled from 2010 to 2020, now with more than 70,000 residents.
Major developments have helped to fuel Dublin’s growth, including the Dublin Transit Center, a mixed-use project near the Dublin BART station.

hed: Phillies pitcher Zack Wheeler sells NYC penthouse for $26M —  a new record for Soho
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Phillies aceZack Wheelerand his wife Dominique have cashed in on a Soho passion project, selling their penthouse at 73 Wooster St. for $26 million, a price that sets a new benchmark for the neighborhood.
The sale works out to nearly $5,400 per square foot, the highest average price per square foot recorded in the trendy neighborhood over the past five years, The Post has learned.
The buyer’s identity remains unknown and was purchased through an LLC.
Penthouse A spans 4,856 square feet of loft living and comes with a sprawling 3,008-square-foot private rooftop terrace, one of the largest and most private outdoor spaces in the neighborhood. The unit initially hit the market for $27 million.
The residence sits inside a boutique, full-service condominium with just six units total.
Inside, the home retains 15-foot ceilings, original casement windows and exposed brick, along with 53 feet of frontage overlooking West Broadway.
The layout includes wide-open living and dining areas, a chef’s kitchen and a climate-controlled wine vault, in addition to the four bedroom suites.
A staircase off the main living space leads up to the rooftop, where the Wheelers built out a pergola, an outdoor kitchen, a bocce court and several separate lounge areas.
Building amenities include a full-time doorman and private storage.
The Wheelerspicked up the property in 2024 for $16 million, then poured money and design work into a full renovation before flipping it for a $10 million gain.
Among the standout features is what’s believed to be the first privately commissioned residential mural by celebrity tattoo artist Mr. K.
Mr. K (Sanghyuk Ko) is a globally recognized, Seoul-born fine-line tattoo artist based at the prestigious Bang Bang NYC studio in Manhattan. Known for his intricate micro-style and single-needle black-and-grey designs, he regularly tattoos an A-list clientele, including David Beckham, Angelina Jolie, Matt Damon, and Ariana Grande,
For Dominique, who spearheaded the renovation alongside interior design firm 1508 London, the sale closes the loop on a project rooted in sentimental territory.
“New York has always been a special place for us. It’s where Zack and I met and where he started his career with the Mets, which is why this penthouse felt like a passion project from the start,” she told The Post.
She made clear the couple never planned to stay long term.
“We never purchased it with the intention of it being a long-term hold. Instead, it was an opportunity to create something truly special and put our own stamp on an incredible property and city,” Dominique said, adding that she was “heavily involved in leading the design vision” and that “every detail was carefully considered.”
With the renovation complete and their vision realized, the Wheelers decided it was time to let someone else take over.
Gavin Shiminski and Jonathan Stein of Douglas Elliman held the listing.
Wheeler, 36, is a veteran starting pitcher for thePhiladelphia Phillieswidely considered one of the most dominant pitchers in baseball, he boasts a Cy Young-caliber track record and signed a three-year, $126 million contract extension with the Phillies.

Nicole Miner, whose father Robert Minerco-founded Oracle, and her author hubby Robert Mailer Anderson are offloading their Pacific Heights mansion to the tune of $65 million.
The philanthropists’  four-bedroom, 11,150-square-foot home — which was once a posh elementary school that closed in 1971 — is believed to be the most expensive home to hit the market in San Francisco this year.
San Francisco is seeing aninsane spike in home prices, particularly at the high end of the market,due to the AI boom.
Described as a “modern estate,” the home at 2916 Pacific Ave. includes sprawling gardens and two separate residences.
Miner and Anderson, who penned the novel “Boonville,” paid just $5 million for three vacant lots in 1999 and spent years building out the showpiece property, according to theSan Francisco Business Times. They reportedly spent $25 million on the project, including the cost of land.

hed: Home of the Week: Perched high, this solar-powered home on 52.6 acres showcases Vermont’s natural beauty
subhead: The owners built it to be energy efficient and private.
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

167 Ward Hill Road, Tunbridge, Vermont

$595,000

Style

Year built2017

Square feet1,484

Bedrooms3

Baths2 full

Sewer/WaterPrivate

Taxes$5,981 (2026)


Christopher M. Young knew his goal: Design an energy-efficient home for his family, one that maximized solar gain, and  could take advantage of the clearing on Ward Hill 1,500 feet above theFirst Branch of the White River.

“I was looking at different shapes and reading about different aspects of different houses, and what I realized is this shape is like a big eyeball,” he said of the trapezoid design he settled on. ”I think we achieved what I set out to achieve. The house faces east, southeast…I kept the ceilings white so that the light would then reflect down once it came into the house. It can be 20 degrees outside, and I can be sitting at 75, 78 degrees in the house.”


The home is on a 52.6 acre lot mostly covered with sugar maples that rises 500 feet above the homestead to a peak with 360-degree views of the mountainous terrain of both Vermont and New Hampshire. Sometimes New York is visible.

The house with green shiplap siding and white trim is solar powered, warmed by aWoodstock Soapstonewood-fired stove, cooled by ceiling fans and nature’s cross breezes.



The front door leads to an open floor plan space of 525 square feet containing the kitchen and dining area with luxury vinyl planked flooring, which is applied throughout the majority of the home. A freezer and refrigerator are white and the propane-fueled range is black. Adjacent to the range are the unique L-shaped counters made of elm harvested from neighboring woodlands by Young’s uncle who sliced them into shape in his own sawmill. A white Italian farmhouse sink is underneath a square window and white floating cabinets on the wall above. A table sits directly across from the range.


The room takes a left hand turn and Young’s design choices are fully in view. The angled ceiling slopes upward, and inset into the wall rising 16 feet to meet it are two large transom windows and below them a pair of large square windows. The greatest solar gain is delivered by a wide glass slider that can be opened for breezes, but does not lead to a deck. Young and his wife, Angie, have placed a couch directly opposite the slider to take in the views.

Built from a 200-year-old barn recovered froma Tunbridge farm,an exposed timber post rises from the floor to meet the horizontal beam crossing the ceiling. Both show their age, as does the window trim throughout the house where the barn wood has also been installed.

Passing past the stairwell with barn wood railings to the lower level on the left, an interior wall sets off the primary suite. Framing the entry is a mural byKatie J. Roberts of the Woodstock Collectivedepicting a Vermont forest scene. The barn doors hang on a black rolling track.



The bedroom is 199 square feet and replicates Young’s solar vision, but on a slightly smaller scale. There is a slider showcasing the view, a transom window above, and behind the area best used for the bed is a set of two square windows. The exposed beams are here, as is the barn wood window trim. A second Roberts mural, this of a Vermont sunset, is above the entry door in the bedroom. There is a built-in wardrobe with a barnyard style door.

The primary bathroom is 110 square feet and features a vintage clawfoot bathtub along with a modern inset shower behind clear glass doors framed by wood. The single vanity stands in front of a shiplap-style knotty pine wall. It has white cabinet and a translucent bowl sink.


The stairwell down leads to a large hallway that ends at a glass slider and the mountainous view. Separated by the hallway are the two secondary bedrooms, both 157 square feet with large windows. Barn wood is used to frame the walls. The floor is corkboard.

The secondary bath is 75 square feet with a single white vanity with a translucent bowl sink. The walls are white and the shower is behind a curtain. The flooring is a luxury vinyl plank.

The lower level has an 118 square foot laundry room.

The home has a poured concrete unfinished basement. One of the outbuildings is a duplicate right trapezoid perfect for office use. The home has wifi and cell service.



Read what follows in the voice of weathered New Englander: To get there from here, a traveler  crosses the Cilley covered bridge. Along with turkeys, the Youngs property contains trails that connect to the Vermont trail system.

The Youngs are selling so they can create a new off-the-grid homestead for themselves.


Some additional facts: The insulation R factor for the interior is R-28 and the roof is R-42. The solar array of 24 panels, paired with 12 deep cycle batteries in the basement generates 6.38 kilowatts. Amid turbulent Vermont weather recently, this home never loses power, according to the Youngs.

The John Deere tractor model 2032R and attachments and a goat shed on pallets are excluded from the sale.

Mary Paino of Coldwell Banker Lifestylesreal estate in Quechee, Vermont, has the listing.

The notorious“Graffiti Towers”in downtown Los Angeles are finally on track for a makeover after a federal bankruptcy court approved a plan clearing the way for their $470 million sale ahead of the 2028 Olympics.
The U.S. Bankruptcy Courtfor the Central District of California on Monday confirmed Oceanwide Plaza’s revised liquidation plan, paving the way for thelong-stalled developmentto be sold to KPC Square, a joint venture between KPC Group and Lendlease.
As part of the court-approved plan, workers must begin removing the graffiti covering the three unfinished towers within 30 days.
“Today’s rulings reflect months of coordinated work across every stakeholder in this case,” a release said Monday. “The withdrawal of objections from the City and County, combined with the court’s confirmation, paves the way for the sale to move toward closing.”

Oceanwide Plazabegan construction in 2015 as a $1.2 billion luxury development featuring a Park Hyatt hotel, condominiums and retail space across from Crypto.com Arena and LA Live. Construction halted in 2019 after parent company Oceanwide Holdings ran out of money, leaving contractor Lendlease with more than $150 million in unpaid bills.
Over the past several years, the abandoned towers became one of Los Angeles’ most recognizable eyesores after graffiti artists covered the unfinished buildings from top to bottom.
Los Angeles initially objected to the sale in May, arguing the proposal lacked a realistic path forward, but laterwithdrew its oppositionafter saying the revised plan included “meaningful improvements that serve the interest of the downtown Los Angeles community.”
“This confirmation is the culmination of a long and complex process, and it delivers exactly what we set out to achieve: a credible path to finally bring this project back to life,” Oceanwide Chief Restructuring Officer Bradley Sharp said.

The site’s location across from Crypto.com Arena, LA Live and the Los Angeles Convention Center has made its future especially significant as Los Angeles prepares to host the 2028 Summer Olympics.
Downtown leaders have long argued the abandoned complex has become a symbol of the city’s stalled development, while stressing that even if the project isn’t completed before the Games, removing the graffiti, improving the site and restarting construction would dramatically improve one of the city’s busiest visitor corridors.

hed: Newly upgraded One Lincoln tower lands its first biotech tenant
content: Biopharmaceutical company Collegium Pharmaceutical is moving its corporate headquarters from Stoughton to the heart of the Financial District, the company announced Monday.Collegium, which specializes in developing medications to treat pain and ADHD, will move into two floors — roughly 40,000 square feet — of One Lincoln Street tower. It will be the first biotech tenant at the recently-refurbished 36-story building.“This move reflects our confidence in where we’re headed as a company,” said Collegium president and CEO Vikram Karnani, in a release. ”Our new headquarters provides an environment that supports how we work together today while positioning us for continued growth in the years ahead.”San Francisco-based real estate investment firm DivcoWest purchased One Lincoln for $400 million in a foreclosure auction in spring 2025 after the previous owner struggled to pay down its $763 million mortgage on the 1.1 million square foot building. Later that year, DivcoWest unveiled $100 million in luxury amenities and upgrades, hoping to attract more tenants to fill 730,000 square feet of vacant space.One Lincoln, situated a few blocks from South Station, served as home to State Street Corp. for two decades before the financial services giant relocated to the One Congress tower near Government Center and City Hall. It’s now home to a variety of tenants, including law firm Sherin and Lodgen, Swedish AI platform Lovable and private equity firm HarbourVest, which occupies 11 floors in the tower. The HarbourVest lease, brokered in 2022, was one of the largest downtown deals in the years post-pandemic and coincided with a $1 billion refinancing then-owners Fortis Property Group had completed.Avison Young principal Justin Dziama, who represented Collegium in the deal, said in the DivcoWest release that companies like Collegium were taking advantage of shifting market conditions to “upgrade their workplace experience, improve accessibility” and “establish a stronger presence in the urban core.”“This relocation reflects a broader trend we’re seeing across Greater Boston,” Dziama said.The office vacancy rate downtown remains stubbornly high — 22.5 percent in the second quarter, according to real estate firm Newmark, though newer and refurbished towers have tended to perform better.Karyna Cheung can be reached at karyna.cheung@globe.com.

hed: Horror as man buys bargain Connecticut home sight unseen — and finds 3 dead bodies inside
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
If a deal seems too good to be true, perhaps it actually is.
Edward Marchion bought a Connecticut home at a foreclosure auction in June — taking a real chance for the spread in affluent Burlington, as the nature of the sale stipulated that bidders could not inspect the interior.
And when Marchion entered for the first time — after placing a winning $525,000 bid for the $650,000-valued home — he found three dead bodies inside, according tothe Wall Street Journal. The horrific surprise even made its way to TV channelWFSB 3.
The skeletal remains, for the two bodies that have been identified, are those of Sally Anne Cash, who would have turned 54 on Monday, and her son Brian, who would have turned 23 this month. The third body remains under DNA testing for identification; Cash bought the Cape Cod-style residence in 2019 with her husband, Paul.
It isn’t clear how they all died or how long they laid inside. Police said the deaths were isolated, that no crime was committed and there’s no threat to the public. Tests also indicated there was no sign of carbon monoxide.
“I don’t know if I’d want the house after that,” Michael NeJaime, who lives nearby, told the Journal.
That said, Marchion has asked a court to delay the closing on the home until the police investigation is complete.
Before the gruesome discovery, the home’s auction lured in some 20 bidders, all of whom inspected the house to the best of their ability only from the exterior. In general, under foreclosure proceedings, residents are legally allowed to remain in their homes and aren’t required to let others inside before public auctions.
After six offers, Marchion was declared the winner of the auction — and even paid a deposit of $82,000 to call the property his own.
The house measures 2,800 square feet and stands on more than 2 acres. The Journal notes it was worth at least twice the amount remaining on its mortgage.
“Why would anyone walk away from that?” Christopher Thogmartin, the court-appointed lawyer who oversaw the auction, told the Journal.
But things had been strange for a bit. Court records show the couple stopped making mortgage payments — about $3,000 per month — in late 2024. That led their bank to file a foreclosure complaint in August 2025, to which the Cashes never responded. Thogmartin believed they had abandoned the property.
But shortly before the auction, signs mysteriously appeared on the lawn, saying “keep out” and “owner occupied.”
Matt Turner, a Burlington resident, told the outlet he still can’t believe no one checked out the home before the sale.
“It seemed like the type of thing where somebody would go into the house and at least make sure there are no dead bodies,” he said.

hed: $33M Wine Country estate that ‘Jeopardy!’ host Alex Trebek owned for 37 years set for auction
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Homebuyers who have dreamed of owning a wine country retreat could well get the chance to snap one up at a bargain price when a luxurious 700-acre estate that was once home to legendary “Jeopardy!” host Alex Trebek is put up for auction—with no reserve.
The extraordinaryranch property known as Windfall Farms, which is located in Paso Robles, CA, was owned by Trebek for 37 years, until he and several other investors sold it to its current owners for $1.6 million in 2001.
In the years since, those owners—Barry and Donna Goldfarb—have transformed it from a working winery into a sprawling family retreat, adding multiple structures, including a stunning primary residence.
They have made several attempts over the years to offload the sprawling estate, most recently listing the ranch for a staggering $33 million.
However, they will now take their chances with what could be a much lower sale price when they put the property on the auction block with Concierge Auctions on Aug. 5.
Because Windfall Farms is being offered with no reserve, it will ultimately be sold to the highest bidder—unless, of course, it secures a buyer before the scheduled auction.
Luckily, there is plenty on offer to help push the price up.
Located along California’s Central Coast, the estate offers far more than celebrity provenance.
The current listing, which is held by Patty Murphy ofSotheby’s International Realty, describes Windfall Farms as a “world-class Central Coast development opportunity with positive cash flow,” emphasizing that it is as much an investment as it is a luxurious private retreat.
Trebek, whodied in 2020 after battling pancreatic cancer, was part of a group of investors that owned the ranch for several years, reportedly helping to save it from bankruptcy,according to the Los Angeles Times.
Trebek—one of TV’s most recognizable personalities during his nearly four decadeshosting “Jeopardy!”—also quietly built a reputation as an investor in California wine country, assembling several agricultural properties far from the bright lights of Hollywood. Windfall Farms reflects that passion.
According to the listing, the ranch “currently operates as a cash-flow-positive premium wine grape vineyard business,” with dozens of acres planted with sought-after varietals that thrive in Paso Robles’ Mediterranean climate.
The productive vineyards are complemented by mature olive groves, creating an estate that blends luxury living with a functioning agricultural enterprise.
The ranch’s equestrian amenities are equally impressive. The listing highlights its “stunning Kentucky-style equine facilities,” which include expansive horse barns, training areas, and a 6.5-furlong racetrack—a nod to the property’s origins as a thoroughbred breeding operation.
Those features help distinguish the estate from the typical celebrity home.
Instead of lavish entertainment spaces or oceanfront views, Windfall Farms offers hundreds of acres of rolling hills, open pasture, and productive farmland.
The sprawling grounds provide exceptional privacy while also creating opportunities for horseback riding, hiking, and outdoor recreation, making the ranch well suited for buyers seeking both a luxury lifestyle and long-term investment potential.
Its location only adds to its appeal.
Over the past two decades, Paso Robles has emerged as one of California’s fastest-growing wine destinations, attracting boutique wineries, upscale resorts, andaffluent buyers drawn to the region’s scenic landscapes and acclaimed vineyards.
The area has developed an international reputation for producing Rhône and Bordeaux-style wines, helping fuel demand for large vineyard estates like Windfall Farms.
The auction also reflects a growing trend across the luxury housing market, where sellers of distinctive, high-value properties are increasingly turning to competitive bidding to reach a global pool of qualified buyers.
Concierge Auctions says bidding is scheduled to begin on Aug. 5 before concluding on Aug. 15 during RM Sotheby’s Monterey Car Week, placing the estate in front of an international audience of luxury collectors and investors.
While Windfall Farms remains one of Trebek’s most notable former properties, it is not the only ranch tied to the beloved TV host.
Earlier this year, another former estate connected to Trebek returned to the market in nearby Creston.
The historic 577-acre property, which he once owned alongside a group of investors, includes producing vineyards,multiple residences, livestock facilities, and event spaces, underscoring his longstanding appreciation for California’s agricultural landscapes.
Taken together, the properties reveal a side of Trebek that many fans never saw.
Rather than building a portfolio centered on glamorous Hollywood mansions, he gravitated toward expansive ranches where vineyards, horses, and open space took center stage.
The listing brands Windfall Farms a “legacy estate” in one of California’s premier wine regions, a fitting description for a property that combines celebrity history with a thriving agricultural operation.
As it prepares to change hands once again, the ranch offers its next owner the opportunity to preserve a unique piece of Trebek’s real estate legacy while writing a new chapter of its own.

hed: Billionaires custom-built homes in this new mountain hot spot to get away from ‘pretentious’ Aspen, Vail, Park City and Telluride
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Forget Aspen. Forget Vail. The ultra-wealthyhave found a Colorado mountain townwhere they can ski all day and never once get recognized — and they’re pouring more than $1 billion into developing it further.
Steamboat Springs, long dismissed as the family-friendly, unpretentious cousin ofColorado’s marquee resorts, has quietly become the destination serious money is choosing instead.
Discovery Land Company — a luxury international developer helmed by George Clooney’s best friend Mike Meldman (who also co-founded Casamigos tequila) — is among the names planting flags there. It’s known for luxury projects in other areas such Hawaii, Dubai and Scotland.
The high-gloss Auberge Collection confirmed in March that its first Steamboat project, the Stockman, will break ground this year at the base of the ski area, a nine-story building with 59 hotel rooms and 95 residences, including 13 rooftop “Barn” units with double-height ceilings. Residential sales launched this summer through a Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices team with prices ranging from $1.6 million to $19 million
Roughly 20 minutes away, Discovery Land Company is pushing forward with Stagecoach Mountain Ranch, a private ski community that would include its own mountain, a high-speed gondola and homesites starting around $3 million. The project remains in the planning and approval phase with Routt County.
Chris Paoli, managing partner of the Agency Steamboat, said the turning point came about five years ago, when hospitality group Alterra Mountain Company started pouring money into the Steamboat Springs resort itself.
“That spurred our first luxury hotel property coming to the mountain in the O’Barrish-Stockman project,” Paoli told The Post, adding that two or three other major projects are rising alongside it at the base area, “which in total is about a billion dollars worth of development happening up there.”
And deep-pocketed buyers really want in. and the proof is in the numbers.
A new mid-year market report shows the median number of days a luxury home spends on the market has fallen 38% year-over-year, while new-construction pricing is pushing toward $3,500 per square foot.
Closed sales above $2,000 per square foot jumped from seven in 2024 to 21 so far in 2026. Another 23 properties are currently under contract above that threshold, not counting the Stockman, which sold $95 million worth of residences before its marketing campaign even launched.
Wealthy buyers on the hunt these days also have some options to browse.
At 1872 Christie Drive, a $12.9 million duplex is the highest-priced duplex on the market and one of the only finished, move-in ready new-construction homes within walking distance of the mountain’s base, a rarity when so much of the town’s new inventory is still under construction.
At Storm Mountain Ranch, a gated enclave of just 14 homesites across 1,100 conserved acres, a 70-acre estate called Meadow House is coming to market for just under $14 million.
Designed by Aspen architect Michael Ernemann, it reflects a growing appetite for legacy ranch estates built to be passed down, not flipped.
At Marabou Ranch, one of Colorado’s premier private sporting communities, two homes are listed between $12 million and $13 million, with ownership carrying private fly fishing on the Elk River, an equestrian center, a mountain club at the Wild Blue Gondola, a spa and concierge service rivaling the country’s top private clubs.
Those homes all stand to crush a big record.
The highest residential sale in Steamboat this year closed at 1870 Christie Drive for $8.2 million, a five-bedroom, six-bath, 5,439-square-foot home built by a well known luxury home builder from Houston who came to town to build his own ski residence.
Paoli would not name names, but described a buyer pool increasingly stacked with chief executives and professional athletes, all drawn by one thing Aspen and Vail can no longer offer: anonymity.
“The nice thing about Steamboat is we see every type of buyer, and the great part is it’s a really great place to come and really not have to show off your wealth,” he said. “A lot of people come here and like it because it’s easy to disappear or just kind of blend in.”
“It’s a very non-pretentious, relaxed environment with all the recreation and dining that people want on their vacation,” Paoli added, describing a town of 12,000 full time residents where “you genuinely are intermingling with people that live here full-time.”
“Steamboat is just different. A lot of people like the fact that you can come here and you have no idea if you sit next to a billionaire or a guy who just mowed your lawn,” Paoli added.
Buyers who plan on six weeks a year rarely stop there.
“I see people buying what they think is going to be six weeks a year type home ends up becoming six months,” he said.
Part of what is driving prices, Paoli said, is simple scarcity. Steamboat has little room left to expand, and most of its luxury inventory was never built to be sold in the first place.
“Most communities like Steamboat are landlocked because of infrastructure,” he said. “We just hit that point where there really isn’t any place to do the next subdivision.”
From here, growth will mean tearing down and rebuilding rather than breaking ground on new land, which tends to push costs even higher.
“I doubt it’s going to get much cheaper over time,” Paoli said. “I think that would be a bad bet.”
He said the town’s building stock has transformed over the past decade largely because buyers from major cities could not find homes that matched what they wanted, so they built their own instead.
“Most of our visitors come from big city markets,” Paoli said. “Your New Yorkers, your Houstons, Boston, Dallas, Chicago. So they bring with them their design expectations and wants from markets that are more in front of design trends.”
Those custom homes, built anywhere from two to seven years ago, are only now starting to hit the resale market.
“We’ve never had homes like those of this quality for sale ever before,” Paoli said.

hed: JD Vance is renting a sprawling property in an exclusive Virginia enclave for his growing family
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It’s not the White House, but it sure is a nice retreat away from the District.
Vice President JD Vance, his wife Usha and their four children are moving to the country.
But don’t expect a“Hillbilly Elegy”kind of hardscrabble country existence.
Instead, the Second Family — whowelcomed their fourth child, Alec Neel, on Sunday — are moving to Middleburg, Va. That’s the “horse and hunt” capital of America, and one of the most elite, under-the-radar and exclusive enclaves in the country.
The Vances are renting a century-plus-old manor house at Wolver Hill Farm, a 500-acre estate owned by federal contractor Charles “Chuck” Kuhn, a data center developer with close ties to the White House, sources told Gimme Shelter.
“It’s a lovely, idyllic place to raise a family,” a source said. “It’s a whole Kennedy-esque compound, with four homes on the property. Usha just had her baby. It’s a great place to nest — a wonderful community. It’s so quiet. You can see why they would want a place like that on a quiet country lane with beautiful trees and stone walls.”
Kuhn did not return calls at press time.
Secret Service security detail will move into an adjacent home on the property, sources said.
If the Vances need help moving, Kuhn can help with that, too.
He’s also the founder of JK Moving Services, which moved President Trump in and out of the White House — twice — as well as other presidents from both parties, including the Clintons, the Bidens and the Obamas.
While the moving company is non-partisan, we hear that Kuhn is keen on backing Vance’s potential presidential run in 2028.
Black SUVs and a helicopter were spotted at the farm a few weeks ago, which got locals buzzing on social media. Many shared concerns that choppers and the Secret Service security will ruin their idyll.
The small town of just 750 people has some wealthy and powerful residents. They include Erik Prince, the MAGA ally and founder of the defunct private mercenary company Blackwater, which is now part of Constellis, a security and defense conglomerate. Prince’s estate, known as Blackwater Ranch, is across the road from Wolver Hill Farm.
One of the world’s richest women, billionaire candy queen heir Jacqueline Mars, also lives nearby, in the Plains, where she operates a working farm and equestrian estate known as Stonehall Farm.
The farm itself is adjacent to the exclusive Salamander Resort & Spa, the flagship five-star luxury resort founded by Black Entertainment Television co-founder Sheila Johnson, the country’s first black female billionaire.
The resort, which sits on 340 acres, is a big draw for DC power players and political fundraisers.
The Vances won’t have much to do in the one-traffic-stop town, just 45 miles west of downtown Washington, DC, but perhaps that’s the point.
For meals, there’s a local Safeway for groceries, and along with Salamander’s offerings, there’s the Red Fox Inn & Tavern, which was founded in 1728 and bills itself as one of the oldest continuously operated inns in the country. It’s where “happy hour” is called the “Middleburg Social Hour,” and offers specials like a half bottle of Thibaut-Janisson with “chips and caviar” for $48.
A White House source said thatVance will keepthe US Naval Observatory in DC as his primary residence. It’s where all vice presidential families have lived since Walter Mondale in 1977.
The Vances’ new Middleburg home is 8,532 square feet and comes with six bedrooms and seven fireplaces. Kuhn bought the property with his wife, Stacy, via an LLC, for $8.5 million in 2020. The Kuhns are also placing a conservation easement on the estate to protect it from future development, according to aKuhn company press release.
A White House source declined to comment on the terms of the lease but said: “It’s a second home. The purpose is to serve as a getaway outside the city for their children and they plan to go there on weekends.”
Real estate sources tell Gimme Shelter that if Vance were to pay a monthly rent for the property, it would cost around $20,000 a month.
Middleburg has also been home to Camelot royalty.
In the early 1960s, President John F. Kennedy and his then-wife Jackie built a home on a massive estate on 167 acres in the area. They called it Wexford.
Jackie was keen on having her children grow up riding horses.
Even movie stars have been drawn to the quiet chi-chi, equestrian life of Middleburg.
Elizabeth Taylor lived just outside Middleburg when she was married to her sixth husband, Senator John Warner. During their marriage, from 1976 to 1982, they lived at Atoka Farm, a 400-plus acre estate in Marshall, Va., where they were married.
In addition to the deal with Vance, Kuhn is also selling a 149-acre parcel of land known as the Middleburg Training Center in Loudoun County to the US Army, to house the army’s famed Caisson ceremonial horses that participate in funeral ceremonies at Arlington National Cemetery.
The controversial sale was opposed by the Virginia Equine Alliance and locals who want to preserve the property for thoroughbred racing and training.

hed: This $1.25 million Gloucester home is like a time machine to the 1600s
subhead: Built in 1678, the William Haskell House looks about the same as it would have back then.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Get ready to fire up the hearth, because Gloucester’s notableWilliam Haskell Houseis on the market for $1.25 million.
Built in 1678,11 Lincoln St.is a four-bedroom, three-bathroom first-period home that carefully toes the line between historic detail and modern function. Impeccably restored, the 3,000-square-foot house was first built byRichard Window, a millwright and joiner who “once was charged for living without a wife and another for cursing, both against Puritan beliefs,” according to the home’s website. He sold the property to Haskell, the forebear of one of Gloucester’s largest families. According to historic documents, he served as a selectman and was one of the first deacons in the first church. The home, which sits on the marshland of the estuary, stayed with the Haskell family for 200 years.
“It’s the same estuary that William Haskell used to chop his hay and then bring it out to the sea,” saidMichael Selbstof Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, who has thelisting.
In the 1920s, the house had a sizable addition put on, and the family that owned it before the current sellers modernized it with up-to-date plumbing and electricity between 2011 and 2013.
Now, the home welcomes you through the back into a foyer. Take a left into the family room, which features all the stunning original wood details from the floors to the beamed ceilings. A fireplace holds center court, and there’s a dining area. That newer wing of the house features the kitchen, filled with wide-plank floors and gray-brown cabinetry. The weathered style manages to flow with the modern black appliances, including a refrigerator, dishwasher, and wine refrigerator.
Back in the foyer, continue straight into the elegant living room, where an oversized hearth warms the gathering space. The neighboring formal dining room also has a large hearth. The spacious primary bedroom, which is also located on the first floor, is filled with rustic charm from the wide-plank floors and beamed ceilings to the oversized fireplace. The bathroom features a unique soapstone sink.
There are two sets of stairs in the home. The first is over the family room in the newer wing of the home. It leads to a bedroom and modern bathroom that are only accessible from those stairs. Head up the main staircase to the second level, and you’ll find a bedroom on each side, as well as another modernized bathroom.
The barn, which dates back to the 1870s, features a 613-square-foot storage area, as well as a 341-square-foot garage. But it’s the 238-square-foot entertainment room that serves as a unique surprise under a white cathedral ceiling, as well as the porch it overlooks through three large windows.
The home has a four-well geothermal system, allowing the owner to heat and cool the house with minimal electricity.
“It has a romantic nostalgia harkening back to the early times in America. And when you’re there, it feels like you’re in a whole different era,” said Selbst. “But it’s been so well restored and stabilized by the previous owners that even though it’s an antique home, it’s really stable and sturdy. The systems are all basically new.”
Megan Johnson is a Boston-based writer and reporter whose work appears in People, Architectural Digest, The Boston Globe, and more.
