hed: New York State house prices reach highest ever recorded — with staggering average cost
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York State house prices are now the highest ever recorded, with the median cost of a home in the Empire State now close to $500,000.
The median price of a home in New York State rose 8% year-to-year, hitting $475,000 in June of 2026, according tofigures from the New York State Association of Realtors.
That price rise came despite increasing inventory in the Empire State, where the number of homes on the market rose for the 16th straight month by 4.4% from 31,124 homes in June 2025 to 32,508 homes in June 2026.
Interest rates also went up slightly between May and June but, at 6.49%, are still lower than the high of 6.82% last year.
New York State saw massive contrasts in sales prices between counties, with homes in some Upstate regions still going for a median price of barely over $200,000.
Genesee County’s median house price was $210,000, and neighboring Orleans County was $221,500,Rochester First reported.
In contrast, downstate counties including Richmond, Rockland, and Suffolk all had median house prices of more than $700,000.

hed: Landlord sues upscale ‘squatters’ in luxe NYC tower who racked up a colossal $78K in back rent
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The rent is too damn high — except when it isn’t being paid.
Two deadbeat residents with an apparent taste for the finestare squattingin a swanky Central Park South tower, having racked up an eye-popping $78,375 plus interest in back rent, a new Manhattan Supreme Court lawsuit alleges.
And, according to other records, this isn’t their first run-in with alleged financial issues.
Daniel and Susan Bancroft have lived inNo. 9GHin the white-gloved 240 Central Park South since August 2023.
The couple signed a two-year renewal on July 1, 2025 at the tower — home to the pricey Marea seafood restaurant — with the monthly rent climbing from $12,500 in the first year to $13,062.50 for the second.
According to the suit, the couple stopped paying rent in full shortly after re-upping at the 28-story, 340-unit landmarked building, which stands in the immediate shadows of the supertall towers alongBillionaires’ Row.
A previous listing for their unit says it spans 1,500 square feet, with two bedrooms and two bathrooms. Its floor plan shows a large dressing room and a study connected to the master suite — as well as a kitchen that leads into a large living room.
The Bancrofts, who didn’t respond to a request for comment, didn’t pay rent for any of it in October or November 2025, paid less than the total in January and February 2026, and then made no rent payments from April through July 2026, according to a court exhibit.
The lawsuit hits the Bancrofts with three separate causes of action: breach of contract, legal fees, and use and occupancy. The owners seek to recoup past, current and future rent — and get an additional $50,000 for legal fees and expenses.
The building owner, the Korein family, named in the lawsuit as Central Park South Associates, L.L.C, “continues to be out-of-pocket paying for expenses such as taxes and other charges, while Tenants lives in his luxury apartment rent-free,” per the suit.
The Korein family, which has owned the property since 1983, didn’t respond to a request for comment, nor did their attorneys.
Susan, 65, and Daniel have had their fair share of other financial troubles.
Most recently, the pair was hit with a $223,873 federal tax lien in July 2024 while living at this Central Park South address, and a $112,718 tax bill in January 2020 when they lived at a penthouse nearby at 160 W. 66th St., court documents indicate. It isn’t immediately clear if these have been resolved.
In late 2017, Malvern Federal Savings Bank sued Daniel in Manhattan Supreme Court for failing to pay $74,107.46, which the bank had mailed to Daniel on or before Jan. 2, 2014, court records also indicate. The matter was dismissed without prejudice a couple of years later.
For his part, Daniel, 66, appears to be a John Hopkins University graduate and leader of thetransportation practiceat WTW, a global professional services firm, since January 2020.
He has also worked as transportation practice leader at Willis Towers Watson, as senior vice president and transportation practice leader atWillis North America in New Yorkand as Philadelphia-based managing director and transportation practice leader for Marsh.
The Bancrofts also filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy in Philadelphia federal court in October 2012, but the case was tossed less than a year later over missed paperwork, records indicate.
Susan said in the bankruptcy documents that she owed money to Bloomingdale’s and Citibank, while Daniel owed money to several banks, including Nordstrom Bank, as well as an attorney, Neiman Marcus, Martha’s Vineyard Hospital and Massachusetts General Physicians Organization.
They listed their assets and liabilities both in the range of $500,001 to $1 million, and their address as 1406 Orchard Way, in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. They owned that property for around 20 years until June 2024.
The luxury high-rise is famed for its prime position overlooking Central Park.
Famous past residents in the Art Deco edifice includeRenée Zellwegerand Angie Harmon as well as broadcaster Bill Boggs and the late Oscar-nominated actress Sylvia Miles.
Three apartments are listed for rent on the building’s website: a 600-square-foot studio for $4,800 per month, a 500-square-foot one-bedroom for $6,000 monthly and a junior four with 1.5 baths that clocks in at 925 square feet and $10,000 a month. The building has a fitness center, and a rooftop lounge and deck overlooking the park.
“It is anticipated that Tenants will not make further payments to Landlord for rent and/or use and occupancy under the Lease unless directed to do so by the Court,” per the complaint, which says that the landlord is entitled to collect ongoing fees until the family regains possession of the unit.

hed: A whopping 30% of Americans would make a surprising romantic decision before moving
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For richer or for square footage? For many modern couples, real estate might outlast romance.
One in four homeowners say their home is more likely than their partner to be in their life in 10 years, and one in five say it would be harder to abandon their house than the relationship, according to a spicy newstudy.
When asked directly, “Which do you think is more likely to still be part of your life in 10 years?” 26 percent selected “my home” over “my partner.”
If push came to shove, one in six would kick their partner to the curb to keep the house — a cold-hearted figure that jumps to 25% for millennials and 28% for unmarried couples.
In addition, 29% say their property gives them a greater sense of security than their significant other does. The same percentage says nothing has strained their relationship more than homeownership.
Even wilder: 21 percent say their house would be way harder to walk away from than their partner — and one in six straight-up admitted they’d choose the home over their relationship if forced to pick. That 16% figure shoots up to 25% among millennials and 28% for unmarried couples.
The findings are based on a survey of 1,000 Americans who bought a home with a spouse or partner, conducted by Clever Real Estate from June 4 to 5, 2026.
“The fact that more than one in four homeowners who bought with their partner believe their home is more likely than their relationship to still be in their life a decade from now speaks to just how significant of a commitment homeownership has become,” Kristen Herhold, writer of the study, told The Post.
“A home is no longer just where people live, but it’s often their largest financial asset, tied to a 30-year mortgage and years of savings.”
Most people who own a home with a partner bought it with a spouse, but a growing share — 13% — buy before marriage or without marrying at all (5%), per the survey.
A fear of being priced out prompted 8% of buyers to pull the trigger on a home before they were ready. Among millennials, that figure ticks up to 35%.
Over a quarter of co-owners end up regretting buying together. That figure nearly doubles among millennials to 50% and unmarried couples to 45%.
Once the ink dries, the honeymoon phase officially ends.
Twenty-nine percent of couples say buying or owning a home is the No. 1 biggest strain on their relationship. For unmarried couples, that share hits 36%. Health issues comes in second for biggest issues that strain a relationship.
Among those who bought before marrying or who remain unmarried, a quarter wished they had waited to buy a home until marriage.
More than 50% say a partner’s annoying habit became 10 times more frustrating after moving in, 24% regularly daydreamed about living totally alone, and 5% said homeownership stress drove them to secretly redownload Tinder. Among millennials, 29% admitted the homebuying strain pushed them back onto dating apps.
Despite the friction, most couples have no plan for their home if they split.
While 36% of buyers believe they deserve to keep the house if things go south, a whopping 66% of couples have never discussed what happens to the property in the event of a breakup. A microscopic 7% actually put a legal agreement in writing.
Couples who bought before marrying are more prepared than married folks.
Thirty-five percent of those who haven’t tied the knot have a breakup plan for their house — more than double the 17% of married couples who do. They’re also nearly three times as likely to get it in writing (14% vs. 5%).

hed: Dying mom leaves grieving son sprawling mythical castle, now filled with her ‘signs’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Los Angeles man is turning his grief into a full-time restoration project, spending his days bringing a storybook Hollywood Hills castle back to life in honor of the mother who left it to him before she died of cancer.
Teva Barnea, who goes by@hollywoodhillscastleonTikTok,has drawn millions of views documenting his slow renovation of the turreted stone property tucked into Laurel Canyon’s Wonderland Avenue, a winding street once home to 1960s and ‘70s rock royalty and now known for one of the neighborhood’s most unusual private residences.
“My mom left me this home after her battle with cancer. I feel her energy and am so grateful,” Barnea, 30,  wrote in one caption.
Built in 1931 and designed with the turrets and stonework of a European storybook cottage, the roughly quarter acre property sits across four lots and has been described in listings as inspired by the architecture ofFrankenstein’s Castle.
The three bedroom home comes with a Moroccan swag chandelier, red sconces, illuminated brickwork and turret lighting, along with a marble steam shower, three fireplaces, heated bidet toilets and multiple courtyards shaded by ancient oaks and bougainvillea.
It has previously been listed for short term rental at $16,750 a month, marketed as a retreat suited to “artists, musicians, and creatives seeking inspiration and escape.”
Dusk with lights off#hollywood#castle
For Barnea, the home has become somethingcloser to a shrine.
“I wanted to show you what the house looks like as the sun is down and it is real calm and all the lights in the house are off too. This is the yard, the flowers,” he said in one video, guiding followers through the darkened property.
His TikTok biography reads simply, “This is my journey to honor my mom through the home she left for me.”
In another clip, he described the strange, almost meditative grief rituals the house has given him.
“I can’t quite explain it, but grief turns you into a bit of a bird watcher. Birds often fly right into the house. I feel it is my obligation to help them get out safety,” Barnea said.
“In this particular occasion this humming bird actually hung out from me for a while. It was a bit like it was thanking me. If you pay attention your loved ones will send you signs. I believe birds are one of the ways they communicate with us.”
He has also opened the door to using the castle professionally.
“My mom passed about a year ago and left me this classic Hollywood Hills home. For a while, I didn’t really know how to handle it. Or what to do. Since, I’ve been updating it. I’m open to shoots, productions and so forth. It’s my dream to carry out my mom’s legacy with the home,” he wrote.
Followers have responded with a mix of sympathy and wonder in the comments, several framing the house and its history in near mystical terms.
“She must’ve been magic,” wrote one commenter.
Another wrote, “I can feel her energy through the screen, this is so beautiful.”
One follower cautioned him never to part with the property because “she left you whimsy,” while another insisted “fairies definitely live there.”
Several others offered condolences alongside the awe, with one writing, “truly magical. I got chills watching this. I am so sorry for your loss.”
The home’s past, however, is not entirely whimsical. In 2010, the property, then rented by tattoo artist and television personalityKat Von D,was heavily damaged by a fire that killed her pet cat, Valentine.
Barnea has said in TikTok videos that Von D kept candles throughout the home and that arson investigators ultimately attributed the blaze to a candle fire, adding that only the home’s stone construction kept it standing.
He has said his late mother Deborah Dresbach, later reached a settlement with Von D that included a non-disclosure agreement, one he said he was not bound by given his age at the time.
Von D has publicly disputed that account, saying the fire began in the basement due to faulty wiring she had already raised concerns about, that she was traveling on a book tour when the fire broke out, and that no NDA was forced on the homeowner.
“I can’t imagine what it would be like to lose a mother that you’re so close with, but at the same time, I didn’t set the house on fire,” she said in her own TikTok response, adding that the fire “was a tragedy and it was out of both of our controls.”

hed: ‘Miami Vice’-style mansion just 90 minutes from LA lists for sale with private boat jetty
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

Can you feel it coming in the air tonight?
In the breezy enclave of Oxnard’s Mandalay Bay sits a house that looks like it was plucked straight out of a 1980s “Miami Vice”art deco fever dream— think bold neon exterior that makes the surrounding properties look like they’re rendered in gray scale, glass bricks as far as the eye can see, dramatic waterfront presence, and unapologetic retro-futuristic flair.
Located midwaybetween Malibu and Santa Barbaraand just 90 minutes from Los Angeles, it offers the best of California coastal living at a price that feels almost reasonable given today’s market.
The striking contemporary home at2150 Napoli Driveis listed at $2.695 million.
What does that price net you?
Nearly 4,000 square feet of living space, four roomy bedrooms, three serene bathrooms, a private 50-foot boat dock easement on one of the wider coveted channels, and — perhaps most impressively —Don Johnsonand Philip Michael Thomas sunning themselves on the Brazilian Ipe hardwood decking.
Full disclosure, that last bit was made up. But with easy access toChannel Islands Harbor, this property will sure make you feel like a dashing TV star, linen suit and pastel T-shirt optional.
What makes this listing particularly interesting is the sheer value. If this exact house were dropped onto LA’s Pacific-facingMarina Del Reyor alongMiami’s prime waterways, there’s little doubt it would command closer to $8 million — maybe even more!

Here, you’re getting that same waterfront lifestyle with significantly more house for the cash you invest — and the perfect combo of views and primo waterway access you can’t find elsewhere on the California coast for anywhere close to that price.
The exterior is pure “Miami Vice”: eye catching, intense, sculptural, art deco lite and impossible to ignore, with custom metal gates, swaying palms, and a tranquil river rock stream greeting visitors at the end of a peaceful cul-de-sac.
Yet once you step inside, the home surprises with a more timeless, understated elegance. Soaring double-height ceilings, open spaces, a muted color palette, walls of glass, and thoughtful architectural details create a light and airy, gallery-like atmosphere rather than garish excess redolent of the cocaine-fueled excesses of the ’80s.
Those aforementioned open living spaces anchored with an artisan fireplace flow chicly toward the water, ideal for everything from lively weekend gatherings à la “The Wolf of Wall Street,” to quiet evenings cozying up on the couch for some tête-à-tête action à la  “The Secret of My Success.”
A chef’s kitchen, games room large enough to fit a pool table (that could easily be converted to a home gym), and multiple outdoor entertaining areas complete the luxe tableau. Upstairs, oversized bedrooms each with a private balcony and a secluded primary suite with its own waterfront terrace add to the property’s star quality.
At a time when true waterfront homes with private docks along the California coast have become increasingly rare and beyond most people’s price points, this home stands out as a rare find — delivering serious panache, sweeping space, and high-glam boating access without the usual seven-figure premium.
And for the Golden State’s highly sought-after coastal real estate, it might just represent the biggest bang for your buck on the market right now.
Sometimes the best real estate deals aren’t the ones everyone’s fighting over in the usual glam zip codes. They’re hiding in plain sight — with a boatload of jetty action and a whole lot of Crockett and Tubbs cosplaying.

hed: Unlucky couple discover their ultimate rural dream home is infested with hundreds of snakes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Imagine you search for years for your dream home and come across a beautiful 1830s stone house in rural Pennsylvania.
There’s only one small problem: a snake infestation. And not just a few snakes, but hundreds.
That’s exactly what happened to Tyler and Lauren Bouldin, who purchased a property in Pine Grove, a small town of around 2,000 people in Central Pennsylvania, in 2020.
The Bouldins bought the 6,000-square-foot, six-bedroom, five-bathroom house at auction in 2020 for $460,000.
The property had sat fallow and unoccupied for more than a decade before the Bouldins and their two children moved in.
That’s apparently when the snakes took up residence.
“When we bought our house, we didn’t realize that we were also buying a large population of snakes,” Tyler joked in one video.
The snakes, as seen on the couple’s TikTok account, appear largely unbothered by their human neighbors.
The Bouldins have caught them slithering up the side of the house, slowly meandering across the front steps of the home, and running roughshod around the property.
“If you find yourself in this situation, the right response is not to burn the entire property to the ground as so many people have suggested,” Tyler said.
Instead, the couple has gone about systematically filling in cracks in their home’s foundation and pulling up stumps on the property that the snakes like to nest in.
Tyler also invested in a “snake grabber” to help him catch snakes on the fly in his yard and remove them to the woods.
The Bouldins originally attempted to let nature manage itself by leaving the non-venomous black snakes largely alone.
“Every time we post a snake video, people say, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the black snakes. Don’t do anything with them.’ And that’s been our policy,” Tyler said in a 2023 TikTok.
The black snakes, said Tyler, are annoying, but serve a purpose: They kept the more venomous Copperheads and timber rattlesnakes at bay.
Or at least that’s what he thought.
He soon discovered that the various snake species were nesting together.
So the family took a different tack, looking to close up any holes in the property that the snakes were slithering into and doing their best to remove food sources —they’ve adopted two cats to help control the rodent population.
Tyler also invested in a “snake grabber” to help him catch snakes on the fly in his yard and remove them to the woods.
Given that snakes love to nest in rotting wood and overgrowth, “We spent whatever free time we had clearing the lawn, stone walls, gardens and woodland of debris, garbage piles, and overgrowth,” Tyler told PEOPLE.
One of the biggest changes they’ve made to the property was removing an ancient in-ground pool that was a cozy home for water snakes.
“We removed our dangerous in-ground pool, restored the pond and installed filters and fountains, and closed up all of the holes in the house and barn, which created homes for mice, etc. We even planted mint around the structures, which naturally deters snakes,” he continued.

The snakes are evidently not keeping the Bouldins from continuing to put down roots.
In 2025, in fact, the couple announced that Tyler’s parents had bought the stone cottage just next door.
If you’ve found your property overrun by snakes, experts recommend first doing everything you can to make the property less inviting for them.
That includes removing debris they might like to nest in and keeping the grass short.
Experts also recommend removing their food sources—snakes feed on mice and other small rodents, so bringing an exterminator in to trap and remove rodents can also help,
Finally, if all else fails, it may be worth hiring a wildlife removal expert who can safely trap and rehome large snake populations.

hed: People keep finding dryer sheets in their mailboxes — here is why you shouldn’t touch it
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A dryer sheet tucked between the bills and the junk mail sounds like a prank. It isn’t, and tossing it in the trash could be a mistake.
Across the country, homeowners are opening their mailboxes to find a Bounce or Snuggle sheet sitting inside, left there deliberately by their letter carrier.
The practice has quietly persisted for years, and it comes down to one thing, keeping wasps out.
Mailboxes make ideal real estate for stinging insects. They’re dark, sheltered from weather, and often go untouched for hours at a stretch, which is exactly what a paper wasp looks for when scouting a nesting spot.
“Insects are always going to be looking for food, water, and harborage,” Brandon Runyon, an entomologist with Swat Pest Management toldRealtor.com.
He added that pests gravitate toward wherever those conditions exist, and mailboxes check every box. Runyon said he has personally discovered paper wasp nests inside his own mailbox.
The dryer sheet trick traces back to a 2010 study that tested Bounce’s “Outdoor Fresh Scent” sheets on fungus gnats, an experiment inspired by gardeners who claimed tucking a sheet in their pocket kept bugs away. Researchers found the sheets held up as a repellent, at least against gnats.
Runyon said the science lines up with what’s inside the sheets. Dryer sheets are loaded with linalool and beta citronella, compounds that occur naturally in lavender, mint, and rose geranium, plants long known to keep insects at bay.
Manufacturers use those same compounds to give laundry products, lotions, and candles their floral scent, pleasant to people, repellent to bugs.
Runyon was careful to note the fungus gnat study doesn’t prove sheets work on wasps specifically, since little formal research exists on that front. Still, postal workers keep swapping the tip on social media, and local news segments keep running it every summer.
Scent may matter more than the sheet itself. A 2015 study found that Victoria’s Secret Bombshell perfume fended off mosquitoes for a full two hours after being sprayed on, while some fruity fragrances appear to draw insects in rather than push them away. One online commenter swore by Dove bar soap as a substitute.
But Runyon isn’t ready to crown the dryer sheet a real solution. He said the concentration of linalool and beta citronella in a typical sheet is too small to meaningfully affect most bugs, and whatever impact it does have will fade fast.
He said a sheet stuffed into a crack where ants are entering a kitchen might scramble their scent trail temporarily, but the insects will eventually reroute or simply wait the smell out.
For anyone serious about keeping insects away, Runyon pointed to sturdier options.
Planting lavender and mint near doorways, window boxes, or garden sheds provides a repellent that doesn’t wash out after one wash cycle. Sprays containing DEET or picaridin work fast, while cedar and lavender oil sprays offer a gentler alternative, provided shoppers match the product to the specific pest they’re battling.
Traps, too, can help, so long as they’re designed for the right target, since ant traps, fly traps, and mosquito traps aren’t interchangeable.
As for the mailbox itself, Runyon’s advice is simple. Close the lid. No opening means no wasp can slip inside, and no unlucky letter carrier gets stung reaching in to drop off the mail.

hed: Beverly Hills rent tumbles drastically as surprising LA County areas spike with huge annual raises
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Are they a bit over the Hills?
In the City Of Angels, it’s noweven cheaper to rentthan buy — especially in the ritzy nabes. LA’s gated Elysium Beverly Hills saw prices for one-room rentals plunge by nearly 9% year over year while rates in more transitional regions surged by as much as 12%, per an eye-opening new survey byZumper.
The study, titled the Zumper Los Angeles Metro Area Report, analyzed listings active from month to calculate the most and least expensive cities in greater LA, as well as the areas where rents are rising — and falling — the fastest.
The findings point to a cooling trend across Golden State — where the median rent for one-bedrooms was $2,057 per month — with 12 of 27 cities clocking in at less expensive than before.
This downward trend was evident in LA Metro Area, where the lion’s share of markets experienced flat or declining annual rents.

Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story
Much of that softness appeared to be concentrated in the region’s priciest neighborhoods.
For instance, costs for single-room rentals in Beverly Hills, where rents cost the second most at $2,750 on average, saw asking rents fall by an average of 4.2% month-over-month — second only to Torrance (4.8%) — and 8.6% year-on-year.
The latter marked the steepest annual decline among neighborhoods where solo-room rentals were $2,000 or higher per month.
The rates for the City Of Dream’s two-bedroom rentals, which set renters back $4,150 per month on average, reportedly dove by 6.1% month-over-month and 12.3% year-over-year.
Other enclaves impacted by the cooldown includedWest Hollywood(single-bedroom rates declined by 1.5% month-over-month, 5.8% year-over-year), Redondo Beach (2.7% month-over-month, 6.9% year-over-year) and Huntington Beach (5.6% year over year).
Not even Santa Monica, which was the most expensive city at $2,830 for a one bedroom, was safe from this cold plunge. The month-over-month dip clocked in at 2.4%.
The reverse was largely true in SoCal’s lower-end locales.
San Bernardino’s single bedroom rental rates amounted to just $1,470 — the most affordable in the region — but it saw a whopping 5% price increase year-over-year (the two bedrooms saw rents climb 6.4% during this same period).
One-bedrooms in Palmdale, which run renters $1,570 per month, saw the greatest year-on-year price hike at 12.1% (4% month-on-month).
Lancaster, where renters pay $1,480 for a one-bedroom, was the one exception. Although rates rose 5.7% from the previous month, they remained 11.9% lower than a year earlier.
Crystal Chen, a seasonedhousing market expertand writer for the Zumper Blog, said these diverging trends boil down to supply and demand.
“In general, new high-end supply coming online in pricier areas like Beverly Hills and West Hollywood gives renters more negotiating leverage, which puts downward pressure on asking rents as landlords compete for a limited pool of top-tier tenants,” she explained. “Lower-end neighborhoods, meanwhile, are seeing price spikes largely because they offer relative affordability.”
She added, “As renters get priced out of city and coastal centers, demand shifts toward these more affordable pockets, pushing prices up there instead.”

hed: Career opportunities are exploding in 5 affordable ‘cities on the rise’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

WhileCalifornia’s Silicon Valleyremains the headline-grabbing epicenter of an AI recruiting frenzy, mid-size—and far more affordable—markets scattered around the US are quietly offering equally impressivehiring opportunities.
The global professional networking powerhouse LinkedIn released its second annual “Cities on the Rise” ranking on July 21, identifying 25 metros emerging as America’s fastest-growing job hubs.
Based on LinkedIn data, the new report focuses on up-and-coming markets beyond traditional hiring juggernauts like New York City and San Francisco, showcasing cities that deliver a combination of career opportunities, affordability, and quality of life advantages. The report also incorporates home listing datafrom Realtor.com®.
“According to LinkedIn survey data, two-thirds of professionals say they work to live, not live to work, reflecting a broader shift inhow people evaluate career decisions,” Andrew Seaman, editor-at-large for Jobs and Careers Development at LinkedIn, tells Realtor.com®. “As a result, smaller and midsize metros with thriving economies, growing employers, and vibrant communities are becoming increasingly attractive places to build a career.”
Fifteen cities fromlast year’s rankingmade a comeback in 2026, demonstrating that many of these metros are maintaining their momentum by continuing to attract a steady stream of professionals.
However, the top of the list underwent significant shifts. Newcomer Augusta, GA, clinched first place, followed by Richmond, VA, which climbed 11 spots from last year to claim silver, and Reno, NV, captured bronze after ranking 22nd in the inaugural report.
Also making its debut in the 2026 ranking, North Port, FL, came in fourth, while Harrisburg, PA, took fifth, having dropped two spots from last year.
Augusta and North Port are among 10 cities making their first appearance in the ranking, signaling that economic momentum is expanding its footprint, with new hiring opportunities emerging across a wide range of regions.
“From growing logistics and distribution centers in Louisville, Charleston, and Harrisburg, to a manufacturingresurgence in Renoand Indianapolis, we’re also seeingAI data centers fuel growthin midsize metros like Augusta and Richmond,” says Seaman.
The South claims the highest share of up-and-coming job centers in the 2026 rankings, with 11 cities, followed by the Midwest, with six, and the West and Northeast with four cities each.
“Each of these markets offers a resilient but also dynamic labor market,” notes Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner, referring to the top five metros on the list. “State governments anchor employment in Richmond and Harrisburg, Fort Eisenhower offers military employment for Augusta, and rapid population growth in Reno and North Port create many kinds of employment opportunities, as well as having outdoor lifestyle perks in those locations.”
Comparing these mid-size markets to larger job hubs in their respective regions, Berner points out that Reno serves as a budget-friendly alternative to the Bay Area, Richmond offers professionals more bang for their buck than nearby Washington, DC, andHarrisburg boasts lower home pricesthan Philadelphia, which is still just a two-hour drive away.

“The combination of robust employment opportunities andlow costs of livingare drawing professionals to these smaller but growing markets,” points out the economist.
Examiningcurrent housing market conditionsacross the top five metros highlighted by the LinkedIn report, Realtor.com data analysis shows that Augusta is the most affordable of the bunch, with the median price in June registering at $315,125, down 4.4% from a year ago.
Harrisburg follows closely with a median price of $350,000, while North Port settled at $485,000 last month.
Reno is a notable outlier among the group: The median price there surged 10% year over year to $685,575, while its inventory of for-sale properties plunged nearly 23%, suggesting that the Nevada city is in the throes of a major supply crunch.
“It may struggle to continue to absorb the increased demand for homes there without prices running up in a major way,” warns Berner.
In contrast, prices in the other four metros are trending downward, offering welcome news to job seekers looking to relocate.

hed: Will Beacon Hill do anything to help the Massachusetts housing crisis? With clock ticking, two ideas are on the table.
subhead: Duplexes everywhere? Religious-land exemption? What housing policy will survive the end-of-session rush?
content: State-level housing reform in Massachusetts is always a hard sell. But lawmakers are feeling the pressure of this state’s ever-rising housing costs — especially after the near-miss earlier this year with a ballot question that would have brought the nation’s strictest rent control policy to Massachusetts. Now, with next week’s close of the two-year formal legislative session fast approaching, the House and Senate are trading proposals for substantial reforms that would make it easier to build multifamily homes in this state that is desperate for more of them. Two significant policies have emerged in negotiations over a major economic development bill. One would allow moderately-dense apartment buildings by-right, or without special local approval, on land owned by religious institutions. The other would allow duplexes by-right on all residentially-owned land in Massachusetts. Neither effort would be a panacea to the state’s housing woes, and it’s not clear what might emerge in final legislation that will be hashed out over the next week. But either could offer a significant boost, perhaps facilitating the construction of thousands of new homes. “This housing problem we have is so pervasive that it is not going to be solved one piecemeal solution at a time,” said Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director of the pro-housing group Abundant Housing Massachusetts. “We need a whole slate of ambitious reforms aimed at immediately making it easier to build the homes we need. Anything short of that is not enough.”Related: Facing empty pews, churches are turning their buildings into low-income housingThe religious-land provision in the House’s version of the economic development bill closely follows similar “Yes in God’s Backyard” — or YIGBY — efforts in other states. It would allow multifamily housing development without discretionary approval from local governments on parcels up to four acres owned by churches, synagogues, temples, and other places of worship. Those developments could be 30 units per acre, and even denser — 50 units per acre — if 25 percent of units are set aside at affordable rents. So the policy could in theory pave the wave for projects as large as 200 units. The provision would tap into what has already been a growing trend: Many churches and other religious institutions have fallen on hard times recently as the number of people attending services has dwindled. That has left many places of worship searching for a second life, and many have settled on housing. It’s a natural transition: Many churches own substantial real estate — acquired when congregations needed space for services, schools, and dormitories — often in premium locations on main streets near town centers where housing development makes good sense. It often fits their mission, too, said Rev. Adam Isbitsky, the legacy pastor of the soon-to-be-closed Second Congregational Church in Beverly.Work is underway to convert a church rectory and former school in Cambridge to an affordable apartment building.David L Ryan/ Globe Staff “Religious institutions are always trying to ask, in this time when the role of the church in society is shifting, how can we continue to serve our wider community?” he said. ”When the cost of housing is a huge challenge facing many people, this is a natural way for us to further our mission.”Isbitsky’s Second Congregational Church will eventually turn their sprawling Conant Street building over to LifeBridge North Shore, a homeless services nonprofit, to be operated as a new resource center. But the process to reach that agreement was at times contentious, with residents concerned it would bring homeless people to their neighborhood.Many other churches making similar transitions or that have opted to build housing on their land have encountered similar opposition. The YIGBY provision could smooth the path.“Churches and religious institutions are deeply rooted in the community,” said Isbitsky. “You’re not putting this power to develop land into housing in the hands of an out-of-state developer. You’re giving it to groups who have a place’s best interests in mind.”Amy Dain, a local zoning and land-use expert and senior fellow at Boston Indicators, the research arm of the Boston Foundation, said the YIGBY proposal could spur the construction of thousands of new homes. An analysis by the Lincoln Land Institute and the Boston-based Lynch Foundation identified some 4,800 developable parcels totaling over 20,000 acres owned by religious institutions across Massachusetts. If even a quarter of that land was developed at a reasonable density, it could translate into 250,000 new homes, according to the Citizens’ Housing and Planning Association.Of course, that level of build out would take time and resources. “But the potential is there,” Dain said. The impact of the duplex provision, which was included in the Senate’s version of the economic development bill, is harder to measure. The idea is simple: there are millions of residentially zoned parcels in Massachusetts, and in a state that needs to build 222,000 homes by 2035 to moderate price growth, allowing two units on those lots instead of one could go a long way.A measure moving through the state Senate would legalize two-family homes on residential lots across Massachusetts.Erin Clark/Globe StaffAnd, importantly, the provision would tackle the state’s thorny history with single-family zoning. Apartments were broadly allowed in many Massachusetts cities and towns as the state grew rapidly in the late 1800 and early 1900s. But many municipalities gradually banned them starting in the 1920s, in part over concerns about immigration and a desire to keep neighborhoods exclusive.Today, 96 percent of the residential land in Massachusetts allows single-family homes by right, according to a report from the National Zoning Atlas, which analyzed the zoning codes of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns. By contrast, duplexes are allowed by-right on 38 percent of the state’s land, and three-unit buildings are permissible on just 7 percent. Related: Spotlight: An American ideal, reimaginedAnd beyond efforts to build more housing, advocates say even something as simple as allowing duplexes on all of that land could help undo that legacy. Other states have done the same, and have been celebrated for “ending single-family zoning.”Either proposal, said Eric Shupin, the chief executive of CHAPA, would also represent a further step to reign in the power of municipalities to restrict the rate of construction in this state. Strict municipal zoning rules are in part responsible for the state’s housing shortage to begin with.“The fact that the House and Senate have taken up these meaningful reforms is both sides acknowledging that we have to do something urgently about our housing shortage,” said Eric Shupin, CHAPA’s chief executive. “And the best way for them to do that, frankly, would be to pass both of these reforms immediately.”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: Cambridge passed one of the most ambitious housing reforms in the US. Now comes the construction, and the backlash.
content: CAMBRIDGE — Depending who you ask, the project at 9 Wyman Road in Huron Village represents either the solution to Cambridge’s stifling housing shortage, or a bellwether of upheaval to the city’s most cherished neighborhoods. The proposal would have a developer knock down a stately single-family house on a tree-lined cul-de-sac of big and expensive homes, and replace it with a 56-unit white and black apartment building, six stories tall and just feet from its shorter neighbors.Those neighbors are not pleased. They’ve started a website to “Stop 9 Wyman” and have asked the historical commission to deem the home a landmark and halt its demolition, to no avail. There are whispers of a lawsuit. “I think every person on this street would agree that cities like Cambridge grow and change and need to build more housing,” said Daniel Cohn, who lives next door. “But it is difficult to see how a project this big can reasonably fit onto our little street.” To many, though, this is what it will take to solve a housing crisis that has made Cambridge one of the most expensive places in the world to live, one that has forced many longtime residents to move away. Projects like 9 Wyman were the goal when the City Council last year near-unanimously passed one of the nation’s most permissive housing laws, in one swoop undoing a thicket of rules that had long dictated what could be built where in this densely packed and desirable city of 120,000. In short, the new rules mean that four-to-six-story buildings can go up on nearly any residential lot, with minimal input from neighbors or city boards.Related: In dramatic overhaul, Cambridge becomes one of the first cities in Mass. to eliminate single-family zoningJust 17 months later, the changes are beginning to take shape: Apartment buildings are cropping up on streets that haven’t seen so much as a home alteration in decades as longtime owners sell to developers eager to utilize the new rules. Hammers and buzzsaws ring out on quiet residential streets. So far this year, the city has permitted around 400 new homes, many of them small and midsized multifamily projects that were not allowed previously. And the docket of planned projects is much larger. A construction crew at 214 Allston Street in Cambridge, where an older two-family home is being replaced with two new high-end condos.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffIt is a meaningful slug of new housing, and change, that has stirred complicated emotions and has Cambridge grappling with how to balance its historic character with a more progressive vision.“If we are serious about building enough housing to support the demand to live in our city and stabilize prices, then we have to be building new homes of all sizes in every corner of the city,” said City Councilor Marc McGovern. “We set out to spur more housing construction in Cambridge. As far as I’m concerned, we’ve achieved that.”Cambridge is one of the most densely populated cities in the US thanks to its blocks stuffed with small apartment buildings, but hasn’t built much in decades, at least beyond large-scale development on its fringes at Alewife and Northpoint. New construction has been particularly slow lately, with building starting on an average of 350 new homes a year between 2023 and 2025, compared to more than 800 units per year a decade ago. There are many reasons — high land costs, tight development sites. But last year the City Council identified what it believed to be a main culprit: Cambridge’s extremely complex land-use rules, which capped building heights in many places at two or three stories, meaning some older homes could not be built today.Their solution? Throw out all of those rules, and allow projects up to four stories tall on nearly every residential lot in the city; projects can be six stories if they exceed 10 units and thus trigger a requirement that 20 percent of units be set aside at affordable rents.Related: ‘The numbers should work, and they just don’t’: Is Cambridge’s affordable housing rule backfiring?The idea was to spread development more equitably across the city, including in neighborhoods that have long resisted new construction. A pipeline is beginning to take shape. While a handful of projects have already received building permits and broken ground, a Globe analysis of a crowd-sourced tracker compiled by City Councilor Catherine Zusy’s office identified more than 70 sites with at least preliminary development plans that, combined, could add more than 600 new homes. There has been a particularly notable increase in four-story projects of three to nine units — a development sweet spot that avoids the affordable housing requirement. One such project, on Ivy Street near Fresh Pond, will put eight condominiums on the site of what was previously one single-family home. Michael Yogman lives on Wyman Road in Cambridge, where a 56-unit housing development is planned for his cul-de-sac of single-family houses.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffSome developers, though, are utilizing the new rules to build bigger luxury homes, a trend that has captured the attention of Zusy and other critics. The lone council vote against the new zoning rules last year, Zusy has been documenting these projects on social media. Last month, she posted a video of an excavator slowly ripping apart a “perfectly good” older two-family at 214 Allston Street in Cambridgeport, to be replaced by two luxury townhouses, likely to be priced well over $2 million each, she said.“What we’ve essentially done is strip away all of the guardrails and let the free market decide what kind of housing gets built and where,” said Zusy. “And not all of the projects are bad, but many of them are replacing good, relatively affordable old homes with more expensive ones.”The developer, Mike Tokatlyan of Boston-based Contempo Builders, has at least eight pending projects in Cambridge, several of them similar townhouse developments that take advantage of the relaxed height and density rules. He did not respond to requests for comment.As cities from coast to coast wrestle with high housing costs, others have tried similar zoning experiments. Portland, Ore., for example allows fourplexes and other “missing middle” housing types citywide. But none have allowed the widespread scale of height and density that Cambridge now does. Related: ‘We love these buildings’: Should developers get to build six stories anywhere in Cambridge?The city’s Community Development Department said projects like the one at 214 Allston Street — with a developer tearing down a small two- or three-family home in favor of the same number of bigger luxury units — are relatively few. And the department and City Council are considering tweaks to the rules for such developments, by limiting the allowable square footage of new units. Zusy and fellow Councilor Tim Flaherty would like to rein it back further, proposing changes that would require larger setbacks and off-street parking and limit six-story buildings to a few major corridors. There are those who argue that even small projects adding one or two more units than what was previously on a lot is a worthy endeavor, even if those new homes are expensive. At 73 Kirkland Street, developer and local architect Martin Cafasso tore down a single-family home that he will soon replace with a geometric four-story, four-family building that he hopes will be inhabited by young families and older residents who are looking to downsize. “Those are big congestion points in Cambridge,” said Cafasso. “The idea is to build an interesting building that will help people stay in the neighborhood.”The AJ Spears Funeral Home and two multifamily buildings next door on Western Ave. in Cambridge will be knocked down and replaced with a six-story, 74-unit apartment building.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffBut if teardowns are perhaps an unintended consequence of the new zoning, projects like 9 Wyman are exactly the point, and roughly 10 developments like it — six-story buildings of 25 to 80 units — are in various stages of the planning process all over Cambridge. In a two-block radius around Ellery Street and Broadway, in mid-Cambridge near the Main branch of the Cambridge Public Library, there are four such projects close to receiving approvals.On Wyman Road on a recent afternoon, Cohn gazed at the “disaster-to-be” next to his house. He and his neighbors, he said, are not altogether opposed to multifamily housing there, and would support something three stories tall and with fewer units. But as it is planned now, the project next door to the single-family house where he has lived since 2012 would not include parking, which Cohn fears would lead new residents to crowd their cars on his narrow dead-end street. Demolition is underway, and if the project receives a building permit, Cohn, a corporate bankruptcy lawyer, said he and his neighbors “absolutely will sue.”9 Wyman Road  in Cambridge, which is proposed to be replaced with a six-story apartment building.David L. Ryan/Globe Staff“We would certainly prefer to talk with the developer about a revised proposal that fits the neighborhood,” said Cohn. “But the City Council has changed the rules in such a way that we no longer have any recourse or input in the development process.”That 9 Wyman’s neighbors have little say in what gets built there is exactly the point of the new zoning rules, said Justin Saif, cochair of the local pro-housing group A Better Cambridge. Cambridge’s affluent and eclectic culture means that a place known for growth and innovation simultaneously has a rich history that people want to protect. Many are willing to spend money to derail development they don’t like — a significant reason why the city has fallen so far short of its ambitious housing goals.At a certain point, the fight over where and how to build housing becomes a question of values, he said. “The question has always been, what’s more important?” Saif said. “The character of our neighborhoods or building the homes we need?”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: A look at Vermont’s new luxury ski-on, ski-off housing developments
subhead: The Green Mountain State is catering to a “growing demand for slopeside ownership.”
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

WhenKillington Resortopens its ski lifts for the 2026–27 season, there will be six new homes at the base ofBear Mountain— one of the peaks (including Pico Mountain) that make up the Vermont ski area known as “The Beast of the East.”

CalledBase Camp at Bear Mountain, the new development offers high-end slopeside housing in a gated community that, besides private heated garage parking, chef’s kitchens, spa baths, and spacious living with mountain views, offers every skier’s favorite amenity: a ski-on, ski-off location. The residents at Base Camp won’t ever need to load their gear into a car, drive to the mountain, or even carry their skis to the lift. They will simply open the door, step into their skis, and take off to the Bear Mountain Quad or Skye Peak Express.


The new townhouses, are the first of an eventual 24; 10 are currently under construction and all are sold, including the six that will be move-in ready this fall. The remaining 14 units that are still available will be completed in 2028.

“We saw a growing demand for slopeside ownership opportunities at Killington Resort, particularly among buyers seeking turnkey, luxury mountain residences,” said Steve Malone, vice president of development of Base Camp at Bear Mountain. The corporation is a separate entity from the resort and purchased the land from Killington. The purchase of a Base Camp condominium does not include lift tickets.

Killington bucked the national trend of corporate ownership in October of 2024, when a local group bought the resort from PWDR, a conglomerate of ski areas. Underindependent ownership, the mountain has launched a $65 million revamp that includes upgraded snowmaking technology, a new base lodge, and new lifts. Killington offers more than 200 trails and 92 miles of diverse terrain, including a terrain park network. The resort also boasts the longest ski season in the area; in 2025, it lasted 183 days.

“It’s too soon to know how independent ownership has affected the numbers, but we know that flexible work has allowed [more] people to stay here,” said Amy Laramie, vice president of marketing and events at Killington. “During COVID, the population at Killington exploded. The new Base Camp development is a real positive for the mountain; We don’t have a lot of lodging that’s close to the ski area.”


The new townhomes at Base Camp, which will have four bedrooms and five bathrooms, are priced at $2,995,000 for the 2,800-square-foot units, and $3,600,000 for the 4,000-square-foot units, which include a walk-out basement. The homes will feature panoramic mountain views through 14-foot windows, gas fireplaces, heated two-car garages, spa bathrooms, and gourmet kitchens equipped with Viking stoves. Homeowners will be able to make their units available to short-term renters, providing they apply for and receive the appropriate license from the town of Killington.

“We also offer a furnishings package in a partnership with Restoration Hardware and Pompanoosuc Mills,” Malone said, noting it’s the only new luxury ski-on, ski-off living development at Killington.



“The market will be very receptive to this development,” said Teresa DiNapoli, associate broker with Four Seasons Sotheby’s International Realty in Ludlow, Vt. “We have seen a lot of walk-to-slope luxury developments at Vermont ski mountains, including at Smuggler’s Notch, at Jay Peak in the Northeast Kingdom, and at Okemo, south of Killington. Okemo is buildingSouth Face Village, a similar luxury development; the mountain has the most walk-to-slope housing of any Vermont ski area.”

SouthFace Village offers chalets and townhomes with direct access to Okemo’s South Face Express Quad chairlift. For year-round and summer residents, the community has an outdoor heated pool. There’s also a spa, fitness center, and outdoor cooking and dining areas.

Current units for salerange from $1,450,000 for a 1,836-square-foot unit to $795,000 for a 1,248-square-foot unit.

Laramie points out that Killington Resort has become a four-season destination.

“In the non-ski season, the mountain offers zip lining, ropes courses, hiking, and scenic gondola rides; people especially love those for the views during fall foliage season,” she said. “Mountain biking has become very big. The chair lifts have bike carriers, and people get a 365-day pass so that they can use them for skiing and for mountain biking.”

But according to DiNapoli, winter remains the market’s biggest draw.

“The market for these kinds of homes is, first and foremost, skiers. While also attractive to people who use them year-round, they are not for people who only come here in the summer,” she said.

For Bryan Rivard, director of communication forSki Vermont, living on one of the state’s resorts isn’t just about luxury amenities.

“In Vermont, the ski areas are community hubs and gathering places, and they become a reflection of the people around them,” he said. “There is a different vibe and attitude at each one; they are so varied in their personality and sizes. we have a huge place like Killington, and at the other end of the spectrum, the Middlebury Snow Bowl, which has four employees.”

“Living slopeside is quite special, especially in the winter,” added Laramie. “When you can see the groomers on the mountain after dark, it’s beautiful.”

Regina Cole writes about architecture and design for national and regional publications, with a specialty in historic architecture and the history of the decorative arts.

hed: Manhattan poker bro sued by ritzy neighbors after ignoring $87K in fines for turning $4M condo into weed den: suit
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A seemingly entitled poker player is taking living the high life a little too literally.
Alleged pot-head Chau Shing Lam has been smoking cigarettes and weed at all hours of the day and night, and burning up his Kips Bay neighbors’ patience, according to an explosive new Manhattan Supreme Court lawsuit.
Property records show Lam paid $4.15 million in August 2022 for a condominium unit in luxury 368 Third Ave. — which has always had a clear non-smoking policy.
Hoping to finally nip his “near-daily” weed habit in the bud, the board at the condo — where a penthouse is currently listed for $8.7 million — is suing the high-flying resident who let $87,000 in fines go straight up in smoke, court records obtained by The Post show.
Lam is an avid poker player who has competed in international tournaments in Monte Carlo, Paris and Barcelona, earning hundreds of thousands of dollars in winnings.
He has allegedly been lighting up pot and tobacco all the time and sending “noxious smoke” wafting through hallways and into neighboring homes.
The secondhand fumes are seeping into the bedroom of a 12-year-old child battling a severe respiratory condition, the suit claims.
The kid in unit 31A, “has been diagnosed with reactive airway dysfunction syndrome, a serious respiratory condition that is directly exacerbated by exposure to secondhand smoke,” court documents state. The child’s father is a practicing physician.
“In the last month, objective air quality monitoring has consistently documented PM2.5 (fine particulate matter 2.5 micrometers or smaller in diameter) in the neighboring unit at dangerous levels, including levels classified by the [US Environmental Protection Agency] as “Unhealthy” for all persons and extremely dangerous for a child with this condition,” per July 17 court records.
That is the same classification used during extreme wildfire events, like the orange haze that blanketed the East Coast from Canadian wildfires, and breathing that air is the equivalent of smoking about seven to 10 cigarettes.
The suit comes as the family with the sick child “will be permanently moving into the adjacent unit the week of July 20, 2026,” public records show.
The lawsuit asks a judge to declare Lam, who didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment, in breach of building rules.
The neighbors above and below Lam, who also goes by the name Andrew Lam, allegedly reported smoke odor made its way into their homes.
To make matters worse, Lam allegedly throws late-night ragers complete with “loud banging, running around, and yelling.” And, there is “loud, incessant dog barking” coming from his unit, per court documents.
Despite neighbor complaints, 16 board violation letters over a roughly two-year period, “escalating fines,” suspension of amenity privileges, and staff attempting to speak to Lam about the issues, the stubborn smoker refused to change his ways.
In total, Lam’s habit ran up an eye-watering $87,250 in penalties over two years, which were applied to his monthly common charges statements.
In 2024, the board levied various fines against him for smoke and dog barking complaints, and stripped him of “non-essential services.” He was also  prohibited from using the building’s amenities including the laundry room, gym, common roof terrace, residents’ storage rooms, the media room and party room and bike storage room for long periods.
Guests, delivery workers, and service people were strictly barred past the concierge desk unless Lam personally escorted them. Doormen were forbidden from calling up to announce arrivals or holding packages other than standard US mail, while all routine unit repairs — except for building emergencies — were flat-out suspended.
By late 2025 and early 2026, the fines surged as the complaints kept rolling in.
Board attorneys called Lam’s behavior “egregious and unacceptable,” and an “inexcusable and unrelenting pattern of willful misconduct,” in court documents.
“Hi, can you please stop making these non sense [sic], I’ve been smoking here the past two year [sic] and the building knows and didn’t say anything about it, and more people smoke in the buildings,” Lam wrote back to the board in an email on June 16, per court documents.
“And after I talk to my neighbor I tried to stop and after our last conversation on the 10th I haven’t even smoke in the apartment, I have weed kept and carried, but that totally fine it my right to do that. So please stop.”
Lam is known to the building staff (and is in the building system) as Andrew Lam, concierge attendant Michael Bonilla told The Post. Lam was not home when The Post paid a visit Wednesday afternoon.
Bonilla said Lam is currently in Asia. Footage of Lam at a poker tournament earlier this month in South Korea saw organizers refer to him as both Chau Shing Lam and Andrew.
Bonilla, who typically works at the building from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., said he personally has had no gripes about Lam, and his access to building services and amenities have since been restored.
On Monday the court issued a temporary restraining order pending the hearing of the motion, which means Lam is court-ordered to cease lighting up in his apartment, on the balcony or in the building’s common areas — at least for now.
“The Board made repeated good-faith efforts to resolve this matter without resorting to litigation, but after exhausting every available avenue, we were left with no choice but to bring this action to enjoin the unit owner’s ongoing misconduct and protect the interests of the condominium community,” the board’s attorney, Jake Bedor, a partner in Fox Rothschild, said in an emailed statement to The Post.
Victor Kamara, senior property manager at FirstService Residential, didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Completed in 2021, Vu condo has 100 units and rises 36 stories. Building amenities include kitchen and pantry for entertaining, a residents’ lounge, a screening room, a fitness center, a studio and a rooftop terrace.

hed: What is the ‘Widow Tax’ — and how could it reshape the great wealth transfer in the US?
subhead: The ‘widow tax’ is not one tax
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
When Evelyn Delgado called her auto insurer after her husband died, she expected the bill to fall — after all, the policy now covered only one driver instead of two.
But after removing her husband, Delgado’s premium jumped by $280 a year.
“You can imagine my shock,” the Central Texas widow told legislators in 2025. “Nothing changed about me or my property, except that I lost my husband. Nothing else changed.”
Pam Kuchta had a similar experience.
“As I grieved the loss of my husband, the last thing I expected was a sudden spike in my insurance bill,” she said.
Texas has since barred home and auto insurers from changing someone’s rate solely because they became widowed, but Delgado and Kuchta’s experiences expose a financial contradiction that is only growing in scale and impact.
Widowhood can reduce a household’s income while leaving the cost of sustaining the same life unchanged — or even higher.
Of the $124 trillion in assets that Cerulli Associates estimates will change hands through 2048, $54 trillion is first expected to pass between spouses.
Of that sum, more than 95% will go to women.
But inheriting the household’s assets doesn’t preserve the income that supported them.
A surviving spouse may keep the house, retirement accounts, and other wealth while losing one Social Security payment and moving into less favorable tax and Medicare thresholds.
Estate-planning attorneys sometimes use the term “widow tax” to describe that collection of disadvantages.
“‘Widow tax’ suggests a single line item, and in my experience it’s really a convergence of several ordinary rules that all land the same year,” explains Jonathan White, an estate planning attorney.
Social Security is often the first hit.
A surviving spouse keeps the larger of the couple’s two benefits, but the household still loses one monthly payment. So while an individual benefit can climb, household income still falls.
That impact has had a dramatic and measurable impact on widows, in particular.
Among women whose husbands claimed Social Security at full retirement age, widowhood increased the probability of falling into the bottom 5% of their pre-widowhood income distribution by 6.9 percentage points, according to a 2026 TIAA Institute study by economist Sita Slavov.
In plain terms, that means becoming far more likely to end up with less income than 95% of women in the study had before widowhood.
What income remains after widowhood also often receives far less favorable treatment.
Just one year after the death of a spouse, the survivor loses the ability to file a joint tax return unless another filing status applies, subjecting required minimum distributions and other retirement income to single-filer tax brackets.
In 2026, the standard deduction is $32,200 for married couples filing jointly but $16,100 for single filers, according to the Internal Revenue Service.
The 22% tax bracket begins above $50,400 in taxable income for a single filer—exactly half the $100,800 threshold for a couple filing jointly.
Medicare’s income-related surcharges also begin at substantially lower income levels for individual filers than for married couples filing jointly.
In 2026, income-related surcharges begin above $109,000 for an individual, compared with $218,000 for a married couple filing jointly—so a widow can cross the threshold even if household income has fallen substantially.
It’s a complicated web of falling income and increasing exposure, but White says surviving spouses should pay attention to two, in particular.
“The changes with the greatest effect are the shift to single-filer income tax brackets and the Medicare IRMAA cliff, because those thresholds for a single filer sit at roughly half the married thresholds, not because the surviving spouse’s income actually falls in half,” he says.
Nowhere is the strain more obvious than the house itself, though.
As many as 35% of recently widowed older homeowners spent at least 30% of their income on housing, the threshold commonly used to define housing-cost burden, according to a 2022 study from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
Among homeowners aged 60 and older overall, the comparable rate was 22%, meaning the housing-cost-burden rate was approximately 59% higher among recently widowed homeowners.
White says it’s something he sees in his own practice.
