“The survivor stays in a house sized for two people, and the carrying costs (taxes, insurance, heating, deferred maintenance) keep draining liquid assets while the equity sits untouched,” he explains.
And in recent years, those carrying costs have become substantially more expensive.
Property taxes rose 31% nationally between 2019 and 2025, while average monthly homeowners insurance premiums increased 72%, according to the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies’ State of the Nation’s Housing 2026 report.
Residential electricity costs rose more than 30% between 2020 and 2025.
Selling the family home and downsizing might seem like the obvious solution, then. But that seemingly straightforward answer runs straight into the hidden home equity tax.
Today, an estimated 13.1 million homeowners have gains above their applicable exclusion limit, according to research from the National Association of Realtors®.
That’s due in large part to long-tenured homeowners remaining in their homes long enough for price appreciation to outpace what the exclusion protects.
But widows who have lived in their homes for decades face an even more unusual exposure: The protection available to a married couple can shrink soon after one spouse dies.
For a surviving spouse, the larger exclusion generally remains available only if the sale closes within two years of the spouse’s death and the other requirements are met.
After that window, the survivor is generally limited to the $250,000 exclusion.
“So a couple who could have sold with no tax consequence while both were alive can find that the same sale, made three years after one spouse dies, generates a real bill, even though the house hasn’t appreciated any further in that time,” White says.
“I tell clients: If you’re going to sell, know that two-year clock and plan around it deliberately. Don’t let it pass by default.”
But allowing the two-year window to expire doesn’t automatically create a tax bill—as a second rule may work in the survivor’s favor.
When one spouse dies, the tax basis of some or all of the home may be adjusted to its fair market value on the date of death. Because taxable gain is calculated against that basis, the adjustment can erase much of the appreciation that accumulated during the marriage and reduce—or sometimes eliminate—the gain on a later sale.
“Two things change at once,” White says. “Part or all of the home’s cost basis gets stepped up to fair market value as of the date of death, which can erase most of the taxable gain built up over the marriage. At the same time, the survivor’s capital gains exclusion on a future sale drops from $500,000 to $250,000 unless the sale closes within two years of the death.”
The survivor then has to weigh both rules together: the possible loss of the larger exclusion and the possible basis adjustment created by the spouse’s death.
But how much of the home’s basis is adjusted can depend on where the couple lived and how they owned the property.
“In a community-property state, both halves of the home get a full step-up in basis at the first spouse’s death, even the half the surviving spouse already owned,” White says. “In Massachusetts and most other common-law states, only the deceased spouse’s half gets stepped up; the survivor’s half keeps its original, often much lower, basis.”
Consider two couples who bought equally priced homes at the same time and experienced identical appreciation. If one home receives a full basis adjustment at the first spouse’s death and the other receives an adjustment only on the deceased spouse’s share, the surviving owners could face very different taxable gains upon sale.
Matt Odgers, a California estate planning attorney, says the distinction can eliminate decades of taxable appreciation in a community-property state.
“When one spouse dies in a community-property state, the home’s entire cost basis resets to its value that day,” Odgers says. “Decades of appreciation can disappear for tax purposes in a single moment.”
But living in a community-property state isn’t necessarily enough. The language on the deed and the form in which the couple held title can affect whether the property receives community-property treatment. That makes the ownership documents nearly as important as the home’s purchase price, current value, and eventual sale price.
Even when a survivor can sell the house with a solid profit, the property’s equity may not reach the couple’s children or other heirs.
Longer life spans and higher costs are expected to consume much of the Great Wealth Transfer’s wealth before it can ever be passed on. Of the $93 trillion in assets that boomers hold today, only $36 trillion could reach Gen X and millennial heirs over the next 20 years, according to Visa Business and Economic Insights.
“Long-term care is the biggest [expense] by a wide margin,” White says. “A surviving spouse who needs assisted living or memory care is often paying $8,000 to $15,000 a month privately, and that draws down savings fast, especially once it runs for several years.”
The home may eventually become the largest practical source of money available to pay for that care, forcing a sale even when the survivor is not emotionally prepared to move, market conditions are unfavorable, or a different timeline would have produced a better tax result.
“In California, the family home often reaches a surviving spouse nearly tax-free,” Odgers says. “What quietly erodes the estate is everything that happens in the years between the two deaths.”
The death of a spouse can start several financial clocks at the moment the survivor is least prepared to make permanent decisions—and that may be the most costly toll.
“I’ve seen families lose real money simply because nobody revisited the plan after the first spouse died, not because anyone did anything wrong, just because grief and administrative fatigue delayed decisions that had actual deadlines attached to them,” White says.
For the millions of women expected to receive wealth from a spouse in the coming decades, the family home may remain their largest asset—and their biggest burden.

hed: $15M Vermont estate with underground tunnel and ‘secret rooms’ goes up for auction
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


A luxurious Vermont mansion that features a climate-controlled underground tunnel, reinforced concrete vault, and a host of over-the-top amenities has been put on the auction block—with no minimum bid and no reserve.
​That means that the homeowners, Adam and Sarah Hergenrother, are handing over the property to the highest bidder, regardless of price.
​Located in Stowe, VT, the property known as The Preserve at Wade Pasture sits behind the gates of one of the town’s most prestigious mountain enclaves, Robinson Springs. Guests are welcomed to the property by an antique red Stowe Mountain Resort gondola.
“An offering of this caliber is seldom available—don’t let it slip away,” the listing teases.
​The extraordinary estate was designed “as a private family sanctuary where craftsmanship, engineering, recreation, and nature exist in remarkable harmony,” a press release states.
​The 10,000-square-foot residence features a concrete underground tunnel that leads to the lavish sports complex. This 7,000-square-foot sports barn is equipped with a heated turf, making it ideal for playing tennis, pickleball, golf, or other activities.
An outdoor court is also available for tennis, pickleball, or basketball. The grounds also consist of a heated pool with a natural stone wall, a winter sledding hill, and a 14-foot-deep spring-fed swimming pond accompanied by a 12-foot diving rock.
“This is not simply another luxury home,” says Stacey Torrey, vice president of Integrity Luxury Real Estate Auctions. “The Preserve at Wade Pasture was built to become a legacy property—one designed for generations of family gatherings, recreation, and unforgettable experiences.
“It offers a level of craftsmanship, privacy, and lifestyle that is exceptionally difficult to replicate today.”
​The first-floor primary suite offers nature views and a spa-level bath experience. A secret door within the suite leads to the underground tunnel.
​Offering five bedrooms and eight bathrooms, the abode is completed with an epicurean kitchen that features a quartz waterfall island, Wolf and Sub-Zero appliances, and a Vero water filtering system.
​The kitchen and living space flow seamlessly together through accordion glass doors and onto 5,000 square feet of bluestone patios.
​A contemporary basement has the “Nordic-inspired wellness wing,” where a full gym, infrared sauna, and Tonal system await.
In addition to the impressive spread of wellness-focused features, the property is equipped with high-security amenities, including four secret rooms and a “reinforced concrete vault.”
​The mountain sanctuary also contains an executive office space, a three-sided fireplace, and a 1,300-square-foot guest apartment.
​This distinct residential offering has a commercial-grade timber construction featuring thick, concrete subfloors and silent hydronic radiant heating.
​Built in 2024, 1084 Wade Pasture Road happily marries the beauty of its natural surroundings with cutting-edge luxury—featuring Douglas fir beams throughout as well as a Crestron smart-home automation system.
Car fanatics will no doubt be drawn to the incredible storage facilities, which include aheatedthree-car garage as well as a detached two-car garage.
​Situated on 11.6 acres with gorgeously clear views of Mount Mansfield, The Preserve at Wade Pasture is only 10 minutes away from the Stowe Mountain Resort.
​“There is something unforgettable about standing on the property,” Torrey says. “The mountain views, the craftsmanship, the peaceful setting, and even the walk through the underground tunnel create an experience that simply cannot be conveyed on a screen.”
​The home was originally listed for $15.8 million in June 2025 but failed to find a buyer—prompting the owners to pivot to anewstrategy. Initially, the ask was lowered to $15 million, however when that decrease still didn’t bring in an offer, an auction proved the next best step.

hed: Retirees in North Carolina community stiffed with $10K HOA fee and massive price hikes — forcing elderly from their homes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Homeowners in a quiet lakeside subdivision outside Charlotte, North Carolina, are bracing for a housing cost jolt that could push some longtime residents right out of their neighborhood.
Families in Magnolia Cove, an 80-home community in Sherrills Ford, are grappling with word that their monthlyhomeowners association duesare set to rocket from $350 to $1,250, with a $10,000 special assessment tacked on for good measure, according toWSOC-TV.
The jump is only the latest in a string of increases that residents say has left them reeling.
Just four years ago,dues in the communitysat at a modest $158 a month, meaning some owners have watched their bills multiply nearly eightfold in that span.
Homeowners, several of them retirees on fixed incomes, told the station they simply won’t be able to keep up.
Many said the dues were originally billed as covering routine lawn maintenance and a community pool, an amenity that residents say was promised but never materialized.
Frustration has curdled into open conflict.
“I spend nights crying because this is just ruining my life,” homeowner Jill Menson told WSOC. “Not what we signed up for.”
Other residents pointed to a deeper structural problem.
Only around 20 of the neighborhood’s 80 homes are still owner-occupied, with the rest converted into rentals, a shift Stephanie Roebuck said she never anticipated when she bought in.
Mike Brokaw went further, telling the outlet that ongoing litigation against the HOA stems directly from a failure to answer basic financial questions, one he believes could have been avoided entirely.
Adding to residents’ unease, the developer behind Magnolia Cove doubles as the HOA’s president, a common setup during a community’s early “declarant control” period, but one that leaves homeowners with scant say over major money decisions.
The association’s attorney, H. Weldon Jones III, offered a different account. He told WSOC the steep hikes are necessary to keep HOA operations funded, noting the developer has effectively subsidized the association for years while some owners fell behind on dues or stopped paying altogether.
Homeowners aren’t taking it quietly. They’ve launcheda GoFundMe campaignto help cover legal costs as the dispute heads further into the courts.
The next HOA meeting, they said, will be held virtually, with questions accepted only in advance and no vote offered on the fee increases themselves.
The fight in Sherrills Ford lands as North Carolina lawmakers weigh legislation that could rein in developer control of HOAs statewide.
One proposal would cap how long a developer can dominate an association’s board, triggering elections once 25% and then 50% of lots have been sold off to individual owners.
A separate measure, House Bill 444, would bar boards from hiking ratified budgets by more than 5% without a majority vote from homeowners, cap fines at $2,500 and route certain disputes to mediation before they reach a courtroom.
For now, Magnolia Cove residents are left waiting to see whether Raleigh acts before their next bill comes due.

hed: New NorCal renting hell unlocked as landlord attempts to charge hefty working-from-home fee
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A rental listing in California has sparked fury for making residentsalready dealing with the nation’s highest gross rentpay even more: by charging a fee for working from home.
The “newly built” furnished one-bedroom and one-bathroom unitis on the marketin Walnut Creek, a city roughly 16 miles west of Oakland.
The 535-square foot accessory dwelling unit — an independent living space located on the same lot as a primary home — is charging $3,250 for rent. But if you’re working from home, you’d need to pay an additional $200.
The listing includes utilities, internet, a private patio and parking. It boasts a “custom sunlit living space, light colored engineered hardwood floors and an updated functional kitchen.”
Many renters on social media did not seem to care about all the features and were instead aghast at the idea of paying extra to work from a space they already paid for.
“That is absolutely insane,” reacted Bay Area resident Julie Crawford. “Is there extra for a stay-at-home mom, too?”
“That is a violation of privacy,” San Francisco resident Aviva Kirsten commented. “They should use the home they see fit as long as it is not a disturbance to the neighborhood.”
According to Zillow, the average rent across the Bay Area is about $3,650 a month, 81% higher than the national average.

Derek Barnes, CEO of the East Bay Rental Housing Association,told ABC7that such fees are unusual but also are within reason. A remote worker uses more electricity, water, internet and air conditioning than an in-office one.
“It’s almost like a utility cost recovery or environmental conservation fee,” Barnes said. “You’re not likely, you know, to be aware of your usage of these precious resources if you don’t see a bill.”
The Post reached out to the owner of the listing for comment.
Such debates over charging more rent for remote workers are becoming more common ever since remote work became more mainstream due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Dave Stickland, an entrepreneur from North Carolina,commented on Xhe encountered a similar request from a landlord there for an extra $300 per month. He, like others, questioned how such a rule can even be enforced without being privacy-invasive.
“Dude also insisted to keep his INDOOR cameras installed,” he said.

hed: Myles Garrett lists Cleveland home for $2.1 million — weeks after shocking trade to Los Angeles Rams
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
NFL star Myles Garrett has put his Ohio home on the market for $2.1 million, just a few weeks after it was revealed that he had beentraded from the Cleveland Browns to the Los Angeles Ramsin what was described as a “landscape-altering” move.
The 30-year-old originally purchased hisCleveland-area home for $1.3 million in November 2018, according to records, just over a year after he was chosen by the Browns as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 NFL Draft.
Garrett, who is originally from Texas, has spent all nine seasons of his NFL career with the Browns, earning the title of Defensive Player of the Year twice during that time—while becoming a local hero in the Cleveland area.
However, the defensive end has also found time to carry out several very impressive upgrades to his private residence, adding an incredibly high-end array of features and amenities, including a detached four-car garage and a custom walk-in closet with a glass display case where he was able to showcase his favorite fashion pieces.
Located on a two-acre spread in Wadsworth, OH, the 4,300-square-foot home—which is listed with Rebecca Donatelli and Natalie Antonelli ofThe Elli Group at Elite Sotheby’s International Realty—sits behind a gated entryway, ensuring maximum privacy.
“We’re thrilled to introduce this exceptional home to the market,” Donatelli told Realtor.com®.
“With beautifully designed living spaces, incredible areas for entertaining, and exceptional craftsmanship throughout, this home is truly one of a kind.
“It offers an unmatched combination of luxury, comfort, and modern sophistication.”
“Sophisticated design, exceptional craftsmanship, and effortless functionality come together in this custom-built home, privately situated on approximately two acres in the prestigious Hidden Lakes of Sharon,” the listing states.
The five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home features several distinctive nods to Garrett’s career throughout its interior, with listing images revealing rooms filled with mementos from his nine seasons in the NFL.
One of thetwobars in the home has been decorated with several images of the athlete on the field during Browns games, while another wall is home to multiple NFL jerseys, including those of former Minnesota Vikings player Danielle Hunter and former Houston Texans star Dameon Pierce.
But it’s not just NFL memorabilia that Garrett collected during his time living in the spacious property.
Images of the “executive office” showcase the custom cabinetry that has been filled with different collectibles, including movie merchandise, action figures, and what appear to be multiple camera lenses.

There is also a large custom gym in the property filled with top-of-the-line equipment that “can convey with the property, along with some select home furnishings,” the listing notes.
Spread across three levels, the home offers ample space for entertaining, particularly on the lower walkout level, which is home to multiple recreation areas, including the gym, a bar, and a movie theater.
On the main level, residents can kick back in several sun-filled spaces, including the open-plan kitchen, which features a walk-in pantry and a spacious island, designed to accommodate multiple people, in addition to a dining area.
That space opens up into the main living area, which has a wall of windows that open out onto the upper deck of the home.
“Designed for both style and function, the kitchen showcases premium appliances, an oversized center island, custom cabinetry, a spacious walk-in pantry, and seamless flow into the adjoining living and dining areas,” the listing states.
The primary suite also features incredible natural light, as well as an array of very upscale features, including a “spa-inspired bathroom” and the “extraordinary” custom walk-in closet, which has been designed to accommodate even the most impressive fashion collections.
In addition to the five bedrooms already available in the home, there is also “an oversized bonus room” that could be used for further accommodations, or as a game room or office.
Outside, the home is surrounded by lush green landscape and offers ample space to entertain, including at the private fire pit or on the upper deck, which boasts a built-in grill area and plenty of room for sitting and dining.
“Completing the property is a three-car attached garage and a separate four-car garage with a finished upper level, ideal for a private office, studio, or hobby space,” the description adds.
The listing comes just hours after it was reported that Garrett had closed on anewhome in Los Angeles—where he is expected to be based for the next few years, having agreed to a restructured five-year contract when he wastraded to the Rams.
In return fortrading Garrett, the Browns received linebacker Jared Verse from the Rams, as well as a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round pick.
According to Sportrac,Garrett’s updated dealis worth a total of $208.2 million, and includes a $35.7 million signing bonus and a guarantee of $99 million.
So perhaps it is unsurprising that he appears to have splashed out a bit more on his new dwelling than he did on his last, with In Touch claiming that he has snapped up an extraordinary $23 million mansion in Hidden Hills—where Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford also resides, along with several members of the Kardashian family.
Records show that the home highlighted by the outlet changed hands for that extraordinary sum on July 13, just over a month after Garrett’s trade was confirmed—and just over a week before he listed his Ohio residence.
The newly-built residence, which appears to have only just been completed, was not listed on the MLS prior to its purchase, suggesting that it traded hands in an off-market deal.
Garrett’s move to Los Angeles, which was described by The Athletic as “seismic,” will not only see him joining his second NFL team, it will also bring him closer to his girlfriend, professional snowboarder Chloe Kim, 26, who grew up in California and has been based in LA for several years.
The couple recently made an appearance together at the ESPY Awards, where Kim presented her partner with the award for Best Record-Breaking Performance in honor of Garrett achieving the most sacks in a single season during his final year with the Browns.
During his acceptance speech, Garrett paid tribute to Kim—while voicing his gratitude that she had managed to keep the news of his award hidden from him.
“Thank you, baby, for keeping a secret like that, because you definitely knew,” he began, before going on to thank Kim and his family for being so supportive throughout his career.
“I want to thank my parents, I know it’s not easy, I can get kind of locked in and focused on my sport, and I know we all try to enter our zone as athletes, and sometimes, the people who mean to the most to us take a bit of a backseat for our journeys that we go on throughout the season, so I want to thank them for always loving me and supporting me in their own ways,” he continued.

hed: The roommate boom is happening in the suburbs — not in cities
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Who says suburban sprawl is just for families and lawn mowers?
Nearly 5.6 million, or 12%, of US renter households now include roommates — a 21% increase over the past decade, according toa new surveyfrom StorageCafe, a nationwide storage marketplace.
But rather than crowding into cities, renters are moving to suburban and secondary hubs like Jersey City, New Jersey, where renters with roommates save a whopping $13,000 per year — more than roomies in any other city.
In Irvine, California; Atlanta; and Raleigh, North Carolina, “living with roommates delivers the greatest financial and lifestyle advantages,” StorageCafe found.
One in four people living in Irvine shares their home, roomies 510 square feet per person and a savings of $12,800 a year.
Next up is Atlanta, where 17% of renter households have roomies. Residents get 535 square feet per person and save $8,900 by sharing a two-bedroom.
In third place is Raleigh, North Carolina’s state capital. There, 17% of renter households have roommates with each person averaging living space of 515 square feet. The rent savings is $8,100.
Nationwide, splitting rent in a two-bedroom apartment rather than living alone in a one-bedroom saves people about $6,700 per year — enough to pay down high-interest debt. That can make a real difference when 43.5 million households spend more than 30% of their income on housing.
“What’s changed is geography,” Victor Maghear, research analyst at StorageCafe, said in prepared remarks. “Shared living used to be concentrated in dense urban cores. Now we’re seeing the fastest growth in suburbs with newer apartment stock, stronger amenities and easier access to regional job centers.”
Shared living isn’t just for twenty-somethings anymore. Millennials now account for over a third, or 1.9 million, of all roommate households, according to the survey, which analyzed the country’s 100 largest cities.
“Roommate living is no longer just about youth culture,” the survey indicates. “It increasingly responds to structural affordability pressures that cut across age groups.”

hed: New Las Vegas strip hotel-casino with atrociously tacky design roasted in the comments
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Vegas is betting bigon hearts.
Sin Cityhas seen plenty of crazy pitches over the years. This one comes with a 265-foot restaurant bolted onto the bones of a dead Ferris wheel — and a giant, glowing heart.
Clark County commissioners approved plans Wednesday for a wild new 752-room hotel-casino directly across from Mandalay Bay, set to rise on one of the Strip’s saddest patches of dirt: the abandoned remains of the never-built SkyVue observation wheel.
The proposal calls for a 29-story tower wrapped in a massive heart-shaped LED screen,along with a casino, restaurants, a pool and a Fremont Street-style covered plaza.
Not everyone is buying the hype.
“Today’s utter bullshit that’s never happening, all due respect to this bulls and shit,” local Vegas insider blog VitalVegas torched in a reply to Clark County’s celebratory announcement on X.
The site has been a punchline for nearly 15 years.
Today’s utter bullshit that’s never happening, all due respect to bulls and shit.https://t.co/FfpwnUXHZd
Developer Howard Bulloch and his firm, Compass Investments, unveiled plans in 2011 for a $100 million-plus spectacle featuring a 500-foot observation wheel, a roller coaster, shops and more,according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal.
Crews barely managed to erect two hulking concrete columns before the money dried up, the newspaper reported.
Bulloch later told the Review-Journal that the property had been “in escrow many times,” but prospective buyers “were just not able to arrange their financing as they had promised.”
What remained were two towering concrete stumps that have loomed over the tourist trudging toward Mandalay Bay ever since — mocked by locals as the Strip’s “pillars of sadness.”
The land was dragged through a bankruptcy auction in 2020, when Seattle businessman Wayne Perry acquired the SkyVue site and neighboring parcels with a $75 million credit bid, according to the Review-Journal.
His family later sold roughly 8 acres along the Strip to the Clark County Department of Aviation for $16.2 million in 2023 before unloading the remaining property this spring, the outlet reported.

That’s where Eli Applebaum and his heart-shaped box come into play.
The developer, working through his Kulik River Capital firm, dropped $70 million in April to acquire the nearly 12-acre parcel.
His answer to nearly 15 years of blight is the towering heart-shaped resort, complete with a gaming floor, restaurants, retail space, a pool, convention facilities and a covered outdoor plaza, county documents show.
The most audacious feature would sit hit above it all: a restaurant perched 265 feet in the air atop the abandoned SkyVue columns.
Instead of tearing down the notorious “pillars of sadness,” Applebaum plans to reinforce them, add a third support column and turn the remnants of one of Vegas’ most recent failures into the resort’s crown jewel, according to the plans.
Even the grand vision has already been scaled back.
Applebaum initially proposed a 874-room resort but was forced to shave roughly 60 off the tower to satisfy the Federal Aviation Administration.
The developer’s land-use representative, Nancy Amundsen, told commissioners Wednesday that the revised project has since received FAA approval.
Amundsen also said she had spoken repeatedly with MGM Resorts, which operates Mandalay Bay across the street, about the long neglected eyesore next door.
MGM’s message was essentially that it wanted to see the property developed or the unfinished columns torn down.
Clark County, naturally, is treating Wednesday’s vote as real progress.
Moving forward with plans to develop land at the south end of the Las#VegasStrip. Commissioners approved permits and reviews for a heart-shaped resort.The project includes a pedestrian plaza and 265 foot high restaurant atop pillars built for a failed Ferris wheel venture.pic.twitter.com/R5tysaHeYO
“Moving forward with plans to develop land at the south end of the Las #Vegas Strip,” the county’s official account crowned on X while touting the approval of the necessary permits and reviews.
But VitalVegas isn’t alone in having heard this song before.
Las Vegas is littered with dazzling renderings of resorts that never made it past the PowerPoint stage. Financing, additional permits and actual construction still stand between Applebaum’s glowing red dream and reality.
Whether the heart beats to life — or merely becomes the SkyVue pillars’ newest roommate in Strip purgatory — is anyone’s bet.

hed: Famed Polo Bar will leave its iconic NYC home for free rent — risking its exclusivity
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This is an offer that could not be refused.
After more than a decade as one of New York’s mostimpossible tablesto book, Ralph Lauren’s Polo Bar is leaving the wood-paneled Midtown perch that made it a fixture of the city’s high-society scene, The Post has confirmed.
Related Companies has secured a deal to relocate the see-and-be-seen restaurant into a 53-story office tower it’s building four blocks north at 625 Madison Ave., according to a person familiar with the leasing negotiations. What’s more, Related is sweetening the deal with a rent break that could stretch on for years, according to a separate person familiar with the matter.
The developer has offered Polo Bar at least two years of free rent to make the move, the source said, as part of a broader push that also includes courting the restaurant’s parent company to expand into Palm Beach, all on the heels of Ralph Lauren’s recent Polo Baropening in London.
This move will take Polo Bar out of its current home just off Fifth Avenue, where it has operated since 2015, and into the ground floor of a brand-new tower expected to be completed in the summer of 2029.
Related declined to comment. Polo Bar did not respond to a request for comment.
Polo Bar’s relocation is viewed internally as one major factor that has helped drive strong leasing demand at the tower.
That demand also includes leases nearing completion with two other companies, General Assembly and software investment firm Veritas, which would be among the first office tenants to commit to the project, the person said. Additionally, there is an undisclosed tenant who is close to finalizing the top two floors of the building, the source added.
“What we’ve seen in New York, the interplay between restaurants and ground-floor retail space acting as an amenity to the office tenants upstairs, has taken on a tremendous importance when landlords are considering either major repositioning of an office building or ground-up new construction, like in the case of 625 Madison,” the source said.
The person familiar with the matter said the new space would give the restaurant significantly more room than its current location, with the small dining space located at basement level, allowing it to accommodate alarger volume of reservations.
Polo Bar has drawn a steady stream of famous faces through its equestrian-lined dining room, fromTaylor Swift and Travis Kelceto the Kardashians. The restaurant has also become a favorite among fashion and entertainment circles.
News of the possible move has already rippled through the exclusive circle of regulars who treat a Polo Bar table as a status symbol more than a meal.
Penn Portman, who recently celebrated a birthday at the restaurant, said she would welcome a change of address if it came with better odds of getting a table.
“If another location helps being able to get reservations easily, I’m extremely down,” Portman, who is in her 30s and resides on the Upper East Side, told The Post.
Landing a table at Polo Bar has become its own small industry of insider knowledge.
Regulars describe a routine in which hopefuls call the restaurant, are told they would check availability and then Google the person before a reservation is confirmed — with availability tightening further as the restaurant’s profile has grown.
Some diners say the best odds come from calling first thing on Tuesday mornings, when same-day cancellations are confirmed and slots can open up.
Employees of Ralph Lauren and Polo brands are also known to have an easier path to a table, according to people familiar with the reservation process, who said openings are sometimes offered informally to those connected to the company.
Molly Friedman, 34, a longtime New Yorker and Polo Bar regular who lives near the restaurant’s current location, said she typically gets her reservations through a family connection rather than calling in cold.
“Because of my uncle I always go with him,” Friedman said of the business strategist and former Estée Lauder executive John Demsey. “Or I would get him to make [a reservation] for me.”
Friedman said she is skeptical the move would preserve what makes the restaurant special in the first place, describing the downstairs space as central to its appeal.
“The point of the downstairs is that it is like a cave … sexy and it brings so many personalities,” Friedman told The Post. “I feel like if they cater to the office type I’m not sure what vibe that’s going to bring. Obviously they will make it stunning and the food will be great. But [it’s] all about the mood.”

hed: Fair housing groups sue HUD over funding changes
content: The Department of Housing and Urban Development is changing a long-standing grant program so significantly that it will vastly curtail fair housing enforcement in much of the country, according to a lawsuit filed in federal court Thursday.Most fair housing law violations are investigated by small nonprofit groups around the country dedicated to promoting fair housing. These groups rely on grants from HUD to cover large chunks of their operating expenses, and for some small groups, HUD grants make up almost their entire budget.According to the complaint, which was filed in the District of Massachusetts, changes to that grant program, announced by HUD this month, would force fair housing groups to significantly cut back on the services they provide or shut down entirely.“This would be catastrophic for our organization,” said Vineeth Hemavathi, the executive director of the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center, one of the plaintiffs on the case. “These fair housing laws are on the books, but they don’t mean anything if there’s no one to enforce them.”HUD did not respond to a request for comment.Nikitra Bailey, an executive vice president of the National Fair Housing Alliance, another plaintiff in the case, said that most complaints investigated by fair housing groups involve disability issues. In one instance, she said, a homeowners’ association outside Philadelphia would not allow a family to modify their own home to accommodate their 8-year-old daughter, who had impaired mobility and hearing.Fair housing groups also investigate sex discrimination claims, Bailey said, like a complaint in Syracuse, New York, against a landlord who offered a rent discount to a woman in exchange for sex. A local group investigated and found more than 40 women with similar allegations against that landlord going back 30 years.“This case does not exist without having a local organization willing to do the work and enforce the Fair Housing Act,” she said.HUD typically awards more than 100 fair housing grants a year, generally for $500,000 or less, according to lawyers representing the fair housing groups. For the 2025 fiscal year grants — which have been extensively delayed — HUD has said it will issue only five of its traditional grants. One will be an award of $25 million, for which law schools are encouraged to apply. According to the complaint, that money could be used to develop a law school curriculum focused on fair housing, including constitutional and statutory limits on its enforcement, and on efforts like expanding the support network for property owners.Because of new restrictions built into the remaining grants, groups will be eligible only if they have a budget of at least $5 million. This would disqualify most fair housing groups, the complaint said, because their budgets are generally between $400,000 to $2 million.For the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center, that would mean foregoing $425,000 of an annual budget that hovers between $700,000 and $800,000.HUD also announced its fair housing grant program for the 2026 fiscal year, which would similarly disqualify many fair housing groups, according to Reed Colfax, a managing partner at Relman Colfax and a lawyer on the case. New applicants will receive preference, and while the grant amounts are much lower, they still cannot make up more than 50 percent of an organization’s budget. Colfax said that many organizations can’t raise more than half their budget from other sources.One year without these grants “would be devastating,” Colfax said. “Two years would essentially be fatal to the network.”Last year, the Trump administration tried to cancel millions of dollars in HUD grants that had already been awarded, then failed to open the application process for the next round of funding. In both instances, fair housing groups sued, and the money was restored.But even gaps in funding that only spanned a few months were enough to damage some organizations. Martie Lafferty, executive director of the Tennessee Fair Housing Council, said that a seven-month gap in HUD funding last year forced her group to lay off two of its four employees and substantially cut back on its work. Usually, the group opens eight to 10 cases every month. In that period, they were able to open just two or three a month.At the Tennessee Fair Housing Council, which was a plaintiff in one of last year’s lawsuits, HUD grants account for $425,000 of its $500,000 annual budget. Lafferty said they were able to make it through the seven-month gap last year because they had built up some reserves.She said that this time, if there’s a gap in funding, that cushion is pretty much gone.This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

hed: SoCal region named the most unaffordable housing market in US — California home to 6 of the most expensive regions
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
There’s no place like home. That is, if you can afford one.
Los Angeles and Orange counties form the mostunaffordable major housing market in America, while California claimed six of the eight worst spots nationwide, according to a grim new analysis.
Southern California News Group columnistJonathan Lasner crunched recent Zillow datafrom 50 major markets, grading each on families sharing homes, the availability of affordable listings and the portion of income consumed by rent.
LA-Orange County landed dead lastoverall.

hed: Ask the Remodeler: Where to donate appliances and fixtures prior to your home renovation in Greater Boston
subhead: Before ripping out your kitchen cabinets and appliances, consider donating them to be recycled in someone else’s home
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Many of our clients have sustainability and energy efficiency at the forefront of their remodel, whether it be energy-efficient doors and windows, lights, appliances, and/or insulation that drive the remodel. Or, it could be sustainable andresponsibly sourced materialsthat are key. That could range from recycled products to sustainably harvested woods to novolatile organic compoundsor off-gassing materials.

There is, however, another element to a sustainable remodel that happens before anything is even installed. That is to donate or sell what you can before the demolition crews even show up. There are many options in today’s social media world that allow people to repurpose items rather than throw them away where they will end up in already overflowing landfills — or worse, somewhere in the environment.

What people may not realize is that prior to aremodel, there are organizations that will take away things like kitchen cabinets (and sometimes countertops), appliances if they are relatively new, and kitchen sinks and faucets. They will also take vanities bath fixtures, and lighting that is in in good shape. Not only will these items stay out of a landfill, but they will go into remodels for people of more modest means.

Two organizations we use areBoston Building Resourcesfor things like cabinets and fixtures, andHabitat for Humanity ReStoresfor furniture and some appliances.

We contact them well before the remodel, send pictures, and typically do a walk-through to make sure the donations are viable for another home. They do charge a fee, but we have found that it is equal to or less than the cost to have our demolition company remove the items and take them to a landfill. Our clients are happy that so much of what we would remove for a remodel can be repurposed in this way. It does take a bit of coordination, but it’s well worth the effort.



A recent column talked aboutrenovating the historic Asa Gray House in Cambridge. As it happens, one of our readers is a Harvard professor emeritus, who specializes in Asa Gray. He took the time to write us back and add additional details and history about this important home. We love reader feedback, so thank you for the thoughtful response that we have included here:


To the Editor,


Having witnessed several renovations of the Garden House (Asa Gray House) in Cambridge, I welcomed a glimpse at what it has taken in this recent renovation to upgrade and protect this important house.


Although as you point out, it was not originally inhabited by Asa Gray (the first occupant was William Dandrige Peck who supervised the Botanic Garden), it was traditionally known as the Garden House. It sat in the Botanic Garden which was located at the corner of Garden and Linnaean Street in Cambridge. The Garden is now the site of Harvard University’s Botanic Garden Apartments. Jane Loring Gray, Gray’s wife, lived in the house until her death in 1909; Gray died in 1888. The house was then sold by Harvard and moved across the street to its current location.


Just to set the record straight, those cabinets that are mentioned are not mahogany, I believe, but rather camphor wood. They were used to store dried plant specimens that were the subject of Gray’s studies. Those specimens came from explorations of the western United States and from around the world, particularly Asia.Camphor wood, with its distinctive chemical make-up and odor, would have been used to protect these precious plants from insect pests. The plants are still available for study at the Gray Herbarium at Harvard where they continue to be used to document the flora of the world. Germination of seeds would not have taken place in these cabinets but rather in the conservatory which was adjacent to the Garden House in the Botanic Garden. The Garden boasted many exotic plants, some of which were the first of their species grown in New England.


Gray, the cabinets, and the house represent a particular period in the development of science in North America. The Grays welcomed botanists from around the world with warm hospitality and botanical treasures, making the Garden House an essential stop for any visiting botanist.


Yours truly,


Donald H. Pfister


Asa Gray Professor, Emeritus


Harvard University Herbaria


Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge. Send your questions to[email protected]. Questions are subject to editing. hed: San Francisco home prices hit eye-popping highs thanks to AI ‘gold rush’ — experts unpack when the madness could end
content:

A tech boom has pushedSan Francisco home pricesfrom expensive to stratospheric — leaving locals wondering when theAI-crazed madnesswill end, and whether there’s any hope left for ordinary folks to buy in.
Median sale prices in the red-hot market hit $1.7 million last month, according toHomes.com, while the prices of single-family homes exceed $2.1 million, far out of reach for many local buyers.
That’s because of a tsunami of AI wealth concentrated in the city, coupled with a lack of inventory — leading wealthy and desperate home buyers to bid up some properties by $1 million or more and evendangle shares of leading firms like Anthropicin exchange for scarce homes.
To underscore the insanity, one relatively shabby 2,400-square-foot home along a noisy street in the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood sold for $3.1 million, seven figures over its original asking price.

The city of roughly 900,000 people at the center of the AI boom is now flooded with housing horror stories as evenmodest rental units aren’t spared.
One North Beach landlord listed a 64-square-foot cell with a shared bathroom and no kitchen accessfor $750 per month. And regular families say they’re being booted from longtime rentals as landlords jack up rates to milk the newfound tech riches.
“There’s very little product to find if you’re a renter or buyer, and that’s why prices are shooting up,’ explained Nigel Hughes, an analyst with Homes.com.
San Francisco’spriciest known home listingis the $67 million Pacific Heights manse of Oracle heiress Nicole Miner and her author hubby Robert Mailer Anderson, built on a plot of land they bought for just $5 million in 1999.
Demand is concentrated in luxury homes in San Francisco’s most desirable neighborhoods — often located within an easy commute to downtown. Below the $2 million range, sale prices aren’t quite as “exorbitant,” Hughes added.

With a slew of AI IPOs expected as soon as this year, Hughes believes there’s “no end in sight” to the elevated prices.
But there may be glimmers of hope yet for the non-billionaire San Francisco buyer.
Prices are a function of supply and demand and there are relatively few homes on the market, and even fewer single-family homes in fashionable neighborhoods, analysts have noted.
That may be partly because sellers are holding onto properties in the hopes that even more buyers will emerge with blockbuster IPOs, according toReal Estate News.
Summer is slow for real estate sales and a new surge in supply could arrive in the fall, Coldwell Banker agent Jeremy Rushton told the outlet, though there are no guarantees.
“We might see some pullback this year if inventory reaches a more normal level,”  Rushton said. “There’s often a glut after Labor Day, but time will tell if that happens this year.”
There are still many ways for buyers without tech riches to own a piece of San Francisco as long as your expectations are realistic, said longtime realtor Bonnie Spindler, who specializes in the city’s quintessential Victorian homes.
Tech-driven real estate frenzies are nothing new in a city that’s known for boom-and-bust cycles dating “back to the Gold Rush,” she noted.
Condos or homes in less-hot neighborhoods may be more accessible to the average buyer, she said, and some put as little as 5% to 10% down on a property or even borrow against retirement savings in order to purchase a property.
“If you can afford rent, you can afford to buy,” she added. “There are lots of ways to get into this market that doesn’t involve being a billionaire.”

hed: Sprawling $128M ranch stretching across 2 states sells days after listing
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A cattle empire spanning two states and nearly 88,000 acres has changed hands for a massive sum — and it barely had time to sit on the market.
Freeman Family Ranches, an 87,953-acre spread stretching across the North Texas and Oklahoma panhandles, sold for nearly its full asking price of $127.7 million after interested buyers began circling right after it hit the market.
The deal closed within a month. Realtor.comfirst broke newsof the sale.
Its sprawling scale isdifficult to picture. For comparison’s sake, it’s roughly six times theland area of Manhattan.
For four generations, the land belonged to the Freeman ranching family, with the earliest deed dating back to 1929 and the rest of the massive holding assembled piece by piece over the decades that followed.
According to listing broker Chad Dugger of Hall and Hall, the ranches were held under a partnership whose operating agreement had expired, prompting the family to liquidate the asset.
Three separate ranches — the Anchor D, the Coldwater and the Frisco — made up the land holding, each with its own identity and purpose, run together as one seamless operation.
It was all combined into what brokers describe as a genuine turnkey enterprise, the rare kind of property that generates income from day 1 rather than requiring years of development.
No livestock changed hands as part of the sale, though historically the ranch was run as a yearling operation carrying around 8,500 young animals at a time.
“You either run mother cows year-round or you run yearlings seasonally,” Dugger told Realtor.com.
“Freeman Ranches was a rare offering, three diverse, well-managed ranches operated as one cohesive unit, the kind of property that simply does not come around every day,” Dugger said in a separate statement to The Post.
Dugger declined to name the buyer but described him as a top 100 national landowner with deep roots in the livestock business.
“He is buying it to ranch,” he said. “Just like his family has for decades. And to expand his land holdings.”
According to Dugger, the Freeman family took comfort in knowing the land would remain in the hands of another Texas ranching family rather than being broken apart.
“It’s always nice when a seller is attached to a place as long as this family has to find somebody who will treat it and use it the way they’ve always treated and used it,” he said. “The buyer will continue the legacy.”
Scarcity is a big part of why the sale moved so fast. Large ranches in this stretch of Texas are frequently purchased and subdivided, and once that happens, the land rarely gets reassembled into a single holding again.
“It’s becoming more and more rare to have these size transactions,” said Dugger, who co-listed the property alongside Sam Middleton of Chas S. Middleton and Son. “The number of large ranches, particularly in this area of Texas, are sometimes bought and divided. Once that happens, they are almost never put together again. So your inventory of places this size is reduced.”
With a quarter century in land dealings, Dugger calls it one of the largest ranches he has ever sold.

hed: San Francisco home prices surge to average $1.7M after sinking to record lows — for 1 big reason
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
San Francisco’s housing market has come roaring back from the depths of theGreat Recession, and the city has one industry to thank for its stunning turnaround.
The median home price in the San Francisco metro area has soared past $1.7 million, marking an increase of more than $1 million since themarket’s rock-bottom lowof $625,000 in March 2012.
By June 2026, that figure climbed even further to $1.72 million, according to a newRedfin analysisof MLS data, representing a gain of roughly $1.01 million over the same month in 2012.
While years of tight housing supply and demand from tech workers laid the groundwork for the recovery throughout the 2010s, it’s theexplosion of artificial intelligencewealth flooding into the Bay Area that has sent prices into overdrive most recently.
The rebound has outpaced the rest of the country by a wide margin.
San Francisco home values have surged 140% since their crash-era low, compared with a 128% bump nationwide and a 122% rise in New York City.
Prices climbed 9.2% year-over-year in June alone, as home sales jumped 23% and the number of new listings on the market fell 16%.
Much of that momentum is being driven by the city’s wealthiest buyers. Luxury home prices in the Bay Area’s most exclusive ZIP codes shot up 13.4% in the two years following the launch of ChatGPT, dramatically outpacing every other price tier as AI industry paychecks fueled a race for high-end real estate.
Pending sales of luxury homes in San Francisco spiked an eye-popping 46% year-over-year in May, the largest jump recorded anywhere in the nation.
The windfall could grow even larger in the months ahead. With AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic both expected to go public soon, their combined employees could theoretically have enough IPO wealth to purchase nearly a third of all homes in San Francisco.
But the AI-fueled boom is leaving many locals in the dust.
Wages in San Francisco have grown just 90% since 2012, a fraction of the 140% surge in home prices over the same period.
Buyers now need to earn close to $300,000 a year to afford a typical home in the city, a bar that puts homeownership increasingly out of reach for anyone outside the tech and AI sphere.

hed: NYC property moguls sue daughter for secretly listing their $3M condo—to fund a legal battle against them
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Parental love has its limits — and, in this case, it can spiral into an absolute nightmare.
A bitter familial feud that has stretched on for years — including pitting brother against brother — has just reached its latest chapter, The Post has learned. And this time, two property-mogul parents who have co-managed a 500-unit Manhattan apartment portfolio are targeting their estranged daughter with legal action.
Arthur and Ester Haruvi, aged 76 and 79, respectively, are trying to halt their 47-year-old daughter Michelle from secretly selling their 1,440-square-foot, two-bedroom Manhattan condo inthe Sheffieldfor some $3 million — claiming it’s for her to “finance and sustain her scorched-earth litigation campaign against” them, according to a bombshell federal complaint filed Wednesday in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York.
They also aim to stop her from making off with all the proceeds, as well as undistributed rental income.
The complaint adds it’s “part of a broader effort to weaponize the family’s assets for her own personal financial gain and to the detriment of her parents, from whom she is now estranged.”
Arthur, Esther and their attorneys didn’t respond to requests for comment, nor did Michelle.
Relations between Michelle and her parents fractured around 2021 due to her conduct with other family members, the parents say in the documents. No other details regarding the ongoing bad blood were provided in the suit.
In November 2012, however, matters between the family members were seemingly quite good. Arthur and Esther gifted Michelle a 99% economic interest in unit 51D atthe Sheffield— a 50-story tower with nearly 600 units that stands near Columbus Circle — as an act of “estate planning and as a gift,” according to the court documents.
Arthur and Esther retained 1%, as well as “their status as the only two members with the authority to manage and direct the LLC [that owns the apartment] and the Unit,” per the complaint.
Fourteen years on, things are quite sour.
Arthur and Esther claim Michelle secretly staged and listed the apartment “to sell the Unit out from under them, without their knowledge, consent or authorization,” according the suit.
The Haruvis claim they discovered the scheme on June 8 from a building-wide notice forwarded by their other daughter, Aileen, that announced a “Private Preview Before Public Listing.” They later learned that Michelle had hired an interior design studio to stage the apartment for prospective buyers, the suit adds.
When the designer, DreamRose Design, posted photos of the staging on Instagram, Michelle demanded the post be taken down to prevent her parents from discovering the sale, according to the lawsuit.
DreamRose Design, which is not named as a defendant, declined to comment, citing the “pending litigation.”
Michelle, who resides in San Francisco, unilaterally assumed the title of “Managing Member,” seized control of the LLC’s bank accounts, and diverted more than $100,000 in annual rental income solely to herself starting in 2021 — all while withholding financial statements and tax documents from her parents, who live on the Upper West Side, they allege.
The unit was rented out from at least 2013 through June 2023, with monthly rents from $9,200 to $9,500. At $9,300 a month, the unit generates $111,600 a year. Arthur and Esther don’t know if there is a renter in place now.
StreetEasy records only showa rental listing from 2015, when the home leased for $9,500 per month — detailing the perch as a “corner apartment” that’s “bright and airy all day,” with added perks of marbled bathrooms and Miele appliances in the kitchen.
The couple says Michelle’s beneficial economic assignment does not give her the right to act on behalf of the LLC, nor does it automatically make her a member of the LLC, which the parents established to buy the apartment in July 2012 for $2.6 million.
The Haruvis are asking the federal court to block the sale, appoint a receiver to take control of the property, compel an accounting of all diverted rent and officially declare that Michelle has no legal authority to act on behalf of the LLC that owns the Sheffield apartment.
“Michelle began to pursue a coordinated campaign to claim a greater portion of Plaintiffs’ estate, including their portfolio of multifamily residential buildings in New York City,” according to the suit.
Still, none of it seems to be stopping Michelle. The unit popped up for sale on Wednesday — the same day the complaint was filed —asking $2.79 million, according to a StreetEasy listing update. Its listing reps from City Zen Realty didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Family feuds, legal and financial troubles haveplagued the family, and their portfolio, for decades.
COVID-19 dealt a major blow to the family portfolio’s bottom line, slashing rental income and driving their $53 million mortgage into default.
When Arthur and his brother Abe restructured their seven-building Manhattan portfolio during the pandemic,the $165 million dealnetted Abe an $80 million payout and brought in landlord Peter Hungerford to manage the properties.
But Michelle, who also held a stake in the portfolio, claimed she was completely blindsided by the deal and promptly sued her father and Hungerford in 2022, the Real Deal reported.
In January 2024, a court dismissed her suit in its entirety, and Michelle appealed that decision. In 2025, an appellate court reversed the decision. The case is ongoing, as abankruptcy case filedby the family company in June 2026 put a pause on the appeal.
Her attorney in the appeal declined to comment.
Arthur andAbehave also had their legal battles, accusing each other in court of stealing from the family business built by their father, Jacob, alongside claims of gross mismanagement.

hed: Detroit developer cites tax hikes as reason big blue cities like NYC are struggling: ‘Socialists are on the march’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s once-iconic industrial hub is primed for an economic comeback as major metropolitan areas continue tobleed residents to lower-tax states, a prominent Michigan developer told Fox News Digital.
Rodney Lockwood, Board Chairman of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, warned thathigh-tax cities like New York City, Los Angeles, and San Francisco are facing serious structural trouble.
“I think we have to look at both sides: what is not working, and then what will work,” Lockwood said.
“Right now, socialists are on the march, andZohran Mamdani in New Yorkis perhaps the best example of that. They’re winning races, and their answer is always the same:more taxesand more free stuff.”
Lockwood’s comments come as progressive-led cities nationwide—including New York, Chicago, Boston, and Los Angeles—struggle with taxpayer flight driven byhigh state and local taxes, lingering crime concerns, and an astronomical cost of living.
A new study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation (NTUF),releasedApril 7, 2026, confirmed that taxpayers are fleeing high-tax environments for more fiscally friendly states.
WhileTexas and Florida remain the top targets, states like North Carolina, South Carolina and Tennessee are also seeing record gains.
Notably, the NTUF “Migration in Minutes” metric found that Texas surpassed Florida in 2022 as the state gaining a new taxpayer most frequently — one every four minutes and 40 seconds.
“I sort of see it as a case of suicidal envy,” Lockwood explained.

“Belle Isle would be on the opposite side of that equation. We would have a taxation system aligned with the best of human characteristics. If you want people to work for the income and dignity of it, don’t tax work—so there’d be no local income tax. If we want people to come, invest, and produce the tools of productivity, don’t tax investments.”
Lockwood is championing a proposal to transform Detroit’s Belle Isle into a self-governing “Freedom City” aimed at setting a new blueprint for urban revival nationwide.
First developed as a public park in the late 19th century, Belle Isle spans 982 acres in the Detroit River—making it roughly 140 acres larger than New York City’s Central Park.
While the city owns the land, it is currently leased to the State of Michigan and operated as a state park under a 30-year agreement signed in 2013.
Under Lockwood’s proposal, private investors would purchase or lease the island from Detroit to build a mixed-use residential, retail, and commercial district.
The goal is to generate massive economic activity and private-sector jobs for a city recovering from decades of population loss.
Lockwood pointed to recent polling by Michigan pollster Steve Mitchell indicating strong interest in bold economic solutions, with 68 percent of likely Detroit voters and 51 percent of voters statewide approving the concept of special economic freedom zones.
Detroit’s economic trajectory highlights the stark reality of post-war urban decline, Lockwood noted.
“We’re trying to restore it back to being the world-class city it once was,” Lockwood said. “Back in 1950, it was the world’s richest city. Today, it ranks among the poorest in the United States. We’ve gone from 1.85 million people down to around 600,000.”
Lockwood believes the island represents a vastly underutilized asset ideal for conversion into a tax-friendly special economic zone designed to draw global capital.
His vision projects a permanent population of 50,000 residents across 20,000 households—all built without relying ontaxpayer dollars.
The “Freedom City” concept, supported by free-market advocates at the Mackinac Center, hinges on courting private venture capital through light-touch regulation and a growth-oriented tax framework.
Lockwood pointed to long-standing socioeconomic challenges across the Motor City as evidence that conventional municipal governance has failed.
“Detroit is stuck,” Lockwood asserted. “Its population has struggled to rebound, and it faces a looming fiscal issue. COVID-era federal relief funds sustained municipal budgets for a few years, but that money is exhausted.”
Lockwood argues that transforming Belle Isle could provide the spark needed to revitalize the entire region.
“What Belle Isle would do with 50,000 residents and $50 billion in private investment is attract an entrepreneurial class,” Lockwood said.
“These are business leaders looking to take proven concepts and expand into the heart of the world’s largest economy.”
