In May 2025,Lydia Rhea, a 26-year-old freelance musician and Juilliard graduate, thought she and her two roommates had found their dream apartment.
​After years of living in cramped student quarters, the group found a newly constructed duplex penthouse at 463 West 125th Street in Harlem.
​For three working musicians who needed space to rehearse, the unit seemed ideal. It boasted a spacious multi-level layout, large windows, two bathrooms, and in-unit laundry. Rhea even scored a second-floor bedroom featuring an ensuite bathroom and a private terrace.
​They signed a 13-month lease offering a one-month free concession, paying a net rent of $5,485 per month. As the very first tenants to occupy the newly built unit, Rhea expected a pristine, modern, hassle-free living experience.
​However, what was marketed as a modern luxury space quickly escalated into a year-long ordeal marked by apparent construction defects, toxic mold infestation, delayed mail delivery, and unresponsive building management, Rhea tellsRealtor.com®.
​“I feel a little bit stupid looking back on it,” Rhea says. “It looked clean, and it had really good access to trains…it looked to be like it was going to be a really good space.”
Public records show the building is owned by an LLC affiliated with ReGlobe founder Tomer Chen,a real estate developer who signed mortgage documents on behalf of the entity. The building was managed by Malek Management, according to emails from the company shared by Rhea.
A person who answered the phone at Malek Management claimed that the company no longer handles the building. Chen did not respond to multiple phone messages.
Mold is a persistent issue for some New York renters. In Fiscal Year 2025, the city’s Department ofHousing Preservation and Development(HPD) received 38,278 mold complaints, according toHPD’s indoor allergen report. That’s a drop of about 8.5% from the prior year’s total of 41,835 mold complaints.
In 2024, Harlem was the moldiest New York City neighborhood, with 397 complaints, according to a report done byRentHop.
Rhea says the red flags started almost immediately upon moving in, and the problems quickly worsened. At first, the issues seemed minor: a bad paint job, leaky faucets, broken doorknobs, and a brand-new, in-unit dishwasher that failed to run from day one.
Fixing the dishwasher alone took four grueling months of bouncing the job back and forth between an electrician and a plumber.
​“It kept going back and forth of the electrician saying it needed to be the plumber, the plumber saying it needed to be the electrician,” Rhea explained. “And then all coming back to the super who’s like, ‘I don’t do this kind of work, and I don’t want to get electrocuted.’”
​In August, Malek Management eventually replaced the broken dishwasher with a working one from an unoccupied apartment. But that ordeal was nothing compared to the missing mail debacle.
​After a few weeks in their new home, Rhea and her roommates realized that they hadn’t received a single piece of mail. As freelance musicians, the roommates were waiting on close to $10,000 in paper checks from gigs.
​Rhea began knocking on her neighbor’s doors, only to discover that no one else was getting mail either.
​Concerned, Rhea marched down to the local post office, where a clerk confirmed that they were holding the building’s mail. However, staff refused to release it over the counter, insisting a mail carrier was legally required to deliver it on-site.
​After returning to the post office almost daily, the roommates finally found a carrier, who revealed that mail delivery had been completely halted because management installed the building’s mailboxes too high,violating federal postal regulations.
​“The whole building wasn’t getting mail, but our management had not told us, ‘Hey, if you want to get your mail, you need to go to the post office between 9 and 10 a.m. Ask for this specific person. We’re working on fixing it,” Rhea said.
​The situation descended further into absurdity when Rhea went back to collect her household’s mail—and the postal worker accidentally handed her the entire building’s mail.
​“So we’ve gone from them being like, no, we can’t have the wrong postal worker hand you your mail for your unit, to being like, sure, let me just hand a random civilian everybody’s mail,” Rhea said.
​Even after management lowered the mailboxes to comply with federal code, they failed to install proper master locks, leaving every tenant’s mail accessible to anyone with a mail key.
​“We had it on security footage, and our management did nothing. The post office did nothing. I think it’s still like that to this day, to my knowledge,” Rhea said.
​Rhea soon discovered that she wasn’t the only person having a hard time in her once ideal apartment.
​“When we moved in, we were optimistic because we were sold this vision of it’s a brand new build,” a tenant who lived in the building said. “At the beginning, though, some of the signs started pointing towards this is not the best.”
​After suffering from mailbox, security, and other amenity issues, it became clear that Rhea wasn’t the odd one out; this was a building-wide problem.
In February 2026, following a series of severe blizzards, a persistent leak developed in the ceiling vent in Rhea’s bathroom. Initially, it leaked only during heavy storms. But soon afterwards, it started to drip every time she turned on the vent.
Management offered only temporary fixes, forcing Rhea to keep a towel permanently laid out on her bathroom floor.
​But on April 8, the situation escalated from simply annoying to toxic. While pulling a laundry basket out of her closet, Rhea found her wall was completely covered in mold.
​She reported the hazard immediately, but with a pre-planned two-week trip to London scheduled, she had no choice but to depart. The mold was so pervasive that she had to wash her packed clothing four times just to remove the stench.
​From London, Rhea called management daily. Yet, management refused to address the mold until the ceiling leak was fixed—a repair that finally took place on April 27. But by then, mold had spread into other rooms, forcing Rhea’s roommates to throw out ruined furniture.
​Other tenants experienced similar structural decay. One tenant reported leaks in their unit–despite not being located on the top floor. Eventually, the issue escalated into a safety hazard.
​“We ended up discovering some mold, which ended up spreading,” the tenant said. “At first, they had a mold company come in, cut it out of the wall, and say, okay, well we cleared it…just because this mold on the surface here [is gone] doesn’t mean that there’s not the conditions that led to its formation in the first place.”
As Rhea and other neighbors’ apartments continued to rot away inside, the world outside became increasingly unsafe.
​When Malek Management leased the building’s ground-floor retail space to a smoke shop, residents submitted repeated complaints about heavy loitering and harassment outside the front door.
​“My wife was getting verbally harassed, especially late at night, and we were told ‘be patient, be patient,’ and it wasn’t fully addressed,” a tenant who lived in the building said. “Meanwhile, the mold issues were still not addressed.”
​The situation escalated violently on April 24 at 6:30 p.m., whena drug-related shootingerupted directly outside the smoke shop. The resulting police shootout with multiple gunmen left neighboring storefront windows covered in bullet holes and police stationed outside the entry 24/7.
Residents say the building now felt like an unsafe, toxic prison.
​”The frustrating part about the shooting…was more to do with the fact that they were not addressing that it happened and not addressing or acknowledging that tenants would like them to be taking measures to be made safe moving forward,” Rhea said.
​With their lease ending in May, the roommates tried to negotiate. They asked to renew at their original rate with the one-month concession. Management immediately denied their request and would be adding a massive pay increase of $715 a month to their rent.
​“We were in a bind because we were like, if they’re not fixing this problem, we don’t really feel like we can resign, but moving in New York City is really expensive,” Rhea explained.
​Three weeks after initially reporting the mold, Rhea says she still had no answers. Though NYC housing guidelines dictate that documentedmold must be correctedwithin a certain timeline depending on the square footage, she says the issue went unaddressed.
​On May 4, Lydia finally filed a formal complaint with HPD. On May 7, she and her roommates notified management that they would be withholding their May rent.
The next morning at 7:30 a.m., Rhea received a frantic call from her super pleading with them not to leave and promising the mold would be resolved.
When contractors finally arrived on May 11, they cut into the closet drywall and made a shocking discovery: the wall, directly attached to her shower wall, contained zero waterproofing.
Water from the shower had been seeping directly through wet tiles into the bare drywall for a year, a direct violation ofBuilding Code 2509.2, which mandates moisture-resistant backing for wet tiling.
Contractors also discovered a complete lack of waterproofing beneath the bathroom tiles, explaining why mold constantly grew under the bathroom floor tiles and why Rhea had to scrub her shower every three days.
“I was honestly not surprised,” Rhea said. “Clearly something was going on if the fact that this unit is a year old and there’s this many problems going on already. I think it just confirmed in my mind what we were starting to discover that it was just really cheaply built.”
​The contractors revealed that the only real fix was to completely gut and rip out both bathrooms. They patched the closet, but within three days, the sickening smell of mold returned.
On May 18, the roommates submitted formal notice that they would vacate the unit on May 31.
Moving out brought one final clash. On June 1, the day after vacating, Rhea received text messages from her super alleging the tenants had damaged the apartment. As proof, he sent photos of the unaddressed mold and bad paint job.
​“I was really exasperated when I got [the messages],” Rhea said. “We’re telling him that these issues have not been resolved, and then he’s doing a walkthrough and he’s sending me photos of mold.”
The next day, a phone call between Rhea, her property manager, and a roommate’s parent descended into a shouting match. Management claimed they would withhold the entire $6,200 security deposit to cover “damages” and the unpaid May rent.
​In response, Rhea compiled a Google Drive containing emails, photos, and text messages that she believed would prove the landlord’s neglect and sent it over.
​After a follow-up email more than a month later, Rhea and her roommates finally received a response that their security deposit would be returned on July 7.
​“It just really opened my eyes in terms of, unfortunately, how corrupt New York City landlords can be,” Rhea said. “I think they expect you to not go to lengths to hold them responsible for things.”
While Rhea recovered her deposit, the musician’s attempt to hold the building owners and management officially accountable fell flat.
​Prior to the contractor’s discovery of the missing insulation, an HPD inspector had visited the unit, verbally confirming the mold as a major violation.
Yet, the HPD case was closed without any follow-up anda message that said: “HPD conducted an inspection of this complaint. The conditions observed by the inspector did not violate the housing laws enforced by HPD. The complaint has been closed.”
Rhea, who had been expecting to go to small claims court to refund the security deposit, tried to reopen the case. Her calls to HPD escalated through various bureaucratic channels until an operator suggested mailing physical photos to the HPD Chief, then gave her a phone contact to report the inspector.
​However, she says she was instead given the number for the Department of Homeland Security.
​Exhausted, Rhea filed formal complaints to the Mamdani Administration and her NYC Council Member.
​“I’m frustrated that there’s nothing really holding people accountable,” Rhea said. “I’m frustrated with how HPD handled it because online it’s showing as just a closed complaint and not a violation.”
Since she moved out, Rhea’s old apartment has already been rented out to other tenants for $6495 per month, according toStreetEasy. She fears they may face similar issues.
“There wasn’t time to fully address the building-wide issues,” the tenant said. “Maybe they finally fixed the rooftop leaking, but I have no idea what’s going on behind the wall.”
Rhea has since secured a new apartment on the Upper West Side after spending the summer subletting in Washington Heights.
“I wanted a pre-war building,” Rhea explained. “I don’t want a new build. I want something with thick walls that has been maintained.”
Despite the nightmare experience, her affection for the city remains intact.
“I still wouldn’t want to live anywhere else in the states for a lot of reasons,” Rhea said. “It’s a really amazing city to live in, but when they say that it makes you tough, they’re not lying.”

hed: A converted hydroelectric plant in Maine hits the market for $750,000
subhead: The 1919 plant was converted to a residence in 2006. The property comes with two buildings.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
“A River Runs Through It” — this former hydroelectric power plant on the Pemaquid River in Bristol, Maine, that is. It’s on the market for $750,000.
The structure at13 Upper Round Pond Roadwas built in 1919, tucked along the edge of the water in a bucolic setting. Back then, the water would go underneath the foundation to generate the power. Converted into a residence in 2006, the space welcomes you through barn doors to a large open cement room. While it could be converted to a living area, the sellers have been using it as a party space that has its own kitchenette.
Walk around to the front to climb a few steps to an outdoor seating area, which leads into the two-bedroom, one-bathroom home. To the right is the kitchen with dark blue cabinetry, a soapstone countertop on the island, and stainless steel appliances. Oversized windows provide views of the river, particularly from the window seat where you can hear the river run through the open the windows. In the corner of the living space, a propane stove provides a cozy setting.
“There’s quite a bit of river frontage on this property. The river is so pretty, and it’s so relaxing to be down there,” saidCrissy Stirrattof Sotheby’s International Realty, who has thelisting, noting that there’s also great fishing. A fire pit and seating area are perfect for soaking up the environment, and there’s a swimming hole for taking a dip.
The primary bedroom fills with light from oversized windows that look down to the river. A double closet provides ample storage.
The property comes with a second structure that previously served as a plumbing supply store, has a two-bay garage. Next to that is an open space that’s ideal for a gallery or exercise  studio. On the back, there’s a spacious workshop area and an insulated space that’s currently being used as a gym. The propane system is new.
The home is close to Pemaquid Beach, and is about 15 minutes from the riverfront town of Demariscotta. Boothbay Harbor is about 45 minutes away.
Megan Johnson is a Boston-based writer and reporter whose work appears in People, Architectural Digest, The Boston Globe, and more.

hed: Beverly Hills property where demented Manson followers murdered Sharon Tate asks $45M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The Beverly Hills property whereSharon Tateand four others were slain by sick-mindedManson family butchershas listed for $45 million, The Post has learned.
Jeff Franklin, the famed producer behind the iconic ’90s TV series “Full House,”has struggled for yearsto part ways with the Mediterranean-style hillside mansion, built on top of the torn-down house where the murders occurred.
Striking in its new iteration, its amenities include a massive 225-foot swimming pool that can fit the Leaning Tower of Pisa — with enough room left for laps.
Still, the Cielo Drive property — most recently asking $50 million — will likely never shake the haunting legacy of what happened almost 60 years ago in August 1969.
That’s when several of Charles Manson’s carnage-craving flunkies cut a path across the 3.6-acre grounds and killed Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her hairstylist friend Jay Sebring in the home’s living room.
They also murdered her guests, the coffee heiress Abigale Folger and her boyfriend Wojciech Frykowski, where the pool now stands, and Steven Parent in an onsite guardhouse.
Efforts to thwart true-crime tourists who still come, some of whom leave strange offerings, have taken several forms over the years — including petitioning the city to change the site’s address, which was an easy lookup for people wanting a view.
Franklin, who now lives in Miami, purchased the property for $6.4 million in January 2000.
Hollywood talent manager Rudolph Altobelli was renting the place to Tate and her husband Roman Polanski at the time of the murders.
What followed, while not as heinous as the murders, did show a dark side of Altobelli and others.
Altobelli moved back into the place three weeks after the killings and then made a move that sickened still-mourning Hollywood. He sued Polanski for breaking the one-year lease on the property when the director moved out after the murders and also billed him for the cleanup costs.
Tate and Polanski lived in the home for less than 6 months, paying $1,200 a month, or roughly $11,000 in today’s dollars.
Years later, Nine Inch Nails frontman Trent Reznor rented the original home and installed a recording studio within. He named the studio “Le Pig,” after the infamous word that Manson’s followers scrawled on the front door in Sharon Tate’s blood.
Reznor took the now-sanded and repainted door with him when he left. But not before Reznor’s now-former friend, the goth shock-rockerMarilyn Manson, who had already taken his stage name from Marilyn Monroe andCharles Manson, recorded there and appeared in Nine Inch Nails’ video for “Gave Up,” which was filmed at this home.
Franklin is listing the estate after trying unsuccessfully to rent it for a colossal $247,500 a month — and it’s a far cry from its 2,300-square-foot, farmhouse-style predecessor.
Within its 21,000 square feet are nine bedrooms, 12 full bathrooms and four half baths. A massive grand foyer entrance opens to 40-foot ceilings and a winding staircase below a dome ceiling and a fountain.
The main bedroom stands in a separate wing and has large dressing rooms, private terraces, a fireplace and spa-styled bathrooms that provide views of Beverly Hills.
There’s also an area that’s home to several sharks, though not as large as the “Jaws” kind. They reside in a 20-foot-long floor-to-ceiling saltwater aquarium that sits between the living room and the dining room. There are several large fish tanks in addition to the sharks’ and a multi-tiered projection room with a stage for performances.
An infrared sauna is part of a beauty salon, and an entertainment area features an arcade room with video games and a photo booth, all surrounded by rich wood-paneled walls and ceilings.
The outside is like a water park, featuring a lagoon-style infinity pool amid three cascading waterfalls. A private river with a current allows residents and guests to float around the property’s grounds. And a 35-foot-long water slide leads to a grotto where guests can watch giant koi fish underwater through reinforced glass.
The property wasn’t always associated with tragedy.
Originally built in 1941, it had a Hollywood patina, with film pioneer Lillian Gish renting there and even the Baron Philippe de Rothschild leasing it when he was in town.
Henry Fonda hid out there from fans during the peak of his popularity. And iconic leading man Cary Grant used the property as a honeymoon nest when he married actress Diane Cannon.
Bennett Bidwell and Adam Rosenfeld of the Resident Group have the listing.

Kendra Wilkinson broke down in tears after her client fired her as their real estate agent.
“When a client fires you… after all the work you put in. Ya, I’m struggling today, guys,” the former reality star wrote on her Instagram Stories alongside an image of her crying with her eyes closed.
Wilkinson, 41, then shared a video of herself shedding tears as she spoke about how difficult it’s been for her as a real estate agent.
“I know that we’re living in a world of struggle right now, I know that. But it’s just … it’s so hard. It’s so hard right now,” she said as she sobbed.
“I feel like I’m doing everything right in my life — I’m raising my kids and putting them first,” the “Girls Next Door” alum, who shares son Hank Jr., 16, and daughter Alijah, 12, with ex Hank Baskett, added.
“I’m doing everything good — I’m a good person. It’s just such a struggle right now.”
Wilkinson described problems she recently faced, including “fighting people that work with me, getting fired, people being rude and mean.”
“It’s taking a toll,” she concluded.

hed: A shocking number of wealthy NYC renters live in stabilized units
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Rich New Yorkers are scoring the city’s best rent deals.
A new analysis by theWall Street Journalof the city’s 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey — the most recent data available — found that some of the sweetest deals in the five boroughs’ rent-stabilization program are landing in the laps of its wealthiest tenants, not its neediest.
Right now, wealthy households make up about 10% of the entire rent-stabilized stock, according to a Citizens Budget Commission analysis of 2023 data. Of those, more than 86,700 households reported earning above $200,000 a year.
High earners in the top 25% bracket who live inrent-stabilized apartmentspay roughly $1,000 less per month than they would at market rate, a savings of 33%.
Top earners in the 10% bracket do even better, pocketing $1,300 in monthly savings, a 36% discount. Compare that to renters in the bottom three income brackets, who save closer to $300 a month, or between 15% and 22%.
Part of the disparity comes down to geography. Wealthier tenants tend to cluster in pricier neighborhoods, where the gap between market rate and stabilized rent is naturally wider, even if the stabilized rate still comes with a hefty price tag.
“You do have people paying $5,000, $6,000 or $8,000 for rent-stabilized apartments,” Allia Mohamed, CEO of the rental data firm Openigloo, told the Journal.
The rest of the gap is baked into the system itself.Rent stabilizationin New York was never designed to check a tenant’s bank account.
“I can’t imagine trying to do an income certification for like a million units,” Brad Greenburg, executive director of NYU’s Furman Center, added. “Administratively, it feels impossible.”
Those well-off tenants are about to get an even better deal, courtesy of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’srent freeze, which kicks in this October.
The borough breakdown shows just how uneven the savings really are. In Manhattan, stabilized units go for about half of what market rate would charge. In The Bronx, that discount shrinks to just 12%. Queens renters save 13%, while Brooklyn tenants land in the middle with a 24% break.
Not everyone in the real estate world is shrugging this off as a quirk of the market. Some see it as proof the whole system needs an overhaul.
“This shows you the system is malfunctioning,” Massimo D’Angelo, a real estate attorney who represents private landlords, told the outlet. “We need to give these apartments to people who actually need them.”
Tenant advocates see it differently. To them, a handful of wealthy outliers in a housing stock of 1 million units is no reason to panic, and definitely not a reason to shrink the program.
“This isn’t a welfare program. That’s not what rent stabilization is. We’re not looking out for just the most needy,” Darius Khalil Gordon, executive director of the Metropolitan Council on Housing, said. “It’s made to make sure that people can afford to live in a city that they love.”
Rent stabilization is often mistaken for rent control, but the two are not the same. Rent-controlled units have their prices capped by the state, while stabilized apartments fall under the watch of theRent Guidelines Board, a city panel that decides how much landlords are allowed to raise rents annually.
Most rent-stabilized tenants are far from wealthy, and the bulk of these apartments sit in The Bronx and Washington Heights, with additional pockets in Brooklyn and Queens.
Still, with a million units scattered across the city, economists say it was only a matter of time before some of that inventory ended up benefiting high earners too.
In neighborhoods like Midtown East, a two-bedroom now averages around $7,500 a month, up 17% from last year according to Zumper, a jump that has made stabilized apartments feel less like a bonus and more like a necessity for anyone hoping to stay in the city long term.
To qualify as rent-stabilized, a building generally has to have been constructed before 1974, when the law took effect, or it must receive some form of public subsidy or tax break. Mamdani made expanding that pool a campaign promise, vowing to add 200,000 new stabilized units over the next 10 years.
There was once a mechanism to catch these cases. If a tenant’s income hit $200,000 for two consecutive years, landlords could convert the unit to market rate. They could also raise rents after a tenant moved out, provided they made qualifying renovations.
Landlords used those tools often. Since 1994, more than 360,000 apartments have exited the rent-stabilization program altogether, according to the city’s Rent Guidelines Board.
That changed in 2019, when the state clamped down hard on those loopholes, a decision the real estate industry has been fighting to reverse ever since.
“There are no current annual income certification reviews,” D’Angelo said. “That needs to be changed.”

hed: Inside the $85M James Bond-inspired Florida mansion designed to wow billionaires
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Just south of the intersection of two main roads in western Delray Beach, Florida, is a hidden community filled with properties “designed to make a billionaire’s jaw drop.”Behind heavily guarded gates patrolled around the clock by former military veterans and Navy SEALs, a new standard of American luxury is quietly taking shape. Welcome to Stone Creek Ranch, where actor Mark Wahlberg, hedge fund billionaire Steve Cohen, Rockstar Energy founder Russ Weiner and NFL star Khalil Mack call themselves neighbors.
Fox News Digital got an inside look at the enclave’s newest flagship listing, “Villa Skyfall,” an $85 million James Bond-inspired estate complete with hidden passages and a poker room, a rainforest-style spa and 2.5 private acres.
“This is literally the most prestigious address in South Florida right now. What’s so extraordinary about the community is that, like you said, eight years ago, it was a hidden gem, not many people knew about it, and it’s truly evolved in terms of the level of A-list celebrity clients who are buying here, business and entrepreneur leaders who have already bought, and also the quality of that we’re now able to offer in this community,” Douglas Elliman Florida executive director and listing agent Senada Adzem, who’s already sold multiple homes in the neighborhood, told Fox News Digital.
“Delray Beach has attracted global wealth now, and it’s a really special destination where it’s much quieter and more private than Miami or Palm Beach, and a lot of our clients really appreciate being in Stone Creek Ranch, where you can have large estates, a lot of privacy. They’re away from the prying eyes,” she continued. “They feel a peace of mind.”Crossing the entrance, guests are greeted by awarm yet modern architectural masterpiecerising behind reflective water features. The single-story estate features a 32-foot-tall grand salon illuminated by crystal chandeliers and backlit onyx, a museum-style automotive gallery, an Amazon rainforest-inspired spa, a hidden poker lounge and a 95-foot-long pool framed by cabanas, fire features and tropical gardens. Every transition appears designed for impact, turning stone, wood, glass, water and light into part of the experience throughout the home.
“It was designed to make a billionaire’s jaw drop,” Adzem said. “What we wanted to do is really follow that theme of very elegant, very sophisticated marketing. We’re not going for a mass audience. So we’re looking for that very specific buyer who appreciates what this property has to offer. And it offers a lot, truly, in every single way — it is one of one. It’s a trophy property.”
A new construction project as grand as Villa Skyfall takes an average of four to five years to complete, according to Adzem, but this estate was built in just 14 months. The $85 million asking price includes all the furniture, fully stocked bars and kitchens, Chanel, Dior and Hermès handbags in the closets, and even electric toothbrushes in each of the home’s 12 bathrooms.“Ultra-high-net worth clients now want top-of-the-line, turnkey properties. They want to come in and worry-free know [that] they’ll only need to bring their clothing, their personal items. Everything else will be provided for them,” Adzem said. “People are accustomed to coming in and having things in a way that they will really appreciate, and I think that’s what adds to the allure.”
There’s active interest coming from high-net-worth buyers fleeing high-tax states, with a heavy concentration of tech founders, finance executives and retiring entrepreneurs looking for private, family-oriented retreats.
“We’re seeing a lot of entrepreneurs who are looking to retire very soon, and they want a sanctuary for themselves and their family and people who really want to entertain… You have tax benefits of being in Florida, so we’re seeing clients from California, we’re seeing clients from New York and Connecticut. They’re primarily in the finance and tech worlds, and we have had a few celebrities as well,” Adzem said of the property’s showings thus far.
Listing a property at an $85 million asking price could set a record for Delray Beach, according to Adzem. At a time when the average American homebuyer is dealing with high interest rates and a tough housing market, she explained that while working families face distinct economic challenges, luxury buyers are exceptionally bullish and confident in South Florida real estate.
“Our clients, both in the ultra-luxury segment, as well as clients who are working… white-collar families who are looking to put their kids through school have different challenges that are facing them. However, what we have noticed is that they’re still very optimistic about the strength of the economy,” she said.
“Ultra-high net worth clients have greatly benefited from the strength of the stock market. So they feel encouraged that this is going to continue,” Adzem added, “and they’re very confident when it comes to investing in real estate, particularly in South Florida.”
While critics and real estate observers frequently question whether South Florida’s soaring luxury home values are approaching a peak, Adzem argued the continued influx of out-of-state capital tells a different story. She said the migration of high-earning families and corporate headquarters from traditional wealth centers has created a structural shift in the region’s economy that extends far beyond a temporary market spike.
“I do believe in the future of the Florida luxury market for many reasons,” Adzem told Fox Digital, highlighting Florida’s zero state income tax and favorable business climate. “There has been a lot of wealth migration into Florida… there’s just a confluence of events that is going to continue helping us attract unique buyers to very special properties.”

hed: Foreclosures spike across California — as new hotspots are revealed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
California foreclosuresare at their highest levelssince the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the latest June 2026 numbers.
The Golden State ranked nine out of the top 10 in worst foreclosure rates last month in the nation with one in every 3,205 housing units foreclosed. The top three states were Florida, South Carolina and Indiana.
Nationwide, one in every 3,656 housing units had a foreclosure fling, according toATTOM Data.
While the national June numbers are an improvement from May, foreclosure rates arestill higher than last year’s numbers.
Of California’s 14,644,735 housing units, around 4,500 foreclosed last month. Lake, Shasta, Sutter and Mendocino counties saw the worst foreclosure rates.
More broadly, in the first half of this year, California had 21,543 homes in various levels of foreclosure activity.
It’s the third-highest total among the states, accounting for 9% of the nation’s 227,548, only ranking after Texas and Florida.
However, expertstold The California Postthat there shouldn’t be much to worry about. Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel said the idea of aforeclosure crisis or housing crash“is very far from the case.”
Instead, Krimmel argued the rise in foreclosures is actually a market “normalization” due to pandemic-era relief programs like mortgage forbearance and payment deferral recently ending.
“We’ve come off really historic lows that any uptick is going to draw some attention,” Krimmel said.
These foreclosures may actually have a bright spot: They help to discount homes especially inCalifornia’s uber-expensive housing market, by up to around a 27% price drop, especially if those foreclosed homes are not in the best shape.
“If it’s selling for 20–30% less than it otherwise would just because it has the foreclosure label on it, for the right first-time buyer it could be a solution in ahigh-cost market like California,” Krimmel told The Post.
Additionally, the data shows that California’s uptick in foreclosures is still relatively modest compared to other states.
The state had the 12th-smallest rise in foreclosures in the last two years, while mortgage payments are surging in states like Colorado or Wyoming.
According to ATTOM analysts, the national monthly decline in foreclosure activity was driven by fewer foreclosure starts, while completed foreclosures continued to increase.

hed: Mamdani publishes names and addresses of all NYC property owners who could be hit with new pied-à-terre tax
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has published a searchable database of Big Apple properties that couldfall under the state’s new pied-à-terre tax, effectively doxxing thousands of wealthy New Yorkers.
The city’s Department of Finance uploaded the comprehensive list – which purports to cover all unoccupied, non-primary residences in the five boroughs worth north of $1 million – including the full names and addresses of every property owner.
The move follows awidely panned X post by the mayor in which he put wealthy residents on noticeto “check your mailbox when you’re back in the five boroughs, because you’ve got mail,” a warning that notification letters were on their way.
“The best city in the world deserves the best parks, libraries, and schools in the world. That’s only possible when we all pay our fair share,” Mamdani wrote Thursday.
The socialist darling has long touted the policy enacted by Gov. Kathy Hochul and Albany Democrats to tax second homes in the city – though critics have warned it could cause property values to plummet.
Mamdani threatened to raise city property taxes by a staggering 9.5% in February unless he was allowed to “tax the rich” to cover a $12 billion budget gap that was later revised down to $5.4 billion.
City Hall estimates the pied-à-terre tax would yield $500 million per year for the Big Apple’s budget.
But Democratic city Comptroller Mark Levine’s office said the real figure would be closer to $340 to $380 million and could diminish over time.
The mayor is just getting started in fulfilling his campaign pledge to siphon funds from rich New Yorkers to bankroll his wealth redistribution agenda.
But it turns outeven the middle-class isn’t safefrom the pricey giveaways on his wishlist, which are being funded by the $23 billion in taxes Mamdani has backed since being sworn in.
He’s also pushing ahead with amonths-long pressure campaign for even more new state taxes, including on city property owners, The Post reported last week.

hed: Inside the Upper East Side’s most expensive rental building — where prices reach $45K/month
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about movin’ on up to the East Side — and to a deluxe apartment in the sky.
A new luxury rental tower on the Upper East Side is drawing tenants willing to pay as much as $45,000 a month — arriving at a moment when deep-pocketed apartment hunters in that area have almost nothing new to choose from, The Post has learned.
The Langdon, a 24-story, 45-unit building at 288 E. 88th St. developed by Alchemy-ABR Investment Partners alongside the Carlyle Group, opened for leasing earlier this month and has already moved a chunk of its inventory off the market.
Asking rents on available units run from roughly $12,400 for a two-bedroom to that $45,000 a month for penthouses unit spanning five bedrooms — making it the most expensive rental building in the neighborhood. Pricing on select apartments has already ticked up since the building’s initial launch.
The residences themselves lean into that same quiet luxury sensibility. Apartments across the one- to five-bedroom layouts favor oversized windows and thoughtful finishes throughout, with recessed lighting, smart climate systems and keyless entry built in as standard rather than upgrades.
Kitchens are outfitted with custom cabinetry, quartz counters, integrated appliances and a dedicated wine fridge, while primary bathrooms lean spa-like, with oversized showers and heated floors. A handful of full-floor penthouses and select residences with wraparound terraces push that further, blurring the line between indoor and outdoor space for tenants willing to pay for it.
The building’s amenities lean into that scaled-down, high-touch pitch. Designed by Hill West Architects, the Langdon includes a fitness center, a multipurpose sports court, a children’s playroom, a media and gaming lounge, co-working space and a landscaped rooftop terrace, spread across a building with as few as two apartments per floor on most levels.
Manhattan’s rental market has been historically tight all year. Citywide vacancy sat at just under 2% in January, and separate estimates put vacancy on the Upper East Side specifically at under 2% as well.
Against that backdrop, brokers say a new building like the Langdon stands out simply for existing.
Keyan Sanai, the top rental broker at Douglas Elliman who represents a competing property nearby, said interest has been strong from the start.
“The Langdon is one of only a few new luxury rental buildings to open on the Upper East Side over the past couple of years, and the demand for these types of buildings has been very strong thus far for sure,” Sanai said.
Sanai credited part of thatshift to the Second Avenue subway line— as the building stands on Second Avenue — reshaping how renters think about the neighborhood.
“The Q train was a complete game changer for Second Avenue. It made getting downtown so much easier and helped change the perception that Second Avenue was somehow less desirable than being closer to the park or the 4, 5 and 6 trains,” he said.
At the Langdon itself, leasing has moved briskly since the building opened. Timothy J. McCarthy, senior sales and leasing director at Alchemy Properties, said the first tenant moved in this month, with the rest of the building filling in through August and September.
“The Upper East Side has been waiting for new luxury rental inventory for years. Once we opened leasing, it became clear just how much pent-up demand was out there. Luxury renters are moving fast because they know if they pass on a great apartment today, it probably won’t be there tomorrow,” he said.
That dynamic has only intensified since the redevelopment of 800 Fifth Ave. got underway.
The Post reported in May that developer Miki Naftali, who paid more than $800 million for the Bernard Spitzer-built tower at Fifth Avenue and 61st Street, isemptying all 208 unitsto make way for a 26-story limestone condominium designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects. Tenants who had paid between $9,000 and $30,000 a month found themselves searching a submarket with almost no comparable rental stock left to absorb them.
McCarthy said the Langdon has picked up some of that overflow, as well as others in the area.
“We have had people that have sold, but they don’t want to leave the neighborhood completely, so they’re renting for that purpose. And we have people coming that say that they’re going to sell nearby, and they’d rather rent at this time,” he said.

hed: A-list New Yorkers named on Mamdani’s potential pied-à-terre tax list include supporters like Cynthia Nixon, Anna Wintour
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A veritable who’s-who of the Big Apple’s upper crust — from movie stars to billionaire philanthropists — were named and had their addressesrevealed on a list of New Yorkerswho might be subject to the state’s new pied-à-terre tax.
Documents posted on the city Department of Finance webpage identified hundreds of thousands of entities who could find themselves in the crosshairs of the Mayor Zohran Mamdani-backed tax on luxury second homes.
The big names spotted by The Post scattered throughout the list included luminaries spanning the worlds of business, politics and the arts — such as actress and failed New York gubernatorial candidateCynthia Nixon, a devoted Mamdani supporter.
Taylor Swift’s Tribeca residence also seems to have made the cut, listed as being owned by the company “Euro Tribeca LLC.”
Oscar-nominated directorDarren Aronofskyis also among the celebrities to appear on the document, along with an Upper East Side residence owned by the “Woody Allen 2005 Revocable Trust” and another owned by Helen Morris Scorsese, the wife of the famed filmmaker Martin Scorsese.
Addresses listed under author and New Age guru Deepak Chopra, legendary journalist Gay Talese and the trust of late “60 Minutes” anchor Morley Safer also appear on the list.
Fashion world icon Anna Wintour is also named on the list, as is her downtown Manhattan address. In April, Wintourfamously gushed she was “full of admiration”for Mamdani’s wife and New York City first lady Rama Duwaji, despite her having liked a deranged social media post calling the Oct. 7, 2023 terror attack against Israel a “mass rape hoax” that the New York Times “fabricated.”
A residence connected to formerMayor Eric Adams‘ first deputy mayor, Randy Mastro, was on the list. As was a home belonging to former CBRE global brokerage chairman Stephen Siegel.
Billionaire businessman and philanthropistLeonard Stern’sabode got a mention along with real estate developers Morris Moinian and Bruce Ratner.
Not one but two City Council members appeared on the document, which was only supposed to list non-primary residences, including District 6 Democrat Gale Brewer, who said of her Upper West Side Brownstone, “I’ve been living in [my place] 365 days a year since 1994. So this whole list must be messed up.”
Joining Brewer was Council Minority Leader David Carr (R-Staten Island) who called the mayor “a shoo-in for ‘Realtor of the Year’ in Texas,” referring to a predicted exodus of wealthy New Yorkers to more tax-favorable states.
City Hall did not comment.
“As per State law, a property roll was released for public inspection,” said a DOF spokesperson. “From this list, DOF will identify properties that may be subject to the new non-primary residence property surcharge.”
— Additional reporting by Craig McCarthy

hed: Home of the Week: Twin cottages on Nantucket are being sold together for $2.5m
subhead: The petite side-by-side studio homes are located in ‘Sconset, a short walk from the water
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

7 and 9 Park Lane, Nantucket

$2.495 million

StyleCottages

Year built1924 (9 Park); 1927 (7 Park). Both updated since.

Square feet384 each

Bedrooms1 each (plus a loft space)

Baths1 full each

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$4,048


The plan: End transient visits to ‘Sconset, the bucolic corner of eastern Nantucket, by investing in a place of one’s own.

The problem: Half the team suffers from apocalyptic snoring.

The solution: Two cottages sitting side-by-side.

Whether or not snoring is the real reason to invest in two island homes, 7 and 9 Park Lane offer the opportunity as they are being sold together.

In large part, the cottages are mirror images. Both are clad in classic Nantucket/Cape Cod style cedar shingling and sage trim, both are single story, both have entry doors flanked by large windows with flower boxes, both are 384 square feet, and both display plaques with the name of the homes. But each has a history of its own.

The cottage at 9 Park was once a primary means of contacting the mainland when it was operated as a telegraph house for summer visitors. Built in 1924, it subsequently was used as a tearoom, a yard shop, and a record store, according to the owners.

The sign above the door reads: “Telegraph House.”


The second cottage, on the right when facing from Park Lane, is named “Right Bank.” One difference from its neighbor is a loft accessed by a ship’s ladder in the bedroom. It’s not an official bedroom and has a small square window to allow natural light.



Both homes have similar floorplans, but differences in the color palettes.

From the street, the front doors open directly into the 242-square-foot bedroom/living rooms with planked pine flooring and support beams crossing the white ceilings. On either side of the screen doors are two large casement windows with decorative divided light muntins. On the right exterior walls are double-hung windows and on the left is a pair of similarly sized windows.



A doorway leads to the other spaces. The 73-square-foot kitchens have electric stoves, white cabinets, and vinyl flooring. The sinks are located underneath a double-hung window and second entry doors are to the right.

The final room in each unit is the 39-square-foot full bathroom with a shower and a stacked washer/dryer. The Telegraph House vanity is white, and the Right Bank one is black.



The window trim in the Telegraph House is Nantucket Red, while the Right Bank trim is soft butter/off-white. The Right Bank has a modest cathedral-style ceiling.

Listing agent Lara Hanson,an eighth generation islander, said the property has a strong rental history with rates between $3,000 and $4,000 a week. Nantucket has its own set of short-term-rental rulesposted on the town’s website.

The cottages can be occupied year-round, Hanson said. But she noted ‘Sconset goes into hibernation with businesses closing doors around September/October and then waiting until April to reopen.


“I can’t speak to what these cottages are like in the winter, but I can tell you the neighborhood that they’re in, ‘Sconset, is very peaceful in the wintertime,” she said. “It’s not a common year-round neighborhood.”

The cottages are on two lots but being sold as a single unit.

Hanson andJen Allen of Fisher Real Estate in Nantuckethave the listing.

hed: California’s first tiny home megaproject ignites fury in idyllic beach town
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New plans for a controversial ADU housing project in Southern California were released in hopes of gaining community support after serious doubt.
The developer of the massive ADU project called Chalcifica is planning on building the homes in the Pacific Beach neighborhood of San Diego.
After facing concerns over culturally sensitive land, developers relocated the project and revised the plan from 136 units down to 125 units spread across six buildings. Parking zones, however, will increase from 70 spaces to 126 spaces.
The sensitive land is associated with the Kumeyaay Nation, the indigenous people native to the San Diego region.
This all comes after a judge granted a preliminary injunction on the original project back in December.
Pacific Beach neighbors sued the city and the developing company, arguing that the plan risked “irreversible harm to the City’s environment” and endangered “public safety by circumventing requirements intended to mitigate wildfire risk.”
“Our goal is to move forward with a project that adds much-needed attainable housing units in Pacific Beach while addressing concerns so everyone can benefit,” theCEO of Infill Innovation Brian Doyle told Times of San Diego.
“We want to turn the page from the past. In many ways, I understand the neighbors’ frustrations, but this is a new company with a new direction and expereinced leadership driving it. We want to work with neighbors and the city to bring something that everyone can benefit from,” he continued.
Infill Innovation, formerly known as SDRE, is the owner and developer behind Chalcifica.
The company’s former CEO, Christian Spicer, stepped down amidst the lawsuit and financial struggles in April.

hed: Yoko Ono to become the longest homeowner inside NYC’s storied Dakota upon sale of $8M penthouse
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Imagine all the people, livin’ for today — and for decades in the same home.
Yoko Ono has long been known as an artist and an activist — and now the 93-year-old is on the cusp of adding another title to her name: the Grande Dame of the Dakota.
Indeed, Ono will become the Dakota’s longest current homeowner whenan apartmentat the building’s tippy top completes its sale, The Post has learned. She moved into the storied Upper West Side property —the first luxury apartment building in America— withher late husband John Lennon53 years ago.
That penthouse, which asked $8 million for sale and is now under contract, was owned by the late art patron Steven Rubin, who bought at the Dakota in the late 1960s and added more space in subsequent years, according to statements by his daughter. The final price to be paid for that perch, as well as its new owner, are not yet known.
With Rubin’s wife, Polly, passing last December, the property listed in June and went into contract this month — a testament to right pricing, deft marketing and the Dakota’s strong cache.
The Rubins’ penthouse began as Gilded Age quarters for maids who worked for the matrons below. Rubin subsequently bought the area above the initial apartment and connected the two spaces with a staircase. Views allowed him and his wife to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade from the coveted comfort of their home, according to the listing from Sotheby’s International Realty’s Roberta Golubock.
While city tax records and transfers show other residents of the Dakota, at 1 W. 72nd St., handing down their apartments to family members,no continuous ownershipby the same person in the 94-unit building is apparent except for Ono.
Her half-century-plus ownership of the seventh-floor sanctuary demonstrates not only staying power, but determination while traversing very devastating, and sweet, times there.
Ono and Lennon moved into the Dakota soon after the Beatles disbanded and the pair created their own oasis by addingan adjacent apartment. The main room was all white, including its Grand Steinway piano where Lennon composed.
Ono and Lennon offset that stark minimalism with other rooms outfitted with heavy, dark wood Asian artifacts, old tapestries and antique instruments from all over the world. Expanses with 14-foot ceilings looked down on custom hand-carved marble fireplaces.
While the amount Lennon and Ono paid for their original apartment in 1973 has not been pinned down, building records show comparable homes in the Dakota selling for between $150,000 and $200,000 at that time. That’s roughly $1.1 million to $1.5 million in today’s dollars.
Individual units like the one the couple initially bought were generally between 2,500 and 3,000 square feet at the time, city Department of Buildings renderings show.
Ono and Lennon bought at least three other units over the years on different floors for guests, and to use for offices and storage.
What’s more, Lennon wrote some of his most textured songs while at the Dakota, including “Mind Games,” “Whatever Gets You Through the Night” and virtually all of his final album, “Double Fantasy.”
The couple raised their son Sean there — and their apartment was whereAnnie Leibowitzshot the famous 1980 photo of Lennon and Yoko nude and curled up, with his arms wrapped around her head while kissing her cheek. Just 5 hours later, Lennon was dead in the Dakota’s archway from the bullet of an unhinged fan, Mark David Chapman, at the age of 40. (Lennon’s “Strawberry Fields” memorial stands just steps away from the building in Central Park.)
While no board memos or policy changes have surfaced after the murder, the Dakota’s board does appear to have hardened towards celebrities in the aftermath. In following years Madonna, Cher and Billy Joel were all left on the outside looking in when they tried to get the very stringent board’s approval to move in, reports say.
The board was more celebrity-friendly in earlier years, giving its nod to Judy Garland,Lauren Bacalland Boris Karloff.
Lennon said he hoped to set the stage for the couple’s board interview by wearing a suit to the meeting and sending Ono back to their apartment to change from the miniskirt she planned to wear.
Ono, now, 93, has downsized her footprint at the Dakota over the years by offloading some of the auxiliary spaces. She nowspends considerable timeat her farm upstate and has given no indication she plans to sell her primary Dakota residence. Real estate platforms and other property portals peg the apartment’s value at around $20 million.
Ono declined a request for comment. Overall, she’s still a true New Yorker.
“New York is like an old friend. It has its moods. But I know them all,” The New York Times reported her saying.

hed: LA landlord sparks renters’ rage after banning common kitchen appliance: ‘It’s a necessity’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Los Angeles landlord is getting cooked online after advertising a $2,400-a-monthSilver Lakeapartment with an odd condition for prospective tenants: “NO stove allowed.”
The one-bedroom unit on North Dillon Street was called out on theLARentals subredditthis week, where a Reddit user questioned whether the unusual restriction could run afoul of a new California law requiring landlords to provide working cooking appliances.
“I thought landlords were required to provide a stove and refrigerator per CA law or is that not right,” the poster asked, claiming the Silver Lake property had been listed and removed three times this year, before recently resurfacing.
Thelistingimmediately fired up Angelenos, particularly since the said pad was asking $2,400 per month. The listing touts hardwood flooring, shared laundry, a “good sized” kitchen with art deco tiles and a full refrigerator.
“I can’t believe these people have the nerve to charge $2400/month for an apartment that doesn’t fully function,” one commenter fumed. “No stove isn’t like ‘no dishwasher’ or ‘no washer/dryer in unit.’ It’s not a nice-to-have amenity. It’s a necessity.”
Another simply asked: “Literally what?? how the how are you supposed to cook?”
The listing appears to be in violation of California Assembly Bill 628, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026, and requires landlords to provide a working stove and refrigerator in residential rental units to meet basic habitability standards. It also added a working refrigerator to the requirements.

There are exceptions for certain types of housing, including permanent supportive housing, single-room occupancy units and housing facilities with communal kitchens.
That made the Silver Lake’s listing apparent ban on a stove especially baffling to Reddit sleuths. “Calling that a kitchen is a bold move,” one commenter quipped. Some suggested that the owner may simply be unaware of the new rule that took effect this year.
Not wanting the unit reported, another argued that a stove-less rental could still work for someone who simply needs a place to sleep or doesn’t cook.
“‘Just a place to sleep’ for $2400? He’s charging luxury prices for a place that isn’t legally considered habitable,” one person fired back.
The firestorm comes as LA’s notoriously brutal rental market has recently offered tenants at least a little breathing room.

hed: Forget the Hamptons — wealthy New Yorkers are making a splash in NJ’s Gold Coast where homes are ‘quietly listed’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
What do New York City real-estate titans Joseph Cayre and Joseph Sitt have in common with reality TV starMike “The Situation” Sorrentino?
A deep love for the Jersey Shore — though Cayre and Sitt’s version involves oceanfront Deal estates instead of Seaside Heights party pads.
Deal, New Jersey— an ultra-exclusive, 1.2-square-mile coastal borough that is known forgolden beaches and coastal charm— is the northern shore’s most expensive ZIP code, with a median listing price of $5.49 million in June,the Wall Street Journal reportedreferencing Realtor.com data. That was up a whopping 57% year-over-year.
The market is tight, with only nine active listings in June, down 10% year-over-year, per Realtor.com.
A 3,856-square-foot home at160 Ocean Ave.is on the market for just under $13 million. The house has eight bedrooms and seven bathrooms. A 4,904-square-foot single-family house is on the market at48 Neptune Ave.for $7.8 million. It has nine bedrooms and six bathrooms.
Beba Realty’s Barbara Gheriani, who’s listing 48 Neptune Ave., noted that oftentime Deal homes are “quietly listed.”
Sixty miles south of Manhattan, Deal is deeply defined by its close-knit Syrian Jewish community. Indeed, roughly one-third of all Deal property is tied to a small group of New York City real estate families, predominantly of Syrian Sephardic heritage, according to aweb postby broker Anthony Licciardello from Prodigy Real Estate.
Deal has a whole host of recreational clubs including the Deal Casino Beach Club, the Conover Pavilion, the Deal Country Club and the Hollywood Golf Club. The Deal Sephardic Network Community Center serves as a hub for the area’s Syrian Jewish community.
A popular summer destination for New Yorkers and New York financiers who reside in Rumson, New Jersey, Deal boasts 900 year-round residents and 6,000-plus summer residents, Licciardello wrote.
New high-speed Seastreak ferry service makes getting from Manhattan directly to the Jersey Shore even easier.

hed: NYC mansion tied up in vicious divorce outed as the city’s priciest home in Mamdani’s pied-à-terre list
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Love may be priceless — but when it all falls apart, it certainly comes with a price.
The Upper East Side mansion at the center of one of New York’s most vicious divorce battles has emerged as the most valuable single-family home in the five boroughs, according to a Post review of the city’spotential pied-à-terre list. That massive data dump, released last last week, inadvertently outed the addresses of thousands of wealthy property owners — and, in certain cases, the big names who own them.
The eight-figure property at 9 E. 86th St., assessed at $75.8 million, now belongs solely to Jenica Paulson, who was awarded the propertyin her settlementwith hedge fund titan John Paulson after years of courtroom warfare over hundreds of millions in trusts and real estate.
The address surfaced in Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s newly released Class 1 property roll, a document meant to identify one- two- and three-family townhouses that could be hit with thestate’s incoming pied-à-terre tax.Instead, it splashed the names and addresses of hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers across the internet, drawing furious backlash from property owners and elected officials alike.
Only one property on the list carries a higher price tag than Jenica’s, a $112 million spread at 7 E. 72nd St. But that property is not privately held.
It is part of a combined megamansion assembled by the government of Qatar, which paid $26 million for the site in 2002 and fused it with the neighboring 9 E. 72nd St. to create a single royal residence, meaning the Paulson townhouse stands as the city’s most valuable home actually owned by an individual.
Jenica paid $30 million in May to keep the mansion as part of the final settlement, capping off an intense divorce saga since John filed to end the marriage in September 2021.
“Jenny Paulson and John Paulson have come to the decision to amicably settle their divorce and trust related litigations,” Jenny’s attorney Robert S. Cohen and John’s attorney Marilyn Chinitz said in a joint statement at the time. “They consider this settlement a private matter and neither party nor any family nor friends of the parties will have any further comment.”
The couple, married in 2000 after meeting when Jenica waited on John at the Bear Stearns cafeteria, spent years fighting over more than $100 million in real estate holdings stretching from the Hamptons to Aspen, Colorado.
In 2022, Jenica filed suit accusing her husband of quietly funneling assets into a trio of irrevocable trusts to keep them out of her reach during the split, seekingat least $1 billion in damages. John’s team denied the claim, arguing the trusts had been set up decades earlier for the couple’s two daughters.
A source with knowledge of the settlement talks said negotiations picked up steam after a judge pushed both sides toward the table.
“The talks began in earnest earlier this year,” the source said, adding that the resolution was “fair to everybody.”
John, whose fortune was built in large part on his legendary bet against the housing market ahead of the 2008 financial crisis, is now engaged to girlfriend Alina de Almeida, with whom he welcomed a daughter last year.
Whether the $75.8 million figure the city has assigned the Paulson mansion actually reflects its worth is another matter. One real estate appraiser, who reviewed the assessment on condition of anonymity, said the number looks inflated based on how the city measures square footage.
“It seems high, it’s about 28,500 square feet including the rear extension, at $1,900 per square foot that’s a little over $50 million,” the appraiser said. “However the city uses gross building area that doesn’t include the rear extension which gives it about 20,500 square feet. At $1,900 per square foot that’s about $40 million.”
“The $50 million is closer to the market value but I don’t know the condition. It was renovated years ago when last purchased. I might be a little low at $50 million depending on how it shows, but $75 million seems very high.”
The mansion’s outsized valuation is only one wrinkle in a document that has caused an uproar since its release.
The database, published by the city’s Department of Finance, lists more than 960,000 residences and owners, dwarfing the roughly 31,000 homes officials originally said would be subject to the new surcharge on non-primary residences.
Other marquee names swept up in the release include Jeffrey Epstein’s former townhouse at 9 E. 71st St., valued at $66.8 million and listed as one of the cities top 10 priciest homes. The properties listed go alongsideprominent New Yorkerssuch as Woody Allen, Anna Wintour and Cynthia Nixon.
City Hall has defended the mass disclosure as a legal requirement.
“As per State law, a property roll was released for public inspection,” a Department of Finance spokesperson said. “From this list, DOF will identify properties that may be subject to the new non-primary residence property surcharge.”
Critics say the rollout has needlessly exposed ordinary homeowners alongside billionaires.
Council Minority Leader David Carr, whose own Staten Island condo appeared on the list, called the move reckless.
Steven Fulop of the Partnership for NYC warned it sets a troubling precedent for how the city treats successful residents, while Councilwoman Gale Brewer, whose Upper West Side brownstone has been her full time home for more than two decades, said her inclusion on the list proves the data cannot be trusted.
Mayor Mamdani has continued to defend the pied-à-terre tax as a matter of fairness. City Hall projects the levy could generate roughly $500 million annually, though the city comptroller’s office has pegged the more likely figure closer to $340 million to $380 million.

hed: Law firm vacating longtime Boston home for South Station Tower
subhead: Greenberg Traurig has operated at International Place since 1999
content: Another law firm is moving to Boston’s South Station Tower. Greenberg Traurig LLP late next year will vacate One International Place, where it has operated since the firm opened a Boston office in 1999. It will move to 76,000 square feet of office space on floors 18 through 20 at South Station Tower, a space about 20,000 square feet larger than its current home.The firm has grown to 120 attorneys, up from around 80 in 2020, Boston co-managing shareholders David J. Dykeman and Terence P. McCourt said in a statement. “South Station Tower’s modern design, first-class amenities, wellness-focused features, and transit connectivity make it an ideal environment for the next chapter of our Boston office’s growth,” Dykeman and McCourt’s statement said. “We are proud to establish our future Boston home in this premier new skyscraper that will become a defining part of the city’s skyline.”Greenberg Traurig has also represented its new landlord, Texas development giant Hines, for the last two decades. Hines’ long-awaited 51-story tower opened last year and has since landed tenants including commercial insurer FM, law firm Jones Day, hedge fund Citadel, and bank JPMorgan Chase & Co. Greenberg Traurig’s lease brings South Station Tower’s 675,000 square feet of office space to about 63 percent leased.The tower has 166 Ritz-Carlton branded condominiums on its upper 16 floors.“South Station Tower continues to attract industry-leading companies seeking an exceptional workplace experience in one of Boston’s most connected locations,” said Sarah Hawkins, head of Hines’ U.S. East market, in a statement. Greenberg Traurig has 3,200 attorneys globally, with 35 offices in the US and 16 international offices.Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: TV’s Maria Menounos shows off her home renovation prowess on Hulu’s ‘Designed to Last’
subhead: The Massachusetts native — along with her husband and dad — is somewhat of a home DIY master, and she shared her best tips.
content:
ByLauren Daley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
When a pipe burst inMaria Menounos’Connecticut home a few years back, “the house had to come down to the bones.”
“Fortunately we were able to rebuild it the way we wanted it, which was great. But it was a painful experience, because it took a long time,” said the Medford native. “It’s just never fun when you’re not in control.”
The Emmy-winning TV journalist and personality — seen on “Extra,” “Entertainment Tonight,” “E! News” “The Today Show” and more — splits her time between Los Angeles and Connecticut. TheHeal Squadfounder andpodcast hostrecently picked up a few home-preparedness prevention tips from hosting Hulu’s “Designed to Last.”
A post shared by MARIA MENOUNOS (@mariamenounos)
The four-episode reality-competition show, made in collaboration with American Family Insurance, saw three teams “of home design innovators face off against the worst Mother Nature has to offer.” “Part competition, part science experiment, each episode tests a different element—until one team reigns supreme and wins the $100,000 prize.” Menounos hosted with contractor Eric Eremita and designer Wendell Holland.
Episode one saw teams fortify tiny homes against hurricane-force wind. Episode two was freezing temps and heavy snow. Episode three was driving rains, and episode four took on fire.
In a phone interview, Menounos shared what she learned from hosting, and talked home renovation tips. Turns out, between her “jack-of-all-trades” dad Costas, her husband Keven Undergaro (they met in Boston) and herself, it’s a DIY-master family.
In hosting the show, what did you learn about protecting your home fire?
I learned about a Japanese technique of pre-charring walls (Yakisugi) —  pre-charred wood is more resilient to catching fire. So it was a cool design feature, where itlooked chic, but also protected the exterior of the home. In terms of design and functionality, I thought that was neat.
… I didn’t know there’s flame-retardant paint,intumescent paint, you can get at most hardware stores.
What about protecting your home from wind?
One team did these sliding barn windows. When wind hit, there was an actuator that would [trip a sensor] to close the barn windows [over the glass windows] for protection. I thought that was cool, instead of having to put plywood on your windows every time there’s going to be a big storm.
Ice and snow?
One team did these heated misters (tubing under the roofline that sprayed saline mist, diluted so as to not stain the house). One team put heating-coils on the roof, and that worked to help melt.
Rain and floods?
Absolutely unequivocally we should always all have big Tupperware bins under our sink, right below our piping. Because inevitably you’re going to have a leak, and you want that water to be captured so you have a minute to figure out that it happened before it’s everywhere.
The blue team created this H2-No drip pan. [They describe it as a “metal catch pan with a float switch so that when the water comes in, the switch comes up…it closes, stops the flow of water.]  I thought that was neat, because the water actually shut off. It’s one thing to just put a bin under the sink and hope you catch the situation in time — it’s another to figure out a way to shut the water off.
What’s another general home safety tip that we should always be thinking about?
For moisture, I saw alot of caulking issues. Melting snow, ice, and rain gets into areas that aren’t caulked properly, so making sure all your windows are really sealed tight, is important.  Also, good drainage systems. Gutters being clear, so that everything can flow out to where it’s supposed to.
Overall, how did you like hosting a home show?
I loved it. My family has been working on homes our whole lives. My dad was a handyman, he installed carpets and tiles, so I learned how to do a little bit of that with him.
… My dad was a jack-of-all-trades. He and his brother had Brothers Carpet Cleaning, they’d install and clean carpets. They did tile. He’s turning 82 this December. He’s a beast, he can outwork any 20-year-old.
Then with Keven, we just went nuts. We’ve done renovations the entire time we’ve known each other — almost three decades. We’ve been renovating homes and properties —sometimes for us, or for friends— and I’ve learned a lot along the way.
So I can hang. It was just fun to have that side of me front and center on this show.
Is Keven a contractor?
Not officially, but we love it. It’s so fun to see something come together. I loved doing home makeovers on “The Today Show” when I worked there, and it’s no different when I get to see a vision come to life at my home.
And my dad is incredible. When we bought our California house, the realtors told us “Don’t buy it,” because it was too much work. I looked at [Keven and my dad] and said, “Are you guys sure you can do this? Because this realtor thinks you’re nuts.” And they turned it into this beautiful piece of property. They know what they’re doing, they love it.
Your dad lives with you now. What are a few recent projects you’ve done at your New England home?
We did raised garden beds — that’s been helpful for all of our backs.  We built a studio there, so that I have space to do my shows.  We’re building garages right now. Eventually we want to be fully on the East Coast, so we’re just kind of slowly making our setup back there appropriate for our needs. We added a side garage to our main garage for all of my dad’s tools and lawn mower and such.
We’re going to build a memorial garden for my mom next to the fruit trees. That’s our next big project.
Keven calls himself the“Regular Guy Contractor.”Have you three come up with creative solutions for problems at home?
Oh my god, consistently. I’m looking now at this berm we built in front of our property in California. We were constantlygetting flooded, and all the sandbags [didn’t help.] My dad, being a genius, was like, “Keven, we just gotta build this little berm so the water just goes around, it doesn’t come in.” We built this little drain, and now if there’s heavy rain, it will go out there. We’re always coming up with solutions.
What do you hope viewers get out of “Designed to Last”?
I hope that they have fun watching it. I think it’s inspiring. Come up with an idea, then ask a handyman or contractor for help. Nothing is beyond your imagination.
The interview has been edited and condensed. Lauren Daley is a freelance culture writer. She can be reached at[email protected]. She tweets@laurendaley1, and Instagrams at@laurendaley1.

hed: What you can get for under $1 million on Cape Cod
subhead: From classic Cape-style shingled homes to condos, buyers can get into the Cape market for well under $1 million
content:

Flanked between the bay and the Atlantic, Cape Cod is all about the water.

“People really live outside. They live on the deck. They outdoor shower,” saidRick Shechtman, senior vice president and realtor at Kinlin Grover Compass in Barnstable.

This desire to be immersed in Cape Cod’s waterfront is largely what differentiates homes above and below the $1 million threshold.

“If you’re right on the water or you have a pool, a lot of those houses, you know, tend to be higher priced,” saidDawn Andalft-Newman, a realtor with Property Cape Cod in Centerville. “The closer [to the water], the higher the price point for sure.”

But every town has bargains. “Certain areas of each town have a lower-priced community,”  Andalft-Newman said.

For those looking for a deal, Andalft-Newman’s has noticed lower prices on Dennisport cottages with minimal square footage — near, but not on the water. Expansive homes and new, modern builds with all the bells and whistles are more likely to break the bank, but classic homes still reign.

“The most popular style is definitely a Cape,” said Shechtman. Cape Cod-style homes — most featuring an outdoor shower or porch — reflect the nature-centric lifestyle many come to the region craving.

hed: Extremely rare LA home hits the market for attractive price — and it’s one of around 40 left
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In a city marked by endless urban sprawl that layers its brief butfascinating architectural historylike rings on a tree, few buildings feel like genuine time capsules.
The Alice Lynch House at 2414 4th Avenue is one of them.
Built in 1922 for poet Alice Lynch, the modest yet striking residence located in the hip and historical neighborhood of West Adams Terrace is a rare Los Angeles example of the true adobe building technique.
No, not the familiar stucco-over-wood-frameSpanish Colonial Revival housesthat began populating the City of Angels in the 1920s, but an actual adobe structure made with traditional stacked sun-dried mud blocks.
With only around 40 truly authentic adobe homes left in the Los Angeles area, this one still stands testament to California’s past.
And it could be yours for the very reasonable (well, by LA standards) asking price of $1,849,500.
Designed byarchitect Henry Harwood Hewittin collaboration with adobe specialist John Byers (who dotted LA with his construction technique from 1916 before retiring in 1946), the house was built using Mexican craftsmen skilled in the old methods.
Byers, who became known for reviving authentic adobe techniques across Southern California, produced many of the materials himself, including the bricks and tiles.
“This type of house can only be arrived at successfully if one builds them much in the same manner as the old days one hundred years or so ago,”Byers wrote of his construction stylein 1946. “The adobes should be made by hand, and laid up preferably by Mexican labor… They can only be done economically if the adobe bricks are made right at the building site with the soil at hand.”
The result of Byers’ painstaking process is this two-story, roughly 2,500-square-foot home organized in a U-shape around a central courtyard — a layout that feels intimate and redolent of a California bygone era drenched in sepia tones.
Thick adobe walls, original timber beams, arched glass doors and a massive brick fireplace define the interior.

Modern updates in the four-bed, three-bathroom home have been handled with restraint: concrete sinks, updated kitchen cabinetry, and refined finishes that complement rather than compete with the home’s historic heart.
Outside, the courtyard remains the hub of the property, framed by adobe walls and offering a sense of seclusion rare in the city.
Los Angeles once had hundreds of adobe dwellings dating back to the Spanish and Mexican periods. Most were lost to earthquakes, neglect or the dogged push of new development.
By the early 20th century, true sunbaked adobe construction had become a romantic novelty rather than standard practice.
The Alice Lynch House, designatedLos Angeles Historic-Cultural MonumentNo. 621 in 1996, is one of the few intact examples left standing from that later revival period.
In a city like LA, wherearchitectural history is often flattened, brutalized or recreated as pastiche, this house feels gracefully defiant.
For those who value authenticity over imitation, the Alice Lynch House is a rare reminder of what SoCal architecture once was — and how little of it survives.
This home is not a clinical museum piece frozen in time, nor a heavily restored dazzler. Rather, it’s a homey dwelling that still wears its original materials well — thick walls that retain the cool morning air, a foreign-feeling courtyard that gathers the afternoon warmth, and a sense of light and understated permanence that most LA new constructions cannot hold a candle to.
