hed: Rare $112M oceanfront California compound stands to break a local home sale record — again
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A sprawling Laguna Beach estate has listed for a massive $112 million — a price that could set a new residential sales record for both the affluent California city and all of Orange County.
The news was first reported inthe Wall Street Journal.
Perched on a little more than an acre of prime oceanfront, the roughly 14,400-square-foot compound, co-is listed by Meital Taub and Jill Lockhart, both with Livel Real Estate. It sits atop a dramatic bluff overlooking the Pacific, with portions of the home extending so far over the water that recreating it today would be impossible under current California coastal regulations.
“One of the most remarkable qualities is how connected you feel to the ocean because the home cantilevers over the Pacific,” Lockhart told The Post. “It’s like you’re suspended on top of the water.”
Another oceanfront estate in nearby Emerald Bay reportedly sold for $110 million, and if this property fetches its full $112 million asking price, it would eclipse that sale and establish a new record for Orange County.
For today’s ultrawealthy buyers, agents say that’s exactly the appeal.
“High-net-worth buyers are increasingly looking for acquiring irreplaceable land rather than simply large homes,” Lockhart said. “This isn’t house just difficult to replicate — it’s impossible.”
The estate — which includes eight bedrooms, 12 full and three half-bathrooms spread across the main house and the guest quarters — was originally commissioned in the early 1970s by financier Boyd Jefferies, the founder of the investment firm that would become Jefferies Financial Group. According to the listing, the ambitious project required so much structural concrete to stabilize the bluff that Jefferies ultimately purchased the concrete company supplying the job.
The architect Fred Briggs, known for luxury coastal residences, created a home that blurs the line between architecture and landscape, wrapping many of its principal rooms in walls of glass with panoramic views stretching to Catalina Island.
Taub said Briggs struck a balance that’s difficult to find in contemporary homes.
“The concrete gives it strength while the wood and the stone bring comfort and livability,” she said. “It’s modern without feeling cold.”
The property’s next high-profile owner was the late Bruce Bastian, the billionaire co-founder of WordPerfect, whose software once dominated the personal computer market and who later became an LGBT philanthropist and civil rights advocate.
The current owner is CEO of Wilson Automotive Group David Wilson, who purchased the home in 2001, in what was then Orange County’s most expensive residential sale. Over the next two decades, Wilson has spent millions of dollars transforming the already iconic estate while preserving Briggs’ original vision.
The renovations expanded the residence with two additional bedrooms and bathrooms, a private movie theater, new entertaining spaces and a detached two-bedroom guesthouse converted from former storage space. Wilson also made significant investments in erosion-control measures and structural upgrades designed to protect the bluffside property while bringing it into compliance with modern building standards.
But perhaps the home’s greatest luxury is something money alone can no longer buy.
Because it predates modern California Coastal Commission setback requirements, significant portions of the residence extend into areas where new construction would no longer be allowed.
The show-stopping primary suite is surrounded by water on three sides, and a staircase links the bedroom to a private library above. At the center of the bedroom is a rotating circular bed sitting beneath a retractable dome that opens to the sky, offering the rare chance to stargaze directly from bed.
Inside the main house, walls of glass and warm teak floors glow in the sunlight, and the chef’s kitchen includes appliances by Wolf, Miele and Thermador.
Elsewhere, the estate is packed with resort-worthy amenities, including more than 2,000 square feet of oceanfront terraces, a swimming pool and spa, a championship tennis court built atop the garage and a 1,000-bottle wine cellar. A wellness center includes a fitness studio, a sauna, a steam room and a waterfall spa.
The compound was also designed for an extraordinary level of privacy. In addition to dual gated entrances, it features separate guest accommodations, discreet security features and direct access to the beach below the bluff.
“Most people drive by it every day and don’t even realize it’s sitting there,” Lockhart said.

hed: Meg Ryan finds a buyer for $15.3M Hamptons mansion—weeks after listing it
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Actress Meg Ryan will have far fewer sleepless nights after securing a buyer for her opulent Hamptons estate—just a few weeks after she listed the propertyfor $15.25 million.
The listing for the picturesque dwelling, which sits on a lush 1.5-acre parcel in Bridgehampton, NY, has now been updated to reflect that it is “pending” sale, meaning that Ryan has accepted an offer from a buyer, although the specifics about that offer are not yet known.
Ryan, 64, who has become almost as well known for her high-end home renovations as her romantic-comedy roles, purchased the picturesque property for $13.5 million in 2024, which means she stands to earn a very tidy profitifshe manages to secure a sale price close to her ask.
The actress—who is best known for her work in “Sleepless in Seattle,” “You’ve Got Mail,” and “When Harry Met Sally”—is no stranger to real estate investments, having recently sold a home in Montecito, CA, for $16.8 million, more than $6 million over the price she bought it for three years prior.
Ryan worked with Evan R. Kulman of Compass on the listing, while Douglas Elliman agents Paul Brennan and Martha Gundersen helped to secure a buyer for the dwelling.
While it’s not yet known exactly what price she has agreed to let her Hamptons home go for, the listing makes very clear the very “rare” features on offer at the dwelling.
“Down a long gated driveway on a secluded and beautifully landscaped flag lot, this exceptional Bridgehampton South residence offers sophisticated luxury living in one of the Hamptons’ most coveted locations,” it states.
“Perfectly positioned near ocean beaches, renowned restaurants, and the heart of the village, the property seamlessly combines privacy, elegance, and convenience.”
Offering nearly 5,000 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and 6.5 bathrooms, the home was originally built in 2016 but has undergone several updates in the years since, upgrades that have carefully preserved its “timeless architecture” while adding several modern touches.
Upon entering the dwelling, guests are greeted with classic Hamptons charmandmodern luxury, offering vaulted ceilings, five fireplaces, a sunken living room, formal dining room, and an expansive chef’s kitchen designed for entertaining.
The residence is packed with custom touches that reflect Ryan’s personal style, including a cozy library that comes complete with its own bathroom.
Moving to the main living spaces, the chef’s kitchen features a stunning marble island, neutral-toned cabinetry, and state-of-the-art appliances.
Adjacent to the kitchen, there is an adorable breakfast nook with French doors that open up to the perfectly manicured grounds.
The dining area offers a much more formal area for guest entertaining, having been stylishly designed around a beautiful fireplace, while glass doors help to flood the space with natural light and offer stunning views of the surrounding landscape.
Additional living space can be found on the lower level, which includes a large guest suite, kitchenette, secondary living area, and a fully equipped gym.
Meanwhile, the primary suite is the epitome of luxury, featuring a private sitting area, steam shower, and a balcony overlooking the picturesque grounds.
The home is also equipped with a geothermal heating and cooling system, offering an environmentally conscious approach to luxury living.
Outside, the property delivers the quintessential Hamptons lifestyle. A heated Gunite swimming pool anchors the backyard, while a covered porch with an outdoor fireplace creates an inviting setting for summer evenings.
The sprawling compound also benefits from a full-property security system, providing privacy and peace of mind.
Seclusion was clearly top of mind when the home was designed, with a long driveway and tree-lined parcel helping to protect the dwelling from any prying eyes—a must for an actress of Ryan’s renown.
However, it’s unclear just how regularly the actress has used the property, having purchased it just two years ago.
“Rarely found in such a premier location, the property also offers room for expansion, further creating the opportunity for a true legacy compound. Combining sophistication, scale, privacy, and future potential, this is an extraordinary offering in the heart of Bridgehampton South,” the listing notes.
The listing comes one year after the actress successfully unloaded another renovated property in Montecito, CA, for $16.8 million—although she earned a much lower profit than she had initially hoped.

The sprawling Santa Barbara area mansion was first put on the market for $19.5 million—exactly $10 million more than Ryan had bought it for just a few years earlier, although shehadmade some very significant updates to it during her ownership of the home.
Ryan purchased the California property for $9.5 million in 2021 via an LLC that she has used for several of her real estate deals over the years. At the time, the property featured 6,500 square feet in five bedrooms, five bathrooms, and a guesthouse.
However, when she listed the home, it was made clear that the Hollywood heavyweight had made some very significant changes, adding two bedrooms, a half bathroom, 3,000 square feet of extra living space, three fireplaces, and a patio.
Ryan previously gushed about her love for renovation projects while speaking with Architectural Digest.
“I know it sounds crazy to most people, the idea of renovating that many houses, but I love renovating. I think it’s tied to living the actor’s life,” she said.
Her son, Jack, 34, whom she shares with ex-husband Dennis Quaid, often teases his mom about her home renovation process and has even branded her work “Meg-anized.”
She added, “As an actor, you are so rarely in control. You’re always saying words that someone else has given you, standing in a room that someone else has designed, to create a reality that someone else wants to see. But with decorating I am in control; it’s a chance for me to bring my vision into the world.”

hed: What America’s most expensive ZIP codes reveal about where wealth actually goes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


When Realtor.com® ranked the country’smost expensive ZIP codesearlierthis year, the numbers were staggering.
Fisher Island, FL, was among the top 3 with a median home price of $10.83 million. Water Mill, NY, and Bridgehampton, NY, two enclaves inNew York’s Hamptons, were close behind, with median prices approaching or exceeding $8 million.
But outside of housing, living in these communities does not cost dramatically more than it does in other affluent parts of the country.
Using county-level data fromUnited for ALICE—a nonprofit research initiative that estimates the minimum income households need to cover basic necessities—a family of four would need about $66,000 a year for essentials in Miami-Dade County and roughly $76,000 in Suffolk County, where Water Mill and Bridgehampton are located.
Those budgets are significant, but they are dwarfed by housing. Financing the median-priced home in Fisher Island, assuming a 20% down payment and a 30-year mortgage at approximately 6%, pushes the annual cost of ownership to nearly $688,000 before taxes, insurance, HOA fees, and maintenance. Comparable totals reach roughly $582,000 in Bridgehampton and $531,000 in Water Mill.
The mortgage alone costs several times more than the annualcost of a family’s basic needs. The difference is not a slightly more expensive lifestyle—it is an entirely different scale of housing expense.
The comparison offers a window into what happens when housing stops reflecting thelocal cost of livingand starts reflecting something else entirely: scarcity, exclusivity, and wealth.
Most everyday expenses are tied to the local economy: Grocery stores compete for customers, child care costs reflect local wages, and transportation and health care expenses vary by region but are shaped by what residents and businesses can afford. Luxury housing follows a different set of rules.
“At the top of the market, the entry barrier is almost entirely the asset itself: land, structure, and a scarcity premium,” says Anthony Smith, senior economist at Realtor.com®. “Local wages and the employment base barely factor in, because a lot of the time, the buyer pool is not local and not income-constrained.”
In other words, thehighest-priced homesare often competing for buyers who are not dependent on the local job market. A household’s ability to purchase a $10 million property may have little connection to the wages earned by people who live and work nearby.
“In these ZIP codes, the wealth divide is the home value, not the cost of everyday life,” Smith says.
That dynamic helps explain why a county-level estimate for groceries, child care, and other necessities can remain relatively grounded while housing costs climb into the hundreds of thousands of dollars per year.
Although Fisher Island and Water Mill sit among the country’s most expensive ZIP codes, they command those prices for different reasons.
Fisher Island’s appeal begins with scarcity. The private island, accessible only by ferry, helicopter, or private boat, has a fixed geographic footprint with little ability to add new supply.
“Fisher Island carries its premium on true island scarcity,” Smith says.
Water Mill’s appeal is different. The Hamptons community has some of the largest homes among the country’s most expensive ZIP codes, with a median home size of more than 6,100 square feet.
“Water Mill can lean into space,” Smith says.
Both command extraordinary prices, but the reasons behind those prices reveal how different forms of scarcity can shape the top of the housing market.
Corey Wayne Ogle, a New York real estate advisor who specializes in the Hamptons, says some clients still want to understand the ongoing costs associated with owning a large property.

“[One client] was asking these questions: How much is the seller spending every month to maintain the lawn, maintain the landscaping? What are these costs actually going to be for keeping the pool clean?” Ogle says.
Those expenses can add up, but Ogle says they are not unique to ultraluxury homes. A buyer with a large property in the Hamptons is still paying for many of the same categories of upkeep as someone with a second home elsewhere.
“If you have a pool and a garden, you have someone that you have to pay to help you maintain it,” he says. “You still have those things.” The difference is that buyers athigher price pointsoften view those expenses differently.
“If I had to put a number on it, it’s probably people buying over like $3 million or $4 million,” he says. “At that point, people kind of are less concerned with the smaller line items when they’re spending $4 million on a home.”
At that level, buyers may still care about maintenance costs, but those expenses are no longer the deciding factor. The question becomes whether the property itself—the location, land, privacy, or lifestyle—is worth the price.
There are important limitations to comparing these budgets.
United for ALICE publishes its estimates at the county level, not the ZIP-code level. That means Fisher Island shares the same non-housing budget estimate as the rest of Miami-Dade County, while Water Mill and Bridgehampton share Suffolk County’s estimate.
Even with those limitations, the pattern is clear: The cost of everyday life rises gradually, even in wealthy communities. Housing can rise without the same constraints.
At the highest end of the market, homes are not priced only as places to live. They are shaped by scarcity, status, investment potential, and access to something that cannot easily be replicated.
That may be the clearest takeaway from America’s most expensive ZIP codes: Wealth does not necessarily make everyday life dramatically more expensive, but it changes what people are willing to pay for a home.

hed: How permanent Daylight Saving Time could affect homeowners
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Currently, most homeowners change their clocks twice a year: forward by one hour on the second Sunday in March and back by one hour on the first Sunday in November.
However, this longstanding ritual may come to an end, thanks to theSunshine Protection Act, which waspassed by the US Houseand aims to make daylight saving time permanent year-round.
If passed by the Senate and signed into law, the act would lead to lighter evenings and darker mornings. And whether it’ll work in your favordepends on where you live.
Homeowners in Alabama, Florida, and Texas, for example, would enjoy more usable daylight while those in Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin could see much later sunrises and limited daylight hours.
Regardless of where you live, it’s important to understand howpermanent daylight saving time might affect your home and lifestyle. That wayyou can prepare for the changesif the legislation does become law.
With more daylight in the evening, you’ll be less reliant on artificial indoor lighting when you’re awake and active. And this could slightly reduce your electricity use.
However, any savings may be offset by increased heating and cooling demands.
“The dark, cold winter mornings that stem frompermanent daylight savingswould mean that your furnace will need to work harder before sunrise,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.
In the summer, the additional sunlight can keep your house warmer later into the evening, forcing your air conditioner to run when energy use is the highest.
“As for the landscaping, additional sunlight can allow you to take care of your lawn in the evening rather than wait for the weekend. You might also have to adjust when you water and maintain your lawn,” Young explains.

More sunlight can also improve the security of your home as most perpetrators commit their crimes at night when it’s dark outside.
Lastly, if you plan to list your home in the future, the extra daylight could help you out.
“Since most buyers look at homes in the evenings, you’ll have more opportunities to show your home in the winter months,” Young says.
Plus, the natural lighting can provide a better view of your home’s exterior, landscape, and overall curb appeal.
There are several ways you can prepare for the darker winter mornings you’ll face if permanent daylight saving time becomes law.
First, start with your smart thermostat.
“Allow it to preheat your house 30 to 45 minutes prior to your alarm clock going off—not all night long,” explains Young.
Marcus Griswold, founder of Little Green Myths in Vallejo, CA, suggests closing the doors and turning off the heat in rooms you’re not using.
“Some smart systems also help you isolate unused rooms by sensing when someone is present. This is known as zoned heating,” Griswold explains.

Also, take advantage of smart shades that can stay open during the day to heat your home and close with the sunset to hold in the warmth in the winter.
Additionally, use the gradual sunrise option on your smart bulbs, which will mimic the increase in brightness. Place the smart bulbs in bedrooms, bathrooms, and hallways to help enhance alertness as you wake up and get into your routine.
Don’t forget to be patient with yourself as it might take some time for your body to get used to the change.
“In our survey, 84% of Americans claim it takes at least one day toadjust to a new time after the time change, while 29% say it takes at least one week. Setting your smart home devices like thermostats and lighting to automatically adjust can make the transition easier,” Young explains.
And if you use time-of-use pricing from your utility company, schedule the dishwasher and the laundry to work outside of peak hours. Doing so can lead to cheaper rates and potentially save you some serious cash.

hed: NYC homeowners sue to stop co-op from evicting their son — whose viral feud with doorman spiraled into racial slurs, assault and arrest
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A toxic, long-simmering feud at an East Side co-op has exploded into a new Manhattan Supreme Court lawsuit, complete with allegations of antisemitic taunts, a viral physical brawl with a doorman — and a desperate bid to block a penthouse eviction.
Irving and Carol Karten bought unit PHC at 339 E. 58th St. for $392,500 in October 2024 to serve as the home for their now 57-year-old son, Kevin, a general contractor with his own Florida-based firm.
Now, the Karten family has filed an emergency lawsuit against 339 East 58th Street Owners Corp. to stop the Sutton Place building’s board from boot-strapping an eviction vote and kicking Kevin — whom they claim is a nuisance — to the curb.
According to court documents, the drama traces back to Sept. 17, 2025, when Kevin submitted a written complaint to management firm New Bedford Management about building doorman Lawrence Montgomery, now 37, and requested intervention.
Kevin, who is Jewish, claimed in the documents Montgomery refused to deliver his mail, twice touched his girlfriend without permission, and subjected him to antisemitic abuse — including pretending to sneeze while saying “a Jew” instead of “achoo,” calling him a “dumb Jew,” and telling him to “f*** your mother.”
The tension boiled over a day later, in a wild, profanity-laced confrontationcaught on cameraandposted on Redditwith the headline, “Tenant threatens, assaults, racially abuses and breaks phone of doorman in NY.”
The court filings allege Montgomery put a phone in Kevin’s face, prompting Kevin to knock it away before Montgomery struck him in the face, inflicting a permanent eye injury.
A New York City DoorMan Got Arrested After he Defended Himself From A Racist Tenant Who  Slapped Him And Called Him The N Wordpic.twitter.com/0TIALCFVrP
“The resident appears to take a swing — while the doorman claims he was struck, the resident later says he only knocked the phone out of the doorman’s hand,” according toEast Side Feed, which first reported on the altercation. “What follows is a back-and-forth dispute over who hit whom. During this, the resident is heard using the N-word multiple times.”
Kevin, who in the video calls Montgomery a “retard” and the N-word at least six times, can then be seen picking up the doorman’s phone and slamming it on the ground several times.
Both men were arrested. Montgomery was charged with multiple counts of assault and one count of harassment, and Kevin with charges of criminal mischief and harassment. It’s not clear where these charges stand, as the District Attorney’s office told The Post the case is sealed.
Montgomery was backed by the co-op board, which issued a notice on Oct. 31, 2025 warning Kevin that further altercations or interference with the “quiet enjoyment or building operations” would be treated as “continuing objectionable conduct.”
“The Co-op and Management possessed or controlled surveillance footage and information concerning the incident, yet did not conduct a fair investigation of Kevin’s complaints, did not meaningfully address the reported anti-Semitic conduct, and did not provide the protection Kevin requested,” the new court documents claim.
In a letter dated Nov. 12, 2025, the Kartens’ attorney disputed the co-op’s account, detailed the alleged discrimination and harassment Kevin received and “demanded that the Co-op cease discriminatory and retaliatory conduct, including any attempt to terminate the Lease,” the court documents say. No real investigation took place following receipt of this letter, the family claims.
Kevin and Montgomery didn’t have any further interactions. Montgomery, who isn’t listed as a defendant, may no longer work at the building. He didn’t respond to a request for comment. The board’s attorney, the building’s management company, the Kartens or the Kartens’ attorneys also didn’t respond to The Post’s requests for comment.
To make matters worse, Kevin was also locked in a feud with his next-door neighbors — one of whom just happened to sit on the co-op board.
In one case it was over plants on their shared terrace, the Kartens allege. In another, “shortly before September 18, 2025, after Kevin complained about another anti-Semitic provocation by Montgomery, [the wife of the co-op board member] allegedly told Kevin, in substance, ‘we don’t want you here’ and to ‘go back.'” the court documents claim.
Kevin reported her conduct to the board and management. The couple is not a defendant in the suit.
A week ago, the board dropped a bomb: a notice scheduling an emergency Zoom meeting on July 28 to vote on terminating the Kartens’ lease, selling their shares at auction and evicting Kevin over vague claims that he harassed a board member.
The notice “does not identify the supposedly harassed Board member, the date, time, place, words, acts, witnesses, evidence, or circumstances of the alleged event,” court documents indicate.
The Kartens’ lawyers immediately fired off an emergency Order to Show Cause to freeze the vote.
“I am Jewish,” Kevin said in a formal written statement submitted to the court. “Before issuing the July 22 Notice, the Co-op did not interview me, ask me to respond to any allegation, identify any witness or evidence, or otherwise request my account of any events.”
Kevin added that the board gave his family just six days’ notice while hiding the specific facts behind the harassment charge.
“Without knowing the alleged event, I cannot identify witnesses, request or preserve surveillance footage, gather responsive documents, or explain what actually occurred,” he alleges.
The legal maneuver bought the family time.
On Tuesday, a Manhattan judge issued a temporary restraining order halting the board’s termination vote until an Aug. 12 hearing.
The Kartens’ lawsuit seeks to toss out the co-op’s notice as “defective” and demands damages for breaching the proprietary lease and its fiduciary duty, as well as damages under New York State and City Human Rights Laws for discriminatory and retaliatory practices.

hed: California exodus to neighboring state plummets as overall migration slows, new data shows
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Californians aren’t betting big on the Silver State anymore.
Golden State residents are still headed for the exits— but far fewer are choosing neighboring Nevada as their new home after years of flooding across the border, new data shows.
Californians surrendered 33,296 driver’s licenses or ID cards in Nevada in 2025, a 14.6% plunge from the 38.970 from the previous year, according to Nevada DMV datareported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal.
That works out to 5.674 fewer Californians trading their IDs for Nevada credentials, according to the Review-Journal.
The outlet reported that even with the sharp drop, Golden Staters still accounted for more than 40% of all out-of-state licenses and IDs surrendered.

Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story
The California slowdown nearly mirrored Nevada’s overall decline in newcomers — as the total decline across the board was 14%.
The turn is especially jarring after Nevada emerged as the biggest per-capita beneficiary of California’s exodus.
For every10,000 Nevada residents, the state gained a net 81 Californianseach year between 2016 and 2025 — more than any other state.
Californians who fled generally landed in significantly cheaper communities, where monthly rents were an average of $672 lower and home prices were nearly $400,000 cheaper.
But the latest DMV figures suggest the once-roaring migration pipeline into Nevada is finally losing steam.
That doesn’t mean California’s broader exodus has suddenly reversed.
The Golden State’s population fell by approximately 54,000 people in 2025 — it’s first annual decline since the pandemic — while Los Angeles suffered a 0.9% population drop.
Instead, fewer Californians appear to be making major moves at all as the pandemic-era relocation frenzy fades.
Brian Bonnenfant, project manager for the Center for Regional Studies at the University of Nevada, Reno, told the Review-Journal that remote work helped “unleash” a wave of migration during the pandemic, but shaky economic and political conditions are not prompting more Americans to stay put.
“Especially now, in times of economic and political uncertainty, people move much less,” Bonnenfant said.
He told the outlet that the slowdown is part of a much larger demographic shit fueled by declining birth rates, reduced immigration and an aging population.
The California exodus hasn’t hit the brakes — but the once bumper-to-bumper road to Nevada is suddenly a lot less crowded.

hed: I’m a successful 70-year-old broker who’s looking for love — so I hosted 2 parties for singles to meet me
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Alan Gabay has found plenty of success in his real estate career. Finding the right guy hasproven trickier.
The Serhant broker turned 70 on June 11 and decided a milestone birthday called for a bold move. Rather thanwait for romanceto find him, he organized two parties. Both weredocumented on Instagram— one on a Manhattan rooftop and one in a Miami cocktail lounge — and he invited every eligible bachelor he could think of to attend.
“I’m 70 and single and so I thought, let’s throw a party and see if we change that,” Gabay told The Post. “And I was telling my friends maybe if you have some eligible people, let me know.”
The New York celebration took place at Inc. 48, a former warehouse turned hotel near 11th Avenue and 48th Street, where Gabay commandeered a corner of the rooftop lounge for his roughly 60 guests.
He timed it for his actual birthday, choosing an outdoor setting during pleasant weather.
“It’s beautiful outside,” he recalled thinking. “So let’s just go outside. Let’s enjoy this.”
For the Miami leg, Gabay skipped the trendy club scene in favor of a friend’s ’80s- and ’90s-themed bar called The Right Hand. He wanted something more intimate, closer to the vibe he’d created on the rooftop.
“I didn’t want to go to some over-the-top Miami restaurant or bar,” he said.
Word spread well beyond his immediate circle. Gabay posted about the parties on social media in the weeks leading up to the events, and the response caught him off guard.
“I must have had maybe 50 or 75 DMs just from people — probably more —  that want to meet me,” he said. Messages arrived from as far as London and Germany.
By the end of the New York party, nothing had materialized. Gabay chalked it up to familiarity.
“Turns out I already know everybody in this city,” he said.
Miami told a different story. There, he connected with a man about 10 years his junior, someone he’d never met, who arrived at the party dressed to impress after seeing a photo of Gabay in his white tie and black suit.
“He came in a tuxedo thinking that he wanted to look as good as I did and dress up for the occasion,” Gabay said. “And I thought that was really sweet.”
The two spent the party talking and hit it off enough that a date followed.
“We felt very, very comfortable with each other,” he said. “I haven’t really been asked out on a date for a long time. I’m usually the one that’s asking. So I was like, ‘oh, this is very nice.’”
As for what he’s looking for, Gabay says it’s quite simple.
“It’s not about age as much. It’s about people that are really comfortable in their own skin,” he said. “I need somebody who’s confident in themselves.”
He described himself as someone who thrives on culture, museums, gallery openings, travel and dining out, but doesn’t expect a partner to share every interest.
“I’m not going to say don’t do it,” he said of hobbies he doesn’t share, like hiking. “You have to be able to give and take in a relationship.”
Gabay has had five serious relationships over the decades, including a six-year run with a man 25 years younger named Cameron. His shortest relationship, less than a year, ended after he discovered his partner was using drugs.
His most recent relationship ended two years ago after three years together, when Gabay realized his partner, a mortgage broker, expected more support than Gabay was willing to give.
“I’m not here to take care of you,” he said. “I’m here to build something together.”
Despite the string of near misses, Gabay says he refuses to give up. He points to his own father, whofound companionship at 90after Gabay’s mother passed away, meeting a woman who lived in the same building for decades without either of them knowing it.
“If he can do it, you know, I’m hopeful that I can do it too,” Gabay said. “I just don’t believe that I have to lose hope.”
He’s tried dating apps but prefers meeting people organically.
“I like meeting people in person,” he said. “I think you get to know more about somebody in person than you do through a dating app.”
“My oldest friend I know is from kindergarten and I have a tremendous amount of friends that go back that far. So I’m not lonely in the sense that I can never find somebody to do something with,” Gabay said. “But,  it’s always nice to be with somebody in a relationship. And I find there’s a lot of people that are still out there that are in the same type of boat for one reason or another.”
For now, Gabay is keeping the Miami connection under wraps until he knows more.
“Whether or not it is the one, I don’t know,” he said, adding their first date is coming over the weekend. “Stay tuned for the hard launch.”

hed: Newly minted millionaires raid LA real estate market after stock sale bonanza — as desired neighborhoods revealed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New-money millionaires — particularly those buoyed by their involvement in Elon Musk’s rising commercial success of SpaceX — are opening theirnewly filled pursesfor the LA real estate market, putting alreadyhighly desired neighborhoodsunder an even brighter spotlight.
SpaceX’s recent historic initial public offering (IPO) debuted June 12 at $135 a share, briefly topped $200, created nearly 4,400 new millionaires, made Elon Musk theworld’s first trillionaire, and raised almost $86 billion.
Now, those fresh LA millionaires are eyeing homes in the South Bay’s affluent beach cities — Manhattan Beach, Hermosa Beach and Redondo Beach — according toThe Ankler.
Hawthorne, where the majority of SpaceX’s thousands of employees still work at the company’s original campus (despite the company moving its headquarters to Texas in 2024), is also expected to see a jump, along with the Palos Verdes peninsula and Westside neighborhoods like Playa Vista, Venice, Santa Monica, Malibu and Brentwood.
Per a Hill.com report, of the 4,400freshly minted millionaires, around 400 of them are projected to earn a whopping $100 million or more.
A former SpaceX employee who spoke with The Ankler anonymously to to his NDA told the outlet that even prior to the initial record-breaking IPO, he and his fellow employees at the time felt “that if the company were to go public, then it was definitely going to be house-buying money.”
Despite SpaceX’sIPO fallingin recent weeks — reaching a record low of $132.50 apiece in mid-July before rallying again — LA real estate professionals are still seeing a burgeoning interest in those with suddenly heavier pockets procuring homes in the area’s notoriously ritzy neighborhoods, as observed in real time by co-founder of Smith & Berg Property Group, David Berg.
“We’re doing a deal right now where the prospective buyer is a longtime [SpaceX] employee and is making a big step up from a modest house on the Westside to a pretty proper house in the $13 million range in Brentwood,” Berg said.
That said, not all SpaceX employees affected have been spending their new money so lavishly.
“I think the price range that we will see affected most dramatically is probably the $2 million to $6 million range,” Lynnsey Ross, an agent with Douglas Elliman, told The Ankler.
Chris Furie, the co-founder of Insignia Mortgage who told the outlet he believed the cash influx would “have a huge effect on the real estate market,” agreed with this assessment.
“I really think we’re gonna see a lot of activity under $10 million,” he added.
While the interest in these luxe living spaces isn’t entirely new — Lakers star Luka Dončić acquired a five bedroom beach house from tennis standout Maria Sharapova for a record-breaking $25 million in Manhattan Beach, perThe Robb Report— the market’s increased activity by the SpaceX sitch (including current homeowners who are hoping to tack on a “SpaceX premium” while selling their properties) is action to watch.
“[The SpaceX effect] “is real,” said Berg. “But is it a wave? It’s too soon to say. Los Angeles is a city that attracts a lot of money. It’s a super-city. You already have so muchmoneyhere. I mean, this is a place where money swirls around.”

hed: I went through the pied-à-terre appeals process and this is how ridiculously complicated it is
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Yes,I am a Manhattan homeownerand, yes, I live in the city full-time — and, yes, my condo is worth a fraction of what will be subject to Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani’spied-à-terre tax.
Still, with the city’s release last week of the list of properties potentially subject to the levy — documents that totaledhundreds of thousandsof names and addresses, a good number of which aren’t even second homes — I decided to find out how complicated the city makes it to apply for an “exemption” to the “surcharge,” as they so euphemistically phrase it.
If you’re a homeowner who has to go through this, I’m sorry. You’re going to be tied up in a number of micro-managed directions spread across multiple websites that doesn’t answer many questions at all. It’s off-putting and exhausting to the point of making you want to give up. Maybe it’s time to start thinking about that move to Florida.
But I can only guess that’s precisely the point.
It all begins witha four-prompt questionnaire.
Among the questions: “Do you use this property as your primary residence?” and “Is the property owned by an LLC, partnership, or corporation and used as a primary residence by one or more individuals who collectively hold a majority interest, or the immediate family member of such individuals?” The middle two questions ask whether a renter uses this home as a primary residence, or if an immediate family member does.
For those who answer yes for that first question, the city — according to theeligibility guideon the “property surcharge” webpage — then requires submission of the most recently filed federal or state tax return to show proof of residence.
If there are no tax returns available, the site notes the owner will have to provide other proof of residence, such as a driver’s license.
For the burning questions, specifically whether the exemption is approved, the city provides no immediate indication as to how long it will take them to respond — or what the penalties are for not paying up.
If a respondent answers no to all four questions, meaning the city classifies the home as a pied-à-terre, the city then directs the site users to pay the tax onCityPay. Of course, it’s not all black and white. What if the home is in probate? What if a local is living in a nursing home? None of those options are available to click.
If you do seemingly owe the tax, don’t think it gets any easier to pay up.
Those who owe are led to two methods for paying property taxes — one password-protected, the other offering guest access.
However, the payment options don’t specify whether they’re for the pied-à-terre tax, which the city —on yet another website— says will be due by Jan. 1, 2027.
If you don’t have an account, the guest access page requires you to find your home using the “Borough Block Lot” tool or simply by putting in the address. The latter option is much easier, without the need of using yet another website to find the home’s block and lot numbers.
Since it all seemed like a general property tax payment search, I plugged in my address. Even though I pay my taxes quarterly and have for years, the CityPay site couldn’t locate my apartment’s records. So for those who must pay, how can they?
But here’s the headache for primary homeowning residents: more and more directions.
If there is an error in the filing with the city mistakenly valuing the property, the initial questionnaire site instructs the user to file a challenge with the city’s Tax Commission. Though that has an option at the top of the site for filing a surcharge appeal, it leads to yet another webpage whose directions are completely lost inbureaucratic word salad.
“Note that you can also ask the Tax Commission to review whether your property is exempt from the surcharge because it is used as a primary residence,” the instructions say. “If you choose to do so, you must also file a challenge to your property’s value, and you will not be eligible for an exemption from the Department of Finance.”
Does any of that make sense? No.
Back on theDepartment of Financesite, there are separate instructions for filing for an exemption. One option is forresidential homes and condos, and the otheris for co-ops. Click on “Begin Filing” for both, but you’ll have to create an account — with a username and a password — to proceed.
Exemption applications are due on Aug. 21 for residential homes — such as townhouses — and condos, and Aug. 24 for co-ops.
Even that may not be enough time to keep the list of websites and log-in portals organized.

hed: What you can get for $1-2 million on Cape Cod
subhead: From condos with pools and tennis courts to an old-school beachfront bungalow, here’s what $1-2 million looks like on Cape Cod.
content:
ByOlivia McKenley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Cape Cod, known as one of New England’s hottest vacation spots, is drawing in more and more homeowners, but not simply for the houses. Rather, buyers are looking to take advantage of the peninsula’s “somewhat unspoiled” land.

“It’s a very finite piece of land. They’re not creating any more of it, so it’s becoming more scarce,” said Joe Hartung, a real estate professional at Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty in Chatham.

While there are a range of residential options and styles along the Cape, location and condition push homes over the $1 million mark. Houses on the Cape that have views and proximity to water, are updated, or move-in-ready tend to be priced in the $1-2 million range.

“If you want to have easy walking distance to the beach, maybe views of the water, of the bay, or the pond, you’re going to pay,” said Bob Sheldon, a broker-associate for REMAX Real Estate Center in Eastham. “Waterfront here oftentimes starts with a two or a three.”

He said that price “runs by town,” with areas like Wellfleet, Truro, and Chatham sitting at the higher end.

With an influx in desire for waterfront living, homeowners are facing new concerns with worseningbeach erosion. Some waterfront developments — specifically in areas along the Cape’s hook, like Truro — have undergone reconstruction further back on the lot or demolition due to eroding coastline.

“[It] doesn’t happen too often,” said Sheldon, but Hartung warned it’s a factor every buyer should keep in mind. “You know, if you have 20 feet of land before the beach, is that going to be 18 feet next year?” he said.

hed: Los Angeles County rents fall to a four-year low, but housing still stretches new graduates’ budgets
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Rentmay be droppingin Los Angeles County — but the difference still doesn’t cut it for most recent college grads.
According to a new report byRealtor.com, LA County rents hit a record four-year low in the second quarter of 2026, with theoverall median asking rent droppingto $2,603 — a decrease of $91, which equates to 3.4%, from the previous year, having not been so low since 2021.
The realty site also reported an area studio’s median asking rent as $2,004, units with zero to two bedrooms at $2,255 (a 3.6% drop year over year), and $3,441 for larger units with larger three-plus bedroom units (a 3.0% drop).
With theshifting habits of the local renting market, which was undoubtedly affected by the height of COVID-19, having finally started to settle since its peak in 2022 — plus additional housing options provided by new multi-family development and accessory dwelling unit (ADU) construction — some renters can finally have some financial weight taken off their shoulders.
California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day.
Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story
But the report also found that with what most recent LA grads are earning, they may not be part of this happy group (neither are New York grads, by the way — even a computer science entry level worker there is projected to spend a whopping 38.2% of their income on a small studio, per anotherRealtor.com report).
“Los Angeles renters are finally seeing meaningful relief after several years of exceptionally high rents, but lower asking rents don’t necessarily make housing affordable for recent graduates,” clarified Jiayi Xu, economist at Realtor.com. “Even with recent declines, many new graduates will still spend around or more than the recommended 30% of their income on rent. While conditions are improving,entry-level workersin many fields continue to face difficult housing tradeoffs.”
Though the rent market is currently generally in favor of new graduates on a nationwide scale — with the average median asking rent for a studio apartment across 50 of the country’s largest cities projected to consume only 20.9% of a Computer Science graduate’s projected national average starting salary, 24.8% of a Business graduate’s salary, 25.8% of a Social Science graduate’s salary and 26.8% of a Communications graduate’s salary, LA grads still have to shell out more than the generally recommended 30% of their income on rent.
While local computer-science grads are in the clear, as they’re currently projected to be spending 25.7% of their on-average $94,000 starting salary on rent, business grads are shelling out 30.4% of their average $79,000 salary, while social science grads ring in at forking over 31.6% of their $76,000 salary. Communications grads are projected to be in the worst spot, handing over an eye-watering 38.2% of their $73,000 earnings towards having a place to stay.
This data was based on Class of 2026 salary projections from the National Association of Colleges and Employers and was adjusted with a 15% geographic premium to reflect Los Angeles wage levels.
Still, Xu advised new graduates who want to put downroots in LAnot to give up hope just yet.
“The increase in rental supply is giving Los Angeles renters more options, especially those looking for smaller, entry-level units,” Xu added. “For recent graduates entering the market, that added supply can create more opportunities to find housing at a time when affordability remains a major consideration.”

hed: Everyday New Yorkers going through hell to prove their homes aren’t pieds-à-terre — even brokers say none of it makes sense
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Under New York’snew pied-à-terre tax, homeowners are guilty until proven innocent.
Karen Young spent three hours just trying tobegin the process of proving her Upper West Side brownstone — her home of 30 years — is her primary residence to avoid the new pied-à-terre surcharge.
In the end, it was a complete waste of time.
“I was planning to upload a few more documents yesterday morning, only to discover the documents I uploaded Monday weren’t saved despite the requirement to set up an account with a password,” Young, president and founder of beauty marketing company the Young Group, told The Post. She also needs to get ownership title/deed for her brownstone from her estate lawyer, whom she has to pay, to continue with the process.
“So I have to start from scratch,” she added. “I will wait till all the documents are assembled. There are a lot of them.”
Young has until Aug. 21 to submit all her documents or else she will be on the hook for a $42,824 surcharge courtesy of New York City’s new annual “Surcharge on Property That Does Not Serve as a Primary Residence,” and levied by the city’s Department of Finance on her Jan. 1, 2027 property tax bill.
“It’s a cumbersome process to prove that I’m a primary resident, which just seems absurd. My jury summons come here, I pay my taxes from here, my utilities,” shepreviously told The Post.
When homeowners get a notice in the mail claiming they owe the tax, the onus is on them to prove the city got it wrong.
The tax — which was framed as a tax on wealthy second-home owners — has caused a whole bunch of confusion. In particular, homeowners were overwhelmed when Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration published asearchable databaseof more than 960,000 residences and owners that couldfall under the new pied-à-terre tax.
“We opposed this tax in part because we warned that determining who is and is not subject to it would be extraordinarily complicated,” said James Whelan, president of the Real Estate Board of New York. “The fact that so many owners appear to be receiving inaccurate notices raises serious questions about the City’s readiness to administer the program. Even we did not expect implementation to be this flawed.”
Signed into law in May by Gov. Kathy Hochul, the Albany legislation targets unoccupied, secondary properties in New York City:one- to three-family homesvalued at $5 million or more, and co-ops or condos worth at least $1 million. Residents who received a bill but don’t meet those criteria can appeal.
“The law was written like Swiss cheese,” high-end residential broker Donna Olshan told The Post. “It is filled with holes. From a legal drafting standpoint it is an example of incompetence.”
Below are some of the issues:
“If you are out of an apartment renovating for a year and still pay New York City taxes, will the apartment be considered a pied-à-terre?” Olshan said. That is common among large homes, she noted.
What happens while a home is in probate, which could take longer than a year, she said. How about if someone has a long stay in a nursing home or assisted living and still owns their apartment?
They “may have to jump through additional complicated hoops, costing them” a lot of money, she said.
What happens if someone is out of their home for over a year due to a fire? “You could be subject to a pied-à-terre tax,” she said.
Olshan brought up a potential issue for homeowners who rent out their apartments.
The tenant has to make the unit a “primary residence,” which carries explicit tax consequences.
If you reject a potential out-of-state tenant because you suspect they won’t be able to substantiate primary residency, it could result in “a fair housing complaint because you’re not supposed to ask people if they pay New York City taxes,” she said. Or if the person is a foreign student and gets turned down, they could file a national origin complaint.
How will the city assess properties that are mixed-use? How will it handle properties that are owned by LLCs, an entity which can’t live in a property, Rosenberg & Estis’Benjamin M. Williamssaid.
And a new owner shouldn’t be penalized because the past owner used a property as a pied-à-terre, Williams said at the Department of Finance’sJuly 9 public hearingon the surcharge.
“Similarly, a purchaser who buys a home with a genuine intent to move in should not be taxed during a reasonable transition period caused by closing, renovation or relocation,” he said at the hearing, noting that taxpayers who are eligible for the exclusion shouldn’t have to go through the whole proof process every year.
For Holland & Knight’s Stuart M. Saft, the biggest flaw is “its Phase 2 valuation system starting in July 2028, which improperly calculates co-op and condo taxes based on outdated building share percentages rather than true unit-by-unit market values. This creates an inaccurate, unfair formula that sets a dangerous precedent for future property taxation,” hewrote.
Phase 1, from July 1 to June 30, 2028, uses values based on current DOF market value and phase 2, from July 1, 2028 to June 30, 2031, applies values based on comparable sales.
Another issue with the law is that homeowners who have more than one home, but live in the city, get dinged on the ones that are not their primary residences.
“This means that the rationale for the PAT Tax that it is directed to the wealthy who do not pay local taxes is not true,” he said.

hed: Luxury homes are selling at a rapid pace — while starter homes pile up as buyers fail to show
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It’s a tale of two markets — and it all comes down to the economy as the rich snap up luxury pads and the starter-home market goes cold.
Starter-home inventory was up 4.5% year-over-year in the US in May and price cuts climbed as economic headwinds like inflation and hiring slowdowns caused starter-home sales to drop 5.4% year-over-year, according to new data from listings giantZillow.
Meanwhile, luxury listings — defined as the top 5% of property values in a given region — slipped 5.2% while sales in this tier increased 6.2% in May, driven by stock market gains.
“Starter homebuyers today have more options, more negotiating power and sellers who are more willing to deal,” Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow, said in a statement. “The challenge is that the same financial pressures making it harder to save for a down payment are also making it harder to take advantage of that opportunity.”
First-time buyers also saw more discounts in June, with a quarter of starter homes cutting prices compared to just 20.6% of luxury properties.
Nowhere was the dynamic more dramatic than in Cleveland, Ohio. While the rich scooped up high-end digs at a breakneck pace in the city — up 23.2% compared to May 2025 — starter-home sales plummeted at nearly the same amount at 24.6% year-over-year. Desperate C-Town homesellers slashed prices in June on 21.5% of starter homes and 20% of luxury homes.
Cleveland was followed by Memphis, Tennessee, with luxury home sales rocketing up 42.4% year-over-year compared to starter-home sales ticking down 1.7%.
Cincinnati, Ohio, was close behind, with luxury homes sales rocketing going up 32.6% while starter-home sales slid 8.4%.
Rounding out the top five were Nashville, then Indianapolis.
“What’s striking is that this divide is so large in comparatively affordable Midwest and Sun Belt markets like Memphis, Nashville, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Indianapolis, which suggests that first-time homebuyer affordability really isn’t just a coastal problem,” Ng told The Post. “In these markets and across the country, luxury home sales are surging while sales in the bottom price tier have fallen. These markets remain relatively affordable when compared to markets on the coasts, but starter home prices here have increased rapidly over the last few years, which has pushed homeownership further out of reach for many buyers.”
Washington, DC, was notable as its starter sales barely nudged up at 0.6%, whereas its luxury sales leaped 23.6%.
Bucking the trend, some markets saw starter homes outperform luxury sales.
In Sacramento, California, for example, luxury sales dipped 3.9%, but the city’s starter-home sales nudged up 7.9%. In San Jose, while luxury sales edged up 2.7%, starter-home sales climbed 10.5%.
“In these markets, starter-home sales are rising while luxury sales have fallen, but when we look at inventory, the number of available starter homes has increased from last year while available luxury homes are declining,” Ng said. “Affordability challenges in these Northeast and West Coast markets have historically been driven by lack of supply, so these recent inventory gains may have unlocked new opportunities for first-time homebuyers.”
Overall, US existing home sales took anunexpected hit in Juneas record-high home prices and sticky mortgage rates kept prospective buyers on the sidelines.

hed: Drama explodes at Billionaires’ Row tower as wealthy homeowners sue for ‘chalky’ water coming from the faucets
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York City’s tap water is famously high-quality — but not in this high-gloss Manhattan tower that’shome to billionaires,according to a new lawsuit.
The building that holds the record for the most expensive home ever sold in America, 220 Central Park South, isbeing sued in Manhattan Supreme Courtby its own board over tap water that’s allegedly tainted with elevated copper, nickel and zinc — and that seven years of plumbing failures have gone unfixed.
The Robert A.M. Stern-designed edifice is wherehedge-fund titan Ken Griffin paid $238 millionin early 2019 for a four-story spread, still the priciest residential sale in US history.
But now, the building is back in the spotlight for another reason entirely.
The case centers on one of the villas in the 117-unit building purchased by 220 CPS International LLC in November 2019 for a whopping $46.5 million. Its owner, an entity connected to Mexican-Israeli businessman billionaire Daniel Jusidman, has complained ever since about water leaving a “whitish, chalky residue” on kitchen and bathroom fixtures, court papers said.
“The Water Issues significantly interfere with Owner’s use and enjoyment of the Unit,” court records say.
The alleged headaches include the owner replacing the kitchen and bathroom filters multiple times to allow clear water to flow through.
A photo from the suit’s exhibits even show someone holding up a finger covered with what appears to be the chalky residue referred to in the court documents.
At present, 220 Central Park South has one home for sale asking $79.9 million for a full-floor dwelling whose bathrooms come clad in marble and whose kitchen has “bespoke detailing,” according to its listing.
But, for the owner of this unit now suing the building, those experiences in his own spaces have been anything but.
“After approximately seven years of experiencing Water Issues and hearing nothing but excuses and promises from the Board, Owner was left with no other choice but to bring suit,” the documents add.
The suit further details that, following that big-dollar buy in 2019, the owner repeatedly raised concerns about the water to the board via emails and letters — concerns the documents claim the board has acknowledged, and even said are due to wider issues throughout the building.
As the water issues persisted, the documents add, the Board brought in AWTC Water Treatment Consulting to test the villa’s water supply, with sampling conducted in June and August of 2024. The documents claim results confirmed elevated levels of zinc, aluminum, iron and copper, prompting a series of building-wide flushings that management hoped would resolve the problem.
But, as the emails show, those efforts brought little comfort to the unit’s owner. Principal Arie Jusidman — who appears to be a family member of Daniel — pushed management for answers as testing stretched on.
“Just wondering if we are still waiting for results from water consultants’ analysis or enough time has pass [sic] to have a plan to solve this embarrassing situation,” he wrote in one email from Aug. 2, 2024, court records show.
“Hope we can soon live like normal people regarding water quality,” Daniel wrote in another email from Aug. 20, 2024, as seen in court records, after back and forth from the board about having pipes flushed out.
Lab results filed with the suit show readings well above federal guidance, the suit alleges.
A February 2026 report from MKM Environmental Consulting found copper at 2,700 micrograms per liter in the unit’s kitchen hot water, more than double the EPA’s action level, the records charge.
Nickel hit 1,600 micrograms per liter in the master bath, 16 times the agency’s health advisory, and zinc reached 16,800, over triple the aesthetic standard, the lawsuit claims.
AWTC Water Treatment Consulting tied the numbers to corrosion from stagnant pipes rather than contaminated source water, pointing to unusually low occupancy on the Villa’s upper floors.
Staff flushed the system repeatedly through 2025, but the complaints didn’t stop.
“I’m letting you know that everything that you have done so far has not improved the quality of the water,” Jusidman wrote that July, as seen in court papers. “Please Inform if you have a plan B or we should look for solution on our side.”
Law firm Cuddy & Feder sent the Condominium a formal demand on July 2, arguing the building’s governing documents make pipe repairs the board’s job since plumbing counts as a shared element.
When the deadline lapsed, the board sued the condominium itself so the owner could pursue a derivative claim, seeking more than $250,000 in damages and a court order forcing repairs.
The Robert A.M. Stern-designed tower also counts Sting andAlibaba billionaire Joe Tsaiamong its owners.
The 220 Central Park South Condominium, through general manager Maria Escallon Duque and property manager Allied Partners, did not respond to requests for comment.
Kempshall C. McAndrew of Cuddy & Feder LLP, attorney for the board of managers and the unit’s owner, also did not respond to a request for comment. Daniel Jusidman also did not respond.

hed: A guide to mint, the plant deer will actually avoid in your garden
subhead: Thyme, oregano, rosemary, summer savory, hyssop, lavender, peppermint, and spearmint all belong to the mint family
content:
ByUlrich Lorimer
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Chances are, most of us are growing a member of the mint family in our gardens. The mint family of plants is large, characterized by square stems and aromatic foliage, with over 7,000 species worldwide and centers of diversity in the Mediterranean, Central Asia, and China.

Thyme, oregano, rosemary, summer savory, hyssop, lavender, peppermint, and spearmint all belong to this cosmopolitan family and originate from the Mediterranean region. Plants like patchouli and shiso, with global economic importance, hail from Asia. Basil can trace its roots to India — its documented use first appearing 5,000 years ago. Tulsi and holy basil hold places of honor in Hindi and Greek Orthodox cultures. These plants are deeply steeped in history for their strongly aromatic foliage, providing plant medicine and complexity to our cooking.

Fortunately, the presence of aromatic oils in the leaves of the mint family that we value so much leads herbivores like deer to avoid them. This week’s column will explore the mint family beyond the culinary and medicinal stars of the vegetable garden, to include stalwart perennials that support a wide range of pollinators, add beauty to the summer landscape, and, most importantly for those of us who struggle with deer pressure, will be avoided by those marauding vegetarians.

I would like to begin with a disclaimer: There are no absolutes in gardening and no guarantees that the following plants will not at least be sampled by deer. Hunger can drive animals to try things they normally avoid. The likelihood of deer browsing on mint family plants is very low, but not zero.

Bee balms, horsemints, wild bergamot, and Oswego tea (Monarda spp.) are highly ornamental and popular garden perennials. The flowers resemble a fireworks display: clusters of narrow tubular flowers, arranged radially and seeming to explode from the center in all directions. Without fail, every year atGarden in the Woodsin Framingham, hummingbird clearwing moths, the most magical of woodland creatures, appear exactly when our wild bergamot(Monarda fistulosa) begins to bloom. The combination of fragrant foliage and floral scent perfumes the air, transporting visitors amid the gentle hum of the moths’ wings.


Jacob Cline scarlet bee balm (Monarda didyma ‘Jacob Cline’) is a top-performing selection with good disease resistance to powdery mildew and vibrant red blossoms that draw insects and hummingbirds alike. Bradbury’s bee balm (Monarda bradburiana) is valued for its small stature — about 2 feet tall — and excellent disease resistance. I personally like spotted horsemint (Monarda punctata) for its unusual silver and pink bracts, its drought tolerance, and its ability to attract every type of insect in the neighborhood.


While not hardy in New England, lemon bee balm (Monarda citriodora)lights up the garden with its hot-pink bracts and pink flowers. I treat this like a summer annual, making sure to collect seeds at the end of the season to resow for next year.

Mountain mints (Pycnanthemum spp.) are another group of excellent garden perennials. I consider them to be a keystone species in that they support an outsized number of pollinators and beneficial insects compared to others at this time of year. When bruised, the foliage is reminiscent of peppermint, basil, or lavender. The flowers are densely clustered atop the stems, and some species feature silvery bracts beneath the flowers, with others lacking the colorful bracts.

Mountain mints can be rambunctious growers in the garden, displaying a quality well known to the mint family: aggressive rhizomes. Broad-leaved mountain mint(Pycnanthemum mutiicum) and Virginia mountain mint (Pycnanthemum virginianum) are most exuberant; be sure to afford plenty of space for them to expand. I find the most well-behaved of the mountain mints to be narrow-leaved mountain mint (Pycnanthemum tenuifolium), which forms tidy clumps that get larger over time.


Giant hyssops (Agastache spp.) are known for the towering spires of lavender and purple blooms, often buzzing with pollinator activity. Black Adder is a selection of the native anise hyssop (Agastache foeniculum) and features dark flower buds and violet-red flowers, whereas Blue Fortune is a hybrid between the anise hyssop and rough-leaved hyssop (Agastache rugosa), a species from Korea. Both are compact selections, disease-resistant, and very floriferous.

Hedgenettles or Betony (Stachys sp.) are excellent garden perennials and quite deer-resistant. They include old favorites like lambs’ ears (Stachys byzantina) and new favorites likeStachys‘Hummelo,’ a late-spring flowering selection introduced by renowned Dutch plantsman Piet Oudolf. Be sure to deadhead spent flower stalks to encourage a second flush of blooms.

Bee balms, mountain mints, giant hyssops, and hedgenettles are but a few of the mints that can add color and diversity to your garden. Catmint (Nepeta spp.), Lavender (Lavandula spp.), Salvia (Salvia spp.), Skullcap (Scutellaria spp.), and obedient plant (Physostegia spp.) are other perennial genera to explore. They are guaranteed to delight, enchant, and engage with every garden visitor from humans to insects to birds — except deer!

Ulrich Lorimer is the director of horticulture at the Native Plant Trust in Framingham. Send your gardening questions, along with your name/initials and hometown, to[email protected]g.

hed: So you want to live on Martha’s Vineyard? Year-round residents give the scoop.
subhead: It’s a tough market — and a tough winter — but one year-rounder’s advice is simple. “Life is short, buy the Vineyard house!”
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

On an October morning in 2021,Keija Minorwas doing what she did most mornings from her home in Oakland, Calif. She was scrolling Martha’s Vineyard real estate listings while having her coffee. A 1980s Cape-style house on nearly 1.5 acres in Oak Bluffs stopped the scroll.

“For years, I’ve always looked at real estate listings on the Vineyard, just to look,” Minor said. “However, when I saw prices skyrocket during COVID, I started to panic that if I didn’t buy soon, I could be priced out.”

She sent the listing to her mother and a family friend, Boston-based developer Duane Jackson, who were both on island and toured the property on her behalf. Minor made an offer from 3,000 miles away and closed two days before Christmas.

From California, she renovated the house with help from Paul Lazes ofRock Pond Studio.

“When I bought my house, it had a small galley kitchen and no dishwasher. On the other side of the kitchen wall was a large dining room. I knew immediately that I wanted to knock down the wall between them and flip the space,” she explained. “What I didn’t know was that to remove the load bearing wall between the kitchen and dining room would take months first to level the floor and then to install a massive steel beam to hold up the second floor. You know how you never want to see sausage being made? That’s how I felt about the beam installation.”


Minor’s route to that home had many stops. A graduate of Howard University School of Law, she practiced corporate law in New York City before jumping to media, where she ran Gotham and Uptown magazines and made history at Condé Nast as the company’s first African American editor-in-chief when she took the helm of Brides. She later served as chief operating officer of Ebony Media Group. Today, she is a real estate agent with thePoint B team at Compass on Martha’s Vineyard— and, as of 2024, she’s a year-round Oak Bluffs resident. But the island’s not new to her; she grew up spending summers there.


“When I was a kid, the Vineyard wasn’t fancy — or at least my Vineyard wasn’t fancy. We didn’t have air conditioning, and on most days you could get on the ferry without a reservation. As kids, we could roam free,” she said, recalling the hours she spent grabbing rings at at Flying Horses Carousel.

“I always thought I’d live here when I retired, but remote work and my move into real estate created a path to making the move much sooner,” Minor said. “With the rise of remote work, more seasonal residents found themselves spending more time in their homes here, which in turn, led to more restaurants and stores staying open longer. More folks discovered how nice it is to be here in the offseason, or spend Thanksgiving here, or come for Christmas in Edgartown.”

The transformation, she said, runs both ways.

“I now wear Hunter Wellies probably five times as often as I wear heels,” Minor said. “I’m gardening for the first time in my life — albeit with mixed results — but as a lady who largely ate out or ordered takeout for the past 20 years, I’m quite proud of my first batch of cherry tomatoes.”


The learning curve to island life got steeper when the temperature dropped. This past winter ushered in levels of snow the island hadn’t seen in years, and Minor found herself hunting down a plow service, riding out a power outage, and pressing a fireplace she once considered decorative into active duty.

“I was Brooklyn condo ready,” she said. “I was not [Vineyard homeowner] ready, but I will not make that mistake again.”

One lesson in particular stuck.

“This winter, I deeply cared that I do not have a garage,” she said with a laugh.

Allison Cameron Parry, aDouglas Ellimanreal estate agent, has lived on the island for 25 years (she arrived as a teenage lifeguard at Chilmark’s famed Lucy Vincent Beach). She offers a longer view of what year-round life delivers.

“The frog noise is just about the loudest noise I hear,” she said of the blissful quiet and natural beauty of the island. Winter, she tells curious buyers, has its own rhythm.

According to the Chamber of Commerce, the island’s nearly 200,000 summer residents whittle down to about 24,000 in the offseason.


“It’s the introspection season,” Cameron Parry said, describing the months when islanders take up photography, mah-jong, or breath work, and when privately endowed programs such asPathways Artsturn the shuttered Chilmark Tavern into a winter hub of music jams and exhibits.Vineyard Haven, she said, has become the island’s true year-round downtown, its restaurant scene energized since the formerly dry town began allowing full liquor sales. Winter in Oak Bluffs is another story.

“The only place to get a coffee in Oak Bluffs is the Keurig machine found in the bank,” she joked


The Vineyard housing market Minor now works in bears little resemblance to the one she grew up visiting — or even the one she bought into. In Oak Bluffs, the median single-family sale price ran just under $635,000 in 2018, according to data from The Warren Group. By 2025, it had more than doubled to about $1.29 million, and through the first half of 2026 it stood at roughly $1.32 million. Edgartown followed the same arc, climbing from $800,000 in 2018 to $1.7 million last year, and Tisbury nearly matched Oak Bluffs dollar for dollar.


What has collapsed is volume. The island’s towns combined had 313 single-family sales in 2018 and nearly 400 during the frenzied 2020 market. Since 2022, annual sales have not cracked 200. Up-island towns are so thinly traded (Chilmark and Aquinnah each recorded just four sales through June) that a single trophy listing can whipsaw a town’s median by millions.

When Minor bought in the Hamptons a decade ago, she noted, the Vineyard was the more affordable of the two markets. On a price-per-square-foot basis, she said, they are now roughly at parity.


Nevette Previd, executive director of the Vineyard Preservation Trust, bought her Vineyard Haven home about 18 years ago with every intention of renovating, flipping, and eventually moving deeper into the woods.

Life intervened, and she and her husband are now raising a teenager (there are six public schools on the island) in that prime downtown location. But when they recently revisited the idea of trading up-island, the math had turned against them. Selling would net a handsome profit, she said, but replacing the house would require significant capital on top of the proceeds, even for a fixer upper.

“There’s no way,” Previd said. “There’s absolutely no way we could get out of the market and in the market again.”



That lock-in effect is one increasingly common in markets across the Cape and Islands and helps explain the island’s vanishing inventory: Even content longtime owners who might otherwise trade up or sideways are staying put. What Previd sees changing instead is the calendar.

“There was the on and off season, but now there seems to be the midseason,” she said, describing residents who arrive before Memorial Day, linger into October, and return for Thanksgiving and for Christmas in Edgartown, a December weekend she calls “massive, massive, massive.”

Cameron Parry is candid about the trade-offs of living on island. Construction and renovation costs run at least 30 percent above mainland averages, she said, thanks to labor scarcity and the price of getting materials across Vineyard Sound, and specialists of every kind — from HVAC contractors to pediatric dentists — require patience. Buyers eyeing historic homes in enclaves such as East Chop in Oak Bluffs face renovation restrictions that can sharply limit expansion. Her formula for making it work is simple.

“If you have a vision and a little extra liquidity, you can overcome anything, really,” she said.

Previd’s counsel for the smitten buyer is blunter.

“Don’t dive in year-round until you’ve spent three months” in the offseason, she said, because the island’s charms in July say little about its realities in March, and because belonging takes work in a place where roots run generations deep.

Volunteering is the fastest way in, she added, with more than 150 nonprofits on an island where showing up at Town Meeting still counts for something.

For Boston-area buyers who fall in love after a week on the island, Minor’s advice is to get pre-approved, as that will make your offer more attractive, and get ruthless about must-haves versus nice-to-haves, because desirable listings rarely wait around, and closings routinely take 60 days.



Her larger philosophy fits on a bumper sticker: “Life is short, buy the Vineyard house!”

“When I bought my house at the end of 2021, I said to friends who bought in 2019, ‘You’re so lucky you bought before the pandemic.’ Now people say to me, ‘You’re so lucky you bought in 2021 when interest rates were so low,’” Minor said. “There will always be someone who bought before you or got a better deal; the important thing is to get in the game.”

“It’s the only place where I want things to stay exactly the same,” Minor added about the Vineyard. “It’s part of the reason I joined the board of Vineyard Preservation Trust. All these century-old buildings take a lot of resources to maintain. In addition to the buildings, we have a responsibility to keep the spirit of kindness and community very much alive here as well. There’s something about the island that makes you cherish it and also want to protect it.”

hed: World’s ‘first motel’ up for sale in sleepy California coastal city
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s first motel — the roadside landmark that helped launch thegreat American road trip— is looking for a new owner.
The historic property in theCentral Coast city of San Luis Obispo, home to the original Milestone Mo-Tel, later renamed the Motel Inn, has officially hit the market for the first time in a generation.
Located just off the historicEl Camino Real, the landmark is widely recognized as the birthplace of the modern motel, offering travelers a place to park their cars and spend the night decades before roadside lodging became an American staple.
The 4.21-acre parcel at 2223 Monterey Street, just off Highway 101, is being offered byHayes Commercial Groupbut without a public asking price.
Highway 101is, in many ways, the modern incarnation of El Camino Real — the old “King’s Highway,” as it was then known, that once stitched California’s 21 Spanish missions together, from San Diego to San Francisco to Sonoma in Northern California.
Laid down centuries later, the freeway still traces that same coastal corridor, carrying today’s travelers along the same historic spine the padres once walked.
