Opened more than a century agoon December 12, 1925 as a labor of love from Pasadena architect Arthur S. Heineman, the Milestone Mo-Tel was built specifically for the new age of automobile travel.
Guests could pull their prized rides right up to the front doors of their motel rooms — a radical and novel idea at the time.
Heineman, who was also an inventor, coined the word “motel” by blending “motor” and “hotel,” and the name stuck. The motel was positioned roughly halfway between Los Angeles and San Francisco, making it a natural overnight stop when a day’s drive still meant exhaustion and numb buns, albeit with far less traffic than endured nowadays.
Hollywood stars, including then-newlywedsMarilyn Monroe and Joe DiMaggio, once passed through in the 1950s. The Mission-style architecture (popularized in California from the 1890s–1920s), complete with its eye-catching three-tiered bell tower and copper dome, turned it into a local landmark.
The motel permanently shuttered in 1991. Over the following decades most of the original buildings fell to ruin and were subsequently demolished. Today, only the refurbished lobby building with its bell tower and the facade of the old restaurant remain, standing behind chain-link fencing as a quiet reminder of a bygone era.
Now, the site is fully entitled for an 83-room boutique getaway featuring 27 bungalow-style guest buildings, a pool and a new sound wall. Construction permits are ready to issue, making it one of the rare rockbreaker-ready hotel opportunities.
California Post News:Facebook,Instagram,TikTok,X,YouTube,WhatsApp,LinkedInCalifornia Post SportsFacebook,Instagram,TikTok,YouTube,XCalifornia PostOpinionCalifornia Post Newsletters:Sign up here!California Post App:Download here!Home delivery:Sign up here!Page Six Hollywood:Sign up here!
“There is no comparable opportunity in California,” listing broker Nolan Tooley said in a release for the property.
“This is a shovel-ready, entitled hotel site on Highway 101 in one of the most supply-constrained lodging markets on the Central Coast.”
Because the motel is listed on theCity of San Luis Obispo’s Historic Preservation List, what’s left of the estate’s historic structure must be incorporated into any future plans.
For a century, the Motel Inn has waited just five miles from the foot of the steep mountain pass that is the Cuesta Grade. Someone new with deep pockets and a big imagination may finally get to bring what was once a trailblazing motel into the 21st century.
All they’ve gotta do is make an offer.

hed: Los Angeles condo sales soar as prices reach record heights
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Condo living is quite the thing.
Sales for the all-inclusive living spaces are on a winning streak in Los Angeles, with a recent report by Compass Developing Marketing Group showing that the City of Angels’ luxury condominium market rebounded in a significant way from a lackluster start to the year during its second quarter.
During that time period, condo sales skyrocketed by a whopping 22.2% quarter-over-quarter, resulting in 760 closings — a number nicely in line with the historic second quarter average of 768.
Though the current average sale price — which rings in at $1.35 million, with average price per square foot sitting at $898 — has stayed on track with the norm of the last three years, the pricing in the ritziest submarkets has continued to climb.
Helen Howe, managing director of Compass Market Development Group, shares that prime addresses that offer full-service and a host of amenities in Rosewood Residences Beverly Hills, Mandarin Oriental Beverly Hills and 8899 Beverly are seeing a wave of “trophy-level closings” and “still commanding premium pricing.”
“[It’s] a signal that today’s most discerning buyers remain willing to pay for the right combination of location, service and lifestyle,” said Howe.
LA’s most elite have been leading this trend towards condo living, with a mystery buyer on track to acquire a half-built penthouse on top of the Aman Beverly Hills set to sell for a whopping$200 million.
If all goes according to plan, the nine-figure closing would more than obliterate the current condo sale record, which sits at $39.2 million for the 2025 purchase of luxury unit at the Century in Century City. If the Aman Beverly Hills penthouse sale goes through, it will beat this record by a staggering 410%.
While the luxe condo has been reserved, the potential buyer’s identity remains a mystery.
While condos sales have historically ranked behind mansion sales in LA’s luxury market, the new wave of residential towers could see this trendbegin to change.

hed: Over 1,000 US public schools shuttered last year: How closings could put your home value at risk
subhead: Buyers pay for access to neighborhood schools
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
More than 1,000 public schools across 700 communities closed last year, according to new data—shuttering a prized neighborhood amenity and potentially putting nearby home values at risk.
Just ask Virginia Morris. She and her family moved to their neighborhood in Oro Valley, AZ, because they saw the local school as a “package deal.”
Copper Creek Elementary was A-rated, close enough to walk to, and deeply tied to the surrounding community—exactly the kind of feature that has shaped homebuying decisions for decades.
But in May 2026, after nearly 40 years in service, Copper Creek closed.
“We never expected in a million years this would be taken away from us,” Morris said at a December meeting of the district’s governing board. “An entire community, and an entire neighborhood, completely gutted.”
Economists have long found that high-performing public schools offer a benefit that extends beyond students. In one landmark study, buyers paid 2.5% more for homes assigned to schools where test scores were just 5% higher.
But that relationship can work in both directions. A strong school can make a neighborhood more desirable. Take it away, and homeowners can lose some of the buyer demand—and the price premium—that came with living near it.
“Public schools and homes are bundle goods: Where people live will decide where kids go to school,” explains Jiayi Xu, economist at Realtor.com®. “In other words, people are not just buying a living space but also a seat in a school district, whether they have kids or not.”
It’s a particularly potent package at the elementary school level. Unlike a high school that may draw students across a large area or a charter school with open enrollment, primary-school attendance zones are generally smaller and more closely resemble the boundaries of individual neighborhoods.
Of the 1,025 closed schools identified by Realtor.com in an analysis of National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) data, nearly half were elementary schools—putting that uniquely personal piece of the housing market in play.
The importance of that connection was on display earlier this year in Sugar Land, TX, as Fort Bend ISD considered closing Sugar Mill Elementary.
“We chose this A-rated school and even bought our home here because of the care, stability, and support Sugar Mill provides,” parent Vicki Haislip told trustees at a January board meeting.
Other residents made the same connection explicitly: One warned trustees that closing a school “completely surrounded by residential homes” would negatively affect the value of those properties.
Research shows why that concern is not purely sentimental.
A 2023 study in Real Estate Economics tracked Atlanta-area homes before and after unexpected changes to elementary-school attendance boundaries. When a boundary change gave a home access to a substantially better-performing school, its sale price rose about 3% and it was sold about a month faster. A move to a worse-performing school pushed demand in the opposite direction.
On March 9, the Fort Bend school board voted 4-3 to close Sugar Mill.
While there are a number of studies that put a specific price on the value strong schools add to nearby homes, the evidence is thinner on what discount, if any, appears when a school closes.
One of the strongest studies examined the sudden closure of a well-performing public school in Cedar Falls, IA. Researchers estimated that the school added about 6.8% to the value of homes within its attendance zone, beyond the value associated with its standardized test scores.
Xu agrees that this is directionally true.
“When a school closes or kids get reassigned, nearby home values typically fall,” she explains. “Sometimes the impact goes further, signaling broader neighborhood decline, which can scare off family buyers and depress prices even more.”
But Humberto Marquez, a licensed real estate broker in Texas, suggests that the impact starts well before a school actually closes.
“The real problem isn’t the school closure itself—it’s the limbo that comes with it,” he says. “The minute a school gets added to an ‘under consideration’ list, buyers with kids in the area start ruling that neighborhood out.”
Of course, that doesn’t mean every closure will produce an immediate or predictable drop in home prices. But the testimony from families shows the underlying mechanism clearly: They had treated the local schools as foundational to their decision to buy.
It also points to a harder question: How does a desirable neighborhood with a strong housing market lose its school in the first place?

Around Copper Creek, nothing about the housing market suggested decline. The median list price was up almost 4% from a year earlier and 11% from three years earlier, according to Realtor.com data.
The same was true in Sugar Land, where median list prices were up 3% from three years prior, even as Texas’ median list price fell about 5%.
But inside the homes, there was a trend line in decline. Fort Bend ISD’s demographer described it as “regeneration.”
Established neighborhoods can lose students as children grow up and empty nesters remain in their homes, while new housing elsewhere adds younger families. The district pointed to new construction as its largest source of enrollment growth.
Arizona officials described a similar process around Copper Creek: Homes were increasingly being purchased by retirees, while some younger families were moving toward less-expensive communities such as nearby Vail and Marana.
In Oro Valley, 35.7% of residents are 65 or older and just 16.3% are under 18, according to U.S. Census Bureau records. The median owner-occupied home value is about $476,000, compared with roughly $414,000 in Vail and Marana. And while Oro Valley’s population grew 2.2% between 2020 and 2025, Marana’s jumped 26.2%.
The numbers hint at a bigger housing-market force behind the enrollment shift: The places where established homeowners have accumulated the most housing wealth are not necessarily the places where the next generation of families can afford to buy.
It’s true that the birth rate has fallen to fewer than 1.6 children per woman, down from 2.1 recorded in 2006—the rate needed to sustain the population. And that is showing up in enrollments.
Nationally, NCES projects public pre-K–8 enrollment to fall about 5% between 2022 and 2031, from 34.1 million students to 32.2 million.
But fewer children is only part of the story—where those children live matters just as much. And housing costs help determine that geography.
A recent study found that if housing costs had remained flat after 1990, there would have been 13 million more children born in the U.S. by 2020. The country’s total fertility rate in the 2010s would have been 77% closer to the replacement rate if those costs hadn’t increased, the research showed.
At the same time, high home prices can push the families who do have children toward cheaper communities—redirecting school enrollment from established neighborhoods toward newer-growth corridors.
It’s a confounding paradox: The school helps make a neighborhood desirable and valuable. Over time, the next wave of young families gets priced out, and the local school has to close.
And once it does, the equation changes again.
A 2022 study using federal school records and Census data tried to answer that chicken-and-egg question.
Across rural U.S. counties, researcherJoseph Sagemanfound that school closures induced additional population loss in many, though not all, of the counties he studied.
That creates the possibility of a feedback loop, according to Xu.
“If birthrates keep falling, the pool of buyers who actually need a school seat shrinks over time,” she says. “That doesn’t mean a decline in housing demand. It means fewer purchasing decisions will be driven by school quality, and more will be driven by other factors such as commute time to work or lifestyle amenities.”
Over time, Xu says, that could “compress the school quality premium, shrinking the value gap between homes with a strong assigned school and those without.”
But, she adds, “national birthrate trends don’t necessarily translate evenly to local markets. Migration patterns can offset the effect.”
That distinction is critical. A region can have plenty of housing demand, while the families driving school enrollment migrate from one part of it to another. Once again, Tucson offers a telling example.
In July 2025, months before Copper Creek would be voted to close, Marana Unified opened Tangerine Farms K-8, built for 800 students in what the district calls the “quickly expanding” Gladden Farms neighborhood.
That same month, Vail School District opened Saguaro Creek K-8, its 22nd school, in the growing Rocking K community.
The contrast is striking. One established community would soon lose a beloved school while growing communities were building new ones.
And it may point to the most valuable takeaway for homeowners. School closures are far from a sign that demand for a particular neighborhood is dropping. Instead, they may signal that the people who want—or can afford—to live there are changing.

hed: Steve Wynn sells $110M Beverly Hills mansion for massive discount as billionaires flee California taxes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Steve Wynn has finally unloaded his jaw-dropping Beverly Hills megamansion, “Villa Lulu” — and the house definitely did not win this time.
The 84-year-old former casino head honcho just cashed out on his 27,150-square-foot Benedict Canyon estate for a final price of $47.75 million, listing broker Leonard Rabinowitz of Christie’s International Real Estate told The Post.
While that sum sounds like he hit the jackpot, for Wynn, it’s a bust.
The 11-bedroom, 14.5-bath castle with multiple kitchens, initially had an eye-watering $135 million whisper price in 2020.
When Wynn officially listed the home in 2021, he put a $110 million sticker on it.
After desperate price chops and no interest, Wynn has sold the home at $87.25 million less than where he started.
Even worse:Monday’s sale pricecomes to $100,000 less than his original purchase price. Wynn bought the 2.7-acre spread from Guess jeans co-founder Maurice Marciano in 2015 for $47.85 million. He sunk millions into an 8,000-square-foot expansion and lavish renovations.
Rabinowitz said the buyer is an “American businessman.”
Rabinowitz blamed the pricing situation on California’s tax rate andtax on billionaires, which is causing residents to flee the Golden State for places like Florida and Texas.
“The buying pool is shrinking so prices start to tumble,” he said.
Still, he said, “I’ll take his win-loss ratio any time.” He was referencing Wynn’s succession of house flips in Palm Beach, where he currently lives, “that were very successful, not to mention his career in Las Vegas.”
A gated property, the home has its own private road off lower Benedict Canyon. The megamansion has a reception area, a bar, a grand living room and an executive office, plus a standalone guest apartment. The owner’s suite features dual amenities, while dedicated quarters accommodate three staff members and two full-time security guards.
The house — which has vaulted ceilings — boasts a 40-seat home theater; a wellness center with commercial-grade gym equipment, a hot and cold plunge and hyperbaric chamber and a hydrating booth; a spa suite with dual massage tables and at a wine room that fits at least 700 bottles, Rabinowitz told The Post.
Wynn, whoForbesestimates is worth $3.9 billion, has relistedhis Ritz-Carlton penthousein New York Cityfor $70 million. He purchased the duplex for $70 million in 2012, listed it for $90 million in December 2022, cut the price to $65 million, then pulled the listing off the market in early 2024 before its current relisting at $70 million.
Wynn was subject to allegations ofsexual misconductin 2018 at Wynn Resorts, which he denied, butstill cost him $20 millionin investor settlement claims. Rabinowitz said this had “absolutely” nothing to do with the Beverly Hills pricing.
He added, “Knowing the man for 30 years I find [the allegations] hard to believe.”

hed: In Waltham, big landlords want to replace an old office complex with new homes. The mayor says no.
content: In the sprawling reaches of the commercial office corridor arrayed along Route 128 in Waltham, a slumping market has forced local officials to confront a thorny new feature of the suburban fabric: empty buildings, one seemingly after another. Two of the city’s biggest owners of those buildings, as well as members of the Waltham City Council believe they have a solution: turn three of the downtrodden commercial districts into more than 2,000 new units of housing. They would be the biggest residential development projects in recent memory in this city of 65,000, bringing a neighborhood feel to what is largely a forlorn stretch of business. But earlier in July, Waltham Mayor Jeannette McCarthy vetoed a measure that would clear the way to redevelop the largest of the three office parks, citing concerns about density, and observed the fact that the project would be “conveniently placed next to a residential neighborhood.”“Why, with all the land that is available on the site, was it placed so close to the existing neighborhood?” she wrote in a letter to the City Council.And she worried big developments would only worsen the city’s already notorious traffic. The mayor declined to be interviewed or answer questions, referring instead to her letter to the council.Related: The next frontier for housing: Suburban office parksMcCarthy’s objection surprised several city councilors, and the panel will now consider overriding McCarthy’s veto at a special meeting Monday. If they don’t, planning for the property will go back to square one, which could put funds for key transportation improvements from the developer and the state at risk.More than that, it would also significantly delay development of up to 1,200 units on a property where little else is going on these days, at a time when Greater Boston is desperate for new homes.“We are at a crossroads in our city — our growth is stagnant,” said City Councilor Cathyann Harris. “And we are in a unique position with all of this underutilized office space to do something about it and transform the city for the future. To waste the opportunity would be a shame.”1000 Winter St. in Waltham in the Bay Colony office complex, which developers are proposing to replace with about 1,200 new homes.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffThe Route 128 corridor in Waltham has long been a commercial hub and was one of the biggest beneficiaries of the boom in life sciences and technology companies, full of shiny new office and lab buildings housing big companies such as AstraZeneca and Boston Dynamics. Today, nearly half of Waltham’s property tax base comes from commercial real estate, a higher share than any where else in Massachusetts except Cambridge and Boston.And while there is still some growth in the business district — Boston Dynamics announced a $100 million expansion there earlier this year — the post-COVID downturn in the suburban office market has hit Waltham hard. Many office buildings are now vacant, and their owners are asking Waltham for tax abatements. This year, the city raised its residential tax rate by 5 percent to account for lost revenue.Waltham’s biggest taxpayer is real estate firm BXP, formerly Boston Properties. Last year the developer approached the City Council with a proposal: rezone three big districts along Route 128 — two owned by BXP totaling 155 acres in all, and the sprawling former Polaroid campus on Main Street owned by local developer J & CO LLC — to allow for mixed-use development that could bring retail and housing to otherwise under-used space.Related: Waltham, long a job growth center, may finally build the housing to matchIn all, the properties could hold 2,100 apartments and condos — a stretch of mostly empty office buildings along Winter Street, known as Bay Colony, could become 1,200 units; 20 acres off Jones Road could hold 300 to 400; the old Polaroid site, now a Market Basket, 600 more.The City Council saw the proposal as an opportunity to push Waltham forward, and in January began workshopping three special zoning districts that could host neighborhood-sized developments. For all its job growth, Waltham has added relatively little new housing during McCarthy’s 22-year tenure, beyond a handful of apartment buildings downtown and nearby along the Charles River. This offered the opportunity to build more, at scale, with relatively little impact on existing residential neighborhoods, said City Councilor Colleen Bradley-MacArthur.“It is incumbent upon Waltham to grow as a city,” said Bradley-MacArthur. “You don’t get many opportunities to build new neighborhoods.”A key part of the negotiations centered around a broader vision for this part of Waltham, which hasn’t had much new residential development and is often deluged with traffic from drivers passing through to reach Route 128.The office parks that line Route 128 in Waltham have long powered the city's tax base, but their values have fallen since the COVID pandemic sparked a push towards working from home. Now developers want to replace some with new housing.Suzanne Kreiter/Globe StaffThat traffic was one of the big concerns from opponents of the projects. Wouldn’t adding housing next to the highway responsible for so much congestion only make the problem worse? The developers agreed to help out with several key infrastructure upgrades, including setting aside land for a new fire and EMS station, upgrading a road through a nearby residential neighborhood, and helping pay for a new connector between heavily trafficked state roads, after the state chips in what the city expects will total $15 million.In neighborhood meetings, there were some concerns about traffic, especially around Bay Colony, Harris said, as well as whether buildings could obstruct views in spots. But the Jones Road site is near the site of a planned new bus hub and commuter rail station, and the Market Basket site has regular bus service. Moreover, Harris said, BXP was responsive and made some changes to its plans. BXP declined to comment for this story.Related: Cambridge passed one of the most ambitious housing reforms in the US. Now comes the construction, and the backlash.All three projects, Harris noted, are intended to be mixed-use developments, less auto-dependent than the office buildings there now. Altogether, she said, they could make western Waltham “a very different kind of transit hub than the car-oriented one we’re used to seeing.” In June, the council unanimously approved the three new zoning districts, which provide a framework for what the projects could look like. Developers would still have to go through a special permit process to actually get project approvals, and buildout could stretch out over a decade. McCarthy approved the Jones Road and Polaroid sites, and there was little hint she was thinking of vetoing zoning for Bay Colony until she sent a letter to the City Council on July 1. Waltham has seen a few new apartment buildings downtown but relatively little new housing elsewhere in recent years, compared with job growth in the city of 65,000.Blake Nissen/The Boston GlobeThat zoning, she wrote, would establish bad development standards, including “dramatically decreasing parking requirements for all uses both residential and commercial, setting a dangerous precedent for the city,” and “redefining height for just these overlays, treating them differently from all other sites in the city.”To some in town, McCarthy’s veto “came out of nowhere,” said Tom Benavides, founder of the local pro-housing group Waltham Inclusive Neighborhoods. If McCarthy had objections, there were opportunities to raise them earlier.“This whole project would not have happened without the mayor being a facilitator in the background,” said Benavides. “She has been attending these meetings. She’s had opportunities to provide input and feedback. And then after the fact without warning, she chooses to veto it. It’s in bad form.”Those concerns, said Bradley-MacArthur, could still be addressed in the special permitting process each project still must go through.The 15-member council’s meeting on Aug. 3 is its only opportunity to override McCarthy’s veto, which both Bradley-MacArthur and Harris said they would vote to do. Several other councilors, including council President Robert Logan, did not return requests for comment.Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: It’s war at NYC’s Pierre — where billionaires could get evicted when shareholders vote on a $2B sale
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Inside the tony halls of the posh Pierre at the corner of Fifth Avenue and East 61st Street, the next chapter of a war raging between some of the wealthiest people in the country — including billionaires Howard Lutnick, Larry Ellison and fashion designer Tory Burch — is being written.
The Post broke news last yearthat the Pierre’s board was in talks with the Sultan of Brunei and the Khashoggi family of Saudi Arabia to sell the historic building — which operates as a hotel and residence owned by a corporation of shareholders — for $2 billion.
Five months later, someoutraged co-op owners led by Burch sued the board, alleging they were secretly plotting a shady deal that would kick owners out of their homes — as the massive deal would also include the sale of their units.
After the board released a non-binding term sheet on the deal and three years of board minutes, thecase was dismissed with both sides claiming victory.
Gimme Shelter can now reveal more details about the $2 billion bid.
The man behind it is Motasem Khashoggi, a Harvard-educated lawyer known as “MK,” who is a cousin of the late Saudi arms dealer Adnam Khashoggi. Khashoggi is the beneficial owner of Sabre Park Avenue LLC, which is making the $2 billion bid, according to a source familiar with the deal. If the deal happens, Khashoggi would hire the Dorchester Collection, a luxury hotel operator run by Brunei’s sovereign wealth fund, to manage the Pierre.
“It’s all him. It’s his money,” the source said. However, some residents tell Gimme Shelter they still don’t know who is behind the purchase: “We are still in the dark. All we have is the name of a shell company. That’s the problem we have,” one said.
The shareholders who own the Pierre’s 77 residences will vote this fall on the bid. If a two-thirds threshold is met, the sale will pass and owners will have to surrender their homes — or they will be evicted and forfeit their share of the sale, sources said.
If the shareholders vote to sell to Khashoggi, they will have the option to buy back into the Pierre after the renovations, which could take five years.
The shareholders also have no say in how much they will receive for their apartments. At one meeting, some residents said they were dramatically handed sealed envelopes that had the sale price they’d be forced to accept if the sale passes.
All of the shareholders, including publishing heir Austin Hearst, Princess Firyal of Jordan, musician Art Garfunkel and Hollywood producer Irwin Winkler, are now waiting for a proxy statement to explain the terms of the sale. But no date has been set for its release, a source for the board’s legal team told Gimme.
Given the lack of information and the absence of a proxy statement, the board called a meeting on Wednesday to deliver a presentation that would provide what little information they could to shareholders about the bid.
About 45 co-op owners attended a three-hour meeting, including Burch, while others, like ex-Disney chair Michael Eisner, attended by Zoom. But the hotly contested meeting turned out to be a “disaster with lots of shouting and tears.”
“I learned nothing,” said one resident. “A lot of it was optics. They didn’t share any numbers.”
At the meeting, the Dorchester Group delivered a presentation about what the Pierre would look like if they would be running it — after the residents had been kicked out of the building.
“It was tone deaf,” the resident said.
“I almost felt sorry for the Dorchester guy. I think they were surprised by the reaction of the shareholders and shocked by the animosity,” the resident added.
A source for the buyer says the purchase price being offered for the homes as part of the $2 billion sale is generous and “three or four times” the value of each residence. Others say the price is too low.
Around 700 people will also lose their jobs at the residence, if two thirds of the shareholders vote to sell the building this fall.
Some of the co-op owners are in their 80s and 90s. They are already rich, and don’t want to move for any price.
Other residents say the board has not been transparent since the talks began a few years ago and improperly rejected an offer from the Taj Group, which currently has a lease to run the hotel and residences — and has been doing so since 2005.
Earlier this week, Taj sent a letter to the board stating that it will invest $300 million for repairs and renovations — without uprooting the residents. (Another insider told Gimme that Taj is not “credible” in part because the building is in need of $400 million worth of repairs that were not made earlier under its watch.)
“This is about morals, ethics and transparency. People should not be forced to leave their homes and have 700 people fired … especially as a result of a deceptive, misleading and opaque process orchestrated by some of the board members and their advisors,” Burch, who has lived in the building for 28 years, told Gimme Shelter.
David Johnson, president of the board, declined to comment on Wednesday’s meeting or the proposed $2 billion buyout, saying: “It was a private meeting among shareholders and it is inappropriate to discuss it.”
The deal would be brokered by Newmark Group, a Cantor Fitzgerald company now run by Lutnick’s sons, Brandon and Kyle, after their father stepped down as Cantor’s chairman and CEO in 2025 to become Commerce Secretary.
That means one of the Pierre’s own co-op owners — Lutnick, who bought the building’s trophy penthouse for $44 million in 2017 but never moved in — has sons whose firm stands to collect a fee on the very sale he’d profit from as a shareholder.
It’s getting ugly.
“Shareholders need more transparency from the board and its agents,” said Hearst.
Added another resident: “It’s an abuse of power and a dereliction of [the board’s] duties. We just don’t know what kind of deals were made on the side. We love our hotel and they want to gut it, change it, and fire the staff and in return we can get a reservation at the Dorchester hotels. They are playing bad pool. I’m so tired of the duplicity.”
People on both sides agree on one thing: the public fight is devaluing the building.
“This is not just a story about wealthy people fighting. If this passes, it will set a precedent for co-ops across the city. Anyone’s home is vulnerable,” the resident added. “We love the Pierre. Yes, it needs work, but we love its old-world charm. We don’t want some marbled new structure. It’s historic and part of New York.”

hed: Sellers are using smart cameras to eavesdrop on homebuyers — but listening in comes with  risks
subhead: Is it legal to have security cameras on during home showings?
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Smart home securitywas designed to keep burglars out, but it’sincreasingly being used to keep tabs on potential buyers—creating a tense new dynamic in the real estate market.
Almost three-quarters (72%) ofrecent homebuyerssay they have either seen or suspected cameras, microphones, or recording devices during a home tour, according to a recentsurvey by LendingTree.
And, at least 56% of sellers surveyed admitted they had recording devices active during a walkthrough.
While most sellers (61%) surveyed said their tech setup is for protection, at least 19% admitted they used the devices to listen in during showings to find out what potential buyers liked or disliked about the home, and at least 18% said they wanted to gauge the buyers’ interest.
Another 6% said they wanted to hear what their real estate agent said about their home.
“Homebuyers todayshould just assume everything they say or do is being recorded when they are looking at homes and plan accordingly,” saysCara Ameer, an agent with Coldwell Banker who is licensed in California and Florida. “The seller is likely watching from somewhere.”
The danger of using security devices as spy cams, though, is that it can stifle the home buying process.
“Once the buyer realizes that there is audiovisual recording, he/she stops talking, tours quickly, and leaves the property without creating any emotional attachment,” saysDaniel Cabrera, owner of Sell My House Fast SA TX in San Antonio.
“In other words, a silent buyer is a buyer that never falls in love with the house.”
One of the first questions that comes to mind for most people is the legality of recording home showings, and with good reason.
Privacy laws vary among federal, state, and even local municipalities.
While a homeowner is absolutely allowed to protect their property with security cameras, if potential buyers don’t know they’re being recorded with audiovisual devices, things can get sticky.
“Video recording inside the private home is a common practice. Audio is a dangerous legal minefield,” saysGreg Field, a specialized Solar Home Realtor® with HomeSmart Realty Pros in Tempe, AZ.
Many states, like Arizona, function under consent statutes that require notification that a recording is in progress, or active participation in a conversation.
As a result, a seller eavesdropping on a buyer may be breaking the law.
“Because a lot of modern consumer electronics such as Ring, Nest, or Blink automatically record HD audio, sellers simply plug them in and then do not pay attention anymore,” says Field, who adds that sellers often believe they have the right to record whatever happens inside their home due to property ownership.
“If the buyer or showing agent does not know that the microphone is recording everything they say, there is no consent from any party in that room. That is not only a violation of the real estate ethics code, but it also becomes a possible wiretapping case.”
To protect clients, some brokerages now require sellers to sign agreements stating that they won’t listen in during showings.
The presence of home security systems are also supposed to be noted in MLS listings as there is a field that asks about audio/video surveillance.
“Some agents also put in the private agent remarks regarding if that is in use as a heads up, but audio should really be disabled to be compliant with the law,” says Ameer.
“However, this isn’t really being enforced based on what I’ve seen yet and it’s hard to police.”
Knowing that they’re likely being monitored as they tour a home,potential homebuyersare now finding themselves on guard.
According to the LendingTree survey, at least 22% ofprospective homebuyerssaid they avoided discussing their offer strategy or budget while inside the home, and communicated with their real estate agent only by text while within the house.
“Buyers should be able to share their impressions of the home as they tour it and openly discuss layout, condition, repairs, smells, noise, awkward spaces, price, and whether the home actually fits their life,” saysSander Scott, a broker and owner of Net Real Estate in Northern Michigan.
“However, the prevalence of these devices have generally made the showing experience for buyers less useful overall because buyers need to refrain from verbalizing their thoughts as they tour the home.”
The saddest part is that potential buyers feel like they have to mask their enthusiasm for a home they like, with 22% avoiding showing excitement for a home so they don’t influence future negotiations. Another 21% avoid saying anything negative for the same reason.
Cameras can also make people feel uncomfortable, to the point that 19% of homebuyers say they’ve left a showing or open house because of the feeling of being watched.
“I remember showing out-of-town buyers one home that had cameras literally in every room staring at us—there was one in the living room on the fireplace mantle and one on the dressers in the bedrooms—it was the most uncomfortable feeling ever,” says Ameer.
“The buyers felt like they had to tiptoe through the house. Needless to say, we were all creeped out and didn’t want to continue the showing.”
There are of course legitimate reasons why sellers want their spy cams on during showings, especially when it comes to protecting their property.
“Many sellers don’t want to disable the audio in their doorbell for safety and security reasons, especially when the home is on display for the world to see,” says Ameer.
However, sellers who do listen in on home tours sometimes get more than they bargained for, and not always in a good way.

“My experience is sellers that watch their house get shown always get their feelings hurt,” saysAmerica Foy, a broker associate with The Grubb Company in the East Bay Area of California.
“They hear buyers complaining about the smell, how cheap the closet mirrors look, how dark the property is, and the occasional, ‘I like the kitchen counters…’ never quite makes up for ‘the bathroom looks like it escaped from 1989.'”
On the other hand, cameras do sometimes protect a seller’s property.
“Once at a showing in Scottsdale, one child knocked over the custom lighting fixture in a foyer. The showing agent claimed that the glass was already on the floor. Footage from the foyer camera showed this kid pulling the fixture,” says Field.
“Game over. Insurance of the brokerage paid the claim without problems.”
Occasionally, however, a seller will hear something that can change the course of a future negotiation, which is probably the biggest concern right now for buyers and their agents.
Before there was audiovisual surveillance, most comments about a home would come from feedback after a showing between the listing and buyers’ agents.
Today, it can happen in real time before a potential buyer has even walked in the door.
“Modern smart doorbells capture crystal-clear audio 50 feet away from the front door,” says Field. “From the moment you arrive to the house, consider yourself in a reality show.”
Ameer says she always advises her clients to check their behavior as soon as they approach the front door. “I tell them to keep their comments/feedback to themselves, and we can discuss when we get back in the car.”
Field adds that he actually saw a deal fail in Tempe because of a recording inside a home.
“There was an active smart hub in the countertop. The buyers came, insulted the interior paint job, said nasty things about the seller, and openly boasted how low their offer will be. And they said this in front of the person who was watching it on their cell phone live,” says Field.
The owner took it personally and two days later, when those buyers made an offer, she rejected it immediately.
“Egos destroy deals way faster than leaky roofs.”
However, the greatest potentially damaging comments a prospective buyer can make “on camera” are financial.
“The comments a potential buyer makes about the cash they have available to buy the potential property, how flexible their timeline is, what their contingencies are and how costly or how far their pre-approval stretches, affect or severely limit the potential buyer’s negotiating position,” saysCody Schuiteboer, president and CEO of Best Interest Financial.
In other words, there’s a reason most buyer’s agents now prep their clients pre-showing not to discuss anything related to numbers, motivation, and strategy inside the property.
“A seller who overhears that a potential buyer has the financial means to buy the property and is also willing to buy the property has the incentive to hold firm or counter the price,” says Schuiteboer.
“The most effective way to ensure you don’t overpay for a potential property is to have discipline about what you say.”
The bottom line is that for now, buyers should go into showings with the assumption that spy cams may be active.
“Treat every home visit as a formal business negotiation held in a public place,” says Field. “Control your emotions until you leave the neighborhood.”

hed: Florida’s famed luxury ‘holdout house’ finally sold — but its next chapter a total mystery
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


On the southernmost tip of Clearwater Beach, FL, a luxurious beachfront cottage whose owners reportedlyrefused all buyout offersfor decades is now the lone single-family house in a sea of large condo developments.
The property’s future is now in question after it sold for nearly $3 million last fall.
In September 2023, the unique property at 887 S Gulfview Blvd., dubbed the “Holdout House,” hit themarket for asmidge under $7 million.
But despite what must have been intense developer interest, the Holdout House didn’t sell. There were multiple price cuts until the property was scooped up by JRP Property Group LLC for $2.99 million in November 2025, according to public records. The seller is listed as Breeze Property Group LLC.
JRP Property Group is registered to James R. Polacek, who is listed as a real estate agent with Charles Rutenberg Realty, Inc in Clearwater.
Reached by phone, Polacek said, “I’m not the one you want to talk to. You’d want to talk to my business partner. If he’s interested, he’ll call you. I seriously doubt he will be, though.”
Cara Ameer, a Ponte Vedra, FL-based Coldwell Banker agent, is familiar with the house and more willing to talk about what might be its future.
“This is a very special home and one of a kind. It is likely for redevelopment on some level, despite it being a treasured piece of history along Clearwater Beach,” she tells Realtor.com®.
“It could be turned into a larger oceanfront estate, condo building or hotel/resort or restaurant. I’m sure the property will be transformed into its highest and best use, despite locals likely not being in favor of that.”
“The price of progress makes it harder to preserve these properties that have so much legacy and history, unfortunately.”
Over six decades, two different sets of homeowners refused to give into the apparent pressure of condo developers who wanted to snap up the last remaining undeveloped oceanfront in the immediate area. This left the house with a small moat of green space holding off dense multistory dwellings.
Built by original owners Carl Wilkens and Mary Ackert in 1963, the four-bedroom Victorian-style gray house with double-tiered terraces is nestled on a .3-acre lot a stone’s throw from Clearwater Harbor.
In 2021, Cathy Salustriwrote about her experienceon a dolphin-watch boat with a captain who had a lot to say about the Holdout House, as well as owner Ackert, nicknamed the “The Holdout Lady.” (It’s unclear why Ackert’s husband did not figure into the David and Goliath narrative.)
“You see, she loved her home and she loved her view. See that gray house right there?” the captain reportedly told the boat’s occupants. “That was her home, and no matter how much money the developer offered her, she politely refused.”
“Then things got-not-so nice,” Salustri recalled the captain telling the enthralled boaters. “As construction started on the condos, things got increasingly nasty. Workers ‘accidentally’ cut her power lines. A bulldozer ‘accidentally’ broke the water main that supplied her drinking water…”
“And still, she stayed in her home, no matter how ugly the developer made things for her.”
According to local lore—or at least this particular boat captain—the “Holdout Lady” then “had the deed to the property changed so that particular piece of land could only ever be used as a single-family home.”
Finally, in 1986, the original owners decided to sell, but reportedly only under the condition that the buyers—local newscaster Joe Mannion and his wife, Elizabeth—not sell the house to developers, according toTampa Bay Creative Loafing.
According to public record, the house changed hands for a mere $133,200.
Reportedly, Mannion and his wife lived there—presumably also fighting off developers—until their deaths and the home passed to their estate, then went to market in September 2023 for $6.99 million.
Listings showed that the boat captain’s declaration of the home’s deed being changed to make it off limits to development was nothing but a tall tale.
In an Oct. 7, 2024 Arc RealtyGroup listing, the property, now discounted to $4.75 million, was advertised as being “zoned for 30 units per acre, making 9 units possible. 2 parking spaces required per unit (to be verified by buyer).”

This was only days after multipleFacebookposts claimed that the house had been “hit hard” by Hurricane Helene.
“Entire porch gone. It’s in CP Marina Pool. All water side windows gone. Total loss damage inside. Minimum 4″ water inside. So sad,” wrote Cindy Yassay, who posted accompanying photos of what appeared to be major damage to both the interior and exterior of the home.
But the home was repaired. Tax assessment records show that $419,706 was poured into improvements, likely in 2025.
It’s unclear why the seller would have put that much money into renovating the house if common knowledge would have it that it would soon be razed for development.
In the new $2,999,000 listing late that same year,photos showeda 2,604-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath house worthy of a spread in a home decor magazine. There are crisp white walls, stainless steel appliances, an open kitchen with stone countertops, a formal dining and sitting area, sunlight-splashed bedrooms, and a spiral wooden staircase to a decked-out third-floor loft.
But it’s the stunning beach views, teal-blue water so close to the porch it feels as if one could reach out and touch it, and 120 feet of private Intracoastal frontage that are the crowning features.
“‘The Holdout Home’ historically resisted development,” begins the original listing, posted by Jim Price ofEngel & Völkers Belleairin Sept. 26, 2023, a few days before Hurricane Helene smashed into the house. “It now stands as the only single-family home on the southernmost point of Clearwater Beach, FL! Over 180 degrees of waterfront warms your soul, as the sun sets in the Gulf of Mexico.
“It is the only home that offers this view. Folks have been boating nearby for decades appreciating the beauty of this historic structure wondering who lives there? Well now, it can be you!”
The listing’s last line proves that the boat captain’s tale about the property being off limits to development was merely good storytelling: “Please inquire about the commercial development opportunities with this unique property as well!”
Co-listing agent Kristin Hallamek of Engel & Völkers Belleair tells Realtor.com that the sellers were the adult children of the Mannion couple.
“They’d had it for years in the family, and it was time to sell,” she says. “The market was up.”
She says the home received multiple offers, but none that were near the $7 million the sellers were asking, so this time it was the Mannion brothers who were the “holdouts.”
However, all that changed when the hurricane hit. “They ended up selling it off market,” she says. “Probably should have taken them,” she says of the offers that were refused.
She adds that she has gone by the house on a boat and that the home appears to have been completely renovated.
“I’m glad it looks like somebody is keeping it as is,” she says. “It would make a very busy Airbnb.”
“To step out a door and you’re four steps into sand is pretty unique.”

hed: Real estate insiders reveal the real cost of Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax — and what it’s really doing to NYC
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Buyers with big budgets are bewildered. Brokers, builders and building boards are apoplectic. It’s only been a month Mayor ZohranMamdani’s so-called “pied-à-terre” taxon second homes valued over $5 million took effect, and the city’s real estate market isalready reeling.
“The numbers are so beyond what people are interested in spending every year that many people are rethinking,” said Pamela D’Arc, a Compass agent who frequently sells luxury city residences to tech and Hollywood execs from California, told The Post. “People are listing things for sale that they don’t use a lot. Buyers are sitting on the sidelines. I have clients that have changed their price point to be just under $5 million.”Highly priced new buildings that lure out-of-town buyers are particularly vulnerable to the tax, which starts at 4% and rises to 6.5% annually in Phase 1. (A second phase will update the calculation in the 2028/29 tax year).
“We had a buyer from Madrid who also has a home in Miami. She was very attracted to the [new] Giorgio Armani Residences at 760 Madison Avenue, partially because of the name, partially because of the location,” Douglas Wagner, Director of Brokerage Services at BOND New York, told The Post. “She had been watching a particular unit pre-market while it was still under construction, and when the price came down, she got serious. But we were coming up on July 1, and we told her about the pied-à-terre tax and what to expect. Around July 11th, she let us know that she was suspending her search because of the extra expense.”That unit, No. 6B at the fashion-branded Lennox Hill condominium has common charges and taxes that add up to roughly $120,000 per year. Based on its city-calculated valuation, the $8.9 million unit would eventually owe another $40,000 to $50,000 in annual tax, Wagner says. That sponsor unit is still for sale as a result.
The many “empty towers” of Billionaires Row, both lauded and lampooned as Swiss bank vaults for the globetrotting elite, are likely to be hit hardest.At 432 Park — where Jennifer Lopez and Alex Rodriguez, as well as billionaires like Saudi property sultan Fawaz Al Hokair, have inked deeds — at least one third of the units will be subject to the tax, the Wall St. Journal reported. That puts owners at the building on the hook for about $3 million in tax on top of the $3.6 million in property taxes owners already pay. Many of the units at that super-tall building are owned by hush-hush LLCs, and if they too turn out to be owned by out-of-towners (which they almost surely are) that figure could be much higher.Another Billionaire’s Row ultra-tower, 220 Central Park South, is also on shaky ground. It’s home to musician Sting and a cache of billionaires, including prime Mamdani target Ken Griffin, who has a $238 million, practically unused, playpen.
In his kerfuffle with the mayor, Griffin has threatened to withdraw his massive fortune from NYC. No wonder: He could be on the hook for another $1 million a year, on top of the $837,000 in property tax he now pays, the Journal reported.
But, as wealthy pied-a-terre buyers change their shopping habits to limit their tax exposure, the real estate market is heating up in surprising places.For decades, co-ops were Manhattan’s most sluggish property category — suddenly they’re hot.“The co-op market is the value buy, as it has been for years,” said D’Arc. “Now, people who had been shopping for condos are looking at co-ops that are pied-à-terre friendly.”The math is simple. In the first quarter of the year the average condo resale in Manhattan with three or more bedrooms (just the kind of plush pad part-time New Yorkers covet) closed for over $6.7 million, according to a Brown Harris Stevens study. The same category of co-op sold for just $3.7 million — coming in under the tax threshold.
And while many prestige co-ops shun pied-à-terre buyers, others welcome them and their share-boosting dollars.New condos towers with amenities a la mode and inventory that skirts the tax threshold are also seeing action. At the 65-unit, 2023-built Mandarin Oriental Residences, Fifth Avenue, broker Peter Zaitzeff credits the tax for sending buyers who would have otherwise spent more his way.In June, the building inked goose-egg deals; but since the tax kicked in Zaitzeff has moved two. Those units 22A and 19A were asking $3.95 million and $4.995 million, respectively, skating just under the number that activates the tormenting tax.“If you look at the building makeup, 95% of the remaining inventory is under $5 million,” the Serhant broker said. “Its actually, sort of, I don’t know… benefited us. We are doing more sales now than we did prior.”
Another building that’s seeing upside to the downside is One Wall St., Harry Macklowe’s ambitious 566-unit residential conversion of an Art Deco skyscraper.“We did a study on what level our existing population would be affected by the tax — and it was close to none,” said Anna Zarro, President of One Wall Street Sales.In fact, Zarro expects to transact off the new tax. Virtually all 32 of the building’s current listings won’t have to pay. At the same time, it has a 100,000-square-foot smorgasbord of swank supplementaries — from a private restaurant, 75-foot pool, fitness center and spa, to  co-working spaces and speciality children’s space. Downstairs there’s the luxury department store Printemps and a Whole Foods. All of that makes it ideal as a home away from home.
“We’re extremely well-suited for those that have multiple homes, with a wide range of residences under the $5 million threshold,” she said.Meanwhile, ultra-luxe rentals are booming.“I’m seeing a ton of activity in the high-end rental market,” says Caroline Bass of Corcoran. “These people, maybe they would have bought. Now, they’re deciding to rent a six-figure apartment.”Top towers like 30 Park Place, 56 Leonard and 111 Murray St. in Tribeca, all loaded with $20,000-plus-a-month rentals, are catnip to this rich, but not insensitive, demographic.
Brokers say these units are already moving. Zaitzeff notes that the penthouse at the Bellemont at 1165 Madison Ave. on the Upper East Side, was rented for $85,000 per month at the start of July.“There are some people who just press pause,” added Zarro. “There are some people who are waiting to see how things play out. And there are some people who are renting very, very high-ticket condos. They’re doing the math on various taxes, including the pied-à-terre tax, and they’re saying, ‘Fine, I’ll rent.’”
But, while some are figuring out their way around the tax and others are finding small benefits, overall, it’s a net loss for NYC and it’s real estate market, insiders insist.“If anything, given the dire strait of the city budget, we should be encouraging more transactions, not less — because the more velocity we have in the market, the more real property tax gets generated, and that goes right into the city’s general fund,” said Jason Haber, a Compass agent and co-founder of the American Real Estate Association. “Instead this tax does just the opposite.”

hed: One-of-a-kind Steamboat Springs mansion with gondola views hits the market for $14M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Many Colorado mountain homes can claim ski-in/ski-out status, butpremier viewsof a gondola gliding just past your windows? That’s a bit more rare — and exactly what the next owners of this Steamboat Springs residence can look forward to.
The sprawling stone estate at 2555 Ski Trail Lane has returned to the market for $13.95 million, offering buyers another chance to own an extraordinary property just steps from the ski base.
The six-bedroom, 7.5 bath residence spans an incredible 11,317 square feet and overlooks the Steamboat Ski Base, Emerald Mountain, the Yampa Valley, and the Flat Tops.
Completed in 2009 after a six-year construction process, the home was conceived as a legacy estate rather than a typical luxury build. According to listing agent Broby Leeds, every detail was selected with permanence in mind, from the locally sourced stone to handcrafted finishes gathered from artisans around the world.
“What has made the home famous locally isn’t a celebrity owner, but the home itself,” Leeds says. “Positioned directly beside the Steamboat Gondola, thousands of skiers and visitors pass by it each winter, making it one of the most iconic private residences in Steamboat Springs.”
That craftsmanship is immediately evident upon entering. Massive stone walls, reclaimed timber beams, handcrafted ironwork, and soaring expanses of glass create interiors that feel equal parts mountain lodge and European manor. Among the home’s most striking architectural features is a custom range hood that rises more than 20 feet through a skylit shaft, flooding the chef’s kitchen with natural light.
The stonework may bethe home’s defining features.
“The exterior stonework was created using locally sourced boulders that had naturally weathered for decades before being individually anchored into place,” Leeds says. But the thoughtful craftsmanship extends well beyond the facade.
“Many of the interior stair railings, exterior deck railings, and even the custom refrigerator handles incorporate reclaimed chairlift cables—an authentic tribute to the community’s skiing heritage that’s unlike anything you’ll find elsewhere,” he says.
Although the residence stretches across three elevator-serviced levels, it was intentionally designed for everyday living, with nearly all essential spaces, including two primary suites, located on the main floor.
The amenities are equally impressive. A temperature-controlled wine cellar stores more than 2,000 bottles, while a private theater, indoor shooting range, hot tub, expansive entertaining deck, and three separate laundry rooms ensure the home is as functional as it is extravagant. Nearly every major room frames panoramic mountain views, while walls of glass keep the gondola and surrounding peaks constantly in sight.
Despite its old-world appearance, the residence has been thoughtfully updated with modern technology, including a fully integrated Savant smart-home system that controls lighting, climate, audio, motorized shades, and entertainment throughout the home.

The location, especially foractive Coloradans, is hard to beat. Owners can walk directly to skiing, mountain biking, hiking, restaurants, and the Steamboat base area while remaining just minutes from downtown.
“It would be extraordinarily difficult, if not impossible, to recreate today,” Leeds said. “You’re buying one of Steamboat’s true legacy estates, something that simply can’t be built again.”

hed: A new steward for Boston’s oldest lighthouse?
subhead: Feds are putting site of Boston Light out for bid. The beacon itself will shine on, though.
content: The federal government is selling Boston’s light. But don’t worry, it’s not going out.The Coast Guard’s historic Light Station Boston at the mouth of Boston Harbor — the country’s oldest continually operating lighthouse — will soon be available for certain organizations to acquire at no cost, federal officials announced Monday. As part of broader efforts to dispose of unneeded property and reduce costs, the feds are offering up complex to state or local agencies, nonprofit or educational institutions, or community development organizations who might want to manage it.“(The US General Services Administration) is dedicated to the responsible stewardship of our nation’s assets, and that includes preserving significant landmarks like Light Station Boston,” said Michael Gelber, acting public buildings service commissioner, in a statement. “It is fitting, as we continue to celebrate our country’s 250th birthday, that we protect and preserve this national treasure for the enjoyment and education of future generations.”Boston Light, in Boston Harbor.Stan Grossfeld/Globe StaffBoston Light, as it’s locally known, dates to 1715 and is considered the first formally authorized lighthouse in the US. American troops burned the lighthouse in 1775 to prevent British troops from using it; the Redcoats in turn blew the lighthouse up when they exited Boston Harbor a year later. The 7-acre Little Brewster Island houses six separate structures, including the lighthouse tower and the keeper’s home. The US Coast Guard and Department of Homeland Security consider it “to be excess to the needs” of the departments, according to a federal notice of availability posted Monday. The light will still shine on, however. The US Coast Guard will continue to operate and maintain the property’s light beacon and fog signal. Interested organizations should submit letters of interest by Oct. 2. This is a breaking story and will be updated.Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Believe it, you can buy a NYC apartment for $130K — but there’s 1 tiny catch
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In a borough where the median price of an apartment hovers over $1 million, landing a Manhattan pad for just 10% of that sounds like a fever dream.
But landing in that price range, which is indeed possible, comes with a big sacrifice in space. Fret not, it’s still easy to live a life of comfort inside them.
Two of the city’s cheapest digs are pint-sized studios asking a mere $130,000 and $155,000 — measuring a cozy 364 and 250 square feet, respectively.
And there’s one that’s even smaller. A 254-square-foot abode in NoMad is on the market for a higher $320,000.
Making shoebox-living work, potential buyers need to consider “what functions you want to perform in this space,” said Laura Cattano, a personal and interior stylist, and professional organizer.
For instance: Do you want a big bed, a place to pray and meditate, a desk?
Beyond professionally, she knows it all personally, too.
“I opted for a twin-size bed because it allows me to have a dining table and proper living space and proper dressing space,” said Cattano of her own 335-square-foot studio apartment.
A king-sized bed? Forget about it. “I mean not if you actually want to live in this place,” she noted.
Her golden rule: get furniture up on legs and mount cabinets on walls.
“When you have a small space, being able to see as much of the floor as possible makes it feel bigger,” Cattano said. “It tricks the eye.”
Here’s how three of Manhattan’s pocket-sized pads stack up — and how the pros would style them.
Apartment 5Dat 35 E. 30th St., a 254-square-foot crib, has multiple exposures and in-unit washer/dryer hookups.
It was bought in October 2019 for $230,000 by a young couple that currently uses it for overflow storage while living in a $2.2 million three-bedroom upstairs, that’salso up for grabs. The pair plans to relocate for work.
At the $320,000 asking price, the home would sell for $1,259 per square foot, according to StreetEasy. The NoMad unit has a maintenance of $1,076 per month.
“You can fit a day bed and add dining furniture or style with a king bed like a hotel suite,” said listing agent Eleonora Srugo of Douglas Elliman, who holds the listing with Bernardo Mensch.
Cattano envisions a twin bed in the corner near the bathroom, a 72-inch sofa catty-corner to the kitchen, a folding screen in front of the bed for privacy, a little living space in front of the washer/dryer, plus shallow cabinets along the long wall between the windows.
Celebrity interior designer Cheryl Eisen said she would do a full wall of mirrors along the entrance wall behind a couch to reflect light into the room and make it appear bigger.
“Mount multiple floor-to-ceiling mirrors next to one another until you’ve covered the entire wall from end to end,” Eisen said. “The result will create the illusion of more space and reflect natural light from the one window you have throughout the room.”
She’d skip the dining table for a full bed, add a room-dividing bookshelf/wardrobe/clothing rack, a mounted swivel TV and a bedside writing desk that doubles as a nightstand.
Snagged in June 2019 for just under $100,000,unit 3Eat 157 W. 123rd St., is an income-restricted Housing Development Fund Corporation property, meaning buyers must live there full-time and cannot earn more than 120% of the Area Median Income, which for a single person is $136,080 per year.
It’s a 250-square-foot studio in an elevator building asking $155,000, or $620 per square foot. Monthly maintenance is just $350 and includes heat and hot water.
For it, Cattano suggested a corner twin bed, a love seat along the main wall, a tiny coffee table in front of the sofa with a chair or two, and a 18- to 24-inch table by the bed that can do double duty as a nightstand and side table for the sofa.
Eisen said she’d do full-wall side mirrors, a full-size bed, an accent foyer table, a love seat, distinct area rugs to define “rooms,” and replace the closet with space-saving “zigzag doors that don’t open up as far into the living room.” Eisen suggested putting a radiator cover across the whole back wall, adding a chair and turning it into a desk. And a coffee table would serve as the eating area.
The largest footprint of the trio, a walk-up studio,No. 4Cat 424 E. 115th St., is a 364-square-foot pad. The East Harlem unit was acquired in 2025 for $95,000. Also subject to HDFC income caps, it has oak hardwoods, a deep cast-iron soaking tub, and a vanity.
It’s on the market for $130,000, with a monthly maintenance of $775.
The owner “loved the location and the price and knew it was a place to get her foothold in New York City,” said Compass’ Gennaro Hathaway who is listing the unit with colleague Karen D. Shenker.
Now that she has settled in for a year, the owner “wants to purchase a larger place to have room to tape her comedy podcast,” the agent said.
For this home, Eisen would place a full-sized bed in the rear nook flanked by nightstands and mirrored walls, place a couch against the entrance wall, facing the bed, and put a coffee table in front of it. She’d have a bookshelf/closet-backed TV console to split the bedroom and living space, and add a narrow kitchen island with stools to also serve as a dining bar.
Overall, she said, “When you’re designing a small space, every square foot has to justify itself. Forget about trying to fit in the most furniture, instead think about choosing smart furniture.”

hed: Palm Springs sees home prices plummet as market finally cools off
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Home prices are beginning to soften in one of California’s hottest luxury markets as the desert real estate market starts to cool off.
Two upscale homes in Palm Springs most sought-after neighborhoods have recently undergone notable price cuts of about $70,000, signaling even luxury sellers are adjusting their expectations after years of soaring demand.
One recently built custom home saw its asking price trimmed by $30,000, dropping from $1.585 million to $1.555 million.
Built in 2023, the 2,907-square-foot residence features three bedrooms, four bathrooms and sits on an oversized 0.41-acre corner lot with mountain views.
The listing boasts 18-foot ceilings, three grand primary suites, custom furnishings, a professionally designed outdoor entertaining space with a barbecue bar, putting green and water feature, along with smart-home features.
The fully furnished property is also marketed as Airbnb-friendly, with short-term rental licenses available.
Another Palm Springs luxury home underwent an even steeper reduction, with its asking price falling $40,000 from $1.638 million to $1.598 million.
The remodeled mid-century modern home spans 1,887 square feet and includes four bedrooms and three bathrooms.
Originally built in 1961, the residence features walls of windows overlooking a south-facing deck and swimmer’s pool, as well as three bedroom suites in the main house and a detached guest wing complete with its own kitchenette and bath.
The listing also highlights owned solar panels and a brand-new roof.
The price cuts come as Palm Springs’ once booming housing market settles down after the buying frenzy during the pandemic.
Back then, low mortgage rates and more remote work led to high demand for second homes and vacation properties.
These factors drove home prices up quickly and created strong competition among buyers.
Today, the market is showing signs of balance. Zillow estimates the average Palm Springs home value is about $619,600, down 1.7% over the past year, while homes are now taking roughly 56 days to go under contract.
