Inventory has also grown, giving buyers more options than they had during the height of the market.
Redfin similarly describes Palm Springs as a “somewhat competitive” market, with homes typically selling for around 3% below their asking price and taking about 70 days to sell.
Just 9.6% of homes are selling above list price, reflecting a market that has shifted away from the bidding wars that once defined the desert oasis.
Although these two listings are just a small part of the market, their combined $70,000 in price cuts highlight a bigger trend.
Sellers are adjusting their expectations, and buyers now have more room to negotiate in one of Southern California’s best-known luxury areas.

hed: COVID-era hot spot flooded with listings after pandemic buying boom grinds to a halt
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The Music City party is over for home sellers.
Nashville has quietly become the second-toughest place in Americato sell a house, according to a new Redfin report, trailing only Miami and beating out three major Texas metros in the process.
Sellers now outnumber buyers by a staggering 128.8%, giving house hunters more choices, less competition and serious room to haggle.
“Buyers are taking their time these days. There are a significant number of listings on the market, people are taking their time and waiting for the right one,” Aaron Glicken, a Redfin Principal agent based in Nashville, saidin the report.
“Buyers feel like they need to get a significant deal. They’re submitting low offers on homes that are already priced well for the market.”
New listings in the metro have jumped 9.4%, dwarfing the national increase of just 0.1%. Homes are also lingering on the market far longer, a median of 78 days compared to 49 days nationwide.
Nationally, sellers outnumbered buyers by an estimated 48.5% in June, meaning the whole country has tilted toward buyers to some degree. But Nashville’s imbalance is nearly triple that national figure.
Redfin agent Kristin Sanchez pointed to a mix of forces reshaping the local market.
“This market is giving homeowners confidence they’ll actually have somewhere to move after selling. Many homeowners with super-low interest rates have delayed life changes for several years. Now, those life events can’t be postponed any longer, so they’re entering the market despite higher mortgage rates,” Sanchez said. “Some sellers recognize that the frenzied appreciation of 2021 and 2022 has leveled off. They’re choosing to sell while home values remain relatively stable rather than trying to perfectly time the market.”
Not everyone is timing it well, though.
“Many sellers are learning the hard way. They’re turning down early offers because buyers are coming in low, only to realize down the road they’re still getting low offers or need to lower the price,” Glicken said.
The shift marks a dramatic reversal from Nashville’s pandemic-era frenzy, when the city was one of the hottest housing markets in the country.
Home prices climbed just 2.8% year-over-year in June, landing just under $500,000. That’s a sharp cooldown from the roughly 20% annual gains sellers were pocketing a few years ago, back when the typical home in the city sold for under $400,000.
Years of new construction have flooded the metro with inventory, while elevated home prices and mortgage rates have chased off a chunk of would-be buyers, tilting negotiating power firmly towardthose still shopping.
Sanchez said she’s still seeing transplants arrive from Florida, California and Chicago, though the wave of New York buyers has thinned out considerably since the pandemic.
Price cuts aren’t the only leverage buyers are using. Closing costs and repair credits have become common bargaining chips too, Sanchez said.
“Many buyers, especially first-time buyers, opt for new construction, where they can get a brand-new home with a super-low mortgage rate and closing-cost assistance,” she said.
Builders are sweetening deals with fixed rates as low as 4.99%, Sanchez said, sometimes paired with temporary rate buydowns. Many sellers, meanwhile, are covering closing costs just to help buyers lower their rates.
In one recent deal, Sanchez helped first-time buyers using a down-payment assistance program land a home for $15,000 under its appraised value, with the sellers covering 100% of closing costs and agreeing to repairs before closing.
“I currently have another buyer under contract for $60,000 under list price right now. A couple of years ago, these same buyers likely would have competed against multiple offers with little negotiating power,” Sanchez said.
With buyers no longer racing the clock, they’re able to shop around and wait for the right fit instead of settling out of fear of losing out.
“Post-pandemic, we were one of the markets where prices skyrocketed and now we’re seeing a correction fueled by higher mortgage rates and lower buyer demand. I do think that prices have corrected enough to bring more buyers to the market than the previous year,” Glicken said.
For sellers, that means the days of naming a price and watching offers roll in are gone. Sanchez said the flood of competing listings has made accurate pricing essential from day one, and sellers should brace for buyers pushing harder on terms than they have in years.
Rising prices have also squeezed out longtime locals, Sanchez said.
“Home prices have risen so much that people who have been here for 10, 15, 20 years can’t afford to buy here anymore,” she said. “Everything has slowed down a bit since housing prices have increased so much.”
Homes that are freshly updated and ready for move-in tend to have an edge, Glicken said.
“The sellers that do upgrades and touch-up work like repairs and paint, tend to sell faster. Buyers today want a move-in-ready home more than ever. They have more choices in today’s market and prices and interest rates are still elevated,” he said.

hed: Aggressive HOAs are running out of money and foreclosing on more residents than ever before
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s homeowners associations are running out of money — and patience.
Amid rising insurance premiums, drained reserve funds and increased safety measures in the wake of theSurfside condominium collapse, the country’s hundreds of thousands of homeowners associations are cracking down on delinquent residents.
Even more startling, HOAs are skipping grace periods and handing delinquent accounts over to attorneys.
HOA foreclosures spiked nearly 40% in two years to 6,376 properties in the first quarter, according to real estate analytics firm Attom, as reported by theWall Street Journal, putting its pace ahead of overall mortgage foreclosure rates.
These foreclosure sales are “like most foreclosures in that they are typically an auction,” attorney Kirk Pearson, who represents homeowners in HOA disputes, told The Post.
“If the property is sold at auction, the homeowner has a 90-day right to redemption where they can buy the property back by paying any delinquent amounts plus any collection fees and costs. If there are no bidders at the foreclosure sale, then the HOA takes ownership of the property. The HOA can then keep the property, sell it, transfer it to the bank where there is a senior lien holder, or allow bank foreclosure.”
A homeowner is often expected to clear their delinquent dues, fees and legal costs during the redemption period following a foreclosure sale.
“In some states, like Pennsylvania, the homeowner has no ‘right of redemption,’ which means at the fall of the hammer at a sheriff’s sale, the homeowner no longer has a right to pay off the debt,” Stephen M. Hladik, who has a Pennsylvania-basedmortgage foreclosure legal practice, said to The Post.
“HOA foreclosure sales can be subject to various liens and encumbrances, and a buyer should do research to see what types of liens there are against the property, and whether those liens survive the foreclosure sale.”
Missed dues are often only a fraction of the bill — the real burden comes from ballooning collection costs, Pearson said. HOAs frequently outsource delinquencies to specialized collection firms that profit by tacking heavy fees onto outstanding balances.
Worse, those firms are often owned by the same corporate attorneys advising the HOA, the California attorney noted. That gives the HOA’s legal team a lucrative financial reason to aggressively pursue foreclosures instead of helping residents resolve their debt.
Millions of Americansare part of HOA communities, wheredues are rising.
“HOAs are being forced into more aggressive collections to avoid their own financial collapse,” Brian Fox, co-founder of real estate technology firm Benutech, told the Journal.
Families inMagnolia Cove, an 80-home community outside Charlotte, North Carolina, are contending with the increase in their monthlyhomeowners association duesfrom $350 to $1,250, with a $10,000 special assessment tacked on for good measure.
In 2025, HOAs filed over 285,000 liens, up about 8.8% from a year earlier, Benutech, which tracks HOA delinquency trends and foreclosures, told the Journal.
Besides delinquencies, costs have been rising for HOAs in insurance premiums, staffing, lawn care and materials. The annual insurance premium at one Long Island HOA surged to $360,000 from $60,000.
Plus, there’s the expense of meeting stricter safety measures, which were instituted in the wake of the partial collapse of the Champlain Towers South condo, a 2021 tragedythat claimed 98 lives.
As unpaid dues trigger legal battles and delayed upkeep, the mounting cash crunch isn’t just threatening individual homeowners — it’s tanking property values for entire neighborhoods.
In many states, “super priority” laws even let HOAs foreclose over unpaid dues before banks can.
At Fairview Condo 1 in Middle Island, N.Y., 15 of its 202 units are allegedly behind on the $595 monthly dues, amounting to a monthly shortfall of roughly $8,900. Ten of them are in foreclosure. The board is handling it by levying special assessments, and postponing upkeep, the WSJ noted.
Floyd Mayweather Jr.’s Las Vegas home was saddled with $25,000 in unpaid dues starting in January 2025, plus interest and legal fees, the WSJ found.
Mayweather’s attorney said the unpaid dues stemmed from an accounting oversight that has since been settled following a recent overhaul of the boxer’s financial team.

hed: Home of the Week: Off a dirt road, this Maine beach house is a private getaway for $1m
subhead: It was built in 1955 before coastal regulations banned homes so close to the shore
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

7 Pond Island Way, Phippsburg, Maine

$1,050,000

StyleCottage

Year built1955

Square feet600

Bedrooms2

Baths1 full

SewerPrivate

WaterWell

Taxes$7,059 (2025)


The nose needs a summer getaway, too.

And this cottagein midcoast Maineoffers olfactory benefits fromfragrant beach rose,potent pitch pine,the salty essence of the Atlantic Ocean, and an earthy landward element added from breezes off theKennebec River.

Built in 1955 before coastal regulations banned homes so close to the shore, this 600-square-foot home offers an outdoor porch and companion deck, an enclosed porch, and a living room with large windows, all positioned to maximizePopham Beachviews. (The public entrance toPopham Beach State Park, one of Maine’s most popular, is also nearby.)


“It’s on a private dirt road,” saidCarrie Logan, co-listing agent.“Nobody is going down there unless they are going to one of the few houses in the neighborhood. … You barely have cell reception. It’s a getaway.”

A path shielded by the foliage meanders back to an entry door between the 16-square-foot porch on the left and the 243-square-foot deck on the right.


The door opens into the 122-square-foot enclosed porch, where the two exterior walls are chock-full of windows that seemingly knit into one large view. The exposed ceiling beams and walls are painted white.

A second door allows access to the interior, starting with the 190-square-foot living room, which is the pivot point for the rest of the home. It’s also where the word rustic roars into the consciousness — the walls are knotty pine, the fireplace is exposed brick, the flooring is beach-friendly vinyl, and the ceiling is white. It should be noted that to the right of the door as one enters, the exterior wall has two large, muntin-free, double-hung windows looking over the deck toward the shore. There is a wood-burning stove insert in the fireplace.




The kitchen is inset into a nook at the rear of the house and features a white, four-burner electric stove, white cabinets on the upper walls, and a window above the sink. Just before the kitchen, a doorway leads to a rear entrance. The hallway, with exposed ceiling beams and walls, is painted white. It’s used for laundry, and three steps up is a so-called cousin’s room, a flat space big enough for a mattress underneath a rectangular window.

The primary bedroom has the premier position among the two bedrooms: It’s on the beach-facing side of the home and overlooks the enclosed porch. The walls are knotty pine as is the ceiling. The flooring is vinyl and there is a closet in the 82-square-foot room.




The second bedroom shares a wall with the primary. It’s a smidge smaller at 79 square feet, has the same planked pine for the walls, and vinyl for the flooring, but no closet. One wall has a pair of casement windows stacked above each other, and the second has a double-hung window.

Also off the living room is the 34-square-foot bathroom. It has a white pedestal sink and teal ceramic tile on the lower half of the wall. The upper level is knotty pine paneling. There is an insert shower with a curtain and a double-hung window. The home also has an outdoor shower.

Nearby islands includeSeguin Island with its historic, functioning lighthouse,constructed at President George Washington’s orders, andPond Island National Wildlife Refuge,a complex of several islands.


Logan said it’s a seasonal cottage on an 1.34-acre lot that includes 200 feet of waterfront. Any expansion plans must be approved by municipal and state regulators.

Logan andPoe Cilleyof Vitalius Real Estate Group has the listing.

hed: Price cuts creep back up as summer selling season stalls
subhead: Western metros lead in price cuts
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
After a strong spring and promising early summer, July saw homebuying stagnate as a result ofrising borrowing costs,forcing sellers to slash prices to revive demand.
The share of listings with a price cut reached 20% in July, nearly even with last year’s levels, after running close to 2 percentage points lower throughout spring, according to the latestRealtor.com® housing market trends reportreleased on Monday.
For the first six months of the year, the dominant theme of the national housing market wassellers pricing realisticallyfrom the outset to meet buyers where they are to avoid listings going stale.
By the end of June, the share of for-sale homes across the U.S. with price cuts was 1.9 percentage points lower than the prior year.
However, as summer entered its peak, price cuts picked up as vacationing would-be buyers pulled back and aging listings piled up on the market.
“We are seeing the housing market run up against some headwinds, especially on the mortgage rate front, at the exact time when buyer demand starts to dip seasonally,” says Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel. “So while the realistic pricing narrative is still there, the story has weakened a bit recently.”
On a month-over-month basis, the share of listings with price reductions rose from 18.8% to 20%.
“July might be hinting at even softer demand than sellers are anticipating,” notes Krimmel. “This will be something to watch as the summer progresses.”
At the regional level, price cuts were least common in the Northeast (13.7% of listings) and Midwest (18.7%), where inventory is tight and demand is robust. By contrast, buyers had better luck finding discounted properties in the more well-supplied West (21.9%) and South (21.3%).
Yet,housing data analysispoints to early signs of market softening in the Northeast and Midwest, where the share of price-reduced listings ticked up by 1 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively, compared to July 2025.
A zoomed-in look at metro-level trends reveals that prices were slashed in July on more than a quarter of homes in 12 of the 50 largest U.S. metros, the vast majority of them located in the West or South.
Portland, OR, reclaimed the title of the metro with the highest share of discounted listings, at 31%, outpacing June’s leader, Denver, which slid to second place with 30.9%, followed by Dallas and Austin, TX, both with 28.3%.
Cory Culpepper, an agent with Douglas Elliman Austin, attributes price cuts to two main seller behaviors. First, some sellers opt to list above market value in anticipation of low offers, or in case they need to pay the buyer’s closing costs.
“Then there are sellers that see their competition selling and feel that their home should capture the same price, even though they haven’t prepared it properly for the [multiple listing service] and potential buyer showings,” Culpepper tells Realtor.com.
While some choose the strategy of listing higher at the outset, with the option of cutting the price down the line, the agent warns that this approach can be a “double-edged sword” and keep savvy buyers away, especially in a market with ample inventory.
“The cons outweigh the pros because sellers take a huge risk of ‘testing the market,’ only later to find their property with too many days on the market and now becoming the problem house,” says Culpepper.
According to the Austin agent, a buyer will always consider days on the market. And if the listing has remained unsold for an extended period of time, they will inevitably start thinking, “What’s wrong with this home and why doesn’t anyone else want it?”
Buyers are taking advantage of Austin’s widespread price cuts to secure better deals, often to the seller’s benefit as well.
“At the end of the day, asmart seller andbuyer typically find a win-win,” says Culpepper. “We are able to negotiate a lower amount and/or closing costs for the buyer to achieve a lower interest rate, which is crucial right now, and the seller is happy, since they technically net the same they would with a much lower offer.”
Echoing the agent, Krimmel says that if price cuts lead to more sales and steady time on the market, they are less of a warning sign and more proof that a market is shifting toward buyers, as reflected in the Realtor.com2026Q2 Market Clock report.
Buyers are facing economic and geopolitical headwinds this summer, as the ongoing conflict in Iran, which ignited in February, continues to drive up oil prices and fuel inflation fears.
During the July meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, policymakers voted 9-3 to hold thebenchmark federal funds rate steadyat a range of 3.50% to 3.75% while keeping the door open for potential hikes later this year to combat inflation.
The news pushed the 10-year Treasury yield higher, and a day later, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans reached 6.66%, the highest level in a year.
Krimmel says that while the spring market showed impressive resilience in the face of accelerating inflation and a mortgage rate roller coaster, these conditions may hit differently in the summer—a time when demand typically slumps.
“Our revised midyear forecast penciled in mortgage rates around 6.3% for the rest of the year, but that view was predicated on easing Middle East tensions,” points out the economist. “With the Iran conflict heating back up and oil prices at their highest level since May, that rate outlook may prove too optimistic.”
Taken together, the monthly housing data paints a picture ofa plateauing market,but not one that’s outright losing steam.
Asking prices fell for a ninth consecutive month at a near-record pace, settling at $428,950, down 2.4% compared to July 2025.
The typical listing spent 57 days on the market, one day less than a year ago, marking the first real annual decline in more than two years.
While active listings edged up slightly, new listings flatlined year over year after tracking above 2025 levels through the spring.
“When the weather gets hot, market activity cools,” concludes Krimmel.

hed: Joni Mitchell’s beachfront Malibu mansion goes on the market for whopping price — but there’s a unique bonus
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Legendary folk singer and songwriter Joni Mitchell’s stunning beachfront estate in Malibu has officially hit the market for a whopping $27 million.
Located on the prestigious Malibu Road, the4,000-square-foot Cape Cod-inspired bungalowdesigned by renowned architect Ron Goldman, offers a slice of coastal paradise that literally cannot be replicated.
Colony #17’s private pool and spa, located mere steps from the sand on the beachfront terrace, is the property’s crown jewel.
Under current strict Malibu coastal development regulations, building a new pool so close to the tide is virtually impossible –– making the property truly one-of-its-kind.
While the house itself is a masterclass in “refined and relaxed” living, it’s the soaring vaulted wood-beamed ceilings, endless walls of glass and sun-drenched floor plan flowing right into the Pacific that make it worth every penny. The property has five beautiful bedrooms and five massive bathrooms.
The property perfectly balances the seclusion of the coveted Malibu Colony with the convenience of being just outside the gates, offering easy access to the area’s top-tier boutiques, cafés and restaurants.
Inside, the home features a massive ocean-facing great room and kitchen, an expansive primary suite with front-row seats to the horizon, and a detached guest house perfect for hosting friends.
For those looking to live like a legend, the estate is being listed jointly by Nanette Iggulden of Coldwell Banker Realty and Jody Katz of Estates and Trusts Realty.
The property listing comes after the folk icon made a rare public appearance at the this year’s Juno Awards in March and shared her health struggles with the world.
While on stage to receive the Lifetime Achievement Award, Mitchell revealed, “[I] had a (brain) aneurysm which changed my life. Oddly, for the better. I went into a coma, which helped me to quit smoking.”
“I was on the road with men for years and years; now I live with a house full of women. So my life has changed for the better out of a catastrophe like a phoenix,” she had said at the time, according to a newsarticle in The Hollywood Reporter.

hed: NYC art gallery sues landlord for $1M and lease termination — for banning indoor cigar smoking
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about a smokeout.
A high-end Soho gallery and event space thought its landlord was fine with cigar smoking — until a sudden notice forced the art space to extinguish its operations after a $1 million renovation and millions paid in rent.
FineArt Fund, operating as Gallery 484, is suing its landlord, Lieberman Holdings, in New York Supreme Court. It claims Lieberman knew and accepted its business model — which featured three rooms of gallery and hospitality space, plus a “cigar-related guest experience” — when it signed a 10-year lease in 2023 at 484-490 Broome St. The building also houses an eight-unit co-op.
But on May 6, Lieberman Holdings abruptly demanded the gallery immediately cease all cigar-related activity following alleged smoke complaints, according to court filings.
Gallery 484 claims the demand came without testing, photos or official violation notices attached. The gallery halted operations and stopped paying rent, claiming the ban rendered the space unusable.
The feud quickly escalated.
Lieberman issued an $81,000 rent demand in May, followed by a civil court nonpayment proceeding in June seeking possession and $162,570 in back rent and fees.
Gallery 484 filed its Supreme Court suit, arguing the landlord breached the lease by taking away the venue’s core business model, ignoring HVAC repair obligations and thwarting the tenant’s ability to obtain a liquor license.
Gallery 484 originally locked in a lease at the building, at the corner of Broome and Wooster streets, with a monthly rent starting at $65,000 — set to scale to roughly $72,000 in the fourth year — and put down a $390,000 security deposit before doing a $1 million buildout.
It isn’t clear if the complaints stemmed from the residents who live above the space. Units inside rarely sell; the most recent deal came in March for a $3.16 million loft with two bedrooms and two bathrooms, according to StreetEasy.
Now, the venue is asking a judge to formally terminate the lease backdated to May 6, force Lieberman to return its $390,000 deposit, and award over $1 million in damages to cover the unamortized cost of its high-end renovations and building repairs.
Attorneys on both sides didn’t respond to a request for comment.

hed: Sudden surge of multimillionaires sees all cash buyers flood superrich California city
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A growing number of wealthy homebuyers are skipping mortgages altogether as all-cash offers flood San Francisco’s luxury housing market amid the city’s AI-fueled resurgence.
Redfin data showed that 30% of home sales across the San Francisco Bay Area between April and June were purchased entirely with cash — a sharp increase from 2021 when fewer than 20% of sales were all-cash transactions.
The region now ranks slightly above the national average for all-cash home purchases,NBCreported.
The shift is playing out in Noe Valley, one of San Francisco’s most sought-after family neighborhoods. Compass Realty agents James Rowbotham and Zara Rowbotham told the outlet that homes priced between $5 million and $6 million are being snapped up quickly by cash buyers.
“It was a couple that bought the house. And that was all cash. That was a cash buy, but just the two of them for seven bed, seven bath,” Rowbotham said.
The increase has coincided with an influx of artificial intelligence wealth flowing into the city, while a limited supply of homes has continued to push prices higher.
Not every buyer is cashing in AI fortunes. Dan Risman Jones of Ascend Real Estate explained that family wealth also fuels the surge, with some parents buying homes outright for their children.
“I have one transaction right now; parents are purchasing the property for the kids using all cash. I assumed that at some point the kids will get loans for it, for the property,” Risman Jones said.
Rowbotham also told NBC that San Francisco has once again become a destination for affluent buyers, with some people who relocated to Texas and Florida during the pandemic now returning as the city reasserts itself as a hub for the AI industry.
“The city is booming. It’s on fire. And I don’t see it going down anytime soon because of the location, the weather, the people,” Rowbotham said.
Both real estate agents acknowledged that competing against all-cash offers can be daunting for buyers who need financing, but said that experienced local agents and flexible offers can still help clients remain competitive.
Meanwhile in Southern California, the historic initial public offering (IPO) hassignificantly impactedthe real estate market as thousands of SpaceX employees recently acquired millionaire status.
While the company moved its headquarters to Texas, SpaceX maintains an active engineering and production hub at Hawthorne in Los Angeles County with over 7660 employees.
Real estate agents from Hawthorne to Manhattan Beach, Venice, and Santa Monica report early inquiries on $5-million-plus properties, raising fears of speculative price spikes and even tighter inventory.
The median single-family home price for California is $930,260 according to the California Association of Realtors – the highest in the country – while the median price in Los Angeles County is around $999,000.

hed: Dazzling $15.65M home inside NYC’s storied Flatiron Building finds its first-ever owner
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A 18th-floor aerie inthe Flatiron Building, one of the city’s most iconic landmarks, has found a buyer.
The three-bedroom, three-bath residence at 175 Fifth Ave. — now in the midst ofa condominium conversion, and one that has been highly successful — was asking $15.65 million, up from its $15.5 million ask in September. The deal — marking the latest inside the storied property — was first reported in theOlshan Luxury Market Report, which named it the highest priced contract of the week.
The name of the buyer, along with the final price to be paid, are not yet known.
At 3,020 square feet, the dwelling is one of only three units in the building to feature arched windows.
Inside, there’s a large, wedge-shaped great room and a roomy primary bedroom with large walk-in closets and a spa-like bath, along with a marble-countered chef’s kitchen.
Design details include white oak parquet floors and lofty ceilings, along with views of the city skyline and the rivers.
Exposed structural steel beams have also been incorporated into the design.
The triangular-shaped Beaux-Arts building overlooking Madison Square Park, at the corner of Fifth Avenue and Broadway, gave the Flatiron District its name.
Built in 1902 for George A. Fuller Construction Co., it served as an office building until its last tenant, Macmillan Publishing, vacated in 2019 after a 60-year run.
By 2023, after the owners fell into disagreement, the historic building was auctioned twice. When the first auction winner failed to pay his deposit, a second group led by Jeffrey Gural’s GFP Real Estate, alongside Sorgente Group and ABS Real Estate Partners, won the second auctionwith a $161 million bid. The Brodsky Organization later bought into the ownership group and is now managing the condo conversion.
Sales quietly launched last year, with move-ins anticipated to begin this fall.
To date, at least 15 units are in contract including a $58.5 million, five-bedroom full-floor residence on the 21st floor.
The 24-story building features large apartments that span up to six bedrooms.
The building, designed by Daniel Burnham and Frederick P. Dinkelberg of D.H. Burnham & Co. in Renaissance Revival style, comes with modern interiors by William Sofield’s Studio Sofield.
The conversion also restored the building’s terra-cotta and limestone facade, as well as the roof’s 6-foot-tall cornice. In addition, more than 1,000 windows were replaced by hand.
Amenities include 24-hour doormen, a 60-foot lap pool, a sauna, a billiards room, a lounge with a kitchenette and bike storage.
Corcoran Sunshine is leading sales and marketing.

hed: Tech billionaire-heavy California town becomes the priciest ZIP code for 1 big reason
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s most expensive ZIP code just changed coasts.
For the first time in two years, Miami’s Fisher Island has been knocked off its perch as thepriciest ZIP codein the country.
The tony 33109 enclave has been overtaken by Atherton, California’s 94027, a Silicon Valley bedroom community now flush with cash from the artificial intelligence boom, according to PropertyShark.com andBloomberg.
The swap says as much about where American fortunes are being made as it does about real estate.
South Florida’s rise was fueled by hedge funders, private equity titans and corporate transplants, a wave that included billionaires like Ken Griffin, Jeff Bezos and Carl Icahn, all of whom helped push Miami-Dade home prices into record territory.
Atherton’s comeback tells a different story, one written by AI executives and engineers suddenly sitting on enormous stock windfalls.
Tucked about 18 miles northwest of San Jose in San Mateo County, Atherton reclaimed its old crown after median home prices there shot up to nearly $10 million in the first half of 2026, a roughly 20% jump from the year before, per PropertyShark’s annual ZIP code rankings.
The town counts venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, WhatsApp co-founder Jan Koum and Golden State Warriors sharpshooter Stephen Curry among its residents, and it’s become ground zero for AI-fueled wealth creation.
Bloomberg reported Atherton has already logged five home sales north of $30 million this year, putting it on pace to match last year’s tally, as workers from OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX cash out stock and pour the winnings into sprawling estates.
The reshuffling at the top is the latest sign that the geography of extreme American wealth keeps shifting. Fisher Island first grabbed the No. 1 spot during the pandemic-era exodus, when droves of wealthy executives and investors fled high-tax states for South Florida’s shores.
Slipping to second place is hardly a demotion for Fisher Island. The 216-acre private landmass, reachable only by ferry, yacht or helicopter, remains one of the wealthiest residential ZIP codes in America. Condos there routinely fetch tens of millions of dollars, and residents get private beaches, a golf course, marinas and a country club most Americans will never set foot in.
The island is dotted with mansions, too, some listed for as much as $85 million. Just last year, Robb Report crowned Fisher Island the nation’s most expensive ZIP code, pegging its median home price at roughly $12 million.
South Florida isn’t ceding ground in the ultra-luxury market either. Bloomberg found that seven of the 11 residential sales that topped $100 million nationwide last year happened in Florida.

hed: New 10,000-seat arena is coming to California — but first, officials want to solve the traffic nightmare
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Rancho Cordova is ready for the big leagues — but they just have to make sure fans can find a parking spot first.
The California city is moving forward with plans for a massive new 10,000-seat arena that could become a sports and entertainment destination for the Sacramento region.
But before fans can pack the stands, the city is putting extra money toward solving one major problem:how everyone will get in and out.
The Rancho Cordova City Council unanimously approved an additional $40,000 for a traffic analysis of the future downtown arena project, bringing the total contract with engineering firm DKS Associates Inc. from $88,000 to $128,000.
The extra funding comes as officials evaluate the “high level of complexity of the project review,” according to a request from DKS Associates included incity staff reports.
The planned venue — located at the corner of Kilgore Road and Trade Center Drive — is expected to seat 10,000 people, with 7,500 fixed seats, and serve as the future home of two Sacramento-area Major Arena Soccer League teams.
But the arena’sambitions go far beyond soccer.
Think less arena, more entertainment takeover. The project could eventually grow into a one-stop destination with hotels, housing, restaurants, shops, a card room, a movie theater and a bowling alley — basically everything except a kitchen sink.
Rancho Cordova, it seems, isn’t just building an arena — it’s trying to build a whole new hangout.
Joshua Wood, a local developer and member of the project’s ownership group, said the arena is continuing to move forward, with the next major step being approval from the city’s Planning Commission.
Woodrecently toldThe Sacramento Bee that “lots of progress” was being made and said updates on a groundbreaking date would come soon. He previously said the privately funded project was expected to break ground this summer.
The deal comes with a few perks, including potential future revenue sharing, waived development and building permit fees, and a slice of a 13-acre city-owned parcel valued at an estimated $6.8 million.
The city has already chipped in nearly $940,000 in waived fees, covering everything from design and infrastructure reviews to zoning checks, grading permits and the legal fine print behind the development agreement.
Wood has previously said the arena would generate new tax revenue for the city, with a portion potentially returning to the project.
Rancho Cordova Mayor Garrett Gatewood has touted the arena as a game changer for the city, calling it one of thecommunity’s most important projects.
Gatewood called the arena the city’s “first chance to have actual full entertainment” and declared to the outlet, “We’re now on the map. We’re not a city that you’ve never heard of before.”
Now, city officials are working to make sure that mapdoesn’t come with a giant traffic jam.
But Rancho Cordova’s big arena dreams come as the Sacramento suburb is already having a growth spurt.

Aspreviously reportedby The Post, the city was recently named one of America’s newest boomtowns, with growth in both housing and its workforce helping push it onto SmartAsset’s list of the fastest-growing cities in the country.
Four California cities made the ranking, with three located in Northern California — but Rancho Cordova wasn’t the only Golden State newcomer making noise.
Menifee, in Riverside County, landed highest among California cities on the list after seeing a 29% jump in housing units between 2019 and 2024, according to the study.
Rancho Cordova followed at No. 70, posting a 21% increase in housing units and a 17% rise in its labor force over the same period.
Santa Clara and Sunnyvale also cracked the list, fueled by their deep ties to California’s tech economy.
SmartAssetanalyzed more than400 cities with at least 65,000 residents, narrowing the list to the 75 fastest-growing communities.
The company noted that “boomtown status does not mean growth benefits everyone equally,” but said the rankings reflect “a city’s expanding economic capacity and the new opportunities that come with it.”
For Rancho Cordova, the arena could be the latest sign that the once-overlooked city is stepping into the spotlight — as long as fans can actually get there.

hed: Dorchester’s Renovation Husbands wrote the book on how to renovate a Maine cabin — literally
subhead: The HGTV winners and Instagram stars renovated a cabin in Midcoast Maine. Their new book on design landed them on “Good Morning America.” Here, they dish on how they do it.
content:
ByLauren Daley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

This is a story about passion and patience. Taking time to listen to a house, letting it slowly tell you what it is, then turning it into your dream home.

In 2017, Western Massachusetts natives Stephen and David St. Russell bought an 1893 Dorchester Victorian that had been gutted by a previous owner. Self-taught, they renovated it themselves, documenting it on Instagram. Today, about a million followers  — along with some 300,000 onTikTok— watch the @renovationhusbandsat work.

(If you’re renovating your home, theirwebsiteis a resource. Every item is labeled, with a link tobuy the product and learn more. They do blog posts where each dollar is accounted for — with tips on how to save money.)

By 2024, they’d been tapped by HGTV to compete on “Battle on the Mountain,” hosted by Milton’s Design expert Taniya Nayak.They won.


They quit their day jobs and now work as full-time content creators and renovators. Thus, fans have been able to watch, step by step, as their second home, a 1975 Midcoast Maine chalet-style cabin they bought in 2023, became their retro nature-enclosed sanctuary. They intended for it to be an investment property but loved it so much, they kept it for themselves.

DK Publishing reached out to the St. Russells for a book on their process, and “Good Character: Design with Intention to Reveal Your Home’s Personality,” is now on shelves featuring looks at the homes they’ve renovated. The couple went on “Good Morning America” this summer to promote it.

Stephen, 35, and David, 38, took some time to talk about their Maine renovation, rural life, a duck obsession, and more.

What do you hope readers get out of “Good Character?”

Stephen: When they asked us what we wanted to write about, this idea of “character”sprang to mind. There are questions we’ve been asking ourselves since we renovated our Victorian: What does character mean? How does it apply to any type of home, be it a new construction or an old home? What are the elements and principles of design that contribute to character? We just explored that, took our lessons and mistakes along the way, and found the narrative.

David: We also interface with people everyday, digitally. We’ve had 10 years of people asking us questions. So we wrote the book in the tone of talking to our friends. We didn’t want it to sound inaccessible or pretentious. We wanted it to sound like if you had come to our house and you’re like, “Hey, why’d you pick this color?”



Your Maine cabin has a retro coziness and a deep color palette — goldenrod and jade. What was your vision?

David: Coming off the heels of the Victorian, we were looking to try something new. The Victorian is high-finish, high-gloss, precious materials, marble countertops. Maine was a great opportunity to flex a new design muscle and create a space that was hearty, where the dogs could be muddy. The goal was to make a home that felt lived in.

Let’s walk through, starting in the main suite with duck wallpaper.

Stephen: We fell in love with our surroundings here in Maine. We’re on a saltwater river surrounded by ducks and wildlife. We’ve become duck-obsessed and really brought that into our primary suite. I’d seen this paper wallpaper for a long time, and was excited to use it and go bold, then create a bathroom that feels like a retreat.

David: When we did the Victorian, our focus was creating an oasis in the city, blocking out city lights and signs. In Maine, it’s the opposite. We’re designing to compliment what’s outside the window. So we use that as inspiration and make the house just an extension of the surroundings and try to enhance what’s so beautiful about Maine.



You mentioned the en suite bathroom.

Stephen: In contrast to the bedroom — busy wallpaper, warm, cozy, saturated — we wanted the bathroom to feel light, airy, a relief from that space. We went neutral. The big feature is the skylight we added over the shower, which makes it feel like you’re showering outside. We love that.

I love the rug.

Stephen: Etsy! That’s a secret: Etsy has so many great vintage rugs. That’s our go-to for anything handmade or old. Our suite rug is also an Etsy find. Finding rugs is a whole journey — it can take a couple of tries.

Let’s go to the kitchen. Youbroke down the itemized costs in your blog post.

David: So much of what you see on Instagram or from interior design firms — the cost isn’t disclosed. So you see these beautiful spaces— but no way for people to understand the actual cost behind it. Wetry to be transparent, even though it’s a little scary — there’s a vulnerability of: “We spent $65,000 on cabinets,” which is ridiculous. But in the absence of sharing, people don’t know. We get a lot of great feedback from that.



What are some tips for people redoing their kitchen?

David: Take your time. In Maine, we were intentional. If we look back at our original kitchen plan, it wasquitedifferent. We spent a full year in the space to understand. What’s the light like in March when you’re stuck inside? What does it feel like in October? How will we use it? Let’s host a party and see how people interact with the kitchen. Do they hang out in there, or do they go towards the living room?

So we hosted a Christmas party. We cooked a lot, the kitchen was a full mess, but nobody was in there. Everyone gravitated towards our living room. Afterward, we realized: Maybe we liked the kitchen being closed — we weren’t worried about the mess.

Stephen: Taking that time really made us especially happy with our decisions. All decisions feel correct because we took the time to listen to the house. Sometimes you have a plan — but once you see a room used in real life, it’s different.

Let’s go to the “Plaid Room.” What inspired that?

Stephen: The Plaid Room is a guest room. It started off as a DIY project. When we first moved in, I painted this plaid mural on a wall, and people resonated with it. So when it came time for us to really do the room the way we wanted to, we wanted to maintain plaid in some way. In this iteration, it’s a wallpaper. It’s almost a novelty room, but we love how playful it is.

David: Guest rooms are a good opportunity to do something fun. They’re not being used every day by the same person, so you can do something out-of-the-box.


What about the living room?

Stephen: It’s a perfect example of elevating what already exists. In ways, that’s almost the same as how we bought it. We redid the floors, we painted the walls, but beyond that, we didn’t change anything architecturally. It’s a funky shaped space — a sunken living room, very ‘70s. It was an exercise of, “What is the right furniture for the space to get the most out of this really unique room?” We wanted to make it a conversation pit you see in mid-century architecture.



You have a fun loft that feels very ‘70s.

David: Yeah, we went hard on the ‘70s up there. Again, this was the experience of living here for a while before starting a project. At first we thought, “Let’s open up more glass in the living room wall, so we have a view from the loft.” Then we found we only use the loft at night. When we’re hosting and hanging, we’re in the living room and the kitchen. We go to the loft to catch up on a TV show, to end the day, wind down. There’s the original wide pine floors. We went cozy. We love the jade marble coffee table.

Stephen: We went with a neutral warm white wall, so you can have a little more fun with the color of the couch and coffee table, go bold.


Tell me about the exterior of the Maine cabin.

David: The exterior is a work in progress. Maine is so naturally beautiful. I don’t want to be out there weeding; I want to be enjoying the water. So, we’re trying to keep high-maintenance gardens more condensed up against the house. Looking out the kitchen window now, it’s all woodland. We’re just letting things grow. It’s been a nice experience. Very different from manicured gardens.


What do you love about Maine?

Stephen: Everything. There’s a bigger connection to nature here. We just went swimming in a quarry.

David: We’re three-and-a-half hours from Boston, in a string of touristy ocean towns. Summer is fleeting, and you really have this sense of soaking it in because winter is always around the corner. We’re rural compared to Boston — but it’s easier to get to the Lowe’s from here than it is to get from Boston to Quincy. No traffic.



Lauren Daley is a freelance culture writer. She can be reached at[email protected]. She tweets@laurendaley1, and Instagrams at@laurendaley1.

Lauren Daley is a longtime culture journalist. As a regular contributor to Boston.com, she interviews A-list musicians, actors, authors and other major artists.

hed: Former Victoria’s Secret angel Martha Hunt asks $3.75M for NYC home in a secret alley
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Top model Martha Hunt is about to list her Tribeca pad on a charming cobblestoned alleyway for $3.75 million, Gimme Shelter has learned.
And it’s sure to make a splash, as the chic spread is in a boutique building with a shared rooftop pool. Plus, the building’s location on a cobblestoned alleyway is “like having your own private street,” said listing broker Taylor Middleton of Douglas Elliman.
“It’s hidden, and tucked away from the hustle and bustle of the city.”
Hunt purchased the condo for $3.45 million in 2017, two years after the building’s construction. She’s now looking for bigger digs with her love, photographer Jason McDonald, and their daughter Emery.
The two-bedroom, three-bath residence is at 5 Franklin Place, between Franklin and White streets, just west of Broadway.
It was reimagined by AD100 designer Giancarlo Valle and had its own 2021 close-up inArchitectural Digest.
The former Victoria’s Secret Angel and top model for designers including Prada and Miu Miu, who was also a formerBulgari ambassador, was also once part of Taylor Swift’s “girl squad” and was in Swift’s 2015 “Bad Blood” music video.
At 1,700 square feet, the loft-like space features three exposures.
“The light is what first drew her here,” Middleton said.
There’s an open chef’s kitchen that anchors the living and dining areas, and custom sage-hued limewashed bedroom walls.
That large main bedroom suite also features custom built-ins, a walk-in closet, and a separate sitting area with a windowed, spa-like marble bath. Design details include 5-inch plank oak hardwood floors and 9.5-foot ceilings.
Furnishings, as per the AD story, include a vintage sofa by Mario Bellini for B&B Italia, and a custom bronze and ceramic dining table and banquette.
Designed byEran Chen’s ODA Architects, the new-construction building features curves and a cantilevered upper exterior, with interiors byAndres Escobar. .

hed: Legendary NYC restaurant long frequented by power players dodges eviction over $89K in unpaid rent
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Gabriel’s Bar & Restaurant — a legendary haunt for power players like billionaire Warren Buffet, and Bill and Hillary Clinton since opening more than three decades ago — has just escaped eviction from its Central Park South home, The Post has learned.
Landlord Atco Properties & Management sought to oust the famous restaurant known for its upscale Northern Italian cuisine at the base of the ritzy 40 Central Park South rental building, and recover $88,246 in back rent and expenses, plus interest and legal fees.
Although Atco said it “recently resolved all issues and are in the process of dismissing this action,” Gabriel’s — where the grilled filet mignon with Bordelaise goes for $89 — defaulted on its roughly $81,000 monthly rent plus nearly $6,000 for water services starting July 1, plus around $2,000 in a previously agreed-upon debt settlement agreement, according to a lawsuit filed in Manhattan Civil Court on July 31.
For now, members of city high society will still have a place to dine and hobnob with their influential counterparts.
Known for private events and full restaurant buyouts — the eatery hosted more than 5,000 functions in its 23 years at the West 60th Street location, perManhattan Sideways— Gabriel’s reportedly hosted former Mayor Michael Bloomberg every Thursday when he worked in the office.
Bloomberg apparently called Gabriel’s his “favorite eatery in the city.”
Bloomberg even held a historic first one-on-one dinner in 2011 with then-newly elected Gov. Andrew Cuomo at the restaurant, theNew York Timesreported, with the pols eating $25 fettucini and $35 yellowfin tuna steak, respectively.
Luminaries from CBS News’ “60 Minutes,” Mike Wallace, Ed Bradley, Bob Simon and Morley Safer, made Gabriel’s a regular hangout — and all four had their memorial dinners at the restaurant, according toWest Side Rag.
In 2019, Gabriel Aiello’s Gabriel’s relocated from just off Columbus Circle into the ground floor and basement levels at 40 CPS, between Fifth and Sixth avenues, sharing an address with long-time fixture Sarabeth’s Central Park South.
But as Aiello — known for personally greeting guests — was building out the 4,600-square-foot dining room, COVID shut down the operation in March 2020, the West Side Rag reported, delaying Aiello’s planned spring grand opening. He still had staff, rent and construction tabs to pay so he “took out more loans and mortgaged his Hamptons house,” the publication said.
He soft launched the CPS location in summer 2021.
Court filings reveal that Gabriel’s entered into multiple rent-relief and lease modification agreements with ATCO between April 2021 and January 2025.
ATCO said it “recently resolved all issues and are in the process of dismissing this action,” via a spokesperson. Gabriel’s didn’t respond to an inquiry.
Upstairs, there have been some famous residents includingLady Gagaliving in a penthouse unitfrom around 2013 to 2017. The building was also formerly home to Lance Armstrong and Rod Stewart.
Monthly rents in the 23-story building, aka 41 W. 58th St.,  for available units start at $6,200 for a 740-square-foot one-bedroom unit and $13,200 for a 1,464-square-foot two-bedroom, two-bathroom pad, according to StreetEasy.
The 139-unit building has two attended lobbies, gym and locked elevator access, per StreetEasy.

hed: Scammers are targeting church land in latest twisted scheme to steal properties from their owners
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A North Carolina church nearly lost the land it spent two decades preparing to build on — after fraudsters forged a dead woman’s signature to pull off a real estate sale the family never agreed to.
Timothy Peppers’ father bought the Orange County property back in the 1960s, laying the groundwork for what was meant to become the new home of West Saint Mark Church of Christ in Chapel Hill. The family had been slowly moving toward breaking ground since 2005.
“Ever since 2005, we’ve been working on developing it to actually build the sanctuary here,” Peppers toldlocal affiliate ABC 11 .
That momentum came to a screeching halt this year when a letter showed up from a law firm informing Peppers it had been retained to handle the sale of his own property, a transaction he never authorized and knew nothing about.
Digging into the paperwork, Peppers found the property had already changed hands for $110,000 on April 17, with a deed filed at the Orange County Register of Deeds.
But one detail on the purchase agreement stopped him cold, a signature belonging to his mother, Molly Peppers, who passed away back in 2021.
“That’s not my signature, and my mother’s deceased,” Peppers said.
The discovery sent him reeling.
“It was just the shock and not knowing what to do next and the panic that you go through when you find out.”
The attorney behind the deal admitted the sale never should have happened. His own client, it turned out, had also been duped, conned by a criminal posing as Peppers himself. The firm scrambled to unwind the transaction and get the deed back into Peppers’ name.
Looking back, Peppers said the timing could have been catastrophic if the scam had gone undetected any longer.
“I was thinking about how big a mess it would have been had we gone through the permitting process, ready to build, and someone walk up and say they owned the property.”
With the title restored, the church’s building plans are finally back on track, including parking lot in the front and the sanctuary set further back on the lot. Peppers said he’s speaking out now so other landowners don’t get blindsided the way he did.
“I think we need to keep raising the flag until people kind of have a sense that that’s what they need to do. Always check.”
He’s far from the only target. A similar scheme hit a landowner in nearby Apex, whose vacant lot was quietly put up for sale without his knowledge.
The pattern has caught the attention of the FBI, which recently put out a warning about criminals hijacking property owners’ identities to sell land they have no legal right to touch, often zeroing in on vacant parcels that sit unmonitored for long stretches.
Investigators say the playbook is consistent: impersonate the real owner, forge the paperwork and push the sale through before anyone notices something’s wrong.
Ways to protect yourself include signing up for free property fraud alerts through your county’s Register of Deeds office, regularly monitor property records for unauthorized filings, be extra cautious with vacant land or property you don’t visit often and report anything suspicious to law enforcement right away.
Fraud alerts won’t stop a scammer from filing bogus paperwork in the first place, but they can flag the activity fast enough for owners to fight back before it snowballs into a bigger legal mess.

hed: Crushing rents drive a shocking percentage of college grads to live with mom and dad
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
They’re walking across the stage to get their diplomas — then walking right back into their childhood bedrooms.
Soaring living costs, paying off debt and low job prospects are prompting college graduates tomove back in with mom and dad.
That said, 30% of young adults have moved back home after graduating from college in the last five years, according torecent numbers crunchedby Clever Real Estate.
Thirty percent may seem like a lot, but it used to be much worse.
In July 2020, “52% of 18- to 29-year-olds were living with a parent, the first time on record above half and higher than the 48% peak in 1940 during the Great Depression,” the study’s author told The Post.
“The most recent Census data puts roughly a third of 18- to 34-year-olds at home today.”
Among the reasons they head back to their hometowns, the biggest percentage — 58% — say it’s due to the high cost of living. That’s followed by 52% who say it’s to save money, then 34% who point to not being able to find a job.
Many returning grads also remain tied to their parents’ bank accounts.
A full 76% of Gen Zers living with their parents still rely on financial support from their parents. That figure drops to 59% for young people who live independently.
Graduates’ hopes are not aligning with reality.
About 61% of recent grads thought they’d become financially independent within a year of getting their diploma, but only 50% achieved it.
Nearly 60% of these people who have failed to launch say they’re actively praying for a housing market crash just to afford a home.
To avoid moving back into their childhood bedroom, 19% of Gen Zers say they would skip meals to afford rent, 12% would live in their car and 11% would move in with a brand-new romantic partner, the study adds.

hed: Donald Trump Jr. spends $7.6M to buy ex Kimberly Guilfoyle out of their Florida mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Donald Trump Jr. has officially severed his last property tie to ex-fiancée Kimberly Guilfoyle, paying her $7.6 million for her share of the waterfront Florida homethey once shared.
A Palm Beach County deed filed August 3 confirms the buyout, which closed on July 25, thePalm Beach Postreported.
The six-bedroom estate is located inside the gated Admiral’s Cove community along the Intracoastal Waterway.
Homes in the exclusive enclave routinely fetch millions of dollars, and the couple’s own purchase five years ago was no exception.
Trump and Guilfoyle paid $9.7 million for the property in 2021, snapping it up after it had spent years on and off the market with an asking price that once topped $19.9 million.
The two-story dwelling spans 11,270 square feet and comes with 11 bathrooms, an elevator and a fireplace.
It was built in 1995 and underwent a major renovation shortly before the couple moved in.
The purchase came just months after Trump and Guilfoyle left New York following the 2020 election, relocating to Florida along with much of the rest of the Trump family.
Jupiter held personal significance for Trump even before the move, since his ex-wife Vanessa and their five children live nearby, not far from Trump National Golf Club Jupiter.
Guilfoyle, 57, now serves asUS ambassador to Greece. She’s listed with a Delray Beach address on the new filing, which also carries a stamp from the American embassy in Athens, whereshe’s stationed.
The buyout comes on the heels ofTrump marriageto Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson, and the newlyweds are reportedly eyeing a move to West Palm Beach.
Trump is also said to be behind a separate purchase of a nearly $15 million vacant lot in the nearby Prospect Park neighborhood, just a mile from Mar-a-Lago, where he’s expected to build a large new family home for his five children and any future kids with Anderson.
As for the Admiral’s Cove estate, the home recently underwent a contemporary renovation, with white walls, white cabinetry and neutral tile and wood floors throughout, plus water views from nearly every room.
Outside there’s a pool, a private dock and a dock lift, all just a short drive from where President Trump and Melania Trump still keep their own Palm Beach residence.

hed: Weezer bassist and his estranged wife ask $3M for LA home where she shot at cops in a bizarre meltdown
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The California hillside retreat where Weezer bassist Scott Shriner’s estranged wifeexchanged gunfire with policelast spring is officially on the market, The Post has learned.
Shriner, who is the longest-running bassist for Weezer, and author Jillian Lauren have listed their gated mid-century compound at 1205 Eagle Vista Drive in Los Angeles for $2.95 million.
Linda Chamberlain of Nourmand & Associates holds the listing.
The 3,035-square-foot home, tucked behind gates on a nearly half-acre lot, was built in 1954 and comes with five bedrooms, four bathrooms, vaulted beamed ceilings and a heated pool set among mature landscaping.
The property also boasts sweeping canyon and mountain views just minutes from Eagle Rock’s Colorado Boulevard shopping strip, according to the listing.
But the sale comes on the heels of a turbulent chapter for the couple — and an unusual encounter Lauren had with cops.
Last April, LAPDofficers shot Laurenin the shoulder outside the home while they responded to reports of a hit-and-run in the neighborhood, in which she was not involved.
Police say Lauren pointed a handgun at officers during the encounter, leading to her arrest on suspicion of attempted murder. She was later hit with lesser charges, including discharging a firearm in a grossly negligent manner, and pleaded not guilty in May.
In September, a judge granted her atwo-year mental health diversion programthat could ultimately wipe the case from her record.
The Los Angeles Police Commission determined earlier this year that officers involved in the shootingacted improperly, with LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell now weighing possible discipline.
Lauren, a bestselling author known for her memoir “Some Girls: My Life in a Harem,” broke her silence on the incident in a December interview withRolling Stone, describing the ordeal as self-defense.
“I was doing the best I knew to protect my family,” Lauren said. “[The] impulse was self-defense.”
She told the outlet the fallout upended her life entirely.
“My world fell to pieces around me in a heartbeat,” Lauren said.
The couplefiled for divorcein early December after 20 years of marriage, with Lauren telling Rolling Stone the split had been building for some time before the shooting pushed things to a breaking point.
“The headlines about the divorce were the ones that really hurt me,” Lauren said. “I was the one who served my husband, but still, to see it in the public was really painful. It was definitely a day [spent] under the covers, blocking out all the noise.”
Despite the upheaval, Lauren said the Eagle Rock property offered a genuine sense of escape during her years there.
“What I’ve loved most about this home is the sense of peace and privacy it provides,” Lauren said in a statement about the listing. “Once you’re behind the gates and surrounded by the trees, it truly feels like your own personal retreat, even though you’re just minutes from the shops and restaurants on Colorado Boulevard and everything Eagle Rock has to offer.”
“Whether spending time by the pool or watching the sunset from the hillside, the house always made me feel connected to the outdoors and it’s been an incredibly special place to call home.”
Reps for Lauren did not respond to The Post’s request for comment.

Maine is Vacationland, as evidenced by the countless rentals listed by online agencies like Airbnb, Vrbo, and Booking.com. Then there are regional iterations: a quick online search turns up a dozen companies specializing in renting Maine properties. Arecent realtor.com reportfound that Maine has the second highest number of vacation properties in the United States, trailing right behind Vermont.

So why would two women start yet another Maine-centered vacation rental company?

“WithTides to Pines, we set ourselves apart from other vacation rental companies,” said Molly Hooper, owner and chief executive officer.

“Our homes are curated; we have standards,” added fellow owner and chief experience officer Paige Teel.


Hooper and Teel, both Maine natives, have deep backgrounds working for real estate and property management companies, including Summer Maine and Vacasa.

“We got to know each other while working for competing companies that are now defunct,” Hooper said. “But, during that time, we learned a lot about what not to do, and often talked about how we would do it if we were running things.”

They got the chance to try in December 2023, when they launched Tides to Pines.

“During COVID, the rental business in Maine boomed,” Teel explained. “People saw this as a safe place to come, and that did not stop after the pandemic.”

By the fall of 2024, Tides to Pines represented 80 homes. Under theCasago umbrella, the company today employs 72 full- and part-time employees and manages a collection of about 475 properties.

Casago (which recently acquired Vacasa), founded in Arizona in 1996, uses a local franchise model and manages tens of thousands of properties across North America, Mexico, and the Caribbean. The company’s Maine properties are now managed by Tides to Pines.

Most are along the Maine coast, while several are near Moosehead Lake and Western Maine’s ski mountains. Several, including a house on Matinicus Island, are remote and inaccessible except by boat or small plane. All, according to Hooper and Teel, have been carefully inspected. They’re required to meet local and state safety codes, such as those calling for smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, reliable railings, adequate lighting, and sound construction.



“Ours is a carefully curated portfolio,” Teel said. “We have a big Rolodex of plumbers, contractors, electricians, landscapers, and people who provide seasonal services like snow plowing or kayak rentals. We make sure that rental properties are safe, spotless, attractive, and furnished with everything guests require, like a kitchen stocked with groceries, including spices and condiments, a crib for the baby, dog sitters, dining reservations.”

Their properties range from simple two-bedroom log cabins to rambling estates with swimming pools, docks, and hundreds of feet of private waterfront. Available Labor Day weekend rentals range from a seven-bedroomhome in Boothbay Harborfor just under $5,000 (Friday to Monday) to a petite studio home inNorthport for $635.

Hooper and Teel do a fair amount of styling in which they edit out superfluous tchotchkes, rearrange furniture, and gently convince homeowners that their grandmother’s décor needs an update.

“We also make sure that each guest is matched with the right property,” Hooper added.


Though their properties are available on Airbnb and Vrbo, Hooper and Teel explain that their business model differs from that of those sites.

“They publish your listing and let people book it through their platform,” Hooper said. “They don’t get involved in the property or a guest’s needs … as a property owner or a guest, you’re on your own.”

Tides to Pines staff, she said, is available to both guests and homeowners day or night.

“We offer concierge services because guests want experiences. For example, we will arrange for chefs to come to properties for private dining events, or we will find a yoga class for you,” Teel added.

The homes are also listed onHomes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy.

In the future, Teel said, the company wants to offer stays in offbeat properties like train cars, yurts, tree houses, or Airstream trailers. “We have a geodesic dome in Boothbay, and we’d like to offer more places like that,” she said.

“That’s what we love to do,” Hooper added. “Offer cool houses in cool locations.”
