hed: Owning a rare Frank Lloyd Wright home isn’t the paradise you’d imagine — but that isn’t stopping some buyers
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Frank Lloyd Wright remains a major figure in the history of American architecture. But when it comes to maintaining his surviving homes — well, that remains a major pain in the neck.
Take Petra Island in upstate New York, with a 5,000-square-foot wood and concrete main house built from Wright’s original plans.
The house was completed in 2007, decades after Wright died in 1959 at age 91, and yet it inherited many of the same quirks as the homes Wright built himself — including a flat roof that leaks and oversized fireplaces that smoke as much as they impress.
“The house is magnificent, but it has some faults in the design,” owner Joe Massaro, 80, a former sheet metal industrialist, told The Post as he stepped into its foyer — where a centuries-old boulder forms one of the walls. “He was not a great engineer, but he wanted what he wanted.”
Frequent, painstaking maintenance is a constant for owners of Wright’s roughly 400 still-standing houses, many of them concentrated in the Midwest. As stewards of the architect’s uncompromising vision, they preserve designs that often prioritized artistry over practicality — an effort that can require serious work.
After all, things were different in Wright’s day. In 1920, while Wright was rising to fame, just 20 states required architects to be licensed, according to theNational Council of Architectural Registration Boards.
Wright founded his own firm in 1893, before Illinois established its law requiring licensing for architects without earning an architecture degree. Instead, he entered the profession through apprenticeship.
Still, what Wright lacked in formal academic training, he made up for with abundant creativity.
“He wanted a more organic structure, for people to feel like they were more tied to nature,” said Dan D’Agostino, principal and founder at New Jersey-basedPLAN Architecture, who’s spent decades studying Wright and his structures. “The idea of bringing stone into a house, that wasn’t really done before Wright.”
To blur the boundary between inside and out, Wright filled entire corners with windows or had grooves cut directly into stone so panes of glass could be fitted without the need for window frames.
“Wright was handed engineering reports with these calculations saying his designs were not going to work, and he would say, ‘You must trust the process. If you’re not going to trust me, I can quit,’” D’Agostino said. “His bravado would get in the way.”
The 11-acre heart-shaped Petra Island in Lake Mahopac — which Massaro purchased in 1996 for $750,000, including the value of a house he traded for it — sits about a mile offshore, boasting two dwellings tied to the mid-century architectural mastermind. Notably, the main house resembles a ship; its 75-foot concrete terrace cantilevers over the water, as though riding a wave preserved in time. Nearby sits its shy sibling, a guest cottage Wright completed in 1949 that’s hidden from the view of passing boaters.
Among the materials used for the main house was five times the amount of African mahogany that Wright used to build the guest cottage.
Every 10 years, Massaro hires a local handyman, Daniel Corbi, to sand and stain the exterior wood enveloping both houses, a project that takes about five years to complete — which costs more than $10,000.
“I’ve been doing this for 20 years or so now, and it’s an honor maintaining it,” Corbi told The Post on a recent break from staining the guest house.
Still, it’s costly — not to mention highly tedious.
Recently, Massaro paid $1,000 each for several 10-foot-by-10-inch slabs of mahogany when some spots needed replacements, he said. To find the correct sealant, he removed a wooden door to the guest cottage and shipped it, carefully, to a specialist in New Jersey.
The challenges of Wright houses resurface in the news every few years, usually when preservationists scramble to save one from the consequences of his uncompromising vision.
Fallingwater, Wright’s highly popular southwestern Pennsylvania tour de force, for example, required an $11.5 million stabilization project to keep it from falling into a waterfall, as its name implies.
In June, Wright’sJ.J. Walser Jr. housein Chicago’s Austin neighborhood finally sold for $150,000 after sitting abandoned and deteriorating for 30 years. The nonprofit Austin Coming Together has taken on the task of restoring the Prairie School-style landmark, built in 1903, whose many tasks reportedly include structural stabilization, along with roof and stucco repairs.
That being said, Wright’s work still attracts a specific pool of buyers.
The lure of Wright’s designs seduced historic architecture preservationists Marika Broere and Tony Hillebrandt in 2016, when they bought the Eppstein House in Galesburg, Michigan for $368,000. Built in 1953 in Wright’s Usonian style, the 2,500-square-foot three-bed, two-bath property was part of a planned community of Wright homes known as the Acres. In 2021, they purchased the 2,200-square-foot two-bed, two-bath Eric and Pat Pratt House next door for $355,000. Both homes had been abandoned for nearly 20 years prior.
“What we love most is how Wright designed not for grandeur, but for harmony,” Broere said. “His homes are meant to live in. They’re human-scaled, light-filled and deeply personal.”
Romanticism aside, they’re also deeply expensive to maintain.
In their years-long restorations of the two homes, the couple invested more than $1.7 million of their retirement savings into the projects, Broere said. This included $130,000 to repair the concrete textile blocks at both houses, $150,000 on woodwork and another $50,000 to replace the roof on the Eppstein house.
The pair assembled a network of specialized craftsmen, largely thanks to recommendations from the community of Wright-house restorers around the country, Broere added.
At one point, they consulted an expert from the Sherwin-Williams paint company who designed a breathable stain for the concrete blocks, Broere said. In another adventure, Broere and Hillebrandt traveled to a warehouse in Battle Creek, Michigan, where they sifted through dust-covered boxes to find the correct bathroom tiles.
“While we tackled much of the work ourselves, we also employed a master carpenter who worked nearly full-time for several years on cabinetry, window frames and doors,” Broere said.
Satisfied with their efforts, Broere and Hillebrandt sold the Pratt House in the spring of 2024 for $1.8 million, including $300,000 for Wright-designed furnishings included with the sale. The Eppstein House is listed bothon Airbnband for sale for$2.1 million. The couple has since hopped across the pond to their next project, restoring a mid-century villa in France.
Preserving and maintaining Wright’s residential treasures is such a celebrated endeavor that the Chicago-basedFrank Lloyd Wright Building Conservancyhands out Wright Spirit Awards at its annual conference.
But John Waters, preservation programs director at the conservancy, noted that all older homes come with their challenges. Many mid-century architects, from Rudolph Schindler to Richard Neutra, built flat roofs that were prone to leaking, he said.
“Wright is the most famous, so he gets the most comments, but any historic house owner is a person who should be lauded for their dedication to preserving the house,” Waters said.
For Massaro, the source of leaks from the roof of the main house are maddeningly elusive.
“I have a leak in the laundry room that leaks when it’s not raining,” Massaro said. “It’s leaked for weeks. I can’t figure it out.”
After a few highly publicized attempts to sell Petra Island, even dropping the price from $20 million in 2012 to$9.95 million in 2019, Massaro went back to his roots as an entrepreneur. He now operates tours to the island, selling tickets at $150 apiece, and has hosted thousands of curious sightseekers, architects and journalists from around the world.
The tours keep him busy, Massaro said, and help recoup some of his financial investment, which includes $120,000 a year on taxes and maintenance for the island and its houses. In between them, he enjoys lounging on the terrace and tinkering with a hologram he built of Wright giving a speech on the design of the main house.
“It’s one of the most comfortable places I’ve ever lived,” Massaro said. “Wherever I am, there’s a view.”

hed: This shady feature makes some neighborhoods 15 degrees cooler
subhead: Trees a major selling point in the city
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Some New York City neighborhoods are much cooler than others, and it has nothing to do with air conditioning, anew study found.
The Nature Conservancy nonprofit studied every neighborhood across the five boroughs for five years and found that those with limited tree coverage can experience temperatures 10 to 15 degrees higher than those with greater coverage.
Trees naturally lower air temperatures, often significantly. In fact,according to Forests News, a single large tree can provide a cooling effect equivalent to 10 room-sized air conditioners operating for 20 hours per day.
TheNew York City neighborhoodswith the greatest percentage of tree coverage, not including major parks or nature areas, ranked as follows:
By borough, Staten Island has the most tree coverage at 33%, followed by the Bronx at 27%, Manhattan at 23%, Queens at 20%, and Brooklyn at 19%.
Mike Plactere, who flips homes in New York City and on Long Island, says he definitely sees a “tree premium.”
“I see the tree premium from the buying side: It shows up in what I pay for a house and what it resells for,” he tells Realtor.com.
“If you want hard evidence that trees carry real value, look at what happenswhen one comes downwithout a permit,” he says. “New York City and many Long Island villages enforce civil penalties for unpermitted tree removal. Nobody writes fines for removing something worthless.”
He notes that the trees that add the most value to a property are “unique specimen trees” such as the Japanese maple and older-growth trees such as oaks, as they tend to be larger, creating more privacy.
“A property that already has a mature screen [of trees] or an old oak canopy has something the neighbor can’t buy at any price this decade,” he adds. “The size matters less than the time. A homeowner can renovate a kitchen in two months.
“Nobody can rush an 80-year-old oak.”
City dwellers with an abundance of trees nearby have not only something pleasant to look at, but also a place to go to instantly cool down. And they’re willing to pay for the privilege.
Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman, who represents Manhattan real estate, says she is seeing a “tree premium” more than she has in years past.
“On the Upper East Side, I have buyers who specifically ask for tree-lined blocks or homes near Central Park because theywant that connection to naturewithout leaving Manhattan,” she says. “For families, it’s about having easy access to green space. I’ve seen buyers pay more for that experience.
Griffith says two apartments with similar layouts and finishes can be valued very differently if one has beautiful green views while the other looks directly into a neighboring building.
“You’re not just paying for the apartment. You’re paying for how it feels to live there every day,” she says.
“I’ve haven’t heard of people saying they want to buy a place near trees because it’s cooler. But when you live in New York City, the energy is so high that any level of proximity to trees or Central Park is calming to the nervous system,” she says.
Manhattan luxury real estate agent Frances Katzen at Douglas Elliman agrees: “When you live in a concrete jungle,access to naturebecomes a luxury in and of itself. Buyers might not always articulate it that way, but they instinctively respond to it.”

She cites a condo at 300 Central Park West that needed a gut renovation but still sparked an intense bidding war.
“Buyers weren’t responding to the finishes. They were responding to the location and the irreplaceable Central Park setting,” she says. “In New York, an unobstructed green outlook is one of the rarest amenities you can own, and the market consistently rewards that.”
So what’s the premium on tree views?
Lisa Lippman of Brown Harris Stevens, who has long represented residences featuring the ultimate New York City amenity—a view of Central Park—pegs it as high as the double digits.
“Listing the property with photos of the trees in bloom [out of a window] can easily command 20% more,” she tells Realtor.com.
Patrick Anderson-Higgins, a Compass agent with The Reisor Team, specializes in Tudor City, a well-known 13-building prewar complex on the East Side near the United Nations. The development is anchored by Tudor City Greens, two small parks with roughly a half-acre oflandscaped greenery. Prices in the complex range from $300,000 to $3 million.
“I can say with certainty that views of the green space are a huge motivation for buyers,” he tells Realtor.com. “Units with park views tend to trade quickly and often command higher purchase prices than those of non-park-facing units.”
Access to greenery commands a premium not just in price, but also in days on the market.
The agent currently represents three units at 2 Tudor City Place with courtyard, not park, views. Each has been on the market for over 100 days, compared to the two comparable units he formerly represented that had park and tree views and were snapped up within 60 days.
“The main difference is theview of the parks and trees,” he says, noting that units on the north side of the building—where the trees are—are rarely available as people tend to hold them longer because of the views. When these tree-facing unitsareavailable, they’re often traded off-market—something allowed by their greater desirability.
Even a lone tree can be immensely treasured. Anderson-Higgins recalls a client who moved to Tudor City in 1959 and planted one outside of her window.
“She still lives in the building and doesn’t want to sell because she doesn’t want to lose the view of the tree,” he says. But if she did sell? No doubt that tree would help her valuation.
The increased demand for cooling trees may have something to do with climate change. Whether or not people understand that trees can lower ambient air temperatures, they can certainly feel more comfortable when they walk down a tree-canopied block on a hot day.
According to theNew York State Climate Impacts Assessment, in the past quarter-century,temperatures have been higher in the statethan in any period in recorded history, and the state has warmed more quickly than the US average. Among cities in the Empire State, New York City typically experiences the most days with ahigh heat index.
From 1981 to 2010, New York City experienced approximately 17 days per year with temperatures topping 90 degrees Fahrenheit. By the 2080s, that number is projected to rise to an extremely uncomfortable 69 days annually, or nearly 20% of the entire year.
Higher temperatures can lead to extreme heatwaves (such as the one much of the countrysuffered through over the July 4 holiday weekend), drought, and wildfires.
More than 1.45 million acres across theWestern US have already been ravaged by wildfiresin 2026, and multiple states are now bracing for what could be one of the country’s most devastating fire seasons, according to theNational Interagency Fire Center.
But there’s hope. Expect more trees—and hopefully cooler temperatures—in New York City’s future.
The city has set a goal of reaching 30% tree canopy cover, up from the current 23.4%, by 2040, through its firstUrban Forest Plan, a citywide strategy focused on planting, protecting, and maintaining trees.

hed: The 6-figure income needed to afford the average US home remains at a record high
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For the first time in years, US homebuying affordability has plateaued. The bad news: You still need to earn six figures to buy a home.
The household income needed to scoop up a typical home in the country — and spend no more than 30% of income on a monthly mortgage payment — sits at $109,796, according to aJune report from Redfin. That is down a marginal 0.5% from an all-time high of $110,382 a year ago.
Six figures is a far cry from reality for many people.
Consider that the median US household brings home just $87,599 annually, though that’s up 4% year-over-year.
“The earnings needed to buy a house have stabilized after several years of deterioration, but that doesn’t mean homes are affordable to the average American,” Yingqi Xu, a senior economist at Redfin, said in a statement. “There’s still a double-digit gap between what the typical household earns and what they need to comfortably buy a home, leaving many prospective first-time buyers stalled on the sidelines.”
For the average buyer, purchasing a median-priced property would consume roughly 38% of their annual household earnings.
On the plus side, the $22,197 affordability deficit — the difference between the $109,796 needed to nab a home and the $87,599 median salary — has shrunk over the past two years, down from $26,125 last year and $28,834 two years ago.
Plus, incomes and monthly housing costs are increasing at about the same rate.
Additionally, there are more options for the average Joe, with 34.2% of active listings now considered affordable, up from 30.5% a year prior.
Entering the market for the first time is a bit easier now. First-time homebuyers need to earn $70,693 to afford the typical US entry-level home, down 1.5% from a year ago.
Nearly half of major US metropolitan areas, like Seattle and San Jose, saw improvements in homebuying affordability.
Typical households make enough to buy a median-priced home in just three major cities: St. Louis, Indianapolis and Pittsburgh.

hed: There’s a strange, giant robot left behind at a pop star’s abandoned mansion — and it’s creeping neighbors out
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A pop star moved out. His 60-foot robot didn’t.
A colossal robot of that massive height has been haunting the English countryside after being left behind at the former estate ofUK pop star Robbie Williams,terrifying unsuspecting locals who stumble across it lurking in the woods.
The mechanical giant, which residents have nicknamed “Om,” once served as the showstopping centerpiece of a $20 million concert set built for Take That, the British boy band fronted by Williams.
The animatronic figure debuted during the group’s blockbuster 2011 world tour, a production so massive it rivaled anything American acts like *NSYNC or the Backstreet Boys ever rolled out.
Williams, one of the UK’s best-selling solo artists, once called the sprawling seven-bedroom mansion in Compton Bassett his home.
(These days, Williams isspending his days in Florida,where he newly purchased a sprawling $40 million Coral Gables waterfront estate, The Post reported.)
But when he sold the Wiltshire property years later, the towering robot apparently stayed put, quietly rusting away among the trees.
Now it’s become an unlikely local legend.
Drivers and dog walkers passing the estate have reported doing a double take at the sight of the hulking figure peering out from the foliage.
Resident Sarah Spencer said the shock of the sighting stopped her in her tracks.
“When I first saw it I had to turn around and go back to see what I thought I’d seen,” Spencer toldTalker News.“It caught me completely off guard but I was intrigued. I thought someone had built a Wicker Man.”
Fellow villager Liz Neve described a similarly eerie encounter, saying the robot’s placement along the road makes it feel like it materializes out of thin air.
“It’s such a perfect location as it just seems to emerge from nowhere and then as you drive alongside it, it seems to withdraw back into the foliage,” Neve said.
Neve joked she wondered “if the locals might be building up to a re-enactment of the Wicker Man.”
Neither Williams nor representatives for the estate have said why the towering prop was never hauled away, or whether there are any plans to finally give the abandoned robot its walking papers.

hed: British homebuyers are quietly flocking to one of Midwest’s most affordable states — here’s why
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


While coastal and Sun Belt states continue to dominate U.S. foreign real estate transactions, Michigan has quietly emerged as one of the top destinations for U.K. buyers drawn by an affordable lifestyle and a long-established job pipeline.
Between April 2025 and March 2026, Michigan was the third most popular landing place for home shoppers from the U.K., capturing 18% of all U.K. purchases nationwide, according to the new National Association of Realtors® 2025 International Transactions in U.S. Residential Real Estate report between April 2025 and March 2026, Michigan was the third most popular landing place for home shoppers from the U.K., capturing 18% of all U.K. purchases nationwide, according to the new National Association of Realtors® 2025 International Transactions in U.S. Residential Real Estate report.
In the NAR report, “foreign” or “international” buyers include foreign nationals living abroad, non-U.S. citizens who are recent immigrants (less than two years at the time of the transaction), and visa holders living stateside.
Only sunny California and Arizona ranked higher than Michigan among British buyers, commanding 36% and 27% of transactions involving U.K. nationals, respectively. Meanwhile, the Great Lakes State outpaced traditional international markets like Texas and South Carolina, which each garnered 9%.
“Michigan’s pull for U.K. buyers likely comes down to two threads,” says Realtor.com® economistJiayi Xu. “On the lifestyle side, the state’s lakefront towns offer the kind of waterfront, second-home living that’s popular back home in the U.K., but at a more affordable price than the U.K. or the Florida coast.
“On the business side, Michigan’s deep, decades-old ties to the auto industry mean a steady flow of relocation opportunities for U.K. professionals in roles tied to Ford, GM, and their supply chains.”
This trend is rooted in strong cross-border economic ties going back decades and anchored in automotive technology collaborations.
According to U.K. government trade data, British subsidiaries employ nearly 40,000 workers across Michigan, making the U.K. one of the leading sources of direct foreign investment in the state.
Overall, U.K. homebuyers accounted for 4% of all foreign real estate purchases in the U.S. in 2026, unchanged since 2024. Meanwhile, Michigan ranked as the eighth most popular destination across all foreign buyer groups, at 3%.
On Realtor.com this spring, buyers from the U.K. made up 6% of international traffic to Michigan, the second-largest group of foreign browsers.
Jaye Sanders, managing broker at Nextpointe Real Estate Service in Royal Oak, MI, has worked with international buyers over the past six years and says U.K.’s ascendance as a major feeder market for Michigan comes as no surprise.
“It makes sense based upon how affordable our market is. It makes sense based upon the fact that we’re a major hub. … You can pretty much fly anywhere you need to fly,” Sanders tells Realtor.com. “And it makes sense because Michigan is a fantastic place to live and bring your family.”
The broker emphasizes that, in accordance with Michigan’s Fair Housing guidelines, she never collects information on her clients’ racial or cultural background, but confirms she has helped U.K. buyers purchase homes in Michigan.
“I have had quite a few buyers who’ve come from other countries, and they’ve specifically been interested in the resurgence of Detroit,” says Sanders.
Motor City, long celebrated as the beating heart of America’s automotive industry, declared bankruptcy in 2013 and became a symbol of urban decay. In the decade since, Detroit has experienced a remarkable economic turnaround highlighted by downtown revitalization, multiple consecutive balanced budgets, and recent population growth.
Many of Sanders’ international buyers, among them British subjects, are drawn to Detroit’s location offering easy access to neighboring Canada, a fellow commonwealth nation. Other crucial selling points include Michigan’s world-class freshwater lakes and its impressive affordability.
She points out some of her foreign clients are shocked that they can afford to purchase a waterfront property in Michigan for a fraction of what it would cost elsewhere.
Michigan’s lower property taxes also play a significant role.
“If you compare our property taxes to a state like California or even a state like New York, it’s a lot more affordable to live in Michigan,” notes Sanders.
The broker explains that many of her international clients work in the automotive sector and arrive on temporary corporate assignments. A large portion of them purchase waterfront condominiums or co-ops in downtown Detroit or Grosse Pointe near General Motors and Ford facilities as part of a long-term investment strategy.
“They look at the price, they look at the location close to the water, and they believe that in a few years, obviously the market will go up and they will sell,” says Sanders.
This cohort of buyers typical look for turnkey, low-maintenance properties in gated communities overlooking the Detroit River or Lake St. Clair that are priced in the $200,000 to $250,000 range.

“They want something that they can move in and immediately ‘plug and play,'” says Sanders.
The idea is that rather than spending money on rent, the expats live in their condos while their work assignment is active, and then convert them into short- or long-term rentals to generate passive income for years to come.
Those who relocate to Michigan from abroad on a more permanent basis and arrive with families tend to prioritize top-rated school districts and single-family homes with backyards, typically shopping in the $250,000 to $400,000 range.
In July, the median asking price in the Detroit metro was $275,000, down 1.8% from a year ago and more than $150,000 below the national median.
Demand for Michigan housing remains strong across multiple international demographics. Beyond ranking third among U.K. buyers, Michigan was the fifth most popular destination for shoppers from Canada and India, and the sixth most popular for Chinese investors, according to the NAR report.

hed: California’s most insane HOA rules revealed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Across the Golden State,homeowners associations are notorious for policing everythingfrom the color of your front door to the calendar dates you can display a holiday wreath.
CaliforniaHOA’shave unleashed draconian mandates that leave residents wondering if they bought a dream home or signed up for suburban probation. Here are some of the most insane HOA rules terrorizing homeowners across California.
In communities like San Diego’s Rancho Santa Fe, homeowners  must choose from an HOA-approved palette to repaint their homes, submit detailed applications, and identify exactly what color will be used.
The community’s broaderdesign guidelinesalso discourage anything too eye-catching, specifically warning against “brilliant” colors — even singling out flamingo pink as an example of what’s considered inappropriate.
Earth tones, oatmeal shades and muted finishes are preferred instead.
“HOA has a lot of rules,” one disgruntled Redditorwroteof the community. “I cannot even remove a tree. I have to get permission to get solar and that has been an issue as well.”
California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day.
Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story
In a display of bureaucratic overreach, residents at the Ambiance townhouse community in San Diego’s San Marcos exploded in anger after theirHOA ordered them to take down their American flags— or face crushing fines.
Just ahead of the Fourth of July, the association cracked down on residents displaying the Stars and Stripes, sparking intense outrage from homeowners who slammed the demand as un-American.
Amy Cooke, 62, told the California Post: “We are outraged, if you want to fly your flag fly it, this is America. We are the land of the free and home of the brave, this is crazy.”
In Orange County, residents are even banned from spreading holiday cheer whenever the mood strikes. At the Auburn Community Association in Irvine, holiday spirit is governed with strict calendar precision.
Christmas and New Years decorations are only allowed from Nov. 15 and must be taken down by Jan. 15, according to theassociation’s official rulebook. If you want to fly a banner or set up festive decor for other holidays like Memorial Day or Chinese New Year, you’re given a 20-day window: starting 10 days before the holiday, and ending exactly 10 days after.
Up north in Danville, the Blackhawk Home Owners Association implemented a rule blacklisting basketball hoops in homeowners’ driveways.
The association’s architectural standards reportedly state: “Portable basketball hoops must be stored in a location out of view of the common areas when not actively in use.”
In a 2023Change.org petitionstarted in hopes of repealing the ban, a resident cited the difficulty of moving a “high-quality portable basketball hoop” given its size and weight and added that the “newly adopted basketball rule is a de facto ban on driveway basketball hoops.”
More than 100 homeowners ultimately signed the petition.
Many California HOAs enforce minuscule time windows for when trash bins can sit on the curb in the name of community aesthetics. In massive developments like Irvine’s Woodbridge, the Woodbridge Village Association enforces strict and detailed garbage rules.
Under thearchitectural rulebook, trash cans cannot be placed at the curb until after 5 p.m. the day before collection — and must be returned to an enclosed storage area and out of view by 8 a.m. the following day.
The rules, which apply to almost 10,000 residential properties, also state that the bins should be thoroughly hidden from adjacent homes so that they can’t be spotted by a neighbor looking down from a second-story window.
HOAs aren’t just making up rules on the fly, though. More than 50,000 homeowners associations in California operate under the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, which gives associations authority to adopt and enforce community rules.
Ironically, many of these nit-picky rules are becoming less financially painful for homeowners thanks to a recent change in California law. As part ofAssembly Bill 130, which took effect on June 30, 2025, the state capped most standard HOA fines at $100 per violation.
The Post has reached out to the HOAs for comment and is yet to hear back.

hed: Florida city breaks ground on its first 3D-printed home — as experts call the technology all hype
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Forget hammer and nails — the latest trend in homebuilding involves pressing “print.”
A Florida city southwest of Tampa has broken ground on its first-ever 3D-printed home, as part of its affordable housing program, according to localFox 13 News.
St. Petersburg city officials said the technology will cut construction time in half.
“You’re talking [about] something that might be a two — or two and a half week process — can be squeezed down into a day and a half, maybe two days,” Nick Bradford, owner of Structures Group, an engineering consultancy firm, toldWFLA News Channel 8.
Developer Bright Community Trust is building the exterior walls using a robotic arm that continuously pours liquid cement layer by layer along the home’s perimeter.
The city leases its vacant lots to developers for a small cost, and they in turn sell the home to a buyer earning up to 120% of the area median income — roughly $96,300 for a single person. The 3D-printed homes still require the typical permitting process and need to satisfy state building codes the same as any standard home.
St. Petersburg’s goal is to eventually erect 150 single-family homes on city-owned land, Fox reported.
Despite the hype framing 3D printing as the “next big thing” for housing, industry skeptics caution that the technology isn’t the magic bullet it’s made out to be.
If it were, why hasn’t there been a “3D printing boom,”posed online edutainer Simon Whistler. Indeed, he said, only hundreds of such homes have been built worldwide.
He pointed to a number of failed projects.
In November 2023, a partially completed 3D-printed home in Muscatine, Iowa, was torn down because the concrete mix failed to hit required structural strength tests.
A deal struck in August 2024 between Prestige Project Management and Cairo, Illinois, to build 30 3D-printed duplexes ultimately didn’t materialize despite a $1.1 million investment in a printer.
On the plus side, Whistler noted, in late 2025, Japan got its first government-approved two-story 3D-printed reinforced concrete house — known as the “O House” or “Stealth House” — in Kurihara City, Miyagi Prefecture.
One of the biggest criticisms of 3D-printed homes stems from what the printer actually builds. A 3D printer cannot lay plumbing, pull electrical wiring, install drywall, frame a roof, or put in windows and doors.
In addition, concrete printers are massive, expensive, and difficult to transport between jobsites.
Skeptics also highlight significant structural and environmental concerns. Concrete is a carbon-heavy material responsible for massive global emissions and printed concrete lacks the structural ductility of framed walls.
As Bradford himself admited, having a limited number of machines creates severe scheduling bottlenecks, and the printers struggle to build multi-story structures.
“As you get more complicated, you start eliminating the cost savings,” Bradford noted.
In addition, 3D projects face regulatory hurdles and hidden costs like buying the printer, Whistler said.
Stewart Hicks said on his“Architecture with Stewart”YouTube channel that 3D-printed homes “look a little weird.”
That could be because of design limitations like the fact that the robot machine laying down the cement can’t make sharp corners.
The greatest challenge, he said, is the “relative inflexibility of the building after construction,” he said.
If anything happens to a part of the structure, it’s “almost impossible” to restore it to its original state.
“The modularity ensures that any part can just be replaced when needed and not leave any visible scars,” Hicks said. “Thinking of a building as one large seamless object is completely antithetical to the realities that buildings face.”

hed: Seann William Scott asks $17.5M for his dream Malibu surfing compound
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Actor Seann William Scott’s Malibu surfing compound is back on the market for $17.5 million — down slightly from its $17.85 million ask with a different brokerage earlier this year.
The “American Pie” actor’s retreat — known as the Vanaya House — in the hills above Zuma Beach, sits on just under 1.5 acres.
The new listing, first reported byRealtor.com, boasts a resort-style pool, a tennis court with a viewing pavilion, covered patios, open air lounges, coastline “glimpses,” plus plenty of room to build new structures for a family compound to span generations.
Scott, a “Lethal Weapon” alum who was also in the stoner comedy, “Dude, Where’s My Car,” is currently starring with Tim Allen and Kat Dennings in ABC’s “Shifting Gears,” which was recently renewed for a third season.
He also voiced Crash, the reckless possum twin in the “Ice Age” franchise.
He bought the five-bedroom, 4.5-bath beach house on Morning View Drive for $3.95 million in 2004, according to property records, around the time that the “American Pie” franchise, in which Scott portrayed the character Steve Stifler, was in full swing.
The gated estate, inspired by Balinese architecture, opens to a gravel motor court anchored by a coral tree.
Built in 1980, the stucco and redwood structure is around 4,100 square feet.
It features floor-to-ceiling glass walls and opens to a pool terrace and serene ocean views.
Design details include interiors featuring natural and organic materials, stone floors, custom millwork and wood-beamed ceilings.
Scott oversaw a remodel that included updating the open living, dining and kitchen areas, and adding custom cabinetry to the chef’s kitchen, which anchors the home. The sunken living room also features a striking stone fireplace that rises to the ceiling.
Upstairs, the main bedroom suite comes with a spa-like bath and opens to a large terrace with prime views.
Outside, there’s an oval-shaped pool and a charming wood footbridge that crosses a cinematic, lily pad-covered pond, leading to the lighted tennis court.
Scott’s custom Venice Beach abode is also back on the market for $4.5 million.
That home, which combines a bungalow with a glass-and-steel-duplex structure, first hit the market for $4.97 million in 2024.
Scott shares a daughter with his ex-wife, interior designer and event planner Olivia Korenberg. The couple,who divorced in 2024, were married for four years.
The listing broker is Sam Plouchart, of Christie’s International Real Estate Southern California.

hed: Charlize Theron’s home builders sell a stunning LA home for $13.2M — a neighborhood record
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Celebrity builders Rob Diaz and Mark Alexander have sold Villa Duir, built this year in Studio City’s Fryman Canyon, for $13.2 million.
That marks a record sale for Studio City on a price-per-square-foot basis.
The builders are known for their fresh “Scandifornian”-inspired designs and the celebrities who buy them, including Oscar-winning actress Charlize Theron and supermodel Amber Valletta.
“Duir” is the ancient Celtic word for oak — an apt name for the home, which is surrounded by century-old oak trees.
The modern two-story, five-bedroom home at 3274 Oakdell Road first hit the market for $13.9 million in March. It sits on just under 0.62 acres, on a rare, flat lot.
It was also delivered fully furnished: The seller bought a vibe as well as a home.
Scandifornian style is a recent term used to describe a design aesthetic that combines a Scandinavian minimalism with a sunny Cali sense of style.
Known for stylish renovations, rebuilds and ground-up spec constructions, the builders have projects that include a renovated 1941 Studio City bungalow that Oscar-winning actressCharlize Theron bought for $2.64 million— $340,000 over the asking price — in 2022.
Supermodel and environmental activist Amber Valletta also purchased a partially finished eco-friendly six-bedroom hilltop home on the edge of a rural canyon from Diaz and Alexander for an undisclosed price;the home was showcased in Architectural Digesttwo years ago.
Another project, known as Casa Mallorca, was showcased on “Selling Sunset,” before selling last year for $4.1 million — down from its $6 million ask.
Diaz and Alexander also built the Fryman Estate, a modern ground-up 17,627-square-foot, seven-bedroom modern farmhouse on property owned by the late “Jeopardy!” host Alex Trebek and his widow, Jean.
The home first hit the market last yearasking a staggering $42 million. In April, the price dropped to $32.5 million. Diaz and Alexander bought the property for $6.45 million in 2022, according to records.
Instead of clearing the landscape to build Villa Duir, the home was built around the trees, so it feels more connected to nature, brokers said. The exterior is clad in limestone and wood, and the interiors are filled with light.
Built for entertaining, the home features two kitchens, two living rooms and floor-to-ceiling glass doors that open to a resort-style pool terrace.
The bedrooms, including one on the main floor, come with ensuite baths.
There’s also a glass bridge “elevated among the trees,” that leads to a private guest suite.
The listing brokers were Jen Winston, of Compass, and Andrew Dinsky of Equity Union. Craig Strong and Lisa Klein, both of Compass, brought the buyer, a local from Los Angeles.

hed: Ask the Remodeler: Backup generator vs. battery backup: Which is right for you?
subhead: What if the power goes out? Backup power typically takes two forms: a fuel-powered generator or a battery backup.
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

We have all seenpowerful stormsbarreling through all parts of New England, bringing heavy rains, high winds, and flooding. That means more power outages, and these seem to be coming through more frequently and throughout the entire year. Add to that an ever-increasingstrain on our electrical gridin general, and it’s making more people consider what to do for backup power. This all comes at a time when our lives are becoming even more dependent on the electric grid. Homes are increasingly using electric heat pumps for heating and cooling, induction ranges, EV car chargers, and we also are working from home more, which requires power and internet. Household electrical needs have never been higher.

So, what if the power goes out? For now, backup power typically takes two forms: a fuel-powered backup generator or a battery backup. Generators have been the norm for many years and are well established. True battery backup on a scale that allows you to power some or all your home is relatively new. Here, a look at the pros and cons of both.


As mentioned, these have been around for some time, and there are many brands out there to choose from.

The pros:

— The initial cost for a backup generator will be less than a quality battery backup system since the products are more established and have been manufactured to scale for some time.

— A generator should give you more than enough power to get you through the outage. The vast majority are fueled by natural gas from your home’s gas utility or a propane tank.

The cons

— Although the initial cost of installation is cheaper, in the long run, it could cost you more with maintenance and fuel costs. There are many variables: How often you lose power and for how long it is out in an average year. Some areas are much more prone than others to losing power.

— The installation and space is pretty invasive. The generator itself takes up a fair amount of room on your property, and it needs to be placed in an area away from windows and doors. If you use natural gas, you will need to connect the gas from your basement and trench the gas line over to the generator. If you use propane, you will need to find a place to put the propane tank. These present challenges in an urban setting.

— They are loud and emit exhaust. Generators have come a long way in terms of decibel level, but they still will let you know when they are running. Again, this can be more of an issue in a tight urban setting.


This technology is newer and doesn’t have the track record that generators do. There are less electricians out there who are familiar with the mechanics of these, but that is changing.

The pros

— Some utilities charge for electricity using what’s called TOU or time of use. The rates are higher during peak hours and go down at night. Most battery backups use smart technology that can allow them to power a home through the day when rates are higher; then the batteries recharge overnight when the rates are lower. (If you combine solar power with battery backup, you are talking about substantial savings. The combination of solar and smart battery power with a utility that charges on a TOU scale can greatly reduce and quite possibly eliminate paying any peak rates.)

— Battery backup is virtually silent and only takes up wall space.

— Battery backup needs little to no maintenance. Once installed, an occasional check when you have the electrician over is probably all you will need for a very long time. Many systems have software updates, but these are done automatically through a Wi-Fi connection.

The cons

— The up-front costs are more to install a proper battery backup system. Over the long run, it will save money, but there is no escaping the higher investment cost.

— The energy they provide is not limitless like a natural gas-fed generator. Even a propane-fed generator has more capacity than you will ever need for a typical power outage. Most battery backups will only get you nine to 12 hours if you are using them for essentials like the refrigerator, lights, some appliances, and device chargers. Trying to run HVAC systems will quickly drain the battery. This can be offset by adding more battery capacity.

Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge. Send your questions to[email protected]. Questions are subject to editing. hed: Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s $100M Los Angeles party palace revealed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The wife of a Google co-founder fighting a plan to make California’s housing more affordable has been caught using her $110 million mansion purely for functions — not even living there.
The Los Angeles estate is larger than the Taj Mahal, dubbed the manor, and has been transformed into a party palace for a “green” mega-billionaire’s nonprofit empire. Now she’steamed up with actress Jane Fondato preserve onerous environmental reviews that make California housing difficult to build.
Wendy Schmidt and her husband, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, splurged on the outlandish former home of famed producer Aaron Spelling, dubbed “The Manor,”last year.
But the power couple won’t be living in the 56,000-square-foot, 14-bedroom and 27-bath estate —  as it’ll only be used for parties, a source revealed to the California Post.
The Holmby Hills manse is undergoing renovations, with property records showing a slew of permits filed since last year to install a solar-friendly roof, rework the HVAC system, and make other interior upgrades.
The couple has also re-christened the 5-acre, 123-room party pad “594,” the Wall Street Journalreported.
The Schmidts — who are die-hard environmentalists with multiple properties in New York, London, Miami Beach and Montecito — plan to host lavish nonprofit fundraisers at the palatial show-home as Wendy rallies opposition toProp. 45.
The measure, supported by the California Chamber of Commerce and fellow Google co-founder Sergey Brin’s Building a Better California, would expedite onerous environmental reviews that critics say have made housing, transit and other infrastructure too costly and difficult to build.
Wendy teamed up with Fonda two years ago to fight oil drilling off the California coast after the industry attempted to roll back coastal buffer zones.

The pals then spun up Clean and Healthy California, an environmentalist PAC that raised millions from a who’s who of Hollywood and Silicon Valley titans.
Fonda and Schmidt co-hosted an arts benefit at posh Gagosian gallery in Beverly Hills that raised $14 million for the cause, according to apress release.San Francisco philanthropist Laurene Powell Jobs, the widow of Steve Jobs, and venture capitalist John Doerr kicked in a cool $500,000 each for the anti-oil campaign.
Actor Sean Penn,Baby2Baby executive Kelly Sawyer Patricofand Maria Shriver, ex-wife of Arnold Schwarzenegger, gave $1,000 each, while actress Kyra Sedgwick kicked in $100.
Clean and Healthy California appears to be using leftover funds from the campaign to oppose Prop. 45, contributing more than $7 million since June to nix the reform that’s designed to make housing and other developments easier to build.
Wendy is a lead opponent of the No on Prop. 45 campaign, contributing more than $5 million to the effort to kill the reform.
Prop. 45 supporters argue it will streamline California’s notorious layers of red tape, but critics like Fonda have labeled it a plot to pollute the environment.
Other opponents include the lefty union Building and Construction Trades Council and a collection of labor and community groups.
The Schmidts founded the Schmidt Ocean Institute and Schmidt Sciences, supporting oceanographic and scientific research with the aim of building a “healthy, resilient, secure world for all.”
The couple has also provided major financial support to Advocacy Action Fund, which bankrolls environmental campaigns and other left-of-center causes.
