hed: Tech billionaire-heavy California town becomes the priciest ZIP code for 1 big reason
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s most expensive ZIP code just changed coasts.
For the first time in two years, Miami’s Fisher Island has been knocked off its perch as thepriciest ZIP codein the country.
The tony 33109 enclave has been overtaken by Atherton, California’s 94027, a Silicon Valley bedroom community now flush with cash from the artificial intelligence boom, according to PropertyShark.com andBloomberg.
The swap says as much about where American fortunes are being made as it does about real estate.
South Florida’s rise was fueled by hedge funders, private equity titans and corporate transplants, a wave that included billionaires like Ken Griffin, Jeff Bezos and Carl Icahn, all of whom helped push Miami-Dade home prices into record territory.
Atherton’s comeback tells a different story, one written by AI executives and engineers suddenly sitting on enormous stock windfalls.
Tucked about 18 miles northwest of San Jose in San Mateo County, Atherton reclaimed its old crown after median home prices there shot up to nearly $10 million in the first half of 2026, a roughly 20% jump from the year before, per PropertyShark’s annual ZIP code rankings.
The town counts venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, WhatsApp co-founder Jan Koum and Golden State Warriors sharpshooter Stephen Curry among its residents, and it’s become ground zero for AI-fueled wealth creation.
Bloomberg reported Atherton has already logged five home sales north of $30 million this year, putting it on pace to match last year’s tally, as workers from OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX cash out stock and pour the winnings into sprawling estates.
The reshuffling at the top is the latest sign that the geography of extreme American wealth keeps shifting. Fisher Island first grabbed the No. 1 spot during the pandemic-era exodus, when droves of wealthy executives and investors fled high-tax states for South Florida’s shores.
Slipping to second place is hardly a demotion for Fisher Island. The 216-acre private landmass, reachable only by ferry, yacht or helicopter, remains one of the wealthiest residential ZIP codes in America. Condos there routinely fetch tens of millions of dollars, and residents get private beaches, a golf course, marinas and a country club most Americans will never set foot in.
The island is dotted with mansions, too, some listed for as much as $85 million. Just last year, Robb Report crowned Fisher Island the nation’s most expensive ZIP code, pegging its median home price at roughly $12 million.
South Florida isn’t ceding ground in the ultra-luxury market either. Bloomberg found that seven of the 11 residential sales that topped $100 million nationwide last year happened in Florida.

hed: New Hamptons mansion aims for a record $162M — 5 months after the property sold for $72M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The sky’s the limit in the Hamptons.
There, the summer of stratospheric listings just booked another contender — a grand $162 million East Hampton compound that will rise from the dunes and replace a storied estate purchased in March for $72 million, The Post has learned.
The five-month quick flip for 43 East Dune Lane comes all-inclusive for the buyer, most notably with the skills of award-winning architects and builders — and all construction permits planned to be in place.
While in former years the purchase would be a shoe-in as the most expensive listed residential property ever in the area, this year there is potentially intimidating competition.
The estate sits between Calvin Klein’s former East Hampton compound, which listed in June for a breathtaking $165 million, and the Sagaponack home of billionaire hedge fund manager Zach Schreiberthat listed the same monthfor $152.5 million. Right now, the record stands withthe $147 million Further Lane buyin 2014 by another hedge fund billionaire, Barry Rosenstein.
The current East Dune Lane home comes with real princess pedigree. Longtime ownerLee Radziwill, the sister of Jackie Onassis, held that title when married to Prince Stanisław Albrecht Radziwill. After their 1974 divorce, the Hamptons upper crust still called her by the royal moniker.
Radziwill bought the property in the late 1980s for a bit over $6 million and lived there for more than a decade with her husband Herbert Ross, who directed the films “Footloose” and “Steel Magnolias.”
When the couple became extremely estranged in the late ‘90s, they stuck a deal to sell the home for $19 million to Jerry Seinfeld. But Seinfeld ended up with “No soup.” The comedian was cancelled after Radziwill and Ross had a rip-roaring fight about the sale and its legacy on the front lawn in front of their brokers and the sale was called off, the New York Observer reported at the time.
The present owner’s $72 million deal marked a steep slide from its original $120 million ask.
Little is known about the buyer because they used a shell company to purchase the property anonymously. Deed and tax roll records provide some information, with the purchaser having ties to a unit in a 134-apartment co-op in the heart of Manhattan’s Flatiron District, at 21 E. 22nd St.
The buyer is working with a stellar “dream team” to create the new home and its guest cottage, said listing agent Terry Cohen of Compass.
It appears plans for the property were in place from the get-go. The design and building team includes architectRobert A.M. Stern, the legendary New York fixture who passed away last Thanksgiving from a brief respiratory illness.
Master custom builder Ed Bulgin is behind dozens of enclaves in the Hamptons, including his redesign and expansion of the sweeping estate that served as sanctuary for Gordon Gekko in the 1987 film, “Wall Street.”
Landscape architect Ed Hollander is also on board. Hollander redesigned exteriors for, among other East Hampton homes, Neil Partick Harris’s 10-acre woodland estate and Candice Bergen’s 2 acres of gardens.
This builder and architects are going to realize “an extraordinary build,” of the new 17,500-square-foot main home, its 3,500-square foot guest house and landscaping, Cohen said.
The team will file building permits within the next two weeks for a home with 270-degree ocean views, a rare basement for Hamptons coastal properties and a short walk to the ocean, Cohen said.
The estate will sit on 3.6 acres with 225 feet of direct ocean frontage and plenty of privacy through its proximity to Hook Pond, and more than 200 acres of manicured golf course.
Nine bedrooms, 11 full and two half-bathrooms will nestle amid its three levels that all have clear ocean vistas. Plenty of mobility is provided by an elevator, dual staircases and a separate second-floor wing with a third staircase.
The first floor unfolds from a gallery foyer that will open into a living hall, and will contain a covered terrace, a sunroom and a dining room — along with a large den and two ensuite guest bedrooms.
The second floor is anchored by the primary suite, complete with a private porch and an office nook, as well as two additional ensuite guest bedrooms.
A separate wing accommodates an en-suite guest bedroom with a porch, and the lower level is designed for recreation and wellness.
That area will include a golf simulator, a gym with a cold plunge, a sauna, a playroom and a snack bar. A nearby sunken tennis court opens to an expansive lawn with an adjoining garden and terrace, as well as the guest house.
Also included are a wine cellar and a bar that opens to an outdoor pergola. If a cocktail party becomes especially buoyant, the nearby 20 by 80-foot rimless pool can fit 140 seated guests.

hed: Princess Margaret’s famous country cottage lists for millions in ‘genuinely rare moment’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The former home ofPrincess Margaretand Antony Armstrong-Jones, better known as Lord Snowdon’s former country retreat, is on the market for the first time in the home’s history.
Known as The Old House, the home, which was gifted to Lord Snowdon by his uncle, designer Oliver Messel, prior to his marriage to Princess Margaret, is listed with Blue Book Agency for about $5.3 million.
Originally built in 1481, the cottage in West Sussex came into the possession of the Messel family in 1890 and was passed down for generations before Oliver gifted it to the royal couple.
Upon receiving the 5,750-square-foot home on the 5.52-acre property, Lord Snowdon transformed the dilapidated home into a private retreat away from the public, often hosting many famous faces, including actor Peter Sellers, ballerina Dame Margot Fonteyn, Bianca Jagger, financier Sir Evelyn de Rothschild and more.
“What Lord Snowdon created here was not simply a private home but an extraordinary creative retreat,” Theo James-Wright, director at Blue Book Agency, said. “This was a place where royalty mixed with artists, actors, writers and designers, where some of the most influential figures of the 20th century gathered behind closed doors. Very few houses can genuinely claim to have witnessed such a remarkable chapter of British cultural history.”
The rich history surrounding this house inspired an episode in season three of thepopular Netflix series, “The Crown.”
Some of the elements Snowdon brought to the home include a redesigned kitchen, a balcony salvaged from Ascot Racecourse’s Royal Box during refurbishment works, a lake he created and a “time capsule of royal, cultural and family life” made up of newspaper clippings detailing royal scandals and major events, put together by Snowdon himself.
The estate features a main house with six bedrooms, as well as a pool house which can be used as a guest suite.
In addition, the grounds include a garden office, library, tractor shed and other amenities.
While this is the first time the home has been put on the market publicly, Snowdon did sell it privately in 2003, and the current owners purchased it off-market in 2005.
“The fact that this is the first time the property has ever been publicly offered for sale makes this a genuinely rare moment,” James-Wright said. “Opportunities to acquire houses with this level of provenance, architectural significance and cultural importance simply do not come along very often.”
Princess Margaret and Lord Snowdon first met in 1958, and their friendship quickly turned into a romance, with the palaceannouncing their engagement in February 1960.
They were married just a few months later in May 1960 at Westminster Abbey.
Their wedding was the first royal wedding to be televised, attracting an estimated 300 million viewers worldwide.
Over the course of their marriage, the couple welcomed two children: their son David Armstrong-Jones in November 1961, and their daughter Lady Sarah Chatto in May 1964.
They were married for 16 years before announcing their separation in March 1976, later finalizing their divorce in July 1978.
Despite ending their marriage, the two are said to have remained good friends in the following years.
Following their divorce, Lord Snowdon married Lucy Lindsay-Hogg in 1978, while Princess Margaret never remarried.
Princess Margaret died in February 2002at the age of 71 due to a stroke, after her health began to decline in the 1990s. Lord Snowdon died in January 2017 at the age of 86.

hed: Elon Musk to build a 100M-square-foot megafactory in Texas — 5 times the size of the world’s biggest building
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Elon Musk is about to build something so big it will make the Pentagon look like a strip mall.
Tesla and SpaceXconfirmed Thursdaythat Terafab, their jointly built semiconductor megafactory, will rise in Grimes County, Texas, just outside Houston, with a first phase price tag of $16.8 billion.
The finished complex is slated to top 100 million square feet, a footprint that would blow past every structure ever built and instantly become the largest building in the world.
Musk, who runs both companies,called the facility“the largest and most valuable building on Earth by far.”
For scale, that beats out the current record holder, China’s New Century Global Center in Chengdu, which tops out around 18.9 million square feet with an indoor beach and ski slope tucked inside.
Terafab would be more than five times that size.
It would also dwarf the Pentagon (6.6 million square feet, making that the current largest building in the US), Apple Park (2.82 million square feet) and the Mall of America (5.6 million square feet) put together several times over.
Whether Terafab ultimately claims the title of world’s largest building will come down to whether it gets built as pitched. Renderings of the facility show a sprawling, wing shaped structure carved into the Texas landscape, with a translucent roofline that Musk has promised will be as striking as it is massive.
“It will be stunningly beautiful,” Musk wrote on X.
Tesla framed the project as an existential supply issue in a post on X.
“Both Tesla & SpaceX will need far more chips than current & future global production can supply,” the company wrote, adding that the goal is “producing over 1 terawatt of compute per year.”
The site will handle logic chips, memory, packaging and testing all under one roof, an approach SpaceX described in a post on its own website.
“The facility will be an advanced semiconductor fab that will bridge the divide between current global chip supply and the compute demand of the future,” the post read.
Semiconductors are needed to control electrical currents, act as the brains of modern electronics, and power everything from smartphones to cars.
Chipscoming out of Terafabwon’t just power laptops and phones.
The company said it “will produce chips optimized for edge computing and inference for use in hardware like Tesla’s Optimus robots and self-driving Cybercabs, along with high-power chips designed for operating SpaceX’s space-based data centers.”
The project is expected to create at least 3,000 jobs, with hiring drawn from Grimes and neighboring Brazos County.
Tesla and SpaceX have said 60% to 80% of new hires at their other Texas sites have come from local residents, a pattern the companies expect to repeat here.
Musk has been eyeing this project since March, when the companies first floated Terafab with a smaller $25 billion headline figure.
The number has since been revised down to the current $16.8 billion first phase, though total investment across all planned phases could still climb as high as $119 billion.
The site itself carries some baggage.
Terafab will sit on the Gibbons Creek Reservoir, a body of water once used to cool a coal fired power plant that shut down in 2018.
With water use for data centers already a sore subject across Texas, SpaceX moved to get ahead of it. The company said it plans to draw water from the reservoir rather than tap local groundwater.
Not everyone in Grimes County is thrilled. Hundreds of residents packeda county meeting Wednesday,a day before the announcement, to raise concerns about the millions of dollars in tax incentives handed to the project and what they called a lack of transparency in how the deals came together.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s office has extended a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant to SpaceX for the project, which also qualifies for the state’s Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program
School officials sounded a friendlier note. Consolidated Independent School District Superintendent Sarah Borowicz called the moment a defining one for the district in a statement.
Intel is also circling the project. The chipmaker has confirmed it will contribute to Terafab, though it has not detailed the nature of its involvement.
The Post has reached out to Tesla and SpaceX for comment.

hed: You need $450M and ‘a set of balls’ to buy this floating doomsday bunker in the Maldives
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A zero-land island spanning 155 acres of deep-water lagoon in the Maldives — designed like an eco-conscious doomsday bunker for the 1% — is on the market for a cool $450 million.
The catch? It hasn’t actually been built.
Dubbed “The Adaptive Atoll,” the eye-watering resort concept calls for a submerged rail infrastructure and Brutalist “Mother-Ship” fortresses enabling mechanically dockable overwater suites — scalable, customizable and designed to rise with the ocean, theDaily Mailreported.
The futuristic concept would “bypass the land-submersion crisis” with technology developed by Private Islands Inc., thelistingon the firm’s website indicates. It provides “a permanent situation in an uncertain world.”
The Adaptive Atoll “combats rising sea levels by decoupling the resort from fixed land,” Private Islands Inc. founder Chris Krolow told The Post. His firm markets hundreds of islands.
Rather than sitting on sinking sand, the island relies on an earthquake-resistant rail system built directly into the lagoon floor. The hidden tracks silently shuttle modular overwater suites across the water, docking them into massive, solar-powered Brutalist fortresses made from raw timber and coralline stone.
While the $450 million price tag is a preliminary estimate and no “ground” has been broken, Krolow insists the underlying technology is solid, drawing on existing heavy-duty offshore engineering.
The 155-acre-deep man-made atoll in the turquoise waters of the Indian Ocean is a real, physical site in the Maldives. The Maldivian government owns the land and the buyer would acquire the lagoon site on a long-term leasehold basis.
Plans call for 10 permanent fortresses, which can be expanded with 30 or more bunk pavilion suites. The circular “Mother-Ship” powers the entire island with 100% solar energy.
To get to and from the site, the layout accommodates fly-in capabilities.
The ideal buyer is an ultra-high-net-worth individual who already owns high-end waterfront properties, Krolow said.
Island buyers “need to be a little crazy,” Krolow previously toldthe Telegraph. “You need to have a set of balls, and you need to have been bitten by that island bug.”

hed: A whopping 79% of home buyers in this pandemic-era Texas boomtown are now selling at a loss
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Homeowners across Austin are learning a brutal lesson about buying at the top of the market.
Ryan McPherson bid $20,000 over asking for a four-bedroom home in East Austin back in 2022, paying $615,000 for a house he’s now bracing to sell for as little as $420,000, a roughly 30% loss.
“Everybody that I worked with, they kept saying Austin only goes up,” McPherson toldBusiness Insiderin an interview.
He’s since moved back to Phoenix and is done waiting for a turnaround. “I’m not going to keep trying to wait this out and pray that there’s a turnaround, because it’s not coming right now,” he said. “I’d rather just stop losing sleep over it.”
He’s far from alone. Austin has postedthe steepest home price dropof any major US metro over the past four years, with asking prices down nearly 25% since the 2022 peak, according to a Realtor.com analysis.
Roughly 79% of homes that sold that year arenow worth lessthan their purchase price.
Remote workers fleeing pricier coastal cities flooded into Austin during the pandemic, drawn by lower taxes and cheap housing. The metro’s population jumped more than 5% between 2020 and 2022, census data shows, making it the fastest growing large city in the country.
“Ironically, affordability was the big draw,” Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told BI.
Asking prices soared 36% year-over-year by August 2021, and typical homes topped $465,000 by spring 2022, Realtor.com figures show. “Prices were getting totally out of control,” Berner said.
Builders piled in, growing Austin’s housing supply by more than 20%, or roughly 211,000 units, between 2020 and 2025, per census estimates. Then the Fed started hiking rates that March, and buyers vanished just as new construction flooded the market.
“Everything was going into multiple offers, and then it really just stopped,” Austin agent Lindsay Neuren said. “That really spooked the market.”
Gary Froniewski bought a North Austin condo in 2022 and figures it’s lost as much as half its value since.
“I expect to take a haircut on this, no matter what,” Froniewski told the outlet. “It’s just a matter of how devastating it ends up being when we’re ready to actually move.”
Others have already taken the hit. Agent Cynthia Mattiza is representing 2022 buyers now pricing their home at a loss.
“We’re just thankful to receive any offer sometimes,” she said. Fellow agent John Mundell recently helped clients in Buda sell for $30,000 less than they paid.
“They’re kind of screwed,” Mundell said. “But they had to move.”
Sellers who once ignored stained carpets and repairs now have to fix things up themselves before listing, Mundell said, and he’s grown pickier about which homes are worth his time.
“I’d take anything before,” he said. “Now I’m just being a little more selective.”
Some owners are listing homes for sale andrent at once,betting that becoming a landlord beats a loss. McPherson tried it in 2025, renting his home for $2,500 a month against a $4,000 mortgage payment. It bought him time, not a fix.
“Life taught me an expensive lesson,” he said. “Hopefully, I don’t repeat these mistakes.”
Not everyone is gloomy. Berner, who bought his own Austin home in 2023, just won a 12% cut on his property tax assessment.
“If I had a crystal ball and saw that my home would basically not appreciate in the three years that I owned it, and I could have continued renting for about two-thirds of what I pay in my mortgage, I probably would have stayed renting,” he said. “But I didn’t have that crystal ball.”
Pending sales rose 11% year-over-year in June and price cuts are growing rarer, per Realtor.com, and Zonda executive Keith Hughes ranks Austin tops nationally for long-term fundamentals.
“The underlying conditions support a comeback,” Hughes said.
Froniewski isn’t second-guessing his 2022 purchase, even if the timing stings.
“I’m a firm believer that you can’t time the market,” he said. “You never know when the peak is, and you never know when the bottom is.”
Still, he admits: “If I had to sell the house today, I would be in shambles.”

hed: Former Bloomberg commissioner blasts pied-à-terre tax with lawsuit filed against Mamdani
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
You’re guilty until you prove yourself innocent in Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s New York.
Former tax chief Martha Stark — who has been trying to fix tax inequities for almost 40 years — is giving NYC’s mayor a big fat “F” on his new pied-à-terre tax.
Stark, policy director forTax Equity Now New York (TENNY), and a former finance commissioner under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, accused the city of overreaching with its data dump and improperly shifting the burden of proof onto innocent homeowners.
Stark’s remarks were submitted as expert testimony in alawsuitbrought by three furious homeowners seeking to halt the city’s controversial new luxurysecond-home tax.
The trio claims City Hall is unfairly forcing them to jump through hoops to prove they actually live in their own homes full-time, all to avoid a luxury tax for second-home owners, according to the lawsuit filed Friday in Staten Island Supreme Court.
The suit demands that a judge declare the city’s actions illegal and immediately scrub the900,000-name listfrom the DOF website, released in July.
“In total, out of approximately 959,710 records published, only 24,218 — roughly two and one-half percent — meet the statutory value threshold,” which taxes one- to three-family homes with market value of $5 million or more; and condominium and cooperative apartments valued at $1 million or more, Stark said in expert testimony.
Release of the names and addresses “caused widespread confusion among property owners who feared they might be liable for the Surcharge when it does not apply to them under the statute.”
The city then mailed warning letters to around 17,000 property owners — 7,218 names short of the homes over the threshold — that were potentially eligible for the tax, but only 5,000 to 6,000 properties actually fit the bill as non-primary residences subject to the tax, she said.
That left 11,000 to 12,000 homeowners with the burden of establishing that they are not subject to the tax.
Rather than use “opaque and unverified unit-value allocations,” Stark said the city could have used tax returns, STAR exemptions and abatement records to accurately determine primary residences.
Stark has pushed for structural property tax reform in the Big Apple for four decades.
Stark was part of a2107 groupthat sued to get the city’s property tax assessment scheme tossed. TENNY claimed the current law and its implementation violate the equal protection and due process clauses of the New York and US constitutions, the state’s Real Property Tax Law and the federal Fair Housing Act.

hed: Historic Maine house selling for $1 — but under one condition or it’ll face demolition
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A historic home in one of Maine’s seafaring towns known as the “City of Ships” hit the housing market for just $1 — but the buyer will have to move it, or it’ll face demolition.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, a shipbuilder,announced Wednesdaythat it is selling two residential buildings for $1 each, including the circa-1900 Deering House at 606 Washington St. in Bath, Maine.
However, the buyer must relocate the buildings to a legally permitted site by Nov. 20, 2027.
The Deering House was originally the home of Gardiner G. Deering, a prominent shipbuilder who helped cement Bath’s reputation as a major shipbuilding center in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The house is currently being used as office space, with tenants under lease through November 2027,WMTW reported.
Bath Iron Works says the buildings are being sold “as is, where is,” with no warranties of any kind.
The buyer will be responsible for “all relocation costs, including permits, approvals, licensed structural movers, transportation, site prep, foundations, utilities, and related services.”
The Deering House will be demolished to make room for a new Bath Iron Works facility if no buyers step in to save the historic residence.
“It’s important for General Dynamics and Bath Iron Works to continue to be able to grow as a company and employ thousands of Mainers. We’re looking for ways to improve our facilities,” Jolene Nickerson, director of facilities capital at Bath Iron Works, said, WMTW reported.
“The hope is that there is somebody that has a viable lot to move this to, and that it’s financially feasible for somebody who is interested in the house to relocate it and preserve the historic nature, which the community is very excited about,” Nickerson added.
Bath was once known as the “City of Ships,” and ranked third in the US in wooden-hulled vessel production in 1854, behind New York City and Boston,according to the city’s government website.
Deering built 99 vessels during his career and operated a shipyard along the Kennebec River that helped make Bath a leading center of wooden shipbuilding before the Civil War ended the boom and “changed. the face of the industry.”
Jack Martin, archivist and special collections librarian at the Patten Free Library, said saving the house would give its new owner a unique piece of Bath history.
“You would have a one-of-a-kind home and a great story,” Martin said, according to WMTW.
“Not only do you have the history of the house that comes with it, then you also have the story of being the person who moved and saved a historic home — and that’s fascinating.”
Bath Iron Works said it has already received several inquiries about the buildings.
The idea of moving a historic Maine house is not unprecedented.
In May, a 6,200-square-foot, three-story house designed by architect John Calvin Stevens in 1899 was moved about one-third of a mile through Augusta,the Kennebec Journal reported.
The 120,000-pound building was split into two sections and transported to a new lot — with the overall project costing more than $500,000.

hed: For $415k, you can live in a New England community library
subhead: Built in 1850, it originally served as the Vestry Schoolhouse for the small farming community of Foster, R.I., before becoming the Tyler Free Library in 1953.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
It’s every bibliophile’s dream: moving into a library.
Built in 1850,81 Moosup Valley Road in Foster, R.I., originally served as the Vestry Schoolhouse for the small farming community before becoming the Tyler Free Library in 1953. In anticipation of the transition of the building from a schoolhouse to a library, Casey B. Tyler donated 2,395 volumes, which were stored in the schoolhouse.
“I feel anxious there be a good library in Moosup Valley as soon as there is a place to keep the books,” Tyler said, according to historic documents.
Fifteen library cards were distributed on that special day. The library was expanded a few times throughout the years to house its growing collection, with its completion being in the 1970s. But its era came to an end earlier this year, and the building is now on the market for $415,000.
Zoned for agricultural/residential use, the 1,760-square-foot property, which sits on one acre, is tucked behind a white picket fence. (Don’t miss the classic book drop on the front of the building.) The building has hardwood floors and open cathedral ceilings. The back room has a half-bathroom and a section filled with bookcases. Steps lead to the former children’s library area, which was originally the one-room schoolhouse.
Head down a flight of stairs, and you’ll find yourself in what was the main part of the library. It’s home to a fireplace that anchors the space.
There is a basement for storage.
“What I would say to you is with little creativity, I don’t think it would take a whole lot to actually change it into something,” saidDawn Wallitschof KEY Real Estate, who has thelistingand took her two daughters to the library when they were younger.
Wallitsch said that when the listing was first posted, endless Facebook commenters had the same question.
“Are the books included?” Wallitsch recalled.
However, the books aren’t included in the sale and will go to the Foster Public Library.
“Tyler Free Library has always been the greatest labor of love and care by the residents of Foster,” the library’s Board of Directors said in a statement. “It is with full and grateful hearts and all of our admiration for every ingenious effort, great and small, in which the town of Foster and its people joined together to build this beloved institution, that we say farewell to our library. A library is more than its books; it is the spirit of place made manifest, and so it has been with Tyler.”
Megan Johnson is a Boston-based writer and reporter whose work appears in People, Architectural Digest, The Boston Globe, and more.

hed: High-flying landowner who said he’d shoot beach ‘trespassers’ finally snared — as he blows up at judge
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
ABay Area real estate investorhas been arrested after allegedly spending more than six months dodging a warrant — before launching into a fiery confrontation with a judge during his first hearing.
Luke “Lucky Luke” Brugnarawas escorted from a federal courtroom last week after repeatedly interrupting US Magistrate Judge Lisa Cisneros, who ordered he remain behind bars while his case moves forward.
The dramatic hearing came days after US Marshals arrested the 62-year-old at his home inSan Francisco’s Sunset District.
Prosecutors say Brugnara attempted to evade authorities by climbing on to the roof of a neighboring church. Brugnara vehemently disputed that account in court.
“I never climbed on any church. The church roof is eight stories tall. OK, how can I go eight stories when it’s a one-story house? It’s a lie,” he told the judge.
He also insisted he had not known about the federal hearing that led to the warrant for his arrest.
“I was not notified by my attorney,” Brugnara said. “I’m legally required to notification by counsel of a court hearing to be held as a failure to appear. OK, I did not appear because I was not notified of the hearing.”
The confrontation marked the latest twist in the legal troubles of the former high-flying San Francisco property developer whose name has now become synonymous with an increasingly bizarre fight overaccess to a Bay Area beach.
Brugnara is facing federal allegations that he fraudulently obtained $422,000 through apandemic-relief programby misrepresenting his company’s size, payroll and number of workers. Prosecutors say he used the money to buy a house.
After he failed to appear at a February hearing concerning his bond, a judge issued a warrant for his arrest. Prosecutors later argued that Brugnara knew about the warrant but did nothing to surrender.
The allegations came into sharper focus after Brugnara became embroiled in a separate controversy at Thornton State Beach.
As previously reported by The California Post, a trust linked to Brugnara acquired an interest in land near the Daly City beach in December.
In January,he fenced off roughly six acresat the entrance to the popular coastal area, despite owning only a fraction of the property.
The move enraged fellow property owners and beachgoers who had long used the trail.
A sign posted near the fence warned that the owner was armed with a 9mm handgun, while another threatened that trespassers would be shot.
The confrontation escalated when Brugnara was accused of threatening people who approached the barrier.
One couple called 911 after alleging he warned, “If you get near the fence, I will shoot and kill you,”ABC7 reported.
Police later stopped Brugnara’s girlfriend as she drove away with a 9mm Glock sitting in an unlocked case on the front seat, according to ABC7.
Brugnara, who was in the back seat, was arrested on allegations including being a felon in possession of a firearm and making threats.
The beach dispute added another chapter to Brugnara’s long criminal history.
The former real estate tycoon previously spent roughly nine years in federal prison for crimes including mail and wire fraud.
His record has also included tax-related convictions and other allegations involving threats and obstruction. During last week’s hearing, Brugnara sought release with a $50,000 cash bond and electronic monitoring.
He also repeatedly raised concerns about his health and blood pressure as the judge considered whether he should remain jailed.
“This my liberty that you’re playing with,” Brugnara told Cisneros.
“I know, but you’re trying to steal from me — possibly my life. I could die tonight from a heart attack or stroke. You don’t care,” he added.

“I do care,” the judge replied.
But Brugnara continued to interrupt as the hearing dragged on.
Eventually, Cisneros indicated the proceeding was over and Marshals moved to take him into custody.
“Am I going to trial?” Brugnara asked.
“Stop talking,” a Marshal responded.
“How can you put an innocent man in jail?” Brugnara said.
A written order issued Wednesday keeps Brugnara in custody through the federal case. His attorney previously sought to withdraw from representing him, and that request remains pending.
His next court appearance is scheduled in about two weeks.

hed: NYC Billionaire’s Row tower where it’s raining ‘chunks of concrete’ losing value fast: ‘It’s too dangerous’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
As drones circle the 1,396-foot tower and repair work begins at 432 Park Avenue, the 94th floor skypad at the beleaguered building has sold for $22 million, Gimme Shelter has learned — a stunning comedown from its original $33 million ask two years ago, and a$3.75 million gut-punchfrom the $25.75 million price it went into contract at earlier this month.
The seller is a trust linked to the late teen science prodigy turned philanthropist Roy T. Eddleman, founder of Spectrum Labs, who paid $31.5 million for the half-floor spread in 2019. Hedied in 2022at age 82.
“The $22 million closing is lower than anyone wanted, but a half floor in the building hasn’t sold since 2024. This is the new market reality,” listing broker Marc Riedel of Serhant told The Post, who shares the listing with Serhant’s Jordyn Nusynowitz.
One broker familiar with the sale said a hit like that barely stings for an owner in that tax bracket.
“You write it off, move on and make more money,” the broker said. “There are lots of bad deals. At least here you get the joy of living in the building.”
Jennifer Lopez and Alex Rodriguez once counted among the glamorous residents at 432 Park.
While sale prices at 432 Park keep sliding, rents are doing the opposite — a split brokers describe as the building’s Jekyll-and-Hyde reality. A certain buyer no longer wants in, but a certain renter still wants the address, repairs and all.
The same 94th floor unit had a signed lease with a renter willing to pay $85,000 a month — a building record for a half-floor unit — before a buyer swooped in and signed a purchase contract first, bumping the renter out.
That set off a chain reaction. Unit 66A, also asking $85,000 a month, ultimately rented for over $90,000. Another unit, 72A, then rented for $85,000. Both 66A and 94A are 4,000-square-foot, half-floor layouts with three bedrooms, three and a half baths and a library.
“I knew I could get $85,000 for 94A, but I didn’t foresee others following in the building,” Riedel said. “It tested the new reality of rising rents throughout the city.”
Two of the three units sold this year went to buyers who already owned elsewhere in the building, sources said.
“It’s one of the most hated buildings in New York, but people love it. It’s comical,” one broker said, noting some renters are drawn by friends already living there — including the pull of dinner together at the building’s private restaurant, run by Michelin-starred Australian chef Shaun Hergatt.
The sale closed as the building’s troubles continue to mount.
On Aug. 4, the building filed a work permit application with the city’s Department of Buildings.
The building’s condo board declined to comment. Building manager Len Czarnecki also declined, telling Gimme Shelter: “We are in active litigation and will refrain from comment.”
Built in 2015 and designed by the late architect Rafael Viñoly, the tower has been dogged by design complaints since it opened. Viñoly oncetold Gimme Shelterthe building “has a couple of screw-ups,” including oversized window frames and a layout that put prime front-facing views in the bathrooms rather than living spaces.
The bigger issue emerged last year, when a report warned that concrete cracks could sendchunks raining downand potentially render the building uninhabitable without a $160 million renovation — one owners hope the courts will force the developer to pay for.
Residents have also complained of swaying, groaning, leaks, power outages, elevator problems and the sound of trash hurtling down the chutes at alarming speeds.
The condo board sued CIM Group, Macklowe Properties and the sponsor entity in 2021, citing more than 1,500 construction and design defects, some of which the board’s engineering consultant flagged as life-safety issues.
A second suit filed in 2025 alleges CIM and Macklowe knew about facade cracking during construction and concealed it from buyers and city inspectors; CIM has denied the allegations and is seeking dismissal. The cracking has allegedly caused flooding and corrosion, and elevators have reportedly gotten stuck during high winds.
The drones circling above are surveying the tower ahead of the $160 million repair effort, as the building’s DOB work permit application moves forward.
“I would never buy in that building,” said one insider familiar with the litigation. “It was built so thin and so tall that it relies on advanced mechanical measures to stop it from swaying in the wind — that’s what caused a lot of the damage.”
“Living there is a gamble. It’s too dangerous for me to allow any of my relatives to live there. I’m a pessimist. This is a real problem — and they’re paying so much to live there!”

hed: Living solo in NYC isn’t cheap — so these single women moved into tiny apartments under 200 square feet
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Every night, Gail Schulman folds down her couch — and folds up her life to fit inside it.
The 32-year-old content creator lives inone of the smallest apartmentsin New York City: a 191-square-foot third-floor Brooklyn studio where a single yellow sofa bed does double duty as her living room and her bedroom.
It’s a tight squeeze, but since moving in this past February, Schulman has turned the space into a cozy home with distinct zones for living, dining and entertaining, piecing it together — and filming it for her nearly 47,800subscribers— one curated detail at a time.
Two matching cushioned yellow chairs, a small table and a new earth-toned rug round out the living area alongside the sofa bed. A small round bistro table with a pendant light fixture marks off the dining space. A cabinet and a built-in ledge in the kitchen do double duty as counters for entertaining — one for food, the other for drinks.
And as the lone tenant on the third floor, Schulman has a private bonus space most New Yorkers would kill for: an 8-by-2.5-foot foyer where she stashes and slips on her shoes.
For comparison, in the US, a standard hotel room averages 300 to 330 square feet.
Renting for $2,151 a month excluding utilities, the home is filled with personal treasures, from family heirlooms to travel finds, sponsored decor and her record player and record collection. Despite the volume of items, intentional sizing and layout prevent any sense of clutter.
“It’s scale,” Schulman told The Post, who stores larger items in a storage closet in the apartment. “I like things being proportioned properly. Visual balance is very important to me.”
Getting a somewhat cheaper apartment was important to Schulman as she left her corporate job to make it as a content producer, posting to her 47,800 YouTube subscribers about decorating her apartment, and didn’t know what her income would look like.
The apartment is outfitted with a full-sized refrigerator, stove, oven, microwave and dishwasher, and a large bathroom.
“It’s the nicest bathroom I’ve ever had in New York,” said Schulman, who has spent the last 10 years in the Big Apple, last living in East Harlem. “This is one of the best kitchens I’ve ever had.”
Inside her kitchen cabinets she has also been selective about what she keeps and how it’s organized.
“I own what I use and I use what I own,” she said.
Instead of using an under-sink cabinet for trash and recycling, Schulman tucked them into a nook concealed by a sliding fabric curtain. The top surface serves as a bar for entertaining.
She said she wanted to “make it look cute with all the ugliness behind it.”
To avoid cabin fever, Schulman works out of coffee shops or the Brooklyn Public Library.
“I make an effort to get out of the apartment multiple times a day,” whether it’s to volunteer in the park on Thursdays, or take a run.
Meanwhile, Exia Stephens, a newly minted real estate agent at Bond New York, lives in aeven smaller place.
Occupying a 156 square feet single-room on the Upper West Side, Stephens moved in with her cat, Superman. But unlike Schulman, Stephens’apartment has no kitchenand no bathroom, but she is grateful to be rid of roommates.
She shares a bathroom — frequently cleaned by staff — on the floor with five other SRO units, and a large communal kitchen on the ground floor with everyone in the building. Because the kitchen is 13 floors down, Stephens, 23, washes her dishes in the bathroom.
The building’s amenities are equally sparse.
The laundry room is stripped of machines, the lobby payphone is dead, and the only functioning elevator is a freight lift that takes forever to arrive. Yet, Stephens takes it all in stride.
“Once I get an instant pot, and once I get a convection oven, I’ll basically have a kitchen,” she said.
Stephens has been slowly furnishing the place. Her bed frame, twin-sized mattress, mini-refrigerator and microwave came with the unit.
She does some basic cooking, mostly oatmeal, sandwiches, microwavable rice and beans. She gets much of her food from her side job working front of house at a restaurant.
Stephens’ rent also comes cheaper — at $1,050 per month — including utilities, on the same block as a$30 million Beaux Arts mansionnear Riverside Park.
“I joke, ‘it’s nice to live in a mixed-income community,’” Stephens said.
Before moving to New York, the Maryland native lived in the UK, where she paid more to rent with roommates.
“This is so much bigger — like I can lay in the middle of my floor and spread out,” she said. “In the UK, neither of the rooms I lived in had enough floor space to even roll out a yoga mat. So this is huge to me.”
After a year abroad, she decided to move to New York.
“Everything in my life imploded, and it was like, ‘Well, why not?'” She said.
Stephens arrived in the Big Apple in January with just two suitcases, subletting furnished rooms before finding the SRO.
Her last spot in Yorkville was barely the length of her bed, cost $400 more per month, and ended abruptly after a literal cat fight between Superman and her housemate’s cat.
Now that she finally has a space to call her own, she has no plans to give it up anytime soon.
“Genuinely I’m not going to leave this apartment until I get married,” Stephens said somewhat in jest. “I’m not even dating anybody right now!”
“I really love this apartment,” she added. “If I ever lose faith in God, I’m like, actually no, because I was led here.”

hed: Bruce Springsteen’s longtime drummer quietly sold $13M Palm Beach land in just days as tech bros race for a spot
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
E Street Banddrummer Max Weinbergand his wife, Rebbecca Weinberg, just sold one of the largest remaining Intracoastal land assemblages in Ocean Ridge, a small Palm Beach County enclave that has quietly become one of the region’s most competitive waterfront markets, The Post has learned.
The adjoining parcels at 7 and 9 Sabal Island Drive traded for $13 million, property records show.
Together, the two lots span more than 33,000 square feet and stretch roughly 325 feet along the Intracoastal, enough room for a buyer to build a sprawling custom estate or a full family compound from scratch.
The site comes with deep-water dockage, a freshly rebuilt seawall, and quick boat access to the ocean through the Boynton Inlet.
A source told The Post the home never hit the open market at all. A buyer simply stumbled onto the listing and snapped it up within days.
The buyer has not yet been identified.
Nick Malinosky and Michael O’Connor of The Exclusive Group at Douglas Elliman brokered the deal, representing both sides of the transaction. They declined to comment on the transaction.
For Weinberg, real estate has long been a second act. The 75-year-old New Jersey native has bought, built or flipped dozens of houses over the years, and he’s not just an investor on the sidelines. He sits on the Planning and Zoning Board in nearby Delray Beach, where he keeps a home and a drum kit in the garage.
“What you try to do as a drummer is keep the conversation going,” Weinberg has previously said of his approach to local governance in an interview with theCoastal Star.“So as a Planning and Zoning Board member I’m trying to keep the municipal planning conversation going.”
Weinberg has anchored Springsteen’s E Street Band since 1974, when he beat out a stack of rivals for the gig after answering an ad in the Village Voice. He later built a second career as Conan O’Brien’s bandleader on both “Late Night” and “The Tonight Show,” a run that lasted from 1993 to 2010.
The numbers explain the appetite. Waterfront landacross Palm Beach Countynow lists at an average of roughly $2.4 million per acre, according to LandSearch data, with the average waterfront listing topping $10.8 million.
Building on the water adds its own premium too: waterfront construction typically runs 15 to 30 percent higher than a comparable inland build once pilings, flood compliance and seawall work are factored in, per SouthShore Builders, a local construction firm.
That math hasn’t slowed buyers down. In Palm Beach’s most extreme case, a private island called 10 Tarpon Islesold for $152 million in 2024,a deal real estate analysts pointed to as proof that in this market, the land itself, not the house sitting on it, can account for the bulk of the price tag.
Ocean Ridge has ridden that same current. Assemblages combining more than 300 feet of contiguous Intracoastal frontage rarely surface on the market, and when they do, buyers looking to build a custom estate from scratch tend to move fast.
Nearby enclaves have drawn a growing roster of billionaires and boldface names willing to pay top dollar for scarce oceanfront and Intracoastal parcels, including Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, WeatherTech founder David MacNeil, Fox News host Sean Hannity, motivational speaker Tony Robbins and pharma billionaire Randal J. Kirk, while Billy Joeloffloaded his own waterfront estatein the area for $43 million in 2024.

hed: NY couple restores abandoned brownstones into coveted guesthouses for Airbnb: ‘They choose us’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


An abandoned New York City building with bricked-up windows, rotting plywood, and rusted chains on the front door would make most prospective buyers run in the opposite direction. But for South Carolina couple Laureta Gjataand James Gale, these forgotten structures are pure gold.
Today, Gjata and Gale operateGale Guesthouses, a hospitality business dedicated torestoring historical propertiesacross the city and converting them into unique rentals on Airbnb.
Long before either of them picked up a sledgehammer, both founders developed the resilience needed to tackle ambitious goals through vastly different life paths.
Gjata, 39, has a background in customer-facing hospitality. She immigrated to Greece from Albania as a young refugee during the war in 1997. While she remembers feeling embarrassed as the kid in school who didn’t speak the language, she credits those challenging years with laying the foundation toovercome tough renovationchallenges.
“Back then, it seemed like the worst thing that could happen to a kid,” Gjata explains. “But looking back, some of the skills that I have have been useful to our journey restoring these buildings.”
Gjata eventually moved to New York to pursue acting, supporting herself from age 17 as a server and bartender.
Originally from Connecticut, Gale, 49, spent roughly 25 years working in the energy industry, specializing in physical natural gas trading and risk management.
While corporate risk management seems distant from historical home renovation, it provided the precise skill set required to evaluate intimidating real estate deals, structure finances, and manage daily operations.
“We both have those qualities that we need for each half of it,” Gale says. “I can’t do the things she does on the hospitality side, and I think she doesn’t have any interest in doing the other aspect of it.”
Together, the couple balance both halves of the business seamlessly, taking their role as hosts deeply to the heart.
“If someone comes to my table and I’m going to wait on them, or they come to our building and we’re going to host them, it’s like a mission,” Gjata explains. “You’re here for a good time. I don’t know what problems are going to come up, but we got it.”
The transition into property management didn’t happen overnight. Around 2015, while living in Astoria, Queens, Gjata found herself responsible for the full rent of a three-bedroom apartment after her roommates suddenly moved out.
To cover costs, a friend suggested listing the spare rooms on Airbnb.
“It was incredible … meeting all these people from all over the world,” Gjata explains. “That’s where the idea started, of what if I can find a place, make it my own, and host all these people and cook for them, and share my favorite spots of the city.”
Later, Gjata experimented with rental arbitrage in Hell’s Kitchen, taking over a neglected unit from a property management company. She agreed to fix up the rundown apartment at her own expense in exchange for listing rights. That project solidified her calling.
“I want to fix places that are not in the best shape and make them nice for people to come and stay,” Gjata shares.
When Gjata and Gale met, their shared love of historic architecture quickly became the focal point of their relationship. The couple spent their early weeks together riding bicycles through Brooklyn and touring open houses.
While Gale evaluates every potential deal through building codes and financial metrics, Gjata relies on an emotional connection.
“I’m the romantic. I’m not the numbers person,” Gjata says. “But you cannot really explain [it]. It’s almost as if we don’t really choose the houses. They choose us. The minute you see it, you know.”
The couple purchased their first property, a Brooklyn brownstone, in 2019. The project—dubbed theMadison Guesthouse—proved to be a true trial by fire.
The abandoned structure suffered from frozen, burst pipes and lacked functional heat and water. Aside from major plumbing work, the couple and their family completed the entire renovation hands-on while living onsite in a ground-floor studio. Through sheer grit and determination, they managed to welcome their first guests within just three months.
While Madison Guesthouse was intended to serve as both their personal residence and a guesthouse, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic made it challenging to balance life and work. Gale was working remotely in the hallway of their tiny studio apartment, guests were knocking for fresh towels, and the couple had just welcomed their first child.
The family relocated to the Finger Lakes to save money while planning their return to the city. In late 2020, they poured their savings into a second Brooklyn brownstone: theMacon Guesthouse.
“The house [was] calling us,” Gjata says. “We saw it, and there goes again the dream of getting our home.”
This second renovation took significantly longer, largely due to needing specialized architects and Department of Buildings permits. Although hiring professional contractors eased the physical burden, the overhaul took nearly two years before it was opened in mid-2022.
Though Macon didn’t become their permanent residence either, the couple cherished the process and the growth that came with it.

“You get into your eyes, you get into your mind what can be done, and I think that grows on you,” Gale explains. “So each iteration has been a better version of the one before, with a bigger eye on detail, a bigger eye on historical significance, a bigger eye on the pieces of what we can do to bring back the old into the new.”
The couple are currently working on their third major renovation: a Brooklyn limestone they are transforming into the Halsey Guesthouse. Even as this project nears completion, another is likely right around the corner.
“I’ve always wanted to tell stories,” Gjata says. “I didn’t know it [was going to be] telling the stories of these old historical buildings. But here we are, and I’m so so happy that we’re doing that.”
While their ultimate goal is to renovate a permanent dream home and relocate back to Brooklyn from South Carolina, Gale admits it isn’t easy to slow down:
“It’s hard when the next project keeps calling.”

hed: Most affordable city in New York has homes for $87K — but no one wants to live there
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Utica, New York wants you. Badly.
The Mohawk Valley city has quietly becomeone of the most affordable placesto buy a home anywhere in the state, with median values ranging from roughly $87,000 to $157,000 depending on the neighborhood, according to multiple market trackers. Rents start as low as $900 a month. Overall cost of living runs about 28 to 33 percent below the New York state average.
For a New Yorker priced out of literally everything, that sounds like a fantasy. So why does the population keep shrinking?
The math is almost cartoonishly lopsided. The average home in Utica — four hours north ofNew York City— now runs $213,412, according toZillow data, up nearly 9 percent in the past year. That’s still a fraction of the roughly $370,000 national average home value.
Median household income sits around $52,000, well below the state median, and the median individual income in Utica was just $30,785 in 2024.
A five-bedroom property 707 Spring St W has listed for only $89,900. And a three-bedroom home is listed for $99,900. On the pricier end for the area, a five-bedroom, 2,500 square feet property at 1527 Mohawk St is on the market for $299,900.
And people keep moving out anyway. Utica is currently losing population at a rate of about 0.74 percent a year, and has shrunk more than 4 percent since the 2020 census.
A recent analysis of statewide migration found Utica among the upstate municipalities outside New York City that lost the most residents, down roughly 1,500 people.
“It’s the cheapest house you’ll ever buy and also the hardest sell to your kids,” one longtime Mohawk Valley real estate agent, who spoke on the condition of anonymity said, describing the pitch to prospective buyers weighing Utica against the Southern Tier or the Capital Region.
“Price isn’t the problem. Everything else is the problem.”
The roots of the exodus go back decades. Utica was hit hard by Rust Belt deindustrialization, with major employers like General Electric and Lockheed Martin shuttering plants and jobs shifting out to the suburbs, hollowing out the city’s tax base and leaving many residents stuck in poverty.
The poverty rate in Utica now sits above 27 percent, nearly double the national figure.
Unemployment hovers around 4.5 to 6 percent, according to the Department of Laabor, and the city continues to bleed residents even as home prices — cheap by any national comparison — keep climbing.
“You can get a whole house here for what a down payment costs in Brooklyn,” a Utica homeowner, speaking on the condition of anonymity, and who recently listed her property said. “The problem is convincing anyone that’s a reason to stay, not just a reason to buy and rent it out.”

hed: Home of the Week: Rhode Island beach house with water views on both sides for under $2m
subhead: The Westerly home has been rented as a vacation spot for up to $9,000 a week
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

408 Atlantic Ave., Westerly, R.I.

$1.780 million

StyleContemporary cottage

Year built1987

Square feet2,724

Bedrooms3

Baths3 full

SewerPrivate

WaterPublic

Taxes$11,125 (2025)


Atlantic Avenue is the last road in Westerly before the waters of Block Island Sound. It’s the way toMisquamicut State Beach, Rhode Island’s most popular public beach,and it’s where this home sits at the crown of a horseshoe-shaped driveway.

The contemporary cottage is across Atlantic Avenue from the beach, but behind the house is another Westerly draw:Winnapaug Pond. As the state describes it, Winnapaug is a“a salt pond that provided a sheltered place to sail and a protected place for a children’ s bathing area.”

From the house, a kayaker can launch directly into the 476-acre pond and then paddle to thebreachway connecting to the Atlantic.

Beauty doesn’t come without some work, which in this house means walking up to the 210-square-foot rooftop deck to admire the full views of both the beach and the pond.



Down one flight of stairs, on the third floor, is the primary bedroom and a white-framed slider to its own 67-square-foot balcony overlooking the pond. The expansive 230-square-foot bedroom has hardwood flooring and a pair of closets with bifold doors. Adjacent is a 192-square-foot family room, a 53-square-foot storage room, and a full shared bath.

The 99-square-foot full bathroom has a single sink in a long vanity with shaker-style cabinets, and the vanity has an unusual feature: a minifridge. There is a curtained shower/bath combination and ceramic tile flooring. The bath doubles as a laundry room with full-size appliances.


Stretching the legs once more, the second floor beckons. The stairwell ends in a foyer from which two bedrooms and a full bathroom flow. The bedrooms, near mirror images at about 180 square feet, each have sliders to the rear deck that runs the length of the home. The 82-square-foot bathroom has a white vanity inset into a shallow nook, white ceramic tile flooring, and a curtained shower.

A door at the opposite end of the foyer from the bath leads to an open floor plan combining the kitchen, dining area, and living room.

The 176-square-foot kitchen (updated in 2024) is on the left and is a U shape with an extra-large stainless steel refrigerator on the left and a six-burner gas stove on the right. The sink is in the middle and underneath a pair of windows. The Shaker-style white cabinets are backed by a white subway tile backsplash. The countertops are Fantasy Brown leathered granite, and the flooring is hardwood. There is a coffee/wine bar.




An 8-foot-long island with seating for four separates the kitchen from the living area, but also presents a great viewing opportunity. The seating is positioned to look directly through the clear glass sliders leading out to this level’s 393-square-foot deck. The living room has recessed lighting, but draws natural light from skylights at each corner of the cathedral-style ceiling. A large ceiling fan assists with cooling. The 123-square-foot dining area has two light sources: a large clear glass window and a pendant light with a lantern-like shape.

A final descent to the first floor leads to the aforementioned horseshoe driveway. Standing outside, there is an attached single bay garage on the left, a 158-square-foot patio in the middle, and an entry door on the right. The door opens into the 249-square-foot recreation room that makes its way to the rear of the home and a slider to the rear 359-square-foot deck. It’s one of the ways to get a kayak in the water from the backyard.


There are also two rooms, both with views of the pond, storage areas, and a full bath.

Listing agentLori Joyalsaid the home has been rented for up to $9,000 a week and that the current homeowner’s annual flood insurance premium for $250,000 in coverage is $1,609.

The homeowner and their guests also have access toMisquamicut Fire District’s three beaches.

Joyal is in the Watch Hill office of Lila Delman/Compass.

hed: Former ‘Real Housewives’ star Dorinda Medley lists part of her Berkshires estate, Bluestone Manor
subhead: Bluestone Manor was prominently featured on Bravo and Peacock.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Dorinda Medley, a former star of Bravo’s “Real Housewives of New York City,” is selling a portion of Bluestone Manor, her famed Berkshires estate.
Medley, 61, skyrocketed to fame on the hit Bravo series thanks to trademark phrases like “I cooked all day! I decorated! I did it nice!” — which was in reference to her stunning Great Barrington home, Bluestone Manor. The Gilded Age Tudor-style estate served as a venue for plenty of drama between the ladies on the series, and Medley is nowselling off 3.7 acres of buildable landon the property for $1.2 million.
Featuring its own private entrance, West Sheffield Road Lot 2 has rolling meadows, mature woodlands, and sweeping mountain vistas. Its prime location combines the solitude of a natural landscape, which is surrounded by conservation land, and proximity to Great Barrington’s cultural institutions and downtown.
“The land is spectacular. It’s open meadowland. It’s flat. It’s gorgeous and private. It sits quite high,” saidShelly Tretter Lynchof Compass, who has thelisting. “She could have divided that property a million different ways, and she chose to preserve the integrity of the site.”
As to why she’s breaking off a piece of her storied estate, Tretter Lynch said that Medley could downsize and “carve away without it affecting her lifestyle.”
Medley herself noted that as she gets her estate in order, she doesn’t need all the land anymore.
“I thought to myself, ‘Why do I need 20 acres?” Medley toldPEOPLE. “I’d been happy with nine! Now I found out I owned 19 and a half! It just felt excessive. And I thought to myself, ‘I don’t want to pay all these taxes on this land I’m not even using.’ It felt wasteful, because the land I own is so far away from the house. I don’t use the land like they did when the home was first built. It isn’t necessarily for the property anymore.”
Last year, Medley gave viewers a video tour the palatial 1902 spread, which her late husband Richard purchased in 2005. The portion of the property she’s keeping features everything from a maze to cornfields. The sale of the land will allow anyone looking for the peace and solitude of the Berkshires to, as Medley would say, “do it nice.”

hed: Home Values in Exclusive Jackson Hole Explode Up to 2,000% in 30 Years
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Since the 1990s, home prices throughout the country have skyrocketed—but the increase in home values in one exclusive, ultraluxury territory far exceeds the national average.
Nationally, home values rose about 300% from 1995 to 2025, according todatafrom the Case-Shiller home price index.
Meanwhile, in the exclusive resort town of Jackson Hole, WY, home values have exploded up to 2,000% over the same 30-year period, according to a new analysis of property transactions in the area.
While the area has become popular in recent years as a world-class destination for hunting, fishing, and skiing, Jackson Hole has a unique feature that sets it apart even from similar resort communities: scarcity.
“In Teton County, we are surrounded by approximately 97% of protected lands. So we have the national forest, we have the national park, we have properties that people have privately put into conservation,” real estate agent Ashley DiPrisco of Evans & DiPrisco tells Realtor.com®.
“So we really don’t have the opportunity to completely explode, like some other mountain towns, as far as urban sprawl because we have such a limited supply. And then that’s just basic economics, right? You have a limited supply and a lot of demand, then your pricing structure just gets crazy,” says DiPrisco.
In its semiannual Jackson Hole Report, the Viehman Group compared more than 100 comparable properties that were sold between 1995 and 1999 and then sold again between 2024 and 2025 in order to identify price trends over 30 years.
The single-family home in the report with the highest appreciation, found in Spring Creek Resort, was sold for $525,000 in 1996. It was sold again in 2024 for $10.95 million—a staggering 2,085% gain.
The single-family home in the report with the lowest appreciation was also located in Spring Creek Resort. The home was sold for $1.595 million in 1999, and again in 2025 for $5.1 million. This home’s value increased by 320%—still higher than the national average for the same period.
The report notes that both properties underwent improvements over the 30-year period, but no changes were made to their square footage. This was consistent among most of the homes included in the study.
Across the valley, single-family homes saw an average appreciation of 1,118% over the three-decade span. Condominium and townhome values appreciated by an average of 742% across the valley.
Even the value of vacant property with no improvements appreciated by an average of 896%. One 5.43-acre parcel of land north of the town of Jackson was sold for $275,000 in 1997 and resold for $5.45 million in 2025: a 1,982% increase despite no changes to the land.
In recent years, Jackson Hole has become an increasingly popular destination for the ultrawealthy, which is reflected in area home values.
The area’s luxury market, defined as condos, townhomes, and vacant residential lots priced at over $5 million and home sales priced at over $10 million, registered 30 sales during the first half of 2026, up 15% from the same period in 2025.
During the first six months of 2026, 33 single-family homes were sold for over $5 million, while only two homes were sold for under $1 million. To compare, 42 homes were sold for under $1 million in the first six months of 2018, according to the Viehman Group.
Of the current available inventory of townhomes and condos, only 16% are listed for less than $1 million.
Both homes and townhouses or condos are appealing to the wide range of people looking to join in the Jackson Hole lifestyle.
“Everything’s desirable. We have a lot of young people coming in their 20s who find the townhome or the condo appealing, and then we have the grandparents looking for the place with the big yard and the wildlife for when the family comes to visit,” says DiPrisco, who grew up and is now raising a family in the exclusive area.
