Wealthy buyers are looking to Jackson Hole not just for its prestigious reputation.
Wyoming doesn’t have a state income tax, which makes becoming a resident very attractive. The state also has no corporate income tax, estate tax, or real estate transfer tax, giving buyers added advantages.
“Wyoming’s tax environment has become an increasingly important part of that demand” says real estate broker Latham Jenkins from Live Water Properties. “I am working with more buyers who are looking not just for a second home, but for a place where they can establish residency and make a long-term investment in their family’s lifestyle and wealth planning.”
Jenkins says that as more states consider measures such as wealth taxes or additional income taxes on high earners, affluent families are becoming much more thoughtful about where they choose to live.
“For the ultrahigh net worth buyer who wants a Rocky Mountain home, estate, or ranch, Wyoming is extraordinarily difficult to compete with,” he says. “You have the Tetons, national parks, national forests, world-class recreation, and an exceptionally favorable tax environment. Then add the fact that private land is incredibly scarce. That combination is what continues to support values.”
The area is also a four-season destination, providing skiing in the winter and access to world-class hiking and fishing during the summer. Fine dining restaurants and art galleries add more amenities for affluent families.
“You can go to the lake, you can go float the river, you can go climb a mountain, and then you can go get a fabulous dinner downtown,” says DiPrisco.
The combination of the attractive lifestyle and tight inventory of buildable land, all while offering impressive tax benefits for residents, has made Jackson Hole the ultimate destination for well-to-do homebuyers.

hed: Rare Gilded Age carriage house from 1850s hidden behind secret NYC gate can be yours for $2.5M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Hidden behind a gate on a bustling Times Square block sits a secluded Gilded Age carriage house that could be yours for $2.5 million.
The freestanding carriage house at 420-422 W. 46th St. is tucked inside Clinton Court, a private courtyard reached through a narrow gated passage off the street, just steps from the nonstop hustle of the Theater District.
The 1,500 square foot home has three bedrooms and three bathrooms across the second and third floors, plus an auxiliary studio with its own office, bedroom and bathroom, two wood burning fireplaces and stained glass details throughout.
The structure dates back to the 1850s, when it housed horses hauling milk deliveries around the neighborhood between shifts. Granite steps lead from the courtyard up to a private roof terrace built above the old stables.
The building later became an art studio for the Menconi Brothers, the sculptors behind the giant flagpole bases outside the New York Public Library.
A 1937 New York Times piece on the courtyard, cited by historian Tom Miller, described the scene as almost too picturesque, like a stage version of Montmartre. Over the decades the courtyard has drawn artists, actors and playwrights, including actress Elizabeth Ashley and playwright Neil Simon.
Listing broker Paul Devlin of Brown Harris Stevens walked buyers through the hideaway in aTikTok tourthat pulled in 410,000 views.
“We’re here in the heart of Hell’s Kitchen on West 46th Street. I’m about to show you a secret carriage house. Here we are in this courtyard between the main building and this original carriage house built in the 1850s.”
All of this in the middle of NYC#house#home#tour
Devlin pointed out the front porch overlooking the courtyard and the private roof terrace above the old stables.
“And then here’s access to the roof of the original stables that could be your own private garden for flowers and vegetables. First you’ll notice these amazing stained glass windows looking out between the buildings and come into this grand room, high ceilings, original windows, wood burning fireplace. This was where the flagpole bases from the New York Public Library at Bryant Park were built.”
He also tied the block to another piece of city history.
“That playground is where the original fight scene of West Side Story was filmed in the 1960s.”
The carriage house has its own Hollywood credits too, showing up in Woody Allen’s “Bullets Over Broadway” and “Deconstructing Harry,” along with “Law & Order” and “Blue Bloods.”
The home has come down significantly in price since it first hit the market.
Per StreetEasy records, it listed at$3.75 million on May 30, 2025, then dropped to $3.25 million that September, $2.95 million in October, and $2.75 million in January 2026. The listing came off the market briefly in April before relisting and settling at its current $2.5 million ask this July — a total cut of roughly 33 percent from the original price.
The carriage house belongs to an 18 unit cooperative, with monthly fees running around $4,000, and commenters on Devlin’s TikTok have plenty to say about it.
One called it “actually a fantastic price for such a beautiful and historic home in NYC,” while another joked “powerball, don’t fail me.”
Not everyone was sold on the math, though, with one commenter griping “the $4400/month HOA and $900/month co-op fees are insane” and another noting that buying in means “you’re not really buying a house you’re kind of signing up to be a historical steward that gets to live where he works.”

hed: Surprising East Coast state named second best in nation to live in — and which came in first
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New Jersey is no longer the“armpit of the nation.”
In fact, the Garden State ranks No. 2 among the best statesto live in the US, driven by strong scores in safety, healthcare and education, according to a newWalletHub study.
The state boasts the lowest crime rate in the country, and ranks high in quality of life, health and education. It also has some of the highest-performing public school districts in the country.
Despite its notoriously high property taxes and cost of living, New Jersey’s high median wages; top-tier health care; and proximity to major economic hubs like New York City and Philadelphia make it a draw, per WalletHub’s evaluation of all 50 states across 51 key metrics.
Broker Lisa Poggi, who leads Douglas Elliman’s New Jersey division, told The Post the state earned its bad reputation from the two-hour drive along the I-95/Turnpike corridor past Newark Airport, industrial docks, ports and oil refineries.
“Nothing looks scenic from that vantage point,” she told The Post. “But you go 40 minutes west of the Turnpike, and don’t forget — it is called the Garden State for a reason.”
New Jersey offers a rare geographic sweet spot, Poggi said, where residents don’t have to choose between the beach, the mountains or Broadway theater — they can hit all three in a single weekend while retaining “a lot more elbow room” than in New York City.
New Jersey, with its 59.41 total score, is bested only by Idaho, which notched the top spot with a score of 60.15.
The Gem State claims a low median real estate tax rate, the eighth-highest homeownership rate, and the country’s highest median income growth. It is also the third-safest state in the nation, behind Wyoming, laying claim to the lowest property crime rate.
Rounding out the top five best states are Wisconsin, with a score of 59.32, thanks to its affordable housing market; Massachusetts, securing 59.28 with some of the country’s lowest homeownership rates; and New Hampshire at 58.89, which is regarded well in economy, education, health and safety.
At the other end of the spectrum, New Mexico came in dead last with a 41.42 score. It rates as the most unsafe state in the country and holds some of the lowest scores for education and healthcare, per WalletHub.

hed: This North Shore city was Realtor.com’s hottest ZIP code in 2026
subhead: Peabody topped the real estate website’s annual ranking, marking the third time the city has landed in the top 10.
content:
ByAnnie Jonas
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Peabody has been namedRealtor.com’s hottest ZIP codein the country for 2026, marking the second consecutive year a North Shore community has claimed the top spot.
Last year, the accolade went to Beverly. This year, the honor went to Peabody, a city of nearly 56,000 people about 20 miles north of Boston. It’s the third time Peabody has appeared on Realtor.com’s list, following top-10 finishes in 2018 and 2021.
The Northeast and Midwest dominated this year’s rankings. Montclair and Sewell, New Jersey, ranked second and third, respectively, followed by Fairport, New York, in fourth and Westfield, Massachusetts, in fifth. The remaining top 10 ZIP codes were in Livonia, Michigan; Lititz, Pennsylvania; North Haven, Connecticut; New Berlin, Wisconsin; and Wheaton, Illinois.
Realtor.com’s annualranking, published Monday, measures buyer interest using two factors: market demand, based on the number of unique viewers per property listed for sale; and the pace of the market, based on how many days a typical listing remains active on the site.
Listings in the 10 hottest ZIP codes received between three and 5.3 times more views per property than the national average during the first half of 2026 and sold 30 to 42 days faster than the national norm of 60 days on the market, according to Realtor.com. The site declined to provide the national average number of property page views.
Peabody stood out on both measures. Listings in the city received 4.1 times the national average number of views and spent a median of just 20 days on the market during the first half of the year.
The city’s median listing price reached $667,000 in June — more than $230,000 above the national average, but still below the Boston metro median listing price of $825,000. Homes in Peabody sold for an average of 0.07% below asking price, compared with 2.3% below asking nationally.
“Its mix of livability, relative value, and easy commuting distance helped make [Peabody] one of the year’s hottest ZIP codes,” Realtor.com wrote in its report.
Much of the interest in Peabody came from within the Boston area. About 70% of the city’s listing views during the first half of 2026 came from viewers in the Boston metropolitan area, according to Realtor.com.
“Buyers are drawn to Peabody by its highway access to Boston, its North Shore setting, and its blend of small-town character with proximity to a major job center,” the site wrote.
The hottest ZIP codes also tend to sit within commuting distance of major cities. Peabody, for example, is about 20 miles from Boston, while Montclair is about 15 miles from Midtown Manhattan and Sewell is roughly 20 miles from Philadelphia.
Who is buying in Peabody?
The median household income in the ZIP code was $101,454, according to Realtor.com. The typical buyer put down about 14%, or roughly $89,000, and had a median FICO score was 747 — close to the national median.
Across the 10 hottest ZIP codes, however, buyers generally had stronger financial profiles than buyers nationally. The average down payment was 19.4%, compared with 13.1% nationally, while the median FICO score of 766, compared with 747 nationally.
The list was limited to one ZIP code per metropolitan area.

hed: A San Francisco home that sold months ago for $2.3M  just sold again for a whopping $5.1M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A San Francisco house flipper just cashed in on one of the fastest, biggest paydays the city has seen in years, and it is a sign of just howhot the markethas gotten at the top.
The mid-century home at 50 Cascade Walk in the Golden Gate Heights neighborhood sold for $2.31 million  in November 2025. Seven months later, after a full renovation, it closed for $5.167 million in June, nearly $1.3 million above its $3.885 million asking price.
That is more than double the sale price from less than a year earlier, on a home that started out as a modest 4-bedroom, 2-bath, 2,203 square foot house.
The listing for the reimagined property promised “unparalleled panoramic views” and “iconic San Francisco living,” with sight lines stretching to the Pacific Ocean, the Golden Gate Bridge, the Marin Headlands, Ocean Beach and the downtown skyline.
Set on a 10,000 square foot lot, described as rare for the hilly, view-driven pocket of the city, the finished home offered 5 bedrooms, 5 baths, a private office and an indoor-outdoor layout built for entertaining.
Golden Gate Heights sits between Twin Peaks and the Sunset District, and it has long been a magnet for buyers chasing wide-open views without the price tag of Pacific Heights or Presidio Heights. That reputation is now colliding with a citywide buying frenzy at the top of the market.
San Francisco’sluxury sectorhas come roaring back after years in the doldrums following the pandemic office exodus. High-end home sales in the city jumped 22.2 percent in March compared to a year earlier, marking five straight months of double digit gains, according to Redfin data.
Non-luxury sales crept up just 3.8 percent over the same stretch, a gap that highlights how lopsided the recovery has become.
The driver is not hard to find. The rapidgrowth of AI companiesincluding OpenAI and Anthropic has minted a fresh wave of ultra-high-earning buyers, many of them plowing outsized compensation packages straight into real estate.
Median luxury sale prices in the city have climbed to roughly $6.8 million, a 9 percent jump from last year, with the priciest homes now moving in a median of just 12 days.
It is a stunning reversal for a city that was written off just a few years ago, when remote work emptied out office towers and depressed home values across the board.
Citywide, the median sale price bottomed out at $625,000 in March 2012 after the housing crash, but by this March it had climbed to $1.7 million, according to Redfin, the first time the gap between trough and current price topped $1 million.
The listing was listed by Shu Pu of Fifty Hills. The Post has reached out to Pu for comment on the sale.

hed: Moving back home after college? All your friends are doing it.
content: When he hadn’t landed a job a few months after graduating from the University of California Santa Cruz, two years ago, Tommy Balmat moved back to his childhood home in the San Francisco Bay Area. He figured looking for a job would be easier with fewer expenses to shoulder. And, perhaps no less important, he was still close with his parents, who were keen to have him back. “I communicate with my parents about every thought that goes through my head,” said Balmat, who majored in literature and anthropology and had hoped for a job in book publishing. “They honestly really encouraged me to come back home if that’s what I wanted.” Balmat is hardly the only recent graduate to have accepted such an invitation lately. Data from economists Stefania Albanesi, Rania Gihleb, and Ning Zhang show that the portion of college graduates ages 23 to 27 living with their parents has returned to the high it reached during the COVID-19 pandemic. More than one-quarter did so as of last year, from a low of about 18 percent in 2001, according to updates to the paper that are not yet online. The fact that so many young adults are living at home reflects persistent weakness in the job market for recent graduates even as the overall economy remains fairly strong. The weakness may be growing as artificial intelligence affects white-collar jobs. Still, some experts wonder if it is all bad news. College graduates may be moving home because they recognize the benefits of conducting a job search from the relative comfort of their childhood bedroom and, as in Balmat’s case, they’re no longer discouraged by social norms from taking advantage of that arrangement. It’s hard to deny that a shortage of good jobs has helped drive the great graduate homecoming even as other economic forces, like the high cost of housing, have also weighed on those just starting out. Over the past decade, young adults with bachelor’s degrees have become more likely to live at home while those with only a high school diploma became slightly less likely to do so, Albanesi has found. Both groups face rising housing costs, but their economic trajectories have diverged. People with less education appear to have made strong gains since the pandemic, while the college-educated have stalled out. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates has increased much more rapidly than the country’s overall unemployment rate over the past four years, to 5.6 percent in the first quarter of this year, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Even graduates in some traditionally lucrative fields have felt the effects. A chemical engineer who had graduated from McGill University in Montreal moved in with her parents in April and said she and many of her classmates had not found jobs in the field. The unemployment rate for chemical engineers who recently graduated more than doubled between 2022 and 2024, to 4.7 percent, while the rate for computer engineers more than tripled, to 7.8 percent, according to data from the bank. Such challenges may be altering the profile of those who live at home after graduation — from the rudderless to the driven-but-thwarted. Alison Yoho assumed that an economics degree from the University of Minnesota, along with solid internship experience, would put her in a strong position to line up a job right out of school. And she moved quickly to capitalize on these advantages. During the fall of her senior year, she prepared to apply for an early career program at a clean energy firm where she had worked the previous summer. But, in a change from past years, the firm did not appear to solicit applications for the program. A few months before graduation in 2025, while having coffee with a former supervisor, she learned that the company had recently gone through layoffs. “That should have been the first clue it would be an uphill battle,” Yoho recalled. She moved home to a suburb in the Twin Cities last August and got her first offer in October. She wasn’t thrilled about the job and felt confident enough to keep searching for a better fit, which materialized two months later. The findings of Albanesi and her co-authors suggest that Yoho will be less likely to take an earnings hit by age 27 than others who struggle to find a job out of school because she could afford to be choosier during her search. Other data suggest that recent graduates are opting to live at home while searching for a job even if they might be able to land a worse job sooner, perhaps because they feel more comfortable doing so. According to the New York Fed, the underemployment rate — the portion of college graduates taking jobs that don’t require a degree — has been relatively low in recent years. Lawrence Katz, a labor economist at Harvard University, cautioned that such data is inexact and difficult to interpret. But Katz acknowledged that shifting norms might help explain why more young people were living at home. “Is there some cultural change in the way people are parenting?” he said. “You see kids today and the degree to which they’re interacting with parents, that’s completely different than the world of 50 years ago, 25 years ago.” The sheer number of people moving home after graduation, and the sense that they are up against economic forces beyond their control, also appears to be normalizing the choice and weakening whatever taboo might have once existed. Betsy Balmat, Tommy’s mother and an assistant school superintendent, said she had observed fewer and fewer recent college graduates living on their own, at least in the Bay Area, where rent is especially high. “I can say from my own social circle of people I work with and know that it is more common than not to have kids moving home,” she said. Balmat said he felt a little pressure from his parents to get a lot of applications out the door, sometimes to the detriment of their quality. He was applying to jobs “just to say I had done it,” he recalled. But, overall, the experience has been a positive one, he said, allowing him to save enough money to move in with a college friend in August. He does not appear to have suffered much stigma from living at home, and for several months dated a woman he had met at a cafe where he worked part time to burn off anxious energy. “We ended up bonding really hard — we’re both writers,” said Balmat, who hopes to publish a novel someday. “We were both really passionate about what we were doing, struggling to figure out how to turn it into money.” When he invited his girlfriend over to hang out, the attention from his parents was sometimes embarrassing. “They would both drop in on us if we’re watching a movie on the couch, to be like, ‘Can I get anybody any snacks?’ ” But his girlfriend took it in stride. It turned out she had moved back home, too. This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

hed: Cruel summer? Rhode Island’s ‘Taylor Swift tax’ went into effect — who’s paying it?
subhead: A new tax on luxury vacation rentals is meant to bolster Rhode Island’s affordable housing, but legacy homeowners say it’s not just affecting “the Taylor Swifts”
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

The cottage in Westerly, R.I.’s Shelter Harbor has no heat. It has 1,800 square feet of living space, a porch on its original columns, and rose bushes that five generations of one family have watched come back every spring. Valerie Uccellani’s great-grandparents built the place around 1909. It has never left the family, and it has never been winterized.

What it has done is quintuple in assessed value in a generation, including a roughly $1 million climb over the past four years, Uccellani said. This year, it also has a new state tax bill.

With Rhode Island’s newNon-Owner-Occupied Property Tax Act— what some have dubbed “the Taylor Swift tax” as a nod to the singer’s Watch Hill mansion in Westerly — thattook effect on July 1, Uccellani’s seasonal cottage is suddenly caught in the crosshairs of a policy aimed at ultra-wealthy out-of-staters — in a cottage that was one of the first two built in the neighborhood. She and her sister own it together and share it with their adult children.

The new lawimposes a quarterly state property taxon non-owner-occupied residential dwellings assessed at over $1 million. At the now-assessed $3.6 million, the cottage owners owe Rhode Island’s new surcharge, pushing the family’s annual property tax burden to roughly $45,000.

Ahead of the tax’s July 1 start, theDivision of Taxationmailed questionnaires to more than 9,000 property owners whose primary residence status it could not confirm, according to theRhode Island Association of Realtors. Its fiscal analysis flagged 8,245 properties as likely subject to the tax, out of 22,431 assessed above $1 million statewide.

Swift’s famed 12,700-square-foot High Watch Hill estate, for example, is assessed at roughly $28 million; the levy adds an estimated $136,000 a year. For others, the math is harder.


Owners must prove they live in or rent a property for more than 183 days a year to avoid the surcharge, which assesses $2.50 for every $500 of value over that $1 million threshold. The tax is intended to fund affordable housing programs for full-time residents, but some longtime homeowners in the area say there are unintended consequences of the new measure.

“To call it a ‘Taylor Swift tax’ or a ‘mansion tax’ I actually think is an unhelpful popular reference … it misleads people as to who is subject to this tax,” Uccellani said. “It’s not just the Taylor Swifts, and it’s not just the mansions.”

As of now, the tax hasn’t cooled the extreme high end of the Rhode Island market.

A 12,200-square-foot harborfront compound at14 Pawcatuck Ave. in Watch Hill— a 2.74-acre estate known as “Home Port” with a dock built for a 70-foot yacht —listed in June for $23.5 million, the highest-priced residential listing in the state, according to the Rhode Island Association of Realtors.It remains for sale. This month, the sale of thepenthouse at Watch Hill’s Ocean Houseclosed at $18.5 million — the most expensive condominium sale in Rhode Island history, according to the brokerage, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices.


“While buyers are certainly noting the tax, the state’s lifestyle appeal continues to outweigh the new surcharge,” said Lori Joyal, an associate broker withLila Delman Compass in Watch Hill.

Nor has the tax made current residents jump to sell off their luxury properties. “We have yet to see any significant influx of new listings triggered by the tax change,” Joyal added.

For homeowners outside the ultra-wealthy tier, the specifics have been harder to navigate. In Jamestown, homeowner Josephine Brak — who has owned her home for 10 years and spends winters in Florida — says the definitions are murky.

“The confusion lies in the term ‘occupancy,’” Brak said.

Brak rents out a room in her four-bedroom home on short-term platforms, but she keeps time slots open to let family stay throughout the year. That doesn’t count.

“We have five kids [and] like eight grandchildren. Someone’s always in the house,” she said. “So, you tell me it’s not occupied.”

She also takes issue with the strict 183-day threshold rather than a scaled assessment.

“I’m taxed the full amount because I didn’t meet the 183 days threshold. That’s really punitive. Why not at least make it pro rata?” Brak said. “Now all of a sudden I’m getting hit with a, what, $5,000 tax for not renting [it out] enough?”

The Rhode Island Division of Taxation and the town of Westerly tax assessor did not respond to requests for comment. The division has issued public guidance, including anine-page FAQin March, a presentation to the Rhode Island Bar Association in June, and a July advisory on payment procedures. None of it addresses how occupancy is counted when a property has multiple owners.

Allison Fleet, an attorney withPartridge Snow & Hahn,said the law added a new procedural step to every closing, and that the first weeks were rocky before the industry adjusted. Under the final rule, sellers must request a Certificate of No Tax Due at least 10 business days before closing to prove there are no outstanding taxes due or an applicable exemption applies.

“It is now a closing deliverable. Closings cannot occur without that form being submitted, and it’s really on the property owner to obtain,” Fleet said.

Proponents of the new tax emphasize that the revenue is urgently needed to fund affordable development. The state projects the tax will generate $24.5 million in its first year for housing programs.

“Any investment into housing is a good thing. That money will help to leverage other programs and other dollars,” said Brenda Clement, executive director ofHousingWorks RI.“We’ve been under-producing housing since the mid 1980s. Our last peak building period was in 1987, so we’ve got a long way to go to catch up.”


Asked about middle-class families with generational cottages facing steep new bills, Clement said the scope of impacted legacy owners remains unclear.

“The data doesn’t give us a sense as to how many people [who] are actually impacted by this are in that category. … If there is some real issue, then we should think through solutions,” Clement said.

Without knowing the scale, she added, “It’s hard to formulate a fix.”

Multifamily ownership remains unresolved. The state has yet to issue guidance on how inherited properties with multiple shared owners will be evaluated for occupancy.

“I think it’s an important question because I think there’s probably a lot of families that are going to have that issue,” Fleet said.

Uccellani’s family is one of them. Their cottage is co-owned by two sisters and shared among their three sets of adult children, and they hired a lawyer simply to interpret the residency rules. Attempts to seek clarity have been met with “stay tuned” responses from state officials, she said.

Uccellani is careful to say she knows what her family inherited.

“It’s not a secret to me that we have been extremely fortunate,” she said. “If everything I say sounds like a victim, that’s not true to the whole picture. I’ve had many years enjoying that property, but my family has invested a lot in it over generations.

“It’s not just money, but we’ve invested a lot of our own energy and care for the area and contributed to the community and the local economy,” she added. “So, we’ve gotten a lot, and we’ve given a lot, and if the state of Rhode Island really wants that to be the end for families like ours, then so be it. But I think they need to really acknowledge the impact of what they’re doing.”

Uccellani’s family financial advisers have already looked at their $45,000 annual tax burden and suggested they walk away. But her children have pushed back, preferring to keep the heritage over cashing out.

For now, the family is holding on, but Uccellani offered a direct question to the lawmakers who passed the bill:

“Look just 10 years down the line, and say, ‘What kind of a picture do you want?’” Uccellani said. “Do you want us and families like ours to be gone, and do you want historic cottages like this one to be demolished? And if you do, then play that out and tell me how that’s going to benefit the people of the state of Rhode Island.”

hed: Manhattan rents reach all-time high of $6,655/month amid Mamdani’s rent freeze and pied-a-terre tax threat
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Manhattan renters, brace yourselves.
The average price tag for a place to live just hit a jaw-dropping $6,655 a month, an all-time high, according to fresh data from Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group.
That’s a brutal 10% jump from a year ago, and real estate pros are pointing straight at Mayor Mamdani’sincoming rent freezeon stabilized units as one of the culprits, along with a looming pied-a-terre tax that brokers say is only going tosqueeze the market harder.The pain is compounded by a record-low number of vacant apartments across the city, leaving desperate renters with almost nowhere to turn.
The median rent, meanwhile, sits at $5,295, up 6% from last July, thoughit held flat month over monthafter climbing 3% in both June and July from May’sprevious recordof $5,125.
Every size apartment is getting hit, with average prices up double digits for two- and three-bedrooms. Studios now average $4,088 (up 8%), one-bedrooms are at $5,486 (up 7%), two-bedrooms have soared to $8,054 (up 13%) and three-bedrooms are averaging a staggering $12,228 (up 12%), all year-over-year. Studios, one-bedrooms and two-bedrooms have all hit all-time highs.
New York’s rental vacancy rate has cratered to just 1.49%, the tightest it’s been since 1968, and down from 1.57% previously. Experts consider anything under 5% a landlord’s market. This is far worse than that.
Separately, state registration data self-reported by landlords shows about57,000 rent-stabilized apartments sat emptycitywide in 2025, roughly 5.6% of the regulated stock and up from 3.7% a decade earlier. Tenant advocates argue landlords are warehousing units rather than renting them at capped rates, while owners say the 2019 rent laws make renovating and re-renting those apartments financially unworkable.
Gary Malin, chief operating officer of The Corcoran Group, points the finger squarely at Albany and City Hall.
“Misguided New York City and State legislation, like ‘good cause’ eviction, the FARE act, and the 2019 rent laws, have in large part created this perfect storm for sky-high rents,” Malin told The Post. “These laws have curtailed the supply of rental housing. This has caused demand to build up to a boiling point and pricing for available apartments to reach all-time highs. Legislators seem to care more about optics versus the actual impact of their policies. Their initiatives may be well intentioned, but there’s been severe unintended consequences, and today’s apartment seekers are literally paying the price.”
And the incoming rent freeze won’t be the relief tenants are hoping for, Malin warned, since landlords still have bills to pay.
“One thing is for certain, landlords’ costs will still go up regardless of the new rent freeze,” Malin said. “While the freeze may be good news for rent stabilized tenants, the bad news for market rate renters is that these increased expenses will likely be passed on to them, in the form of higher rents when it’s time to renew their lease.”
And brokers say that shift is already underway, well before the freeze officially kicks in on October 1. Landlords who know their rent-stabilized units are about to be locked in place are padding rents on their free-market apartments now to cover the gap.
He also sees the new pied-a-terre tax scaring off would-be buyers and pushing them straight into the already-slammed rental pool.
“The new pied-a-terre tax may have an impact on the rental market as well, especially at the high-end,” Malin said. “People who were in the market to purchase a part-time home in New York, may instead look to rent — to avoid the liability and hassle associated with the surcharge. In addition, current homeowners now faced with the tax may choose to sell their pied-a-terre and rent as an alternative. Overall, both new policies will likely cause additional demand to hit a rental market that’s already incredibly stressed.”
Douglas Elliman’s top-producing rental broker, Keyan Sanai, says it’s a collision of forces: high mortgage rates keeping buyers on the sidelines, a housing shortage that never gets fixed, and policy blunders piling on at the worst possible moment.
“It is not supernatural, but it is the ‘perfect storm,’” Sanai said. “There is no single reason Manhattan’s average rent has reached $6,655. It is a collision of economic headwinds, a structural housing shortage and public-policy mistakes, all pushing rents up at breakneck, or in this case, wallet-breaking speed.”
With 30-year mortgage rates back up near 6.69%, Sanai says plenty of would-be buyers are staying renters instead, especially when the stock market has outperformed Manhattan real estate for a decade. He also blames the FARE Act, which shifted broker fees onto landlords, for quietly fueling rent hikes as owners folded that cost into monthly rents instead of eating it.
He also says tenants are just plain exhausted by it all.
“They walk into a listing already frustrated even when they genuinely want the apartment because they feel that, year after year, they are paying more and receiving less,” Sanai said. “The same apartment may now be listed for $500 to $1,000 more per month than it was just one year ago, so tenants often arrive disgruntled before the showing has even begun.”
Even Sanai admits the old rules of the game have flipped.
“I used to tell clients, ‘In life, you get what you pay for and in Manhattan, you get a little less than that.’ At today’s prices, even that may be optimistic,” Sanai said.

subhead: Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
California’s gold is going for dirt cheap.
The state’s luxury housing is getting more affordable — withmillion-dollar homes flying off the market.
Four California metro areas landed among the 10 markets with the biggest year-over-year drops in luxury home prices in July, according to a newRealtor.com report.
San Francisco led the California declines, with the threshold to enter the top 10% of local listings falling 8.6% to about $2.49 million. San Diego dropped 7.3%, San Jose fell 6.9% and the Oxnard-Thousand Oaks-Ventura market slid 6%.
And those California homes are moving fast.
Million-dollar properties in San Francisco sold in a median of just 37 days in July — the fastest pace among the luxury markets analyzed. San Jose wasn’t far behind at 38 days.
And San Jose remains the country’s million-dollar listing capital, with nearly 62% of its active listings priced above $1 million.
“A lower luxury threshold doesn’t necessarily mean demand has weakened,” Realtor.com senior economist Anthony Smith said. “In some markets, declining thresholds reflect prices adjusting after rapid growth. In others, like San Francisco and San Jose, Calif., homes are selling so quickly that inventory is turning over faster than it’s being replenished.”
Los Angeles is still one of America’s priciest luxury markets, with the top 10% of listings starting at nearly $4 million. The market’s luxury threshold nevertheless fell 3.8% from a year ago.
Nationally, the entry point for luxury housing dropped 2.7% to $1.25 million, marking the 29th straight month of annual declines.
Yet the wealthy are still buying. Luxury homes in the top 10% sold three days faster than they did a year ago, while ultra-luxury properties — the top 1% — sold five days faster.
“The national luxury market continues to normalize, but the forces driving prices vary significantly from one market to another,” Smith said.

hed: Elizabeth Taylor’s home saved from demolition — bedroom will be preserved as she left it in $47M restoration
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Cue the klieg lights.
Storied builder Ardie Tavangarian has high hopes his rehab and buildout ofElizabeth Taylor’sformer Bel Air estate will command the same drawing power as the actress herself, in what appears to be his swan song as a decades-long uber-luxury developer.
The 1.3-acre property where the legendary actress lived for 30 years is becoming a Taylor/Tavangarian manor, with restoration of the original home to shore up its 60-year-old frame and much of the interior remaining as when Taylor lived in it, right down to the huge room where she kept her fabled jewelry in velvet lined cases.
Newness is coming from a large addition that will blend with and connect to the existing home, Tavangarian said in discussions with The Post — put­ting to bed persistent reports, and the resultant public outcry, that the legendary home wasalready torn downor was on its way to being so.
Instead, it will be a melding “from the heart,” Tavangarian said. “We’re trying to create something that is a continuation of Elizabeth Taylor and her legacy while creating a phase 2 to enhance the beauty that is already here.”
Taylor was an iconic actress andhumanitarian activistwho provided people decades of exceptional performances and much needed pathos.
She bought the estate for $2 million in 1981 from Frank Sinatra’s first wife, Nancy, and lived there until herpassing in 2011, at age 79.
Some parts of the original 7,000-square-foot home will serve, in essence, as the Elizabeth Taylor wing, with rehab planned for her master bedroom and bath, her beauty center and other areas she treasured.
“We’re just modernizing it from a point of view of functionality,” Tavangarian said.
Tavangarian also plans a gallery for the home filled with Elizabeth Taylor-related artwork.
The rest of the home is being remodeled to smoothly transition to an additional 12,000-square-foot buildout that has already seen a massive hill next to the house leveled to create an area that will include Tavangarian-signature touches.
These include subterranean framing and deep foundation footings that will allow walls, floors and ceilings to be built underground and shored up like a heavy-duty bunker to hold back thousands of tons of shifting earth.
There will also be a 4,500-square-foot retractable roof for stargazing, as well as an expansive grass overlay.
Taylor’s ranch-style home is 2 levels, with 5 bedrooms, and the addition will stand that tall and 3 levels in some areas. The existing home’s brick exterior will remain and continue onto the new structure to create visual continuity.
The new structure will have 3 bedrooms, a high-end screening room, a spa and other wellness amenities, as well as a family “pajama room” where residents and guests can kick back and enjoy entertainment on a huge-screen TV while munching on popcorn and other treats from well-placed canisters in surrounding comfort.
Tavangarian vows to keep much of the estate’s original landscaping, removing only the thick bamboo that was on the now-defunct hill.
The outside will still boast Taylor’s striking sapphire-colored pool, which reflected the color of her eyes, amid natural landscaping and tall trees. The koi pond and shell-shaped fountain that her nephew built is being rehabbed and arbors of climbing roses and a bright pink hybrid tea rose named “Elizabeth Taylor” will still dot the area.
Tavangarian said he is restoring some areas of Taylor’s home to their original state after they were outfitted as a showroom and offices for a high-end audio/visual firm that rented the place from former owner Rocky Malhotra, and for a bit after Tavangarian bought the property from the razor blade tycoon in the summer of 2021.
The designer and builder said he paid $15 million for the compound and expects to put at least another $47 million into its rehab and buildout. The project does not have a buyer lined up, Tavangarian said, and he declined to say what he might list it for when it is finished next year. His custom mansions often trade north of $100 million.
Tavangarian’s uber luxury properties include the $135 million, 35,000-square-foot Bel Air mega mansion, Villa Siena. He told The Post he had a buyer for the long-listed and often price-reduced compound last month, but the deal fell through when the prospective purchaser reconsidered and determined they “didn’t want that kind of footprint in LA.”
The compound relisted this month at $135 million after originally being put up for sale in the fall of 2024 for $177 million.
Tavangarian said non-disclosure agreements keep him from saying more about the almost purchase, except that the prospective buyer was not part of the tech billionaire influx that had been accounting for many sales in the area.
Tavangarian’s scores of uber projects have broken real estate price records as they catered to the world’s most ultra-wealthy individuals over the past 4 decades. But building modern day palaces is no longer viable, the developer said. “First there was Covid, then the LA fires and now global unrest,” in addition to knots of local legislation making mega homes unappealing to developers and buyers.
After the Elizabeth Taylor property buildout, Tavangarian said he will continue building hotels, and more affordable “fire-proof” homes that can help rebuild the more than 16,000 structures that burned to the ground, or were left standing and uninhabitable, as fires tore across over 50,000 LA-area acres last year.
Tavangarian has already rebuilt one of these protective places in the Pacific Palisades for one of his daughters. Given the vast need for these very fire-resistant homes and the positive reception to his approach, “this is the direction we are headed in,” for his Arya Group design and building firm.
Right now, though, it’s about harkening back to Hollywood’s heyday with a modern twist through a property with a unique patina that Tavangarian feels Taylor “would be comfortable living in.”
“I’m approaching this as though she is my client,” he said.

hed: I scour Manhattan’s trash for junk like broken $1K strollers and $20 coffee grinders — then fix and give them away for free
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
One man’s trash really is another man’s treasure.
Darrick Lo’s neighbors throw out everything from broken strollers to coffee grinders to chairs. He’s the guy whodigs through their trashand fixes it all himself.
Growing up in New Jersey, Lo liked to watch his mother sew on her Singer Stylist 534, circa 1975.
One day, it stopped working.
“It needed its hook and feed gears replaced because the original parts were made of materials that degrade over time,” Lo told The Post. Once he found the service manual, he repaired it.
Lo went on to earn undergraduate and graduate degrees from Cornell University in mechanical and biomedical engineering. Now, finding joyin the forensic workof figuring out what’s wrong and correcting it, he solicits broken toys, gadgets and appliances from his Manhattan neighbors — things that would otherwise be thrown away — sohe can repair themand teach himself as he goes.
Most items come from Craigslist or his local Facebook Buy Nothing group. He admits to taking things off the street on recycling night.
It’s not a repair service, he said, because he doesn’t want the pressure or logistics of fixing things on a timeline.
“I view these items as machines that follow the basic laws of physics,” said Lo, whose day job is at a medical-device company. “The core engineering principle that was instilled in me is to break down complex systems into their simplest forms. Failure can be caused by one specific thing, but it is usually a multitude of things and is not very obvious.”
As a high-schooler, Lo had a part-time job at an electronics store. After college, he took his motorcycle apart and reassembled it.
“I have done house calls for friends to repair washers, dryers, refrigerators, ovens, water heaters and furnaces,” he told The Post.
Lo recently found himself with two broken UPPAbaby strollers. They were “structurally compromised,” he said. “They have complex features and brake mechanics. The body construction is aluminum but it is also susceptible to fatigue and it is difficult to reweld.”
Unlike steel, which can withstand minor repetitive strains, “aluminum weakens with every bump and curb it encounters, until it eventually breaks,” Lo said. Rewelding destroys the metal’s strength, making it prone to breaking again. He researched the two strollers and found that despite being two model years apart, they shared many of the same components.
“I decided to take them both apart — to essentially cannibalize the two strollers — and combine them into one fully working unit,” he said.
Lo has reverence for product design and the work that goes into making user-friendly items. He calls headphones “a modern miracle,” available for a reasonable price after enormous amounts of time and money spent in development.
“That is the framework I cherish about every product that comes into my hands,” he said. “It is an acknowledgment of the hands that have touched it before me.”
On Craigslist, he spent $20 on a coffee grinder advertised in “questionable condition.” The motor, caked with coffee grounds, had stalled.
“The seller was very honest,” Lo said. “They said, ‘I don’t know if it works.’” He didn’t know either, but figured he could make it work.
If a grinder isn’t regularly cleaned, fine coffee dust combines with the bean’s natural oils to create a kind of glue inside the machine. “This mixture hardens into a solid brick that physically locks the paddle wheel and burrs, causing the motor to jam,” Lo said. All it needed was a good cleaning.
The grinder, which now lives on his kitchen counter, inspired him to become more of a coffee connoisseur. He later found a broken espresso machine for $35, also on Craigslist. Such machines intrigue him for their fluid mechanics.
“Fundamentally, an espresso machine can be boiled down to three basic systems — a water heater, a high-powered pump to push that water with intense force, and an overpressure valve to keep that force under control and regulate the hydraulic pressure to the espresso puck,” he said. “An espresso machine is a modern marvel.”
His machine’s problem was solved with a new overpressure valve.
“And now I drink too much coffee,” he said. “A lot of my family and friends would call me a home barista at this point. I am kind of a perfectionist.”
Lo gives away the items he doesn’t keep — to his Buy Nothing group, a nearby thrift store or friends. He once fixed an old chair with a broken seat that concealed an array of perimeter holes, revealing that the chair originally had a hand-woven cane seat.
“I purchased raw materials, taught myself the meticulous art of weaving and successfully restored the piece to its authentic design,” he said.
Lo, who has three toolboxes, laments today’s throwaway consumer culture. He prefers high-quality items that can be repaired if broken. Still, not everything can be fixed.
Cellphones once opened with a screwdriver, and parts such as the camera, microphone or battery could be replaced, he said. Now they’re tightly sealed.
“For most modern cellphones, you need a heat gun to melt the adhesive so you can take the glass off and access the internals,” Lo said. “A lot of people are comfortable throwing their old phones out.”
It’s also simply more convenient to toss old things than to get them repaired. There are so few repair shops left that people don’t even know where to take a broken item, said waste expert Anna Sacks, known as the Trash Walker, who scours the city’s trash for reusable items herself. People might have to wait for a part to arrive. Or it might cost as much to repair the item as to replace it.
Repairing something is doubly valuable, Sacks said.
“You are preventing things from going to landfills, but you are also preventing the need to buy a new one,” Sacks told The Post.
Lo’s own sewing machine is a Singer Fashion Mate 258, circa 1974 — a model that does decorative stitches — that had been missing several parts. A sewing machine is complex, and a lot can go wrong.
“Some of the gears are made from polymers, but they oxidize and crack over time,” Lo said. That was the problem his mother’s machine had. “There is a whole segment of science called tribology — the science of friction.”
Lo uses his Fashion Mate for fabric repairs and projects.
“Every intricate stitch, feed cadence and needle swing is choreographed through gear trains, rotating cams and interlocking linkages,” he said.
“These sewing machines do require electricity, but everything else is mechanical. These systems rely entirely on the laws of physics and metallurgy. There are no circuit boards or microprocessors, and that is exciting to me. It’s magical.”

hed: An Easton church has been converted to a $1.3m home
subhead: Built in 1892 by the Swedish Evangelical Lutheran Church Society, 16 Williams St. in Easton served as a community space for young Swedish immigrants.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
They say the home should be your sanctuary, and this Easton church makes that literal.
Built in 1892 by the Swedish Evangelical Lutheran Church Society,16 Williams St. in Eastonserved as a community space for young Swedish immigrants, according to historic documents. It was there during the late 19th century that the women of the church formed a society called the Golden Links to share in the support and maintenance of the church during World Wars I and II. By 1960, the building became a Masonic Temple for the Freemasons. Now, it’s a transformed home that maintains the design elements of its original use, and it’s on the market for $1,300,000.
Measuring 5,730 square feet, the four-bed, three-and-a-half-bathroom home was converted into a residence in 2008. Step inside the main doors to the entry, which immediately greets you with the grandeur of its days as a church. There’s a spacious room on the first floor that could serve as a large bedroom, as well as a full bathroom with three faucets, a urinal, and a glass and stone shower. Another large room on the first floor currently functions as a gym and media area, and doors lead to an outdoor patio. Also on the first level is the kitchen, equipped with a Viking range, double ovens, a professional-grade hood, and granite countertops.
Two staircases in the home lead to the oversized great room that once served as the main church area. Soaring curved ceilings cascade overhead, while walls of windows stream in natural light through stained glass. The great room is currently divided into several settings with hardwood floors running throughout. There’s a dining area as well as a cozy fireplace nook. A wet bar is set up for entertaining. Past the dining area is the family room.
Stairs lead up to the primary suite, which has a walk-in cedar closet and a spa-inspired bathroom with custom double vanities and a steam shower. It overlooks the rest of the great room from the Juliet balcony. Under the primary suite is a media room, which has a small attached office with black walls covered in chalkboard paint.
There’s a bit of green space close to the street that’s fenced in. On the opposite side of the home, there’s a driveway. With a prime location close to Main Street, there are restaurants, a library, and churches nearby.
“It’s a great space,” saidBobby Morgenstern, Vice President of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, who has thelistingwithBob Hershman.

hed: The Hamptons have competition and it’s a ‘secret’ tiny NJ coastal town 45 minutes from NYC with $20M listings
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Rumson, New Jersey has spent decades as Monmouth County’s best kept secret. Not anymore.
A sprawling waterfront compound on the Navesink River just hit the market for $26 million, which could stand as the highest asking price in Monmouth County history if it closes anywhere near list. It’s not an isolated blip.
Just down the road, a home sold this year for $20 million and the buyers are tearing it down to rebuild.
Zoom out further and the town’s entire market has been climbing steadily upward, with the median list price now sitting at $3.22 million and closings in the $3 million to $4.5 million range showing up on a near weekly basis, according to listing data.
The $26 million listing, at 100 W River Rd, includes four separate residences spread across more than five private acres, and it’s the clearest sign yet that this tiny riverside enclave 45 minutes from Manhattan has quietly transformed into one of the priciest zip codes on the East Coast.
The main house is a custom four story residence with six bedrooms, seven full baths and three half baths, plus a private elevator. The kitchen is stocked with Sub-Zero, Gaggenau, Wolf and Miele appliances, and the lower level has a cedar sauna, an exercise room and a hot tub. The primary suite comes with its own sitting room and library, along with a spa style bathroom finished in Perrin & Rowe fixtures and Ann Sacks tile.
Beyond the main house sits a five bedroom guest residence, a staff house and a carriage house. Down by the water there’s a boathouse topped with a fiberglass rooftop deck and an Ipe dock with a boat lift, opening straight onto the Navesink. The grounds also include an infinity edge pool ringed in travertine, English style hedged gardens, a mature apple orchard, a greenhouse and an eight car garage.
The beach, area yacht and country clubs, and NYC ferry service are all just minutes away.
If the deal closes near ask, it would set a new high water mark for the town.
Rumson’s current record belongs to Long Point Estate, an 18,000 square foot waterfront property on the Navesink that sold for $12 million, a deal that stood as the largest residential transaction in Rumson history at the time.
More recently, Villa Paradiso, a 17,425 square foot mansion on the Navesink with 200 feet of private waterfront, hit the market for $17.5 million, another sign that Rumson’s ultra high end has been creeping toward eight figures well before this latest listing.
Laura LoPresti of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices, who holds the listing alongside Mario Venancio, said the number is new territory for the area but not out of step with where the market has been heading since the pandemic.
“When COVID started in 2020, any inventory that was on the market cleared off the market,” LoPresti told The Post. “And since then, it’s just gone upward.”
And $26 million isn’t even the ceiling. LoPresti said a house just a handful of doors down from the listing recently traded for $20 million, and the buyers are tearing it down.
Rumson has alwaysdrawn Manhattan moneylooking for a shortcut between office and ocean. LoPresti described it as a longtime “bedroom community for New York,” where a SeaStreak ferry ride puts commuters on Wall Street or in Midtown within roughly 45 minutes to an hour.
“It allows people to have your cake and eat it too, if you will,” she said. “You can work in the city and in 45 minutes or an hour tops, your home in your dining room having dinner with your family.”
What’s changed, LoPresti said, is visibility. Rumson isn’t a new discovery, it’s a formerly quiet one.
“It just wasn’t talked about,” she said. “And the numbers that you’re seeing fly around now, as far as sale pricing, you weren’t seeing that before because it was really kind of like a secret almost. We used to say the best kept secret in Monmouth County is Rumson and the whole peninsula area.”
The geography does a lot of the selling. The town sits between the Navesink and Shrewsbury Rivers, with the beach at Sandy Hook roughly seven minutes from the $26 million compound. Add Hartshorne Woods, a 400 to 500 acre stretch of hiking and biking trails less than five minutes away, and LoPresti argues Rumson offers a Hamptons style lifestyle without the Hamptons style traffic.
“Comparatively to the Hamptons, the beach is maybe seven minutes from this house, if that,” she said. “What are you getting there that you’re not getting here? Nothing, once you discover it.”
Like much of the country, Rumson’s market has been squeezed by thin inventory since the pandemic, and LoPresti said that scarcity is doing a lot of the work behind the eye popping prices.
The numbers back her up. Recent closings around town include a six bedroom house on Buena Vista Avenue that sold for $4.55 million in June, a four bedroom on Ridge Road that fetched $4.4 million the same month, and a five bedroom on Lauriston Court that traded for $3.9 million in July. Even the smaller sales are climbing, with a three bedroom on Evergreen Drive closing for $2.28 million earlier this month.
The family has owned the land since the early 1990s and is selling as it enters, in LoPresti’s words, “just a different chapter.”
Rumson already has a quiet celebrity pedigree. Bruce Springsteen,Jon Bon Jovi,Richie Sambora and Patti Scialfa have all had ties to the area over the years, and Queen Latifah and singer Charlie Puth have also called the town home, according to public records. Fox News anchor Bret Baier and actress Siobhan Fallon Hogan round out the list of notable residents tied to the address.
LoPresti sees room for that list to grow, particularly as construction continues on Netflix’s roughly 292 acre production studio a short drive away on the former Fort Monmouth Army base in Eatontown and Oceanport. The streaming giant has committed close to $1 billion to the project, which will eventually house 12 soundstages.
As for how longtime locals feel about their secret getting out, LoPresti said the adjustment period is mostly behind them.
“Locals at this point, we’re used to it,” she said. “As all things go, people get used to things after a few months or maybe a year. And it just becomes the new way.”

hed: After 25 years, sprawling 950-acre equestrian estate that trained Kentucky Derby winners lists for $58M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
We’re not horsing around.
A 951-acre landmark Kentuckyequestrian estatethat once was home to 1896 Kentucky Derby winner Ben Brush and legendary sire Domino is on the market for a cool $57.5 million, Bluegrass Sotheby’s International Realty announced in a press release.
Located in rural horse country in Lexington, near the Kentucky Horse Park, 2469 Iron Works Pike belongs to the family of the late Irish billionaire Tony Ryan, who co-founded Irish ultra-low-cost airline Ryanair in 1984.
The property is anchored by a Greek Revival mansion dating to 1840 that spans 13,500 square feet and has seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms, according to thelisting.
If it doesn’t sell on the open market, the estate will be auctioned off as the final lot of the invitation-only Keeneland Championship Sale on Oct. 28, just before the Breeders’ Cup World Championships.
Called Castleton, the property has been associated with notable Thoroughbred champions, like Eclipse Award winner Gio Ponti, Grade 1 victors Jack Christopher and Gormley, and Longines Test Stakes winner Chi Town Lady. After retiring from his legendary racing career in 1966, Standardbred Bret Hanover became one of the most successful harness racing stallions in history while at Castleton.
With a bloodline that dates back to 1793, the estate includes an 1840 Greek Revival mansion flanked by ornate ironwork gates, as well as 16 barns housing 268 stables, staff quarters, a guest house, a covered bridge and an equine cemetery.
Regarded as one of the most photographed farms in the Bluegrass region of Central Kentucky, Castleton was featured in the 2005 Disney film “Dreamer,” starring Kurt Russell and Dakota Fanning.
“Castleton has existed as an equine operation for more than two centuries, whether with Standardbreds, Saddlebreds or Thoroughbreds, and we have been the sixth stewards of this historic farm,” said Ryan’s son, Shane Ryan, in prepared remarks.
Tony acquired the site in 2001 for $14 million and made subsequent upgrades before his death in 2007. Shane, who has run it as a horse-breeding operation while living on an adjacent site, is now ready to pass the reins.
He is now selling the historic farm because he spends most of his time in Europe and his children aren’t as passionate about equestrian life, listing agent Ken Donworth of Bluegrass Sotheby’s told the Wall Street Journal.

hed: New status symbol for Long Island’s elite: A home that grows wine, harvests honey and lays its own eggs
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Forget the home theater. Forget the bowling alley. The new flex among Long Island’swealthiest buyersis a dozen fresh eggs and a glass of wine you grew yourself.
Across the East End, from the vineyards of the North Fork to the wellnesscompounds of the Hamptons, real estate agents describe a buyer pool that has quietly rewritten what luxury means.
It is no longer about how much house you can fit on the lot. It is about how self sufficient, and how restorative, that lot can make you.
The latest and most striking example just hit the market in Jamesport. Starry Night Farms, a 6.3 acre spread at 1810 Main Rd listed for $3.795 million, comes with two barns and ten horse stalls, a working Merlot vineyard, Flow beehives, 16 raised garden beds, a chicken coop with 20 hens, and a wine barrel sauna with steam and hot rocks.
There is also a heated saltwater pool, a putting green and an outdoor kitchen. The listing describes a property where “luxury is no longer defined simply by what you own, but by how you live.”
It is exactly the kind of estate agents say has become the new gold standard for wealthy East End buyers, and it is not an isolated taste.
Elsewhere on the South Fork, brokers describe an outright arms race in wellness amenities, now treated as essentials rather than novelties.
Evenbrand new construction in East Hamptonis being built around the ritual. A Georgica spec home completed this summer includes a private wellness wing with steam, sauna, a full gym and a garden built around a hot tub and cold plunge, the kind of layout Sotheby’s agent, Keith Green, called a shift driven by a younger generation with a different view of what defines a well lived life.
But Starry Night Farms represents something a step further. It is not biohacking. It is farming, and the family behind it built the whole operation from scratch.
Owners Bo and Heidi Magnussen bought the property five years ago after relocating from Northern California so their daughter, Zoe Bliss Magnussen, could join the New York City Ballet program at 14. Zoe, later featured in Disney+’s “On Pointe,” now designs the gardens, keeps the bees and chickens alongside her father, and works in an on-site pottery studio.
“We were kind of looking for something by the beach in the Hamptons, but we found this place and just fell in love with it,” Magnussen said. “It’s so quiet and peaceful.”
Growing up gardening in Northern California, the family found something familiar in the North Fork’s soil and salt air. “We sort of felt like this was a little bit like Napa on the North Fork,” Magnussen said. “I was surprised you could even grow grapes out here.”
For the Magnussens, the point was never simply accumulating amenities.
“It’s not just likelux amenities,like bowling alleys and pools, but really like healthy way of living, growing your own,” Magnussen said. He described a daily ritual most homeowners never experience, gathering fresh eggs and honey before the day even starts. “It just felt so wholesome and grounding.”
He said the property does something a spa membership can’t.
“It just has all these healthy amenities that make your body feel good and your spirit and soul sing,” Magnussen said, describing the wine barrel sauna and a saltwater pool he keeps open through winter for cold plunges.
The family is selling because their younger daughter was accepted to Cal Poly and they want to be closer to relatives back west. “It’s time for a new chapter,” Magnussen said.
What they built along the way has become something guests don’t want to leave.
“Everything you’d ever want is right here,” Magnussen said. His wife grew up riding horses, and the estate’s caretakers occasionally give the family lessons.
“They’re just incredible animals,” he said, though he’s had to set limits on how far the farm fantasy goes. “The kids want to have goats and sheep and llamas and I’m like, ‘slow down, that’s enough.’”
The vineyard yields roughly 20 cases of Merlot a year, shared with friends and poured at gatherings on the property, including Magnussen’s recent 60th birthday party.
“All of that sort of feeds into that wellness, organic, fun-filled lifestyle,” Magnussen said.
Douglas Elliman listing agent Kristy Naddell, who represents the property, said what the Magnussens built by instinct is now something buyers are actively seeking out.
“There’s been a very distinct trend towards wellness and lifestyle living, where it used to just be, ‘okay, I want a big fancy house on the water with a pool,’” Naddell said. “But now they want more of this wellness style.”
She said the archetype driving demand isn’t who people assume.
“These are young entrepreneurs. These are people in the tech industry, AI industry, finance people who have done very well for themselves,” Naddell said. “They are purchasing these properties as a fully immersed and sustainable way of life.”
None of the Starry Night Farms amenities were part of the original purchase, Naddell said. The Magnussens added every bit of it after closing in 2021.
“What was there was just really the riding stables and the house and the pool,” she said. “Since they purchased it, they added the sauna. They added the gym. They added the vineyard. They added all of the organic gardens and the orchards.
The takeaway for Long Island’s luxury market, agents say, is that the pool and the private beach access are no longer the finish line. The finish line is a property that can feed you, calm you and occasionally hand you a fresh egg before 8 a.m.

hed: San Francisco’s cheapest one bedroom apartment is a jaw dropper
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

A relative ”deal” on a one-bedroom apartment in ridiculously expensive San Francisco has been unearthed.
The latestanalysis from Zumperfound rents in the city haveskyrocketed 22.9% year over year, fueled by a limited supply and an AI boom that’s driving up salaries.
That means a one-bedroom in the city carries a median price tag of $4,180 a month, almost twice what a similarpad costs in Los Angeles.
Yet, amid thesurge in housing costs, a rare and relative “deal” on a one-bedroom apartment in San Francisco has been unearthed.
To find the holy grail,KRON4combed residential listings on Zillow and Apartments.com, limiting their search to one-bedroom units with at least one bedroom and a kitchen.
Their report excluded income-restricted units, as well as shared and co-living spaces.
In an effort to avoid scam listings, only units represented by management companies or real estate agents with verifiable contact information were considered.
Zillow delivered the winner in the form of a one-bedroom apartment at 245 Leavenworth St offered at$2,195 per month.
No square footage was provided, and though the unit, which is managed by J. Wavro Associates, does not include laundry facilities or parking, it features hardwood floors and ample natural light.
A one-year lease is required, and pets are permissible with a monthly “pet rent” of $75.
