According to J. Wavro Associates, “Residents enjoy elevator access and a convenient location near public transit, shopping, dining, and downtown attractions.”
The apartment is located in SF’s Tenderloin neighborhood, which ranks dead last for safety in the city, withSafemapreporting elevated levels of crime in the area, which has historically been associated with open drug use and a significant unhoused population.
Safemap reports that cases of assault and battery account for 19.6% of all criminal incidents in the Tenderloin, followed by drug offenses at 9.5%
Still, the neighborhood boasts sterling scores for walkability, bikability, and access to public transport
KRON4 verified the listing, and the California Post has reached out to the management company for comment.
The Post recently reported that desperation for affordable housing has prompted SF landlords to take advantage of shelter shoppers via micro studios described as “a dystopian fever dream.”
For example,a $750-per-month “apartment” in North Beachwas listed on Zillow, though it’s no more than a tiny box with a shared bathroom, no kitchen and no sink.
The apartment is just 64 square feet; a different unit in the same building priced at $800 a month is a paltry 70 square feet.
Renters can fare better in other corners of California.
Arecent reportfrom real estate platformHouzeorevealed the 10 most affordable places to live in the Golden State.
Each city was given an overall affordability score out of ten, based on three main factors: median home value, median house rent, and cost of living compared to the state average.
The list was dominated by Central Valley cities, with Porterville, Fresno, and Bakersfield claiming the top spots for affordability, with the median rent in all three falling below $2,000.

hed: The worst time to sell a home is right now, dire figures show
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It’s crickets out there for home sellers.
The pool of active US homebuyers has dwindled so drastically due to affordability concerns pushing would-be house hunters onto the sidelines.
The number of buyers in the market sunk to about 967,000 in July — the lowest level recorded since Redfin began tracking the metric in 2013. That marks around 34% fewer homebuyers than sellers, giving buyers a leg up as inventory swells, according to a new Redfinreport.
That’s because “mortgage rates were falling in July 2025, which helped bring more buyers into the market later in last year’s homebuying season,” Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, told The Post.
Compared to last July 2025, however, the buyer pool is down 5.5% year-over-year from 1.02 million buyers.
“Home prices remain high, andmortgage ratesrose to their highest level in a year in July, making monthly payments difficult for many would-be buyers to stomach,” Fairweather said. “Economic uncertainty is also causing some buyers to hold off.”
From June to July, the estimated number of buyers fell 2.5%, while the number of sellers fell just 0.3%.
“That left nearly half a million more sellers than buyers nationwide,” Fairweather said. “With more homes competing for fewer buyers, the buyers who remain can be choosier and have more leverage to negotiate on things like price and concessions.”
Home sellers dominated the market in July, outnumbering buyers by a staggering 51.3% — up from 47.9% in June, and coming dangerously close to the record peak of 51.8% set in December.
More than three-quarters of US metros — 39 of the 49 markets analyzed — were ranked as buyer’s markets, per Redfin, led by areas that were hot for sellers during the pandemic — Miami, thenNashville, followed by a trio ofTexascities.
Those Sun Belt markets are facing the same affordability challenges as other areas, but in Miami and Nashville, pandemic-era home building and investing is coming online now, Fairweather indicated. And in Houston, San Antonio and Austin, they have “some of the country’s most active homebuilding pipelines,” the economist said.
In each of those five markets, seller supply outpaced buyer demand by over 100%.
On the flip side, there were just six seller’s markets in the US in July, withNassau County, New York, leading the charge with 36% fewer sellers than buyers. The suburban area benefits from its proximity to a major job center, Redfin said.
Nassau County was followed by Newark, New Jersey, with 21% fewer sellers than buyers, and then, Providence, Rhode Island, with 17% fewer. The seller’s markets are mainly in places where construction of new homes has been constrained for years, the report indicates.

hed: Waltham’s mayor vetoed 1,200 units of new housing. The City Council said to do it anyway.
subhead: Proposal would convert an obsolete office park to 1,200 units of new housing.
content: The Waltham City Council Monday night overturned the objections of Mayor Jeannette McCarthy to advance new zoning that could replace a stretch of mostly vacant office buildings with up to 1,200 new homes in a new neighborhood-scale mixed-use development.The 15-member council voted overwhelmingly to override McCarthy’s recent veto of a special zoning district for the 135-acre office complex off Winter Street. More approvals are needed, but the move means that landowner BXP — formerly known as Boston Properties — can push ahead with plans to put what would be Waltham’s largest housing development in recent memory there.Redeveloping the district, known as Bay Colony, is part of a broader effort aimed at transforming the commercial corridor near Route 128 in western Waltham, where a faltering office market has left the city — which has the third-highest commercial property tax base in the state, behind Cambridge and Boston — with many vacant properties and an out-of-balance budget. “We have significant office vacancies, acres of parking lots built for employees who are no longer coming into these buildings every day,” City Councilor Cathyann Harris said at Monday’s meeting. “Overriding this veto, Waltham has a once in a 10-year cycle … opportunity to reposition its commercial land, increase its value, restore and grow tax revenue, and make these properties productive for Waltham and Waltham taxpayers again.”Related: In Waltham, big landlords want to replace an old office complex with new homes. The mayor says no.Bay Colony is the largest of three districts the council voted in June to rezone. The other two — a 20-acre site off Jones Road, also owned by BXP, and the sprawling former Polaroid campus on Main Street owned by local developer J & CO LLC — are planned to hold 300 to 400 units and 600 units respectively, totaling up to 2,100 new homes across the three sites. They would be the biggest developments, including residential units, in recent memory in this city of 65,000, at a time when Greater Boston is desperate for more homes.The council had spent the first six months of the year working with BXP and J & CO to establish parameters for the sites. The two developers approached the council at the end of 2025 with preliminary development plans, and the zoning districts unanimously passed in June are meant to serve as an outline for what projects on the sites could look like. The developers will still need to submit formal project filings and go through the special permit process before they can move forward. McCarthy approved the zoning for the Jones Road and Polaroid sites, but her early-July veto of the Bay Colony district caught several councilors by surprise. She cited concerns about density and that the project would be too close to a small single-family neighborhood on the city’s border with Lincoln. And she worried about such a large development’s impact on the city’s traffic, and said the decreased parking requirements in the zoning set “a dangerous precedent for the city.” Mid-rise office buildings line Route 128 in Waltham.Suzanne Kreiter/Globe StaffHer veto temporarily threatened to send planning for the site back to square one, or perhaps derail it altogether. But the council was nearly unanimous again Tuesday morning, with 12 of the 13 members in attendance voting to override McCarthy’s decision. The lone vote against was council Vice President Randall LeBlanc, who said he was “not against the project, not against the housing,” but that he was hoping the council would more thoughtfully consider the points McCarthy raised. McCarthy did not speak about the zoning districts or her veto at the meeting.Related: The next frontier for housing: Suburban office parksUltimately, the council saw the rezoning as a rare opportunity to pivot key stretches of land away from office properties and revitalize the city’s tax base. Nearly half of the city’s property tax base comes from commercial properties. But with many of those buildings vacant, the city this year was forced to raise its residential tax rate by 5 percent to account for lost revenue. Waltham has built relatively little housing during McCarthy’s 22-year tenure. Rezoning the three districts offers a chance to build three new neighborhoods from scratch. Part of the negotiations around the projects centered on a broader vision to transform this part of Waltham, which is home to little residential development and where roads are often snarled by traffic from drivers passing through from other towns to reach Route 128. The projects would also bring several key infrastructure improvements, including upgrading a road through a nearby neighborhood and funding from BXP and J & CO for a new connector between heavily trafficked state roads, after the state chips in what the city expects will total $15 million.City officials have been talking about the connector project in particular for years, and some have worried that rejecting the zoning for the Bay Colony development could mean losing state funding or BXP’s contributions for the infrastructure upgrades. The new developments, which will include retail and commercial uses, could also help ease traffic in the area, councilors hope, with new residents who are able to shop and work near where they live needing to take fewer trips through the city by car. The Jones Road site is near the location of a planned new bus hub and commuter rail station, and the Market Basket site has regular bus service. “These are not small benefits,” said Harris. “These are game changers for the city. They represent major public and private investment [in] infrastructure that Waltham needs now, and it’s an opportunity to generate new economic value from commercial [development] today that is not reaching its potential.”1100 Winter St. in Waltham is part of an office park that its owner would like to redevelop into what would be the city's largest new housing complex in decades.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffAndrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: Aaron Rodgers looks to flip his New Jersey mansion for $15M after a failed Jets career
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Legendary quarterback Aaron Rodgers is set to score big — at least in the New Jersey real estate market.
Rodgers, who is playing for the Pittsburgh Steelers for the final season of his 22-year career in the NFL, hopes to sell his Montclair-area home for a cool $15 million, 57.9% more than the price he paid for it just three years ago.
The 42-year-old MVP, who left the New York Jets after a disappointing two-year stint in 2025,dropped $9.5 millionfor the sleek eight-bedroom, 9.5-bathroom at 349 Crestmont Rd. in summer 2023. The home was a new-construction build at the time.
Billed as “an extraordinary contemporary estate on the Cedar Grove/Montclair border,” by listing agent Cindy Mistretta of Coldwell Banker Realty, the two-story, 18-room abode boasts an open-floor plan, a two-story living room and “unobstructed views of the Manhattan skyline.” The 2-acre property is less than an hour away from Manhattan.
The listingwas first reported byNorthJersey.com.
Rodgers’ home has a gourmet kitchen with a center island and bar seating.
All bedrooms have ensuite bathrooms. The primary suite includes a custom dressing room and closet with an open-concept spa bath featuring an oversized glass shower and soaking tub.
Fun amenities include a wine cellar and cigar lounge, meditation room, media room, wet bar and fitness center, all on the lower level.
Outside there is a heated salt-chlorinated freeform gunite pool and spa and a “resort-style outdoor living area” with a fire pit, a sauna and a cold plunge.
A cutting-edge property, Rodgers’ place has an advanced AI-integrated security system, motorized privacy shades and radiant heated floors throughout.
The four-time MVP famously led the Green Bay Packers to a Super Bowl title in the 2010 season — a high-water mark he never quite matched again, despite four subsequent NFC Championship appearances.
Rodgers’ time with the Jets was defined by massive hype followed by profound disappointment. Traded from the Green Bay Packers in April 2023, his tenure lasted two seasons —highlightedby a torn achillesfour snaps into his 2023 debut and a 5-12 record in 2024 — before the teamreleased him in early 2025.
Rodgers has accrued a number of properties around the country, including a 3.5-acre Wisconsin compound in Oneida, a $28 million Malibu oceanfront pad, alongside properties in Tennessee, Texas and his hometown of Chico, California.

hed: Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax has a winner — Greenwich, CT, where condos just hit $12M for the first time ever
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For the first time in Greenwich history, condos are selling for as much as $12 million, blowing past the town’s previous record condo sale of $6.75 million by nearly 50 percent.
The prices are coming out of Chilston Court, a new luxury development in downtown Greenwich from Caspi Development, the team behind Tribeca’s celebrity-favorite hotelFouquet’s New York.
Founder Josh Caspi said the numbers are unprecedented for the market.
“It turns out that it’s exactly what people want because it’s never existed,” he told The Post.
The timing is no accident. New Yorkers are increasingly eyeing Greenwich as an escape hatch from Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new surcharge on high-value secondary homes.
The pied-à-terre tax levies an annual charge on one to three family homes, condos and co-ops valued above $5 million when the owner keeps a separate primary residence outside New York City.
Caspi said the policy is now a direct driver of sales at Chilston Court.
“I’d say about a quarter of the buyers have places in New York City and several of them have made the move already where they’re selling their New York City place and buying here as their secondary home instead of being in the city for that reason exactly,” he said.
For many of those buyers, Greenwich isn’t a downgrade so much as a strategic repositioning. Caspi said some owners are shifting what used to be their full-time home into secondary status once they establish residency elsewhere for tax purposes.
“It would become, by default, their secondary residence, but it’s where they raise their kids and family,” he said.
The pace of demand since the launch just last week, caught even Caspi off guard. Units priced between $9 million and $10 million sold first, and he raised prices repeatedly to keep up.
“We started raising prices immediately and we’re now getting close to breaking $12 million,” he said.
Competition got fierce enough that he pulled the remaining top-tier units to release later in the sales process rather than let buyers keep bidding each other up.
Even Caspi admitted he wasn’t sure the market would support it.
“I was nervous and my brokers said look this is new territory. And we didn’t know what the response was going to be,” he said. “It was very reassuring.”
Mamdani’s tax rollout, meanwhile, has hit turbulence in court. A Staten Islandbriefly blocked enforcementearlier this month aftera group of homeowners sued,arguing the city had wrongly flagged their primary residences as subject to the surcharge. An appellate court in Brooklynlifted that blockon Thursday, clearing the city to resume the rollout while the underlying case continues, with the next hearing set for later this month.
The back-and-forth in court hasn’t slowed the exodus Caspi is capitalizing on.
Chilston Court, designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects with interiors by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, is leaning into hospitality-style amenities to justify its price point, including a private speakeasy with individual wine lockers, a 55-foot lap pool, and concierge-run in-unit delivery closets.
Units, which range from mid $4 to $5 million two-bedrooms to penthouses starting at $11.5 million feature custom millwork, bespoke lighting, single-slab marble kitchens, unique parquet flooring, and ceilings exceeding nine feet throughout the living spaces.
Caspi said he modeled the building on what he’s seen resonate withguests at Fouquet’s.
“It really gives you all the benefits of what you would get in like a high-end hotel or a condo building in New York City. But it’s in downtown Greenwich,” he said.
The development is slated for completion in 2028.

hed: With a $4M price cut, infamous Paul Castellano mob mansion on Staten Island relists
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It’s an offer buyers keep refusing.
The ornate Staten Island mob mansion that just can’t find a buyer is back on the market, again.
This time it has a price tag of $13.995 million, a steep markdown from its $18 million ask that flopped in 2024.
Built in 1980 by Gambino crime boss Paul “Big Paul” Castellano, the Todt Hill “White House” — called such as he had the residence designed to resemble the White House with a pillared portico and circular drive — at 177 Benedict Road spans 33,000 square feet with eight en-suite bedrooms and 17 bathrooms.
Castellano’s former propertyaimed to fetch$16.8 million in October 2023, and then came back online with an$18 millionprice in late-2024.
The 25-room mansion, which sits on nearly 1.6  acres with sweeping Verrazzano Bridge views, boasts indoor and outdoor Olympic-sized pools, a 13-car garage, a home theater, a gym with a sauna, a beauty salon, a wine cellar, a solarium and a lot of marble.
Anywhere near the new asking price would still shatter Staten Island’s single-home sales record, which was set by 176 Benedict Road, directly across the street from Castellano’s property. That closed in 2025for $8.5 million.
“At $13.995 million, we believe we’re positioned much more consistently with the market and with where we ultimately expect the property to trade,” listing agent PreReal Real Estate’s Rob Nixon, who marketed the property along with Anthony Volpe, told The Post. “At the same time, it’s important to put that number in perspective; we estimate the replacement cost of an estate of this scale and caliber today would be upwards of $30 million.”
The Staten Island Advance was the first to report onnews of the listing.
Castellano commissioned it in 1976, after succeeding his brother-in-law, Carlo Gambino, as the syndicate’s don. Completed in 1980, Castellano lived and ran the family from there, until his 1985 death. John Gotti had him whacked outside of Sparks Steak House in Manhattan.
The owner, Selim “Sal” Rusi, bought Castellano’s former home for $3.1 million in 2000. An immigrant from Albania, Rusi built his success as a self-made entrepreneur.
While Rusi doesn’t want to lean into the house’s notorious past, Nixon said its history “can’t be ignored.”
He pointed out the modern face-lift given to the estate since its mob-boss days, including tripling the size of the former residence on more than twice the property from Castellano’s days.
“Most recently,” Nixon said, “they completed an over $1 million kitchen on the lower level of the home. Importantly, this is the estate’s second kitchen, not its primary kitchen.”
As for listing the home during the slow summer season, Nixon said, “With a conventional home, seasonality can certainly play a larger role. We don’t view 177 Benedict Road as a conventional listing.”

hed: Third-oldest home in New York — visited by George Washington, King Philippe, and friendly ghosts — hits market for $8M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A slice of really cool New York history is up for grabs.
Glen Sanders Mansion,the riverfront estatein Scotia, NY, believed to be thethird-oldest surviving dwellingin New York State, has hit the market for $8 million, The Post has learned.
The 75,000-square-footproperty traces to 1658,when Scottish merchant Alexander Lindsay Glen built a stone dwelling on the Mohawk River and named the settlement Scotia, after his homeland.
That one-room structure still stands, folded into the mansion around it, and the family held the estate 266 years until it was sold in 1962.
“That room is still part of the house, which would make it the third oldest,” listing agent Angelo Michael Mazzone Jr, son of the mansion’s current owner, confirmed to The Post.
Restaurateur Angelo Mazzone Sr bought the estate in 1988, opening it a year later as the flagship of what became Mazzone Hospitality.
“We used to cater on their lawn. So when the house went up for sale, I said, well, we can make this a great restaurant and banquet hall,” Mazzone Sr said.
Now 75, he said the decision to sell comes down to age.
“I’ve worked 40, 50 years struggling, working really hard to keep everything up and running,” he said.
His son isn’t taking over: “I’m an opera singer and a real estate agent,” Mazzone Jr said. “I decided not to do this.”
Mazzone Hospitality, the operating company, was sold to Compass International five years ago, but Mazzone Sr remains sole owner of the real estate itself.
“It was my baby. I grew a company from this facility to a $70 million food and beverage company,” he said. “But there’s really no one in my family that wanted to do it.”
The mansion’s calling card is its list of storied visitors.
George Washington stopped there while surveying the region’s northern defenses in 1775, though historians have long noted he slept across the river at the John Glen House in Schenectady’s Stockade District.
“It’s been verified that he was there for a tea party. Possibly stayed, but there’s no written documentation that he slept there,” Mazzone Jr said.
A young Louis Philippe, the future King of the French, is said to have stayed at the mansion during his American exile in the late 1790s, decades before he took the French throne in 1830, in a room still known as the Louis Philippe Bedroom.
The historic dwelling maintains it’s original windows, floors, beams, staircase and the rock walls that hold up the beams, according to Mazzone Sr.
“All the original doors are here,” Mazzone Sr added. “So the doors that were put in in 1713, they’re all still working. But the doors that I put in, in 1989, I replaced 10 times.”
Family tradition holds that the mansion’s basement once sheltered freedom seekers as part of the Underground Railroad, with a passage said to connect the main house to a building across the street that later became the Scotia library.
A visible mark on the original staircase banister is attributed to an Indigenous visitor, according to Mazzone Jr.
“There’s actually a tomahawk mark in the banister from one of the Indians,” he said.
Staff and family say the mansion has its share ofunexplained activity,including a recurring sighting of a woman in a red dress some associate with Deborah Glen — the granddaughter of Alexander.
Mazzone Jr recalled an odd episode from when his father first bought the property.
“We pulled up, and every light was on in the house. So the three of us went in, turned off all the lights, and crossing the river, the whole house just lit up again.”
A painter who worked alone in the mansion reported similar moments, he said, seeing “drapes moving and things like that she couldn’t explain.”
John Lawrence of Douglas Elliman who is co-listing the property alongside Mazzone and Rick Rosa said the family doesn’t dwell on the stories out of respect.
“They’re friendly ghosts, and we don’t really like talking about them because they don’t want to be noticed.”
The listing includes roughly three acres, with the historic core measuring about 2,800 square feet inside the complex, which includes a 22-room inn. The mansion is not on the historical register, so there’s technically nothing stopping a buyer from tearing it down, though Mazzone Sr doubts the village would allow it, calling the house “really like the logo of the village.”
The sale also comes with a sweetener: entitlements for a previously approved 95-unit apartment complex with a ground-floor restaurant.
Mazzone Sr had planned to develop it himself before changing course a month ago and deciding to sell instead.
“If somebody was to purchase this and keep the historical house, it has been granted that we have some very strong entitlements that we would sell if somebody does want to develop and keep the original house,” Lawrence said.
For Mazzone Sr, the hope is simple.
“I just hope they keep the old building. I just hope they preserve the old building the way we did. It’s really pretty incredible because the rooms are all exactly like they were.”

hed: Newly minted mega-millionaire unmasked as buyer of $70M estate at just 31 years old — see his stunning pad
content:

The likely buyer of a jaw-dropping Bay Area estateinspired by Lake Comohas been unmasked as an obscure 31-year old mega-millionaire who’s cashing in bigon the AI boom.
“Tony” Yuhuai Wu, a co-founder of Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI, has been linked to the $70 million, 12-acre property in the San Mateo County town of Hillsborough that shattered local sale records, theSan Francisco Standardreported.
The property at 3000 Ralston Avenue is modeled after alakeside Italian villa.
Images of the secluded property, dubbed Villa de Verano, show off its a vast front lawn, reflecting pool and lush trees shrouding the 12,000-square-foot, six-bedroom main home and 4,600-square-foot guest house.
Even more eye-popping is the sports complex featuring a tennis court, golf course, putting green, horseshoe pit, and pickleball, volleyball, and bocce courts. There even is a 150-seat amphitheater, a reflection pool, a koi pond, a large saltwater aquarium, and fountains inspired by the Bellagio casino.

The seller was private equity investor Ted Kruttschnitt and his wife.
Daikon no Hana Capital LLC is the new listed property owner, who was represented by an investment firm official named Jia Xu.
Xu is reportedly tied to only one other major property transaction, a $12 million Los Altos home bought by Wu.
The LLC’s manager, attorney Steven Anderson, is also tied to the Los Altos home. Anderson put that property into a family trust shortly before the Hillsborough sale closed on Aug. 6, the Standard reported.
Wu is a scientist who, despite his young age, has an impressive resume that includes gigs at OpenAI and Google’s DeepMind, according to his LinkedIn profile.
He then co-founded xAI, Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence project that spawned the controversial AI tool Grok, which is embedded in the social platform X.

“It’s time for my next chapter. It is an era with full possibilities: a small team armed with AIs can move mountains and redefine what’s possible,” Wu said then on X. He later joined the board of an aging-focused startup.

hed: AI data center boom minting new class of 6-figure jobs — what it means for housing: Nvidia CEO
subhead: The labor needs of data centers
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Workers in America are eyeing blue-collar trades—such as construction, plumbing, and steelwork—with new interest.
Even CEOs like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang are on that list.Huang recently predictedthat the next wave of six-figure jobs won’t come from Silicon Valley, but from the crews building the data centers powering it.
These jobs pay over $100,000, require no college degree, and are desperate for bodies: hundreds of thousands of electricians, laborers, and supervisors, with nowhere near enough people to fill the roles.
Skilled trades are already stretched thin, and the same shortage now competing for data center construction crews isone more strain on a housing industrythat can’t build fast enough.
“The shrinking and aging construction labor force is a major issue in the homebuilding industry right now, leading to increased labor costs and longer construction timelines for new homes,” says Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner. “Where zoning may completely prevent some projects from being started, the labor shortage could prevent them from completed profitably and on time.”
So, the question becomes, can the country push its young workforce toward these jobs—and will housing markets feel the difference as workers potentially move from data centers to homes?
It depends who you ask.
Huang’s prediction is already playing out in paychecks. Workers moving into data center construction are seeing pay jumps of 25% to 30% over their previous jobs,according to the Wall Street Journal, and sometimes far more: An Ohio drywall contractor who took a supervisor role overseeing 200 workers at a data center site now makes over $100,000 a year, while an electrician managing crews across six sites inNorthern Virginiatops $200,000.
Those wages are a function of scarcity. Data center construction starts approached $80 billion nationally in 2025, nearly triple the previous year’s figure,according to ConstructConnect. If this work is going to continue at pace, the industry will need more workers: TheInformation Technology and Innovation Foundationputs the sector’s worker shortage at roughly 439,000 people this year alone, specifically noting the lack of electricians, pipe layers, and HVAC techs.
And the buildout isn’t confined to a few tech hubs—much of the country is experiencing the data center boom. According to Realtor.com data, theshare of U.S. home sales within 5 miles of a data centeris ticking up rapidly, with low-income areas seeing a particularly high influx.
“Texas and Virginia are home to the most current and proposed data centers, but Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Ohio are close behind,” says Berner.“Pennsylvania and Ohio especially could benefit from an influx of tradespeople as their homebuilding levels are lower than the Southern states mentioned here.”
What makes data center wages climb so high is who’s paying for them: Meta, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are spending billions of dollars on these projects. Homebuilders have no equivalent backer. They’re selling into what buyers can actually afford, on far thinner margins, which limits how far they can chase the same workers upward.
The question is, if data centers can pull tradespeople in with pay homebuilders can’t match, does any of that labor eventually flow back toward the country’s other, more urgent construction problem?
The optimistic case is straightforward: Moretradespeople trained todaymeans more tradespeople available to build homes tomorrow. The reality, according to the people who watch this labor market closely, is more tangled.
“Given such tepid residential demand, it’s a bit of a stretch to say that there is fierce competition today for skilled labor between data center and residential construction,” says Kathryn Thompson, founding partner and CEO of Thompson Research Group. Residential construction has been in its own three-year slump, she says, which means the two sectors aren’t yet fighting over the same workers — but that could change quickly if residential demand recovers.
Where the sectors do overlap, it’s narrower than the headlines suggest.
“A carpenter constructing a house would not make the switch to a data center project,” says Sean Plunkett, a home advisor and realtor with Triple Crown Homes, “but there could be competition among electrical contractors relied upon by homebuilders competing for the same limited pool of licensed electricians.” That competition shows up less in headline worker counts, he says, and more in how long a homebuilder waits on a single specialty subcontractor to become available.
Ryan Starr, a principal architect at Starr Designs & Architecture, sees a different risk. Large-scale data centers require concrete, cranes, and multi-ton building sections handled by specialized crews, he says, not the smaller, more improvisational teams that build single-family homes. Because most local contractors can’t handle a project that size, general contractors and their preferred subs typically arrive from out of town, creating a temporary population surge in the small communities hosting the buildout, then leaving again once construction wraps in three or four years.
“This kind of cyclical stress is not helpful,” Starr says. “It temporarily makes the housing issue much worse.”
Whatever the labor math ultimately shows, the housing shortage it might help solve isn’t waiting. The U.S. is short roughly 4 million homes, and builders added just 1.3 million last year, a gap the Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap Report says the country isn’t on pace to close. That urgency is the premise behindLet America Build,a campaign Realtor.com launched at SXSW this year alongside the National Association of Home Builders, pushing for lighter permitting rules and fewer zoning barriers to new construction.
The Realtor.com state report cards on affordability and home building show where that fight is furthest along, and where it overlaps with the data center boom. Texas remains the nation’s largest permit issuer by far, and several metros flagged among the top new-construction markets, including Austin, TX; Nashville, TN; and Raleigh and Charlotte, NC, are also seeing real data center investment nearby. But building a lot and building affordably aren’t the same thing: Arizona, another major data center market, earns only a middling affordability grade despite solid construction activity—a reminder that more permits don’t automatically mean more accessible homes.
Let America Build is pushing for more homes, faster. The data center boom is pulling for more electricians, plumbers, and equipment operators now. Whether those two efforts end up feeding each other may come down to a few key factors.
“I buy this long-term upside if the individuals who chase the high-paying data center jobs remain in their trade when the projects become less lucrative,” says Berner. “If the pipeline from data center electrician to home electrician is robust and delivers lots of talent, then this benefit may exist. If instead data center electricians chase other high-paying jobs later on instead of working on homes, the benefit to homebuilding could be minimal.”
Plunkett, for his part, sees a real if distant payoff.
“In the long run, the boom could assist housing by convincing more people to enter apprenticeships and skilled-trade careers,” he says. “The problem is timing.” Training takes years to catch up to demand, but as it does, “the short-term competition for workers might eventually create a greater pool for homebuilding as well.”
Thompson is willing to bet on that pipeline paying off: “We expect there to be at least a few bumps in the road, but ultimately, this will benefit the residential end market.”

hed: Florida’s historic rainbow beach cottages torn apart by Hurricane Ian in 2022 now being rebuilt as multimillion-dollar homes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WhenHurricane Iantore through Florida in 2022, it destroyed not just thousands of homes, but decades of history—particularly in Fort Myers,where a collection of beloved rainbow-hued beach cottages were decimated by the horrifying storm.
The properties, which made up an idyllic beachfront community called Paradise Point, had originally been built in the 1960s and had become a local treasure in the six decades before the Category 5 hurricane touched down in the Sunshine State.
Further devastation came when the owners of those cottages,DennisandLisa Greenspon, announced that they would not make an effort to rebuild, saying in a statement that the structures were “no more.”
“We will miss all the close friendships that we have formed over the past 20 years,” the couple wrote on Oct. 4, 2022. “We will not be rebuilding. Cottages of Paradise Point is now a beautiful, cherished memory.”
But nearly four years later, it seems a rainbow is set to rise on Fort Myers Beach once again—with work now underway to restore the brightly colored homes, albeit as part of a very hefty investment that will see the once-quaint cottages turned into multimillion-dollar abodes.
Work—which is being overseen byMarvin Construction—on one of the cottages began in January, with at least two more planned to begin construction this year. But the newly built cottages will look far different from what stood on the Greenspons’ property before.
The old dwellings were dedicated as old-world Florida rentals; the new builds will be modernized and listed for sale, with prices starting at $2.6 million.
They will also be designed to withstand extreme weather, perched much higher above the ground in a bid to protect them from potential flooding.
“The cottages, like many on Fort Myers Beach, were built in the late 50’s and early 60’s and as such they were built to the codes of that time,” Marvin Homes PresidentRichard Durlingtells Realtor.com®, in an email. “Constructed on wood piles and elevated slightly off the ground they survived over the decades, weathering storm after storm.
“But that was until Hurricane Ian came ashore on September 28, 2022. The little neighborhood of Paradise Point on the North end of Fort Myers Beach was hit hard. The 12 cottages there were completely destroyed.
“What was once colorful little beach cottages was now a pile of debris buried in the sand.”
Durling notes that the Greenspons are also ready to begin a new chapter of their lives, explaining that, while the couple is happy to rebuild the community where they enjoyed such success with rentals, they are planning to sell the cottages that will be built in their place.
“They were quite successful with those rentals,” Hurling explained toBusiness Observer. “But at this point in their lives, they’re thinking they just want to rebuild them and sell them. And then whoever buys them can rent them.”
Work on the first cottage—a bright pink structure spanning just over 2,100 square feet—is nearly completed, and construction on several other dwellings—one measuring 3,600-square feet and another that will be 2,053 square feet—is underway.
There are a total of 12 lots, with three rows and four lots in each, spanning from Estero Boulevard to the Gulf. The Greenspons own eight of the 12 lots, having purchased the first one in 2001.
Marvin Homes has already built a new home on one of the lots for the owner, and another is currently under construction for another owner under a different contractor. The other two lots remain vacant.

Built in the 1960s, the original cottages were constructed very low to the ground on wood pilings. While this method is typically acceptable, they aren’t as resilient as modern guidelines.
The new cottages will be built 15 feet above the ground on concrete pilings and reinforced to withstand 160-mile-an-hour winds. They will also feature hurricane-impact windows, doors, and metal roofs.
In tribute to the culture of Fort Myers Beach, the homes will each be brightly colored and have a uniquely designed floor plan.
“The look and the feel we wanted to convey is that it is a beach home, a beach community, similar to what was there, but, obviously, not the same construction,” Durling explained.
The high-end reconstruction of the Cottages of Paradise Point follows the same pathway that much of Fort Myers Beach has undergone after Hurricane Ian, as the traditional, old-world community is being remodeled into a more modern, luxurious neighborhood.
The Fort Myers Beach Town Council is working to redevelop the destroyed community, holding its first reading and public hearing on Aug. 3 on a proposal to reconstruct the Silver Sands Resort on Estero Boulevard as well.
The proposal would rezone the property to permit a six-story, 60-room boutique hotel with ground-level parking, retail space, and a rooftop pool that overlooks the Gulf. Developers also would include access to Margaritaville’s facilities, such as the beach club and restaurants.
The original Silver Sands Resort had 22 small cottages but was destroyed by the hurricane. The Aug. 3 public hearing will be followed by a second reading and vote on Sept. 9, where approval would mean the project is slated to move forward.

hed: California mansion asks $4.7M — with scenic views of a giant condo construction site: ‘What a dump’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Not in your future backyard.
Most real estate listings boast about “tremendous views,” but a $4.7 million Newport Beach home in Cliff Haven is selling something far less serene –– a front-row seat to a massive condo construction site.
The elevated property,according to Zillow listing, offers “tremendous views of Fashion Island, Saddleback Mountain and the Castaways,” along with the promise of “even more vistas through future expansion or redevelopment.”
But, the mansion currently offers depressing views of barren land with a backhoe loader as the main attraction. A sign of the abysmal times in the crisis-stricken California housing market, it seems.
Jerry Zaiden, Vice President of Strategic Partnerships at MagnaFlow, took to Instagram to share a video of the property Saturday.  “This is what you get in Newport Beach, California for $4.7 million dollars. 3500 ft.² on a 9100 square-foot lot built in 1953,”he captioned the video.
Instagram users quickly jumped in with their views with one user saying, “What a dump.” One of the bathrooms in the home even has an awkwardly positioned toilet which is partially buried in the wall.
“A $4.7M purchase to rebuild with a dirt lot/condo view sounds like luxury,” Orange County resident, Juliana Vittoria Kiesselbach commented.
Another user, who said they had moved to Tennessee from the Golden State, said “Hell to the no no and that’s why I moved to Tennessee six years ago… 40 acres 4300 square-foot home for $700,000 and now worth double.”
Others online found the listing way too overpriced for the multi-million dollar price tag.
“What a friggin joke. I’ll give ya $600,000 and not a goddamn penny more. When the condos go up you’ll lose that beautiful view of the highway,” another user commented.
The five-bedroom, 3.5-bath house, spanning more than 3,500 square feet on a 9,000-plus-square-foot hillside lot, is being marketed as a “move-in ready” opportunity in “one of Newport Beach’s most coveted areas.”
The address sits just off 17th Street, near shops and restaurants, and a short hop from the Castaways trails, Newport Harbor, local beaches, Fashion Island, and Balboa Island.

hed: Hayden Panettiere’s LA home purchased at the height of her fame torn down — with the lot asking $7M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Two years after her breakout in “Bring It On: All or Nothing,” a 19-year-old Hayden Panettiere used her rising star powerto buy a homein the Hollywood Hills for herself and her mother, Lesley Vogel — a nest for the pair during one of the most successful stretches of the young actress’s career.
Now, nearly two decades later, that home is gone.
The house, at 7640 Curson Terrace, has been demolished, and the half-acre lot is on the market for $6.99 million, marketed not as a home but as a fully entitled development opportunity for someone else’s dream mansion, The Post has learned.
Panettieredied Sundayat the age of 36. She was found unresponsive at theJudson Mill Lofts apartment complexin Greenville, South Carolina, where police and EMS responded around 1:51 p.m. to a report of anunresponsive female.Despite attempts to resuscitate her, she was pronounced dead at the scene less than an hour later.
Police said the preliminary investigation has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances, and the Greenville County Coroner’s Office was scheduled to perform an autopsy Monday to determine the official cause and manner of death.
In happier times, Panettiere and Vogel paid $2.63 million for the property in March 2008, property records show.
The pair briefly listed the home for rent — first at $9,500 a month in August 2009, later dropped to $8,000 — before pulling the listing that September and holding onto the house themselves, records show.
Panettiere owned the property through her star-making run as cheerleader-turned-superhero Claire Bennet on NBC’s “Heroes” and her starring role in the 2009 comedy “I Love You, Beth Cooper,” before selling it in February 2014 for $3.075 million — more than $400,000 above its final asking price of $5.79 million that August.
The buyer, an LLC called Thrasher NK, kicked off more than a decade of ownership changes and financing deals.
The property changed hands again in October 2016, selling for $5.5 million to an entity called Curson NK LLC, which financed the purchase through 7640 Curson LLC. By 2023, that entity had defaulted on more than $12 million in debt tied to the property. A notice of default for $12.82 million followed in January 2024, and by July of that year, the property had been seized in foreclosure, with a trustee’s deed transferring it to Knight Development Group LLC for $13.45 million.
At some point after the foreclosure, the house Panettiere and her mother once shared was torn down. The current listing touts an approved, “Ready-to-Issue” plan for a roughly 14,705-square-foot contemporary estate — complete with a cantilevered infinity pool, a private wellness spa, a rooftop sky terrace and an entertainment lounge — designed by Roman James Design with structural engineering by KOR Engineering.
Whoever buys the empty lot can break ground immediately.
Meanwhile, Panettiere’s many fans continue feeling the shock and sadness surrounding the star’s abrupt death.
Panettiere had reportedly flown from Los Angeles to South Carolina with heron-and-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson,the day before she died. Her “Nashville” co-star Charles Esten had performed a show at a venue sharing an address with the apartment complex two nights earlier, though police have not said whether that was connected to her presence in town.
Panettiere had spoken openly in recent years aboutstruggling with alcohol, opioids and postpartum depression,chronicling the journey in her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.” Her younger brother, actor Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 at age 28 from complications related to an enlarged heart.
Her father, Alan Panettiere, asked for privacy in a statement: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
It is unclear where Panettiere was living at the time of her death.

hed: California cities most exposed to wildfire risks in new analysis — LA takes the top spot
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Californialeads the nation in wildfire exposureby a significant margin and over 1.28 million properties are facing moderate or greater wildfire risk.
According to2026 data from Cotality, the Golden State accounts for $850 billion in potential reconstruction cost value (RCV), highlighting the massive economic exposure concentrated within its borders.
California’s wildfire exposure dwarfs that of other Western states, carrying more than five times the number of at-risk properties compared to second-place Colorado, according to the report.
The property-data analytics firm evaluated 6.8 million California homes on wildfire mitigation measures like fire-resistant roofing and cleared brush using a regulatory-approved insurance rate scoring model.
The analysis revealed that the top 10% most-prepared properties in the Golden State experience 78% lower losses than average while the bottom 10% face losses over 10 times the average.
A poorly prepared home is roughly 47 times riskier and expects $47 in damages for every $1 lost by a well-prepared home, according to the Cotality analysis.
The report highlights that 6 of the nation’s 10 most exposed metropolitan areas are also located in California. High property values and dense populations near wildland-urban interfaces drive these totals.
Cotality scientists noted that El Niño events in 2026 will redistribute wildfire risk across regions rather than eliminate it entirely.
“Conditions in the Southwest should ease once winter precipitation arrives, while the Pacific Northwest dries into conditions associated with larger, more extreme fires,” the report said.

hed: Flatiron Building nears sellout as wealthy buyers race to claim a rare piece of NYC history
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York’s most-photographed landmark just became its hardest apartment to snag.
Nearly every unit publicly listed for sale at Manhattan’s famed Flatiron Building has already found a buyer, cementing the century-old triangular landmark as the most sought-after residential conversion in Manhattan just as it prepares to open its doors this fall.
Of the 22 residences StreetEasy has shown as listed for sale at 175 Fifth Ave., only four remain unsold, putting the building at roughly 82% absorption on its public listings. That kind of pace for a building still finishing construction has stunned brokers who track the city’s luxury new development pipeline, where units routinely sit for a year or more before finding takers.
The latest proof came last week, when the Flatiron Building notched its second straight appearance atop Olshan Realty’sweekly contract report.
Unit 17-North, a four-bedroom spanning 4,626 square feet with a 63 by 27-foot great room overlooking Madison Square Park, went into contract asking $23.95 million. Its final price, as well as its forthcoming owner, are not yet known until the deal closes.
It marksthe second time in three weeksthat a unit inside the building has claimed the No. 1 spot in the report, a rare feat for any single address. It’s also one that puts the successful conversion ahead of the ultra-exclusive new-construction towers it finds itself competing against for the city’s wealthiest buyers.
Few buildings anywhere carry the instant global recognition of the building’s razor-thin silhouette, a shape so famous it lent its name to the entire neighborhood surrounding it. Built in 1902 to a design by Daniel Burnham, the 22-story tower spent well over a century as commercial office space before Macmillan Publishing, its last major tenant, moved out in 2019 and left the building largely vacant.
What followed was a saga befitting the property’s outsized reputation. When the Flatiron Building’s owners couldn’t agree on its future, the property went to auction in 2023, where a little known bidder named Jacob Garlickwon with a bid of $190 millionand then vanished without ever putting down his deposit.
A second auction that spring produced a winning bid of $161 millionfrom those existing owners, which then partnered with the Brodsky Organization to reimagine the office relic as residential real estate.
The developers tappedStudio Sofieldto handle the interiors, a decision that has become central to the building’s marketing pitch. The firm reworked the awkward angles created by the building’s wedge-shaped floor plates into a layout of one north-facing and one south-facing unit per level, plus two sprawling full floor residences on the top two stories.
Pricing across the 36 sellable units ranges from just under $11 million for a three bedroom to$58.5 million for the penthousespanning the 21st floor. But not all units have hit the market yet, a representative for Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group told The Post.
Sales launched quietly last fall, publicly early this year, and momentum has only built since.
In March, a buyer signed for the seventh floor at anasking price of $30.5 million,a unit originally planned as two separate apartments before the developers combined them into a single 7,700-square-foot home with ceilings over 10 feet tall. That deal briefly stood as the priciest inked at the building, a record since eclipsed as contracts have piled up on higher floors.
Amenities inside include a 60-foot lap pool, a fitness center, a sauna, a cold plunge pool, a billiards room and a residents’ lounge with a kitchenette — all tucked into a structure that was never designed to house any of it.
Construction crews have spent recent monthsreplacing roughly 1,000 windowsto landmark preservation specifications and installing the building’s first-ever exterior lighting scheme, details that have required extensive sign off given the Flatiron’s protected status.
Residences are expected to be move-in ready this fall, with the building’s full amenity package, including the lap pool, slated to open in early 2027.

hed: Home of the Week: Somerville condo with parking (and a short walk to some great food) for $520k
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement

Send this article to your social connections.

170 Highland Avenue Apt. 2, Somerville

$519,900

StyleCondo

Year built1880; converted 1980s

Square feet638

Bedrooms1

Baths1 full

Sewer/WaterPublic

Fee$329 monthly covers water, insurance, grounds maintenance and snow removal

PetsAllowed with some restrictions

Taxes$4,208 (2026)


It’s about a nine-minute walk to theMagoun Square stationon the MBTA’s Green Line, but probably more importantly, it’s less than two minutes to reach the Highland Kitchen,once described by the Globe’s food critic, Devra First, as the “perfect neighborhood restaurant.”

These are two of the perks of becoming a resident in the city’s Spring Hill neighborhood, specifically in this condo unit, one of five created out of a Victorian-era home with a Mansard-style roof in the 1980s.

The sidewalk leading to the front porch passes garden beds framed by cast iron fencing before arriving at the front portico supported by two Grecian-like columns. An entry to the unit is on the right side of the portico.

The entry leads directly into the living room. It’s 128 square feet and full of natural light, as three double-hung windows, with a natural wood finish, fill one wall. A closet has a style of its own with a solid, not louvered, door. The floor is carpeted, and there is a ceiling fan and window air conditioner.


A rectangular arch leads to a dining area and office nook, both of which have carpeted floors and white walls. The wood trim has a natural finish, and louvered doors are installed on closets. The combined spaces are 113 square feet. The closet with the louvered door is also the in-unit washer/dryer. (There is also an entry door from the interior foyer if one uses the main front door.)


Passing through the dining area, the kitchen is located on the right, segregated by a mid-height pass-through with a wood top. Flooring shifts over to vinyl, but the overall design choice — white and natural wood — continues. The cabinets are white and the pulls, instead of metal, use wood edge trim. There is a four-burner electric stove and dishwasher, both black, along with a stainless steel refrigerator. The sink is also stainless steel.

Privacy lies at the end of the hallway, where you’ll find the bathroom on the left and the bedroom.

The 38-square-foot bathroom is petite, as expected for a home this size. It has a single vanity with a natural finish and a white porcelain sink, white mosaic tile flooring, and a curtained shower/bath combination with white subway tile backsplash.


The bedroom is carpeted and, given the summer’s heat, a propeller-like ceiling fan provides helpful support to the window air conditioner. It’s 188 square feet, and natural light comes from a bay window-style bank of three double-hung windows with natural finish wood framing. Lacquered bi-fold doors with louvers guard the 10-square-foot closet. Storage is available above and in a second, narrow closet with a louvered door.


There is an extremely welcome add-on for the condo, especially in Somerville, which has thousands more vehicles than on-street parking spaces. It has its own parking space in the rear of the building, where there are also spots for the four other units.

The unit has electric heat via baseboards. There is separate storage.

The unit can be rented, according to the listing agent.

S. Brett Sillari of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Commonwealth Real Estatehas the listing.

hed: Rentals now allowed in historic water tower on King Charles’ Sandringham Estate where royals spend Christmas
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Have you ever wanted to join the Royals while they celebrate Christmas at Sandringham Estate in England?
Well, now you can! Sort of.
The more than 150-year-old estate in Norfolk, around 100 miles north of London, recently renovated the historicWater Toweron the property, and it is now available to rent.
Prices start at around 151 pounds a night — a little over $200 — but can be much more expensive for shorter visits. The price tends to decrease per night with a longer stay.
The neo-Byzantine water tower was originally built in 1877 to provide fresh water to the royal residence, and it was a functional part of the estate for nearly 100 years.
“THE WAIT IS OVER … IntroducingThe Water Tower,” Sandringham wrote on social media on Tuesday while sharing footage of the classic renovation.
“Rising majestically above the Norfolk countryside on the historic Sandringham Estate, aremarkable pieceof Royal history is being unveiled for a new chapter.”
Photos and videos of the “romantic retreat for two” give glimpses of an elegant living room replete with traditional British décor, including a fireplace, chandelier and royal and historic paintings showing the estate.
The lush bedroom upstairs, which has its own fireplace, offers stunning views of the surrounding countryside, and a medieval-looking back staircase heads to the roof where even better views of the rolling English hills will have you thinking fondly of Jane Austen.
“Designed by renowned engineer James Mansergh, the Tower’s distinctive neo-Byzantine architecture, circular form and intricate brickwork have stood proudly above the Norfolk landscape for almost 150 years,” Sandringham added.
The water tower joins two other places on the estate — the Gardens House, which sleeps eight, and the Folly, which sleeps six — that are available to rent.
There are also several places wherethe royals gofor their summer retreat, such as Balmoral Castle in Scotland, available for rent.
Charles inherited Sandringham and Balmoral, both of which are private estates, from the late Queen Elizabeth II. Queen Victoria bought Sandringham in 1862 as a retreat for her son, King Edward VII.
Around 200 people work at the estate, which includes farms, a sawmill, a juice pressing plant, formal gardens, a restaurant and the Sandringham Exhibition & Transport Museum.

hed: See why a majority of Manhattan home listings are hidden from view — and how that costs sellers thousands of dollars
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
You’re supposed to be able to find a home anywhere.
But thanks to Compass’acquisition of Anywhere Real Estate, you can only do that if you hire one of the conglomerate’s agents.
The country’s largest independent real estate brokerage is using its weight — controlling 21.6% of the market nationwide, and up to 80% in major markets — to keep private listings off public databases, leavingclueless buyers out in the cold.
“When a consumer sits down and uses a website like Streeteasy [in New York City], they don’t know if they’re getting all the listings,” Jonathan Miller, a housing analyst at StreetMatrix, told The Post. “And when you have the largest brokerage firm in the world putting a large amount of listings behind a paywall you’re forced to go through an agent of a particular company rather than anybody you want. This is a major setback in the homebuying process to the 1950s.”
Compass’ three-stage marketing pitch promises big gains for sellers. Listings start in-house with Compass’ 340,000 agents as a “Private Exclusive,” to test the market confidentially, move to a “Coming Soon” preview on select sites, and then go fully public. According to Compass, skipping the immediate public launch helps homes sell 34% faster and fetch 4.6% more money.
Compass, which declined to comment, markets the approach as a seller’s choice, providing adisclosure formabout informed consent to wait to post their home on a Multiple Listing Service.
But critics say the promise is a farce.
“You cannot determine what a home is worth unless you expose it to the broader market,” James Dwiggins, CEO of Compass rival NextHome, told The Post.
Also, Miller said, “Consumers don’t understand what a private listing is, what an MLS is. It’s just somebody you work with that says, ‘just do this.’”
The practice — which some say allows Compass to “double-dip” by collecting a commission from both the buyer and the seller — carries massive implications in major metros where Compass dominates.
Fueled by its $1.6 billion Anywhere merger, Compass controls 60-plus% of transactions in Redwood City, California; San Francisco; and San Mateo, California — far surpassing the 30% threshold that invites federal antitrust scrutiny.
In Manhattan, that concentration jumps to a staggering 80%, meaning buyers relying on standard portals miss out on the lion’s share of inventory while the homes are hidden.
When Caitlin Bigelow and her husband decided to sell their 1,690-square-foot two-bedroom, two-bathroom San Francisco condominium in 2025, they had “a magic number in mind.”
At their agent’s suggestion, the couple posted the Cole Valley listing as a Compass Private Exclusive, Bigelowwrote on LinkedIn.
After two private showings they got their target number.
“SF real estate is a strange beast,” Bigelow wrote in the responses section of her post. “I think [the agent] truly believed that us hitting our magic number was basically impossible. So when that happened in the off market I think he was happy for us and excited we were getting what we hoped for.”
But Bigelow, CMO at artificial intelligence-backed content platform Blazel, grew uneasy, wondering if a public listing would have yielded higher offers. When the buyer backed out, the couple listed the condo on the regional MLS — a cooperative database where competing agents share information about properties for sale with each other — and Zillow.
Six days later they got an offer for $100,000 above their hoped-for price, selling the home for $2.15 million in April 2025, she confirmed to The Post.
“A free and open market is what allowed us to get top dollar and ultimately, walk away with a much bigger win,” Bigelow wrote, later saying, “I would not recommend private exclusives.”
Buyers are feeling the heat, too.
Even Dwiggins, despite running a national real estate franchise, is struggling while searching for a primary residence with his wife in Northern California.
Stalled by sparse public inventory, he was forced to leverage personal connections at Compass just to view the full gamut of all available properties — something the average house hunter could not do.
Seymen Usta, founder and CEO of Modern Chandelier in St. Petersburg, Florida, spent weeks searching for a home in December. Driving around, he finally stumbled upon a Craftsman house on a corner lot on Beach Drive with a coveted porch swing, only to be told it was a “Compass Coming Soon” listing that was “not officially on the market yet.”
“I was calling listing agents directly, thinking I was being efficient,” Usta told The Post. “What I didn’t realize was that without an agent plugged into Compass’ internal network, I was invisible to their ‘Coming Soon’ inventory.”
It took him three weeks to find the home on Zillow, where he could only view a photograph before it was snatched up.
“The house sold for $40,000 less than I would’ve paid,” Usta said.
States are beginning to crack down on private listings, with legislatures in Washington, Wisconsin and Connecticut moving to ban or restrict off-market listings, and similar measures are pending in New York, Illinois and Hawaii.
In New York, the Attorney General’s antitrust division launched an investigation into Compass’ footprint, which is still ongoing, her office confirmed.

hed: California’s population is shrinking — one of just 5 states losing residents
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Californians are ditching the Golden State.
A new research revealed that nearly 10,000 residents left California in 2025, reducing the state’s population by 0.02%.
SmartAsset analyzed year-over-yearpopulation changes in 50 states across the USand found that only five states lost residents in 2025 as compared to the year before that.
With 39,355,309 residents, California remains the most populous state in the US, despite a slight year-over-year decline. The state had a population of 39,364,774 in 2024.
The state has shown persistent decline in population in the past decade and a half. Between 2010 and 2024, nearly 10 million Californians left for other states while just over 7 million moved in,according to a report by CalMatters.
The downward momentum reached its sharpest point between 2020 and 2021, when California lost arecord 374,900 residents in a single year.
Among the five states that recorded decreases in population, Vermont lost the largest share of its residents at roughly 0.3%, followed by Hawaii at 0.2%.
The report revealed that South Carolina and North Carolina were among the nation’s biggest population gainers with a growth of 1.46% and 1.32%, respectively.
“The U.S. population continues to grow, but that growth has slowed dramatically, with the year-over-year increase now below 1%,” according to SmartAsset.
Utah emerged as the nation’s youngest state in the research, with a median age of 33. The Beehive State also has the highest share of kids under 5 (6.5%) and the lowest proportion of seniors 65 and older (13%).
By contrast, Northern New England has the oldest population. Maine leads the country with a median age of 45 and the highest share of seniors, while Vermont and New Hampshire closely follow with median ages of 44.
“A growing population can increase labor availability and expand the consumer base, supporting economic growth. At the same time, negative population growth may reduce pressure on housing and infrastructure, potentially improving affordability for current residents,” the report said.

hed: Affordability crisis fuels bidding wars for abandoned homes in beleaguered US city — reducing vacancies in a stunning reversal
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Long-blightedBaltimorehas a blooming new future in store.
Thousands of vacant homes within the city, which for years stood as eyesores and scared investors away, are now seeing a stunning moment in the spotlight thanks to big buyer demand and bidding wars,the Wall Street Journal reports. And while not every city neighborhood is seeing such success, the activity is helping Baltimore see a notable vacancy reduction — nearly a third — over the last decade.
Not only are the city and Maryland showering Baltimore with billions of dollars in funding, but nonprofits are also rehabbing full blocks at once — all while violent crime makes historic drops.
Still,the languishing affordability crisisis making Americans in pricier cities have a look at Baltimore. It doesn’t hurt that the city’s median sale price is $235,333, according to Zillow data, well below the $381,333 national median.
Alex Queen, a Baltimore native, left Los Angeles after repeatedly losing out on California homes in bidding wars. She and her family ultimately bought a vacant property that had been rehabbed by Parity Homes, a nonprofit developer.
Similarly, Alex Kovach and Ella Miller purchased a home in East Baltimore’s Johnston Square, where a nonprofit developer, ReBUILD Metro, has made big strides reducing the sum of vacant properties. It’s close to downtown Baltimore and transportation options.
“Johnston Square is at the perfect location,” Kovach told the Journal.
Buyers like these are helping the city mark massive milestones. For many years, the city saw vacant homes hit a stagnant high of 16,000. That number has since lowered to less than 12,000.
“Vacant housing was everywhere,” Baltimore’s mayor, Brandon Scott, told the Journal. “When people see a bunch of vacants, no one wants to live there. No one wants to invest there.”
The recent activity traces its origins to the COVID years, whenlow interest rateslured in buyers, helping prices grow and renovations become more doable. Then people from pricier areas, namely Washington, DC, began eyeing Baltimore as a more affordable alternative.
Now, more than ever, investors are swooping in. Plumber and part-time investor Chris Waldron had to raise his auction bid to $45,000 for a vacant property with boarded-up windows and a peeling facade — after competitors doubled what he wanted to shell out.
“What did I get myself into?” Waldron told the outlet of his thoughts when he visited the property after winning the sale. But then he figured out his plan — flush it with $130,000 for a five-month renovation before selling it for more than $300,000.
Not every neighborhood benefits currently. For instance, Carrollton Ridge — home to some of the worst homicide rates in Baltimore — has 750 vacant homes, 40 more than it had a decade ago.
Elsewhere, the change is hard to believe, locals said. In Johnston Square, the purchase activity has made a community garden replace a drug market, while formerly vacant blocks are now home to families.
“There was nothing but rows and rows of boarded-up houses,” longtime neighborhood resident Regina Hammond told the Journal. “Now it’s a whole different story.”

hed: Popular NYC brunch staple shutters 2 locations — as landlord sues another outpost for unpaid rent
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Sarabeth’s is closing in on two fronts.
The beloved brunch brand pulled the plug on its Park Avenue South and Greenwich Village locations last weekend, with both restaurants serving their final plates on Sunday — all as the chain’s Upper West Side eatery is being hauled into court by its landlord over alleged months of unpaid rent.
Sarabeth’s, founded by Sarabeth Levine in 1981, has been in business for 45 years, having started as a jam-making operation out of her apartment before opening its first Upper West Side restaurant that same year and later expanding.
However, time has not proven to be kind to the brand.
In a statementposted to Instagram, Sarabeth’s thanked “the teams, guests, and neighbors” who made the two now-shuttered locations “such vibrant, beloved parts of New York City.”
But the company said the math no longer worked, writing that “despite everything that was working well, the economics of running these two locations are no longer sustainable.”
Further specifics surroundings those closures were not available by press time.
The brand, a fixture of the city’s weekend brunch scene for its classic American comfort food, said it will keep operating its two remaining locations, Central Park South and the Upper West Side, and “look forward to welcoming” loyal customers there.
But the Upper West Side outpost, at 423 Amsterdam Ave., has troubles of its own.
Landlord 423 AMCO sued the restaurant’s operator, BSWR Inc., also known as BWRS Inc., in Manhattan Supreme Court in late July, accusing Sarabeth’s of blowing off rent payments and refusing to report sales figures required under its lease.
According to the landlord’s complaint obtained by The Post, Sarabeth’s owes $43,432.16 in back rent, additional rent and percentage rent, covering shortfalls from May, June and July of this year.
The suit alleges the restaurant violated its 2020 lease modification by “failing to report Gross Sales within thirty … days of end of each month” and by failing to pay base rent “in the amount of $10,000.00 per month ($120,000.00 per year) or 8% … of monthly sales.”
Under that 2020 agreement, Sarabeth’s had negotiated a hybrid rent structure tying its payments to sales performance, along with an additional 1% of sales earmarked to repay rent that had previously been abated.
The landlord claims it sent a default notice on June 11 giving the restaurant until June 22 to catch up, then followed up with a formal notice of lease cancellation on July 1 after the restaurant failed to cure the default. The lease was terminated effective July 13, according to the filing, though the restaurant “remains in occupancy of the Premises beyond the Termination Date without Landlord’s consent.”
The landlord is seeking a laundry list of remedies from the court, including a money judgment for the unpaid rent, an order forcing Sarabeth’s to resume reporting its sales, and — if the restaurant doesn’t fall in line — the right to eject the tenant with the help of the city sheriff.
The case escalated in August. On August 5, attorney Norman Flitt of Rosenberg & Estis, P.C. notified the restaurant’s operator that the landlord was seeking a court order with a temporary restraining order attached, warning “we will be filing a motion by order to show cause, containing an interim order and temporary restraining order.”
The following week, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Lyle E. Frank signed off on a temporary order directing Sarabeth’s to start paying up. Under the order, the restaurant must pay $17,810.72 in use and occupancy for August, and continue paying that amount “on or before the first … day of each calendar month thereafter,” while the case plays out.
Frank’s order also bars Sarabeth’s from destroying sales records and requires the restaurant to hand over monthly gross sales figures dating back to March.
A hearing on the landlord’s broader request, which includes posting more than $43,000 to cover the arrears, is scheduled for Sept. 8. Justice Frank has directed that the matter be argued orally.
Sarabeth’s did not respond to The Post’s request for comment.

hed: Mortgage rates rise for 5th straight week, hitting levels not seen since 2025 for 2nd week in a row
content: CHICAGO — The average long-term US mortgage rate rose for a fifth consecutive week to its highest level in just over a year, marking the latest strain for prospective homebuyers who are facing steep borrowing costs.The benchmark 30-year fixed rate mortgage rate rose to 6.69 percent, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday, up slightly from 6.66 percent reported last week. By comparison, the average rate was 6.63 percent at this time last year — and hadn’t been higher than its current level since July 2025.Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power. As rates rise, that can lead prospective home shoppers to delay buying a home, one reason US home sales have been sluggish this year.Meanwhile, borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages — which are often sought by borrowers looking to refinance a home loan — fell slightly this week. That rate averaged at 6.01 percent, down from 6.04 percent last week. A year ago, it was at 5.75 percent, Freddie Mac said.Mortgage rates are influenced by several factors, including inflation, broader policy rate decisions from the Federal Reserve, and expectations from bond market investors for the economy. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.Rates have been mostly rising this year as the US war with Iran, which has fueled expectations for hotter inflation as crude oil prices soared. Despite easing oil prices recently, long-term bond yields remain steeper than they were before the conflict began in late February, pushing mortgage rates to tread higher.The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.65 percent as of midday Thursday on the bond market. Before the war, it was just 3.97 percent in late February.

hed: Sprawling ‘Love Island’ estate quietly lists for sale in Hawaii: ‘Hard to beat’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A “Love Island” bombshell hits the market in Hawaii.
A Big Island estate that once played host to reality TV’s most infamous test of loyalty is now looking for a buyer of its own for $3.25 million, The Post has learned.
The Royal Palms Estate, a nearly 13-acre spread along Hawaii’s Hamakua Coast, served as the Casa Amor villa during Season 3 of “Love Island USA,” which shot there in 2021.
The show sent contestants to the property to tempt fate, and now the sellers are hoping its second act on the market gets just as much attention.
The four-bedroom, 5.5-bath home spans just over 3,700 square feet, wrapped in the kind of privacy that reality producers and second homebuyers alike seem to crave.
Listing agent Paul Stukin, founder and CEO of Deep Blue Hawaii, pitched the property as a standout even among the coast’s famously beautiful homes.
“This isn’t just a home, it’s one of the most special properties on this part of the island,” Stukin said.
The estate’s centerpiece is an infinity-edge pool that spills toward panoramic ocean views.
“The pool alone is one of the best I’ve seen, and paired with those ocean views, it’s hard to beat anywhere on the Hamakua Coast,” Stukin said.
Beyond its brush with reality TV fame, the property functions as a working farm.
The orchard produces more than 25,000 pounds of lychee a year alongside avocados and a rotating cast of tropical fruit.
“There’s an old donkey barn on the property dating back to the sugarcane plantation days. It’s a real piece of island history, and it gives the whole place a character you just can’t build new,” Stukin said.
Stukin said the departing sellers are ready to hand off the property, memories and all.
“My sellers have loved this home for years and made some incredible memories there, but it’s just time for them to move on. They’re excited for the new owners to enjoy it as much as they did,” Stukin said.
Season 3 was the only installment of “Love Island USA” to film in Hawaii, relocating the franchise from its usual tropical backdrops to the Big Island for a single summer before the show moved on to California and eventually settled in Fiji.
The season, hosted by Arielle Vandenberg, ran 40 days and pulled in 34 islanders across its run. Korey Gandy, a 28-year-old from Virginia Beach, and Olivia Kaiser, 29 and from Anchorage, Alaska, were crowned the winning couple on the Aug. 15, 2021 finale, taking home a $100,000 prize.
Casa Amor itself was where a rotating cast of bombshells arrived to test the original couples’ loyalty, a twist that has become the show’s signature gut punch each season.
