hed: Ari Emanuel’s company to acquire 7 Broadway theaters and 10 in the West End
content: Ari Emanuel, a Hollywood power broker who is building a live events company that already has holdings in visual art, tennis, collector cars, and theater ticketing, announced Tuesday that his venture had agreed to acquire ATG Entertainment, a British company that operates theaters on Broadway and in London’s West End.Emanuel’s company, MARI, reached a deal to buy ATG from US private equity firm Providence Equity Partners, which has owned a controlling stake since 2013. No financial terms were disclosed, but The Financial Times reported in June that the price tag was expected to be about $6 billion.The acquisition will require regulatory approval.ATG is the smallest of the big three Broadway landlords, controlling seven of the district’s 41 theaters. It has also become increasingly active as a producer of Broadway shows, including a Dolly Parton musical that is scheduled to open in January. (ATG is facing litigation from an investor over its production of a 2024 Broadway revival of “Cabaret,” which said it had lost all its money despite grossing $90 million at the box office.)The company is a bigger player in London, where it operates 10 theaters in the West End. It has a global footprint, operating 70 venues in Britain, the United States, Germany, and Spain. It also has a financial affiliation with a production company run by the London-based Sonia Friedman, who is one of the more prolific producers in the West End and a significant player on Broadway.ATG also operates Boston’s Emerson Colonial Theatre.MARI already has a foothold in the theater business: Last year, the company acquired TodayTix, a growing player in the theatrical ticketing business in the United States, Britain, and Australia.Emanuel said that “this is a long-term bet on where live goes next.” MARI said that “ATG will continue under its existing brand and leadership.”In New York, ATG has long owned the Lyric, one of Broadway’s largest venues, which has for years housed “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.” The company also owns the Hudson, one of Broadway’s smallest venues. That theater has been home to some recent successes, including two starring Daniel Radcliffe: a revival of “Merrily We Roll Along” and the one-performer play “Every Brilliant Thing.”ATG assumed control of five theaters previously operated by Jujamcyn in 2023. The former owner of Jujamcyn, Jordan Roth, has retained a minority stake in ATG.This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

hed: Inside the strange history of an unsellable NYC home tied to a mob-linked poker scandal — now the stage of a blue-chip design showcase
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A 189-year-old West Village townhouse that once housed the composer of “The Stars and Stripes Forever;” a Pulitzer-winning novelist; and Travis Scott and Kylie Jenner — all before it became the site of an allegedmob-run poker scandal— keeps marching on.
In its latest chapter, the landmarked red-brick Georgian townhouse at 80 Washington Place is now the site of this year’s blue-chipKips Bay Decorator Show House, which since 1973 has been known in the design and residential architecture worlds as the preeminent showcase for high-end interior designers, while raising more than $33 million for the Kips Bay Boys & Girls Club.
Twenty-two top designers including Carrier and Company, Peter Dunham, TORREY, Marmol Radziner, Ten Plus Three and Nicole Fisher Interiors are currently transforming the property into a modern, month-long creative dreamscape that opens to the public on Sept. 16.
“When we saw 80 Washington Place, we immediately saw the potential,” said Nazira Handal, director of special events and corporate partnerships at Kips Bay Boys & Girls Club. “It’s a beautiful historic townhouse with so much character, but it also offers six levels, terraces, a wellness floor and a rooftop overlooking Washington Square Park, giving our designers an interesting range of spaces to work with. Most importantly, it felt like a house that could be completely reimagined, and we were excited to show visitors what our designers did with it.”
The residence was most recently on the market for $21 million before it was taken off in June.
It’s slated to go back on the market once the showcase ends, listing broker Melissa Olson, of Douglas Elliman, told Gimme Shelter.
“It’s currently a construction site, filled with designers running around and lots of plywood. But it’s going to be amazing,” Olson said, adding that when the home returns to market, it will be at a new, still-to-be-determined price.
While the exact designs are currently under wraps, they will include upgrades to the kitchen and bathrooms, she said.
“Some of the top designers in the world are making it amazing. It benefits everyone, including Kips Bay,” Olson said.
The current owners purchased the six-story spread for $17 million in cash in 2024 after it had lingered on and off the market for 12 years. It originally asked $31.5 million back in 2012.
The owners, who wish to remain anonymous,then listed the home for $22.5 milliona few weeks after the poker bust last year — and around eight months after they bought it.
“They didn’t buy it as an investment, but their plans changed,” Olson said.
The six-bedroom home is around 8,700 square feet, and comes with six baths and three powder rooms. It also features four landscaped terraces totaling 1,566 square feet.
Reimagined after an architectural restoration, the home is now a mix of historic brick, original stone, glass, steel and wood.
The townhouse’s past lives “make for great cocktail conversation,” Olson said.
The home’s glossy present is far from its reality just a few years ago, whenneighbors were calling 311, and the ritzy residence was the site of multiple mob-linked assaults, according to anunsealed 2025 federal indictmentand related court filings.
From 2021 to 2023, the townhouse was allegedly the site of rigged poker games backed by the Gambino and Genovese crime families, with the Bonanno family sharing in the proceeds after the game merged with one of its operations in 2023. The games were fronted by NBA stars and coach Chauncey Billups to lure victims, according to the accusations that broke last year.
Two assaults happened at the home, according to federal prosecutors in the Eastern District of New York. In November 2022, Bonanno associates allegedly assaulted a gambler over an unpaid debt — and around a year later, two mobsters armed with a gun and a baton allegedly stormed the home and assaulted the game’s organizer.
The home’s history includes ownership in 1919 by the American composer and band leader John Philip Sousa. It later became a boarding house, where one of its tenants was the Pulitzer Prize winning novelist Willa Cather. In 2021,Scott was renting the townhousewhile Jenner, then pregnant with their second child, was mainly residing in LA with their daughter Stormi — although shewas spottedstaying at the townhouse with Scott during the time he rented it. The now-former couple had no involvement in the alleged poker scandal.
History aside, details inside the six-floor townhouse include a skylight that floods all floors with light — down to the basement media lounge.
A garden floor features a foyer that opens to a chef’s kitchen, along with a double-height great room with a gas fireplace and floor-to-ceiling glass doors leading to a garden made for indoor-outdoor living and entertaining.
Two guest suites take up the third floor, while the entire fourth floor is devoted to a primary bedroom with a fireplace, a private terrace, a spa-like bath and a walk-in dressing room.
The fifth floor is for wellness, including a home gym, a glass-enclosed sauna and a terrace.
The crown jewel is the roof deck, with a grill, a bar, a dining area, a lounge — and views from Washington from Square Park to One World Trade Center and the downtown city skyline.

hed: New owner stands to get the $48M Malibu mansion that Kevin Garnett once owned — but never lived in
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This Malibu house still has game — and plenty of avocados to spare.
A modern beach residence thatNBA legend Kevin Garnettcommissioned — but never lived in — is back on the market after a four-year renovation, asking a cool $48 million.
Mansion Globalwas the firstto report the listing.
The ultra-modern residence, at 27715 Pacific Coast Highway, features a large infinity pool, wide ocean views and, yes, no fewer than 50 avocado trees.
It’s also part of a small, ultra-exclusive blufftop stretch of the highway that is one of the most compressed high-net-worth corridors in the country.
Beyoncé and Jay-Zpaid a record $200 millionfor their similar sized estate in 2023, at 27712 Pacific Coast Highway in an all-cash deal, while billionaireMarc Andreessenpaid $177 million for his estate, which also sits on around 7 acres, at 27740 Pacific Coast Highway in 2021.
Garnett’s former home is on 6.74 acres, a triple lot, standing adjacent to an equestrian center.
One of the three lots that is part of the sale is currently vacant, comes with its own address, and could be used to build a second home or perhaps a family compound, brokers said.
At 11,000 square feet, the six bedroom mansion feels more like a year-round home than a weekend beach retreat — and it comes back to market as more folks are making Malibu their permanent residence, brokers added.
Garnett had purchased the property for $6.4 million back in 2003, when he was with the Minnesota Timberwolves.
But he never completed his dream house and ended up selling it in 2021, which is where the story gets messy.
Garnett, known as one of the NBA’s greatest power forwards, agreed to sell the home, unfinished, to Ando Hacopian of Hacopian Design & Development Group for $16 million in 2021. As part of the deal, Hacopian agreed to cover Garnett’s closing costs and prior leans, leaving Garnett with $6 million, including $2 million in cash at closing,according to the Real Deal.
But Hacopian, Garnett alleged, didn’t have the funds to close.
Garnett filed a lawsuit against Hacopian alleging fraud, followed by a second lawsuit against the title and escrow companies.
Vladimir Valsky, CEO of VIG Private Lending, who held senior debt on the property, took ownership in 2022,the Real Deal reported. Valsky then hired Swiss architect Roger Kurath, of LA-based Design 21, to overhaul the design, gut renovate and meet new fire codes.
Kurath, whose celebrity clients have included Gene Simmons and Kathy Griffin, spent the next four years upgrading the property, built with materials including fiber cement, stucco and aluminum windows.
In addition, Kurath also oversaw the home’s interior design, furniture and art curation.
A long driveway leads to the gated home, where glass doors open to a large foyer with 21-foot-high ceilings.
The residence is anchored by a large chef’s kitchen with a wine fridge.
Three “guest suites” have 10-foot-high ceilings, custom closets and ensuite baths — while the upstairs main bedroom suite includes a projector, a spa-like bath, an expansive terrace and views from the landscaped garden to the Pacific Ocean.
Outside there’s a 65-by-30-foot infinity pool.
There’s also a pickleball court, a barbecue area, and a home theater and gym. A separate structure on the property works as a yoga or art studio.
The listing brokers are Tomer Fridman and Aaron Kirman of Christie’s International Real Estate Southern California, and Chris Cortazzo of Compass.

hed: It was once New England’s largest building. A New York developer wants to turn it into housing.
content: A block-long Back Bay office that was once New England’s largest building is set to become Boston’s largest office-to-residential conversion project.Vanbarton Group, a New York real estate firm, this month applied to create up to 490 apartments at 31 St. James Ave. The 11-story, 540,000-square-foot property, known as the Park Square Building, stretches a full block between Arlington and Berkeley streets. If approved, the project would cost up to $410 million and be by far Boston’s largest office-to-residential conversion to date. “The location speaks for itself as one of Boston’s most desirable neighborhoods,” Gila Cohen, managing partner of Vanbarton Group, said in a statement.The building has struggled financially since the pandemic and in April sold at foreclosure for $96 million to LNR Partners, a Miami-based subsidiary of commercial real estate giant Starwood Property Trust. That $96 million almost matches its mortgage from two decades ago, property records show, though it’s a far cry from the $160 million mortgage New York’s Capital Properties Management took out in 2017. It’s also 19 percent less than the property’s assessed value, which itself is down 33 percent in the past four fiscal years. It’s not immediately clear whether Vanbarton will assume the mortgage, or whether it might buy the property outright from LNR. The conversion would be Vanbarton’s first development in Boston. The ground-floor tenants at 31 St. James include French furniture retailer Roche Bobois and restaurant Fire + Ice. Vanbarton said it plans to keep about 30,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space.The ground level will also include “amenities for residents,” wrote Adam Baron, the head of East Coast acquisitions for Vanbarton, in the property’s conversion application. Baron declined to comment for this story.Vanbarton has completed a 588-unit office-to-residential conversion project at 160 Water St. in New York, and has another 1,511 units under construction in three other buildings there. One of those projects is located at the longtime headquarters of New York’s Archdiocese.In Boston, developers have proposed converting some 2 million square feet of underutilized office space into residential projects. Less than 20 percent of the 2,331 units proposed for conversion have been built or are under construction.At 31 St. James Ave., Vanbarton proposed a unit mix ranging from studios to three-bedroom units. It’s proposing a rent range of $6.50 to $7.50 per square foot for the 80 percent of the building that’s not set aside at affordable rents, equating to roughly $5,425 for a 775-square-foot unit.Nearly two dozen office tenants occupy 31 St. James Ave. now, though they’re “expected to vacate” within a year, Baron wrote in Vanbarton’s conversion application.Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Inside the gruesome history of Mark Zuckerberg’s Irish castle —where people were tortured and hung down a ‘murder hole’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Mark Zuckerberg just bought himself a piece of Irish history that comes with a body count.
The Meta mogul and his wife, Priscilla Chan, quietly closed on Strancally Castle, a 440-acre Gothic-revival estate in County Waterford, Ireland, in an off-market deal valued between $23 and $35 million, according to theIrish Times,which broke the story.
But long before the Facebook founder set his sights on the riverside pile, the ground it sits on was the stuff of nightmares.
The original Strancally Castle, situated about 2 miles from the current structure, was reportedly the site of a medieval killing floor known as the “murder hole,” where unsuspecting guests were said to be trapped, bound and dropped to their deaths.
Legend has it the original castle was once seized by Spanish occupiers who lured local landowners inside under the guise of a banquet, only to drop them through a hidden trapdoor into a flooded cave below. Word of the slaughter eventually got out, and the occupiers were driven off and the castle torn down.
English writer William Howitt immortalized the legend nearly two centuries ago in his 1847 book “Homes and Haunts of the Most Eminent British Poets,”describing how victims met their grisly end.
“The unwary, when decoyed within the castle, were tied hand and foot, and hung down the murder-hole,” Howitt wrote. “The rapid river hurried by, and soon carried away their gasping shrieks, and the dead told no tales.”
Howitt himself was skeptical of the lore, chalking it up to local legend, but not before adding his own eerie caveat.
The castle standing today bears no resemblance to that blood-soaked ruin. It was built around 1830 for John Keily, a Tory member of parliament, and designed by brothers James and George Richard Pain, the same architects behind Dromoland Castle in County Clare and Blackrock Castle in Cork.
The three-story, 16,000-square-foot mansion was constructed on such an extravagant scale that it reportedly took a 4.5-minute walk just to get from the kitchen to the dining room.
The estate changed hands over the following century, passing to the Whitelocke-Lloyd family around 1855 before eventually landing with the Irish Land Commission.
It was purchased 25 years ago by Michael Alen-Buckley, a co-founder of London investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife Giancarla, who poured two decades into restoring the property before handing over the keys toSilicon Valley’s most famous billionaire.
The sellers said goodbye to their longtime home with a statement to the Irish Times.
“We leave our home of 25 years fondly and are grateful for the opportunity we have been given to save and restore Strancally Castle,” the Alen-Buckleys said.
“We are delighted that Mark and his family intend to build on our stewardship by continuing to invest in maintaining and enhancing the property and grounds as their home in a sustainable manner. We wish them and their family much happiness in this unique and blessed place.”
A rep for Zuckerberg confirmed the purchase and struck a decidedly cheerier tone than the castle’s bloody backstory might suggest.
“Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” the spokesperson said.
Zuckerberg and Chan plan to keep their primary residence in the US and use Strancally as a landing pad when doing business in Ireland, where Meta has run its international headquarters since 2009 and employs roughly 1,500 people.
The Meta chief isn’t the first tech titan to go castle shopping along the River Blackwater.
Strancally sits near Ballynatray House, snapped up by Dyson founderJames Dysonfor about $34 million in 2024, and Lismore Castle and Salterbridge House, owned by British property magnate Stephen Vernon. Stripe co-founder John Collison also grabbed the 1,100-acre Abbey Leix estate in County Laois for roughly $23 million back in 2021, making Zuckerberg at least the third tech billionaire to plant an Irish flag in five years.
It’s also not Zuckerberg’s first swing at Irish real estate.
Last year, Liberty Media chairman John Malone told theWall Street Journalthat Zuckerberg had made a play for his Castlemartin House and Estate in County Kildare, once home to the late businessman Tony O’Reilly. That deal never materialized.

hed: Notoriously cramped NYC apartments are actually getting larger in 1 borough
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Renters chasing extra elbow room in New York City have exactly one borough to thank.
Queens is the sole district where new apartments have grown over the past decade, according to a fresh analysis fromRentCafethat tracked square footage across the 100 largest cities in the country.
What’s more, Queens lands at fifth nationally for the biggest gains in living space during that span of time.
The typical new Queens apartment now clocks in at 732 square feet, a 16-square-foot bump from where things stood a decade ago.
That’s part of a broader national trend, with the average US apartment now sitting at 910 square feet after every unit type picked up extra space in 2025.
Queens’ growth outpaced the national gain of 13 square feet, even as the borough still ranks in the bottom tier for overall size compared to the rest of the country.
Brooklyn and Manhattan did not fare nearly as well.
Brooklyn ranks fourth among thecountry’s smallest markets, with apartments averaging 714 square feet, 6 square feet smaller than a decade ago.
Manhattan landed just behind at 735 square feetwith sizes barely budgingsince 2016.
Both boroughs are getting squeezed by the same forces reshaping cramped cities everywhere. Developers are leaning hard into studios and one-bedrooms because they can pack more units into a single building, a strategy that drives down the average square footage even as it puts more apartments on the market.
“When we see average apartment sizes decrease in a city, it doesn’t necessarily mean renters are getting less value,” RentCafe research analyst Veronica Grecu said in the report.
“In high-demand markets, developers often prioritize studios and one-bedrooms because they can deliver more apartments per building and meet the needs of a growing number of single-person and smaller households,” she added. “The trade-off is a lower average square footage, but the upside is more availability in markets where inventory has historically been tight.”
Even with its gains, Queens is far from spacious by national standards.
The borough still trails the national average by more than 175 square feet, and comes nowhere close to Tallahassee, Florida, where new apartments average a roomy 1,156 square feet —  the largest in the country.
Still, in a citywhere square footagehas become the ultimate luxury, Queens renters can at least say their apartments are headed in the right direction while their neighbors across the East River keep losing ground.

hed: ‘Arthur’ creator Marc Brown sells Martha’s Vineyard home for $6.4 million. Take a look inside.
content:
By Shannon Larson, The Boston Globe
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Author-illustrator Marc Browndrew plenty of inspiration from his Martha’s Vineyard home.

The creator of the best-selling “Arthur” children’s books, he completed about half the series there. After the adventures of the beloved aardvark ended, Brown brought the stone bridge leading to the entrance of the compound to life as the home of a troll named Helga in his animated television show “Hop,” listing agents said.

Brown and his wife, artist Laurene Krasny Brown, purchased the nearly 8-acre property in Vineyard Haven in 1988 for $700,000, property records say. Over the years,they restored the circa-1730 farmhouse and several outbuildings.

She converted a former horse barn into an art studio; he transformed the space above the carriage house into his own. They furnished the home with carefully curated American folk art and antiques. And Brown painted most of the wood floors himself, according to their listing agents.

But after 37 years, they felt their work was done. They were eager to take on a new project.

Recently, they sold the home in the Pilot Hill Farm enclave for $6.4 million, a year after it waslisted for $6.9 million.

TheWall Street Journalfirst reported the sale.



When the Browns bought the property, which had originally been part of a 225-acre dairy farm, it was in a state of disrepair, said listing agent Elle Lash of Tea Lane Associates/Forbes Global Properties. She had the listing with colleague Alexis Holden.

“But being two artists, they really had a vision for this old house,” Lash added.

In the 1930s, oceanographer Columbus Iselin purchased the farm and built a homestead,according to its ownership history, compiled by Holden and Lash. The Iselin family maintained the farm for four decades and housed refugee children there during World War II. His children later sold the original farmhouse, preserving 75 acres as conservation land and dividing the rest into smaller lots sold to buyers.

The community became Pilot Hill Farm, which now consists of 25 homes, said Holden, who lives in the private residential and agricultural enclave.




The Browns were living in Hingham when they bought the original farmhouse. They enjoyed being surrounded by trees and ocean, and the serenity the area offered, Lash said. They were excited to make the space their own while preserving its history.

By the time they began renovating, “Arthur” was beginning to soar in popularity. Years earlier, in 1976, Marc had lost his job after his employer,Garland Junior Collegein Boston, went belly up. His young son, Tolon, asked him for a bedtime story one night,and Arthur was born.

The young aardvark became the central character in his massively successful children’s book and television series. The award-winning PBS show ended its 25-season run in 2022.




“Marc and Laurie just adored working on the house, and so much of the work they did themselves,” Lash said. “It was their great joy to do together.”

The roughly 3,700-square-foot main home has five bedrooms and four bathrooms. It features a spacious screened porch overlooking a heated saltwater pool, which was added by the Browns. A guesthouse features two bedrooms and a bathroom. The carriage house has room for three cars. Both art studios are big and open.

Although the Browns renovated much of the compound, they still kept many features intact, including gunstock posts, a Dutch door, and four fireplaces. The coupletold the Wall Street Journal last yearthey spent millions of dollars in improvements.




The interior color palette was chosen by Laurie “to mimic colors in nature,” Lash said.

While the property is considered “down island” — where the shops and bustling downtowns are — it’s located in a rural setting, said Holden, “so you have the best of both worlds.”

The home is surrounded by nature. There are two ponds, perennial gardens, fruit trees, and raspberry bushes.




“Obviously, the question is, why are you selling? Marc said to me: ‘It’s been like a piece of art, and it’s finished now,’” Holden said. “So, he said, ‘It’s on to the next one’.”

The Journal reported the Browns have purchased a home in New York’s Hudson Valley for their next restoration project. Their primary home is in New York City.

hed: Alex Trebek’s  ginormous California ranch sells at jaw-dropping discount
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Thesprawling California ranch and vineyardonce owned by beloved “Jeopardy!” host Alex Trebek has fetched $16.9 million after hitting the auction block—going for nearly half of staggering $33 million price tag it carried when it hit the market last year.
Known as Windfall Farms, the 724-acre mega-estate in the rolling hills of Paso Robles went to the highest bidder during Monterey Car Week last week after languishing on the market. The sale is now pending, according toConcierge Auctions, which sold the estate in partnership with Sotheby’s International Realty.
The TV titan, whodied in November 2020 at age 80, used the compound as a thoroughbred horse breeding haven. The ranch retains its equestrian glory, anchored by a 6.5-furlong racetrack, large paddocks and enough open turf for a regulation polo field. It also houses an industrial-grade, three-bay machine shop outfitted with heavy-duty hydraulic lift, 480V three-phase power, and natural gas lines.

The main house is an expansive, 10,000-square-foot primary residence with eight bedrooms, offices, conference rooms, large kitchen, dining and living areas, a media room, 12 bathrooms, and two separate manager residences.
The property is also awine country goldmine, with 387 acres of planted wine grapes, which operates as a “positive cash flow business in production today,” according to the listing, through contracts with other wineries.
A whopping seven wells pumping out more than 7,000 gallons per minute keep the dirt green, plus the Huero Huero Creek slices through the grounds. With 76 approved, buildable 10-acre lots, it’s also a developer’s dream.
Hundreds of acres of rolling hills, open pasture, and productive farmland help distinguish the estate from the typical celebrity home.
The location is also a draw for buyers, since Paso Robles has emerged as one of California’s fastest-growing wine destinations over the past two decades, withaffluent buyers drawn to the region’s scenic landscapes and acclaimed vineyards. The estate is managed by agricultural giant Limoneira, and is situated near wine-country legends like Justin and Halter Ranch.
Windfall Farms was owned by Trebek for 37 years, until he and several other investors sold it to its now former owners for $1.6 million in 2001 to Barry and Donna Goldfarb. Since, they have transformed it from a working winery into a sprawling family retreat, adding multiple structures.

hed: Rare Frank Gehry-designed LA loft asks $2.39M and comes with storied history: ‘People painted on the walls’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Now is your chance to buy a coveted California residence designed by the legendary architectFrank Gehry— less than a year after his death.
ASanta Monicaartist’s loft in a six-unit building that the Pritzker Prize-winning architect designed in collaboration with his friend, the artist Charles Adnoldi, has listed for $2.39 million, Gimme Shelter has learned.
The sleek, minimalist triplex — more of a townhouse than a condo — is located at 1643 12th St., delivering views of the ocean.
At 2,565 square feet, the three-bedroom, two-bath space is currently set up as an art gallery and a private residence.
But it can be configured in whichever way works best for the next owner, listing broker Brandon Assanti of the Agency told Gimme Shelter.
Built in 1992, the units were originally designed as artist studios for Gehry, Adnoldi and their friends — in a minimalist manner with high ceilings and large open wall spaces for art displays.
“Over time, people bought and transitioned them into live-work spaces,” Assanti said.
“Back in the day, people painted on the walls directly as huge canvasses. It has a very cool vibe inside, and out, which is especially unique in Santa Monica,” Assanti said.
The sellers purchased the loft for $1.33 million back in 2014. Sales in the building are so rare, Assanti said, that there has only been one deal in the building since then — in 2024.
“If they had their choice, they would never leave. But they recently relocated to New York for work,” Assanti said.
The dwelling comes with industrial-scale windows and oversized skylights that showcase the views.
Inside, it features large open living spaces and 17-foot ceilings on the main floor — plus a mezzanine level, a second floor with 12-foot ceilings and a third floor with 15-foot ceilings.
A middle level comes with an open living room, a dining area and a custom chef’s kitchen with millwork, concrete countertops and stainless steel appliances
The main bedroom takes up the entire upper floor, and features panoramic Pacific vistas. There’s also a large walk-in closet and a spa-like bath with marble slabs.
The building is also gated and comes with two spaces in its underground parking garage, as well as storage.
Gehry-designed residences are in high demand. ActorPatrick Dempseyonce owned the “Tin House” in Malibu — a corrugated metal Gehry design from the 1960s. He bought it for $7 million in 2009 and sold in 2015 for $15 million — $500,000 over its asking price, at 29715 Cuthbert Road.
Gehry himself lived in a deconstructed home in Santa Monica at 1002 22nd St. — where he passed away last December.

hed: Tiny Cape cottage offers 294 square feet of living space in Eastham community
subhead: The house is part of the Cranberry Cottages condo complex.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
What this Eastham cottage lacks in square footage, it makes up for in character.
Located in the coveted Cape Cod hamlet of Eastham,unit 9 at 785 State Highwayis a 294-square-foot seasonal home tucked inside the 14-unit Cranberry Cottages complex right off Route 6. Built in 1952, the home has been transformed in the last few years into a stylish tiny cottage. Now it features hardwood floors and freshly painted walls and is on the market for $279,000.
“It’s been completely reimagined. Every single square inch of the whole 294 square feet is taken advantage of,” saidCallie Zaglioof Christie’s International Real Estate Brokerage, who has thelistingand has already sold three other cottages in the same complex.
The home is set toward the back of the Cranberry Cottages complex. It has a home’s front parking space. Upon entering, you’ll find a queen-size bed on the right.
The kitchen was redone in 2022 and features a retro-style mint green refrigerator and quartz countertops. White cabinetry is above and below the sink, and there’s an area for small appliances in the corner. Under the window, there’s a dining nook.
The bathroom was redone in 2020 and has a step-in shower and porcelain tile floors, as well as new cabinets, a sink, and a mirror.
A door to the right of the bed leads out to the back deck, the backyard, a shed, and an outdoor shower. The yard, which has an exclusive-use area, is surrounded by leafy trees. A shed contains two Cannondale bikes and two stand-up paddleboards that come with the home. The back of the complex leads to a bike path.
“If you’re coming for the summer and you have to rent a hotel room, a hotel room is like $300 to $400 a night. I would much rather have something like this instead,” said Zaglio. “You can literally just pack your bags and go.”
Almost everything inside the cottage is included in the sale, except for some artwork. The buyer will be buying into a piece of the 5.67-acre complex, which is collectively owned by the residents.
The annual HOA fee is $1,295.00, and it includes landscaping, town water, basic cable, Wi-Fi, and trash. There is a new roof and a new water heater.

hed: Earth-sheltered Ohio home that is built almost entirely underground comes with a roof you have to mow
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The future owner of a newly-listed Ohio residence will never need to worry about shopping for roof shingles—but they should take care to ensure that their lawnmower is in good condition.
Because the earth-sheltered property, which is locatedin Huron, Ohio,is built almost entirely under the ground, complete with a dirt- and grass-covered roof that provides spectacular protection from the elements, butdoesrequire the odd trim now and then.
“We’ll call it an earth-sheltered home because about 90% of it is underground,” said listing agent Laurie Brill with Keller Williams Citywide. “[The sellers] built it in the side of the hill and then they covered it with dirt, so the roof is ivy and myrtle and they literally mow the roof.”
The home is on—or, rather, under—about eight acres on the Huron River and was recently listed for $850,000, an ask that Brill admits was not easy to come up with, largely because there arenosimilar properties in the area to compare it to.
“Trying to price it was really difficult… it’s not like any other home. There are other earth-sheltered homes across the country, but I’ve never seen one here in northern Ohio,” Brill says. “There are not comps for this.”
The sellers have lived in the solid concrete underground home since they built it in 1977.
Initially, Brill saus, they weren’t intending to create such a unique structure, but the beauty of the natural landscape inspired a different design.
“He bought a piece of land and he was just going to build a regular house on it,” Brill explains, adding the seller told her he was walking the land one day and had a type of epiphany, wondering if the house could go underneath the ridge. “So he went and talked to a contractor that could do a concrete home, and that’s what they did.”
Brill says she didn’t know what to think when she firstsaw the place.
“I’m a 40-year veteran selling real estate and this is clearly the most unique listing I’ve ever had, and I’ve had some weird ones,” she admits with a laugh.
However, after she walked inside the home, she breathed a sigh of relief—because for all of its unique quirks on the outside, the interior is very much that of a traditional residence.
“When you go inside the home, it feels exactly like a normal little 2,100-square-foot ranch floor plan,” she says, adding there is actually a lot of natural light from windows on two sides and skylights throughout.
“In the living room, dining space, and kitchen, you’ve got natural light coming in, just like you do in any other normal house.”
There are two bathrooms and three bedrooms, one of which would make a perfect room for napping at any time of the day.
“There’s only one room in the house that does not have any windows, and it is the third bedroom,” Brill explains. “If you turn the light on, it looks normal, but definitely there is no light coming into that particular room.”
The entire home is almost hiddenunder a tree canopy.
“You would never know that house is back there unless you knew it’s back there,” she says. “If you want to live like a hermit or a hobbit, there you go.”
But while much of the house is hidden, part of it still has a view.
“In the main living area, when you’re standing at the kitchen sink, you can look right outside,” she says. “There’s this beautiful gazebo out there, so you can look right into the yard and into the gazebo and the patio.”
There are also two other above-ground structures on the property, a log cabin and a workshop. The parcel has about 250 feet of waterfront and it is about a 30-minute boat ride to Lake Erie and open water.
The home itself could use a bit of updating but is in good shape. Keeping it up is different from other homes which are above ground.
“There’s no roof. There’s no gutters. There’s no siding. There are no downspouts, so [the sellers] have never had to replace any of those items,” Brill says, adding the sellers have been doing all of the property maintenance themselves, which is getting harder for them as they get older.
“[It’s] a unique property and they’ve enjoyed it, and they’ve loved it, and they’ve taken care of it. Hopefully, we’ll find another buyer that will love it just as much as they have.”

hed: Architect’s ‘upside-down wedding cake’ home hits the market for first time
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A strikingly modern Michigan property that was designed by late award-winning architect Ken Neumann, FAIA,as his personal residence has been listed for $3.25 million—marking its first time on the market since its 1987 construction.
The five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom masterpiece is located in Franklin, MI, where its sleek design clearly sets it apart from the carefully preserved 19th-century homes that have inspired the Detroit suburb’s nickname, “The Town That Time Forgot.”
For nearly four decades, the glass-walled home has intrigued and delighted locals who have only been able to admire the dwelling from a distance—until now, with its listing providing members of the public with their first real opportunity to see inside the spectacular structure.
Although Neumann primarily worked on commercial projects, his work skewed residential, as well. Inspired by Bauhaus design principles, his 7,348-square-foot Franklin residence is an excellent marriage of both ends of the architectural spectrum he worked on, touting clean lines and modern materials.
Over the years, the home has been featured in countless publications, gracing the pages of Elle Decor and books including “Architects House Themselves” and “Dream Homes Michigan.”
Ken and his wife, Beverly Neumann—a prolific artist who now resides in a senior community but still paints daily and created most of the pieces displayed in the home—purchased the lot from another architect who claimed it was “unbuildable.”
Because of its sloping landscape and dense trees, many believed that the parcel could not house a residential property, only for Neumann to prove them very wrong.
However, Linda Hiller Novak and Frank Novak—the mother-son real estate team who have listed the home—tell Realtor.com® that, because of those difficult circumstances, it was quite some time before the architectural masterpiece came to life.
“They sort of marinated on it, trying to decide what to do and what to build,” Linda explains. “It was 15 years before they built this house.”
The home was certainly worth the wait, with that 15 years spent ideating a home that could naturally fit within the existing landscape. Linda says the home was “built like an upside-down wedding cake,” noting it’s unusual shape spared any trees from removal during the process.
While some may be tempted to turn a challenging lot into a blank slate before building, Ken and Beverly let the surrounding area inspire the home.
“They chose these horizontal lines of the house because they wanted it to contrast with the vertical lines of the trees,” says Linda. “That’s the kind of thing that only an architect and an artist would think about.”
25850 Romany Way has undergone a handful of updates over the years, primarily to accommodate the family’s needs as they grew over time. Aesthetic changes made the list, too. The home was originally white; Ken opted for a natural red-brick color in later years.
Though not immediately obvious from the exterior’s brick facade in the front of the home, expansive windows steal the show across the entire back of the structure, providing peaceful panoramic views of the artesian pond located on the 1.24-acre lot and flooding the interior with beautiful natural light.
Standing in the driveway of the dwelling, you could be forgiven for thinking that the property was a single-story abode—but walk through the door to the back of the home and it tells a very different story.
Having been designed to follow the slope of the land on which it was built, the structure appears to cascade down the hillside, with the enormous wall of windows stretching well below the first floor of the property.
In certain lights, it creates the illusion of a waterfall steadily tumbling down the hill. Yet, thanks to the dense trees surrounding it, the home still feels incredibly private.
Inside, the space is well-suited for entertaining, but also allows for privacy and relaxation.
The remodeled gourmet galley kitchen includes new Viking and Miele appliances. A useful pass-through window connects to a spacious living area and is surrounded by a statement-making wall of built-in shelving, which the Neumann family lovingly filled with their enormous collection of books, art, and black-and-white photographs.
There are seemingly endless built-in bookshelves throughout the house, constructed of rare Bird’s Eye maple. An assortment of over 10,000 books was removed from the home and sold to Detroit’s John K. King Books.
The home is an excellent residence for creatives, like Ken and Beverly. In addition to the various displays that are integrated throughout and the inspiring outdoor views, there’s an artist’s studio, which Beverly worked out of each day.
Marked by bold black-and-white-checkered floors, the studio is connected to the luxurious primary suite, and includes a private staircase.
The suite features heated floors, a recently updated bathroom, and a spacious walk-in closet that Linda jokes could qualify as a bedroom in some Southeast Michigan spots.
The four additional bedrooms in the home also include ample windows, giving each member of the family their very own view of the tranquil retreat. There’s not a single window treatment in the home.
Amenities are plenty, with an elevator that provides access to all three levels. A weather-resistant EPDM roof was installed in 2025, and a full-home generator provides peace of mind. There’s also an intercom system, closed-circuit cameras, and exterior video surveillance.
There’s even a heated patio and driveway—invaluable perks during a harsh Michigan winter.
“This is more than a home—it is a work of art, a legacy of design, and a living environment unlike any other in Franklin,” the listing notes.

hed: Popular NYC Chabad congregation facing eviction in brutal fight with landlord over lease dispute
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For six years,Chabad Lofthas served as a hub for Jewish life in Greenwich Village, operating from the bottom of a quaint rowhouse at 10 E. Eighth St.
Now, the space — aptly dressed with painted exposed brick, gold-tone light pendants and plush jewel-tone furniture for its trendy young congregants — is facing eviction.
Rabbi Jerry Bankhalter is embroiled in an acrimonious fight with his landlord over ambiguous lease terms that involve the validity of a lease extension that was never signed.
Bankhalter, known as Rabbi Yakov, claims he has two years remaining on the lease. But the landlord claims the synagogue is a month-to-month tenant paying far below market rate.
In June, the landlord sued for eviction in housing court in Manhattan. And now, a window sign even says the space is available for rent — a total of 2,800 square feet on two levels.
“The whole street is filled with vacant storefronts,” the rabbi told The Post. “The space is weird. There is not much interest in a seven-step walk down with 9-foot ceilings and pillars in the middle of the space. It is not handicapped accessible. It is a very hard sell. We are perfect tenants to them.”
The monthly rent for what is known as “the Kavanah Space” is $7,000.
“The landlord is trying to bully the rabbi out of there,” said Angelo Bisceglie, the rabbi’s lawyer, who in July sued the landlord in Manhattan Supreme Court for promissory estoppel, breach of contract, fraud, deceit and negligent misrepresentation.
Not so, according to Gregory Bougopoulos, the lawyer for the landlord, then known as Lynch Family Associates.
“This is a disagreement over the legal status and appropriate terms of a commercial tenancy,” Bougopoulos said in a statement to The Post.
“The tenant has, for years, paid well below market rate and currently has no lease in effect,” he said. “When the property owner sought to resolve the expired lease and negotiate new terms, the tenant repeatedly indicated that he would engage in that process. Ultimately, however, he declined to enter into discussions regarding a market-rate tenancy. The tenant disputes this account, and that disagreement is appropriately a matter for the legal process to resolve.”
The rabbi, who formerly lived near Union Square, came to the building just before COVID shut down the city, occupying the top-floor residential space for a rent of $8,500. That rent dropped during the pandemic and settled at $7,000. The rabbi now resides there — above a hair salon called Salon V — with his pregnant wife, his mother-in-law and his three young sons.
During COVID, the nascent congregation used a nearby empty storefront whose landlord was an observant Jew, Rabbi Yakov told The Post. “We didn’t have a real synagogue. We had more of an online community.”
So when the space below his home came available, he happily signed on, also for $7,000 a month. The original two-year commercial lease was signed in 2021, as the city was emerging from the pandemic and the previous tenant, the MNDFL mediation studio, departed. That lease came with a five-year option to renew, until mid-2028.
The Lynch family bought the building for $8 million from New York University in 2008, according to city records. The space had once been thelong-time homeof the Patricia Field boutique.
“Over the past several years, this location has developed an identity as the Kavanah Space,” Rabbi Yakov told The Post. “People can find hospitality, a meal, friendship, learning, spiritual connection and a sense of belonging. For many people, particularly those who may not have family or an established community in New York, it has become a second home.”
Over time, the rabbi spent around $30,000 on improvements that involved floors, walls, kitchen counters and boiler parts — and he did so while relying on the ability to stay until the 2028 expiration date, according to court papers.
Both parties agree that the five-year option to renew was never signed. That’s about their only point of agreement.
“I find it appalling that the rabbi gets assurances until 2028 and invested money to improve the facility and now they want to evict him,” his lawyer, Bisceglie, told The Post. The landlord accepted rent, he said, “so it was reasonable to rely upon that assurance.”
The relationship was cordial until early this year, after “an apparent restructuring of the landlord entities and a refinancing of the building,” according to Rabbi Yakov’s complaint.
At one point, the rabbi received an alarming phone call from the elderly owner, Michael Lynch, Sr., who suffers from dementia and lives in a senior-care facility. He owns the building with his sons, Michael Jr. and Frank.
In the call, “Lynch Sr. threatened Rabbi Yakov and told him repeatedly to get out of the building. . . that he [Lynch Sr.] didn’t care about the law . . . and that Rabbi Yakov would instead have to deal with ‘Lynch rules,’” according to the complaint.
“Rabbi Yakov was alarmed by the call and left with great concern for the safety and well-being of himself and his family,” the complaint further alleges.
The commercial rent — $7,000 from the start — never rose.
“The landlords say they can get a higher rent,” the rabbi said. “They made it seem like they would negotiate but they wouldn’t go below $15,000. But their broker is asking for $12,000. That made it pretty clear that the $15,000 number was not really a serious attempt to negotiate with us.”
The disputed lease extension expires anyway in two years. “Two years gives us time to find something else,” the rabbi said.
“There is presently no substitute location available to us where all of our activities could simply be relocated on short notice. What exists here is a living community that has developed organically over many years around this particular location. It is not simply a piece of commercial real estate.”

hed: Tennis star Mike Bryan gets $2.35M in cash for his waterfront Florida home
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It’s not a tennis court, but it sure is a nice place to claim a win.
Tennis legendMike Bryan, who reached the top of the pro tennis ranks in doubles withhis twin brother Bob— and with whom he won an Olympic gold medal in 2012 — has sold his waterfront Florida home for $2.35 million in an all-cash deal, according tothe Business Observerand a release from the listing brokerage.
Located in St. Pete Beach near St. Petersburg, the three-bedroom dwellinglisted for $2.59 millionearlier in the year. Its new owners, according to the publication, are a Minnesota couple named Sheri and Thomas Karnowski.
Bryan, 49, along with his wife Nadya, had owned it only since 2024, buying it at that time for $1.9 million in an LLC named Beyond the Baseline Coaching.
They reportedly purchased it as a vacation home, then spent a cool $300,000 on renovations. Their permanent base is roughly an hour’s drive away, in Wesley Chapel.
The home spans 2,182 square feet on Boca Ciega Bay. What’s more, it draws its aesthetic inspiration from the Soneva Fushi resort in the Maldives.
It stands replete with wood finishes and a split-roof design, which allows sunlight to flood throughout the interior. That design also allows the exterior to resemble the sails of a ship.
Nearly every room looks out to water views, while double-height ceilings and wide-open layouts provide modern comforts. A central courtyard with palm trees also helps bring the outdoors in.
The couple’s recent upgrades include new flooring, upgraded bathrooms and a redesigned kitchen. A custom area for kids has a catamaran-style hammock and play features — while outside perks include a private beach, a nine-person hot tub and a dock. Multiple balconies and terraces also add to the waterfront experience.
Johane Bucaille and Daniel Francis, of Coldwell Banker Realty, had the listing.

hed: Logan Paul’s infamous ex-psychedelic retreat hits the market for $3 million — and it comes with a wild hippie backstory
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Influencer turned boxing star Logan Paul has listed his storied, psychedelic California property for just under $3 million dollars, three times the price he paid for it.
Paul purchased the remoteMountain Center, CA, retreat known as the “LSD ranch,” in 2019 for $1 million, a half century after counterculture icon Timothy Leary used it as his heady, hippie headquarters.
An ex-Harvard professor turned LSD-evangelizing high priest of the late 1960s, Leary coined the mantra, “Turn on, tune in, drop out.”
Leary, who President Richard Nixon once described as “the most dangerous man in America,” is alleged to have produced the pure and potent LSD strain “Orange Sunshine” whilst at the ranch which he occupied with his devotees, the Brotherhood of Eternal Love.
The property’soriginal listingmade no secret of the ranch’s storied past.
“With more hippies, as they were referred to by the locals, joining the Brotherhood, this often unpredictable group would later operate vegetarian soup kitchens, oppose the Vietnam War and preach to others that the regular use of LSD would create a more sensitive human race,” read the listing, noting that the compound grew to include 30 members, a ranch house, several outbuildings and teepees.
In 1972, federal agents raided the compound, where they reportedly found Leary making said sunshine under the canvas of one of those fabled teepees.
Far out and in deep.
At present, the property is registered to a trust named for Paul and his brother Jake and has undergone serious upgrades since the pair acquired it.
The listing is held byBill Church of So Cal Coast Real Estatewho described the rebranded Fobes Ranch as “a truly extraordinary piece of California mountain history” and the ultimate “off-grid retreat.”
When Paul purchased the property the primary residence had two bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms.
However, the new listing reveals that the residence now boasts four bedrooms.
To boot, the listing notes that Paul is offering the property, with “most of the furnishings, ranch vehicles and equipment.”

In addition to the primary residence, the 78-acre spread includes a caretaker’s home, a bunkhouse, a horse barn, green house, gymnasium, garages and sheds, and a 300-yard shooting range.
“For the outdoor enthusiast, the possibilities are endless-horseback riding, dirt bike riding, four-wheeling, hiking, wildlife watching, ranching, or simply enjoying the peace and solitude of your own private mountain retreat,” the listing continues.
The home is equipped with solar power, batteries, a propane backup tank, and a “gravity-fed water system.”
Though the Logan brothers did not utilize the property as a working ranch, it is outfitted to support the endeavor.
“The property features expansive, level acreage suitable for cattle grazing, a seasonally full pond, and miles of four-wheel-drive trails winding throughout the ranch,” the listing notes.
The remoteness of the Fobes Ranch is underscored in the listing: “Reached by a secluded four-mile drive from Highway 74, with no other residences along the way, Fobes Ranch is surrounded by the San Bernardino National Forest.”
Idyllwild, the closest town is roughly 25 minutes by car while the property is an hour from the Palm Springs Airport.
Since 2021, Paul has continued to pull up stakes in California and cement himself as a permanent fixture, and resident in Puerto Rico citing the commonwealth’s boxing training camps and favorable taxes as the reason for his retreat.
“I went out there to scout it, and I fell in love with it,” Paul said about Puerto Rico in an episode of his “imPaulsive” podcast. “Obviously, I’m impulsive, and I trust my gut, my instincts. I feel like it’s the closing of a chapter and the opening of a new one.”

hed: Home of the Week: In Roxbury’s Fort Hill neighborhood, a 3-bedroom in a ‘twin home’ Colonial for $650,000
subhead: The neighboring unit is also for sale
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

49 Norfolk St., Roxbury

$649,900

StyleColonial

Year built1900; updated

Square feet1,688

Bedrooms3

Baths2 full

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$7,408 (estimate without residential exemption)


Dorchester Heights makes history books for its role in the1775 Siege of Boston, but what has become known asFort Hillin what was then the independent town of Roxbury was a player, too. In its more recent history, Fort Hill has become a neighborhood drawing interest.

This attached single-family — sometimes called a twin home — has a covered front porch protecting two matching doors with entry to different units.

Both properties are on the market, with the 1,712-square-foot home at51 Norfolk St. listed for $699,900.

On the right, is the entrance to 49 Norfolk St. Upon entering, the foyer is 74 square feet and shares space with a stairwell to the second floor. The common space of this home is arrayed on the first floor in three successive rooms: the living room, the dining area, and kitchen.


A door on the right side of the foyer opens into the 220-square-foot living room. It evokes an earlier time in one of Boston’s oldest neighborhoods with a central light fixture that resembles a candelabra. There is a nonfunctioning fireplace with a mantle extant, crown molding, and a three-pane bay window. The hardwood flooring is original to the home.


The dining room follows, and is slightly larger at 221 square feet. There are two large double-hung windows with natural-toned staining on the walls and a drum-shaped pendant light in the center of the room. The walls are painted a butter yellow, and the floor is carpeted.


A French door opens to the 172-square-foot kitchen with maple cabinets in a variation of Shaker design. There is space in the center for a two-person dining table underneath a central light fixture and recessed lighting. There is also a skylight. The flooring is ceramic tile, and the countertops are quartz. Appliances are stainless steel, includinf the gas stove. In a corner is a second stairwell to the upper floors.



The 175-square-foot primary bedroom is at the front of house on the second floor and has three double-hung windows on its three exterior walls. The window trim and doors are white, and the walls are painted red with painted crown molding. There is a ceiling light fixture and wall sconces. Signaling its spot as the primary bedroom is the 56-square-foot walk-in closet. There’s also a 66-square-foot office next to the bedroom.


The second bedroom is 155 square feet, has two double-hung windows, a central light fixture, and hardwood flooring. The window trim is white, and the walls and crown molding are painted a gentle shade of olive.

The shared bathroom is 54 square feet. The mirror trim, faucets, and shower head are gold tone. The bath walls and shower backsplash are cloaked in cream tile with a vine and flower accent line.

The third floor qualifies as a quiet space, should one be looking for it. It’s the spot for the third bedroom — among the largest rooms in the house at 417 square feet. The ceiling lines mirror the slope of the roofline, the flooring is original to the home, and the walls are painted white.


The last full bathroom is on the third floor too, and it is fully updated with black and white hexagon mosaic tile flooring, a single vanity underneath a light fixture with three globes, and marble-like ceramic tile wainscoting. The shower is nested behind rolling plates of glass with steel framing and has two shower heads and a marble-like backsplash. There is a window in the shower.

There is a private deck off the back.


The home has central air conditioning and forced air gas heat. Bonuses include rooftop solar panels to help reduce utility costs, two off-street parking spaces, and an unfinished basement for storage.

Kellyanne Swett of Allison James Estates & Homesis the listing agent for both 49 and 51 Norfolk St., which are separately owned.

hed: $13.9M NYC townhouse at center of ‘squatting’ lawsuit sells — months after live-in housekeeper evicted
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In less than a year, this Manhattan townhouse has gone from an alleged squatting scandal to a multimillion-dollar sale.
Mansion Global reportsthe townhouse at 111 E. 81st St., which hit the market in May for $15 million, has entered into contract after most recently asking $13.99 million.
The identity of the forthcoming owners — and they price they’re paying — are not yet known, but it will be a new chapter following the drama that embroiled the property earlier this year.
In February, a California-based neurologist named Sarah Shalev — who’s tied to the LLC that owns the 6,650-square-foot townhouse — filed a Manhattan Supreme Court lawsuit claiming that the home’s live-in housekeeper, Hilarie Page, was squatting inside and preventing Shalev from entering.
Shalev’s estranged husband, the direct-to-consumer mattress executive, Craig Schmeizer, died in the home last November.
According to the complaint at that time,as The Post reported, “Page was a licensee occupying space in the Building with the permission of Schmeizer,” but the “said license of Page to occupy space in the Building was terminated by virtue of the death of Schmeizer.”
It added, “By reason of the termination of her license … Page has no right to use or occupy any portion of the Building.”
The primary issue at hand, court documents alleged, was that the impasse between Shalev and Page was jeopardizing valuable assets inside the home, such as wine and artworks to be inventoried for insurance and estate reasons. What’s more, the building had to be sold due to no income being generated, the documents added, which required brokers and inspectors to access the interior.
Not long after Schmeizer’s death, Shalev called Page, according to an affidavit at the time, and the talk didn’t go well.
“She was extremely hostile, told me she was not going to leave the house because Craig was dead and it was clear that I would not be allowed into the Building,” Shalev claimed in the filing.
Come February, after attorneys’ letters went unanswered and the interiors remaining dark, Shalev and a legal representative attempted to enter.
“We rang the doorbell many times. [sic] pounded on the door and even threw snowballs at windows to get the attention of anybody who might be inside,” Shalev added in the affidavit.
When no one responded, a locksmith was called.
According to the complaint, once the door was opened, Page “ran toward the door, screaming,” and both sides contacted the police, who ultimately instructed the estate’s representatives to leave.
However, the ordeal ended rather quietly. A month after the lawsuit, Page was served with an eviction notice and vacated the residence shortly after,according to the Daily Mail.
Schmeizer purchased the townhouse in February 2022 for $13.25 million. He was 52 years old at the time of his death. It has five bedrooms, an elevator, a garden and roof terraces.

hed: Beloved Kips Bay movie theater to shutter at the end of 2026
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
That’s a wrap on a popular Kips Bay movie theater.
The curtain is closing on theAMC Kips Bay 15after becoming a staple for moviegoers for nearly three decades. The theater opened back in 1999 with five screens on Second Avenue and then moved to its current location — 570 2nd Ave — in 2006.
AnAMCemployee has confirmed to The Post that no date has been set for the closure and the location will operate until the end of the year. The plot thickens, as the employee said not even its manager was told their last day.
According toABC News, the property owner is ending the lease before its scheduled expiration and “details are still being finalized.”
“The theatre has been an important part of the Kips Bay community and surrounding neighborhoods, providing guests with a place to enjoy the magic of the movies together,” a statement from the spokesperson read.
Movie lovers can still catch flicks at the three nearby locations: AMC Empire 25 IMAX in Times Square, AMC Lincoln Square and AMC 34th Street 14.
It’s not clear what is taking its place, as no information has been released. However, a website calledSave Kips Bayis urging cinephiles to sign the petition to keep the neighborhood favorite as its the only IMAX in the area.
It goes on to claimNYU Langonewill be taking over the lot, insisting that the block doesn’t need another “institutional medical space.”
“NYU Langone already dominates huge portions of Kips Bay. Now our neighborhood’s only movie theater, a 15-screen AMC and the only IMAX on Manhattan’s East Side, is reportedly threatened by yet another NYU medical expansion,” the website reads.
The owner of the theater is Kips Bay Development Limited Partnership, care of M.D. Carlisle Construction Corp. Neither NYU Langone nor the property owner has publicly stated whether NYU is taking over the space.
The post reached out to NYC Langone for comment but has not heard back.
“Kips Bay did not lose its theater to streaming, or to a bad quarter, or to a landlord who couldn’t fill the space. It lost it because someone decided this block is worth more as something other than a neighborhood,” the site read.
AMC currently has 860 theaters across the globe and is the largest theater chain in the world. But in a February earnings call, CFO Sean Goodman revealed that AMC will be closing “underperforming locations.”
Goodman also said that since 2020, AMC had shut down 213 locations, while opening 65 new theaters in the same timeframe. Since 2025, the company has closed six theaters.

hed: Inside Dolly Parton’s $2M California ‘weekend escape’ home in Solvang
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Dolly Parton’s secret California hideaway where the rhinestone-loving country queen could escape from the spotlight is still on the market — asshe dies aged 80.
The singer’s modestformer retreat, which she quietly owned from around 2004 to 2014, is tucked away in the town of Solvang — known as the “Danish capital of America” — and is available for $1,995,000.
The white farmhouse in Santa Barbara County, which was listed in April, is a far cry from thelarger-than-lifeimage of the music icon, whose death was heartbreakingly announced by her family Tuesday.
Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security, Bryan Seaver, confirmed her passing in an Instagram post on behalf of the Parton and Owens family.
“I am representing the Parton and Owens family today, announcing the passing of my Aunt Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean,” Seaver said.
“Sister, sis Aunt Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next,” he continued. “This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality.”
Parton’s publicity team also confirmed her death, remembering the beloved singer for a life that extended far beyond her music.
“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” her reps said.
Away from her rhinestone-filled public life, Parton created a quiet refuge in the heart of California’s Santa Ynez Valley.
The singer reportedly bought the 1920s-era property through Dolly Parton Enterprises in 2004 and quietly kept it as a getaway for nearly a decade.
Sitting on the corner of Alisal Road and Maple Avenue, just a short walk from downtown Solvang, the farmhouse was built to blend in rather than announce that one of the world’s most famous women was inside.
Inside, Parton reportedly went to extraordinary lengths to keep her visits private.
The windows were made to reflect the scenery outside so that curious passersby couldn’t see in. A latticework corridor led to the back door, creating a “paparazzi-proof” tunnel for Parton to come and go without being noticed.
Her main bedroom could reportedly be locked from the inside with seven locks.
“She paparazzi-proofed the whole house,” current owner Cris Lapp previously told SFGate.
Parton also left behind many touches that were unmistakably hers.
A small “wig room” remains in the garage, said to be a miniature version of the elaborate wig-storage setup at her Tennessee home.
One of the most obvious signs of her presence is above the front door: a stained-glass window that spells out “Dolly” next to her trademark butterfly.
A plaque on the white fence also marks the property as Parton’s former home.
The home’s celebrity history stayed mostly hidden for years, until property records and building permits eventually linked it to Parton’s company.
Lapp, a real estate broker with Black Oak Homes and Mortgages, bought the property for about $1.3 million in 2022 and later found signs of its famous past.
Since then, the former retreat has been turned into three long-term rental units and has become such a local curiosity that people call it “Solvang’s Dollywood.”
The property includes a three-bedroom, two-bathroom front home, another three-bedroom, two-bathroom residence in the upper rear and a one-bedroom lower unit with a three-quarter bathroom. Each has its own enclosed patio.
But Lapp has said he isn’t just looking for someone who sees the place as an investment.
“That is just me, I want a mega fan,” he previously told Noozhawk.
Another of Parton’s properties, her former cabin retreat, returned to the market less than a year after a charity sold it for $585,000, following her donation in November 2023.
The mountainside home in the picturesque town of Idyllwild, CA, belonged to Parton, 79, and her late husband, Carl Dean, for decades before she gifted it to Ronald McDonald House Charities of Southern California, which sold it in July 2024, records show.
The listing describes the three-bedroom cabin—now on the market for $768,000—as “Dolly Parton’s former Idyllwild retreat—a home as iconic as the legend herself,” perRealtor.com
“If walls could sing, this charming three-story mountain retreat would be belting out a country classic,” the description continues, noting that “nearly everything inside remains just as Dolly left it.”
Now, in the wake of Parton’s passing, both homes offer a rare window into the private world of one of America’s most cherished icons.

California homebuyers searching for the state’s strongest real estate market may want to skip Los Angeles and San Francisco — and set their sights on Irvine.
TheOrange County citywas named California’s best real estate market and the 10th-best nationwide in WalletHub’s 2026 ranking.
Irvine earned a score of 64.28, ranking eighth for the strength of itshousing marketand 85th for affordability and economic conditions. It also finished second among large US cities, behind only Charlotte, North Carolina.
Roseville was California’s next-best bet at No. 12 nationwide, followed by Santa Clara at No. 29, Clovis at No. 33, Ontario at No. 34 and Elk Grove at No. 39.
Rounding out the Golden State’s top 10 were Murrieta at No. 58, Sunnyvale at No. 66, San Diego at No. 70 and Santa Maria at No. 72.

WalletHub compared 300 cities across 17 measures, including home-price appreciation, affordability, foreclosures,mortgage delinquencies, building activity and job growth.

hed: California city goes rogue, plots 1,200 new homes at high-speed rail site
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
California’sbeleaguered, over-budget high-speed rail linenow has one more thing to worry about: A city and housing developer wants to build homes right in the train’s projected path.
Shafter, a city near Bakersfield, and developer Lennar Homes are plowing ahead with 1,200 homes in the same area off Highway 99 where thestate’s rail authority plans to build tracks.
The development, calledGossamer Grove, is a “master-planned community” that will be equipped with a picnic area, playground and dog-walking trails, according to Lennar’s website.
The homes planned by Lennar, one of the largest builders in the Central Valley, will have three to four bedrooms, with prices in the high $300,000s.
“It’s raw land, we own it, we plan to develop it,” Walter Diamond, Lennar’s director of entitlement, said at an April city planning meeting.
Shafter officials have a history of opposing the high-speed rail project, calling for the tracks to be built outside its boundaries.
Mayor Chad Givens said the housing project may force the high-speed rail authority to moves its trains,telling The Fresno Beethe city would go to court to defend the planned property development.
“You’ve got a city and a pretty high-volume developer willing to fight against high-speed rail,” Givens said.
The rail authority opposes Lennar’s map of the development. It told the Bee that the rail’s plans to run through Shafter were decided after a 2018 environmental lawsuit from the city was settled. The authority could sue over the development, but the agency told the Bee it would be open to negotiations.

Lennar said at the April meeting that it was done trying to negotiate.
“We made the attempts,” Diamond said. “We’re looking forward to moving forward.”
City officials said they’re legally obligated to approve the project, pointing to housing laws and the fact the rail authority has yet to buy land in the area.
Any actual construction of the rail in Shafter is likely a long ways off.
A risk analysis of the rail endeavor projects completion of the Merced-to-Bakersfield segment in September 2034. But officials warned that even that deadline may not provide enough breathing room because the authority is relying on “overly optimistic assumptions.”
The project is far from complete since workers broke ground in 2015. Only this year did the ill-fated project enter what officials called the“track-laying phase.”
Republicans have criticized the rail line as a fantasy project that’s wasting taxpayer money.Costs for the original plan have ballooned past $200 billion,though the rail authority insists the reassessed project cost is $126.3 billion.
“I’ve been saying this for years now, but this is the most wasteful government project in probably world history,” state Sen. Tony Strickland (R-Calif.) told the California Post.

content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
California’s housing markethas become synonymous with eye-watering prices, but it turns out you can still find a bargain.
While buyers in Los Angeles,San Franciscoand other pricey parts of the state are known for sky-high home prices, remote Trinity County is hanging onto a distinction that has all but vanished elsewhere: a median home price of just $250,000.
The rural Northern California county was the cheapest market tracked by the California Association of Realtors’July 2026 Home Sales and Price Report, with its median price clocking in at exactly $250,000 in July.
That makes the wooded enclave, tucked between Redding and the North Coast, one of the last places in the notoriously expensive Golden State where roughly a quarter of a million dollars can get you a typical home.
The prices are moving in favor of the buyer, dropping a whopping 29.1% from the previous month, when it hovered at $352,480, according to the report. Compared to a year earlier though, the mean was up about 4%, from $240,500 in July 2025. The dramatic monthly swings may be common in smaller counties like Trinity, with the report cautioning that “many of the outsized gains and losses were likely driven by low transaction volumes, rather than broad changes in underlying market conditions.”
Those prices look like bargains stacked against the statewide median of $887,680, which actually fell 1.9% from $904,640 in June.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, the median home price in July sits above $1.2 million, while in theLos Angeles Metro Area, homes carried a median price of $849,450. In Trinity County, that same amount of cash could get you between three and five homes.
The tradeoff for a bargain home seems to be remoteness. Home to the Gold Rush town of Weaverville, Trinity is a world away from California’s coastal cities, and is characterized by mountains and wilderness. Unsold inventory spent a median of 118 days on the market on July, which ballooned from 43.5 days in June.
For house hunters priced out in other parts of the state, Trinity may just be the last affordable refuge that also gives buyers the luxury of time when shopping around.
