hed: A $16.9M listing for rare Old Hollywood mansion is exposing a bitter family feud — pitting dead brother against dead brother
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about a grave injustice.
One of Old Hollywood’s last stately mansions, connected to deceased real estate investor Paris Nourafchan, is on the market for $16.9 million — all while his name remains embroiled in a vitriolic legal dispute involving his also-deceased brother, Richard.
As the case involving Richard’s death rattles through California Superior Court, accusations of forgery, fraud, elder abuse and a bat mitzvah that allegedly went off the rails are flying.
The suit does not name this listed Holmby Hills home at 1196 Brooklawn Dr. or the legal entity that owns it — but the legal tussles between Paris and his nephew, Nicholas Rahban, over alleged actions by Richard on his deathbed could cast a pall over the mansion’s sale.
Both Paris and Rahban are claiming the right to Richard’s holdings after separate visits just days, if not hours, before the dying 78-year-old man lapsed into a coma from which he never emerged. He died in 2024.
Paris and Rahban both say they came away from their visits with valid will and trust documents that made them the stewards of Richard’s estate.
Rahban filed the suit against Paris individually and as the trustee of Richard’s assets before Paris passed away last year, and the battle continues in his Paris’s name. Paris, in his own legal action, has contested Rahban’s probate petition.
Both sides have presented wills and trusts to the court that they say are legit, while accusing each other of using unsavory tactics to get the documents. These include allegedly faking the fading Richard’s signature and strongarming him.
Rahban got his authorization after pulling a make-a-will kit from an online site and photoshopping his uncle’s name and initials on it, Paris’s papers claim.
Rahban, for his part, contends that his uncle Richard loathed his brother, alleging that Richard refused to join Paris and their other brother George for a candle-lighting ceremony during a grandniece’s bat mitzvah, and yelled to the rest of the family, “I’m not getting on the stage with those crooks.”
Both men have denied the other’s claims and say in court papers their close relationship with Richard compelled him to leave them his assets.
Paris suggests Rahban is the family’s black sheep and an opportunist, noting in court papers that he has not been successful in business endeavors and claims Richard wanted his estate to be divvied up by giving Paris and George each a third and the rest to go to other relatives — while Rahban “is desperate to obtain the entirety of Richard’s wealth.” The three brothers had been in business together.
Rahban wants the court to award him double the “at least some tens of millions of dollars” he says the estate is worth, and wants the extra amount to come from Paris personally. Rahban’s suit bases his request on the assets’ own value and penalties through a California statute involving elder abuse Paris allegedly committed by bullying Richard into signing. Or, Paris forged his brother’s signature, Rahban’s suit says.
Rahban has a lot at stake, with his inheritance going from 100% to around 8% if his uncle’s lawsuit prevails, according to his filings.
Rahban did not return calls requesting comments about the suit.
Paris’s son Marc Nourafchan, who is one of his heirs, told The Post the mansion “is in no way” connected to the suit, although word about the family fracas could put “a cloud” over its sale.
Estate planning attorney Nicole Israel, who is not involved in the case, pointed out that “when someone in a probate case is named individually,” as Paris was, it can “open the door to their assets being laid claim to by the plaintiff.”
Another estate planning attorney, Craig Redler, who is also not involved with the suit, agreed, though neither would comment on the specifics of this case. Marc added that the home has seen a lot of foot traffic since his decision last month to cut $2 million from the $18.9 million he listed the mansion for in the spring.
The parties are due back in court in January.
Meanwhile, Marc continues his efforts to sell the 6,477-square-foot Holmby Hills mansion, known as Villa d’Este, and its separate onsite 4,000-square-foot theater, both of which were built in 1929 as magnificent examples of Old Hollywood flare.
The five-bedroom Spanish Colonial home and its 1.6-acre grounds “are spectacular, with the kind of Hollywood glamour that doesn’t exist anymore,” said Drew Meyers of Westside Estate Agency, who shares the listing with colleague Kurt Rappaport.
The artisans of the home’s intricately hand-carved living room ceiling replicated the one they created for publisher William Randolph Hearst’s architecturally awarded San Simeon estate.
Stevie Nicks was into the vibe and rented the estate in the 1980s. Clint Eastwood chose the huge theater for a key scene in his film, “Firefox,” Marc Nouafchan said. Eastwood, as director, turned the theater into a pyrotechnics-filled airplane hangar which he, playing elite pilot Michael Gant, tries to fly out while a MiG-3 next to him is exploding, and electrical systems and fuel lines are erupting in flames.
The home had a much more sedate beginning, commissioned by Fox Film Corp. production chief Winfield Sheehan while he was successfully steering the studio from silent films to talkies.
Under Sheehan’s stewardship, Fox Film launched the word vamp into the vernacular through its film “A Fool There Was,” with Theda Barra playing a no-holds-barred seductress. The studio’s “Regeneration” was the first full-length film about gangsters.
Later on, the estate was a busy hub for celebrity social gatherings, with guests ranging from Shirley Temple to John Wayne, who shared the same stature in their Hollywood heydays. Neighbors included Walt Disney, Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Becall, Clark Gable and Carole Lombard, and Frank Sinatra. The Playboy mansion was minutes away by car.
Architect Burton Schutt designed the mansion around the same time he was working on the nearby Bel-Air hotel.

hed: A Maine town, once dependent on a paper mill, tries to move on
content: The state of Maine is about 89 percent forest and has an $8.3 billion forestry industry. Besides logging, papermaking has always been a large part of that. At the industry’s height, there were 35 paper mills in the state. Today, there are six.The paper mill in Madison, a rugged town of about 4,700 residents where it’s not uncommon to see trucks stacked with logs coming and going, shut down in 2016. For over a century, the mill, home to Madison Paper Industries, had been responsible for a majority of the town’s good-paying jobs with benefits. Even as the company was being revalued in 2013, partly because of the decline in paper sales, the mill still made up 46 percent of the town’s tax base.When it closed, no one was surprised. The newspaper industry had been declining for years, and Madison Paper Industries, makers of the glossy paper used by The New York Times for inserts, struggled too.“The handwriting was on the wall, so it wasn’t a shock,” said Rick Veinotte, who had worked for 25 years at Madison Paper, which was owned by a joint venture of UPM-Kymmene and Northern SC Paper, a subsidiary of the Times.“But it was sad for the more than 200 employees who would be out of work,” Veinotte added. “And it was devastating to the town.”A decade later, Madison is still trying to figure out what it is without the paper mill, another example of a small town dependent on a shrinking industry that’s had a rough go of moving on. And the mill’s new owner has struggled to revive manufacturing in the town, a sign of just how hard it is to make things on a large scale in the United States when manufacturing jobs across all industries have been scarce.TimberHP acquired the defunct paper mill in 2019. Matt O’Malia, an architect, and Joshua Henry, a chemist, paid $2.3 million to buy the 600,000-square-foot plant and refurbish it into one making wood fiber insulation panels from wood chips and other wood waste.Workers monitor the company's production inside the TimberHP facility in Madison, Maine.RYAN DAVID BROWN/NYTThe move seemed like a win for both the community, which got a new employer and big taxpayer, and TimberHP, which got the wood from Maine’s forestry industry and had access to seasoned manufacturing workers.Wood fiber insulation, a product that is made in Europe but had not been produced in the United States until TimberHP came along, could also address America’s much-needed housing construction and sustainable building efforts, the company said.The founders said they wanted to help revitalize Madison. Both grew up in working-class towns — O’Malia in Belfast, Maine, and Henry in Pittsburgh — and they wanted to replace  the lost paper mill jobs.But seven years later, keeping the doors open at TimberHP hasn’t been easy. The pandemic snarled supply chains, delaying deliveries on things the company needed to refurbish the mill, such as copper and transformers. A few years later, soaring inflation and construction delays stemming from those disruptions slowed the development of TimberHP’s production lines — enabling the company to make only two products instead of the three originally planned.And, broadly, the difficulty of keeping the plant alive and saving even a fraction of the jobs it once supported highlights the hurdles to a manufacturing revival that policymakers from the local level to the White House say they want to encourage.The founders tried to sell TimberHP without success. Burdened by debt and running out of cash, the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2025. Its CEO, Henry, left abruptly last fall. He told the Times he was legally “really not allowed to talk about why I left.”TimberHP’s challenges were mostly related to money. Despite raising $122 million in two fundraising rounds and also receiving $3 million in grants from the state, it wasn’t enough to weather the storms the pandemic had set off.Venture capital funding wasn’t an option because those investors were used to making returns that were orders of magnitude more than their investments in technology companies and other fast-growing firms. Manufacturing wasn’t that.“Venture wants these really outsized returns,” said O’Malia, now the company’s CEO.The company was running out of cash, O’Malia said. It took more than a year to get out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, pay back investors and start producing the wood fiber boards.“Chapter 11’s not cheap,” O’Malia said, referring to legal fees and exit financing while still having to remain operational.In 2025, TimberHP paid about $196,895 in taxes to the town of Madison. It was something, but it was still “a far cry from the $3.7 million Madison Paper Industries paid in 2013,” said Tim Curtis, Madison’s former town manager.In November, TimberHP announced it was out of bankruptcy. Since then, the company and the town have started to find their footing. The company has about 80 employees, about half its original goal.An exterior view of the TimberHP facility in Madison, Maine.RYAN DAVID BROWN/NYTTimberHP is also finding some success. Its products are being used on a multifamily project by Avesta Housing, a Maine-based affordable-housing provider; Amazon is using its products in an Elkhart, Indiana, delivery station, as is Meta for its Richland Parish Data Center in Louisiana; and D.R. Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder, is using TimberHP’s insulation on town houses in the mid-Atlantic.The company also is being supported by investments from FTAI Infrastructure, a clean energy investor, and other investors and finance partners including BlackRock and the Finance Authority of Maine.Even as the town’s manufacturing future seems hopeful for now, Madison is still coping with losing an industry that had been the lifeblood of the town. People still speak of the mill’s loss as if it had been the passing of a living being. “I’m not a real emotional person, but I could have just stood there and cried,” Veinotte said about its closing.Denise Ducharme, the town’s manager who has lived in Madison since 1983, calls it “the kind of community where you can’t sneeze without a neighbor knowing.”“For so long, our community’s identity was tied to being a paper mill town,” she said. “We had to figure out who we were without a paper mill — who we wanted to be — sort of an identity crisis.”This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

hed: On 13 acres, ultramodern Manchester-by-the-Sea house lists for $6.9m
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Set at the top of an isolated wooded hill, surrounded by 12.8 acres of land in the picturesque North Shore town of Manchester-by-the-Sea, a dramatic modern house is for sale. It has total privacy with wide ranging views of marshes, inlets, and the ocean, and notable contemporary architecture.
The five-bedroom, five-bathroom house’s 4,925 square feet are encased in metal, clapboard, and glass. Built in 2006, the house at370 Summer St.was designed by architect Marcus Gleysteen ofConnecticut-based MGA. It expresses modernism with projecting wings, contrasting siding materials, a steel and glass curtain wall shaded by a trapezoidal canopy, arching rooflines, angled support beams, and irregular decks. There are no right angles: the house is a livable contemporary sculpture.
In a town of handsome historic buildings, this ultramodern structure is unique. It’s on the market for $6,900,000.
A long private drive rises 150 feet to the site, which commands sweeping views of Kettle Cove and Crow Island. A large glass entry door leads to the interior. Individual elements include maple live-edge stairs, bubinga paneling, and enormous pieces of local granite that serve as room dividers and framing for a stainless-steel freestanding fireplace under a 23-foot high living room ceiling. Just as the exterior, the interior expresses modernism with a mixture of materials, colors, and shapes, all flooded with natural light. Lena Fransioli ofZoe Designcontributed detailed wall and ceiling coverings. None of the rooms are simple boxes.
The large chef’s kitchen is equipped with high-end stainless-steel appliances, a large island, stone countertops, and custom-built cabinets. The dining room has a private deck and separate exterior access. There is a family room as well as a living room that could also function as a home office. The bathrooms are outfitted with stone and ceramic tile, each en-suite to one of the five bedrooms located on three levels.
In the garage, there are two parking spaces; the surrounding area provides room for another 25 vehicles. Patios, decks, and porches make for indoor-outdoor living, and there is a hot tub. The property’s 12.79 acres abut Hooper Trask Conservation Pasture, which provides another 2,000+ acres of protected land complete with wildlife and hiking trails.
Manchester-by-the-Sea, roughly 30 miles north of Boston, is a scenic community famous for its rocky coastline, historic architecture, a picturesque downtown, a yachting harbor, and the popularSinging Beach. Knowledgeable Bostonians ride the commuter rail from North Station to the train station in the center of Manchester-by-the-Sea, and walk to Singing Beach from there. In fact, the town is small enough to be walkable in every way — the shops of the downtown and the beaches are within walking distance of this house.
Amanda Armstrong of Compass has the listing.
Regina Cole writes about architecture and design for national and regional publications, with a specialty in historic architecture and the history of the decorative arts.

hed: Inside the lavish NYC penthouse that Dolly Parton shared with her former manager: ‘He’s gay … We were like Will and Grace’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Dolly Parton may have been country to her core, but for a glittering stretch of her rise to stardom, the Tennessee songbird brought a little bit of the Smoky Mountains to Fifth Avenue.
Her unlikely Manhattan roommate? Her gay manager and close confidant Sandy Gallin — the powerhouse talent manager who also represented Michael Jackson and Cher — a living arrangement Parton later summed up perfectly.
“He’s gay — he had one end of the house and I had the other,” Parton toldthe New Yorkerin 2009. “We were like Will and Grace.”
Though in Parton and Gallin’s version, “Will” apparently did the decorating.
For years, Parton and Gallin shared a Fifth Avenue pied-à-terre, a Manhattan home base that neither occupied full time.Vanity Fairwas still describing it as the Fifth Avenue apartment the pair shared when the magazine interviewed Parton there in 1996.
The apartment was reportedly at 800 Fifth Ave., a luxury rental tower overlooking Central Park at East 61st Street, where no units are presently available, according to StreetEasy.
And despite Parton’s rhinestone-studded, larger-than-life aesthetic, the place was far more Sandy than Dolly.
“Everything you see is Sandy’s taste,” Parton toldthe New York Timesduring a 1979 visit to what the newspaper described as her New York “office-apartment.”
Parton said she had personally chosen only “the bed and the piano.”
Gallin furnished the place and assembled its contemporary art collection, introducing the self-described country girl to a decidedly more highbrow Manhattan aesthetic.
“What little dab of culture I have is because of Sandy,” Parton later told Vanity Fair, describing the two of them as “burlap and satin, Tennessee and Manhattan!”
The aerie even appeared in a 1980 episode of CBS’ “Country People,” which showed the typical trappings of luxury decorations from that era — among them round glass tables, maximal floral wallpaper and a massive cushioned headboard for her bed that made a true statement.
The apartment was more than a glamorous crash pad.
Parton and Gallin used it as a hybrid home and workplace where she could conduct business, make music and entertain industry friends without the formality of a traditional office.
Most of its wall space was even covered in sound-absorbing fabric, according to the Times.
There was just one problem: It apparently wasn’t enough to contain Dolly.
“We play music too loud and we’ll probably get thrown out that window,” Parton predicted to the Times while working on a new album.
Parton said she respected the neighbors, but sometimes forgot about them after cranking up a track and contemplating whether it needed horns or strings.
Then, as she put it, she would suddenly remember that “the neighbors don’t particularly want horns.”
The shared pad also came with one amenity that made the Tennessee native feel a little more at home: Central Park.
From high above Fifth Avenue, Parton could look out over its sprawling greenery — a little patch of country in the middle of Manhattan. After all, she grew up ina humble two-room cabinin the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee — a tiny home that still stands, and which she shared with her parents and 11 siblings.
800 Fifth Ave. is a towering structure with 208 units, perStreetEasy.
Completed in 1979, the building sits directly across from Central Park and just blocks from the Plaza Hotel. It remains a rental nearly five decades later — though living at Dolly’s alleged old address doesn’t come cheap.
Recent listings include a 1,475-square-foot two-bedroom that last asked $16,000 a month before going off the market in August 2025. A 1,025-square-foot one-bedroom asked $10,000, while a sprawling 2,040-square-foot three-bedroom sought $22,500 a month.
Parton’s road to a Fifth Avenue address had started considerably less glamorously.
She first came to New York in 1964 on a senior-class trip from Sevier County High School, according to the New Yorker. It was her first stay in a hotel — and included her first, and apparently only, subway ride.
A return trip with her best friend Judy Ogle in 1970 went even worse.
The pair stayed near the then-seedy 42nd Street and quickly discovered their flamboyant clothes attracted plenty of attention.
“We were overdressed — lookin’ like I do now, we did look like trash, and so we looked the part,” Parton recalled to the New Yorker.
After one man pushed her against a wall — prompting Parton, who was carrying a gun, to threaten to shoot him if he touched her again — she and Ogle headed for the airport.
“We just went to the airport,” Parton said. “We swore we’d never come back to New York.”
That vow clearly didn’t stick.
By the end of the decade, Parton had gone from fleeing 42nd Street to looking down on Central Park from her Fifth Avenue digs.
Her roommate era with Gallin lasted for years. The 1996 Vanity Fair profile found Parton sitting in the living room of the Fifth Avenue apartment they shared, while Gallin’s2017 obituaryin the magazine described the apartment as his only longstanding residence.
And even after the pair’s real-life “Will and Grace” arrangement ended, Parton kept her own foothold in the Big Apple.
By 2009, she told the New Yorker she had an apartment of her own on York Avenue.
There was just one problem with her Manhattan perch.
“It’s on a high floor, and I get a little leery,” she admitted.
Despite having her own place in Manhattan, Parton sometimes preferred sleeping across the Hudson River on her tour bus parked in Newark, she told the magazine.
Naturally, this was no ordinary bus: It came equipped with a mirrored wig closet and a refrigerator stocked with homemade meatloaf and mashed potatoes.
Only Dolly could have a home high above Manhattan — and sometimes decide she’d rather sleep in New Jersey.

hed: Inside the 2-room cabin where Dolly Parton grew up — a humble home she recreated for Dollywood
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Dolly Parton embraced her roots throughouther 80-year life— and that includes the Tennessee cabin where her storied journey began.
The country legend’s originswere as humbleas her childhood home — a two-room cabin in Locust Ridge in the Great Smoky Mountains, located outside of Sevierville in east Tennessee. It’s the small residence she shared with her parents and 11 siblings.
The cabin had a kitchen and a single bedroom, andno electricity or running water. For nighttime visibility, the family caught fireflies in jars and placed them throughout to illuminate the interior.
The home still stands, though it’s closed to the public. But during Parton’s upbringing, it had a kitchen with a table for six, a washing basin between the kitchen and the bedroom — and just a partial wall separating it all.
Parton was proud of this home, so much so that she had it recreated forher Dollywood theme parkin Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Parton’s brother Bobby handled the design, while Parton’s mother, Avie Lee, offered her stamp of approval.
“These mountains and my childhood home have a special place in my heart,” reads a sign just outside of the replica. “They inspire my music and my life. I hope being here does the same for you!”
The Dollywood cabin lets visitors see what Smoky Mountain life was like for the family in the 1940s and 1950s.
Images of the bedroom show several beds, and even a baby’s crib, standing side by side.
Meanwhile, the kitchen has a vibrant floral wallpaper, curtains on the windows, cast-iron skillets hanging from hooks and a standalone stove for heating. The eating space is wallpapered with newspaper clippings, while a table is topped with a gas lamp.
Despite the crippling poverty in which the family lived, the replica shows a cozy reality — giving a glimpse into the happy family who resided inside.

hed: J. Paul Getty’s grandson William Paul Getty scoops up $20M Dallas mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
William Paul Getty, the grandson of oil magnate J. Paul Getty, and his wife Vanessa have scooped up a nearly $20 million Dallas mansion as thebillionaire heirsets his sights on expanding his business interests in Texas.
The couple purchased the sprawling Crescent Avenue estate in ritzy Highland Park in June, according to deed records reported byThe Real Deal— adding another trophy property to the Getty family’s impressive real estate portfolio.
But the move doesn’t mean the couple is giving up its West Coast roots.
“Mr. Getty is in the process of opening an office in Dallas. Billy and Vanessa have spent and plan to continue to spend a great deal of time there. Billy has been looking to further expand his portfolio and is excited about the business opportunities in Texas,” a spokesperson for the Gettys told the California Post.
The timing of the move is interesting, considering so many ultra-wealthyCalifornians are leavingthe state as the possibility of thebillionaire tax looms. However, the couple still has a home in the Golden State.
“The Gettys have not sold either their San Francisco or Hawaii properties,” the spokesperson added.
William Getty — also known as Billy — is the son of Gordon Getty. California Governor Gavin Newsom grew up among the four sons of Gordon.
Newsomclaimed in his memoirthat his friendship with Billy collapsed over Billy’s resentment of Newsom’s close financial and personal ties to Gordon, who ultimately sided with Newsom.
Their new 11,400-square-foot spread, which was most recently listed for just under $20 million, sits on a half-acre in Highland Park and comes with seven bedrooms and nine-and-a-half bathrooms, per the outlet.

hed: Faneuil Hall managers sue tenants over more than $2 million in alleged unpaid rent
content: This story was published originally on boston.com.Managers of Faneuil Hall Marketplace have sued seven current or former tenants over more than $2 million in alleged unpaid rent and other fees, adding another challenge for the historic marketplace as it struggles to fill vacant storefronts.The lawsuits were filed in Suffolk Superior Court between July 2024 and July 2026. Most of the businesses named in the cases have since left Faneuil Hall, leaving the marketplace with a growing number of empty spaces.J. Safra Real Estate took over management of Faneuil Hall at the beginning of 2024. Since then, the company has filed lawsuits against tenants including FoMu, Lovepop, Ghirardelli Chocolate, Boston Halal, Popular Properties Realty, Imagine Exhibitions, and Boston Sugar Factory, which is the only named business still operating at the marketplace.The cases vary, but the lawsuits generally allege that the businesses failed to pay rent or other fees required under their leases.The case against Lovepop, which allegedly owed more than $165,000, was dismissed in April.J. Safra Management said that it does not comment on litigation filings.Popular Properties Realty, which J. Safra alleges owes more than $366,000, disputed the claims and said it left its space because of problems with the property.In its response to the lawsuit, the real estate company said loud music from a retail business beneath its office interfered with client meetings. It also cited ongoing construction, large gatherings in an outdoor space, mice and other rodents, and accessibility problems with the building.The company denied breaching its lease and said that after it left, it believed the managers were able to find a replacement tenant.FoMu founder Deena Jalal told the Boston Business Journal, which first reported on the lawsuits, that the ice cream company stayed current on its rent during its three-and-a-half years at Quincy Market.Jalal said the only rent FoMu did not pay was money the company believed was covered by an agreement with the previous landlord. She said the agreement was related to unexpected demolition costs stemming from a severe pest infestation and damage to the building.Other tenants named in the lawsuits did not respond to requests for comment.In response, J. Safra Real Estate said that it is investing in a multiphase improvement plan led by Boston-based firm Commodore Builders.Phase one was completed this summer and focused on maintenance and repairs such as resetting granite pavers, cleaning the exterior of buildings and glass sheds, and other physical repairs to the site.The legal disputes come as Faneuil Hall Marketplace continues to search for a new identity and fill empty storefronts.In March, Mayor Michelle Wu convened a two-day workshop with city officials, outside experts, and Harvard professors to brainstorm ways to reimagine the historic marketplace and make it more appealing to visitors and businesses.The city did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked whether additional meetings or plans are in the works.The marketplace’s struggles have prompted calls for a change in direction. As one business owner previously put it, Faneuil Hall “needs a shot of adrenaline.”However, the firm said that it is in the process of bringing in more tenants, pointing to the recently opened Tree House Brewing Company at Quincy Market, to other local businesses including Smashed by BRED, The Maharaja, Azul Mexican Kitchen, Mona Sweets, and more.“We look forward to sharing more updates on the progress of the Marketplace’s evolution to ensure it continues to be welcoming, best-in-class gathering place for residents and visitors alike,” a spokesperson for J. Safra Management said.

hed: Moving in Boston is hard. Gen Z will turn to anything — even Facebook.
subhead: Young people are using the social network not to keep up with friends, but as a utility to combat Sept. 1 moving day competition
content:
ByDaisy Levine
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

The film “Single White Female” scared generations of prospective roommates from putting a want ad in the paper. But desperate for a Sept. 1 lease, Gen Z is feeling safe on their parents’ social network — Facebook.

Move-in day will never not be chaotic. But in a college hub like Boston, everyone’s day of stress is the same day, which is not typical of all other cities. Tens of thousands of leases start and end on the same day. The turmoil of Sept. 1 — the day of 70 percent of Boston-area apartments’ turnover,the city told Boston 25 News— datesback to 1899. It not only makes it difficult to find a U-Haul, but also turns move-in day into a competition.

It’s a big problem for Gen Z, which ranges in age from 14 to 29. It’s college, the job market, the housing crisis, and inflation all wrapped up into one. They often can’t live with their friends (because it seems like the universe only doles out one to two job offers per friend group), they can’t afford to buy brand new furniture, and they’re deciding whether enough people in TikTok comments can tell them if a particular realty group is a scam.

Their answer to finding real people and real advice? It’s Facebook, their parents’ favorite app. The social media site has turned a corner on Gen Z as a utility — less so to keep in touch with people, but often as a lifeline during the torturous housing process, especially in Boston.

A network where the user doesn’t usually hide behind a screen name, as on Instagram, Reddit, TikTok, or Snapchat, Facebook groups and Marketplace are a saving grace for people relocating in the Boston area.

Betches of Boston HOUSINGis a private Facebook group with more than 40,000 members. Most of the group’s activity comes from young women looking to join existing leases or find potential roommates with similar interests.


“Real people can connect with other real people that are verified,” said Gabby Hanley, a Boston-based real estate broker and moderator in the group. “A lot of the people are posting there and saying, ‘Hey, I’m moving from Kansas. I want to live with another girl that will become friends with me.’”

Hanley said Betches screens both prospective tenants and real estate professionals. She said members need profile pictures, and Hanley cross-references brokers’ license numbers. She also said the moderators and members are diligent about reporting spam.

“People feel a little bit safer [in Betches] because we do such a good job,” she said. “We do actually monitor and make sure that people are who they say they are.”

She doesn’t get paid for this, but she hopes the people who ask her questions may become her clients. She wants to help young people understand real estate.

She said she sees a lot of, “Hey, is this allowed?” when a broker may be taking advantage of them.

“A lot of people don’t trust real estate professionals,” Hanley said. “They want another female to say what’s a great neighborhood for me to move into, stuff like that.”

Aryan Singh moved in with strangers at 20 years old. He needed a place on Mission Hill. So did practically every other off-campus hopeful at Northeastern University (the neighborhood had become an extremely popular off-campus housing hub at his school).

But his new roommates didn’t feel like strangers because his mom found them on the Northeastern parents’ Facebook group. Another mom had posted that her son was looking for a fourth roommate. Singh ended up living with this group for two years until graduation, and they all became friends.

He never thought to use Facebook. He said he didn’t even have an account until his junior year of college, and he now uses it exclusively for housing groups and to find cheap furniture on Marketplace.

“I think I share a thought with a lot of Gen Z that Facebook is this app for older people,” he said. But a lot more people he knows use it religiously around Sept. 1.

“The fact that everyone moves on the same day is the dumbest thing ever,” he said. “I don’t know who set it up like that … No matter what neighborhood you’re in, it’s just absolute chaos.”

Elizabeth Scholl, 23, didn’t have a Facebook profile until she made one for move-in season.

Many people post their initial query in a Facebook group, she said, but encourage respondents to contact them outside of Facebook Messenger, often through a more popular site for their age group: Instagram.

Scholl would not feel comfortable meeting roommates on any other social media site, since Facebook is the only one that seems to verify names, she said.


“They’re sharing their Instagrams, they’re sharing their numbers, they’re posting photos of themselves,” she said. “It was really easy to see who these people were, and basically it’s like, ‘You look pretty normal and cool.’ And I think that is what makes that platform [work].”

Another big draw is Facebook Marketplace, where college students can find used, cheap furniture.

Talia Lubie, 21, recently bought a desk on Facebook.

“I’ve never had to buy any furniture, and I figured there’s no way I’d be able to furnish my whole apartment and not break the bank,” she said. “I thought [Marketplace] would not just be good for the environment, but good for my wallet.”

Getting to the closest IKEA on Aug. 31 would likely be a waste of time, since, she assumed, everything would probably be bought out by then.

Madeline Andrews, 22, said it was a culture shock, cost-wise, moving to Boston from rural North Carolina a month ago. She said her brother told her about the advantages of Marketplace, since he’s lived in Boston for three years. He told her it was his lifeline for all things moving, from the couch he bought to finding a mover.

“My money needs to go to keeping the lights on,” she said. “[Marketplace] feels like the cheat sheet.”

Kahan described Boston as a transient city, which means regular furniture turnaround on Marketplace. Their current home is also made up of almost entirely Marketplace finds, as well as the results of Kahan’s annual celebrations ofAllston Christmas, Boston’s unofficial Sept. 1 yard sale.

Kahan also found their first housing situation on Facebook.

“Craigslist feels scary. No one is verified,” they said. “I think having the name verification on Facebook … you can see maybe they share the same political beliefs or they’re a real person and not a bot.”

They searched in one of the LGBTQIA+ housing groups, with their biggest priority being feeling safe and comfortable in a gender-affirming space.

“Folks utilize these groups because they’re trying to find their people,” they said.

hed: Ask the Gardener: Rethinking weeds — which to pluck and which to admire
subhead: Too often we reach for poison with a false notion that we can kill weeds forever and not have to deal with them. How can deeper knowledge help us create better strategies to manage them?
content:
ByUlrich Lorimer
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

“What is a weed? A plant whose virtues have never been discovered,” quipped Ralph Waldo Emerson in his 1878 essay,“The Fortune of the Republic.”

We may not all take such a transcendental view on unwelcome guests, yet weeds, as a broad category, can tell us much about our gardens. They can forecast soil conditions, tell us how we maintain our plots, and reveal clues about the soil seed bank and wildlife dispersal patterns. Some are unsung ecological heroes, while others can cause harm and reduce biodiversity. Their growth patterns vary from annuals to biennials and perennials. Some are vines, others shrubs or trees. All have unique stories to tell of their relationships with humans or how they arrived on these shores. Above all, they are living organisms that command respect for their tenacity, persistence, and tolerance, their prodigious growth, and ability to appear almost out of nowhere.

Too often we reach for poison with a false notion that we can kill them forever and not have to deal with them. How can deeper knowledge of weeds help us create better strategies to manage them, ideally without chemicals or herbicides? The aim of this week’s column is to group weeds into categories: ruderals, annuals, biennials, woodies, and ecologically harmful plants — each corresponding to a different management strategy. When is cutting seedheads effective, and when is using herbicide the best option after exhausting all other techniques?

The well-tended vegetable garden I left at the beginning of my family vacation in early August was not the garden I returned to two weeks later. Abundant sunshine, rampant animal dispersal, and rainfall all conspired to create an explosion of growth. Not only were my cherry tomatoes loaded with fruit, but I discovered bittersweet vines along the deer fence, nut sedge in the pathways, and lambsquarters, amaranth, and wood sorrel mingling with my raspberries. In the planting beds, horseweed, foxtail grass, fireweed, and smartweed were crowding my perennial plantings. Spotted spurge, violets, and crabgrass were pushing through the cracks in the pavers. Where do I get started?

First, let us connect disturbance with the soil seed bank. Every time I pull a weed, the soil is disturbed, and new dormant seeds are brought to the surface. This does not mean that pulling weeds is a bad idea, just that managing the seed bank can help reduce weed pressure in the future. Ruderal is a term for plants that grow in waste areas or recently disturbed landscapes, like after a new road is built or a new home is constructed. Not always, but frequently, they are annuals, which means cutting their flowers or seed heads off before they disperse results in less seed getting into the seed bank and therefore fewer weeds in future years. Horseweed and fireweed (so named as it appears quickly after wildfires) are both annuals, so cutting them is all I have to do. Similar weeds include the foxtail grasses, the smartweeds, lambsquarters, and amaranths. I cut as close to the ground as possible. They may resprout, but cutting repeatedly saps their energy reserves.


But not all annuals are weeds. Some provide important resources for pollinators like fleabanes, Black-eyed Susans, partridge pea, wild flax, or rabbit tobacco. By their nature, these annuals need some disturbance to continue to seed into the garden. They may be abundant one year and scarce the next. If they ever become out of balance with other plantings, simply cut half before the seed can disperse.

Cutting perennial weeds can result in less seed, but because they can overwinter, you will need to be vigilant and consistent with cutting. Nut sedge produces small underground nutlets that break away when you pull the plant out of the ground. Nutsedge prefers compacted and poorly drained wet soils, so improving drainage will help reduce its spread. Pulling the plants early in the season before the nutlets have formed is also effective. It is also known as chufa, or tiger nut, and is cultivated in Asia for the sweet, almond-like flavor of the nutlets.

Lastly, woody plants and vines like bittersweet, honeysuckle, or buckthorn can be challenges. If the bittersweet is small, I still hand-pull, looking for the bright orange roots as evidence I removed the whole vine. Once thicker in girth, pulling or repeated cutting becomes less effective. For especially thick vines, I recommend the cut-and-paint method: cut the stem and immediately apply a judicious, targeted dose of herbicide to the stump. This method works for honeysuckle, buckthorn, and even the dreaded Japanese knotweed. Repeat applications may be necessary, as these plants are tough! Bittersweet, buckthorn, and honeysuckle get around thanks to birds. It is a cruel cycle that causes further ecological harm. Adding native fruit-bearing shrubs like dogwoods, viburnums, winterberries, or elderberries ensures birds have choices and helps spread these natives, too.

Keeping up with weeds is challenging, even for professional gardeners. You have to admire them for continually coming back — their drive to survive is fierce. While New England is not the tropics, the amount of life our gardens can support, desired and undesired, is staggering. Even when I feel overwhelmed, I remember that weeds are a human construct, and by shifting how we see them, they can lead us to appreciate their abundance.

The book “Weeds of the Northeast” is a comprehensive and indispensable guide to learn more about potentially problematic plants in your garden. TheUMass Weed Herbariumis another online tool for identification and info on life cycle.

Ulrich Lorimer is the director of horticulture at the Native Plant Trust in Framingham. Send your gardening questions, along with your name/initials and hometown, to[email protected]g.

hed: Angelina Jolie’s $29.85M LA mansion may have a prospective buyer — Madonna
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Angelina Jolie’s glamorous California estate has caught the eye of Madonna, who may soon be back in the City of Angels, Gimme Shelter has learned.
The music superstar,who just celebrated her 68th birthday in Greece, expressed interest in viewing the“Couture”star’s Los Feliz estate even though she wasn’t in LA to see it in the flesh, Gimme Shelter can reveal exclusively.
Brokers, we hear, arranged for Madonna to tour the $29.85 million property by way of video.
“Madonna’s people called up and the tour was arranged,” a source said, adding that the neighborhood is a “wonderful colony in the upper Hollywood Hills with a lot of celebrity power.”
Co-listing brokers Ernie Carswell, of Sotheby’s International Realty and Jon Grauman of Resident Group, did not return calls at press time. Spokespersons for Madonna and Jolie also did not return calls.
While Madonna and Jolie don’t appear to have any kind of long-standing friendship, they are both iconic, independent, culture-defining talents who are each mothers to six children — a combination of biological and adopted kids.
Joliefirst listedthe property at 2000 De Mille Drive in May. It does not yet appear that she is looking to purchase anywhere else.
“I don’t think she knows” where she wants to be yet, a source said.
Brokers told Gimme Shelter they’re not surprised to hear that Madonna eyed the home. It’s been just over three years since shesold her Hidden Hills estate for $23 million— after buying it from Canadian R&B star the Weeknd for $19.3 million in 2021.
At the moment,Madonna’s properties includea triple-wide, 57-foot townhouse on East 81st Street on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. It’s a combination of three townhouses. She also owns a Georgian townhouse in London and a horse farm in Bridgehampton that was formerly owned by Kelly Klein, the model and ex-wife of fashion designerCalvin Klein— as well as a property in Portugal.
Jolie’s gated property is part of Hollywood history. It was owned by filmmaker Cecil B. DeMille and his family for more than half a century.
DeMille, who died in 1959 at the age of 77, was a film pioneer. “The Squaw Man,” which he made, was the first American feature film to ever be released and led, ultimately, DeMille co-founding what is now known as Paramount.
His films include grand epics, such as the 1953 Oscar winner, “The Greatest Show on Earth,” as well as “The Ten Commandments,” “The King of Kings,” “Samson and Delilah” and “Cleopatra.” He also appeared as himself in Billy Wilder’s “Sunset Boulevard,” where the famous last line — from Gloria Swanson’s character, Norma Desmond, looking straight into the camera — is: “Alright, Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my close-up.”Jolie, the property’s latest Oscar-winning steward, bought the estate in June 2017 for $24.5 million, around nine months after she filed for divorce from Brad Pitt. In an interview, Jolie said she would leave LA when her children were adults. Her youngest kids, twins Knox and Vivienne, turned 18 last month.
Celebrities love the neighborhood because “it’s quiet and inaccessible. There are no tour buses up there, and there’s a sneaky way to get down to Sunset without going through Laurel Canyon,” a broker said.
The estate is anchored by a Beaux Arts mansion with a white stucco exterior and a red tiled roof — all in an elegant and refined, minimalist style, and built in 1913. There’s also a pool, a pool house, and a guest house/studio, a tea house and a garage with a security gate, all on 2.1 acres surrounded by rolling lawns, century old trees — and views of the Hollywood Hills and the Griffith Observatory.
DeMille bought the home in 1916. In 1920, he expanded the estate by purchasing the property next door, which was once home to Charlie Chaplin. The two homes were then joined by a glass corridor, although they are now separate properties again. The DeMille family retained the property until the late 1980s, according to the listing.
A winding path leads to the dwelling, with stairs up to the front door, surrounded by stately columns. Inside the five-bedroom main house, there’s a chef’s kitchen, a formal mahogany-paneled dining room, a step-down large living room, arched windows and a library.
There’s also a primary bedroom suite with a marble fireplace, a sitting room, a spa-like bath, a dressing room and a closet, plus French doors that open to a terrace.
The estate is at the highest point inside Laughlin Park — a gated enclave of around 60 homes across De Mille Drive, Linwood Drive, Cummings Drive and Laughlin Park Drive.
There, past and current residents include Natalie Portman, Kristen Stewart, Brie Larson, Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard. During the golden age of Hollywood, the enclave’s residents also included Carole Lombard and Lily Pons.

hed: Yayoi Kusama wasn’t only displayed in museums — but also in other unexpected buildings across NYC
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese art icon whose hypnotic polka dots, whimsical pumpkins and dazzling “Infinity Mirror Rooms” made her a global sensation,died Aug. 14at a Tokyo hospital. She was 97.
But nearly 6,800 miles away, Kusama’s work lives on in some unexpected corners of New York City — where seeing it doesn’t require a museum ticket, an advance reservation or hours spent waiting in line.
One of the most striking examples is hiding in plain sight beneath Midtown Manhattan.
At Grand Central Madison, commuters pass every day by “A Message of Love, Directly from My Heart unto the Universe,” Kusama’s sprawling glass mosaiccommissionedfor the Long Island Rail Road terminal.
The permanent 2022 work sits along the Madison Concourse between East 46th and 47th streets, filling the passageway with bold colors, lines and fantastical forms. The work expands on Kusama’s “My Eternal Soul” series, which she began in 2009.
The MTA says the mosaic conveys themes of love, the universe and peace central to Kusama’s work — and that the artist hoped it would “bring joy” to people encountering it as they passed through the station.
On Thursday, just hours after news of Kusama’s death broke, The Post found commuters and visitors doing just that.
Sandrine Gold, a 51-year-old teacher from Port Washington, stopped and began snapping photos — without realizing she was looking at the work of one of the world’s most famous contemporary artists.
“I was just walking by in the subway and noticed this amazing art on the wall,” Gold told The Post. “I love how rich and inspiring the colors are.”
Gold, who teaches Spanish and French at the Long Island School for the Gifted and also leads an after-school art class, said the work immediately gave her ideas to take back to her students.
“The colors were really catching my attention and started to inspire me for my classes,” she said.
Her chance encounter captures something unusual about Kusama’s presence in New York: Some of her art can be stumbled upon entirely by accident.
That’s a sharp contrast with the frenzy surrounding Kusama’s blockbuster exhibitions.
Kusama’s “Infinity Mirror Rooms” became an international sensation, drawing huge crowds for the chance to step inside her mirrored, seemingly endless spaces.
Her 2013 David Zwirner exhibition in Chelsea featured “The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away,” one of the installations that helped propel her to an even wider popular audience.
But Kusama’s footprint in New York has extended beyond galleries and museums — and beyond Grand Central.
For years, one of her signature pumpkins also greeted residents at SKY, the massive 1,175-unit rental tower at 605 W. 42nd St.
The custom bronze “Pumpkin,” installed in 2016, sat in the building’s cobblestoned motor court, bringing Kusama’s unmistakable polka dots to the base of the glass-and-steel tower. The more than 2,600-pound sculpture is no longer at the property.
Kusama’s connection to New York stretches back nearly seven decades.
Born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, she moved to New York in 1958 and became part of the city’s avant-garde art scene, developing her “Infinity Net” paintings while experimenting with sculpture, performance and installations. She returned to Japan in the 1970s.
Decades later, her work would return to New York on a vastly different scale — filling galleries with crowds and commanding millions of dollars in the international art market.
But for New Yorkers like Gold, Kusama’s legacy can still appear much more unexpectedly — simply on the way to catch a train.

hed: How Floyd Mayweather landed a $100K/month NYC apartment in 1 day — before he allegedly stopped paying rent
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
When a grand apartment at the Baccarat Hotel & Residences caught the eye of boxing legendFloyd Mayweather Jr., he agreed to rent it for a year — for a hefty $100,000 a month. At the time, it wasMidtown’s most expensive rental, as Gimme Shelter reported exclusively.
There was just one condition: The deal had to be signed that very day, so Mayweather could move in that evening. It was just before Christmas in 2024.
Mayweather, the undefeated boxing champ who earned more than $1.1 billion over the years and became a real estate investor, is one of the best paid athletes of all time. But that hasn’t stopped Mayweather’s former landlords at the Baccarat, who are suing the boxing champ in New York State Supreme Court for breach of contract over allegations of unpaid rent.
Mayweather’s lawyer, Bobby Samini, declined Gimme Shelter’s request for comment.
In addition, Mayweather iscurrently facing a $7.27 million IRS lienfor unpaid federaltaxestied to 2018 and 2023, and in May,Mayweather sued his former investment advisor, Jona Rechnitz, and others for $175 million amid allegations of fraud, theft, and mismanagement of funds and assets including jewelry, a jet and real estate.
(Rechnitz denies wrongdoing. In a statement, his lawyer Morris Missry said Mayweather’s claims “are utterly baseless” and that Mayweather has “gambling issues, prolific spending habits, monies owed to third party creditors and IRS tax liens and levys [sic].”)
It appears Mayweather’s most recent financial disputes may have begun at the Baccarat home.
On the day that Mayweather decided he needed to rent the Baccarat residence, he was staying nearby atthe Plaza Hotel.
He had seen apromotional videoof the 18th-floor aerie starring reality TV’s Brooks Nader, of “Love Thy Nader.” The cast of “Emily in Paris” had also done a photo shoot there.
“He was in a big rush. Floyd was adamant that he needed the keys. He’s a very impulsive guy and decided he just had to have it right then,” said a source close to the deal.
Known as the Gemstone Terrace, the five-bedroom, 4,178-square-foot spread at 20 W. 53rd St. came with an eat-in chef’s kitchen, five marbled baths, two marbled powder rooms — and a pickleball court on its massive 3,100-square-foot terrace.
“It was a lot of work, but we made it happen,” Compass broker Brian K. Lewis, who at the time shared the Baccarat listing with Ryan Garson, also of Compass, told Gimme Shelter.
“Jona spearheaded the search,” Garson said. “He saw the apartment at 8:30 a.m. and said the deal was contingent on having Floyd move in that day. We negotiated all day using creative strategies to accelerate the approval process and move him in the same day.”
Added Lewis: “We did right by our clients, the owners of the apartment, and served our fiduciary responsibility. I’m proud of that.”
Mayweather arrived around 6 p.m. that evening, clad in Versace and carrying a Gucci duffle bag. He wrote a check to the owners for $200,000 — the first month’s rent and a security deposit — and he signed a separate agreement with a staging company for the furniture, the brokers said.
“He was dressed well and looking good. He was a really nice guy,” Lewis said.
“He moved right in then and there. The staff loved him. There were no complaints,” Garson added.
At the time, Mayweather even invited the brokers and the unit’s owners,Miami entrepreneurs and philanthropists David and Leila Centner, to his 48th birthday party, which was to be held two months later, in February, at the former Gianni Versace mansion in Miami. Mayweather allegedly said he owned it. (In fact, Mayweather had put down a $250,000 deposit to own a part of it, and hosted his birthday party there before declining to close on the deal, after which the deposit was returned,the Real Deal later reported.)Mayweather has not commented publicly on this deal.
Meanwhile at the Baccarat, everything was going fine with the rental for the first six months; rent was paid from December through June.
That’s when Mayweather allegedly stopped paying and broke the lease, said the brokers and their clients.
In a summons with noticefiled in Januaryin New York State Supreme Court, the Centners — through their two LLCs, Perpetual Love Investments LLC and Perpetual Love Condo LLC — claim that Mayweather signed a settlement agreement, which was submitted as an exhibit in the court documents, acknowledging $515,834.25 in unpaid rent and damages.
It also claims that Mayweather agreed to pay the amount in full and vacate the apartment by Dec. 2, 2026.But, the Centners allege, while Mayweather left the apartment, and made one single $100,000 payment, he never paid the full amount that he owed. Mayweather has not commented on the allegations and his lawyer did not return calls.
The summons also noted that the Centners sued Mayweather for $337,736.13 for breach of contract. In an interview with Gimme Shelter, Leila said she had hoped the issue would have been resolved without a lawsuit. That amount subtracts the $100,000 payment plus the $100,000 security deposit from the amount owed, Leila said.
“After [Leila Centner] spoke to him, [Mayweather] signed an agreement to take care of it [to pay what he owed]. He left the apartment, but he failed to make the payments that he had committed to,” said a source close to the rental deal.
Today, the apartment — which Mayweather had told the Centners that he wanted to buy, is being rented for $140,000 to another tenant, sources said. What’s more, it’s also in contract to sell, Gimme Shelter can reveal exclusively.
While the final price is not yet known, it was last asking $24.99 million with listing broker Rena Kliot of Pulse International Realty, who declined to comment.
Mayweather’s rental deal with the Centners was negotiated through Mayweather’s investment advisor Rechnitz, a former FBI informant who had once been a top campaign donor to Bill de Blasio — whocalled Rechnitz a “brother” in emails. That was before Rechnitz was accused of trying to bribe NYPD officials with hookers onprivate jets; he pleaded guilty in 2016 for his role in the so-calledNYPD corruption scandal.
Before Mayweather allegedly stopped paying rent, Garson said he ran into Mayweather and Rechnitz at a Lakers game in LA.
“I was randomly right behind Jona and Floyd. They were courtside and I was behind them. I went up to say hello and we talked about the apartment. Floyd said he really wanted to buy it. We talked about putting a pool on the terrace. It was amazing,” Garson told Gimme Shelter. “He also wanted to buy the apartment next door, which we had [as a so-called pocket, or whisper listing] off market, and combine the two using Robert A.M. Stern Architects.”
At first, the monthly rental checks stopped coming in because Mayweather said he would purchase the unit. The rent payments would supposedly be tied to a sale, said the brokers and other sources.
But as it became clear that Mayweather wasn’t going to buy the apartment, the Centners wanted him to pay the rent and damages they were owed. Although Mayweather moved out when he said he would, he never paid what he owed, and the Centners sued for breach of contract in New York State Court in January, according to the summons.
“We were the intermediaries. The owners came to us and we went to Jona. He was our contact. He said the money was coming but it never came,” Garson alleges.
“Floyd is really nice, friendly and hospitable, a great guy. But Jona was calling the shots. They were talking about buying the apartment and the one next door. There was no reason to believe it wouldn’t happen, but it was all hot air, and then the balloon deflated,” Garson said.
In an interview with Gimme Shelter, Leila said that when she ultimately reached Mayweather, he seemed genuinely surprised to hear that the rent payments had stopped.
“I think that may have tipped him off that something was wrong,” Leila told Gimme, alleging that Mayweather then made one payment, and thensimply stopped paying.
The case is ongoing.

hed: Zillow’s latest AI staging tool allows users to ‘redecorate’ potential homes
subhead: Could a computer-fabricated coffee table or sofa convince house hunters to place an offer?
content:
ByOlivia McKenley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Fluffed pillows and a potted plant might seem like trivial touches in the grand scheme of home buying, but industry professionals hope they help buyers envision life inside a listing.

Boston’s housing market hadover 12,000 active listingsin July, according to Zillow market research, and agents are going the extra mile to stand out.

In The National Association of Realtors2023 Profile on Home Stagingpublished by the Washington Post, over 80 percent of agents said that staging a property made it easier for a buyer to visualize it as a future home.

Now, buyers are enhancing aesthetics themselves before even setting foot inside a home using Zillow’s latest AI staging feature, which allows browsers to redecorate a home virtually in their preferred style.

Inside a listing withZillow’s Showcase package— a paid-for special listing with interactive photography, floor plans, and virtual tours — users can navigate to a virtual staging icon with a panel to try on different curated styles like “farmhouse,” “Scandinavian,” “mid-century,” “coastal,” and others. A combination of photography, computer vision, and generative AI redesigns the original room with decor from the specified style. A Showcase listing fee varies based on the property’s location and an agent’s purchasing arrangement.

Over his decade with Zillow, Vice President of AI Product Nicholas Stevens had repeatedly tried to implement AI-powered staging, and when generative AI and image models materialized, the prospect became “a huge opportunity.”

With Zillow’s acquisition of the company Virtual Staging AI in 2024, it was able toofficially launchthe virtual staging feature last September as part of its Showcase package.

For agents, the feature capitalizes on a home’s potential. And on the buyer’s end, it helps jog imagination.

“I think people before AI were trying to do that in their heads,” said Stevens. “But with virtual staging and the style specifically, they can do that more actively.”

Boston brokerKelly Roche with Kelly Atlantic Realtystarted using Zillow’s Showcase package and its virtual staging feature about six months ago. She paid $750 for a Showcase listing at99-105 Broad St. in Boston, which is priced at $1,549,000.




Inside the luxury penthouse unit listed by Roche, the original cream accent chair in the corner of the primary bedroom becomes wicker in the “coastal” style. In that same corner, the chair morphs into a sleek dresser within the “industrial” design.

A slider allows users to shift between the original and staged space for side-by-side comparison. Users are even able to remove existing furniture to see a blank slate.

Roche said Zillow’s virtual staging is compelling users to explore a single listing rather than doom-scrolling.

“They’ll spend more time in each room … so it kind of keeps their attention on the specific property,” she said.

She hasn’t made a full switch to virtual staging, but said Zillow’s feature is a go-to to save time and money. Real, non-virtual, staging — depending on property size — can take days, versus on Zillow, where media is uploaded within 24 hours.

National and New England-based virtual staging companies are surfacing, but Zillow’s operations remain in-house.

Roche is expecting the usual rise in real estate activity in Boston this fall, and to prepare, she said realtors are opting to elevate listing photos with virtual staging.

But the imaginative appeal of AI has challenges of accuracy and misrepresentation.





In the early stages of development, Stevens said the generic image models would “hallucinate,” creating defects like an extra window or wall.

Roche does worry that the stagings can be misleading for buyers in an already confusing marketplace. “I like it, but as long as things are realistic,” she said.

Even she’s been deceived by an overly enhanced home.

“I went to show a house the other day and I drove right by it because they had completely virtually staged,” she said. “It was great to get us there, but then once you’re there, you’re already like somewhat disappointed off the bat.”

Responsible use of AIis a priority at Zillow, and according to Stevens, the company hasspecific standards— like aligning with MLS disclosure rules, photo screenings, including original content, and clear labeling.

He and Roche agree that it’s essential for listings to disclose when things have been virtually enhanced. That’s why Zillow chooses not to lead off its user experience with its AI tools. Rather, the virtual staging tool is an optional feature at shoppers’ disposal. When first entering a listing, the obtained images from agents and through MLS feeds are what’s on display — though browsers should note that those may have been virtually staged outside of Zillow. Zillow spokesperson Claire Carroll said transparency falls to agents at the start of the selling process.

“Agents and brokers bear the front-line responsibility for accuracy,” she said. “We support clear disclosure and believe shoppers should be able to see the original alongside the altered version where possible.”



The effects of AI and virtual staging could be more than aesthetic. According to Carroll, among online listings, those of its Showcase package aregenerating over 75 percent more page views, saves, and shares on average compared to non-Showcase homes in similar areas.

Carroll said Showcase listings are also more likely to go pending within two weeks of listing, and AI could even explain the difference in sale price, with Showcase listings selling for 2 percent more on average — about $7,000 more than non-Showcase listings.

Roche still plans to use traditional and virtual staging for a multifaceted approach, and while she remains optimistic about Zillow’s AI-based staging, she’s still waiting to attest to its selling success.

“It hasn’t helped me sell a house yet.”
