hed: Socialite Libbie Mugrabi loses Hamptons mansion at wild court-ordered auction — after paying nothing on its $3.5M mortgage
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Socialite Libbie Mugrabi lost her Hamptons mansion on the steps of Southampton Town Hall in a public, and wild, court-ordered auction held Friday morning — a rare occurrence in the tony East End.
The auction pulled in just $5.864 million for the Bridgehampton estate. That’s a far cry fromthe $25 million she soughtfor the 10,687-square-foot spread in May, not to mention a stunning about-face after winning a hefty $100 million inher fractious divorcefrom the billionaire art collector David Mugrabi in 2020.
The winning bidder, who showed up to the sale dressed to the nines with his wife, would neither comment on the purchase nor provide his name. Mugrabi, for her part, was not present.
The Mugrabis for years have been knownfor their particularly acrimonious split, which began in 2018 when David, now 54 — son of the Israeli industrialist Jose Mugrabi —filed for divorcefrom Libbie, now 46.
They had no prenup in place, and the proceedings spiraled into a circus. Among the antics, Mugrabi lugging a 25-pound, and $500,000, Keith Haring sculpture into a 2018 Manhattan Supreme Court appearance that she and David had “wrestled” over, according to a witness.
The former couple share two children and were married for 14 years — and were said to have spent $3.5 million annually. Rumors of infidelity had also circulated around the husband and wife, including allegations that David — whose family is known for owning the world’s largest collection of works by Andy Warhol — had a 26-year-old mistress.
More recently, Mugrabi’s drama centered on this East End estate, which carried a $3.5 million mortgage — which she admitted she hadn’t paid a cent toward. The lender, a shell company affiliated with REO Assets of America of Great Neck, N.Y., had sued Mugrabi over the property after she didn’t keep up with mortgage payments. This home is one of the most expensive assets Mugrabi got in the divorce.
Fast forward some years, and Friday’s sale was just as packed with bizarre behavior.
Some 10 interested bidders gathered for the auction, including Mugrabi’s sister, Mia Rowe, who initially won with a $7.8 million bid — but without a check in hand. After saying she was going to a nearby Chase to retrieve $780,000 for a deposit, she never returned.
That drew very loud objections from the other bidders, as interested parties had to appear with certified checks. A friend of Mugrabi’s family then turned to them and said, “This is a family matter. [Rowe will] beat any number you put out.”
The sale wasn’t shy of other television-worthy drama. Also present was Mugrabi’s mother,Jane Scher— along with her dog named Botox — who told the lender’s attorney, Ryan Mitola, “Your client is a d–k.”
That was before police arrived at the sale with lights flashing, over complaints Scher was being disruptive. When they arrived, they took Scher aside, telling her she was out of control, and escorted her back to her car.
“I go to lots of these things, and this one is hands down the most entertaining,” bidder Eddy Bellacera told The Post.
Despite the sale, Mugrabi still finds herself in a $9 million-plus hole to cover repayment of the mortgage, penalties and at least $140,000 in legal fees she racked up after blowing off payments.
It’s not clear how she has found herself in such debt despite winning a nine-figure divorce settlement. Still, she is known for her very high-end and money-burning tastes, including jetting off to Europe for fashion spending sprees and making it a priority to pamper herself.
Her inaction on the loan sparked a two-year legal donnybrook, whose ultimate aim was for her to turn over the keys to the 7-acre Middle Line Highway estate.
The auction’s proceeds will go toward paying off the loan, back interest and other costs.
Mugrabi earlier attempted to sell the home througha public listingin late spring. The listed price was $25 million, with two quick subsequent reductions to $19 million.
Even that proved to be a pie-in-the-sky number, given Mugrabi telling The Post the estate was listed at the “high end” of its value and her attorney, Claude Castro, telling a court the property was worth “between $10 million and $12 million.”
The listing resulted in only one offer, $7 million from a purported Nigerian prince with an allegedly sketchy background that Castro and Mugrabi were not comfortable with.
Still, Friday’s auction sure brought in more than the $500 her lender, a shell company affiliated with REO Assets of America of Great Neck, N.Y., paid for it in a February 2025 auction for the estate that was held online. The lender was the only bidder present.
That auction was held after Mugrabi first defaulted on the loan in October 2024 — and after vehement protests by Mugrabi and Castro over the move, the two sides struck an accord that the home was to be sold by Aug. 25, as well as many other considerations, to ensure the lender was paid back.
The attorneys agreed to go the auction route if the estate was not unloaded during that time through a real estate listing. The deed was destroyed when Mugrabi missed the deadline, Mitola said Thursday.
The auction came just 24 hours after Castro told a court that Mugrabi should be given more time to sell the home because she has lined up a new lender for an $8 million mortgage to purchase the property herself. In the early-morning hours of Friday, Castro filed an appeal in court seeking to prevent the sale from proceeding — an effort a judge denied just 2 minutes before the auction’s start time.
Mitola, for his part, told bidders before the sale “You’re buying litigation,” as he charged there are still legal issues with it.
Mugrabi offered as collateral a Jean-Michel Basquiat artwork worth $40 million, based on an assessment from an outside appraiser she submitted to the court. Mugrabi won back rights to the painting two weeks ago after tussling over its ownership in court with fine art financier, Art Capital LLC, which was extending her money on it for a separate loan.
The question now is if Mugrabi will file for bankruptcy. Attorneys for both sides have discussed the prospect, although Mugrabi had not taken that step as of early Friday morning, according to a check with the US Eastern District Bankruptcy Court, the district where the home stands and where Mugrabi has been living.
Mugrabi seems to relish the idea of legal tangles. “I feel great every time I’m in court,” the New York Times reported her as saying around the time of her divorce. “I love court.”
That’s probably a good thing, since there are still at least six cases she is currently involved in that haven’t been resolved. One of them, brought by art critic and cartoonist Anthony Haden-Guest, claims Mugrabi has 97 of his drawings in this Bridgehampton home that she won’t give back.
She is on the cusp of losing her wingman for that suit, though. Her attorney, Michael Regan, of Regan and Associates, is petitioning the judge on the case to free him from working with Mugrabi, citing “an irreconcilable breakdown in the attorney-client relationship and communication,” records show.

hed: America’s pandemic-era cash-buying boom is fading — but it’s still king for certain home sales
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s pandemic-era love affair with buying homes in cold, hard cash is finally cooling.
All-cash purchases accounted for 31.4% of US home sales during the first four months of 2026, down from 32.3% a year earlier, according tonew Realtor.com research.
And cash buyers are retreating faster than the housing market as a whole: The number of cash sales dropped 11.2% year-over-year, compared with an 8.5% decline in total home sales.
That’s a shift from the pandemic years, when buyers routinely ditched the mortgage to elbow their way to the front of bidding wars.
But don’t declare the death of the cash buyer just yet.
Cash remains more common than before the pandemic — and in certain cities, and at both extremes of the housing market, buyers are still plunking down the entire purchase price without borrowing a dime.
“We’re really just in this holding pattern,” Hannah Jones, senior economic research analyst at Realtor.com and author of the report, told The Post.
During the pandemic, cash was a battering ram.
With buyers fighting over scarce listings, an all-cash offer could vault one bidder over a pile of competitors.
Today, buyers have more options in many parts of the country as inventory has recovered and competition has cooled.
“In a lot of the country, the market is a lot less competitive,” Jones said. “You don’t have to come forward with cash in every situation.”
But cash hasn’t lost its appeal to sellers. Its superpower has simply changed.
During the pandemic, Jones said, sellers viewed cash as “the best offer of a lot of really good offers.”
Today, with financing harder for some buyers to secure, cash can instead be “the most solid, stable, reliable offer” — one that isn’t going to collapse because financing falls through.
Cash used to help buyers win the race. Now it can help sellers make sure they actually cross the finish line.
The national decline hides a striking divide over who is still reaching for the checkbook.
More than two-thirds of homes selling for less than $100,000 were purchased without a mortgage.
Jump to the opposite end of the market and cash comes roaring back: More than 40% of $1 million-plus homes were bought in cash, while a majority of $2 million-plus purchases required no financing.
In between are ordinary buyers who remain much more dependent on mortgages.
But the people buying a $75,000 fixer-upper and a $5 million mansion aren’t exactly shopping from the same playbook.
At the lower end, investors, financing difficulties and credit barriers can push transactions toward cash.
At the top, the explanation is simpler: The buyers have the money.
Jones said the divide reflects what economists call a “K-shaped housing market,” where different groups of buyers are experiencing vastly different realities.
“People on the high end are living in a different world than a lot of the people in the middle,” she said.
Nowhere is cash more prevalent among major metrosthan Miami.
Some 43.2% of sales in the Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach metro were completed without a mortgage in early 2026 — the highest share among the major metros analyzed.
The city’s mix of affluent buyers, retirees and second-home owners helps keep cash king even as its popularity fades nationally.
But the cash map gets considerably stranger from there.
Kansas City, Houston, San Antonio and St. Louis also ranked among the country’s most cash-heavy major metros — showing that the phenomenon isn’t confined to millionaire playgrounds.
And some cities are actually bucking the national retreat. Pittsburgh saw the number of cash purchases surge 22.6%, the largest increase among major metros, while San Francisco posted a 7.7% jump.
San Francisco’s increaseis particularly notable because buying a home there outright requires significantly deeper pockets.
Cash transactions there increased 7.7% even with an average sale price north of $1.1 million.
Realtor.com said the trend is consistent with an injection of wealth from the artificial-intelligence boom — including fundraising, IPOs and stock compensation that can leave newly flush tech workers with enough liquidity to bypass financing.
The data doesn’t prove AI wealth caused the increase, but it offers another potential glimpse at how the tech boom is spilling into housing.
Closer to home, cash buyers are moving in the opposite direction — and financed buyers may finally be getting an opening.
Cash accounted for 32% of sales across the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro from January through May, down 3.2 percentage points from the same period last year, according to additional Realtor.com data provided to The Post.
The number of cash sales plunged 25%, compared with an 18.5% drop in overall transactions.
That’s a notable reversal for a market where cash buyers have proved remarkably resilient.
In 2025, 34.7% of metro-area purchases were made in cash — 3.7 percentage points higher than in 2019 — even as the median sale price soared 64% over that period.
But the landscape has begun to shift.
Inventory in New York City has climbed year-over-year since February 2025, while prices have generally eased. Combined with lower mortgage rates earlier this year, those conditions have created more opportunities for buyers who need financing, according to Realtor.com.
The numbers suggest more financed buyers have been able to make their way back into the market.
The shift is even more pronounced across the Hudson.
Just 24.6% of New Jersey home sales were all-cash from January through May, down 3.7 percentage points from the same period last year.
That’s happening even as the Garden State’s housing marketremains painfully expensive.
New Jersey’s median sale price soared 75.5% between 2019 and 2025, while overall sales plunged 27.9% as rising prices and scarce inventory squeezed the market.
Cash buyers initially weathered that squeeze slightly better than their mortgage-dependent counterparts. But this year, cash sales have fallen faster than overall transactions.
The reason may be that buyers who need a mortgage finally have a little more room to breathe.
Inventory in New Jersey has increased year-over-year since April 2024, while asking prices have fallen for the past 14 months, according to Realtor.com.
Jones said the changing cash numbers suggest there is now “a little bit more slack in the New Jersey market,” allowing financed buyers to compete after several punishing years.
Still, conditions remain far more challenging than they were before the pandemic.
The shift in New York and New Jersey reflects a broader possibility for Americans who don’t happen to have hundreds of thousands of dollars sitting around.
A falling cash share can mean buyers no longer need cash to compete as aggressively — or that financing has become accessible enough for mortgage-dependent buyers to return.
“Both of those things are good news,” Jones said.
For much of early 2026, mortgage rates were lower than a year earlier, giving financed buyers some breathing room.
But that progress is fragile. Rates have since climbed again, Jones noted, potentially pushing would-be buyers back to the sidelines.
So the housing market hasn’t suddenly become buyer-friendly.
Instead, Jones said, it is inching “towards more balance.”
For buyers who spent years watching cash offers sail past them, even that may be a start.

hed: Texas is welcoming cheaper homes — but some cities are pushing back
subhead: Why Texas is betting on manufactured housing
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
When Millard’s Apple Park was platted in Nacogdoches, TX, in 2002, the 69-lot subdivision was designed to accommodate both traditional houses andmanufactured homes.
But only two years later, the city stopped allowing new manufactured homes by right in its residential districts. Homes already there could remain, but they became legally nonconforming—limiting owners’ ability to replace or expand them.
It’s a common pattern across the state: 33% of cities don’t explicitly allowmanufactured housingand an additional 11% subject it to a special permit or public hearing, according to arecent analysis from the National Zoning Atlas.
Nacogdoches, for its part, understood the trade-off at the time. Its2003 comprehensive plancalled manufactured housing “one of the most affordable means of entering intohomeownership,” but seemed to put more stock in the concerns from local residents about its potential effect on neighboring property values.
Then, in early August, Nacogdoches reversed course.
The City Council unanimously created a new residential district where manufactured homes are permitted by right—including all 69 lots of Millard’s Apple Park.
It was a win foraffordabilityadvocates, and especially for owners of the manufactured houses that had been built before the laws changed.
“They don’t have to wait till it just completely falls apart to replace it,” Mike Neu, the city’s executive director of development and infrastructure, told council members. “This gives them options. They didn’t have that before.”
But Nacogdoches was not acting entirely by choice. Beginning on Sept. 1, a new state law (Senate Bill 785) requires Texas municipalities with zoning to allow new HUD-code manufactured homes by right in at least one residential district.
The change will require nearly 400 cities to update their codes to comply, according to an estimate from the Texas Manufactured Housing Association—making Nacogdoches an early glimpse at what could soon play out across the state.
The city offers a clear case for why state lawmakers are betting on manufactured housing to deliver mass affordability.
By national standards, the city looks relatively inexpensive. But buying remains badly mismatched with what local residents earn.
The median home was listed for about $325,500 in August, according to data from Realtor.com®, while the median household income of $39,281 is roughly half of what someone would need to qualify for a mortgage that size. As a result, fewer thanfour in 10 households own their homes.
Renting doesn’t offer residents much relief, either. City officials have described the rental market as “tight,” while Realtor.com data shows the median asking rent reached $962 in August—up 13% in three years.
Manufactured housing, meanwhile, could offer a much lower entry price. A new single-section manufactured home sold for an average of $87,300 in 2025, while a multi-section home averaged $151,500.

Those figures exclude land and taxes, so they don’t offer a perfect comparison to a site-built home. But further research suggests that a new manufactured home installed on a foundationcan cost roughly 35% to 73% as much as comparable site-built construction.
Texas has already adopted manufactured housing at an enormous scale, too. The state received17,458 manufactured homes in 2025, more than 2.5 times the number sent to second-place Florida.
But despite the clear need and demand for wider adoption, manufactured housing has run headlong into a patchwork of local rules that can make them legal in one community, discretionary in the next, and outright impossible in another.
And while SB785 is designed to close that gap, it’s also where the limits of the law are already beginning to show.
While an earlier version of the legislation required cities to allow manufactured homes across a “substantial area of land” and prohibited other regulations that directly or indirectly amounted to a citywide ban, neither provision survived intact.
The final law requires only that the qualifying district apply to “an area of land,” without quantifying how much.
In Nacogdoches, city planners identified three areas that could potentially receive its new R-3M manufactured-home zoning. But only Millard’s Apple Park was actually rezoned. For the changes to span more widely, property owners would have to request the change themselves.
“Theoretically, there could be no other property owners requesting a change to R-3M beyond tonight,” Neu told council members in May.
That means Apple Park’s 69 lots could conceivably represent the full extent of the city’s response—a drop in the bucket compared to the 1,300 units the city needs in thenext five years to adequately address demand.
Bellmead, a small city outside Waco, offers an even sharper example. The city created a new manufactured-housing district but requires a tract to contain five contiguous acres before it can be rezoned into it.
For Amber Haliburton, that was the difference between building new housing on her family’s property or moving on.
“Because we have chosen a manufactured home, there is currently no clear or practical path for us to move forward in Bellmead,” she told theCity Council in February.
Haliburton also questioned why a rule ostensibly intended to open the city to manufactured housing seemed better suited to developers assembling subdivisions than someone trying to place a single home.
City staff acknowledged some of that tension. The new district, Community Development director Fred Morris said, was intended to comply with state law and facilitate development projects, “not to address individual residential lots.”
Bellmead eventually identified a 13.98-acre tract beside an existing manufactured-home development as appropriate for the new zoning. But even that didn’t automatically open the land to manufactured homes. The city’s own memo emphasized that the designation “does NOT rezone the property.” Its owner still has to request the change.
The NZA analysis warned about that possibility before SB785 was passed. Researchers recommended requiring cities to rezone in “good faith,” noting that a municipality could otherwise satisfy the law with land unlikely ever to host a manufactured home.
How the complications play out will matter far beyond the Lone Star State.
By September 2025, the Pew Charitable Trusts had identified nine states that had enacted zoning reforms designed to expand manufactured housing. Some have gone further than Texas, requiring qualifying manufactured homes across single-family residential zones rather than guaranteeing them a foothold in only one district.
At the same time, Washington is attacking other pieces of the problem.
Thebipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in July, includes a series of reforms intended to expand manufactured and modular housing. But it stops short of overriding local zoning, leaving opponents with a powerful tool to continue to limit where manufactured homes can be built.
The resistance is rooted in part in an outdated stigma. Manufactured homes have long been treated as a lesser form of homeownership—cheaper to buy, but also assumed to be a worse investment.
The numbers tell a different story. Realtor.com research found that manufactured homes sold with land appreciated 70.1% from 2019 to early 2026, compared with 58.6% for single-family homes. Even manufactured homes sold without land appreciated 51.6%.

hed: Waterfront Queen Anne in Provincetown has remained in one family for 110 years
subhead: It was the summer home of artist Max Bohm, who became one of the founders of the artist colony in Provincetown.
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
At one point, the road heading into Provincetown splits and separates into Bradford Street and Commercial Street. Just before the split is a property whose 1.2-acre lot is one of the biggest residential parcels in town. CalledGrand View, the house also has an important place in American art history.
Grand View, at676 Commercial St., is an elegant Queen Anne cottage with a porch that wraps around three sides, the house was built in 1880 by Charles E. Perry and Matilda M. Perry, who once owned large tracts of property in the East End. In 1916,American artist Max Bohmbought the house to serve as a summer residence; he became one of the founders of the artist colony in Provincetown. He died only seven years later, but the house has remained in his family ever since. His wife, Zella Bohm, also an artist, summered here until 1956, a year before her death. The Bohms’ artistic legacy continues through their granddaughter,Anne Packard, and her daughters Cynthia and Leslie.
The price was recently reduced from $4.9 million to $3.99 million.
Its site atop a bluff makes for beautiful views of Provincetown Harbor, Long Point, and Cape Cod Bay, and adjoining municipal conservation land provides added space and privacy. The 2,166 square foot house has four bedrooms and two bathrooms.
“It is built like a ship,” said Gregg Russo, a realtor forWilliam Raveis who has the listing. “It has been well-maintained through the years, and though it is old, the house is structurally sound. And, like many Victorian houses, it has big rooms on the first floor.”
One of the features of the large downstairs rooms is a five-sided living room window bay with a deep window seat — a welcoming place to read or look at the ocean view. While bays are typical in Queen Anne houses, its five window sides make this one unusual. One of the bedrooms also has a bay window with water views.
The spacious kitchen has white appliances (the stove is gas) and cabinets and room for a dining table. The two full bathrooms are also roomy; each has a shower/tub combo, one being a clawfoot tub.
“While the kitchen and baths need updating,” said Russo, “You can move right in; everything works.”
Although Max Bohm did not live here in the winter, his descendants did, and the house has central heating, insulated windows, and a fireplace converted to a wood-burning stove inset. A former coal-burning fireplace in the dining room has been covered over, but the graciously proportioned fireplace mantel, fireplace surround, sconces, and mirrored overmantel remain.
A laundry room is located on the first floor; there is also a full pantry, a linen closet, and — suitable for a house overlooking the beach — an outdoor shower. Stairs lead from the house down the bluff to a gate on Commercial Street (Route 6A).
Regina Cole writes about architecture and design for national and regional publications, with a specialty in historic architecture and the history of the decorative arts.

hed: Dolly Parton’s cottage may soon sell amid a flurry of ‘serious interest’ from around the world
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Dolly Parton was a down-home gal even when far from eastern Tennessee — with her California homes stocked with Spam, collard greens and abundant coziness.
Indeed, her two Golden State dwellings shrugged off the sea and the sand in favor of hilly and mountainous areas. Their Fort Knox-like builds, which included solid steel doors, panic buttons in every room and camouflaged windows, also show the lengths celebrities go to feel protected.
Parton owned a small cottage in the foothills of Solvang, Calif., down the road from Michael Jackson’s opulent Neverland Ranch, and a large mountainside home in Idyllwild some 240 miles away.
Now, the former stands to turn a new chapter.
The Solvang cottage, Parton’sformer weekend escape, may be on the cusp of selling following her passinglast week at age 80aftera brief battle with cancer. And the new owner may be a way out-of-towner.
“Serious interest” is coming in from people in the UK, France and Australia, as well as “all parts of the US,” its co-owner Chris Lapp told The Post.
Lapp, who listed the property for $2 million in April with his business partner Daniel Ferguson, said mushrooming interest following Parton’s passing even landed a firm offer. But it was an astonishingly lowball gesture; the pair rejected it while continuing to field interest from other potential buyers.
The price after Dolly’s passing “is staying the same,” Lapp said. Potential buyers now need to show proof of funds before setting foot through the door for a showing — in an effort to avoid looky-loos trying to get a peek into Parton’s onetime inner sanctum.
Lapp said he would come down “a smidge” if the City of Solvang, known as “the Danish capital of America,” bought the place for Parton’s fans to visit.
“I would love to see them own it,” said Lapp, who is an area resident.
Solvang Mayor David Brown quashed that prospect.
“We didn’t buy Neverland when Michael Jackson died,” Brown said. “We will all always love Dolly. It doesn’t take a physical property for that.”
Parton, a celebrity loved by all who was known for her iconic hits including “Jolene,” owned this property between 2004 and 2014.
When using the cottage, Parton “would come here with Judy” pretty much exclusively, Lapp said. He was referring to Judy Ogle, whom Parton is said to have met in her rural third grade classroom — and who was her lifelong friend, confidante and personal assistant.
“The caretaker had two instructions when Dolly was coming,” Lapp said. “Lots of fresh flowers and the refrigerator filled with Spam.Dolly loved her Spam.”
The home is surprisingly small — about 1,100 square feet over two stories — and is part of a three-house compound with about 2,500 square feet of living space total, plus seven bedrooms and six bathrooms.
Parton’s dashes of flair and design acumen are apparent throughout the main house where she stayed. The home retains a farmhouse feel through hand-carved woodwork, including lots of lattice, as well as a living area with stately furnishings.
Parton’s wig room is still onsite and spreads in and around a converted garage measuring 12 by 13 feet.
Her dressing room remains “a totally glam area, with all colors of lipstick, a lot of pinks, reds and spangly things,” said Ladd, who covers them when showing the house.
Parton was no slouch when it came to security at the place. Her bedroom door was solid industrial-grade steel and so heavy it took three people to take it out. Lapp said he replaced it with a wooden door.
The home’s exterior looked inviting, but was like a fortress. The frame was reinforced and, while it seemed like someone could view inside, it was an illusion. All the windows were actually blacked out as part of the property’s “pap proofing,” Lapp said.
The outside includes a small birdhouse modeled after a traditional chapel and a dog run installed by Parton,a staunch animal advocate. A miniature windmill and wooden tulips are a nod to Solvang, which is also called “the Tulip Capital of the US.”
The amount Dolly paid for the complex has remained under wraps. Solvang property records show the owner before her paid $185,000 in April 1999.
Lapp bought the home for $1.3 million in 2022, and said he put in roughly $100,000 for rehab to turn all three homes into rentals.
Lapp said he didn’t know the place was Parton’s until late in purchase process, when he was in escrow and having the title searched as part of the closing.

hed: NYC landlord sues sanitation department over trash-placement fines — because there’s nowhere to put it
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A clash over trash is playing out in Tribeca — where plenty of small buildings have no choice but to set out their garbage in plastic bags rather than bulky bins.
In such small buildings, there is simply no space for the sanitation department’s required bins, which consume far more space than bags alone.
Regardless, late last year the sanitation department slapped landlord Robert Moskowitz with three “receptacle violation” tickets — for using garbage bags rather than the requisite “rigid receptacles with tight fitting lids.”
Moskowitz paid $150 for those three counts of “failure to containerize.” His efforts to fight the tickets failed, and he is now suing the city’s sanitation department, DSNY.
It is both “physically and legally impossible to comply” with the bin requirement, wrote his lawyer, Nicole Waknine, in papers filed last week in Manhattan Supreme Court.
“We have no objection to the use of trash cans,” she told The Post. “Our issue is a practical one. The goal is to push the city to implement a waiver program for building owners who have tried in good faith to comply and truly can’t comply.”
With no yard or storage space, there is simply no place to put the bins, except for a building’s entryway, where people would need to shimmy past. Even if there were space, the fire code prohibits the storage of rubbish in lobbies.
Nor is there space for another allowed option, a fenced-in storage area within 3 feet of the building, which would block the doors.
Moskowitz — whose company, Only Properties, owns about a dozen small downtown buildings — was issued tickets for three historic Tribeca properties. All are small walkups, with lofty rental residences atop narrow ground-floor commercial spaces, and open directly onto the sidewalk.
Large buildings and massive skyscrapers are in a very different situation, with plenty of space and resources to handle garbage, Moskowitz said in a statement to The Post.
“The law places a disproportionate burden on [small buildings], forcing us to purchase only DSNY-approved trash cans and to create storage space out of thin air.”
The current situation is “an example of a ‘one size fits all’ rule really failing,” Waknine said.
About two years ago, as part of itswar on rats, the city required buildings to containerize their trash, specifyingcertain requirementsfor the bins used.
(As of Sept. 8, the sanitation department will start fining small buildings, defined as having one to nine residential units, that do not use thespecific official NYC bins, which are available at Home Depot.)
“This is not a matter of storing a small waste bin in the residential lobby,” the complaint reads, “but rather having enough space for storage of the amount of garbage that accumulates within the entire building over a 72-hour period,” which the law requires.
The buildings in question have trash picked up three times a week.
At 277 Church St., one of the ticketed buildings, the commercial tenant is the French restaurantFaux, scheduled to open next month by George McNally, son of legendary restaurateurKeith McNally. The restaurant will occupy both the ground-floor and basement levels.
One obvious problem: The building’s residential lobby is 50 inches wide, and storing two 45-gallon bins would consume no fewer than 45.2 inches.
“Residential tenants cannot safely enter and exit the building with only 5 inches of space,” Waknine wrote.
Even if the bins were slightly smaller, “regardless of size, we are completely prohibited from storing bins in the lobby,” she told The Post. The buildings also don’t have space for recycling or compost bins, but they have not been ticketed for those failures.
Building residents put their own garbage out, with the super organizing it to be sure it is neatly and correctly bagged.
Moskowitz lost an appeal because “no evidence was presented to indicate whether Respondent made aby [sic] effort to place refuse out for collection in a rigid container” and also “failed to prove that the containers could not be stored in other areas, including the commercial space,” the hearing officer wrote.
Waknine was incredulous. “The court is making decisions that are not addressing reality,” she told The Post.
“The notion that a restaurant would want large garbage cans stored on site and would accept the building’s residential tenants going in and out to dispose of their garbage when they are not required to under their lease agreement is preposterous,” Waknine wrote in court papers.
What’s more, “is the hearing officer arguing that Respondent should have proven it cannot store these garbage cans within one of the residential apartments? There is no court in New York State that would compel a residential tenant to submit to the public storage of garbage in its home.”
At 31 Walker St., the Mexican restaurantAñejo TriBeCauses a hatch for deliveries, and there is also signage outside for the building’s sprinkler system. Neither can be blocked.
At that building, approved trash bins in the lobby would leave residents squeezing past with only 22 inches of clearance. If stored behind the stairwell, the bins would block the freight elevator.
Interior storage space is also missing at 92 Reade St., where the ground floor is occupied byHeyday Skincare. “There, we were directed to build a fenced-in enclosure,” Waknine told The Post.
But there is no place to do so without obstructing doors or setting the enclosure in the middle of the sidewalk, thereby impeding pedestrian flow in a busy commercial area, where thesidewalk widthon the block is just 9.1 feet.
The City Council has recognized the absurdity of the bin requirement, and is consideringa billthat would exempt some small buildings that don’t have adequate bin space.
“I’ve heard from deli owners, barbers and landlords who have no alley, no yard, no storage space — but are still getting fined for not having a place to put these bins,” the bill’s sponsor, Councilmember Frank Morano of Staten Island,told SI Livelast October. “That’s not good government; that’s bureaucracy gone wild.”
Sanitation spokesman Joshua Goodman declined to comment on pending litigation, but emphasized that using bins instead of bags “actually works” as far as cleaner streets and fewer rats.
“Looking at enforcement data, these three buildings appear to have been caught not using a bin about 80 times since the rules went into effect,” Goodman wrote in a statement to The Post. “That’s 80 nights with an all-you-can-eat rat buffet outside the buildings.”
Since the start of 2025, DSNY has issued about 170,000 summonses for failure to use a bin, and 30,000 written warnings, he told The Post.
He further insisted that DSNY does have a process for buildings to apply for exemptions.One formis for “extremely rare cases” where using a bin would pose “a public safety risk to pedestrians.”Another formis for property owners who have a disability making the use of a bin impossible.
“We do not appear to have a record of these property owners applying for an exemption or reaching out for assistance,” Goodman said, adding that DSNY is “very proud to be such an accessible and responsive agency.”
Those forms are irrelevant, Waknine said. “Our issue is a practical question of how small building owners can realistically store cans between collection days — not an argument that putting trash cans out on collection days will pose a threat to public safety.”

hed: Ultra-private $16 million island with own helipad available in Florida Keys: ‘Salt-life lover’s dream’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An idyllic private island retreat in the Florida Keys that is accessible only by water or air has returned to the market for $16 million, offering up a rare opportunity to enjoy the best of both worlds: “extraordinary privacy”andmetropolitan proximity.
The beautiful isle sits just a quarter-mile off the coast of Marathon, FL, and is surrounded by beautiful turquoise waters that serve as the ideal spot for “snorkeling, swimming, kayaking, paddleboarding, fishing and watersports.”
And, while boats, jet skis, and helicopters are the only real methods of transport to the island, residents and guests can be on the mainland in mere minutes using one of those options, creating a level of convenience rarely enjoyed at properties of this kind.
According to Vladimir Rochebrun, who isco-listing the propertywith Aaron Rosenthal, both of The Chad Carroll Group at Compass, the island’s location on the Atlantic Ocean side of Marathon also comes with several other advantages.
“It’s on the ocean side so you don’t have a lot of the issues that you deal with on the Gulf side, where you’re dealing with all these bugs and all these things that impede on your quality of life,” Rochebrun explains.
“If you do own an island on the [Gulf] side, there’s so many more things that are nuisances that kind of impede on the value of being able to freely be outside and be comfortable.”
The impressive property is currently home to a three-bedroom primary residence and a separate one-bedroom guesthouse, as well as a private helipad and a large dock that can house a sizable boat. Yet there is much more to the property than meets the eye.
In addition to the land that is easily viewable above the water, the property also comes complete with approximately 5.8 acres of seabed that surrounds the island—creating a private underwater paradise that only a few have had the chance to enjoy.
“You have to factor in the surrounding seabed, which you have ownership and rights to, so all that reef, everything like where people are snorkeling, that’s all owned under this folio for this property,” Rochebrun explains.
“It has just enough depth to where you can come in with a substantial boat, but it’s not so deep to where you can’t comfortably snorkel with a bunch of people and go lobstering.”
The sellers have done a lot of updates to the 2,304-square-foot main home since it was last listed for $11.7 million in 2021, including a major kitchen renovation.
“I think my favorite part about the island is just how much it’s been cared for,” Rochebrun says. “You feel the love on that island. It doesn’t feel like a spec property that someone built to sell. You can tell that it’s something that’s been cared for and maintained in excellent condition. It’s just such a special property that you can tell it feels like something that’s generational.”
The main home has two bathrooms and there is also a bathroom in the guesthouse, with the total living space spanning about 5,000 square feet.
The home has no public utilities but is certainly not primitive.
“It has its own solar and wind system entirely, so it’s completely off grid and self-sustained,” Rochebrun says. “I were a buyer, it’s definitely a place that I would have a lot of pride in owning. You’re giving your family something that is just so special and irreplaceable.
“The energy of the island is just unreal. We didn’t want to leave our first time there. It felt like home. You feel like you’re at home instantly.”
In addition to the sleeping spaces, there is also a pool, a protected snorkeling area, and a fishing pier.
“My favorite thing about this property is you can literally catch fish off the dock and filet the fish because everything’s fresh from the ocean,” Rosenthal says. “My other favorite thing is you can have multiple boats on the property. You can have your tender and you can also dock your fishing yacht.”
The island is only accessible via helicopter (there is a helipad) or boat (the listing includes a dock on the mainland), but it’s a short ride either way.
“You’re about a quarter-mile offshore, so it’s easy to get to and from,” Rochebrun says, adding it’s even swimmable if you wanted.  “Once you’re [on the mainland], you have dock space and space to park cars, and then the grocery store is literally a three-minute drive from the dock.
“Literally everything you need is maybe within a 10-minute drive once you’re on the mainland, so it’s really ideally located.”
The island has also been a successful business venture over the years as well as a family getaway.
“[The sellers] historically have used this as an investment property and they have repeat business, which makes it very special,” Rochebrun says. “It’s very lucrative from a business standpoint and whenever it’s not rented, they can easily just go and stay there, so it’s generating a substantial income, but it’s also something that’s been in their family for over 30 years.”
According toone rental listing, the place rents for a standard weekly rate of $13,500 with a $1,000 discount during September and October. The rate goes up to $17,500 for holidays like Christmas and New Year’s.
The location is ideal for many kinds of buyers.
“This is one of the most unique properties there is. Just by the accessibility and how easy it is, and you’re really close to civilization and you’re away from civilization at the same time,” Rosenthal says.
Rochebrun agrees.
“It’s for someone who wants their privacy but doesn’t want to be so far away from the mainland to where it’s going to feel like a trek,” he says. “It’s literally every boater’s and salt-life lover’s dream.”

hed: Entire California town with 35 buildings goes on the market
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
If you have a spare $7 million, you could be the new owner of an entire town in California — just an hour awayfrom San Diego.
Downtown Campo, a historic unincorporated community and former World War II military base is up for sale for $6,600,000. The sprawling 15.75-acre property at 431 Jeb Stuart Road is a mix of 28 residential and 7 non-residential buildings.
The town has its own local Post Office, a Border Patrol facility, a church, a VFW post, and multiple specialized workshops such as a cabinet shop and metal shop.
“The opportunity extends to revitalizing currently vacant buildings within the town, a move that could add substantial income by introducing new or enhanced services like gyms, laundromats, daycares, or community centers, directly responding to the desires and needs of the local population,” readsthe real estate listing.
Las Vegas real estate investor John Ray has owned most of Campo since 2000 and nearly all of the town has been on the market since 2019, according tothe Orange County Register.
The sale arrives amid a period of steady growth for the area, which saw its population increase by 10.1% between 2010 and 2020 as more residents look to balance rural tranquility with proximity to urban job centers.
The location originally rose to prominence in 1885 when the Gaskill brothers constructed the fortress-like Campo Stone Store on-site using four-foot-thick walls to protect against border raids.
Decades later, the property underwent a massive transformation during World War II when the U.S. Army absorbed the land to construct Camp Lockett, building a sprawling network of military barracks to garrison the legendary Buffalo Soldiers of the 10th and 28th Cavalry Regiments — the last horse-mounted units in U.S. military history.
Following the war, these exact military structures were preserved rather than demolished, transitioning into private ownership in the late 1950s where they were converted into the residential apartments and long-term commercial spaces that still stand at the address today.

hed: Meghan Markle has wild demands for her new UK home — 9 bedrooms and a film studio among them: report
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Meghan Markle’s wish list shows she’s not downsizing her US lifestyle for the “English countryside dream.”
Markle, 45, touched down in Britain this week with a very specific number in mind: nine.
That’s how many bedrooms the Duchess of Sussex is insisting on for the family’s new countryside estate, according to theDaily Mail, and it just so happens to match the exact bedroom count atthe $15 million Montecito compoundshe already owns.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed at Birmingham Airport on Wednesday with Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, arriving by private jet before being driven off in a convoy of blacked-out SUVs.
Rather than moving into a home of their own, the family is currently holed up “indefinitely” in the spare house ofa wealthy friendon the edge of the Cotswolds while the real estate hunt plays out.
And it’s a hunt with a very specific shopping list.
Meghan reportedly wants nine bedrooms and a film studio, while Harry wants “a lot, and I mean a lot, of land, and no footpaths going across it to protect their privacy.”
Three separate sources have told the Daily Mail that despite earlier reports of a $16.2 million property being locked in, no deal has actually closed.
Money doesn’t appear to be the obstacle. The couple is reportedly working with a “gargantuan budget,” even as their Hollywood ambitions have cooled and their big-ticket production dealshave dried up.
Friends insist they’re not selling the Montecito place either, meaning the Sussexes could soon be juggling three properties: the California mansion, an $8.5 million vacation home in Portugal and whatever nine-bedroom trophy house they land in the historic Cotswolds.
That math has raised eyebrows across the pond. A person in the Santa Barbara luxury market told The Post there “have been rumblings” that the couple might quietly offload the Montecito estate, noting “every broker wants that listing.”
It’s not hard to see why the pressure is on.
The Postfound the 7.4-acre property carries a mortgage and tax bill north of $600,000 a year, with the monthly mortgage payment alone landing somewhere between $40,000 and $43,000 and 2025 property taxes totaling $149,668, before factoring in security, insurance or upkeep.
Douglas Elliman broker Jason Streatfeild told The Post he has “a strong feeling that it’s already being discussed and shown,” and explained deals like this typically happen off-market, saying “many times properties like this will trade off-market with a nondisclosure agreement signed and all of the terms sealed until the property records at the county.”
Despite the financial juggling act, insiders describe the move to England as a full reset for the couple, something friends are calling “Finding Freedom 2,” a nod to the 2020 biography about their original royal exit.
One friend told the Daily Mail the appeal this time is that Harry gets to live in the UK as a private citizen rather than a working royal, explaining “they will have more freedom now — it is like finding freedom again.”
Another associate close to the couple was more blunt about why California didn’t work out, telling the outlet “he had no life in California, no friends. There was no common ground with anyone.”
Meghan, meanwhile, is reportedly eyeing that future film studio as a way to keep her As Ever brand alive from British soil, even though the product line currently doesn’t ship to the UK.
One source predicted she “won’t be able to resist building a film studio at their new home” and will end up producing “home making content” once she’s settled, adding “that is the heart of who she is.”
The kids’ schooling appears to be the one area where the couple is dialing back the showbiz instincts. A friend told the outlet that academics are “very low on the list” for Archie and Lili, with the priority instead being “a nurturing atmosphere” and an “outdoorsy and sporting ethos” that mirrors Harry’s own happy years at Ludgrove prep school.
Still, for a couple who left Britain in 2020 describing the royal family and British press as hostile, the return comes with familiar baggage.
Harry has said publicly he’s not rejoining royal life, just bringing his children back for the British school experience, and a source says he intends to be a “full-time dad” while Meghan continues splitting time between continents to keep her business interests running.

hed: State Farm pocketed $1.4B as weather and roof claims worsened, unsealed records show
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It seems State Farm has not been a good neighbor for quite a while.
Worseningstorms battered Oklahoma roofsfor years. State Farm’s payouts, it turns out, didn’t exactly keep up.
A trove of internal documents unsealed by a Comanche County judge, first reported on byNBC News,shows the insurance giant quietly rewrote its own rulebook on hail and wind damage starting in 2020, squeezing nearly a billion and a half dollars out of policyholders in a single year.
The paper trail now sits at the center of a legal war engulfing nearly 1,000 Oklahoma homeowners and the state’s top law enforcement officer.
One internal email spells out the bottom line in blunt corporate math.
“Volume down while severity up quite a bit,” a State Farm claims manager wrote. “About a $1.4B decrease in indemnity from 2020 to 2021.”
The same message tracked how roof replacement ratios cratered under the new approach.
“When we started this work, we were replacing roofs at a rate of 5.6 to every 1 we repaired. In 2021 we landed at 2.0 for every 1 and 2022 increased to 2.2 to every 1,” the email continued.
Another executive calculated that trimming approvals by a single percentage point was worth a staggering sum across the company’s claim volume.
“Each % point difference is about 5k claim, so if we didn’t pay for 1% of claims that did not have damage and were not covered but would have been paid for before based on lack of skill/will, that is 5k claims at $15,768 avg severity of $78.8 million,” the executive wrote.
The operation traced back to an internal hunch that State Farm was too generous compared to competitors on small hail and wind claims. A 2020 business plan flagged roofs as the biggest lever the company could pull, noting they made up 70% of claims and 57% of what State Farm paid out.
“If in fact Full Roof Replacements is our biggest bucket of opportunity,” one exchange between claims managers read, “We think our best option is to first focus on small hail/light wind.”
State Farm brought in outside consulting firm Haag Engineering to retrain adjusters, but Haag’s damage metrics didn’t match State Farm’s own policy language, according to internal correspondence.
“The information provided by Haag does lend an engineering perspective in some instances and not an insurance coverage/damage perspective,” one March 2020 email read. “While their perspective is not inaccurate, it is not State Farm’s understanding and should be noted in advance of viewing the videos.”
It wasn’t just customers getting blindsided. A Kentucky-based agent wrote directly to leadership in 2021, warning the claims process was destroying the business.
“This system is not only broken it is taking us down quicker than you can imagine. Its gone from bad to worse in record time,” she wrote. “Inspectors are being sent out to measure and photo roofs and hand out a very small estimate to REPAIR knowing that in a lot of cases it should be much more than that. They are afraid to get their hand slapped and are in the pockets of State Farm so they are low balling at best and almost NEVER replace a roof.”
Even company insiders acknowledged the fallout privately.
“The roof thing is a problem,” one representative wrote. “We have not done ourselves a favor there and claims leadership needs to clearly communicate the philosophy change to agents.”
Ryan Graff, a Wisconsin attorney who has represented policyholders against insurers, told NBC News the documents show a company applying standards it never disclosed to customers.
“You can cut costs through claims. What you can’t do is sell one thing and provide another,” Graff said. “In every jurisdiction, insurance policy interpretation cannot be more restrictive than what is in the policy. That is a huge no-no.”
Peter Kochenburger, a visiting law professor at Southern University Law Center, was more cautious in his own remarks to NBC News.
“These records certainly suggest areas to inquire about and possibilities of improper conduct,” Kochenburger said. “There’s nothing wrong with trying to get the quickest result and the most accurate result. That’s fine, but it has to be the actual. You can’t lowball your policyholder.”
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond sued State Farm in June, accusing it of running a “Denial Enterprise” under the state’s anti-racketeering statute.
“This case is about more than individual claim disputes,” Drummond said. “The allegations describe a corporate scheme that threatens the integrity of Oklahoma’s insurance market place and undermines public confidence in an industry families rely on when disaster strikes.”
Drummond suggested the case could turn criminal.
“There may be a scheme inside of State Farm’s leadership to intentionally defraud Oklahomans, and if that can be proven, that RICO will cross into the criminal world.”
A company lawyer, during a hearing over the records, insisted the documents show nothing more than routine business analysis.
“State Farm believes a plain reading of the documents shows that it was only evaluating if they were properly paying claims,” the lawyer said, adding that in some cases the company had been paying claims with “no evidence of damage.”
“Plaintiff’s counsel make statements and they misconstrue documents as if that scheme theory is fact. It’s not fact. It’s merely argument,” she said.
A company spokesperson added, in remarks to NBC News, that so-called bad-faith suits make up roughly 1% of the 30,000 claims State Farm handles annually, and that the insurer has paid out more than $1 billion to Oklahoma customers for wind and hail damage over the past two years.
“Each claim is fairly and diligently evaluated based on its specific facts,” the spokesperson said.
Only 31 documents have been unsealed so far, with hundreds of thousands more still under wraps. Internal emails from 2023 obtained by NBC News suggest leadership had no plans to abandon the strategy.
“We need to go back to what worked in the past to quickly make an impact,” one executive wrote.
With more than 1,000 lawsuits pending and Oklahoma’s attorney general now circling with racketeering claims of his own, State Farm’sroof reckoning is far from over.

hed: The happiest city in America revealed — and the others in the top 5 may surprise you
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Happiness has an address — and it’s in California.
Fremont, Calif., has been crowned the happiest city in the country, according toa new WalletHub studyranking 182 of the largest US cities.
The Bay Area city took the No. 1 spot after WalletHub compared cities using 29 measures of happiness spanning emotional and physical well-being, income and employment, and community and environment.
And Fremont certainly has reasons to smile.
The city, located on the southeast shore of San Francisco Bay, ranked first for emotional and physical well-being, helped by its walkability, mild weather, high sports participation and an average life expectancy of nearly 82 years, WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo told theNew York Times.
Its residents also have some financial cushion: 80% of Fremont households earn more than $75,000, according to the study, even though the city ranked 89th in the income and employment category.
But the rest of America’s happiness map comes with a few surprises.
Bismarck, ND, took the No. 2 spot, followed by Scottsdale, Ariz.; South Burlington, Vt.; and Fargo, ND — putting two cities in frigid North Dakota among the five happiest places in America.
Apparently, sunshine isn’t a requirement for a sunny disposition.
Bismarck topped the community and environment category, with the study pointing to residents’ strong sense of connection and satisfaction with their community.
Locals also devote plenty of time to leisure — and have wide-open spaces where they can actually enjoy it.
“It’s not as hustle and bustle as it would be in a major metro area like New York City or Washington, DC,” Lupo told the Times, noting that residents have more opportunities to unwind, spend time with family and pursue hobbies.
Rounding out the top 10 were Overland Park, Kan.; Charleston, SC; Irvine, Calif.; Gilbert, Ariz.; and San Jose, Calif.
And New Yorkers searching for a little more joy don’t necessarily have to head all the way to California — or brave a North Dakota winter.
Just across the Hudson, Jersey City came in at No. 31, while Yonkers landed at No. 38.
Both punched well above their overall rankings when it came to emotional and physical well-being: Jersey City placed 16th in that category, with Yonkers close behind at No. 18.
Jersey City had even more reason to smile: It recorded the lowest depression rate of all 182 cities analyzed and the second-lowest suicide rate, according to WalletHub.

hed: Home of the Week: Expanded mid-century 4-bedroom in Cohasset for $1.45m
subhead: It was built in 1960 as a ranch before being expanded and reconfigured by a prior owner
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

25 Virginia Lane, Cohasset

$1.45 million

Stylemid-century

Year built1960; expanded and updated since

Square feet2,405

Bedrooms4

Baths2.5

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$12,621 (2025)




To be clear, Jennifer L. Chu is not a moth.

But Chu says it was the light flooding into this mid-century modern that lured her into buying it in 2015. Another attraction was the arboreal cloak covering the 1.87-acre lot.

“The feeling was this is like a million miles away from the city, but it’s less than an hour away from downtown Boston,” said Chu.

Chu is ending her stewardship of the home, which began in 1960 as a ranch before being expanded and reconfigured by a prior owner into its current shape. After updating key rooms including the kitchen and the bathrooms, Chu is moving to be closer to relatives.



From the driveway, which is partially covered by broadleaf trees, a curving walk of pale gray ceramics leads to the porch and the primary entry door, which has three panes of glass and two others on each side, is painted a bright orange, (Chu’s favorite color), and is protected by a roof. The sidewalk also offers a view of the addition — a trapezoid with a sloping roofline — that redefined the architectural identity.

A second entry is on the extreme left side of the house and also has an orange door, opening into a mudroom with white cabinets and a built-in bench.

Stepping inside, the foyer shoots in a straight line to the rear of the home. Moving to the right, one enters the 307-square-foot living room, which occupies the front of the trapezoid. It has a cathedral ceiling — some 13 feet at the front peak — and exposed white beams below. But it’s the plate glass windows and the natural light they pull inside that entranced Chu. There is a ribbon of three clerestory windows near the ceiling, and a second collection of three casement windows seemingly large enough to step through with ease. On the opposite wall, as it descends to 7 feet, is a white floor-to-ceiling entertainment center. Flooring is white oak, original to the home and refinished by Chu with a water-based stain.



The living room also serves as the fulcrum for a full bathroom and the access point for three bedrooms that range in size from 142 square feet to 167 square feet. (One is currently being used as an office.) All three have their own collections of large, clear-plate glass windows and propeller-style ceiling fans. The 63-square-foot full bathroom has a shower with a river stone floor, a single vanity, and ceramic tile floor and backsplash.

Following the foyer’s path, it leads to the kitchen and dining area as well as a full bathroom and the primary suite, which is an island unto itself, occupying the remainder of the right side of the home.



The updated kitchen has quartz countertops with a marble appearance on the island, which has an overhang on two sides, creating seating for five. Above are three pendant lights with clear glass globes. The cabinets in the 315-square-foot area are white, and the backsplash is large formatSpanish Porcelanosa tiles.The inset sink is underneath windows, and the appliances are stainless steel. A half-bathroom is off the kitchen and doubles as the laundry room.


The flooring is white oak, and it continues through a large archway into the 378-square-foot dining area, a space that seems to require sunglasses on a bright day. There are sliders to a 304-square-foot deck on one wall, and two adjoining sliders leading to a three-season porch. For the colder days, there is a wood-burning fireplace, original to the home, on the interior wall of the dining room near the kitchen.


The 162-square-foot porch is yet another room with windows, windows … and more windows. It also has white oak flooring and in a holdover from earlier owners, part of the roof is corrugated translucent plastic, more commonly used for greenhouses.

The primary bedroom is 285 square feet with white oak flooring. There is recessed lighting along with a bank of three clear glass windows and a fourth rectangular window on the other wall. A clear glass door opens to the private deck overlooking the rear yard.



There is a 122-square-foot walk-in closet with built-in shelving, and two square plate glass windows. The primary bathroom is 121 square feet with a deep white oval soaker tub positioned in front of white Spanish Porcelanosa tiles. The shower area is behind the white tile wall and has entrances on either side. It’s a direct entry without any shower doors. The backsplash is ceramic.

There is a garden with beehives installed and maintained byFoxRock Farms, which is aiming to rebuild the populationof the essential pollinators. Chu also said a fox passes by between 6:45 a.m. and 7:15 a.m. nearly every day. “He’s got an agenda,’’ she said.

Andrea Hulme of Corcoran Property Advisershas the listing.
