hed: NYC’s biggest builders are circling a $360M vacant lot that could become the city’s next supertall tower
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A long-stalled Upper East Side development site once envisioned as the home of a 1,000-foot-plus skyscraper is back up for grabs — this time with a $360 million price tag.
The six-parcel assemblage at 143-161 E. 60th St., directly across from theBloomingdale’sflagship and steps from Lexington Avenue,last tradedfor $300 million in 2015.
Now, more than a decade later, the seller is seeking $60 million more for the roughly 20,000-square-foot site, which offers about 283,000 square feet of development potential.
And unlike the last time the property changed hands, the old buildings that stood on the lot are now gone, leaving developers with a cleared site and a rare chance to make their mark on the Manhattan skyline.
The property’s zoning allows for residential or commercial development and, crucially, has previously been marketed as allowing a tower without a height limit — opening the door for a future developer to once again shoot for the sky.
But buying the dirt could be just the beginning of the bill.
Listing broker Marlon Schwarcz estimates that developing a high-end project on the site could require roughly $500 million on top of the land acquisition.
“Usually, you look at 2 times from whatever the acquisition price is” as a typical indication of the capital needed for a project, Schwarcz said. “Now, for the ultra-luxury, you go 3 times the original acquisition.”
At the $360 million asking price, that could put the overall investment needed for an ultra-luxury project in the neighborhood of $1 billion.
At the other end of the spectrum, Schwarcz said the site could be developed as affordable housing, which he estimated could cost roughly $100 million to $300 million to build.
Some of New York’s biggest builders are already circling.
Schwarcz said he has received offers from major developers, including players with projects on nearbyBillionaires’ Row.
“I can’t say the names,” he said. “But what I can tell you, it’s top 10 — often people that are doing projects on Billionaires’ Row.”
Offers began arriving roughly 30 days after the property hit the market, he said, and Schwarcz believes a deal could be reached within about 90 days.
Chinese developer Kuafu Propertiesbought the six-property assemblagefrom World Wide Group for $300 million in 2015, when its low-rise buildings included the longtime home of the belovedSubway Inn, which had been forced to relocate as redevelopment plans took shape.
Kuafu, led by Shang Dai and Zengliang “Denis” Shan, had much bigger ambitions for the corner.
The developer commissioned prominent architecture firms to dream up competing visions for the site — several of which could have extended the supertall boom that transformed Billionaires’ Row northeast toward Lenox Hill.
Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners devised a 62-story, 1,000-footresidential towerin 2015, with a slender glass design rising above a retail base. Kohn Pedersen Fox later produced its own potentialsupertall conceptas part of a private design competition, envisioning an exceptionally slender tower broken up by a series of setbacks and cutouts.
Archilier Architecture proposed perhaps the most audacious version: a roughly1,240-foot towerwith an inverted-taper design that widened as it rose, putting its largest floors — and prized Central Park views — near the top. At that height, it would have ranked among New York’s tallest residential skyscrapers.
None made it off the drawing board.
The project then became tangled up in a shakeup at Kuafu. In 2016,the Real Deal reportedthat Shan was leaving the development firm to launch his own venture, with the East 60th Street site among the projects going with him.
The assemblage ultimately ended up underShan-controlled Sumi Properties.
The sheer amount of money required to build on the site helps explain the challenge facing any developer hoping to finally turn those sky-high ambitions into reality.
“If you don’t have enough investors that want to invest alongside with you, everything is on your shoulders,” Schwarcz said. “Regardless of how wealthy you are or how big you are, it’s very unlikely you’re going to accomplish this development.”
Years of work have nevertheless changed the property dramatically since its last sale. The six buildings have been demolished, leaving the assemblage cleared and ready for its next act.
The seller, meanwhile, isn’t desperate to make a deal.
“It all comes down to numbers,” Schwarcz said.

hed: I live above a noisy NYC laundromat whose vibrations and fumes are ruining my life — and I have nowhere to go
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Last fall, when Dorian Solomon viewed theEast Harlemstudio apartment she now calls home, construction kept her from noticing the commotion from the Miss Bubble laundromat on the ground floor, directly below.
Since moving in, however, the disruption from the laundromat has been tormenting her with noise, vibration and fumes during all waking hours, while a boiler ticks noisily around the clock.
“I feel like a zombie,” Solomon told The Post. “In a small studio, there is nowhere to escape.”
The low-frequency vibration is a “heavy hum that resonates in your chest and penetrates right through earplugs and white noise,” said Solomon, 42, whose $2,550 monthly rent at the East 118th Street building is paid by a city housing assistance program.
“I walk outside for hours daily simply to escape,” she said. “I am exhausted, distressed and emotionally drained.”
Miss Bubble, sometimes labeled Ms. Bubble, has 32 branches in Manhattan and Brooklyn, with a website calling it “New York’s best laundry service,” stating that “all of our work is done on our premises — we don’t use off-site services. This way we can manage and oversee every aspect of our cleaning process ensuring best practices for you and for us all.”
Solomon wonders whycommercial laundromatsare even allowed inside residential buildings.
“Behind that business listing is a tenant living with constant vibration, combustion fumes and chronic health symptoms, and a city enforcement system where every agency treats the problem as someone else’s job,” she said.
Last spring, Solomon sued the landlord, Akari Equities, to obtain repairs. The landlord’s lawyer, Eric Kahan, wrote in court documents that the landlord “never failed or refused to correct any violations in the subject premises,” but is also “willing and ready” to correct any that do exist.
And if the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development did issue any violations, the landlord “does not concede or agree that any report or violations as written or issued by HPD are accurate or that same constitute violations of law,” Kahan wrote.
He also wrote that no other residents of the 20-unit building have complained, and that Solomon didn’t grant access “to inspect the alleged conditions.”
Solomon, who was unable to obtain legal aid, withdrew the lawsuit because the issues she broached are not generally enforced through housing court, which deals primarily with maintenance concerns such as leaks, lead paint and lack of heat.
Kahan didn’t return requests for comment, nor did a Miss Bubble representative.
Desperate for relief, Solomon then spent months scrutinizing city records and attempting to navigate an uncaring bureaucracy. She has contacted multiple city agencies and officials, the main result being inspections marked “resolved” that resolve nothing.
“My goal is a livable home,” she told The Post.
Records from the Department of Buildings show that the certificate of occupancy allows for a tenant laundry room, which doesn’t currently exist, plus an eating and drinking establishment on the ground floor.
But, according to a DOB spokesman, the property has a “letter of no objection” that allows for the space to be legally converted into a laundromat.
At one point, a building inspector did issue a violation for the laundromat, but “the summons issued by the inspectors was reviewed by DOB attorneys, who determined that it was issued in error,” the spokesman said.
Solomon complained to the DOB that “the laundromat is making the building shake,” but the DOB claims otherwise.
“We have inspected this property multiple times in response to the constituent’s complaints and have not observed the shaking or vibration of the building … nor issued any enforcement actions for alleged unpermitted or illegal occupancy,” the spokesman said.
Though the 2023 building code has certain sound transmission standards for structure-borne noise, including an “impact insulation rating” for dwelling units sharing a floor or ceiling with a mechanical equipment space, “these modern code requirements are not retroactive,” and existing buildings need not comply, the spokesman said.
Severalother complaintsabout Miss Bubble were received before Solomon moved in. One neighbor complained about the laundromat ventilation “blowing toxic dust into my apartment … it is effecting [sic] my health.” Another complained of “air quality … so bad that it is affecting my love one causing asthma and other health issue.”
The fumes persist, said Solomon, who was frustrated by the Department of Environmental Protection’s response to her complaints about noise and air quality.
Last month, the DEP conducted an inspection, and “the complainant did not answer the door, so the inspector left a voicemail,” according to a DEP spokesman.
But nobody buzzed, Solomon said. “I got a call from an unknown number and missed it. They left a voicemail, but there was no number for me to call back.” The morning of the inspection was uncharacteristically quiet, she said, likely because management had been notified in advance.
“I came out of the shelter system through a city housing assistance program, and this apartment was supposed to be stable housing,” Solomon said. Her miserable situation shows “a systemic tenant protection failure.”
That’s true, saidAndrew Scherer, a professor at New York Law School and an expert in landlord-tenant law. “The system is wholly inadequate,” he told The Post.
“We haven’t made decent, affordable housing a reality for everybody. If the building doesn’t violate any codes, the city agencies almost never do anything affirmative or proactive. There is no routine enforcement or inspections. It’s all complaint-driven.”
The housing-court approach — going to court with a common-law nuisance or warranty-of-habitability case — is tough for someone with few resources and the inability to pay a lawyer, Scherer said. Free legal services prioritize people facing eviction.
“It’s not so much that there’s nothing that can be done,” Scherer told The Post. “It’s that there aren’t the resources to actually do it. Potential solutions would take significant effort on the part of this tenant. The system doesn’t have any automatic resolution to things like this, which is very unfortunate.”
A person can keep complaining, but “nothing is a sure shot,” Scherer said. In some cases tenants join forces, but Solomon believes the neighbors are afraid to complain too vociferously.
“MayorMamdani says‘government only works when it answers to the people it serves,’” Solomon said. “I spent months asking his agencies why their own records contradicted one another. I couldn’t get answers. So by the mayor’s own standard, who was government answering to?”
The mayor’s housing spokesman didn’t return requests for comment.
Solomon’s landlord has offered a penalty-free lease break, she said, and she would be glad to move, but it’s tough to find apartments that accept rental assistance and are in acceptable condition.
“I cannot resolve a health crisis by relocating into another one,” she said.

hed: Manhattan’s luxury rental market skyrockets — reaching $100K a month amid pied-à-terre tax
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Manhattan’s wealthiest residents just found a new way to dodge Mayor Zohran Mamdani’spied-à-terre tax: Don’t buy at all.
The city’s luxury rental market is shattering records as wealthy New Yorkers who could easily afford $20 million or $50 million trophy homes are choosing to rent instead, brokers say, a trend accelerating since the new tax on high-value second homes took effect.
Manhattan median rents hit $5,295 a month in July, a record high, up 6% compared with last July and unchanged from June’s plateau, according to a Corcoran Group report obtained byThe Post,with the average rent citywide up 10% year-over-year to $6,555.
But the real action is at the top.
The average price for luxury rentals, the top 10% of the market, soared 35% over the past year to $17,464 a month, or roughly $121 per square foot.
The number of apartments renting for more than $50,000 a month has more than doubled compared with 2025. Units renting for more than $100,000 a month are up sevenfold.
“The $100,000-a-month number is almost normal now,” Laura Klein of Bespoke Real Estate, who recently brokered a Chelsea penthouse rental for $177,000 a month, toldCNBC.“These are renters who want turnkey, unique, trophy properties.”
Two recent examples — a four-bedroom, five-bathroom penthouse in Tribeca at 161 Hudson St. just hit the market for a whopping $99,000 per month, listed with the Deborah Grubman Team at Corcoran. And a duplex penthouse with sweeping views overlooking Central Park at 988 Fifth Ave. listed for $95,000 per month, listed with Noble Black of Corcoran.
“To some degree, there are New York homeowners who’ve opted to lease out their luxury properties to avoidthe pending pied-à-terre tax, thus increasing the pool of high-end rentals,” Gary Malin, chief operating officer at the Corcoran Group, told The Post. “Leasing appeals to wealthy people who want to avoid the responsibilities that come with homeownership. As I like to say, renting is like dating a home but buying is like marrying it. When there’s any uncertainty around the future of the city, people are less inclined to make a serious long-term housing commitment.”
Keyan Sanai, a broker at Douglas Elliman, said he didn’t handle any rentals approaching $100,000 a month this summer, with $35,000 the priciest deal he closed. But he noticed what he called “one of the more surprising trends” of the season.
Luxury apartments that historically took longer to rent because of a smaller tenant pool “moved remarkably quickly,” he told The Post, while several more conventionally priced Manhattan units took longer to find tenants than usual.
The pattern, Sanai said, “suggested that demand at the high end was unusually decisive, while renters in the broader market were becoming more price-sensitive and selective.”
Historically, renters were people who couldn’t yet afford to buy. Now the opposite is happening. A record low supply of high-end properties for sale has pushed cash-flush buyers into rentals while they wait for their dream home, and falling or flat resale prices have made ownership look like a worse investment.
Adding to the calculus is Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax. The levy applies to one-, two- and three-family homes, condos and co-ops valued at $5 million or more where the owner’s primary residence is elsewhere.
For the first two tax years, properties assessed between $1 million and $3 million face a 4% annual surcharge, those between $3 million and $5 million face 5.25% and those above $5 million face 6.5%.
The tax is projected to raise at least $500 million a year for the city, and roughly 17,000 letters have already gone out to property owners who may owe it, though many can contest the designation by proving the home is a primary residence or a rental.
Brokers say the tax has added fresh fuel to the shift toward renting.
“The sharp increase in rentals following the pied-à-terre tax announcement suggests that some prospective purchasers may already be choosing flexibility over ownership,” Pam Liebman, president and CEO of the Corcoran Group, said.
Klein said none of the ultra-high-end rentals she handles are publicly listed. They move quietly through a small network of brokers to wealthy clients. She currently has a $175,000-a-month rental in Tribeca and a $95,000-a-month unit on the Upper East Side.
“There is so little inventory. And they don’t want to compromise,” Klein said of her clients, who she said can easily afford $20 million to $50 million trophy homes but are opting to rent instead.
The owners renting out these properties don’t need the income, Klein said, but are cashing in on demand.
“They say to me, ‘If the number is right, I’ll rent,’” Klein said. “These are properties that if they were on the market would be listed for tens of millions” of dollars.
The tax has not been without controversy. President Trump, whose Trump Tower apartment could fall under the new levy, hascriticized it publicly,and Mamdani’s administration has spent recent weeks clarifying who is actually on the hook as confused homeowners flood the Department of Finance with questions.

hed: Artists scooped up this SoCal beach retreat for $10K in the ’60s — now it’s listed at a wild 43,000% markup
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A modest Southern California tract house that was built in 1960 and sold during that decade for under $11,000has hit the market for the first time in six decades— now listed at $4.25 million,representing a nearly 43,000% price increase.
Long before coastal San Diego real estate became a seven-figure game, artists Wayne and Barbara Chapman purchased their home inSolana Beachfor the princely sum of $10,900.
But the Chapmans didn’t simply own the house: They transformed it into a highly personal, living, breathing work of organic architecture.
After marrying in 1969, the couple hiredvisionary San Diego organic architectKendrick Bangs Kellogg to completely reimagine the house, turning it into what can only be described as a tropical retreat filled with magic and whimsy.
The Chapmans purchased the property simply as an affordable home. They then had Kellogg completely reinvent it during the 1970s. The couple didn’t just hand over the keys — they got their hands dirty and helped build it.
In an interview withSan Diego Magazinein 2025, Wayne Chapman told the outlet, “We dreamed of having a house like this where we could work at our crafts. [Kendrick Bangs] Kellogg designed this house; Barbara was friends with his wife. A fireman who lived nearby and I built it together. Every piece of wood in this house has got my fingerprints on it. Barbara did the interior design.”
True to Kellogg’s collaborative style, the Chapmans took a hands-on role. Ceramist Wayne Chapman managed construction and worked the site himself alongside his firefighter friend and community fixture Jim Baker, who had been the fire chief of the Del Mar Fire Department.
Wayne Chapman sourced massive utility poles and thousands of feet of rough-sawn redwood boards from a local lumber yard. Barbara — a craftswoman and fiber artist who taught crafting at an Encinitas gallery for more than 40 years — shaped the interiors with her exceptional eye for color and texture.
When it comes to the renovations, property expansions and a heartbreaking rebuild in 2001, this works out to a 42,650% increase in the listing price, one of the more eye-catching yet worthy appreciation stories onSan Diego County’s north coast.
What makes the price jump even more eyewatering is what the house became.
The result is a roughly 3,900-square-foot, three-bed, three-bath multi-story, split-level composition of wood and glass that feels more like a live-in sculpture than merely a conventional beach house. Decorative short stairs replace traditional walls, creating a flowing sequence of levels coupled with bright, open spaces.
Kellogg’s signature sculptural fireplaces are sprinkled throughout. Hand-carved doors open onto lush Japanese-inspired gardens. A dedicated ceramics studio and ocean views from the living room complete the picture.
Listing agent Keith A. York describes the home to The California Post: “The Chapman home elicits emotional responses from all visitors as they delight in the garden sculptures and plantings through to each and every interior space bathed in natural light.
“Exemplifying the unique architect-client relationship, Ken Kellogg’s detailing was brought to life by the client’s sweat and handiwork. The home therefore is as much artistic-creation as it is architect-design.”

For decades the home served as both residence and creative workshop. The Chapmans filled it with their own ceramics, textiles and global folk art, and for more than 40 years they hosted pottery sales on the property.
A serious fire in 2001 damaged the wood-heavy structure, but the couple extensively repaired and continued living there.
Wayne Chapman, a former Marine who later worked as a San Diego police officer and probation officer before dedicating his life to his art, kept making pottery into his mid-90s. Barbara Chapman, a skilled craftswoman who once had work shown at the Louvre, passed in 2022 after nearly 54 years of marriage. Wayne Chapman died in 2025 at age 94.
Now, after a lifetime of art, craft and careful stewardship, the house the couple transformed will finally pass those keys to a new owner.
For a property that began its life as the cheapest home a young couple of artists could afford in Solana Beach, it has evolved into a one-of-a-kind architectural statement in collaboration with one of the Golden State’s most distinctive organic architects.
The leap from under $11,000 to multimillion-dollar retreat stands as one of the more dramatic yet deserved real estate appreciation stories on the SoCal coast.

hed: AI’s overnight millionaires create absurd mansion shortage in San Francisco
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
San Francisco’s artificial intelligence boomhas created a new class of tech millionaires so quickly that the city is now facing an unlikely problem — a shortage of mansions.
Wealthy AI execs and workers are entering the city’s cutthroat housing market, driving bidding wars, record sales and sky-high prices as companies expand their local workforces.
The frenzy comes as companies like OpenAI and Anthropic prepare to go public, a process that has unleashed a wave of new wealth with more to come, according toNPR.
At the top of the market, buyers making all-cash offers of $25 million or more have still been outbid for coveted properties.
The mix of newly wealthy buyers and a limited supply of single-family homes has become so extreme that real estate brokerage Compass and others call it a “mansion shortage.”
The median San Francisco home sale price has jumped 25% from a year ago, according to Compass data cited by NPR.
In June, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million above their asking prices, Compass chief economist Mike Simonsen told the outlet.
Competition is intense even for less expensive homes.
Part of the buying spree comes from ageneration of AI executiveswho are now looking for larger homes.
Many are in their mid-30s or early 40s with young children, creating urgency to secure homes in desirable neighborhoods near schools, according to Simonsen.
So far, some of the most dramatic price increases have been concentrated in San Francisco’s wealthier enclaves.
The rise in AI wealth is also making it harder for people who aren’t looking for mansions.
San Francisco rentersare facing bidding wars as well-paid tech workers in their 20s move in, some able to spend up to $10,000 a month.
Listings get a lot of attention within hours, and renters say that bids often go hundreds of dollars above the listed price.

For people who don’t work in tech, the sudden jump in housing costs is making an already expensive city even harder to afford.
Alex Brenner, 29, who works in healthcare, said he and his fiancée encountered lines of prospective tenants at open houses and saw the rent on one apartment rise twice by $500 before they even viewed it.
“It’s actually ridiculous,” Brenner told NPR.
Market analyst Jonathan Miller explained that San Francisco is increasingly undergoing a “New York-ification” of its real estate market.
The prices no longer reflect just the property itself but also the premium buyers are willing to pay to be at the center of a powerful economic hub, he told NPR.
“It’s like buying a one-bedroom apartment without great views in Manhattan and it costs you $3 million, and you tell that to somebody in Des Moines, Iowa, and they’re like, ‘There’s something wrong with you,'” Miller said.

hed: Middle-aged renters are ‘speed-roommating’ to find housemates amid California’s sky-high cost of living
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Who says bunking up is only for the young?
Digitally fatiguedCalifornians in their 40s, 50s and 60sare flocking to monthly “speed-roommating” events in Hollywood, searching for the perfect housemate amidincreasingly high costs of living.
The trendy event is hosted by SpareRoom, an online roommate-finding platform that operates in the US and the UK. For many attendees, living alone has become unrealistic even as they age.
Amanda Hart, 46, has leased her three-bedroom Valley Village apartment for nine years. And though her apartment is rent-controlled, she still needs help.
“Two years ago, I was able to have my three-bedroom all to myself. The way the economy is, I definitely have to have roommates now,” Hart, a film industry professional who says her industry has “tanked because our mayors let us down,” told The California Post.
“I probably will live in my apartment forever because it is rent-controlled, which we definitely need,” said Hart.
“We sadly need it, I wish we didn’t, but we have to because I’ve heard of friends that their rent will go up $300 to $500 after their year lease ends.”
Loosely based on speed-dating, participants at SpareRoom’s speed-roommating events each wear a name tag filled out with their budget, neighborhood, and whether they’re looking for a roommate or a tenant.
The platform started hosting the events in the UK in 2007, and has since expended the mixers to London, Los Angeles and San Diego.
At the gatherings, participants are free to mix, mingle, and if they’re lucky, exchange details of their properties.
“You immediately get a sense of what people need, what their intentions are,” said Leetal Platt, 40, a tailor looking for a roommate to help her pay to live in her “fairly large” space in Hollywood.
“It kind of is cutting out some of the fat, and being like very direct, ‘Who are you? What are you looking for? What’s the price? Do we vibe?’”

In LA, the event happens monthly at Sassafras Saloon, a Western-themed bar in Hollywood.
Most of the guests at a recent night there said they showed up because the process of finding a roommate is much easier in person than digitally.
“I’ve tried online, and you kind of meet a range of people. I prefer to try and engage with someone in person because I feel like what you can’t see behind a camera, you can see in person,” said Nwabudike Washington, 36, a fundraising professional who lives in downtown LA.
Still, certain demographics prevail. SpareRoom says their events are popular among older renters.
“We’re seeing people not only sharing for longer, but people living with roommates in their 40s, 50s, 60s, and actually the older groups are growing faster than the younger groups because people just can’t afford to live either on their own or look to buy a place,” said Matt Hutchinson, director of SpareRoom.
“The events are particularly interesting for some of the older renters who might feel a bit intimidated, thinking that living with roommates, they’re going to have to deal with a bunch of people in their 20s and 30s, and they’ll feel a bit awkward about that. And actually, you get in the room and you see the range of people there.”
A July report from Realtor.comshowed that rents in LA County hit a four-year low in the second quarter of 2026, with the overall median rent falling to $2,603.
Despite this, Realtor.com says renters, in particular young ones, are still likely tospend a large portion of their income on rent.
“Even with recent declines, many new graduates will still spend around or more than the recommended 30% of their income on rent. While conditions are improving, entry-level workers in many fields continue to face difficult housing tradeoffs,” said Jiayi Xu, economist at Realtor.com.
While many came to speed-roommating on a mission, others were just looking for someone to keep them company.
“I can afford to live in my place by myself, I just prefer to have someone around,” said Johnny Yamamoto, 54, of West Hollywood.
But even those looking for temporary accommodation bemoaned the rising cost of living.
Albrik Keshishian, 66, who splits his time between Europe and LA, typically stays with his niece while in SoCal. But the retiree is now looking for a rental for his next visit, with a monthly budget of $800 to $1,000.
Keshishian lived in LA for decades, purchasing a property in Glendale in 1989 before selling it in 2022. Today, the property’s worth stuns him.
“I sold my property in 2022. My property now is worth $2.5 million, and I sold it for $1.2 million. It’s crazy,” said Keshishian. “Good luck to the person who bought it, but what I’m saying is the average American is going to find it very tough if they don’t have help from their families for a down payment.
“The whole world has become so expensive,” Keshishian continued. “It’s going to be very difficult for the new generation. I’m retired, but it’s going to be tough. Something has to give.”

hed: Mysterious Bitcoin investor quickly sells Miami mansion for $51.5M as his whereabouts remain unknown
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A 41-year-oldGeorgian Bitcoin investorand financier whose life reads like a John Le Carré spy novel has sold his just-built Miami mansion on guard-gated Hibiscus Island for $51.5 million.
The sale is a record for Hibiscus and Palm islands, surpassing a 2024 sale, when“mysterious Miami party boy”Daniel Liburdi paid $40.25 million for 101 North Hibiscus Drive.
Before listing this property, Giorgi “George” Bachiashvili fled Tbilisi, Georgia shortly before he was sentenced in absentia to 11 years in prison on March 10, 2025, for allegedly embezzling cryptocurrency from his former boss — Georgia’s most powerful man, Bidzina Ivanishvili, the former prime minister. Bachiashvili denied the charges and called them politically motivated.
Bachiashvili was then allegedly abducted from Abu Dhabi on May 24, 2025, and brought back to Georgia, where he was imprisoned by his ex-boss. His sentence was suspended following a plea deal, and he was released from prison after less than a year, in February.
Bachiashvili’s whereabouts remain secret, his lawyer, Peter J. Sahlas, of Amsterdam & Partners, told Gimme Shelter.
In mid-August, around six months after his release from prison, Bachiashvili listed this Miami home for $55 million. It sold 11 days later to a mystery buyer for $51.5 million.
The sale wasfirst reported by the Real Deal.
The modern mansion at 270 South Hibiscus Drive comes with five bedrooms, a maid’s quarters, six full baths, two half baths, a home office, a gym and 120 feet of water frontage. Inside, there’s also a large foyer, a double-height great room and a chef’s kitchen.
Bachiashvili bought the property for $19 million in 2021, according to records. At the time, it was “an incomplete shell of a home still under construction,” a source said. He later hired South African firm SAOTA to design the property.
Extravagant features include a soundproof home theater with a bar. There’s also a pool and two private docks — as the home sits on two bayfront lots — that can hold at least one 105-foot-long yacht.
The listing broker was Jordan Karp of Jordan Karp LLC; the buyer’s broker was Dora Puig of Luxe Living Realty.

hed: Travis Kelce bought a sprawling lakefront mansion months before marrying Taylor Swift
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Travis Kelce closed on an Ohio mansion for $5.35 million back in March, snapping up the Lake Erie estate months before hemade Taylor Swift his wifeat Madison Square Garden in July.
The Bratenahl property initially listed for $5.99 million after being freshly renovated, and the deal closed on March 2, according to listing records reviewed by theWall Street Journal.
Built in 1895, the sprawling 21,140-square-foot compound sits on 3.5 acres along the water and comes stacked with eight bedrooms, eight full and three half baths, and a five-car garage.
The Cuyahoga County native grew up just a few miles away in Cleveland Heights, and the home’s location near a private airstrip should make life easier for a couple juggling a real estate footprint that’s already climbed into double digits.
Swift broughther own collectioninto the marriage, including a Manhattan condo and homes scattered across Rhode Island, Nashville and California, while Kelce arrived with his own place in Kansas City.
David Ayers, who brokered the deal alongside Nick Zawitz of The Agency Cleveland, said the Gilded Age property blends old world charm with a serious glow-up.
“Meticulously restored original details paired with its exceptional modern amenities has created a truly rare Great Lakes estate,” Ayers told The Post in a statement. “We’re thrilled for the new owners and so excited for Cleveland.”
The mansion buy wasn’t the only headline out of Kelce’s world this week. He and Swift also introduced the world to their new Samoyed puppy Wendy, who made hermodeling debut in a Tommy Hilfigercampaign shoot on the roof of the Plaza Hotel.
Kelce told Vogue the brand needed a dog for the shoot and he didn’t hesitate to volunteer his own.
“We figured, why not her? She crushed it and actually really fit into that Tommy aesthetic, too,” he said. “Those are some of my favorite shots.”
Of his new pup, he added simply, “She lights up my day.”

hed: Furious backlash over $5K San Francisco rental listing: ‘These landlords are literal demons’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
San Francisco renters are once again asking:How much?!
A one-bedroom apartment in the ritzy Pacific Heights neighborhood has sparked a firestorm online after being teased for a jaw-dropping $5,495 a month — despite what commenters described as a dated kitchen, dingy carpet and a small patio.
Real estate agent Thomas Baboinposted about the upcoming listingfor the apartment at 2321 Scott St., pitching it as an “SF Icon” in “Prime Pac Heights.”
The internet was not impressed.
“$5,500 for something that hasn’t been updated since ‘Guess who’s coming to Dinner?’ With a prison cell patio?!” one commenter wrote.
Another added: “Almost $6k and no in-unit laundry? These landlords are literal demons.”
The apartment’s carpet took a particularly brutal beating.
“Diabolical with that carpet,” one commenter wrote, while another called it a “CARPETED DUNEGON FROM THE EARLY 90s AND NO WINDOWS FOR NEARLY 6 GRAND?!!!? WHACKKK.”
Others questioned who could possibly afford the place. “1 bedroom and 5k… read that again,” one person wrote. “This is what a mortgage cost on a $1 million house,” another added.
One Pacific Heights resident claimed their own one-bedroom costs less than $4,000 and comes with 700 square feet and Bay views.
“I live in PAC Heights in a one bedroom and can tell you that this looks like a 70s renovation with old carpets.
“My place is not even $4,000 and it has views of the bay and 700 sq ft. This is a terrible price and I feel bad for anyone forced to be paying this.”
The listing’s comment section quickly piled up with dozens of reactions, ranging from disbelief to outright fury.
“This has to be the worst apartment for the price I’ve ever seen. Bravo,” one commenter wrote. Another summed up the mood: “$5495 for CARPET??? Nobody wants that.”
The sticker shock comes as San Francisco continues to grapple with some of the nation’s most punishing housing costs.
A recent Zumper analysis found the median one-bedroom rent in the city had climbed to more than $4,000, with limited housing supply and the booming tech sector helping fuel prices.
And apparently, $4,000 is just the starting point.

hed: San Francisco’s drug-addled Union Square gets a rebirth with $75M bet from rookie real estate investors
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Just two years ago, downtown San Francisco’s commercial real estate was in a grim position.
Retailers fled, and empty storefronts had turned Union Square — once the city’s crown jewel — into a state of disrepair, withopen-air drug markets, homeless zombies and crime pushing out customers.
Downtown office real estate sales in 2024 slumped to $310-per-square-foot on average — almost two-thirds below the $861 average of 2018, according to CBRE.
However, Union Square’s fortunes are now in the process of adramatic reversal— thanks togood governanceand private investment.
Clothing brand Uniqlo, which had left Union Square in 2021, has signed a lease and is set to reopen later this year. Zara is set to expand to a four-story, 40,000-square-foot flagship store. They will join a Nintendo store, which has commanded lines around the block, The RealReal, Aritzia, Pop Mart and AT&T. Kith has signed a lease and Nordstrom and Bloomingdale’s are said to be eyeing space.
In the middle of that remarkable turnaround is a nascent firm, Uris Acquisitions, helmed by Max Raskin, 36, and Ian Jacobs, 49. The pair began snapping up real estate just months after Mayor Daniel Lurie took office in Jan. 2025.
Their conviction was that San Francisco wasn’t dead, but struggling — with problems they believed Lurie could rapidly fix. They began raising capital ahead of his campaign and have deployed almost all of it, $75 million, in just the last 15 months.
“Forget blood in the streets,” Raskin joked — a reference to a popular investment maxim. “We bought when there was feces in the street.”
Jacobs is from a family of real estate investors, but had first focused on finance at Goldman Sachs, then later as a Warren Buffett analyst, picked after writing him a fan letter.
Raskin worked as a journalist at Bloomberg and Morgan Stanley before landing at law school, then the Treasury Department. He has a good head for politics — and a belief that the greatest cities in the world always make a comeback. Although he now only occasionally writes, he met Lurie when interviewing him for a story.
Their relationship with Lurie has proven key to their success. “We feel a real partnership with the city,” Raskin explains. “It’s just, ‘Hey, what can we do to help out?’
“It’s not rocket science. It just takes a lot of willpower… You just arrest the criminals and you don’t give them drugs.”
Mayor Lurie, for his part, is clear that, “If we make the streets safe and clean, people will want to be here. When people don’t feel safe, nothing else matters.”
“Government needs to do its job, which is providing the basics. If we provide the basics, the city can sell itself.”
Lurie isn’t only taking Raskin’s calls. When Jamie Dimon was in town for JPMorgan’s 2025 annual healthcare conference — an event which, in 2021,The Post reportedexecs were “pleading” with the company to cancel due to the out-of-control crime — Lurie invited him to City Hall afterward. It was Dimon’s first time inside the building.
JPMorgan then recently announced it’s not just expanding its office but also making San Francisco its 24th corporate center and putting $200 million into a waterfront housing project.
All of those calls have helped Lurie implement common-sense reforms — like making it far easier to get building permits, which previously had stood in the way of new development.
“Retailers have been dating San Francisco, waiting to fall in love again … waiting for an indication that the time was right and that the frog had turned back into a prince,” joked Julie Taylor, the realtor Uris has used to purchase property.
“It’s really a full gut remodel of Union Square…  We’re going to have fresh brands in every door.”
Since early 2025, Uris has acquired five buildings in and around Union Square: 200 Powell, 35 Powell, 71 Powell, 120 Maiden Lane and 233 Grant. They are also under contract for two more buildings in Union Square.
Of course, there are still challenges with homelessness and crime and people who are wary of change. And while Uris made the bet that effective government could resolve the biggest problems, there is not a guarantee that type of governance will last.
But Raskin says his optimism and positivity have helped.
“We didn’t know it was going to be the AI boom, but we knew something was going to boom… We just bet on people. We bet on smart people, and we bet on cities.”

hed: Chris Evans fetches $5.38M for the LA home where he trained to become Captain America
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Chris Evans has officially assembled a buyer for his longtime Los Angeles home — but the deal came with a super-sized discount.
The “Captain America” star sold his secluded Hollywood Hills estate for $5.38 million, more than $1.6 million below the $6.99 millionhe originally soughtlast year, according toRealtor.com.
The home also comes with some serious superhero history: Its detached guesthouse contains the gym where Evans trained to transform into Captain America for the Marvel blockbusters.
Evans, 45, first listed the home in May 2025 before pulling it from the market that November. He brought it back in June at the reduced price of $6.39 million — meaning the final deal still landed roughly $1 million below its latest asking price.
But the actor did not exactly walk away empty-handed. He purchased the property for $3.52 million in 2013, leaving him with a gross gain of about $1.86 million before accounting for renovations and other costs, according tothe Wall Street Journal.
The sale marks Evans’ long-planned departure from California as he settles on the East Coast with his wife, Portuguese actress Alba Baptista, and their daughter, Alma.
“The West Coast is beautiful, and I’ve spent more than a decade in this home enjoying Los Angeles,” Evans told The Post when the property was listed last year. “But I’ve decided to spend more time on the East Coast. It feels like the right moment to pass this beautiful property to the next owner.”
The Massachusetts native and Baptista married during a private ceremony on Cape Cod in 2023. They reportedly also own a home near Evans’ hometown of Sudbury, outside Boston.
Built in 1940, the approximately 4,600-square-foot Hollywood Hills residence sits on 0.76 acres and offers sweeping views of Laurel Canyon and the Santa Monica Mountains.
The four-bedroom spread features an open-plan living area with a fireplace, a formal dining space with a wet bar, and a kitchen equipped with a 60-inch Wolf range, marble countertops and skylights.
Evans’ primary suite comes with its own terrace, a walk-in closet and a spa-like bathroom featuring a soaking tub and a steam shower.
Outside, landscaped terraces and stone pathways lead to a swimming pool, a spa and a fire pit overlooking the canyon.
The detached guesthouse — home to Evans’ Captain America training ground — also includes a bedroom, a kitchen and an office.
Evans made a number of upgrades during his 12 years at the property, including adding a retaining wall that expanded the usable outdoor space, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The home was listed with Scott Moore of Christie’s International Real Estate Southern California. The buyer’s identity has not been disclosed.

hed: New images reveal Michael Jordan’s North Carolina lakefront mansion — now nearing completion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Michael Jordan is rebuilding his North Carolina lake life from the ground up, literally.
Fresh aerial shots reveal the NBA legend’s under-construction estate on Lake Norman in Cornelius finally has a roofline and frame, more than a year after the bulldozers leveled the previous mansion on the site.
The Jordan Family Gift Trust snapped up the original property back in 2013 for $2.8 million, a six-bedroom, eight-bath spread with its own pier.
By last spring the wrecking crews had moved in, clearing the way for whatever custom build Jordan had planned next.
The plot sits tucked inside the exclusive Peninsula Club, with one shot capturing a tee box and fairway practically brushing up against the property line. It’s a fitting flex for the six-time champion, who has quietly built one of the most eye-popping real estate portfolios in sports.
North Carolina remains a cornerstone of that empire. Beyond the lakefront project, Jordan owns a 7,000-square-foot spread in Uptown Charlotte, stitched together from two penthouse condos he grabbed in 2010 for a combined $3.15 million.
But his true home base sits far south, inside Jack Nicklaus’ guarded Bear’s Club enclave in Jupiter, Florida, where his original 28,000-square-foot compound comes loaded with a private court and a full athletic setup.
He doubled down there in 2024, dropping millions more on a five-bedroom secondary house nearby to expand his footprint in the neighborhood.
The portfolio tells the story of a man constantly upgrading. Long before Jupiter, Jordan and wife Yvette Prieto started small with a modest three-bedroom place in Miami picked up for around $281,000.
He’s also cycled through a Park City, Utah mountain retreat he sold in 2020, and a Lake Michigan penthouse from his Bulls dynasty years that eventually went to ex-wife Juanita Vanoy in their divorce settlement.
And then there’s the crown jewel of them all, the 56,000-square-foot Highland Park, Illinois compound famous for its number 23 gate, whichfinally found a buyerin December 2024 for $9.5 million after more than a decadelanguishing on the market.
While his real estate game stays red hot, Jordan’s broadcasting gig is cooling off fast.
The Hall of Famer’s brief run as an NBC Sports “special contributor” appears to be over almost as soon as it began, with reports suggesting he won’t be back for the 2026-27 season.
Fans expected regular commentary when the deal was announced last spring, but Jordan delivered just one interview with host Mike Tirico all season, doled out in pieces across several weeks.
Tirico pushed back on the criticism that followed, telling Sports Illustrated, “Michael doesn’t talk much, as you know. Michael still has so many interests in the game, business interests, with a piece of the [Charlotte] Hornets and obviously his involvement with [Jordan Brand].”

hed: Before and after: Two bathroom renos for under $91k — one landed in Architectural Digest
subhead: Dreaming of green tile since high school, here’s how a Cambridge couple made the most of a double bathroom (plus pantry) renovation
content:
ByLauren Daley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Cambridge’s Nick Andersen and Luke Massa were in San Francisco for a friend’s wedding, but they just had to make a pit stop to see their tile source.

The couple had just finished renovating their condo with two dream bathrooms tiled inHeath Ceramics. While checking out with a vase, Andersen told the cashier about the bathroom renovations, and she said, “‘Oh my God. I know your bathrooms. Everyone here knows your bathrooms.’”

The couple’s bathrooms — both a green-tiled main bathroom and a blue-tiled powder room — are now featured on Heath’s site as thedefinition of bathroom inspiration.

“I was ashamed of how affirming it was that the people at the tile warehouse knew our bathroom, but it absolutely was,” said Andersen.

The main bathroom also landed in aJanuary Architectural Digest roundup, along with a few other Massachusetts bathrooms.

After meeting in 2015 at a local potluck dinner, Andersen, an audio producer/cheesemonger, and Massa, a software engineer at TripAdvisor, moved into a spot right on the Cambridge/Somerville line. Literally. The town line runs through their home. “It’s a nightmare,” Andersen quipped.

They bought the condo in 2019, and by 2024, they wanted to renovate their main bathroom and turn part of the pantry into a powder room. Through an ex-boyfriend of Andersen’s, they connected with Doug Jack of Boston-basedNidify Studioto create two dream bathrooms and a pantry for under $91,000.



“Nick sent the most beautiful program email I’ve ever received. It had such clear vision and purpose. I gravitated towards it because they wanted to do something visionary,” said Jack. “For most people, the program email is a quantitative list: ‘I need a bedroom, a big kitchen, etc.’ Nick’s was qualitative with design detail. He said he’d loved a particular lobby at his [Michigan] high school, with greenPewabic tile. I had to look it up.”

“Luke makes fun of me because he’s like, ‘I don’t know if I remember the lobby of my high school — and I certainly wouldn’t want our bathroom to look like that,’” Andersen added.

They ended up not using Pewabic tile — a 123-year-old Detroit-based pottery maker — but the inspiration remained.

“From the start, I said if we’re building a bathroom around special tile, we can’t just find some random cheap tile from a big factory. The tile itself is part of the narrative,” said Jack. “I thought of [California-based] Heath Ceramics. Everything is handmade, one batch at the time.Each tile is unique. From a distance, it looks united. But close up, each tile feels different. You can tell it’s not from a big factory.”




The powder room took space from the existing pantry, which is underneath the home’s staircase. Gravitating toward primary colors, they chose a bright cerulean blue. The remaining smaller pantry space was outfitted with closed cabinetry to keep everything tidy.

Speaking of looking tidy, Jack said they made conscious design choices to “curate the view” of the spaces.

“You’ll notice in the photographs the toilet doesn’t appear — that’s by design. Basically, it’s rotated 90 degrees, and tucked around the corner,” he said.

In terms of staying on budget, Jack’s advice is to choose just a few focal design elements that will have a high impact and not cheap out on them. Andersen and Massa splurged on some luxuries: the tile, radiant heat in the full bathroom, a shower that allows users to choose their exact temperature, and a yellowconcrete sink from Kast for the half-bath.


“Where we saved: we scrapped the idea for a second window in the main bathroom. It’s a little darker in that area — it would’ve been nice to have light — but [we saved there],” said Andersen. “We also saved on the structure. Some of Doug’s original ideas would’ve changed the physical structure, like moving a wall. In the end, we saved and stayed with the same footprint.”

“At one point, the bathroom door was getting really tight on the jam trim with new finishes. Instead of replacing the door, we slimmed down the plaster,” added Jack. “A renovation in an old home like this, those forks in the road happen frequently, and Nick and Luke were good at sticking to the more frugal options.

“Also, the yellow sink sits on stone. We saved money by going to a local stone yard,Dover Stone,and looking through the remnant pile,” said Jack. “You can find smaller pieces at a really great rate.”

“Doug gave us an array of options, which made us feel good about the choices that we went with— it didn’t feel like we were being stingy or extravagant,” said Massa


Final advice to aspiring remodelers:

“Looking back, we probably shouldn’t have done both bathrooms at once because we had no bathroom for a very long time. We’re very grateful that a friend of ours in this building let us shower for seven months,” said Andersen. “We had a Bath Ball to celebrate when renovations were finished … We crowned our upstairs neighbor the Queen of the Bath Ball with a tiara because she let us use her bathroom for so long.”


Designer: Doug Jack,Nidify Studio— Boston

hed: Lou Dobbs’ 283-acre NJ farm asks $6M — where the late anchor hosted his storied July 4th parties
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A 283-acre New Jersey farm owned by the late television personalityLou Dobbsis on the market for $6 million, its listing brokerage told Gimme Shelter.
Hickory Hollow Farm is where Dobbs and his wife, Debi, a former CNN sports anchor, hosted their annual Fourth of July parties.
Those all-day celebrations, where media stars and political consultants mixed with locals and newsroom staff, featured a live band and fireworks — along with scavenger hunts, swimming and pony rides for the kids.
“We wanted to share our unique farm and all it had to offer,” Debi told Gimme Shelter.
Those who attended the glam festivities over the years included Fox Business host Stuart Varney and his family, as well as political consultant Ed Rollins and top Douglas Elliman real estate broker Shari Scharfer Rollins — as well as the entrepreneur, political activist and former US Ambassador to Poland Georgette Mosbacher.
The massive estate was fitting for such a larger-than-life personality, friends said.
“The parties were always fabulous,” said one friend who attended, but declined to be named. “It’s a beautiful farm.”
The estate is anchored by a five-bedroom Colonial home. There’s also a two-bedroom guest cottage, a two-bedroom caretaker’s cottage, a pool, a tennis court, plus an 11-acre pond stocked with fish.
Dobbs, who passed away at age 78 in 2024, was an original CNN anchor and chief correspondent for the network when it launched in 1980. He was known for hosting his show, “Moneyline,” which was later renamed “Lou Dobbs Tonight.”
By 2011, Dobbs had moved to the Fox Business Network, where he hosted “Lou Dobbs Tonight” until 2021. Throughout his career, he remained ahead of his time when it came to championing conservative issues.
“There’s nothing fair and balanced about me,”said Dobbsin a New York Times interview in 2006. “Because there’s nothing fair and balanced about the truth.”
Hickory Hollow Farm’s main house was built in 1977 and acquired by the Dobbs family in 1984. It has been expanded over time to its current 283 acres.
New owners can determine what’s next, notes the listing — from Weichert Realtors’ Jaime Luongo — suggesting the addition of potential amenities like a helipad and a golf course.
The property is categorized as farmland assessed, not preserved, which means there are development options, the listing also notes.
Outside, there is also a spring-fed well water and a generator with a 2,000-gallon propane tank.
Inside, a family room features floor-to-ceiling windows that overlook an 11-acre pond, while the back wall of windows looks to the pool, a tennis court with a half basketball court and the back paddock.
A chef’s kitchen features a two-tiered breakfast bar that looks out to the garden. There’s also a home office off the kitchen, a dining room and a sunroom with bluestone floors.
Downstairs, an unfinished basement awaits new vision. The grounds also include a main barn with 12 large stalls and a hayloft. There’s also a sand ring and a fenced riding area.

hed: Billionaire pharma heir wants $35M for LA mansion as he prepares to build the world’s biggest yacht
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
He’s looking to “seas” the day.
Billionaire pharmaceutical heir Frank Binder is lifting the anchor on his dazzlingLenny Kravitz-designedHollywood Hills mansion as he prepares to build the world’s largest yacht.
Binder listed the cliffside estate for $35 million late last week, a 10,700-square-foot combination of rock-and-roll swagger, and unparalleled views extending from Los Angeles to the Pacific Ocean.
Simultaneously, Binder is launching construction of his Nimitz-sized “residential yacht,” a more than $2 billion project that will offer ocean adventures and permanent digs to the ultra-wealthy.
Back in LA, the home comes with plenty of Kravitz flavor.
The four-consecutive Grammy winner, not surprisingly crafted a killer sound system and installed a 12-foot-long digital video wall and a floor-to-ceiling TV.
Binder reportedly spent $2 million for retractable doors throughout the mansion’s three levels that contain four bedrooms and seven bathrooms, all perched just above the storied Sunset Strip.
Living areas feature deep crimsons, amber glow lines and smoky accent mirrors that reflect the neon lights of los Angeles.
Getting into the home is half the adventure. Heavy bronze entry gates lead to the front door through a walkway bored through a massive wall of raw Hawaiian lava rock.
A 12,000-pound granite boulder has a firepit as its center and a 15-foot-wide gas fireplace sits in the home’s upper living level. Twenty-one-foot-high ceilings frame retractable glass walls that open onto a cantilevered balcony overlooking Los Angeles. A 70-foot-wide half-moon infinity pool faces that way as well.
In addition to its very high-end sound system, the home’s subterranean night club takes a “space themed retro” approach, while a climate-controlled wine cellar capable of 1,200 bottles is nearby.
An unobtrusive air-conditioned five-car garage conceals autos by using a hydraulic lift, and there are additional spaces nearby.
Binder, who holds the Hollywood Hills home through a shell company, paid $33 million for it in 2018. The mansion was offered at $38 million through a private listing.
It’s not clear whether Binder will keep the adjacent 4.5-acre parcel at 1 Electra Ct. that he holds through a separate corporate vehicle. He won that property for $29.5 million at auction in 2018 as part of the dissolution of Woodbridge Group of Companies. The development company was implicated and liquidated on the heels of an alleged $1.2 billion Ponzi scheme that defrauded more than 8,400 people. The Electra Court home, which Binder tore down, was owned by Larry Ellison’s daughterMegan Ellisonbefore that.
By listing the main house for just $2 million more than he paid for it six years ago, Binder may be among the first to accept the deflated reality of selling a mega-mansion in the Los Angeles area. He is also looking at a $1.92 million haircut based onthe 5.5% mansion taxthat Los Angeles City levies on residential sales.
“The owner is being realistic in this marketplace,” said Branden Williams of the Beverly Hills Estates, who has the listing withMauricio Umanskyof the Agency.
Umansky and Kravitz are also part of the team for Binder’sresidence-on-the-sea Ulyssia, with the former launching the craft’s marketing campaign on his “Buying Beverly Hills” Netflix show and the latter lending his design hand.
The Ulyssia is expected to cost more than $2 billion to build and be 1,060 feet long — about the length of modern US Navy aircraft carrier. The ship will have 15 decks with 122 private residences and 22 guest suites.
High-rolling residents will pay between $10 million and $90 million for rooms that will range in size from 1,184 square feet for a one-bedroom to 10,258 square feet for a six-bedroom penthouse. Outdoor terraces are included.
The ship will sail under the Swiss flag year-round and provide access to helicopters, two submarines, a school for residents’ children, a hospital and a dental facility.
Binder has told boating publications he already has more than $1 billion in commitments. He will be aboard as owner of the ship’s largest unit, a 10,700-square-foot top deck penthouse.
Binder expects to begin calling “Ahoy,” to those mateys in 2031.
Most landlubbers will have to stay behind, though. “We will, of course, select [the residents] and it’ll be the most exclusive club in the world,” he told Forbes.

hed: Nobody wants to live in our nation’s capital, dire figures show
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
DC home sellers are bleeding out, and buyers still won’t bite.
Washington’shousing market has hit a grim milestone. Nearly one in five homes for sale in the nation’s capital is listed for less than the owner originally paid, the worst mark in the country, according to fresh data from real estate analytics firmParcl Labs.
The number, 17.8%, dwarfs every other state and territory tracked. Colorado is a distant second at 11.8%.Floridaand Hawaii are tied at 10.9%. Arizona rounds out the top five at 10%. The national average sits at just 6.9%.
The numbers ask a very obvious question: Why are so many DC home sellers willing to walk away at a loss?
Parcl Labs’ own research points to an answer that has little to do with a flood of new construction and everything to do with buyers who simply aren’t showing up.
In an August report titled “Washington, DC: The Housing Correction Enters a New Phase,” the firm found that unlike overbuilt Sunbelt markets in Florida and Texas, DC’s slump has been driven primarily by weak demand rather than oversupply.
District home prices were down 1.6% year-over-year as of mid-August, marking a multiyear stretch of underperformance against both the broader DC metro area and the national market, which climbed 3.6% and 3% annually over the same stretch, respectively.
Sales, meanwhile, are still running about 45% below where they stood in 2021, when the market peaked.
The pain is not evenly spread. Condo-heavy pockets of Downtown, Southwest and Southeast Washington are absorbing the worst of it.
In the ZIP code covering the Southwest Waterfront, the Wharf and Buzzard Point, prices have cratered 11.5% year-over-year, wiping out nearly a third of the neighborhood’s value since its 2024 peak. The Golden Triangle and Dupont Circle area aren’t far behind, down 8.1%.
Entry-level condos and townhouses under $500,000 are getting hit hardest of all, with 45% of those listings taking a price cut and nearly 15% qualifying for Parcl’s “fire-sale” designation, roughly double the rate of any other price band.
Luxury is a different story entirely. Northwest neighborhoods like Foxhall and the Palisades have actually seen prices climb 4.6% year-over-year, and Brookland is up 5.5%, a divide that tracks with broader reporting on the resilience of DC’s high end even as the middle and bottom of the market struggle.
“DC has quickly shifted from a market where buyers felt pressure to act to one where sellers are competing for their attention,” Mark Rutstein of Compass, who has worked in the DC real estate market for nearly 25 years, told The Post.
“We’re seeing fewer showings across the board, and with high interest rates, uncertainty around the federal workforce and significant pressure on the condo market, buyers have more leverage than they’ve had in years — although well-located single-family homes and parts of the higher-end market continue to hold up better.”
One group isn’t waiting around for a rebound. Investors have ramped up their share of DC home purchases from 12.3%to 19.2% this year, scooping up 1,121 properties through July against just 840 sales, a net gain of 281 homes.
It’s the clearest sign yet that someone believes the District’s bloodletting is closer to a bottom than a bottomless pit.
Whether that bet pays off may come down to supply. Housing permits authorized in DC have collapsed 79% since 2022, from 7,705 units down to just 1,591 last year, almost entirely driven by a pullback in multifamily construction.
Fewer new units hitting the market in the years ahead could eventually give the District’s beleaguered sellers the floor they’ve been waiting for.

hed: Surging AI wealth is creating a ‘mansion shortage’ in San Francisco
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Artificial intelligenceis minting a new class of millionaires in San Francisco — and they’re running out of mansions to buy.
A wave of wealth tied to the city’s booming AI industry is sending home prices soaring, triggering bidding wars with as many as 50 offers and leaving even buyers armed with $25 million in cash out in the cold,NPR reported.
The frenzy marks a stunning turnaround for a city whose housing market slumped during the pandemic as tech workers scattered and offices emptied.
Now, AI companies are rapidly expanding, employees are returning to their desks and startups including OpenAI and Anthropic are generating enormous paper wealth for workers and investors — with potentially even larger windfalls ahead.
That said, the median home sale price inSan Franciscohas jumped 25% from a year ago, according to Compass data cited by NPR.
Compass agent Paul Kitchen told NPR that some listings have attracted as many as 50 offers. At the very top of the market, buyers offering $25 million or more in cash have still been outbid.
“You have to laugh just because it is so ridiculous and so beyond the pale,” Kitchen said.
In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million above their asking prices, Compass chief economist Mike Simonsen told NPR.
The collision of newly wealthy buyers and a limited supply of large, move-in-ready properties has produced what industry insiders are calling a “mansion shortage.”
Many of those buyers are AI executives in their 30s and early 40s who need homes quickly as their children reach school age, Simonsen said. Their urgency, combined with their ability to make enormous cash offers, is intensifying competition in San Francisco’s most affluent neighborhoods.
The mansion frenzy is an extreme expression of San Francisco’s broader housing shortage, which is squeezing buyers at nearly every income level.
Only 2.1% of the city’s listings in March 2026 were affordable to a household earning about $75,000, leaving a deficit of approximately 2,475 homes within reach of those buyers, according to aMay 2026 analysisfrom Realtor.com and the National Association of Realtors.
San Francisco received a listing-to-income alignment score of just 66%, meaning the distribution of homes for sale remains badly mismatched with what residents at different income levels can afford. The score improved by 4.5 points from March 2025 and 8.3 points from March 2019, but remained well below a balanced market.
Renters are feeling the same supply pressure. NPR reported that highly paid young tech workers who can afford rents as high as $10,000 a month are flooding the market, with some apartments receiving hundreds of inquiries within hours.
One couple took a $5,200-per-month apartment sight unseen after repeatedly watching other listings disappear, while another prospective renter encountered bidding that raised an apartment’s monthly price by $1,000 before he had even toured it.
The surge has renewed fears of displacement in a city where previous tech booms already drove out residents who could no longer afford to stay.
Whether it is a $25 million mansion or a modest starter home, the underlying problem is the same: San Francisco has too many buyers chasing too few properties — and the AI boom is raising the stakes.

hed: Amanda Seyfried asks $3.19M for longtime LA home — after moving to a New York farm with her family
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
“Mamma Mia!” star Amanda Seyfried, who is living her dream on an animal rescue farm in upstate New York with her actor husband and their two kids, has listed her Hollywood Hills home for $3.19 million.
The Emmy Award–winning actor had purchased the 110-year-old property, a 1916 traditional gated home, for $1.85 million from her 2009 “Jennifer’s Body” comedy/horror film co-star, Adam Brody, in 2011.
It had formerly been owned by Limp Bizkit frontman Fred Durst.
The new listing, which hit the market on Aug. 27, was first reported byRealtor.com.
The Hollywood Hills home is near Runyon Canyon and sits on just under a quarter of an acre.
Thoroughly updated, it comes with three bedrooms, two and a half baths, tree-top views and old-fashioned charm. A wide wraparound porch overlooks a pool, a lounge area and landscaped gardens. The property’s privacy is also protected by high hedges.
Inside the 2,738-square-foot home, the vibe is traditional country, updated for LA.
It all opens to a formal living room with a fireplace. There’s also a chic white and blue chef’s kitchen with a breakfast nook, a sunroom and a home office. Outside, a detached garage has been converted into a gym.
Seyfried, who won an Emmy for portraying fraudsterElizabeth Holmesin Hulu’s “The Dropout” series now spends most of her time in the Catskills with her husband Thomas Sadoski of “The Newsroom,” and their two kids Nina and Thomas.
The family’s home base is a 1930s farm, which she bought in 2013. It’s also been home over the years to a menagerie that has included horses, including a retired NYPD horse named Herman.
The “Mean Girls” star also has a “farmhouse inspired”pied-à-terreat the historic Apthorp —which she toured for Architectural Digest— on Manhattan’s Upper West Side.She bought itfor $2.52 million in 2019.
These days, upstate New York is where she feels best.
The listing broker of the Hollywood Hills home is Justin Paul Huchel, of Carolwood Estates.

hed: Middle-class co-op on Billionaires’ Row dodges 450% rent hike, appeals court rules
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Carnegie House just bought itself another round in its fight for survival.
A state appellate panelunanimously wiped out the arbitration awardthat would have jacked up ground rent at the Billionaires’ Row co-op by 450%, handing the 324-unit building a rare win against the ultra-wealthy investors who own the dirt beneath it, The Post has learned.
The Appellate Division’s ruling sends the dispute back to square one on rent talks, sparing more than 300 middle-class families at 100 W. 57th St. from an outcome that board president Richard Hirsch has previously called financial ruin.
The land under Carnegie House is controlled by an entity tied to real estate investors Rubin Schron and David Werner, along with Dell Technologies founderMichael Dell.
Last summer, an arbitration panelsided with the landownersand set new annual ground rent at roughly $24 million, up from $4.36 million, a jump co-op residents said would have been impossible to absorb without triggering defaults, foreclosures and wiped-out equity across the building.
Making matters worse, the landlords then tried to collect on the increase immediately, demanding more than $10 million in back rent with only 20 days’ notice.
Carnegie House cried foul, arguing the arbitration itself was compromised.
According to the Appellate decision, the neutral umpire overseeing the case failed to properly disclose a job offer from the landowners’ co-counsel while the arbitration was still underway, an omission the court found raised a legitimate question of bias.
That was enough for the Appellate Division to throw out the award entirely.
Hirsch framed the decision as a lifeline, not a finish line.
“Today’s decision is a critical victory for over 300 Carnegie House families who have been backed into a corner by real estate tycoon Michael Dell, our other billionaire landowners, and a corrupt arbitration award,” Hirsch told The Post in a statement.
“While this ruling is a temporary stopgap, it gives us a fair shot at negotiating reasonable rent terms, or arbitrating before an impartial panel, instead of being bound by a flawed process that would have cost us our homes. We look forward to a fair process in order to reach an outcome that works for both parties and keeps our co-op intact for generations to come.”
But owners of the ground lease see it differently.
“These tenants — largely investors — can seek all the delays they want, but the numbers are the numbers and we are confident that the next arbitrator will come to the same conclusion,” a spokesperson for 57th & 6th Ground LLC told The Post.
The case is being closely watched well beyond West 57th Street.
Carnegie House is one of roughly 100 ground lease co-ops across New York City, home to an estimated 25,000 residents, many of whom bought in decades ago under land leases now colliding with sky-high 21st century real estate values.
More than half of those buildings sit in Queens, Brooklyn and The Bronx, in neighborhoods where household incomes hover close to the citywide median of $76,000.
Legislative fixes have stalled. A bill aimed at protecting ground lease co-op residents statewide cleared the state Senate last year but the Legislature adjourned in June without sending it to Governor Hochul’s desk, leaving an estimated 12,000 homes exposed to the threat of deconversion.
For now, Carnegie House gets to renegotiate, or take its chances with a new, impartial arbitration panel. But the underlying standoff between a middle-class co-op and its billionaire landlords is far from resolved.

hed: The RealReal’s Julie Wainwright wants $7.88M for her NYC home in the world’s first skyscraper

The RealReal founder and former CEOJulie Wainwrightis taking another shot at selling her Manhattan condo.
Just ahead ofNew York Fashion Week, the luxury resale entrepreneur has relisted her 34th-floor condo inside the landmarked Woolworth Building — the world’s first skyscraper — for $7.88 million, according to StreetEasy.
Wainwright previously offered the home for the same price in June 2024 before taking it off the market later that year.
The three-bedroom, 3½-bath residence spans 3,282 square feet and commands panoramic city, skyline and river views from 2 Park Place in Lower Manhattan.
Wainwright paid $6.75 million for the condo in 2020, shortly after taking the RealReal public. The Postcovered the purchasewhen the home had most recently been asking $7.19 million.
Her latest asking price is roughly $1.13 million more than she paid.
The residence carries nearly $13,916 in combined monthly common charges and property taxes.
The renewed listing follows another notable deal for Wainwright. In November 2024, she sold her five-bedroom Beverly Hills home for $10.7 million after initially asking $11.99 million. She purchased that property for $9.65 million in 2021, as The Post previously reported.
Wainwright founded the RealReal in 2011 and led the luxury consignment company through its 2019 initial public offering before stepping down in 2022.
Kane Manera of Corcoran holds the listing. He declined to comment.

hed: Ask the remodeler: Creative storage ideas for back-to-school season and beyond
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Labor Day weekend is here, and that means switching over to school clothes. Where to put all those clothes that are out of season can be a real struggle. In an urban home, space can be tight, and in older homes, basements can be a challenge. And what about school gear, books, and backpacks? Every home is different, so the solutions to storage will be different. The following are a few solutions that we have created with our clients by thinking outside the box.
Often this is the first place we start when working with a young family with school-age children (and pets). In most homes, we cannot build out a new mudroom space — or if we can, it is very limited space because of proximity to property lines or the sidewalk out front. What we have done in the past with great success is carve out a space near the door and create a half wall for cubbies and storage, often with a bench to encourage kids to take their shoes off and also provide shoe storage below. Staggered coat hooks can be put on the wall if there are no windows that prevent this. We also will put a receptacle in the new entry for a phone or laptop charging area.
This is an often-overlooked area for storage. We have installed small powder rooms underneath a set of stairs, and for storage, we have used them in several ways. We have built and installed cubbies with slide-outs or baskets to help organize the day-to-day gear. Since many urban homes have the main stairs by the front door, this makes it a fantastic grab-and-go location. A more involved twist on this idea is to build drawers into the space that would allow more organization, but less bulky storage. We have also put receptacles in these spaces for a charging station or used the space for a more traditional coat closet. This would have us installing a door of some kind which can take two main forms. In some homes, we installed a smooth, flush door with no visible hardware that would have push button openers to access what is inside. This would get painted the wall color and was meant to simply blend into the wall. More often than not, we would install a door that would match the style and trim of the house with the goal of trying to make it appear as though it was always there.
This is always a challenge since clients often need far more bedroom storage than was ever incorporated by the original floor plan. It is sometimes possible to take an adjacent bedroom and carve a primary closet out of that space. Not everyone has that luxury, however, and that’s when we have to get creative. The second floor in many urban homes has eaves. The eave is where the sloped ceiling connects to a short 3-foot by-5-foot knee wall. If the eave space behind that short wall isn’t filled with utilities like AC ducts, that space can be captured for storage. This can be a little complicated because the space needs to be conditioned, meaning insulated and closed off from attic space above. Once that is done, the space can have open shelving with baskets, bookshelves, etc. We think the best use of this space is to create deep drawers for clothes and linens. That will free up floor space because you would need less furniture pieces such as dressers or bureaus. We have also built wardrobes into a bedroom, typically in an unused or less busy corner. These would be trimmed out to match up with baseboards and casings so it looks like it was built into the space originally.
One of the more interesting projects we had was creating a primary suite in a Queen Anne Victorian. There was very little leftover space after creating a beautiful primary bathroom. Being a Queen Anne, it had a turret in the corner that extended up into the second-floor primary bedroom. The clients weren’t terribly interested in keeping the turret space as a reading area, but also didn’t want to give up the light that splashed through the east-facing windows. Our solution was to fabricate and build custom cabinetry around the inner perimeter of the turret with tall cabinets between the windows and seats with storage underneath the windows. It added a substantial amount of storage without compromising the beauty and architectural integrity of the room.Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge.
