hed: ‘Morbidly obese’ NYC man takes co-op to court over new rules threatening his prime parking spot
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A disabledEast Villageresident with morbid obesity is suing his co-op over new rules he says threaten a parking spot his family has used for decades — as the board moves to sell the lot for residential development.
Steven Andruseaski, 61, is suing Village View Housing Corporation over a new parking agreement he says would give the co-op the ability to boot him from his space in Parking Lot 7, next to his apartment in the seven-buildingMitchell-Lamacomplex just south of Tompkins Square Park.
Weighing about 375 pounds, Andruseaski said he uses a cane and can only walk about 200 feet. He depends on his car — and the nearby parking spot — to get to doctors’ appointments and buy groceries on Long Island.
“It’s hard for me to be mobile because I can’t walk too far and I can’t stand still at all,” Andruseaski told The Post. “If I stand still — my knees, my back, my hips — they just start hurting right away.”
A doctor’s note filed with the Manhattan Supreme Court suit says Andruseaski has been diagnosed with “morbid (severe) obesity” and osteoarthritis in both knees.
Andruseaski said his family has used the parking spot for more than 40 years and that he currently pays $200 a month for it.
The suit comes after Village View gave residents until Aug. 31 to sign a new agreement expanding the circumstances under which they could lose their parking privileges — or face having theircars towed.
Andruseaski claims the agreement violates state human-rights law and is asking a judge to permanently bar Village View from removing his car or denying him access to the parking space.
His parking fight comes amid a broader battle overVillage View’s plan to sellthe 110-space Lot 7 for residential development — a connection Andruseaski makes in his lawsuit.
His complaint alleges the co-op plans to sell the lot to a developer and eventually eliminate its parking spaces.
Hundreds of shareholders at the 1,236-unit complex have demanded more transparency about the proposed redevelopment of Lot 7, one of seven parking lots at Village View, and questioned why the board is moving ahead without a shareholder vote.
But the board doesn’t need shareholder approval to proceed, only a green light from the city Department of Housing Preservation and Development.
The co-op received bids for rental developments starting in the mid-$30 million range, Jodi Stein, the board’s attorney in the potential sale, previously told The Post.
Stein disputed that the parking litigation is connected to the lot’s proposed sale.
“The litigation filed by Mr. Andruseaski has nothing to do with the sale of the parking lot,” Stein said in a statement to The Post. “I would avoid conflating these issues, as they are completely separate.”
Kagan Lubic Lepper Finkelstein & Gold, the law firm representing the co-op in Andruseaski’s case, didn’t respond to a request for comment. Neither did Andruseaski’s attorney.
Andruseaski isn’t the only shareholder challenging the new parking agreement at the 110-spot lot.
Sebastian Kot told The Post he filed his own challenge to the agreement, with a hearing scheduled for October.
Kot said residents could lose their spaces under several circumstances, including moving to another apartment within the complex.
“They can also kick you out [of the spot] for basically no reason,” he claimed.
Resident George Jarema claims he is already caught in another provision.
He said he tried to submit succession paperwork for the three-bedroom apartment where he grew up shortly after his mother died in 2022, but management allegedly refused to accept it.
Jarema claimed to The Post the co-op is now using the succession restriction to prevent him from keeping his parking space.
“It’s a little shady, them doing this parking agreement roughly at the same time when it came to light they’re trying to sell the parking lot,” Jarema said.
“It’s my belief that it’s easier for the board and management to take spots away from people to make it easier to sell the parking lot.”

hed: Martha’s Vineyard home sale breaks Massachusetts record at $43 million
subhead: Known as “Great Point,” the new record holder is 7,190 square feet with nine bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, boasting Edgartown’s scenic views.
content:
ByDaisy Levine
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

A massive Edgartown property broke the record for highest home price in the state.

This home, sitting on 18.6 acres, just closed for $43 million, toppling the previous record set by aKatama Bay property at $37.5 million.

Known as “Great Point,” the new record holder is 7,190 square feet with nine bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, boasting Edgartown’s scenic views. Nestled in Herring Creek Farm, a coastal enclave equipped with a functioning farm, the property also has 2,500 feet of private shoreline, along with a nearby space to land a private aircraft.


The coastal compound wasoriginally listed for $49 millionin June by Boston tech giant Michael Bronner of Digitas. He invested more than $19 million into the site, according to property records.

There’s an outdoor sauna, a massive kitchen equipped for a private chef, and an abundance of panoramic views.


Listing agents Maggie Gold Seelig of MGS Group Real Estate and Brian Dougherty of Corcoran Property Advisors did not disclose the home’s new owner, but, whoever it is, the buyer joins Herring Creek’s exclusive neighborhood of about a dozen homes. An agent described it as the “’Billionaires’ Row’ of the Vineyard” to the Globe in June.

Residents include late-night legend David Letterman,according to the Wall Street Journal. Letterman helped save a plot next to 61 Butlers Cove from being developed in a $64 million deal back in 2001.

This property is “the best of all worlds,” one of the agents to told the Globe in June. It has privacy, yet vast amounts of nature alongside it, with its own walking trails, and is only a short bike ride away from Edgartown.


“This is not a property meant to be admired from within. It is meant to be lived,” Bronner said in a statement to the Globe in June.

“What we continue to see when advising high net-worth buyers … is that aside from privacy, the thing they value most is time,” one of the agents said when the listing first went up. “We find that Great Point is a place where it just feels like time stands still, and it’s yours to kind of reclaim.”

hed: 4-island package on US-Canada border hits market fully loaded for $2.3M — boats included
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Why settle for one private island when you can have four?
A sprawling 520-acre compound nearly strattling the border between Michigan and Ontario, Canada has hit the market for $2.3 million, offering Burnt, Wilson, Claw and Harris islands — along with a three-bedroom home and much of the equipment needed to live there.
The unusual spread sits in the St. Marys River near Drummond Island, with the main residence tucked on a peninsula between two bays. The views look out to our neighbor to the north.
And while private-island living might conjure visions of being stranded miles from civilization, listing agent Anna DeCamp of Gaslight Group said the trip from the American mainland is surprisingly manageable.
“It’s about 20 to 30 minutes, depending on weather, from DeTour up to the island,” DeCamp told The Post. “It looks much further on a map than it actually is in person.”
The sellers keep a boat slip in DeTour Village and make the journey from there, occasionally sharing the waterway with freighters traveling through the St. Marys River.
For major grocery runs, island dwellers can head farther afield to St. Ignace or Sault Ste. Marie, according to DeCamp.
Once home, however, the closest neighbors may have four legs.
Wildlife is abundant across the islands, with foxes, otters, beavers, coyotes and sandhill cranes among the visitors. “You can hear the loons calling,” DeCamp said, describing how they call to one another from the bays on either side of the house.
But despite all that wilderness, the roughly 2,131-square-foot house isn’t exactly roughing it.
The three-bedroom, two-bath home has electricity and water, as well as a sauna and gas stove.
That renovation was considerably more complicated than your average gut job: With the property accessible only over water, construction materials had to make the journey by boat.
“They had to completely gut it,” DeCamp said. “For the next owner, it’s already done.”
The current owners have held the property for roughly a decade and use it as a vacation retreat rather than their primary residence. They “absolutely love it up there,” DeCamp said, but are selling as they get older.
Most of the 520 acres are protected by a conservation easement held by the Little Traverse Conservancy, leaving roughly 100 acres outside the protected area. Any future development would still be subject to applicable restrictions and regulations.
And whoever buys the four-island package won’t have to bring their own fleet.
The sale includes a Kubota tractor and other maintenance equipment, plus two boats — including a 2006, 32-foot World Cat catamaran used to make the crossing from DeTour.
The listing has already drawn several prospective buyers. DeCamp said there have been a couple of showings, with one potential buyer “pretty interested” and another showing scheduled for next week.
So far, interest has largely come from people who already know the region but want something more secluded than nearby Drummond Island.
“They don’t want to be on Drummond,” DeCamp said. “They want to have their own place.”

hed: No HOA is as strict as the rules for the ‘Billionaire Bunker’ island where Bezos and Zuckerberg live
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Money talks in Indian Creek Village. It just can’t talk its way out of a 103-page book stuffed with rules and regulations that deep-pocketed residents of this “Billionaire Bunker” must follow.
The 300-acre island off Surfside and Miami Beach has quietly become the address of choice for theplanet’s wealthiest,but nobody gets a pass on the fine print — not even the guywho owns Amazon.
Jeff Bezos,Mark Zuckerberg,Tom Brady, Carl Icahn, and Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner all call the enclave home. And all of them answer to a code written back when the community was incorporated in 1939 — one that still governs a population that clocked in at just 84 people in the last census.
For starters, these billionaires can’t land their choppers in their own backyards. And when it comes to the size of the mansions they call home, the rules also mandate strict minimums for square footage.
Break it and it’ll cost you.
Willful violations of the Land Development Regulations carry fines up to $500 a day, on top of the threat of court enforcement or a yanked building permit.
Village Manager Guillermo Olmedillo oversees compliance, and the enclave backs it up with its own police department that one broker has described as openly hostile to anyone without clearance to be on Indian Creek.
As for those on the island, they have some real regulations to follow.
Yes, forget landing the chopper in the backyard. Helicopters and helipads are banned outright as an accessory use, full stop, regardless of how many private jets are parked at the airport.
Want a mansion instead? Better make it big, not small. The code sets a floor, not a ceiling, requiring at least 5,000 square feet of gross floor area, three quarters of it under the main roof. There’s no such thing as a modest starter home on Indian Creek.
Even the lawn has rules. Grass can’t grow past 6 inches high, and building coverage is capped at 25% of the lot — including hard surfaces, such as driveways, pools, tennis courts and patios. That leaves at least 55% of every property as landscaped or open space, whether the owner wants a lawn or not.
Waterfront mansions can’t hug the shoreline either. Principal residences need at least 100 feet of setback from the bay, front and side setbacks run 50 and 25 feet away, and accessory buildings have to stay 50 feet back from the water.
Pools get a little more leeway — they’re allowed to dip into that waterfront setback — but they can’t rise more than 3 feet above yard grade, and putting one in the front yard is banned outright.
Guest houses, cabanas and pool houses are permitted, up to two extra structures per lot, but they’re capped at 800 square feet and can’t be built to function as a standalone residence unless it’s for staff.
Fences and walls top out at 7 feet, have to sit back 10 feet from the property line and need landscaping to screen them from the street. Privacy, yes. Fortress walls, no.
Hurricane generators get their own paragraph entirely. Enclosures are capped at 18 feet wide, 20 feet long, and 12 feet high — and they have to sit 100 feet from the front property line, 100 feet from the water, 25 feet from the side line, and 10 feet from the house, with zero variance allowed on any of those numbers.
Subdividing a lot to squeeze out extra land is off the table completely, the code requires at least 200 feet of water frontage per residential site.
And even the pets are regulated: No packs, herds, litters, bevies or flocks larger than three without a village resolution approving it first.
The takeaway is simple. On Indian Creek, the water views come free. The exemptions don’t.

hed: Home prices dropping fastest in major US cities — and they’re not the ones you think
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
While the US housing market cools down and enters a seasonal late-summer transition,price drops are hitting some metropolitan areasmuch harder than others—and it might not be where you think.
High mortgage ratesand shifting local supply-and-demand dynamics have driven down list prices across the country, though more slowly in August than in previous months.
Sellers are trending toward more realistic pricing, and the market is seeing broader price corrections. Metro areas that saw explosive, COVID-19 pandemic-era growth are now experiencing some of the deepest cuts in the price per square foot.
In August, the price per square foot—a measure that controls for the size of homes on the market—decreased year over year for the 10th straight month.
Nationwide,housing pricesper square foot are down 1.8% year over year, and median list prices fell year over year in three of the four regions (-3.6% in the Northeast, -2.6% in the South, and -2.1% in the West), while prices remained flat in the Midwest.
At the metro level, the median list price per square foot fell in 36 of the top 50 metros in August, another sign that it’s “game over” for unrealistic seller demands.
The largest price-per-square-foot declines were in Austin, TX (-8.1%); Tampa, FL (-5.6%); and Memphis, TN (-4.1%). The largest gains were in Providence, RI (+9.3%); Indianapolis (+4.4%); and Chicago (+3.6%).
Among the 50 biggest metro areas, these saw the biggest annual declines in listing price per square foot in August:
Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel says some of this market shift in these cities may be due to continual readjustment following theCOVID-19 pandemic.
“One common thread for most markets—including Austin, Tampa, San Antonio, Denver—is 2020–22 boomtowns continuing to give back some of their pandemic-era gains. These are also, by and large, places with much more inventory now than pre-pandemic norms,” he says.
One outlier is San Francisco, where the market saw a 3.9% decrease in price-per-square-foot costs, despite its status as an ultracompetitive market.
In July 2026, active listings fell 16.3% from the previous year, tightening up the housing market even further. And while the median listing price in the market remains high—$908,700—it has decreased by 5.2% year over year.
Veronica Peter is a real estate agent with Compass serving the Fremont area, which is on the southeastern edge of San Francisco and close to Silicon Valley, where most of her clients work. She says the market is being affected by the shifts in the tech industry. Many of her clients are quietly reeling as AI transforms their industry.
“A huge portion of our workforce in Fremont holds tech-related jobs such as software engineers, data analysts, and web developers,” she tells Realtor.com. Many heavy tech hitters, including Oracle, Meta, Dell, Microsoft, and Amazon, have implemented “quiet layoffs” as they restructure with AI in mind.
The encroaching instability in the tech workforce has meant that while the housing market “has certainly not crashed, pricing [has] adjusted to meet buyers where they are today,” she adds.

At recent open houses, she’s heard similar sentiments: Tech workers are uncertain about their employment and feeling the strain of high interest rates. Many also invested heavily in tech stocks, which haveslumped this year.
“A softer stock market depleted the funds buyers were planning to use for their down payments,” she says.
There’s been a marked shift in the housing inventory in the metro area, Krimmel adds.
“It’s not about San Francisco homes losing value, but rather how expensive the available inventory is this year relative to last,” he says.
“There are fewer small, pricey homes in the center of the city for sale. They are scarce and selling fast. On the flip side, this year there are relatively more large, less expensive per-square-foot homes coming up for sale in outer suburbs,” he says.
Real estate experts note that these downward adjustments offer a welcome silver lining for prospective buyers who have felt sidelined by affordability constraints over the past few years.
As active inventory continues to build nationally—climbing toward levels not seen since late 2019—sellers in these cooling markets are increasingly forced to reevaluate their pricing strategies to attract a more selective pool of financially qualified buyers.
Whether these double-digit or near-double-digit pullbacks represent a temporary normalization or the beginning of a broader regional shift will depend heavily on local economic momentum and upcoming changes in mortgage rates as the autumn buying season approaches.

content:

A million-dollar mansion perched along Los Angeles’legendary Mulholland Drivehas become anything but a dream home — with squatters and trespassers turning the unfinished property into a late-night party pad.
The abandoned house at 7711 Mulholland boasts sweeping views of the city, but neighbors say its biggest attraction after dark is the empty property itself.
“It’s just right under the Universal Overlook, and people come at night, use it to party,” said Ted, a local resident who lives near the property,told FOX11. “There’sgraffiti all over it, beer cans, and everything.”
Neighbors say the calls for help have been piling up while the mansion has deteriorated into an eyesore and nuisance.
“The house on the top of the hill has been an issue for a while,” community member Paul Sterntold NBC Los Angeles.
The home was last sold in 2022,according to Zillow, which describes the property as a three-bedroom, three-bathroom mansion spanning more than 4,000 square feet.
Its estimated market value is now upwards of $1.47 million.
Photos show a luxurious glass room and deck overlooking Los Angeles — a jaw-dropping perch that would be the envy of anyHollywood Hills homeowner.
But now, the property is covered with graffiti and several of the home’s windows are gone. Property records show Walking Media Inc. as the current owner of the property, NBC reported.

The mansion is in fact not actually finished. When it was last sold, it had no kitchen, no sewer connection, no bathroom and no driveway or off-street parking. However, that work could begin soon as the owner was issued a building permit in May,according to Realtor.com.
Until then, neighbors say the property has become a magnet for partygoers.

hed: Private Mediterranean island boasting its own Napoleonic fort on sale for $7.5M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.
A private islandless than 5 miles from Venice with a Napoleonic fort is on sale for $7.5 million.
The Island of Crevan, nestled in the Venice lagoon, has views of the floating city as the islands of Torcello, Murano and Burano.
The 5,700 square-mile property boasts the 215 square-mile fortress — now converted into a small villa with vegetable gardens.
With an internal canal and two private boat moorings, it’s easily accessible by air or water.
It was restored in 1996 and offers four principal rooms and two bathrooms.
DuringNapoleonic rule, Crevan became part of the defensive system created to protect the Venetian Lagoon.
The military redoubt was built in 1806 and subsequently enlarged and reinforced under Austrian rule.
In 1866, along with the rest of the Veneto region, the island became part of the Kingdom of Italy, retaining its military function until after World War I.
It later passed into private ownership and was converted for residential use.
New owners will have the opportunity to consolidate the caretaker’s quarters, creating the opportunity for a larger, more contemporary home.
Founder and CEO of Lionard Luxury Real Estate, Dimitri Corti, says: “In ultra-prime real estate, a private island represents one of the purest expressions of ownership: its boundary is not a wall, but the horizon.
“Crevan offers the privilege of withdrawing from the world without leaving behind the universal allure of Venice.
“What is acquired is not simply a residence and a piece of land, but space, privacy and an entire landscape to preserve.”

hed: A Big Dig titan planted his family in North Reading. Their estate is for sale.
subhead: The daughter of Les Marino, founder of Modern Continental, is selling her longtime family home.
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Every May, the pear trees bloom in Ridgeway Estates.

Lelio “Les” Marino planted them himself, lining the streets of the North Reading development he began first carving out of the woods in the late 1970s. May 6 was his birthday, and more than two decades after his death, the trees still mark it.

“Every May 6, they bloom, and it’s the most beautiful thing you would ever want to see,” said his daughter, Laura Marino. “Every time I see those pear trees, I think of him.”


Marino, the founder of Modern Continental — the Cambridge construction giant best known for its work onthe Big Dig— died in 2004 at age 69.

During his career, Boston knew Marino as a builder of tunnels and the owner ofa farm in Natick, a restaurant in Cambridge, and an integrative health center. Ridgeway Estates was something more personal: his first big development in North Reading, and the place he decided his family would stay. When he laid out Ridgeway, he set aside three lots for his children.


Now, his daughter Laura’s house, a nearly 11,300-square-foot house at the center of the development,4 Wren Circle, is on the market for $3.85 million through Marina Tramontozzi and Kristine Pecora ofTrue North Realty. The Marino family designed the house with Modern Continental’s architect. Between the main house and an addition, there are five bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and three half-bathrooms on 10.6 acres.

“As Italian families do, they always end up moving in close to each other,” Laura said. “He wanted his kids close to him.” Her father was born in Chieti, Italy, and her mother is from Rome.

Laura filled much of the home with her design eye in 1998. A salmon-colored dining room is reminiscent of a palette she fell in love with in Italy, there’s Italian artwork throughout, and the kitchen was designed for family feasts of all sizes.




“I wanted the kids to have a warm home to bring their friends home to,” she said. “As it turns out, that’s exactly what this house represented.”

That is evident over the family’s 28 years in the home. Grandbabies bathed in the island sink, two daughters descended the main staircase in their wedding gowns, and there were graduation parties, retirement parties, and Christmas parties. The party spills outside, too; the grounds include a heated pool, a cabana, a stone patio, and a fire pit.


“You can put 75 to 100 people in this house, and you won’t even know it,” Laura said. “It’s cozy when there’s two, but yet it can handle 75 people, and I still don’t know how that’s possible.”

The night Marino died at his own house two minutes away, the family compound gained its final wing.


“The next day, [my mother] said, ‘Do you mind if I build just something small next to you?’” Laura said.

The something small became a 4,000-square-foot addition with its own entrance, kitchen, and bedroom suite, where Anna Maria Marino has lived for more than two decades — close enough to help keep the traditions, and to watch four generations pass through the house. No longer in need of so much space, Laura is moving to a town house.


“It’s going to give me a chance to decorate, which I love,” she said. “That’s the part of my father that I have, and my mother says it all the time.”

She hopes whoever buys the house uses it the way her family did — at full capacity. She also remembers the line her father left her with after one visit. “He said, ‘Baby, this is a beautiful house. I’m happy for you. But never forget where you came from.’”

hed: Cipriani tops off Miami’s tallest tower south of Manhattan with $53M penthouses and a black book to match
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Cipriani Residences Miamiis putting the finishing touch on its Brickell skyscraper with a pair of penthouses so lavish they come with their own zip code in the sky, The Post has learned.
The Italian hospitality empire unveiled The 1931 Collection this week, a two-unit offering perched atop the 950-foot tower that now stands as the tallest residential building south of Manhattan.
Together, the penthouses carry a combined price tag of $53 million, with the larger unit listed at $33 million and its companion at $19.8 million.
Named for the year Giuseppe Cipriani first opened the doors of Harry’s Bar in Venice, the two residences sit on the building’s uppermost floors and are meant to channel nearly a century of the family’s hospitality instincts into full time living spaces rather than hotel suites.
The pricier of the pair, dubbed The San Marco, unfolds across three levels and 9,677 square feet of combined indoor and outdoor space. A 24-foot Great Room anchors the home, while a chef’s kitchen finished in lacquered wood and Calacatta marble, an integrated wet bar and a dedicated wine display round out the entertaining areas.
The real showstopper sits upstairs, where a private rooftop delivers an infinity pool, summer kitchen, cold plunge, hot tub, massage pavilion and even a putting green with sweeping views of Biscayne Bay.
Its sibling unit, The Torcello, trades scale for intimacy at 6,703 square feet. Buyers still get their own infinity pool, gym, wellness room, cold plunge and hot tub outdoors, plus a private screening room and wine storage inside.
A standout feature is The Midnight Bar, a dedicated space built for cocktails and late night gatherings.
Both homes come stocked with the kind of perks money alone can’t always buy elsewhere.
Residents get in-home dining prepared by the Cipriani culinary team, along with reservation privileges across the brand’s international network, from the original Harry’s Bar in Venice to Cipriani outposts in New York, Monte Carlo, Dubai, Hong Kong and Punta del Este.
“Cipriani has never simply been about a place, it is about what happens within it and what people carry with them long after they leave,” Giuseppe Cipriani told The Post. “Harry’s Bar, Piazza San Marco and Locanda Cipriani have been part of our family’s story for generations, but also of the lives of so many others.”
“With The 1931 Collection, that spirit finds a new expression in Miami, where these residences can become the setting for celebrations, rituals and memories that belong entirely to the families who call them home.”
The timing lines up with a milestone moment for the tower itself. Cipriani Residences Miami recently topped out at 950 feet, and the building is already 85 percent sold to buyers hailing from more than 30 countries ahead of its planned Summer 2027 occupancy.
Soccer star Lionel Messi, who recentlyannounced his retirement,are among those whopurchased several unitsin the building.

hed: California lake town to be transformed with world-class race track, luxe condos and private club
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Start your engines Riverside County.
NASCARveteran and road-racing legend Boris Said is behind bombshell plans for “Elsinoring” — a Nürburgring-inspired private motorsports playground near Lake Elsinore where wealthy motorheads can race around a track with 22 turns — then park them at their own luxe “garage villa.”
The name is a cheeky, palm-tree-lined homage to Germany’s infamousracing venueand plans call for a 3.2-mile, 22 turn circuit designed to FIA Grade 2 standards with three different configurations allowing separate portions of the track to potentially operate at the same time.
The track promises a mix of technical corners, sweeping sections, and passing opportunities, with drivers divided into sessions based on experience and the type of vehicle they’re driving — according to an AI-driven marketing package blasted across the project’s flashy website.
The paradox of unapologetic mega-wealth coming to a down-on-its-luck lake town is hard to miss. Plagued by toxic green algae blooms, Lake Elsinore has a less than glamorous reputation, and is better known for aninfamous serial killerorwild brawls at In-N-outthan multi-million dollar cars and fancy homes.
“The city loves us,” Said toldAutoweek. The sentiment was echoed byLake Elsinore‘s economic development director, Gina Gonzalez, who touted the town as the “actions sports capital of the world.”
The Elsinore Ring project is also plotting a well-heeled auto enthusiast’s dream version of a condo, with plans to reportedly offer 275 garage condominiums and trackside “villas,” envisioned with 1,300 square feet of climate-controlled garage space capable of holding six to eight cars. In addition to storing their Ferrari’s and McLarens there, members can live there year-round if they want.
Each private luxury retreat is “finished to the standard of a luxury custom home,” complete with a kitchen outfitted with “premium designer appliances, stone countertops with waterfall edges, and custom cabinetry.” Plus, the villas feature private balconies with a full view of the track.
Other amenities read like an upscale resort, with its clubhouse boasting a swimming pool with a glass floor and panoramic views of the circuit, a luxe spa and gym, among others. A dedicated helipad will sit right on top of the clubhouse roof so high-roller can easily bypass SoCal traffic.

Since Lake Elsinore has long branded itself as a off-road and water sports mecca, flanked by skydiving fields and motocross tracks, the location of Elsinore Ring is ideal.

hed: California condo owners face massive $19M HOA assessments for repairs
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Californiacondo ownersare fighting back after theirhomeowners associationapproved a multimillion-dollar emergency assessment that they say could financially cripple them.
The uproar comes from a Torrance condominium complex, where residents were hit with assessments of more than $49,000 each to help pay for sweeping repairs,ABC7 reports.
The 499-unit property is facing at least $19 million in work, including a $13 million overhaul of the building’s podium, along with re-piping and elevator repairs.
It follows a similar battle in San Clemente, where owners at the 198-unit Villa Moura complex were ordered to pay more than $26,000 apiece for an assessment — totaling more than $5 million.
Stephen Wang, who lives in the Torrance complex, said: “I was shocked, as most of the residents here are.”
He continued: “The HOA decided to redo the whole podium, the entire podium, and that became a $13 million project, and plus the re-piping and the elevators, so it came up to $19 million.”
He added the massive bill came after theHOAdecided to tackle several major projects at once, leaving residents scrambling to figure out how they could possibly afford their share.
In San Clemente residents have argued the work should not have been classified as an emergency and the association should have given homeowners a greater say in how the repairs were handled.
Noah Martin, who lives there, said the roof project did not qualify as an emergency under California regulations.
He added: “It didn’t fit under the California Code of Regulations, 5610. Clearly, it was not an emergency; it’s a deferred maintenance. And so, then we as members should have a vote on how we want to take care of the roofs.”
Residents also say the HOA has threatened to place liens on properties belonging to owners who fail to pay the assessment.
“They have pushed back, arguing the roofs were not leaking and that replacing the underlying material could be sufficient instead of tearing out all the tiles.
Adam Dubin, another homeowner, said residents want the HOA to shop around before committing to such an expensive project.
“What we would like to do is have multiple bids competitively submitted and actually negotiate those bids in the best interest of the homeowners. As the board should be doing with their fiduciary responsibilities to us,” Dubin said.
For some residents, the payment options have done little to ease the financial pain. Homeowners in San Clemente were offered the choice of paying the assessment upfront, splitting it into two payments or adding more than $2,000 to their monthly bill for six months, followed by another $400 monthly payment.
“Retired, single, what, lose my house? I wouldn’t qualify for a loan to refinance. So where do you go?” homeowner Albright said.
HOA attorney and expert Michael Kushner said special assessments have become increasingly common, pointing to soaring insurance costs and California’s balcony-inspection requirements as factors.
But he cautioned that associations can sometimes push beyond their legal authority.
He said: “It is a very lopsided relationship, just by virtue of the fact that the HOA has got everybody’s money to play with, and the HOA has authority to issue discipline.”
California homeowners also face an unusual hurdle when disputes erupt: there is no state regulatory agency specifically overseeing HOAs.
The Davis-Stirling Act lays out rules governing associations and provides protections for homeowners, but Kushner said portions of the law could be strengthened and clarified.
The Torrance homeowners have taken their fight to court and are also seeking to recall their HOA board.

hed: California city fumes over planned skyscraper linked to Russian oligarch
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A wealthy California city is in revolt after the son of a Putin-alignedRussian oligarchdemanded approval to build a gigantic skyscraper in the middle of their quiet suburb.
Residents from Menlo Park, near San Jose, are opposing the 80 Willow Road project that is owned by Vitaly Yusufov –– the son of former Energy Minister Igor Yusufov.
Attorney General Rob Bonta, however, essentially backed the project after his office sent a letter to Menlo Park asserting that the city was violating state housing laws in stalling the plans.
Resident Maria Kleczewska said: “I urge you to fight the 80 Willow project despite the risk of massive legal fees. This project will be the ruin of our beautiful city.”
“How many residents will be looking at that monstrosity from their streets and yards instead of the open sky and trees that we love to see? How many houses will be in shadow? How many streets will experience a dramatic increase in traffic?”
“Argue back at the Attorney General. He ain’t the only lawyer in town. Reject the developer’s deadline. Who died and made him God?” another resident said.
The former Russian Energy Minister was worth about $1.1 billion,according to Forbes, and is the founder of an investment vehicle called Fund Energy.
The billionaire is sanctioned by international countriessuch as Canadaand Ukraine, but his name has been notably absent from the US and the European Union.
The80 Willow Road propertywas purchased for $72 million in 2018 and is located on a 6.7 acre site. The project is planning on constructing around 665 residential units, 332,000 square feet of office, three buildings ranging from 301 to 458 feet tall, and more.
Previously, the oligarch’s son purchased a German shipbuilding company called the Wadan Yards in 2009 after then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel helped broker a deal.
Residents are also voicing opposition against the plan due to potential environmental impacts.
A group calledMenlo Forwardthat was created to oppose the 80 Willow Road project wrote that the “environmental impact of such an immense project right next to the San Francisquito Creek cannot be ignored.”
“The need for housing across the region is serious and demands serious proposals to address the shortage — but proposals such as this, that include buildings taller than any in San Jose, undermine the good work of housing advocates and create more problems than they address and should not be seriously considered,” the group also wrote on their website.
Under California law, every city needs to turn in its housing plan to the state on time. 80 Willow may normally violate the city’s building codes but Menlo Park failed to turn in its housing plan.
Since Menlo Park missed the deadline, Yusufov can proceed with his plan under the Builder’s Remedy –– but only if he includes a portion of his units as subsidized housing.
The city council is set to hold a special meeting on Tuesday to discuss the attorney general’s letter and to formulate a response after the project’s developer set an October 27 deadline for approval.
The Attorney General’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Post.

hed: ‘I will get ICE and the police to your house’: Immigrant workers say they increasingly face wage theft, deportation threats
subhead: Such actions, despite being illegal, are adding to a climate of fear and powerlessness among immigrant workers across the state
content: Three construction workers said they completed three jobs without seeing a single dime last fall. Their employers, masonry subcontractors, insisted that the money — roughly $10,000 — was coming. It never did. When one worker confronted his employer over text, saying he would file a report alleging wage theft, the employer wielded a threat that immigrant advocates say has become increasingly common since the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown started. “You can file whatever you like,” the employer wrote, in messages viewed by the Globe. “I will not pay you nothing because you threaten me [sic] now [expletive] off or I will get ICE and the police to your house to bring you back to the dusty taco eating place you come from … I know where you live.”The workers lacked work authorization. For them, the deportation threat was real. Such cases are a growing problem, immigrant advocates say, with groups that help undocumented workers saying they’ve seen an uptick in complaints, particularly in the construction industry, of employers not paying agreed-upon wages and then, when confronted, threatening to call Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Such actions, despite being illegal, are adding to a a climate of fear and powerlessness among immigrant workers across the state.“Employers who want to exploit workers seem to feel like they have the green light to continue exploiting,” said Leela Ramachandran, co-director of the Metrowest Worker Center in Framingham, an advocacy group that helped the workers in the masonry case. “The environment does not carry consequences for their threats.” Before Trump’s second term, the center handled one to two wage theft cases a month. Now, it receives about seven cases each month, she said. “There’s no doubt that employers are taking advantage of workers’ fears to get away with not paying wages … and not following the law with respect to workplace injuries,” said Audrey Richardson, managing attorney at Greater Boston Legal Services, a nonprofit organization that provides legal assistance to immigrants and refugees, including on wage theft cases.  Even as many immigrants are scared to speak out, wage theft cases — in which workers allege their employer didn’t pay them enough for work performed — have spiked since the immigration crackdown began in early 2025. Workers filed 3,384 wage theft complaints to the Massachusetts attorney general’s office from January through May. That’s a roughly 16 percent increase over the same period in 2025 and a 10 percent rise over 2024.Most complaints filed with the AG’s office by May of this year came from the health care, restaurant, and service industries. About 7.7 percent of all complaints, or 261, came from the construction industry, one of the industries that employs the most undocumented workers in the state. In many of these industries, advocates say, workers are often paid in cash and have to negotiate with their employer to receive the full agreed-upon amount. In the construction industry, for instance, workers are often paid only at the end of a project, which allows employers to undercount hours and pay below prevailing wages. Renato, 48, a construction worker who lives in Everett, said he doesn’t know a single person in his industry who hasn’t experienced wage theft. “But now if anything happens, the first thing that [employers] do to pull threats is call ICE,” he said. Renato, who is originally from Brazil and requested to be identified only by his first name for fear of retaliation, worked for a decade on building maintenance projects. When the business dissolved, Renato looked through dozens of past invoices and discovered that he was missing a sum of about one paycheck a month for the past 10 years, amounting to $22,000. Renato confronted his employer in March to request the unpaid funds. Massachusetts law allows workers to demand payment for wage and hour violations up to three years after the violation. Renato could legally sue the employer and — if he won — get triple damages. The employer refused to pay any of the owed amount, Renato said. “I can solve this problem with one phone call, just like I did with the other employee,” Renato recalled the employer saying. According to Renato, the employer had regularly boasted about getting a previous worker deported. “So I just stood up, put the chair back, and walked away,” Renato said. Renato reported his case to the attorney general’s office, which is investigating. Notifying immigration authorities about a worker who complained about labor rights violations is considered retaliation, according to the attorney general’s office, and is subject to penalties such as fines or jail time. But the lingering threat continues to burden Renato. “I can’t sleep,” Renato said. “I have to drink energy drinks to stay awake during the day, and at night I cannot sleep.” Many of the workers who arrive at the Framingham center, also called Casa, allow the organization to contact their employers and negotiate on their behalf, but refrain from filing an official complaint, said Ramachandran. “Workers have never felt less protected and scared, and the people who usually support them have less capacity,” she said. “It’s a perfect storm.” “Employers who want to exploit workers seem to feel like they have the green light to continue exploiting,” said Leela Ramachandran, co-director of the Metrowest Worker Center in Framingham.John Tlumacki/Globe StaffThe pervasive fear is also reflected in the falling number of wage theft cases workers are taking to Greater Boston Legal Services, Richardson said. Such cases were down by almost 50 percent for 2025 and 2026, compared to the same period in 2024. Similarly, the Brazilian Worker Center in Allston has seen the number of legal cases it helps workers pursue against employers be cut in half to about 50 per year since President Trump returned to office, said André Simões, the center’s workers’ rights program manager.Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell said in a statement Massachusetts law protects all workers, regardless of immigration status. The office does not request immigration-related information when investigating. “We do not tolerate employers who retaliate against workers for asserting their rights or reporting violations,” Campbell said.Employers who don’t play by the rules hurt the entire industry, said Bert Durand, communications director at the North Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters. “If your competition is cheating and cutting 30, 40, or 60 percent off of their labor costs, you’re at a significant disadvantage just by following the rules,” Durand said. Even business partners can be vulnerable to deportation being used as a weapon. In another case handled by Ramachandran, a Framingham resident, 25, wanted to disentangle himself from a construction business partner in New York who Ramachandran said was taking company funds for personal use and drugs, including roughly $33,000 the Framingham man said he was owed. Last year, the man traveled to New York with his wife and baby to return company equipment and demand the missing funds, Ramachandran said. When he arrived at the meeting spot, his former business partner pointed at him and said, according to Ramachandran, “This is the guy I have problems with.” A squad of ICE agents swarmed the group, shoving the man’s wife and baby and detaining him, according to Ramachandran. Family members, with the help of Casa, paid bond for the man, who is awaiting further immigration proceedings and had no prior criminal record. “This is highlighting the contradiction of the system … and upends the narrative that ICE is detaining the worst people and making our country safer,” said Ramachandran. In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said: “ICE does not comment on unverified, anecdotal scenarios. The Trump Administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.”Maria, 27, a Casa worker whose family works in construction and asked to use only her first name to protect from retaliation, said her brother-in-law went unpaid for six months’ worth of overtime but didn’t report it for fear of ICE. “Sometimes I feel sad,” she said in Spanish. “Because we lack papers or documents, we stay silent.” Yogev Toby can be reached at yogev.toby@globe.com.

hed: A Big Dig titan planted his family in North Reading. Their estate is for sale.
subhead: The daughter of Les Marino, founder of Modern Continental, is selling her longtime family home.
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Every May, the pear trees bloom in Ridgeway Estates.

Lelio “Les” Marino planted them himself, lining the streets of the North Reading development he began first carving out of the woods in the late 1970s. May 6 was his birthday, and more than two decades after his death, the trees still mark it.

“Every May 6, they bloom, and it’s the most beautiful thing you would ever want to see,” said his daughter, Laura Marino. “Every time I see those pear trees, I think of him.”


Marino, the founder of Modern Continental — the Cambridge construction giant best known for its work onthe Big Dig— died in 2004 at age 69.

During his career, Boston knew Marino as a builder of tunnels and the owner ofa farm in Natick, a restaurant in Cambridge, and an integrative health center. Ridgeway Estates was something more personal: his first big development in North Reading, and the place he decided his family would stay. When he laid out Ridgeway, he set aside three lots for his children.


Now, his daughter Laura’s house, a nearly 11,300-square-foot house at the center of the development,4 Wren Circle, is on the market for $3.85 million through Marina Tramontozzi and Kristine Pecora ofTrue North Realty. The Marino family designed the house with Modern Continental’s architect. Between the main house and an addition, there are five bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and three half-bathrooms on 10.6 acres.

“As Italian families do, they always end up moving in close to each other,” Laura said. “He wanted his kids close to him.” Her father was born in Chieti, Italy, and her mother is from Rome.

Laura filled much of the home with her design eye in 1998. A salmon-colored dining room is reminiscent of a palette she fell in love with in Italy, there’s Italian artwork throughout, and the kitchen was designed for family feasts of all sizes.




“I wanted the kids to have a warm home to bring their friends home to,” she said. “As it turns out, that’s exactly what this house represented.”

That is evident over the family’s 28 years in the home. Grandbabies bathed in the island sink, two daughters descended the main staircase in their wedding gowns, and there were graduation parties, retirement parties, and Christmas parties. The party spills outside, too; the grounds include a heated pool, a cabana, a stone patio, and a fire pit.


“You can put 75 to 100 people in this house, and you won’t even know it,” Laura said. “It’s cozy when there’s two, but yet it can handle 75 people, and I still don’t know how that’s possible.”

The night Marino died at his own house two minutes away, the family compound gained its final wing.


“The next day, [my mother] said, ‘Do you mind if I build just something small next to you?’” Laura said.

The something small became a 4,000-square-foot addition with its own entrance, kitchen, and bedroom suite, where Anna Maria Marino has lived for more than two decades — close enough to help keep the traditions, and to watch four generations pass through the house. No longer in need of so much space, Laura is moving to a town house.


“It’s going to give me a chance to decorate, which I love,” she said. “That’s the part of my father that I have, and my mother says it all the time.”

She hopes whoever buys the house uses it the way her family did — at full capacity. She also remembers the line her father left her with after one visit. “He said, ‘Baby, this is a beautiful house. I’m happy for you. But never forget where you came from.’”

hed: Palatial Hudson Valley estate once asking $30M heads to auction — and could sell for millions less
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This mansion couldn’t find a buyer. Now it’s going once, going twice.
A storied 151-acre spread in one of New York’s most guarded old money enclaves is about to find out what it’s really worth.
Renamor, the sprawling French Provincial estate at 120 Ridge Road in Tuxedo Park,hit the market last Augustasking $29.5 million. A year later, with no taker in sight, the price got sliced to roughly $25 million. That didn’t do the trick either.
Now the property is headed to the auction block withConcierge Auctions, with bidding open from Sept. 16 through 29, and opening numbers expected to land somewhere between $5 million and $11 million. But there is no minimum bid set, so it could potentially sell for even lower — a brutal discount.
Mansion Globalfirst reported newsof the sale.
The estate dates back to 1928, built by George S. Amory, a major stockholder in the Sea-Land Freight shipping empire, and his wife Marion Renee, whose combined names gave the property its title.
The couple split their time between New York City, France and Denmark, tucking their Tuxedo Park retreat in among the rolling hills of the exclusive gated village, which happens to be the first private residential community in the country.
Most recently the home belonged to the late Robert S. Dow, a longtime financial industry heavyweight and 1972 Olympic saber fencer, who died in 2024. His widow Christina Seix Dow, a former asset manager, held onto the property until listing it last summer.
The main house alone runs about 14,000 square feet, packed with a great hall, a grand salon, a banquet-sized dining room, a library, a wine cellar and a onetime chapel that’s since been converted into a sitting room.
There’s also a fumoir, the old fashioned term for a smoking room, a detail that dates the house as much as its clay tile roof and dormer windows do. Sixteen bedroom suites and 20 bathrooms round out the main residence, with 19 fireplaces scattered throughout for good measure.
Beyond the front door, the grounds sprawl across three additional structures totaling more than 22,000 square feet combined, including a 3,700-square-foot guest house and a 4,700-square-foot carriage house.
Outdoor amenities include two pools, a tennis court, a putting green, a boathouse perched on Tuxedo Lake, a tea house, a spa building anda one-room log cabinwith its own stone fireplace.
The sellers reportedly sank more than $1 million into geothermal heating and a hidden solar array over the past decade, enough to let the entire estate run independent of the local power grid on its own microgrid system.
Tuxedo Park itself carries plenty of history worth bragging about. The private club there is widely credited as the birthplace of the modern tuxedo, and residents in the community’s earlier days would reportedly roll up in their own private railroad cars.
Etiquette writer Emily Post once summered there with her family. Fewer than 400 people call the village home today, and its historic houses are protected under the National Register of Historic Places.
Estates of this scale typically sell at auction for well under their original list price, though sellers often come out ahead anyway once they factor in the taxes, insurance and upkeep costs of sitting on a property that isn’t moving.

hed: First town ever sold on eBay will return to market
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Bridgeville, CA,made history in 2002 as the first townever sold on eBay, and soon, it will be up for grabs again.
TheNorthern Californialocale—positioned along the Van Duzen River, 45 miles southeast of Eureka and 26 miles east of Fortuna, with an estimated population of just 25—is an 80-acre property surrounded by beautiful redwood trees.
It’s been quite a journey to find an ideal owner for Bridgeville.
When Bridgeville was initially listed oneBayby its former owner, Elizabeth Lapple, the minimum bid was set at $775,000.
The monthlong bidding war—which garnered 250 bids—saw the price soar to $1,777,877.
The winner backed out upon learning how much work the town needed, andSF Gatereported that “a dozen more deals” similarly fell through.
Two years later, in 2004, an Orange County, CA, financial adviser named Bruce Krall purchased Bridgeville for $700,000. At the time, the deal included 10 houses, four cabins, a post office, a cemetery, and a few additional structures.
Krallreportedly had plans to transform the town into a health spa, but helisted it on eBayonce again in 2006, upon the realization he could no longer afford to make restorations.
The next owner was Daniel LaPaille, a 25-year-old entertainment manager from Los Angeles who acquired the town for $1.25 million in 2006. LaPaille had plans to reinvigorate Bridgeville, turning it into a self-sufficient, off-grid destination.
He died by suicide months after the purchase.
Now, LaPaille’s family owns the property, but they’re looking to offload it to a buyer who can see at least some version of his vision through to completion.
“It was all about community for him,” Cindy LaPaille, Daniel’s mother and the current owner of Bridgeville, tells Realtor.com®.
“I would like to see somebody who is really wanting to see the community flourish,” she continues. The ideal buyer would be able to live in the town, which is not possible for her as a Southern California resident, she adds.

Currently, Bridgeville’s rural community is small but mighty.
The community uses the town’s school as a meeting space—which allows them to be “really active,” but it limits the kinds of meetings that can be held.
“There are a lot of great people out here. They all love community, they all love nature. They probably wouldn’t live out here if they didn’t,” the elder LaPaille adds.
Pear, plum, and apple trees, along with blackberry bushes, can be found throughout the town, as well as a variety of wild animals.
“We have two resident bears, lots of deer, wild turkey … if you’re sitting out here, you can always just look across and see something. … We have it all,” LaPaille details. “I’m told we have a bobcat. But that I haven’t seen.”
LaPaille says the family received plenty of suggestions on what to do with Bridgeville over the years—mostly encouragement to “make [it] an Airbnb” destination to attract nature enthusiasts.
“We kind of held out a few times trying to fulfill his dream. It’s an interesting process here,” she says.
Bridgeville has been on and off the market since 2014. The asking price has not since surpassed the near-$1.8 million bid from 2002, peaking at $1.5 million in 2023. Most recently, it was listed in March 2025 for $1.2 million.
Later this September, Bridgeville will be listed by agent Derek Baca of Madrone Realty, who has a handful of recommendations, too.
It is not yet confirmed which structures will be included in the listing, or what the asking price will be.
Noting that he’s received inquiries about the property’s zoning from potential buyers interested in a wide range of endeavors from adding cabins to creating an RV park, Baca confirms that, “yes, you can absolutely do all those things.”
“Humboldt County is very open to economic growth,” he says. “So even if it’s not zoned properly, you can go through planning and building to actually have it rezoned and reclassified to suit your needs.”
Although Daniel LaPaille’s original vision was to support an off-grid community, there is currently public power.
“It is a place that if somebody had the money to develop and turn into something, I think it would flourish 12 months out of the year,” Baca continues.
He also points out that Bridgeville’s unique location—between Highway 5 and Highway 101—qualifies it as “a good middle ground” for a stopover. A gas station, a food truck, or even a solar-powered electric vehicle charging station could be very impactful for travelers passing through.

hed: Their condos burned down 5 years ago — but the pricey HOA bills never stopped: ‘Unconscionable’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about getting burned twice.
Nearly a dozen Texas condo owners whose homes were destroyed in a massive fire more than five years ago are still shelling out hundreds of dollars every month in homeowners association fees — even though their units have yet to be rebuilt.
Eleven owners at Bayfront Towers, a waterfront condominium complex in Nassau Bay outside Houston, have been displaced since a March 29, 2021 blaze reduced their units to rubble,Houston Chronicle reported. Another 26 units sufferedheavy smoke and water damage. No one was injured.
But the HOA bills never stopped, despite the tragedy.
Resident Sarah Arends, whose first-floor corner condo was among those destroyed, is still paying $767 a month in association fees — nearly $10,000 a year — for a home that no longer exists.
Arends told the Chronicle that continuing to pay the fees while having no idea when she can return is “absolutely preposterous.”
Another displaced owner, May-Ying Lam, has paid just under $50,000 in association fees since the fire. Lam described paying for a “nonexistent apartment” as “unconscionable.”
And those monthly charges aren’t the only expense.
After insurance proceeds and reserve funds proved insufficient to complete the reconstruction, the Bayfront Condominium Association levied three special assessments totaling $38,249 per unit, raising more than $2.8 million from the complex’s owners, according to the Chronicle.
The rebuilding process has dragged on for years. The association has worked with at least four contractors and consultants, while its current contractor, Sunrise Certified Services, has missed six promised deadlines over two years, residents told the outlet. Sunrise did not respond to the Chronicle’s requests for comment.
The association maintains that even owners who cannot occupy their homes remain responsible for their share of the property’s expenses.
Gwen Curlee, treasurer of the Bayfront Condominium Association, said maintenance and insurance costs have continued — and risen — since the fire. The association’s bylaws also contain no provision allowing it to suspend fees following a disaster, per Chronicle.
The saga has left some displaced owners ready to cut their losses.
Arends said she plans to sell once her unit is finally completed and receives a certificate of occupancy. Two of the 11 destroyed units have already been listed for sale, including one asking $200,000 — more than $50,000 below its appraised market value.
The ordeal comes in a metro where association living is particularly widespread. Roughly 55% of Houston-area housing units are governedby an HOA, according to Census data cited by the Chronicle — nearly 1 million homes, the most of any US metro.
Meanwhile, the 11 Bayfront owners are still waiting for the homes they lost in 2021 to rise again.

hed: Half of Americans would overpay to live in a gated community for safety, study shows
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Forget granite countertops. The hottest home upgrade in America right now might be a locked gate at the end of the driveway.
A new study finds that half of US adults would pay above market price for a house in a neighborhood witha gated or controlled entrance, and nearly a third say they’d shell out at least 6% more for the privilege.
The numbers come from a survey of 1,000 American adults conducted byTri-State Gate,a Westchester County company that installs automated driveway gates.
Real estate data backs up at least part of the trend. Homes in gated communities already carry a roughly $30,000 premium over comparable ungated properties, according to prior research from the American Real Estate Society.
What makes the survey notable isn’t just the price tag buyers are willing to eat. It’s the disconnect between how dangerous peoplethink their neighborhood isand how safe they actually feel inside it.
Sixty nine percent of respondents said crime where they live hasn’t gotten any worse. Yet 72% admitted they don’t feel fully at ease at home. Only 28% picked the option “very safe, I feel genuinely protected,” while the majority landed on a more hedged answer, “mostly safe, but I stay alert.”
“What stands out to me in this data is that people aren’t necessarily reacting to crime. Most of them said crime in their neighborhood hasn’t changed. What they’re responding to is a lack of control,” Matthew Prato, president of Tri-State Gate, told The Post.
“A gate doesn’t change what’s happening in the neighborhood; it changes who can pull into your driveway without you knowing. For a lot of homeowners, that’s the difference between thinking about their home when they’re away and not thinking about it at all.”
That unease is showing up in behavior, not just survey answers.
Sixty nine percent of respondents now own a security camera or video doorbell, and checking the footage has become something close to a nervous habit.
A third of camera owners say they check their feed multiple times a day, and when you add in people who check daily or whenever an alert goes off, more than eight in 10 camera owners are monitoring their homes constantly.
Despite all that vigilance, most Americans are strangely passive when it comes to acting on it.
Fifty six percent said it would take an actual break-in or a visible pattern of crime nearby before they seriously invested in physical security upgrades, rather than doing it preemptively. That’s a striking number given that break-ins remain rare.
Just 8% of households reported experiencing one or an attempted one in the past two years. Package theft is a far more common headache, with 23% of respondents saying a delivery has been swiped off their doorstep.
The takeaway is less about actual danger and more about the psychology of feeling watched, or unwatched.
Crime rates nationally have been trending down for years, and separate polling from Gallup has found only a small share of Americans call crime in their area a serious problem.
But that data hasn’t translated into peace of mind. If anything, the rise of doorbell cameras and 24/7 footage may be feeding the anxiety it was supposed to cure, turning homeowners into round-the-clock monitors of their own front steps.

hed: ‘Cottage in the sky’ crowns $7.5M NYC penthouse — offering a rare rooftop house right in Manhattan
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
It looks as if a tornado picked up a Cape Cod cottage and dropped it on an East Village rooftop.
Perched above 203 E. 13th St., an unlikely cedar-clad house in the sky — complete with pitched rooflines, terraces and greenery — has hit the market as part of a $7.5 million penthouse.
The three-bedroom, three-bath duplex spans roughly 2,000 square feet indoors, plus nearly 1,000 square feet of private outdoor space. But its defining feature is upstairs: a cottage-like structure that appears strikingly out of place against the surrounding Manhattan skyline.
And many may not even know it exists.
“Generally speaking, when you’re adding a pop-up to a building, you have to have it set far enough back that you don’t see it,” listing broker, Serhant’s Corrin Thomas, told The Post. “Now, this was done at a time when it got approved, so you get the really unique charm of it.”
“Seeing something that has this cottage aesthetic is very rare,” he added. “I’ve seen maybe one or two in the entire city.”
The unusual aerie wasn’t always so quaint.
According to Thomas and fellow listing broker Violetta Weddepohl, an earlier, far plainer rooftop structure was transformed in the mid-1980s into the cottage that crowns the building today.
The result is a home with something of a split architectural personality.
The lower level has the bones of a classic downtown loft, with exposed brick, high ceilings and windows facing multiple directions.
The lower level also features four working woodburning fireplaces, including a pair positioned on opposite sides of the main living and dining areas. A fifth fireplace is currently being used to hold furniture but could potentially be made functional, according to Thomas.
Climb the internal staircase, however, and the apartment takes on an altogether different character.
The penthouse has two private outdoor areas surrounding the upper house structure, including planted and irrigated terraces. From there, the cottage’s improbable setting becomes particularly apparent: shingles and greenery in the foreground, Manhattan rooftops beyond. Adding out-of-city charm to the mix, the house even has a chimney.
The cottage retains an A-frame roof, although its full height is currently concealed by the interior ceiling.
The unidentified owner purchased the apartment for $4.44 million in 2015 and has used it as a primary residence for more than a decade, according to StreetEasy and the brokers.
At $7.5 million, the asking price works out to $3,750 per interior square foot. The brokers noted that the figure doesn’t assign any value to the outdoor space.
“It has all the warmth of a townhouse, but you’re completely bathed in light and you’ve got a view out every window,” Weddepohl said. “The arches, the brick, the fireplaces — it’s a very magical place.”

hed: Home of the Week: In Marblehead, a charming 3-bedroom antique for $759k
subhead: Framed by New England classics — broadleaf and yellow cap hydrangeas — sits this New England antique, circa 1850
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

14 Linden St., Marblehead

$759,000

StyleAntique

Year built1850

Square feet1,205

Bedrooms3

Baths1 full

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$6,375 (2026)


On a narrow street in one of the first European settlements in the region, framed by New England classics broadleaf and yellow cap hydrangeas sits this New England antique, circa 1850. A stairwell on the left side leads to the main entry located off the driveway.

The black door is framed by a white pilastered surround with windowed sidelights. The same colors are used for the windows that reinforce the classic New England look — black louvered shutters adjacent to white framed windows with decorative muntins. The shingled exterior is grey.


Stepping inside is a lateral hallway leading on the left to the dining room and on the right the living room. A key feature in the living room is the brick-faced, functioning wood-burning fireplace original to the home. To one side of the fireplace, which has a white wood mantle, is a built-in cabinet with storage and shelving. There are four double-hung windows on two walls and thin crown molding throughout the room.

Flooring here and through all but the one bathroom is original hardwood, now with a glossy finish, and interior doorways are framed with white trim original to the home.


Turning left from the front door, a doorway framed with white trim leads to the dining room. There are exposed support beams painted white to blend in with the ceiling. The lower half of the walls are covered with raised panel wainscoting, and there is a decorative brick fireplace. To the right is a floor-to-ceiling white china cabinet. There is a central light fixture and currently a table for four underneath.


The dining room flows into the kitchen where there is a three-window bum-pout opposite a the electric stove, white cabinets, the sink, and a small countertop prep space. A double-hung window is above the counter. On the interior wall are more cabinets — two layers with a deck in between. The flooring is refinished hardwood.


This leads to the final room on this floor, an updated room that serves as a mudroom with heated ceramic tile flooring as well as a laundry room. There are exposed beams crossing the cathedral-style ceiling with a skylight. A half-door connects to the kitchen.

The home’s full bathroom is nicely situated among all of the first-floor rooms. It has a curtained shower/bath combination. There is ceramic tile flooring and a single vanity. A wall-mounted paneled radiator sits underneath a window.



The three bedrooms are on the upper floor and they alone comprise that level. The largest, considered the primary, has a large skylight on the angled ceiling and a double-hung window on one wall. There are two double-door closets with a shelf in between. The floor is hardwood. The two secondary bedrooms are similar in design with hardwood flooring but with a single window.



There is a fenced-in yard, an outdoor shed and mature trees on the property and surrounding it. Cooling is by window air conditioners. There is oil heat.

Lindsey McCarthyof Coldwell Banker Real Estate has the listing.
