hed: Quiet Louisiana enclave becomes a magnet for wealthy buyers — as luxury home prices have doubled
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Forget the Hamptons. The smart money is heading to a stretch of Louisiana most Americans couldn’t find on a map.
The Northshore of Lake Pontchartrain, anchored by the towns of Covington, Mandeville and Slidell, has become one of the hottest luxury housing markets nobody’s talking about.
Prices for the priciest homes in Covington have shot up 94% over the last decade, while Mandeville isn’t far behind at 80%, according to fresh data fromRealtor.com.
Compare that to the national luxury market, where top-tier home values have climbed a comparatively modest 57% over the same stretch.
Realtor.com senior economist Anthony Smith says the seeds of the boom were planted two decades ago, in the aftermath ofHurricane Katrina.
“Households who wanted to stay near New Orleans moved north across the lake,” Smith told theDaily Mail.“Over the years, St. Tammany Parish stopped being a suburb and became its own metro, though it keeps close ties to New Orleans.”
These days the buyers pouring in aren’t just locals. Out-of-state money is flowing in from Dallas and Chicago, where house hunters are cashing out on markets that no longer stretch as far as they used to.
In Louisiana, that same budget buys a lot more square footage, along with the kind of old-money aesthetic that’s made cities like Charleston and Savannah into buyer magnets.
“The area also has the Southern charm ingredients buyers look for: walkable downtowns, historic cottages and old oak trees lining the streets,” Smith said. “Buyers here can capture the same character for less.”
Covington has crowned itself the region’sluxury capital. The median price for the top 10% of homes there now sits at $1.13 million. Climb into the top 5% and that number jumps to nearly $1.87 million. At the very top, the top 1%, homes are trading for an average of $3.74 million.
Roughly 11.2% of Covington’s listings, or 82 homes, are currently priced above the million-dollar mark, the highest share on the Northshore. Mandeville trails close behind at 9.4%.
Part of the draw is geography. Covington sits along the Tchefuncte River, the Bogue Falaya River and Lake Pontchartrain itself, giving buyers waterfront access for boating and fishing that’s hard to find at these prices elsewhere.
A wave of high earning professionals has also settled in as medical employers like St. Tammany Parish and Ochsner continue to expand their footprint.
There’s a catch, though. Homeowners insurance in the region can swing wildly depending on a property’s age and how close it sits to a flood zone, something Smith flagged as a major factor for anyone eyeing a home near the water or in an older neighborhood.
The market’s roots go back generations. Covington has long served as a warm weather escape for well-heeled New Orleans families, and their old estates now sit shoulder to shoulder with sleek new construction.
One current listing captures that mix perfectly: a $3.2 million midcentury modern spread on the Tchefuncte River, set on 3.4 acres with a dock built to handle yachts up to 80 feet, a private boat lift and a detached garden house.
Another, a $4.5 million Colonial dating back to the 1860s, comes with white columns, a sprawling veranda, a tennis court, a pool and 2 acres of oak canopied grounds overlooking the Bogue Falaya.
Alexis R. Foster of 10/12 Properties, who has the $3.2 million listing, says the growth has outpaced what the parish was built to handle.
“Both residential and commercial has grown so much. The parish can’t keep up with the amount of people moving to the area,” Foster said.
Smith cautions that the eye-popping percentage gains are still concentrated in a narrow slice of the market.
“When we look at areas like Covington, the growth at the very top is high, but it’s still a narrow segment,” Smith said. “The parish overall has room to grow, particularly in areas like Folsom and Bush where land is still available and new supply can be added.”
Translation: this Louisiana land rush is just getting started.

hed: New York couple claps back on viral claim they spent $2M on a home renovation for their dog
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
No, they didn’t spend $2 million renovating a house just for their dog — despite what many may think.
Howard and Suze Rubin are listing their midcentury-modern Pound Ridge retreat for $2.9 million — and pushing back on a viral narrative that they poured a cool $2 million into the property solely for Buster, their 9-year-old bearded collie.
“We didn’t spend $2 million renovating the house for the dog,” Howard Rubin told The Post.
He said the renovation bill covered a sweeping overhaul of the property — from major mechanical systems and appliances to internet infrastructure and an additional garage that cost a few hundred thousand dollars on its own.
Headlines regarding their listing even prompted angry messages from people criticizing the couple for supposedly spending millions on their dog while others were struggling.
But listing agent Sally Slater of Douglas Elliman, who has worked with the Rubins for more than 25 years, said the upgrades have to do with Rubin’s own personal nature.
“He’s so meticulous in his whole thinking,” Slater told The Post.
The property has 16 cameras monitoring the house and grounds, two full-size house generators in case one fails and two separate internet feeds. Rubin even installed a termite protection system despite an inspection finding no termite problem.
Rubin, a professor emeritus of computer science at Hunter College and founder and CEO of technology research and advisory firm Rubin Worldwide, has a simple explanation: “I just like things to work.”
Buster still got plenty of perks when the couple renovated the spread.
The four-bedroom, 3½-bath home, spanning 4,442 square feet on 2.76 acres, is fully fenced to keep Buster safely separated from deer and coyotes, with pet-friendly turf and plenty of shade.
Because Buster likes the water but isn’t much of a swimmer, the couple reworked the pool with a shallow sun shelf where he can splash around.
Indoors, there are nine TVs throughout, and Rubin said Buster likes to plop down in front of one to watch his favorite show, “Paw Patrol,” until he falls asleep.
The home’s floor-to-ceiling windows even let him lie on the floor and keep tabs on the deer outside.
The Rubins bought this residence in 2019 for $1.82 million after finding Florida summers too hot, initially envisioning it as both their own getaway and a pet-friendly rental. COVID shelved the rental plan.
But building a life around animals was nothing new for the couple.
Rubin grew up in The Bronx and Suze in Queens, and over their 56-year marriage they have kept everything from dogs and cats to rabbits, hamsters and horses. Suze worked as a veterinary technician and an EMT.
When their son started riding at age 6, the family bought Peas and Carrots, a small stable in South Salem, NY. Slater helped them buy and later sell the property.
Rubin said members of the 1996 Olympic team trained there and “Superman” actor Christopher Reeve was among its clients.
Now 9, Buster has developed arthritis, one reason the Rubins have decided to sell.
The couple plans to consolidate at their one-story Florida home, where Buster won’t have to contend with hills, stairs, snow or ice.
“He’s part of the family,” Rubin said.
The home, which hit the market last Wednesday, is already drawing interest — including at least one prospective buyer who brought along her own four-legged companion.
“One couple came — she had a dog in her pocketbook,” Slater said.

hed: Buffalo and Houston are the next big landing spots for priced-out renters, Zillow finds
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For-sale home prices refuse to budge, and it’s pushing an army of would-be buyers back into the rental market — a trend quietly reshaping which cities are about to boom.
New data from Zillowshows renters nationwide are increasingly hunting for apartments outside their own metro areas, and the cities pulling in the biggest crowds of outsiders are Buffalo, Chicago and Houston, followed by New Orleans and Dallas.
In markets like Salt Lake City,Raleigh, Hartford and Nashville, out-of-towners searching for rentals now outnumber locals altogether, a sign that the migration wave that hit those cities has already matured into full-blown demand.
That matters more than it seems.Rental searchestend to predict where home sales heat up next, since renting is often the test run before a purchase.
“Renting is often how people try out a new community before committing. When we see a market with a growing share of rental searches coming from outside the metro, that tips us off to a developing pipeline,” Mischa Fisher, chief economist at Zillow, said in the report.
“A year-over-year surge in out-of-town browsing in places like Buffalo and Chicago tells us a wave of newcomers may not be far behind.”
Buffalo is the clearest case study. The average home value in the city sits at $249,040, a fraction of the $434,100 national median for an existing home sold in July, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Homes there are also moving fast, going to pending in about 10 days, and prices have climbed 104% since the start of the pandemic, according to Parcl Labs data.
Despite that run-up,Buffalo remainsone of the more attainable markets in the entire Northeast, and renters testing out the city before buying appear to be catching on early.
Houston tells a slightly different story, one built on jobs rather than sheer cost. The metro’s median sale price was $360,000 over the three months ending in July, up 2.2% year-over-year, according to Redfin, while Zillow put the average home value closer to $260,000.
Houston’s economy added roughly 18,000 jobs on an annualized basis over the three months ending in May, according to the Dallas Federal Reserve, with growth spread across energy, construction, manufacturing and healthcare.
Relocation buyers from expensive coastal states, particularly California, New York and Illinois, have increasingly viewed Houston as their landing pad, and the rental search data suggests many are trying the city out first.
Chicago is the outlier in the group, since it is not cheap by comparison to Buffalo or Houston, but it is still far more affordable than the coasts. The city’s average home value stands at $315,024, and depending on the data source, the broader metro’s median sale price ranges from the mid-$300,000s to as high as $425,000.
Even so, Chicago ranked first for annual median price growth among the nation’s 40 largest markets in a recent Homes.com analysis, evidence that renters flowing in from outside the metro are arriving at a market already gaining momentum rather than one still cooling off.
The pattern lines up with the broader math. Rents, meanwhile, are creeping back up after years of relief. August marked the first month-over-month increase in four years, according to Apartment List, even though prices were still running slightly below where they stood a year earlier.
New York Citystands apart from the rest of the country’s renters in one key way. While most tenants elsewhere are searching just across state lines, New Yorkers are looking south, with Raleigh and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando and Tampa pulling in outsized shares of their attention.
Fisher said the direction of the traffic tells its own story.
“When we see strong out-of-town interest flowing into a smaller market, it’s often an affordability story. So renters in pricier places are choosing or discovering that they can get a lot more for their money somewhere new,” Fisher said.
“When the flow goes the other direction, into a major metro, it’s frequently regional pull, people drawn to a big city’s job market or opportunities from nearby.”
Even with the wave of pandemic-era arrivals already reshaping Southern cities, the region has held onto its price advantage over the coasts, keeping the migration alive on both a financial and lifestyle basis.
RentCafe’s latest“Best Cities for Renters”ranking backs that up, with 37 of the top 50 spots going to Southern cities and McKinney, Texas, Huntsville, Alabama, and Austin, Texas, taking the top three slots.

hed: Dallas skyscraper scooped up by California-based firm as investment pours into Lone Star State
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A San Francisco investment firm is doubling down on Texas as money continues to pour into the Lone Star State from California.
Shorenstein Investment Advisers announced Tuesday that it has acquired Sherry Lane Place, a 20-story, 300,000-square-foot office tower in Dallas’ prestigious Preston Center, for an undisclosed price.
The purchase is Shorenstein’s fourth in less than two years, and gives the firm control of about 20% of the Class A office space in one of Dallas’ strongest-performing business districts,according to Dallas News.
The 93%-leased tower at 5956 Sherry Lane, which is worth $120.2 million, is home to the Park Cities Club and once housed an office for President George W. Bush.
Shorenstein bought the 320,000-square-foot Sterling Plaza in Preston Center in July 2025 and purchased The Tennyson in Plano, Texas, in June.
The firm has owned International Plaza II, a 15-story tower along Dallas Parkway, since late 2024.
The shopping spree comes asTexas continues to attract businesses, residents and investment from California — where high taxes, housing costs and regulation have helped fuel an exodus of companies and residents to lower-cost states.
Since 2024, Shorenstein has acquired 13 office properties across the country in deals totaling roughly $2 billion.

hed: Whoop plans to lease additional space in Boston before going public
content: Whoop, a Boston company that makes wearable fitness trackers, plans to double the size of its Kenmore Square headquarters ahead of going public, its chief executive said this week. Chief executive Will Ahmed said in an interview with Bloomberg published Wednesday that he expects the initial public offering to come in about 18 months. The company plans to lease 107,000 square feet of office space next to its existing headquarters, an expansion that “can accommodate 1,000 employees,” Bloomberg reported. Whoop garnered a valuation of $10.1 billion in March. “It’s hard to know at an early stage if a company is great, but you want to create an environment where they can continue to flourish,” Ahmed told Bloomberg. A Whoop spokesperson declined to comment beyond the Bloomberg article. Whoop opened a 121,000-square-foot headquarters in the heart of Boston’s Kenmore Square three years ago. The company has steadily grown in valuation since launching in 2012, and earlier this year announced plans to hire 600 more employees in 2026, on top of its existing 800-odd workers. Bloomberg reported that Whoop has so far made almost 400 hires this year, more than 70 percent of which were Boston-based roles.Whoop’s headquarters sign, where the company name is spelled out in all-caps white letters facing Kenmore Square, for years blocked the city’s famed CITGO sign. Suffolk Construction crews have demolished and are in the midst of replacing the historic CITGO sign 30 feet higher than its prior home, a move that should be complete by mid-November. Boston biotech AI Proteins earlier this year leased 40,000 square feet at 660 Beacon St., a building that’s part of Related Beal’s 471,000-square-foot One Kenmore Square redevelopment of former Boston University buildings. “We are committed to creating spaces that inspire innovation and foster growth for companies across Boston’s life science and technology sectors,” Alex Provost, the company’s development vice president, said earlier this year. Whoop’s latest fundraising round came in at$575 million, and the company’s most recent investors include the Qatar Investment Authority and Macquarie Capital. The company’s Boston employees are expected to be in the office four days a week, Ahmed told Bloomberg.Due to incorrect information provided to The Globe, an earlier version of this story misidentified the location of AI Proteins’ Kenmore Square headquarters. The company earlier this year leased 40,000 square feet at 660 Beacon St. Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Can AI be your interior designer? Not quite, but it can act as an assistant.
subhead: Boston-area interior designers are embracing the benefits of AI in their work — with a critical eye
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Eva Barbier was overwhelmed with options while renovating her home office.
The “fairly large” third-floor space of her home in Newton’s Waban village needed to serve multiple functions: as a guest suite for visiting family during the holidays and a spot for Barbier to work as a marketing consultant running her own business,Eva Barbier Consulting. While Barbier had gathered pictures for inspiration, she wanted to give her interior designer, Jessie Sheehan ofJessie Sheehan Interiors, a stronger idea of what she was looking for.
“When I can see something installed, I can say I like it, or I don’t. But when I’m looking at various tiny swatches, it’s really hard to visualize them in the room,” said Barbier.
For an accent wall with two windows behind her desk, where Barbier generally sits to log into Zoom meetings with clients, Sheehan and Barbier had settled on a leafyLewis & Wood wallpaperwith beech trees. But still, Barbier wanted to see what it would look like.
“She just really wanted to make sure that the tree composition and the branches’ locations would look the best,” said Sheehan, who had the wallpaper installer, Jim Arena ofArena Wallpapering, draw branches on the wall with pencil to give Barbier a visual. “But she still couldn’t quite get her head wrapped around it.”
Barbier plugged a photo of the room and another of the wallpaper into Google Gemini to visualize the composition, specifically where to put the branches on the wall. She played around with the layout and was so pleased with the AI image that she told Sheehan to move forward.“I hate to say it, but she was able to create what it would actually look like as opposed to just a pencil sketch on the wall,” said Sheehan. “Both the wallpaper installer and I sort of looked at each other and were like, ‘Oh wow … that’s good.’”
Barbier isn’t the only homeowner who has turned to AI for design help. According to amarket research company S&S Insider, the AI interior design marketsize was worth $1.47 billion in 2024, and it’s projected to reach $6.96 billion by 2032 thanks to the growing use of tools like 3D visualization, augmented reality, virtual reality, and machine-learning algorithms. But interior designers are quick to say that while AI can be helpful, it doesn’t prevent your next renovation from becoming a nightmare reminiscent of the 1986 Tom Hanks’ comedy, “The Money Pit.”

According to amarket research company S&S Insider, the AI interior design marketsize was worth $1.47 billion in 2024, and it’s projected to reach $6.96 billion by 2032 thanks to the growing use of tools like 3D visualization, augmented reality, virtual reality, and machine-learning algorithms. But interior designers are quick to say that while AI can be helpful, it doesn’t prevent your next renovation from becoming a nightmare reminiscent of the 1968 Tom Hanks’ comedy, “The Money Pit.”Lindy Lowney, ofLindy Lowney Designhas seen a variety of AI disasters cross her desk since its rise in popularity. There are the funny examples, like an area rug that looks like it’s the size of a beach towel under a dining room table courtesy of ChatGPT.
“They’d send me a photo of a dining room, and the dining room chairs are missing legs,” said Lowney, who is based in Rhode Island.
Then there are the scary ones, like in kitchens where everything from building codes and safety violations to electrical and plumbing problems are ignored by AI. When people attempt to assume the role of a contractor, problems are imminent.
“Everything that we do is done with measurements, budgets, and codes, and that plays into safety, health, and your environment,” said Lowney. “A lot of contractors want an old-school setup of technical documents and drawings, and these basic AI programs may not have somebody driving it with the technical experience.”
Still, many designers are in favor of AI’s presence for creating simple visualizations. Vivian Robins ofArketa Design Studiofinds AI helpful in assisting clients who need a quick visual of a change. While she sees a vision clearly in her head, she recognizes that the client doesn’t always have the same innate ability.
“I feel that if anything, it can aid us in trying to get something to somebody quicker,” said Robins. “That’s our superpower, right? We see everything in our head. But that’s not a client’s superpower. So, we can drop that fabric onto a photograph of an existing chair that we’re reupholstering and be specific and tell [AI] it’s a vertical and horizontal repeat, so that the computer knows it’s not enlarging it on the existing fabric. But once you show that to the client, they’re like, ‘Oh, that looks awesome!’”
Despite the changing tide in opinions about AI in the interior design industry, some designers recognize that their fellow professionals have some trepidation about AI’s spread.
“I think a lot of designers are seeing it as an enemy, like ‘it’s going to take my job.’ I do see a lot of resistance,” said Lulu Friedman ofDidi Interiors + Architecturein Needham, who is openly embracing AI for some projects. “I think people think that it’s cheating. But I see it more as a tool to make designers better and more efficient.”
But for Barbier’s attempt to see her wallpaper in place, AI served its purpose. After she settled on the wallpaper, paint, and furniture, she completed the space and, with the help of a Wellesley-based art consultant,Libby Silvia Artstyle, she chose a piece by artistHayley Mathewesto hang between the windows. With her home office finished, she is thrilled with the results. And when she’s not working or busy with her kids, she finds herself seeking out some quiet time in the peaceful oasis.
“I love it up here. It just makes me really happy. In the little spare time that I have, I like to draw and paint,” she said. “I will come up here and do all that creative thinking because it’s a very soothing and relaxing space for me.”

See more of our coverage in your search results.
It could be a scene from a Nicolas Cage film.
A giant, expanding sinkhole swallows up part of an Oscar-winning actor’s oceanfront Malibu escape,leading to the evacuationof 31 homes on an exclusive, gated street.
But the scene is real — and only in Malibu could residents just shrug it off.
“We had three back-to-back hurricanes in a row. That’s why this is happening. Stuff happens. It’s nature!” said broker Irene Dazzan-Palmer, of the Agency, who shared the four-story home’s listing with her son Sandro Dazzan when Cage bought it, on exclusive Sea Level Drive, for $10.5 million in 2024.
But sinkholes aren’t the only issues Malibu homeowners presently face.
More than a year after theJanuary 2025 Palisades Fire, which scorched 600 Malibu homes, giant waves up to 10 feet high are crashing into oceanfront homes. In some cases, they’re “taking away decks and even a pool,” one resident told Gimme Shelter. Another described the crashing waves in front of her home as “violent.”
“Eight-foot-high waves may not seem huge, like a tsunami. But if you are on the sand and the wave is 8 feet high, that is considerably taller than you, and you would be engulfed by it if it came to shore,” said brokerErnie Carswell, of Sotheby’s International Realty.
But Malibu residents are a resilient, hardy lot, used to dealing with all sorts of issues — all while their homes slowly sink into the Pacific.
“There is so much that those tough Malibu people have to endure, so many geological traumas, tsunami warnings, mudslides, floods, fire, earthquakes — our whole region is susceptible to that — as well as slowly sliding into the ocean and now this,” Carswell said.
“It’s typical Malibu risk,” he added.
Once, Carswell said, when he sold the late actressLoretta Swit’sMalibu home, the deal came with a disclosure, so that the buyer was aware that the home “was moving one half an inch toward the ocean every year.”
“That’s a lot of movement,” Carswell said, “and when you drive down Malibu Road, it becomes a little undulating. It wasn’t built that way, but the soil underneath the road is moving, like it’s a serpent.”
Cage’s sinkhole, however,can be attributed to the weather.
“This happens to our coastal region because of the hurricanes. The most recent one was not far from Hawaii. It created massive waves, and there were washouts all the way down to Newport Beach,” Carswell said.
The area around Cage’s home — the Broad Beach/Point Lechuza corridor of western Malibu — is very susceptible to losing its sand barrier. “It lost all the sand around 20 years ago, and it had to be trucked back in,” Carswell said.
Malibu, Carswell added, is also notorious for its frequent fires, where hundreds of homes are lost — and yet people remain.
Still, the rebuilding — from the Palisades to Malibu — is tough to navigate, and home sale prices and the frequency of sales in Malibu are falling.
The median price of single-family homes in Malibu fell 7.3% year-over-year in June 2026, according to Realtor.com. At the same time, active listings across Malibu rose 7.1%, compared with a 5.5% decline across California as a whole.
Even so, Malibu residents and their brokers remain undaunted.
“Malibu has been there for well over 100 years. It’s always been one of the most desirable locations in California. Sometimes you just get the perfect storm, or in this case, bad things happening all at once. But by no means do I believe that Malibu won’t recover. It’s quicker and easier to rebuild here than in the Palisades after the catastrophic events. Prices have been impacted — they’ve come down — but they will recover once people see construction,” said broker and reality star Josh Flagg, of Compass.
Carswell added, “People still pay a premium to live in Malibu. It’s where the highest sales in our state are happening. Malibu is a mindset, and you pay for the risk of living there.”

hed: 25 years after 9/11, the World Trade Center’s last tower finally rises
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Larry Silverstein was 70 years old when he tooktitle to the Twin Towers, posing for photos with a giant set of cardboard keys. He figured he had finally arrived — and he could start thinking about retirement. Seven weeks later, on Sept. 11, 2001, his optimistic site became one of tragedy.
Now 95, Silverstein still goes to his office every day at 7 World Trade Center,the first tower his company rebuilt, and watches the final piece of his 25-year project rise a few blocks away.
“New York has always been a city that refuses to walk away from a challenge,” Silverstein told The Post. “After 9/11, I made a promise to New Yorkers that we would rebuild the World Trade Center, commemorate those we lost [and] restore commerce to Lower Manhattan.”
Ground broke in Julyon 2 World Trade Center, a 55-story, nearly 2-million-square-foot tower at 200 Greenwich Street that will become American Express’snew global headquarters.
It is the last commercial office building called for in the original master plan; when it opens in 2031, every site on the 16-acre campus will be finished or under construction, according to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which owns the land.
“Every one of these other buildings kind of had to be built first,” Dara McQuillan, chief marketing and communications officer for Silverstein Properties, told The Post, explaining why 2WTC is only now going vertical.
Money was the first obstacle. Silverstein bought the lease on the Twin Towers for $3.2 billion in 2001, then spent five years fighting more than 20 insurance companies over payouts, a fight that only ended after then-Gov. Eliot Spitzer threatened to bar insurers from doing business in New York if they didn’t pay up.
That money, plus federal Liberty Bonds, went first into 7 World Trade Center,One World Trade Centerand 3 and 4 World Trade Center — necessary steps to prove the site could attract tenants, before anyone would finance another speculative tower. Bureaucracy compounded the delay. The land belongs to the Port Authority, controlled by the governors of New York and New Jersey, and, at one point, 19 government agencies had oversight over the project, McQuillan said.
The turning point came only this year,when American Express agreed to serve as anchor tenantfor the entire building, giving Silverstein the guarantee it needed to secure financing. The excavation and foundation work for 2WTC was actually finished back in 2013, tied to construction of the Oculus transit hub, so this summer’s groundbreaking involved no new digging.
American Express will not just anchor the new tower, it will own the whole thing outright — making it the only building at the World Trade Center Silverstein will not lease out. For AmEx, the move is a homecoming of sorts. The company has been headquartered across the street, at 200 Vesey, for nearly 40 years, and traces its Lower Manhattan roots back nearly two centuries.
“We witnessed firsthand the tragedy of September 11 and mourned the loss of 11 cherished colleagues,” Denise Pickett, President of Enterprise Shared Services at American Express, said at the July groundbreaking. “When many questioned what the future would hold, American Express chose to stay. [With the tower] we reaffirm that choice, and our confidence in the future of this remarkable neighborhood, by building here once again.”
The tower will hold up to 10,000 employees across 55 office floors, more space than the company occupies today, though a spokesperson said the extra room reflects more space per employee rather than a hiring surge. Its signature feature is an acre-plus of outdoor terraces and gardens woven through the building.
Interior plans, including restaurants, are still being worked out. The next milestone is topping out, expected around 2029.
Each tower was shaped by the same instruction, drawn up in architect Daniel Libeskind’s 2003 master plan for the eight acres of memorial site and eight acres of office towers.
“Every building faces the 9-11 Memorial,” McQuillan said. “That’s where the office lobbies are.”
The louder, more commercial parts of each building — retail, restaurants, signage — are pushed to the side streets.
Individual architects have layered in their own gestures. At4 World Trade Center,the glass was chosen because it seems to vanish at certain times of day. At 2WTC, architect Norman Foster built the tribute into the outdoor gardens themselves.
The broader campus is now 97% leased, McQuillan said, with just a handful of floors left. Most are stacked at the top of 3 World Trade Center, where a temporary exhibit tells the rebuilding story through photographs, models and news clippings, including decades of coverage from The Post.
The last open question is5 World Trade Center,envisioned as a roughly 1,200-unit residential tower on a parking lot that once held the Deutsche Bank building, which was badly damaged on 9/11 and dismantled piece by piece — a process so difficult two firefighters lost their lives during the deconstruction.
Financing has stalled amid rising construction costs, with Port Authority officials telling a Manhattan Community Board earlier this year that certain costs have jumped as much as 50%, a spike one official tied partly to instability in the Middle East.
“The Port Authority remains fully committed to delivering a world class tower at Site 5, including the goal of one third of the units being affordable,” the agency told The Post.
McQuillan said Silverstein is working with the Port Authority to figure out a path forward, but there is no firm timeline yet.
Twenty-five years after the towers fell, and with a single office tower left to complete the vision drawn up in the chaos of 2003, McQuillan, who has spent more than two decades telling this story for Silverstein — the man who insisted on rebuilding — put it simply.
“There’s an enormous amount of pride in not just working at the World Trade Center, but completing the final office building here is of major significance,” he said. “Nearly everyone has a personal connection to this place one way or another.”

hed: Steph Curry offloads massive SF property as speculation swirls over future with Warriors
content:

Golden StateWarriors legend Steph Curryappears to have scored millions after offloading a massive property in the Bay Area.
The 38-year-old point guard purchased a two-story masonry building in San Francisco at the corner of 20th and Illinois streets, close to the waterfront at Pier 70, for $8.5 million in 2024.
On Tuesday, the place sold for $11 million to a Utah Corporation with an office in the area, according to property records obtained by theSan Francisco Chronicle.
The purchase was to be a flagship headquarters for his off-court business Thirty Ink, but the project was halted in 2025 over a reported dispute with a local union over the use of workers for the construction.
Plans for the property initially entailed renovating the 25,000 square foot building into an impressive five-story office space, complete with an event space, office and lab space. It was also slated to have a roof deck and a three-bedroom penthouse for clients visiting the area.

hed: San Francisco’s deserted shopping palace heads for sale with staggering fall in value
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An empty shopping mall that was once the crown jewel ofdowntown San Franciscois again seeking a buyer after a prior deal to sell the desolate property imploded this year.
Sellers are likely to offload the 1.5 million-square-foot San Francisco Centre, whichbooted its few remaining tenantslast year, at a pitiful fraction of its former worth — no more than $130 million, compared to a valuation of $1.2 billion a decade ago,per the WSJ.
The ornate nine-level complex, known for its rare spiral escalators and 102-foot diameter glass-and-steel dome, once housed a Bloomingdale’s, Nordstrom, a nine-screen movie theater and a posh day spa in additional toseveral floors of retailatop a BART station at the center of downtown.

It was one of the top shopping destinations in California before the pandemic hollowed out the area, replacing commuters and tourists with open drug use and petty crime.
Now the deal mall has become a glaring symbol of collapse in the once-bustling shopping district.
Nordstrom and Bloomingdales announced the closures of their San Francisco Centre locations in 2023 as foot traffic in the area struggled to recover. Soon after, the mall’s owner, Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield, stopped paying its loan and turned theproperty over the lenders.
A $130 million deal to offload to property to Presidio Bay and Prado Group fell apart in July after the developers determined that the mall, which sits on land owned by San Francisco Unified School District, would be too costly to redevelop.
The property costs millions of dollars per year just to maintain, per the WSJ, and is expected to run out of cash within months.
Meanwhile, developers and others have floated wild ideas to repurpose the cavernous former shopping mecca.
One possible bidder, Urban Land Development, is reportedly eyeing a massive sports complex at the site that could include volleyball, soccer and basketball facilities. Architectural firm Gensler proposed a massive soccer stadium at the mall.
Design students at Stanford and UC Berkeley “reimagined” the mall as a mixed-use development that blends housing with entertainment amenities such as a trampoline park and go-kart track, alongside green space, a food court, a concert venue and immersive art, the SF Chroniclereported.

hed: Tory Burch’s ex Chris Burch asks $39.5M for revamped Hamptons estate — seeking a hefty profit
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Billionaire investorChris Burchis looking to turn a tidy profit on his Hamptons retreat — after giving the sprawling waterfront estate a major makeover.
Burch, the founder and CEO of Burch Creative Capital who co-founded the Tory Burch fashion label with his then-wife,designer Tory Burch, has listed his Water Mill estate for $39.5 million.
He purchased the spread, known as Listowel, for $28 million in 2021, property records show, marking his return to the Hamptons just months after unloading another Southampton estate for $15.5 million.
The Post reportedon Burch’s purchase at that time.
The deal was one of several big-ticket real estate moves by the serial entrepreneur.
Burch bought a waterfront Miami Beach estate for $14.2 million in 2020, extensively renovated it and later listed it for $49 million, according tothe Real Deal. He has also rented at Manhattan’s glossy220 Central Park Southand has owned homes in the Hamptons and near Paris.
His property interests have extended overseas, too. Burch and hotelier James McBride acquired the Indonesian resort now known as NIHI Sumba in 2012 and transformed the former surf retreat into a luxury resort,Forbes reported.
Back in Water Mill, the nearly 7-acre property at 258 Horsemill Lane sits directly on Mecox Bay, with roughly 360 feet of water frontage.
Since Burch bought the estate, the shingle-style home has undergone an extensive renovation. The work transformed the interiors and reconfigured the floor plan.
The seven-bedroom home was originally designed by architect Katherine McCoy, with interiors by Daniel Romualdez. The original project took five years to complete.
Among its more distinctive features is a two-story library. The property also has a pool overlooking Mecox Bay, a private dock and a carriage house.
Approvals are also in place for a three-bedroom guesthouse.
The property is surrounded on three sides by farmland, with Mecox Bay forming its fourth boundary.
Listowel has had a long journey through the Hamptons luxury market.
The property first hit the market for $39 million in 2017. Its asking price was eventually slashed to $29.5 million before Burch bought it in 2021,according to previous reports.
Now, following his renovation, Burch has brought the estate nearly full circle — asking $39.5 million, slightly more than its original price nearly a decade ago and $11.5 million above what he paid.
Tim Davis of the Corcoran Group holds the listing.

hed: Mystery buyer of Libbie Mugrabi’s Hamptons mansion for $6M steal unmasked
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Give in or get gone.
Those are the options for the socialite Libbie Mugrabiafter recently losingher luxe Bridgehampton estate in a humiliating auction to a hopeful Queens politician.
Court records reveal thatHenry Ikezi, an investor who made a failed run for Queens borough president last November, has emerged as the winner of last month’s auction for Mugrabi’s 10,687-square-foot mansion, with a $5.86 million commitment. That sum is a far cry from the $25 million Mugrabi aimed to fetch earlier this year.
The purchase was made in Ikezi’s name, but it was his brother, Stanley, who appeared to be the one bidding at the auction and placing the required 10% down payment for the property on his behalf.
Depending on the legal structure of the sale, Ikezi has 30 or 45 days to complete his purchase, and then take over the property. If Mugrabi,who has livedat the estate throughout the court proceedings, refuses to leave, she can physically be evicted by Suffolk County sheriffs, per state law.
Ikezi, when contacted by The Post in the wake of the dramatic late-summer sale, said “no comment” when asked about the transaction or his plans for the property.
Mugrabi did not return requests for comment. Her mother, Jane Scher, said only that her daughter “is doing good.”
Ikezi has a net worth on paper of $23.4 million, based on his roughly 40% holdings of shares in Solidion Technology, an early-stage growth company developing advanced batteries. The company and its predecessor Honeycomb Battery Co., which was established in 2015, have never turned a profit and had generated minimal sales, filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show.
Ikezi’s holdings in Solidion are through his own investments and those of investment vehicles he oversees. One of these vehicles was used to provide the down payment for Mugrabi’s home.
Outside of tech,Ikezialso serves asNew York GOP State Committeemanfor the 24th Assembly District covering parts of eastern Queens including Flushing and Queensboro Hill. He is also listed as a district leader with theQueens County Republican Party.
Ikezi ran for Queens Borough President last November, receiving roughly 30% of votes, with winnerDonovan Richardsgetting about 70%.
Meanwhile, Mugrabi has used extensive litigation to try to hold onto the property she got as part of her late 2020divorce settlementfrom the billionaire art collector David Mugrabi, son of the Israeli industrialist Jose Mugrabi.
Mugrabi previously claimed to The Post she got $100 million in the split, but that number is not verified.
The auction for her Bridgehampton property came after Mugrabiadmittedly did not pay anythingon a $3.5 million loan that used the property as collateral. The lender, an entity affiliated with REO Assets of America, Great Neck, N.Y., then took matters into its own hands and bought the 7-acre spread for $500 in an online auction in February 2025, at which it was the only bidder.
The subsequent outcry from Mugrabi and her attorney Claude Castro, of Castro Law Group, later led to a proposed settlement between the two parties. It gave Mugrabi a two-and-a-half-month window this year to sell the home through a public listing, with an agreement to allow the property to be disposed of by the lender immediately after her Aug. 25 deadline if she wasn’t successful.
The court-ordered auction provided over-the-top theatrics in a raucous display that had locals trying to get into Town Hall – as well as Town Hall employees — stopping to watch.
Mugrabi’s mother, Jane Scher, who attended the auction with her dog named Botox, told the lender’s attorney, Ryan Mitola of Vallely Mitola Ryan, “Your client is a d–k.”
The circus-like behavior extended to the bidders, including Mugrabi’s sister, Mia Rowe, who furiously raised her offer each time she was outbid and initially won with a $7.8 million commitment — but without a check in hand. After claiming she was going to a nearby Chase bank to retrieve $780,000 for the required deposit, she never returned.
Mugrabi, who wasn’t present at that August auction, has lived in the Bridgehampton home throughout the litigation and has made no qualms about wanting to hold onto it. A family friend at the auction emphasized her position telling bidders, “She’ll never leave that house.”
Castro has previously indicated to a court that he has discussed a bankruptcy filing with Mugrabi. While that action would open up another whole host of issues for her, it probably would not save her home.
Castro had told the court Mugrabi is in a $9 million-plus hole to cover repayment of the mortgage, penalties and at least $140,000 in legal fees she racked up after blowing off payments.

hed: Rare mid-century home designed by famed architect John Lautner hits the market in Pasadena for $2.6M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
That’s one cool pad.
Pasadena’s only home designed by beloved SoCal architect John Lautner has hit the market for $2.595 million — giving one mid-century buff the chance to live in one of the visionary’s early works.
The legendary Lautner became a household name in Los Angeles for his jaw-dropping, gravity-defying Hollywood villain-esque lairs — like thesaucer-like Chemospherein the Hollywood Hills, and the Elrod House in Palm Springs featured in the James Bond classic, “Diamonds Are Forever”.
But the Dahlstrom House, at 780 Laguna Road in the San Rafael neighborhood, shows a young architect flexing a warmer, rounder design muscle.
The 1949 two-bedroom, two-bathroom, west of the Arroyo property spans about 1,900 square feet — but what it lacks in mega-mansion sprawl it makes up for in geometric wizardry.
Sitting on a triangular shaped lot, the house was commissioned by book designer Grant Dahlstrom, who owned Pasadena’s Castle Press.
Right from the start, visitors are greeted by a projecting semi-circular steel overhang, which creates a carport. The rounded details continue inside, and guests enter through a wood-paneled foyer before following a curving hallway into the living room, where a steel ceiling appears to float above walls of glass.
A cylindrical concrete fireplace anchors the living space, alongside built-in bench seating and a revolving bookcase — cleverly concealing part of the home’s steel structure. With the glass walls, the boundaries between inside and outside vanish, and make the garden feel like an extension of the living room.
Even the primary bedroom gets in on the disappearing act.
The semicircular suite features a massive curved sliding wall that rolls back to merge the bedroom directly with the living room.
Outside, curved landscaping disguises the sharp boundaries of the three-cornered, 10,441-square-foot lot.

Lautner started out studying under Frank Lloyd Wright as an apprentice — and the Prairie School pioneer’s influence is readily apparent here.
Pasadena recordsspecifically point to the home’s “the cantilever of its roof above expanses of glass, as well as the rounded carport overhang” as evidence.
While plenty of beautiful vintage homes in the Los Angeles area have been subjected to remodels over the years, the Dahlstrom House remains intact.
After buying the home in 2009 for $1.35 million, the seller undertook a careful restoration, refinishing surfaces with materials considered appropriate to the home’s architectural pedigree, listing agent Rob Moore of Compass toldMansion Global.
“It’s all very quiet,” he said. “Nothing is flashy, but really beautifully crafted.”

hed: Record 42% of all listings in the US get price cuts — as Western hubs see the most dire discounts
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Home sellers across America are throwing in the towel on their asking prices at a record clip.
A staggering 42% of all active home listings in the United States are currently undergoing price reductions, according to fresh data released this week byreal estate analytics firm Parcl Labs.
That figure marks a 24 basis point jump from just one week earlier, with the national inventory of active listingssitting at 1.57 million homes.
The cuts aren’t landing evenly. A cluster of Western and Sun Belt markets have blown past the 50% mark, meaning more than half the homes for sale in those cities are now priced lower than when they first hit the market.
Colorado Springs is leading the pack with 56.3% of its listings slashed. Austin isn’t far behind at 54.1%, followed by San Antonio at 53.4%, Denver at 53.1% and Kingsport, Tennessee at 51.1%.
On the flipside, even sellers in a handful of smaller Northeast and Midwest markets holding firm and barely budging on price still have a good chunk of cuts.
Rochester hasthe lowest share of price cuts in the country at 17.8%, trailed by Atlantic City at 18.9% and Lincoln, Nebraska at 22.1%. Those markets have largely avoided the glut of inventory piling up elsewhere, giving sellers there far more room to wait out a buyer willing to pay closer to asking.
Zoomed out to the state level, the Parcl map shows the deepest red concentrated in the Mountain West and Southern states.
Colorado and Oregon are both hovering just under the 50% threshold statewide at 49.6% and 49.7% respectively, while Texas sits at 47.9%, South Carolina at 46.8% and Arizona at 46.8% as well.
Tennessee, Florida and Louisiana are all clustered in the mid 40s too, reinforcing just how broadly the discounting has spread across the Sun Belt.
New York, by contrast, sits at a comparatively modest 28.9%, putting it closer to the more insulated markets than the fire sale conditions out west. Connecticut is even cooler at 25.1%, and New Jersey checks in at 28.4%, suggesting the tri-state area’s tighter supply is still giving sellers there some breathing room.
Illinois stands out as one of the lowest in the country at 28.2%, while nearby Indiana runs hot at 46.7%, a reminder that even within the same region, price pressure can vary wildly.
Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman saidbuyers simply aren’t playing alongwith aggressive pricing anymore.
“Buyers today are incredibly educated and they are willing to wait. If a seller comes to market too aggressively, buyers aren’t afraid to sit on the sidelines and let the property come to them. That’s when you start seeing price reductions,” Griffith told The Post.
She added that many reductions are less a sign of weakness than a correction.
“The properties that are priced correctly from the beginning are still trading, and exceptional properties can still command a premium,” Griffith said.
“You want to come to market at a price that creates urgency. The longer a property sits and the more reductions it takes, the more leverage you ultimately hand to the buyer,” she said.
Ali Wolf, chief economist at NewHomeSource and Zonda, pointed to a broader affordability squeeze driving the trend nationally.
“There’s a bit of a panic among home sellers. The hope going into this year was that interest rates were going to go down, but as time has gone one, we’ve seen the complete opposite. Real-time mortgage rates are back in the 7% [range]. This means that prospective buyers are facing higher monthly payments,” Wolf told The Post.
“For existing homeowners trying to sell, lowering the home price is one way to at least help offset the higher costs for shoppers. Areas that are very expensive (like the Mountain West) or oversaturated with supply (like the Southeast) are bound to see more price adjustments to encourage a sale,” Wolf said.

hed: The most affordable college towns in the US — offering young graduates easy paths to homeownership
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
AsLabor Dayrecedes in the rearview mirror and the fall semester gets underway, now is a good time to examine the nation’smost budget-friendly college townsoffering recent graduates and young professionals a realistic path tohomeownershipin a vibrant market without breaking the bank.
Realtor.com® economists analyzed 2025 median listing prices for residential properties in towns anchored by a Division I university.
While 365 institutions make up the NCAA’s elite athletic division, markets with fewer than 15 listings were excluded from the list to ensure a reliable estimate.
The remaining 231 markets were then ranked from lowest to highest median asking price, showing where house hunters can still find reasonably priced real estate in vibrant communities that offer economic stability, cultural diversity, and strong local amenities.
Unsurprisingly, the affordable South dominates the list, accounting for roughly 38% of all ranked markets, followed by the Midwest at approximately 30%.
The West and Northeast, which are typically higher-priced housing regions, account for 20% and 12% of the rankings, respectively.
Topping the Realtor.com list of America’s most affordable Division I college towns are Detroit, Jackson, MS, Pine Bluff, AR, Macomb, IL, and Peoria, IL.
“These towns tend to have lower land and construction costs, flatter or slower-growing populations, and housing stock that was largely built out before the last two decades of price appreciation,” says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.
“That combination keeps home prices tethered to what local wages can actually support, rather than being pulled upward by demand outrunning supply.”
Three of the five—Detroit, Macomb, and Peoria—are nestled in the heart of the Midwest, where the typical home is still within reach for a household earning the median salary.
Other notably budget-friendly DI college towns boasting impressive levels of housing affordability include Toledo, OH (University of Toledo); Carbondale, IL (Southern Illinois University of Carbondale); Youngstown, OH (Youngstown State University); Akron, OH (University of Akron); and Cleveland (Cleveland State University).
By far the largest market in the top five with a population of nearly 650,000 residents, Detroit anchors its college town status through the University of Detroit Mercy, a private Catholic institution sponsoring 17 NCAA Division I teams, including basketball, cross-country, and lacrosse.
Once America’s economic engine driven by the booming automotive industry, Detroit fell on hard times at the turn of the century, ultimately declaring bankruptcy in 2013.
In the years since, however, the Motor City has undergone a striking transformation fueled by downtown revitalization and renewed population growth.
A key indicator of Detroit’s changing fortunes is its appreciating real estate market: The metro’s median asking price surged more than 12% from 2024 to 2025, a shift reflecting its growing appeal among budget buyers.
Yet despite those gains, Detroit remains one of the most affordable housing markets among the 50 largest US metros.
“Home shoppers there do face more competition than in past years, but prices are still well-calibrated to local income levels, which lets young buyers get into the market sooner and pair affordable housing with the built-in amenities college towns offer,” notes Jones.
Ranked second on the list, Jackson offers similar affordability, with a median asking price avereging $106,654 in 2025, down more than 12% from the prior year.
Jackson, Mississippi’s state capital, is home to Jackson State University—one of four higher education institutions located within the city, and its sole DI school.
For homebuyers looking to relocate, Jackson offers a rich blend of Southern culture, vibrant art and music scenes centered around museums and concert venues, as well as ample career opportunities in government and business.
The second Southern entry in the top five, Pine Bluff, AR, is known for its strong sense of community centered around the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff, a historically Black university (HBCU).
With a population under 45,000, Pine Bluff retains a tight-knit, small-town feel offering residents walking trails, fishing piers, and parks.
Last year, the median asking price in Pine Bluff registered at $106,980, up more than 7% year over year but still a bargain compared with the national figure.
“Modest population growth and ample housing stock relative to demand has kept a lid on price growth,” explains Jones.
Located 75 miles southwest of Peoria, Macomb is a quintessential small-town community that revolves around the historic Western Illinois University (WIU).
Over the 127 years since its founding, WIU has shaped Macomb’s identity, from its architecture to its open green spaces, including the university’s Horn Field Campus, with its acres of woodlands for hiking.
Macomb’s downtown features a historic central square with coffee shops and boutiques. Residents also enjoy theatrical productions, live music, art shows, and sporting events tied directly to WIU.
In 2025, the median listing price in town increased by 3% to $107,125.
Bradley University, a private institution known for its NCAA DI basketball team, imbues the city of Peoria with youthful campus energy.
Cafes, quaint shops, live music venues, and walkable neighborhoods give the city its vitality, while a low cost of living keeps it accessible for students and recent grads.
In fact,a 2026 study by CoworkingCaferanked Peoria No. 7 nationally for launching a career after college.
“Our colleges partner very well with employers across all industries, providing many opportunities for college students to become involved in the communities prior to graduation,” Leslie Rothan, the broker leadingThe Rothan Group at eXp Realty, tells Realtor.com.
