“This allows for a better chance of postgrad employment and lets students continue the roots they established while studying,” adds Rothan, a Bradley alumna who chose to remain in Peoria after graduation.
For homebuyers, the value proposition is undeniable, with the median listing price last year coming in at $118,462.
“Peoria has been called ‘a big small town.’ In comparison to other larger metropolitan areas, we have very similar amenities while offering a lower cost-effective way of living than the larger cities,”says Rothan. “The cost of dining and entertainment is lower, making it an affordable, budget-friendly college town.”
Peoria’s housing market also offers diverse options across budget levels and preferences.
“We see buyers purchasing a condo for the simplicity of maintenance-free living while also exploring budget-friendly, single-family homes that could eventually become an income-generating asset, should their living needs change,” adds the broker.
Overall, these top five education hubs offerwould-be homebuyerssomething that few markets can at a time of economic headwinds and persistent affordability hurdles.
“At a time when starter-home inventory is scarce nationally and young-professional wages make both renting and buying a stretch, these five towns stand out as places where recent grads and early-career professionals can still access the wealth-building potential of homeownership,” concludes Jones.
Notably, the appeal of affordable college towns like Jackson or Macomb goes beyondnewly minted graduates and young professionals.
These markets typically attract a diverse mix of people, including faculty, parents of students, alumni, and active retirees.
Michael Lyon and his wife, Jane, recently relocated from rural Virginia to Durham, NC, home of Duke University—ranked 172nd on affordability—in their pursuit to spend their golden years in a dynamic, culturally diverse city.
“One of the things about Durham that, I think, leads to that diversity and attraction is Duke University,” Jane tells Realtor.com.
“It has, obviously, cultural opportunities, educational opportunities.”
For Jane and her husband, a college hub like Durham strikes the ideal balance between urban energy and small-town approachability.
“We consider ourselves in the city, but it’s a small enough city that it’s all right here,” she says. “It’s easy to access, the entertainment, the performing arts center, baseball, Duke sports.”

hed: Home sales tumble to lowest level in over a year as high mortgage rates scare off buyers
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Sales of previously occupied US homes declined in August to their slowest annual pace in more than a year as home shoppers grappled withrising mortgage ratesand home prices.
Existing home sales fell 2% last month from July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday.
This is the third straight monthly decline.
Sales also fell 1.2% compared with August last year. The latest sales tally is just shy of the 4 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet.
“It’s not a surprise home sales and mortgage rates move in the opposite direction and we have seen mortgage rates rising, rising, rising from February,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist.
Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2-million.
The last time the annual sales pace came in below 4 million was June 2025.
Despite the latest pullback, existing US home sales are running 1.6% higher through the first eight months of this year than they were in the same stretch of 2025, NAR said.
The housing market has been stymied in large part by rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the US and Iran started in late February.
Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, pushing up mortgage rates.
The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 6.71% last week, its highest level in more than a year.
Yun noted that rate could soon reach 7%, given that mortgage rates tend to follow moves in the10-year Treasury yield, which continues to climb.
The yield was at 4.92% on the bond market as of Thursday morning.
Even as sales slowed, home prices continued to rise nationally last month.
The US median sales price increased 1.6% in August from a year earlier to $429,100, an all-time high for the month of August based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 38 months in a row.
The US housing market has been in aslumpsince 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied US homes were essentially flat last year, stuck ata 30-year low.
Years of soaring home prices, especially in the early part of this decade when rock-bottom mortgage rates fueled a buying frenzy, have left many would-be homebuyers frozen out of the market.
And a chronic shortage of homes for sale nationally, due partly to years of below-average new home construction, has helped prop up home prices even in a multiyear sales slump.
Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in July and June, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.66%.
The sales slowdown is leading to unsold properties sitting on the market longer, helping boost the number of available homes.
Although home inventory levels remain well below historical norms, there were 1.62 million unsold homes at the end of last month, up 3.2% from July and up 5.9% from August last year, NAR said.
That’s still short of the roughly 2 million homes for sale that was typical before the COVID-19 pandemic.
Still, August’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.9-months’ supply at the current sales pace. That’s the highest level in over 10 years.
Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers.

hed: Rebels keep blowing up luxury vacation homes to scare off foreign buyers on this ‘French Hamptons’ island
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Masked rebels are bombing million-dollar vacation homes on theFrench island of Corsica, and buyers are still lining up to purchase there anyway.
Since October 2023, 34 homes across 20 towns were bombed or torched in a single, and disturbing, overnight spree.
Corsica’s armed independence movement, which doesn’t appear to have killed anyone, has kept up a steady campaign of attacks on second homes, mostly empty vacation properties owned by mainlanders and foreigners. Another home was blown up as recently as March 2026, according to theNew York Times.
The National Liberation Front of Corsica, the paramilitary wing of a 50-year-old independence movement, wants outsiders off the island for good.
Last month roughly 15 masked, armed members of the group held a press conference to say so directly, warning tourists and second-home buyers to stay away.
“Until our national rights are recognized and respected, we have only one message to send them,” one member read from a prepared statement. “Stay home. And, if that’s not the case, do not consider yourself safe on our national territory.”
The threats have not slowed the market. Second homes now account for 37% of Corsica’s housing stock, and as much as 50% in some coastal towns, according to a 2026 report from the Corsican Assembly.
Only about 61 Americans live on the island full time, according to a 2020 report from the Local, making it the least popular region in France for US expats, largely due to its lack of a major city and pricier travel links to the mainland.
Politically, the bombing campaign has paid off. The French Senate votes next month on a constitutional amendment recognizing Corsica’s distinct language — far more similar to Italian than French — culture and history, and granting its local government new authority over zoning and waste management. It would be the first time any French region received that status.
“It was a tactical success,” André Fazi, a political scientist at the University of Corsica, referring to the bombings, told The Times.
Still, the amendment stops short of giving Corsicans control over who can buy property there, the central demand of hardline separatists. Petru Antone Tomasi, a spokesman for the independence party Nazione, which opposes the amendment as a diluted compromise, said the land fight cannot be separated from the broader independence push.
“We consider the fight for the land intertwined with the struggle for Corsica,” Tomasi told the outlet.
The Liberation Front has claimed responsibility for thousands of attacks since forming in 1976, including a 1991 operation that hit more than 80 vacation homes and a 2012 incident in which masked gunmen dragged a Parisian financier and six others from his villa before blowing it up.
Fifteen homes have been burned or bombed since 2024 alone. A Paris counterterrorism investigation into the 2023 attacks has led to 10 arrests, and prosecutors have opened a separate probe into last month’s press conference.
Buyerskeep coming regardless.Madeleine Michaud, a 65 year old retiree from Lyon, paid 2.5 million euros for a home in southern Corsica, including 150,000 euros for a retractable glass wall overlooking the sea. She noticed nationalist tattoos on some of her construction workers but said her ties to local friends make her feel protected, though she asked to be identified only by her middle and maiden names as a precaution.
“They don’t care about me,” she told The Times.
Real estate agent Irène Valentin said she regularly hears from anxious prospective buyers.
“Some of them are very afraid,” she said. “They know somebody who had a house in the village and the house was burned. They want to come here and they want to be reassured.”
Not every buyer takes the threat seriously, she added.
“They can be very arrogant,” Valentin said. “I say to myself, if they behave that way here, they’ll get their house burned.”
Mona Wingate, whose family bought a Corsican olive mill in 1975 amid an earlier wave of bomb threats, moved back to the property in 2019 and has taken the opposite approach, opening her land to locals and attending village events.
“It’s their land and they had access to it for hundreds of years,” she said.
So far, she said, she has had no problems.

hed: San Francisco declares ‘rent emergency’ as prices for dingy one-bedrooms top $5,000
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on Thursday declared a “rent emergency” and proposed several actions to combat evictions — amid shocking headlines ofrents in the city hitting more than $5,000for one-bedroom apartments.
Lurie said he will support legislative actions to forestall evictions by an additional month, limit the size of rent increases and amp up funding for lawyers on eviction cases.
“Today, most San Franciscans feel our city is finally moving in the right direction, but many are also asking whether they can still afford to live here,”  Lurie saidin a statement.“Today, we are taking action to tackle San Francisco’s rent emergency head-on and help San Franciscans stay in their homes.”
The declaration won’t actually let the mayor bypass laws and regulations to enact his agenda, but is instead aimed at focusing on providing resources for tenants.
Rents in San Francisco are spiking more than anywhere else in the country, the mayor’s office said. According toApartment List,the apartment vacancy rate in the city fell to just 2% in August, while rent prices have skyrocketed 26% in the past year.
“This leads the nation and represents the fastest post-pandemic rent growth captured by our model,” the Apartment List analysis said.
Much of the rental price jumps have been attributed to the city’sartificial intelligence boom, driven by soaring valuations and incomes of startups and workers in Silicon Valley.
Part of Lurie’s initiative includes multiple pieces of city legislation that involve putting more money into supporting displaced tenants. For instance, he wants to increase by 25% the amount of required payments to tenants being displaced, factoring out to nearly $3,000 per person,
The city will invest $1 million and partner with private employers to launch a “Know Your Rights” campaign, educating renters and property owners on their legal protections and responsibilities, Lurie said.
Legislation will also be introduced to cap annual allowable rent increases from banked increases and capital improvement charges at 10% for rent controlled tenants.
Many city supervisors and other leaders threw their support behind the mayor.
“San Francisco is facing an eviction crisis, and we’re excited to see the mayor and Board of Supervisors act with urgency to go to bat for tenants,” said Gail Gilman, Eviction Defense Collaborative Executive Director.
But not everybody agrees there is a “rent emergency” in San Francisco.
Oz Erickson, a member of the San Francisco Apartment Association, toldthe New York Timesthat the city’s rents are only climbing now because prices fell hard during the COVID-19 pandemic. The real crisis, he said, is the cost of building affordable housing.

hed: NYC penthouse forged from a famed copper roof finds its first-ever owner for a fraction of its $40M ask
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A raw Billionaires’ Row penthouse once asking as much as $40 million has finally landed its first-ever owner, The Post has learned.
The sprawling triplex tucked beneath the copper roof of Hampshire House at 150 Central Park South is pending sale for a considerably discounted $6.76 million following a July auction, according to a press release from Concierge Auctions, which handled the sale in partnership with listing brokerage Nest Seekers International.
The deal comes after years of attempts to unload the unusual property, which spans roughly 9,000 square feet beneath the landmark co-op’s distinctive mansard roof but remains largely unfinished. That’s because it was always an attic used as mechanical space, and never for a residence.
The identity of the new owner won’t be known until the sale closes.
The Post toured the penthouse shortly before it hit the auction block, getting a firsthand look at the enormous gap between what exists today and what could eventually rise in its place.
Architectural renderings done by SPAN Architecture show soaring living spaces, sleek interiors and sprawling terraces overlooking Central Park.
In reality, much of the upper two levels remains former mechanical and storage space, with exposed concrete, aging ventilation ducts and decades-old building infrastructure still in place.
Getting to the roof currently means climbing a narrow staircase through the unfinished space. At the top, however, is the payoff: sweeping views across Central Park.
The raw bones come with an ambitious blueprint.
Pre-approved plans by SPAN Architecture envision transforming the shell into a five-bedroom residence with four private terraces overlooking the park — including a rooftop entertaining area and a wet bar perched between Hampshire House’s twin copper chimneys.
Securing co-op approval for the ambitious redesign took roughly three years, listing broker Tal Reznik previously told The Post.
The penthouse has had a long and rocky journey to a buyer.
It first hit the market in 2018and at one point carried a $40 million asking price before later returning with an $18.75 million price tag. An attempted auction in 2022 never got off the ground after bidding failed to reach the minimum threshold required to launch the sale, said Reznik.
This time, the property returned to the block with a $6 million starting bid. After bidding concluded, Concierge Auctions announced that the penthouse was “pending sale for $6.765M.”
If it ultimately closes at that figure, the price would be roughly 83% below the penthouse’s one-time $40 million asking price.
Still, whoever ultimately takes possession won’t exactly be getting a move-in-ready bargain.
Converting the existing structure into a white-box shell alone is expected to take roughly 18 to 24 months before interior finishes can begin, Reznik previously told The Post. The scale of the undertaking has long been one of the property’s biggest hurdles, he said, as many ultra-wealthy buyers prefer turnkey homes over taking on years-long renovations.
The landmark building has had its share of boldface residents, including opera legend Luciano Pavarotti.
Meanwhile, Hampshire House is also still locked in litigation over neighboring supertall111 W. 57th St., alleging that construction there caused roughly $25 million in damage to the historic co-op. A judge granted Hampshire House partial summary judgment on liability in 2024, while the amount of damages remains unresolved.

hed: Ask the gardener: How to ‘work smarter, not harder’ in your gardens and yards
subhead: Leaf season is almost here. Ulrich Lorimer offers advice and insight into making yardwork an enjoyable pastime rather than a cumbersome chore
content:
ByUlrich Lorimer
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

As a teenager, yard work was presented as a chore to complete. The lawn had to be mowed, the leaves had to be raked, and mulch was to be spread as directed. Perhaps due to my interests lying in other places, I bristled at the strain on my adolescent time. Rarely did I take the time to enjoy the fruits of my labor.

Later, as an adult and as a professional gardener, I understand the tension between the time needed to complete garden projects and affording the moments of enjoyment, respite, and calmness that time spent in gardens gives us. I suspect I am not alone in struggling to find the right balance between efficiency and enjoyment.

Phrases like, “work smarter, not harder” and “learn to work with the process” come to mind, but what do they really mean? Surely, no one is suggesting hard work is unintelligent or unworthy. And exactly which processes are being referenced? This week’s column seeks to unpack these phrases a bit further, along with how our garden aesthetics contribute to the workload. Furthermore, I will suggest ways in which we can gain more time to experience our gardens and less time feeling overwhelmed by the amount of work.

Let’s start with some perspective about plants. It may appear simple, but plants are individual living organisms with a drive to survive all their own. I am not suggesting plants have a will of their own, but that they are exquisitely attuned to their environments and react accordingly. Sometimes, they grow exactly in the way we intend, more often, though, they have their own designs and don’t follow our instructions.

In short, gardens are dynamic and always will be. All gardens require a range of maintenance — informal gardens involve deeper understanding of plants and ecology while formal gardens require static regiments intended to keep them looking the same. These larger cycles unfold over longer time spans, highlighting that working with plants is really a long-term planning exercise and that some understanding of how plants grow will help us gardeners to anticipate what might occur in the future.

Formal gardens


Humans have long sought to impose order over nature, and the history of formal gardens represents such efforts, tracing back to its origins in Western Asia, Persia, Egypt, and ancient Greco-Roman cultures. These gardens used symmetry and geometric shapes to separate human spaces from the chaos of nature beyond. They were status symbols of wealth and power.

Maintaining formal gardens requires a lot of time and repeated tasks like edging, weeding, and clipping hedges — often multiple times a year. Looking at suburban landscapes now, I see miniature versions of that formality.

To save time on such repetitive, and frankly unexciting garden tasks, why not replace your clipped hedge with a dwarf or slow-growing selection? The shrub grows to the desired height, and you no longer spend time pruning it into unnatural shapes.

I am intentionally contrasting formal gardens with informal ones to draw attention to the maintenance tasks needed to keep a garden looking the same, year after year. This garden ideal stands in opposition to the reality that gardens are dynamic.

Informal gardens


But informal gardens need maintenance, too. Weeding, editing, learning to work with the abundance and exuberance of plants is integral to shaping the future of informal gardens.

In my last column, we discussed managing the weed seed bank by strategically cutting some weeds and pulling others. Even desirable plants can become too much in an informal design, so the same approaches apply. Cutting seed heads before they disperse helps reduce the amount of new seedlings the following year. Editing or transplanting helps keep design intent intact while embracing that gardens will change over time.

Observe where leaves accumulate and plan for perennials that can push through the deep layers. Conversely, if wind patterns keep an area of soil bare or mossy, use that as an opportunity to plant small, delicate blossoms that would otherwise be swamped or covered by leaves. Informal, less tidy-looking gardens generally support more wildlife, especially if managed without pesticides or fertilizers. All of these examples are working with the process rather than against it.

Lawns


Let us talk about lawns next. They have utility as gathering spaces for family and friends and surfaces on which to pursue sports or a serious game of tag with your children. They should, however, not take up all your time.

First, consider small pathways or odd corners where you have to push and pull the mower inefficiently. Aren’t these areas ripe for conversion to a lawn alternative? Steep slopes, where pushing a mower is difficult, if not dangerous: these areas are also good candidates to convert to a groundcover or lawn alternative. By streamlining the area that needs to be mowed, you will spend less time doing it and more time enjoying the possibilities a lawn affords. This is an example of working smarter, not harder.

A garden is never finished, rather always a work in progress. Loosening our tolerances and thresholds for weeds, and for the perception of untidiness, will help us focus on the aspects of our gardens that bring us the most satisfaction and joy. Spending time among plants deeply benefits humans physiologically and psychologically, often in subtle and unseen ways. Access to gardens creates joy, especially knowing you have had a hand in its creation and continuing evolution.

Ulrich Lorimer is the director of horticulture at the Native Plant Trust in Framingham. Send your gardening questions, along with your name/initials and hometown, to[email protected]g.

hed: Perez Hilton drops price of Las Vegas home as he remains hospitalized — and in financial struggle
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Perez Hiltonjust took a $350,000 haircut on his Las Vegas mansion, and insiders say the blogger needs the cash fast.
The 48-year-old media personality, still hospitalized aftera gruesome self-harm livestreamlast month, has cut the asking price on his six-bedroom Sin City spread from $4.25 million down to $3.9 million, theproperty listingshows.
The listing, handled by Kathryn Winterton of Las Vegas Sotheby’s International Realty, has sat on the market since June without a buyer.TMZwas the first to report on the price cut.
The 6,600-square-foot house on Olive Creek Court in the gated Prado community comes loaded with six en-suite bedrooms, a detached casita, a multigenerational suite and a backyard built for entertaining.
It’s also where Hiltonraised his three kids, filmed countless TV hits and cranked out documentary work, including a recent project on theBlake Lively and Justin Baldonilegal saga.
But the good times apparently didn’t pay the bills. Sources told The Post Hilton was scraping by even before his August meltdown, unable to land new television deals despite pitching multiple reality show concepts that stalled at the pilot stage.
Back in July, Hilton called the Vegas dwelling “a beautiful home, and it served me well personally and professionally.”
He added, “I was in the house for two-and-a-half years but now it’s time to leave Las Vegas as I want to focus on my health while with my family back in my hometown of Miami. Miami is where I need to be.”
The financial squeeze reportedly got worse aftera brutal health scareearlier this year. Hilton spent three weeks in the hospital battling sepsis, undergoing two surgeries while doctors treated fluid in his lungs, a blood clot, kidney trouble and heart arrhythmia.
Helater admitted the ordeal drained his savingsand pushed him to launch a religious-themed clothing line just to stay afloat.
“You don’t want to know how much I had to pay in hospital bills with insurance,” he said in one Instagram clip, where he promoted his new merchandise line. “That’s why your boy is in hustle mode.”
Then came August 4, when a TikTok livestreamshowed Hilton bloodiedand holding a knife inside his Miami home.
His sister Barbarafound him in the bathroom;police say he chased his own children into the street as she drove them to safety. He’s since been treated for lacerations, an overdose and significant blood loss, and doctors also uncovered lingering complications tied to his earlier sepsis fight.
Hilton hasn’t seen his three children since the incident. His mother, Teresita Lavandeira, hasfiled for temporary custody.TikTok has pulled the video and suspended his account.
If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-TALK (8255) or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.

hed: Why so many new Pacific Palisades homes look the same
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The Pacific Palisades in Los Angeles has long been known for its distinctivehomes and innovative architecture, but as one ofAmerica’s most expensive communities rebuildsafter the2025 Palisades Fire, it’s starting to look a little more cookie cutter.
Instead of designing completely custom homes from scratch, more homeowners are choosing from catalogs of predesigned houses, sacrificing some uniqueness for a faster, simpler path home.
“When you look around the Palisades now, there’s been great progress. What do you notice? All the homes look the same,” said Matt McRoskey, head of growth at homebuilder Builders Workshop. “You’re not seeing a whole lot of design diversity.”

Never miss a story
McRoskey lives in the Palisades. His parents and relatives all lost their homes, and he’s now dedicating his career to the rebuild.
Builders Workshop just debuted four home designs for Palisades survivors to choose from, under a new program called RESET.
RESET is Builders Workshop’s first catalog of predesigned homes, designed to meet the growing demand for a faster, simpler way to rebuild in the Palisades.
RESET says its designs are ready to submit to the city for permitting. It has a set price range, a predictable timeline, and underwriting commitments from insurance companies.
The homes are also built using cold-formed steel, amore fire-resilient alternative to timber.
“This hasn’t been our business,” McRoskey said. “We’re a custom home builder. We’re really good at it, we love doing it. But we didn’t have a catalog of homes.”
For families desperate to rebuild their lives, architectural individuality may not be the first priority.
To build a custom home, it can take years to hire the right team, design the home within budget and secure permits.
And many Palisades survivors are racing against another clock: The expiration of insurance money that’s paying for temporary housing.
“Our solution is the easy button,” McRoskey said. “The first thing you do is you look at the four homes that we’re providing, and if one of them speaks to you, it’s as simple as signing a contract, and then we start building right away.”
McRoskey says RESET also chooses the colors, wood, finishes and appliances.
RESET is competing with the likes of Thomas James Homes, another one-stop shop homebuilder that says it’s working with more than 30 families in the Palisades.
The company is behind the first fully rebuilt single-family home to receive a certificate of occupancy in the Palisades fire zone.
Thomas James Homes offers 12 predesigned home options, with guaranteed pricing and completion within 12 months of the start of construction — plus compensation for every day the project exceeds that deadline.
“We do not have to send plans out to bid. We do not have to hire an architect. We don’t have to hire an engineer nor an outside design team,” said Thomas James Homes’ VP of sales Jeffrey Sandorf. “All of that is under one roof and one price, guaranteed price. That’s it.”
The companysays its predesigned plans and in-house team are helping it secure building permits in 54 days, less than half the average time cited by the company for Palisades permits overall.
“Homeowners are dealing with paying their mortgage while they can’t even occupy a house, and they just have dirt, and they have living expenses,” Sandorf said. “Soon that insurance is going to run out. I mean, the faster the better.”
That also means sacrificing to some extent on customization and uniqueness.
“If a property owner wanted to design an extremely unique house to their very specific taste, they probably are not the best fit for Thomas James Holmes, nor a lot of the people rebuilding here,” Sandorf added.
That’s where the traditional custom-design process still has appeal.
Architecture firm Bureau Namas is designing custom homes for clients who are deeply attached to aspects of the home they lost. It’s an emotional process that can involve many months of design revisions, as people’s desires and feelings change.
“The most stressful process for them is not to lose those memories,” Bureau Namas Founder Daniel Shurinov said. “Not to lose those moments in the home that they loved so much, while we’re designing basically a brand new home for them It can be a tiled floor in the kitchen that they all enjoyed cooking barefoot or a porch at the back where they spent countless evenings together.”
It’s a glimpse into how extreme weather is reshaping the character of some of America’s most iconic neighborhoods.
As the Palisades rebuilds, homeowners are choosing between the time and complexity of rebuilding something uniquely theirs, and the speed and certainty of a predesigned home.
And those decisions could determine not just how quickly one of America’s wealthiest neighborhoods comes back — but what it looks like when it does.

hed: Squatters accused of terrorizing ultra-exclusive SF neighborhood, ‘stealing’ $4M mansion — as wild criminal history revealed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A $4 million San Francisco mansion has becomeground zero for what neighbors and officials say is wild squatter takeover— with the bizarre saga unfolding for over a year while thecity failed to act.
The home on 32nd Avenue in the Sea Cliff neighborhood, one of the most elite, affluent, and visually stunning neighborhoods the City by the Bay has to offer, has apparently become a revolving door of unfamiliar faces, with neighbors reporting unwelcome activity at all hours.
“I go to bed nervous. I wake up nervous,” one neighbortold ABC.
“It really has been a 24-hour surveillance that’s going on,” another neighbor said. “People are at a breaking point.”
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story
And the midnight madness isn’t just talk.
Neighbors say surveillance footage captured unknown people at around 4 a.m. loading suitcases into a car, another claims her scooter was also stolen. The neighborhood is so panicked they’ve organized into a WhatsApp group named “watch 250” to fight back and collect surveillance footage.
Luxury vehicles have also been spotted outside the property, with some appearing to have no license plates. Apparent break-ins, theft, sketchy characters and a major flooding incident have plagued the incredibly well-to-do neighborhood where Robin Williams once lived since around May 2025. Though the house has set empty since 2019.
What’s happening inside the house remains a mystery, but the how the squatters came to be there is a crazy story involving a convicted fraudster, allegedly dodgy property deeds and an absent wealthy Chinese owner, reports theSan Francisco Standard.
Property records show the deed bounced between two people, convicted fraudster Brandon Aadee and a felon named Diana Peng, at least seven times over the past year, including four times since July. Each now claims the other person is not the legitimate owner. Aaadee even tried to sell off the home, but failed when the realtor smelled a rat.
Aadee’s criminal past stunned neighbors when they found out the accused squatter’s name and began looking him up online. He was federally charged in 2008 with stealing more than $48,000 in Hurricane Katrina relief, though he wasn’t a New Orleans resident or a victim. FEMA paid him out over $34,000 and the Red Cross covered $13,000 for his hotel stays.
He was also charged with credit card fraud, after lifting a Visa from an envelope in an SF apartment hallway and running up more than $11,000 over six months, much of it at Aladdin Bail Bonds locations in Marin and San Mateo, the Standard reported.
Aadee pleaded guilty to both federal charges in 2009 and was sentenced to a year and a day in federal prison, roughly $60,000 in liens, before being in and out of custody on probation violations through 2012.
In September last year, San Mateo County charged him with five felonies, including identity theft and possession of a forged driver’s license, over an alleged August incident. The arrest warrant is still active.
Peng is no stranger to a courtroom either. She was convicted of felony perjury in San Mateo County in March 2008 and sentenced to three years’ probation and 90 days in jail. In 2012, facing five felonies including forgery and using another person’s ID, she pleaded to identity theft and commercial burglary and served seven months.
Three years later, charged with four more counts, including forging a driver’s license, she was sentenced to two years.
Neighbors say the property appeared to have been abandoned by its owner in 2020. But over the past year, a group of roughly a dozen people began showing up at the house, with some apparently moving in.
“Then one day the front door of the house was broken down…” a neighbor told ABC. “Then a deed was recorded in an individual’s name and that started this whole process.”
Peng and Aadee both used allegedly forged documents to fool police on several occasions when they were detained trying to gain access to the home.
The San Francisco Police Department said the District Attorney’s Office is investigating the case.
And now, after neighbors say they complained to the city over the past year and a damaged water main  outside the disputed mansion caused huge flooding, the City Attorney’s Office has finally gone to court.
The office filed a lawsuit against both alleged squatters, accusing them of an “unlawful scheme to obtain ownership of a property located at 250 32nd Avenue… through the recording of forged deeds with the San Francisco Assessor’s office that were fraudulently notarized.”
“Defendants are effectively trying to steal a house and sell it to make millions in profit. That is fraud, and they are trying to profit off that crime,” City Attorney David Chiu said when announcing the lawsuit.
The alleged deed scheme has also raised concerns about notaries being caught up in fraud.
“It’s tragic,” Bill Anderson, vice president of Government Affairs of the National Notary Association, told ABC, adding that the notary becomes a victim in these alleged deed frauds.
“What we’re finding at the National Notary Association… 12% of our $100,000 insurance claims since 2023, those have been seal fraud cases,” Anderson said.
The property belongs to Wei Wang, an absentee Chinese owner, according to what investigators say is the legitimate deed. Wang has apparently been struggling to enter the US to secure the property and is years behind on taxes for it.
San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors was asked on Tuesday by the city’s tax collector to auction off the home as it is more than five years behind on property taxes — the opening bid would start at a relatively cheap $500,000, but if someone, anyone, pays off the more than $324,000 taxes, then the auction gets canned. The board also has to approve the auction, leaving stressed-out neighbors in limbo for now.Meanwhile, California’ssoft-on-crime lawsprevent police from immediately removing trespassers, leaving homeowners trapped in lengthy court processes.

hed: More people are leaving LA than moving in, and one glitzy state neighbor is their top destination
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New data from online real estate marketplace Zillow reveals that there are fewer renters looking to move to Los Angeles than Angelenos looking to move elsewhere — and one glitzy city is a top destination.
Zillow looked at itsrental page viewsacross real estate markets around the United States.It determined where prospective renters searching in each city were coming from. Multiple cities had Los Angeles as the biggest source of out-of-town rental page views.
According to the data, nearby Las Vegas was the most attractive out-of-state option for Los Angeles renters, who made up about 5.4% of rental page views there.
Next up was Phoenix, with 2.3% of its viewers coming from Los Angeles. Salt Lake City saw 2.1% of page views from the City of Angels.
It’s not a surprise given Los Angeles’s notorious reputation for becoming increasingly unaffordable. According to a new report byRealtor.com, LA County rents hit a recordfour-year lowthis year, but theoverall median asking rentwas still a whopping $2,603.
“You are going from an area where, on average, you’re severely rent-burdened, to an area where not only can you afford rent, but you’ve got considerable savings left over, and it’s still sunny and warm,” Zillow’s Chief Economist Mischa Fisher toldthe Los Angeles Times.
“You don’t have the ocean, but it has other benefits.”
Shane Phillips, with the UCLA’s Lewis Center for Regional Policy, told the Times that there has also been an exodus of Angelenos moving southern states such as Florida and Georgia. The Midwest is also seeing an uptick in Angelenos.
“Given that the Midwest is not a particularly strong market, not great job prospects for many people, I think it’s just notable that there’s outmigration to there,” Phillips said.
The Zillow data shows that even if Los Angeles renters can’t afford to move out of state, they’re heavily looking at moving to cheaper places within California.
Riverside, about 55 miles east of Los Angeles, saw a notable 21.3% of page views coming from LA. San Diego had almost 9% of its rental page views from Los Angeles.
On the other hand, rental listings in L.A. attracted the second-lowest percentage of out-of-town search traffic, just after New York City. Just 27% of viewers were from outside L.A.
The data echos a broader exodus that saw54,000residents leave L.A. County. The region recorded the largest population drop of any county in the country between July 2024 and July 2025, according to recent estimates from theU.S. Census Bureau.
Experts have blamed a lack of housing as a main driver.
“If you’re not increasing the supply of housing in your neighborhood, you are probably losing population,” Phillips said.

hed: Donald Trump’s NYC childhood home sells for $1.93M after a $500K, 8-month renovation
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Donald Trump’s childhood home has officially changed hands — and the presidential pedigree appears to have paid off.
The Tudor-style Jamaica Estates housewhere Trump spent his earliest yearshas sold for $1.93 million, listing agent Joe Zhu of RE/MAX Edge confirmed exclusively to The Post.
That’s nearly $1.1 million more than the $835,000 developer Tommy Lin paid for the rundown Queens property last year — before pouring more than $500,000 intoan eight-month gut renovation.
The final price also came within $70,000 of its most recent $1.99 million asking price.
The deal closes the loop on a saleThe Post first reported in July, when the five-bedroom home went into contract but the agreed-upon price had not been revealed.
At the time, Zhu said the offer was “very close” to asking.
Turns out, it was.
Zhu said the home’s connection to the president was a major draw for prospective buyers, with many interested in the property for more than just its bricks and mortar.
“There were quite a lot of people” interested because it was Trump’s former home, Zhu told The Post, adding that some saw additional historical value in owning the property.
The roughly 3,100-square-foot residence at 85-15 Wareham Place has come a long way from the condition Lin found it in.
When he bought the property for $835,000 in 2025, it had sat vacant for years, suffered damage from a burst pipe and mold — and had even become home to a colony of feral cats, as The Post previously reported.
Lin’s renovation brought in a chef’s kitchen, herringbone floors and spa-like bathrooms while leaving its distinctive Tudor-style exterior intact.
The five-bedroom, four-bath property initially returned to the market for $2.3 million before being taken off the market and later relisted. After another price cut, it was asking just under $2 million when it found a buyer this summer.
But no renovation can replicate the house’s biggest claim to fame.
Trump’s father, real estate developer Fred Trump, built the brick-and-stucco residence in 1940. The president lived there until he was about 4, when the family moved to a larger Jamaica Estates home nearby.
The Wareham Place property has since had a colorful real estate history of its own.
It sold for $2.14 million in 2017— shortly after Trump entered the White House for his first term — and was later offered to tourists on Airbnb before eventually falling into disrepair.

hed: Selena Gomez lands a buyer for her LA home once owned by Tom Petty — with his touches intact
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Selena Gomez is saying goodbye to the Los Angeles mansion where she once cooked up a storm on “Selena + Chef” — though the final sale price came in a little underdone.
The singer and actress has sold her longtime Encino estate for $5.39 million, roughly $1.1 million shy of the$6.49 million asking priceit carried when it hit the market in May.
But no need for a sad song: Gomez, 34, still came out ahead of the $4.89 million she paid for the sprawling compound in 2020.
The nearly 11,500-square-foot home sits on just under an acre and comes with six bedrooms, 8½ bathrooms — and enough celebrity history to rival its square footage, asThe Post previously reported.
Long before Gomez moved in, rock legend Tom Petty had the home custom-built in 1989 and owned it until 2017, when it was sold just months before his death.
The house still carries traces of its rock ’n’ roll past, including a vocal booth on the lower level believed to have been part of Petty’s original recording studio.
That level is practically a compound of its own, with a creative work area, a wine cellar, a gym, a massage room, a den, a kitchen and a guest suite.
Then came Gomez, who added another dose of pop culture to the property.
After buying the home in 2020,she turnedits kitchen into a familiar TV backdrop, filming the first three seasons of her HBO Max cooking series “Selena + Chef” there.
The property had already undergone a major renovation before Gomez bought it and was pitched as a private celebrity compound when it returned to the market this spring.
Inside are soaring ceilings, multiple living and entertaining spaces, two primary suites and a movie theater.
The backyard is equally ready for showtime, with a swimming pool and spa fed by a cascading waterfall and stream, plus a cabana and bar, a fire pit and an outdoor dining area.
And Gomez isn’t exactly downsizing.
She has moved on to considerably pricier digs with her husband, music producer Benny Blanco.
The couple purchaseda $35 million Beverly Hills estate in an off-market deal in December 2024 — the same week they became engaged.
Spread across two lots, their new compound includes a seven-bedroom, 12-bath main residence and two separate guesthouses. One comes with its own studio, while the other houses a home theater.
The blockbuster purchase ranked amongBeverly Hills’ priciest deals of 2024.
Gomez has since teased glimpses of her new surroundings on social media, including a colorful kitchen with blue cabinetry and vibrant shelving, along with a lush backyard and rose-covered patio.
So while the Encino home may have sold below ask, Gomez is leaving with a profit — and closing the book on a house that has served as both a rock star’s recording retreat and a pop star’s televised kitchen.

hed: Georgia home where US Marshals forced out Kim Zolciak and Kroy Biermann quietly sells for a loss
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Kim Zolciak and Kroy Biermann werehauled out of their Georgia mansionby US Marshals — and now the house has quietly sold, The Post has learned.
The Milton estate known as The Manor closed earlier this summer, on June 30, for $3.67 million, property records show — the final gut punch in a saga that dragged the 15,600-square-foot property from a $6 million fantasy down to a fire sale in less than three years.
Zolciak and Biermann bought the place for a mere $880,000 in October 2012, months after their wedding, and filled it with six kids, a private arcade and a 500-bottle wine cellar.
Themarriage crateredright along with the mortgage.
By early 2023, the couple had defaulted on a $1.65 million loan against the property. Truist Bankmoved to foreclose,and Biermann filed for divorce for the second time that August.
What followed was a two-year fire sale. The home hit the market in October 2023 asking $6 million. The price bled out over the next year, sliding as low as $3.65 million, before the exes finally unloaded it for $2.75 million in a deal that closed just ahead of a scheduled foreclosure auction in December 2024.
Biermann later accused his ex in court filings of blowing up the sale process, claiming her spending habits had left the house as their only shared asset and that she rejected any offer under $3.85 million because she worried it would not leave her enough to buy a new place. He asked a judge to cut her out of the sale decisions entirely.
Even after the deal closed, the couple would not leave. The new owners had to go to court, and on April 8, 2025, US Marshals showed up and physically removed Zolciak and Biermann from the property.
A legal filing obtained by The Post accused the pair of overstaying “premises over and beyond the term for which they rented to them.”
The eviction played out over roughly three hours that afternoon, and Zolciak was reportedly selling off furniture from the house on Instagram the same day, including her daughter Ariana’s bedroom set for $10,000.
The home’s new owners waited less than a year to try again. They relisted The Manor in February 2026 for $4.65 million, a steep markup from what they paid, betting on the property’s amenities to do the talking.
The listing leaned hard into the seven bedrooms, the wine cellar, the home theater, the private massage room off the gym and a detached garage suite once used as a salon, now pitched as flexible space for an au pair or a home office.
The market was not as generous as the sellers hoped. The price dropped to $4.19 million in March, then to $3.89 million in May, before finally settling at $3.67 million in June, a loss of nearly $1 million off the relist price and barely half of what Zolciak and Biermann originally sought in 2023.
Zolciak has said she has moved on to a smaller home in Georgia.
“I just moved into a brand new home that I love at the end of February,” she said on “Watch What Happens Live” in July 2025. “I’m happy, it’s great, it’s perfect.”
The divorce has not cooled off since. Biermann hassought sole custodyof the couple’s four biological children, accusing Zolciak in filings of being “wholly unavailable to parent the children in any fashion” and leaving the country for weeks at a time. Zolciak has denied these claims.
“These accusations are completely false and nothing more than a deliberate attempt by Kroy to defame my character,” she said in a statement. “I spent five weeks away working on two TV shows to support my family and make sure my children are cared for, something I will never apologize for.”
The family’s legal troubles have only deepened since.
The couple’s eldest son, Kroy “KJ” Biermann Jr., 15, was accused on Friday ofhaving sex with an underage relative,according to prosecutors. The allegation surfaced during a bond hearing in Georgia’s Fulton County Superior Court, where KJ is facing seven felony charges in aseparate alleged sexual assaultinvolving a female classmate.
Deputy District Attorney Caitlin McGillicuddy told the court that investigators previously discovered videos on KJ’s cell phone allegedly showing “multiple encounters” involving penetrative sex with a family member under the age of 12.
McGillicuddy also alleged the footage captured KJ using “predatory, derogatory” language toward the child.

hed: NYC suburb is now the toughest place in America to buy a house
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Long Island homeowners looking to cash in have never had it better, even as sellers everywhere elseare getting squeezed.
Newdata from Redfinshows the New York City suburbs are swimming against a national tide that has turned hard against sellers.
Redfin found 39 of the 50 biggest metros in America are now buyer’s markets, meaning house hunters from Miami to Houston are finally catching a break after years of getting outbid.
But Long Island just got crowned the single strongest seller’s market anywhere in the country, bucking that trend completely. The reason: big demand for being near Manhattan.
Nassau and Suffolk counties are seeing 36.2% fewer sellers than buyers, an imbalance so severe it dwarfs every other market Redfin tracked.
Northern New Jerseylanded at No. 2 nationally with a 20.7% buyer surplus, while Central Jersey rounded out the top five at 12.9%.
It’s a split screen. While sellers nationally are cutting prices and waiting out longer days on market, three of the only six true seller’s markets left in the country happen to surround Manhattan.
Even the city itself is merely “balanced,” with 5.3% more sellers than buyers, according to Redfin, which makes the suburban numbers even starker by comparison.
Redfin agent Sandra Glaser, who works the Long Island market, said homes priced right don’t sit for long, a sharp contrast to what agents are describing in most of the country right now.
“I’m seeing multi-generational buyers looking to purchase single-family homes so they can live with their families,” Glaser said.
She’s watched a wave of buyers flee Queens in search of bigger backyards without giving up their commute into Manhattan. One listing she has on the South Shore, a three-bedroom, two-bath fixer-upper, started drawing calls before the open house even happened.
“I initially tested this property below the price that other homes in the neighborhood have been selling for because it needs work. It’s in a great area but it has been neglected,” Glaser said.
She’s since fielded five offers and expects a sixth any day. The open house pulled dozens of lookers, she said.
“At the open house, we had dozens of people show up to see the house. I’m sure we will be able to sell it quickly,” Glaser said.
It’s not just about square footage. Glaser said Long Island still sells a lifestyle that’s tough to find close to the five boroughs.
“People want to be in a neighborhood where their children can ride bikes, play outside, and not have to worry about much. Everybody here looks out for their neighbors. There is a real sense of community,” Glaser said.
One couple she worked with toured more than 50 homes and lost multiple bidding wars before finally landing a four-bedroom in Wantagh. The offer got accepted the same day their baby was born.
Across the Hudson, the picture is more nuanced, but sellers still have leverage that’s disappeared elsewhere. Redfin agent Natasha Bartolomeo said it depends heavily on what you’re shopping for.
“If you’re looking for a super-desirable single-family home in the suburbs, it’s a seller’s market. But if you’re looking for a condo in Jersey City or surrounding towns close to Newark, there is more inventory,” Bartolomeo said.
She’s seeing transplants arrive from as far as Los Angeles chasing relative affordability without sacrificing proximity to the city. A three-bedroom townhouse she listed in Newark got two offers and sold for thousands over ask.
“It offers a good balance between accessibility to the city and having more space. You don’t have to sacrifice anything here. You can be in a place that has so much available to you,” Bartolomeo said.
Her advice to sellers hoping to cash in while the window is open is simple: don’t overprice and don’t cut corners on presentation.
“Buyers are looking for move-in ready homes. If buyers see good value in the property, the home will sell,” Bartolomeo said.
Buyers, meanwhile, are being told to come prepared for a fight that most of the country has already stopped having. Redfin recommends getting preapproved, digging into comps beforehand and being ready to pounce the moment a listing hits. Glaser said price sensitivity hasn’t disappeared just because inventory is tight, especially near the million-dollar mark.
“People want move-in conditions, especially if sellers are asking for at or around that $1 million price point. For buyers, it’s important to know what you can afford before you start going out to look at homes,” Glaser said.

hed: Pierce Brosnan forced to flee $100M Malibu compound over fears of quakes, fire and sky-high costs
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Pierce Brosnan is ready to say goodbye to his slice ofMalibuparadise, after decades of dodging wildfires, worrying aboutearthquakesand shelling out a fortune to keep his sprawling $100 million compound afloat.
Theformer James Bondstar, 73, and wife Keely Shaye Smith, 62, are preparing to move on from the spectacular oceanfront estate they have called home for more than two decades, with Brosnan admitting that life along California’s famously volatile coastline has begun to lose some of its luster.
“We’ve been spared by the fires a few times now. But I think it’s time to move,” Brosnan toldThe Times. “Everything changes, everything falls apart.”

Never miss a story
The actor said living beside the Pacific Ocean, in an area vulnerable to earthquakes and devastating wildfires, has created an underlying sense of unease.
“We live by this body of earth’s water on a fault in a ring of earthquakes. That creates a fear,” he told the outlet.
Those fears are hardly hypothetical.
Malibu was hammered by the catastrophic Los Angeles wildfires in January 2025, which destroyed the homes of celebrities including Mel Gibson, Paris Hilton and Jeff Bridges.
Brosnan’s own home has already had a frightening brush with flames. In 2015, a fire erupted in the property’s garage while the actor and his family were home, causing an estimated $1 million in damage.
Now Mother Nature is once again rattling Malibu’s millionaire playground.
Amonster sinkholerecently tore through Sea Level Drive, a private beachfront road in an exclusive enclave associated with wealthy residents including Nicolas Cage.
The collapse ballooned to an estimated 25 to 30 feet deep and roughly 30 by 60 feet wide, cutting off the road’s only entrance and exit and forcing evacuations.
Cage’s $10.5 million, four-story oceanfront mansion was left alarmingly close to the crater.
“I don’t think this is a single, isolated event for Malibu,” City Manager Joseph Irvin warned.
Brosnan also acknowledged that maintaining his extravagant California lifestyle hasn’t come cheap.
The actor said there have been periods during his career when mortgage payments and school costs for his sons made landing his next role a financial necessity.
“There are definite moments of, oh, this boat is not quite sinking, but [it might] if we don’t get a job soon,” he told The Times.
That sometimes meant accepting projects he wasn’t particularly passionate about.
“You make the commitment because you need the money, then you show up on time and do good work,” Brosnan admitted.
Brosnan and Smith created their Southeast Asian-inspired estate after purchasing two neighboring Broad Beach properties for a combined $7.35 million in 2000.
Spread across more than an acre, the compound reportedly contains two residences totaling five bedrooms and a staggering 14 bathrooms.
Its centerpiece, dubbed the “Orchid House,” spans nearly 12,500 square feet and took more than a decade to complete. The lavish spread includes a movie theater, gym, music room, spa and climate-controlled wine cellar with room for roughly 200 bottles.
The couple has previously tested the market, at one point offering the property as a $120,000-per-month rental and later listing the compound for sale before pulling it off the market in 2021.
Brosnan and Smith currently divide their time between Malibu and Kauai, Hawaii and the islands increasingly appear to have won his heart.
“I love Malibu,” Brosnan previously toldThe Wall Street Journal, saying the California beach community “has my heart.”
But he added that “home is very much here in the islands.”
After 26 years and more than a few close calls, Bond may finally be ready to make his Malibu escape permanent.

hed: Home prices skyrocket in mountainous western state,  leaving 91% of renters unable to buy
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Home prices in Utah continue to increase, putting 91% of renters out of the running to becomehomeowners, according to a new report.
The median sale price across all housing types in Utah rose to $520,000 in the first quarter of 2026, an increase from the median price of $500,000 a year earlier, according to the 2025–26State of the State’s Housing Market reportconducted by the University of Utah’s Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute.
This exceeds the state’s previous high median sales price, which was $502,000 in 2022, after which prices temporarily dropped back into the high $400,000s.
“Rapid post-pandemic growth drove housing prices to record highs in 2022 before entering more stable periods. Since 2024,Utah’s marketincreased by 3.6% across all housing types,” the report reads.
Utah ranks as the 10th most expensive market for single-family homes, which had a median sales price of $559,900 in the first quarter of 2026. In 2016, the median price for a single-family home was $249,900.
To afford a median-priced home in Utah with a 10% down payment in 2026, the annual income required is $146,800, much higher than Utah’s median household income of $96,658.
Renter householdsin the state have a median income of just $64,000, and only 4.9% of homes sold in 2025 were affordable to buyers at that income level, the study found.
Renters in apartments saw a glimmer of relief this year, as there were more apartments available than renters.
For every 100 households earning no more than 80% of the area median income, 108 affordable rental units were available in 2025, an increase from the 100 units available in 2023.

Please provide a valid email.
