Never miss a story.
This led to a 2.3% decline in asking prices for apartments from March 2024 to March 2026. Over the same period, however, rents for single-family detached homes and townhomes increased 8.5% and 8.3%, respectively.
From 2010 to 2016, paying a monthly mortgage was more affordable than renting a comparable rental. In 2017, that number flipped, pricing renters out of the housing market.
Since 2023, monthly mortgage payments have fluctuated between $4,000 and $4,500, not including maintenance costs associated withhomeownership.
The average asking rent has remained between $2,500 and $2,700 during the same period, giving renters an immediate cash-flow advantage and fewer monthly expenses.
Because monthly mortgage payments have continued to increase in recent years, the State of the State’s report showed that 91% of Utah renters could not afford a median-priced home in the first quarter of 2026.
Only 4.9% of homes sold in 2025 were within the budget for a renter household with the median income of $64,000, the report found.
There are programs in the state to helpfirst-time homebuyerswith the initial cost of buying a home, including the First-Time Homebuyer Assistance Program.
Backed by the Utah Housing Corporation, this program offers up to $20,000 to assist with down payments, closing costs, and interest rate deductions.
It is available for buyers who have resided in Utah for at least one year before closing and can be applied to properties valued below $450,000.
Those looking to save for a down payment should budget around the actual monthly median income in their area and add the surplus after expenses to a specific savings account, according to financial experts, rather than making a loose savings plan.
“The renters I work with who succeed usually stop thinking of it as ‘saving what’s left over’ and start treating it like a fixed bill—automating a transfer the day they get paid, before anything else touches that money,” Matthew Scarborough ofScarborough Realty Grouptells Realtor.com®.
“It sounds simple, but it’s the difference between having $0 and having $15,000 saved in two years.”

hed: ‘Shark Tank’ star slams Kylie Jenner’s lengthy renovation on $15M mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


“Shark Tank” star Barbara Corcoran has some thoughts about reality TV personality Kylie Jenner’s yearslong home design project.
When asked to weigh in on the 29-year-old makeup mogul’s build-in-progress, which has been in the works since 2020, the 77-year-old real estate tycoon gaveTMZa candid response.
“Not worth it,” Corcoran said. “You should see my house. It’s much nicer.”
Corcoran elaborated on her advice, explaining, “You don’t enjoy the home when you’re too particular about the design. When you finally get it, it’s like a showcase, and you don’t really live there.”
The entrepreneur insisted she speaks from experience, adding it’s a lesson that she’s “learned over the years.”
Corcoran recently completed a major home renovation of her own, transforming the$16 million Manhattan penthouseshe purchased in October 2025.
On Aug. 26, Corcoran shared an Instagram post, noting she’s still getting ready to reveal the full renovation.
In the months leading up to the project’s completion, she shared a few behind-the-scenes progress updates, providing a look at some of her favorite existing details—from the original century-old tile in the bathroom to the sky-high ceilings and wood-burning fireplace.
Fresh off of a home makeover, Corcoran recommended spending some time in a new home to “get the feeling of the space, then finally decorate and do it fast.”
While Corcoran’s approach to renovation may seem to prioritize speed over anything else, she’s previously opened up about the sentimental value a dream home can hold.
When she listed her “dream” penthouse in 2025—which wasquickly snapped up for $1.5 million over asking, at a final sale price of $13.5 million—Corcoran told the New York Times, “It’s easy to spend money when you’re building a lifelong dream. For me, real estate is emotional.”
Corcoran called the palatial Upper East Side penthouse home for a decade, investing an estimated $2 million in sprucing it up as an ideal place for her family to live before making the difficult decision to move when her husband, Bill Higgins, became unable to safely navigate the staircase.
Like Corcoran, Jenner has also taken to social media to share the progress of the “beautiful dream Italian home” she’sbuilding on a $15 million 5-acre lotin Hidden Hills, CA.
“I’m so excited. I feel like I’ve been working on this for so long, and I’m just ready for it to be done and to move in,” Jenner admitted in aSept. 6 vlogin which she took followers along for a day of design approvals.
Jenner gave a first-look at a few of the home’s latest features—some of which she was seeing for the first time herself.
The entrance of the property has been outfitted with an “unreal” reclaimed cobblestone driveway and lush landscaping completed by Jim Hyatt, who Jenner explained is known for his work on the San Ysidro Ranch, a boutique resort in Montecito, CA.
Her own slice of paradise has been designed to “kind of” copy the legendary location, emulating the same look with lavender and ancient olives.
Inside, reclaimed wood floors run throughout the abode, which will soon be paired with a neutral white plaster for the walls, a decision Jenner made in real time in her vlog.
Reclaimed materials seem to be a theme throughout the project, as Jenner has chosen “an old fireplace” for the entry and vintage tile for a guest bathroom.
“It’s the only bathroom right now that has a tile moment,” the mom-of-two explained. “I think it’s going to be very, very fab.”
Fabulousity aside, that room isn’t even Jenner’s favorite bathroom on the property. A stunning stone space takes that title.
The kitchen seems to be coming along, with the room taking shape through custom cabinetry that is soon to be stained.
A trip to the basement unveiled more of the property’s Italian-inspired design, as Jenner showed off the soaring arched hallways, doors, and windows.
The outdoor space is underway as well, with plans for a rose garden.
“I just want to be a princess,” she quipped.
A sport court is in progress, as well as an ambitious outdoor dining project nestled in a tree-lined space of the backyard that will eventually feature a pizza oven and host “dinner parties and birthdays.”
The backyard even includes a sweet nod to Jenner’s older sister Kendall, who realized she needed to get rid of several young olive trees while doing construction at one of her properties.
“She was like, ‘Does anyone want them?’ And I said, ‘Absolutely,’” Jenner recalled. “Not only are they so beautiful, it reminds me of my sister every time I look at them.”
Jenner is no stranger to home renovation, having made her mark on plenty of properties over the years.
The star boasts an impressive real estate portfolio andcurrently has two homes on the market: an $18 million Hidden Hills home that served as her primary residence for years and a $38.5 million brutalist concrete fortress in Holmby Hills.
She recently reflected on her habit of snatching up expensive real estate, tellingWho What Wearthat she’s “changed” her mind about “having an enormous life.”
“When I was younger, I got really excited and I got the craziest house I could in Beverly Hills, and I just kind of went for it,” said Jenner. “I realized that my life got too big, and I said, ‘Yeah, never mind.’”

hed: Inside the massive Kennedy family ‘Camelot’ compound — passed down since 1928
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For nearly a century, the Kennedy family’s sprawling Hyannis Port compound has served as the backdrop to countless summer celebrations, where days were spent sailing on Nantucket Sound, swimming off the Cape Cod coastline and taking part in fiercely competitive games of touch football.
The waterfront retreat became so synonymous with the political dynasty’s warm-weather traditions that images of the Kennedys gathered on its sprawling lawns or setting sail from its private pier helped cement the family’s idyllic “Camelot” image.
And as summer drew to a close, the Kennedys could often still be found embracing the activities that had defined their months in Hyannis Port.
It was there thatJohn F. Kennedyspent his final Labor Day holiday in 1963, enjoying an activity-filled weekend with wife Jacqueline Kennedy, their children, relatives and friends just months before his assassination.
Archival footage from that weekend captures the family swimming, boating and spending time along the waterfront—offering an intimate glimpse at the traditions that made the compound much more than a collection of impressive homes.
Long before the Kennedy name became synonymous with American politics, summers in Hyannis Port were centered around family—and plenty of competition.
The Kennedy children grew up swimming, sailing, playing tennis, riding horses and facing off in games of touch football, activities that became deeply intertwined with the family’s time on Cape Cod.
Kathleen “Kick” Kennedy, one of Joseph and Rose Kennedy’s nine children, was known to enjoy horseback riding, tennis, swimming, sailing and touch football during the family’s summers in Hyannis Port, according to the National Park Service.
Those activities were hardly limited to one member of the family.
Joseph Kennedy encouraged a competitive spirit among his children, and the expansive outdoor spaces and waterfront setting surrounding their summer home provided an ideal playground for the growing brood.
Touch football, in particular, became one of the family’s most famous pastimes, with photographs of Kennedys tossing a football across the grass becoming nearly as synonymous with the compound as its shingled homes and ocean views.
The water was equally important. Sailing became a fixture of Kennedy family life, while swimming, boating and trips out onto Nantucket
Decades later, those same activities were still unfolding around the compound when JFK returned as president for Labor Day weekend in 1963.
The Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port holds almost as much lore as infamous political dynasty itself.
This home was purchased in 1928 by family patriarch, diplomat, and businessman Joseph P. Kennedy for his wife, Rose, and their nine children, including JFK and Sen. Robert F. Kennedy. Over the years, the residence has become closely intertwined with the family’s storied history.
It was at the Cape Cod retreat that JFK planned his presidential campaign in the summer of 1960, and it was there that his wife, Jackie, fled after he was assassinated in 1963 at the age of 46.
Hyannis Port would be where Jackie crafted the image of Kennedy’s presidency as “Camelot” in the wake of his death, taking inspiration from the late politician’s favorite Broadway musical and telling the media in her first official interview after his passing: “Don’t let it be forgot, that for one brief, shining moment there was Camelot.”
The home had been the site of many happy vacations for JFK and Jackie—and it went on to serve as a much-needed retreat for other family members over the years, becoming the site of an annual Fourth of July reunion for many of their descendants.
The Kennedys might never have come to Hyannis Port if it hadn’t been for one pastime Joseph and Rose loved: golf. In 1926, and already a millionaire, Joseph went in search of a home near a golf club.
He explored a membership at the Cohasset Country Club, on the South Shore and close to Boston. However, he was iced out, reportedly as a result of his Irish Catholic faith.
Instead, the couple found Hyannisport Club on Cape Cod—then run by an Irish Catholic—and the Kennedys were welcomed. They proceeded to rent Malcolm Cottage, as it was then known and, in 1928, purchased the property for $25,000, according to thewebsitefor the JFK Museum in Hyannis.
The 3-acre property on a dead-end street directly faces Nantucket Sound.
While the Kennedy family spent time at other homes in New York, Maryland, and Florida, Hyannis Port is where they would create a multigenerational compound. Joe Kennedy expanded the main house, dubbed the Big House, toreportedlyinclude 21 rooms, 12 bedrooms, a steam room, and a 50-person theater in the basement.
The grounds offer a tennis court and pool, and other recreation options including golfing at the local club and sailing on the sound. Touch football, played on the grassy lawn, was also a favorite.
JFK bought a home behind his father’s Big House in 1956. It became known as the President’s House. Robert F. Kennedy and his wife, Ethel, bought another adjacent home; and those three properties made up the compound, which now spans 6 acres of waterfront property.
It was in the main house that JFK decided to run for president, and the home subsequently served as his campaign headquarters.
The morning after the election, it was his young daughter, Caroline, who woke him up in their Hyannis Port home to announce, “Good morning, Mr. President.”
During JFK’s presidency, the compound became the “seaside White House.” Heonce saidof his Cape Cod home, “I always come back to the Cape and walk on the beach when I have a tough decision to make.”
The place became iconic when images emerged ofJack and Jackie spending time therewith their children during the White House years.
It’s also a place where family members have retreated to grieve tremendous loss over the years, from the deaths of Joe Kennedy Jr., the eldest son, in World War II, toJFK’s assassination in 1963to RFK’s assassination in 1968, after he won the California presidential primary.
Another tragedy, decades later, took JFK’s son,John F. Kennedy Jr., who died in a plane crash with wife Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in 1999.
In 2019, another tragedy struck: A granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy, Saoirse Kennedy Hill, died of a suspected overdose at the Kennedy family compound. Her death occurred in the home of her grandmother, Ethel Kennedy, who was 91 at the time.
The compound was designated a US National Landmark in 1972—not surprising for a property that embodies so much American history.
It was against that storied backdrop that JFK returned to Hyannis Port for what would ultimately become his final Labor Day holiday.
The president and his family spent the long weekend there from Aug. 29 through Sept. 2, 1963, with official White House photographs and home-movie footage preserved by the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum offering an intimate glimpse into their final days of summer.
And despite JFK’s position as president, much of the weekend appeared remarkably similar to the Cape Cod vacations the Kennedys had enjoyed for decades.
Caroline and JFK Jr. spent time along the beachnear the compound, where they swam with other children. JFK Jr., who was just 2 years old, was also captured helping to guide a small motorboat into the bay, where the presidential yacht “Honey Fitz” sat anchored offshore.
Elsewhere, JFK watched as the children rode horses and later ventured into town with his close friend Paul “Red” Fay and John Jr. for a visit to a local toy store before the trio drove back to the compound.
The family also took to the water aboard theHoney Fitz, with footage showing the Kennedys and their guests making their way down the pier before embarking on a cruise.
Yet even during the holiday weekend, presidential duties were never far away
JFK sat down with legendary CBS newsman Walter Cronkite on the lawn of his Hyannis Port residence, where cameras captured the pair waiting as crews made the final technical preparations for their televised interview.
When the weekend came to an end, the cameras captured one final family scene: JFK Jr. running up the walkway of his grandfather’s home to greet Joseph Kennedy Sr., who was sitting on the porch.
The toddler was later filmed running toward a waiting helicopter that would carry him and his father away from Cape Cod and back toward Washington.
JFK would never celebrate another Labor Day. Less than three months later, on Nov. 22, 1963, the president was assassinated in Dallas at the age of 46.
His death forever changed both the Kennedy family and the public perception of their Hyannis Port sanctuary.
The homes that had once simply provided a summer escape became physical reminders of a lost era, while photographs of the family sailing, swimming and playing together took on an increasingly nostalgic quality.
Yet the compound’s significance was never rooted solely in its connection to JFK’s presidency.For the Kennedys themselves,Hyannis Porthad been home long before the White House entered the picture.
Generations learned to sail there. Children and cousins crowded onto the lawns and beaches. Family members competed against one another in sports and piled onto boats for trips across the water.
And during JFK’s final Labor Day weekend, many of those traditions were still playing out just as they had for decades.
The surviving footage shows a president, but it also shows a father watching his children, a toddler maneuvering a boat, youngsters swimming off the family beach and relatives gathering for a day on the water.
More than six decades later, those scenes offer a glimpse inside the Kennedy Compound at perhaps its most famous moment—not as the seat of an American political dynasty, but as the family playground it had been built to be.

hed: How do you measure value of a garden? The emotional heft of selling a labor of love
subhead: “If we’re going to do anything in life, it’s to leave something better than we found it,” one homeowner said. “And I think, at least with this garden, that we’ve done this.”
content:
ByLindsay Crudele
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Fifteen years ago, Mary Kernan and her husband moved from a condominium into a big house in Bedford and took on a gut renovation for the 4,200-square foot house. And then there was the yard, all 1.5 acres of it.

“The only things growing wereinvasives,” she said. “There was lily of the valley. There was buckthorn. There was bittersweet. There was knotweed. There were junk trees. It was an absolute mess.”

Kernan didn’t know much about gardening at the time, so she hired a landscaper. It didn’t go well.

“I spent the next 15 years undoing everything he did because so much of it, I realized, was wrong,” she said. “And along the way, I learned a lot.”

Over time, Kernan added a vegetable garden. Then came fruit trees, includingpawpawandmulberry, followed by hundreds of native plants. She leveled up by installing drip irrigation, so she could spend more time gardening and less time watering. Kernan learned so much that she began teaching others, sharing plants, and joining theBedford Garden Club.

“It kept growing and growing,” she said. “And then the more it grew, the more I started sharing with other people.”



But when they bought the home, Kernan and her husband promised each other they would spend 15 years — no longer —there. That time is now up. The two have purchased a condominium with only a small outdoor space for gardening. And while Kernan said she accepts what feels like a practical and necessary downsizing, her ambivalence as she prepares for the sale is palpable.

“I’m sitting here on my front step watching the bees in my front garden, and right now, they went from the thistle to the bee balm to the echinacea, and they’re just kind of buzzing all over the garden,” she said. “I’m mourning the loss of this space, and we’re trying to figure out if we can find the right buyer who will appreciate what it is versus somebody who might come in and tear it all out.”

Ultimately she said, maximizing value will be the sale’s determining factor, and from there, she must let go.

Selling a home with an established garden adds complexity to already daunting work — it can carry emotional heft, along with practical considerations. Can a garden be quantified in numerical value? Maybe.


Investing in outdoor, curb appeal-oriented improvements is a good idea for sellers, and it can return value, said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist for theNational Association of Realtors.

“For standard lawn care service, landscape maintenance, overall landscape upgrades, and outdoor kitchens, sellers are estimated to receive at least 100 percent cost recovery on the project,” she said via email.

But landscape design is a wildly variable field: trim lawns and boxwood rows are different from naturalistic native plantings, and may attract different buyers. For established gardens maintained as a labor of love by a homeowner over years, resale value is much harder to quantify.

“Our data shows that the more specific and functional the garden feature, the better it performs on price,” said Amanda Pendleton,Zillow’shome trends expert. “For instance, homes with fruit trees sell for 0.7 percent more than expected, while homes with a generic ‘garden’ actually sell for 0.4 percent less than expected.”

Buyers favor value and low maintenance, not just any greenery, she said.

“The most rewarding outdoor features tend to be ones that are productive, purposeful, or planet-friendly,” said Pendleton.


When Mary Huff prepared to sell her1.26-acre property in Atlantabefore moving to Littleton, Mass., the $3,000 native landscaping plan provided by the designer she hired was a budget-friendlier option than traditional landscaping quotes that topped $5,000. The designer’s plan detailed plant species and the wildlife that each would attract and support.

“I think our real estate agent was a little apprehensive about it,” she said.

But buyers responded enthusiastically to the climate-resilient, lower-maintenance plantings, aided by renderings of how the garden would look once further established. The four-bedroom, three-bathroom house sold for nearly 11 percent over its asking price, and the agent attributed part of that success to the garden.

Finding the right buyer for a longtime garden is just a matter of matching tastes, like any home feature, said Judy Chauvin, a Realtor withCape Landing Real Estate. She said she isn’t seeing sellers do much to modify yards such as these.

“I think when you are a gardener … you take pride in that garden and you just leave it as is and hope somebody will come along that loves it and admires it as much as you have,” she said.

For instance, Chauvin is currently representing7 Cranberry Road in Plymouth, which is nestled among blueberry bushes in a coastal setting.

“There’s a lot of natural plantings there that kind of just mix in with the environment,” she said. “It’s kind of like ‘my little secret garden.’”



Since 1986, writerSuzanne Strempek Sheahas lived near Springfield in Palmer, where she’s grown flowers so tall you can wander through corridors among them. But after many seasons hosting writing workshops in Ireland, she and her husband have decided the time is right to try living abroad full time. She hasplaced the three-bedroom home for sale, and, she said, she can’t take the plants.

Forty years ago, the garden was all grass. Now, Shea said, the winding avenues and places to sit are a wildlife haven.

“If we’re going to do anything in life, it’s to leave something better than we found it,” she said. “And I think, at least with this garden, that we’ve done this.”

“People who are familiar with our yard here have said, ‘I hope it’s not someone who’s just going to plow it over,’ and I would hope that too,” she said. “But you know, you really have to just let that go.”

Billie Jean Petrieis the realtor tasked with selling the home. She said that for her, it’s a chance to emphasize the retreat-like atmosphere in her marketing. A garden of this scale is an anomaly, she said.

“It’s just beautiful everywhere you look all the time,” she said.

Ariana Lymberopoulos grew up inher father’s Needham home, where he transformed the yard into an abundant mirror for his earlier years gardening in Greece, lush with flowers and edible plantings.

“My relationship to that garden was very entrenched in my parents’ identity, which became my identity, and it was something that I saw my dad just pour his time into all summer,” she said.

The garden nurtured her own sense of patience, discipline, and responsibility.



(Ariana Lymberopoulos’ father transformed his Needham home’s yard into a lush garden of flowers and vegetables. Photos:Ariana Lymberopoulos)

“It was also a dramatic, massive garden,” she said.

Drivers would slow down to marvel at tall plumes of flowers spilling down the driveway wall, and a hill of giant tomato plants rose each summer.

As her father aged, Ariana and her brother took the house over legally, but when she moved to Hingham, and her father came to live with her, it was time to pass the house on to a new owner.

“I almost wanted to make sure that the next people that came in were green thumb people,” she said. She received pressure from her agent to trim things back, and remove some of her father’s fencing.

“They were like, ‘Is there any way you can bring some landscapers in here to kind of clean this up?’” she recalled. “And we were like, ‘Yeah, we don’t think that’s necessary …’”

An interested family emerged, moving from the Midwest, who added a letter to their offer explaining that the garden reminded them of home. In 2023, they closed on the house.

Lymberopoulos has driven by to peek at what became of the garden. At last look, it was smaller, but still there.

“Like an altar,” she said.

hed: After 46 years, a Hingham family has listed the Abby Bradley Estate, an 1860 Victorian, for $2.8m
subhead: The neighborhood kids once thought of it as a haunted house. Today, it’s a well maintained 19th-century time capsule.
content:
ByDaisy Levine
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

The Abby Bradley Estate used to be a creepy, boarded-up house.

Current owner James Wechsler’s coworker told him he used to sneak into the house as a kid when it was abandoned. Kids like him, he said, would play in the home but try not to move anything. They were sure it was haunted.

Built in 1860, it was originally the home of Abby Bradley, part of Hingham’s storied Bradley family, who ownedBradley & Hubbard Manufacturing Companyin the 1800s.

The Bradley family was a “major presence” in Hingham, said Wallis Bowyer, one of the Coldwell Banker Realty agents who has the listing. Today, there are three streets and neighborhoods in Hingham named for the family: Bradley Hill, Bradley Woods, and Bradley Park.

James and Eva Wechlser settled at the Hingham house in 1980, which they bought for $130,000, according to Zillow. They raised three children in their 46 years at the home and put iton the market this August for $2,849,000.


“We really enjoyed living in it,” said James Wechsler, 83. “We did redecorate things, but we never did anything to alter the things that [Abby] had done. We wanted to keep it as true to the original house as we could.”

Located at the end of a cul-de-sac at 60 Bradley Hill Road, much of the six-bedroom, five-bathroom house remains a time capsule of its original era. There are seven fireplaces, original wood paneling, and handcrafted molding. The house has all its original windows, many of which are bowed, or rounded — a rarity with today’s craftsmanship.


The staircase, with its hardwood banisters and vintage spindles is “very grand feeling,” Bowyer said. “It goes up and then it goes around and it heads to the third floor. And when you look down from the third floor, you can see all the way down to the first. It’s incredible.”


Bowyer points out an especially notable room in the 5,770-square-foot Victorian: the intricate sunroom. “I don’t even know who I would pay to do this for me in present day,” she recalled a builder once commenting. Abby Bradley hired a French artisan who spent 18 months hand-carving the sunroom — incredibly expensive details to recreate today, Wechsler said.

“No one would do this nowadays, but in those days, that’s what they did,” James Wechsler said. “So [Abby] spared no expense to fix the place up.”


The house also has some quirks that could have contributed to the neighborhood kids thinking it was haunted. For one, there’s a secret door — possibly the old servants’ quarters, Bowyer said — that can be pressed to reveal a passageway to the basement and the backside of the house.

Walking down to a circa-1860 basement can, admittedly, be a little scary, Bowyer said, but this one has high ceilings and is actually “clean as a whistle.”

The Wechslers put on an addition for the kitchenand  modernized the home a bit.


James Weschler, a self-proclaimed history buff, spent his retired years researching the home’s centuries-old inhabitants and uncharacteristic features. When ripping off a piece of interior wallpaper, he found an inscription dated 1898.


The house sites on 1.3 acres. Previous owners filled a sizable pool outside the home, so Bowyer noted there is a large amount of yard space.

“When you look at that wraparound … porch, it goes around two sides and it looks over the whole property, which is stunning,” she noted.


Additionally, the sale comes with a buildable lot at 109 Thaxter Street.

“The whole house, it’s truly architecturally amazing,” Bowyer said.

hed: More Americans are drowning in underwater mortgages — and 1 state just saw a staggering surge
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
More American homeowners now owe substantially more on their mortgages than what their properties are worth, as a key measure of housing-market distress moves in the wrong direction.
The share of US homeowners who are “seriously underwater” on their mortgages climbed to 3.2% in the second quarter, up from 2.7% a year earlier, according to a newstate-by-state analysisfrom real estate data firm ATTOM.
That means the combined balance of loans secured against the property is at least 25% greater than what the home itself is estimated to be worth.
The problem worsened year-over-year in 33 states and Washington, DC — but nowhere was the shift as dramatic as Minnesota.
The North Star State vaulted to the top of the nation’s underwater rankings, with a whopping 12.1% of mortgaged homes seriously underwater in the second quarter.
That’s up from just 3% in the first quarter and 2.6% a year earlier — meaning Minnesota’s rate has more than quadrupled in just 12 months.
Louisiana ranked second, with 10.3% of mortgaged homes seriously underwater. Unlike Minnesota, however, the state’s situation has actually improved: Its rate fell from 11.8% in the previous quarter and 11.9% a year earlier.
Iowa landed in third place at 7.8%, up from 6% in the first quarter and 5.9% a year ago.
Mississippi and Arkansas rounded out the five states with the highest shares, at 6.4% and 6%, respectively.
The deterioration comes as another measure of homeowners’ financial cushion is also moving in the wrong direction.
Just 41.1% of mortgaged US homes were considered “equity rich” during the second quarter — meaning the amount owed on the property was no more than half its estimated value — down from 43.3% during the first quarter and 47.4% a year earlier.
That marked the fourth consecutive quarterly decline and brought the share of equity-rich homes to its lowest level in nearly five years, according to ATTOM.
“These two measures of home equity strength, the rates of equity-rich and seriously underwater homes, remain healthier than they were prior to 2020,” ATTOM CEO Rob Barber said in the report.
“However, both have been moving in less favorable directions over the past year, suggesting a trend worth watching.”
New York homeowners, meanwhile, are largely bucking the troubling national trend.
Just 1.5% of mortgaged properties in the Empire State were seriously underwater in the second quarter, down from 1.9% during the first quarter and 2% a year earlier.
New Jersey also fared relatively well, with 1.6% of mortgaged properties seriously underwater, down from 1.8% the previous quarter and 1.7% a year ago.
Vermont recorded the lowest underwater rate in the country, at just 0.9%.

hed: NYC outskirts crowd out top 6 in America’s 20 Best Suburbs ranking
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Where do New Yorkers go after the rat race is won?
While there is nowhere that compares to New York City, the call of the quaint and the quiet, not to mention the lure of lawns and leafy streets, has long drawn urbanites to the outskirts.
To help city slickers choose an aspirational outskirt,HGTV ranked the top twenty in the nation— and unsurprisingly, the top six slots are dominated by NYC suburbs.
“Though city living has its perks, living in a suburban neighborhood has plenty of advantages, too,” said HGTV.
“Suburban neighborhoods often offer residents more indoor and outdoor space and, in many instances, a lower cost of living,” they continued, noting that trading traffic for trees need not come at the expense of quality dining and recreation options.
“In fact, many suburban neighborhoods have top-notch entertainment, seasonal festivals and enriching theater programs,” they promised.
With the know-how of real estate experts atSuburban Jungle, the top spots are spread across New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.
A quaint hamlet 30 miles north of NYC, Chappaqua is beloved for its expansive nature trails and walkable downtown, which helped it earn the number one spot on HGTV’s list.
A less-than-an-hour commute to Manhattan makes Chappaqua an easy choice, while the promise of educational excellence is pure parent bait, as the small town boasts some of the best schools in the country.
The tightnight community of roughly 3,000 is bound together by wealth and a predictable love of seasonal festivals and farmers’ markets.
Though Chappaqua might be best known for septuagenarian residents Bill and Hillary Clinton, the median age is just 45.8.
The median household income is $220,139, while the median home value is $740,300, per GOBankingRates.
Larchmont, on Long Island Sound, was also recognized for its suburban superiority.
Just 30 minutes from Manhattan, Larchmont’s culture centers on water sports like boating, paddleboarding, and kayaking.
Residents and visitors alike favor Larchmont Manor Park, framed by 5,000 feet of shoreline and famed for its natural stone sculptures carved by glacial rock.
The Larchmont food scene is good and getting better; Michelin-starred Chef Michael Psilakis is slated to open his Greek-inspired restaurantKlēmain the coming weeks.
True to its name, Summit made the top 3 for covetable suburbs.
Just under an hour from NYC, Summit has grown increasingly popular over the past two decades.
“This Union County suburb has long been a favorite for city dwellers seeking a little breathing room – but not at the expense of culture, coffee, or community,” reports Suburban Jungle.
“With its walkable downtown, top-rated schools, and tree-lined streets, this Union County suburb tops countless city families’ lists – many who start planning a move as soon as they visit.”
Port Washington, on Long Island’s north shore, is chock full of literary lore: The Sands Point Peninsula inspired the East Egg neighborhood in F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel,The Great Gatsby.
The former sand-mining town, located just 17 miles from NYC, also draws commuters with its renowned school system and waterfront charm.
Port Washington is home to 15,846 residents who call the town simply “Port.”
“Known for its walkable downtown, buzzy restaurant scene, and serious waterfront vibes, Port has long been a top pick for New Yorkers craving space without sacrificing style,” praisesSuburban Jungle, which describes the town’s aesthetic as “suburbs but make it chic.”
Rich and renowned, Greenwich is not only an aspirational NYC suburb but one of the most sought-after communities in the United States.
Known for its constellation of mansions and the occasionalhigh-profile murder,Greenwich is home to roughly 63,000 people, the majority of them well-heeled nature lovers who find refuge from city life in the town’s 300-acre Bannock Preserve and the Audubon Center.
Earlier this summer,Greenwich condos began selling for as much as $12 million, blowing past the town’s previous record condo sale of $6.75 million by nearly 50 percent.
Meanwhile, last year,25 homes priced over $10 millionsold in the idyllic town, representing the highest sum for any full year since 1999.
Westport, Connecticut, has long held commuter cachet thanks to its small-town feel, abundant access to nature, and a legion of cultural centers and activities.
Home to 27,840 residents, the town ranked a stately 6th in HGTV’s best suburbs ranking.
“Just one hour outside of midtown and rich in countless resources, Westport is known as a center of creative energy and has been for more than a century, when artists, actors, musicians and writers first descended on the town,” saidSuburban Jungle.
“The results are a vibrant community that enjoys tremendous vitality—and draws attention from Manhattan elite looking to call the suburbs home.”
Indeed, Westport was the fictional residence of Ricky and Lucy Ricardo (“I Love Lucy”) and Darrin and Samantha Stephens (“Bewitched”), and the real home of many a celebrity, most famously, Martha Stewart and the late Paul Newman.

hed: Booming Sun Belt city revealed as America’s top pet-friendly rental market
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Charlotte has officially claimed the crown as the most welcoming rental market in the country for furry tenants with four legs, according tofresh data out of Zillow.
The North Carolina metroposted a staggering 91.6% pet-approval rate among its rental listings, narrowly outpacingAustin, Texas, which came in at 91.5%.
Denver, Dallas and Nashville rounded out the top five, continuing a pattern in which Sun Belt and Mountain West cities dominate the leaderboard, largely thanks to newer apartment complexes built with pet policies baked in from day one.
Nationally, landlords have clearly gotten the memo.
Three-quarters of all rental listingson Zillownow allow pets, a dramatic jump from where the market stood just a few years back. Zillow Home Trends Expert Amanda Pendleton put the shift in stark terms, telling HGTV, “The rental market has undergone a dramatic shift for pet owners.”
She noted that only a little more than half of listings allowed pets as recently as three years ago, adding, “Today, that number has climbed to 77%.”
The demand driving that shift isn’t hard to explain.
Nearly six in 10 renter households now have a pet in the home, edging out the share with kids and even the share with houseplants.
Two-thirds of renters call pet-friendliness a dealbreaker when apartment hunting, a number that’s climbed steadily as more Americans opt for a dog or cat over, well, anything else.
But not every city is keeping pace, and New York is one of the worst offenders.
The five boroughs allow pets in only 61% of listings, good for second-to-last among the nation’s largest metros.
Only Providence, Rhode Island, trails further behind, with just 54% of its rentals opening the door to Fido.
That reluctance may be costing New York landlords real money. Pet-friendly units in the metro rent a full 26 days faster than those that ban animals, the widest such gap of any major market in the country.
Listings that welcome pets also pull in significantly more views, saves and shares than the ones that don’t, according to Zillow’s research, suggesting Gotham’s holdout landlords are leaving both time and cash on the table.
Elsewhere, the numbers are moving fast. Salt Lake City posted the single biggest jump of any metro over the past year, climbing nearly eight percentage points, with Louisville, Cleveland, Miami and Indianapolis also showing meaningful gains.

hed: Malls are making a shocking comeback — becoming the top performer in commercial real estate
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Zombie malls are having the last laugh.
After a decade of doom-loop headlines, Instagram-video obituaries and dead-mall photo essays,America’s shopping centersjust posted the hottest numbers in commercial real estate.
Mall values shot up 13% in the past year, according to real-estate research firm Green Street, crushing every other property sector and doubling the pace of the broader commercial market’s recovery.
The comeback isn’t just Wall Street math. It’s Gen Z dragging their moms to the food court, luxury brands moving into old Sears boxes and landlords finally figuring out that a mall without a movie theater or a Din Tai Fung is just a warehouse with parking.
“In terms of how we think about the malls today fundamentally, this is probably the best it’s felt post-COVID,” Ronald Kamdem, who heads US REIT and commercial real-estate research at Morgan Stanley, told theWall Street Journal.
It’s a wild reversal from five years ago, when lockdowns gutted foot traffic and department-store closures were already bleeding malls dry.
Roughly 200 mallshave shuttered nationwidesince 2008, Green Street data shows, leaving about 900 still standing.
And the survivors left standing aren’t just surviving, they’rebecoming tourist attractionsin their own right. As for the top five, based on foot-traffic alone, they’re booming.
Minnesota’sMall of Americapulls in a jaw-dropping 40 million visitors a year to browse its 500-plus stores and 50-plus restaurants. New Jersey’s American Dream matches that same 40-million-visitor number thanks to an indoor ski slope and DreamWorks Water Park, one of the largest indoor water parks in North America, alongside more than 300 retail stores.
Houston’s the Galleria draws upward of 30 million shoppers a year, many of them lured by its center-court ice skating rink and more than 400 stores. Pennsylvania’s King of Prussia Mall, home to one of the country’s deepest luxury retail lineups across 450-plus stores, pulls about 25 million visitors annually. And South Florida’s Aventura Mall rounds out the top five with roughly 25 to 28 million annual visitors browsing its 300-plus stores.
Simon Property Group, the mall king of America, is riding the wave straight to the bank. Its stock blew past its old 2016 record high in July and has outpaced the S&P 500 over the last year.
Even landlords who swore off American malls are crawling back. Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield ditched plans to exit the US market just four years ago. Now it’s spending close to $1 billion this year to buy out partners and take full control of Westfield UTC in San Diego and Westfield Southcenter near Seattle.
“We see the type of rent growth that we haven’t seen since the beginning of the 2010s,” URW chief executive Vincent Rouget told the Journal.
Rouget said the American portfolio is now outgrowing the rest of the company’s holdings worldwide, with tenant sales and income climbing faster than average even after URW sold off a slew of underperforming properties in recent years.
It’s not just the trophy properties cashing in either. Chattanooga-based CBL Properties spent a year in bankruptcy after the pandemic hit and has since clawed its way back, shedding more than two dozen weaker malls since 2013 while snapping up five new ones since last July. Its stock has climbed 48% since January.
“It’s really been, I think, even better than we had hoped,” CBL chief executive Stephen Lebovitz added.
And it turns out the kids never left. At Tysons Corner Center in Virginia, shopper Heather Eilers-Bowser watched her 13-year-old daughter hunt down sweatpants from the online-famous brand Edikted while she picked out sneakers for her husband and son.
“She has more expensive makeup than I do,” Eilers-Bowser said of her daughter. “And a lot more.”
Not everyone is buying the hype. Bob Neighoff, a portfolio manager at Mariner Investment Group, thinks the sector’s newfound swagger has a shelf life, especially since so many malls filled their empty anchor spaces with restaurants and entertainment venues that would be brutal to replace if they ever went under.
“Unlocking the dirt is the true value of the mall,” Neighoff told the Journal. “I’m a little more cautious on the actual retail experience of the mall being something to hang your hat on.”
Still, CBL’s West County Center outside St. Louis shows just how far the turnaround has come. Back in 2022, the 1.2 million-square-foot mall couldn’t even refinance its debt as lenders fled midtier malls. Values there had sunk 30% over the prior decade, three of four prime restaurant spaces sat empty and a rival mall was stealing shoppers from anchor tenant Nordstrom.
Fast forward to today and Nordstrom’s old rival location has closed, Macy’s has renovated, and Cheesecake Factory and Urban Outfitters are both moving in later this year. Tenant sales at the property are up 13% since 2023, and Lebovitz says he expects to close on a refinancing within 60 days.
“We’ve just seen this real strengthening of the property,” he said.

hed: Boston Red Sox staff moving out of Fenway Park offices
subhead: The move consolidates the Sox and Fenway Sports Group offices
content: The Sox are leaving Fenway Park. Or, at least, their office staff is getting new digs.The Boston Red Sox have leased the top three floors of a 13-story Boylston Street office steps from the ballpark, and will vacate their offices inside the historic venue itself.The move is a consolidation that will bring office employees of the Sox, its ownership conglomerate Fenway Sports Group, and marketing company Fenway Sports Management together under one roof. They’re currently spread among three offices in the ballpark at 4 Jersey St. and at nearby 82 and 98 Brookline Ave. “This is an interim office solution and does not change our long-term plans for the proposed Lansdowne Street building or our broader commitment to the Fenway Corners project, which we continue to advance,” Sox spokesperson Zineb Curran said in a statement. Fenway Sports Group last year proposed a seven-story office on what’s now a two-story parking garage between the Green Monster and the Massachusetts Turnpike. That 250,000-square-foot office would be the first phase of the $1.6 billion Fenway Corners mixed-use project, planned in partnership with WS Development, which calls for eight new buildings on the streets encircling Fenway Park. John Henry, The Boston Globe’s publisher, is principal owner of Fenway Sports Group. The Sox will be moving into the Boylston Street office as another neighborhood stalwart departs. Chef Tiffani Faison, citing “challenges and dynamics of the restaurant industry,” said restaurants Sweet Cheeks Q and Fool’s Errand at 1381 and 1377 Boylston St. will close this fall.The 13-story mixed-use building at 1325 Boylston St. opened in 2015 and includes office space, 172 apartments, and a three-level, 170,000-square-foot Target store. Its developer, Boston-based Samuels & Associates, spearheaded the redevelopment of much of the modern Fenway neighborhood.“We are delighted to welcome the Red Sox operations team to 1325 Boylston Street, where they will be joining a diverse array of innovative companies that value The Fenway neighborhood and its robust mix of amenities and opportunities for connection and collaboration,” said Peter Sougarides, Samuels’ co-president and principal, in a statement.The 100,493-square-foot lease includes exclusive rights to a portion of the building’s roof deck and “non-exclusive rights regarding signage,” indicating the building could eventually see Sox, FSG, or FSM branding join the large Target logo on the building’s facade.The lease is dated June 30 but was not recorded in Suffolk County property records until this month. The five-year lease begins Nov. 1 and extends through 2032, though the Sox have an option to extend for another five years after that. The Sox have not yet finalized plans for the future use of their office space inside Fenway. Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Home of the Week: Near Harvard Square, a sunny 2-bedroom condo is a garden oasis for $900k
subhead: The Cambridge unit has a private deck and a shared, landscaped backyard
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

391 Concord Ave., Unit 1, Cambridge

$899,999

StyleCondo

Year built1920

Square feet1,058

Bedrooms2

Baths1 full

Sewer/WaterPublic

HOA fee:$220 month

Taxes$4,961 (2026; without residential exemption.)


Behind a white picket fence at the end of a short sidewalk awaits a 23-foot-wide porch in a classic farmhouse style that is exclusive to Unit 1. It has a beadboard ceiling painted light blue and views of the small garden in the front yard and the tree-shrouded city sidewalk beyond.

It’s in the city’s West Cambridge neighborhood,also known as Neighborhood 10. Better yet, this home is near Harvard Square.

The front door opens into an enclosed stairwell connecting to the two units that make up this condo building.


A door on the right opens into Unit 1, making the arrival point the 260-square-foot living room and its glistening hardwood floors believed original to the 106-year-old building. The ceiling, however, has a mark of more recent occupation in the form of recessed lighting. Directly opposite the entry is a key source of natural light: a three window bump-out of double-hung windows with white trim. To the right, more light is pulled in through an accent window with diamond shaped muntin, and finally on the front wall, a set of double-hung windows overlook the porch.


A door near the end of the living room leads to the primary bedroom. It’s a 111-square-foot rectangle with a bank of two double-hung windows on the right side. Behind sliding mirrored doors is a 30-square-foot walk-in closet. The flooring is refinished hardwood.

There is a private door connecting the primary bedroom to the home’s one full bath. The 70-square-foot bathroom has a shower/bath combination with jets. The backsplash is tile, and the flooring is handmade Spanish tiles. There is a single vanity.

The end of the living room is the start of an 18-foot-long hallway where there is another entrance to the bathroom.


Almost directly across the hallway is the 88-square-foot second bedroom, which is a nearly perfect square. The current owners converted it into a sunny home office with the help of a pair of double-hung windows. But the key addition is the installation of a Murphy bed behind shelving on the right side of the room. The left side has a desk and more shelving.


In the hallway, a bit beyond the bedroom, is a closet and then the final interior areas: the kitchen, dining area, and laundry closet. The dining room is 117 square feet and has the footprint of an enclosed sunroom — and the benefits of having that as its antecedent. The left, center, and right walls are full of double-hung windows, with all the trim painted white. There is a sill running underneath large enough to host tchotchkes. The ceiling has recessed lights and two drum-shaped pendant lights. The flooring is a darker shade than the rest of the hardwood.


The kitchen is 107 square feet. One would be forgiven for staring at the floor in this room; it features charming Spanish tile of greens and blues in a diamond pattern. There are two layers of wood cabinets with raised panel doors. Countertops are quartz and the backsplash is white subway tile. Appliances, including the double ovens, are stainless steel, and there is a gas cooktop.


The dining room also provides access to the 67-square-foot farmhouse-style deck, private to this unit. The shared backyard is a gardener’s delight that has been developed over the past seven years into a green refuge.



The home has forced hot air for heating. The unit does not come with an off-street parking space.

Elis Aguilar-Becker of William Raveisin Boston has the listing. As of press time, an offer has been accepted on the property.

hed: House hunt stories: He dreamed of a South End brownstone for 12 years. It took 90 days of chaos to get one.
subhead: Boston resident Kris Moore shares the ups and downs that led to condo ownership
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Twelve years ago, not long after Kris Moore moved to Boston, he settled on a real estate goal as he explored his new city: “Someday I want to live in a brownstone in the South End,” he said.

Last spring, the dream came true. The 40-year-old, who works at a downtown law firm, finally got his keys after a bidding war with 12 offers, a seller who could legally walk away at any moment, and a brief, unplanned stint as a landlord to two frustrated tenants.

“I kept taking on added risk and complexity because the fundamentals of the place were strong, even if the process itself was stressful,” Moore said.

Budget:$750,000

Search radius:South End or bust.

The find:a 711-square-foot, two-bedroom, parlor-level condo near West Canton Street and Columbus Avenue, listed at $700,000 in December 2024.

Purchase price:$780,000.

The challenges:

·Went over budget; high interest rates

·Sellers were rolling the proceeds into a1031 exchange, which can allow deferring capital gains taxes on sales of investment properties

·Unit was tenant-occupied

·Historic brownstone required renovations



Moore was no rookie. He previously owned a condo on the East Side of South Boston for nearly three years, sold it in 2021, and set aside the profit. After several years of renting in the South End, he decided in the fall of 2024 that he was ready to buy again. His lease ran through the spring, so there was no rush. The plan was simply to hit open houses through the winter and get a feel for what his money could buy.

At first, the answer was sobering. His first stop was a one-bedroom condo on Warren Avenue in the low $700,000s that needed work. But open house number two was the one.

The two-bedroom condo had been a rental for years, and it showed. The listing photos were dim and the tenants’ oversized furniture crowded every room. The December open house was mobbed anyway. Moore looked past the mess and saw a parlor-level unit with nearly 12-foot ceilings, a bowfront window, exposed brick in every room, a fireplace, and a small back deck, sitting between two parks (Hayes Park and the recently reopened Crite Park), and a short walk to Back Bay Station.


The rental-grade condition was an opportunity, he figured. Having renovated before, he knew what paint, refinished floors, and properly scaled furniture could do. And the listing price, set low in part because of those unflattering photos, was under his ceiling.

“What’s the catch here?” he remembered thinking.

That catch arrived quickly. The condo drew 12 offers, including all-cash competition. Moore’s agent,Brett Campbell of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, had done a deal with the seller’s agent before, and that track record helped Moore’s financed offer prevail. But winning meant going to $780,000 — $80,000 over asking, and past the top of his budget.

Then came a wrinkle Moore had never encountered: the unit was an investment property, and the sellers were rolling the proceeds into a1031 exchange, making the entire sale contingent on their finding a replacement property, he said. Partway through negotiations, the property the sellers had identified fell through, pushing out the closing on Moore’s dream home. Open house to closing took roughly 90 days.

“Ride this ride. There are going to be highs and lows,” Moore said of his mindset at the time. “It might fall apart, and we just have to be okay with that, because the upside was still ultimately there.”


The unit was also tenant-occupied, with a lease running through the end of May — a problem since Moore’s lender required him to take occupancy within 60 days of closing. The sellers negotiated an earlier move-out with their tenants, but because the closing and lease still overlapped, Moore briefly became a landlord. On advicethat Massachusetts’ technical requirements around deposits, he didn’t collect a security deposit from the tenants, who were understandably unhappy about leaving early, and just hoped for the best.


Moore’s down payment came from the sale of his Southie condo, but the rate environment for a mortgage stung.

He locked in at 6.6 percent — accepting that 2021 rates were “never coming back” — and that his purchasing power had shrunk accordingly. About nine months in, he refinanced into a five-year adjustable-rate mortgage at 5.75 percent. Between the refinance and the city’s residential exemption, which kicked in partway through the year, his monthly housing costs dropped by roughly $1,500.



The first year delivered a full curriculum in brownstone ownership. The building’s shared pipes froze twice during an exceptionally cold winter, once leaving him without hot water for nearly two days during a snowstorm — “a memorable lesson in dripping the faucets when temperatures drop below 20 degrees,” he said.

The washer died; the delivery crew then discovered corroded shutoff valves that required a plumber before the new one could be hooked up. A declining backyard tree needed removal, another shared expense. Parlor-level living beside the front door came with a soundtrack of comings and goings.

The location, though, has over-delivered.

“I can be at the Pru in five minutes,” Moore said, and his commute is now a few blocks to Back Bay Station and four Orange Line stops to his office.


Before moving in, Moore painted every room, installed matching hardwood in the previously carpeted bedrooms, and refinished the floors in dark walnut. Since then, he has turned a cluttered nook off the kitchen into a proper dining room with a round table, an oversized mirror, and a dramatic pendant light, and transformed the second bedroom with a custom Murphy bed and aCalifornia Closets wardrobeinto a guest room/office. Up next is the installation of ductless mini-splits, adding built-in wardrobes for the primary bedroom, and, over time, restoring the crown molding and mantel the unit lost somewhere along the way.

“I’m really glad I trusted my gut that the fundamentals were there,” Moore said. “This sounds cliché, but it’s been better than I expected.”



“Just accepting that these high rates mean you’re going to be paying a lot of interest. You can always refinance after the fact,” Moore said. “You likely will have to take on a fair amount of risk in the transaction. That’s just a reality in the market today. If you calculate the risk and how much you really have a tolerance for it, it ultimately is worth it — if the fundamentals are there.”
