hed: HOA seizes man’s $450K home over $977 debt — and sells it for just $8K
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An Arizona man lost the home he bought for nearly half a million dollars after falling just $977 behind on homeowners association fees — with the property ultimately selling back to the HOA for a mere $8,172.
Toby Newton purchased the four-bedroom Mesa home for $475,000 in 2022, but ran into financial trouble two years later after losing his job and being diagnosed with diabetes, according tothe Mesa Tribune.
Newton fell behind on his quarterly HOA assessments, which were around $170, eventually owing $977 in fees and interest.
“I bought the house and then I got sick,” Newton told the outlet. “I got diabetes and I was out of work.”
Newton said he contacted the Superstition Springs Community Master Association in an attempt to work out a payment plan.
He initially offered to pay $50 per month toward his debt while keeping up with his regular assessments. After that was rejected, he increased his proposed payments — eventually offering $200 a month — but said the HOA rejected those offers as well.
By November 2024, the association had initiated foreclosure proceedings.
As the case dragged on, the relatively modest HOA debt ballooned.
Court filings showed that by July 2025, Newton owed $1,311 in missed assessments and late charges, along with $1,042.09 in plaintiff’s fees and $3,345 in attorney fees.
The home was ultimately sold at public auction in October 2025 to the Superstition Springs Community Master Association for just $8,172. Newton’s total debt stood at $6,579 by then.
The case unfolded as Arizona lawmakers moved to give homeowners greater protections against HOA foreclosures.
In April 2025, Arizona enactedSenate Bill 1494, which significantly raised the bar for when an HOA can foreclose over unpaid assessments.
Under the new law, homeowners must be delinquent for at least 18 months or owe $10,000 or more in assessments before an HOA can foreclose — up from the previous thresholds of one year or $1,200.
The law also requires HOA boards to make reasonable efforts to communicate with delinquent homeowners and offer a reasonable payment plan before filing a foreclosure action.
Newton’s longtime partner, Sherrie Patten, laterlaunched a GoFundMefor the couple, writing that the ordeal had taken an “emotional and financial toll” on them.

hed: ‘The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air’ mansion returns with a 25% listing discount — and stands to be demolished
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about a re-run.
Will Smith’s opulent home in “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” is back for sale following a king-sized price cut of nearly 25%, to $22.95 million. That’s afteran initial listing early this yearasking $30 million attracted lots of looky-loos, but no commitments.
The property snoops at Realtor.comfirst reported newsof the listing’s return.
A sale would be bittersweet since the nearly 100-year-old home’s heyday has passed — and it would likely be torn down by its new purchaser. That’s because it would require a massive amount of work and money to revitalize instead of just building a new, personalized mansion there.
Farhad “Frank” Rahbanhas owned the estate for nearly 50 years as part of his expansive real estate holdings in the Los Angeles area. He and his wife, Parvin Nourafchan Rahban, raised their two sons, Nicholas and Sasha, there.
Sasha, in an interview with The California Post in January, said he was able to watchO.J. Simpson— who lived two blocks over — begin his slow Bronco ride down a Los Angeles highway in a still-notorious media spectacle before cops arrested him.
If a buyer were inclined to hold onto the home’s history and keep it standing, its entire nearly 6,500 square feet of interior space would have to be gutted and rebuilt. The outside, so frequently seen in the 1990s pop culture landmark show, would need to support that work.
Until any decisions are made about the property, it has found a new cast of characters, but with a much less buoyant storyline. The estate is a prime exterior for the Hulu/FX summer hit, “The Shards,” a dark erotic thriller set in 1981 in which a serial killer is hunting rich prep school kids.
The estate’s pool is featured as one of the male leads gets drunk by it, strips while walking over broken vodka bottle shards, plants a kiss on his costar’s lips, and then cannon balls into the water and is pulled out unconscious. The property is also where one of the females leads gets attacked, presumably by the serial killer.
“Capitalize on the expansive, flat corner footprint to build a (larger) world-class, multi-structure private estate compound,” the listing says of the land’s practical use.
As it stands now, the home “is not in move-in shape,” said Christophe Choo, who has the listing with Coldwell Banker Realty.
The property, though, “Is one of the finest locations in all of Los Angeles,” Choo said.
Choo said he is already seeing interest since listing the property late last week, with a Beverly Hills couple “flying home early from their European vacation to see it,” and other viewings planned.
The mansion still carries its Colonial Revival grace, including a two-story columned front portico framed by sprawling lawns and towering trees.
The property is advertised, as is stands, as one with six bedrooms and seven bathrooms. Listing images don’t show much of the interior, though certain shots reveal handsome moldings, beamed ceilings, arched doorways and fireplaces. A curved bridal staircase connects the levels. Massive windows also flood the space with sunlight throughout the day.
Upstairs, the primary suite has sitting areas, two bathrooms and massive closet space.
Outside, expansive stone terracing, a garden gazebo, a stone arbor and a pool house pavilion are enclosed by lush hedging.
It all dates to the 1930s, and stands behind secure entry gates.
“This is not merely a home; it is one of the finest land and lifestyle opportunities available on the Los Angeles market today,” the listing adds.
These are the shots that are very familiar to the millions of viewers who watched “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” from 1990 to 1996. The series boasted an impressive 148 episodes, andlaunched Will Smithinto international superstardom.
The property has a slew of princely neighbors, with some of the most prominent names in sports, politics and Hollywood surrounding it. A-listers have included “40-Year-Old Virgin” directorJudd Apatow, who lived next door for many years.
LeBron Jameshas a $23 million mansion in the neighborhood, while actor and former California GovernorArnold Schwarzeneggerhas lived in a sprawling multi-acre Brentwood compound for decades. “Star Wars” and “Indiana Jones” heroHarrison Fordis the longtime owner a private $12.6 million estate, and Oscar-winner and Goop founderGwyneth Paltrowhas a compound there.
They are in good company. As Smith sang at the show’s open, “Looked at my kingdom, I was finally there, to sit on my throne as the Prince of Bel-Air.”

hed: The best time to buy a home is almost here — with tons more listings to browse and thousands in savings
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
House hunters who spent the summer getting outbid or balking atsky-high pricesmay finally be getting their moment.
The best time to buy a home in 2026 is the week of Sept. 27 through Oct. 3, when buyers are expected to find a rare combination of lower prices, more homes to choose from and fewer rivals fighting over them, according to a newRealtor.com analysis.
And for buyers ready to make a move, the seasonal slowdown could translate into some serious savings.
A typical home shopper could save roughly $14,000 compared with this year’s summer price peak, based on a median-priced home of about $416,000.
But price isn’t the only advantage.
Buyers are expected to have 13.3% more active listings to choose from than during an average week — and nearly 32% more than they had at the beginning of the year.
At the same time, competition from other house hunters historically drops 30.1% from its annual peak during the best buying week.
That means buyers who spent the spring and summer racing to open houses and worrying about competing offers may have more room to take their time — and potentially negotiate.
Homes are expected to sit on the market for roughly 64 days during the sweet spot, about 13 days longer than during the year’s fastest-moving period.
That slower pace can give shoppers more time to inspect a property, weigh their options and potentially negotiate with sellers who have watched their homes linger on the market.
Price cuts are also more common around this point in the calendar. Historically, an average 5.7% of homes see their asking prices reduced during the best week.
So how should buyers take advantage?
For those whose biggest priority is having choices, the answer may be to start shopping sooner rather than later.
Fresh listings tend to be more plentiful earlier in the fall, meaning buyers with a long wish list — whether that’s a certain neighborhood, school district or number of bedrooms — are more likely to find a home that checks their boxes.
But bargain hunters willing to sacrifice some selection could benefit from waiting.
Prices typically continue to soften as the holidays approach, according to Realtor.com, potentially giving late-fall buyers an opportunity to squeeze out additional savings. The trade-off is that fewer new homes will be coming onto the market.
Either way, buyers may want to start preparing now by getting pre-approved, setting a firm budget and watching listings in their target neighborhoods so they can recognize a good deal when one appears.
There is one major wildcard:mortgage rates.
Unlike home prices and inventory, rates don’t follow a predictable seasonal pattern and weren’t included in Realtor.com’s calculation of the best buying week. A cheaper house doesn’t necessarily mean a cheaper monthly payment if borrowing costs move higher.
And the magic date isn’t the same everywhere.
Realtor.com analyzed the country’s 50 largest metro areas and found that 42 have their best buying week within a month of the national sweet spot.
For the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro, the best week arrived earlier, Sept. 6 through Sept. 12. Buyers there historically see 7.9% more listings than during an average week, 24.3% less competition than at the market’s peak and listing prices about 3.2% below their seasonal high.
Other buyers still have more time.
Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston, Philadelphia and Atlanta all share the national Sept. 27 to Oct. 3 sweet spot, while San Francisco’s best week arrives Oct. 11 to 17 and Phoenix’s falls Nov. 1 to 7.
And sun-seeking buyers can wait even longer:Miami and Tampadon’t reach their most favorable buying conditions until Nov. 29 through Dec. 5.
Ultimately, there isn’t one perfect day to snag a house.
Buyers looking for the widest selection may be better off moving earlier, while those focused squarely on price could gain leverage by waiting as inventory lingers and sellers become more motivated.
But for shoppers who have been waiting all year for the market to tilt a little more in their favor, their window is opening.

hed: Nazi-looted painting surfaced in a real estate listing must be returned to its rightful heirs, judge rules
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A stolen masterpiece that vanished during the darkest days of World War II has finally made its way home, and it tooka house-hunting websiteto crack the case wide open.
An Argentine federal judge signed off on the return of “Portrait of a Lady,” an 18th-century canvas by Italian baroque painter Giacomo Ceruti, known as Il Pitocchetto, to the heirs of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker.
The ruling brings a bizarre and decades-spanning saga to a close, one that involves fleeing Nazis, a shady South American hideout and, of all things, a real estate photo shoot gone wrong.
Goudstikker built one of Europe’s great private art collections, more than 1,100 pieces strong, before he was forced to flee the Netherlands in 1940 as German troops rolled in.
He died during the escape, and his gallery was systematically stripped by Nazi officials.
Among those officials was Friedrich Kadgien, a financial fixer who later slipped away to South America — as many Nazis did — and settled in Mar del Plata, Argentina, a resort town on the Atlantic coast.
That’s where his daughter, Patricia Kadgien, was living decades later when a real estate agency listed her house for sale online. Buried among the interior photos was an image of the living room, complete with a green couch and a painting hanging above it that had been on international missing art registries for 80 years.
A Dutch journalist chasing leads on the Goudstikker collection spotted the resemblance and eventually connected with attorney Yael Weitz at the New York firm Freedman Normand Friedland. Weitz brought the case to Argentine authorities, and police soon raided the Kadgien property, only to discover the painting, and the incriminating photo, had already been scrubbed from the listing.
Investigators didn’t come away empty-handed. They seized phones, unregistered guns and a stash of 1940s-era documents that helped build the case.
The painting is one of hundreds seized from the collection of Goudstikker, who assisted fellow Jews in escaping mainland Europe once the Nazis took control of the Netherlands. Roughly 800 works were snatched up by Hermann Goering, the Luftwaffe commander and one of the Third Reich’s most influential figures, according to the Telegraph.
Kadgien and her husband, Juan Carlos Cortegoso, were charged with concealment, but ultimately cut a deal, surrendering all claims to the painting and agreeing to donate roughly $3,200 to a Mar del Plata children’s hospital in exchange for having the criminal case against them suspended.
Attorney Juan Ignacio Pascual, who represents the Goudstikker heirs, called the outcome a watershed moment for a country with a complicated postwar history.
“As far as we know, this is the first time that the Argentine justice system has recovered and restituted a painting looted by the Nazis during the Second World War,” Pascual toldthe Art Newspaper.
The painting had long been misattributed to fellow Italian artist Giuseppe Ghislandi, but a court-ordered examination by Argentina’s National Academy of Fine Arts determined Ceruti was the true creator. The painting is valued at $288,000.
For Goudstikker’s family, the recovery is one small victory in a fight that has stretched across generations. More than 200 works from his collection were returned by the Dutch government back in 2006, but hundreds of other pieces remain scattered around the globe, their locations unknown.
Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s daughter-in-law and sole heir, said the ruling carries weight far beyond the canvas itself.
“I am thrilled with the court’s decision to restitute this important artwork,” von Saher told theNew York Times.

hed: NYC co-op in hot water over $30M parking lot sale after $16M in reserves allegedly vanishes
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A legal battle over an East Village co-op’s proposed$30-million parking lotsale is escalating, with a shareholder going to court to pry loose financial records as he questions a nearly $16 million plunge in the complex’s reserves.
Village View resident Sebastian Kot filed a books-and-records proceeding in Manhattan Supreme Court involving the seven-building Mitchell-Lama complex just south of Tompkins Square Park.
His petition alleges years of governance problems, including missing or inaccurate meeting minutes, conflicting financial disclosures and repeated refusals to provide corporate records.
“It’s an important step toward restoring transparency and lawful governance at Village View,” Kot told The Post. “The issues raised in the petition are all documented, statutory matters, and having them under judicial review ensures they can no longer be ignored or minimized.”
A Sept. 3 reserve collapse presentation delivered by the board of directors of Village View Housing Corp. shows the co-op’s reserves plummeted from $18.6 million in 2021 to $2.9 million in 2026, per a court exhibit. That has happened without explanation, per Kot.
Once Kot gets the documents, he said, “shareholders can evaluate next steps based on the facts.”
Attorneys for Village View’s board didn’t respond to a request for comment, but in a letter sent to residents, the board’s attorneys said the requested documents “are privileged and/or constitute confidential and sensitive corporate records,” per an exhibit.
Village View — sprawling between East Second and East Sixth streets and First Avenue and Avenue A — seeks to sell Parking Lot 7, adjacent to 40 First Ave., potentially netting about $30 million after taxes.
The goal of the sale, the board says in a presentation Kot filed with the court, is to get the development out of annual debt in recurring expenses, cover increasing expenses, contribute to the reserves and preserve the affordability of the 1,236 units.
Kot contends the parking-lot deal requires approval from two-thirds of Village View shareholders under New York’s Business Corporation Law and challenges whether the transaction can move forward without such a vote.
Village View’s land-use attorney, Jodi Stein, previously told The Post the irregular lot measures about 100 by 230 feet and contains roughly one-third of the complex’s 345 parking spots, representing a fraction of the property.
Helmed by Kot, hundreds of shareholders in June signed a petition seeking transparency around the proposed sale and redevelopment of the lot.
In early September, a morbidly obese disabled resident, Steven Andruseaski,sued Village View Housing Corp.over a new parking agreement he said would give the co-op the ability to oust him from his space in Parking Lot 7, next to his apartment.
That, he said, would in turn make it easier for the co-op to sell the lot to a developer and eventually eliminate its parking spaces.

hed: Botox and a brownstone? Boston-area real estate agents are hosting lavish open houses.
subhead: Realtors have offered everything from oyster shuckers, tarot card readers, and a full-blown holiday market in the spirit of getting feet in the doors of their listings
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Thinly sliced mortadella covered the dining room table at an open house for a penthouse condo in a modern, six-unit East Boston building.

After rolling out craft paper, Alexis Cervasio, owner ofEast Boston Oysters, draped about 10 pounds of the meat across the table. On top, she placed shells filled with bright green Castelvetrano olives. Her new thing is adding dollops of burrata and laying fresh baguettes diagonally. From a distance, the layout resembles a pale pink tablecloth.


“The host feels so good because the guests are saying, ‘Oh my God, this is the best showing we’ve ever been to,’” said Cervasio.

She was hired to turn a realtor’s open house into a curated event. During the COVID pandemic, agents couldn’t host open houses for about two years. That happened at the beginning of a cycle of volatility in the real estate market that continues to shift due to everything from wars and oil prices to elections and housing shortages.

“It’s been an uphill battle, at least on the sales side,” saidSarah Maguire, principal of the Aronson Maguire Group at Compass. “So we started to have to get very creative.”


Throughout Boston, real estate agents are getting savvier when it comes to getting potential buyers and their agents through the doors of open houses. But a free glass of cheap wine and a cheese board doesn’t pull the weight that it used to. As a result, agents are going to tremendous lengths to curate custom events that engage the community, attract unlikely guests, and satisfy builders who want to see a successful return on their investment.

Realizing that free beers and a gift certificate weren’t going to do the trick, Maguire’s team leaned into special events. To highlight a new build in Dorchester, it hiredRed Oysterto walk around the open house shucking oysters with pails of empty shells hanging from their matching aprons. The event was a hit.


“They were running around literally shoving oysters down people’s throats with all the accouterments,” said Maguire. “People loved it.”

For another listing that went up between Thanksgiving and Christmas, Maguire needed to drum up interest for three units in a Jamaica Plain development.

“It’s the absolute worst time to sell anything,” said Maguire. “We’re like, what the hell are we going to do? No one’s buying anything. Rates are through the roof.”

Maguire and her team came up with the idea of hosting a holiday market inside the development featuring local makers from Jamaica Plain, West Roxbury, and Roslindale. Vendors sold everything from knitted hats to homemade dog treats throughout the three units. Ultimately, the sale of the units set price records.


“Our sellers need to see that we’re trying to do everything we possibly can to get people through the door,” said Maguire, who has also hosted open houses featuring bouquet-making bars, Botox, a gelato stand, and a tarot card reader.

When the builder ofDiana Lannon’s listing told her they wanted the open house for a recently constructed $2.8 million home to be “something like the ones on ‘Million Dollar Listing,’” the popular Bravo real estate show, she knew she had her work cut out for her.

“The reason 100 people show up to an open house on ‘Million Dollar Listing’ is that they’re going to be on TV,” said Lannon, an agent with Gibson Sotheby’s Realty. “I needed to get the most attention on this property.”

But the $2.8 million listing was on the pricier side for Sudbury, and it was in the middle of January, when getting people to leave their homes is tough. Lannon knew she’d have to come up with an unusual idea to reel in attention from people in neighboring suburbs and the city. Knowing a new medspa was opening in town, she came up with the idea for a “Botox and Bubbles” event. She paid for the first few units of Botox and asked interested people — who were invited to the open house on Paperless Post invitations — to sign up ahead of time.

“People from the local area were going to come, but I needed people from the city,” Lannon said. “I needed agents who have higher-end buyers that are selling their $1.5 million or $2 million condo in the city, and want to come to the suburbs, but they want something brand new and luxury.”

There were a few negative reactions. Lannon even received a few “nasty” emails. But on the day of the event, attendees were greeted by champagne and a spread of food fromBaker’s Bestin Needham. The fireplace glowed, and music played in the background. The medspa was set up in the home office, so guests could get injections in privacy. For a broker open house that typically yields eight agents, around 40 people came through the door, including agents from nearby towns like Wellesley and Lexington.

“They never would have come if I didn’t do that,” she said.

So is investing the time — and significant money — in turning an open house into a custom event worth it?

“It depends on what it is that you’re trying to sell,” said Maguire. “What’s the product? What’s the price point? Where’s the location? Sometimes we have to do these things to appease our sellers. The potential commission that we’re making from it has to be enough for us to cover the cost. These things cost thousands of dollars. The risk has to be worth it.”

Megan Johnson is a Boston-based writer and reporter whose work appears in People, Architectural Digest, The Boston Globe, and more.

hed: Home search: A family of four toured three homes west of Boston. Here’s what they picked.
subhead: The criteria: Under $900,000, neighborhood with quiet streets and a welcoming community, plus a big backyard
content:
ByMadeline Bilis
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Ten years ago, Pamela Bathen, a broker associate withOak Realty in Ashland, helped her clients buy their first single-family home: a charming Cape in Shrewsbury. Though they’d spent the last decade renovating it, they approached Bathen again recently, this time for help finding a larger house.

The couple now had two boys, ages 3 and 6, plus two dogs. Add in sports equipment and one son’s newfound interest in piano, and they realized they’d outgrown their once perfect home. Next, the goal became finding a place with some of the things they loved about their current house — namely a close-knit neighborhood — and more square footage for everyone.

“They were really shoehorned into the home after they had kids. They had no garage, and one small addition that functioned as a dining room, storage area, mudroom, and entryway,” Bathen said. “It was just getting very crowded.”

One parent works in tech and commutes into Boston once or twice a week, while the other parent works in education.

With a budget cutoff of $900,000 they made their list of priorities:

The couple wasn’t afraid of cosmetic work, either. They’d successfully renovated their current home and knew they could do it again. That meant they could look past paint colors, old flooring, and dated kitchens to prioritize the location and other things they couldn’t change.

Here’s how their house hunt went.



$840,000

4 bedrooms

2.5 bathrooms

2,903 square feet

This home came on the market in a nearby Shrewsbury neighborhood, helping the clients envision what living in a larger home could be like. While excited at first glance, they realized this particular house, listed for $840,000, had several downsides, including a non-traditional floorplan; a large portion of the home’s square footage was taken up by a sunroom on the first floor. The house did, however, have things they liked: energy efficiency, central air conditioning, and a neighborhood they already loved.



$929,900

4 bedrooms

3.5 bathrooms

2,740 square feet

This $929,900 home in Shrewsbury stopped the buyers in their tracks. It was huge, and the photos were gorgeous. “They were anxious to see it,” Bathen said. But when they arrived to tour the place, the roar of traffic on Route 140 filled their ears. They hadn’t realized the house was on a corner so close to a busy road, not to mention it was positioned strangely on the lot. The front of the house faced some trees separating the yard from Route 140, while the garage-facing side faced the street. “It wasn’t really a neighborhood feel,” Bathen said.



$880,000

4 bedrooms

2.5 bathrooms

2,790 square feet

By this point in their house hunt, the couple knew they wouldn’t find a perfect fit. And this $880,000 home in Westborough certainly wasn’t perfect. It needed cosmetic updates like new flooring, and the kitchen was fairly small. Still, “the home was built beautifully and solidly,” Bathen explained. It also had all-electric heat, a holdover from when the house was built in the ‘70s. This meant each room had its own thermostat, which turned out to be fairly energy efficient. Best of all, the finished walkout basement had been updated with floor-to-ceiling windows, window benches, a fireplace, and space for a home office.



Though they had a few home projects in mind for it, the couple settled on the third option in Westborough, closing for $860,000.

“It’s a beautiful little cul-de-sac with the homes situated so there’s privacy, but neighbors definitely can see each other in the driveway, say hello, and get to know each other. They wanted that, too,” Bathen said. After moving in, their 6-year-old started kindergarten. Instead of taking the bus or hopping in a car, his parents walked him down a path beside their new cul-de-sac toward his new school. “They were just over the moon,” Bathen said.

Madeline Bilis is a freelance journalist and editor who covers real estate, travel, design, architecture, and New England lifestyle.

hed: Famed Jersey Shore pier lists for $85M in rare opportunity: ‘offers the chance to own the Atlantic itself’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Atlantic City’s famed Steel Pier is hitting the market for $85 million — offering the supremely rare chance to buy an operating amusement park perched overthe Atlantic Ocean, along with rights to build even farther out to sea.
The historic attraction, directly across the boardwalk from the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino, spans roughly 5.2 acres and is being listed byRyan Serhant, Michele Zyska, and Kevin Bergin of Serhant.
Today, the nearly 1,000-foot-long pier remains a classicJersey Shoreamusement park, with a towering Ferris wheel, rides, games and food — plus the unusual perk of a built-in helipad.
But beneath the carnival attractions is a unique piece of developable real estate.
The existing pier measures 150 feet wide and 965 feet long, while a perpetual riparian grant permits it to extend as far as 2,850 feet into the Atlantic.
“How often does someone get to own a piece of the ocean? That’s exactly what this offers,” Serhant said in a statement announcing the listing.
“The Steel Pier isn’t just 5 acres on the most famous boardwalk in the world, it actually offers the chance to own the Atlantic itself and build something unforgettable on top of it,” he added.
Speaking separately with The Post, Serhant called it “developable American history that extends straight into the Atlantic Ocean.”
And there is plenty of history.
Constructed in 1897 and opened in 1898, Steel Pier was once billed as the “Showplace of the Nation,” stretching nearly 2,300 feet at its historic peak. It has since appeared in films including “The Long Kiss Goodnight” and “The Bounty Hunter,” as well as television productions including “Cake Boss.”
The pier was rebuilt with steel-reinforced concrete in the late 1980s and is anchored roughly 90 feet into bedrock, remaining intact throughSuperstorm Sandy, according to listing materials.
For the Catanoso family, the sale would mark the end of a decades-long run at Steel Pier.
The longtime South Jersey amusement operators ran the attraction for nearly two decades before an ownership group including brothers Anthony, Charles and William Catanoso purchased it for $4.25 million in 2011.
But after 15 years as owners, succession has become an issue.
“The next generation is pursuing other passions,” Zyska told The Post. “So rather than keep it in the family, they’d rather see it go to an owner who can really realize its full potential.”
The $85 million asking price is 20 times the 2011 purchase price, though the owners have since made substantial capital improvements. Zyska said the property was appraised at $87 million last year.
“If this were in Palm Beach, it would be $400 million, and someone would have bought it already,” Serhant told The Post. “The fact that it’s even available and there’s an opportunity to purchase it, I just think is super, super special.”
Despite its long amusement history, Steel Pier doesn’t necessarily have to remain an amusement park.
The approximately 40,000-square-foot front building and sky bridge carry an easement into the neighboring Hard Rock’s convention floor, while the existing pier footprint could potentially be expanded by 25%.
The property was approved and permitted for a condo-hotel entertainment complex in 2008 — a concept Serhant said would be his first choice if he were developing it.
“Executing on a condo-hotel plan would probably be my first plan,” he told The Post. “You have the rare ability to build out over the ocean itself.”
He said the brokerage has already had “soft conversations with a handful” of potential players and sees an opportunity for the kind of branded hospitality and residential projects proliferating elsewhere.
“If you’re a high-end, high-net-worth hospitality builder, I think Atlantic City is incredible value,” Serhant said.
Zyska said other possibilities include music and entertainment uses.
“If it lands in the right hands, it can really transform the boardwalk, and even that stretch of the Atlantic,” she told The Post. “It’s really a premier opportunity.”
The listing comes as Atlantic City undergoes another wave of development, with new residential projects from Kushner Companies, K. Hovnanian Homes and other developers rising around the resort town.

hed: Gillette buys back parking lots for nearly $20 million more than its 2021 sale price
content: Five years ago, amid a regional life sciences laboratory boom, Gillette’s parent company shaved off a slice of parking lots directly next to its longtime World Shaving Headquarters in Fort Point, and sold it to a lab developer. Now P&G Gillette has bought the land back — for nearly $20 million more than its 2021 sales price. Cincinnati-based consumer products giant Procter & Gamble, Gillette’s parent, has re-purchased 232 A St. for $99.3 million and now plans to use the property as part of its $1 billion overhaul of the razor maker’s home campus. Life sciences real estate developer Breakthrough Properties bought the 2.4-acre swath of parking lots in 2021 for $80 million, and later secured city approval to build a 325,000-square-foot research and development lab and 1.2-acre waterfront park there. The 24 percent value swing in the past five years — a period where the region has grappled with a glut of lab vacancy — reflects both Gillette’s future development goals and the value that comes with city permits to build a 150-foot-tall commercial building there.Now, instead of lab space, that building will serve as Gillette’s headquarters.“As we planned for the next chapter of our longstanding campus, it was a priority to find a location that would allow us to transform our operations and continue our deep commitment to this neighborhood,” said Kara Buckley, vice president of community affairs for P&G Gillette, in a statement. “232 A Street is an ideal fit — honoring our heritage, providing the perfect space to build the cutting-edge capabilities we need for the future and positioning us at the heart of this special community for generations to come.” The Boston Planning and Development Agency board in 2024 approved Breakthrough’s proposed lab project, including 125 underground parking spaces and a public park facing Fort Point Channel. Gillette is planning a large-scale redevelopment of its longtime home along Fort Point Channel and recently bought back a slice of previously sold parking lots.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffAs part of an effort to mitigate future flooding damage, Breakthrough committed to building a vegetated “resiliency berm” that would help manage stormwater and “serve as elevated flood protection from the Fort Point Channel . . . and contribute to flood protection in the immediate area and larger South Boston neighborhood.” The new Gillette facility “will incorporate new green spaces, sidewalks, bike lanes and Harborwalk improvements,” according to a press release. Though the sale closed at the end of July, according to Breakthrough Properties spokesperson Bud Perrone, it does not yet appear to be recorded in Suffolk County property records. Breakthrough is a joint venture of Bellco Capital and developer Tishman Speyer.“Gillette’s commitment — a major, long-term investment in Boston — is further testament to the city’s enduring appeal as a hub for innovation and economic development,” said Jessica Hughes, the managing director for Tishman Speyer in Boston, in a statement.Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Historic NYC synagogue and longtime home for pioneering artists asks $11M — with stunning architectural details intact
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about divine inspiration.
A former Lower East Side synagogue that later became a creative haven for generations of New York artists has hit the market for $10.95 million.
The roughly 6,800-square-foot building at 80 Forsyth St. has served as the studio of fiber artist Dana Barnes since 2013 — but its artistic pedigree stretches back decades, with traces of its religious and creative past still embedded throughout the three-story property.
Before Barnes moved in, the building was the longtime home and studio of Abstract Expressionist artists Milton Resnick and Pat Passlof, who took over the space in the 1960s.
And before the artists came, there were worshippers.
The 25-foot-wide brick building was originally erected as a synagogue in the 19th century for an early Eastern European Jewish congregation in the neighborhood, according to the sellers.
Remnants of that chapter remain throughout the property — including a former mikvah, or a Jewish ritual bath, on the lower level, along with pointed arch window forms dating to its synagogue days.
The building’s evolution from a house of worship into an artist enclave began during a transformative period for the Lower East Side, when artists were increasingly moving into the neighborhood’s former industrial, commercial and religious spaces.
Resnick, a Russian-born painter who became associated with the Abstract Expressionist movement in New York, and Passlof, an American painter who studied with Willem de Kooning, made 80 Forsyth their home and workspace.
The pair transformed portions of the old synagogue to suit their work while retaining much of the original structure.
Some of those changes are still there more than half a century later.
Hand-built pine walls installed by the two remain, as does an upper gallery mezzanine dating to the 1960s. Original casement windows, cast-iron columns, skylights, and wood and concrete floors also survive.
In places, the floors are still splattered with paint from the artists who worked there before Barnes — evidence of the building’s creative history that the current owners deliberately chose not to remove.
Barnes, a former fashion designer known for large-scale fiber sculptures and wall hangings, and her husband, private investor Dale Westhoff, purchased the property for $6.4 million in 2013.
Rather than scrubbing away its past during their ownership, the couple preserved much of what previous generations left behind.
Barnes has since used virtually the entire building as her studio, filling the expansive rooms with coiled, knotted and woven textile works that range from sprawling floor pieces to towering sculptural installations.
The setting gives her plenty of room to work.
Ceilings rise to more than 18 feet in portions of the property, while large windows and skylights bring natural light into the studio spaces.
The building also comes with two vintage kitchens, 2.5f bathrooms, laundry and storage areas, and two woodburning fireplaces.
A bedroom-office area occupies the top floor, while the upper levels look out over Sara D. Roosevelt Park, the nearly eight-block green space stretching along the eastern side of Forsyth Street.
There are also about 225 square feet of fenced outdoor space at the rear of the property.
Despite its unconventional history, the building isn’t frozen in time — and its next owner could take it in an entirely new direction.
The sale includes approximately 10,000 square feet of additional air rights, according to the listing, potentially giving a buyer substantially more room to work with than what currently stands on the site.
The building and its block are also not landmarked, according to the listing, opening up possibilities for alterations or future development, subject to city approvals and zoning requirements.
That means a buyer could preserve the unusual live-work setup that has defined the property for decades — or explore something altogether different.
The property is being marketed for uses ranging from another private residence and artist’s studio to a gallery, foundation or other creative space.
Its combination of scale and history makes it particularly unusual in a Lower East Side that has changed dramatically since Resnick and Passlof first began working there in the 1960s.
Today, the surrounding blocks are packed with new residential developments, galleries, restaurants and nightlife, while 80 Forsyth still bears the physical fingerprints of several very different eras of downtown New York.
For Barnes, the building became the latest chapter in that lineage.
Her works have been shown in galleries and exhibitions in the US and abroad, and the artist increasingly divides her practice between New York and Amsterdam.
That shift is now prompting Barnes and Westhoff to part with the Forsyth Street property after more than a decade of ownership.
Jonathan Hettinger, Mark Amadei and Megan Hait of Sotheby’s International Realty hold the listing.

hed: Wealthy ‘Roblox’ widow bought $16M love nest for escort who allegedly scammed her
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A grieving widow sitting on a “Roblox” fortune recently shelled out nearly $16 million on one of Manhattan’s grandest mansions to build a life with the male escort she claims laterfleeced her for millions, property records reviewed by The Post show.
Marianne Flippo, 49, closed on the landmarked house in Kips Bay on April 30, plunking down $15.9 million for the Gilded Age Beaux-Arts showpiece mere months before accusing her companion Gregg Starr, 38, of draining her bank accounts.
The 1903 mansion, built for banker James F.D. Lanier and his socialite wife Harriet, spans six stories and 11,638 square feet with 12 bedrooms and nine-plus bathrooms, a wine cellar, an oak-paneled elevator, and a wellness floor complete with a cold plunge pool and a cedar sauna.
The property initially hit the market in 2023 for a whopping $29.2 million. It last listed for $16.5 million before closing at a slight discount, property records show.
Flippo’s attorney Larry Hutcher confirmed to The Post that the purchase was not a solo indulgence.
“She bought that house because she thought it was a beautiful property,” Hutcher said. “She thought it would be a nice home for them to live in.”
The mansion buy landed squarely inside the same window Flippo now says Starr and an escort agency handler were pressuring her to fork over millions more under a bogus “buyout” scheme, according to her Manhattan Supreme Court filing.
Hutcher added that despite splurging on the Murray Hill trophy home, Flippo — whose husband, Chad, died by suicide in 2024 — hadn’t fully relocated her life to the city.
“She still does live in New Hampshire as well,” he said.
Property records paint a portrait of a woman who restructured her entire geography around a man she’d met barely a year earlier. Flippo had spent decades in New England, with a documented address in Walpole, New Hampshire dating back to the late 1990s, before Starr moved into her New York apartment last December, according to the lawsuit.
The relationship began innocently enough in December 2024, when Flippo — who suffers from a rare genetic condition — needed an Italian-speaking companion for a trip to Italy. She was steered toward Cowboys 4 Angels — an agency she says she believed offered personal assistants, not paid companionship. She didn’t realize the outfit was actually a male escort service until well into their entanglement, the suit claims.
By this spring, prosecutors’ version of events and Flippo’s lawsuit allege, Starr and the agency were pressuring the medically fragile widow, plied with alcohol and recovering from surgery, into signing a $10 million “Exit Agreement” so he could supposedly buy his way out of his contract with the agency.
She wired $5.95 million into a joint Charles Schwab account before Starr allegedly moved most of it into an account under his sole control and threatened to disappear with the cash. According to her own court filings, it ended with her bank balance reduced to just $12.61.
The Lanier House itself is no ordinary address. Designed by architects Hoppin and Koen, the same firm behind the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Presidential Library, the mansion was commissioned for a couple who ranked among the exclusive 400 guests said to fit inside the Astor family’s Fifth Avenue ballroom.
It is both a New York City landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, with only two owners in its 120-plus year history before this sale.
Other features of the home include a fitness room,  and an oak-paneled library.
Monthly carrying costs on the property run north of six figures, with property taxes alone estimated at roughly $14,000 a month, according to listing data.

hed: Inside Lena Dunham’s London ‘Home Base’ and Connecticut ‘Forever Home’ as ‘Girls’ creator welcomes first child
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.
Writer and director Lena Dunham has welcomed her first child with husband Luis Felber—five years after leaving Los Angeles behind for a new life in London.
The “Girls” creator, 40, revealed in an op-ed for Vogue that she and Felber hadwelcomed a daughter via surrogate, sharing intimate details about the moment she became a mother.
Despite having traded the palm trees of Los Angeles for the bustle of London, Dunham revealedthat she and Felbertemporarily relocated to New York City ahead of the birth, staying in an Airbnb close to their surrogate.
“13 days late, in the face of a solar eclipse and a meteor shower, she announced herself. I sat on a hospital bed, between the legs of a woman I hadn’t known a year ago, waiting for a glimpse of this person who I had been waiting for with something related to patience, but also none at all,” Dunham penned of her daughter’s arrival.
She added, “I saw her face, gasping just as she did. Her eyes, wide and unfocused, taking in the light and shadow, blinking rapidly.”
Dunham described her first moments with her daughter as leaving her “bashful and dizzy with joy.”
“’Hello,’ I said, ‘I’m your mama. You look nothing like I thought you would, but exactly right. We’ve been waiting for you, do you know that? It was so nice of you to come,’” she recalled.
But the joyous milestone wasn’t without some logistical difficulties—particularly when it came to the couple’s temporary living situation.
Dunham admitted thatshe and Felber had failed to extend their Airbnb reservation because they hadn’t anticipated their daughter arriving nearly two weeks after her due date.
“It had occurred to me she might come early, but it had never occurred to me she would come late. Our Airbnb in a state not our own, just down the road from where our surrogate lives, ran out, and we hadn’t bothered to check if it was booked for the next two weeks (it was, by frat boys on vacation). As we passed her due date, the days became liquid and squishy, too long and without any form,” she explained.
Although Dunham and Felber, who tied the knot in 2021, largely kept their surrogacy journey private, the filmmaker has previously spoken candidly about her desire to become a mother and expand their family.
“It was a grief but it was also a relief. I thought I would have the opportunity to experience my fertility and my cycle waning and it never was,” Dunham told The Times following her 2025 hysterectomy.
“Instead it was a very quick, sharp cut-off… I will say we’re in the process of expanding our family in new ways. I want to safely meet our children and then figure out how to talk about it,” she added.
The arrival of their daughter marks another major chapter for the couple five years after Dunham left Los Angeles and sold her primary home there in favor of a life across the Atlantic.
After relocating, Dunham and Felber snapped up a four-story townhouse in North London, which has served as their primary residence and what Dunham has described as both a “home base” and “creative escape.”
The eclectic property is filled with bold design choices, including various shades of green and pink that reflect Dunham’s colorful aesthetic.
Dunham has previously opened up about how moving to London offered her a fresh start.
“London shocked me with its reassuring differences—streets so wide that the buildings seemed to be stepping aside for me to pass, the blank slate of it all,” she said.

The house was built during the COVID-19 pandemic and has memorably been described as looking as though “a kindergartener drew a house.”

Dunham later explaining that the finished home demonstrated just how well her mother understood her.“[It was] showing me just how well [mum] knew me. I felt a shocking amount of gratitude to have these parents and this home,” she said.

hed: More than 1 in 5 NYC homes are selling in bidding wars — with prime Brooklyn nabe at the center of the frenzy
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Bidding wars are back in New York City  — and Brooklyn is ground zero.
Higher mortgage rateswere supposed to cool the housing market. In the Big Apple, something very different is happening.
Despite average 30-year rates sitting at roughly 6.7% in August, 21.8% of NYC homes sold for more than their asking price, according to a new market report fromStreetEasy.
The month before was even more wild, with 25% of sales closing above ask in July, the highest share the city has seen since 2022.
Fueling the frenzy is ashrinking supply of listings,with total inventory down 5% year-over-year citywide and Manhattan alone seeing an 11.2% drop.
A recent draft from the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development estimated that New York would needa whopping 700,000 new housing unitsover the next 10 years just to keep up with demand.
For Frances Katzen at Douglas Elliman, the figures confirm what she’s already telling clients on the ground. Rate headlines and actual buyer behavior, she said, are two very different stories right now.
“The biggest thing I’m telling sellers right now is, don’t confuse higher interest rates with a weak market. They’re not the same thing.”
“I would much rather launch into a market where inventory is constrained, even with higher mortgage rates, than wait for rates to come down and suddenly find myself competing against five other sellers who had exactly the same idea,” Katzen said in a statement.
Brooklyn is where that scarcity is most visible. Nearly a third of homes in the borough sold above ask, and in Park Slope the number jumped to three in five sales closing over asking price.
Greenwich Village saw an even sharper spike, with 40% of homes selling above ask.
Brooklyn properties are also moving the fastest anywhere in the city, spending a median of just 69 days on the market in August, six days quicker than a year earlier, while the citywide median sits at 77 days to contract.
Sellers appear to be leaning into the imbalance rather than fighting it. Instead of pushing prices as high as the market might bear, many are setting asks a notch lower to spark competing offers and let bidding wars do the heavy lifting.
The tactic shows up in the data too, with the citywide median asking price slipping 2% to $980,000 even as sale prices climb past that mark.

hed: Is fall a good time to buy and sell houses in Greater Boston?
subhead: Spring and fall tend do be real estate’s high seasons — what exactly does that mean for local buyers and sellers?
content:
ByRobyn A. Friedman
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Spring may be the traditional home buying and selling season in many markets across the country, but it probably doesn’t come as a surprise that the real estate market in Greater Boston is slightly more nuanced. After all,Sept. 1 is the official move-in dayfor renters as the vast majority of leases turn over on that day.

But what aboutbuying or selling a home? Some studies, such asa Zillow analysis of 2025 home sales, have found that homes sell for 3.4 percent more in Greater Boston in late May — a $25,300 boost on average. But local real estate professionals say that it’s actually the fall that may yield better results for both buyers and sellers.

“During COVID, timing didn’t matter; everyone was buying because the interest rates were so low,” saidMelvin A. Vieira Jr., a real estate agent with ReMax Real Estate Center in Boston. “But we have shifted, and now we are moving toward two seasons for buying in Greater Boston — the spring and the fall.”

Of course, buyers who need a new home because of a job relocation or birth of a child shouldn’t try to time the market, nor should sellers who need to move. The median expected tenure in a home is now 15 years, according to the2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellersreleased in November 2025 by theNational Association of Realtors, and the transaction costs for buying or selling are high, so buying or selling decisions should be made with care.

But local statistics do show patterns that should be of interest tobuyers and sellers in Greater Boston.

According to theMassachusetts Association of Realtors(MAR), the median sales price of a single-family home in Greater Boston hit its lowest point of 2025 during December, when the median was $875,000. In September ($880,000) and October ($905,000), median sales prices were slightly higher. It’s important to note, however, that these are closed values and that the actual prices of these homes were locked in about two months earlier when the parties signed a sales contract. So, the lowest median sales price in December 2025 actually reflects single-family home prices negotiated in October, during the fall. That means that buyers may be able to get their best deal during the fall months.

Chuck Silverston, senior vice president ofGibson Sotheby’s International Realty in Brookline, said one of his favorite times of the year for buyers is the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Few people list their homes that week, he said, so any available properties were probably listed months earlier.

“Sellers will be motivated,” he said. “So, buyer deals are more likely.”

For sellers, however, Silverston said that their decision to list “depends first on what their needs and goals are.” He noted that some Greater Boston neighborhoods see their heaviest listing activity immediately after Labor Day, so sellers planning to list need to price their homes correctly due to the competition.

“This market is much less forgiving of aspirational pricing than it was before,” he said. “That means that sellers have to get the pricing right and not overprice.”

According to MAR, the highest median sales price for a single-family home in Greater Boston in 2025 occurred in June, when the median was $1,007,000. Remember, however, that the sales price for that month was locked in during April — in the spring, when the sales contracts were executed. So, while September may be best for buyers seeking the best deals, sellers in Greater Boston may want to stick with the traditional advice of listing in the spring, especially if they want to shoot for the highest sales price.

The dynamics of the local submarket are key to choosing the best time to buy or sell. “You can be in a strong sellers’ market in one neighborhood and then drive 10 minutes and find a strong buyers’ market, so it’s varied here,” said Silverston.

Robyn A. Friedman is an award-winning freelance writer who covers real estate, homeownership, and personal finance.

hed: Before falling in love on a home tour, watch out for these 5 red flags
subhead: Here are a few things to keep an eye on when touring a prospective property
content:
ByRobyn A. Friedman
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Imagine this. A house wasstaged to perfection— flowers in the beds, the aroma of fresh bread in the air, and the furniture arranged to show off how spacious the rooms were. It presented so well that buyers missed the smell of mildew in the basement and the cracks in the wall. By the time their home inspector informed them that these are signs of significant problems, the buyers had fallen in love with the home and decided to buy it anyway.

It’s not an unheard of scenario.

Home inspectionsgive buyers a professional, objective opinion about the condition of a house. But, by the time the inspection is done, many buyers have already emotionally connected to the property — and overlooked its flaws. In a competitive market, where there might bemultiple buyers biddingon every house, it can be difficult to let go no matter what the inspection discloses.

That’s why buyers need to keep their eyes wide open from the first time they step into any house they’re considering.

“There are always issues that come up when buyers walk through a house,” saidErin Freeman, a real estate agent withGibson Sotheby’s International Realty in Hingham. “It’s common to encounter things that should give buyers pause, to make them dig in to see what’s behind them.”

AFebruary 2026 survey by Zillowfound that 75 percent of those who successfully purchased a home in the past two years have at least one regret. The top regret: About one-third of buyers said the home needs more work or maintenance than they expected.

So, what are these red flags that should cause buyers to think twice about whether they even want to make an offer?


These include actual signs of water intrusion as well as ceilings that have been recently repainted. “Water is the scariest thing to me,” said Freeman. “It could be damage from an air handler, a leaky roof, or bad plumbing.” And, once there’s water damage, there’s also the possibility of mold or structural damage.

Alex Steinberg, owner and president ofJBS Home Inspectionsin Watertown, said that buyers should be wary of houses in low-lying areas, especially if you see a sump pump in the basement. “Water management is critical,” he said. “If a house looks wet, feels wet, or seems like the water isn’t draining off properly, that’s something that could require a lot of work right off the bat.”


Settlement cracks are common, especially in older homes. But when they are wide — greater than 1/8th to a quarter inch — horizontal, or are around windows or doors, this can be a sign of a serious issue. “Foundation cracks don’t necessarily mean that you should run away from the house,” said Steinberg. “But they can be a sign of a big structural issue that can be really expensive to repair.”


If you smell mold, mildew, or feces, that could be a huge red flag. Steinberg said that cigarette smells can also be an issue because they leach into the walls and can be difficult to remove.

“If people use air fresheners or light candles before a showing, it sets a lovely mood, but it always makes me wonder what they’re covering up,” said Freeman.


If it’s obvious the roof is old and or that the heating system is in poor repair, this should put you on notice that you may have to invest a big chunk of money right off the bat for repair or replacement of major systems in the house. That increases your purchase price right from the start.


“Termites are hard to pick up [on] unless you know what you’re looking for, but you can definitely see mice or mice feces, and that would be a red flag depending on where the house is,” said Steinberg. Houses in the suburbs are more prone to mice, so they’re less of an issue, he said. But if your home is in downtown Boston, mice should give you pause.

So, what happens if you encounter one of these red flags when you first tour a house? At what point should you walk away?

“It’s up to the buyer and their comfort level,” said real estate attorneyNikolaos (“Nik”) Ligris, co-managing partner ofLigris & Associatesin Newton Centre. Two factors matter: How much of “a stomach” a buyer has for undertaking risk and the possible severity of the issue. Issues that would impact the buyer’s ability to get a mortgage or insurance, such as knob and tube wiring, which is still found in many older homes in New England, would be severe enough for a buyer to walk away from the deal, he said.

Of course, abuyer’s decisionalso depends on the status of the local market and how badly they want that home. It all depends on the facts and circumstances of each deal.

Anything is fixable, Steinberg said. It just boils down to how much risk you are willing to undertake and whether you want a turnkey home you can move right into or have an appetite for repairs or renovations.
