hed: A private island in Maine can be yours for a bargain $450K
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Aprivate islandin Maine has hit the market for $450,000 — offering buyers an entire secluded escape for less than the price of many New York City apartments.
The Moosehead Lake escape comes with a renovated cabin and spectacular sunsets — but buyers will need to bring their own dock, as well as a boat to keep it company.
Located in Lily Bay, the pint-sized island come with a one-bedroom, one-bathroom cabin surrounded by water, towering pine trees and mountain views.
The 660-square-foot retreat has been renovated from the studs in 2022, according to the listing, giving therustic Maine campa modern update while preserving its woodsy character.
Inside, an open-concept living area features warm wood finishes, large windows overlooking the lake and a stone accent wall anchored by a wood-burning stove.
The adjoining kitchen has an island of its own — fittingly — along with wood cabinetry, open shelving and stainless-steel appliances.
The cabin’s bathroom also received a polished update, with a glass-enclosed walk-in shower finished with tile and a pebble-stone floor that nods to the natural landscape outside.
Despite its off-grid setting, the well-insulated home isn’t entirely roughing it. The property is equipped with generator power, water drawn from the lake, and both Rinnai and wood heat.
The roughly 0.1-acre parcel also boasts about 200 feet of waterfront, according to property listings.
Still, reaching the hideaway requires a little more planning than hailing a cab: The listing notes that a new dock will be needed for seasonal access and use.
Moosehead Lake, in northwestern Maine, is the state’s largest lake and the largest lake located entirely within New England. The sprawling body of water is known for boating, fishing and wildlife — including, true to its name, moose sightings.
The property’s annual tax bill was just over $562 for 2025, records show, and there isno homeowners association.
Nicole Hilton of The Folsom Realty Group holds the listing.

hed: Jersey City Loew’s Wonder Theater to reopen following a $130M renovation — and decades of neglect
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
There was a time when, instead of audience members in the Loew’s Jersey Theatre, there were only pigeons nesting in the rafters.
Now, after 40 years of neglect and at least one potential brush with a bulldozer, Jersey City’s grandest roomis roaring back.
The 1929 movie palace at Journal Square reopens Nov. 13 with a Trey Anastasio Band show, followed a night later by The War on Drugs, marking the finish line on a two-year, $130 million restoration and the start of what its operators hope is a permanent second act.
“This reopening represents far more than the return of a historic building, it’s the revival of a landmark that has inspired generations,” Bruce Wheeler, general manager of Loew’s Jersey Theatre, said. “This marks the beginning of a new era for live entertainment in Jersey City and the entire metropolitan region.”
The building has earned the reputation.
Designed by Rapp and Rapp, the Chicago firm behindhundreds of American movie houses,the Loew’s Jersey opened its doors on Sept. 28, 1929, just weeks before the stock market cratered.
It was built as one of five so-called “Wonder Theatres” that Loew’s Corporation scattered across the New York area — including theUnited Palacein Washington Heights — and the only one of the five constructed outside the five boroughs.
Architect George Rapp reportedly described the philosophy behind the gilded, over-the-top palaces this way: “opulence unbound, but opulence with a purpose.”
The idea was to make a factory worker feel like a duke for the price of a movie ticket. A three-story lobby rotunda, a Baroque Rococo facade dripping in terra cotta and a 3,021-seat Italian Renaissance-style auditorium made good on that promise, and the venue went on to host acts ranging from Duke Ellington to The Four Seasons.
But the postwar suburban exodus and the rise of the multiplex hollowed the place out. It was chopped into a triplex in 1974, went dark in 1986 and spent years staring down a wrecking ball, That was all before Jersey City bought the building and a nonprofit called Friends of the Loew’s launched a volunteer-driven rescue.
Even that effort could only do so much heavy lifting, and the theater limped along for decades on borrowed time.
“There were some spot usages of the theater 10, 12, 15 years ago. Some music videos were shot, some concerts and book signings were done,” Wheeler told The Post, adding that for the most part the last 40 years amounted to an empty, abandoned building.
The turnaround came in 2023 when Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment stepped in, teaming with the city, the Jersey City Redevelopment Agency, and the New Jersey Economic Development Authority to fund and execute a full-scale rebuild. Asked why now, after decades of false starts, Wheeler kept it simple.
“It’s … that the city really felt that making an investment and bringing this building back, again, to a state-of-the-art facility was a way to anchor the Journal Square neighborhood,” Wheeler said.
“And just as Jersey City and others have made investment and reinvestment in other areas of the city,  it seemed like it was the time for Journal Square. And the mayor’s office and pretty much all the government entities are very excited about the theater coming back online.”
None of it came easy. Renovating a 97-year-old building meant confronting problems that no blueprint could predict.
Wheeler said, “When the general contractor first went in, there were things that went smoothly and according to plan. There were also likely some areas where they had to take a step back and rethink. But at the end of the day, it all seems like it’s in a great lane now, and we’re getting ourselves prepared to open up in November.”
Sean Saadeh, who’s overseeing booking strategy for the venue, said the reaction to Monday’s lineup announcement has already exceeded expectations, even with tickets not yet on sale.
“The response have been really, really positive,” Saadeh told The Post. “People are super excited about the property because it’s such a beautiful theater and it’s in an incredibly important spot in Jersey City, so a lot of people that have had history with the theater are super excited to see it really come back to life in its full use.”
That’s all after years of painstaking work.
The restoration team chased period accuracy down to the paint chip.
“The restoration is down to matching the colors, the original colors and the original flow of the theater,” Wheeler said. “There’s really not that many properties out there that we can point to that will not only bring in that more classic feel, but really be state-of-the-art with respect to its audio and lighting, and really the patron and the fan experience really is going to be second to none when you combine those two elements together.”
The venue was also engineered for flexibility that few historic theaters can match. Fully seated, capacity tops out around 2,700, but pulling the orchestra-level seats opens the room up to 4,000, giving promoters room to scale a show up or down depending on the act.
“That’s something that is a bit of a rarity in the market and gives artists and agents and managers the flexibility to be able to scale their show accordingly,” Wheeler said.
Location doesn’t hurt either. The theater sits directly across from the Journal Square PATH station, putting Midtown and the World Trade Center each roughly 10 to 20 minutes away.
Tickets to the opening weekend shows go on sale Friday at 10 a.m. via Ticketmaster and LoewsJersey.com, alongside a lineup that also includes Jodeci, Derek Hough, Jeff Dunham, and a World of Warcraft concert next May.

hed: Gen Zers are fleeing NYC faster than any other US metro — flocking to a city just 90 miles away
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York may still be the city where young people come to make it — but a growing number of Gen Zers are making their exit.
The Big Apple lost more members of Gen Z than any other US metro in 2024, posting a net outflow of 29,554 young adults, according to a newRedfin analysisof Census Bureau data.
And many aren’t venturing far.
A whopping 9,284 Gen Zers traded the New York metropolitan area for Philadelphiajust 90 miles south, making it the country’s second-most-popular migration route for the generation, behind only trading Los Angeles for nearby  Riverside, California.
The move comes with a considerable housing discount. The typical home in the New York metro sells for about $832,000, compared with just $309,000 in Philadelphia, according to Redfin.
That means buyers heading to Philly could theoretically purchase nearly three homes for the price of one in New York.
The migration pattern suggests young Americans aren’t necessarily cutting ties with their existing regions as they hunt for less expensive housing and better job prospects.
Instead, many are making relatively short moves that allow them to remain within reach of family, friends and professional networks.
“Younger adults are gravitating toward cities where they can launch careers and their social lives, while millennials are more focused on places where a paycheck stretches further and buying a home is attainable,” Redfin principal economist Sheharyar Bokhari said in the report.
“But young Americans aren’t fleeing expensive cities for the cheapest place they can find: Most are making relatively short moves, suggesting they want a better job or lower cost of living without giving up their existing networks.”
The most common Gen Z move was from Los Angelesto Riverside, with 10,261 people making the roughly 60-mile shift. The New York-to-Philadelphia route came next, followed by Los Angeles to San Diego, which attracted 9,237 movers.
New York also experienced the largest millennial exodus of any metro, recording a net loss of 42,698 members of the generation. Los Angeles followed with a net millennial outflow of 31,107, whileMiami lost21,373.
But Gen Zers and millennials appear to be chasing different versions of the American dream.
“Gen Zers are chasing opportunity, while millennials are chasing space,” Bokhari said.
Millennials favored metros where larger homes remain relatively attainable.
Houston led the pack with a net millennial inflow of 16,365, followed by Dallas, Baltimore, Las Vegas and Atlanta. All five metros had median home-sale prices below $450,000.
The analysis used the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey. It defined adult Gen Zers as those ages 19 to 27 and millennials as those ages 28 to 43.

hed: UES residents fume nearby homeless shelter quietly kept operating despite city order to shut down
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A luxury Upper East Side hotel has spent years serving as aquiet homeless shelter,and neighbors say the city cut them out of the loop entirely.
The Bentley Hotel,a 21-story tower at 500 E. 62nd St. where rooms once fetched more than $200 a night, is housing 197 people under a taxpayer-funded contract, according to Highland Park Community Development Corporation, the Brooklyn nonprofit running the operation,Upper East Sitefirst reported.
It is not the building’s first rodeo as a shelter. Thehotel took in homeless New Yorkersdisplaced from crowded congregate shelters back in May 2020, part of the city’s pandemic-era push to spread people out and slow the spread of COVID-19 inside dorm-style facilities.
The Bentley resurfaced as a shelter in 2023, this time designated a Humanitarian Emergency Response and Relief Center for asylum seekers arrivingamid the migrant crisis, with Highland Park landing a $32 million contract to run it, Upper East Site reported.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered the city’s last remaining HERRC, in The Bronx, be shuttered by the end of this year. Yet the Bentley never closed. It simply got a new label.
Highland Park’s marketing materials now brand the property a “Tier 2 family shelter” called “Yorkville Sanctuary,” even though the building sits in Lenox Hill, not Yorkville. The pitch promises to helpresidents land on their feet.
“A Tier 2 family shelter, providing a safe and secure environment to families,” the materials read, according to Upper East Site. “The goal of the program is to assist the families in locating affordable housing.”
This has theUpper East Side localsfuming. The Department of Homeless Services has a track record of alerting Community Board 8 when new shelters open nearby, notifying the board about a 92-bed site on East 91st Street and a 200-bed high-rise on First Avenue. The Bentley got no such heads up, Upper East Site found.
Tyler Hollinger, owner of Festivál Café on Second Avenue and a founding member of the East Side Accountability Alliance, said the building’s status was never exactly a mystery to those paying attention.
“We always knew that it was a shelter,” Hollinger told Upper East Site.
He argues the silence from officials fits a pattern.
“It’s very clear that the community board and the government doesn’t really care what the people think, and they’re just going to do whatever they want,” Hollinger said.
Richard Barcia, who lives on East 62nd Street, said he has no beef with the people staying there, just with the city dodging basic disclosure.
“I don’t have anything against these people — I know they need a place to live,” Barcia told the outlet.
He wants the city to come clean rather than let residents piece it together themselves.
“Why don’t they just put that out as a press release and just acknowledge what’s going on?” Barcia said.
Michael Bailey, a member of the East Side Accountability Alliance, accused the city of stonewalling.
“It seems like they’re intentionally misleading us,” Bailey told Upper East Site.
A Department of Social Services spokesperson confirmed migrant-specific shelters have been phased out citywide but would not say what the Bentley is currently being used for, citing confidentiality rules around shelter addresses. The agency stopped short of denying the building is operating as a shelter, and did not answer follow-up questions about the terms of its contract with the hotel or what happened to people who were living there when the migrant program wound down.
Highland Park CDC and the Bentley Hotel did not respond to requests for comment.

hed: ‘You cannot do real estate without marketing yourself’: This Newton agent is also an influencer
content: NEWTON — At Moments Cafe, a sleek new Newton coffee shop, Newton Mayor Marc Laredo posed for a picture between owners Tai Huynh and Phuong Nguyen. In front of them, Katherine Kranenburg lifted her pointer finger. Taking two steps back, she positioned her phone for the most flattering angle. “I’m very picky about my photos,” said Kranenburg, a longtime real estate agent, with a chuckle. “I don’t like the sun.”Kranenburg snapped a few shots and recorded the hubbub, later posting a clip to her Instagram profile, with the account name movemetoboston. Soon after, she left the coffee shop and drove 10 minutes down the road to film in a $2.1 million newly constructed townhouse in Newtonville, where she is hoping to court buyers. Her phone was out as she walked through the living room and kitchen. A video from there, too, later ended up on her Instagram.Katherine Kranenburg, a real estate agent, began regularly posting on social media in 2023.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffOne post was designed to sell a neighborhood; the other, a house. But Kranenburg’s Instagram account, with nearly 30,000 followers, is in service of a singular goal: To give her an edge, in a saturated real estate market, as the one doing the selling.“You cannot do real estate without marketing yourself,” said Kranenburg, 55. “Your goal is to talk to your audience.”Kranenburg is one of many real estate agents in Boston and beyond using social media as a new way to reach that audience, in hopes they will become clients. Social media was a top tool for drawing “quality leads” in 2024, according to the National Association of Realtors. That stands in contrast to more traditional alternatives, like online listings, or cold-calling and door knocking.But Kranenburg, who is affiliated with The Real Brokerage, knows that it takes more than a tasteful clip of a fireplace or a kitchen island to get real eyeballs and, ultimately, close deals. That’s why she, for one, has veered closer to full-blown influencing, vying for the favor of algorithms by posting hyperlocal content that doesn’t necessarily have to do with housing — news about Mike’s Pastry, and Sail Boston, and Back Bay elephant sculptures. “No one wakes up thinking they’re buying a house from Katherine Kranenburg,” she said. “They want to know what is happening in Boston.”Katherine Kranenburg walks through a Newton property.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffThe idea? Hook users with an aesthetic or an inside scoop, and then reel them in with a walkthrough of a $13 million Cambridge six-bedroom. Gain a view, gain a client, gain a sale.“It boils down to: Do you want a realtor that is selling a home first, or themselves first?” said Marc Savatsky of the real estate firm Choose Boston Brokerage. He began posting his listings on Instagram about a decade ago, and cohosts a podcast about real estate. The landscape has became so crowded, he said, that having a unique personality is as important as the strength of the listings. For Kranenburg, this strategy has paid out handsomely. Over the past few years of building her social media presence, with many videos gaining tens of thousands of views, her buyer pool has grown by 80 percent, she said. Buyers regularly flood her direct messages because they, or a friend, saw one of her social media posts. Many of her recent deals, with values in the seven-figures, have been spurred by her posts, she said.Content creation is not something that came naturally to Kranenburg, who lives in Newton. She has worked in real estate for 20 years, eight of them in Boston, but spent most of that time relying on old-fashioned networking and cold-calling for leads. She only started posting to social media regularly in 2023, ramping up slowly, starting with Instagram, then later uploading to YouTube and TikTok.To stay ahead of the curve, Kranenburg has courted help. An editor in the Philippines now produces her YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok content. Her Instagram videos last no longer than a minute, with plenty of fast cuts. “We’ve got it down to a science,” Kranenburg said. “We know what style we’re going for.”She also said she often turns to AI tools, such as Claude and ChatGPT, to vacuum the internet for real estate news, fact-check her content, and refine ideas. When she has accidentally posted inaccurate content — such as saying a Cambridge development was actively being built despite it being completed weeks earlier — she has corrected or removed the posts once realizing her mistake. But the high-tech help is still worth it, she said. “If realtors are not incorporating AI into their content, then they’re missing the mark,” Kranenburg said. “It buys back my time.”Katherine Kranenburg stands in a Newton property, where she was filming content for social media.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffKranenburg isn’t the only one in the real estate industry reaping the benefits of social media. Ali Joyce, who has been a real estate adviser for nine years, said buyers frequently message her about her seven-second videos that show luxury listings across much of Greater Boston, such as in Westwood, Needham, and Dedham. Savatsky, who works mostly in East Boston, said he sold five units in a multifamily property that is currently under construction off of consistent Instagram posts that showed renderings and the build-out. “Realtors have the opportunity to show people listings that are not normally in their consideration, because they would be filtered out by platforms like Zillow,” said Carey Morewedge, a professor of marketing and chair of the marketing department at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business. Back in the Newtonville townhouse, Kranenburg’s heels clacked through the empty hallways as she walked through each room, moving a dish towel here, pillows there. The beads on her phone’s lanyard rattled as she began to capture pictures and videos of gold hardware and a luxe electric range. In the video that ended up on her Instagram, she sits on the kitchen counter as text-box graphics pop up around her, listing off the things she most likes to hear from clients.“I shared your post,” one reads. “We found you on social.”Katherine Kranenburg goes over some listing paperwork while in the kitchen of a Newton property.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffRedmond Bernhold can be reached at redmond.bernhold@globe.com.

hed: Even fully leased Seaport office buildings are selling for less than they used to
subhead: As it plans a big project nearby, Oxford Properties bought an 18-story tower on Fan Pier $435 million, 10 percent less than the building sold for in 2019
content: In a deal reminiscent of pre-pandemic days, a Seaport District office has changed hands for $435 million. Still, in a hallmark of the post-COVID real estate environment, the $435 million price tag is 10 percent less than the building sold for before the pandemic upended where and how we work. Toronto-based Oxford Properties Group on Tuesday closed on its acquisition of One Marina Park Drive on Fan Pier and the parking beneath the 18-story tower, according to Suffolk County property records. New York’s Clarion Partners sold the property, which it acquired in late December 2019 for $482 million. The 492,000-square-foot building is 99 percent leased, with tenants including legal and technology companies.The acquisition comes at a time when Oxford is planning a mammoth mixed-use project with up to 22 buildings, built in three phases, further out in the Seaport between Pappas Way and E Street along the Reserved Channel. The buildings would be a mix of residential, hotel, laboratory, and office, and could range in height from four to 17 stories, according to a recent public presentation. An artist’s rendering of Oxford Properties Group’s proposed residential building along Pappas Way and West First Street near South Boston’s Reserved Channel. The building would be part of the first phase of a mammoth mixed-use development, which could bring up to 22 buildings on what’s now industrial property.Skidmore, Owins & Merrill/ScapeCity planners are reviewing the project’s first phase, a residential development with 287 units — built in either one or two buildings — at 370 West First St. One of the buildings could rise 183 feet. One Marina Park Drive opened in 2010 and was among the first wave of modern glass development along the Seaport’s waterfront. It “exemplifies” an investment that’s “well-located, well-amenitized, and positioned to benefit” from the flight-to-quality office leasing trend among top-tier tenants, said Ankit Bhatt, head of Oxford’s US investments. “It combines a premier waterfront location, a diverse occupier ecosystem, and exceptional connectivity within one of Boston’s most desirable office districts,” Bhatt said in a statement. “Its strong income profile and high-quality tenancy provide a solid foundation for long-term performance.” The real estate arm of a large Canadian public employees pension fund, Oxford is among the largest commercial landlords in Boston. Its local property holdings include 225 Franklin St. in the Financial District, a laboratory building that once held nation’s largest WeWork at 745 Atlantic Ave. near South Station, and the conjoined 222 Berkeley St. and 500 Boylston St. in Back Bay. The firm has city approvals to build a 13-story laboratory with three levels of underground parking on the site of an old parking garage at 125 Lincoln St. just outside Chinatown.But One Marina Park Drive marks Oxford’s first major office purchase in nearly a decade, following its July 2017 acquisition of two Washington, D.C. buildings in a joint venture with the real estate arm of Norway’s central bank. Oxford is owned by OMERS, a Toronto-based pension fund for Canadian municipal workers including firefighters, police, and paramedics. Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: The top things that drag out a home renovation project
subhead: While all remodeling projects have their hiccups, a lot can be done to avoid or minimize disruptions
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

We have all heard the horror stories. A remodeling project that starts off swimmingly, then gets bogged down and grinds to a halt before mercifully limping to the finish line — way past schedule and over budget. While all remodeling projects have their hiccups, a lot can be done to avoid or minimize disruptions. The vast majority can be ironed out before the work starts, which helps the project run smoother once things get rolling. Below are a few things that tend to stall renovation projects.


Well before the work starts and the permitting process is taking shape, it’s important to have plans from your builder that will give the building department what they need to not only approve the permit, but lay the groundwork for the inspection process. Nothing will slow a project down like a failed inspection. Building officials looking at any serious renovation will want to see that builders are licensed and insured and that architects are certified. It is possible a structural engineer will also be needed. Sketch-up plans are not what a building department is looking for and will bog down the whole process.

Lack of understanding what city or town departments are involved with the permitting process is also a major hinderance. Again, a builder/architect should know this, but it is important to understand who will be involved in the permitting and inspection process. It could be zoning, historical, or perhaps the conservation committee that will weigh in on things. If a plot plan is needed from zoning, that could take four to six weeks to get researched and drawn up. It’s not something you want to be dealing with at the last minute.


The development schedule lays out milestones for the owners, builder, and architect. There are a set number of meetings to draft the plans and layout — typically anywhere from three to six. Among the three main players, and each has tasks with deadlines within the overall schedule. These all run concurrently on parallel tracks as development moves forward.

The homeownermust make final decisions on overall plans and schematics. We lay out the product selections they need to make and in what order. Product selections can greatly affect the cost of installation, and the lead times have to work within the parameters of the project. For instance, we would need kitchen cabinets and appliances chosen first since those impact so many other choices. Then we would want all the plumbing, electrical, and HVAC chosen and ironed out since those are critical path items. Further down would be tile selection, paint colors, etc.

The builderbrings all the subcontractors and suppliers through to review the project, map out routes for all the utilities, and manage service upgrades if necessary. Having all the key subs and suppliers through gets a better handle on budget and length of time needed for each component of the project. This leads to a more accurate production schedule. The builder should be continuously monitoring the budget and scope of work. The project can change over the course of development; as long as the client is made aware of changes to scope and budget, the process should move along smoothly. The builder should also be nursing the project along with the building officials to make sure there aren’t stumbling blocks once work starts.

The architectis modifying drawings as needed during development. The goal being that when the contract is signed, a full set of permit-ready plans are good to go. The architect may stay involved in the interior design work, which is not something that has to be on the building permit plans.


As much as we do not like changes once a project has begun, they are an inevitable part of any remodel. It is important to have a system and protocol in place when they do happen. On our projects, we immediately fill out a change order form with pricing and submit that to owners before any additional work is done that isn’t in the initial contract. Change orders generally happen for two reasons:

The first is what we call “the house talking,” and it happens on most every project. We may open up a house and find rot or that past contractors have drilled through structural beams and/or joists. We would drop what we are doing, get the solution written up and priced, then submit that to the owner. We would shift gears and work on another part of the remodel while the change order is submitted, discussed, and signed.

Sometimes homeowners change their minds about something and add or modify elements that change the scope of work. This will likely lead to delays in the project. These would also be written up as a change order, signed, and incorporated into the product schedule.


Having all three players in the development process working together and in parallel with each other while holding each other accountable is the only way to pull all the pieces together in an efficient manner. Doing it right is a lot more work than people realize. Virtually everything we go over in the development process will have to be discussed and debated at some point. It is always better to do that over the dining room table with a cup of coffee and the plans in front of us, rather than having those discussions once your house is opened up and there are contractors standing around waiting for answers. That is a recipe for cost overruns and scheduling delays.

Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge. Send your questions to[email protected]. Questions are subject to editing. hed: Room to love: A backyard barn in Newton finds new life as a gathering space
subhead: Dover-based Cara Fineman of DAG Design transformed a once “frat house”-style barn into a coastal family room
content:
ByMarni Elyse Katz - Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Paint

The first thing designer Cara Fineman did to transform the barn in her clients’ Newton backyard was paint the entire interior white. “This dark brown barn looked like a frat house” said Fineman, founder ofDAG Designbased in Dover, said. “Now it’s a cheerful and inviting gathering space.”

Lights

Oversized rattanpendants from Serena & Lily, $598 each, are an instant wow that fill the top of the room and set the tone. “The organic material has a casual, coastal sensibility— the barn may be used as a pool house later — without feeling out of place in the suburbs,” she said.

Drapery

Fineman used shibori-patterned fabric designed by local artistAnnie Damphousse of Housse Studio, for the drapery panels, made byMakkas Workroom in Sudbury. “The drapes introduce multiple blue tones and a bohemian vibe that plays off the pendants,” she said.

Game Tables

A pool table and a game table — both white to blend into the background — offer alternatives to screen time.Doc & Holliday’s Santorini pool table, from $7,599, comes in various finishes and felt colors.

Sofa

Crate & Barrel’s Gather sectional, starting at $4,447, provides ample seating while the bench cushion configuration is ideal for napping. Durable performance upholstery protects against spills. Fineman added a custom pillow made from Katie Ridder’s Turtle Bay Belgian linen. Or, try a sea turtle print pillow fromEtsy vendor Ethan Taylor Home, starting at $22.77.

Coffee Table

The white oak coffee table brings natural wood to the middle of the space and anchors the seating area.Quince sells a similar onefor $300.

hed: Inside the ultra-exclusive Disney World community where families watch fireworks from bed and get private rides to the parks
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Florida family has found a way to make every day feel like a fairy tale — by owning a storybook-inspired home within the gates of Walt Disney World.
Cristie Anne, the 39-year-old creator behind the travel account The Traveling Red, splits her time between her primary residence in Miami and a vacation home in Golden Oak, Disney’s ultra-exclusive residential community in Lake Buena Vista, Florida.
The gated enclave was designed by Walt Disney Imagineering and is composed of individually designed luxury homes — including Cristie Anne’s cottage, which takes its cues from Belle’s provincial home in the live-action “Beauty and the Beast.”
She told the Daily Mailthat the inspiration is immediately apparent when the home’s exterior is compared with the cottage seen in the film. Inside, Imagineer-designed details continue the theme without making every room feel like a theme-park attraction.
Her parents purchased the four-bedroom, 3,600-square-foot cottage in 2020 for an undisclosed sum, although buying within the resort was never part of their original plan.
They had been searching for a family beach house when her parents visited friends who had recently purchased a place in Golden Oak. On the same day Cristie Anne’s future home hit the market, her parents toured it and showed the property to her and her brother over FaceTime.
Her daughter was just 3 years old at the time, making a “Beauty and the Beast”-inspired Disney cottage especially difficult to resist. The family saw it as a place where she could grow up while they built traditions together.
Golden Oak properties occupy a rarefied corner of the Orlando market. Other homes currently available within Walt Disney World are asking about $8 million, while past reports have placed prices across the community between roughly $2 million and $20 million. Cristie Anne has not disclosed what her family paid.
Living on Disney property comes with perks that most parkgoers can only dream of.
Depending on which park the family wants to visit, they can arrive within minutes by car or use private Disney transportation that drops them near the entrance. That means they can head out for dinner, squeeze in a favorite ride or catch a fireworks show without turning the excursion into an all-day production.
The family visits most frequently during Florida’s more temperate winter months. Because they can return whenever they want, Cristie Anne said there is no need to race through every attraction in a single trip.
Homeowners received complimentary park admission for several years when her family bought the property, she told the outlet. Once that benefit expired, they purchased annual passes like other guests.
Cristie Anne has now visited the parks hundreds of times. But one of the home’s most enchanting amenities requires no ticket at all: The family can watch Magic Kingdom’s nightly fireworks from the property in their pajamas.
Despite sitting inside one of the world’s busiest tourist destinations, the neighborhood itself is notably secluded.
Only residents and their registered guests can enter Golden Oak, meaning vacationers cannot simply drive through to look at the homes. Short-term rentals are also prohibited, helping the enclave retain the feel of a private residential community rather than an extension of the resort.
Cristie Anne said she is careful not to film neighboring properties when sharing her Golden Oak life with her more than 200,000 Instagram followers, limiting her tours and posts to her family’s own home.
The community does not contain everyday necessities such as supermarkets or schools, so residents must travel a few minutes beyond Disney property for groceries and other errands. But restaurants, resort hotels, golf courses, spas and entertainment are all practically on their doorstep.
For Cristie Anne’s family, that combination of real-world convenience, privacy and Disney magic makes the home a keeper.

hed: Couple fights HOA to save home from foreclosure after disputed $8K bill balloons to $20K
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Georgia couple is fighting to save their first home after a disputed homeowners association bill ballooned to roughly $20,000 — even though closing documents reportedly showed no outstanding balance when they bought the property.
Tatiana Pimentel poured her life savings into a townhouse at the 100-unit Whitehall Forest community in DeKalb County in 2024, hoping to become a homeowner after spending 25 years in the US.
But less than a year later, the Whitehall Forest East Condominium Association moved to foreclose on the property over nearly $8,000 in allegedly unpaid dues, according toAtlanta News First.
The association now claims Pimentel and her fiancé, Obren Cicmil, owe about $20,000 after adding monthly assessments and legal fees, Pimentel told the outlet.
“I have no idea” how the amount became so high, she said.
The association’s original October 2025 foreclosure filing sought nearly $8,000 in dues that Pimentel claims were never disclosed before the purchase. Court documents reportedly claim she is more than four years behind — despite her having owned the home for less than two years.
Her closing documents showed a zero-dollar HOA balance, while state records indicated that the association had been dissolved in 2021 and was not active when she purchased the property, the outlet reported.
Dean Heard, who owns two units in the community, reinstated the HOA in 2024 and assumed its presidency about one month after Pimentel’s purchase, according to nonprofit records cited by the outlet.
But residents told the station they do not recall electing Heard or receiving notice of a community vote. Heard acknowledged that homeowners did not elect him, saying he had been vice president and took over after the board removed the previous president.
The couple struggled to find an attorney willing to handle the case until Candace Sneed, working through DeKalb Pro Bono, agreed to represent them without charge.
Sneed said she was stunned that a homeowner could potentially lose her property over an assessment she had allegedly never known about. Although the organization does not ordinarily handle HOA disputes, she took on the case after private firms declined it.
The couple appeared in court on Aug. 24 and asked for a jury trial. An attorney representing the association opposed the request, and the judge postponed a decision while reviewing the case. Pimentel and Cicmil are due back in court Sept. 23.
Their title insurer has offered a $9,600 check to help cover the disputed dues and prevent foreclosure, but the association is still seeking thousands of dollars in attorneys’ fees, according to the report. Pimentel said she is holding the check as a show of good faith while the litigation continues.
The foreclosure battle comes amid a wider financial and infrastructure crisis inside Whitehall Forest.
As of March, the community had accumulated astaggering $5.1 million past-due water balanceand owed another $24,000 for trash collection, DeKalb County confirmed to Atlanta News First.
The HOA charges each household $143 per month for water, trash collection, lawn care and roof repairs. But Heard said roughly 60% of the community’s 100 homeowners withhold their dues, while residents maintain they do not trust or remember electing the association’s leadership.
The development’s monthly water charges reportedly run between $16,000 and $20,000, while the HOA pays only about $1,000 to $2,000. Persistent leaks may have added to the costs, although their financial impact remains unclear.
County officials said the unpaid balance is being absorbed by a shared fund supported by all DeKalb County water customers.
Heard maintains that the association has acted according to its bylaws and that foreclosure decisions are made by its attorneys. Sneed, however, said its financial records do not support the debt claimed against Pimentel.
Georgia has since passed a law increasing HOA oversight, but it will not fully take effect until January 2027.

hed: Former Disney CEO Michael Eisner grabs $10M NYC home — after ditching the embattled Pierre hotel
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Michael Eisner isn’t waiting around to see how the war at the Pierre ends.
The former Disney chief, already a two-time owner inside the embattled Fifth Avenue co-op, just closed on a $10 million off-market apartment at the Sherry Netherland hotel, property records show.
The move puts him a block away from the building where he and dozens of other wealthy shareholders are facing the possibility of losing their homes entirely.
Eisner and his wife Jane bought unit 25T from the Broad Revocable Trust, tied to the family of the late art collector Eli Broad and his widow Edythe.
The two-bedroom, 2.5-bath spread runs 2,500 square feet inside the 38-story tower at 781 Fifth Ave., steps from Central Park and known for its white glove service, including attended elevators, daily housekeeping and room service from Harry Cipriani.
The timing is hard to ignore.
The Pierre has spent the better part of a yearlocked in a bitter fightover a proposed $2 billion sale that would hand the historic building to Saudi buyer Motasem Khashoggi and put it under the management of the Dorchester Collection, owned by the Sultan of Brunei.
If two thirds of shareholders approve the deal this fall, every resident, no matter how long they’ve lived there or how much they’ve spent renovating, will have to give up their apartment or be evicted and forfeit their cut of the payout.
Eisner, who last year spent $4.3 million buying a second Pierre apartment and picking up more co-op shares along with it, joined a July 29th shareholder meeting on the sale by Zoom rather than in person, as tempers flared inside the hotel’s Cotillion Ballroom.
The gathering, meant to finally answer residents’ questions, instead turned into what multiple attendees described as a “s–tshow.”
Investor Austin Hearsttold the room representativesfrom Dorchester and Khashoggi Holding had done “a miserable f–king job” laying out the terms.
Fashion designerTory Burchpressed them on the roughly 400 hotel employees whose jobs hang in the balance, saying “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line every five minutes.”
Longtime resident Tina Beriro, 85, put the math on aging owners bluntly, warning “many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”
And Eisner isn’t the only Pierre name hedging.Larry Ellisonbought two units from Shari Redstone for $24 million in an off-market deal in November, another sign that some of the building’s richest residents would rather cash out quietly than wait for a shareholder vote that could upend their lives.
Commerce SecretaryHoward Lutnick, who owns the Pierre’s trophy penthouse but has never lived in it, sat out the July meeting entirely, tied up at the Oval Office the same day.
His absence didn’t sit well given his sons now run Newmark, the brokerage that stands to earn a fee on the very sale their father would profit from as the co-op’s largest shareholder.
Board president David Johnson has declined to comment on the meeting or the terms of the bid, calling it a private matter among shareholders.
As of now, the Pierre’s board still hasn’t set a release date for the long-promised proxy statement laying out the sale’s actual terms.

hed: Libbie Mugrabi refuses to leave the $25M Hamptons mansion she lost in a humiliating public auction
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Heck no, she won’t go.
Libbie Mugrabiis staying put in the Hamptons mansion she lost in a court-ordered foreclosure auction last month.
As the one-time socialite digs in her heels, the attorney who repped her throughout the lengthy battle to keep the property has filed an action in a Suffolk County appellate court to invalidate the auction, which the court has not yet acted upon.
Mugrabi and the attorney, Claude Castro of Castro Law Group, told the court they have lined up a lender willing to provide a loan that would save the home and allow her to stay. Mugrabi would use as collateral a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that is appraised at $40 million. She recently won the artwork back in a separate legal battle.
It isn’t clear, however, whether Castro will pursue the matter because Mugrabi has now parted ways with him, according to court documents. In a handwritten note to the court, with hearts over each “i” in her name, Mugrabi said that she wants to handle situation herself from this point henceforth.
This marks the latest twist in a lengthy melee that has papered the court with thousands of pages of legal claims. Over the past two years, Mugrabi has tried to convince the court she should be allowed to keep the home despite defaulting — by admittedly not paying anything — on a $3.5 million loan that used it as collateral.
Mugrabi got the 10,687-square-foot Bridgehampton mansion and its surrounding 6.8 acres as part of an equally fraught settlementin her divorcefrom the billionaire art collector David Mugrabi — an heir to an Israeli industrial fortune — in 2020. Mugrabi previously told The Post she received $100 million in cash and other assets from the settlement, although the figure has not been verified.
Mugrabi, speaking from the home, told The Post she has not set a time to leave the property. “I don’t know what’s going to happen,” she said.
Her mother, Jane Scher, said she “Wants this all over,” so her daughter can, “make a fresh start as the artist she truly is.”
Pressure is also coming from her lender’s law firm, which on Sept. 11 responded to Mugrabi’s motion to the appellate division to stop the sale and give her more time to pay off the loan.
The filing is on behalf of lender REO Assets of America, in Great Neck, N.Y. It contains 72 pages of other reasons to bolster its case, especially highlighting the settlement Mugrabi agreed to with the lender in the spring that gave her 90 days, until Aug. 25, to sell the home through a traditional listing — or give up all rights to it.
The effort started witha $25 million asking pricethat quickly reduced by two price cuts to $19 million.
Because Mugrabi didn’t sell the home, “and actually consented to the eviction in the settlement, she gave up virtually all of her rights to appeal,” said Maria Beltrani, a partner at Schwartz Sladkus Reich Greenberg & Atlas in the firm’s real estate and litigation department. Beltrani is not involved in the case but reviewed it at The Post’s request.
Last month’s auction itselfhad every carnival elementexcept for corn dogs. Mugrabi’s sister, Mia Rowe, first won the property with a $7.8 million commitment after furiously topping all offers from roughly 10 other bidders. But Rowe never returned after saying she was going to a Chase bank branch to get the required 10% down payment. And the bidders, who had been left cooling their heels for close to an hour without shade in the 82-degree swelter, were furious that she was even allowed to participate empty-handed.
When the tumult died down,Henry Ikezi, a hopeful Queens politician and real estate investor, won the property with a $5.86 million bid made on his behalf by his brother, Stanley. Mugrabi herself was not present at the Southampton Town Hall sale.
Ikezi had 30 or 45 days, depending on how the sale is legally structured, from the Aug. 28, auction date to pay the balance of sale amount and then begin legal efforts to get Mugrabi out of the home if she doesn’t leave of her own accord.
Ikezi did not respond to requests for comment about whether he has completed the purchase.

hed: Divorce-battling billionaire buys $72M Palm Beach palace — and moves in with younger girlfriend
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about trading up.
While hisestranged wife battles himfor a fortune in aNew Jersey courtroom,hedge fund titan John Overdeck has settled into a $72 million Palm Beach waterfront palace with a new partner.
The Two Sigma co-founder, 56, bought the 16,000-square-foot spread through a Delaware shell called Avocado Enterprises, according to records reviewed by theDaily Mail.That is nearly triple the roughly 6,000-square-foot Short Hills, NJ, home he once shared with his ex-wife Laura.
He shares the Florida residence with Kimia Shadrokh, 42, a Peakstone managing director and former commercial real estate executive at the Moinian Group. Both gave the address when they registered to vote this spring, Florida records show.
Overdeck’s attorney, Jonathan W. Wolfe, confirmed the romance.
“John has been going through his divorce for more than four years,” he told the Daily Mail. Overdeck “is now in a committed relationship with someone who he met long after this divorce process began.”
The nearly 1-acre Neoclassical compound sits on the island’s exclusive north end, where Sylvester Stallone is among the neighbors.
It reportedly got a $20 million makeover before the couple arrived. It boasts six bedrooms, 7.5 bathrooms, a great hall with 26-foot ceilings, a travertine pool with a cabana and 165 feet of waterfront with a dock deep enough for a serious boat.
The paper trail leads back to Overdeck’s old shop. The LLC’s manager, Matthew Siano, spent about 20 years overseeing legal and compliance work at Two Sigma, according to his LinkedIn page.
The move comes as the couple’s divorce, filed in March 2022 after nearly 20 years of marriage and no prenup, grinds through New Jersey Family Court.
Overdeck, worth about $8 billion per Forbes, has offered Laura $723 million in tax-free cash. He testified that the figure is “fair.” She wants 35% of his Two Sigma stake, which herlawyer values at $6.2 billionand his lawyers put at $4.9 billion.
His camp argues the firm was founded before the 2002 wedding and is not marital property. Laura’s lawyer, Theresa Lyons, told the court he “methodically and strategically” plotted for decades to shield his wealth.
Laura’s filings also accuse him of shuffling billions into Wyoming trusts with help from Two Sigma staffers.
Laura’s own position is shaky. Judge Bruce Buechler barred her from testifying or presenting evidence after finding she accessed her husband’s private P.O. box and computer and photographed his emails with his lawyers, as The Post reported. Her team is appealing, so her best shot is grilling Overdeck on cross-examination.
The stakes reach beyond the couple. Overdeck and co-founder David Siegel each own roughly half of Two Sigma and are locked in a fight over control of it.

hed: Living near a Costco may increase your home value — but it depends on where you live
subhead: What Costco means for home values
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Few brands have the kind of legendarydevotion that Costco has cultivatedover the past few decades.
Shoppers love thebulk deals, the store’s Kirkland Signature products, and the cheap hot dogs—which is why any given Costco parking lot is likely to look like a zoo whenever you visit, especially in this economy.
A Costco run can be good for your wallet, if you like buying honey by the bucket or gumballs by the hundreds.
But the benefits may go beyond that: According to research from the Vancouver School of Economics,Costco openingscan have an impact on nearby property values, especially in already densely populated areas.
That’s some great potential upside forhomeownersand potential buyers.
Just keep in mind that living close to any high-traffic amenity comes with its own trade-offs, such as more cars, more noise, and more foot traffic on the weekends.
In the abstract, living within a short driving distance of Costco is a good thing. But can you put a number on it?
Silas Kwok at the Vancouver School of Economics conducted research on this question. It turns out that the overall impact of living near a Costco is negligible.
In looking at Costco openings from 2002 to 2020 across the US,the research showedthat the openings “caused no significant changes in property values on average.”
That said, there were certain parts of the country where Kwok finds Costco did drive values—namely, in high-density and high-income areas.
“Costco openings caused a 7.9% increase in property values within five miles in counties with above-average population density, and a 5.2% increase within five miles in counties with above-average household income 2.5 years following store openings,” writes Kwok.
Consider a Costco opening in a dense, high-income area like Brooklyn, NY, versus one in a lower-density, lower-income market like Birmingham, AL. The research suggests the first is more likely to see a bump in nearby property values than the second.
There are a few possible reasons for this. One is that wealthier Americans tend to prefer Costco,according to YouGov, and may be willing to pay for easy access to it on a regular basis. Another is that Costco simply brings more value to people’s lives than the typical big-box store.
“A Costco nearby equals convenience and savings in the minds of many consumers. A household can join a Costco and go get gas for their car, groceries for their home, and holiday decorations all in one trip. Not to mention there is likely an optometrist and even a section to get new tires,” says Christina Rordam, a real estate agent in the Orlando, FL, area.
“Busy familiescan save hours every month, not to mention cheap gas these days is worth its weight in gold.”
Yet another view of the data is that Costco doesn’t necessarily create value—it confirms what already existed.
“Home values only increased in areas that were already high-density or high-income. That suggests the Costco effect is not universal but is highly dependent on the pre-existing economic and demographic characteristics of a neighborhood,” says Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality.
“Costco strategically targets areas with specific economic profiles that may already be on an upward trajectory.”
Hepp also contends that some of what makes Costco unique is also what makes living near it minimally valuable.
“Costco functions as a destination store. Its business model is built on a membership base willing to travel, often by car, for less frequent bulk-shopping trips. When you are already planning to drive 15 or 20 minutes, the value of living one minute away is minimal,” she says.
“That convenience premium does not get capitalized into the home’s price the way it would for a daily-visit amenity like a grocery store or a coffee shop.”

It’s true that a new Costco may simply be part of a larger economic upswing in a given area.
For example, in August, Advenir Azora acquired 18 acres in Franklin, WI—a suburb of Milwaukee—to build a 166 build-to-rent residential neighborhood, spending over $51 million. The biggest perk? It’snear a future Costco.
The mayor of Franklin, John Nelson, says that the Costco will bring a “spark” to the area and potentially attract other large tenants to the area.
That spark may be enticing to homebuyers seeking property in an area that will soon see rising prices, and want the Costco as a vote of confidence in the neighborhood’s economic future. And these days, a quick drive to Costco’s gas station is a true benefit considering the current price of gasoline.
As with any amenity, there is a limit to the benefits of being near a Costco.
Anyone who has ever visited one of its stores on a weekend knows just how busy the parking lot and the surrounding areas can get. And that’s not even the full picture.
“When we evaluate a house that backs up to or faces a big-box site, we have to price in what the next buyer will feel: delivery trucks before sunrise, parking lot lights at night, weekend traffic, and a backyard view of a loading dock,” says Andy Kravchenko, founder and CEO of Sterling Home Offer.
“The sweet spot is being minutes away, not next door.”
If a Costco moves in nearby, be prepared for the potential for noise, light pollution, and loss of neighborhood feel. These can be real downsides to living, and buying, nearby.
The clearest takeaway from Kwok’s research is that living near a Costco is more of a boon in high-density, high-income areas than elsewhere.
Whether that applies to any specific house is still a case-by-case question, and Kravchenko recommends doing some on-the-ground homework before deciding.
“For buyers weighing it, visit at the ugly hours, 6 a.m. on a delivery day and Saturday noon. Stand in the backyard and listen. Then pull up the county parcel map and check the undeveloped commercial land nearby, because today’s green buffer can become tomorrow’s expansion,” he says.
“If the house passes those tests, being close to a Costco is a plus that pays you back when you sell.”
And if you’re not sure a nearby Costco will do much for your home value, it’s worth considering how the store actually fits your life, says Rordam.
“Consider how much time shopping there would or would not save you,” she says.
“If you are a single or smaller household, maybe you won’t have much use for those gallon jugs of ketchup or 50 packs of noodles anyway.”

hed: $1.25m Brookline condo in converted church features full rose window
subhead: Saint Mark’s Methodist Church is a Brookline landmark that you can live in.
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
The congregation of Saint Mark’s Methodist Church first assembled in Brookline in 1873; by 1891, it had grown to the point where its members purchased 25,000 square feet of land at the corner of Vernon and Park Streets and hired one of Boston’s best-known architects to design a church building for them. George A. Clough, who also designed Boston’s Suffolk County Courthouse, drew up the plans for an 8,000-square-foot Romanesque Revival church that would become a landmark in the residential neighborhood, according to theBrookline Historical Society.
“The church was dedicated in 1896; the cost of construction was $160,000,” the historical society details.
By the 1970s, the congregation merged with another, and the church at 90 Park St. stood empty. The residents of Brookline came together to save it from demolition and got it listed on the National Register of Historic Places, according toHKT Architects of Charlestownwho eventually converted it to condominiums.
Condo conversions of churches were rare at the time, and other developers had found the project too challenging, according to HKT, who came up with a plan that preserved the exterior architectural features as well as many interior details.
Unit 35, a two-bedroom, two-bath condolisted for $1,250,000 million this September, is an example of this with original rosewood flooring, vaulted ceilings, and molded plaster details.
“There are 20 units in the building; each one is different,” said Sanda O’Brien, a sales associate with Coldwell Banker Realty, who hasthe listing. “This is the only unit in the building that has a whole round window. There were two huge rose windows in the church, this one was on the back side. The front one has been divided in two, and two separate condominiums each have half. But this unit has the whole round window. It is a dramatic focal point.”
Originally, both of the church’s rose windows had stained glass. Some panes were damaged during the years it stood empty, and others were broken during the construction process, O’Brien said. Now the window featuring one large central round pane and seven surrounding round panes holds clear glass.
The 1,163-square-foot unit is three levels, with an iron and metal staircase connecting the lower story, which has a bedroom and bathroom, to the main floor’s living room, kitchen, and dining room. From here, a spiral stairs lead to the primary bedroom and its adjoining bath. Above that is a loft, reached by a ladder, that overlooks the drama below.
The unit has all the modern conveniences, including central air conditioning, a gourmet kitchen with granite countertops, luxury marble baths, a private laundry in the unit, separate storage, and two parking spaces. While the neighborhood is quiet, leafy, and residential, the building is only two blocks from the dining, shops, and cafés of Coolidge Corner.
As of press time, the unit was under contract.
Regina Cole is a freelance writer who covers architecture, design, historic homes, and the decorative arts.

hed: ‘Rare’ private island on Minnesota lake lists for $7.2M — first time being sold in 50 years
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


An extremely “rare opportunity” to buy a private island onLake Minnetonkahas just hit the market for $7,250,000.
Located in Shorewood, MN, the2-acre legacy compound on Gale Island, surrounded by 1,841 feet of luxurious lakeshore, features several structures:
“Lake Minnetonka is the lake in Minnesota,” says listing agentJeffrey Dewing of Coldwell Banker Realty. “It’s a very storied and sought-after destination, and it’s very rare for an island to come to market. This one has been in the same family for 53 years, which makes it even rarer.”
It is also located just a short boat ride from Excelsior and Wayzata, which have lots of restaurants, shopping, and a vibrant scene.
“The property will likely be used as a secondary residence based on logistics, but it potentially could be a year-round property,” says Dewing. “There are three main cabins that were used by different family members, so it is beautifully suited for multigenerational living.”
Dewing says the buyer pool he is seeing has been unique.
“It could be acquired by another family and used like this was for a family retreat, or it could be used in a multitude of different ways,” he says. “There have been weddings on the island, and it has such a fun history.”
The island was originally purchased from the federal government in 1871 by Harlow A. Gale, a Minneapolis real estate developer, and remained in the Gale family for nearly a century. It was later owned by St. Olaf College and used as a retreat before returning to private ownership.
“There aren’t many island estates like this that become available,” notes Dewing. “It’s an incredibly unique opportunity.”

hed: Gold-domed NYC penthouse fetches barely a third of its $25M ask
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The Fifth Avenue aerie that sat for more than 500 days finally found a buyer — and the markdown is brutal.
A 40-foot golden dome. Views of the Empire State Building from a private roof deck. A front-row seat next tothe Flatiron Building. None of it was enough to land a buyer at $25 million.
The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom penthouse atop the Sohmer Piano Building at 170 Fifth Ave. has sold for $9 million, The Post has learned.
That marks a 64% drop from itsNovember 2024 debut,and only a little more than the $7.2 million tech mogul Greg Carr paid for the raw space back in 2001.
The purchaser is keeping a low profile. Records list the buyer as White Piano LLC, an entity with an East 20th Street mailing address.
The price slide was steady. After hitting the market at $25 million, the two-floor home was cut to $14.9 million and lingered on the market for 530 days.
Rather than keep waiting, Carrhanded the keys to Concierge Auctions, which projected opening bids between $6 million and $9 million.
Bidding opened at $8.25 million after the reserve was met, and the hammer fell live July 29 at Sotheby’s New York. Concierge later announced the sale as pending at $10.147 million.
Listing broker Claire Groome of Sotheby’s said the traditional route had run its course.
“Auctions are really exciting, and people like doing them,” Groome said. “It’s the better way to move something that usually sits on the market otherwise.”
Carr built Boston Technology and once chaired Prodigy. He spent nearly 25 years hosting guests beneath the gilded cupola, and has saidLauren Bacallonce danced there.
These days Carr’s attention sits half a world away. He has steered more than $100 million toward wildlife conservation at Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique, and every dollar from this sale goes to the Gorongosa Project.
He previously told The Post the home’s history was the draw from the start.
“What initially drew me to this penthouse was the fact that it represents an extraordinary chapter of New York City’s architectural history,” Carr told The Post. “From the moment I acquired it, we were committed to preserving its character while thoughtfully reimagining it for modern living.”
Carr has described the chapter in theatrical terms.
“If life is a three-act play, that was act two for me, and it was a magnificent act,” he has said. “I loved that place and got a lot of use out of it.”
The roughly 5,700-square-foot duplex comes with more than 40 oversized windows, an 80-foot greenhouse-style window expanse, two grand foyers joined by a circular limestone staircase and a privately deeded roof deck. The corner primary suite includes more than 35 linear feet of closet space and a spa bath with a Waterworks soaking tub.
Sotheby’s Lawrence Treglia, who co-listed the property with Groome, pitched it as more than a typical luxury apartment.
“Whether you’re entertaining beneath the golden dome, enjoying sunset views from the private roof deck or simply taking in the natural light that pours through the home’s expansive windows, every space feels connected to the energy and beauty of New York City,” Treglia said.
After the sale, Concierge Auctions CEO Chad Roffers framed the auction as the right tool for the job.
“The auction process delivered the competitive, time-defined environment this landmark property deserved,” Roffers said in a statement.

content:

Anentire California townhas hit the market for a cool $4.75 million.
Nestled along Northern California’s Feather River Canyon, Belden was once the site of a bustling mining camp during the gold rush. But by the 20th century, the area’s economy had faltered.
Since, 1989, the town has been owned by Ivan Coffman, Belden’s unofficial mayor, who’s turned the town into a picturesque tourist destination.

The four-acre property contain’s an owner’s quarters, seven guest cabins with 2-3 bedrooms each, an 18-room hotel, 16 RV spaces, a full service restaurant and bar, and multiple outdoor event spaces.
“Whether envisioned as a boutique resort, event venue, music destination, retreat center, glamping property, RV resort, corporate getaway, outdoor recreation hub, or a combination of hospitality uses, Belden Town offers infrastructure and character that would be difficult — and extraordinarily expensive — to replicate today,”the town’s websitereads.
“Properties of this scale, uniqueness, and historical significance rarely come to market,” the website continues.
A nearby five-acre parcel that is currently used for extra parking and event support is available separately for $500,000.
With a population of just 15, Belden is not an official town. The nearest incorporated ton is Portola, about an hour away.
Coffman first visited Belden in 1970 in search of gold.
“That year, we had a terrific flood that washed a huge bar of gravel off down into this hole, and that’s what left all that gold layin’ there,” Coffman toldSFGATE. “It’d been hidden for all them years.”
At 87, Coffman told the outlet he still mines for gold in the river almost daily.
Just off highway 70, a red steel bridge over the Feather River leads you to Belden. The Belden Town Resort and Lodge contains the restaurant, a bar, general store, hotel rooms, and private apartment.
The charming town is full of character. Murals and painted wooden signs can be found throughout, as well as brightly-painted cabins. There’s also a mechanic’s garage built in the mid-20th century, and and an abandoned schoolhouse, overgrown with bushes and vines.
Trailers and RVs parked on the property’s grounds house the people who work in the area, Coffman told SFGATE.
The restaurant is a time capsule decorated with taxidermy, artwork, an old slot machine, a leather saddle, rows of glass bottles and vases, and an oversized rooster.
Coffman decided to sell the property partially because of the death of his son earlier this year from health complications. Flowers were planted by the gazebo in his son’s memory.

hed: Nearly half of US homebuyers are scoring seller perks — but NYC buyers are getting almost nothing
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Homebuyers across the country are persuading sellers to sweeten the deal with cash for repairs, closing costs and mortgage-rate buydowns — but buyers in the New York area are largely being left empty-handed.
Sellers provided concessions in a whopping 44.7% of US home sales in August, up from 42.6% one year earlier and the highest share recorded for the month since at least 2020, according to a newRedfin analysis.
In the New York metro area, however, concessions appeared in a paltry 5.7% of sales — the second-lowest share among the 29 major metros analyzed.
Only San Jose, Calif. ranked lower, at 4.2%.
That means buyers nationally were nearly eight times as likely as those in the New York area to receive a seller perk.
Seller concessions can include money toward repairs or closing costs, mortgage-rate buydowns and even appliances. They do not include reductions to a home’s listing or final sale price, Redfin noted.
The national rise comes as a glut of homes for sale gives buyers more choices and greater negotiating power. August marked the strongest buyer’s market in Redfin records dating to 2013, with sellers increasingly willing to offer incentives to get deals across the finish line.
“Buyers know they can be picky. They’re asking for every concession under the sun,” Amanda Peterson, a Redfin Premier agent in Dallas, said in the report.
The perks are especially common in the Sun Belt, where pandemic-era building booms have collided with softer demand.
Atlanta topped the list, with sellers offering concessions in a staggering 72.8% of transactions. It was followed byCharlotteat 67.9%, Phoenix at 67.4%, Las Vegas at 66.7% andRaleighat 66.3%.
Nashville, Houston and Las Vegas now rank among the country’s five strongest buyer’s markets, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers, according to Redfin.
New York, by contrast, remains a balanced market with roughly equal numbers of buyers and sellers — giving house hunters less leverage to demand extras. Its concession rate also slipped by 0.9 percentage points from a year earlier.
Other markets where concessions remained relatively rare included San Francisco at 18.6%, Chicago at 21.9% and Philadelphia at 25.5%.
Some buyers are managing to score two discounts at once. Nationwide, 15.8% of homes sold in August received both a price cut and a seller concession — also the highest August share in Redfin’s records.
The analysis was based on deals submitted by Redfin buyers’ agents and covered the three-month period ending Aug. 31.

hed: Massive Northern California vineyard goes up for sale after Canada booze ban
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A massive family-run California winery has fallen victim to Canada’s ban on booze imports — listing 11 vineyards amounting to 3,500 acres for sale as a wave ofbankruptcies and closures rock the industry.
McManis Family Vineyards, a 36-year-old winery business, is offloading its main facility and vineyards as it faces a steep decline in its export business, theSacramento Bee reported.
The company is offering its real estate assets for $22 million, accordingto an online listing, with 11 individual vineyards across San Joaquin and Sacramento counties ranging in price from $800,000 to $14 million.
“It was a very hard decision for myself and my family,” Ron McManis, president and co-owner of the company, told the Bee in a statement.
The firm once did brisk business exporting wines to Canada, mostly Ontario, as well as growing and crushing grapes for bulk production. Sales to American’s northern neighbor formerly made up 40% of its export sales, the paper reported.
Much of that evaporated when Canadian provinces slapped bans on American booze in response to President Donald Trump’stariffs on the country.
The sale is only the latest sign of turmoil in the California wine industry, which is struggling with a combination of falling booze consumption, rising costs and excess inventory.Modesto-based Gallo, one of the country’s largest winemakers, revealed plans in June to shutter a San Joaquin crush facility and lay off 20 employees in June.Jason Smith, CEO of Valley Farm Management,said last monthhe sold his land and set fire to vineyards because they were no longer worth maintaining.“There’s literally no way for me to make money,” the 57-year-old Smith told theNew York Times.Wine sales have plunged over the past two decades as Americans have grown more health-conscious about the risks of alcohol and Gen Z drinkers increasingly favor alternatives like hard seltzer.
Fifty-four percent of American adults said they drank alcohol in anOctober 2025 Gallup poll— the lowest percentage since Gallup began tracking the stat in 1939.

hed: Millions of California homeowners to be hit with higher costs under new law
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Get ready to pay up.
Californians may have to pay even higherhomeowners associationfees thanks to a law that could be signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom before the end of the month.
Assembly Bill 2050 would requireHOAsto maintain a 30-year reserve fund and conduct a study of the reserve account.
If an HOA’s reserves fund is projected to fall below zero at any point during the 30 years, the association must transfer at least 15% of its gross annual budget into reserves each year beginning January 2032.

Never miss a story
If the HOA’s budget can’t cover the required transfer, the bill requires the HOA to raise fees on homeowners through a “special assessment.” It’s not clear how much the bill could raise monthly fees for homeowners.
The law would affect millions, as nearly a quarter of California households pay HOA according to U.S. Census Bureau data.
Newsom has until September 30 to sign the bill into law or veto it.
The Consumer Federation of California criticized the bill, saying a better policy would include capped fee increases.
“We’re not against reserving, but it ought to be combined with some reasonable limitations on what could be increased and how rapidly, along with some important guardrails on financial protection and responsibility so the residents don’t get ripped off because the board acts like a kangaroo court,” Robert Herrell, the ogranization’s executive director told theSan Francisco Chronicle.
“I don’t know that you want to sign a bill that’s essentially going to directly lead to massive assessment increases on 14 million Californians,”  he continued.
Proponents of the bill say it would make sure HOAs are better able to keep up building maintenance and other costs. Robert DeNichilo, legislative co-chair at the Community Associations Institute’s California Legislative Action Committee, told the SF Chronicle that the bill budgets “the actual cost of ownership.”
In California, HOAs can can increase regular dues by up to 20% per fiscal year without a vote from community members.
The bill would beespecially tough on condos. Fannie Mae will require condo associations to put 15% of their annual budgets toward reserves starting next year, an increase from the current 10%.
Nathan Godin, a doctoral student at the UC Berkeley Haas School of Business who conducted research on a similar 2022 law enacted in Florida, told the SF Chronicle that the bill could make HOA fee increases more fair to future homeowners.
“You don’t want to be basically passing the buck on to future owners,” Godin said. “You want to have this month-to-month payment instead of expecting some future special assessment. It’s just better practice.”
