hed: Condo owners are getting trapped in homes they can’t sell — as HOA costs and financing woes pile up
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Condo owners across America are discovering that their supposedly affordable homes may come with an expensive catch: They can be extraordinarily difficult to sell.
Soaringhomeowners association fees, costlyspecial assessmentsand insurance problems are scaring off buyers and making it harder for some to obtain mortgages — leaving existing owners stuck in properties they no longer want,MarketWatch reported.
Will Hudson, 43, bought a two-bedroom condo in Golden, Colorado, sight unseen for $260,000 in July 2024, according to the outlet.
The public employee had previously lived in the complex in his 20s and hoped to return to a place he remembered fondly.
Instead, he now calls the purchase “the greatest mistake of my life.”
Hudson told MarketWatch that recurring water shutoffs, flooding in common areas and rising HOA fees — now nearly $470 per month — left him wanting out within a year.
But selling could prove just as painful.
Another unit in the complex languished on the market even after its asking price was slashed from $270,000 in May 2025 to $149,000 this month. The property is now under contract, but the sale has not yet closed.
Hudson estimates that selling his own condo could wipe out the $58,000 he put down — and potentially cost him even more after broker commissions and closing expenses.
“I feel trapped,” he told the outlet.
His predicament reflects a broader squeeze facing condo owners as buildings’ growing expenses are passed down to individual residents.
Among condo buildings constructed before 2000, 8.5% imposed a special assessment in 2025, with affected owners receiving a typical bill of nearly $2,500, according to data from HOA-management platform Vantaca.
Across buildings of all ages, the median special assessment has risen from $930 to $1,100 over the past four years, the data showed.
The pressure may soon intensify: Some 54% of community associations plan to raise their fees to cover expenses including insurance and new reserve requirements taking effect in 2027, according to the report.
That is undermining one of the condo’s traditional selling points.
Condos have historically offered a less expensive entry into homeownership than detached houses. But once monthly HOA charges and special assessments are factored in, buyers may find that a lower-priced unit is not necessarily cheaper to own.
National condo and co-op sales fell 2.7% year-over-year in August, according to National Association of Realtors.
Meanwhile, condos now represent 15% of active inventory across the Mid-Atlantic region served by Bright MLS, stretching from New Jersey to Virginia. Before the pandemic, they accounted for less than 10%, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant told the outlet.
Insurance is making the problem even worse.
As insurers raise premiums — or refuse to cover some condo buildings altogether — associations are passing those expenses to owners through higher monthly fees and assessments, according to MarketWatch.
Buildings without sufficient master insurance policies can also fail to meet federal lending standards, preventing prospective buyers from qualifying for conventional mortgages backed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.
Hudson encountered that issue when he purchased his unit, he told the outlet. His initial lender rejected the property because the HOA’s master policy did not provide adequate roof coverage under federal guidelines.
He eventually found another lender, but only after putting 20% down. Now, he worries a future buyer could face the same financing roadblock.
The result is a vicious cycle: Rising building costs push up HOA fees, higher fees deter buyers and insurance or reserve problems further restrict the pool of people capable of financing a purchase.
Andrew Lester, president of FirstService Financial, advised prospective buyers to examine a condo association’s reserve studies, insurance coverage, structural reports and the age of major systems such as the roof, plumbing and elevators.
Missing documents or delayed answers should be treated as red flags, he told MarketWatch, because buyers are taking on not only an individual unit but also a financial stake in the condition and management of the entire building.

hed: Rare $2.1M Frank Lloyd Wright home is back on the market after a 2-for-1 deal failed
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Frank Lloyd Wright home in Michigan is back on the market for $2.1 million after failing to find a buyer aspart of a bundled deal, The Post has learned.
The Samuel and Dorothy Eppstein House in Galesburg, Mich., is listed with Sotheby’s International Realty.
The 1953 Usonian residence is built from roughly 3,000 hand-cast concrete blocks and sits on 2 acres inside The Acres — a 70-acre enclave of Wright-designed homes near Kalamazoo that is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
In fall 2023, the property was offered alongside its neighbor, the Eric and Pat Pratt House, as a $4.5 million package billed as the first time two adjoining Wright homes were sold together.
No buyer came forward for the pair. The Pratt House later sold on its own in June 2024 for $1.8 million, leaving the Eppstein House to be marketed alone.
Co-owner Marika Broere said in an interview with The Post that the bundled approach hurt the sale.
“That format limited the buyer pool,” Broere said.
Broere and her partner, Tony Hillebrandt, bought thedeteriorating house in 2016and completeda major restorationthe following year. Broere said that work should ease a common concern among Wright buyers, who often worry about costly upkeep.
“The roof, plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling, drainage, glazing and woodwork have all been addressed,” Broere said. “There is no restoration project awaiting the next owner.”
Even so, the home’s location and its price tag present hurdles. Galesburg is a small Michigan city about a two-hour drive from Detroit, far from the coastal markets that typically drive top-dollar sales of architectural landmarks.
Broere said the unusual nature of the property makes it hard to price against other sales.
“Its $2.1 million asking price must also be considered in light of the scarcity of comparable sales for properties of this kind,” Broere said.
She said she expects the eventual buyer to be a specific type of collector.
“Its eventual owner will likely be someone seeking an important piece of American architectural history rather than simply a three-bedroom house near Kalamazoo,” Broere said.
Made up of three bedrooms and two full bathrooms, the home occupies 2,500 square feet and can be used a business opportunity as well.
“This property is used part time as a profitable short-term rental. The home generates significant income through Airbnb to enthusiasts around the world,” the listing notes.
Wright properties can outperform expectations. The Shavin House in Chattanooga, Tenn., listed for $1.6 million in June and sold for $4 million in August after competing bids came in. That sale, however, was driven by a family lawsuit and a court-supervised process, making it an imperfect comparison.
Still, Broere pointed to the Shavin sale as evidence that demand exists.
“These results demonstrate that there is a market for exceptional Wright houses when they reach the right buyer,” Broere said.
She said the couple is hoping the new Sotheby’s listing will widen the pool of prospective buyers.
“For Tony and me, selling the house is bittersweet,” Broere said. “We have always regarded ourselves as its custodians.”

hed: Home of the Week: Retreat to the Berkshires in a high-end log cabin on 3.14 acres for $1.6m
subhead: With a pool and pool house, expansive views, and an updated rustic interior, this property can be accurately called a “retreat”
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

4 Glendale Road, West Stockbridge

$1.625 million

StyleLog cabin

Year built1987

Square feet3,185

Bedrooms4

Baths3.5

SewerPrivate

WaterShared well

Taxes$11,370 (2026)



Like brokers labeling nearly every property a “must see!,” identifying a home as a “retreat” can seem overdone. But there are instances where the appellation is appropriate, and that’s the case with this West Stockbridge home.

It’s a log cabin enshrouded by broad leaf trees on a 3.14-acre lot at the foot of the Berkshire Hills — visible from the front porch — in what’s called theWilliams River Subwatershed of the Housatonic River Valley.


There’s a heated in-ground Gunite saltwater pool with an integrated hot tub and an updated pool house that’s its own retreat (or home office), all framed by a rustic locust fence and bluestone tiles. A firepit is built next to towering irregularly shaped bouldersalongside landscaping that includes a children’s play set, a fenced garden, and an extensive mowed lawn.



The home itself is set on a slight rise and the wrap-around porch adds to the atmosphere with round log columns supporting the roof while rubblestone piers and more round log columns support the porch. An overhanging creates an entry to the unfinished concrete basement, now mostly used as an exercise area by the current owners.


Stepping into the house, a sense of high-end rural living explodes into view. The flooring for the dining area is cherry, rough hewn logs zip across the ceiling, and the stairwell to the right is honey-toned wood that includes a curved shelf built into the stairwell. The angled ceiling ends in four transom windows with natural wood trim. A rustic-looking railing is installed in front of a second-floor landing.


Just steps beyond the dining area is a counter with seating. The kitchen lies behind an archway on the right. It’s a festival of pine. The expansive cabinets and the central island all use the wood, and the country style is reinforced by flat-faced cabinet doors. The central island and the countertops are topped with soapstone. The flooring is slate, and there are two pairs of pendant lights. Natural light arrives through two large, double-hung windows with natural wood casings. Appliances are stainless steel, including the gas range.


Nearby and behind a sliding barn door is a half bathroom/laundry room. There is also a three-season porch with views of the surroundings.


The house flows into a great room that evokes a ski chalet or a hunting lodge of yore. The vaulted cathedral ceiling is lined with roughly hewn square beams offset by a white ceiling, and crossing from one side of the room to the other are rounded log beams barely scraped of bark, setting the visual stage for the room’s dominant feature: a floor-to-ceiling fieldstone fireplace. Functioning and wood-burning, a rough hewn mantel furthers the rustic look. Flanking the fireplace are large, knotty pine bookshelves. Multiple French doors open out to the porch.


The first floor’s large primary suite is in the private corner of the home, and the use of logs and pine that dominate the other rooms on this level is dialed back. The walls are painted a charcoal gray and the white ceiling is smooth, unbroken by beams. There is a walk-in closet, and a French-style door opens to the front porch, adding views to the suite’s attractions.


The primary bathroom can also be considered something of a personal retreat. There is an oval soaking tub and a separate stand-alone shower behind a clear glass door with a tile backsplash. The single vanity underneath a double-hung window incorporates the sink and a linen closet, but in the shape of knotty pine cabinets. The floor is tile and there is also a bidet.


The second floor has three bedrooms, one of which is now set up as a home office. There are also two full bathrooms, both with single vanities; one has a shower/bath combination and the second is shower-only with a glass door and tile backsplash.

Heat and hot water is fueled by propane. There is central air conditioning.

Elle Villetto of William Pitt Sotheby’s International Realtyin Lenox has the listing.

hed: Longtime Celtics voice Mike Gorman lists Boston penthouse for $1.5 million
subhead: The Hall of Fame broadcaster, 78, who started giving his play-by-play commentary of the Celtics in 1981 is saying goodbye to his unit in Lovejoy Wharf.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Mike Gorman, who is best known as the former voice of theBoston Celtics, just listed his North End penthouse with the best commute ever.
The Hall of Fame broadcaster, 78, who started giving his play-by-play commentary of the Celtics in 1981 and officially signed off in 2024, is saying goodbye to his unit in Lovejoy Wharf, the luxurious building that sits mere steps from the Celtics’ home base at the TD Garden.
The two-bedroom, two-bathroom unit at100 Lovejoy Wharf PH 3C, which measures 1,244 square feet, is officially listed at $1.495 million after going on the market earlier this year with different agents. Gorman purchased the unit from the developer in 2017.
“It’s a really great location. I can’t say enough about the building and the people,” Gorman said in asocial media interviewwith George Sarkis of The Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman. He also noted that the proximity to the Garden was a boost, adding, “I would say it added on 10 years to my career.”
A post shared by George Sarkis (@georgesarkisjr)
“You cannot buy that same size unit with the views it has in a full-service building pretty much anywhere in Boston,” said Sarkis who has thelistingwith Karen Navarette.
Sitting at the top of the building and boasting sweeping views of the Boston skyline through oversized windows, the unit welcomes you into a sprawling open living and dining area. Hardwood floors run throughout, and there are custom built-in bookshelves. In the custom kitchen, there are Bosch and Gaggenau appliances, a wine refrigerator, and a comfortable breakfast bar for a morning meal.
A spacious primary suite features four closets and a spa-inspired bathroom with dual vanities, a glass-enclosed shower, and a separate soaking tub. The second bedroom, which is also quite roomy, has corner exposure and could easily function as a guest suite, private office, or den.
The unit comes with additional storage, one parking space, and valet parking. The building offers 24-hour concierge service, a fitness center, entertainment lounge, children’s playroom, dog spa, and rooftop terrace with grilling stations. There’s also on-site water taxi stop making stops at Logan Airport or various other spots in the city.   The North End, TD Garden, and Harborwalk just a few steps away.
As to where the legendary broadcaster is headed, Sarkis noted that Gorman will be going somwhere a bit more serene.
“He has a place somewhere else, more like a vacation place, and he just wants to travel and be closer to his family,” said Sarkis. “He has grandchildren now. He’ll always have a piece of Boston, but he just doesn’t need this place.”
Megan Johnson is a correspondent who covers real estate, distinctive homes, architecture, and interior design.

hed: No one wants to buy Tribeca Film Festival co-founders’ NYC apartment —  now $27M discounted from its original ask
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The famedDakota co-opassembled piece by piece by Tribeca Film Festival co-founders Jane Rosenthal and Craig Hatkoff justgot cheaper again.
The 6,000-square-foot spread at 1 W. 72nd St., which the exes spent more than three decades and 20 separate transactions stitching together into one home, dropped to $12.5 million on Monday, The Post has learned.
That’s down from the $13.9 million The Postreported in May,and a steep comedown from the original $39 million price tagthe apartment carriedwhen it first hit the market in 2016.
Rosenthal — Robert De Niro’s longtime producing partner behind films like “Meet the Parents,” “The Irishman” and “Wag the Dog,” co-founded Tribeca with De Niro and Hatkoffin the wake of 9/11.
She and Hatkoff, a real estate investor, split in 2014 after 19 years of marriage but held onto the apartment together, a unit listing broker Ben Dixon of Douglas Elliman says has more Central Park frontage than anywhere else in the building.
The sale also includes a separate 400-square-foot unit across the hall with three windows and its own bath, which had been asking $15 million on its own last year.
Selling a piece of the Dakota is never simple.
The building’s landmarked status makes renovations a bureaucratic slog, brokers have said, and that’s part of what’s kept this listing lingering.
Dixon’s answer was to commission a new floor plan, developed with architect Elena Frampton after conversations with the building’s own architect, John Wender, that reimagines the apartment entirely.
“I asked Elena to come up with the craziest plan to turn this residence on its head,” Dixon told The Post.
“Buyers looking to modernize need to be up for a renovation,” he told The Post. “This is set to be one of the most iconic homes in Manhattan for the buyer who chooses to invest the time and money to reimagine it for today.”
Dixon hopes the new price tag will give buyers the chance to invest more money into the renovation process.
The reimagined layout would turn the home into a five-bedroom with ensuite baths, though any changes would still need co-op board sign-off.
“I think the big change is that we have more information on what you can do with the apartment. Before, it was presented as a finished product. Now we have an alternative floor plan so [potential buyers] with bigger budgets can create something with a more modern layout for today’s lifestyle,” Dixon said.
The bones are still pure old New York. Eleven-foot ceilings, coved archways and two woodburning fireplaces remain, tucked inside a building where John Lennon was shot dead in 1980 andwhere Yoko Ono still ownsa unit one floor below this very apartment.
Lauren Bacall, Roberta Flack, Judy Garland and Boris Karloff all once called the Dakota home too.

hed: Baby Boomers are pouring into Eastern seaboard state — rejecting cities’ unaffordable taxation
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The migration to Delaware’s beaches is no longer just about retirees hunting for a cheaper place to spend their golden years.
As residents continue to flock to the First State’s tiny coastline, the influx is reshaping everything from the homes being built to the farmland surrounding its beach towns.
Low property taxes, no state sales tax and access to the beach have been major draws, particularly for residents arriving from high-tax New York and New Jersey — and even neighboring Pennsylvania.
Indeed, as The Postpreviously reported, more than 40,000 people have moved to Delaware’s Sussex County since 2020, swelling its population by 17% — roughly five times the national growth rate.
Delaware’s population of residents 65 and older, meanwhile, surged 23% over the same period, more than any other state, as retirees increasingly looked beyond traditional destinations such as Florida.
Maggie, 64, and Vince Dominici, 70, are among the Northeasterners putting down roots along the Delaware coast. Vince is retired and lives fulltime in Delaware, while Maggie still works and divides her time between Bethany Beach and Bethlehem, Penn.
The Pennsylvania couple discovered Bethany Beach in July 2020 while searching for a family beach house. After spending a day exploring coastal Sussex County, they returned for a weeklong rental in August, bought the house in September and closed that November.
The home needed work, and Vince initially preferred moving farther inland, where their money could buy a newer property. Maggie held out for the location.
Vince now calls it “the best thing we ever disagreed on.”
The couple later downsized to a smaller residence in Bethlehem and expanded and remodeled the Bethany Beach house, which has become the family’s primary gathering place.
Their younger son, Devon Dominici, took the Delaware plunge even further.
After living in his parents’ beach house while working remotely during the pandemic, Devon built a four-bedroom, 3½-bath home of his own  in Ocean View, about 2 miles from Bethany Beach.
Property records show the newly built home transferred for nearly $600,000 in April 2023. A bank appraisal conducted in May valued it at 39% more than what it cost him to build, Devon said.
He believes proximity to the water will continue to underpin values in communities such as Bethany Beach, Ocean View, Dewey Beach and Rehoboth Beach, where developable land close to the coastline is limited.
“There’s really nowhere else to go,” he said. “So you’re buying existing inventory.”
The Dominicis are part of a much larger Northeast migration into coastal Delaware — one that local brokers say predates the pandemic by years.
Lee Ann Wilkinson, who has worked in Delaware real estate for decades, said buyers from other states have been retiring to the Delaware beaches for roughly 20 years. What has changed visibly is the amount and type of housing being created to accommodate them.
Sussex County itself issued 3,885 building permits in 2025, according to Census Bureaudata.
Many retiring buyers want low-maintenance communities where landscaping is handled for them, along with clubhouses, pools and social activities. First-floor primary bedrooms are another priority.
Developers have even adapted their floor plans to Northeastern transplants.
“A lot of people are looking for basements now, which we didn’t 20 years ago,” Wilkinson told The Post. “Now there’s a lot of homes with a basement because the people that are moving here are accustomed to having basements, so they had to start building basements here.”
Jen Barrows, a coastal Delaware broker, said a typical retiree she works with has a budget of roughly $400,000 to $800,000.
Even buyers who sell a New York-area home for $1 million or more frequently don’t want to pour all of the proceeds into their next house, she said.
“They want to bank some of that money,” Barrows said. “They don’t want to spend it all on their next house.”
Instead, many look several miles inland, where large planned communities offer amenities while keeping residents within reach of the coast.
Asked where buyers can find the best value, Wilkinson singled out Milton.
Barrows agreed, calling Milton “the one town that I think is probably the best value and has the most going on for the money.”
She pointed to its historic downtown, library, theater and nearby Dogfish Head brewery, along with a mix of new construction and existing homes.
“Milton’s just really a gem,” Barrows said. “There’s a lot of communities that are still very reasonably priced, from new construction to resale.”
Recent sales data bear out the price gap. Over the three months ending in August, the median sale price was about $439,000 in Milton, compared with roughly $774,000 in Lewes, $859,000 in Bethany Beach and $909,000 in Rehoboth Beach, according to Redfin.
Prices across coastal Delaware, however, are no longer the bargain they once were.
The Federal Housing Finance Agency’s home-price index for Sussex County climbed about 57% from 2020 through 2025. More recently, the market has begun to normalize: The county’s median sale price was about $439,000 in August, down 1.9% from a year earlier, according to Redfin.
For New Yorker Diana Rohan, a former member of the New York City Police Department who now works as a flight attendant, and her husband, also a former NYPD officer, the tax savings demonstrate why Delaware remains difficult to resist.
The couple bought a Delaware townhouse about five years ago after previously owning a second home in North Carolina.
Their annual Delaware property-tax bill is just $1,071, Rohan said.
Their property and school taxes back in New York? Nearly $17,000 a year.
“It’s a big difference,” Rohan told The Post. “We save a lot of money by purchasing here.”
The townhouse remains a second home shared with their children and other relatives. Delaware offered the couple a beach retreat considerably closer to their family in New York than their former North Carolina property.
Five years after buying, Rohan said they are “very happy” with the decision.
Still, she has watched the landscape around her change.
“I feel like they’re overdeveloping, though, because people are just buying like crazy,” she said. “There’s a lot of farmland that is turning into development.”
“Everywhere you go, you see the trucks and they’re building all over the place.”
That building boom is one of the growing pains accompanying Delaware’s newfound popularity.
Rapid population growth has brought worsening beach traffic and strained access to doctors and dentists, while rising incomes and housing costs threaten to make Sussex County increasingly difficult to afford for teachers, healthcare workers and other year-round employees.
The Dominicis have experienced those shortages firsthand.
Maggie and Vince said they had to rely on a personal connection to secure Vince a doctor’s appointment. Even then, an appointment they arranged in April was not available until the following February.
Traffic has become another persistent frustration, with ordinarily short drives turning into lengthy crawls during the summer.
Yet those drawbacks haven’t been enough to push the Dominicis away.
Bethany Beach, Devon said, remains something of a quiet bubble between more nightlife-heavy destinations such as Dewey Beach to the north and Ocean City, Md., to the south.
The town’s family-oriented character — along with restrictions on building heights, noise and late-night activity — was part of what attracted his parents in the first place.
Still given the perks of Delaware, Rohan isn’t ready to abandon New York entirely
Her 88-year-old mother remains there and relies on her for help with shopping, appointments and other daily needs. The couple’s daughter and other close relatives also live in New York.
For Rohan, the ability to keep one foot in each state is the point.
“We won’t leave New York full-time,” she said. But Delaware has given the couple a second life by the beach.
“When my husband and I are here, we go out to eat a lot. We go to the bars,” Rohan said. “We walk on the boardwalk. There’s a lot to do.”

hed: Baltimore homes jumped from $40K to $200K in months with no renovations in alleged ‘extensive real estate fraud scheme’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Baltimore rowhouse sells for $40,000. Just months later, it changes hands again for around $200,000.
There’s just one problem: According toa new lawsuit, virtually nothing happened to the house in between.
That dramatic leap in value was allegedly repeated across dozens ofBaltimore propertiesas part of a sprawling mortgage fraud scheme that one lender says left it with more than $14 million in losses.
AmeriTrust Mortgage Corp.filed a federal lawsuit in Maryland, accusing a network of real estate investors, a mortgage broker, appraisers and title companies of working together to make inexpensive properties appear far more valuable than they really were.
The alleged playbook was surprisingly simple.
Companies tied to the scheme would buy homesin and around Baltimorefor roughly $40,000 to $50,000, according to the complaint. Within months, and allegedly without making improvements, the properties would be sold to other shell companies for around $200,000 — a roughly 300% markup.
The much higher sale price could then support a much bigger mortgage.
AmeriTrust claims the new buyers applied for financing using appraisals and title reports that failed to disclose those recent, far cheaper transactions. In other words, the lender alleges it was being shown a $200,000 house without being told that the same property had recently been a $40,000 or $50,000 house.
Once the loan closed, the proceeds went to the seller.
Then, according to AmeriTrust’s charges, some borrowers barely bothered making payments.
The lender alleges the buying companies never intended to repay the mortgages and defaulted almost immediately, in some cases failing to make even the first few months of payments.
That left AmeriTrust in a bind. The company had sold the mortgages to investors, but once the loans went bad, it faced losses tied to mortgages that it alleges were far larger than the homes securing them were actually worth.
Multiply that process across roughly 90 loans and AmeriTrust says the damage reached about $14.1 million.
The lender is now accusing the defendants of fraud, conspiracy to defraud, breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation and civil racketeering under the federal RICO Act.
The defendants include mortgage broker FirstLoans Inc., title companies REXTAR Title Services and Fidelity National Title, as well as appraisers, investors and numerous LLCs.HousingWire reportedthat the defendants did not immediately respond to its requests for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.
At the center of the case are DSCR loans, a type of mortgage that has become popular with real estate investors.
Unlike a traditional home loan, where a lender focuses heavily on the borrower’s salary and personal income, a DSCR loan is underwritten based on how much rental income the property itself is expected to generate.
That can make it easier for landlords to finance investment properties — but AmeriTrust alleges the Baltimore operation paired those loans with inflated appraisals and title reports that concealed earlier, lower-priced transactions.
And the lender claims its own loans may represent only a fraction of the alleged activity.
The lawsuit alleges the same basic scheme was repeated hundreds of times across Baltimore, while earlier reporting found that hundreds of investment properties had been purchased at sharply inflated prices using hundreds of millions of dollars in DSCR loans from dozens of private lenders. More than half of those loans ultimately defaulted, according to HousingWire.
The fallout, AmeriTrust alleges, is now being felt on the ground: foreclosures could drag down surrounding property values, while some abandoned homes tied to the troubled loans have become occupied by squatters — further destabilizing neighborhoods already dealing with vacant properties.

hed: Quiet Florida fishing town undergoing a $2B luxury makeover is emerging as the next Palm Beach
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For decades, Pompano Beach was the sleepy South Florida alternative to its glitzier neighbors — a fishing town where waterfront living could still be had without Miami orPalm Beach prices.
Now, the secret is out.
The Broward County city is in the throes of a multibillion-dollar transformation, with a $2 billion downtown overhaul and a wave of ultra-luxury developments from Waldorf Astoria, Ritz-Carlton, W and Armani/Casa reshaping its once-low-key skyline.
At the center is a 75-acre redevelopment led by RocaPoint Partners in partnership with the city. Plans envision roughly 4 million square feet of residences, shops, offices, hotels, civic facilities and public spaces, anchored by a new City Hall.
But some of Pompano’s biggest changes are happening along the sand.
Miami-based Related Group has made a multibillion-dollar commitment to the city, beginning with a gamble it took long before Pompano became a magnet forluxury developers.
“We saw the fundamentals early: incredible oceanfront, a great location between Miami and Palm Beach, and pricing that was still accessible relative to other South Florida coastal markets,” Patrick Campbell, senior vice president of Related Group, told The Post.
“We actually bought the oceanfront site that would eventually become Solemar at a courthouse auction in 2011 and held onto it for nearly a decade,” Campbell said. “At the time, Pompano wasn’t yet viewed as a luxury destination, but we believed the ingredients were there.”
They were. Solemar, Related’s first project in the city, sold for an average of about $900 per square foot, Campbell said. Its latest sales at the under-construction Waldorf Astoria Residences Pompano Beach are now averaging roughly twice that, at $1,800 per square foot.
Related also soldtwo Waldorf penthousesfor $17.1 million and $18.1 million this summer, setting new benchmarks for Pompano.
“Those numbers tell us buyers are willing to pay for exceptional product here, but there’s still asignificant pricing gapbetween Pompano and comparable branded oceanfront residences in Miami or Palm Beach,” Campbell said. “That’s what gives us confidence there’s still room for the market to grow.”
The 28-story Waldorf tower, developed by Related and Merrimac Ventures with Hilton, will contain just 92 residences and is expected to be completed next summer. More than 85% of its units were under contract when the building topped out in May. It is also Waldorf Astoria’s first standalone residential development.
The project’s amenities are decidedly more resort than sleepy beach town, including a 20,000-square-foot oceanfront pool deck, spa and wellness facilities, concierge service and in-residence dining.
Related is also behind W Pompano Beach Hotel & Residences, while other developers have brought Ritz-Carlton and Armani/Casa projects to the area.
The new construction is attracting a broader group of buyers.
“We continue to see strong interest from the Northeast and Canada, along with a significant local component — South Florida and inland Florida buyers who want to be directly on the ocean,” Campbell said.
But he said interest is increasingly coming from Latin America and other overseas markets, particularly at the W development.
Despite the influx of big-money buyers and luxury brands, Campbell doesn’t think Pompano needs to turn itself into another Palm Beach.
“I don’t think Pompano needs to become the next Miami or Palm Beach…that’s what makes it interesting,” he said. “It still has that relaxed, Old Florida beach-town character, but the level of product and hospitality is changing dramatically.”
That balancing act could determine what Pompano becomes as billions of dollars pour in.
“Five years from now, I think you’ll have a much more established luxury destination while still being able to walk down to the pier, go fishing and feel like you’re in a real beach town,” Campbell said.
“The city is changing, but it’s retaining its character — and that balance is what will continue to differentiate Pompano.”

hed: How homebuyers can ‘rate-proof’ their budgets in a volatile mortgage market
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Homebuyers facesevere uncertaintythis fall amid surging mortgage rates and stubbornly high living costs, but those who prepare and take stock of their finances early can shield their budgets from unexpected spikes.
Last week, the average rate on 30-year fixed home loanssurged to an 18-month high of 6.95%, propelled by climbing 10-year Treasury yields as the Federal Reserveincreased its interest ratesfor the first time in three years.
These developments have made home shoppers question whether they can manage monthly payments on their purchase, as reflected in a slowdown in August’s existing-home sales.
To offer jittery buyers guidance on navigating market uncertainty, Realtor.com® researchers analyzedmonthly mortgage rate shifts dating to 2000, establishing clear benchmarks for how much rates typically fluctuate over time—and how risk-averse buyers can adjust their budgets accordingly.
“Rate-proofing for potential buyers right now is super important because they can’t build assumptions for their finances on the chance that interest rates may go down,”Ralph DiBugnara, president of Home Qualified, tells Realtor.com.
“They need to be comfortable with the monthly payment, whether the rates go down or up, and build their budgets around that. This is not a market where you can time for the best rate and the best price that’s the best fit for you.”
If their purchase window extends over the next 12 months, buyers are advised to be ready for a mortgage rate to move as much as 100 basis points in either direction of today’s rate, a range that covers 80% of historical scenarios considered in the analysis.
For example, if the current 30-year fixedmortgage rate is roughly 7%, a home shopper should be equally prepared for the rate to drop to 6% or surge to 8% by next September.
As Realtor.com senior economistJoel Bernerexplains, this mathematical exercise carries major real-world consequences.
For a buyer with a monthly budget of $2,000 for mortgage payments, the difference between a 6% and an 8% mortgage rate determines whether they can take on a loan balance of $333,583 at the low end or $272,567 at the high end.
“The potential variability in rates one year out can create a range of over $60,000 in homebuying power for this hypothetical buyer,” says Berner.
Tania Jhayem, a real estate agent atKeller Williams The Marketplace‘s luxury division in Las Vegas, says that in the current environment, where buyers’ affordability is already stretched thin, “rate-proofing” for the future is the smart approach.
“Buyers shouldn’t build a home search around the assumption that the rate they see today will still be available three, six, or 12 months from now,” she tells Realtor.com. “Rather than asking, ‘What can I afford at today’s rate?’ I would encourage buyers to ask, ‘What can I still comfortably afford if rates are higher when I actually purchase?'”
An aspiring homeowner starting to plan six months in advance should budget for mortgage rates to move up to 75 basis points up or down.
For the buyer operating on a $2,000 monthly budget, a rate jump to 7.75% lowers their loan capacity to $279,169.
On the other hand, if mortgage rates retreat to 6.25%, that purchasing power expands to $324,824—a buying power boost of more than $45,000.
“The further out buyers feel they are from actually closing on a home, whether it be 60, 90, 120, or 180 days, the bigger the payment buffer they are using as a variable should be,” says DiBugnara. “I would always want a buyer to be very conservative on the low side and use the high side of interest rate and monthly payments to make decisions on homes they want to purchase.”
According to Jhayem, building a rate buffer into a budget helps buyers identify a price point they can actually afford.
“If someone is six months away and planning around a 75-basis-point swing, we can establish their comfortable monthly payment first and then determine the price range that still works under that higher rate scenario,” says the agent. “The goal isn’t necessarily to qualify for the maximum amount. It’s to make sure the purchase still feels financially comfortable if the market moves against you.”
Shoppers who have a narrower timeline of three months to make a move have a better sense of where the rates will land when they go toobtain a loan.Historically, 80% of the time, rates fluctuate 40 to 45 basis points in either direction over the course of three months.
To be on a more conservative side with an extra cushion, Realtor.com experts suggest that buyers allow for 50 basis points of movement from the current rate.
In other words, a buyer looking to secure a home just before Christmas this year should budget for the 30-year fixed mortgage rate to edge down to as low at 6.5% or rise to as high as 7.5%.
For the hypothetical $2,000-per-month buyer, this range of rates translates into loan balances of $316,422 and $286,035, respectively.
“This roughly $30,000 difference is still sizable, a sign of how much buyers need to be flexible,” notes Berner.
Consider a home purchaser three months away from closing on the median-priced property of $424,500, assuming a 10% down payment. If the rates stay at around 7%, the buyer’s monthly principal and interest payment would amount to $2,542.
If the rate edges down to 6.5%, that monthly payment would shrink to $2,415. However, should the rate rise to 7.5%, where it was in November 2023, the payment will increase to $2,671.
To rate-proof their homebuying budget, the shopper should be prepared to pay $129 more or $127 less per month, depending on how the rates move.
Mortgage volatility is a constant feature of the homebuying process, no matter the state of the economy. What a buyer can afford continuously shifts: a dream home that was within budget just a week ago can suddenly become out of reach today depending on rate ups and downs.
But experts maintain that following these guidelines makes these shifts more predictable, allowing shoppers to be better prepared and more empowered to take control of their homebuying.
“Currently, homebuyers need to be very cautious on how much they gamble on interest rates for the homes they’re interested in,” says DiBugnara. “They move much faster up than they will down. Interest rates coming down any significant amount will take a long period of time, and it is very tied to how fast inflation can come down.”

Both DiBugnara and Jhayem agree that trying to time mortgage rates is next to impossible.
“Instead, buyers should know their payment at several different rate scenarios before they write an offer,” suggests the Vegas agent. “They should also understand what options may be available if rates move higher, including permanent rate buydowns, seller concessions where appropriate, adjusting the down payment, or simply changing the purchase price.”
Meanwhile, the Home Qualified president urges shoppers to “control their own controllables,” meaning to prepare for a home purchase by reducing their other monthly debt obligations and boosting savings.
Jhayem describes this process as creating “financial breathing room” by paying down revolving debt to improve debt-to-income ratios to give the buyer more flexibility if mortgage rates swing up.
