hed: Soccer legend Thierry Henry asks $25M for his eye-catching all-glass NYC penthouse
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Soccer legendThierry Henryis taking another shot at selling his sprawlingSohopenthouse — this time asking $25 million for the Manhattan spread he and his partner once loved too much to let go.
The former Arsenal and FC Barcelona star and his partner, Andrea Rajacic, have relisted their penthouse at 39 Crosby St., according to theWall Street Journal.
It’s a stunning, roughly 6,086-square-foot residence with five bedrooms, five full bathrooms, two powder rooms and some 3,400 square feet of private outdoor space.
The asking price works out to roughly $4,108 per square foot.
Henry purchased the penthouse and the apartment below for $14.85 million in 2010, the same year he left Barcelona to join theNew York Red Bulls, according to the Journal. The couple subsequently combined the units into the massive, glassy residence they have today.
The purchase came after an exhaustive day of apartment hunting in Manhattan that almost ended without a winner.
Their agent convinced them to squeeze in one final showing — the Crosby Street penthouse, with sweeping views that include the Brooklyn and Williamsburg bridges.
The couple immediately fell for it.
Henry and Rajacic lived in the home full-time for roughly five years before relocating to London following his retirement from professional soccer in late 2014. They held onto the Manhattan property and continued using it during trips to New York, though those visits became less frequent over time.
They first tried to part with the home last year, asking $26.75 million, but ultimately pulled it from the market. The penthouse returned this week with a $25 million price tag — $1.75 million below its previous ask.
“We were and still are in love with the place,” Henry told the Journal, adding that leaving New York had been “very difficult.”
The home has undergone several renovations over the years, including another update this year.
Its main living level features roughly 14-foot ceilings, walls of glass, a gas fireplace and an adjoining terrace, with views stretching from the Brooklyn Bridge to One World Trade Center and across Soho’s historic rooftops.
The private rooftop adds a pergola, a barbecue area, and spaces for outdoor dining and lounging. Altogether, the residence has four private outdoor spaces and nearly 360-degree exposures.
But one of its biggest luxuries may actually be downstairs.
The property comes with two deeded parking spaces and keyed elevator access, allowing its owner to go directly from the garage to the residence — an especially rare setup in Soho. It also includes about 250 square feet of private storage.
The primary suite occupies its own level and includes a private terrace, while the residence also offers multiple living and entertaining areas spread across several floors.
The penthouse crowns a boutique cast-iron and brick building originally designed by architect Edward H. Kendall in the 1870s and converted into condominiums in 2010.
Joshua Judge, Glenn Norrgard and Samantha Sitinas of Sotheby’s International Realty hold the listing.

hed: Nick and Vanessa Lachey list their LA house again — after buying it back from tennis star Naomi Osaka
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Obsessed “Love is Blind” fans can now get a sneak peek inside power couple — and show hosts —Nick and Vanessa Lachey’sstunning Los Angeles home.
The couple loved their Tarzana dwelling so much that they bought it twice. But now, they’re looking to sell it again,Realtor.com reports.
The gated home, which comes with San Fernando Valley views, is now on the market for $8.19 million. The listing comes as the couple and their three kids — Camden, 14, Phoenix, 9 and Brooklyn, 11 — are leaving California “to start a new chapter,” said listing brokers Mauricio Umansky and Craig Knizek of the Agency.
The couple first bought the property for around $5 million in Dec 2020 from NFL wide receiverRandall Cobb, who was last with the New York Jets in 2023. But in February 2022, the Lacheys sold it for $6.26 million in an off-market deal to tennis superstarNaomi Osaka, according to records.
Under Osaka’s ownership, the home’s footprint expanded significantly. She added an 800-square-foot one-bedroom guest house and gym with a spa bath and a kitchenette.
But the Lacheys loved the home so much — including Osaka’s reimagining of it — that they bought it back for $7.95 million in August 2025 . (Before they bought the house back, the Lacheys had purchased a home in Encino for $6.8 million in July 2024. It sold at a loss in June for $6.15 million.)
Built in 2014, the listed East Coast-traditional-style home sits on a coveted cul-de-sac on three quarters of an acre.
At 6,855 square feet, it features five bedrooms, five baths and two powder rooms. Entertaining amenities include an “entertainer’s bar with a wine room” that holds more than 500 bottles. There’s also a home movie theater that seats eight, a home office, multiple fireplaces, hardwood floors and glass walls showcasing mountain and valley views.
A roomy, eat-in chef’s kitchen that comes with two center islands anchors it all. There’s also a formal dining room and a living room with coffered ceilings, a fireplace, built-in bookcases and pocket doors that open to a covered outdoor area.
Upstairs, a primary bedroom suite boasts a private balcony with panoramic views of the San Fernando Valley as well as two walk-in closets and a spa-like bath.
Outside there’s a full-length lighted basketball court — it can double as a pickleball or volleyball court — a pool, an outdoor kitchen and a firepit.



“It’s rare to have some many coveted attributes in one house. It has everything that every buyer wants – views, land and private security,” Knizek told Gimme Shelter.

hed: Wealthy Hamptons homebuyers set their sights away from oceanfront mansions — but not because they can’t afford them
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In the Hamptons, $20 million no longer necessarily buys you the Atlantic Ocean.
For decades, the rule of thumb in Hamptons real estate was simple. If you wanted to spend big, you bought on the beach. But that math is starting to change.
A rarefied group of deep-pocketed buyers is increasingly shelling outoceanfront-level money for estatesfarther inland, trading direct access to the surf for something even harder to find on the East End these days: space.
The emerging shift is showing up north of the highway, on bays and across sprawling interior parcels where buyers can get the privacy, acreage and elaborate amenities that have become increasingly difficult to create along the heavily regulated coastline.
“We’re seeing numbers in the $20 million range north of the highway,” Douglas Elliman broker Kyle Rosko told The Post.
Exhibit A is 29 Wills Point Road in Montauk. The brand-new seven-bedroom bayfront spec mansion is roughly 10,000 square feet. It sold this month for its full $23 million asking price after landing a buyer just three days after hitting the market in July. Public listing records show the deal closed Sept. 7.
The sale set a new high-water mark for a non-oceanfront Montauk home, according to Rosko, who represented the listing.
“The demand for that is higher than ever … people want that space,” he added. “And if they can accomplish that space, they’re willing to go away from the ocean and away from south of the highway.”
And he would know. Rosko said he also handled the previous $17 million record last year at 18 Maple St., after earlier setting the benchmark at $14 million.
The jump is especially striking because $23 million was oceanfront territory in Montauk as recently as last year.
For perspective, Rosko said he closed three Montauk oceanfront deals over the past year, and every one of them went for less.
But 29 Wills Point isn’t exactly a consolation prize for someone who couldn’t land a house on the ocean.
Set on 1.6 acres overlooking Fort Pond Bay in Culloden Point, Italian architect Piero Lissoni designed the house. It has glass walls running floor to ceiling and a courtyard built around a mature Japanese maple. Outside there’s a rooftop lounge, a 56-foot infinity pool and a private path down to the bay.
So why pay beachfront money for a bay view? It comes down to space, and the rules that govern it.
In late 2024, East Hampton Town, which includes Montauk, cut the maximum size of a single-family home in half, from 20,000 square feet to 10,000. A separate formula now caps how much can be built based on lot size. Oceanfront parcels also face an extra gauntlet of FEMA and coastal regulations.
Rosko said Wills Point was permitted before the tougher limits took hold, and that a house like it could not realistically rise on the ocean today.
“It’s pretty much impossible to amass a piece of oceanfront property that would allow for this type of house to be built,” he said.
The bigger story, Rosko said, is what the property’s record price says about what ultra-rich buyers now value.
Buyers with a wish list that runs to barns and tennis and padel courts rarely find the acreage on the sand. Instead, they are heading inland, where bigger parcels still exist.
“There’s only so much land left,” Rosko said.
“A one-of-one location isn’t always the ocean,” Rosko said. “A one-of-one location can be in a setting that gives you a view and a vista that’s incredibly unique and very powerful.”
Jonathan Miller, president and CEO of appraisal firm Miller Samuel, said the shift remains relatively new.
“Over the last five years, sales at or above $20 million were largely those with ocean front views. Beginning last year, we began to see a few $20 million or higher sales north of the highway,” Miller told The Post.
He attributed the change partly to tight supply at the top of the market and strong Wall Street compensation, while cautioning that ultra-luxury sales can swing significantly from year to year depending on which properties become available.
He also agreed the town’s size crackdown is sending buyers elsewhere.
“The limits on home size construction force a growing number of buyers to look for alternative locations to create a house the size they want, and that seems to be north of the highway,” Miller said. “Teardowns in the East End almost always result in a new home that is substantially larger than the original.”
Rosko has more on deck. He is preparing to list a $27.5 million spec mansion north of the highway, and said a couple of nearby homes recently went into contract above $20 million.
Still, nobody should write off the beach.
Miller cautioned that the inland megadeals are “still a very small niche of the super luxury market, in the very early stages of evolving.”
“Oceanfront pricing continues to expand faster,” he said.
Scarcity is doing the heavy lifting there. Owners rarely build on the ocean on spec, so few homes come up, and the ones that dofetch staggering sums.Earlier this year, a contemporary oceanfront home on Beach Lane in Wainscott changed hands off-market for $59 million, up from $45 million in 2021.
Rosko is quietly shopping a 10,000-square-foot Montauk oceanfront estate for $60 million, a figure that would set a record for the hamlet.
He added that some off-market oceanfront asking prices across the Hamptons have climbed north of $275 million. As for why so many of these trophies never hit the open market, “It really has to do with privacy,” he said.
Demand isn’t cooling with the weather either. Rosko said he got seven or eight requests to touroceanfront homesin his portfolio in a single recent weekend.
“That’s a lot of requests for oceanfront, especially when it is not the summer season,” he said.
In other words, the richest buyers aren’t being priced out of the beach. Many of them just want more house than the beach will allow.

hed: NYC gets crushed in affordability ranking for renters — but nearly tops the list for 1 huge perk
subhead: Manhattan costs a fortune — but quality of life is near the top
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York City may have world-class transit, walkable neighborhoods and endless cultural amenities — but renters are paying dearly for those perks.
Manhattan, Queens and Brooklyn all landed near the bottom ofRentCafe’s 2026 rankingof the 150 best US cities for renters, which analyzed 20 metrics spanning housing and cost of living, the local economy and quality of life.
Manhattan ranked No. 137 overall, while Queens came in at No. 147 and Brooklyn at No. 148 — putting two of the city’s biggest boroughs just a few spots from the bottom.
Manhattan’s biggest problem probably won’t surprise anyone who has written a rent check there.
The borough ranked dead last at No. 150 for housing and cost of living,with expenses runninga whopping 138.9% above the national average. Apartments average 759 square feet.
But renters are getting something for all that money.
Manhattan ranked No. 3 nationwide for quality of life, with more than half of its apartments located in top-rated areas close to transit, green space and everyday amenities.
It also took the No. 1 spot nationally for public transit and walking, with 61.1% of residents getting around that way, while ranking No. 25for school quality.
Its economic showing was considerably stronger, too. Manhattan ranked No. 33 for its local economy, with 336 business applications per 10,000 residents and nearly half of residents classified as highly educated.
Brooklyn fared even worse overall, ranking No. 148, and came in at No. 149 for housing and cost of living.
Its cost of livingis 63.9% above the national average, while apartments average just 735 square feet. Still, 15.6% of its apartment stock is new, and renter incomes have surged 39.1% over five years — the strongest growth among the three boroughs.
Brooklyn also performed considerably better for quality of life, ranking No. 58 nationally. Some 55% of residents use public transit, the second-highest share in the country.
Queens finishedjust one spot ahead at No. 147 overall. It was the least expensive of the three boroughs, although its cost of living remains 53.8% above the national average — and its apartments are actually the smallest, averaging 730 square feet.
Queens ranked No. 3 nationally for public transit and walking and No. 22 for school quality, the best showing among the three boroughs.
But getting around can still be a slog: 62% of Queens residents face long solo commutes, the third-highest share in the country.
Elsewhere in New York, renters had better luck. Albany ranked No. 64 nationally, the state’s best showing, followed by Buffalo at No. 131and Rochesterat No. 134.
For city renters, the rankings highlight a familiar tradeoff: some of the country’s best transit and big-city amenities come with one of its steepest price tags.

hed: The Globe’s housing reporter thought he’d have an edge finding an apartment. He had no idea what was coming.
subhead: Finding a place required wading through thousands of listings, unresponsive brokers, and fierce competition with other tenants
content: It was a beautiful Thursday evening in April — one of those first sunny spring days that makes you remember why you live here — and I was running down the sidewalk in East Boston.A few hours earlier, I had toured a distinctive apartment near Magoun Square in Somerville with my partner. I was expecting an email from the landlord any second, and my phone was about to die. In Greater Boston’s cutthroat housing market, nice, well-priced apartments frequently go to one of two kinds of applicants: Those who make a boatload of money, or those who move fast.So there I was, with neither a boatload of money nor sufficient sleep, weaving between pedestrians on Bennington Street, desperate to fill out an application before someone else did.This is what it takes to find an apartment around here.As The Boston Globe’s housing reporter, I spend my professional life writing about Massachusetts’ intractable housing problem, and how it warps the lives of so many people in this state — especially renters. But the ever-rising cost of housing is big in my personal life, too. Countless friends have moved away because rents are too high; others complain about the city’s notorious Sept. 1 shuffle — when about two-thirds of all the leases in Boston turn over.Finding a new apartment is, in a word, a nightmare. Every decent listing seemingly has 50 interested applicants. Some brokers still try to charge steep (and mostly now-illegal) fees. And the rent itself soars higher every year. Related: Landlords can no longer require renters to pay the middlemanFor years, I have managed to avoid the anguish of a housing search here by staying put in my charming-if-slightly-tattered apartment in an East Boston three-decker. But I have finally outgrown that place, and my partner — Globe transportation reporter Diti Kohli — and I decided in March that it was time to look for somewhere new.I initially dismissed the seriousness of this endeavor, and volunteered to head our search. As someone who writes about housing for a living, I figured I would be uniquely equipped to navigate Boston’s frenetic rental market.I had no idea what lay in store.Apartment buildings in Union Square in Somerville in 2018.Craig F. WalkerThe apartment in Magoun Square was a great find — a first-floor unit in a little multifamily building steps from the Green Line extension. It met much of what we were looking for: Outdoor space, a good kitchen, plenty of windows for our cat, Mittens. With friends nearby, Somerville was our preferred neighborhood. And at $2,700 a month, it was in our price range.The challenge, of course, would be beating out dozens of other applicants.Half the trouble of apartment hunting here — if you want to avoid a several-thousand-dollar broker fee, that is — is poring through the sheer volume of listings online. There are dozens of websites, from local brokerages to national sites like Apartments.com, with thousands of apartments to choose from. It’s no simple feat to figure out what is a real, available apartment, and what isn’t. It requires backgrounding landlords and brokers, finding an actual person to set up a tour, ensuring move-in timing works — all while hoping that some better-financed renter doesn’t beat you to the punch.As it turned out, shockingly few of the thousands of apartments listed online were available on our timeline, or fit even a few of our criteria we had established. For those, competition was fierce. And many landlords and brokers didn’t return messages.When they did, there were often issues, like that some were charging broker fees, which was a nonstarter. (Massachusetts mostly outlawed tenant-paid broker fees last year, but some brokers still charge them, sometimes through a loophole with so-called “open listings” that are shared by multiple brokers, or in apparent violation of the law in other instances.)“Does the landlord have any flexibility on the broker fee?” I had asked the broker of one Somerville apartment.This broker actually wrote me back. “No.” Related: Massachusetts finally banned broker fees. Why are renters still stuck paying them?Before long, apartment-hunting became something of a full-time job. I turned on Zillow notifications for new listings in our preferred neighborhoods — Somerville, Jamaica Plain, perhaps Dorchester. Each buzz of my phone sent my heart rate soaring. Maybe this was the place? But our search quickly fell into a tiresome pattern: Either a listing would be for a place that wouldn’t work for us, or it would be somewhere that looked right, but the landlord would already be swamped with applications. March drifted into April, and apartments available for Sept. 1 move-ins were quickly getting scooped up.A "for rent" sign in Mission Hill in 2025.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffSo when Bethany, the owner of that apartment in Magoun Square, messaged me back to set up a tour, the stakes suddenly felt very high.It may sound ridiculous, but I spent two days rehearsing what I would say to her.The night before the tour, I could barely sleep.When we arrived at the apartment, a woman who looked to be around 30 and had clearly just finished her own tour was outside chatting with Bethany, laughing and looking very personable. I muttered something to Diti about her apparent charm offensive, and offered the woman a smile as we walked in. She did not smile back. Without a word, it felt like she was telling us: “This place is mine.”Bethany, a kind woman whose arms were full of tattoos and appeared very much like the sort of person who would own a building in Somerville, explained that she already had more than a dozen tours lined up, with more to come. We tried our best to be charming. We asked questions and chatted about Bethany’s impending move to Portugal. I sprinted home from the Blue Line and returned our application as soon as it landed in our inbox.But I just had a feeling that we weren’t getting this place. And sure enough, three days later, Bethany wrote back.Good afternoon,Thank you for the application. We just signed a lease.Good luck in your search!Ouch. I realized at that point that I had probably let the search process get to me more than was reasonable. But this is an experience shared by many Boston 20-somethings, including those who make significantly more money than Diti and me.There is an argument to be made that a tight housing market is a good thing — a sign that, despite the region’s recent struggles, demand to live here remains high. Indeed while rents have been dropping in some other high-cost rental markets lately, they’re still rising in Greater Boston. At the same time, when 20- and 30-somethings with professional jobs can’t find an apartment, it’s a clear sign the region simply doesn’t have enough homes for the people who want to live here. When young professionals struggle to find housing at their tier of the housing market, it puts even more pressure on working-class families, who are leaving the region due to cost pressures in increasing numbers. Related: Forever renters: For many in Greater Boston, the American dream of homeownership ‘no longer exists’I decided after the Magoun Square debacle that I needed to shift my strategy away from Zillow searches, and perhaps focus on Jamaica Plain, where I hoped competition might be less intense. I started wandering neighborhoods hunting for “for rent” signs, and even turned to a platform I had previously shunned: Craigslist.There, small landlords were advertising units in old multifamily buildings — the sort of buildings that Diti and I love. After a few failed attempts, I stumbled upon a broker who seemed to exclusively work with small landlords. I perused her portfolio and found a unit that almost seemed too good to be true: A 1,000 square-foot two-bedroom in an old triple-decker near an Orange Line station. It had a front porch, a walk-in pantry, and some interesting built-in quirks like a stained-glass window.New and old housing side-by-side in Jamaica Plain in 2019.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffThe broker answered her phone after one ring, and offered to show us the place the following day. On the tour, she said the apartment had been on the market for a few weeks, and while a couple of people had liked it, no one had yet applied.She handed us a paper application form and told us to email the completed version to her as soon as possible.Driving home, Diti and I talked about how much we both loved the place. So we pulled over at a Dunkin’, filled out the application by hand, and emailed it back.A few days later the broker texted. The owner wants to meet you on Sunday . . . to go forward!A few days later, we met our new landlords — a couple who have lived in Jamaica Plain and owned the triple decker for decades — at JP Licks on Centre Street, and signed the lease.We recently got the keys, and though we aren’t moving for a few more weeks (to avoid the peak Sept. 1 moving costs), we stopped by the other day to plan and clean.As we sat there munching on a pastry from what will be one of our new neighborhood cafes, I realized that there was still one thing I had forgotten to do.I pulled out my phone and deleted the Zillow app. Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: ‘The idea is to build as fast as possible’: Developers seek to build nearly 2,000 units in Southie
subhead: Could a grocery store come to Dorchester and Old Colony avenues?
content: A development team behind one of New York’s tallest residential skyscrapers intends to build 1,945 homes on a prime South Boston site — property where Southie native Andrew J. Collins long dreamed of building.New York-based J.T. Magen & Co. and Extell Development in March successfully bid $75 million at a public foreclosure auction — held on St. Patrick’s Day — to buy a collection of industrial property along Dorchester Avenue where it splits from Old Colony Avenue. The site, located midway between the Broadway and Andrew MBTA Red Line stations, is at the heart of a decade-old city plan that called for a corridor of dense, tall development in what is now a low-slung industrial zone. Now the group has kicked off the city’s formal development-review process, with local partner Thomas O’Brien of The HYM Investment Group this month alerting Boston officials of the plan to build 1.8 million square feet of residential and retail space at 314-420 Dorchester Ave. In terms of space, that’s just a tad larger than the former John Hancock tower in the Back Bay, though the Southie project will be developed as multiple buildings.Collins, the identical twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, spent years cobbling together multiple parcels along the Dot. Ave. corridor and pitching a life-science campus there. Despite persuading a number of investors to funnel money toward a project, Andrew Collins never got a development off the ground. Collins has faced a number of lawsuits in state and federal court from investors claiming he owes them around $150 million. The city of Boston in 2016 highlighted the Dorchester Avenue corridor between the Broadway and Andrew MBTA stations as "an opportunity to build a 21st-century district." Here's a rendering from the 2016 Plan: South Boston Dorchester Avenue showing the conceptual buildout of the district.City of BostonThe J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM development is one of the largest new housing projects proposed in Boston in years. The group envisions a collection of four 200-foot residential buildings with about 45,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and is exploring the potential to bring a grocery store to the site. None of the buildings would rise higher than 200 feet, O’Brien said. At that height, the buildings would be roughly 18 stories. The project would have underground parking, which costs about $350,000 per space to build.O’Brien, who last year briefly considered challenging Mayor Michelle Wu’s reelection, declined to share an estimated total development cost. However, new high-rise residential construction in Boston these days can cost more than $1 million per unit to build. The development team hopes to have all permits in hand by early next year.“The idea is to build as fast as possible,” O’Brien said. “Not much housing is being built right now. ... You’d be delivering those units into a market that has not had much new product, and that’s a really important consideration.” The anemic pace at which Boston is permitting and constructing housing is a top concern for many residents and the regional real estate development community, many of whom have sought to build outside city limits given the expense of developing in Boston. Approving 2,000 units would help the Wu administration’s preliminary goal of adding 3,000 new units annually over her second four-year term, which started in January. Capping the buildings’ height at 200 feet aligns with the city’s adopted plan for the Dot. Ave. corridor. Still, because the plan’s guidelines were never incorporated in Boston’s zoning code, the J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM partnership would need additional approval in order to build anywhere near that high.The first building would likely be situated on a triangular-shaped parcel, currently home to a parking lot and vacant Castle Self Storage facility. The distinctive shape gives Boston-based architecture firm CBT “an opportunity for a really beautiful design,” O’Brien said.A St. Patrick's Day foreclosure auction of 10 parcels in South Boston was held in the triangular-shaped parking lot of the Castle Self Storage facility. Suzanne Kreiter/Globe StaffExtell has built in Boston before, but not for decades. In 2006, the firm built the waterfront Intercontinental Hotel and Residences in downtown. “These are two groups who are very familiar with Boston, and they understand the basic dynamics of what makes our city great,” O’Brien said. As for the drive-through Dunkin’ located at 75 Old Colony Ave. in the center of the site, the Extell, J.T. Magen and HYM team intends for it to “stay for as long as possible,” O’Brien said. Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: US judge blocks Trump overhaul of funding for fair housing groups
content: A federal judge on Wednesday blocked President Trump’s administration from restructuring a federal grant program to redirect money away from over 100 non-profit organizations that had historically received funding to help prevent and investigate housing discrimination.US District Judge Myong Joun in Boston ruled that the US Department of Housing and Urban Development had failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its decision to implement “sweeping changes” to a decades-old grant program run by the agency designed to combat housing discrimination.HUD did not respond to a request for comment.The judge, an appointee of President Biden, said that Congress had long recognized the need to provide funding for fair housing organizations to help support the work of HUD, which had funded them through multi-year grants.Yet he said HUD in July upended that system of enforcing the Fair Housing Act by announcing it would not allocate any of its congressionally appropriated funding for the 2025 fiscal year to private enforcement initiatives or to multi-year grants issued through the Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP), which Congress created in 1987.In the past, HUD would typically award more than 100 grants ranging from $75,000 to $425,000, according to lawyers for several fair housing groups, including the National Fair Housing Alliance that sued over the changes in July.HUD instead planned to use $46 million of the $56 million that Congress had appropriated for just five grants, $25 million of which would go to a law school. The remaining $10 million could go to a state or local agency.“The effect of HUD’s restructure effectively bars the very housing organizations that have been effectuating FHIP’s mission year after year since its enactment,” Joun said. The Trump administration also sought to force grant recipients to sign onto unrelated conditions to receive funding, by imposing requirements that they not use any funding to support “gender ideology” or “illegal immigration.”HUD had argued it had the discretion to impose those conditions and that the changes it was making to the grant program were part of a large-scale modernization effort designed to broaden participation.But Joun said that “pithy description falls woefully short of the mark in both form and substance,” and that it was “hard to see how or where defendants relied on relevant data in crafting these changes.”

hed: In bid to boost Boston housing supply, Wu proposes tax relief that could jumpstart more than 1,000 units
content: Mayor Michelle Wu Monday proposed short-term tax relief for a handful of market-rate housing projects, in a bid to jumpstart the city’s sluggish development pipeline and speed at least 1,400 new units into construction by 2027. The tax breaks, proposed for four projects that have already been approved by the Boston Planning Department, are part of a broader effort that will see officials deploy “targeted, time-limited tax abatements” for residential developments 100 units or larger that have been unable to break ground due to financing constraints. The total tax relief for those four projects will be worth roughly $31.5 million, city officials said. “Residents urgently need more housing now, and we can’t afford to let approved projects that are ready to build remain stalled because of today’s tough economic headwinds,” Wu said. “Boston is open for business and we’ll keep using every tool available to get more housing built for our residents.”The proposal will be considered by the BPDA board in October after a 30-day public comment period. It marks a distinct shift for Wu, who in 2023 briefly considered tax breaks for newly built market-rate housing projects before backing away from such a move. Her approach to housing has instead focused heavily on boosting the production of subsidized homes in the city, and some developers have complained that those policies have contributed to their financing difficulties. Boston relies heavily on tax revenue from development to balance its budget, and the construction of new homes has fallen off significantly over the last few years amid rising interest rates and construction costs. Today, thousands of units permitted by the city are stalled because developers can’t finance them. Only two projects of 100 units or more started construction in 2025. The challenges are so significant that city housing officials are considering lowering their housing production target for Wu’s second term, the Globe reported last week. Meanwhile, rents and home prices have continued to rise as demand outpaces supply, and political pressure to address the cost of housing has ratcheted up. With the new proposal, Wu is throwing financial help to market-rate housing developers. It is an indication, advocates and officials said, that her administration is willing to work with developers to get housing built. The four projects for which Wu proposed relief Monday include: a 16-story, 408-unit development across from the Sullivan Orange Line station in Charlestown, a 16-story, 318-unit project on Pratt Street in Allston, a 333-unit development on Leo Birmingham Parkway in Brighton, and a 341-unit mixed-use project across from the Mass Pike near Boston Landing. With the tax break, New England Development would aim to start construction on the next phase of work at Allston Yards, said John Twohig, the company’s executive vice president, in a statement.“In this difficult fiscal climate, we have been working hard to find a path to deliver more housing at Allston Yards,” Twohig said. “The city’s proposed abatement is a critical tool to help move that housing forward.” Representatives for the other three developers behind the projects that could receive tax breaks — Fulcrum Global Investors, Hines, and Nordblom Co. — did not respond to requests for comment by press time.Kairos Shen, the city’s planning chief, said Monday that tax incentives will only be available on a limited basis, and that any such relief would be “modest and prudent.” City officials are only considering abatements for large projects that meet the city’s subsidized housing and energy-efficiency standards, and are “right on the goal line” of working out their financing, Shen said, and would be able to begin construction in 2027 with the help of a tax break. And officials will closely review projects to ensure developers aren’t receiving more relief than they need.Shen said the mayor “recognizes that this is a difficult and in some respects unprecedented economic time, and that we have data that have shown that it is time for us to deploy this last sort of tool that we have available to get construction going.“ ”The goal is to let people know that Boston is interested in investment and that we’re really open for business, but we’re going to be prudent in making sure that this is something that can actually lead to action,” Shen said.In total, Wu is willing to spend around $100 million on tax relief, which officials believe could accelerate as many as 4,000 units. Officials are currently in discussions with around one dozen other projects about the prospect of relief. There are 47 projects in the development pipeline 100 units or larger that could meet the city’s criteria for relief, but Shen said a fair number of those have financing gaps too large to be jumpstarted by the level of aid officials are willing to offer. Currently, the administration is offering two tracks of abatements, both of which would allow projects to keep their property tax rate as-is during a roughly three-year construction period. A shorter-term option would increase property taxes by a flat 2.5 percent rate for five years after a project finishes construction, while the longer-term option would allow for a tax rate that starts lower and ramps up over a 10-year period.The Pratt Street project in Allston, which is being developed by Houston-based Hines and Framingham-based Calare Properties, is the only of the four projects that chose the longer track. Related: After a surge of affordable housing development in Boston, the money that helps pay for it all is drying upNearly three-quarters of the city’s operating budget comes from property taxes, and commercial buildings like offices have lost value for the last two years running. Amid a development slowdown, the prospect of forgoing revenue could raise eyebrows. But city officials said the agreements would not result in any revenue loss because they only constitute temporarily delayed tax increases, as opposed to reducing a property’s tax bill. And when the projects are eventually built and paying their full bill, it will bolster the city’s tax base. In other words, the city is forgoing some revenue in the short term to bring in more in the future. “It’s really important that the city is always increasing our tax basis,” said Sheila Dillon, Boston’s housing chief. “We’re really creating basis for future generations. … We’re not collecting taxes right now, but we really are setting up for financial health down the road.”Giving tax breaks to developers is inherently a tradeoff, but in the midst of a housing crunch, that tradeoff is well worth making, said Josh Zakim, a former Boston city councilor and head of the advocacy group Housing Forward MA. “From a public policy perspective, the biggest need right now in the City of Boston is more housing,” said Zakim. “So giving a little help right now for something that is undeniably for the public good is what the government is here for.”The offering is modest, but appreciated, said Tamara Small, the chief executive of CREDA Massachusetts, a commercial real estate industry group.“It has become crystal clear that developers of market-rate housing are simply unable to build housing in Boston,” Small said. “We would hope that, looking forward, recognizing the housing crisis that Boston faces, the city continues to think creatively on how we can jumpstart housing production.”Some developers have been skeptical of short-term tax breaks. The Globe reported in June that some developers considered a five- or 10-year term to be too short to make a significant difference in whether their projects were financially feasible.In 2023, the Wu administration announced deep tax breaks for projects that would convert defunct offices into apartments, with developers eligible to reduce property taxes by up to 75 percent for as long as 29 years. Some of those projects have now started construction. The hope, officials said, is that the relief proposed Monday could be similarly effective at getting shovels in the ground.“The key is to try to jumpstart construction,” Shen said. “We need more housing, and we’re sitting on this pipeline, and … the mayor wants us to actually get these housing units built.”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker. Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: ‘Ambitious but possible’: Wu plans on new tax breaks, reworked zoning to tackle Boston housing crisis
subhead: City officials are drafting a plan to tackle one of Boston’s thorniest challenges: The cost of housing
content: Over her five years in office, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has pledged to rein in the city’s sky-high cost of housing, to little avail. Rents continue to climb, construction has slowed, and residents continue to trickle away for places they can better afford.Now, her administration is considering a host of changes in hopes of finally cracking the problem, including tax breaks for “high-priority” projects struggling for financing and zoning to encourage more affordable housing developments in key neighborhoods.At the same time, housing officials are preparing to lower expectations for how much housing can realistically be built amid the current economic conditions.A draft of the Wu administration’s new plan, obtained by the Globe, indicates the city hopes to permit 3,000 new housing units annually over her second four-year term. That’s fewer than the 13,000 she set out to build over her first four years in office, but roughly on pace with construction over the last 18 months.Boston officials stressed the plan is preliminary — drafted by the city’s top housing officials, it has not been finalized by the mayor herself. But a draft was shared with developers and advocates last week, and it outlines how Wu might address one of Boston’s thorniest challenges in her second term.The new goal of 3,000 units per year is a relatively low bar for a city with more than 675,000 residents that built far more than that just a few years ago. The goal would, though, mark an uptick from the deep lull of the last three years, the slowest period for new development in Boston since the Great Recession.That modest target is an acknowledgement of the broad market forces that are slowing housing construction across the country, officials said, as well as the lagging growth in the population in Boston itself.“Our discussions have been framed by: how do we stretch our goals because production is such an important piece of the puzzle?” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “But we also don’t want to put out a big round number that we couldn’t achieve in these economic headwinds. We’re trying to thread that needle of something that’s ambitious but possible.”Boston Housing Authority administrator Kenzie Bok, with Mayor Michelle Wu, in 2024.John Tlumacki/Globe StaffThe high cost of housing is a major issue for Boston, warping the lives of residents across the income spectrum. And the biggest factor keeping prices high and driving them upward, many economists agree, is that there simply aren’t enough homes for everyone who wants to live here.Rents have declined in cities such as Austin, Texas, that have added a significant number of new units recently. But in Boston, where the rate of building has slowed, rents are still going up.Wu has, at times, been hesitant to set targets for new construction, citing a commitment to what she describes as a more holistic approach that prioritizes housing for everyone — targeting all the “different stages of life we’re trying to house,” as Bok put it — instead of numerical goals for market-rate building. Related: Amid housing crisis, Boston’s building boom has gone cold. How much of that is due to Mayor Wu?This plan follows that same tack. But developers have frequently complained Wu’s policies — particularly around affordable housing and energy efficiency requirements — have driven up the cost of building and slowed development.To that end, the draft housing plan includes measures the city hopes may lower costs and boost production, including short-term tax breaks for “high-priority” projects that have been approved but are not financed due to prohibitive construction and borrowing costs. One challenge is making incentives, such as property tax abatements, meaningful for developers without undermining city finances. “Tax revenue is what our city runs on, so we have to be really careful about how any abatement is given out,” said Sheila Dillon, the city’s housing chief. “But we are working seriously on using that tool in a targeted way to advance specific, high-quality projects that are truly ready to go if they get that relief. We need housing now, and we need to grow as a city.”The draft also says City Hall would consider “offering flexibility for how projects meet” Boston’s requirement that 17 percent of units in most new buildings be set aside at affordable rents, plus another 3 percent for Section 8 tenants. Importantly, it stopped short of saying officials would lower the 20 percent target, as some developers have urged. (Wu increased the affordable threshold from 13 percent under her predecessor, Martin J. Walsh.) Boston would also continue to rework stringent zoning rules to allow for taller and denser housing developments near key transit nodes and in major squares and corridors, the draft plan says, though details were limited. While Boston has moved forward rezoning efforts in some neighborhoods recently, progress has been gradual, and at least one such effort in the Codman Square section of Dorchester was delayed due to pushback from residents. Wu’s more measured approach to housing development is a shift from Walsh, who preferred to set high long-term goals, at one point saying the city would need to add 69,000 units over a 16-year period, citing population trends. But growth in Boston has slowed significantly since the COVID-19 pandemic, and when Wu has set housing production goals, they have been more modest. Her Boston Housing Strategy 2025 said the city would aim to build 13,000 units — 8,300 market rate and 4,700 income-restricted — during her first four years in office.Those years coincided with rising interest rates and higher materials and construction costs that discouraged construction nationwide; Boston missed its goal by about 1,200 units, permitting 11,804 new homes during that period.Indeed, 2023 and 2024 were the two slowest years for new housing permits since 2011, with fewer than 2,400 in each. Last year was slightly higher, but still slow, while the first half of 2026 was better yet, with  1,643 units permitted.That is roughly in line with the goal outlined in the administration’s draft plan, which says that while it’s harder to build now than before, Boston continues to remain ahead of its neighboring communities.“Boston has far exceeded its share of housing production, while so many others in the region have fallen short,” the plan says.Much of the strategy focuses on affordable housing, which has been Wu’s top housing priority. Under her tenure, Boston has built a wave of new subsidized units — funded in part by hundreds of millions of dollars of federal pandemic relief funds. That money is running out, and affordable housing funding generated by new commercial and market-rate housing development is dwindling amid the broader development slowdown.An apartment building under construction in East Boston earlier this year.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffTo offset those losses, the plan says, the city may consider an effort to boost the Community Preservation Act levy it charges property owners. It will also consider tax breaks for affordable housing projects and plans to tweak its Housing Accelerator Fund, a $100 million effort to unlock stalled projects that has not been widely utilized.The plan also suggests citywide zoning for affordable housing, allowing projects that meet certain affordability requirements in designated locations to build at higher densities. That idea is modeled on a policy Cambridge adopted in 2020 allowing fully-affordable buildings up to 12 and 15 stories tall in key corridors without special approval from a zoning board. And officials said the Boston Housing Authority will continue expanding its affordable housing footprint in the city. Related: After a surge of affordable housing development in Boston, the money that helps pay for it all is drying upWhile Boston has policy levers it can pull on its own, many of the Wu administration’s preferred housing solutions — namely, rent control and a small fee on high-dollar real estate transactions to fund affordable housing — hinge on approval from a Legislature that has thus far been skeptical.Winning over lawmakers and moving forward a broad array of new housing policies, the plan said, is essential to the city’s long-term vitality.“Boston needs additional market rate housing, but it’s more than this,” said Dillon. “We need a more nuanced, comprehensive plan that also focuses on increased affordability and making sure that all of our populations — including seniors, families with kids, and students — are safely and appropriately housed.“Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: Julia Child’s Cambridge home hits the market for $6.475 million
subhead: Famed chef Julia Child was a staple of the Cambridge area where she lived for 40 years and filmed some of her shows in her personal kitchen.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Get ready to say “Bon Appétit” like Cambridge’s most legendary chef because Julia Child’s former home is officially on the market.
The house at 103 Irving St., where the iconic author, TV host, and culinary queen lived for 40 years, was just listed for $6,475,000. Child rose to notoriety as the author of “Mastering the Art of French Cooking” and later became a TV icon as the host of “The French Chef,” the beloved WGBH cooking show. But she was also a staple of the Cambridge area, where she shopped for her groceries at Savenor’s, dined at Harvest, and called her peaceful oasis on a tree-lined street home.
Built in 1889, the soft purple six-bedroom, six-bathroom (four full, two half) home became a culinary epicenter for Child and her husband, Paul, upon his acceptance of a job in Cambridge in 1961. She remained in the 6,321-square-foot home until 2001, when she moved to a retirement community and donated the house to Smith College, which later sold it, according toHistory Cambridge.
A post shared by Cambridge & Somerville (@incamberville)
The Cambridge City Council voted this summer in favor of putting up a historical marker at Child’s former home, where she filmed some of her PBS shows.
Now, it’s time for a new owner to make it their own.
Just a few blocks from Harvard Yard, the home is tucked behind a white fence. A brick walkway, gracious front yard, and a few steps lead up to the house, which welcomes guests through a grand entry. Inside, to the right, is a space that is currently set up as a living and dining room combination. Back in the hallway, there’s a family room on the left with French doors, a bay window with a built-in seat, a fireplace, and endless shelves.
In the kitchen, don’t expect to find anything that resembles what it was in Child’s day when she filmed some of her later shows like “In Julia’s Kitchen with Master Chefs” and “Julia and Jacques Cooking at Home” right in her home kitchen, according to theJulia Child Foundation. She donated her kitchen to the SmithsonianNational Museum of American Historyin Washington, D.C. (“Charmingly, a sticker for one of her favorite local restaurants, Eat, is still visible on her refrigerator door,” History Cambridge writes.)
Now, the space has been adapted for the modern era, with Poggenpohl cabinetry, a six-burner cooktop, marble countertops, and a Sub-Zero refrigerator. A large island is the anchor, and the eat-in area is surrounded by a wall of windows that embraces the natural setting. In the Butler’s pantry, where Paul Child once stood making martinis, you’ll now find further Poggenpohl cabinetry, Sub-Zero refrigeration, and a beverage cooler. The kitchen provides easy access out to the yard.
“The feel of her is still in there,” saidEd Feijoof Gail Roberts, Ed Feijo, and team at Coldwell Banker, who has thelisting. “Even though obviously it’s been renovated, you still get that sense of why she wanted to be there. It’s just very tranquil and relaxing.”
Head up to the second floor to find four bedrooms, including the primary bedroom suite. It features a fireplace, walk-in closet with built-in cabinetry and pocket doors, and an ensuite bathroom with a double vanity. A private balcony feels nestled in the trees.
On the third floor are two more potential bedrooms, one of which easily functions as a media room with a fireplace. There’s an office space and there’s plenty of additional storage. On the finished lower level, there’s an exercise room, a laundry room, a half-bathroom, a wine room, and several storage spaces.
The outdoor space is one of the most unique aspects of the home. Many of the same plants are the ones that were planted by the Childs themselves.  Feijo notes that the property is a “garden-style house,” and that a lot of the properties on Professor’s Row are set sideways, specifically designed to take in the garden from every angle. There are two covered porches, a patio, a stone wall, and a fenced-in yard surrounded by mature plantings that create an environment of tranquility.
The home has its own porte cochère,in addition to the driveway parking, where Child once parked her old Volkswagen after returning home from the market with fresh ingredients.
Megan Johnson is a correspondent who covers real estate, distinctive homes, architecture, and interior design.

hed: Inside Gavin Newsom’s San Francisco childhood home — now listed for $4.5M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A leafy San Francisco retreat with a direct line toGov. Gavin Newsom’sfamily tree is up for grabs — and it will set a buyer back $4.5 million.
The two-bed, two-bath house at 1284 Stanyan St. hit the market Wednesday with Compass. It sits across the road from the hiking paths of Mount Sutro Forest, with Cole Street’s cafes and shops, UCSF and Golden Gate Park all close by.
The political pedigree goes back to the fall of 1967. That year, his father Bill Newsom ran for the city’s Board of Supervisors, and his candidate blurb in the official booklet for the Nov. 7 election gave Stanyan as the address he shared with his wife, Tessa Menzies.
She had inherited the place from her father, Arthur Menzies.
Their son Gavin arrived Oct. 10, weeks before voters hit the polls, according to California State Library birth records. Bill Newsom lost that race, though he later became a state appellate judge.
How long the future governor actually lived there is murkier. The Compass team says he spent ashort stretch there as a boy,but the paper trail only places his parents at the address. And Newsom’s 2026 memoir, “Young Man in a Hurry,” says the family was living in an apartment on Octavia Street when he was born.
The house itself is a woodsy throwback. Built in 1951, it got new Marin County redwood siding in 1979, and the current owner has since overhauled the kitchen and both bathrooms.
There’s a deck on the top level, patios tucked into the garden, stone retaining walls and city glimpses through the trees. The primary suite boasts a big walk-in closet, a dedicated meditation nook and views stretching to the Golden Gate Bridge and downtown.
Out back there’s a Japanese soaking tub, plus a little cabin on the second lot, and the combined 9,600-plus square feet leaves room to grow if the city signs off.
“It is a true urban getaway in nature surrounded by trees, plants, insects, animals and fresh air,” Compass agent John DiDomenico said in a statement.
The seller, who went unnamed in the Compass announcement, sounds sorry to go.
“As a country girl asked to live in the city, I found the best of both worlds at 1284 Stanyan,” she said. “I loved having that sense of escape without leaving the city.”
The property has been on the move lately. It was listed for $3.6 million back in 2019, and it changed hands in 2025 for $3.9 million, according to public records, meaning the owner is looking for roughly a $600,000 bump.
The Post has reached out to Newsom for comment.

hed: Homeowner wins 3-year war with HOA — and forces association to pay her $33K legal bill
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
As homeowners across the country find themselves locked in bitter battleswith their HOAs, one Texas woman has emerged victorious — securing more than $33,000 in damages, legal fees and other awards after a nearly three-year fight with her association.
Elizabeth Luna owned a rental townhome in Oaks Northwest, a tiny 11-unit community near the San Antonio Medical Center, which she purchased when there were no restrictions preventing her from renting it out, according toKSAT’s report.
That changed in 2023, when HOA President Terri Thomure pushed to prohibit short-term rentals in the community.
Luna alleged in her lawsuit that Thomure called a special meeting in March 2023 to approve the restriction without complying with notice requirements under Texas law — a procedural failure that Luna argued rendered the amendment void.
Still, Luna tried to play by the new rules.
She secured a tenant on a 12-month lease — only for another confrontation with the HOA to ignite.
According to Luna, Thomure approached the tenant’s assistant in the parking lot without identifying herself and demanded personal identification and information about the visit.
Days later, Luna said, the tenant backed out of the lease.
The dispute then followed Luna when she decided to sell.
After she listed the property, the HOA filed a legal claim against the home that prevented the sale from moving forward, Luna told KSAT. A judge later threw out the claim, clearing the way for Luna to finally sell the property in May 2024.
“What was going through my head when all of this was happening is the abuse of power of the homeowners association,” Luna told KSAT.
But selling the home didn’t end the fight.
Luna pursued the HOA in Bexar County’s 438th District Court, and this year a judge ruled in her favor.
The Oaks Northwest HOA was ordered to pay Luna $10,743.39 in damages and $10,000 in attorney’s fees, while Thomure was separately ordered to pay $12,500 for interfering with Luna’s rental contract, according to KSAT.
Together, the judgments total $33,243.39.
Luna told the station that both judgments have since been paid.
After nearly three years of fighting, she said she hopes the victory encourages other homeowners to scrutinize whether their HOA boards are actually following their own rules.
“If you find that your board members are not following the rules, hold them accountable,” Luna told KSAT. “Hold them to a higher standard.”
The case comes as homeowner associationshave faced increasing scrutinyover the considerable power they can wield over residents’ properties — from rental restrictions and mounting fees to liens andforeclosure actions.

hed: Famed NYC co-op stands to become a luxury loser — as $67.5M home faces a $55.5M discount
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A Fifth Avenue co-op could become the biggest loser in New York City real estate history — and it’s in a building already flooded with discounted home sales. But perhaps that’s why members of Manhattan’s high society are now looking to live there.
A full-floor residence in the Sherry-Netherland wherean alleged Chinese spy once livedis in contract — its last asking price was $12 million. In 2015, its owner paid $67.5 million cash for it.
That’s a staggering $55.5 million loss on the unit if the deal closes for that sum.
Another apartment that last sold for $11.1 million in 2011 is listed for $1.6 million, marking an 85.6% drop, according to StreetEasy.
“At these prices, the apartments are being given away,” quipped one broker with listings in the building, a skip away fromthe posh Plaza Hotelat Fifth Avenue and 59th Street.
Another broker who has traded there for 20 years added: “It’s getting to the point where owners are asking if they can just leave their keys at the front desk and walk away.”
The nearly century-old building’s sales prices are in freefall as its monthly maintenance fees soar to some of the highest that the city has ever seen.
In context, that in-contract $12 million unit comes with an extraordinary $85,654 a month in maintenance fees for the regular operation of the building. And that’s on top of additional one-time “assessment” fees for things like fixing the building’s brick exterior, or fixing the old wood-paneled elevators, brokers said.
Experts told Gimme Shelter that those ever-rising monthlies are having a direct impact on pricing inside the famed building, which has been home toDiana Ross,Francis Ford CoppolaandJudge Judy Sheindlin.
Those fees have almost doubled in the past 10 years, from $6.67 per square foot in 2016 to $12.15 in 2026, according to data compiled by appraiser Jonathan Miller, of StreetMatrix.
The fees also pay for hotel-style services, including daily housekeeping and evening turn-down service.
That’s a rare perk in New York, and people really love having it.
Prince Lorenzo Borghesewho lived at the Sherry-Netherland for 10 years in a one-bedroom owned by his family, calls it “the most beautiful building in New York City.”
“It’s my absolute favorite building,” the reality star and entrepreneur told Gimme Shelter. “The staff is the nicest and most professional. It’s not a regular apartment. They really take care of you.”
“There are fresh new sheets every day and fresh towels. They take care of everything, even the toilet paper. I never had to buy a roll of toilet paper or towels the entire time I lived there,” Borghese said.
Still, it all comes at a price.
Miller puts the Sherry-Netherland in an elite class of co-op buildings with hotel-like services that includes the Pierre at 795 Fifth Ave. andthe Carlyle, at 35 E. 76th St. Miller found that The Carlyle has the highest monthly maintenance fees, at $18.53 per square foot, followed by the Sherry-Netherland.
And soon, the latter will get its newest resident.
The $12 million unit belongs tojailed Chinese national Guo Wengui, who is also known by names including Ho Wan Kwok and Miles Kwok.
His unit is held through shell companies and is now being sold by a bankruptcy trustee to pay some of the roughly $374 million in debts Guo listed when he filed for bankruptcy in 2022.
Guo, a onetime ally and business associate ofSteve Bannon, was charged in 2023 with defrauding investors of more than $1.3 billion for varying media and crypto scams. In June, he was sentenced to 30 years in prison after being convicted in July 2024 on nine of 12 counts, including racketeering conspiracy, wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering. Guo, currently held at a low-security prison in Danbury, Conn., maintains his innocence and appealed his conviction and sentence in July. His lawyer, Melinda Sarafa, declined to comment.
In 2018, Guogave Gimme Shelter a tourof the sprawling property. The 7,000-square-foot apartment was impressive, with lots of wood paneling, terraces with extraordinary views of Central Park, and a chef’s kitchen where Guo enjoyed cooking up noodle dishes for his American guests. Sources said it’s the second largest unit in the building.
Miller told Gimme Shelter the Guo apartment sale, if it closes, “will be the largest loss on an individual residential sale on record in New York City. Nothing comes close to $50 million.”
The apartment’s listing broker, Douglas Elliman’s Sabrina Saltiel, declined to comment.
Broker Jenny Lenz, of Dolly Lenz Real Estate, who has many clients in the building, and whose mother Dolly once had Guo as a client, said that the apartment “has been gutted to its shell, and restoring it will require an extraordinary investment on top of maintenance approaching $100,000 a month.”
And yet, the low prices and a billionaires’ war over the fate of the nearby Pierre,as Gimme Shelter exclusively reported, may have finally kickstarted renewed interest in the building, and buyers are slowly returning.
The latest is former Disney CEO Michael Eisner,who paid $10 million off-marketfor a unit sold by a trust tied to the late billionaire Eli Broad.
ActressMarlo Thomasalso recently bought a unit for $2.75 million at the Sherry in August, Gimme can reveal. The three-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bath unit had last been purchased for $8.5 million in 2012, according to records, and extravagantly decorated by famed designer Geoffrey Bradfield. It features domed, coffered and tray ceilings, marble floors, custom moldings and millwork and stunning Central Park views. Its latest reported maintenance fees were $26,432 a month, plus $1,362 for a storage/staff room; there is also a $2,679 additional monthly assessment fee through September 2027, according to a past listing.
The building’s management did not respond at press time.

hed: Legendary California oyster enclave on sale for $13M after 101-year run
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Well, shucks.
A stunning Northern California coastal property has hit the market for roughly $13 million — but it’snot your typical high-dollar waterfront spread.
The prime, 16-acre parcel at the heart of theMarin Countyoyster farming village of Marshall includes a string of commercial and residential buildings by the side of Highway 1 — and one legendary seafood restaurant, The Marshall Store.

The Tomales Bay-facing plot roughly 60 miles north of San Francisco was purchased just over a century ago in 1925, by Croatian immigrants Nickola and Nickolina Vilicich — and has never been up for sale since.
Other tenants on the property include Point Reyes Oyster Co., Marshall Boat Works and the local U.S. Post Office.
Opened in 2006, The Marshall Store is a small bivalve spot with a big reputation. The restaurant was featured in The New York Times’ top 50 restaurants in America in 2021.
Owner Shannon Gregory said the secret to her success is keeping things casual.
“It’s expensive to go and eat oysters — why do you want to go sit at some rustic restaurant on the bay and have dine-in service and have it be more expensive? I think people like the fact that it’s casual,” Gregory toldSFGATEin 2021.
“Anybody can come here. We’re not just for the blue collar workers, we’re not just for the wealthier people. We’re for everybody.”
A brochure for the listing, obtained by SFGATE, reveals the combined properties yield $400,000 in operating income — set against $250,000 in expenses.
Three of the property’s parcels are zoned for commercial use, and the listing says the land comes with “multiple income-producing and development possibilities.”
The scenic shoreline is also home to the Tomales Bay Oyster Company. Co-owned by Gregory’s sister Heidi, the company is the longest-running oyster farm in California, first opening in 1917.
Once a local secret, the oyster farming town has seen an increase in development in recent years.
Just up Highway 1, Nick’s Cove, an popular restaurant and waterfront inn, underwent a major refresh in 2022, transforming the picturesque resort into a four-star hotel where minted tech workers pay hundreds of dollars a night to stay.
Also in Marshall is the original location of Bay Area legend Hog Island Oyster Company — an oyster farm that started on Tomales Bay in the early 1980s.
Hog Island has since become known for their trendy chain of upscale oyster bars, with high-traffic locations in San Francisco, Napa and other area cities.
