hed: Homebuyer’s ‘crazy’ $899K bet on a crumbling Nantucket cliff is still standing 5 years later
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
He asked the Atlantic for five years. So far, the Atlantic has kept its end of the bargain.
Massachusetts car dealer Charles Fotopoulos and his wife, Miglena, snapped up 93 Baxter Road, a 1951 cottage clinging to the edge of Nantucket’s storied Sconset Bluff, for $899,000 in September 2021.
On an island where eight-figure price tags barely raise an eyebrow, it was one of the rare deals that year to come in under seven figures.
Five years later, the house is still up there. Barely.
Just a few feet of ground now separate the back of the home from a 40-foot plunge to the sand. When it was built, the ocean sat hundreds of yards away. Over the decades,the retreating bluffhas swallowed a string of the neighbors.
The Fotopouloses, who run dealerships in Lowell and Westwood, went in with their eyes wide open.
“It was cheap and I said ‘hey, I’ll buy it’,” Charles told theNantucket Currentback when the deal closed. “The foundation is structurally sound, and with the geotubes there, unless we have a killer storm, I think we’re safe. A lot of people think I’m crazy, but if I get five years out of it, I think I’m good. I’ll take that any day.”
Five years later, it appears Fotopoulos’ gamble has paid off.The house is still standing, as are the geotubes (although they are damaged due to alleged vandalism).Here’s how the property at 93 Baxter Road looks today:pic.twitter.com/a6BoRkP5qy
From the living room, there is nothing to see but open water.
“It’s both a great view, and a scary view,” he said.
The sellers took a beating. Steven and Erin Freeman paid $1.53 million for the place in 2007, when a comfortable 50 to 70 feet of land still stood between the house and the drop. They walked away roughly $631,000 poorer.
Their broker, Jamie Howarth, said nobody was fooled.
“They knew the risks going in,” Howarth said in 2021. “I was clear with him and we were clear with him that there was serious risk.”
The Freemans didn’t surrender quietly. In 2010 they hauled the house back toward Baxter Road, and in 2017 they took a DIY approach to shoring up the top of the bluff, work the island’s Conservation Commission never approved and slapped them with an enforcement order over. The couple were also active in the Sconset Beach Preservation Fund, the well-heeled homeowner group bankrolling the geotubes.
Howarth figured the Freemans probably clawed back their loss and then some through summer rentals, with peak weeks fetching up to $10,000.
The new owners may have tried a similar play. Listing records show the home was advertised as a rental in September 2025 at $10,000 a month, and this past summer, it rented for $29,500 per month.
Fotopoulos, for his part, insisted the numbers penciled out.
“It is what it is. It’s a hole in the ocean on Nantucket. It’s really worth $8 million if you really think about it. The next comp down the street is $8.4 million,” he said at the time.
Today, similar comps on the island with oceanfront views have homes listed between $11.5 million to $29 million.
His safety net was the geotubes, massive fabric sacks packed with sand and parked at the base of the bluff to absorb the surf. They have slowed the erosion along that stretch. They have also become the most bitterly contested pile of sand on the island.
The Conservation Commission voted in 2021 to rip them out. The preservation group simply ignored that order.
This year has been brutal for the barrier. Afterfresh collapsesleft big sections stripped bare, the commission’s chair warned in March that the project could be nearing “complete failure.”  A winter storm packing gusts above 80 mph scoured away even more sand.
The fight over expanding the wall has zigzagged ever since. Voters at the Town Meeting narrowly shot down the expansion this spring, a vote that blocks the 3,000-foot extension no matter what happens in court or at the state level.
A Superior Court judge nonetheless sided with the expansion permit in August, and the commission has signaled it may let the group patch a section damaged in what officials called suspected vandalism back in January. Then state environmental regulators fired off an Aug. 31 letter flagging a dozen unresolved problems with the proposal, and the Select Board has so far refused to promise voters a second crack at it.
The stakes reach beyond one cottage. Opponents argue that old homes like 93 Baxter are precisely what keeps the whole armoring project legally alive.
“The presence of that pre-1978 house is what provides the legal justification, in part, for the permitting of hard armoring,” Nantucket Coastal Conservancy’s D. Anne Atherton said at the time of the sale.
The Fotopouloses have no ties to the preservation group.
For now, the cottage still has its view, and its owner still has his five years. What comes next is anyone’s guess, including his.
“How long does it last? You and I don’t know that,” Fotopoulos said.

hed: Tech billionaire’s wild mansion war with neighbors who battled him over dog poop takes new turn
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A years-long neighborhood war involving a tech billionaire, an 11,000-square-foot Utah mansion and two 100-plus-pound Bernese Mountain dogs has taken another dramatic turn.
A judge tossed two lawsuits Wednesday challenging Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince’s sprawling Park City property.
It’s the latest development in a bitter property battle that previously spiraled into accusations of dog poop, snarling canines and “Save Sasha and Mocha” stickers plastered around the ritzy ski town.
Prince and his wife, Tatiana, have spent years trying to build the massive residence on King Road overlooking historic Old Town, while downhill neighbors Eric Hermann and Susan Fredston-Hermann have fought the project over its size, height and design.
The feud took a particularly bizarre turn in 2024, when Prince sued the Hermanns over their two Bernese Mountain dogs, Sasha and Mocha.
AsThe Post reportedat the time, Prince alleged the dogs were allowed to roam unleashed, poop on his property and “aggressively” approach his family and guests.
His lawsuit claimed the dogs harassed his then-82-year-old mother and “barked, snarled and charged” at his infant daughter while she sat in a stroller.
The Hermanns denied the allegations and described Sasha and Mocha as “well-behaved, polite and nonaggressive.”
The canine clash erupted shortly after the Hermanns and other neighbors challenged approvals for Prince’s mansion, eventually prompting locals to rally behind the dogs with “Save Sasha and Mocha” stickers.
Now, two of the lawsuits tied to the mansion itself have been thrown out.
Utah’s 3rd District Court Judge Richard Mrazik dismissed the cases after ruling that a deal approved by the Park City Council earlier this year superseded the previous land-use decisions the Hermanns were challenging, according toKPCW.
The City Council voted 3 to 1 in January to approve a consent agreement with Pesky Porcupine LLC, the entity associated with Prince’s project.
The agreement relied on a Utah law that took effect in November 2025 allowing municipalities to settle litigation over land-use decisions with property owners through such agreements.
“The respective petitions to review regard land use decisions that have been superseded by something, the consent agreement specifically,” Mrazik said, according to KPCW.
The Hermanns had raised objections to the mansion’s height, floor area, roof, parking and whether it complied with Park City’s historic-design rules.
Construction, meanwhile, appears to be moving ahead. TownLift photographed excavation underway at 220 King Road on Sept. 16.
But Prince’s long-running neighborhood battle isn’t over just yet.
The Hermanns filed a separate lawsuit after the City Council approved the consent agreement, arguing in part that Park City could not use the deal to eliminate their independent legal challenges without their consent.
That case remains pending.
Attorneys for the Hermanns, the Princes and Park City are due back in court Dec. 29 — meaning the years-long mansion saga still has at least one more fight left.

hed: Ask the Gardener: Mums aren’t the only stars of autumn — these flowers thrive in the fall
subhead: To keep your New England garden blooming through October, look to these two flower varieties
content:
ByUlrich Lorimer
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Welcome to autumn, fellow gardeners! The days bring cool mornings and pleasant afternoons. A sweet fragrance fills the air as the late-day sun warms the blossoms of goldenrods, asters, gentians, tickseeds, sunflowers, and grasses. Unlike spring and summer blooms, these plants demand patience; we have given them space in our gardens and waited for their time to shine.

Planning for flowers to bloom from April through the end of October can be tricky. Fortunately, many asters and goldenrods grow in a variety of conditions. Beyond their beauty, these flowers provide crucial end-of-season resources for pollinators and seed for migratory and resident birds. I could not imagine a group of plants that fits New England landscapes better. Many species and varieties are available. Here are a few of my favorites.



Many of you have likely heard this before, but it is worth repeating. Goldenrods do not cause hay fever. Goldenrod pollen is heavy, sticky, and gets moved around by pollinators. The culprit for seasonal allergy sufferers is ragweed. It blooms at the same time as goldenrod, and its pollen is tiny, lightweight, and easily blown into the air.

For dry shade, wreath, also called blue-stemmed goldenrod (Solidago caesia) is a top choice. Growing up to 3 feet, the arching, blue-tinged stems bear clusters of yellow blooms nestled in the leaf axils. Drought-tolerant once established, this goldenrod may seed itself around in the garden, but it can be easily edited as needed.


For shade and slightly moister soils, I recommend zig-zag goldenrod (Solidago flexicaulis). This species features rounded clusters of blooms, also held in the leaf axils, and has rounder leaves with prominent teeth. I have found it quite well-behaved in the garden, with the clumps growing ever larger with each passing season.

For full sun and poor soils (i.e., sandy and rocky), I like how gray goldenrod (Solidago nemoralis) performs. It is among the shortest of the goldenrods, only reaching 2 feet in height and topped with a dense plume of golden blossoms. It spends most of the summer as a tidy clump of grayish-green basal leaves before erupting into bloom in September. The plant spreads slowly via rhizomes or seeds.

My final goldenrod recommendation is a selection of rough goldenrod (Solidago rugosa) called Fireworks. This selection has been on the market for a long time, first discovered in the 1970s and made available to gardeners in the early 1990s. It forms a tidy, bushy clump about 3 feet tall, with overlapping, arching stems covered in yellow flowers; the overall effect is like a firework exploding in your garden. Most importantly, it is not aggressive. Several other goldenrods spread and seed vigorously, and not all suit smaller gardens. They play an important role in supporting wildlife and pollinators, but are best left for abandoned fields, roadsides, and places where ample space balances their exuberance and growth.



Easily recognized by their cheerful yellow center and spectrum of colorful petals, asters are widely distributed across the United States and heavily represented in New England. Most are very floriferous, from New England aster (Symphyotrichum novae-angliae) with blooms nearly 3 inches across to bushy American aster (Symphyotrichum dumosum) with individual blooms less than an inch in size.

White wood aster (Eurybia divaricata) is common and extremely tough. It thrives in dry shade conditions, growing in woodlands and forests along trailsides and openings. Largely unassuming during the summer months, this aster shines during early autumn with clouds of starry white blooms.

Equally outstanding is heart-leaved aster(Symphyotrichum cordifolium), a stout, branched part-shade denizen that sports dense wands of light blue flowers from mid-September into October. “Avondale” is a popular selection for its slightly smaller stature and long-lasting blooms.

For full sun, I recommend flax-leaf stiff aster (Ionactis linariifolius). This aster has thickened, narrow leaves similar to rosemary in appearance without the fragrance. It is short, reaching only a foot in height, and topped with pale blue blossoms.


Lastly, we have New England aster (Symphyotrichum novae-angliae), a graceful plant with large flowers ranging in color from pink to purple. Characterized by clasping leaf bases and a generally pleasant odor to the foliage when bruised, New England aster could easily be the region’s most recognized wildflower. Breeding efforts have produced several dwarf selections such as Purple Dome and Vibrant Dome, both growing to less than 2 feet in height and spread.

As we look forward to the blazing colors of fall foliage, asters and goldenrods are the perfect complement in the garden. We grow them for their beauty as much as for their ecological significance, and because our autumn landscapes would not be the same without them.

Ulrich Lorimer is the director of horticulture at the Native Plant Trust in Framingham. Send your gardening questions, along with your name/initials and hometown, to[email protected]g.

hed: This Sudbury home’s formal gardens boast global inspiration and 25+ years of memories
subhead: Many of the outdoor plants — even the trees — are portable, so they can come inside a winterized structure during cold weather
content:
ByDaisy Levine
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.

Drive past and you might miss it.

The 5-acre oasis at82 Old Garrison Road in Sudburyhides behind its surrounding greenery. Among lush, labyrinth-like gardens is a four-bedroom, four-bathroom home nestled in the storied Wayside Inn historic district.


Listed for $2,495,000, the 4,561-square-foot house was built in 1961 and almost entirely redone in 2004 by the current owners, who first settled on Old Garrison Road in 1999. The owners’ love of travel transformed it into a globally influenced home.

“It was originally a very different little Cape house,” said current owner Karen Brandse.



“It’s taken decades to cultivate and create such a magnificent property. It’s not just the structure itself … but it’s also the grounds,” saidPeace Nguyen, of Engel & Völkers Wellesley, who has the listing.

And the grounds certainly stand out.

“You can meander through different pathways, and, around each corner, discover something new,” said Nguyen.



A walk around the property shows off fountains, waterfalls, a pool, and even a small orchard. Originally from South Africa, Brandse said there are “a lot of different theme gardens … we basedifferent garden sectionsdepending on where we’ve traveled.”

The indigo tiling and paintwork along thegarden— that’s from Morocco. The Buddha is from Cambodia (which was quite a task to import, Brandse said). One of the bells is from Thailand. Almost every ornament has been imported.



Brandse and her husband have put more than 25 years of work into the grounds, so she said they now require minimal upkeep. Two of their children held their weddings in the scenic gardens outside their childhood home. And now, the owners have decided to downsize and perhaps relocate somewhere warmer.

The house is designed to embrace the gardens. Inside are high, vaulted ceilings with skylights to allow intense light to pour through. Many of the outdoor plants — even the trees — are portable, so they can come inside a winterized structure during cold weather.


Brandse described it as a West Coast-style house where there’s more focus on the outdoor elements.

“It is definitely a house for somebody who enjoys an indoor-outdoor kind of living, even in winter,” she said. “If you’re indoors, you’re seeing out.”


Brandse said the house really doesn’t look like anything else she’s seen on the East Coast. And, there’s an accidental wine cellar. The room was left unheated, but now it stays at the perfect natural temperature to store wine.


“Every once in a blue moon, there is a property that comes to market actually unlike anything else,” Nguyen said. “What you have to see in person to appreciate is the indoor-outdoor flow.”

hed: Joe Jonas finds a buyer for his $6.75M NYC home — as Taylor Swift drops a song that fans swear is about him
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Talk about timing.
Joe Jonas has lined up a buyer for hisBrooklyn sky perch,and the deal landed a day before his most famous ex released a new single that Swifties are convincedtakes aim at him.
The Jonas Brothers singer’s three-bedroom condo on the 26th floor of Olympia Dumbo went into contract Sept. 24, according to StreetEasy. It had asked $6.75 million since June, when The Post first broke news of the listing, which he had quietly put on the market.
Then on Friday, Taylor Swift unleashed “Patient Zero,” and the internet did what the internet does.
Swift revealed the new trackon Sept. 22 as part of “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore.” The song is written as a message from one woman to another who is now with a man the singer once dated. Swift casts herself as the first person to catch the emotional sickness he spreads, and offers to help the new girlfriend recover.
Fans quickly pointed to “Game of Thrones” star Sophie Turner. After the actresssplit from Jonas,Swift let Turner and her kids stay in herdowntown Manhattan apartmentduring custody talks. The two women were photographed together around New York again and again after the breakup.
And Swift and Jonas go way back. They dated briefly in 2008, and the romance ended over the phone. Swift later told Ellen DeGeneres about “the boy who broke up with me over the phone in 27 seconds” and moved on.
Not every Swiftie is sold. Some lines seem to fit other exes better, and a reference to social climbing makes little sense for someone as famous as Jonas. Swift has not named Jonas, Turner or anyone else as the song’s muse.
As for Jonas’s unit, the final sale price won’t be public until the deal closes and hits city property records. But Jonas was never chasing a windfall. He bought the residence in May 2024 for $6.5 million, so his ask sat just $250,000 above what he paid.
Once broker commissions and transfer taxes are paid, that margin could shrink to nothing, or flip into a loss.
The 2,654-square-foot corner unit faces the Manhattan Bridge, the East River and the lower Manhattan skyline through a wall of glass.
The showstopper is a lounge done up in lipstick red, with a walnut bar and a vinyl station, a space that could revert to a fourth bedroom for a buyer who needs guest space.
The kitchen is dressed in Fior di Bosco marble and hand-blown Bocci light fixtures. Common charges run $3,590 a month. Carl Gambino of the Gambino Group at Compass represented the seller.
The buyer is moving into one of Brooklyn’s buzziest addresses.
Olympia, a Fortis Property Group tower finished in 2024, counts former Nets guard Ben Simmons and “Frozen” songwriters Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez among its buyers.
Its 32nd-floor penthouse alsoplayed Denzel Washington’s homein Spike Lee’s “Highest 2 Lowest,” and sold for $16.25 million. The only other penthouse in the building remains available for $15 million. The 33-story waterfront tower holds 76 residences and more than 38,000 square feet of amenities, including indoor and outdoor pools and a tennis court.
Jonas picked up the unit shortly after his 2023 split from Turner.
He now divides his time between the US and the UK to be near the two daughters they share. He unloaded his longtime Nolita apartment for roughly $5.3 million, and was spotted scouting new digs in Greenpoint in January 2025.

hed: NYC ranks fifth-hardest metro for first-time homebuyers — 7% mortgage rates are squeezing them even more
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Buying a starter home in New York was already a stretch for the average household.
Now mortgage ratesare back above 7%— adding yet another hurdle for would-be homeowners already contending with stubbornly high prices and a shortage of homes for sale.
The New York metropolitan area is the fifth-hardest place in the country to get on the property ladder, according to new research from personal-finance company Achieve.
An entry-level home in the metro costs about $489,359, while the median household earns $99,155.
Assuming a 10% down payment and keeping mortgage payments to 30% of gross income, Achieve calculated that a household would need to earn $114,380 a year to comfortably afford that home — 15.4% more than the typical household actually makes.
And that calculation comes as borrowing costs are heading in the wrong direction.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage climbed back above 7% this week after years of languishing inflation, further eroding the purchasing power of buyers who need financing.
For buyers, however, the problem is much bigger than the mortgage rate alone.
Appraiser Jonathan Miller, of StreetMatrix, told The Post that an acute shortage of homes for sale is preventing the normal market correction that might otherwise give buyers some relief.
“When we think about affordability, I think the influence of inadequate inventory is more powerful on the affordability topic than actual rates themselves,” Miller said.
Normally, Miller explained, a sharp increase in borrowing costs would cause sales to fall, inventory to build and prices to soften.
This time, that last part isn’t happening.
“Mortgage rates are over 7%, and prices are still rising, right? That’s not logical to many people,” Miller said. “But the reason it’s not logical is because the limited inventory is distorting everything.”
Part of the problem is the so-called mortgage “lock-in effect.”
Millions of homeowners secured ultra-low mortgage rates in previous years and now have little financial incentive to sell their homes and take out a new mortgage at around 7%.
“You’ve got to get all the people that are sort of locked in because they’ve got a 2.75% mortgage,” Miller said. “There’s no way they’re gonna trade that for a new house with a 7.2% mortgage. They’re gonna sit tight.”
The result isa vicious circle: higher rates make buying more expensive, but they can also discourage existing owners from selling, restricting inventory and helping keep home prices elevated.
“The bigger problem for affordability is rising rates keep inventory from coming into the market,” Miller said.
Jessica Peters of Douglas Elliman said buyers who expected higher borrowing costs to bring substantially cheaper homes have largely been disappointed.
“Buyers are being squeezed from both sides,” Peters told The Post. “Borrowing costs remain elevated, but New York home prices have remained resilient, particularly in desirable neighborhoods where inventory is limited.”
And the mortgage is only one line on a New York homeowner’s bill.
“New Yorkers also have to account for maintenance or common charges, taxes and closing costs, so the monthly carrying cost can become substantial very quickly,” Peters said.
Buyers are responding by recalibrating rather than necessarily giving up altogether, according to Peters — increasing down payments, lowering their budgets, expanding their searches into different neighborhoods or choosing a smaller apartment or co-op instead of a condo.
But those with the least cash have fewer options.
First-time buyers who rely more heavily on financing “feel every movement in mortgage rates,” Peters said, while buyers with proceeds from a previous sale or greater liquidity have more room to maneuver.
That divide is especially stark in Manhattan, where Miller said the upper half of the market is currently performing better than the lower half.
“As you move higher in price, there’s less reliance on mortgage rates, and as you move lower in price, there’s more reliance on mortgage rates,” Miller said.
Donald Brennan, broker/owner of Engel & Völkers New York City, Brownstone Brooklyn, North Fork and Hoboken, said the divide has become striking among his firm’s current New York clientele.
The buyers currently working with advisers in his New York City office are all paying cash, Brennan said — compared with a more balanced mix of cash and financed buyers in the past.
“The people that are still buying are the cash buyers,” Brennan said.
For buyers struggling to make the numbers work, waiting for mortgage rates to fall might seem like the obvious answer.
But a lower rate doesn’t necessarily translate dollar-for-dollar into greater affordability.
“A lower mortgage rate absolutely helps the monthly payment, but it doesn’t solve the affordability equation by itself,” Peters said.
If rates fall and more buyers rush back into a market where inventory remains scarce, that new demand could put additional pressure on prices.
“For affordability to meaningfully improve, buyers need not only cheaper financing but also more housing options at a wider range of price points,” Peters said.
Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel also cautioned against looking at a mortgage rate in isolation. For buyers, what ultimately matters is the rate in relation to the price they’re paying and their overall housing budget.
Realtor.com researchsuggests buyers three months from closing should prepare their budgets to withstand roughly 50 basis points of movement in either direction, rather than assuming today’s rate will still be available when they close.
And the old real-estate mantra of “buy now, refinance later” isn’t a guarantee either.
Miller said that strategy made more sense a few years ago, when there was a stronger case that buyers could refinance into a lower rate down the road.
Today, he said, “you’re gambling on more affordability later on.”
“If you’re waiting for rates to come down, I think that’s gonna be a long wait,” Miller said.
That’s because many of the forces currently putting upward pressure on borrowing costs aren’t disappearing, he said, pointing to inflationary pressures, the federal deficit and geopolitical and trade uncertainty.
While the Federal Reserve doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, its monetary policy and the broader inflation outlook influence the market in which mortgage rates are determined.
Miller believes those conditions could keep borrowers in a “higher for longer” mortgage-rate world for at least the next several years.
“There’s no expectation that any of those will be leaving us over the next couple of years,” he said.
The outlook is murky enough that Miller has another way of describing the current housing market:
“Our uncertainty has uncertainty.”
Higher mortgage rates can also make life more expensive for people who aren’t buying at all.
“Rising mortgage rates make rental prices rise,” Miller said.
Would-be buyers who can no longer afford to purchase remain renters for longer, he explained, leaving fewer apartments available for newcomers and adding pressure to an already expensive rental market.
“When we talk about impacting affordability, it’s not just the purchase market,” Miller said. “It’s the rental market as well.”
That leaves some New Yorkers caught between an expensive purchase market and an expensive rental one.
And for families who genuinely need more space, waiting indefinitely isn’t always an option.
“Children generally don’t stop growing just because the borrowing rates have increased,” Brennan said.
For those buyers, the question isn’t whether the market will suddenly become cheaper — but whether they can make the numbers work under the conditions that exist today.

hed: Libbie Mugrabi reveals when she’s leaving the Hamptons mansion she lost at auction — and where she’s going
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Libbie Mugrabi is packing up her bags and planning to bag a very rich new spouse in the Sunshine State.
Mugrabi has set Oct. 1 as the move-out date from the Hamptons residence she lost at auction last month. She’s relocating to South Florida to look for a new, and very rich, husband, she told The Post.
Mugrabi’s comments, made from the mansion, are an about-face from last week,when she indicatedshe planned to stay put at the Bridgehampton property. But with the deadline for the sale to be completed nearing, if not already passed, Mugrabi said she doesn’t “want to be thrown out” — which she physically could be if she refuses to leave.
The departure would end a two-year odyssey that took Mugrabi from ownership of a grand Bridgehampton estateto losing itat a riotous court-ordered auction on Southampton Town Hall’s steps for $5.86 million.
Mugrabi gotthe 10,687-square-foot Hamptons mansionand its surrounding 6.8 acres as part ofher 2020 divorce settlementfrom art patron David Mugrabi, whose billionaire family is said to have the largest collection of Andy Warhol works in the world.
The subsequent dispute over the dwelling stems from Mugrabi admittedly paying nothing on a $3.5 million loan she took out against the home. Her lender had battled her in a Suffolk County court to receive the proceeds back.
Mugrabi said her priorities from here on out are getting more deeply into the art world and “interviewing (prospective) husbands who will take care of me.”
She wants, “an older billionaire. I’ve been going around with these young, hot models, but no more.”
The way Mugrabi sees it, “A woman my age shouldn’t not be married.”
Mugrabi, who is in her mid-40s, added her new spouse will have to understand, “I’m not going the way of Diana,” to whom Mugrabihas compared herselfin terms of the princess’s claims the royal family tried to keep a tight rein on her by controlling how she dressed and generally presented herself.
Mugrabi said arrangements she is making include shipping the cars she got in her divorce settlement,said to includea Ferrari and a Porsche.
The question remains whether the auction winner, area politician and real estate investor Henry Ikezi, has wrapped uphis purchaseof the home.
Ikezi declined to comment on the status of his plans to pay the auction price. Suffolk County Clerk records as of Friday morning showed the owner to be the company that made the loan to her, an affiliate of REO Assets of America, in Great Neck, N.Y. This could mean the transaction has not been completed or the new deed has not been processed through the system.
Ikezi sent The Post photos of bags stuffed with clothing and sheaves of legal papers he said are evidence of Mugrabi packing. They could not immediately be verified.
Ikezi, who likes to refer to himself as Sir Henry Ike, has a worth of $24 million on paper as the biggest single shareholder of Solidion Technology, an early-stage advanced battery developer. Ikezi also had an unsuccessful run for Queens Borough President and invested in residential properties.
The countdown for Ikezi to complete the purchase began at the Aug. 28 auction and gave him 30 or 45 days, depending on how the sale is legally structured.
Despite the drama surrounding the home’s sale, Mugrabi said there are some bright spots.
“There are still a lot of good memories here,” Mugrabi said, which includes raising her two children in the home.

hed: ‘The Gateway to the Rockies’ suddenly becomes America’s most in-demand ZIP code
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Pack the U-Haul and point it toward the runway.
A far-flung corner of Aurora, Colorado, out by Denver International Airport, is now themost popular landing spotfor movers in the country, according to the September edition ofMovingPlace’sHottest ZIP Codes report.
The ranking, built on 890,131 moves logged in August, measures how many newcomersa ZIP codeabsorbs relative to its size, which lets small, fast-growing enclaves punch well above their weight.
Aurora’s 80019 ZIP leapfrogged from a tie for eighth place in the previous month’s list to the top slot.
The lesson from the leaderboard is simple. Build it, or send people there for a job, and they will come.
“The new September Hottest ZIP Codes Report indicates that the strongest moving activity in the last month is tied to places where there’s either a lot of new housing being built or a steady pipeline of people relocating for work,” Daniel Cobb, senior editor at MovingPlace, told The Post.
In Aurora, known as “the Gateway to the Rockies,” it’s the bulldozers doing the recruiting. Master-planned neighborhoods such as Painted Prairie and High Point have been soaking up buyers who can no longer swing a house closer to downtown Denver. The typical home there is valued at $529,300, and the median household pulls in $129,154.
“Aurora is a good example,” Cobb said. “The 80019 suburban corridor is still relatively new, with a lot of housing being added around Denver International Airport. Lower land costs have helped keep both rents and new home prices relatively affordable compared with other parts of the Denver area.”
The runner-up is a different animal entirely. Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, the Army installation on the Missouri River that houses the Combined Arms Center and the Command and General Staff College, held the No. 2 position for a second consecutive month.
Nobody is fleeing Brooklyn for the Kansas prairie.
“Kansas tells a completely different story,” Cobb said. “Fort Leavenworth is heavily influenced by military moves, so its appearance near the top of the ranking isn’t necessarily about people choosing Kansas as a lifestyle destination, but likely more to do with the influx of service members and their families.”
Because the post’s population is so small, even a routine rotation of officers can send its numbers soaring.
“Coming out of the peak summer moving season, that effect can be even more pronounced as activity in other areas starts to slow,” Cobb added.
Then there’s Florida, which grabbed three of the 10 spots.
Port Saint Lucie’s 34987 ZIP code landed third, powered by the sprawling Tradition development, a longtime draw for retirees and remote workers ditching the Northeast. Homes there carry a median value of $430,100.
Coming in fourth was Inlet Beach, the ritzy Panhandle hamlet on scenic Highway 30A next door to Rosemary Beach and Alys Beach. It’s the priciest ZIP on the list by a mile, with a median home value of $947,700, and its bounce back into the rankings likely reflects wealthy buyers scooping up vacation homes.
Bradenton’s 34211, which takes in the booming Lakewood Ranch area east of Sarasota, rounded out the Sunshine State’s haul at No. 6, where new construction keeps the moving trucks rolling and homes are valued at $601,300.
Texas planted two flags, both in the Dallas-Fort Worth exurbs. Lavon, a small Collin County town near Lake Lavon, came in fifth, a regular on the list in recent months. Justin, a Denton County community along US-377 where developments like Union Park are sprouting from former ranchland, cracked the top 10 at No. 9 for the first time in months.
City dwellers aren’t entirely out of the picture. Richmond, Virginia’s 23230, a renter-heavy stretch of the West End near Willow Lawn, cooled to seventh after leading the entire country in July.
Downtown Hartford, Connecticut’s 06103 debuted at No. 8, a jump fueled by office-to-apartment conversions in a neighborhood with few full-time residents. And Nashville’s 37203, covering Midtown and Music Row, grabbed the 10th spot thanks to a crop of new rental towers luring young professionals.
Not everyone held their ground. Richmond’s 23219, El Paso’s 79908 and Nashville’s 37228 all tumbledout of the top 10after making the cut the month before.

A San Franciscorenter has been offered$35,000 to walk away from her apartment, but the eye popping check has not been enough to make her say yes.
Serabeth Mullaney is facinga very San Francisco dilemma.
Her landlord wants the apartment back and is willing to pay five figures to get it, but Mullaney saysthe nightmare of finding another placecould make the deal a bad bargain for her.

She has beendocumenting the situation on TikTok, where she explained what is keeping her from accepting the offer.
“The one thing I think that is stopping me from accepting it is the apartment hunt,” Mullaney said.
Mullaney described the prospect of finding a new home in the city as a “nightmare,” and said there is another string attached to the deal because her landlord is also asking her tosign a nondisclosure agreement.
Tenant buyouts are a familiar feature of San Francisco’s heavily regulated rental market, where strict protections can prevent landlords from simply raising rents dramatically on existing tenants.
Paying a renter to leave can give a landlord a way to regain the unit and then charge a price that better reflects current market rates.
For Mullaney, however, the problem is what happens after she takes the money.
The average one bedroom apartment in San Francisco now costs $4,500,according to Zillow, while fierce competition has created a particularly painful trend for renters as bidding wars break out over available apartments.
Mullaney has kept her exact location private, althoughSan Francisco Rent Board datashows that many of the city’s high value tenant buyouts have occurred in historically rent controlled, high demand neighborhoods such as the Mission, Castro, Haight Ashbury and Pacific Heights.
Her $35,000 offer might sound like a fortune, but it is actually right around San Francisco’s historical median for tenant buyouts, meaning some renters have walked away with vastly larger sums.
The biggest recorded buyout in the city went to a couple in their 60swho received a staggering $475,000to leave their seven bedroom rent controlled apartment in Presidio Heights.
They had lived there for 30 years while paying $12,500 a month for the sprawling luxury flat, which came with sweeping views ofthe Golden Gate Bridge.
That history puts Mullaney’s offer into perspective, particularly as she weighs the possibility of giving up an apartment in a city where replacing it could prove painfully difficult.Real estate lawyers have described buyouts in the $35,000 to $50,000 range as“chump change”for landlords.

ASuper Bowlwinning quarterback is behind a new community nicknamed “Gridiron Grove.”
David Carr, aformer NFL signal callerfor the New York Giants and Houston Texans, is one of the partners for a newdevelopment in Clovis, California and he says he’s taking it all the way to the house.

“This is America to me, family is still valued here,” Carr exclusively told the California Post.
Traditions at Heritage Grove kicked off sales earlier this month starting at $400,000 for a three bedroom two and a half bath home, which is way down from the Golden State average of $900K.
California Post News:Facebook,Instagram,TikTok,X,YouTube,WhatsApp,LinkedInCalifornia Post SportsFacebook,Instagram,TikTok,YouTube,XCalifornia PostOpinionCalifornia Post Newsletters:Sign up here!California Post App:Download here!Home delivery:Sign up here!Page Six Hollywood:Sign up here!
Clovis sits just north of Fresnoin California’s agricultural rich Central Valley, not far from where Carr was a Bulldog at Fresno State before becoming the NFL’s 1st overall draft pick by the Texans in 2002.
In a time where successful athletes find wealthy enclaves by the sea, Carr, who won the 2012 Superbowl with the Giants, has chosen to move back to the landlocked area where his NFL career was shaped.
“It’s still home.  It’ll always be home for us. You’re in New York, you’re in the Bay Area but this place in particular is special, there’s always something on your plate grown in this area,” Carr said.
Clovis, referred to as the “Gateway to the Sierras” has had its struggles economically. The area consists of wealthy agricultural land owners farming cattle, while others are often left behind.
“Not everyone can have a farm, so you need starter houses with a community feel. You can open your garage doors and meet people, talk to your neighbors. That’s how I grew up, playing football in the street, using light posts as end zones,” Carr said.
Carr and his wife Melody are partnered with the experienced Bonadelle Family who have been building homes in the Fresno Valley for 80 years.
“I believe in what they’re doing, I believe in this area. I want it to grow,” Carr said.
The Traditions at Heritage development features four homes to choose from ranging from just over 1200 square feet to almost 1900 square feet.
The largest homes in the community dubbed “The Encore” feature up to 4 bedrooms and two and a half baths.
Amenities include 9 foot ceilings, abundant windows, kitchen island with sink and breakfast bar, and phone charging stations in the kitchen and master bedroom.
The gated neighborhood located on Cherry Lane near Minnewana Avenue also features a pool and pickleball court in case you want to trade in your pads and helmet for a racquet.
Carr says his brotherDerek Carr who played for the Saints and Raidersalso has a house nearby.
The ex-Giant revealed his son Austin and his wife, Kaleigh are expecting a baby boy “any minute”, and looking to move into “Gridiron Grove” so they can be close to the dozens of Carr’s in the area.
“It’s a little slower than when he was hailing cabs at six years old, ” Carr said referring to the time when he was playing in New York with family in tow, “Now he’s hand feeding cows instead, and we’re about to pass that on to a new generation.”
“This is where I’m supposed to be,” he added.

hed: Powerful nor’easter pounds dozens of vulnerable shore homes in North Carolina’s Outer Banks — with 100 more at risk
subhead: Years of erosion have put more homes at the water’s edge
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An early-seasonnor’easter is pounding a stretch of North Carolina’s Outer Bankswhere dozens of homes are already threatened by the advancing ocean — and officials warn the next row may not be far behind
On Thursday, Cape Hatteras National Seashore closed the beach from the northern edge of Rodanthe to the town’s pier because “multiple threatened oceanfront structures pose risks to public safety,”according to the National Park Service.
For locals, it’s an all-too-familiar scene. Since 2020,32 homes have collapsed,as erosion has steadily redrawn the shoreline.
The losses have been concentrated around Rodanthe and Buxton, two small villages on Hatteras Island, one of the narrow barrier islands that make up the Outer Banks.
At a state meeting last November, officials said they were tracking 100 threatened structures in the two towns, and warned more could follow.
“If every one of those structures falls in,” Cape Hatteras National Seashore Superintendent Dave Hallacsaid, “there would be another 100 right behind them.”
Already, at least five more homes have collapsed since Hallac’s warning, according to NPS records. Andthe latest stormis putting the remaining threatened properties through another round of punishment.
On Thursday, extreme tides broke through protective dunes on Pea Island, just north of Rodanthe, damaging roughly 500 feet of pavement and forcing the closure of N.C. 12. The National Weather Service warned of breaking waves peaking at 10 to 15 feet through Saturday evening.
The pounding surf is hitting a coastline that looks radically different from when many of its beachfront homes were built.
Michael McDaniel bought his Buxton beach house for about $500,000 in 2011, when roughly 250 feet—nearly the length of a football field—of dune separated its front porch from the Atlantic.
But in the 15 years since, erosion has erased that buffer and left his home uninhabitable.
That retreat is not unique to McDaniel’s property. The Outer Banks are barrier islands—narrow ribbons of sand that naturally shift as waves and currents move sand up and down the coast.
Erosion itself is part of that natural process.
In parts of Rodanthe, the shoreline has retreated an average of about 13 feet per year, according toDare County. Around parts of Buxton, chronic erosion historically exceeded 20 feet per year.
Those long-term averages can hide much more abrupt losses during bad weather, too.
DuringHurricane Erin in August 2025,for example, 75 residential structures were damaged in the two villages. Over the following two months, 16 homes collapsed during a succession of offshore storms.
And as the shoreline moves inland, it’s colliding development built decades earlier. County records show that most of the homes now threatened were built in the 1980s and 1990s when the ocean was much farther away.
Homeowners facing this slow-moving threat have few options.
While flood insurance typically covers direct physical damage caused by flooding, it may not pay simply because erosion has put a home in danger.
“The NFIP policy pays for a direct physical loss from flood,” Lisa Sharrard, a North Carolina flood insurance agent and Certified Floodplain Manager, tells Realtor.com®. “So there has to [be] a flooding event, not normal high tide.”
“The SFIP does not cover damage caused by gradual erosion,” Sharrard adds.
That can leave homeowners like McDaniel in between a rock and a hard place: Stuck with a home they may no longer be able to safely use but one that has not yet suffered the kind of damage an insurance policy is designed to cover.
“If they have a policy, the policy may pay if the house collapses due to erosion,” Sharrard explains. “In the meantime, they have a house they cannot use and debris to clean up after. Most are trying to move if they can.”
Even when federal flood coverage does apply, the standard NFIP policy provides no more than $250,000 in building coverage for a single-family home—a sum that falls woefully short of what impacted homeowners need.
One Rodanthe couple previously told Realtor.com they spent more than $200,000 to move their house roughly 100 feet inland after erosion brought the ocean dangerously close. And they had something many threatened homeowners don’t: enough land left behind the house to put it somewhere else.
So where does that leave the homeowners farther back from the water—and the communities trying to keep them from becoming the next ones at risk?
One option is to try to keep the shoreline from reaching them.
But North Carolina prohibits most permanent seawalls, leaving communities to rely heavily on beach nourishment: the practice of pumping sand onto an eroding beach to try and rebuild a buffer in front of homes and roads.
Buxton spent about $18.1 million replenishing 2.9 miles of shoreline in 2022. Two years later, a coastal storm stripped away an estimated 175,000 cubic yards of sand. Engineers estimated replacing that loss alone would cost another $10.2 million.
So this summer, the dredges came back. By Sept. 16, crews had placed about 1.5 million cubic yards of new sand along Buxton—just over a week before the current nor’easter began pounding Hatteras Island.
Even under normal conditions, Dare County says nourishment projects generally last about five years before more sand is needed.
In Rodanthe, officials say even that solution is too expensive.
“In Rodanthe there isn’t enough money to solve the problem with beach nourishment,” Dare County Manager Bobby Outten told state coastal officials in November.
Meanwhile, the ocean is expected to keep rising. TheFifth National Climate Assessment projects15 to 22 inches of sea-level rise around the Outer Banks by 2050, allowing future high tides and storms to reach farther inland.

hed: Home of the Week: Elevated views of the Arnold Arboretum from this $700k Jamaica Plain condo

It’s kind of like Boston’s Formula 1 racetrack — the 1.6-mile Arborway that parallels theArnold Arboretumas it curves from Forest Hills to Pond Street in Jamaica Plain.

But this story isn’t aboutthatroadway. It’s about a third-floor condo on the less traveled carriage road that parallels the Arborway. Given its elevated location, it provides views of the ever-changing arboretum greenery.

The red of the brick building is contrasted by the white window framing and private decks with white railings that pop out on the front of each floor. From the street, a wide sidewalk on the right leads to the building and a common stairwell that corkscrews to the third floor. (This is not an elevatored building.)


From the landing, there are two ways into the unit: A door into the living room and a door into the front bedroom, which is currently configured as an office.

This room is also the access point to the private front deck from which the views encompasses the 281-acre arboretum.

“With the arboretum just across the street, some of our favorite moments have been the nearly daily walks there with our two young children,” the current owners wrote in an e-mail provided to the Globe by the listing agent.


The 144-square-foot bedroom/office is one of the brightest in the home, compliments of a pair of updated double-hung windows located in the front of the unit. Flooring is refinished hardwood and believed original to the home. The room has two closets.


A doorway at the rear of the office connects to the 156-square-foot living room, which occupies the remainder of the area in the front of the home. On the front wall is a three-part composite window, with a larger one in the middle, flanked by smaller double-hung windows. On the second exterior wall, a rectangular window adds to the flow of natural light. Flooring is refinished hardwood.


A wide cased opening leads to the dining room where a feature original to the home is the standout. On the left is a triangular built-in china cabinet with glass doors and drawers. The cabinet, trim, and raised panel wainscoting are all painted white, as is the ceiling. The walls are a light gray, and there is a central light fixture. On the right is a bank of three double-hung windows, and the flooring is refinished hardwood.


A door opens into the 156-square-foot kitchen. On the left is the gas range nestled on each side and above by cabinets. The countertop on the cabinets on each side of the range is black granite. The microwave is located above the range. On the right is another set of cabinets and the sink. The exterior wall has two large, double-hung windows, and between the windows is an island with an overhang that provides seating for two. The refrigerator is stainless steel. The full-size washer/dryer shares the 34-square-foot room. Off the kitchen is a second porch.


A door from the kitchen enters into a hallway occupied by the primary bedroom, a secondary bedroom, and the one full bath. The 48-square-foot bathroom, which has refinished hardwood flooring, features a white clawfoot tub with an attached showerhead behind a curtain. There is a white pedestal sink and subway tile on the lower half of the walls.



The primary bedroom is reached by turning left from the kitchen. It’s 144 square feet and has a pair of windows deep into the right corner of the space. There is a six-panel door guarding the closet, and on the ceiling, there is a propeller-style fan with light. The flooring is refinished hardwood.


The final room is the secondary bedroom at the rear of the home. It’s 144 square feet, and has double-hung windows on each of the walls. Like the primary, there is a propeller-style ceiling fan with light. The floor is hardwood.


Karen McCormack and Paula Callaghanof the Insight Realty Group in Jamaica Plain have the listing.

hed: Julia Child’s former Cambridge home — where she filmed shows — on market for $6.4M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

A historic home in Cambridge, MA, boasting an impressive culinary pedigree has just hit the market near Harvard Square for $6,475,000.
Theformer homeof legendary chef Julia Child is where the cookbook author and TV host of “The French Chef” lived with her husband, Paul, for 40 years.
“The home is a garden-style house, so the front of the house is on the side, and the home itself is surrounded by gardens,” saysEd Feijo, who is co-listing the property withGail Roberts of Coldwell Banker Realty. “The house is set in the middle of the lot, so you enjoy views of the gardens from every room.”
Built in 1889, the six-bedroom residence offers a spacious 6,321 square feet of modern living.
Child lived in the home until 2001, when she moved to a retirement community in California and donated her house and office to Smith College, which later sold it, according toHistory Cambridge.
While the shows “Cooking with Master Chefs,” “In Julia’s Kitchen with Master Chefs,” “Baking with Julia,” and “Julia and Jacques Cooking at Home” are all said to have been filmed in her Cambridge home, Child donated her original kitchen to theSmithsonian’s National Museum of American History, where it remains on display.
“The whole property has been updated since then,” Feijo noted. “The house is a stone’s throw from Harvard Square but is located in a suburban environment.”
The light-filled residence boasts hardwood floors, wainscoting, a bay window with built-in seating, French doors, and four fireplaces.
A grand foyer opens up to the living area and family room with built-in shelves.
Child’s former cooking spothas been transformed into a luxurious chef’s kitchen with Poggenpohl cabinetry, marble countertops, dual dishwashers, and a butler’s pantry (where Paul perfected his signature upside-down martini) that now doubles as a caterer’s kitchen. From here, there is also access to two covered porches.
An upstairs primary suite has a gas fireplace, a walk-in closet with built-in cabinetry, a spa-inspired bathroom with a soaking tub, and access to a private terrace.
The third floor features an office with a built-in desk. On the lower level, there’s a wine room and a bonus area that could be transformed into a fitness center, entertainment room, or guest accommodations.
A brick patio framed by a stone wall overlooks the lushly landscaped, fenced-in yard. There is also a porte-cochère that offers sheltered parking.
“The next buyer could be a family, someone who teaches at Harvard, or someone who loves to entertain,” he adds.
Because of its prime location and walkable convenience to restaurants, shops, and cafes, Feijo believes the property will likely be used as a primary residence.
“It is located in a neighborhood called Professor’s Row, which is located behind the Divinity School and Harvard Law School,” he notes. “It’s a neighborhood steeped in history with lots of interesting people, so it speaks to a lot of different buyer pools.”

hed: Inside Spirit Halloween’s real estate maneuvers — and why locations pop up where they do
subhead: How did Spirit Halloween get here?
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The arrival of fall also means the arrival, in many places, of a Spirit Halloween store.
The pop-up retailer that specializes in costumes, decorations, and party supplies forspooky seasonis almost ubiquitous during September and October, with over 1,500 seasonal locations in shopping centers and strip malls across North America. The brand’s ability to set up shop quickly and then disappear in November is the stuff of legend.
But thetemporary nature of a Spirit—and the way they tend to inhabit big, empty storefronts—can leave people with mixed feeling.
Some might look at Spirit taking over a former Party City as the work of an involved landlord, seeking to keep foot traffic up until another long-term lease is signed. Others might worry that a Spirit is a last-ditch effort to squeeze a few bucks out of a dying area. And either direction could be a sign of things to come for the broader market and your home directly.
There’s no definitive answer to that uncertainty here. Experts say it comes down to the broader context of the area, rather than just the Spirit itself.
Spirit Halloween has been offering its pop-up retail experience since 1983. The heart of its strategy lies in finding large, vacant commercial spaces, and convincing the landlords to agree to short-term leases. An empty Party City or Bed, Bath, and Beyond is a prime opportunity for Spirit to move in, even temporarily.
“We like to locate our stores in power centers, strip centers, free-standing stores, major downtown retail locations and in major malls surrounded by a national retailer mix,” says theSpirit Halloween website.
It also notes they look for communities with a population of approximately 35,000-plus, living within a 3-5 mile radius, and a car count of at least 25,000 cars per day.
So whileSpirit’s physical footprintonly lasts a few months, the effort to locate the right places to set up shop is a year-round endeavor. Don’t let the gaudy costumes and masks fool you: this is a savvy operation.
“Spirit is an opportunistic real estate player,” says Todd Drowlette, the managing director of TITAN Commercial Realty Group in Albany, NY.
“They target busy, regional locations with high traffic counts and traffic generators in the center or retail corridor like Target, Walmart, or grocery stores. Landlords will do deals with them, because they are short term deals and Spirit typically takes the locations ‘as is’ so it is basically some cash flow for the property owner while the vacant space is being marketed.”
In short, a Spirit Halloween is often a win-win-win—for the business itself, for the landlord of the building they inhabit, and for shoppers looking for an accessible way to find costumes ahead of trick-or-treating.
Just because Spirit’s model is savvy doesn’t mean it’s not kind of funny.
A Bed, Bath, and Beyond in a space may have once signaled something like adulthood and maturity—while a Spirit Halloween is kitschy and silly. And to top it off, the store literally “haunts” an abandoned retail space. You can forgive people for thinking that a Spirit arriving isn’t necessarily a sign of economic strength.
“I think Spirit is the visible indicator that consumers see and think ‘retail apocalypse’ and can be the butt of jokes,” says Stephanie D’Amico, VP at CrossMarc Services, a commercial real estate advisory in Winter Park, FL. But those who understand commercial retail know that an empty storefront with a temporary tenant is just part of the business.
“Having a vacancy is not a harbinger of the death of retail. Retail is just evolving,” she says. “It could end up being filled long-term by a new grocery concept, a new online retailer looking for brick and mortar like a Wayfair, or just another relocation of a similar tenant in the market.”
D’Amico also argues that a shopping center that invites a Spirit is better than one that leaves the space empty.
“Halloween is a huge industry, so a Spirit or similar type use is a great way to bring in shopping center traffic,” she says.
Where a Spirit could be seen as a sign of decline is when you see it pop up in the same place more than once—like deja vu.
“If Spirit rents the same vacancy two years in a row, that is a serious red flag for that shopping center and market potentially,” says Drowlette. “Most spaces rented by Spirit are leased by the time the following Halloween season comes back around.”
If that same space is still empty by spring, it’s fair to worry about that location’s long-term viability.
And sometimes it’s the absence of a Spirit that should bother locals, says Drowlette. If you have multiple shopping centers with several larger vacancies where a Spirit could live, that could be the sign of a domino effect of business failure. Better to see four Spirit Halloween’s in one high-density city—even if it feels like overkill—than four empty storefronts.
So what does it mean if a Spirit Halloween, or even more than one, moves into your neighborhood? On its face, not much.
“A Spirit Halloween store near you does not have any direct impact on your home’s property values,” says Drowlette. “Spirit Halloween themselves never cause a market decline. They don’t hurt markets, the markets are in trouble if they have too many vacant boxes to choose from in any given season.”
Like any other business, especially one that has been around for over 40 years, Spirit has standards. The brand will pass on a location if the traffic, income, and demographic don’t meet their minimum requirements, says D’Amico. So maybe a little haunting of your nearby vacant commercial space is a good thing.
Not only that, but Spirit is likely to expand its offerings:Spirit Christmas, which the company has run intermittently over the company’s lifespan, returned in 2024, and expanded to 30 locations in 2025.

New Yorkers searching for an escape from the city’s punishing housing costs are increasingly eyeing a familiar neighbor — Philadelphia,where homes costless than half.
The New York metro posted a net outflow of 27,143 prospective movers during the second quarter, meaning significantly more people were looking to leave the region than move in, according toa new Redfin analysisof home-search activity.
That was the second-largest net outflow among the country’s 100 biggest metros, trailing only Los Angeles, at 28,652. (Angelenos, for their part,headed to the Sin Cityof Las Vegas in search of cheaper housing costs there.)
And for New Yorkers looking elsewhere, the most popular destination wasn’t Miami, Orlando or another sunny southern city.
It was Philadelphia — just 90 miles south.
The reason may come down to a whopping half-million-dollar difference in home prices.
A typical home in the New York area costs about $832,000, compared with just $309,000 in Philadelphia — a roughly $523,000 gap, according to Redfin.
Philly may be the top destination for New Yorkers considering a move, but the Sunshine State continues to exert a powerful pull.
New York was the most common origin for people looking to relocate to Orlando, Miami and Tampa, which ranked third, fourth and seventh, respectively, among the metros with the biggest net inflows.
Florida dominated at the state level, too.
The Sunshine State recordeda net inflow of 38,922 prospective movers during the quarter — more than Arizona, South Carolina and Tennessee, the next three most popular states, combined.
South Carolina followed with a net inflow of 13,764, while Arizona gained 11,929 and Tennessee gained 9,872.
New York sat on the opposite end of the spectrum, posting a net outflow of 29,838 at the state level, second only toCalifornia’s whopping 56,548.
Illinois, Washington and Massachusetts rounded out the five states with the largest net outflows.
The trend reflects a broader reshuffling of where Americans are willing to live as high housing costs continue to push would-be buyers and renters beyond their home markets.
Nationwide, 18.7% of Redfin users searched for homes outside their current metro during the second quarter, up from 18.1% a year earlier and the highest second-quarter share in records dating back to 2021.
Ongoing trends in remote and hybrid work have made it easier for Americans to consider farther-flung destinations, Redfin noted, while the huge differences in housing costs give residents of pricey coastal metros another reason to look elsewhere.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean Americans are packing up the U-Haul in record numbers.
Overall homebuying remains sluggish, so the total number of people actually relocating is likely still below the pandemic-era levels seen in 2021 and 2022, even as relocation searches account for a larger share of the market.
Redfin’s figures measure home-search activity rather than completed moves. Its analysis covers users who viewed at least 20 homes for sale or rent in a destination metro during a month, and can include searches for second homes and investment properties.

hed: Solo renters must earn nearly $154K annually to afford a studio, per new ‘Carrie Bradshaw Index’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Living alone in New York City still requires a veryCarrie Bradshaw-sized fantasybudget — or, more realistically, a six-figure salary.
A solo renter in New York would need to earn $153,600 a year before taxes to comfortably afford the city’s typical studio, according to The Economist’s latest “Carrie Bradshaw Index,” named for the “Sex and the City” heroine famousfor living alone in Manhattanon a columnist’s salary.
The typical studio payment in New York is $3,840 a month, according to the index, which assumes renters should spend no more than 30% of their gross income on housing.
For comparison, Los Angeles renters face a steep solo-living hurdle, too. A typical studio in LA County rents for about $2,004 a month, according toRealtor.com data, which translates to roughly $80,000 a year to stay within the 30% affordability rule — still far below New York’s $153,000 threshold.
There is better news for renters nationally.
The number of America’s 100 biggest cities that the index considers unaffordable for an average earner has fallen to 30 — the lowest since The Economist began the index three years ago.
Nationwide, renters who want to live alone now need to earn about $150 less per month than they did a year ago.
A surge of newly completed apartments has helped ease the squeeze. The US added 695,000 apartments in 2024 — a 40-year record — followed by another 531,000 in 2025, according to The Economist.
At the same time, softer demand has helped slow rent growth and prompted landlords to dangle incentives such as free months or waived fees.
The improvement has been particularly noticeable in some smaller and less expensive markets. Cities including Oklahoma City and Lexington, Ky., posted some of the biggest affordability gains, while 11 cities crossed into affordable territory.
In Oklahoma City, one of the biggest gainers in The Economist’s index, a studio averages $735 a month, according toZumper.That would require an annual income of about $29,400 under the index’s 30% rule. In Lexington, Ky., the average studio costs $984 a month, requiring about $39,400 a year.
The picture is similar in three other cities. Studios average $945 in Phoenix, $944 in Detroit and $875 in El Paso, requiring annual incomes of roughly $35,000 to $38,000.
New York’s $3,840 studio, by comparison, requires $153,600 a year. Nationally, the median studio rent was $1,595 a month in August, according toApartmentAdvisor.
That makes the index’s namesake especially fitting.
Carrie Bradshaw famously lived by herself in a rent-controlled Upper East Side apartment despite working primarily as a newspaper columnist — a lifestyle that has long raised questions about how she actually paid for it.
And the national rental reprieve may prove temporary. The Economist notes that new construction starts have fallen sharply from their 2022 level and are now at their lowest quarterly total since 2011, potentially limiting future supply.
For now, solo renters across much of America are finally catching a break.
New Yorkers hoping to trade in their roommates for their own Carrie Bradshaw apartment? Not so much.

hed: Luxurious home in “Ghostbusters” building offers Central Park views — but only for $8.9M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
A sprawling 4,400-square-foot home with direct views of Central Park has opened up in theprewar co-oppop culture mavens will recognize from the 1984 film, “Ghostbusters.”
In the film—which stars Bill Murray, Dan Akyroyd, Sigourney Weaver, and Harold Ramis—the 19-floor building is named “Spook Central,”but in real life, it’s known as 55 Central Park West or The Shandor Building.
Although the professional Ghostbusters from the movie determine that the building—which is home to residents possessed by demons—was built by a cult leader, the truth is that the iconic art deco high-rise was constructed in 1929 by renowned architects Schwartz and Gross.
55 Central Park West’s design is considered to be a pivotal build for the art deco movement, and the original interiors of residences inside were also innovative when it opened in 1930.
Originally filled withapartments touting three to nine rooms, the units featured newly developed dropped living rooms that set the homes apart from anything else.
The unit available is an $8.9 million five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom residence which boasts 60 feet of Central Park frontage and from the inside, its 13 rooms create an atmosphere that feels more like a spacious suburban house than a New York City condominium.
The listing is represented byLisa K. Lippman of Brown Harris Stevens.
The abode features a park-facing, grand sunken living room with herringbone floors and is flooded with light, thanks to a massive picture window. Coffered ceilings, sleek crown molding, and unique light fixtures add to the home’s grandeur.
The formal dining room strikes the perfect balance between the building’s original prewar character and modern luxury, with the size and layout well suited for entertaining or intimate family gatherings.
Equipped with ample storage space and a wine refrigerator, the newly renovated kitchen is just steps away and offers an additional dining space for more casual dining.
Bedrooms are arranged in two separate wings for optimal privacy, with the primary suite situated in the south side of the home,facing Central Park.
The primary suite includes lots of closet space and an oversized bathroom with double vanities and more park views. In fact, all of the home’s 5.5 bathrooms have windows.
Depending on how a buyer may choose to utilize the layout, the home’s north side can host three or four additional large bedrooms. There’s also a sizable den, which hosts access to a kitchenette and laundry room.
The remaining rooms in the home can be leveraged to suit just about any lifestyle.
Potential buyers can prioritize a work-life balance with a dedicated library and office, young families can thrive with a playroom, or a fashion-obsessed resident can take advantage of the home’s opportunities to add additional closet and dressing spaces.
In addition to its starring role in a legendary supernatural comedy, The Shandor Building has been called home by a handful of notable individuals.
Designers Calvin Klein and Donna Karan have each lived there, as has film entertainment mogul David Geffen.
Billionaire businessman Marc Lasry and the late “Hello, Dolly!” composer Jerry Herman resided there, as well.
With an impressive offering of amenities, it’s no surprise that 55 Central Park West has drawn the attention of so many distinguished residents.
The 109-unit building promises “white-glove, full-service” and has a full staff, including two full-time doormen and a live-in resident manager.
There’s a bicycle room, storage bins, laundry facilities, a dedicated generator, and a newly added community room in the lobby. A new state-of-the-art fitness center has been added, as well.
55 Central Park West permits pied-à-terres and welcomes pets.
The building is conveniently located near the world-famous Lincoln Center, a destination for fans of music, dance, opera, theater and cinema.
Some of Central Park’s most exciting attractions—such asTavern on the Greenand the Central Park Carousel—are also within close reach.

hed: Supermodel Linda Evangelista gets $6.75M for the NYC penthouse she rented to Keanu Reeves
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Canadian supermodel Linda Evangelista’s West Chelsea penthouse has sold for $6.75 million, according to property records.
News of the dealwas first reportedby Curbed.
The industrial-chic home, which comes with a 2,500-square-foot terrace, was rented last year by fellow CanadianKeanu Reeves for around $45,000 a month, when he was in town starring in Broadway’s “Waiting for Godot,” as Gimme Shelter exclusively reported at the time.
The penthouse is inside 525 W. 22nd St., a six-story elevator edifice known as the Spears Building.
A West Chelsea real estate pioneer, Evangelista purchased the swanky aerie in a then-burgeoning arts district for $1.4 million back in 2001 — eight years before the first section of the popular High Line opened, transforming the area.
The Canadian beauty had first listed the four-bedroom, two-bath nest for $9.45 million in 2024. The price had then droppedfirst to $8.19 millionand then to$7.99 million earlier this year,as Gimme also reported.
Listing broker Steve Gold, of Corcoran, once told Gimme Shelter that the price was a “value buy” because he has sold “north of $5,000 a square foot nearby.”
The 4,022-square-foot ritzy residence comes with lots of open spaces and custom built-ins.
A large living room is warmed by a fireplace. There’s also an eat-in chef’s kitchen.
Industrial design-style details include high ceilings, skylights, polished concrete floors and exposed brick.
As for the pièce de résistance, the main corner bedroom suite features High Line views, a spa-like bath and a grand dressing room fit for a supermodel — with six floor-to-ceiling custom closets.
In 1990, Evangelista famously told Vogue that she and fellow supermodel Christy Turlington wouldn’t “wake up for less than $10,000 a day.” Back then, she was part of a supermodel cabal that included Turlington, as well as Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford, Claudia Schiffer and Tatjana Patitz.
Although Evangelista is leaving West Chelsea, she is not leaving New York. Last year, Evangelista paid $5.24 million for a three-bedroom unit not too far away — at 35 Hudson Yards, according to property records.
