hed: Julia Child’s Boston-area home asks $6.47M — where she filmed her shows and her flowers still grow
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Julia Child’s former home of four decades — a late-19th-century residence just blocks from Harvard Yard — is on the market for $6.47 million.
Child’s world-famous home kitchen was preserved and now stands in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. But this updated home still has her stamp — including her plantings in the irrigated, landscaped garden and Floribunda roses, Coldwell Banker’s Ed Feijo, who shares the listing with Coldwell’s Gail Roberts, told Gimme Shelter.
The listing was first reported onBoston.com.
Child wasn’t just a national culinary treasure known for introducing the American home chefs to the delights of cooking butter-and-cream-rich, delicious French cuisine. She was also an American intelligence official working directly for General William J. Donovan, the head of the OSS — the precursor to the CIA — in places including China and Sri Lanka during World War II.
Her work included creating a synthetic chemical shark repellent to save sailors from shark attacks after ships and planes went down and to keep sharks from setting off underwater explosives intended to detonate German U-boats.
The OSS is also where Julia McWilliams, born in California in 1912, met her husband, Paul Cushing Child. In 1948, the couple moved to Paris, where Paul was posted with the State Department’s Information Service; that’s where she first discovered and studied French cooking.
The couple returned to the US in 1961 after other foreign stints and bought this Cambridge residence.
Built in 1889, it’s where Child filmed her TV shows, including “In Julia’s Kitchen with Master Chefs” and “Julia and Jacques Cooking at Home,” helping Americans learn to make the perfect omelet, quiche Lorraine and roast chicken, among other dishes.
The sellers, who have declined to be named, bought the dwelling for $3.7 million in 2009, according to property records.
Child lived in the home from 1961 to 2001, when she moved into a California retirement home. She died in 2004 in Montecito at the age of 91.
She donated the house to her alma mater Smith College in Western Massachusetts, while donating the kitchen, separately, to the Smithsonian, according to History Cambridge.
The six-bedroom residence, at 103 Irving St., is known as a “garden-style” home.
“The home was built in the center of the lot so all the rooms look out onto the gardens, bringing the outside in,” Feijo told Gimme Shelter.
Behind a white fence and a brick walkway, front steps lead to the entrance.
At 6,321 square feet, the renovated spread includes a new chef’s kitchen with a pantry in a space where Paul once prepared martinis for Child and their guests.
Because Child was a striking 6-foot-2, Paul designed the original kitchen to accommodate her so she could easily reach for higher shelves in a way that would not be awkward for her tall frame.
The residence opens to a grand entry that leads to a large living and dining area. Along with the chef’s kitchen, there’s a family room with French doors and a bay window that comes with a built-in seat. There are also four gas fireplaces, including one with an original stone mantel, Feijo said.
Upstairs, the main bedroom suite features a fireplace, an ensuite bath and a balcony on the second floor. Additional bedrooms are on this floor and the third floor, which also boasts a home office. The basement holds a gym, a laundry room and a wine room.
The property also comes with solar panels, as well as charming covered porches, a patio and a stone wall.

hed: Larry Ellison quietly bought 8 homes for his staff to be near his sprawling Florida mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Larry Ellison’s Florida real estate empire apparently comes with its own staff housing.
The Oracle billionaire quietly bought eight houses in the a single gated Boynton Beach community, shelling out nearly $10 million to put members of his family’s household staff within commuting distance of his sprawling Manalapan estate.
The buying spree unfolded over just weeks in 2023 at Palm Meadows Estates, a 288-home enclave about 30 minutes from Ellison’s oceanfront compound, according to property records.
And Ellison wasn’t shopping for investment properties.
The homes were intended for employees who help keep the billionaire’s household running, including tutors for some of the five children he shares with his wife, Jolin Ellison, people familiar with the arrangement told theWall Street Journal.
The unusual setup offers a window into how the ultrawealthy are expanding their real estate footprints beyond mansions and vacation homes, increasingly securing separate housing for the employees who make their lifestyles possible.
For Ellison, 82, that meant effectively creating a satellite neighborhood for staff near his own South Florida base.
Ellison made a splash in Manalapan in 2022 whenhe paid $173 millionfor Gemini, a roughly 15-acre estate stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Intracoastal Waterway. The blockbuster deal set a Florida residential sales record at the time.
About 30 minutes away sits Palm Meadows Estates, a guarded community in West Boynton Beach surrounded by South Florida horse country. Itshomeowners associationsays the development contains 288 homesites that all boast water views along with 24-hour staffed security and a clubhouse.
Ellison’s arrival there began with a mysterious house hunt.
Around March 2023, Palm Meadows resident and LuxeIQ real estate agent Kimmie Cruz said she received a request from another broker seeking immediate access to her listings for an unidentified buyer interested in acquiring roughly 10 houses.
The search wasn’t limited to properties already for sale.
Cruz said the buyer’s team was particularly interested in single-story ranch homes and eventually began pursuing houses whose owners hadn’t put them on the market.
That sent Cruz knocking on doors.
“I said, ‘Look, this is the chance to sell it without having to have it on the market,’” Cruz told the Journal. “‘This is a chance to have somebody very viable. The money is there.’”
The mystery didn’t last long.
Days later, Cruz was told the buyer himself wanted to tour the properties. Ellison showed up accompanied by bodyguards, and signed contracts soon followed.
An LLC connected to Ellison ultimately closed on all eight houses in May and June 2023, spending nearly $10 million in total, according to property records.
The homes themselves are a far cry from Ellison’s trophy estate in Manalapan. They are relatively modest suburban properties with tidy yards, with some featuring private swimming pools.
For several owners, however, Ellison’s buying spree produced a hefty payday.
Paul and Yvonne Carozza sold their roughly 2,100-square-foot, three-bedroom home for $1.2 million after purchasing it for $567,000 in 2019, according to property records.
The arrangement is part of a broader luxury real estate phenomenon as billionaires, hedge fund executives and other wealthy homeowners increasingly secure nearby accommodations for nannies, tutors, chefs and other household employees.
Providing housing can also be a powerful recruiting tool in expensive markets where employees might otherwise face long commutes or steep housing costs.
“If you want them to get to work quickly and have a reasonable commute, investing in lodging can be a very smart decision,” Peter Mahler of Mahler Private Staffing told the Journal.
Keeping employees nearby but outside the main residence can provide another commodity prized by billionaires: privacy.
The concept is increasingly finding its way into luxury condominium developments as well, with smaller units sometimes incorporated into buildings to accommodate household employees separately from owners’ primary residences.
YouTuber Jimmy Donaldson, better known as Mr. Beast, for example, purchased an entire neighborhood for his staff and family in North Carolina for the same reason, The Postpreviously reported.
At Ellison’s Manalapan estate, some of the buildings include areas used to homeschool his older children, who have multiple tutors and are learning several languages, according to people familiar with the family.
But buying eight houses in one relatively small community did not sit well with everyone.
Some Palm Meadows residents objected to one owner amassing such a large concentration of properties, andthe homeowners associationsubsequently adopted restrictions designed to stop a similar buying spree from happening again, according to Cruz.
Ellison’s footprint remains visible around the neighborhood.
Residents said people living in at least some of the staff houses drive Teslas. County records also show permits were filed for Tesla Powerwalls at all eight properties after the purchases.
Ellison served on Tesla’s board from 2018 until 2022.
Meanwhile, his South Florida holdings have continued to grow far beyond staff accommodations. His $173 million Manalapan purchase helped put the tiny barrier-island town on thebillionaire real estate map,part of a broader influx of technology and finance wealth into the region.

The 1933 home located at 1856 Jewett Drive is listed for $849,000 — yep, you read that right — and offers something increasingly rare in the highly sought-after canyon: Two separate houses on one terraced lot.

Down an outdoor staircase sits a completely independent second unit, tucked into the hillside and surrounded by greenery with canyon views galore — and resplendent with an outdoor clawfoot tub. Although not hooked up, the tub is perfect for a rustic soak under the stars.

In a market where starter homes are more often than not well above the million mark, the Jewett Drive listing stands out as a genuine anomaly — a quirky, character-filled foothold in one of Los Angeles’ most storied and historical neighborhoods, priced to sell under $850,000.

hed: Rare Lake Placid ‘70s time capsule’ hits market for first time in half a century — complete with groovy living room spa
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This Lake Placid home is still partying like it’s 1977.
A sprawling Adirondacks time capsule built just before the 1980 Winter Olympics has hit the market for $1.39 million — complete with soaring ceilings, shaggy retro interiors and, yes, a hot tub in the living room.
The five-bedroom, six-bath home at 33 Evans Lane spans a whopping 7,026 square feet on 4 acres in Lake Placid’s aptly named Olympic Hills neighborhood.
Built in 1977, the chalet has remained in the same family for nearly 50 years and still wears much of its original personality proudly.
But the home’s connection to Lake Placid history runs deeper than its vintage décor.
Original owner Harold Evans was a pilot and airplane executive who also served on the executive committee for the 1980 Lake Placid Olympic Games, listing broker Bob Miller of Bob Miller Real Estate told The Post.
Evans built the home as a residence for his family during a period when the tiny Adirondack village was gearing up to host the world.
“He built it to have a place here for the Olympics,” Miller said, noting that the house itself was never used for an official Olympics purpose.
One of its quirkiest features came directly from Evans’ other passion: flying.
“He designed the carpet,” Miller said. “It’s all weaved together to look like the landscape from when he was flying planes over the Adirondacks.”
The unusual flooring — showing varying tones of browns, greens and blues — remains one of the property’s biggest conversation starters.
And the carpeting doesn’t stop in the living area.
Some of the bathrooms are carpeted, too — a design decision that might horrify modern buyers but wasn’t so unusual when the house was built.
“It was a thing back in the ’70s that, thankfully, went away,” Miller joked.
Beyond its retro flourishes, the house has some serious bones.
Its centerpiece is a massive great room with vaulted, beamed ceilings, walls of windows and a dramatic double-sided fireplace — off to the side of which is that indoor spa tub. An open layout connects the great room to the dining room, kitchen and family room, while a deck wrapping around much of the home takes advantage of its elevated mountain setting.
The primary suite is also on the main level and includes a spa and sauna, while the upper and lower levels contain additional bedrooms, bathrooms and shared spaces. There’s also a potential apartment and a two-car garage.
Still, anyone hoping to step straight into a perfectly preserved ’70s fantasy should probably bring a renovation budget.
The listing itself describes the property as requiring “extensive renovation,” and Miller said he expects the eventual buyer to make substantial changes.
“I would certainly expect that whoever purchased it would be doing very significant updates,” he said, pointing particularly to the kitchens and bathrooms.
The home first hit the market for $1.99 million in June 2025 before that listing expired. It returned this June asking $1.69 million, before receiving a $304,000 price chop this month to its current $1.39 million ask.

hed: Get in a witchy spirit with these vibey Victorians for sale in New England
subhead: On a windswept, moonlit night, it wouldn’t take much to convince you that at least several generations of witches like those of “Practical Magic” or “Sabrina the Teenage Witch” live here in antique splendor.
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Oh, the shivery charm of approaching a tall, intimidating Victorian house whentrick or treating…the towers and turrets, the ornate gingerbread, the formal, vertical orientation. On a windswept, moonlit night, it wouldn’t take much to convince you that at least several generations of witches like those of“Practical Magic”or “Sabrina the Teenage Witch”live here in antique splendor.
Many of the 19thcentury houses for sale today do, indeed, display antique splendor, carefully preserved by owners who value historic architecture and its stylish place in our streetscapes. But many also have updated systems, new kitchens, and spa baths.
Here is a short list of some atmospheric Victorian properties on the market today. Whether the vibes are witchy or not is for the homeowner to decide.
Listing price: $879,000
Year built:1872
Square footage:3,136
Bedrooms:5
Bathrooms:2.5
“In 1995, this was supposed to be a tear-down,” said Daniel Donoghue, who islisting the historic James W. Mort House. “It was built as a farmhouse atop Christian Hill, overlooking the city, circa 1869, for a Lowell cigar manufacturer. Though it was in rough shape 30 years ago, it was lovingly restored by people who cared about its historic value.”
Today, it is a meticulous example of the Second Empire style, displaying the characteristic mansard roof, eyebrow-like window heads, a verandah, and projecting central pavilion. In its 1980 architectural survey, the City of Lowell singled out the house for its two-story pavilion bay, “heavily ornamented,” rising into “an octagonal tower with a concave cap.”
The interior, too, is a showcase of Victorian high style, with modern amenities tucked in. The quarter-acre lot includes landscaped gardens and a two-car garage. It is topped by an expansive deck that features a central cast-iron gazebo that opens to the house’s sunroom.
Listing price: $899,000
Year built:1896
Square footage:6,270
Bedrooms:6
Bathrooms:3
Built for prominent local banker and shoe manufacturing magnate Myron Whitcomb, this Queen Anne house has been lovingly preserved. A prominent Haverhill landmark, it still has the ornate 19thcentury workmanship that is so valued today, including richly detailed mahogany woodwork, intricate carvings, leaded glass cabinetry, stained glass windows, oak parquet flooring, and six fireplaces. It’son the market for about $900,000.
Features also include original wainscoting, including sections accented by Grecian columns, crown molding, and beamed ceilings. There are elements that rarely survive, including original hardware and light fixtures.
Listing price:$1,799,000
Year built:1885
Square footage:4,927
Bedrooms:6
Bathrooms:2.5
This impressive Queen Anne house ison the market for the first timein over 30 years.
“This is probably one of the largest single-family homes in Dorchester,” said Daniel Lewis, a realtor with Herringbone Realty who has listed the impressive three-story house. “It is not only large and architecturally important. It is also located in Dorchester Center’s historic Carruth Street/Peabody Square neighborhood, one of South Dorchester’s most established and desirable residential enclaves near Ashmont and Davis Square.”
The Ashmont Red Line is approximately half a mile away, making for an easy commute to downtown Boston. The house features rich architectural details, including five fireplaces and multiple porches on every level. The third floor presents possibilities for future expansion or conversion: the space features a kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, and living room, and may be used as a potential separate apartment, which it once was.
Listing price:$1,495,000
Year built:1898
Square footage:5,739
Bedrooms:8
Bathrooms:3
In the 1890s, George Pepper, the third owner of Salem’s Ye Olde Pepper Candy Company, sold it and, in 1898, built this grand Queen Anne house. With two towers and impressive front and rear foyers that connect to a grand central stairway, it is a rare survivor that still has all the original ornate interior features, including beautiful millwork, high ceilings, and arched doorways.It’s listed for $1.5 million.
It has the space today’s homeowners want, including a butler’s pantry, a mudroom with laundry facilities, and an updated kitchen. There is also a substantial two-story carriage house. The exterior was recently extensively repaired and painted.
Listing price:$1,249,000
Year built:1875
Square footage:6,437
Bedrooms:9
Bathrooms:2 full, 3 half
“New Hampshire is becoming a tax haven for people from Massachusetts,” said Jim Nadeau, a broker with LandVest | Christie’s International Real Estate, who islisting what is known as The Hayes House. “Dover is ‘The Lilac City,’ which describes it as a quiet, residential refuge just across the river from Portsmouth.”
Built in 1875, the Hayes House is one of Dover’s beloved architectural treasures. It was built by Civil War Union Quartermaster Andrew Young in the fashionable Second Empire style. The three-story house has many of the hallmarks of the style, including a mansard roof, eyebrow window heads, a central tower, and a verandah-like porch. The exterior also boasts corner quoins and butted-board siding. The interior has many of the original features, including ornate chandeliers with decorative medallions, stained and leaded glass, and beautiful woodwork that has never been painted or stained.
Regina Cole is a freelance writer who covers architecture, design, historic homes, and the decorative arts.

hed: Tyler Perry lists $57M Beverly Hills mansion where Prince Harry and Meghan Markle hid after fleeing the palace
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Tyler Perry is saying goodbye to one seriously star-studded piece of California real estate.
The billionaire filmmaker has listed his sprawling Beverly Hills estate — which once served as a temporary home forPrince Harry and Meghan Markle— for a whopping $57 million as he prepares to relocate to Puerto Rico.
The 22.5-acre spread, tucked inside the gated Beverly Ridge Estates community, centers on a roughly 24,500-square-foot Mediterranean-style mansion with eight bedrooms, according tothe Wall Street Journal.
Perry purchased the land for just $4.3 million in 2004 and completed construction on the massive residence in 2012.
The sprawling Tuscan-style villa has eight bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, along with a library and grand entertaining spaces. Outside, the grounds feature a swimming pool and fountain, according toArchitectural Digest.
Privacy is also a major part of the package. The home sits on more than 22 acres inside the exclusive gated enclave, creating a secluded compound in the middle of Beverly Hills.
And there is plenty of space beyond the main residence. The property also comes with a separate one-bedroom guesthouse and staff quarters — accommodations that have come in handy for Perry’s famously high-profile guests.
The estate has reportedly hosted a string of A-listers over the years, including Oprah Winfrey and former President Barack Obama, according to Architectural Digest. Among its notable temporary residents were the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who stayed there after moving to the US in 2020. They’vesince returnedto the UK afterseveral years in California.
“We needed a house and he offered security as well,” Markle later said of Perry during the couple’s 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, during which she announced her pregnancy with her youngest child.
And the Beverly Hills estate isn’t the only trophy property Perry is putting on the market.
In June, he listed his sprawling Jackson Hole, Wyo., retreat for $39.5 million. That property includes a roughly 10,988-square-foot custom log home sitting on 37.62 acres.
Together, the two listings are asking a staggering $96.5 million.
The selloff comes as Perry, 57, prepares for a major lifestyle change.
Earlier this month, the actor, producer and studio mogul revealed that he plans to move to Puerto Rico at the beginning of 2027 while scaling back his famously relentless work schedule.
“Yep, moving to Puerto Rico at the top of the year, and I’m pulling back a whole lot,” Perry said during an appearance on “Today with Jenna & Sheinelle.”
“He’s spending less and less time” in California, listing agent Santiago Arana of the Agency told the Journal.
Perry still commands a formidable real estate empire.
His holdings include a megamansion near Atlanta, as well as Tyler Perry Studios, his enormous 330-acre production complex built on a former Army base. He has also owned property in the Bahamas’ Exuma Cays.
His Beverly Hills listing arrives as Los Angeles’ high-end housing market continues to contend with the effects of thecity’s mansion taxand this year’s wildfires.
Beverly Hills itself, however, has proved more resilient. The median sale price there hit $4 million during the three months ending in August — up 34.1% from a year earlier, according toRedfin.

hed: Luxury LA condo towers at risk of losing utilities after developer stops paying bills
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Any day now, worried the residents of the luxury Metropolis towers in Los Angeles, the building’s power and water could be shut off.
The residential towers, located near the Crypto.com Arena and the LA Convention Center indowntown LA, had been heralded as the best in upscale living, with luxury amenities and access to all the city had to offer.
But somehow, thecondo towershad racked up thousands in unpaid utility bills, and residents were concerned they might lose electricity.
And that wasn’t the only problem. Maintenance on the buildings had slipped.
The elevators in Tower II were constantly out of service, and the gym’s HVAC unit hadn’t worked in months.
First Service, the property management company in charge of the buildings, warned developer Greenland USA in June 2019 that the development’s homeowners associations were “now officially out of money,” vendors would “not perform services,” and utilities were “at risk of being shut off,” according to an email included in court filings.
That was how Oleg Pariser, a long-time resident of Tower I in Metropolis, discovered that the developer had given itself an abatement that exempted it from paying thousands of dollars in HOA dues each month on the roughly 300 unsold units it still owned.
Pariser said he was shocked to learn that Tower I, with an operating budget of around $4 million, had less than $200,000 in reserves, and that Greenland hadn’t paid any HOA dues since 2018.
The developer’s total unpaid tab with the HOAs now totals $6.8 million, residents have claimed in court filings.
The discovery set off a chain of events that led to multiple lawsuits, HOA liens, and ultimately a “desist and refrain” order from California’s Department of Real Estate preventing Greenland from selling any additional units.
That order may be why so many Metropolis units remain empty today, as Realtor.com® reported earlier this month.
At the heart of the conflict between Metropolis homeowners and Greenland is whether the developer improperly used its control of the complex’s HOAs to avoid paying assessments and other fees.
“The directors—even though they’re representing the developer—have a legal fiduciary duty to act in the best interests of the homeowners,” says Chad Cummings, an attorney and CPA with experience handling HOA cases, who is not connected with the Metropolis case. “The people that are serving on that board are actually exposing themselves to personal legal liability because they’re putting the interest of the developer ahead of the homeowners.”
Greenland USA, an American subsidiary of the Chinese state-backed real estate developer Greenland Holding Group, broke ground on Metropolis in 2014, and began selling units in 2017.
Construction on the complex, which includes two condo towers, an apartment building, and a hotel, was completed in 2019.
Oleg Pariser was among the first to buy in the complex. He bought a one-bedroom in Tower I on an upper floor for more than $800,000.
Pariser, a senior software developer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says he wanted to try out high-rise living in downtown L.A.
“The whole area was going away from being just basically a commercial center, to also being a residential community,” he tells Realtor.com.
He watched as the building slowly filled up, and noted that many of the other owners actually lived in mainland China and subleased the units out to local students and professionals.
Condo owners in the development contributed to two homeowners association funds: the Met Master Association, which covered the overall complex, and their individual building’s subassociation.
Pariser joined the board of Met I—the HOA of Tower I—in 2019. Tower I is smaller than Tower II, with around 308 units, 50 of which Greenland still owns, while Tower II has 514 units, around 250 of which Greenland owns, according to public records reviewed by Realtor.com.
Early on, Pariser says he raised issues on the board about the lack of reserve funds in the Met Master Association account, but says he found it difficult to make headway.
“I was seeing that a big component is still that this foreign corporation is owning a big portion of the development, and they are just not paying” HOA dues on those units, he says.
In 2023, Pariser filed a complaint against the Metropolis Master Association, the governing HOA of both Metropolis Towers, in small claims court. In it, he asked that the previous year’s board elections be voided because “Greenland maintained wrongful control of the Met Master Board in reliance on illegal abatement agreements, offsets, and credits that were the product of unfair and unreasonable self-dealing transactions.”
In essence, the complaint argued, because Greenland had given itself an assessment exemption on the units it owned, it was not in good financial standing with the association.
And under the Metropolis Master Declaration of Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions, board members had to be in good standing to be elected. Because of this, Pariser argued, the “association must disqualify all candidates or directors who are delinquent in the payment of assessments absent compliance with an agreed-upon payment plan.”
How delinquent were they? In 2020 alone, the board granted Greenland more than $1.2 million in abatements, according to the lawsuit.
“On at least one occasion, the entire Metropolis I high-rise tower was within hours of losing water and electricity, because Master HOA had no funds to pay the utility bills,” Pariser’s lawsuit noted. “Also, Metropolis I has on multiple occasions experienced utility disconnections such as inoperable elevator emergency phone lines, phone lines in the common area, and intercom at the garage entrance due to Master HOA’s repeated failure to timely pay its vendors’ invoices.”
Pariser won his small claims case in 2024, and the 2022 election of Greenland representatives to the Met Master Association board was voided. But that wasn’t the end of developer control at Metropolis.
Then in 2025, David Nealy, a resident of Tower II, challenged the Master HOA’s 2024 election, in which three representatives of the development company were elected to the board.
He argued it violated association election rules and guidelines.
In April 2026, a Los Angeles County judge agreed, and told the developers they would need to hold a new election within 90 days of the order. That election has yet to happen, though the Master HOA now says it will take place in December.
Also in 2025, Nealy and fellow Tower II resident Nitin Bhatnager filed a separatelawsuitin the Superior Court of the State of California against the Metropolis Master Association, property management company FirstService, and several current and former board members who represented Greenland on the Master HOA board.
The suit argued that Greenland-backed board members were in breach of fiduciary duty and in breach of contract by failing to collect assessments from developer-owned units.
To make up for the lack of income from the Greenland units, the lawsuit argued, “it is reasonably certain that Master HOA will have to specially assess the non-Greenland owners in Metropolis I and II millions of dollars just to catch up financially.”
Nealy says that process has already begun. In 2025, homeowners were required to vote on an increase in assessment fees of more than 20%.
Nealy and Bhatnager’s suit estimates that Greenland owes more than $6.8 million in unpaid assessment fees.
They are asking for damages to be paid, and asking that any agreements made to abate the assessments are voided.
When Nealy and Pariser took on Greenland, the California Department of Real Estate took notice. In 2023, the regulator issued a rarely used “desist and refrain” order against Greenland USA, ordering them to stop selling units in both 889 Francisco St. and 877 Francisco St.
The DRE took issue with amendments Greenland had requested to its Final Subdivision Public Report.
A Final Subdivision Public Report is a disclosure document for prospective buyers that the DRE issues and that legally authorizes a developer to sell in the state.
It wasn’t what was in the amendments, but what was left out, which set off alarm bells for the DRE.
Greenland’s amendment requests included an updated budget and provisions for a reciprocal easement agreement, but they failed to mention its developer-owned condo assessment abatements.
Thanks to Pariser’s lawsuit, the DRE learned about everything the amendment requests allegedly left out.
The DRE was not happy. Per its ruling, “Respondents entered into an assessment abatement agreement with the Metropolis I Condominium Owner’s Association (“Association”) to lower the expenses it was to pay on unsold units, which constitute material changes in the setup of the offering of interests in the subdivision” and failed to notify the DRE of the changes.
Greenland USA resubmitted its public report filings, and in December 2025 the DRE issued a new public report—but only for Tower II. This unblocked the sale of properties in that building. However, sales of properties in Tower I are still prohibited. Nealy and Bhatnager’s case is still moving through the courts. The next hearing is in March 2027.
Even as Greenland has once again been granted the right to sell units in Tower II, it hasn’t aggressively moved to do so.
One possible reason may be that, until recently, all 300 or so units owned by Greenland USA were delinquent on their property taxes. All of the units reviewed by Realtor.com received delinquency notices in 2024 and 2025.The units are listed as “current” and paid up in full as of today, though a review of property tax records only showed payments for 2025 and not 2024.
“Certainly, if I were representing a buyer, I would want to see proof from the seller that property taxes were actually paid that year and would not allow a client to close on the purchase until we had independently validated whatever documentation was provided,” said the attorney Cummings.
Similarly, all 50 developer-owned units in Tower I currently have HOA liens against them—because the developer is no longer in control of the sub-HOA for that building. Tower II doesn’t have liens, but only because the developer still controls Tower II’s HOA.
Holding on to the units in Tower II prevents a full turnover of the building to non-homeowner developer control, according to the HOA’s governing documents. And that’s sort of the point.
“Placement of liens requires board’s approval,” explains Pariser. “Greenland employees sitting on these boards routinely approve placement of liens for regular homeowners, but Greenland-controlled boards do absolutely nothing with regards to non-payment of assessments on Greenland’s unsold condos. Not only are liens not placed, but late fees and interest are not assessed.”
The liens matter, because when a lien is attached to the property, any past debts must be cleared before a property can be sold or refinanced.

Which is why, Cummings says, any real estate agent that sees an HOA lien or a delinquent property tax bill will tell a buyer, “you need to run, not walk, in the other direction.”
If Metropolis homeowners really want to push the issue, he recommends they file a foreclosure action to enforce the HOA liens. “If there’s not a lien, liens need to be placed, but that’s not going to magically happen. Somebody has to hire an attorney, pay a retainer, and start placing liens on the units.” Cummings acknowledges that it could cost millions for that type of action to wind its way through court.
Until then, he says, Greenland “has every incentive to just sit still and do nothing. They probably know that these units are going to be foreclosed at some point, so they have every incentive to sit still, do nothing, and just drag things out.”
“I’m sure they’d love to sell these units if they didn’t have to bring a whole crap load of money to the table to do it, but there’s no way around that,” says Cummings.
In the meantime, Pariser says the impact on the units’ value has been catastrophic. He purchased his one-bedroom apartment in Tower I in 2017 for more than $800,000. Now, similarunits are selling for less than $600,000.  Many units in Tower II for sale have been on the market for more than a hundred days and have undergone multiple price cuts.Nealy says he’s less concerned about the money. His goal is for homeowners to have a genuine voice, for the building to be well managed, and for the community to thrive. He admits rising dues and largely unsold inventory are suppressing values, but says his main aim is to make the area a good place to live.
“I’m hoping that doing everything I can do gets to the point where people love where they live,” he says. “And we have a lot of promise here. We have some beautiful amenities, but we just kinda need it to be a situation where homeowners have a voice, and we can manage things in a responsible way.”

hed: Stunning $1M California home with a 2-story wall of glass quickly becomes the most-viewed listing in the US
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This California home is shattering the glass ceiling of real estate.
A striking glass-walled house tucked into the Berkeley Hills has become an unlikely internet sensation, drawing nearly 12,000 views on Redfin in just four days as house hunters swarm the listing.
The two-bedroom, three-bath home at 141 Fairlawn Drive hit the market Sept. 23 for $1.08 million and quickly landed as the most viewedlisting on Redfin.
As of the platform’s latest publicly available count, the 1,625-square-foot pad had attracted 11,946 views and 1,051 favorites.
And listing agent Elizabeth Lee of eXp Realty is in no hurry to pull the plug on all that attention.
Asked why the heavily trafficked home had not already been snapped up, Lee said she deliberately planned additional opportunities to get buyers through the door.
“There’s a reason why — because I’m having two open houses and I’m having a twilight party Thursday,” Lee told The Post.
She is also hoping the eye-popping attention translates into a sale well north of the asking price.
The Bay area market has seen aflurry of buyersoutbidding for homes.
The property is scheduled to host that twilight open house Thursday from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., followed by additional weekend showings.
But the home’s sudden viral fame is about more than its price.
Built in 1972, the residence is an early work by then 28-year-old architect Andrew Batey, who designed it for architectural photographer Henry Bowles. Bowles trained under noted California photographer Morley Baer and photographed projects for Condé Nast, according to the listing.
The result is a house that looks almost more greenhouse than home.
A soaring, two-story grid of glass dominates the facade, putting the leafy surroundings on full display from inside. The main living space rises beneath exposed structural beams, while an open staircase leads to a mezzanine-like upper floor. Sliding glass doors spill onto a broad deck shaded by mature oak trees.
Batey also designed the home around its hillside setting rather than leveling the property, creating a multi-level floor plan that unfolds along the slope.
Upstairs, a primary suite spanning more than 400 square feet includes a black-tiled bathroom that Batey returned to design in the late 1980s, according to the listing. Two skylights bring additional natural light into the space.
There’s another piece of the property’s photography pedigree beside the garage.
A roughly 300-square-foot standalone space, originally used as Bowles’ darkroom, now has a sink, a full bathroom and a skylight, making it suitable as a studio, office or guest quarters. The property also comes with a detached garage, EV charging, central heat and an updated kitchen with quartz counters.
The home’s history suggests Berkeley buyers have been willing to pay a premium for it before.
The current owner purchased the property for $725,000 in 2004 after it had been listed for $595,000, becoming so captivated by it during an open house, public records show. It previously changed hands for $358,000 in 1988 and $210,000 in 1981.

The 11,152-square-foot estate at 1754 Sunset Plaza Drive became infamous in 2024 for being the site of repeated vandalizations while it was owned by John Powers Middleton, whose father owns the Philadelphia Phillies.

The six-bedroom, twelve-bathroom mansion has sweeping views of Los Angeles, with amenities including an elevator, a ballroom, two gourmet kitchens, and a spa room.
The home’s primary suite comes complete with dual bathrooms and closets, and glass doors that open to one of the home’s two pools.
Photos of the now cleaned property show its ornate exterior, complete with arches and detailed stone fencing.
The vacant property became notorious in the neighborhood when was repeatedly taken over by squatters and taggers who covered the property’s exterior in bright graffiti.
The property earned the ire of neighbors, who branded it a nuisance and an eyesore.
“It’s tragic,” neighbor Alexander Gorbis, who was friends with a previous owner’s son, toldKABCin 2024.
“I [virtually] grew up in that house. I saw it when it was very small, and there wasn’t too much to it. I grew up with the son of the previous builder — and to see how it is now is just beyond words.”
In September 2024, the LAPD toldFox News Digitalthat the Hollywood Hills area responded to 17 calls for service on the 1700 block of Sunset Plaza Drive so far that year.
Just miles away,another vacant property owned by Middletonwas also overtaken by squatters and decorated in graffiti.
Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman blasted Middleton for the conditions of both properties.
“This is a public safety issue with serious consequences for both neighbors and the surrounding community,” Raman said. “Irresponsible property owners must take accountability for their property or face action from the city.”
In September 2024, Middleton released a statement apologizing to the city of Los Angeles for the conditions of his properties, saying he would be compensating community members for any fees incurred by residents because of his homes.
“I would like to apologize to the people of Los Angeles, and especially to my neighbors. What’s happened to the two properties I own is unacceptable, and no matter what caused it, I own the houses,”  Middleton, film producer, said in a statement sent toFox News Digital.
“I will also repay any and all taxpayer funds used to gate, fence or board the houses and to pay all tax bills. I want to thank the city of Los Angeles for working with me to rectify this horrible situation.”

hed: Ask the Remodeler: So, you want to go into construction? Options for students going into the trades.
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

The school year has started andfall is officially underway. While autumn in New England is just as magical as summer, our mindsets shift to parts of our lives other than, “Do I have enough SPF 30 in my beach bag?” For some who have seniors or juniors in high school, the thoughts may turn to college and important life choices for our children.

For years, those of us running construction-related companies tend to wonder, “Where have all the young men and women who are the future of the industry gone?” This has been our lament for many years: not enough young people are coming into the trades to be trained and become tomorrow’s skilled workers. That is slowly changing, and parents and younger students/workers are starting to pay attention.

One could write a book on the root causes of this shift. You can’t look past the pandemic as one of the leading causes of people rethinking a four-year degree — add to that the ever-increasing cost of higher education, and you have a perfect storm for a shift in career choices. I came across this statistic fromNorth American Trade Schoolsthe other day:

“Student loan debt in the U.S. now exceeds $1.8 trillion. The average borrower carries more than $43,000 in student loan debt … The trades, meanwhile, can’t find enough workers to keep up with demand.”

This was a bit sobering to read. Add the fear of AI replacing entry-level workers in various industries, and it is no surprise that we have seen a shift in career choices. In an ironic twist, the demand for construction workers, electricians, and HVAC techs has soared with theneed to build the data centers that are powering AI. The projected shortage of skilled trades is so acute that investment firmBlack Rock pledged $100 millionto support the training of skilled trades this year.

So where should parents or students turn to if they want to consider the trades as a career path?

Trade schools

This is the time-tested route. A trade school could be something a student takes advantage of while still in high school. If a technical or vocational school is part of the public school system, there is no tuition outside of some fees for specialized clothing or equipment. If a student takes this route, they could walk into a job right after high school with zero debt, jump into an apprenticeship role, and start working their way up the ranks.

Another trade school route is a for-profit training academy that one would enter after high school. These schools do charge a tuition for typically a two-year program depending on the skill set students are learning. While there is a cost associated with this, the amount is often manageable, and students would be working within two years, not four. Do your homework on these; not all for-profit trade schools are created equally.

Trade unions

This route has a lot of appeal for those worried about carrying any debt. You can “earn as you learn” as the saying goes. In a trade union, members start at the bottom and get hands-on training while also taking classes for a particular skill set. Pay increases as they move along and gain experience. Because they are working within the union, they will get a benefit package along with a paycheck.

Private construction companies

For students with no vocational training or desire to join a union, simply applying to companies looking for apprentices is always an option. This is more common in the carpentry end of things, but not unheard of in some of the other fields. There is an acute shortage of carpenters in this country, and jobs are plentiful for those who want to put in the time and energy to learn. This route is similar to that of unions, but far less structured. The pay and benefit packages will vary from company to company. The well-respected trade groupPRO New Englandsponsors and hosts a career day for students considering jumping right into the trades.This year’s is on Oct. 14.

This article is most definitely not intended to dissuade anyone who has a dream of pursuing a four-year degree and the college experience. It is all to say that students today have options in this ever-changing economy. In much of the world, apprenticeship programs are an honor that many people aspire to achieve. It seems we here in this country are finally catching up and recognizing the importance of a robust workforce in the skilled trades.

Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge. Send your questions to[email protected]. Questions are subject to editing. hed: Why Miami is flunking homebuilding and affordability while the rest of Florida booms
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


While Miami continues to attract deep-pocketed transplants and institutional capital from across the globe, beneath the surface,the city’s housing market is failing on two key fronts: new construction and affordability.
Dotted with palm trees and bristling with amenity-rich luxury condominium towers, “Magic City” earned the dubious distinction of being 1 of 13 major U.S. metros to receive an F grade in the newly released 2026 Realtor.com® Metro Report Cards.
Out of a possible 100 points, Miami earned an overall score of just 29, weighted down by a lackluster affordability component score of 18.9, combined with a slightly better homebuilding component score of 39.1.
For context, best-in-class Des Moines, IA, which received an A+ in the ranking, earned a total score of 83.4, propelled by affordability and homebuilding component scores of 88.3 and 78.4, respectively.
Although Miami is not the worst-performing market in the nation, with Los Angeles comfortably claiming that title, it neverthelessholds a unique distinction: It is the sole failing metro located in a state that earned a passing grade on the Realtor.com State Report Cards.
“We gave the whole state of Florida a B, butMiami behaves differently, with many more restrictions on geographic expansion than other metros in the Sunshine State given the Everglades to the west and the Atlantic Ocean to the east,” says Realtor.com senior economistJoel Berner.
Experts agree that when it comes to new construction, land scarcity is Miami’s Achilles’ heel relative to the rest of the state.
“There isn’t much room for Miami to growexcept up, which is why we see a large share of condos on the market there generally and a large share of luxury condos in the new-construction space,” says Berner.
This severe land constraint directly dictates the economics of residential development in Miami.
“Land is expensive, construction and labor costs are high, financing is still costly, insurance has become a major expense, and permitting and approvals can add significant time and uncertainty to a project,”Daniel Ickowicz, CEO of Elite International Realty in Miami, tells Realtor.com. “When you put all of that together, developers may still build, but it becomes very difficult to deliver new housing at lower price points.”
To put it simply, because the baseline cost of building in Miami is so high, developers watching their bottom line naturally focus on delivering luxury units at the expense of budget-friendly options.
“That’s part of the reason you can look around Miami and see cranes everywhere while still having an affordability problem,” says Ickowicz.
Data analysis confirms the divide: Miami leads the 100 largest metros in its new-construction premium—the extra market cost of buying a brand-new home versus an existing one. Today, the typical new build in Miami carries a price tag 248% higher than the median-priced resold home.
“Miami is not a market where nothing is being built,”Ana Bozovic, a Miami-based real estate agent and founder of Analytics Miami. “It is a market where the cost basis makes it extraordinarily difficult for new privately financed construction to be delivered at prices affordable to the median household.”
On the affordability front, Miami’s emergence as a magnet for global wealth plays a defining role for better or worse. Ickowicz notes that the city’s real estate is increasingly priced for international buyers, detaching housing values from local incomes.
“Local buyers are competing with people and capital coming from Latin America, the Northeast, Europe, and many other markets,” says the CEO. “That is very different from many other cities.”
The median earner in Miami currently spends nearly 47% of their $74,274 median annual income on a monthly payment for the median-priced home of $507,237, well above the recommended 30% affordability threshold, effectively putting homeownership well beyond reach for average working families.
“If the cost of producing a new unit is substantially above what a median-income household can afford, simply adding units does not immediately solve the affordability problem,” notes Bozovic. “Lower-income and first-time buyers are competing primarily for existing housing stock, while much of the new supply enters at significantly higher price points.”
She stresses: “This is why it is important to distinguish between housing supply and affordable housing supply. Miami can add thousands of units and still have an affordability problem if the cost of producing and owning those units is substantially above what local incomes can support.”
So why is Miami dramatically underperforming compared to the rest of Florida? Both Ickowicz and Berner largely attribute the gap to land availability and cost.
“If you go to Central or North Florida, there are areas where developers can still acquire larger parcels and create entire communities,” points out Ickowicz. “Miami has much less room to expand, land is considerably more expensive, and demand is coming not only from the local population but from buyers around the country and the world.”
Berner notes that Miami’s new-home inventory also has to contend with location-specific affordability challenges that inland suburban new builds escape, including skyrocketing coastal property insurance and heightened scrutiny over condo building reserves in the wake of the deadly Surfside building collapse.
“We are dealing with a different combination of land, development costs, and demand,” confirms Ickowicz.
Elsewhere in Florida, the picture looks different.In fact, two markets—Jacksonville and Palm Bay—scored above 70 points overall, driven by high homebuilding marks that secured them A- grades and top 10 national rankings.
Lakeland, Cape Coral, North Port, and Orlando, FL, likewise acquitted themselves well on affordability and homebuilding, each receiving a grade in the B range.
According to Berner, these metros owe their impressive performance to rapid suburban expansion on low-cost land that Miami simply cannot replicate.
Despite the bleak report card, Berner emphasizes that the state has done well to preempt local zoning codes to allow for taller and denser residential construction in commercial areas through theLive Local Act, and he believes that more creative solutions like this one are needed.
“When land is scarce, building tall and dense affordable inventory is the only solution. So rezoning parts of the metro for multifamily homes and continuing the push for accessory dwelling units will make the biggest difference.”
Ickowicz agrees, arguing that while there is no one policy that would solve affordability in Miami overnight, the key to unlocking more budget-conscious housing is greater density around transit and employment hubs.
Other crucial levers include making it easier to redevelop underused properties and reducing unnecessary delays in permitting and approvals to make the process more predictable and streamlined.
“For a developer, time is money. If a project takes significantly longer because of uncertainty in the approval process, those additional costs eventually become part of the price of the housing,” says the CEO. “Miami is always going to have some natural limitations on supply and very strong demand. We can’t change that. What we can do is make sure we’re not making housing even more expensive by making it unnecessarily difficult or costly to build.”
Bringing the conversation back to market fundamentals, Bozovic says the key thing to remember is that “Miami cannot manufacture more land.”
“The long-term solution is to use the land we have more efficiently, make it faster and less expensive to build appropriate density, and preserve as much of the existing attainable housing stock as possible,” she concludes.

hed: Peter Thiel outed as the billionaire who purchased LA’s most expensive mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The mystery bidder who walked off with one of America’smost famous mansionshas a very famous name.
Tech billionaire Peter Thiel is the man behind the $130 million purchase ofCasa Encantadain Los Angeles, the legendary Bel-Air estate that sold at a foreclosure auction in July, theWall Street Journalreported.
A limited liability company linked to the 58-year-old venture capitalist placed the winning bid, according to the paper’s sources, keeping his name under wraps for roughly two months.
The setting was hardly fit for a trophy home. The sale played out outside of the city of Los Angeles at Pomona’s Civic Center Plaza, beside an unremarkable fountain, with an auctioneer in casual denim calling the bids.
Thiel had his eye on the property for months before the gavel fell, per the report. But don’t expect him to unpack. He views the hilltop spread as an investment and plans to spruce it up, a source told the Journal.
The deal ranks as the biggest home sale in Los Angeles this year, even though it landed far below the prices once floated for the place.
Casa Encantada first hit the market in 2019 for $225 million and returned in 2023 asking $250 million — making it the most expensive home in America at the time. After a series of chops, it was listed at $170 million asrecently as February,The Post reported at the time.
Set on roughly 8.5 acres overlooking the Bel-Air Country Club, the 1930s mansion has seven bedrooms and about 40,000 square feet. It has twice smashed the record for the priciest private home sale in the US, fetching $12.4 million in 1980 and $94 million in 2000.
Hotel titan Conrad Hilton once owned the estate and nicknamed it “The House Where Dreams Come True.” It later went to billionaire David Murdock, who sold it to telecom mogul Gary Winnick in 2000.
Winnick, who built Global Crossing on a pitch to circle the globe with undersea fiber-optic cable, and his wife, Karen, spent more than two years and millions of dollars on a makeover led by architect Peter Marino.
Once billed as LA’s wealthiest man, Winnick died in 2023. His death exposed a fortune in far worse shape than outsiders knew, with the financier short on cash and buried in debt.
At the center of the mess was a 2020 loan from CIM Real Estate Credit, secured by the mansion, that swelled past $150 million. Karen and her son Alexander accused the lender of running a loan-to-own scheme that left her “effectively destitute,” and she maintained she didn’t grasp the terms.
CIM fired back in court papers, arguing that Karen personally signed a guaranty and later put her name on multiple amendments and advance requests tied to the loans. The lender rejected claims of fraud and financial elder abuse, casting the arrangement as a hard-nosed commercial deal between savvy players, and called the family’s allegations “fantastical.”
A foreclosure auction slated for December 2025 was frozen at the eleventh hour.
“At Karen Winnick’s request, the California Court of Appeal granted a temporary stay of the foreclosure on December 16, 2025,” a lawyer for Winnick told The Post in February.
The reprieve didn’t hold. By July, the auction went forward and the estate went to the highest bidder.
Casa Encantada now joins a globe-spanning Thiel portfolio that includes homes in Washington, DC, Miami, Buenos Aires, a Hawaii compound and property in New Zealand, where the German-born investor is a citizen.
Thiel, who was also Facebook’s first outside backer, moved his primary residence from California to Miami late last year.

hed: Huge 514-home tower that would change WeHo’s skyline forever heads for approval
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Is WeHo movin’ on up?
A mammoth 34-story mixed-use tower that would dramatically reshapeWest Hollywood’s skylineforever is heading to the West Hollywood Planning Commission this week.
On Oct. 1, the commission will consider a proposal for a 514-apartment development at1000 North La Brea Avenue, on the northeastcorner of La Breaand Romaine Street.

The proposed development, brought forward by CIM Group, would replace a former CEMEX concrete batch plant and vacant warehouse with an approximately 352-foot-tall building containing 514 residential units and about 30,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial space.
If approved, the tower would stand far above the current height limits, which are capped at 90 feet, or eight stories.
The proposed project would reach 34 stories with a floor-area ratio (FAR) of 9.85, well above the standard maximum FAR of 3.0.
Of the 514 apartments, 128, or 25%, would be designated affordable. That includes 51 very low-income units, 51 low-income units and 26 moderate-income units.
In the city of WeHo, which ispart of Los Angeles County, larger residential developments with 11 or more base units are typically required to set aside 20% of those units for affordable housing under the city’sInclusionary Housing Ordinance.
The remaining 386 apartments would be market-rate. The affordable apartments would be located on floors 8 through 11 and share the same common amenities as the rest of the building.
The development would also feature six billboards integrated into the building’s facades, including one full-motion digital display.West Hollywoodwould receive 20% of the adjusted net billboard revenue under the proposed development agreement.
Lucky residents would get access to landscaped gardens, a pool deck, indoor amenity spaces and rooftop open areas. The project includes 674 parking spaces and more than 260 bicycle spots.
So far city staff have received 68 pieces of public correspondence, all in support of the project. The Planning Commission will make a recommendation to the City Council, which holds final approval authority.
The project has been in the works for several years and would help West Hollywood move closer to its state-mandated housing goals.

hed: Iconic, bankrupt LI wedding venue heads to auction — with doors open to residential development
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Long Island’s famed Oheka Castle will sell to the highest bidder next month — finishing its transition from grand Gilded Age manor to a gavel-ending auction.
The Concierge Auctions sale, where prospective buyers must pony up $750,000 to even have a chance at the 113,000-square-foot mansion, will take the estate out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy — and give the buyer not only bragging rights as new lord of the manor, but also open doors to lucrative building opportunities.
Curbedfirst reported newsof the sale, which will conclude on Oct. 27.
Located in Huntington, the town has approved 95 luxury condos for the easternmost 5 acres of the 23-acre property. At an expected $1.8 million and much morea pop, the residential addition could pull in millions annually and spur more condo development on a site adjacent to the Oheka property.
The auction will leave by the wayside former owner Gary Melius, a local developer and political heavyweight who filed for bankruptcy last summer to try and keep his creditors at bay.
The filing showedjust how direOheka’s financial picture was — with the hotel, restaurant and event space having less than $60 in its bank account, no cash on hand and carrying more than $63.5 million in debt.
Because Melius couldn’t pay off the massive balances under the Chapter 11 filing, the federal bankruptcy court signed off on a public auction. Leading up to this outcome, Melius spend decades as Oheka’s owner, pouring millions into its restoration, even dodginga mid-day assassination attemptthere in 2014.
“Forty years here, $50 million in, and now nothing,” the 81-year-old Melius told The Post.
Melius said he is still living at the 127-room estate and did not indicate what his future plans are.
Hedge fund Taconic Capital is considered the frontrunner for the property since it holds the mansion’s $60 million defaulted mortgage. It can also use the amount as bidding currency while others will have to start from scratch, according to US bankruptcy code.
Taconic Capital, started by former Goldman Sachs partners Frank Brosens and Ken Brody, has even more skin in the game as owner of an adjacent 13.3-acre development site purchased in December from the country club next door, property records show.
With Taconic owning the Oheka Castle land and the adjacent property, it isn’t a stretch for the parcels to be put together and revive a proposal that Melius and golf legend Jack Nicklaus tried to float years back, for 100 units to be built on the parcel next door.
Whoever wins the property will apply their $750,000 deposit to their purchase price, while other bidders will get their outlays back.
Banker Otto Kahn, a billionaire in today’s dollars, built the massive estate for himself and his family just before the Roaring Twenties kicked in and Oheka Castle helped set the decade’s chaotic pace. Kahn’s dinners, often for 50 or more guests — each assigned their own personal valet — turned into parties that could last for days, featuring a high-society mix of Hollywood stars, opera singers, European aristocracy and an abundance of flappers.
Oheka Castle started the, “Can you top this?” craze in megamansion building over 100 years ago, as bankers and robber barons couldn’t import French limestone and Italian marble fast enough trying to outdo each other in opulence along Long Island’s North Shore.
Oheka topped them all as the biggest estate along the Gold Coast, beating neighbors including the Vanderbilts and the Morgans by tens of thousands of square feet.
The castle maintains its status as the largest residence ever built on Long Island, even withstandingbillionaire Ira Rennert’s110,000-square-foot Sagaponack spread, completed in 2003.
Oheka Castle is extraordinary, from its French-style exterior to its 34 guest suites featuring period-style furniture and high-backed beds under crystal chandeliers. Its 2,300-square-foot ballroom overlooks grounds that include reflecting pools and fountains set amid formal French gardens.
After being a party palace in the 1920s, Oheka engaged in more serious pursuits, as a school for radio operators during WWII and a vacation retreat for low-paid NYC sanitation workers before the war.
Orson Welles used the mansion and grounds for Xanadu in “Citizen Kane,” where thinly veiled newspaper publisher William Randolph Hearst hosted Hollywood’s elite in the 1930s.
NYC society and old-money families have long held their weddings at Oheka Castle and its grounds. Celebrities who also held their nuptials there includeKevin Jonas, who married his sweetheart Danielle, with his brothers Nick and Joe serving as his best men.
Former politician Anthony Weiner married Huma Abedin there in a service officiated by former President Bill Clinton, although that onedidn’t work out so well. In April, New York Giants wide receiverDarius Slaytonwed Olympic track-and-field star Anna Hall wed there in April in a “fairytale-style” ceremony.

hed: Former Connecticut housing authority exec charged with $16.2 million loan fraud
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The US Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut has indicted the former executive director of a Connecticut public housing authority onnine counts of fraud and money laundering.
Robert Cappelletti of Middlebury, CT, was charged with committing the crimes while heading up Meriden Housing Authority, which served the communities of Meriden and Groton. He pleaded not guilty and was released on bail.
Cappelletti served as MHA’s executive director from 2009 to 2025 and also served on the board of the Maynard Road Corp., a nonprofit that undertook redevelopment projects on behalf of the MHA.
Prosecutors say that in 2022, Cappelletti took out a $16.2 million loan, alleging it was on behalf of the Maynard Road Corp., but did so without authorization from the MHA or the MRC.
According to the indictment, Cappelletti issued a promissory note on behalf of the MRC and guaranteed it on behalf of the MHA without authorization from either entity’s board of directors.
He then allegedly funneled a portion of those funds to himself through various accounts and shell companies.
The indictment claims he transferred $450,000 of the funds to a personal brokerage account, used more than $374,000 on mortgage payments on his personal residence, and spent additional funds on credit card expenses related to personal travel.
To repay the loan, he then made a series of wire transfers totaling around $1 million from the Groton Housing Authority and its subsidiary LLCs, telling the Gro­ton Hous­ing Author­ity that the payments “were related to a forth­com­ing bond for a devel­op­ment project in Gro­ton and would be reim­bursed.”
To back up his story, he allegedly created forged invoices to the Gro­ton Hous­ing Author­ity.
“It has been a long pro­cess, and I’m glad we have reached the next step in allow­ing the facts to come to light,” Gro­ton Town Man­ager John Burt toldThe Day.
“Mr. Cap­pel­letti viol­ated the trust placed in him by the Gro­ton Hous­ing Author­ity and the res­id­ents that it serves,” Michael J. Rose, an attorney for the Groton Housing Authority, which has since separated from the Meriden Housing Authority, said in a state­ment.
“Today’s arrest and indict­ment begins the pro­cess of hold­ing Mr. Cap­pel­letti crim­in­ally account­able for breach­ing that trust and viol­at­ing his oblig­a­tion to those indi­vidu­als who rely on the Hous­ing Author­ity to meet theirhous­ing needs.”

Cappelletti was indicted after a joint investigation by the FBI and theUS Department of Hous­ing and Urban Devel­op­ment.
If convicted, Cappelletti faces up to 20 years on each count of wire fraud and up to 10 years on each count of illegal monetary transactions.
The former housing exec has also been named in a separate civil suit brought forth by the Groton Housing Authority.
A complaint filed in Connecticut Superior Court accuses Cappelletti and property manager Jamie Lee of fraud and conspiracy and violating Connecticut’s Unfair Trade Act.
In that suit, Cappelletti is accused of making unauthorized property purchases under the auspices of the Groton Housing Authority.
Lee is accused of preventing housing authority officials from accessing her computer files.
