hed: Former owners of Wonderland site secure $16.5 million settlement with Revere over eminent domain taking
subhead: The property was seized in 2022 for construction of a new high school
content: Revere will pay the former owners of the shuttered Wonderland dog track an additional $16.5 million to resolve a dispute over the value of the nearly 34-acre property the city seized by eminent domain for construction of a new high school.The resolution heads off a jury trial that was set to begin in Suffolk Superior Court under Judge Anthony Campo, with as many as 18 witnesses lined up to testify. The trial, initially set to begin last week, was postponed until this week as the two sides worked to strike a deal.The years-long saga began in the fall of 2022, when then-Mayor Brian Arrigo signed an order to seize the Wonderland parcel. City officials decided to pay $29.5 million to owner CBW Lending, then consisting of business partners including Joe O’Donnell and New York firm Vornado Realty Trust. CBW sued the city the following February, saying the price dramatically undervalued the land. The legal fight continued after O’Donnell, a prominent local businessman philanthropist, died of cancer in January 2024.The final resolution was filed with the court on Tuesday, and the trial was canceled. The settlement includes around $500,000 for a separate issue involving unresolved parking fees for the site, which had been used as a parking lot.Revere Mayor Patrick Keefe Jr. was on the City Council at the time of the original taking and said city officials withheld those disputed parking fees, limiting the actual payment to $29 million to CBW. Keefe said the final bill to the city — $29 million plus $16.5 million — is still well within the realm of what council members anticipated paying at the time.“This is a win for Revere taxpayers,” Keefe said. “Ultimately, you want to walk away with zero [in new payments] but when the delta is anywhere between $10 million and $70 million or $80 million, you’re happy when it’s closer to the $10 million range.”If the trial proceeded, CBW’s lawyers would have had to persuade jurors that the city should pay even more for its new high school, whose price tag is already nearly $500 million.However, Keefe said the city has already found around $24 million in savings in the high school project, so the final price tag shouldn’t go up. The city, he said, will need to issue new bonds to pay for the settlement. He noted that the trial could have lasted three weeks.“We felt very strong in our case but you never know what’s going to happen with a jury,” Keefe said.At the time the lawsuit was filed, CBW had argued the Wonderland site could have been worth as much as four times what the city paid. The nearby 50-acre NECCO factory site, for example, sold for $355 million three years earlier. “CBW of course would have preferred a larger amount,” Peter Flynn, a lawyer who represents the former landowners, said of the $16.5 million settlement. “But we are certainly aware of the public purpose nature of the [high school] project and how jurors might react to that.”Flynn said the looming trial helped motivate both sides to strike a deal that valued the property at nearly $46 million, combining the city’s original payment plus the new settlement.“In the end, once we knew we were going to get somewhere with it, the city of Revere and CBW starting working together pretty well,” Flynn said. “In the last few weeks, we’ve been pretty unified in just trying to get this done and behind us.”The legal issues might not be over yet for CBW: In July, the state Appeals Court ruled in favor of E. Mark Noonan, a lender that had sued CBW, arguing he is owed money for the property. That case is now before the Supreme Judicial Court.O’Donnell and Vornado were also business partners at the nearby Suffolk Downs horse track-turned-simulcasting center. The partners had invested in the Wonderland property — the dog track closed following a 2008 state ballot question outlawing greyhound races — as they unsuccessfully chased Greater Boston’s sole resort casino license. However, the Massachusetts Gaming Commission ended up picking Wynn’s Everett proposal over a Suffolk Downs casino plan. O’Donnell and Vornado started marketing the Wonderland site, across the street from the Blue Line’s Wonderland terminal, after losing the casino vote in 2014. In 2019, after tearing down the old dog track grandstand, CBW tried pitching it for a mixed-use development with offices, shops, and apartments — akin to Assembly Row in Somerville — right before the pandemic hit. In 2025, the city held a ground-breaking at the property for its new high school, and construction remains ongoing, with a goal of finishing two years from now. Keefe said the project is on track to be done by the end of 2028, with students expected to start attending classes there in early 2029.Jon Chesto can be reached at jon.chesto@globe.com. Follow him @jonchesto.

hed: Fully restored 1840s Brooklyn Heights townhouse hits market for $12.75M — and it could be yours
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Standard-issue historic restorations often require years of patience, but anewly listed historic 178-year-old Brooklyn Heights townhouseoffers all the 19th-century charm without any of the architectural heavy lifting.
Listed with Carl Gambino of the Gambino Group at Compass, the asking price for the six-bedroom, seven-bath home is $12,750,000.
“The current owners purchased this in 2023 and undertook an extensive renovation,” Gambino tells Realtor.com®.
Spanning 6,000-square-feet, it’s stocked with luxuries that include Bianco Carrara marble countertops in the kitchen, solid white-oak floors, and Forbes & Lomax hardware.
The next owner will have access to the Bertazzoni, Sub-Zero, and Miele appliances to whip up chef-grade meals or entertain in style.
But the “guts” of the home have also been updated. Now there’s new electrical, mechanical, plumbing, and HVAC, as well as an all-electric LG heat-pump system and eco-friendly insulation born out of mostly hemp.  Similar to other Brooklyn townhouses, the width is only 25 feet, but the property features a lot of height as there are five levels.
“It is unusual to find a 25-foot-wideBrooklyn Heights townhousethat preserves its 1848 Greek Revival character while offering a fully rebuilt interior,” says Gambino.
“The historic facade and restored details sit alongside new mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems throughout.The renovation was extensive,including a reconstruction of the rear wall and new systems throughout the home.”
ASH, a firm recognized by Architectural Digest on its AD100 list of the world’s top designers and talent, worked with the sellers to reimagine the rooms so they sparkle, and show just how wow-worthy this home can be for the next owner.
At the same time, original architectural details throughout the home, such as restored millwork are intact and have been carefully preserved, making this property a true gem as it straddles historical architecture with modern-day living.
One level is tied into wellness, with a gym, sauna, and steam shower. Another healing sanctuary is the home’s garden level, where a one-bedroom suite with a private kitchen and laundry area could host a guest or live-in staff. There’s even room for a wine cellar on that lower level, in a power-ready space, to attract an oenophile.
Another entertaining-friendly feature is the eight-foot-deep ipe terrace, accessible from the parlor floor, above a fully landscaped garden and bluestone patio.
The last time this home was on the market, in 2023, it sold for $5,350,000.
This new price reflects all of the costly updates and the fact that you just can’t find a listing like this very easily in Brooklyn Heights.
“The combination of a 25-foot width, approximately 6,000 square feet, and private outdoor space is compelling in this neighborhood,” says Gambino. “The finished cellar has a gym and sauna, while a separate suite with its own kitchen gives the next owner valuable flexibility.”
In addition to the home’s amenities and modernized design, what also makes this a stand-out listing is the neighborhood.
“Buyers come to Brooklyn Heights for its preserved architecture and residential streets, with Brooklyn Bridge Park, the Promenade, and Manhattan close by,” says Gambio. “It offers a strong sense of neighborhood without giving up access to the city.
“I see this appealing to someone who wants the scale and privacy of a substantial townhouse, appreciates historic architecture, and values a home ready for contemporary living.
“Its six bedrooms and flexible suite could serve a family, frequent guests, or a household with changing needs.”

hed: Once America’s hottest housing market, popular state is now the hardest place to sell a home
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

If you’re planning to cash out in Florida, you might want to pack your patience.
The Sunshine State is the single worst place in the countryto sell a homeright now, according to a fresh ranking fromUnderwood Law Firmthat pits 48 states against each other on how brutal their markets are for sellers.
Florida sits at the bottom of the barrel with a staggering 206,508 homes up for grabs, the biggest glut of any state studied.
The typical property there lingers for 73 days before a buyer bites, and bidding wars have all but vanished. Only 10.9% of homes fetched more than their asking price.
This essentially means buyers in Florida are calling the shots.
The firm crunched Redfin Data Center figures across seven yardsticks.
Those include median sale price, total homes sold, median days on market, annual price swings, active inventory, the share of homes selling over asking and the share of listings that had to slash their price.
Each factor carried a different weight depending on how much it matters to sellers. The scores were then blended into a single difficulty rating, and states were lined up from most punishing to most forgiving.
Texas grabbed the No. 2 slot. The Lone Star State has 180,524 homes on the market and a median wait of 68 days. Nearly a quarter of sellers there, about 23%, were forced to cut their price, putting Texas near the top of the study for markdowns.
South Carolina landed at No. 3. Homes in the Palmetto State sit for a median of 74 days, and 22.1% of listings took a price chop. A mere 13% sold above asking.
Montana placed fourth and holds the dubious distinction of the slowest market in the ranking. Homes there sit for a median of 85 days, close to three months. Even more jaw-dropping, the data shows zero homes in Big Sky Country selling for more than list price.
Arizona closed out the five toughest markets. Properties there wait a median of 66 days, and 21.4% of sellers had to lower their price.
Now head to the Northeast andthe picture flips.
Connecticut earned the gentlest score in the entire study, landing dead last at No. 48. Well over half of its homes, 55.8%, sold above asking, the highest rate in the nation.
Rhode Island placed 47th. There, 45.4% of homes went for more than list price, and the typical property was snapped up in just 31 days, less than half the Florida wait.
New Jersey ranked 46th. Buyers in the Garden State paid over asking on 48.3% of homes, even with a hefty median price tag of $587,553.
Massachusetts came in 45th despite some of the steepest prices in the study, with a median of $657,263. Still, 43.6% of homes there drew offers above list price.
Illinois rounded out the seller-friendly end of the list. The Prairie State logged 11,526 home sales, a median of 52 days on market, and 35.8% of homes sold over asking.

hed: Chelsea Piers founder asks $6.6M for NYC townhouse with a massive English garden
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This statement Manhattan home has no real “pier.”
A four-story limestone-clad Upper West Side townhouse with an extravagant English-style garden is on the market for $6.6 million — down from its original $9.5 million asking price in 2023.
The sellers are film financier, developer, author and Chelsea Piers founder Roland Betts — who once co-owned the Texas Rangers with his dear friend and Yale classmate, former President George W. Bush — and his wife Lois.
The Betts bought the 20-foot-wide residence at 313 W. 102nd St., between Riverside Drive and West End Avenue, for $150,000 in 1972 — $1.22 million today. It is one of four surviving townhouses built in 1892 by developer Charles G. Judson and designed by architect Clarence Fagan True.
The Betts loved the townhouse so much that they got married there the year they bought it, Compass listing broker Miryam Tesfaegzi told Gimme Shelter.
Over the next five decades, the home hosted many parties, with guests including Bush.
Roland Betts founded Chelsea Piers after looking for a new ice skating practice rink for his daughter, who was a competitive skater. In 1992, Betts formed Chelsea Piers L.P. with partners Tom Bernstein and David Tewksbury, winning a 30-year-lease to redevelop the run-down, abandoned piers on Manhattan’s West Side. The complex launched in 1995 on more than 28 acres of crumbling waterfront infrastructure — with sports facilities including an ice hockey and skating rink, a gymnastics studio, and a gym — attracting more than 4 million visitors a year.
In Hollywood, first as president of International Film Investors and then as co-founder, with Bernstein, of Silver Screen Management, Betts produced films including “Pretty Woman,” “Beauty and the Beast,” “Gandhi” and “Honey, I Shrunk the Kids.”
Long before the Betts bought the 313 W. 102nd St. residence, it had been home to First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt’s father, troubled Gilded Age socialite Elliott Bulloch Roosevelt — the younger brother of future President Teddy Roosevelt — who lived there until his death in 1894 at age 34.
Addicted to alcohol, morphine and laudanum, and devastated by the deaths of his estranged wife, Anna Hall Roosevelt, and their son less than two years earlier, Roosevelt jumped out of one of the home’s many windows. He died the next day,according to the National Park Service.
By the time the Betts bought it, the house had been divided into apartments, but they restored it to a single-family home and raised their two daughters there: Maggie Betts, a movie director and Jessica Betts Dreyfuss, who works at Chelsea Piers Management.
When they bought the residence, the Betts were working as teachers in Harlem, where they had met.
More than 50 years later, the Betts have moved to a nearby residence, in part because the house has a spiral staircase and no elevator. They also own homes in Connecticut, Jackson Hole and the British Virgin Islands.
But the Betts still come around to tend the garden.
“I think the beautiful garden really reflects how much care Mr. Betts still puts into it. He personally takes care of the garden,” Tesfaegzi said. The Betts could not be reached for comment.
The 6,000-square-foot home has four bedrooms and 4.5 baths. Outdoor space totals 1,337 square feet.
Inside the home, design details include casement windows and three fireplaces.
The garden level opens through a rock-faced limestone arch to a gut-renovated chef’s kitchen with pastel blue accents, restored exposed wood beams, limestone tiles and custom white shaker cabinets.
The kitchen leads to the dining room, with a woodburning fireplace, original hardwood floors and white French glass patio doors that open to a covered patio for private outdoor dining.
A parlor floor has a living room with 11-foot ceilings and its own fireplace — while, on the third floor, the main bedroom overlooks the garden. A lower level has a cedar-lined closet, laundry, pantry and storage rooms.
But there is nothing quite like the garden, Tesfaegzi added, which boasts “hostas and ferns, with white hydrangeas standing out in the back. There are also large pink caladiums and on the sides there are vibrant gold and pink lantana and colorful mums too.”

hed: They spent $700,000 renovating a Brookline basement. Now it brings in $4,500 a month in rent.
subhead: Basement renovations carry a special advantage. They allow historical homes to be preserved while also expanding the housing supply.
content:
ByCarey Goldberg
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

It was dark, musty, and dusty, with low ceilings and rough walls unchanged for more than a century.

Cobwebs and tangles of old wires hung from exposed beams, and some mysterious substance emanated from its depths, suffusing our entire Victorian house with an odor of age, a hint of rot.

No longer. These days, our family’s formerly nasty basement is a gleaming, modern 1200-square-foot apartment filled with light and (odorless) air,easily rented outfor now and available as an age-in-place option for later.

When longtime broker Geoffrey Wells of Harvard Real Estate stopped down for a look recently while out dog-walking, he said, “This is the nicest basement I’ve ever seen in my life!”


Honest — he was just a passerby, not a paid marketer. We didn’t need much marketing: we found wonderful tenants within days of offering up the fully furnished, two-bedroom apartment on a rental site for $4,500 a month.

Overall, our recentbasement renovationexperience certainly seems to contradict the old wisdom that it makes little financial sense to invest much below ground. In fact, it seems to make quite a bit of sense right now, at least in areas like ours — Coolidge Corner in Brookline — where rents and sale prices remain sky-high.

To be sure, below-ground space still carries stigma, and it routinely goes for significantly less than higher floors. But thehousing shortageand the huge increase in property values have changed the basement-renovation equation, said Michael Kim ofMKA Architecture LLC, which designed our project.



His take: “If extra space on existing real estate can be converted into first-quality space, the value of new living space now vastly exceeds the cost of its construction.”

Our basement conversion could likely be “replicated by the hundreds in Brookline alone,” and elsewhere, said Kim, whose firm has designed several similar projects. “It does require some extra thought and care,” he added, “which has always been in short supply.”


But basement renovations also carry a special advantage, he argues. They allow historical homes to be preserved while also expanding the housing supply.

Density can be added “without sacrificing the urban fabric that is so valued by the community,” he said — a feat not usually achieved with a tear-down and new building.

One more social benefit: no market-rate apartment in our neighborhood can possibly be considered “affordable.” The median condo price in Coolidge Cornertopped $1.2 millionthis year, according to Newton-based Centre Realty Group. But below-grade spaces can at least be a bit less unaffordable.

“They often are really good options for you if you want more square footage or a neighborhood you might not otherwise be able to afford,” said agentFran Hoy of Coldwell Banker, whose colleagues nicknamed her “the queen of basements” because she has sold several in recent years.

“And they’re often as bright as any above-grade unit,” she said, despite the stereotype that all below-grade spaces are inevitably dark and depressing.


For me, the decision to renovate the basement stemmed from the conviction that in our astronomically priced neighborhood, it made no sense to leave 1,200 square feet to molder vacant — even below ground. Added inspiration came from a friend who bought a nearby duplex consisting of a main floor and a finished basement that was as elegant and bright as any above-ground space — and priced accordingly.

“Don’t call it a basement,” she corrected me. “That connotes hot-water tanks and mold. Call it ‘the lower level.’”

Such duplexes have been proliferating in parts of Brookline and beyond for the last dozen years or so, Hoy said. Developers convert big single-family houses into two units: the first floor and basement, often priced at about $2 million; and the two upper floors, which lately can reach $3 million or more.


Another factor in our renovation decision was that a central stairwell meant our 1895 house couldn’t be easily split into smaller units. The basement, on the other hand, was just sitting there.


Sitting there, sure, but no easy job for our general contractor, Marcos Coelho ofMega Construction Services, even though he has managed dozens of old-house renovations.

Challenge after challenge in a projectlike our basement involves finding ways to impose a new order on an old house never made for it. Nineteenth-century builders just never intended for basements to be used as living space. “It never crossed their minds,” he said.


So, Coelho has become well-versed in the solutions.

Ceiling too low? Dig down a couple of feet (not cheap) and add new walls to shore up the foundation.

Brick pillars cluttering up the space? Carefully tear them out and, with a structural engineer’s help, install new steel beams to support the house. (One of those moments when you really, really want contractors who know what they’re doing.)


Plumbing posed particular challenges. Hundreds of feet of new pipe had to be installed, both for the basement and the main house, but there was no room to drop the basement ceiling to hide it. That meant a great many pipe contortions and extra fittings for Jeff Snow of Somerville Plumbing and Heating.


“A renovation is 20 times harder than a brand-new construction job because you have to deal with a lot of things that are existing,” Snow said. For example, “you have two giant chimneys throughout the basement, and you have to find a way around them.”

The most important challenge, of course, was light. How could we bring as much natural light as possible below ground?



Kim’s team took an “every trick in the book” approach: windows wherever possible, dug-out “light wells” around two big windows, and restoration of a rotting wood-beamed sunroom for use as a glassy entrance. Most dramatic of all, the design called for digging out a roughly 60-square-foot section of the sideyard and installing five south-facing skylights to illuminate the living room.

Over the year-plus that this basement project took, I reaped plenty of non-financial benefits: the pleasure of watching experts successfully perform difficult work, the honor of doing right by this beautiful old house, and the comfort of setting up options for our family’s future.


But did it really pay off? Here’s some tentative math.

All told, the renovation cost roughly $700,000. Themedian price per square footfor a Coolidge Corner condo is reported at $850, so our 1200-square-foot apartment could theoretically be worth just over a million — except that it’s below ground.


Wells, the broker, estimates that the price penalty for below-grade space is roughly 20 percent. For example, he figures that our $4,500-a-month apartment could fetch a thousand or two more per month if it were higher up.

So, this $700,000 investment likely yielded $800,000 or more in value. The broader lesson, Wells said, is that for the many homeowners who do not have as much to invest or as big a basement, spending much less could still yield an apartment nice enough to generate $2,000 or more in monthly rent.



At the very least, I tell myself, this big basement project isn’t looking like financial folly.

Here’s hoping the rental income will remain reliable. So far so good. A potential tenant came for a viewing the other day and paid the ultimate compliment: “It doesn’tfeellike a basement at all!”


MK Architecture + Design, Brookline

Mega Construction Services, Framingham

Jeff Snow of Somerville Plumbing and Heating

Carey Goldberg, a contributing writer for Globe Ideas, is a former Boston bureau chief for The New York Times and Bloomberg News, and a former health and science reporter for the Globe and WBUR.

hed: US home prices are finally cooling — but a Mid-Atlantic region just surged 6.3%
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Think the housing market is finally giving buyers a break? Not around one East Coast region.
Home prices across the US rose a relatively modest 2.6% over the past year, but New York and its neighbors are stubbornly bucking the slowdown, according to new federal data.
Prices across a Middle-Atlantic region — New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania — surged 6.3% from July 2025 to July 2026, the biggest increase of any region in the country, according to the latestHouse Price Indexfrom the Federal Housing Finance Agency.
And buyers hoping the region is finally starting to cool aren’t getting much relief yet.
Home prices in the three-state area jumped another 1.5% in July alone, five times the 0.3% increase nationwide and once again the largest gain among the country’s nine census divisions.
The numbers paint a strikingly different picture from the one emerging in some other corners of the country, where the pandemic-era housing boom has increasingly given way to slower price growth — and, in some cases, outright declines.
Nowhere is that contrast clearer than in the Mountain West.
Prices across the Mountain division — Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — fell 0.8% in July, marking the weakest monthly performance of any region in the country.
Over the past year, prices there managed to rise just 0.6%, also the smallest increase nationwide.
That means homes in New York’s three-state region appreciated at more than 10 times the annual pace seen in the Mountain West.
The divide is particularly notable after years in which pandemic-era migration helped fuel housing booms across many Western markets, as buyers sought more space and took advantage of remote work.
But the latest FHFA figures suggest there’s no longer one national housing market moving in lockstep.
Across the country as a whole, home prices increased 0.3% between June and July, after remaining flat the month before. On an annual basis, prices were up 2.6%.
Every US census division still recorded an annual increase, according to the federal data, but the size of those gains varied dramatically — from the Mountain region’s barely-there 0.6% rise all the way to the Middle Atlantic’s 6.3%.
For buyers around New York, that’s an especially frustrating split.
A broader national slowdown might ordinarily be expected to offer house hunters some breathing room after years of soaring prices. Instead, homes in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania continue to appreciate considerably faster than the country overall.
And while the FHFA numbers don’t mean every individual market or home across the three states rose 6.3% — the index tracks the broader region — they show just how differently housing markets are behaving depending on where buyers are looking.
The result is a tale of two housing markets: buyers in parts of the West are beginning to see prices slip, while those around New York are still watching them climb at the fastest pace in the nation.
For Northeast house hunters waiting for the national housing cooldown to finally reach their neighborhood, they may have to keep waiting.

hed: Charming NYC rooftop farmhouse lists for $10.5M — with a porch and front yard looking to skyline views
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Who needs a weekend house upstate when you can have one on the roof?
A West Village penthouse topped with an eye-catchingporch-fronted cabin,a carpet of greenery and a working vegetable patch has hit the market for $10.5 million, offering farm-life fantasies six floors above Greenwich Street.
The top-floor co-op at 719 Greenwich St. belongs to developer David Puchkoff, 87, and his wife, writer Eileen Stukane, who have lived there for decades and even exchanged their wedding vows in the living room back in 1988.
Now the couple, who have three daughters, say it’s time for a new chapter.
“I think as we’re aging, a lot of our attention is redirected now to our children and our grandchildren,” Puchkoff toldthe New York Times.The pair may stay in Manhattan or decamp for the Hudson Valley.
“Right now, it’s all in flux,” he said. “We think of it as an adventure,” Stukane added.
Puchkoff snapped up the six-story brick building, which once operated as a basket warehouse, in 1974 for roughly $220,000. He carved it into a co-op and held onto the top floor for himself.
The rooftop dream came later, sparked by a visit to a friend’s lake house in rural Pennsylvania. With architect pal Lawrence Tobe, he crowned the apartment with a cabin and blanketed the roof in soil, which was shot up the side of the building through a tube. Puchkoff did much of the labor himself.
Getting to the “country” takes about a minute. The elevator opens directly into the apartment, and a gleaming steel staircase with a seafaring look rises from the middle of the living room into the cabin and its compact kitchen.
Push through the screen door and you’re on a wooden porch with a swing and a family-size dining table, gazing past a Japanese maple and beds of sedum toward the Midtown skyline.
Stukane runs the farm side of the operation.
“I’m the herb and vegetable gardener,” she said. “We really do well with eggplant, zucchini and lettuce. And there are lots of tomatoes and a big section of basil.”
The porch doubled as the family’s favorite hangout.
“It made us very popular with our relatives,” she said.
Below the greenery sits about 3,060 square feet of loft living with four bedrooms and two baths. Think exposed brick, chunky timber beams, oak floors and big windows framing both Midtown and Lower Manhattan.
The living room centers on a woodburning fireplace Puchkoff built from old cobblestones he said were lying “all over the streets in the ’70s.” The kitchen pairs butcher block counters with a mahogany breakfast bar, and the primary suite comes with a hot tub and views of Hudson Yards. Monthly maintenance runs $5,468, with taxes rolled in.
“It’s an interesting juxtaposition between country and urban,” Compass broker Jim St. André, who has the listing with Michael Maniawski and Trevor Stephens, said.
“We’re not in Kansas anymore, but we pretty much are,” he added.
The math may also tempt buyers. The ask works out to about $3,431 per square foot, while the median asking price for a four-bedroom in the neighborhood sits at $21.75 million, according to StreetEasy.
The pastoral perch hasn’t always been peaceful. In 2018, after an anonymous neighbor complained, city regulators slapped Puchkoff with a $1,200 fine and claimed he never had permission to build.
The Department of Buildings also demanded a new certificate of occupancy, and Puchkoff took the city to Manhattan Supreme Court.
“I haven’t done any other work in there except to water my garden, so who am I annoying?”he told The Post at the time, noting he filed permits in 2003.
“It isn’t fair, I’ve already met all the rules and regulations,” he said. “Somebody doesn’t like it.”
The hideaway can’t be spotted from the sidewalk, but it’s no secret. It has turned up in the Times and National Geographic, and it went viral in 2015 when aerial photographer George Steinmetz caught it from a helicopter.
Puchkoff, who developed several residential buildings around the neighborhood, has watched the Village transform.
“We saw this area evolve over the last 50 years from a wild, unruly area to what it is today,” he said.
As for the garden, he’s ready to hand over the trowel.
“I had the good fortune to be part of this garden and now it’s up to someone else to do what they want with it,” he said.

hed: NYC renters can save $31K per year instead of owning — as the gap widens nationwide
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For Americans dreaming of ditching their landlord and buying a home, the price of ownership is increasingly difficult to swallow.
Renting a typical home in the US was $1,066 a month cheaper than buying one in August — a gap that has widened as homeownership costs rise far faster than rents, according toa new Zillow analysis.
The typical US asking rent stood at $1,948 a month, compared with $3,014 for a new homeowner’s monthly mortgage payment, taxes and insurance.
That leaves renters with a whopping $12,792 annual advantage over buyers.
And the divide is growing.
Over just the past six months, the typical monthly cost for a new buyer has jumped $140, while rent increased by just $32 — meaning ownership costs rose more than four times as much in dollar terms.
Renting is now cheaper than buying in every one of the 50 largest US metro areas, according to Zillow.
The difference is particularly eye-popping in pricey coastal cities.
In San Jose, Calif., the typical rent was $3,815 in August, while a new buyer faced an estimated monthly payment of $11,698 — an extraordinary $7,883-a-month difference, or $94,596 over a year.
San Francisco renters faced a $3,409 monthly bill compared with $8,822 for buyers, leaving them $5,413 ahead each month.
In Los Angeles, the gap was $4,441 a month — $2,941 to rent versus $7,382 to buy — while San Diego renters paid $2,994 compared with a $7,229 estimated monthly cost for buyers, a difference of $4,235.
Seattle also posted a sizable $3,511 monthly gap, with typical rents of $2,278 compared with $5,789 for a new homeowner.
New Yorkers, meanwhile, aren’t exactly getting a bargain by renting — but buying is considerably more expensive.
Typical New York metro rent hit $3,615 in August, up 4.2% from a year earlier. A new homeowner would face an estimated $6,244 monthly payment, leaving a $2,629 gap between renting and buying — equivalent to $31,548 a year.
New York was also the country’s least affordable major rental market relative to local incomes. Zillow estimates a median-income household would have to spend 40.6% of its income on a new rental, compared with 36.9% in Miami and 34% in Los Angeles.
Boston renters saved an estimated $2,829 a month compared with buyers, while the difference was $2,640 in Salt Lake City, $2,540 in Portland, Ore., and $2,504 in Denver.
The renter advantage stretched well beyond expensive coastal markets.
In Austin, the typical $1,622 rent was $2,054 below the estimated $3,676 cost of buying. Phoenix renters saved $1,634 a month, Dallas renters $1,522 and Philadelphia renters $1,420.
Even in Pittsburgh — which had the smallest gap among the metros included in Zillow’s analysis — renting was still $536 a month, or $6,432 a year, cheaper than buying.
Zillow’s calculation assumes a new buyer puts 10% down on a typical home and takes out a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.67%, with estimated property taxes and homeowners insurance included.
The analysis does not include some other costs associated with ownership, such as closing costs and maintenance.
The financial divide extends to the salaries Americans need to comfortably afford each option.
Zillow estimates a household needs an annual income of $77,919 to afford the typical US rental, compared with more than $120,500 to afford the typical mortgage payment with 10% down — a difference of more than $42,000.
Rents themselves, however, remain far from cheap.
The typical asking rent rose 2.5% from a year earlier and is now 38.5% higher than at the beginning of the pandemic.
Single-family rents have climbed even faster, soaring 47% since the pandemic began to $2,289 a month in August. Multifamily rents rose 30.2% over the same period to $1,774.
There are signs of relief for some renters.
Nearly four in 10 — 39.2% — rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in August, such as free rent or another landlord incentive. That share was 2.5 percentage points higher than a year earlier.
And rents actually fell month over month in eight of the 50 largest metros, led by Boston, where they dropped 0.7%.
But rent growth remains particularly hot in parts of California.
San Francisco rents surged 10.8% from a year earlier, the largest increase among the 50 biggest metros, followed by San Jose at 7.6%, Virginia Beach at 6.6%, Milwaukee at 5% and Chicago at 4.9%.
Zillow also calculated what could happen if renters invested the money they saved instead of spending it.
A renter who invested the national $1,066 monthly difference at the 4.68% yield on the 10-year Treasury would earn an additional $322 during the first year, according to the analysis.
Assuming rents and buying costs remained unchanged, the accumulated savings and investment returns could total about $72,000 after five years.
In San Jose, where the rent-versus-buy divide is largest, Zillow estimates investing the difference could generate another $2,381 in returns in the first year alone.
The widening gap underscores just how much today’s combination of elevated home prices and borrowing costs has changed the traditional financial calculation between renting and owning — even as renters continue to grapple with housing costs that remain well above pre-pandemic levels.

hed: Mamdani’s $607M NYCHA makeover costs taxpayers a staggering $528K per apartment
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani just inked a public housing rehab so pricey it works out to more than half a million dollars for every single apartment — on city taxpayers’ dime.
The cityclosed financing Tuesdayon a $607 million overhaul of Nostrand Houses, the aging NYCHA complex in Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn.
Spread across the development’s 1,148 units, the math lands at roughly $528,700 per apartment. That’s nearly $38 million for each of the campus’s 16 buildings and north of $300,000 for every one of its roughly 2,000 tenants.
Jay Martin, head of the landlord group Community Housing Improvement Program, didn’t mince words either.
“My criticism is not about NYCHA getting needed repairs,” Martinwrote on X.“It’s not that those repairs cost $522,000 per unit. It’s not even that the average NYCHA unit costs 80% more per month to operate than a pre-1974 rent-stabilized unit.
“It’s the inability to acknowledge that hundreds of thousands of private rent-stabilized units have rents that don’t cover operating costs.”
Those units get a rent freeze and show trials. Public housing getsbillions of dollars. City Hall, meanwhile, was popping champagne.
“This $607 million investment means new kitchens, safer and healthier apartments, modern building systems and the dignity of a home that works the way it should,” Mamdani said in a statement.
So what exactly does half a million bucks buy in Sheepshead Bay?
Kitchens and bathrooms will be gutted down to the studs and rebuilt with quartz countertops, new appliances, fresh plumbing and scratch-resistant floors. Every apartment gets double-pane windows, new intercoms, laundry hookups and window heat pumps that let tenants control their own heat and AC. Crews will also scrub out lead and mold hazards.
Building-wide, the money covers new elevators, boilers and hot water systems, rewired electrical, expanded security cameras and an on-site guard. Officials said 81 units will be retrofitted for residents with mobility needs and another 48 for those with vision or hearing loss. A new management office will house more than 40 staffers.
The project is the first to cross the finish line under the Public Housing Preservation Trust, a state-created entity that lets NYCHA developments swap traditional federal funding for the more generous Section 8 pipeline while staying in public hands.
Nostrand residents voted to join back in December 2023. City officials said the switch roughly doubles the federal operating subsidy the complex collects.
“This $607 million investment gives us the resources to deliver the modernization residents have been waiting for while keeping Nostrand fully public and preserving resident rights and affordability,” Trust President Vlada Kenniff said.
The deal pulls in money from the Office of Management and Budget and the Housing Development Corporation (HUD), Merchants Capital and the AFL-CIO Housing Investment Trust, with the city’s building trades unions signed on as labor partner.
The administration has not released a line-by-line breakdown showing how much of the $607 million goes to actual construction versus financing, reserves and other soft costs.
Construction is slated to start this fall.
“Residents have helped shape these plans from the beginning, and now we are one step closer to seeing the improvements we’ve been waiting for become a reality,” said Miriam Rodriguez, a Nostrand tenant who sits on the Trust’s board.
The timing is raising eyebrows in the private market.
The bill lands just as Mamdani’s hand-picked Rent Guidelines Board slapsa two-year freezeon roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments, taking effect on leases starting Thursday. Owners of those buildings, many of them pre-war walk-ups, say they’re being squeezed between flat rents and soaring bills for insurance, fuel and upkeep.
“Older rent-stabilized buildings are already struggling under rising operating costs, yet the Board chose to disregard those realities,” Real Estate Board of New York President James Whelan said after the June vote.
Mamdani has made NYCHA the centerpiece of his housing agenda, pouring $5.6 billion in capital funds into public housing in his first budget. Three more developments, Bronx River Addition, Unity Towers and Hylan Houses, have already voted to follow Nostrand into the Trust.

hed: Massachusetts is looking for a curator to rehabilitate a historic Hyde Park house – and use it for 25 years
subhead: A house inside Stony Brook Reservation is the latest project from the Massachusetts Department of Conservation and Recreation
content:
ByOlivia McKenley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Tucked inside Hyde Park’s forest landscape lies the Massachusetts Department of Conservation and Recreation’s latest project. DCR’s Historic Curatorship Program is scouting for a curator fit to restore the house at 12 Brainard St. atStony Brook Reservation. The organization currently has arequest for proposalsout for the “rehabilitation, reuse, and maintenance” of the site. Proposals should also include planned use for the space, which can be anything from residential to commercial or nonprofit.

The program strives to rehabilitate the Commonwealth’s most vulnerable and underutilized properties, often holding historical value. Kevin Allen, DCR’s senior preservation planner, said the hope is to “preserve the building, not just for the time being.”

The program’s public-private partnership allows curators to lease a one-of-a-kind historic property in exchange for long-term rehabilitation and maintenance. Under the lease, curators can transform the space for their own use — they can live in it, operate a business, or any other use approved in their proposal.

DCR is behind restoration projects like the wedding venueWillowdale Estateat Bradley Palmer State Park in Topsfield, theCharles River Speedwaymarketplace in Brighton, and the Wachusett Historic Superintendent’s House which now operates as an eatery and event space calledMountainsidein Princeton, about an hour west of Boston.

In 2019, CBS Local reported that the Wachusett Mountain space was vacant for 30 years until the DCR curatorship transformed it. “Thanks to a unique program offered by DCR, [Katherine Huck and Robin Springfield] will invest hundreds of thousands of dollars of their own money to bring this old building back to its former glory. In return, they will get a long-term lease to operate a second location of their business, The Mountainside Market, at the site,” the site reported.


The curator doesn’t gain any property ownership, but holds a lease that typically lasts 25 to 30 years. A fair market rent is established as a base, but outside of the cost of renovations and the sweat equity put in, the curator is not responsible to pay rent.

The fair market rent set by DCR for the Hyde Park house is $3,526 a month ($42,312 annually) through a 25-year lease. According to DCR’s request for proposals andconditions assessment reports, the estimated cost of the baseline required improvements is $862,737. Curators hold responsibility for all rehabilitation and maintenance costs, including applicable taxes, fees, insurance, and utilities.

Ethan Parsons, the DCR’s historic curatorship program manager, envisions the house returning to its residential roots or being used by a small-scale business or nonprofit. But he said he and the rest of the curatorship program are open to every possibility.


During its original construction in 1898, the Stony Brook Reservation home served as the park superintendent’s residence. Over time, it shifted into a general office space for DCR staff. Parsons estimates the property has been vacant for roughly a decade. Artifacts of DCR’s office use have been uncovered in the past few years — internet equipment, desks, filing cabinets — most beyond repair.

The structure, one of the oldest remaining builds by the Metropolitan Parks Commission (now DCR), sits on Stony Brook Reservation’s southwest edge. The reservation — roughly 600 acres of forested space — surrounds the property, with idyllic trails and ponds.

The home is also near the Hyde Park Community Center, a commuter rail station is under a mile away, and a tennis court sits just adjacent to the property.

Inside the two-story Dutch Colonial, original details like built-in cabinetry and window seats, trim, flooring, and an oil-fired furnace have stood the test of time.


State officials note that the structure is in “fairly good condition.” To Allen, the soundness of the 128-year-old home makes it a rare candidate for curation.

“Folks don’t need the same amount of investment and resources, as in time,” he said. “Hopefully that means we do have a broader range of applicants.

“Sometimes the harder part is the ongoing maintenance. That’s kind of why we get in the position we’re in with some of these in the first place,” he added.

DCR anticipates replacing the plumbing and electrical systems and improving accessibility. The bulk of the restoration — and timeline — will depend on what new use the curator imagines for the structure.

The DCR’s overarching hope is that the restoration “invites the public to use the property from time to time, has some programming that engages with the neighborhood, with the reservation, and really restores the vibrancy and life that this building has the potential to provide.”

Hopeful curators can submit proposal requests through Dec. 28.

hed: HOA threatens to sue Texas resident over oil stains allegedly left by its own landscapers
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Texas homeowner is pushing back after a neighborhood association allegedly demanded payment for a driveway the resident says was ruined by the HOA’s own landscapers.
The owner, whoposts on Redditas HOUSEofBEAST84, said the Preston Oaks HOA in Austin mailed a notice seeking repair costs and warned of a legal fight if the work isn’t done.
“They park their mowers and they leak oil everywhere,” the homeowner wrote. “Asking them to stop made it worse and they left trash everywhere.”
The post did not say how much money the association wants or include a copy of the notice. The resident said the mess has been documented and that fed-up neighbors have launched a petition against the board.
When the matter came up at a recent board meeting, the homeowner said, leaders promised only to circle back.
The complaint, posted to a forum devoted toHOA grievances,drew dozens of replies within days. Most urged the owner to take the association to court, and one commenter claimed to have sued an HOA in small claims over a water main its landscaper broke.
“Sue the HOA, which is a legal entity,” another wrote. “It’s on them, or their insurance, to recoup from the landscapers.”
Another commenter skipped the legal talk entirely and recommended an enzyme powder that dissolves oil stains over several weeks.
State law gives owners some cover. In subdivisions governed by Chapter 209 of the Texas Property Code, an association must send written notice by certified mail before it can bill an owner for property damage. The notice has to describe the damage and state the amount owed, and the owner has 30 days from the mailing to request a hearing before the board.
Those rules do not settle who caused the damage, but they give an owner a formal chance to contest a charge before it sticks.
Owners who would rather go on offense can turn to aTexas justice court,where small claims cases are capped at $20,000 and hiring a lawyer is optional.
Disputes like this one touch a huge slice of the state. Texas has roughly 23,500 community associations housing about 6.4 million residents, according to the Foundation for Community Association Research.
That footprint keeps growing. Nearly two thirds of new single-family homes started nationwide in 2024 sat inside an association, according to a National Association of Home Builders analysis of Census Bureau data. In the region that includes Texas, the share topped 70% .
Who pays in a fight like this usually comes down to an association’s governing documents, which lay out who maintains driveways and lawns and when a board can pass repair costs to an owner.
Preston Oaks HOA did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

hed: San Francisco rent crisis hits staggering new highs as median rent now nearly $1k more than NYC
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
San Francisco renters are getting squeezed harder than ever — and the city’slatest apartment pricesare starting to look downright outrageous.
The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the city hit a record $4,400 a month in September, according to a new reportfrom real estate site Zumper.
That’s a staggering 25.4% jump from a year ago, putting San Francisco just $180 behind New York City, where themedian one-bedroomcosts $4,580.

But renters don’t have to look far to find listings that make the $4,400 median look almost like a bargain.
Last month, The California Post profiled a San Francisco one-bedroomasking a jaw-dropping $5,495 a month, sparking outrage from renters who questioned how such a tiny apartment could command such a massive price.
And the latest numbers show that listing was hardly an isolated case.
The median price for a two-bedroom apartment in San Francisco has now climbed to $6,340 a month — the highest in the country and nearly $900 more than the median two-bedroom in New York.
Two-bedroom rents have jumped 26.8% over the past year, with the median price blowing past $6,000 in July.
The surge is being fueled in part by abooming artificial-intelligence sector, according to Zumper, which said AI hiring is creating a wave of new demand in a city where housing supply remains tight.
The rent spike is also far outpacing much of the rest of the Bay Area.
In San Jose, the median one-bedroom costs $2,890, while Oakland renters pay a median $2,100 for a one-bedroom. Those prices are also up over the past year, but nowhere near San Francisco’s 25.4% increaseaccording to CBS.
Nationally, the median one-bedroom rent rose just 0.1% over the past year to $1,518, while the median two-bedroom increased 0.5% to $1,903.
“There really isn’t one U.S. rental market right now,” Zumper CEO Shawn Mullahy said in a statement. “The common denominator is supply: markets still absorbing the building boom are competing aggressively for renters, while markets that avoided it are tightening quickly.”
The housing crunch has become such a problem that San Francisco Mayor Daniel Luriedeclared a “rent emergency”earlier this month, citing soaring rents and evictions that are expected to hit their highest level in a decade.
“For thousands upon thousands of San Franciscans, the most immediate pressure right now is rent,” Lurie said at a Sept. 10 briefing. “And that pressure is rising rapidly.”
Lurie has proposed measures including a 10% cap on rent increases and roughly $55 million for a legal fund to help tenants fight to remain in their homes.

hed: One of the first post-wildfire homes inside the Pacific Palisades burn scar lists for sale — asking $14M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In thePacific Palisades, one of the first post-wildfire new-construction homes within the burn scar has hit the market for $13.99 million, Gimme Shelter has learned.
The five-bedroom home, at 837 Muskingum Ave., is on a street that largely survived the devastatingJanuary 2025 wildfires, said listing broker Ryan Jancula, of Compass.
It is one of 14 dwellings that Alison White, of Alison White Homes, is currently developing in the Palisades.
Eight of the others are currently under construction and “well underway,” while the remaining six are “in design and permitting,” White told Gimme Shelter.
Muskingum is the only spec house of the 14, and the first to be completed, as its permits were secured beforethe fires tore through.
“We are building all of the other ones for the homeowners … All will get people back into their homes,” White said.
Eleven lost their homes and two others bought burned-out properties, and are now building their dream homes and moving to the Palisades, she added.
The Muskingum home was built on a vacant lot, “as the former home was torn down a month before the fires and acted as a fire break, more or less, saving the entire neighborhood. Below it, everything burned, and above it, everything was saved,” Jancula said.
While construction has begun on more than 1,100 new homes in the Palisades, only 43 have received a post-wildfire certificate of occupancy, according tothe Palisadian-Post’s Pali Rebuild Map.
On social media, Jancula calls the Muskingum listing “the first residence of its caliber to be offered for sale since the fires.”
There’s also an option to buy the home fully furnished.
Jancula believes the home will appeal to people who lost their homes to the wildfires but are too overwhelmed to deal with permits and other issues.
As the listing notes, the home offers something “rarely possible in a community at such a pivotal moment: immediate ownership … at the forefront of Pacific Palisades’ next chapter.”
But the rebuild is just beginning, and prices reflect that.
Some luxury homes that launched post-fire inside the Palisades — but outside the burn scar, Jancula noted — have already dropped their prices significantly.
For example, 1072 Amalfi Dr. — which, unlike Muskingum, is still under construction — launched in April at $19.99 million. It was chopped $2 million, to $17.99 million, on Sept. 24, according to websites.
Another home outside the burn scar at 990 Corsica Dr. first listed in April for $18.99 million and is now asking $16.9 million, another $2 million drop.
Like many developers, White is using wood to build instead of fireproof steel — and offers “a number of fire safe options. It depends on how far clients want to go,” White said. “A lot of our clients believe a fire of this magnitude will never happen again.”
White cites a “state-of-the-art” exterior fire suppression system with sprinklers on the roof, and fire-safe vents “not required by building code,” among other things.
Jancula told Gimme Shelter that Muskingum comes with fire-safe features including a “top-of-the-line whole house and exterior sprinkler” system.
At 6,511 square feet, the residence opens to a grand entry with a sunroom overlooking the grounds.
A chef’s kitchen, which anchors the home, includes a 60-inch range, a custom wet bar and a walk-in pantry.
Upstairs, a main bedroom suite features a fireplace, vaulted ceilings, paneling, a roomy walk-in closet and a spa-like bath.
There’s also a movie theater, an upstairs laundry room and a three-car garage.
Annette Tatum Design, whose clients include Owen Wilson, Minnie Driver and Marcia Cross, curated the interiors, which have been staged and customized thanks to a partnership with Serena & Lily.
Outside, there’s an infinity pool, a wellness deck with a sauna and cold plunge, and an outdoor kitchen with a dining area, lounging spaces and a fire pit.
The home is by Palisades Village, which just reopened and is now at 99% leasing capacity — a good sign for the community, brokers said.
Many people who lost their homes are still nervous to jump back into the real estate market.
“It’s taking a long time to rebuild. The permits are coming faster, but the water has still not been put back in the reservoir,” Jancula said, referring to the Santa Ynez Reservoir that was empty during the 2025 wildfires, was filled in April 2025 and then drained again in April 2026, according to reports.
In addition, rebuilding takes a psychological toll that is often not taken into account.
“If you have lived in your home for 30 or 40 years, the emotional cycle of thinking about where you want to spend the rest of your life is also quite a challenge,” he said. “People aren’t factoring that in. It’s not just waiting for insurance payouts. Buying a piece of land in a neighborhood that is not yet completed, and designing your next forever house after you lost what you thought was your forever house.”
On a lower luxury end, Jancula is also bringing to market two properties in the burn scar: 744 Iliff St., asking $4.99 million, in the Alphabet Streets, and 605 Erskine Dr., asking $4.29 million. The Erskine home was the first purchased post-fire and rebuilt as a spec house, Jancula said.
Added White: “Every day there’s more construction popping up. It’s heartwarming and wonderful to see.”
