hed: AI millionaires are dropping mega bucks on San Francisco houses — comically free from tech
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
They made their fortunes inartificial intelligence. But that doesn’t mean they want a mansion filled with smart gadgets.
San Francisco’snewly minted AI millionaires are seeking warm woods, handmade furniture and wellness amenities, brokers and designers told The Post — with some even forgoing smart-home features in a stunning about-face.
Their vision of a dream home puts natural materials, calm interiors and room to unplug high on the list.
Think saunas, cold plunges, red-light therapy, private gyms and libraries.
“Ten years ago, everybody wanted a wine cellar or a wine room,” Annie Williams, a veteran San Francisco broker with Sotheby’s International Realty, told The Post. “Everybody’s asking for, ‘Where can I put my sauna?’”
The frenzy is unfolding amid what Williams, who has worked in San Francisco real estate for 25 years, called the hottest market she has ever seen.
“We took off in January and nobody seemed to see it coming,” she said.
Williams said the phenomenon stretches beyond founders and employees at companies such as OpenAI. Surging technology stocks have created a much broader “wealth effect” among investors, longtime tech workers and families whose portfolios are heavily exposed to AI-related companies.
Lisa Smith, a founding agent at Serhant in San Francisco, said she began feeling the surge particularly strongly around May. Smith said AI buyers have also toured a $20 million off-market property she is marketing in Mill Valley, about 10 minutes from San Francisco. The remodeled historic home has five bedrooms and four bathrooms across roughly 3,800 square feet and sits on a half-acre lot within walking distance of downtown Mill Valley.
“Right now, I’m feeling a little bit like I’m in a tsunami,” Smith told The Post. “The request of what they want right now is just outpacing what we can get them.”
The problem is that San Francisco hasonly so many mansionsto go around.
Once they find one, the new generation of tech wealth is putting its own stamp on luxury.
Smith said wellness features — particularly saunas, cold plunges and red-light therapy — have become increasingly common requests.
Just before speaking to The Post, she had toured a home where red-light therapy had been installed directly on the wall of the primary bedroom.
Jennifer Jones, principal designer at Niche Interiors, who is currently working with several AI-industry clients, said she is seeing the same shift from the other side of the transaction.
Clients who buy homes with wine rooms are increasingly asking her team to turn them into spas or saunas, she said. Others want full gyms, plunge pools and even dedicated rooms for at-home massages.
Those amenities are increasingly showing up in homes drawing interest from the AI crowd, too.
One such property they can consider is att 827 North Point St. in Russian Hill — a three-bedroom condo asking $2.95 million, listed by Neal Ward and Neill Bassi of Sotheby’s International Realty. The 1,643-square-foot home has its own private wellness setup, with a sauna and cold plunge opening onto a private deck.
Another penthouse, at 18 Lansing St. in Rincon Hill, takes the idea to the roof. The $2.39 million, roughly 1,940-square-foot home, listed by Justin Goldberg of Compass, has more than 1,000 square feet of private outdoor space, including a rooftop sauna and hot tub, along with a fire pit and an upper observation deck with panoramic views of downtown San Francisco and the Bay.
“Most buyers touring our penthouse work in AI or tech, with offices just a few blocks away,” Goldberg told The Post. “With a significant IPO market anticipated in the coming months, buyers are looking to get ahead of the potential liquidity expected to enter the neighborhood in 2027.”
Daniel Kavanagh, principal of Rogue Sauna, said he has installed high-end saunas for a number of Bay Area clients working in AI and tech. Residential projects can run from around $40,000 to $100,000, he said, with cold plunges often part of the setup.
For clients who spend their working lives immersed in technology, Kavanagh said the appeal is often getting away from it.
“The irony is that they want something to decompress from tech,” he said. “They want a break from technology.”
A sauna, he added, is “one of the few places in the house that nobody checks email.”
The aesthetic beyondthe sauna— and into the general design of the homes — has changed, too.
Where previous generations of Silicon Valley wealth often gravitated toward shiny metals, crystal chandeliers, dark wallpapers and other conspicuous displays of luxury, many of today’s younger clients are asking for something softer.
“Quiet” and “calm” are words Jones said she hears repeatedly.
The look is heavy on warm woods, handmade pieces, organic shapes, textured fabrics, muted palettes and sculptural furniture — a kind of California modernism meets “quiet luxury.”
“They want light. They want airy,” Jones said. “They do not want dark, moody rooms.”
And quiet luxury doesn’t mean quiet spending.
Jones said AI clients have shelled out $150,000 for a custom glass-and-bronze chandelier and more than $100,000 for a hand-knotted silk-and-cashmere rug.
The six-figure purchases reflect a particular appetite for custom craftsmanship, she said, even when the finished room is deliberately designed not to scream wealth.
Of course, AI itself is also increasingly shaping what those homes look like.
Jones said clients now arrive at the beginning of projects armed with their own ChatGPT-generated renderings — something designers would traditionally create much later in the process.
“They’re like, ‘Here’s an idea. Here’s an idea,’” she said, describing clients rapidly generating different versions of rooms in their new homes.
That has accelerated expectations for the rest of the process, too.
“They want these projects done fast,” Jones said.
The trouble is that the physical world doesn’t always move at AI speed.
“We can’t make a hand-knotted rug in Nepal any faster,” she said.
Jones said “speed is something that’s become a new currency” among this generation of clients.
In one particular request, an AI client challenged her team to compete against artificial intelligence to design a custom piece of furniture. Both sides received essentially the same brief, and the client compared the results.
“We won that challenge,” Jones said. “I’m not worried that AI is taking over a job as an interior designer anytime soon.”

hed: NYC now ranks as the hardest place to buy a home for first-time buyers
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New Yorkers hoping to buy their first home may need to start saving decades before they get the keys.
New York City isthe hardest major market in Americafor first-time buyers to scrape together a down payment, with a typical household needing a staggering 65.2 years to save enough, according toa new analysis from Rocket.
The median first-time buyer in the Big Apple puts down $265,000 — a 30% of the $883,333 purchase price, the analysis found.
That puts New York well ahead of even notoriously expensive California markets.
InSan Francisco, a typical household would need 57.2 years to save the median $400,000 down payment, equivalent to roughly 27% of a $1.5 million purchase.
Los Angeles came in third, requiring 41.5 years to accumulate its $170,500 median down payment on an $852,500 home.
Boston followed at 37.8 years, with first-time buyers typically putting $185,000 down, while Anaheim and San Jose, both in pricey California, tied at 33.6 years. First-time buyers in San Jose put down a median $249,000 on a roughly $1.1 million purchase.
The calculation assumes a household saves 5% of its income every year. Rocket combined 2024 Census household-income data with down payments made by its first-time buyer mortgage customers between May 2025 and May 2026.
That means the eye-popping 65-year figure isn’t how long New Yorkers actually spend saving. Rather, it illustrates just how far the typical household’s income is from the amount first-time buyers are putting down in the city.
In New York, the median household income used in the analysis was $81,228, meaning saving 5% annually would amount to just over $4,000 a year.
The picture changes dramatically hundreds of miles west.
In Warren, Michigan, the median first-time buyer puts down just $8,797, or 5% of the $175,940 purchase price. A typical household could theoretically save that amount in only 3.1 years.
Nearby Detroitwas second-fastest at 3.9 years, where buyers put down a median $7,600 — also about 5% — on a $152,000 home.
Virginia Beach and Fort Worth followed at 4.3 years each, while Indianapolis and Milwaukee both came in at roughly 4.4 years.
The vast divide isn’t solely the result of coastal homes costing more. Buyers in expensive markets are also putting a much larger share of the purchase price down.
In New York, first-timers put down a median 30%, six times the 5% share seen in Detroit and Warren.
New York’s notoriously demanding co-op market may help explain the difference. Many co-op and condo buildings require buyers to put 20% to 30% down, according to Redfin agent Jason Warner.
“The price point is so much higher in New York City than it is in most of the country,” Warner said in Rocket’s report.
He said the hurdle has changed the profile of the city’s first-time buyer.
“Since it takes a bit longer for first-time home buyers to save here, I’m now often helping mid-career professionals in their late 30s and early 40s to buy their first home after decades of renting,” Warner said.
And bringing more cash to the table can matter beyond simply satisfying a lender or building.
With inventory tight and sellers weighing which deals are most likely to make it to closing, a hefty down payment can make an offer appear stronger, Warner said.
The findings come as first-time buyers nationwide continue to face a daunting affordability equation.
The typical US homebuyer put down $64,000, or 15% of the purchase price, in March, according to a separateRedfin analysis. That’s roughly double the dollar amount buyers were putting down before the pandemic, largely because home prices have soared.
And despite some recent improvement in affordability, the typical American household still earns substantially less than what’s needed to comfortably buy a home.
Redfinestimated in Junethat a household needed to make about $109,800 a year to afford the typical US home, compared with an estimated median household income of about $87,600.
For New Yorkers, the gap is even wider: Redfin estimates a buyer needs to earn roughly $233,000 to afford a typical home in the metro, while its estimated median household income is about $98,000.
For would-be buyers who don’t have decades to wait, family assistance has increasingly become part of the equation.
Rocket’s analysis cited a Redfin survey finding that nearly a quarter of young recent homebuyers had used family money toward their down payment.
Others are widening their searches or adjusting their expectations.
But for buyers determined to stay in New York, the numbers illustrate the extraordinary amount of cash it can take just to get through the front door.

hed: Miami’s $100M club swells in size as chapel-equipped Coral Gables compound asks $148M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Miami’s nine-digit house party just got a new guest.
A waterfront compound in Coral Gables has hit the market for a stratospheric $148 million, an ask that would nearly triple the city’s sales record if met. It is one of five single-family homes in Miami-Dade now publicly priced at $100 million or more, The Post has learned.
The spread at 8901 Arvida Lane covers 2.38 acres at the head of a lagoon in Gables Estates, a gated enclave of fewer than 200 homes and lots. Dennis Carvajal of ONE Sotheby’s International Realty has the listing.
Coral Gables has never logged a home sale north of $100 million. The current high is $55 million, set last year elsewhere in Gables Estates. Carvajal is betting this one clears that bar by a mile.
The property “will reset the market,” he told The Post.
So what does $148 million buy? Start with a Rafael Portuondo-designed main house that the brokerage puts at upward of 14,000 square feet, with six bedrooms, nine full bathrooms, three powder rooms and 25-foot ceilings. Inside are a wine room kept at cellar temperature, a theater, a billiards room, a pair of offices and an elevator. The primary suite has a terrace, its own bar and a bathroom wrapped in onyx.
Then come the extras.
The estate packs a chapel fitted with stained glass, plus a guest villa with a full kitchen and a standalone gym at the water’s edge topped by a sun deck. The pool is lined in mosaic tile and ringed by marble. Out back, 245 feet of shoreline and an 86-foot dock offer a straight shot to Biscayne Bay with no bridges to duck under.
The landscaping is its own flex. More than 600 species of palms, trees and plants cover the lot, which tracks with the seller’s day job. The owner has been identified as Manuel Diaz, founder of Homestead nursery Manuel Diaz Farms. The property tax bill alone ran $260,235 last year, per the listing.
This is not the home’s first trip to market. Diaz sought $45 million in 2017 and $55 million a year later, then tried $48.5 million in 2020 and $52 million in 2021 before pulling it in 2022. The new number is roughly triple those earlier asks.
What changed is the ceiling. In 2022, Ken Griffin made the Adrienne Arsht estate on Brickell Avenue set a record at $106.87 million. This March, Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan paid $170 million for anunfinished Indian Creek mansion, a new county high.
“A few years ago, we rarely saw homes even testing a $100 million price point,” Carvajal told The Post. “Now there are multiple properties publicly listed at or above that threshold, and there are buyers with the ability and appetite to transact at that level.”
The competition is stiff. Topping the pile is a $237 millionKey Biscayne estatewhose listing touts its turn as Frank Lopez’s house in “Scarface.” A two-home compound on the Sunset Islands is asking $110 million, as is a 1.61-acre bayfront propertyon Brickell Avenue.A new build on North Bay Road with an 18-car garage wants an even $100 million .
A sixth contender has already blinked. John Ruiz’s $175 million mansion, also in Gables Estates, appears to have come off the market, according toThe Real Deal.
Carvajal’s camp pegs the current tally at a 500% jump from 2022 and says it undercounts the action, since estates at this level are often shopped privately before any public listing.
The broker chalks it up to supply. “It’s the scarcity effect,” he said. “There are only a limited number of trophy estates in Miami with this scale, water frontage, privacy and prime location.”
He doesn’t see it cooling off.
“Miami is only going to become more important as a global epicenter for wealth,” Carvajal said. “We’ve already seen an enormous amount of capital move here, and the demand has not stopped. The ultra-wealthy aren’t just looking for a great house anymore. They want compounds with multiple combined lots, more land, more waterfront and complete privacy.”
“I think we’ll continue to see records broken because there simply aren’t enough of those properties to meet the demand,” he added.
But these figures only tell one story. Despite the luxury market in Sunshine State taking off, the regular market has seena steep decline. Florida currently sits at the bottom of the barrel when it comes to selling the average home, with about 206,508 homes sitting on the market — many of them which have undergone severe price cuts.

hed: US mortgage rates brush 7 percent, weighing on buyers, sellers and further straining a bleak housing market
content: Home shoppers holding out for relief from rising mortgage rates may be in for a long wait.The weekly average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate home loan has been rising for months and this week climbed to just below 7 percent — its highest level in more than 19 months.The benchmark 30-year fixed rate mortgage rose to 6.95 percent from 6.76 percent last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.26 percent.This is the fourth week in a row that mortgage rates have moved higher. The average rate hasn’t reached this level since Jan. 30, 2025.Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate increased to 6.26 percent from 6.09 percent last week. A year ago, it was at 5.41 percent.Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month to borrowers’ costs, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power. As rates rise, that can also lead prospective home shoppers to delay buying.In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98 percent, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The nearly 1 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional $255 a month cost for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate.The housing market has been stuck in a rut this year in large part because of rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have kept marching higher in the months since the war between the US and Iran began in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher.Mortgage rates are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy, and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield. That yield, which was at 3.97 percent in late February, before the war began, breached 5 percent on Monday for the first time since 2023. It was at 4.94 percent at midday trading on the bond market Thursday.Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve’s decision Wednesday to increase its key interest rate for the first time in three years in a bid to tame surging inflation could also put upward pressure on mortgage rates.While the central bank doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately affect the yield on 10-year Treasurys. The Fed also signaled Wednesday that another rate hike could occur later this year.“The rate hike all but guarantees that mortgage rates will remain stuck at or above the 7 percent threshold, which creates a psychological and financial barrier that will sharply squeeze affordability and sideline even more prospective buyers,” said Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist at Bright MLS.The US housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied US homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. US sales of those homes slowed again last month.And the latest monthly tally of home purchase transactions that have yet to be finalized points to potentially more sluggish home sales in coming months.Pending US home sales inched up 0.3 percent last month from July and fell 4.7 percent from August last year, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday. There’s usually a month or two lag between a contract signing and when the sale is finalized, which makes pending home sales a near-term bellwether for the housing market.A sharp run-up in home prices, especially in the early years of this decade, and a chronic shortage of homes nationally worsened by years of below-average home construction have left many aspiring homeowners priced out of the market.That has many would-be homebuyers keeping an eye on mortgage rates, which can boost home shoppers’ purchasing power when they come down, but also reduce how much homebuyers can afford when rates rise.Depending on a borrower’s income, credit, and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average.The Fed rate hike and other factors already driving up mortgage rates this year could set the stage for a further slowing in the housing market this year.Still, it’s not clear how much mortgage rates will move up from here, as their rise in recent weeks may already reflect, at least in part, expectations that the Fed would elect to begin hiking interest rates.“That matters because it tells us how mortgage rates and the bond market might respond to potential Fed hikes,” said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.

hed: LA’s ‘mansion tax’ backfires spectacularly as thousands of homes and jobs vanish
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
LA’s “mansion tax,” sold to Angelenos as a way to tax the rich and boost housing, has instead blocked the building of 9,100 homes, wiped out 16,650 full-time construction jobs and cost $452 million in revenue.
A damning new report says the tax, officially known asUnited to House LA, or ULA — has had a negative impact on the city’s high-end and multi-family real estate markets and collected less than half what it was expected to generate to tackle the city’s housing crisis.
The ULA was expected to raise about $900 million a year, or $2.7 billion over its first three years. Instead, it brought in about $1.2 billion.

The tax — which went into effect in April 2023 and was championed by socialist mayoral hopeful CouncilwomanNithya Raman— means if a property in LA sells for more than $5.4 million, the seller is taxed 4% of the price at closing. If it sells for more than $10.9 million, it increases to 5.5%.
Despite its nickname, LA’s “mansion tax” applies far beyond luxury homes. Apartment buildings, offices, warehouses and vacant land can all trigger the tax if they sell above the thresholds.
About 1,000 of the 9,100-plus new homes lost would have been affordable units — the very thing the tax was supposed to create — according to RAND corporation, a non-partisan, nonprofit research group.
Westside real estate broker Danny Brown told The California Post the tax was ”another disaster initiated by the incompetent socialists who run our city.”
“ULA has chopped the legs from under the residential and commercial real estate industry, which is one of the largest parts of our city’s economic engine,” Brown said.
Mayor Karen Bass did not take a position on the mansion tax, but Raman has since said she was in favor of reforming the tax.
RAND found the ULA slashed high-value property sales by an estimated 31% through early 2026, with apartment and commercial sales falling by more than 46%.
Simply put, the tax has discouraged some owners from selling and developers from pursuing projects that, because of the tax, no longer make financial sense.
“Measure ULA has the noble aspiration of delivering more affordable housing inventory to Los Angeles, but its negative repercussions may outweigh its benefits. A transfer tax of this type adds friction to the housing market and slows the number of home transactions,” Joel Berner, a senior economist atRealtor.com, told The Post.
Realtor.comis owned by News Corp, the same parent company that owns The Post.
“Builders are already dealing with high costs of labor and materials, so this added expense when they go to sell a completed or revitalized project squeezes their margins even further,” Berner added. “This will lead some to decide that the deals simply are not worthwhile.”
New research has documented a significant hit to high-value property sales and housing development since ULA took effect in 2023.
The tax also wiped out the equivalent of 16,650 full-time construction jobs and cost government agencies $452 million in lost revenue, according to RAND.
And the City has barely touched the cash, spending just $114 million as of May — less than 10% of the money raised. The City Council voted 13-0 last Tuesday, Raman included, to put a record $466.6 million toward affordable housing, with $324 million of that — nearly 70% — coming from ULA.
But when the tax passed, Raman couldn’t stop bragging.
“This is truly the first housing initiative of its kind anywhere in the United States that will have such a widespread, immediate, and long-term impact on the housing and homelessness crisis,” she said.
One property in Brentwood, the Westside enclave long favored by Hollywood stars and pro athletes, shows how the tax can play out in the real world.
The property sold for about $5.3 million in February 2023, weeks before ULA took effect.
The original house was torn down and replaced with a new 8,990-square-foot, seven-bedroom home with a pool, screening room and guest house. It hit the market last December at $19.995 million. After three price cuts, it’s now listed at $15.995 million.
If it sells at that price, the ULA bill would be about $880,000.
Brown showed The Post around the block and said even the modest older houses next door could get hit because the land beneath them alone is worth more than $5 million.
“It’s 2,000 feet. Not a mansion, even though it’s $5.5 million, because of the land it’s sitting on,” Brown said. “Sounds good to tax the millionaires and billionaires. Everyone says, ”great,” but it’s so far from reality of what happens.”
For builders, that additional cost reality hits even harder.
Developer Barry Cassily said developers already operate on threadbare profit margins, and now have to factor in an additional 4 to 5.5% bite out of qualifying sales, potentially making some projects financially unworkable.
“You are taxing housing to pay for housing,” he said.
Critics say the result is builders have stopped building and owners stop selling.
Fewer sales also means less property tax revenue, because in California, a property is reassessed to its current market value when it changes ownership.
A study by UCLA’s Michael Manville and USC’s Mott Smith, covering about 338,000 LA County property sales, has found a sharp decline in transactions above ULA’s threshold.
“If in the meantime, you’ve deterred hundreds or thousands of market-rate units, you have not helped affordability,” Manville, who chairs UCLA’s urban planning department, told The Post.
He called it “robbing Peter to pay Paul.”
Manville says the report takes into account other economic factors such as high interest rates. Researchers at Occidental College, meanwhile, argue broader economic conditionsbetter explain the declinein multifamily development.
Their analysis suggests that the slowdown in apartment construction was part of a wider trend affecting development, making it difficult to isolate the tax’s impact from other economic pressures.
Jason Oppenheim, the luxury broker who stars on Netflix’s “Selling Sunset,” claims RAND’s numbers through September show as many as 10,600 apartments were deterred, against roughly 1,900 new units ULA has helped fund.
“City Hall is celebrating the housing it funds from Measure ULA while ignoring the far greater number of apartments its tax is preventing,” Oppenheim told The Post.
Even those 1,900 units come with an asterisk, with the ULA only typically funding one part of affordable housing projects.
Manville compared the city’s claim to old TV ads calling Froot Loops “part of this nutritious breakfast.”
“It is a part of that breakfast,” he said. “But, like, how big of a part really?”
Raman has since tried to change the tax, proposing earlier this year to exempt newly built apartment, commercial and mixed-use projects from ULA for 15 years.
“A policy that unintentionally stalls housing production ultimately undermines the very goals voters asked us to achieve,” Raman said.
However, her proposal failed to make the June ballot amid fierce opposition from labor and pro-ULA groups.
Bass hasn’t been a ULA purist either.
Last year, the mayor tried to rewrite the tax in Sacramento, then pulled the bill at the last minute after ULA backers revolted.
Weeks later, after meeting with billionaire developer Rick Caruso, she asked the council to give Palisades fire victims a three-year break from the tax.
And some of the money isn’t building anything new.
In April, the city steered $55.5 million toward preserving 3,713 existing affordable units. About $2 million went to 11 buildings run by SRO Housing Corp.
One of them, the 96-unit Renato Apartments, got $100,000. In a 2024 lawsuit, tenants alleged they lived with bedbugs, cockroaches, rats, sewage leaks and human waste, court papers show.
SRO Housing has lost $27.8 million since 2022 and has warned the city it will collapse without more public money, Politico reported this month.
Manville said keeping existing units livable isn’t automatically a bad use of the money.
“If for a small amount of money we can take some units that are at risk of being declared uninhabitable and keep them on the market, that could very well be a policy win,” he said.
Councilwoman Imelda Padilla, who took over the council’s new Housing Committee in August after the committee Raman chaired was broken up, has pushed for quarterly reports on where the money goes.
“We must follow these dollars and ensure they are producing the affordable housing Angelenos deserve,” Padilla told The Post.
ULA’s citizen oversight committee did not respond to The Post’s request for comment.
Applications for the $466.6 million funding round open Oct. 13 — three weeks before voters decide whether Raman gets the keys to City Hall.

hed: State’s highest court renews its support for MBTA Communities Act, deeming it a ‘valid general law’
content: Two years ago, a controversial housing law stirred a small uprising of cities and towns against the state.Known as the MBTA Communities Act, the law requires municipalities served by the T to make room for more multifamily housing. Many towns had spent years actively shutting out housing development, and the new law led to heated public meetings, contentious referendums, and a flurry of lawsuits. That uprising was dealt a significant blow Friday, when the Supreme Judicial Court again ruled in support of MBTA Communities, concluding for a second time that the housing measure is “a valid general law.”The unanimous ruling came in a challenge to the 2021 law by the Select Board of Marshfield, one of 177 communities required to make way for more multifamily homes under the law. But now, nearly every legal challenge to MBTA Communities has been dismissed.The law is one of the most ambitious attempts to boost housing production in Massachusetts in decades. The act has become a cornerstone of Governor Maura Healey’s efforts (though it was passed by the Legislature under her predecessor, Charlie Baker) to address the state’s housing shortage and rein in high rents and home prices that are prompting some people to leave Massachusetts.But with its simmering unpopularity within some town halls, MBTA Communities could also be a campaign issue in the gubernatorial race this November.Healey has embraced it and has sought to crack down on noncompliant municipalities as part of her goal to build 222,000 homes in Massachusetts by 2035. But the Republican challenger, Mike Minogue, has said he would eliminate state MBTA Communities enforcement and offer legal support to cities and towns that oppose it.“I’m disappointed by the SJC’s decision and continue to have serious concerns about the MBTA Communities Act and the way it has been forced on municipalities,” Minogue said in a statement. “We believe local communities should have a meaningful voice in determining how and where housing is developed, based on their own infrastructure, planning for schools, and the needs of their residents.”The latest court ruling arose out of a lawsuit filed last year by Marshfield and eight other communities, asserting the law was an “unfunded mandate,” in that it imposed requirements on municipalities without providing new state funding to implement them. The communities also claimed that more multifamily development would strain local infrastructure such as roads and sewer systems.Writing for the SJC, Justice Serge Georges Jr. dismissed the unfunded mandate contention and concluded the Select Board did not have legal standing to invoke the constitutional voting rights of Marshfield’s Town Meeting, which twice rejected the law. A Superior Court Judge had rejected the towns’ lawsuit last year; Marshfield appealed the decision to the SJC. Marshfield town counsel Robert Galvin said in a statement that while the ruling leaves open the unfunded mandate issue, it makes clear that “the subject of the law falls within the state’s reserved authority,” and that “the Town does not have the authority to exempt itself from state law.”He called the ruling “helpful guidance” but said it “does not make local communities feel better about recent state action restricting traditionally local zoning authority.”The SJC decision is the latest in a series of rulings in favor of the law that have significantly stunted efforts from cities and towns to skirt its requirements.Last year, the SJC ruled Attorney General Andrea Campbell has the authority to enforce the law, after a direct challenge to it from the town of Milton.On Friday, Campbell cheered this latest ruling, saying it “reaffirms that the Law is constitutional and compliance is mandatory.”Since it was passed five years ago, the law has generated a pipeline of more than 7,000 new homes, but the action has not come without controversy. Several cities and towns have held referendums over the zoning rules that town officials proposed in line with the law. In Milton, for instance, voters rejected a zoning plan in 2024 that would have aligned the town with the law after a heated campaign that pitted neighbors against each other. Some local elected officials have been voted out of office over their support for compliant zoning plans. Marshfield filed its lawsuit after State Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s office issued an opinion in 2025 saying the law “does not provide a funding mechanism for compliance with its provisions.”A claim central to Marshfield’s lawsuit was the town incurred expenses designing, reviewing, and ultimately voting on new zoning rules required under the law. The court did not agree with that assessment. “The complaint alleges Marshfield incurred costs from evaluating and preparing proposed zoning amendments, and presenting those proposals at town meetings, but it does not allege facts that suggest those costs were involuntarily incurred and exceeded incidental local administration expenses,” Georges wrote.Cities and towns also have frequently complained new multifamily housing would strain their infrastructure, in the form of more traffic on their roads, more children in their schools, and potentially greater strain on emergency services. The court found Marshfield’s claim to that end “too conclusory and speculative.” Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director of the housing group Abundant Housing Massachusetts, said the ruling Friday affirms the state’s authority over local zoning rules.And, Kanson-Benanav argued, it is through restrictive local rules that towns have limited growth, so a key to meeting the Healey administration’s lofty housing production goal should come at the state level with broad land-use reforms.“This ruling reiterates the fact that cities and towns in Massachusetts exist under the authority of the state,“ said Kanson-Benanav. ”The housing affordability crisis in our state isn’t limited to one single community. It reaches across the entire state. Therefore the state has a legitimate role in ensuring every city and town is doing their part to meet our residents’ housing needs.”Ultimately, most towns have fallen in line with the law; just nine have yet to pass zoning rules that comply with it. Earlier this year, the attorney general sued those towns, many of which have lost access to some local funding programs due to their opposition.Even Marshfield last year enacted more permissive building rules, after two previous Town Meeting votes rejected compliance plans.The ruling, said Eric Shupin, chief executive of the housing advocacy group Citizens’ Housing and Planning Association, means the state “can move on and refocus our efforts on doing everything we can to tackle the housing crisis.” “The SJC found that the housing crisis is a statewide concern that falls squarely within the Legislature’s responsibility to deal with,” Shupin said. “We’re looking forward to seeing the Legislature do that.”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker. John R. Ellement can be reached at john.ellement@globe.com. Follow him @JREbosglobe. Jeremiah Manion can be reached at jeremiah@globe.com.

hed: Home of the Week: With views of Okemo Mountain, a Vermont ski chalet for $585k
subhead: Killington, Stratton, Pico, and Magic Mountain are all within reasonable driving distance of this Ludlow home
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

350 Bixby Road, Ludlow, Vt.

$585,000

StyleA-frame chalet

Year built1985

Square feet3,093

Bedrooms3

Baths3

Sewer/WaterPrivate

Taxes$6,614 (2026)


Here are five reasons to choose Ludlow, Vermont: Okemo,Killington, Stratton, Pico, and Magic Mountain. All thoseski areas— including Ludlow-based Okemo — are within reasonable driving distance of the Windsor County town.

TheOkemo resortis an integral part of this A-frame chalet perched on a hillside at the end of a gravel driveway as it’s visible across the valley from nearly every spot on the 11.8-acre lot. Plus, it’s just a five-minute drive away.


From the driveway, entry to the home is through a white insulated door into a basement mudroom with knotty pine paneling and a long wooden bench and hooks for jackets, boots, and gloves.

The mudroom connects to a 400-square-foot recreation room and, in one corner, a wood-burning stove sits on a raised platform with a surround of fieldstone that runs to the ceiling. Nearby are two sets of large casement windows looking out to Okemo Mountain. The flooring is carpeted. Off the room is the first of three full bathrooms. It features a single vanity and a shower behind a curtain along with tile flooring.


A carpeted stairwell leads to the main attraction of the ski chalet: The 400-square-foot living/dining room and its collection of windows that together combine into a floor-to-ceiling gable-end glass wall with views of Okemo and the surrounding natural landscape. The angled cathedral ceiling is cloaked in the knotty pine planking, as are the walls. The space has a wood-burning stove with a fieldstone wall behind.



To the left of the stove, a clear glass slider opens into a 60-square-foot room now occupied by a hot tub sitting in front of four floor-to-ceiling window panes. In the right corner of the room, there is a slider leading out to the deck that runs the width of the house, giving an unobstructed view of the downward sloping lot.

The floor on this level, except for the kitchen and the full bath, is vinyl plank.



The 103-square-foot kitchen is adjacent to the dining area. It’s in the shape of a U and has a peninsula on the right that creates a breakfast bar with seating for three. The appliances — including the electric stove — are black and are framed by pine cabinets. The stainless steel sink, located underneath a window, is a double bowl design. The floor is white tile.

The two secondary bedrooms are in the rear of the house — the largest is 129 square feet, the smaller, 116 square feet. Both have wood-planked ceilings and flooring along with a casement window and a closet. The second full bathroom in the home is 60 square feet and has a single vanity, tile flooring, and a curtained shower/bath.



Another carpeted stairwell leads first to a 58-square-foot landing — another great viewpoint of the nature that surrounds this home — overlooking the living room before a door connects to the primary suite, which alone occupies the third floor. The primary bedroom is 196 square feet and has a carpeted floor and knotty pine planking on the angled ceiling. There is a skylight above the best spot for a bed and a casement window. The en-suite bathroom is 62 square feet, with tile flooring, a single vanity, and a curtained shower/bath combination.

The home has electric heat.

Sarah Sheehan of Vermont PropertyTeam/William Raveis has the listing.
