hed: NYC’s priciest rental is $250K-a-month — but what’s inside might surprise you
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The city’s most expensive rental has just hit the market.
It’s a $250,000-a-month condo inside troubled 432 Park Ave., Gimme Shelter can reveal.
The 8,100-square-foot skypad spans the tower’s entire 88th floor. It comes with five bedrooms, seven baths, two powder rooms, oak floors, 12½-foot ceilings and a library with a wood-burning fireplace. Panoramic views stretch across three states, from the city skyline to the rivers and the Atlantic Ocean.
A private elevator landing opens to an entry gallery that leads to a corner living room. There’s also a corner dining room and a windowed eat-in chef’s kitchen with marble floors, a wine cellar and a pantry.
The main bedroom suite boasts a sitting room, dressing rooms and two windowed baths clad in marble, with radiant heated floors.
“It’s one of the most beautiful apartments in New York,” said a source familiar with the residence, which is also for sale at $88.5 million. “Spectacular, understated and elegant.”
The sellers are Lewis “Lew” Sanders, the former chairman of AllianceBernstein and the founder and CEO of Sanders Capital, and his wife, Alice. The couple bought the unit for $60.8 million in 2016, property records show.
“It was a raw box when they bought it, and they put around $10 million into it,” the source said. The interiors are by Andrew Sheinman of Pembrooke & Ives.
Despite it being the most expensive rental currently on the market, according to StreetEasy records, it is not the most expensive listing ever.
Back in 2015, a full-floor Presidential Suite on the 39th floor of The Pierre Hotel was briefly listed for rent for awhopping $500,000 per month, before returning to the rental market for the same price in 2017.
The Sanderses also own a Palm Beach mansion beside Howard and Beth Stern, a home in East Hampton and a$19.4 million West Palm Beach condothey bought earlier this year.
Listing broker Richard J. Steinberg of Compass declined to comment.
So how did they land on the astronomical rent?
“Lew decided to list the apartment at a premium. He doesn’t need the money. He isn’t an anxious seller or renter. He doesn’t care. That’s the truth,” a source said, adding that rental income is an enticing way to offset the city’s pricey new pied-à-terre tax.
“It is appealing to someone moving to the city from the West Coast or internationally, not a New Yorker,” the source said.
But there’s a catch. The Billionaires’ Row building, once the tallest residential tower in the world, has a notoriously rocky history.
Completed in 2015, the 1,396-foot tower was designed by the late architect Rafael Viñoly and developed by Harry Macklowe and CIM Group. The supertall, superskinny design was inspired by the city’s grid and by a trash can that Austrian architect Josef Hoffmann designed in 1905.
The building drew buyers like Jennifer Lopez and Alex Rodriguez, who sold after about a year. But structural flaws have since led to major problems.
The tower is so skinny that it sways and makes noise in the wind, and residents have long complained that the garbage chute sounds like a bomb when trash goes down.
There are also leaks and elevator problems. And the experimental white concrete exterior is cracking, which could endanger pedestriansif chunks fall.
Work to fix the building has already begun, sources tellGimme Shelter.Repairs are estimated at around $160 million.
The owners have also filed two lawsuits. The first, in 2021, demands that the developers pay for about 1,500 alleged construction and design defects. The second, in 2025, seeks at least $165 million in damages for alleged fraud, charging that the developers hid the cracks in the exterior concrete. The developers have denied wrongdoing.
“All of the complaints are true,” a broker with listings in the building tells Gimme Shelter. “The elevators make noise. There’s rattling, and on windy days you can hear the clanging. It all goes back to Harry [Macklowe] and Viñoly. It was the perfect storm. They chose form over function. They were fanatical about design and didn’t care about how people lived.”
Viñoly once told Gimme Shelter that the building “has acouple of screw-ups,”including oversized window frames and a layout that gave bathrooms the best views instead of living spaces.
Even a garage promised 10 years ago has yet to be built. “There’s nothing there! Just empty space,” a source said.
Even so, brokers in the building say buying there beats renting right now because prices are so low, even if the cost of repairs isn’t factored into the purchase price.
Amenities include an 8,000-square-foot private restaurant with a 5,000-square-foot dining terrace, helmed by Michelin-starred Australian chef Shaun Hergatt.
There’s also a 14-seat boardroom with a marble table, office suites, staff suites, storage units, climate-controlled wine cellars, a residents’ lounge, a library, a gym, a 75-foot pool, a billiards room, a screening room, a children’s playroom, a concierge desk, in-suite dining and room service.
But all of that is moot if the problems aren’t fixed. The building could become “uninhabitable,” structural engineer Steve Bongiorno told theNew York Timesin October 2025.
He also urged the Department of Buildings to investigate. The DOB said the building has passed inspections.
Still, “People who live in the building love it,” says one of the building’s brokers.
“They love the restaurant and the lounge, the daily breakfast, and the great location,” the broker said. “For those who can afford it, I encourage them to buy. The prices are depressed, the problems will rectify and the prices will go up. Every building has problems. This one just has more than most. But it’s still the best location on Billionaires’ Row.”

hed: Manhattan rent smashes record at $6,865 as Brooklyn logs busiest September since 2020
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

New York’srental marketisn’t cooling down with the weather.
Manhattan’saverage monthly renthit a new record of $6,865 in September, whileBrooklyn logged its strongest Septemberleasing activity since 2020, according to Corcoran’s latest rental reports.
The median rent in Manhattan also reached an all-time high of $5,395 — up 2% from August and 9% from a year earlier — as available apartments dwindled.
The borough had 5,015 active rental listings, down 16% annually and the fewest for any September since 2019. Inventory has now declined year-over-year for two straight years.
“Manhattan’s rental market remains defined by a lack of available apartments,” Gary Malin, chief operating officer of the Corcoran Group, said in a statement.
“With demand continuing to outpace supply, competition remains frustratingly intense across much of the borough.”
Larger apartments saw some of the steepest increases. Average rents for two- and three-bedroom units posted double-digit annual gains, with two-bedrooms reaching a record of nearly $8,500 a month.
Even one-bedrooms, which recorded the smallest annual increase at 6%, averaged $5,436 — just $50 below their July peak.
Manhattan’s vacancy rate stood at 1.54%, marking a fifth consecutive month around 1.5% — the longest stretch at that level in nearly six years.
But the squeeze isn’t translating into more signed leases. Manhattan recorded 3,841 new leases in September, down 19% from August and 5% from a year earlier. Corcoran attributed the slowdown to scarce inventory and record rents discouraging tenants from moving.
Apartments also took longer to find tenants, averaging 48 days on the market, up 12% annually, as renters spent more time weighing their options.
Across the East River, Brooklyn’s rental market bucked the usual seasonal slowdown.
The borough recorded 1,407 signed leases, up 10% annually and 3% from August. Since Corcoran began tracking the market in 2019, September leasing had fallen from August every year, by an average of 24%.
Two-bedrooms drove the increase, with 434 leases signed — up 21% from a year earlier. Studio signings were essentially flat at 248, but still marked the strongest September on record for that apartment type.
Brooklyn’s median rent eased to $4,300 from August’s record $4,368, though it remained 5% above its year-earlier level. Average rent rose 3% annually to $4,946.
The modest monthly dip came alongside a sharp decline in available apartments. Brooklyn had 3,428 active listings, down 25% from a year earlier and 11% from August, marking its lowest September inventory since 2022.
“These conditions continue to prop up pricing and create urgency among renters who are searching for new homes throughout the borough,” Malin said.
Brooklyn one-bedrooms averaged $4,218 a month, while studios cost $3,521 and two-bedrooms reached $5,708. Three-bedrooms were the only category cheaper than a year earlier, slipping 1% to $6,885.
Despite stronger leasing activity, Brooklyn apartments spent an average of 53 days on the market — 13 days longer than a year earlier — reflecting more listings that lingered before securing tenants.

hed: Former Olympian accused of squatting in $26K-a-month NYC luxe condo as owners fight to evict her
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


A former Olympic luger is in a race to stay put.
Erica Terwillegar and her partner, Peter Molinari, are fighting to hold on to their $26,000-a-month condo at one of New York’s most exclusive addresses.
The owners accuse the pair ofliving rent-freeafter their lease expired and scuttling a $6.75 million sale of the unit.
The standoff is playing out at 150 Charles Street, the celebrity-favored West Villageluxury building.
Terwillegar, a jewelry designer who competed for Team USA at the 1988 and 1992 Winter Olympics, isstill living in the apartmentwith Molinari as owners Cathy Crane and Salvatore Trentalancia try to take it back.
A doorman confirmed to The Post on Thursday that the couple still live there. Outside, chauffeurs waited in front of the upscale property, which has attracted buyers including Ben Stiller and Jon Bon Jovi, according toCurbed,who first broke the story.
Behind the luxury-building doors is a familiar landlord-tenant fight — with decidedly unfamiliar price tags.
According to the owners’ July complaint, Terwillegar’s lease ran from Aug. 22, 2024, through July 31, 2025, at $26,000 a month. Her mother, Andrea, also lives in the apartment and is named in the suit alongside Molinari.
The owners acknowledge that the base rent was paid during the original lease. But they allege utilities went unpaid — and that rent payments stopped after the lease expired.
Terwillegar says she renewed for another year, according to the complaint. The owners say she needed their agreement to do so.
Now they want $624,000 for the year through July 2026, pointing to a lease provision that doubles the rent for tenants who overstay. Alternatively, they’re seeking $327,600 in rent or payment for the occupants’ continued stay.
They’re also demanding at least $30,000 for utilities and other charges, at least $100,000 in legal fees and $250,000 in punitive damages.
But the biggest number on the bill is $6.75 million.
The owners allege they had a buyer willing to pay that amount — provided the buyer could actually see the apartment. They say the occupants repeatedly refused access, torpedoing the deal.
The tenants tell a very different story.
In an interview with The Post, the couple and their attorney, Colleen Kerwick, maintained that payments were made on time and described an apartment cluttered with the owners’ belongings which meant the occupants couldn’t use the cabinets and drawers. Kerwick also questioned whether the prospective buyer was real.
The owners dispute the couple’s description of the apartment.
Whatever his complaints about the place, Molinari was clear about wanting to keep the address.
“Once I got into 150 Charles,” Molinari told the Curbed, “I wasn’t leaving.”
The couple’s courtroom history stretches beyond Charles Street. The Post counts 19 lawsuits.
At their previous rental at 166 Perry Street, the landlord also alleged in a May 2023 complaint that they stayed after their lease expired in November 2022.
That apartment cost $11,000 a month. The landlord sought at least $66,000 in unpaid charges, ongoing monthly payments and at least $25,000 in legal fees.
Terwillegar argued that they had been negotiating to buy the apartment and had become month-to-month tenants. That the fight ended in an undisclosed settlement in August 2024, according to court documents obtained by The Post.
And the couple isn’t always on the receiving end of a lawsuit.
In 2007, Molinari sued over a sidewalk fall outside a different building, at 167 Perry Street, where he was a co-op shareholder.
He alleged that uneven pavement caused a January 2004 fall that left him with a broken ankle. A judge refused to throw out the suit against the building’s owner and manager in 2012, saying disputed facts needed to be sorted out at trial. That ruling does not show whether he ultimately received any money.
In July 2025, the couple sued Barry Leistner, a New York construction executive and investor who heads structural-steel company Koenig Iron Works, for at least $30 million in lost earnings over a disputed debt.They allege he obtained a judgment against them in November 2012 by physically cutting and pasting their signatures from another document onto a “confession of judgment” — a document acknowledging a debt — and submitting forged papers claiming they had been served.
Terwillegar had given Leistner jewelry and gemstones they value at roughly $750,000 as security for that debt, according to their complaint. They now want those items returned and say the judgment was vacated in March 2024 on grounds of fraud and forgery.
A September filing shows Leistner was seeking dismissal of their lawsuit and that the parties had discussed a settlement.
Meanwhile, their eviction case at 150 Charles is headed for a December trial.

hed: Murder-suicide NJ dad moved family to Princeton for ‘special-needs’ daughter, then sued realtor over tainted mansion
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Years before authorities say hegunned down his wife and daughterinside their New Jersey mansion, David Grodnick went to court claiming a real estate agent stashed his family’s $33,800 deposit in her own bank account after luring them into a hazardous rental.
The insurance executive and his wife, Lora, said they chose the Princeton area because of “the benefits of its school system for their daughter, who has special needs,” according to a lawsuit they filed in 2018 and obtained by The Post. The complaint does not give her name or age.
The house they rented had arsenic in the well, electricity that “continuously shorted out” and a living room fireplace that “emitted carbon monoxide fumes,” the couple alleged.
Specifically, the Grodnicks sued real estate franchise giant Keller Williams, franchisee Adele DeMoro LLC and agent Hong Jing in Mercer County Superior Court under the state Consumer Fraud Act, seeking triple damages. The landlord, Xiaoying Wang, was not named.
The dispute dates to 2016, when the family settled on 28 Morris Drive, a 4,257-square-foot house with four bedrooms on just over half an acre.
According to the complaint, Jing held herself out as the property manager and said a certificate of occupancy and a fire inspection had been applied for, smoke detectors and extinguishers had been bought and well testing was underway. The suit claims those assurances proved false.
The couple signed a lease on June 3, 2016 and gave Jing two checks made out to the landlord. One was a $26,000 “initial deposit” equal to five months of rent. The other was $7,800 in security. New Jersey caps deposits at a month and a half of rent, the filing says.
The money belonged in a brokerage trust account, the Grodnicks alleged. They claimed Jing instead deposited it in her personal checking account, “comingling the funds with her personal money.”
The well was tested on June 30, 2016 after the couple demanded it.
“Astonishingly, the results revealed that the well water contained high levels of arsenic,” the complaint states, adding that the readings exceeded the state limit.
The family said the contamination blocked the home’s treatment system and kitchen faucet, and that they paid to fix the well pump and tank, water heater, furnace, refrigerator and plumbing.
When they raised the electrical and fireplace problems, they were told the issues were “petty,” according to the suit. They cited what they called Jing’s “elusiveness” and said they were “forced to immediately pay out of pocket.”
Jing, Adele DeMoro and Keller Williams answered jointly in February 2019. They denied that Jing presented herself as the property manager or that her unavailability forced the couple to pay for repairs. They acknowledged she had no management agreement with the landlord.
They said Jing was a licensed salesperson working as an independent contractor for Adele DeMoro, which runs a Keller Williams office in West Monmouth. Keller Williams said its local offices are “independently owned and operated” and denied “any agency relationship” with its franchisees.
On most other allegations, including the reason for the move, the arsenic results and the handling of the deposit, the defendants said they lacked enough information to admit or deny them.
Their 30 listed defenses included that the suit came too late, that any losses stemmed from the couple’s own negligence or a third party’s, and that the Grodnicks had “unclean hands” and “suffered no damages.”
A one-page stipulation filed Sept. 4, 2019 dismissed the case for good “without costs to either party.” It does not say whether money changed hands and contains no admission of wrongdoing.
The Morris Drive house sold for $837,000 in January 2021. That August, the Grodnicks closed on a nearly 6,000-square-foot home in Montgomery Township on Wild Azalea Ln for $1.345 million listing records show.
Nearly eight years after the couple sued, police entered that house on Oct. 2, a day aftera welfare checkwent unanswered. They found Lora, 62, and the couple’s 24-year-old daughter, Sloane, in separate bedrooms with gunshot wounds to the head. David, 61, was also dead inside with a firearm in his possession, prosecutors said.
The medical examiner ruled the women’s deaths homicides and his a suicide. No motive has been given, and prosecutors have called it an isolated incident with no danger to the public.
David was a senior vice president and underwriting counsel at Land Services USA, a Philadelphia-based insurance agency that works on commercial real estate deals. Sloane, a 2020 graduate of the Hun School of Princeton, earned a degree from the Savannah College of Art and Design in 2024 and was pursuing a master’s at the Rhode Island School of Design.
The Montgomery Township home is not on the market. Real estate sites estimate its value at about $2 million

hed: A San Francisco home listed for $7.9M just sold for a whopping $15M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Forget a bidding war. This was a blowout.
A 112-year-old house on the lip of San Francisco’s Presidio has traded for $15 million, a jaw-dropping $7 millionmore than its sellers asked.
The four-bedroom at 2 Sixth Ave. came to market in late September with a $7.999 million price tag. It closed Oct. 7 at an 87.5% premium, about two weeks after its debut.
That pencils out to roughly $3,340 a square foot, about triple the $1,108 a typical San Francisco house fetched in August.
“We received 9 strong offers,” listing agent Maureen Terris of Compass told The Post. “This exceptional property was a once-in-a-generation opportunity and the market responded.”
Ronda Priestner, also of Compass, brought the buyer, who has not been publicly identified.
The appeal starts with the dirt. The 4,490-square-foot home sits on a 9,233-square-foot parcel on a dead-end block above Lake Street, with gardens that run right up to the national park. In a city where houses are wedged shoulder to shoulder, this one stands alone.
“This house featured well-preserved architectural elements from 1914, was fully detached and set back from the street, and was situated on an oversized lot with front and back gardens bordering the Presidio National Park,” Terris said.
The residence is a product of the First Bay Tradition, a homegrown style that favors timber and handiwork over flash. The redwood trim dates to the home’s construction, the dining room has a coffered ceiling and both it and the living room have fireplaces that burn real logs.
A library wrapped in bookshelves looks out over the Presidio and its golf course. The kitchen has a Wolf range set into a brick wall, timber beams overhead and a butler’s pantry,  with doors leading to a patio and the back garden.
Upstairs are four bedrooms and a covered porch. The primary suite swallowed a former bedroom to create a dressing room lined with closets. There are four bathrooms, two of them half baths.
Then comes the real San Francisco flex. A detached two-car garage sits at the end of a brick driveway with room for at least five more vehicles.
The deal is extreme even for a city where the list price has become an opening bid.
Compass counted 144San Francisco homesthat sold for at least $1 million over asking in the first half of 2026. The same stretch of 2025 produced eight. June alone accounted for 44.
The brokerage’s chief economist has pinned the surge on theartificial intelligence boom,which has minted a class of buyers flush with cash and short on patience.
The frenzy has not cooled. In August, 85% of houses in the city sold above list, an 18-point jump from a year earlier. The median house price hit about $1.855 million, up roughly 24%, while the supply of houses for sale shrank 31%.
Sellers that month collected an average of 124% of what they asked. The Sixth Avenue sellers got 187.5%.
The closest recent rival is a Union Street mansion that sold in May for close to twice its $8 million ask.
Nor was the Sixth Avenue home obviously lowballed. Zillow’s own estimate had pegged it at about $7.36 million  before the offers rolled in.

hed: Jane Fonda’s idyllic former home, once surveiled by the CIA, hits the market for a steal
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


An idyllic Hollywood Hills home where Jane Fonda once lived is now on the market for $1.99 million, The Post has learned.
Built in 1924, the gated, five-bedroom Mediterranean Revival-style villa is at 2001 Holly Hill Terrace.
It’s where Fonda lived for a time during her marriage to the French film director Roger Vadim (they were married from 1965 to 1973), according to the listing. It’s also where Fonda lived with her second husband, the late political activist and politician Tom Hayden, whom she married days after her divorce from Vadim was finalized,according to LA city planning documents.
While living in the house, which she rented rather than owned, Fonda came under surveillance by the CIA for speaking out against the Vietnam War. They famously intercepted and opened Fonda’s mail — four letters written to her from the Soviet Union.
According to a document seen by Gimme Shelter — declassified in 2018 — Fonda’s name and Holly Hill Terrace address appear in CIA files as number 22, in a list of 50 names and addresses tracked by the agency in 1971.
The CIA opened mail sent from the Soviet Union to American citizens living in the US from the 1950s to 1973, according to National Security Archive documents.
“That is illegal and we stopped it in 1973,” then-CIA Director William Colby reportedly told President Gerald Ford in 1975,according to reports.
But nevertheless, it remains a fascinating part of the history of the house.
The home itself a majestic stucco-clad residence at the end of a cul-de-sac in Whitley Heights, one of Hollywood’s most historic residential neighborhoods.
It was also the last project of developer H.J. Whitley, who built the neighborhood to look like an Italian hillside village.
The historic district was once filled with Old Hollywood legends including Rudolph Valentino, Bette Davis, Jean Harlow, Rosalind Russell, Janet Gaynor, Carmen Miranda and William Faulkner.
The home features a two-story veranda that was added in 1941, and it comes with two entrances.
The seller is Kathleen Whyte, the daughter of the late Hollywood character actors Bryan Clark and Jo Deodato Clark, who owned the home for 41 years. The Clarks bought the home for $234,180 in 1985. It first hit the market for $2.79 million in 2024.
Bryan often portrayed President Ronald Reagan in films and, ironically, “Reagan lived nearby when he was a working actor in a mansion on top of the hill in Whitley Heights,” said listing broker Edward Piechocki of Douglas Elliman. He added that he doesn’t think the actors ever met. Bryan, who was also a national spokesperson for Folgers Coffee, also appeared in films like “All the President’s Men,” Piechocki said.
At 4,241 square feet, the home opens to a formal foyer with a grand staircase. There’s also a separate entrance from the top of the home through a two-car garage, with steps that lead down to the pool and terraced gardens with mature fruit trees.
On the main level, there’s a living room with a fireplace that leads to a home office, along with a formal dining room, an eat-in chef’s kitchen, and a library that opens to a patio with canyon views. Throughout are hardwood floors and high ceilings.
A main bedroom suite is upstairs and includes a sitting room, private patio with canyon and treetop views, and a spa-like bath.
Outside, behind the house, terraces lead to a pool and a summer kitchen with an outdoor grill and plenty of room to entertain.
There’s also a guest suite on the lower level with its own entrance, laundry and full kitchen.

hed: The region’s housing crisis is raging on. Should cities ease requirements on builders to help spur more construction?
content: For years, Greater Boston developers have repeated the same complaint: City-mandated affordable housing requirements, however well intentioned, are bad for business, cutting into their bottom lines by requiring builders to set aside units at below-market rents. But now, amid a slump in new construction, their complaints are finding a more receptive audience — to a point.Earlier this year, Waltham and Chelsea lowered their targets for affordable housing units that are built under what’s known as inclusionary zoning, in hopes of getting shovels in the ground again. While Boston, Cambridge, and Somerville have yet to follow suit, some councilors in those cities have publicly challenged their officials to be more flexible in their various requirements. So far those cities aren’t budging, saying the zoning requirements are a powerful tool to force construction of more affordable housing.“This mayor has made it very clear that we should be building for the future,” Kairos Shen, Boston’s planning chief, said at a press briefing last week announcing tax breaks to help get stalled developments moving. “We don’t think compromising inclusionary development and compromising energy performance, climate resiliency is smart.”Related: ‘The numbers should work, and they just don’t’: Is Cambridge’s affordable housing rule backfiring?A popular option for Greater Boston municipal leaders, inclusionary zoning requires housing developers to set aside a certain percentage of units in new developments at affordable prices as a condition of building. Developers foot the bill for the rent-restricted units, which are generally less profitable than market-rate homes. Effectively, the zoning policy allows cities and towns to generate affordable housing without having to fund it with taxpayer dollars. During the building boom of the 2010s and early 2020s, with luxury towers sprouting up in Boston and beyond, advocates began to press city officials to raise those affordable housing targets. In their view, the additional units would allow the broader public to benefit from the glimmering new developments catering primarily to wealthier residents. Somerville and Cambridge hiked their affordable requirements a decade ago to 20 percent, among the highest levels in the country. Mayor Michelle Wu followed suit in 2023, increasing the target in Boston to  17 percent of units in new buildings that have to be set aside for low- and middle-income residents. An additional 3 percent are to be set aside for low-income households that receive federal Section 8 housing subsidies.Clouds hang over Boston as seen from the Longfellow Bridge on July 30.Suzanne Kreiter/Globe StaffAnd while inclusionary zoning has created thousands of new affordable homes across Boston, Cambridge, Somerville, and other cities in the region, the economics of homebuilding have shifted significantly over the past few years, with higher interest rates and higher costs for construction contributing to a dramatic slowdown in new building. In Boston, 2023 and 2024 were the two slowest years for new housing construction since 2011, according to city data, with 2025 only slightly better. Developers complaining about having to build affordable units as part of their projects is an old story in Boston. And now, with projects stalling, developers are attributing at least part of the blame to the 20 percent requirement. These days, the rent for the an average two-bedroom “inclusionary” unit in Boston is around $1,740, according to city data, compared to $2,550 for a market-rate unit, according to the rental listing website Apartment List. Many places rent for far more. In Cambridge, builder Old North Development sued the city earlier in September, saying the requirement forced it to “surrender” 14 of the 71 units in a building planned on Massachusetts Avenue near Porter Square to below-market rents.It’s the second such lawsuit, following one filed by Cambridge attorney and developer Patrick Barrett last year, in which he argued the inclusionary zoning requirement would cost him $11.4 million — the approximate value lost if the units are rented at below-market prices. That cost, Barrett argued, effectively made his redevelopment of a commercial building near Inman Square into  condominiums nearly impossible to finance. “What drives me crazy is that the city talks constantly about how badly it wants to build enough to ease housing costs,” Barrett said. “Yet in this instance, they have all of these developers showing them the numbers, telling them this policy is killing housing development, and they won’t budge.”Related: How a developer’s lawsuit against Cambridge aims to topple affordable housing rules across MassachusettsIt’s proved so difficult to finance projects in Cambridge lately that some builders say they are throwing in the towel. Daniel Sibor, managing partner of local developer North Cambridge Partners, said he decided earlier this year to cut his losses and sell a parking lot at 2400 Massachusetts Ave., which he had planned to build 60 condominium units just a quick walk to the Red Line. Developers of market-rate housing must generate a certain rate of return to attract the investors who fund most projects — an array of institutions, including pension funds, private equity, life insurers, and banks. Higher costs — and lower revenues —make that more difficult.Sibor’s firm acquired the rights to the parking lot in 2022 and paid more than $1 million in interest for it over four years. It was largely interest rates and construction costs that drove the finances of the project so out of whack. But the affordable housing rule is something cities control. “We looked at this piece of land every which way,” Sibor said. “But there are all of these external factors that are beyond the control of any developer or local government driving up the cost of development right now. Repeatedly, we came back to the lever that was there to pull, which was always the inclusionary housing ordinance.”Sibor estimated the 2400 Mass. Ave. project could have been financed last year if the affordable housing target was dropped from 20 percent to around 8 percent, and he told city officials as much. Daniel Sibor, managing partner of local developer North Cambridge Partners, said he decided earlier this year to cut his losses and sell a parking lot at 2400 Massachusetts Ave., where he had planned to build 60 condominium units just a quick walk to the Red Line.John Tlumacki/Globe StaffLast year, he figured he would sell the market-rate units at close to $1,500 per square foot, a steep figure partially driven by high construction costs and the need to offset the discount on the affordable units. The price for affordable units, under the city’s rules, would have come in closer to $275 per square foot.Cambridge officials did not directly comment on their complaints, saying of one lawsuit that they are “evaluating next steps.” A long-awaited city study on the feasibility of Cambridge’s inclusionary housing rule is set to be released this month. But to some housing advocates, developers like Sibor and Barrett struggling to get projects off the ground in tough financial times is not a reason to lower hard-fought inclusionary rules. Advocates battled for years to get higher affordable housing targets; many saw it as one of the only ways to ensure that a slice of expensive new developments would be accessible to working- and middle-class families increasingly being priced out the housing market, said Kathy Brown, executive director of the Boston Tenants Coalition. “It is hard to feel a lot of pain for these developers who have made so much money over so many years,” said Brown, whose group is part of the Coalition for a Truly Affordable Boston that has fought for the higher levels of affordable housing. The inclusionary zoning requirement “is such a small cost in the grand scheme of all of the factors that are making it so expensive to build right now,” Brown said. “It’s hard to believe it is really a big part of the problem.”Related: In bid to boost Boston housing supply, Wu proposes tax relief that could jumpstart more than 1,000 unitsIn Boston, Wu has largely held the line on the affordable housing policy, despite a recent push from developers and City Councilor Ed Flynn to lower it. In an interview, Flynn said returning to a previous level, 13 percent, would be a good place to start. But recently, Wu said she is not considering lowering the requirement. She has opted instead to pursue tax abatements to help get struggling projects off the ground. That stance has pleased advocates.“We fought for this long and hard,” Brown said. “Look at the need for affordable housing in Boston. This policy is the only reason some people can stay in Boston at all.”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: For some New Englanders, a second home is an ocean away
subhead: Despite logistical obstacles, some Massachusetts natives buy second homes abroad. Here’s how they make it work.
content:
ByCameron Sperance
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Emily may have gone to Paris, but plenty of New Englanders are looking to the south of France and beyond when it comes tobuying a second home.

Jane Freedman, a lawyer from Newton, majored in French, studied abroad, and spent years wondering how to get back. The answer arrived in 2013 on a visit to a colleague’s home in Eygalières, a village in Provence.

“My husband and I were riding bikes along this beautiful path with our friends, and we looked at each other and we were like, ‘Yeah, this is what we want,’” Freedman said.

It took more than a decade to make the numbers work. In April 2025, the couple closed on a five-bedroom house on 4 acres in the Bandol wine region, about 45 minutes east of Marseille, with a vineyard, an olive grove, a pool, and a pétanque (lawn bowling)court.

They have company. AGallup poll last Novemberfound that one in five Americans would like to move abroad permanently, roughly double the share a decade earlier. TheAssociation of Americans Resident Overseas estimated in 2024that 5.5 million U.S. citizens already live outside the country. For New Englanders who want a foothold more than a full exit, Delta made the commute easier in May when itlaunched a nonstop between Boston and Nice.

Megan Driscoll of Duxbury is furnishing her foothold now. The 51-year-old, who founded a recruiting firm at 25 and later sold it, picked up the keys on Sept. 15 to a new two-bedroom apartment in Nice’s Libération neighborhood, a 10-minute walk from the train station and steps from the city’s largest outdoor market.


Driscoll grew up in Duxbury, so the Cape nearby wasn’t as much of a draw for a second home, and she wanted awinter basein a city that stays lively after the summer crowds leave.

“They still eat outside on the streets in February,” she said.

Recently divorced and with her youngest child headed to college next year, she liked the name of the neighborhood as much as the location.

“I’d be starting off in this neighborhood that sort of represents my next chapter,” she said.

Purchases don’t look much like a closing in Massachusetts. France has no equivalent of the Multiple Listing Service. Notaries handle the transaction in place of the attorneys a Massachusetts buyer would expect.


Freedman searched broker by broker and town by town throughthree scouting trips. When a listing in a town she had never heard of popped up on Facebook, she didn’t wait.

“I said to my husband, ‘We’re getting on a plane this weekend and going to look at this house,’” Freedman said.

They made an offer on that trip.

Closing took nine months. A legal complication on the seller’s side required a French court to sign off on the sale, and an ownership structure an adviser had recommended for tax reasons ended up blocking the European mortgage the couple had counted on, Freedman added. They financed through their U.S. bank at a less favorable rate.

Driscoll took the opposite route. She speaks no French, so she paid a fixed fee to work withAdrian Leeds, the property consultant familiar to viewers of HGTV’s “House Hunters International,” whose team lined up the notary and still makes phone calls in French on her behalf. Having spent most of her life in a Duxbury house built in 1812, she insisted on new construction.

“I just had had it with the renovation and the issues and the constant upkeep of an older place,” Driscoll said.

“New” came with its own lesson. Apartments in new French buildings are typically delivered without kitchens, Driscoll spent about $25,000 on hers.

Bill Searles, who grew up in Hudson and retired to southern Italy with his wife, Barbara, found the same bare room there and lived off hot plates until a kitchen went in.

Filippo Cori, an international property consultant with the Italian brokerage Great Estate who works in Umbria and Tuscany, said about 95 percent of his American clients want a house that is turnkey or close to it.

“It’s not easy to follow work on the house from abroad,” he said.

Cori, who has worked with clients from New England in the past, walks U.S. buyers through three costs that tend to surprise them when purchasing a home in Italy: The buyer pays the notary’s fee in full. A purchase tax is not calculated on the property’s assessed value in the land registry instead of its sale price. The buyer and the seller each pay an agency commission, usually 3 percent to 4 percent.

Sellers expect to negotiate, he said, and typically come down 5 percent to 10 percent from the asking price. Most of his American clients pay cash, and those who borrow from an Italian bank can usually finance 50 percent to 60 percent of a second home.

The typical client, Cori said, wants a place to spend two or three weeks a year with family and friends and then rents it out for five to 10 weeks to cover running costs. Rising prices in Tuscany once sent bargain hunters over the border to Umbria in Italy.

“Now Umbria is no longer [as much of a value play],” he said, calling Le Marche in central Italy on the Adriatic coast the next frontier.


The price of entry varies widely. Asking prices in Umbriaaveraged about €1,189per square meter (about $1,339) in late 2026, less than half theTuscan average of €2,700per square meter (about $3,040), according to the Italian real estate portalImmobiliare.it. In Nice, apartments averaged €5,216 per square meter (about $5,873) this year, according to theFrench listings site SeLoger, which puts a 750-square-foot two-bedroom near €365,000 (about $411,000). For comparison, the median condo price in Greater Bostonreached $750,000 this spring, according to the Greater Boston Association of Realtors, with citywide Boston medians hovering around $850,000.

Some buyers want the purchase to come with the right to stay.

Americans are the largest source of residence and citizenship applications at the housing advisory firmHenley & Partners, accounting for 22 percent of its global total, and their applications rose 52 percent over the past 18 months compared with the 18 months before. Massachusetts accounts for about 3 percent of the U.S. total, and 91 percent of this year’s American applicants still have a U.S. address, the firm said.

“From what I’m seeing with families and advisers across New England, most clients are not looking to permanently leave the U.S.,” said Simon Gabbay, the firm’s director of private clients. “They are looking to create options.”

A house alone rarely delivers those options. Greece still counts qualifying real estate toward its golden visa residency-by-investment program, Gabbay said, while Portugal no longer does and Spain closed its investor residence program in 2025. Neither France nor Italy grants residency for buying a home.


Americans without a visa are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across Europe’s Schengen zone, so both women are planning around the calendar. Freedman and her husband aim to spend less than six months a year in France, a month or two at a time in spring and fall. Driscoll plans to apply for a long-stay visa once her son leaves for college.

Then there is upkeep from 3,500 miles away. Among other upgrades, Freedman has redone a septic system, upgraded the electrical and internet, and learned what high season does to a repair schedule.

“If your air conditioning breaks in July, you might have to wait 10 days for the repairman to show up,” she said.

The Searleses waited two years for a connection to town water, filling a cistern every other week in the meantime, and they received a surprise bill of about €2,000 for a municipal property tax.

“You really have to stay there to oversee renovations,” Barbara said.

The couple now lives in Italy full time, a move that let them retire at 62 when they had expected to work until 67.

“Moving to Italy meant we could retire earlier because the cost of living is so reasonable for us, and we have no mortgage,” she said.

So what do international homeowners in the know wish they understood when they started the process?

Learning the language and hanging out with the community are crucial, Freedman said.

“Show people in your town that you are there with them, even if you’re not there full time,” she said.

Driscoll’s apartment came with a garage, which she plans to inhabit with a Mini Cooper — a convertible, of course — so she can bop around the Riviera.

Her advice?

“You only live once.”

hed: Soap hunk’s former Hollywood Hills chalet ‘feels like Disneyland’ and it can be yours for nearly $3M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


AHollywood Hills homethat looks like an Aspen chaletplunked down in Los Angeleshas hit the market for $2.99 million.
The all-wood spread at 8497 Harold Way was once home to soap star Peter Reckell, the original Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives.”
“It looks like you are in Aspen,” listing broker Bianca Fields of Carolwood Estates told The Post.
“But it feels like Disneyland, like it’s not even real,” added Carolwood co-listing broker Adriana Yedidsion.
The pair share the listing with Mark Cianciulli and Patrick Sweeney of The CREM Group.
Built in 1954, the “chalet-inspired” house comes with a peaked roof and a “country and rock-n-roll vibe,” Yedidsion said.
Reckell played Bo from 1983 to 1987 and returned to the role on and off until 2023. He owned the 4,598-square-foot home for 19 years, from 1984 to 2003.
That stretch covered his marriage to Dale Kristien, a “Days of Our Lives” co-star who went on to star in “The Phantom of the Opera.” The two wed in 1987 and divorced in 1991. Reckell married singer-songwriter and documentary filmmaker Kelly Moneymaker in 1998.
Also a musician, Reckell built a soundproof recording studio in the house.
“Everything is thought out with intention. [Reckell] spent a lot of time tinkering with the house and being playful,” Yedidsion said.
Robert Kelker-Kelly, who took over as Bo after Reckell’s second stint, died Oct. 3 in Missouri at age 62,Page Six reported.
The seller is a trust tied to the late celebrity plastic surgeon Stephen Pincus.
Framed by mature trees, the rustic three-bedroom, five-bath retreat is packed with exposed beams, custom woodwork and ironwork.
It’s also filled with eclectic furnishings and art, plus one-off touches like a corrugated iron art wall along the main entryway.
A stone fireplace anchors the sunlit living room, which has tall windows, glass doors, wood floors, built-in shelves and a high ceiling.
The open kitchen and dining area has “integrated wine and glass storage,” per the listing, and windows that look out on the trees.
For entertaining, there’s a family room and a separate billiards room.
A main-floor bedroom currently serves as a home office.
Upstairs, the large main bedroom suite has vaulted ceilings, a fireplace and French doors that open to a private deck, along with a custom walk-in closet and a spa-like bath.
An open gallery overlooking the living room offers an “inviting place to read or unwind,” the listing notes.
Multiple decks, balconies and a stone patio round out the indoor/outdoor flow.

content:

California’shousing crisis has made it very difficultto buy a home, but one rare opportunity has opened up giving a few lucky families the chance to buy 3- to 4-bedroom homes at prices far below the local median of $1 million.
The Bay Area city of Walnut Creek has ahomeownership programthat will offer three homes to households with at least three to four people that meet “very low” to “low” income requirements — all for prices ranging from just $262,750 to $377,000.
In contrast, the average home in Walnut Creek is valued at over $992,000, according to Zillow, which is more than three times the below-market price.

Each of the homes has a value estimated at $1.2 million to $1.5 million,KTVU reported, making it a sweet deal.
One of the properties has been revealed as a 2,466-square-feet two-story, four-bedroom home within Shea Homes’ Abigail Place development. It has 3.5 bathrooms and a landscaped backyard.
According to the listing, the $262,750 home is in close proximity to public transportation and Highway 680, schools, nearby parks and trails, and local attractions such as Walnut Creek’s year-round farmers market.
The two other below-market homes will be available to applicants and will be part of a separate lottery. They will be priced in the mid-$300,000s, KTVU reported.
According to thecity’s website, the future homes may be inEsperanza Place, offering 1 to 4 bedrooms, solar powered capabilities, parking with electric vehicle access, and close proximity to public transportation.
The homeownership program is run by the nonprofit Bay Area Affordable Homeownership Alliance. Mechanics Bank will provide additional down payment assistance subsidies and a loan subsidy to qualified buyers.
To qualify, one must be a first-time homebuyer with no ownership in the past three year. There are income requirements, with a family of four that should not make over $81,400 per year. The other two homes have slightly higher income maximums, such as $135,740 for a family of four.
Credit scores, debt and other finanicial qualifications will also be checked.
One must entera lotteryby the end of this month, anda virtual informational workshopwill be held on Oct. 21.
There will be strings attached once the home is owned, such as a prohibition on renting the place out and pre-approval from the city of any future home sale.

Dolly Parton’s former Los Angeleshideaway could be yours for a whole lot of 9 to 5 paychecks.
The late country legend’s formerHollywood Hills home has hit the market for $7.95, according toPeople.
Parton and her husband, Carl Dean, bought the four-bedroom, six-bathroom property in 1985 for $750,000 and sold it five years later for $1.2 million, according toRealtor.com.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Now, the 4,689-square-foot pad is back up for grabs — with a price tag more than 10 times what the couple paid for it. Kurt Rappaport of Westside Estate Agency alongside Edward Tinney of Nourmand & Associates are the listing agents for the property.
The home sits on a 0.35-acre lot in the Bird Streets, the celebrity-favored enclave tucked above the Sunset Strip.
It is hidden behind an unsuspecting garage, giving it the kind of privacy fit for one of music’s most recognizable stars.
But inside, the views are anything but subtle.
The living and dining rooms are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows that look out toward Downtown Los Angeles and the Pacific Ocean.
Those rooms open to a terrace overlooking the home’s pool and spa, with outdoor space meant for entertaining.
The primary suite is its own mini-retreat, with a coffee bar, two bathrooms, a steam shower, an office, a gym, a walk-in closet, a fireplace, a private spa and a deck with panoramic city views.
The kitchen comes with Miele double ovens, a six-top burner, a 48-inch Sub-Zero refrigerator, a microwave and a wine fridge.
The property also includes a Zen trail and garden at the top of the lot.
There’s a two-car garage with private access, custom cabinets and wiring for an EV charger, along with four additional parking spaces.
Parton and Dean’s years in the Hollywood Hills home came during their famously private marriage.
The couple met in Nashville in 1964 and married two years later.Dean died on March 3, 2025, andParton died August 25, 2026, at age 80.
Though Dean stayed mostly out of the spotlight, the pair renewed their vows at their Nashville home in 2016 to mark their 50th wedding anniversary.
The Hollywood Hills spread if one of several homes Parton owned over the years,including a California weekend escapein Solvang anda lavish New York City penthouse.

hed: A once doomed city beats Miami and Manhattan as America’s toughest rental market
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Chicago may have lost some of its biggest billionaires, but finding an apartment in the Windy City has never been more competitive.
Despite years ofheadlines about violent crime,corporate departures and wealthy residents heading for sunnier pastures, Chicago has overtaken Miami to become America’s most competitive rental market, according to a newRentCafe report.
An average of 17 prospective renters competed for every available apartment during the peak 2026 leasing season, with vacancies filling in just 27 days.
It’s a remarkable climb for a city that ranked fifth during the2024 peak rental seasonand second in2025.
Just four years ago, Chicago was making headlines for an entirely different reason.
Billionaire hedge fund founder Ken Griffin moved Citadel’s headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022, citing concerns over crime and political leadership, and hassince been selling off his Chicago real estate holdings, including his final home in the city.
The departure came amid a wave of high-profile corporate relocations, including Boeing’s decision that same year to move its headquarters from Chicago to Arlington, Virginia.
But while some of Chicago’s wealthiest residents and major employers have headed elsewhere, competition for the city’s apartments has only intensified.
“Chicago’s rise is primarily a supply story reinforced by steady demand. The city did not suddenly experience an unprecedented influx of renters,” Doug Ressler, a senior analyst at RentCafe, told The Post.
“Instead, apartment construction slowed dramatically while renters continued to compete for a very limited number of openings.”
Chicago’s housing shortage is nothing new. But the latest figures suggest the squeeze is getting worse.
Newly built apartments accounted for just 0.27% of Chicago’s rental inventory, according to RentCafe’s analysis.
Apartment construction across the Chicago region is expected to fall to its lowest level in more than a decade this year, while the metro area faces an estimated shortage of 165,000 homes, according to the report.

Never miss a story.
Mark Brown, a Chicago real estate broker with HotSpot Rentals who specializes in luxury high-rise apartments, said the shrinking supply has made finding desirable units increasingly difficult.
The shortage is also driving up prices. Brown said one-bedroom apartments that rented for roughly $2,800 to $2,900 three years ago are now commanding as much as $3,800 to $4,000.
That squeeze has left more than 95% of apartments occupied, with nearly two-thirds of existing tenants renewing their leases rather than moving out.
Chicago also offers something increasingly rare in major American cities: relative affordability.
Compared with coastal markets such as New York and San Francisco, the Midwestern hub offers big-city jobs, restaurants and cultural attractions without the same sky-high housing costs.
“Affordability is part of Chicago’s appeal, especially relative to New York, Miami and other coastal gateway markets,” Ressler said. “But we should not overstate migration as the sole explanation. The stronger evidence is that Chicago has a very limited supply of available apartments.”
Meanwhile, Miami, the city that welcomed Griffin and Citadel, has lost its grip on the top spot.
The Florida hotspot ranked first in RentCafe’s2024and2025year-end reports.
But it slipped to second place this summer, with 16 prospective renters competing for each available apartment, compared with Chicago’s 17.
“Miami has not become an easy rental market. It remains nearly 96% occupied, roughly 70% of renters renew, and about 16 renters compete for each opening,” said Ressler.
“What changed is that Chicago’s available apartments began leasing even faster. Chicago’s average vacancy period dropped to 27 days, compared with 36 in Miami, giving Chicago the edge in the overall index.”
Even Manhattan couldn’t match Chicago’s rental frenzy.
The New York borough tied for fourth nationally, with 12 prospective renters chasing each available apartment and 96% of units occupied.
Elsewhere in New York City, Queens jumped 10 spots to No. 22 nationally, overtaking Brooklyn, which fell to No. 26.
The findings come as rental competition has eased slightly nationwide, with an average of nine prospective renters competing for each available apartment.
But with apartment construction slowing across the country, renters in some of America’s biggest cities may still face an uphill battle finding a place to call home.
The report analyzed rental conditions across 139 US markets through July 2026.

hed: Is Ken Griffin building his own city inside Miami?
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.




Plenty of billionaires buy a mansion in Miami. Ken Griffin seems to be buying the parts list for a city.
The Citadel founder, whose fortune Forbes pegs at about $60 billion, already controls most of a block in the financial district, aseven-lot spread on Star Islandand a private dock for his 308-foot yacht. On Sept. 30, he added a college campus.
Griffin closed onroughly 30 acres of Wynwoodfor $1.1 billion in cash, a purchase the seller’s company billed as the biggest land assemblage Florida has ever seen. That same day, Carnegie Mellon University said he was giving it $3 billion, which the school calls the largest gift an individual has ever made to higher education. Two-thirds of that money is earmarked for a Miami outpost on the site, planned for more than 3,500 students and nearly 300 faculty. Construction is slated for 2027, with the first students due in 2028.
One source likened his continuing investments in Miami as “a man building his own city within a city.”
Griffin himself is not underselling it.
“The opportunity to bring one of the greatest universities in the United States of America to Miami will change the very fabric of this city for centuries to come,” he said in public comments last week. “This may be the most impactful investment I will make in my lifetime — both for Miami and for our nation.”
So is one man stitching together his own town inside the Magic City?
Some brokers wince at the label.
“I think building his own city is kind of a provocative way of putting it,” Douglas Elliman broker Devin Kay told The Post. “But when you look at the scale of what’s happening, you understand why people are kind of phrasing it that way.”
Corcoran’s Mick Duchon offered a gentler version.
“It’s not that he’s building a city within a city, but he’s helping the city evolve and creating depth,” he said.
The receipts back up the hype. In Brickell, Griffin paid $363 million in 2022 for a 2.5-acre bayfront lot where a 54-story Citadel headquarters is planned. He spent another $286.5 million on the office tower next door, bought out every unit in a neighboring 22-story condo building he intends to raze and added 300 apartments to the blueprint. In July, the city agreed to sell him a historic cottage for about $3 million, the last holdout on the block.
A few miles north, he teamed with Goldman Properties in January to buy the 545wyn office building for roughly $180 million. Then came the Wynwood land from developer Moishe Mana, who has said he spent about $70 million piecing together his holdings there starting in 2009.
Then there is where Griffin sleeps. He paid$106.9 million in 2022for a Coconut Grove estate, the first Miami home to crack nine figures. HisStar Island lotsran about $169 million. And because a boat that size needs parking, he won approval for aprivate marina on Terminal Island, where a proposed helipad has nearby condo owners up in arms over noise.
Brokers say the shopping list matters less than what it adds up to.
“Griffin isn’t just simply buying Miami real estate, he’s investing in the infrastructure of a city, whether that be business, education, housing, and talent,” Kay said.
The school plugs a hole that has long dogged the city’s corporate ambitions, according to Duchon.
“Part of the reason some larger corporations historically haven’t moved their headquarters to Miami is because of the talent pool,” he said, adding that Griffin is “baking in future growth” and “bringing permanence to the market.”
Kay said the money that flooded in during the pandemic now has reasons to stay put, since “the infrastructure is being built around that wealth.”
For Lourdes Alatriste, a Douglas Elliman agent who came to Miami young, the shift is hard to overstate. She recalled the drug-money years of the 1970s and ’80s, then the ’90s wave of models and A-listers.
“We had all those celebrities coming in for a second home, never to stay full time,” she said.
Now the buyers stay year-round, and she credits Griffin, whom she has met, with setting the pace.
“He doesn’t hesitate. He moves and gets it done,” Alatriste said. “I think he is one of the biggest assets we have here right now.”
She expects Wynwood, long a district of murals and bars, to follow the path of a far tonier neighbor.
“I see it transforming like what Coconut Grove was many, many, many years ago,” she said, before adding a caveat. “It needs more walkability.”
Where Griffin goes, other fortunes tend to trail.
“He came in, Jeff Bezos came in, Larry Page came in,” Alatriste said.
Kay traced the luxury boom to Griffin’s early bets, calling him “the first one to raise the bar in South Florida” and noting that “all the other smart money follows.”
The sales job has gotten easier, too.
“We’re not pitching Miami anymore. Miami speaks for itself,” Duchon said.
Not everyone gets a seat at the table. Kay said homes priced at $10 million and up have soared, while buyers a rung or two below are getting squeezed.
“A lot of people that are in the one to five million dollar price point have gotten priced out of a lot of these markets because it’s just gotten way too expensive,” he said, adding that many are being “edged out by cash buyers.”
“With more people moving here than there are properties to even sell them, that’s putting pressure on pricing and pricing a lot of people out of the market,” Kay said.
Some of his own clients have started shopping outside Miami and Palm Beach altogether, he added.
There are other reasons for caution. The campus is years from opening, and no one has yet produced numbers showing it has moved home prices. Griffin’s record here isn’t spotless, either. He paid $60 million for twoFaena House penthousesin 2015 and later unloaded them at a $13.8 million loss.
His cheerleaders are already sold.
“He has touched things that nobody else had touched,” Alatriste said.

hed: Sleepy Hollow homeowners brace for spooky season onslaught of Halloween crowds
subhead: How Sleepy Hollow became a seasonal destination
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Every October, thousands of tourists descend uponSleepy Hollow, NY,for “spooktacular” celebrationssurrounding Halloween. In fact, last year the area, located about 25 miles north of midtown Manhattan, had around 200,000 visitors for its fall festivities.
While videos on TikTok highlight the massive crowds that descend on the the area each weekend in October, many Sleepy Hollow homeowners still seem to embrace the season and everything it entails.
Sleepy Hollow resident and Compass real estate agent Trevor Goodman, who closed on his townhome in the area on Oct. 31 last year, says that while there are downsides to the annual Halloween rush, for him it was part of the draw.
“Yes, there is some frustration among Sleepy Hollow residents during the Halloween season, mostly related to crowds, traffic, limited parking, and occasional disrespectful behavior from visitors,” he says. “However, much of that frustration seems to come from longtime residents and families who have lived here for generations and have watched tourism grow dramatically, fueled in part by social media.”
“For newcomers like myself, the Halloween season is often part of what we expect when choosing to move here, and many of us try toembrace the energyand traditions that make Sleepy Hollow so unique,” he adds.
Residents also stress that there is more than just spooky season making this little town of approximately 11,500 people so special.
“People tend tothink of Sleepy Hollowas a perpetual Halloween destination, or as ‘exurbia,’ even more remote than suburbia. It’s neither. It’s a very distinctive suburban community,” saysJan Maier, who moved to Sleepy Hollow from Bronxville, NY, seven years ago. “The benefits of living here are the beautiful scenery, the access to culture and nature, and the view of the river everywhere you look, all day long.”
Formerly known as North Tarrytown, residents voted to officially change the town’s name to Sleepy Hollow in 1996. The rebrand was enacted to reflect the region’s deep history while also offering a hat-tip to the famous short story “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” written about the area by former Tarrytown resident Washington Irving in the 1820s.
What came next, however, was even more fame than the area could have imagined. While social media has amplified its spooky vibes (TikTok and Instagram influencers besieged Sleepy Hollow in recent years), the town has also leaned into its reputation with a bevy of festive Halloween activities all season long.
“Sleepy Hollow celebrates the season with roughly seven weekends of events, beginning in September and continuing through November 1st with Día de los Muertos festivities,” says Goodman. “There’s a real sense of community pride in having something so unique to our village, and it’s wonderful to see so many people out enjoying everything it has to offer.”
Though Goodman also acknowledges that crowds can bring some frustration for locals, particularly with parking and traffic over an extended season, overall, he finds there’s plenty of enthusiasm among the residents. Local businesses benefit from the tourism boost and add to the fun with special events and pop-ups as well.
The fallcalendar of eventsin Sleepy Hollow is packed, meaning residents (and visitors) can find festive outings daily if they want to take them.
“I first attended the nearbyGreat Jack O’Lantern Blaze[an area event displaying over 7,000 hand-carved pumpkins] years ago and have enjoyed going back with friends and family every year since,” says Barbara Schainman, who moved to the Kendal on Hudson retirement community in Sleepy Hollow about four years ago from Mount Kisco, NY. “This time of year, I also enjoy strolling through the famousSleepy Hollow Cemetery, a reminder of our town’s fabled history and the ghostly story of the Headless Horseman.”
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Please provide a valid email.
By clicking above you agree to theTerms of UseandPrivacy Policy.
Never miss a story.
Some of the other entertaining events on the docket include theTarrytown Halloween Parade, the Sleepy Hollow Haunted Hayride, and even a SUP Witches Festival, “which features more than 100 witches paddle-boarding on the Hudson,” adds Goodman. “We’re especially excited for that one, since the festivities will take place right behind our home.”
Interestingly, though Sleepy Hollow is frequently listed as one of themost haunted areasin the world (thanks tomany paranormal reportsbeyond the famous headless horseman), it’s also been named as thesafest small cityin the U.S.
Put those unique attributes together, and it’s little wonder the people who live there find it interesting while also being comforting. Plus, its location and vibrancy make it a coveted place to establish roots.
“’We have it all here! Riverside walks along the beautiful Hudson, the enormousRockefeller State Park Preservewith its miles of carriage trails, and a quick express train to the delights of New York City,” says Betsy Anderson, who moved to Sleepy Hollow from New Canaan, CT, about a year ago. “And don’t forget to add in the cute shops of our historic downtown, the films and arts programs at the nearbyJacob Burns Film Center, and Westchester County Airport close at hand. Plus, October here is gorgeous, with spectacular fall color.”
With all of these positives even beyond the Halloween spectacle, it’s no wonder the area continues to be in high demand with homebuyers and renters alike.
And that demand also makes living in Sleepy Hollow a pricey proposition. According to Realtor.com® listing data, the median listing price in the ZIP code that covers Sleepy Hollow and Tarrytown was $1.2 million last month.
Inventory is incredibly scarce, with just 44 active listings across the two towns in September, and 10 new listings hitting the market that month.
“Sleepy Hollow continues to be a desirable place to live, and the limited inventory reflects that,” says Devin McCrossan, a real estate broker in the area with Douglas Elliman. “Currently, there is only one single-family home on the market, which speaks to the demand and limited availability in the historic community.”
The fact that demand remains consistently strong, while available inventory is often limited also means that the market frequently moves fast.
“Securing a home in Sleepy Hollow can be highly competitive, particularly in its most sought-after neighborhoods and developments,” says Francie Malina of the Francie Malina Team at Compass which covers Westchester County. “With charming neighborhoods such as Philipse Manor and Sleepy Hollow Manor, along with stunning riverfront developments including The Daymark, Ichabod’s Landing, and Edge-on-Hudson, Sleepy Hollow offers an impressive range of places to call home.”
The village is also not even 3 square miles, further limiting who gets to live there, which is yet another reason why those who do make Sleepy Hollow home tend to embrace it in all seasons.
“While Halloween can be a bit too busy for some to be in town, we truly appreciate the heritage that makes Sleepy Hollow unique,” says Lois DeStefano, director of marketing for Kendal on Hudson. “There’s real depth to the demand, and people keep coming here looking to make Sleepy Hollow home.”

hed: Michael Dell’s $875M bet in Boca Raton is paying off as $9M condos get snapped up
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Michael Dell’s investment inBoca Raton’sluxury real estate market is proving successful.
Buyers have claimed roughly 40% of the condos planned at The Boca Raton in just a few months, a rep for the project told The Post.
The 75 homes, located at 501 E Camino Real, mark the first time the 100-year-old Florida resort has sold residences on its grounds. Prices run from $8.95 million to more than $20 million for three to five bedrooms.
The cheapest unit now costs more than twice what was first floated.Bloombergpreviously reported a starting price of $4 million, and a May sales announcement put the floor at $5 million with two-bedrooms in the mix.
The lineup includes terrace units, penthouses and three villas that come with their own gardens, plunge pools and outdoor kitchens, according to the resort. Owners get butler service at home, with childcare and pet care on the menu. Newly released photos obtained by The Post show renderings of the residences being built.
The building’s private perks include a rooftop pool with cabanas, a spa with a hammam and thermal suites, a gym with a Pilates studio and a golf simulator. There is also a card room and a residents’ lounge with its own bartender.
“Homeowners will enjoy a highly amenitized lifestyle serviced by the resort, which includes 45,000 square feet of private indoor and outdoor amenities and a one-of-a-kind Residential Club Membership that extends to owners’ parents and children,” Sabrina Gleizer, a partner at developer BDT & MSD Partners, said in a statement.
She called the project “a truly unique offering.”
The membership may be the real prize. The resort says it created a new top tier for condo owners that covers relatives from grandparents to grandchildren and stays attached to the home.
Architect Addison Mizner opened the resort in 1926. Today it has about 1,000 rooms spread across five hotels, plus a beach, golf course, marina, spa and tennis courts. It bills itself as the only Forbes quadruple five-star resort in the Americas.
Dell’s MSD Partnersbought the property for $875 million in 2019 and later merged with Byron Trott’s BDT & Co. The combined firm has put some $375 million into upgrades. It also landed a $1 billion refinancing.
The overhaul repainted the famously pink main building beige and brought in the New York team behind Carbone to run restaurants. Rooms can now top $1,000 a night.
The eight-story condo building won city council approval in March. Construction is set to start late this year and wrap in 2029.
Hart Howerton is the architect. The exterior will be ivory stucco and shell stone with bronze accents. Pembrooke & Ives designed the interiors with a nod to Mizner. Units will have terraces 12 feet deep, full-height glass, white oak, marble and kitchens fitted with Sub-Zero, Wolf and Cove appliances.
The neighbors are not hurting for cash. Just south is the gated Royal Palm Yacht & Country Club, where Travis Kelcerented a $20 million, six-bedroom mansion during the 2025 offseason for a reported $100,000 a month. Taylor Swift, now his wife, was said to have joined him.
A spec mansion in that community sold for $75 million in May, a Boca record. Actor Kevin Jamespaid $17.15 millionfor a house there earlier this year.
Douglas Elliman’s Senada Adžem is leading sales. The developer says this will be the only time homes are sold on the property.

hed: She DIYed a ‘Miami Vice’ pink palace in Hull complete with a ‘Scarface’ nursery. It went viral.
subhead: Miranda Miele's 1980s Miami-inspired Hull home is the antithesis of Millennial gray. And the nursery? No "sad beige mom" here.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Miranda Miele spends her days as an audiologist, but her internet persona is a whole lot more colorful.
Miele, 34, said she’s always been crafty. After getting laid off for a couple of months at the beginning of the pandemic, she decided to channel that creative energy into starting something fun on social media. She began bedazzling things left and right, doing DIY tutorials, and up-cycling furniture and clothing around her house. She started an Instagram account,Pineapple Princess Creations, to show off her work, and five years later, it boasts 264,000 followers. In her bio, she describes herself as a “DIY princess” and a “tropical Barbie.”
Growing up in Weymouth, Miele was obsessed with all things tropical. After all, what’s more elusive to a kid in Massachusetts than palm trees? Add in her parents’ affinity for Jimmy Buffett music, and Miele was enamored by anything tinged with heat waves and sandy beaches. The Millennial gray era only enforced her love of color.
“I want the opposite of that,” she told herself.
In her previous home, a rental, she said she went for a tiki/Margaritaville theme. And when she purchased her current home in Hull, she decided she wanted to continue the tropical motif — but kick it up a notch. She decided on a luxury Miami ’80s penthouse aesthetic for her primary bedroom. But sourcing the items was not so easy.
“That’s the thing that a lot of people don’t realize. It is a lot of hard work, especially up in Boston,” said Miele. “I have sourced pieces from all over the country.”
With the aesthetic nailed down, she secured a bed frame online before she even closed on the Hull home she shares with her husband. She found the piece in poor condition in Tampa, Florida, and hired a shipper to bring it up to her. She now goes on Facebook Marketplace throughout the country, moving the location around depending on the item she’s searching for. She knows New York has a lot of postmodern ‘80s decor, while New Jersey favors a casual beach vibe. But Florida is, naturally, where she finds that ‘80s Miami look.
The bedroom result: a pink palace reminiscent of Barbie’s dream house of the 1980s and ’90s, complete with white lacquer furniture, columns, swans, and palms.
A post shared by Miranda Miele | DIY Princess | Tropical Barbie (@pineapple_princess_creations)
One of the postschronicling the DIY transformation — “paht six” as she quotes her dad saying — ended up going viral, racking up 4.6 million views and over 271,000 likes.“Paht” 17got 3.8 million views.
Her father can be seen in many of the videos, helping her drill the walls, create her next unusual masterpiece, and saying his catch phrase, “looks like it grew theah.” Miele has even designed a couple of pieces of furniture herself, since the style is extremely limited. (In the future, she’d love to create a line of ‘ 80s-inspired lamps, rugs, and mirrors.) Miele’s husband, who doesn’t appear in most videos, is “always behind the scenes doing the heavy lifting on things.”
Miele admits her husband has been skeptical about some of the designs. In particular, he had doubts about the columns in the bedroom and the “Scarface” Cadillac-inspired dresser in the nursery. “Yet [he] still drove an hour each way with me to pick the columns up from [a Facebook Mrketplace listing] and even sanded the dresser,” she said. “But [he] ended up loving both in the end and ultimately loves having all these crazy things in his house.”
He does have his own office color drenched in green. “I’m not allowed to put any pink in there,” Miele said with a laugh.
The transformation didn’t stop at the bedroom. The living room walls are also painted pink, and the room features a curved pink sofa, palm tree mirrors, and accent chairs straight out of the ’80s that she had shipped from Las Vegas. She calls this room the“Miami ’80s Sky Lounge.“Hull may not be the Sunshine State, but the windows look out to the water, adding to the Miami fantasy.
When Miele discovered she was pregnant, she knew she wanted to come up with a fun theme for the baby’s nursery. Since half the house was covered in pink already, she thought she’d lean into an ‘80s Barbie motif.
But when she discovered she was having a boy, she decided to challenge herself.
She came up with the idea of a “Scarface”-themed nursery. Her family said the idea was a little outlandish, but she went for it. Determined to put in some references to the movie in a baby-friendly way, she thought of the catchphrase, “The World is Yours” — which refers to Tony Montana’s pursuit of the American Dream and ruthless ambition in the film — and crafted a sign emblazoned with the phrase. For the door, she created another sign that says, “Say goodnight to the little guy.”
Miele says she doesn’t have anything particularly against the “sad beige mom” era, but this nursery, in a red, black, and gold motif, is anything but that. There’s a panther lamp that came from New York, and a giant mirror behind the crib from Miami is adorned with a baby panther she painted herself. A special-order cheetah-print carpet was the perfect finish. Now, her infant son is lulled to sleep under a mobile that says, “The World is Yours.”
Her favorite part of the home project has been having followers tell her she’s inspired them to infuse a bit of color into their lives. People come up to Miele around in Hull, she said, recognizing her and her creations from social media.
“The whole purpose of my page really is to inspire people to get out there and get creative,” said Miele. “If I can do a Miami ’80s time capsule house in Boston in 2026, then you can do anything.”
Megan Johnson is a correspondent who covers real estate, distinctive homes, architecture, and interior design.
