hed: House flippers are cashing in big in one Upstate NY metro— while Texas gets burned
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.



Home flippers across America are watching their profits shrink, with the typical flip bringing in just $60,526 before expenses in the second quarter of 2026 — down from $71,000 a year earlier, according to anew reportfrom real estate data firm ATTOM.
That’s a return of 21.5% on what investors paid for the property, down from 27.6% a year ago.
And that’s before paying for renovations, closing costs and other expenses — meaning the actual payday could be a whole lot smaller.
“Flippers are still making money in most markets, but the typical return continues to narrow,” ATTOM CEO Rob Barber said in the report.
“The second-quarter numbers continue the general downward trend in profit margins and gross profits we have seen over the past two years.”
It’s a far cry from the days when soaring home prices made flipping houses look like an easy way to get rich.
Now,with homes already expensiveandbuyers watching their budgets, investors have less room to make a quick buck.
And fewer people are getting in on the action.
Some 77,991 homes were flipped nationwide during the second quarter, making up 6.2% of all home sales, down from 7.3% a year earlier.
That’s roughly one in every 16 homes sold.
But while some investors are struggling to turn a profit, others are still laughing all the way to the bank.
InBuffalo, New York, house flippers are hitting the jackpot.
The upstate city delivered a whopping 76.6% return on the typical flip, the second-highest among major metropolitan areas with populations exceeding 1 million.
Buffalo’s relatively affordable homes and competitive housing market offer some clues to its strong showing. According toRedfin, the city’s median home sale price stood at approximately $233,000 in September, about 42% below the national average, while nearly 60% of homes sold above their asking price.
The uptick is credited to career professionals and remote workers increasingly moving to Buffalo in the last few years. The regional economy has diversified past its industrial roots into healthcare, education, technology, research, and financial services.
Only Pittsburgh did better, with an eye-popping 81.5% return.
New Orleans wasn’t far behind at 75%, while Virginia Beach clocked in at 63.4% andPhiladelphiaat 62.8%.
In other words, there’s still plenty of money to be made — if you know where to look.
But the picture isn’t quite as rosy everywhere in the Empire State.
Rochester had the lowest share of flipped homes among major metro areas, with just 2.7% of all sales involving properties bought and resold within a year.
Tight housing inventory in the western New York city may be limiting opportunities for investors. According toRealtor.com, the metro had just 1,151 active listings in July, with homes spending a median of only 32 days on the market, compared with 57 days nationally.
And down in Texas, the house-flipping dream is looking more like a nightmare.
San Antonio was the only major metro in the report where the typical flip actually lost money, with investors selling for slightly less than they paid — a negative 0.3% return.
Dallas wasn’t much better, with a paltry 1.8% return.
Austin came in at 2.8%, while Houston managed just 3.7%.
The weak returns come amid a much tougher selling environment across the Lone Star State, where buyers have gained the upper hand.
According toRedfin, sellers outnumbered buyers by 130% in Houston, 116% in San Antonio, 112% in Austin and 99% in Dallas in July, with sellers increasingly cutting prices and offering incentives to compete with an overflow of newly built homes.
Those razor-thin margins don’t leave much wiggle room for a leaky roof, an unexpected plumbing disaster or a renovation that goes over budget.
And because ATTOM’s figures don’t include the cost of fixing up a property, even flippers who technically made money on a sale could have ended up in the red.
The report also suggests that bigger — and cheaper — isn’t always better.
Homes purchased for between $100,000 and $200,000 delivered the strongest returns nationwide, averaging 28%.
Properties bought for $200,000 to $300,000 weren’t far behind, at 26%.
But investors who went bargain hunting at the very bottom of the market weren’t so lucky.
Homes purchased for $50,000 or less ended up losing a typical $15,000 on resale.
Turns out, the cheapest fixer-upper on the block isn’t always the bargain it appears to be.
There was at least one small bright spot for flippers: They’re getting deals done a little faster.
The typical flip took 161 days from purchase to resale, down from 166 days a year earlier.
That’s five fewer days of waiting for a buyer — though it hasn’t done much to stop profits from sliding.

hed: Most Americans won’t be able to afford a house until 2031 — and it’s even worse if you’re on Long Island
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


America’shousing affordability crisiscould drag on for at least another five years — and for New Yorkers, the wait could stretch well beyond a decade.
Housing costs nationwide could return to their 2018 levels relative to household income by 2031, according to a newRedfin analysis— but buyers in New York City, Long Island and roughly half of the major metropolitan areas studied could face another decade of financial pain.
That optimistic national scenario assumes mortgage rates fall to 6% while annual home-price growth holds steady at 2.1%.
If rates remain around 7.5% but home prices stop rising, affordability could recover by April 2032 instead.
And in an even rosier — though unlikely — scenario, where rates drop to 6% and prices flatten, housing costs could return to their pre-pandemic benchmark by February 2029.
But the picture is considerably bleaker in the Northeast and Midwest, where stubbornly rising home prices continue to outpace wage growth.
Long Island is feeling the squeeze particularly hard.
Nassau County, ranked the nation’sstrongest seller’s market by Redfin, has seen home prices climb 5.3% over the past year, outpacing projected annual income growth of 3.6%.
That’s a 1.7-percentage-point gap between home-price appreciation and expected income gains, leaving prospective buyers struggling to keep up in an already fiercely competitive market — even if mortgage rates fall to 6%.
That imbalance means affordability could take at least 10 years to return to 2018 levels, even if mortgage rates fall to 6%.
New York City, Newark, New Brunswick and Philadelphia face similarly lengthy recoveries, along with Chicago, Boston and several other major markets.
Chicago home prices, for example, have surged 5.5% year over year, compared with projected annual income growth of 3.9%.
“It may seem counterintuitive that housing costs could return to normal sooner in the country’s most expensive markets than in a place like Chicago or Philly, but it comes down to the direction of home prices and incomes,” Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said in the company’s published analysis.
Redfin defines “normal” as a return to August 2018, when the typical American homebuyer needed to spend about 30% of household income on monthly housing payments, including mortgage principal and interest, property taxes and insurance, assuming a 20% down payment.
“But in many Midwest and East Coast markets, home prices are still climbing faster than incomes — so even if rates were to drop meaningfully, a buyer’s monthly payment wouldn’t return to something that feels normal anytime soon,” he added in the report.
Ironically, some of America’s notoriously expensive West Coast markets could recover much faster.
San Jose, California, is closest to returning to its 2018 affordability levels, thanks to a 3.2% annual decline in home prices and projected wage growth of 6.5%.
Under a scenario with mortgage rates at 7.5%, San Jose could return to its previous benchmark by October 2027.
Austin, Texas, could follow in February 2028, while Oakland could reach that point by April 2028. Seattle and Portland are also among the markets positioned for relatively quick recoveries.
San Francisco presents an unusual case. Its housing costs briefly returned to 2018 levels when mortgage rates were around 7.25% in September, but soaring home prices — up 9.7% annually amid an AI-fueled wealth boom — threaten to push affordability further out of reach.
At 7.5% mortgage rates, San Francisco could face another decade before costs normalize.
Crucially, that doesn’t mean homes would suddenly become cheap. In expensive markets such as San Jose and San Francisco, returning to 2018 affordability levels could still leave homeownership beyond the reach of many residents.
The analysis examined 46 major metropolitan areas and modeled different combinations of mortgage rates, home-price growth and projected income gains.
And while the scenarios offer some hope for frustrated house hunters, they are hypothetical projections rather than forecasts of what will actually happen.
“Many house hunters feel stuck between two bad options: Stretch themselves to buy at today’s rates, or wait for lower rates only to see prices climb further out of reach,” Khan said in the published report.

hed: Wall Street titan’s $80M bulletproof UES mansion could set Manhattan townhouse record
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.





Talk about horsepower.
Former Morgan Stanley honcho John Mack and his wife, Christy, have put their converted Upper East Side carriage house on the market for a jaw-dropping $80 million, making it themost expensive townhousecurrently for sale in New York City.
If a buyer pays up, the deal would smash the borough’s townhouse record, set in June 2019 when 14 East 67th Street, a 22,000-square-foot mansion,traded for $77.1 million.
“If this listing ends up selling for $80 million, it would be the highestManhattan townhousesale on record,” appraiser Jonathan Miller of Miller Samuel told The Post.
“If any home deserves that record, it’s this one,” listing agent Mike Fabbri of The Agency told The Post.
The Macks scooped up 165 East 70th Street for $13.5 million in 2009, according to property records, back when John was still steering the Wall Street giant. At the time, the 33-foot-wide building had never been a home at all.
“It was a distressed property,” Fabbri said. “It was always used as a garage.”
What followed was a six-year gut job, with Christy leading the design, according to Fabbri. The couple kept the landmarked limestone facade, added a floor and reinforced the guts with steel beams, transforming the bare-bones stable into a roughly 16,000-square-foot mansion with 20 rooms.
“It took our client six years to do this and build this,” Fabbri said.
The Macks had hunted for roughly a decade for a move-in-ready townhouse before settling on building their own, he said. Now the couple is cashing out and retiring to North Carolina, where both grew up.
John, who led Morgan Stanley as CEO through the 2008 financial meltdown, gave up the chairman’s seat in 2011.
Security was baked in from the start, down to a bulletproof front door, a state-of-the-art alarm system and dedicated security offices.
“I think everything was thought of in this home, even safety and security,” Fabbri said, adding that the house was “built like a fortress.”
The creature comforts are just as serious. A snowmelt system keeps the sidewalk clear in winter.
“So when it snows outside, the sidewalk in front of the house melts away the snow,” Fabbri explained.
Inside, the radiant heat runs everywhere. “Not just the bedrooms and the baths, like every single floor is heated,” he said. The HVAC was swapped out this year.
The cellar works as a private wellness club with a hot tub, cold plunge, steam room, sauna and massage room. There’s a 13-seat screening room, a wine cellar for 6,319 bottles, two elevators (one of them high-speed), six wood-burning fireplaces and three landscaped terraces, including a 480-square-foot perch on the roof.
Then there’s the rarest Manhattan luxury of all, a private curb cut leading to a garage that doubles as party space.
“You’re usually giving up something to live in a townhouse,” Fabbri said. “You’ve got it all in this house.”
The building dates to 1902, when society architect C.P.H. Gilbert, the talent behind some of Fifth Avenue’s grandest mansions, designed it for banker Henri P. Wertheim.
“It’s not like you can recreate a C.P.H. Gilbert home,” Fabbri said.
Only five owners have held the keys in more than a century, according to Fabbri. The roster includes Singer sewing machine heir Stephen C. Clark and Paul and Bunny Mellon, who used it as a private garage before selling to the Macks.
Rather than erase the building’s horse-and-buggy past, the renovation worked it right into the design. The old ramps, scarred by decades of hooves, turned out to be slabs of virgin chestnut. They now wrap the lower-level gym as wainscoting.
For Fabbri, the real selling point is that the next owner won’t have to lift a finger.
“It’s completely turnkey, which is the magic word,” he said. “It’s not just a showpiece, which it is. It’s also somewhere that’s really functional.”

content:

Home field advantage just got real. That is,primo real estatefor all you football fanatics.
Football season is in full swing, and these West Coast homes currently listed for salelet you tailgatein your own driveway, sizzle a sausage with your friends, then stroll to your seat — without ever risking a DUI.
For die-hard NFL fans and season ticket holders who have too much common sense (and a little cash to splash) to battle thatgame-day traffic, overpriced parking and the eternal risk of a traffic ticket, a handful of homes put the biggest stadiums in the West practically in their backyard.

So, if you’d rather strut to kickoff than sit in a highway parking lot or gamble on an Uber surge, these listings are for you.
The least expensive entry point to living a life in football heaven is in Seattle and sits right across from Lumen Field and is a seven-minute stroll to T-Mobile Park.
A 529-square-foot junior one-bedroom condo at the aptly named Gridiron (590 1st Ave. S, Unit 702) is asking just $339,000, whichis a steal in Seattle, a city of tech bros where the average home price reportedly falls around $833,192.
Gridiron’s listing boasts floor-to-ceiling windows, in-unit laundry, rooftop deck with stadium and Elliott Bay views, and you’re literally steps from Seahawks and Mariners games — perfect for walking over after a parking-lot tailgate (or just taking the elevator downstairs). No rental cap, either.
Inglewood is fast becoming a cultural and entertainment hub in Greater Los Angeles. A bright two-bedroom, two-bath condo at 3859 Thorncroft Lane Unit E is listed at a steal — at least, by LA standards — for just $575,000.
Not only does the gated Carlton Square community give residents access to a pool, spa and tennis courts, it’s situated just moments from the biggest and most recognizable stadiums in California: SoFi Stadium, Intuit Dome and the Kia Forum. Jocks and wannabe WAGs rejoice!
Sin City fans can snag an 11th-floor two-bedroom condo at Panorama Towers. 4575 Dean Martin Drive Unit 1103 could be yours for $475,000. True to its name, the 1,054-square-foot space delivers floor-to-ceiling panorama views of the Vegas Strip, Allegiant Stadium, Aria and Vdara, plus a private terrace perfect for pounding the pre-game brews.
Lucky residents also get access to 24-hour concierge, valet, resort-style pools, a fitness center and secure gated access — all just minutes from kickoff.
In Glendale, Ariz., a fully upgraded three-bedroom, two-bath house at 8307 W McLellan Road is pending at $454,900. It’s listed as for sale by owner, and with no pesky HOA, new everything and minutes from State Farm Stadium and the Westgate entertainment district, Arizona has never been cooler.
At the other end of the price spectrum and higher up the real estate food chain, a comfy three-bedroom, single-family home at 2199 Avenida De Las Flores is listed at $1.599million. Close enough toLevi’s Stadiumthat game days become a neighborhood stroll instead of a fraught freeway battle.
Lastly, a tastefully restored 1886-built Victorian at 2021 Eliot Street is asking for a hair over a mill, at $1.1 million.
Tucked on a quiet cul-de-sac in Jefferson Park, it’s just blocks from the stadium and packed with character: original architectural details, a cozy fireplace, renovated kitchen with oversized island, two primary suites (one with a private deck and skyline views), finished basement and front porch.
Plus, if you love to splash and float, there are multiple options for bathing — think private spa bath, clawfoot tub and sexy outdoor hot tub.
Fully paid-off solar panels and plans for a future garage with ADU add extra upside. Pre-game hangs here would feel special — and the walk to kickoff is short enough to skip the parking chaos entirely.

hed: At 281½  Main St. in Charlestown, a hidden home for $1.2 million
subhead: The single-family house has three floors and a private patio
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

281½ Main St., Charlestown

$1.195 million

StyleSingle-family

Year built1920

Square feet1,293

Bedrooms2

Baths2 full

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$9,362


Well-known neighbors include the Bunker Hill Monument and the Phipps Street Burying Ground, but this Charlestown home is sort of hidden from the world.

It’s what some Canadians call a laneway house and Australians label a battle-axe development‚ but for Boston it’s numerical — a house built on land carved out of a larger lot is designated with the ½ fraction.

In this iteration, a black gate between a coffee shop and an insurance office opens to an alleyway ending at a paving stone patio, and the home that occupies a petite 779-square foot lot. Beyond a red door is the first of three floors with an open floor plan stitching together the living room, dining room, and kitchen.


The 164-square-foot living room is on the right. It has a white ceiling crossed by dark beams and a circular central light fixture, refinished wide-planked flooring, and thin crown molding. Natural light arrives from French doors that opens to the front patio. On the opposite side of the room is a fireplace (not used by current owners) nestled between built-in book shelves.


The dining area, to the left of the front door, is 65 square feet, and a narrow table for four sits underneath a double-hung window. It then extends into one of the distinctive features of this home: a glass bump-out overlooking the private rear patio.


The U-shaped kitchen has Shaker-style cabinets with a natural finish that allows the wood grain to stand out. The range is cloaked in a custom wood surround and the appliances are stainless steel, including the Bosch five-burner gas range. On two walls, there is open shelving and the countertop is Brazilian White Pearl quartzite.


Directly across from the front door is the main stairway, and on the second floor is an 88-square-foot office. It’s in an alcove that is one of the sunniest spots in the house. On the left wall is a double-hung window, and then the space ends in a bank of three tall windows with a view of the surrounding greenery. There is recessed lighting. Another living room, at 192 square feet, has its own French door that open to a Juliet balcony. Flooring is refinished hardwood, and there is a fireplace that current owners have not used.


The final room on the second floor is a 57-square-foot bathroom with a coffee-colored single vanity that has a stone countertop underneath a wood-framed mirror with three light vanity bars. There is a shower, and the flooring is tile. This bathroom also serves as the laundry.


The third floor has the two bedrooms that are across the central hallway from each other. The 152-square-foot primary has the refinished wide-planked flooring, a large rectangular skylight, and a built-in bookshelf. There is a closet with double doors. More natural light arrives from a double-hung window. Both the window and skylight have blackout shades installed.


The secondary bedroom is currently being used as a nursery. It’s 83 square feet with refinished flooring, a double-hung window, crown molding, and a ribbon-style window with the appearance of stained glass.

Both bedrooms have direct access to a bathroom. The updated space has a white casement-style sink with shimmering exposed brass piping and a gooseneck faucet. The walls are white subway tile with a pencil-style black accent line. Flooring is classic style black-and-white hexagonal tile.


The shower/bath combination is behind a frameless slab of glass. The fixtures are brass, matching the sink, and include a rain shower head at its peak. At the opposite end is a brass towel rack. A clear rectangular window is above the bath.

Recent upgrades include a ductless Buderus gas boiler and mini-split systems for air conditioning. Storage is available in the 179-square-foot unfinished basement.

hed: Jack Dorsey’s $32M San Fransico compound has been under construction for 14 years, and his billionaire neighbors are losing it
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Even billionaires can’t buy peace and quiet.
Twitter co-founderJack Dorseyhas spent nearly 14 years transforming his sprawling $32 million San Francisco estate into a luxury retreat — complete with a massive sauna complex, plunge pool and rooftop gardens — while his affluent neighborhood has turned into a seemingly endless construction zone.
And his utlra-wealthy neighbors are over it.
“I’ve been listening to 24-7 construction noise in the distance for years now,” one local told The Post on the condition of anonymity. “One day it will end. I hope.”
The tech mogul’s two adjoining properties in the exclusive Sea Cliff enclave overlook the Pacific Ocean and Golden Gate Bridge, occupying a combined 1.21 acres along El Camino del Mar.
But instead of the tranquility that comes with a multimillion-dollar oceanfront address, the neighborhood has been filled with the sounds of jackhammers, cement mixers and construction trucks for over a decade, according toSFGate.
Dorsey, 49, who now heads financial technology company Block, purchased his first property at 830 El Camino del Mar in February 2012 for $9.99 million.
The 3,734-square-foot modernist residence, built in 1965, originally featured just two bedrooms and two bathrooms.
Construction began within months of the purchase and has continued in various forms ever since.
City records show that a major redevelopment application submitted in December 2013 proposed $3.7 million worth of improvements, including seismic upgrades, additional living space, roof decks and a planted roof.
That permit alone took three and a half years to secure.
Another redesign submitted in 2020 brought changes to the property’s windows, courtyard and exterior finishes, with approval arriving in July 2022.
And the paperwork kept coming.
Subsequent applications covered everything from solar panels and landscaping to fire sprinklers, retaining walls, an underground water tank and a cold plunge pool.
Architectural plans reveal an elaborate coastal sanctuary featuring three vegetation-covered roofs, reclaimed redwood siding, stonework and expansive windows overlooking the ocean.
The primary bedroom opens onto a private hot tub perched above the Pacific, while other amenities include a steam room, a plunge pool and an extensive sauna complex with its own vestibule and dedicated passageway.
There’s also a gym with a punching bag, an outdoor fire pit, cedar benches and 34 solar panels.
The home’s fire protection system alone required plans for 122 sprinklers and a dedicated 145-foot water line.
As the renovation dragged on, Dorsey expanded his real estate holdings.
In November 2018, hepurchasedthe neighboring property for $21.9 million, bringing his combined acquisition costs to approximately $31.9 million. That five-bedroom, three-bathroom residence spans roughly 3,588 square feet and sits on 0.62 acre.
Although restrictions separating the properties were subsequently removed, the architectural plans do not show the two houses being combined into a single building.
Dorsey is hardly the only tech titan assembling a sprawling residential compound.
Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg hasacquiredneighboring estates in Lake Tahoe, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has assembledmultiple adjoining propertiesaround his San Francisco mansion.
But Dorsey’s seemingly never-ending renovation is only part of a much bigger construction frenzy in Sea Cliff.
The prestigious neighborhood, which has counted late comedianRobin Williamsand actress Sharon Stone among its residents, is also home to Salesforce co-founder Marc Benioff and billionaire investor Tom Steyer.
Along the eight-block stretch of El Camino del Mar, at least 24 homes have filed building permits since the beginning of 2025, according to planning documents.
During a recent visit, the outlet documented mansions covered in scaffolding, construction crews occupying sidewalks and heavy equipment operating outside multimillion-dollar homes.
Even the spectacular views have become a source of irritation.
When a visitor stopped to photograph the Golden Gate Bridge through a gap between two houses, a nearby resident complained about the constant attention.
“This always happens,” the neighbor told SF Gate. “It’s so annoying.”
The Post has reached out to reps for Dorsey for comment.

hed: Midtown massage parlor busted for alleged $100 happy endings, a decade after owner swore off sex trade
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The city wants to padlock a Midtown massage parlor where workers allegedly offered undercover copssex acts for cash,more than a decade after the building’s owner agreed to a court order barring prostitution there.
Twice in late May, a worker at East Garden Spa, on the third floor of 23 W. 45th St., agreed to perform a sex act on an undercover officer for an extra $100 on top of a massage, according to a nuisance abatement suit the city filed Sept. 30 in Manhattan Supreme Court and obtained by The Post.
On May 21, the officer was offered an hourlong massage for $80, plus the $100 add-on, the suit says. On May 30, it was a 30-minute rubdown for $60, with the same $100 extra.
A 911 caller hadreported prostitution at the spa,according to the suit, which cites NYPD records reviewed in February.
Online ads for the spapromise “Young Hot Beautiful Asian Girls” and declare “I’m ready to give you the HOT!!” One escort-site listing says the spa is open seven days a week until 1:30 a.m. Another touts a “4hand special.”
The city is suing the building, 531 Central Park Avenue Associates LLC, which the suit identifies as the owner, and the spa’s unnamed operators. It wants the unit closed for a year, its contents seized by the sheriff and each defendant fined $1,000 for every day it intentionally allowed the nuisance.
But the building had already changed hands. An entity called 21 W 45 LLC bought it on Sept. 16, two weeks before the suit was filed, property records show.Our Town NYreported in early September that the developer plans to demolish it and put up a new building spanning 21 and 23 W. 45th St.
It’s not the first time the city has gone after the unit.
In November 2013, a woman inside the same third-floor space agreed to perform a sex act on an undercover detective for $40 and was arrested, court records show. The detective returned in February 2014 and paid $60 for a massage from a woman who couldn’t produce a valid massage license. She was arrested, too.
The city sued 531 Central Park Avenue Associates and the tenant at the time in November 2014. A city lawyer warned in court papers that “the community and neighboring businesses have severely suffered and continue to suffer, as a result of the illegal activity occurring at the subject premises.”
The landlord settled and agreed to an injunction barring prostitution in the unit, which a judge signed off on in March 2015. That history means the owner should have been on alert, the new suit argues.
The spa may already be finished. A woman who answered its phone said it had closed and been locked up because the building was sold. When The Post visited Monday, the elevator wouldn’t stop on the third floor.
The historic hobby shop The Red Caboose, which occupied the basement, closed for good in October after more than 50 years in business, 32 of them on West 45th Street.
The building directory lists Seville Real Estate Services as its manager and leasing agent. A woman who answered the phone there said the firm was “not associated with that building anymore.”
The deed in the 2014 exhibits appears to be from 2004, which would mean 531 Central Park owned the building for about 22 years.
Neighbors said they had no idea anything seedy was going on at the spa.
A manager at Sophie’s Cuban Cuisine next door said she hadn’t heard anything, and neither had an employee at the souvenir shop on the other side of No. 23.
A bartender at The Dawson, the family-owned Irish pub on the building’s ground floor, said the bar caters to a corporate crowd and she had never seen any riffraff tied to the massage business.
Dr. Igor Kletsman, founder of NY Medical, the primary care practice on the second floor, said in an email that his office has “no affiliation” with the spa “and no firsthand knowledge of its operations or of the allegations.”

hed: Soho House to open huge NYC clubhouse — with a brand new super-luxury amenity
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Soho House is finally hitting the gym.
The jet-setmembers’ clubis planting its fourth New York City location on Broadway in NoMad, and this one comes with something none of its Manhattan clubhouses has ever had. It will have a full-blown fitness floor.
The new outpost is slated to welcome members in early 2028. It will give two entire floors over to sweating it out and recovering afterward. The company is pitching the space as its most ambitious Soho Health Club yet. The 20,000-square-foot facility will include saunas, ice baths, a hammam, instructor-led classes and a smoothie counter where members can refuel and mingle after a workout.
“Our New York members have long told us they would value a gym and wellness facilities as part of our commitment to give them a membership that suits their lifestyles morning noon night.
“We’re really happy to finally make this happen and open a world-class Soho Health Club,” a Soho House spokeswoman told The Post.
The club’s three existing city locations are housed in buildings that couldn’t be reworked to fit a fitness operation of this size, according to the company.
Soho Housesays it had been hunting for another New York site for a while. NoMad’s revival and its growing creative crowd made the neighborhood an easy pick, and so did its location, a short trip for members based near the other three Houses.
The address carries some serious pedigree. The 12-story building sits on the southeast corner of Broadway and West 28th Street and takes its name from its original owner, Caroline Johnston — a prominent late 19th and early 20th-century developer. It has a limestone Beaux-Arts facade and counts as part of the landmarked Madison Square North Historic District.
Built in 1903, it later became the NoMad Hotel, which helped turn the surrounding blocks into a destination for modern New Yorkers. Today it’s home to The Ned NoMad, a sister brand that was redesigned by Soho House’s own design team.
Soho House is reworking the first four floors for its members. Plans call for a club bar, a drawing room with views of Broadway, a separate bar and lounge, a pantry for late-night nightcaps, a tucked-away terrace and a stage for live shows.
At street level, Cecconi’s and the Little Ned wine and cocktail bar aren’t going anywhere. The Ned will keep running 120 hotel rooms on floors five through 12, and anyone can book them. Ned’s Club NoMad will also stay put.
Just don’t call it a two-for-one. Soho House insists the two brands are not connected, even though they share a roof. Each will have its own front door and its own members-only space. Members who want both won’t get a bundle deal or a discount.
Access to the new club comes through the Every House membership, which costs $6,000 at every New York location. That membership also unlocks more than 50 Houses around the globe. Members pick a home club based on where they live but can drop into the others, and each one runs its own events and menus.
The expansion follows a turbulent stretch for the brand. Soho Housereturned to private handsafter a $2.7 billion take-private deal that nearly fell apart,  with Ashton Kutcher putting in fresh equity and taking a board seat.
The NoMad news also comes on the heels of a splashy citywide flex. On Oct. 3, Soho House threw itsfirst-ever New York festivalat Pier 17. Alanis Morissette headlined, Questlove brought out Pusha-T and A$AP Ferg, and MGMT closed out the night.

hed: Most haunted town in America revealed — and a Jersey Shore city ranks top 10
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The city that never sleeps apparently has nothing keeping it up at night.
New York City finished 68th out of 74 destinations in a new ranking of America’sspookiest places,making it the seventh-least frightening city in the study.
The crown went to a Comstock-era boomtown that, with a population of roughly 855, could fit inside a single Manhattan high-rise.
Virginia City, Nevada, topped the 2026 Spookiness Index fromhome security company Vivint,which scored cities on seven factors including reported ghost sightings, haunted places, haunted house attractions, psychic and spiritual businesses, funeral services and eerie Google searches.
Tombstone, Arizona, placed second and Eureka Springs, Arkansas, took third, followed by Galena, Illinois, Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, and Cape May, New Jersey.
Most of those metrics are measured per 10,000 residents, a formula that gives tiny tourist towns a big edge. Virginia City racked up roughly 10,870 spooky searches per 10,000 locals, the highest rate in the study, plus about 124 haunted house attraction listings for the same population.
Vivint acknowledges its Yelp counts can sweep in businesses outside city limits, which helps explain how a town that size logs more than 1,100 funeral service listings per 10,000 people.
The raw tallies paint a different picture. Austin, Texas, led the country in reported ghost sightings with 115, ahead of Dallas at 64 and Houston at 48. Los Angeles claimed the most reported haunted places, with 61.
Travelers are also increasingly looking to sleep with the dead. Searches for haunted hotels soared 315% from 2023 to 2025, while interest in haunted houses nearby slipped about 11%.
NYC actually logged more reported ghost sightings than any other New York city studied, with 16, along with seven haunted places. It still finished last in the state, trailing Poughkeepsie (44th) and Buffalo (49th).
The Big Apple’s problem is appetite. New Yorkers ran about 104 spooky searches per 10,000 residents, the second-lowest rate in the nation, beating only Ipswich, Massachusetts. The five boroughs also posted the third-lowest concentration of spiritual shops in the country and just 1.5 psychic and astrologer listings per 10,000 people.
Amityville, meanwhile, landed 13th nationally to claim the state title despite a single reported ghost sighting, tied for the fewest in the study, and no reported haunted places at all. The Long Island village rode its business density instead, posting about 78.6 haunted house attraction listings per 10,000 residents, second only to Virginia City, and roughly 176.6 psychics and astrologers. That was enough to outrank New Orleans (22nd), Savannah (28th) and Salem (41st).
Amityville’s reputation rests largely onone Dutch Colonialon Ocean Avenue. Before the 1979 film made it famous, the house was where 23-year-old Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed his parents and four younger siblings in 1974.
A year or so later, George and Kathleen Lutzbought the placeand moved in with three kids and a dog, then fled in less than a month, and their account fueled the bestselling book and the franchise that followed.
Owners have spent decades trying to shake the gawkers. The original address, 112 Ocean Avenue, was switched to 108 to discourage onlookers,  and the signature quarter-round windows were removed years ago.
The stigma has shown up on the price tag. The home hit the market in May 2010 at $1.15 million and sold that September for $950,000. It came back in 2016 at $850,000, offering five bedrooms, 3 1/2 baths, a boathouse and a slip on the Amityville River, and it last traded in March 2017 for $605,000.
Not every owner bought the hype. James Cromarty, who lived there for a decade after buying in 1977, told Newsday, “Nothing weird ever happened” beyond the parade of curious visitors.
The nation’s top scare sits on Nevada’s Comstock Lode, where silver money, saloon brawls and frontier violence left plenty of material for ghost tours.
The Silver Queen Hotel, built in 1876, is the town’s oldest,  and legend says a prostitute named Rosie worked there during the Comstock boom and took her own life in Room 11 in the late 1800s. Her spirit is said to show up in that room and on the staircase. Guests who book Room 11 have described tapping at the door, whispering and even growling, and the hotel has hosted paranormal TV crews, including Zak Bagans’ “Ghost Adventures.”
Down the street sits the infamous Suicide Table, an 1860s Faro bank table blamed for the deaths of three owners. The first, a gambler known as “Black Jake,” supposedly shot himself after losing $70,000 in a single night of cards. The furniture has proven tougher than its owners. The Delta Saloon, its longtime home, exploded on March 11, 2019, but the table came through nearly untouched and now resides at the Bonanza Saloon.
Then there’s the Bucket of Blood Saloon, raised in 1876 after the Great Fire of 1875 leveled most of the town. Lore holds that the name came from blood-soaked sawdust hauled off the floor after nightly shootings, stabbings and fistfights. Its real history is arguably more striking. In 1997, historians discovered it was built atop the remains of the Boston Saloon, the only Black-owned saloon in the West at the time.
Tombstone, which posted the study’s highest rate of psychics and astrologers at 625 per 10,000 residents, needs little introduction. On October 26, 1881, a roughly 30-second shootout involving the Earps left Frank and Tom McLaury and Billy Clanton dead, and the corral is said to be haunted by the cowboys to this day.
Nearby, the Bird Cage Theatre ran around the clock from 1881 to 1889, saw 26 deaths and still bears 140 bullet holes, with locals claiming as many as 31 resident ghosts.
In Eureka Springs, the 1886 Crescent Hotel carries the darkest résumé. Norman Baker, who had no medical training, bought it in 1937 and turned it into a cancer hospital peddling miracle cures, complete with a psych ward and a morgue.
He was later convicted of mail fraud and sent to Leavenworth for four years after bilking patients out of roughly $4 million. Guests seeking a fright request Room 218, known as “Michael’s Room,” and Room 419, tied to a woman named Theodora. Michael is said to be an Irish stonemason who plunged to his death during construction, and general manager Jack Moyer, a onetime skeptic, has collected more than 5,000 reports of unexplained activity since arriving in 1997.
Cape May, which ranked second nationally for spiritual shops, mixes Victorian charm with a long roster of ghost stories, many dating to the Great Fire of 1878 that destroyed more than 40 acres of the resort.
Ghost tours have run since 2004 at the 1879 Emlen Physick Estate, and that tourism is credited with keeping the house standing.  At the Hotel Macomber, an elderly woman’s mischievous ghost is said to linger in Room 10, while visitors to the Southern Mansion on Washington Street report a well-dressed female spirit.
The Cape May Lighthouse, guiding sailors since 1859, has its own Lady in White, and some locals tie the restless spirits of Higbee Beach to Thomas Higbee, who died in 1879 and was entombed near the shore.
At the other end of the list, Santa Fe, New Mexico, finished dead last.

hed: He’s not moving. How an 82-year-old Gloucester resident created his accessible ‘forever home.’
subhead: Interior designer Lisa Bonneville, who specializes in designs that accommodate physical limitations, melds beauty and safety in Tom Baker’s home.
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Tom Baker’s Gloucester home is proof that safety and beauty can coexist.

A visitor may be struck by a creative mix of paintings, sculptures, textiles, posters, books, rugs, and furniture from all over the world. It takes longer to notice, but equally important to thedesign is its accessibility. There are no sills or trip hazards; the doorways are wide enough for a wheelchair to pass; any change in elevation has a hand rail nearby; bathrooms are equipped with curbless shower floors, grab bars, and multilevel shower heads; and the kitchen has reachable storage space and work surfaces. Best of all, an elevator just big enough for one wheelchair and a caretaker opens to all three levels of his condominium.


Baker, 82, doesn’t use a wheelchair, but he is concerned about his diminishing ability to walk, and he’s not taking any chances.

“I don’t want to ever move again, no matter what happens,” he said. “This is my forever home.”

The marriage of artistic furnishings with Universal Design is the work of Manchester-by-the-Sea interior designerLisa Bonneville, who specializes in homes that accommodate physical limitations and issues of aging. She is the author of “The Safe Home: Designing for Safety in the Home,”published by the American Society of Interior Designers (ASID) in 2007, and she has lectured on the subject all over the country. She and Baker met via a mutual friend when he moved here in 2020.


“I started out working in advertising in New York; it was very much the life portrayed in ‘Mad Men,’” Baker said, smiling. “Then I moved to California and worked as the travel manager for Reader’s Digest. I traveled constantly, all over the world, until I retired in 2010.”

Since leaving the corporate world, he has written and published three novels, a book of short stories, and, in 2024, a collection of prose poems entitled “A Book of Common Flowers.”

In 2011, his partner of 35 years died.

“By then, Santa Monica, where we lived, had changed. It was discovered by movie executives, who moved there, and that changed the funky, low-key vibe. And then there were the fires,” he said.


Baker decided to move back east.

“I was not downsizing. I knew that I needed space for my things. I wanted something all on one floor, but nothing like that was available. I liked this place when I saw it, but I knew I would need the help of a skilled interior designer. A friend introduced me to Lisa, and she said to me, ‘You have great stuff to work with.’ We had an instant connection.”

Bonneville headed up an extensive building project in which the kitchen and bathrooms were gutted, and walls were reconfigured to provide wide turning spaces.


“We did one floor at a time, starting with the top floor,” she explained. “That way, Tom could live relatively undisturbed while we worked. The hardest part was aligning the elevator for all three levels.”

On the top floor, the elevator door is in the hall beside the primary bedroom suite. On the main floor, it opens to the hall between the living room and the kitchen. On the ground floor, the elevator is next to the door leading into the garage.


“Originally, the door into the garage was where the elevator door is now,” Bonneville said. “We took the space for the elevator from a closet and put a new door to the garage into the blank wall next to it.”

“Right now, five steps lead up to the door; they have handrails, a shallow rise, and are 11 inches deep,” Bonneville added. “In the future, if needed, we will put a ramp where the steps are.”


Once inside the house, the only other level change is two steps down into the sunken living room. The lowest level also has a family room, a home office, a bathroom, and a movie theater complete with twinkling ceiling lights and a 96-inch screen.

“This was the model unit when they were first building these condos,” Baker said. “They had installed the theater and, since it came with the house, I decided to keep it.”

He also keeps architectural elements that are important to him, as evidenced by the barn board that lines the wall of the downstairs bath. Originally found in New Hampshire, it traveled to California where it lined a different bathroom wall, and back to the East Coast.

Baker likes to tell the stories behind his home’s furnishings. The kitchen walls, for instance, wear the famous – and much copied – wallpaper usually called “Banana Leaf.” Actually named “Martinique,” it was created in 1942 by the design houseCW Stockwelland was extensively used in a 1949 redesign of the Beverly Hills Hotel, with which it has been associated ever since. When Baker worked in advertising, the hotel was one of his agency’s clients; he keeps a framed advertisement for the hotel on a kitchen wall.


In a corner of the living room stands the glowing skeleton of a modern chair, a piece that noted neon artist David Otis Johnson made specifically for Baker. You clearly can’t sit in it, but it is a delightful companion to a pair of tubular steel and cowhide Le Corbusier Sling chairs pulled up to the fireplace.

Bonneville asserts that beloved objects are an important part of aging in place.

“Beauty and nature around us provide a sense of emotional wellbeing and nurture the spirit,” she said. “Yet, it is the ease of function inside our homes that nurture a sense of safety.”

Among the mobility-friendly elements Bonneville installed are soft lights under the primary bathroom’s vanity. They act as nightlights as well as making the floor more visible. She designed chair rails that camouflage grab bars, pointing out that they need not look institutional.

“There are so many good-looking products on the market now that we have a lot more choices than we did even a few years ago,” she said.

She says that, while an extensive construction project like Baker’s is costly, it is important to compare costs before deciding to leavea familiar and beloved home.

“Once a home is accessible and safe, it is less expensive to stay there and to have help come in,” she said. “Until you require eight hours of care a day, you spend less than you would inassisted living.”


Baker loves his Gloucester home. He loves being surrounded by his books, his art, and his cherished objects, and he loves feeling safe there. He uses a walker much of the time, made easier by wide halls and doorways without sills.

“What I love best is the elevator. At this point, I can climb stairs, but it’s not easy. Because of the elevator, I move around a lot more than I would otherwise,” he said.

“And,” he added with a grin, “We put gold wallpaper on the ceiling of the elevator, and I’ve got some favorite pictures in there. It’s functional, but it’s also a pretty space.”

Project team

Interior Designer:Lisa Bonneville, FASID,Bonneville Design, Manchester, MA

General Contractor:Robert Marshall & Sons, Inc., Danvers, MA

Millwork:Dean Richards Custom Woodworking, Essex, MA

Electrician:Bolduc Electrical Service, Danvers, MA
