In the fall, when the flurry of East End festivities are finito, it’s hard to return to real life — and apartment living.
That’s when our envious eyes wander north, where the leaves are drenched in color and a flush of dramatic estates are now on the market.
Behold, Arrow Hill at 2525 Purchase St. in Westchester County. Built in 1927 on 40-plus green acres, it’s one of the most significant properties to list in the area in years.
“In almost three decades of being in the real estate industry, I have never experienced a more inherently unique and versatile property than Arrow Hill,” says broker Louis Katsoris of Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, who has it listed at $28.5 million.
And dig this for grandeur: The recently reno’d neoclassical pile expands over 14,000 square feet in the main house with eight bedrooms and nine full bathrooms.
The grounds have two guest residences, a do-what-thou-wilt “hanger,” a pool house and formal landscape architecture with enough fountains and garden statuary to make a duke feel at ease.
The tennis court, indoor sports court, gym and, yes, “catacombs” offer all the venues needed for your own game of “Traitors.”
Follow your compass about 18 miles northeast to the town of Pound Ridge for a completely different take on a surreal estate.
Here lies 51 Old Stone Hill Road, an award-winning rectangular home built into 19.5 acres of wooded and boulder-strewn landscape by Philly-based designer KieranTimberlake.
Reflect upon its mirror, glass, steel and zinc-coated copper jigsaw facade. Compass broker Brian Milton calls it “a rare, collectible work,” and like a lesser Rothko, has it listed for $15 million. Inside, the four-bed, four-bath, 4,485-square-footer has “gallery-like interiors,” floating staircases and walls of glass blended with natural materials like stone and warm woods.
Of course architecture isn’t enough, so how about a 2,400-bottle wine cellar, an outdoor kitchen and a media room built by audiovisual pros?
Additional autumnal attitude can be attained by driving another two hours north and turning right.
Sneak just five miles over the Massachusetts border to find another estate that’s a once-in-a-generation buy. Designed in 1893 by Peabody & Stearns in the style of a 16th-century Florentine palazzo, with 21-acre grounds by Frederick Law Olmsted, the Wheatleigh at 11 Hawthorne Road in Stockbridge is a rare surviving example of a Gilded Age “Berkshire cottage.”
It hit the market asking $14.5 million in July after five decades operating as a boutique five-star hotel.
It has 19 bedrooms, 25 bathrooms and almost 20,000 square feet of space, plus a cellar ready for 6,500 of your best bottles. Pool, tennis court, gym, it’s got it all.
Does it need a residential redo after years of gallivanting guests? Sure it does. But that’s just turning over a new leaf.

hed: NBA star Precious Achiuwa purchases lavish $1.8M condo in Miami
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Sacramento Kings forward Precious Achiuwa is expanding his real estate portfolio after signing a contract for a$1.84 million condoinside a lavish Miami development that has already attracted several high-profile athletes.
The 27-year-old NBA star is set to become one of the newest residents of Jean-Georges Miami Tropic Residences, a 49-story luxury condominium building located between Miami’s Design District and Midtown neighborhoods.
Achiuwa signed a contract for a two-bedroom, two-bathroom unit that was listed for $1.84 million, according to an announcement from developers Terra and Lion Development Group.
The basketball player, who was represented by Simon S. Mass of Altariss & TCS, is no stranger to investing in Miami real estate, having previously purchased property at Five Park, another development by Terra.
“Miami has always felt like a second home to me, and when Simon walked me through what Jean-Georges and Terra were building at Miami Tropic, it was an easy decision,” Achiuwa said in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.
“I already invested in Five Park by Terra with his guidance, and this was the same instinct.”
The NBA star explained that the development’s focus on fitness, nutrition, and luxury living played a significant role in his decision to invest in the property.
“The combination of world-class wellness, Jean-Georges’ culinary vision, and the location between the Design District and Midtown is unlike anything else in the market,” he added.
Achiuwa is joining an increasingly star-studded list of athletes who have secured residences inside the development.
Argentinian polo champion Nacho Figueras and his son, Hilario Figueras, recently purchased a three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom unit spanning 2,951 square feet, which was listed for $3.116 million.
Meanwhile, Alpine Formula 1 driver Pierre Gasly secured a sprawling four-bedroom, four-bathroom sky residence measuring 3,712 square feet, with a listing price of $4.9 million.
While Achiuwa’s future home is more modest in comparison, it will offer access to the same expansive collection of luxury amenities available to the building’s residents.
The development, which will house 338 condominiums, marks Michelin-starred chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s first foray into residential real estate.
Designed by architecture firm Arquitectonica, with interiors envisioned by Yabu Pushelberg, the tower will feature more than 80,000 square feet of indoor and outdoor amenities spread across five floors.
Among its most notable features is The Well Club at Miami Tropic, a dedicated wellness destination designed to help residents prioritize their physical health and recovery.
The facility will offer infrared saunas, steam rooms, hot and cold contrast therapies, compression and percussion treatments, and private treatment rooms.
Fitness enthusiasts will also have access to strength-training equipment, cardio facilities, yoga and barre offerings, squash, and personalized training services.
Elsewhere, residents will be able to enjoy an eighth-floor swimming pool and private restaurant and bar, as well as a rooftop pool, juice bar, private dining room, library, and multiple lounge areas.
Vongerichten has also played an integral role in shaping the building’s culinary offerings, which will place an emphasis on fresh, seasonal ingredients and farm-to-table dining.
The chef’s influence will extend beyond the communal dining areas and into the residences themselves, with his vision helping inform the design of the in-home kitchens.
The ground floor will house abc kitchens, a restaurant concept combining elements of Vongerichten’s abcV, abc cocina, and abc kitchen.
Meanwhile, the building’s interiors will draw inspiration from Miami’s tropical surroundings, incorporating greenery, natural woods, stone finishes, and textured materials to create a calming atmosphere.
The tower’s location will also place residents within walking distance of the upscale boutiques, restaurants, and cultural attractions that have helped transform the surrounding neighborhood into one of Miami’s most sought-after destinations.
For Achiuwa, the combination of location, wellness amenities, and luxury hospitality appears to have made the development an appealing addition to his growing property portfolio.
“Precious is joining a rapidly growing Miami Tropic community of residents with a shared appreciation for wellness, hospitality, and culture,” Terra CEO David Martin said in a statement.
“In partnership with Jean-Georges, we’re building a lifestyle destination that blends world-class dining, holistic wellness, and elevated service—a combination that deeply resonates with globally-recognized athletes, food connoisseurs, and art and culture enthusiasts.”
Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor’s degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers’ moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

hed: Inside Athens oasis Kimberly Guilfoyle forced to leave — as sources reveal she’s heading back to Florida
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Kimberly Guilfoyle is losing more than a title. She’s losing one of the most coveted addresses in Athens and will likely be heading back to the Sunshine State, a source told The Post.
The former Fox News star and Trump loyalistagreed Tuesday to step downas US ambassador to Greece once the White House asked her to go, which means she’ll have to give up Jefferson House, the government-owned estate that comes with the job.
“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia announced at her first briefing.
“She will not be there. I didn’t like what I read,”President Donald Trump told reporterson the South Lawn.
The residence sits on Panagi Kyriakou Street in Kolonaki, the city’s toniest neighborhood, tucked at the base of Lycabettus Hill and an easy stroll from Syntagma Square.
It’s a pricey postcode. Homes in Kolonaki-Lykavittos are the most expensive in Athens, averaging roughly $660 per square foot, and the best properties command close to $1,000 per square foot.
For comparison, a 3-bed, 3-bath Kolonaki townhouse of about 2,000 square feet is currently listed for $2.17 million. Renters pay a premium too.Kolonaki ties Santorini and Thessaloniki’s Old Waterfront for Greece’s highest average rents..
Jefferson House meanwhile is a sprawling, gated diplomatic compound. Washington keeps the specs close to the vest. Details on the home’s history, layout and interiors are scarce for security and privacy reasons.
What is known is the architecture blends stately Greek touches with a breezy Palm Beach vibe, featuring columns and a symmetrical facade that echo the neighborhood’s old-world look. Outside, the grounds include manicured gardens, a pool and a veranda.
Inside, the home splits private family quarters from official space, with formal reception rooms, dining areas and meeting rooms decorated to showcase American culture alongside Greek artistry.
It’s built for entertaining. Then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo stopped by in October 2019, and the grounds have hosted several Fourth of July bashes. Guilfoyle’s predecessor, George Tsunis, threw a reception there for Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew and hosted the Fulbright Commission’s awards ceremony in June 2022.
Guilfoyle put her own stamp on the place. As the first woman to serve as America’s ambassador to Greece, she featured three portraits by Françoise Gilot in the residence’s State Department art collection.
She also wanted a game room of sorts.The Daily Mailreported that she requested a $58,000 basketball court next to the pool and gardens.
And then there were the self-portraits. Oversized images of Guilfoyle hung on the walls, and that in her final days visitors found her looking past them at a soundless TV airing coverage of her growing scandal.
It remains unclear where she is heading following her move out of the Athens residence. Sources, however, told The Post she is expected to return to Florida. The Post has reached out for comment.
A trio of Wall Street Journal investigations did her in. The first, in late September, said she had been talking up a Greek construction firm while working hand in glove with its chief lobbyist. A second surfaced texts showing she asked Trump donor Eric Deters for $100,000to pay off her AmEx billbefore her confirmation hearing. A third detailed private jet trips and five-star European hotel stays paid for by shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos.
Deters told CBS News she wanted the money wired directly to her American Express account so the balance wouldn’t show up on her financial disclosures.
Guilfoyle fought hard to hang on, working the phones with Trump allies at all hours and telling White House officials the Deters texts were AI-generated. The Journal said it confirmed they were authentic.
In her goodbye post, Guilfoyle said the job “has been the honor of a lifetime”  and denied the allegations, pledging to fight to clear her name.
The White House hadn’t floated a replacement as of Tuesday.  Until it does, a low-key career diplomat is expected to run the embassy as chargé d’affaires.

hed: West Palm is making waves in luxury real estate
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Not so long ago, the Intracoastal was the Berlin Wall. On the island side, charity luncheons in mega-villas flashed with Tory Burch and tennis bracelets.
And on the mainland, West Palm was known largely for its dog track. Then, mega-developer Related Ross came and tore down that wall. The developer is behind a massive redevelopment of West Palm that includes the construction of homes so luxurious they’re luring persnickety island buyers across the water.
For now, the action is concentrated on South Flagler Drive.
“When we broke ground on South Flagler House, no one had tested whether an entire building could be absorbed at this price point in the West Palm Beach market,” says Bryan Cho, executive vice president, Related Ross, of their 105-unit, 28-story towers designed by Robert A.M. Stern at 1355 S. Flagler Drive. “What we’ve learned is that buyers respond to quality … and we’re on pace to sell out before we open early next year.”
But act quickly and you can still nab the south tower’s duplex penthouse, on the market asking $70 million with Suzanne Frisbie of the Corcoran Group.
Spanning the 27th and 28th floors, it has seven bedrooms and eight full baths spread over 13,904 square feet, with nearly 2,000 additional square feet outdoors.
Three miles down the coast, at 6315 S. Flagler Drive, a newly built modern mega-villa is ready for those who don’t need to live above it all and can’t stomach the $100-million-plus asks across the Intracoastal.
“People are leaving the island to come to West Palm Beach looking for similar estate-style homes at a much lower per-square-foot price,” says Hilary Musser, star of Netflix’s “Members Only: Palm Beach” and developer of the seven-bed, nine-full-bath home. She’s selling it alongside Douglas Elliman superstar Fredrik Eklund for $42.5 million.
“At South Flagler, they’re getting upward of $6,000 a square foot. I’m running at $3,100 a foot, making my $42.5 million look like a bargain,” she says. Located directly on the water with a dock that can handle a 90-foot yacht, it’s 13,370 square feet of “full-blown luxury” inside, Musser says, with a private cinema, fine art and furnishings by Poltrona Frau.
Musser also handled the home’s interior design. “I think that there’s a lot of upside to West Palm over Palm Beach,” she says. “For instance, if you live in the estate section of Palm Beach south of Mar-a-Lago, you can’t drive north when Trump is in town. You have to cross the bridge, and then turn around and go back. It’s sort of ridiculous. From this location, it’s actually much faster to get to Worth Avenue.”
Steps down the street is 6709 S. Flagler Drive, a traditional mansion that hit the market after a meticulous redesign last year by Caroline Rafferty Interiors.
With 120 feet of water frontage, the five-bedroom, five-full-bathroom home has 6,706 square feet, a pool, a garden and, most importantly, a private dock.
It’s asking $19.95 million with Brown Harris Stevens’ Whitney McGurk and Liza Pulitzer. That’s roughly a decimal place less than what a home could cost half a mile across the waterway.

hed: Impeccably preserved Frank Lloyd Wright-designed Usonian lists in Minneapolis for $2.5 million
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Designed to blend into the landscape with strong horizontal lines and an abundance of natural light,Frank Lloyd Wright’s Usonian homeswere built from the 1930s until his death in 1959. Today, they can be foundacross the Midwest and from coast to coast.
One of those, the Freida and Henry J. Neils House inMinneapolis, MN,completed in 1951, is now seeking only its third steward. There are nine Usonian homes designed by Wright in Minnesota, including this one.
With an asking price of $2,495,000 it’s nearly identical to another Usonian that recently re-listed—the Eppstein House in Galesburg, Michigan, with an asking price of $2,100,000.
David Stickney of Coldwell Banker Realty Stickney Real Estate is listing the three-bedroom, three-bath home in Minneapolis’ Calhoun Isles neighborhood, set on a half-acre and overlooking Cedar Lake.
“It is an incredibly quiet and peaceful location, with the home situated on a private half-acre overlooking Cedar Lake and adjacent parkland. The way the home relates to its surroundings makes Cedar Lake and the parkland feel almost like an extension of the living space,” says David Stickney.
“Much ofFrank Lloyd Wright’soriginal design and craftsmanship remains intact, which is part of what makes the home so special.”
Like his other Usonians, the home boasts a floor-to-ceiling fireplace in the living room, vaulted ceilings, walls of windows and built-in furnishings that were custom-designed, including a built-in desk spanning half the width of a wall in one of the bedrooms. And yet, as the listing states, “the home is distinguished by materials rarely found inWright’s work, including cull marble bearing walls, larch interior paneling, and aluminum-framed windows and doors.”
Stainless-steel countertops in the galley-like kitchen are typical of Wright’s homes, with sunlight streaming in through the windows, as well as numerous storage areas.
Then, on the exterior, is a carport, another iconic Usonian feature. This one can hold up to three cars. But what takes it to the next level—particularly during harsh Minnesota winters—is the detached two-car garage added by the seller, along with a new synthetic shake roof and HVAC, as well as improvements to the landscaping.
“The work has been approached with great care to preserve the integrity of Wright’s original design while ensuring the home functions well for modern living,” says Stickney.
One reason for the impeccable preservation is that the house only changed hands twice.
“The original owners, Frieda and Henry J. Neils, later passed the home to their daughter, Mary Louise Neils McGee,” explains Stickney. “Her estate sold the property to the current owner in 2007.”
The seller snapped up the home for $2,400,000 that year, then put it on the market in 2018 with an asking price of $3,400,000, only to delist it seven months later after a price reduction to $2,950,000.
This new price is just $95,000 more than what was paid 19 years ago.
As with any Wright-designed home, the type of person compelled to put in an offer is likely someone already familiar with the late architect’s portfolio and legacy.
“The ideal buyer is someone with a strong appreciation for architecture and design who is looking for something truly unique and special,” says Stickney. “It is particularly compelling to someone who understands the significance of owning an important piece of architectural history but also wants a home that can be enjoyed and lived in today.”
Whoever buys this will become the owner of a true gem not just in Minnesota or the Midwest, but nationwide.
The home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and this architectural landmark offers a rare opportunity for the next owner to become the next steward of an “exceptional” piece of architectural history, according to the listing.
“This is far beyond your typical city home and would be extremely difficult to replicate anywhere in the local market,” says Stickney.

hed: NYC-area luxury buyers shell out $2.6M and up, yet their kids’ public schools rank near the bottom nationally
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A multimillion-dollar home may come with sweeping views and lavish amenities — but a toppublic school rating isn’t necessarily part of the package.
The New York-Newark-Jersey City metro ranks ninth among the most expensive luxury housing markets tracked inRealtor.com’s September luxury housing report, with the priciest 10% of listings starting at $2.62 million.
Yet public elementary schools assigned to those properties average 6.7 out of 10 onGreatSchools,placingthe metro among the bottom10 of the 43 markets studied.
The findings suggest that buying at the top of a housing market doesn’t necessarily mean getting a public elementary school rated among its state’s best.
GreatSchools ratings compare schools with others in the same state, rather than using a single nationwide academic benchmark.
According to GreatSchools’ published methodology, ratings reflect state test results and academic progress relative to other schools in the same state. Realtor.com averaged the overall ratings of public elementary schools assigned to luxury listings in each metro.
The New York result covers the broader metropolitan area, including communities in New Jersey. It is not a rating of all New York City public schools.
Realtor.com examined markets that averaged at least 500 million-dollar listings over the previous 12 months. Within each metro, it defined luxury homes as September listings priced at or above the local 90th percentile.
Each property received the average GreatSchools rating of its assigned public elementary schools. Those property-level scores were then averaged across the market, excluding homes without an assigned school rating.
Naples-Marco Island, Florida, led with an average school rating of 9.3. Its luxury listings started at $3.69 million, making it the third-most-expensive market in the analysis.
Crestview-Fort Walton Beach-Destin, also in Florida, followed with a 9.1 average and a $2.87 million luxury threshold.
Closer to New York, Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury, Connecticut, ranked third for school ratings at 8.5, with luxury listings starting at approximately $3.6 million.
But some markets with substantially lower luxury price thresholds also stood out.
Jacksonville, Florida, ranked 11th for school ratings, averaging 7.8, despite a luxury entry point of $900,388. San Antonio-New Braunfels, Texas, placed 15th with a 7.4 average and a threshold of $780,487.
Both thresholds were below the national luxury entry point of approximately $1.2 million.
“Some really affordable areas really popped out here in the top 15,” Smith said. “That was really intriguing to me.”
Their placement indicates that schools assigned to luxury listings can rate highly against their state peers even in markets where the top tier of housing costs considerably less.
At the other end, Kahului-Wailuku, Hawaii, had the second-highest luxury threshold, at $3.79 million, but the lowest average school rating, at 5.0. Urban Honolulu followed with a 5.7 average.
The analysis also excludes private schools, school-choice programs and lottery-based admissions, capturing only part of the educational picture families may consider when purchasing a home.
School ratings are often a starting point for buyers, but other priorities can carry more weight, said Seth Keslow, an associate real estate broker with Compass’ Keslow Hurwitz Team in Westchester.
“Most of my clients rely on their online searches to obtain general school ratings,” he told The Post.
He added that a home’s location within a town and proximity to work or loved ones can matter more than its school district.
“In any event, the definition of a ‘great school’ varies from person to person,” Keslow said, adding that online ratings are “usually a starting point but not always an ending point.”
Strong school ratings weren’t a shield against falling luxury asking prices, either.
Despite its third-place school rating, Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury’s luxury threshold fell 15.6% from a year earlier — the steepest decline among the 10 most expensive markets.
New York’s threshold dropped 11.3% annually, although it rose 1.1% from August.
Nationally, the luxury entry point fell 3.6% to $1.199 million marking the 30th consecutive month of year-over-year declines. The threshold now sits 14.1% below its May 2023 peak.
Those figures measure listing prices rather than completed sale prices — and, like the school ratings, offer buyers one piece of a much larger decision.

hed: Brooklyn Heights eyesore reborn as sprawling mansion and carriage house, asks $20.99M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


A 174-year-old Brooklyn Heights mansion that was once deemed a“derelict eyesore”the city partly tore down nearly two decades ago is hitting the market, paired with the carriage house next door, for a combined $20.99 million, Gimme Shelter can reveal.
The 1852 Greek Revival corner house at 1 Monroe Place, in New York City’s first historic district, is listed at $14.99 million. The three-story carriage house at 94 Clark St. is asking $6 million.
Serhant’s Mallory and Brandon Bogard, a husband-and-wife team, have the listings.
Before a buyer moves in, the public gets a look. The mansion is hosting this year’s Brooklyn Heights Designer Showhouse, the fifth edition of the Brooklyn Heights Association’s biennial fundraiser, which runs through Nov. 1. Nineteen design studios took over the rooms, giving them a playful, sometimes quirky retro spin.
Participants include Jess and Jonathan Nahon of Sugarhouse Design & Architecture, Hannah Blumenthal of Studio Olivine, Poonam Khanna of Unionworks and Isy Runsewe of Isy’s Interiors.
The seller is developer Margaret Streicker, whose firm paid $1.25 million in cash for the wrecked properties in 2010.
“When I acquired 1 Monroe and 94 Clark Street, the properties were vacant and partially demolished,” Streicker tells Gimme Shelter.
She described the rebuild as a regulatory puzzle involving landmarks rules, shifting building codes, the pandemic and the buildings’ tangled past.
“We unlocked it with a multi-phase, multi-year strategy and rebuilt One Monroe from the ground up, brick by brick,” she said.
Streicker, a Republican, is the daughter of the late real estate mogul John H. Streicker. She ran for Congress in Connecticut in 2020 and lost to longtime Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro. She also redeveloped 86 Bedford St., the former Chumley’s speakeasy in the West Village, now home to Catch Hospitality Group’s hard-to-book steakhouse The Eighty Six.
The Monroe Place house had been rotting for years. In 2008, the Buildings Department declared it structurally unsound, forced out its last three rent-stabilized tenants andlopped off its upper floors.The owner at the time sued to block a full teardown. A court tossed the suit in 2010, and the property sold to Streicker’s firm months later. Lingering claims from the displaced tenants dragged out the rebuild.
NV Design Architecture, which handled the restoration,says on its websitethe job ran from 2016 to 2026 and that masonry, woodwork and ornament had to be re-created from a “limited collection of historic photographs and archival documentation.”
“As we have been preparing it for market, people have been commenting on what an amazing milestone it is to bring the home back to life. It’s important for the neighborhood,” Mallory Bogard said.
The five-story, roughly 7,200-square-foot mansion has a red brick facade, oversized bay windows, a stoop and a mansard roof. Inside are seven bedrooms, seven full baths and four powder rooms, plus an elevator, multiple fireplaces, wide-plank hickory floors, a marble chef’s kitchen and a full-floor primary suite with its own gym.
There’s also a wine cellar, wet bar, playroom and home office, along with two garden-level studios, each with a kitchen, full bath and private entrance. Outside, there’s 1,100 square feet of space plus a roof terrace with a gas grill and sweeping views.
The carriage house, also built in 1852 and fully renovated, adds 2,100 square feet with three bedrooms, three and a half baths, a skylit kitchen, a gas fireplace and a home office. The third floor is a primary suite with a spa-style bath, and the basement holds a wine cellar, laundry and media room. A terrace and roof deck add another 800 square feet outdoors.
Marketed together as the Monroe Place Estates, the pair could work as a family compound or a live-work setup, according to the listing.

hed: Surprising Midwest city beats NYC, Miami, and San Francisco for the biggest jump in home values
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


Home prices are climbing in some unlikely corners of America — and most, are surprisingly, from modest Midwestern cities.
While home values declined in most major US cities over the past year, some unexpected places have bucked the trend.
Toledo, Ohio, recorded the largest annual increase in typical home values among 100 major US cities, rising 5.6%, according to aSmartAsset studypublished in April.
Lincoln, Nebraska, followed with a 4.1% increase, while New York City and San Francisco each saw gains of approximately 4%.
Toledo’s relative affordability may help explain its strong showing. The Ohio city’s typical home value stood at just $126,270 in February, according to SmartAsset, making it a comparatively affordable option for buyers. Local brokerageWiens & Roth Real Estatepointed to tight inventory, with roughly 1.5 months of housing supply, and interest from buyers priced out of larger metropolitan areas as factors supporting demand.
Lincoln, Nebraska typical home value now averages to $285,359 in February, according to SmartAsset. The city’s housing market has remained competitive.Realtor.comclassified Lincoln as a seller’s market in September, with median sale prices up 6.5% year over year, even as active listings increased 11.4%.
The increases stand out against a broader backdrop of falling prices, with 70% of the cities analyzed experiencing declining home values between February 2025 and February 2026.
San Francisco’s gains were particularly striking given that nearby Oakland recorded the steepest decline in the study, with typical home values falling 9.1%.
Florida also saw some of the largest drops, with St. Petersburg declining 7.5% and Naples falling 6.4%, while Austin, Texas, recorded a decrease of approximately 6%.
Meanwhile, at the uppermost reaches of the housing market, some of America’s wealthiest communities are reaching unprecedented heights.
Atherton, California, the Silicon Valley enclave favored by tech billionaires, became the first ZIP code in the country to surpass a staggering $10 million median home sale price, according to aPropertyShark reportreleased Tuesday.
The exclusive community reclaimed its title as America’s most expensive ZIP code, with a median sale price of $10.725 million — a 29% jump from last year.
More than two-thirds of the ZIP codes in PropertyShark’s ranking recorded rising median sale prices.
“Generally speaking, on the top end of the market is more resilient,” Eliza Theiss, the report’s author, told The Post.
She explained that wealthy buyers tend to be better positioned to withstand economic downturns and affordability pressures, helping some luxury markets sustain price growth even when broader housing conditions weaken.
In the Hamptons, Sagaponack reclaimed the nation’s No. 2 spot with a $7.35 million median sale price, up 24% from last year. The milestone comes asHamptons homebuyers increasingly look beyond beachfront properties, reflecting shifting preferences in the luxury market.
Nearby Bridgehampton landed at No. 4 after its median sale price skyrocketed 114% to a record $6.15 million, while Water Mill ranked seventh at $5.75 million.
It marked the first time Suffolk County placed three ZIP codes among the nation’s 10 most expensive.
ButBridgehampton’s extraordinary increasecomes with an important caveat.
Theiss told The Post that just 30 homes changed hands during the study period, compared with 49 a year earlier — a nearly 39% drop in transactions.
Rather than a handful of unusually expensive deals pulling up the median, she explained, fewer lower-priced properties sold, leaving transactions concentrated at the highest end of the market.
“It’s not that a couple of sales just pulled the number up,” Theiss said.
Atherton, by contrast, recorded relatively stable activity, with 55 sales compared with 59 last year, suggesting its record-breaking increase wasn’t simply the result of a dramatic shift in sales volume.
Elsewhere, Newport Coast, California, reached a record $6.1 million median sale price, up nearly 20%, while Beverly Hills’ famed 90210 ZIP code returned to the top 10 at $5.39 million, a 24% increase.
The New York metropolitan area also made a strong showing, tying the San Francisco Bay Area with 31 ZIP codes among the nation’s most expensive.
Westchester County placed three ZIP codes in the top 100 for the first time, while New York City itself had just three, led by Tribeca’s 10013 at $3.85 million.
Still, not every wealthy enclave experienced rising prices.
Fisher Island, the ultraexclusive Miami Beach community that topped last year’s ranking, slipped to third after its median sale price dropped 24% to $7.22 million.
Theiss noted that even luxury markets aren’t immune to downturns, pointing to 2023 as a particularly weak year following the pandemic housing boom.
The two studies measure different aspects of the housing market: SmartAsset tracks changes in typical home values across major cities, while PropertyShark examines median prices from completed transactions in the country’s most expensive ZIP codes.
Together, the findings show how differently home prices are moving across America — from relatively affordable Midwestern cities to exclusive coastal enclaves where multimillion-dollar properties are the norm.

hed: Home Depot billionaire family nabs Carl Fischer’s storied UES carriage house for $10.75M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The Home Depot fortune just bought a piece of photo history.
A trust linked to billionaire Home Depot co-founder Ken Langone has shelled out $10.75 million for theUpper East Side carriage housethat legendary lensman Carl Fischer used as his home and studio for decades, The Post has learned.
The deed, dated Oct. 2 and recorded with the city on Tuesday, lists the buyer as the Article IV Trust for Bruce Marshall Langone, which was set up under a 2025 irrevocable grantor retained annuity trust. Ken, his wife Elaine and Bruce are all named as trustees.
GRATs are a favorite estate planning tool of the ultra-wealthy, letting families shift assets to the next generation while keeping the gift tax bill to a minimum.
Bruce is one of the couple’s sons. Ken and Elaine Langone have three children, Kenneth G. Jr., Stephen and Bruce. The elder Langone, a Wall Street veteran, arranged the financing that allowed Bernard Marcus and Arthur Blank to launch Home Depot, and his name graces NYU Langone Health.
The seller was Carl Fischer Photography, Inc.
The deal closes the book on a three-year sales saga. The Postexclusively revealedin September 2023 that the 121 E. 83rd St. property was hitting the market for $13.5 million, shortly after Fischer died at 98. The ask was later slashed to $10.75 million, and the house went into contract on May 29.
That works out to roughly 20% below the original price tag, or about $1,373 per square foot.
The Langones are getting plenty of house for the money. The 25-foot-wide building spans 7,825 square feet, with medical offices on the ground floor and basement and a four-bedroom duplex upstairs. The ground level boasts 13-foot ceilings and a curb cut, a rarity in Manhattan, and zoning allows the new owners to bulk the place up to 10,420 square feet.
Architects Hamilton & Mesereau designed the brick structure as a private stable for five-and-dime king Frank W. Woolworth. Murray Guggenheim of the mining and museum dynasty later lived there.
Fischer took over the lower floors for his studio in 1965 and went on to shoot some of themost famous magazine coversof the 20th century under its lofty ceilings. Among them was his Esquire image of Muhammad Ali, and Fischer also photographed Andy Warhol with a Campbell’s soup can in 1969. His subjects included political heavyweights Lyndon Johnson and Robert Kennedy.
His sons, Doug and Ken Fischer, grew up in the house and rubbed elbows with the stars who came through.
“I got to be there when Ali was there,” Doug told The Post in 2023. “It was like meeting God.”
Doug even recalled discovering the boxer’s iconic white trunks years later, buried among his brother’s things after being pressed into service for pickup basketball.
Ken described his father’s setup as a dream arrangement.
“He used to say that he lived above the candy store, so to speak, because his photo studio was on the ground floor, which had very high ceilings,” he said.
Jed Garfield of Leslie J. Garfield represented the seller.

hed: 3-D printed homes of the future built by robots are being snapped up in Texas for $600,000
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
In early 2024, Daniella Glaeze and her husband were under contract to buy a new, traditional three-bed, two-bath home on the northern shore of Lave Travis, 20 miles outside of Austin, Tex.
“Nice and simple,” Glaeze said.
Then they saw a social media post about some 3D-printed homes 15 minutes away in Georgetown. The Glaezes, who both work in tech, decided topay a visitand tour Wolf Ranch, the world’s largest community of 3D-printed homes. They fell in love with the preciseness of the layer-patterned walls and the sturdiness of the foundation, which they believed would hold up well in potential floods.
“We almost couldn’t believe what we were looking at,” Glaeze said.
The following month, she and her husband were moving in.
There are only several hundred 3D-printed homes in America today — making up less than .0001% of the housing market — but that number is steadily growing. Globally, the market for 3D-printed homes was valued at about $60 million in 2024 and isestimated to reach over $4.5 billion by 2033.
Young buyers like the Glaezes are drawn to home ownership without the heavy maintenance of a traditional home. Plus there’s the energy efficiency. Most of the world’s 3D-printed homes, like those at Wolf Ranch, are made out of a concrete-based formula. Compared to drywall, sheetrock or wood, the material is highly effective at keeping internal temperatures stable.
Wolf Ranch’s 100 homes were constructed by ICON, the world’s leading 3D home printer. In addition to the 270 houses the company has printed in the US and Mexico, ICON has also built barracks at Fort Bliss for the Department of War and is working with NASA to design robots that can print infrastructure on the moon.
And that’s just the beginning. This October, the company raised $200 million from BlackRock and Baillie Gifford.
For Glaeze and her husband, the four-bedroom home they settled into was priced similarly to the traditionally constructed home they were previously under contract to buy. While they did not disclose the exact closing price, four-bedroom homes at Wolf Ranch list around $550,000, according to the community website.
There are eight different models of homes at Wolf Ranch, all of which are one-story and were designed in collaboration with world-renown architect Bjarke Ingels. They are ranch-style and instantly recognizable as 3D-printed because of their curved, ridged walls. It’s a byproduct of the 3D-printing process used to construct them, in which successive layers of concrete are squeezed out like toothpaste from an oversized nozzle.
“It’s almost [like living in] a cave,” Glaeze said. “These homes are built to withstand the test of time and environmental changes — there have been a couple of rainstorms and hurricanes but [we’ve never not felt] safe and secure.
“We have no issues with mold or rodents or any of the other typical things [homeowners deal with],” Glaeze continued. “And it’s not like the big bad wolf is gonna come and blow it away with a strong wind.”
The Glaeze’s home, like the other seven models at Wolf Ranch, has an attached garage, standing seam roof (the only part of the home not made of concrete) and floor-to-ceiling windows. They outfitted theirs with solar panels, though their heating and cooling needs are minimal.
For construction companies like ICON, the appeal of 3D-printing homes lies in the breakneck speed and comparatively low costs at which they can be built.
“Technology has upended every industry, but we’re still building homes the way we did in the middle-frickin’ ages,” Will Hurd, a former Representative from Texas, now President of ICON, told The Post. “We have a tool that can address cost, labor, time and scale — all at once.”
The exact price- and time-savings of an ICON build versus a traditional build vary depending on the type of construction, but the company said it can reduce construction time by an average of six weeks and come in roughly 40% cheaper than the national average.
ICON also said its homes are safer than traditional constructions, with walls that can withstand winds up to 175 miles per hour vs. an industry average of 40. A typical home’s fire rating, which measures how long a barrier can block fire and heat, is about 30 minutes. ICON’s is nearly 180.
Homes like Glaeze’s were printed by Vulcan, ICON’s first generation machine. It looks like an oversized 3D printer with two long parallel tracks and a vertical arm that runs between them.
As the wall-systems are being printed, space is left for electrical, heating and plumbing, which are dropped in after the print is complete.
ICON’s $200 million raise is being used, in part, to fund the rollout of its second generation robot: Titan. It can be set up in under an hour and is ultra-mobile because it’s not constrained to tracks. Titan’s massive crane-like arm, which extends out of the base, can pour concrete walls up to 26-feet tall.
Starting next year, ICON will sell the machine to third-party construction companies across the country for about $1,000,000.
“I am excited to build as many 3D-printed homes as possible,” Hurd said. “This is a way to meet demand, address the affordability issue and [help more] Americans achieve the dream of homeownership.”

hed: California is home to America’s most expensive zip code — where homes cost over $10M
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Atherton is back on top, and this time it made history. That is,ultra-wealthy history.
The teeny-tiny Silicon Valley enclave beloved by tech bros and wealthy professionals in fleece vests reclaimed the No. 1 spot onPropertyShark’s annual ranking of the priciest ZIP codes in the US.
Atherton’s 94027 ZIP code posted a median home sale price of $10.75 million through the first nine months of 2026, according to the ranking. It represents the first ever ZIP code in the United States to clear the $10 million median threshold.

Prior to Tuesday’s ranking results,Fisher Island in Miami Beachhad been king of the gold-dipped hill, but has since slipped to third, with a median of about $7.21 million, behind second-place Sagaponack in the Hamptons, New York.
The Bay Area’s Atherton has now held the top ranking in nine of the past 11 years.
Located in San Mateo County and just a stone’s throw from Stanford andMeta headquarters in Palo Alto, the posh town of fewer than 7,000 residents  is a favorite of tech founders, venture capitalists and the nouveau riche AI crowd.
Atherton is a purely residential sanctuary with strict one-acre minimum single-family lot sizes and zero commercial zoning. It leans rural, with no commercial restaurants, downtown shopping streets or retail stores.
That unique combo of scarcity, privacy and proximity to Silicon Valley’s business and tech hubs has long made Atherton a magnet for eight- and nine-figure deals.
The real estate boom is mostly being fueled by AI wealth. Stock windfalls from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX have sentnewly minted millionaires and cashed-up billionaires hunting for trophy estatesclose to Silicon Valley’s epicenter, and further afield to San Francisco.
Notable Atherton residents have includedbillionaire tech investor Marc Andreessen, WhatsApp co-founder Jan Koum andGolden State Warriors’ Stephen Curry.
Indeed, several real estate sales above $30 million have already closed in 2026.
California still dominates the overall list of the 100 most expensive ZIP codes, though its slice of the pie has slightly thinned since the COVID pandemic as wealth has spread to New York, Florida and other coastal retreats and mountain pockets.
“The demand is among the strongest I have seen in my career,” luxury realtor Ken DeLeon toldBloombergearlier this year.
Even so, the Golden State’s signature ultra-luxury market just set a new national benchmark.
In Atherton, the price of entry for a typical home is now more than $10 million — and rising.

hed: AI firm Blitzy signs Cambridge’s largest office lease this year
subhead: Other tenants in the building include AI giant Anthropic
content: Blitzy, a Cambridge-born artificial intelligence firm, has signed a 52,000-square-foot office lease at One Kendall Square, the largest office lease in Cambridge this year, according to a news release Thursday. “We’re choosing to keep building where we were founded and making an investment in the future of the AI community here,” Brian Elliott, Blitzy’s chief executive and cofounder, said in the release issued by the real estate company JLL, which represented Blitzy in the transaction.Blitzy’s two-floor lease is the second one by a major AI firm to be signed at the office and lab space complex owned by Alexandria Real Estate Equities. Earlier this month, Anthropic signed a 24,000-square-foot lease, saying at the time that Cambridge was “a natural place for Anthropic to put down roots.” AI companies now represent more than 60 percent of the new leasing volume across the city, said Bryan Sparks, senior managing director at JLL. “It’s no mystery that the Cambridge office market has been particularly hard hit during the last six years, but the green shoots are there,” he said, indicating the beginnings of a recovery. Blitzy was founded in 2023 by two Harvard Business School students and is known for developing autonomous software. In May, the company said it raised $200 million through venture capital backing and local investors, which valued it at $1.4 billion and made it a unicorn. The company expects to move in to the space in the second quarter of next year following a 39,000-square-foot build out. The lease will run for five years and is slated to support more than 350 employees for the company’s expansion. The company now has 200 workers, it said in a LinkedIn post Thursday. This anticipated growth comes as Blitzy is positioning itself as a homegrown player. Last week, the company announced it will become a presenting sponsor at the Boston Celtics Shamrock Foundation Tip-Off Gala, a major fund-raising event that supports underserved communities in the region. Tanner Powers, Blitzy’s vice president of finance and operations, said the wave of announcements signal the company’s fast growth and commitment to the local market. “This is our home, and for us to be deeply embedded in the community means a lot to us,” he said in an interview Thursday. “Our hope is that we can be kind of an enduring pillar of the community.” Yogev Toby can be reached at yogev.toby@globe.com.

hed: Beacon Hill’s iconic Halloween decorations can cost $25k. ‘It’s a big game.’
subhead: One landscaping company is upping the ante on Halloween decor.
content:
ByDaisy Levine
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Take a walk through Beacon Hill around Halloween and you might stumble across a house so magnificently decorated that you ask yourself, “How do they do it?”

The answer might be a professional Halloween decorator.

For nine months of the year,Parterre Garden Servicesin Billerica is a landscaping company. But once October hits, and gardens die down, it becomes a full-time, above-and-beyond professional holiday decorating service for exclusive clients — those who can afford the fee.

The idea started about 10 years ago. A client asked if the company would be willing to decorate their home for Halloween.

“I was like, ‘Oh, this could be fun,’” said Vanessa Tropeano, Parterre’s creative director. “We came up with a more artistic and creative way of doing it.”

And this did not mean a typical superstore’s plastic cobwebs.

Each home that Parterre does has a theme — spooky under the sea, a dramatic spider takeover, a home infested by dragons. Their most popular design is a home that, each year, shows plastic skeletons putting up the decorations themselves. Almost all their designs have gone viral on social media.



Most designs come from Tropeano, but she happily brainstorms with clients if they have specific visions.

The company never advertised as decorators. Word-of-mouth — or Instagram — spread like wildfire and got their name out there. Tropeano said the company makes hundreds of thousands of dollars from Halloween alone, despite having only 20 to 30 jobs each season. The installations cost upward of $25,000.


A post shared by yara and abigail | boston food and events (@foodiesof617)

They range from the most expensive large-scale installations to smaller ones, and decorations come from everywhere. Some items are custom-made while others are sourced; Tropeano goes to trade shows to find unique pieces. It starts with the idea, she said, then she goes out to find it. Large-scale Parterre designs must be booked about six weeks in advance. Clients do not pay for the installation alone; they are buying the pieces. So, they end up owning the decor and Parterre stores it for them.

“It’s a big game,” she said. “People want to be the best at Halloween.”

Each year, installation crews dodge passersby while hanging toy witches from trees, scaling bay windows three stories up to strategically place plastic skeletons, climbing ladders on vertical streets to place orange string lights in challenging spots of million-dollar historical brownstones.



This year, a job on Mt. Vernon Street in Beacon Hill was the brainchild of 4-year-old Fallon who wanted a not-so-scary home makeover that matched her Halloween costume: a butterfly.

Homeowner Mary DiLeo originally reached out to Tropeano with a since-scrapped idea of the butterfly graveyard. Tropeano thought the whole thing was too sad, so she revised it, and came up with a story of butterfly migration that, of course, also has some elements of the undead.

“We included these skeletons here that the butterflies are swarming to turn into. They’re more like zombie butterflies,” Tropeano said.

The brownstone became a work of art after a two-day installation process that started Oct. 8. Not everybody who passes DiLeo’s home will get it, and that’s indicative of the complex art Parterre hopes to achieve, but Tropeano wants people to at least get something out of it.

“It starts from a visual place and then you try and create a story to make it a little more interesting because, to me, you want to have all these different little special parts,” she said. “When you’re walking by a display like this, you’re able to notice little things that are going on with them.”


DiLeo knew she had to up the ante from last year when she underestimated the neighborhood-wide celebration Beacon Hill truly becomes (her 80 pounds of candy for trick-or-treaters was all gone by 8 p.m.). Since moving to this address, she has seen her neighbors’ homes transformed with help from Parterre and said she just had to hop on the bandwagon.

“We said go big or go home this year,” she said. “I can’t tell if I’ve lost my mind or if this is the best thing I’ve ever done.”

hed: He’s not moving. How an 82-year-old Gloucester resident created his accessible ‘forever home.’
subhead: Interior designer Lisa Bonneville, who specializes in designs that accommodate physical limitations, melds beauty and safety in Tom Baker’s home.
content:
ByRegina Cole
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Tom Baker’s Gloucester home is proof that safety and beauty can coexist.

A visitor may be struck by a creative mix of paintings, sculptures, textiles, posters, books, rugs, and furniture from all over the world. It takes longer to notice, but equally important to thedesign is its accessibility. There are no sills or trip hazards; the doorways are wide enough for a wheelchair to pass; any change in elevation has a hand rail nearby; bathrooms are equipped with curbless shower floors, grab bars, and multilevel shower heads; and the kitchen has reachable storage space and work surfaces. Best of all, an elevator just big enough for one wheelchair and a caretaker opens to all three levels of his condominium.


Baker, 82, doesn’t use a wheelchair, but he is concerned about his diminishing ability to walk, and he’s not taking any chances.

“I don’t want to ever move again, no matter what happens,” he said. “This is my forever home.”

The marriage of artistic furnishings with Universal Design is the work of Manchester-by-the-Sea interior designerLisa Bonneville, who specializes in homes that accommodate physical limitations and issues of aging. She is the author of “The Safe Home: Designing for Safety in the Home,”published by the American Society of Interior Designers (ASID) in 2007, and she has lectured on the subject all over the country. She and Baker met via a mutual friend when he moved here in 2020.


“I started out working in advertising in New York; it was very much the life portrayed in ‘Mad Men,’” Baker said, smiling. “Then I moved to California and worked as the travel manager for Reader’s Digest. I traveled constantly, all over the world, until I retired in 2010.”

Since leaving the corporate world, he has written and published three novels, a book of short stories, and, in 2024, a collection of prose poems entitled “A Book of Common Flowers.”

In 2011, his partner of 35 years died.

“By then, Santa Monica, where we lived, had changed. It was discovered by movie executives, who moved there, and that changed the funky, low-key vibe. And then there were the fires,” he said.


Baker decided to move back east.

“I was not downsizing. I knew that I needed space for my things. I wanted something all on one floor, but nothing like that was available. I liked this place when I saw it, but I knew I would need the help of a skilled interior designer. A friend introduced me to Lisa, and she said to me, ‘You have great stuff to work with.’ We had an instant connection.”

Bonneville headed up an extensive building project in which the kitchen and bathrooms were gutted, and walls were reconfigured to provide wide turning spaces.


“We did one floor at a time, starting with the top floor,” she explained. “That way, Tom could live relatively undisturbed while we worked. The hardest part was aligning the elevator for all three levels.”

On the top floor, the elevator door is in the hall beside the primary bedroom suite. On the main floor, it opens to the hall between the living room and the kitchen. On the ground floor, the elevator is next to the door leading into the garage.


“Originally, the door into the garage was where the elevator door is now,” Bonneville said. “We took the space for the elevator from a closet and put a new door to the garage into the blank wall next to it.”

“Right now, five steps lead up to the door; they have handrails, a shallow rise, and are 11 inches deep,” Bonneville added. “In the future, if needed, we will put a ramp where the steps are.”


Once inside the house, the only other level change is two steps down into the sunken living room. The lowest level also has a family room, a home office, a bathroom, and a movie theater complete with twinkling ceiling lights and a 96-inch screen.

“This was the model unit when they were first building these condos,” Baker said. “They had installed the theater and, since it came with the house, I decided to keep it.”

He also keeps architectural elements that are important to him, as evidenced by the barn board that lines the wall of the downstairs bath. Originally found in New Hampshire, it traveled to California where it lined a different bathroom wall, and back to the East Coast.

Baker likes to tell the stories behind his home’s furnishings. The kitchen walls, for instance, wear the famous – and much copied – wallpaper usually called “Banana Leaf.” Actually named “Martinique,” it was created in 1942 by the design houseCW Stockwelland was extensively used in a 1949 redesign of the Beverly Hills Hotel, with which it has been associated ever since. When Baker worked in advertising, the hotel was one of his agency’s clients; he keeps a framed advertisement for the hotel on a kitchen wall.


In a corner of the living room stands the glowing skeleton of a modern chair, a piece that noted neon artist David Otis Johnson made specifically for Baker. You clearly can’t sit in it, but it is a delightful companion to a pair of tubular steel and cowhide Le Corbusier Sling chairs pulled up to the fireplace.

Bonneville asserts that beloved objects are an important part of aging in place.

“Beauty and nature around us provide a sense of emotional wellbeing and nurture the spirit,” she said. “Yet, it is the ease of function inside our homes that nurture a sense of safety.”

Among the mobility-friendly elements Bonneville installed are soft lights under the primary bathroom’s vanity. They act as nightlights as well as making the floor more visible. She designed chair rails that camouflage grab bars, pointing out that they need not look institutional.

“There are so many good-looking products on the market now that we have a lot more choices than we did even a few years ago,” she said.

She says that, while an extensive construction project like Baker’s is costly, it is important to compare costs before deciding to leavea familiar and beloved home.

“Once a home is accessible and safe, it is less expensive to stay there and to have help come in,” she said. “Until you require eight hours of care a day, you spend less than you would inassisted living.”


Baker loves his Gloucester home. He loves being surrounded by his books, his art, and his cherished objects, and he loves feeling safe there. He uses a walker much of the time, made easier by wide halls and doorways without sills.

“What I love best is the elevator. At this point, I can climb stairs, but it’s not easy. Because of the elevator, I move around a lot more than I would otherwise,” he said.

“And,” he added with a grin, “We put gold wallpaper on the ceiling of the elevator, and I’ve got some favorite pictures in there. It’s functional, but it’s also a pretty space.”

Project team

Interior Designer:Lisa Bonneville, FASID,Bonneville Design, Manchester, MA

General Contractor:Robert Marshall & Sons, Inc., Danvers, MA

Millwork:Dean Richards Custom Woodworking, Essex, MA

Electrician:Bolduc Electrical Service, Danvers, MA

hed: Iconic Plaza Hotel to close for four years as broker warns selling there is ‘gonna be tough’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Eloise isn’t the only one who kept a Plaza secret.
The Plaza’s big shocker wasn’t so shocking to the people who live there.
Condo owners at the Fifth Avenue icon were in the loop for months about the hotel’s coming marathon shutdown, well before Fairmont Hotels & Resorts broke the news to the rest of the world this week, The Post has learned.
“The residents have known about this for many, many months now,” Corcoran broker Kane Manera, who has two penthouse listings in the building, told The Post.
Manera said he first heard about the plan “early this year.”
Fairmont revealed Wednesday that the 119-year-old landmark will go dark in January so crews can restore its storied exterior, a job expected to take at least four years and possibly stretch into 2031.
According to a statement fromPlaza management:the timeline estimated is “due to the complexity of this undertaking and significant intrusion to operations.”
The operator has stayed mum on what the work involves, how much it will cost and whether anyone living in the building’s 181 condos will be forced to clear out.
Brokers with clients inside say the answer is no.
Douglas Elliman’s Michael Passoro said owners he works with went straight to building staff once word got out. “They had confirmed with the doorman and management that residents will continue to live there,” he said.
Owners come and go through their own entrance on the 58th Street side, cut off from the hotel.
“The residential lobby is in a completely different space to the hotel,” Manera said.
What residents do lose is the glamour. The Palm Court, the hotel’s event spaces and the white-glove perks that come with living above one of the planet’s best-known hotels will all vanish for the duration. Scaffolding is also likely to wrap the building’s marble and brick facade for years.
The bigger fallout may be on the sales floor, where The Plaza wasalready a tough sell.
“I think there’s 29 units currently on the market and I’m sure there’s a few shadow inventory that’s not yet listed,” Passoro said.
He closed a $10.625 million deal in the building in February 2025, and said the sale came with a cloud hanging over it. “I think there have been rumors for the last couple years that this might happen,” he said.
“That person who purchased that apartment actually has it back on the market for sale,” Passoro said, noting the buyer relisted roughly a year after closing. “I don’t know if [the shutdown] played into their decision at all, but it’s gonna be tough.”
Now bargain hunters smell blood.
“I think it is going to be difficult to sell in the building over the next couple years,” Passoro said. “Negotiability, I think it’s just gone up for anybody that’s looking possibly to purchase in the building.”
He expects nearby trophy towers along Billionaires’ Row and Central Park South to scoop up shoppers who’d rather skip the hard hats.
“I don’t think many people are gonna be too thrilled about going to look at the Plaza in the near future,” he said.
The building has already seen some painful exits. Russian billionaires Valery and Olga Kogan offloaded their roughly 5,000-square-footspread last year for $21 millionwhile facing foreclosure, about 45% below their original $38 million ask. They recentlylisted their Plaza hotel penthousefor $45 million. Smucker’s heir Tim Smucker took a haircut on a one-bedroom he sold at auction.
Owners also face a second renovation problem that Fairmont’s facade fix won’t touch. Many units date to the mid-2000s condo conversion and need serious updating, and that bill lands on individual owners, not the hotel.
Still, both brokers argue the patient money wins.
“It’s a blip in the ocean, at least from where I stand,” Manera said, pointing out that most Plaza buyers plan to stay put far longer than four years.
“The thing is that buildings need maintenance, they need care, they need upkeep. And if they don’t get them, then they fall into disrepair,” he added.
Once the scaffolding comes down, Manera predicts a rush.
“Once people experience The Plaza in its renovated format, it’s going to be a slingshot for sales,” he said.
Passoro agreed. “It’s a short-term inconvenience for a long-term gain,” he said.
Both brokers said they hope the work eventually revives the beloved underground food hall, which has sat dark for years and remains a sore point for buyers.
The Plaza’s 378 union workers will be allowed back at the same pay when it reopens, according to the Hotel & Gaming Trades Council, which says it will try to place them elsewhere in the meantime.
Until then, New Yorkers and tourists have one final holiday season to get their fix, whether that’s tea at the Palm Court or a night in the pink Eloise Suite, which runs north of $4,000.
“Short term, there may be a little bit of pain, but long term, it’s going to be a gain, not just for the residents and the hotel guests, but for all of New York City,” Manera said.
Fairmont did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

hed: The ‘Costco effect’: How living near the warehouse giant boosts your home’s value
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Forget good schools, spacious backyards and fancy kitchens. For some American homebuyers, the hottest neighborhood amenity is a Costco down the road.
The wholesale gianthas become such a draw that house hunters are increasingly factoring the distance to their nearest warehouse into where they choose to live — a phenomenon dubbed the “Costco effect.”
Real estate agents say the sweet spot is typically a five- to 15-minute drive, close enough for a quick grocery run but far enough to escape the traffic, delivery trucks and parking lot chaos, according toUSA Today.
And sellers are catching on.
An analysis by Zillow found that roughly 3% of active home listings across 606 ZIP codes containing a Costco explicitly mention the retailer in their descriptions, marketing proximity to the warehouse as a lifestyle perk.
In Pensacola, Florida, one three-bedroom home listing advertised its location just 2.6 miles from the city’s first Costco alongside its proximity to downtown and nearby beaches.
In Austin, Texas, broker Sean McCormack of Nice Move Realty has even incorporated Costco into his home-search tools, allowing prospective buyers to filter properties by their distance from the warehouse chain.
For some shoppers, the obsession goes well beyond convenience.
Adam Staley, a Kansas City, Missouri, resident who visits Costco at least four times a week, told USA Today that living near the store was a major factor in choosing his family’s rental home.
The property was just five blocks from the warehouse, putting his favorite shopping destination a three-minute drive away.
But that convenience recently disappeared when the location closed to transition into a Costco Business Center, leaving Staley facing a roughly 25-minute drive to the next traditional warehouse.
The attraction may also have financial implications for homeowners.
AsThe Post previously reported, research from theVancouver School of Economicsexamining Costco openings nationwide between 2002 and 2020 found that new warehouses had no statistically significant impact on nearby property values overall.
However, homes within five miles of a new Costco in counties with above-average population density saw values rise 7.9%, while those in higher-income counties experienced a 5.2% increase over the 2½ years following an opening.
The findings suggest that while having a Costco nearby could be a selling point, the potential boost to property values depends heavily on the local market.
There are also trade-offs. While easy access to bulk groceries and discounted gas can make a neighborhood more appealing, living too close to a busy warehouse can mean dealing with traffic congestion, crowded roads and delivery trucks.

hed: America’s home sellers now outnumber buyers by 63% — the biggest gap since the housing crash
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The tables are turning in America’s housing market, withhouse hunters gaining the upper handin much of the country — though some pockets remain fiercely competitive.
There were 62.6% more home sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in Redfin’s records dating back to 2013, when the housing market was recovering from the Great Recession and housing crash, according to a newreportreleased Wednesday.
The imbalance has widened for four consecutive months, up from 56.9% in August, as high housing costs and economic uncertainty continue to keep prospective buyers on the sidelines.
An estimated 928,892 Americans were actively looking to buy a home in September, the lowest level on record and down 2.4% from August. Meanwhile, the number of sellers climbed to 1.51 million, the highest since March 2020.
The result is a housing market where buyers who can afford to enter have more properties to choose from and greater leverage to negotiate.
“This is a buyer’s market born out of caution, not strength,” Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said in the report.
“Buyers have tremendous negotiating power in most of the country because so many other would-be buyers have been priced out of the market, or scared off by economic uncertainty,” he added.
The shift is especially pronounced across the Sun Belt, where years of robust homebuilding have added inventory even as demand has cooled.
Of the 50 major metropolitan areas analyzed, 41 were classified as buyer’s markets — the most in Redfin’s records.
Miami led the nation, with 158.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 134.5% in August. Nashville and Houston followed, while Tampa’s seller surplus jumped to 103.7%, up from 82.2% just a month earlier.
Florida’s housing market has faced mounting pressurefrom rising home insurance premiums,homeowners association feesand an influx of new listings, giving buyers more options and leaving sellers competing for a shrinking pool of house hunters.
“Sometimes, when buyer demand drops, seller activity drops right along with it—so the overall balance of power barely budges,” Khan said in the report. “But that’s not what we’re seeing this month. In every single metro where the number of buyers fell from the month before, the gap between sellers and buyers increased, causing the market to tilt further in buyers’ favor. That’s because sellers didn’t pull back nearly as fast, or pull back at all.”
But the picture looks dramatically different in the New York City suburbs.
Nassau County onLong Island ranked as the nation’s strongest seller’s market, with 28.6% fewer sellers than buyers — meaning competition remains fierce despite the nationwide slowdown.
Redfin estimated that Nassau County had 11,120 prospective buyers and 7,935 sellers in September, underscoring the area’s tight housing supply.
Nearby Newark, NJ, also bucked the national trend, with 18.5% fewer sellers than buyers. Montgomery County, PA, Milwaukee and San Francisco rounded out the country’s five seller’s markets.
Redfin attributed the resilience of the New York metropolitan area’s housing market to years of limited construction and persistent demand for homes near a major employment hub.
San Francisco, meanwhile, has benefited from theartificial intelligence boom, which has generated new wealth and intensified competition among buyers.
The divide is also showing up in home prices. Across the five seller’s markets, sale prices rose an average of 6.4% year over year in August, compared with just 1% across the nation’s buyer’s markets.

hed: Wrecking ball comes for Pablo Escobar’s abandoned Medellín lair after it became a den of drugs, sex and satanic rituals
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The devil finally got evicted.
Medellín officials started tearing down a long-abandoned house tied to Pablo Escobar on Tuesday, afterthe decaying compounddevolved into a nighttime hangout fordrug users, hookupsand what authorities describe as satanic rituals.
The property sits on a roughly 20,000-square-foot lot in El Diamante No. 2, a pocket of the upscale El Poblado district.
Escobar’s wife, Victoria Eugenia Henao, bought it in 1979,  back when the cocaine king was building an estimated $30 billion fortune by supplying as much as 80% of the planet’s cocaine.
City officials reported finding graffiti and other items pointing to occult activity inside, along with signs of drug use. Photos of the interior show a red star daubed on a tiled wall and floors buried in trash.
Neighbor Lina María Echeverry said groups regularly met at the house for sex, rituals and drugs.  Its notorious history also drew foreigners and other visitors on so-called narco-tours, which cash in on the Escobar legend.
“In Medellín there is no place for glorifying drug trafficking,” actingMayor Manuel Villa Mejía,who also serves as the city’s security secretary said.
Villa said the city can’t keep letting “places tied to the criminal past” be used to promote narco-tourism, and framed the teardown as a step toward leaving behind spaces that feed “notions of violence, of darkness and worship of criminal structures.”
The government has been circling the property for two decades. Prosecutors froze it in 2004, and in 2018 it was handed to Frisco, a state fund for seized criminal assets run by the Special Assets Society, or SAE. A court finalized the forfeiture in 2020.
Before crews moved in, the city’s disaster risk agency inspected the structure and gave its blessing, and a local coexistence inspector signed the final demolition order. The land stays with the SAE for now, though it could eventually pass to the city for an infrastructure project.
It’s not the first Escobar landmark Medellín haswiped off the map. In 2019, the city imploded the Monaco, the eight-story concrete fortress where the drug lord’s family lived in the 1980s, using 180 detonators as roughly 1,600 people watched.
The site was slated to become a park and memorial, and then-President Iván Duque said history would now be written “in recognition of the victims.”
Escobar was killed on a Medellín rooftop in December 1993 during a joint US-Colombian operation.

hed: Historic NYC churches and landmarks at risk of being razed for the sake of ‘affordable housing’: sources
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York City has stopped awardinghistoric landmark designations, leaving some of the city’s most notable old buildings at risk of being razed.
According to city records, no buildings are currently even under consideration by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC), the department charged with protecting sites of beauty and significance from bulldozers.
That puts this year on track to be the worst ever for preservation since the department began in 1965.
“Without landmark protection, it’s very likely that eventually all of the historic buildings, the tenements, the old synagogues and churches, the institutional buildings will be demolished and turned into luxury housing and expensive hotels, the way things are going,” Richard Moses, president of the Lower East Side Preservation Initiative, told The Post of the current climate.
The socialists who have taken over have a dim view ofpreserving old buildings, particularly houses of worship, because they’d rather see more affordable apartments. They claim keeping churches from being torn down isn’t “equitable.”
Preservationists are particularly alarmed over the fate of Most Holy Redeemer church on East 3rd Street in Manhattan’s East Village — a granite and limestone cathedral built in 1851 by German missionaries.
The building, owned by the Catholic diocese, has been closed to regular service in recent years, only occasionally hosting events, said Moses.
“I would call it the most important landmarking situation in the East Village. It’s really a beautiful church and the interior is really magnificent,” said Moses, adding that designation doesn’t usually protect the inside of buildings.
“The Lower East Side really is one of the most important historic areas in the country in our view. At one point, about a third of Americans could trace their routes through the Lower East Side,” he added.
If the church were given a preservation order, then even if sold its façade would be required to remain as it is. East Village Catholic, the diocese that operates Most Holy Redeemer, did not respond to requests for comment.
However, it may not meet requirements. Citing “the killing of George Floyd” and “attacks on democracy” LPC announced an “equity framework” in 2021 to “ensure diversity and inclusion in designations” and focus on “prioritizing designations that represent New York City’s diversity.”
Shortages in housing across New York City have pushed rents to record highs, with median monthly rent in Manhattan reaching $5,300 in June, up 8% from a year earlier, according to Corcoran real estate.
Developers and city planners alike are looking forany places they can to buildand help ease the crisis. “NYC’s housing affordability crisis is at DEFCON 1,” City Comptroller Mark Levine said over the summer, adding: “We need to push harder on every front to address our housing shortage.”
Preservationists are particularly worried about buildings being demolished to make way for affordable housing, after a bill called the“Faith Based Affordable Housing Act”was introduced by Brooklyn Democrats Andrew Gounardes and Brian Cunningham.
It targeted houses of worship to have their landmark protections amended to allow developers to add-on or completely demolish sites of historic religious significance as long as they offered a fraction of the units they build at below market rates.
“There’s a certain feeling that landmarking is detrimental to affordable housing,”Richard Moses, president of the Lower East Side Preservation Initiative, told The Post said of the current climate.
The “Faith Based Affordable Housing Act” worked its way around Albany for two years, but died in the last legislative session. However, New York’s Democratic Socialist mayor Mamdani — who frames housing as a guaranteed public good rather than a speculative commodity — recently targeted 12 neighborhoods with the “lowest rate of affordable housing production,” including the Upper West Side and Bay Ridge in Brooklyn for fast-track development.
