“The housing crisis is a symptom of the affordability crisis, and to solve it… all corners of the city need to step up,” Hizzonor warned at an Oct. 1 press conference.
“Culture is low on the totem pole. If the mayor really wants an affordable housing complex to go on a historic site, it’ll probably happen,” Michele Bogart, former vice president of the New York City Art Commission under Mayor Rudy Giuliani, told The Post.
The city currently boasts over 38,000landmarked properties.The vast majority of those are contained within 159 landmarked districts — entire blocks or neighborhoods that have been preserved through the decades after tedious review.
Three buildings wereofficially landmarkedthis year — West 30th Street’s Lithuanian Alliance Building; Grand Street’s Church of Saint Mary, both in Manhattan, and Brooklyn’s Public School 15 Annex — but those had been put on the schedule under former Mayor Eric Adams’s administration.
Other sites preservationists are angling to get protected include Our Lady of Guadalupe Catholic Church on West 14th Street. Founded in 1902 it was the city’s first Spanish-speaking congregation, where radical activist Dorothy Day and 1950s beatniks like Jack Kerouac attended worship. It has been de-commissioned by the diocese, putting it at risk.
Various preservation groups are also lobbying for landmark recognition of 2nd Avenue’s New York Ear and Eye Infirmary, an 1856 Italianate brownstone; Church of the Transfiguration in Maspeth, Queens, built in 1962 which blends mid-century modern design with traditional Lithuanian folk architectural; and the 1857 Church of St. Michael in Chelsea.
New York City’s LPC was established in response to the 1963 demolition of the original Penn Station to make way for Madison Square Garden, an architectural loss that still outrages many New Yorkers today. But after decades of robust preservation, which has included famed sites like the Plaza Hotel and Grand Central Terminal, efforts have slowed to a trickle in recent years, with just 11 designations in 2024 and only four last year. The LPC did not respond to The Post’s request for comment.
“It’s a nightmare what’s happening with the churches,” Bogart, author of “The Politics of Urban Beauty,” said.
“I don’t see the merit of tearing down a church in favor of putting up some anodyne glass building.
“You lose something significant in that. But the city will gain more for its coffers, presumably, in tax money.”

hed: Mortgage rates hit 7 percent as Iran war crushes a weak housing market
content: Mortgage rates jumped to 7 percent this week for the first time since January 2025, squeezing housing affordability when many Americans are grappling with higher energy costs and economic uncertainty brought on by the war with Iran.The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rate, the most common home loan in the United States, rose to 7.03 percent, up from 6.3 percent a year ago, mortgage giant Freddie Mac said Thursday.Mortgage rates fell below 6 percent in late February, offering a glimmer of hope that the housing market was recovering from a yearslong slog. But they began steadily rising again after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.“A move from 6 to 7 is a big change,” said Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a finance professor at Columbia University’s Graduate School of Business, “and it will further dampen an already weak housing market.”Since war broke out in the Middle East, oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have dwindled, pushing up prices for energy products like gasoline, diesel fuel, and heating oil. Economists worry that higher energy prices caused by the war will spread to other parts of the US economy.Those concerns have materialized in the government bond market, which underpins mortgage rates. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond — a benchmark for a range of consumer borrowing costs — has climbed above 5 percent, a level not seen since before the global financial crisis two decades ago.Overall inflation has remained stubbornly elevated, at an annual pace of 3.4 percent in August, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this month.Higher mortgage rates in turn are weighing on a moribund housing market. Sales of existing homes fell 2 percent in August from July and are at their lowest level since June last year, the National Association of Realtors reported. Home prices rose 1.5 percent annually in June, up from a 1.2 percent annual gain the previous month, according to Cotality, a housing market data provider.“Nobody can afford to buy a house anymore at these high prices and at these higher mortgage rates,” said Van Nieuwerburgh, who added that the cost increases had locked up the housing market.Mortgage rates had dipped as low as 2.65 percent in January 2021, setting off a stampede of homebuying that ignited bidding wars and drove up prices. But as rates began to rise again about a year later, the housing market settled into a malaise as homeowners became reluctant to move and give up their ultralow rates.With the housing market stagnating, developers are delaying building homes. “Higher mortgage rates, rising construction financing costs, and affordability challenges continue to weigh on the market and limit momentum for new-home construction,” Bill Owens, chair of the National Association of Home Builders, said in a statement.Eric Orenstein, a senior director at Fitch Ratings, said that he expected home sales and mortgage refinancing to slow for the rest of the year, but that the market would eventually begin to thaw as homeowners were forced to move because of major life events, like a job change.“There’s a psychological aspect: At what point do consumers just accept that rates are not going back to 3 percent?” Orenstein said.And as owners build more equity in their homes, losing a low rate will have less impact, he added. Americans have amassed a record $35 trillion in home equity, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.Van Nieuwerburgh said he was hopeful that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which Congress passed in June, would add to the supply of homes to local markets by easing regulations for builders.This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

hed: Ask the Remodeler: Heating your home is expensive in New England — should you get a heat pump?
subhead: The question that inevitably gets raised when we talk about heating systems as part of remodel is, “Should we swap our system from fossil fuels to heat pumps?”
content:
ByMark Philben -- Globe Correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

As the days get shorter and the air cools, we all start to think about heating our homes this comingwinter. These thoughts seem particularly ominous now with thecost of heating fuel going through the roof. The cost of electricity has been equally affected given that most of our electric power is still generated by natural gas. At the moment, there does not seem to be any relief in sight.Governor Maura Healy has expanded heating assistancefor low-income families and those who heat with oil. However, much of the state will have to pay the market rates for our heating requirements— and hope it is not a bad winter.

The question that inevitably gets raised when we talk about heating systems as part of remodel is, “Should we swap our system from fossil fuels to heat pumps?” The short answer, unfortunately, is that it depends.

It’s a huge investment and may take decades to recoup the cost, if ever. From a purely monetary perspective, that doesn’t make sense. If you have an old oil or gas-fired boiler that you are concerned about and are considering replacing anyway, then you should consider an air source heat pump. It will cost more toinstall a new heat pump systemthan to replace the boiler, but you will gain the benefit of also having a whole-house air conditioning system. The heat pump systems also allow you more control over the heating and cooling of the space using remotes or Wi-Fi apps. There are some monetary incentives left from Mass Save for replacing your fossil fuel systems with heat pumps, but it is a relatively small dent in the total cost for a new system. There are little to no federal tax or rebate incentives left to take advantage of; those expired at the end of 2025.

If you are considering replacing your system with a heat pump for environmental reasons and combining that with solar power on your home or purchasing your electricity from a solar farm (which subsidizes the building of more solar farms to feed the Massachusetts grid), then switching to heat pumps makes sense for altruistic reasons as well as monetary reasons.

So, what are the things to consider if replacing an older fossil fuel system with a new heat pump system?

Boiler replacement cost:The cost to simply replace the boiler (oil or gas) and keep in place the existing heating elements would be approximately $12,000 to $15,000 in Massachusetts. That is for a system typically with an efficiency rating around 97 percent. There are very few other associated costs in other parts of the house when swapping out a boiler, assuming radiators or baseboard heating elements are in good repair.

Heat pump installation cost:Installing a new air source heat pump system for the entire home will run $50,000 on average.


Electrical power coming into the house:Homes today have a higher and higher demand for electricity. Car chargers, induction ranges, and the like require large amounts of electricity. Heat pumps are no different, with the added amperage needed to run a heat pump system, you may need to upgrade your service that comes in from the street.

Old radiators and/or baseboard heating elements:Once you have installed your new heat pump system with wall or ceiling units, you, in all likelihood, will want to remove the radiators and baseboard heating elements. That is an expense that needs to be considered — not just removing the heating elements but patching the floors and walls after they are gone.

Don’t forget the bathroom:Other areas that are often forgotten when considering heat pumps are bathrooms, mudrooms, or small areas of the house that still need heat. Bathrooms are the best example. These are typically too small to warrant putting in a ceiling or wall unit, but they still need heat. We typically do either electric radiant heat if the space is being remodeled, or we install a small, energy efficient wall heater. We useEnvi wall heaters from Eheat; they use  convection to silently take in cold air from below and distribute warm air from above.

Our clients are always asking about the cost comparisons to actually heat the house regardless of installation costs. The Department of Energy provided a table to make an apples-to-apples comparison of which energy source is most cost effective. The calculations are a little wonky, but below is a simple break down using common fuel sources in our area. It is based on fuel cost per million BTUs. (A BTU is British Thermal Unit and is the standard measure of energy used worldwide.)

Fuel oil at current price of $6.12 per gallon:$51.91 per million BTU

Natural gas at $2.50 per unit or therm:$25.77 per million BTU

Electric air source heat pump at $.36 per kwh:$36 per million BTU

(Mass.gov provides a list of current home heating fuel prices.)

Natural gas has always been the most efficient and probably will be for some time to come. Oil will presumably come down at some point, making the efficiency cost above come down. Given the volatility of extracted energy sources, something like heat pumps that can be combined with renewable energy sources like solar should be strongly considered long-term, despite the initial cost outlay. Incentives and rebates can offset the cost.

Mark Philben is the project development manager atCharlie Allen Renovationsin Cambridge. Send your questions to[email protected]. Questions are subject to editing. hed: This Nantucket estate just hit the market with a $45 million price tag. Take a look inside.
subhead: The 13,500-square-foot Cliff home features a hidden "speakeasy" and an underground tunnel to a spacious guest cottage.
content:
ByClaire Thornton, Globe correspondent
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

The nine-bedroom mansion perched inNantucket’s coveted Cliff area has it all: a movie theater, a cozy speakeasy, even a tunnel connecting the spacious main residence to a guest house.The owners never intended to sell it, according to the listings agents, so they made it their dream home.

But now the property has hit the market for $45 million — a price that could break records.

The family that built the estate at33 Cliff Roadover the past two years spared no expense, said listing agent Greg McKechnie.

“When you go into this house, you can just feel that it is so well built, so solid. You understand the quality from the minute you walk into it,” he said.

The home went up for sale this month because, at the last minute, the builder-owners decided they didn’t want to move out of theirotherNantucket home, which is located on a part of the island that’s “a bit more rural,” McKechnie said.


“Typically, a home like this wouldn’t come on the market,” McKechnie said. “But it just happened to be that this family changed their mind about where they want to be on the island.”

The 13,500-square-foot Cliff home is minutes from the heart of downtown and up the road from some of the island’s most picturesque beaches, like the sloping dunes of Steps Beach. To the west are the breathtaking Nantucket Cliffs, and the harbor is to the east.

“It’s brand new, which is really unusual on the Cliff,” McKechnie said. “There’s nobody building brand new homes and putting them on the market.”

The mansion was designed by Botticelli & Pohl Architects and built by Hehir Group Custom Builders.

If the property sells for its $45 million listing price, it will break the Massachusetts record for private home sales, which was set just last month by a$43 million sale on Martha’s Vineyard, listing agent Bobby Sabelhaus said.


The Nantucket home boasts 23 rooms, 10-plus bathrooms, and is being offered fully furnished, with new appliances and fixtures, according to itslisting.

The Cliff property’s many vantage points are of its best features, McKechnie said. To the north, the home has views of Nantucket Sound. The bustle of downtown’s cobblestone streets and historic facades can be seen to the southeast.

The family that built the home intended to spend time there throughout the year, so 33 Cliff Road was designed with a movie theater, billiard room, and many other indoor amenities, including a gym.

An underground tunnel connects a gym space in the main house to the guest cottage, McKechnie said, making the compound feel more united.

The underground hallway is not the only hidden feature. Enter through a door camouflaged into the wall between the living room and dining room and you’ll find yourself in what listing agents call a “speakeasy.” It features built-in banquette seating, wraparound counter with bar stools, and softly lit shelves.


“You wouldn’t even know it’s there,” Sabelhaus said.

The home’s current owners have a large family and like to entertain, McKechnie said. So they designed the home with many different gathering areas, as well as more private nooks for private time, he said.

“They’ve created quiet areas where they can be apart,” McKechnie said.

The widow’s walk on top of the home is large enough to accommodate several people for firework-viewing gatherings or a sunset cocktail hour, the agents said.

Sabelhaus added: “It’s incredible how much it brings together in one property.”

hed: NYC sees biggest wave of homes for sale in four years
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

It’s a seller’s sprint in the Big Apple.
New York homeowners flung open their doors in September, putting 4,951 propertiesup for saleacross the five boroughs, according to a newStreetEasy report.That’s the biggest monthly haul since the spring of 2022 and a 7.6% jump from a year earlier.
The timing is no accident. Owners are betting that eager buyers and a bone-dry supply of homes will keep prices propped up, even as the cost of borrowing keeps creeping higher.
“Sellers are running to take advantage of a market where buyer competition is still hot and inventory is still tight,” Kenny Lee, senior economist at StreetEasy, told The Post. “Even with mortgage rates climbing, more than one in five homes sold above asking in September, so sellers see a window and are moving.”
That window could be narrowing. The national 30-year fixed mortgage rate punched past 7% in late September for the first time since January 2025, then climbed to an average of 7.28% at the start of October, up from roughly 6.3% a year ago, per Freddie Mac.
Buyers are already feeling the squeeze. Signed contracts fell 5.4% citywide to 1,528 last month, with Manhattan down 6.8% to 660 and Brooklyn tumbling 11.5% to 415. Homes arealso lingering longer,with the typical property now sitting 88 days before a deal, two weeks more than last fall. The citywide median asking price slipped 5.2% to $995,000.
Queens was the rare bright spot. Contracts there rose 9.3% to 353, powered by a 12.4% spike in co-op deals.
But don’t call it a buyer’s market just yet. More than 21% of homes still fetched above their asking price, a slight uptick from a year ago. And despite the listing bonanza, overall inventory dropped 4.9% to 16,737 homes, extending a losing streak that has run every single month of 2026.
Long Island City blew every other neighborhood out of the water. New listings there more than tripled, soaring 205.4% to 113 homes asa string of new developmentsopened sales. The median ask came in at $1.14 million.
Flatiron grabbed the No. 2 spot with 99 new listings, a 67.8% leap, at a median price of $2.725 million. Tribeca followed with 81 listings, up 30.7%, carrying an eye-watering median ask of $5.1 million.
On the more affordable end, Washington Heights saw listings climb 42.1% to 54, with a median price of just $539,500. Astoria jumped 28.4% to 95 homes at a median of $999,000, while Williamsburg added 109 listings, up 26.7%, at $1.45 million.
The Upper East Side remained the volume king by a mile, with 603 new listings, up 17.5%.
In Manhattan, the action is coming from people who already own. Resale condo listings surged 15.8% to 1,054, while brand-new sponsor units shrank 18% to just 155 as fewer towers make it out of the ground.
“While neighborhoods like Long Island City saw surges in new listings driven by new development launches, the pipeline of new developments across the city is starting to dry up,” Lee said. “That means that many neighborhoods, like the Flatiron District, are seeing jumps in new listings primarily from condo owners cashing in on resilient demand for resale condos.”
Meanwhile, would-be buyers spooked by rates are staying put as tenants, and that’s making life miserable for everyone hunting for a lease.
Rental inventory plunged 15.3% to 29,029 units, the steepest annual drop in four years. Manhattan’s median asking rent held firm at $4,995, up 8% from last year and shrugging off the usual post-summer dip. Brooklyn’s rental supply shriveled 18.4%, with the median rent there climbing to $3,945, while Queens hit $3,400.

hed: The state desperately needs more housing. Could an old Army barracks at Devens be part of the answer?
content: It’s the kind of field trip that would be fun for an architect, or maybe a historian.The nearly century-old buildings that comprise Vicksburg Square drew a different kind of visitor last month: government officials from the towns of Harvard, Ayer, and Shirley. They came to get a closer look at this impressive but weather-beaten brick campus, and to dream aloud about how to fill it up again.The 400,000-square-foot-plus barracks complex, empty now for three decades, straddles the Ayer and Harvard town line while actually sitting in the jurisdiction of a quasi-public state entity, MassDevelopment. Their tour guide was Michael Sweeney, MassDevelopment’s relatively new appointee to oversee all the former Devens base properties, spanning some 4,400 acres across the three towns.The bad news: It will cost $44 million for environmental remediation in Vicksburg’s four main buildings to get them ready to be converted to apartments. The good news: MassDevelopment seems more eager than it has in a long time to make such a conversion happen. The 90-acre innovation and technology district where Vicksburg is located at Devens still needs to be rezoned for housing. Toward that end, MassDevelopment is drawing up a rezoning proposal that would go to all three towns for their approval in the spring of next year. It’s all part of a broader effort by the Healey administration to turn unused state parcels into residences, to address the state’s pressing need for more housing construction.Although repurposing state land has been done under previous administrations, these projects seem to be gaining momentum lately. Consider the groundbreaking by Vivmark (formerly AvalonBay) for nearly 500 apartments at Salem State University on Friday, or Trinity Financial’s plan to finally launch on a similar complex at the old Medfield State Hospital, hopefully later this year. Last month, the Healey administration put out a call for developers interested in building several hundred units at a former reform school in Lancaster. That followed the decision to work with Concord officials to reimagine the foreboding, shuttered prison that butts up against Route 2 as a new neighborhood.Perhaps nowhere on state-controlled land is there more potential for new housing than at Devens. Thirty years after the Army base closed, Devens is now a booming industrial park with nearly 100 employers, ranging from drugmaker Bristol Myers Squibb to metals manufacturer VulcanForms, collectively drawing more than 7,500 workers. Getting housing built in Devens has been a much trickier proposition. Until the Legislature interceded in 2024, a strict cap in state law essentially kept development at fewer than 300 units. Now that the cap has been lifted, MassDevelopment is seeking developers for the remaining residential land. It just designated Metro West Collaborative Development to build on a 6.6-acre parcel, though it still hasn’t awarded the bigger prize: rights for 63 acres along Grant Road.More potential awaits in the “innovation district” area of Devens that includes Vicksburg Square, if MassDevelopment can finally succeed with a rezoning. To pull it off, a majority of voters in each of the three base towns of Shirley, Ayer, and Harvard need to approve at simultaneous town meetings — the so-called super town meeting. In 2012, Shirley went along with a plan by Trinity Financial to convert Vicksburg into apartments, while Harvard and Ayer voters did not.To streamline this quirky system, Governor Maura Healey included language in her newest economic development bill that would have combined these votes into one town meeting, to be held at Devens, and open to all three towns’ voters. That didn’t go over well with the towns, so state lawmakers kept this provision out of more recent versions of that legislation — a controversy that’s now apparently in the rearview.SusanMary Redinger, Harvard’s Select Board chair, says officials in her town are encouraged by MassDevelopment’s reengagement on Vicksburg, as well as broader jurisdictional questions around Devens that need to be answered in the coming years. Redinger says Sweeney and Navjeet Bal, MassDevelopment’s chief executive, have shown they want to work collaboratively with the towns to resolve both of these hot-button issues. Likewise, state Senator Jamie Eldridge, whose district includes much of Devens, says he’s cautiously optimistic that Vicksburg can be reborn now that MassDevelopment under Bal’s leadership is reestablishing good relationships with the communities. But he is not sure if enough state and federal funds can be found to remediate the old Army barracks, given that $44 million price tag.Now, it’s up to MassDevelopment to craft zoning changes that are palatable to all three communities and also allow for enough development to make home construction in and around Vicksburg financially feasible. It will take far more than a fun field trip to pull that off. However, as Redinger put it after returning home, the Vicksburg visit was a good start to what will be a long process.Jon Chesto can be reached at jon.chesto@globe.com. Follow him @jonchesto.

hed: Maine’s ‘endangered’ blueberry theme park is up for sale
content: This story was published originally on boston.com.An endangered roadside blueberry attraction in Maine is up for sale.Wild Blueberry Land in Columbia Falls opened in 2001 and includes a 26-foot tall blueberry-shaped geodesic dome. The quirky attraction just landed on the state’s list of most endangered historic places in 2026, released by Maine Preservation.The property along Route 1 in Washington County is owned by blueberry farmers Dell and Marie Emerson of Wescogus Wild Blueberry in nearby Addison, who have dedicated their lives to the blueberry industry.A “for sale” sign is posted on the land, but there’s no online listing and the sale price has not been made public, reported The Bangor Daily News. The couple asks that interested buyers contact their farm.The property, open seasonally from June to October, sees 15,000 to 20,000 visitors per year, according to Maine Public. Inside the blueberry-shaped dome, guests can shop for blueberry merchandise in the retail shop, buy scratch-made pies, pastries, jams, and other sweets in the bakery, and learn about the state’s official berry in the blueberry museum. Outside, there’s a blueberry-themed miniature golf course and a whimsical yellow brick road.“A day doesn’t go by that someone doesn’t tell me a wonderful story about Wild Blueberry Land,” Marie Emerson told The Bangor Daily News. “It means a lot to the people that have visited … and people love the building.”Dell, a legend in Maine’s blueberry industry, is an 11th-generation farmer who worked for more than 50 years for the University of Maine at the nation’s only wild blueberry research farm, Blueberry Hill Farm. That’s where he met Marie, an award-winning chef who taught at Maine Community College System for 30 years and makes the blueberry treats sold on the property, according to the farm’s website.In 2016, Dell and Marie helped found the nonprofit Wild Blueberry Heritage Center, which has managed Wild Blueberry Land and expanded its educational programming. The board recently voted to dissolve the organization, according to Maine Preservation, and the remaining money was given to the Passamaquoddy Nation for the opening of museums in Sipayik and Motahkomikuk.Wild Blueberry Land, which is an hour drive past Acadia National Park, has experienced a decline in tourism, according to Maine Preservation. However, the Downeast Maine National Heritage Area, designated in 2023, includes Washington and Hancock counties and “represents an exciting opportunity to leverage celebration of the wild blueberry in shaping the future of the region,” wrote Maine Preservation.The geodesic dome is structurally sound, noted Maine Preservation.“Their ideal owner for Wild Blueberry Land would be the Passamaquoddy Nation, who were the original stewards of the land where the property now sits. Dell and Marie are open to considering any potential buyers who agree to maintain the structures of Wild Blueberry Land and to continue its important educational work,” wrote Maine Preservation.“I don’t want to see the building destroyed,” Marie Emerson told Maine Public. “It has to be the right person.”

hed: Inside the $12.5M Colorado estate with hidden mountainside car gallery
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


A Colorado estate with a car gallery built into the mountainside has hit the market for $12.5 million.
Set on nearly 7 acres along the eighth fairway of Castle Pines Golf Club, 3 Elk Pointe Lane in The Village at Castle Pines spans about 13,800 square feet. The property is poised to become the highest-priced residential sale in Castle Rock.
The owners, Lewis and Rebecca Kling, built the home with architect Don Ruggles and the builder Montare.
“The owners haven’t made any updates, as they were very precise with their design 16 years ago,” says listing agentStacie Chadwick of LIV Sotheby’s International Realty, who shares the listing withJustin Joseph.
That precision is evident from the moment you step inside, where an 8-foot-wide gallery runs 140 feet beneath 21-foot ceilings, lined with walnut floors and limestone pillars, before ending at a floor-to-ceiling wall of glass.
“The architect thoughtfully positioned the residence on its nearly 7-acre site to capture the surrounding landscape, even shifting the home inches during construction to perfectly frame Pikes Peak through the center of its dramatic entry gallery,” Chadwick says.
Solid walnut carries through the floors, doors, cabinetry, and coffered ceilings. A two-story water feature accompanies a floating walnut-and-steel staircase, and there are a total of 11 fireplaces, seven inside and four out.
The dining room seats 12 beneath three crystal chandeliers and opens to a 400-bottle wine room. The kitchen features Gaggenau appliances, bar seating for six, and a TV that rises into view.
The primary suite includes a fireplace, a private deck, and a bath with a three-sided steam shower. Four lower-level en suite bedrooms each open to a deck or patio, part of roughly 8,000 square feet of outdoor space connected to every room in the house.
There’s also a theater with a 108-inch screen, a fitness suite with a sauna, and a panic room. A Crestron/Vantage system controls about 620 interior and exterior lights.
The showpiece, however, remains hidden. The roughly 3,400-square-foot subterranean gallery holds about 10 cars, which reach the circular drive by hydraulic elevator. It has its own kitchen, bar, fireplace, and bathroom. There’s also Hermès-inspired etched glass and a fire pit overlooking the fairway.
Outside, a trail leads to a heated treehouse, and commissioned sculptures by Colorado artist Jim Vilona dot the grounds. The home was a 2016 Colorado Homes & Lifestyles Home of the Year finalist, and its landscape earned a Grand Award from the National Association of Landscape Professionals.
Residents of the community have access to two Jack Nicklaus–designed golf courses, trails, and tennis and pickleball courts.
“The combination of architectural vision, engineering, art, privacy, and extraordinary amenities creates a property that would be exceptionally difficult to replicate today,” Chadwick says.

hed: Killer tides pummel Malibu’s ritziest enclave as celeb homes sit unsold: ‘It’s so depressing’
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Inside Malibu Colony on Saturday, the guard-gated enclave’s high-powered homeowners were cleaning up afterhigh tides tore awaymany of their oceanfront decks and the stairs leading down to the beach.
Wood planks and rusty nails churned in the surf. Shards of glass from blown-out windows piled up on battered deckslike a Hollywood crime scene— the aftermath of Tropical Storm Rachel’spunishing wavesand unusually high tides.
Other residents weremopping up seawaterand sand that had seeped into their homes and prized tea houses. A Colony association meeting was canceled Saturday so neighbors could tend to the damage.
“It’s so depressing, first you have to drive through where the wildfires were and now this. Anybody who comes here for Thanksgiving is crazy. You’d only be able to cook half a turkey before the electricity is turned off [due to high winds],” one Colony board member told The Post.
The Colony got off easier than Newport Beach and Long Beach, where waves crashed over seawalls and flooded streets. But the enclave is still hurting. Sales have stalled as residents and buyers sit tight, and brokers expect three more king tides before year’s end.
“Malibu Colony is low-key but everybody here is super rich. Whenever anyone talks about the fires, they never mention Malibu. Everyone thinks, ‘F–k you, you are already rich and this is probably your second home even though so many homes burned down,’” a resident said.
Malibu is often dubbed the “wildfire capital” of North America, and roughly 700 homes inside city limits were destroyed in the 2025 Palisades Fire. Flames returned to the Malibu hills late Thursday afternoon, when the Bryson Fire broke out in brush near Encinal Canyon Road and Mulholland Highway.
Fanned by fierce Santa Ana winds, it scorched 200 acres by evening with zero containment. Evacuation orders and warnings were issued for parts of the area, though no structures had burned and no one had been injured at press time.
Known as the Colony, or the original Malibu, the enclave has been a Hollywood power base since the days of Gloria Swanson, Mary Pickford and Charlie Chaplin, and later Jack Warner, Bing Crosby, Jane Fonda and Frank Capra. Past and present residents include Tom Hanks and Rita Wilson, Ridley Scott, Chris Columbus, Spike Jonze, the late Rob and Michele Reiner, Jim Carrey, Paul Reiser, Ed Norton and Red Hot Chili Peppers bassist Flea.
Jonze is among the Colony’s current sellers. The Oscar-winning filmmaker and music video director behind “Being John Malkovich,” “Adaptation,” “Where the Wild Things Are” and “Her” paid $18 million for the home in 2023. The seller was “Touched by an Angel” actress Roma Downey, who bought it years before her 2007 marriage to “Survivor” and “The Apprentice” producer Mark Burnett.
The five-bedroom Cape Cod-style house, built in 1963, is now asking $22 million. It has ocean views and a pool, a rarity in the Colony.
The main suite comes with a fireplace, sitting areas, a sundeck and a skylight, while a third floor could work as a screening lounge, home office or extra sleeping space. Beamed ceilings and ample room for indoor-outdoor entertaining round out the package.
Still, the threat of coastal flooding has injected fresh uncertainty into the deal, sources say.
“I considered buying it, but now with all of this weather and the unknowns, I’m going to hold off,” one prospective buyer told Gimme Shelter. “No-one’s buying now.”
Listing broker Damon Skelton of Compass declined to comment.
Flea, whose real name is Michael Peter Balzary, has also listed his Colony home. It’s asking $7.995 million, down from $8.495 million in March. The bassist paid $7.55 million for the four-bedroom, built in 1959, in 2020. Listing brokers Sandro Dazzan and Irene Dazzan-Palmer of The Agency declined to comment.
The next high tides are expected in late October and November.
“[This period] will bring a lot of damage with it as there is not a lot of time to put in protective measures,” a resident said, adding that a full moon around Christmas could push tides to between 6 feet 7 inches and 7 feet 2 inches.
“If this happens in Malibu and no one has been red-tagged, then tragedy is coming,” the resident added. “[The king tides] will cause damage on top of damage and no one will be down here to see it. That’s all I know, as this danger is a new reality.”
As for the full moon, the resident said, “They are usually lovely to watch. Not this year.”

hed: Long-lost Keith Haring mural that spent decades hidden behind drywall hits market in $25M Tribeca loft
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

For years, downtown diners ate dinner a few feet from a Keith Haring and had no clue.
Now that long-buried mural,painted by the pop art iconback when he was a broke art student, is the main attraction in a $25 million Tribeca triplex that just landed on the market.
The 8,000-square-foot maisonette sits inside the American Thread Building at 260 West Broadway, a Renaissance Revival landmark built in 1896. Ian Slater, Michael Koeneke and Eduardo Martinez of Trove Partners at Compass are shopping the seven-bedroom, nine-bathroom spread.
There’s just one wrinkle for buyers. The Haring stays put.
“It’s a piece of New York City’s art history that can never be recreated or moved,” owner Adam Zoia told The Post.
Haring made the black-and-white work in 1979, when he was enrolled at the School of Visual Arts and the school ran a student gallery out of the building’s lower floor. He didn’t splurge on supplies. The future art star brushed on a homemade concoction of black shoe polish and alcohol, sending his trademark tangle of lines across two walls, the ceiling and a cast iron column that helps hold up the building.
“TheKeith Haring muralis one of a kind,” Zoia said, adding that “it’s in a corner painted on both walls and even the ceiling, its scale is large, it’s painted in part over a cast iron column and it was painted by Keith before he was famous when he was only 20.”
The piece very nearly vanished. After SVA cleared out in the early 1980s, the space was turned into a restaurant and the mural was sealed behind sheetrock, where it sat in the dark for decades. That cover turned out to be a lucky break, shielding the fragile work until the unit’s previous owners tore into the walls during a 2007 renovation and found it largely intact. The Keith Haring Foundation later confirmed the unsigned piece as an early Haring.
Zoia, the CEO of Glocap Tech, snapped up the loft in 2021 and spent two years gutting it. Crews overhauled the HVAC and other guts of the home, laid marble floors, added Venetian plaster and reworked both the main level and the primary closet.
Protecting the Haring drove the redesign. Zoia built a custom bar in front of part of the mural to keep guests from brushing against it or splashing drinks on it, while the artwork keeps climbing up the wall and over the ceiling behind the bottles.
So what’s a shoe polish masterpiece worth? Nobody will say. Because it’s painted right onto the building’s columns, beam, ceiling and walls, the mural can’t be pried loose or sold on its own, according to reps for the sellers.
“You can put a price on real estate, but it’s nearly impossible to put a value on something this rare,” Slater said. “What makes this property so exceptional is that the artwork is inseparable from the home itself, creating a rare opportunity for a buyer to own an irreplaceable work by an artist of such significance.”
The developer who first spotted the mural told Slater the artwork runs “well beyond that little area” that was exposed, stretching across much of the wall in the home’s main room. That means whoever buys the place could, in theory, go looking for the rest.
The rest of the pad isn’t too shabby either.
The main floor centers on a 45-by-45-foot great room with 28-foot ceilings, three massive arched windows, white oak floors and designer lighting. There’s a chef’s kitchen with doubled-up appliances and room to seat 22 for dinner. A curved, marble-inlaid staircase leads up to two guest suites, the primary suite and a home office walled in curved glass that peers down over the great room.
The primary suite plays like its own apartment, with a five-piece bath, a powder room and a huge custom closet.
Downstairs, a nearly 2,000-square-foot lower level holds three more en-suite bedrooms and a kitchenette, plus a home spa and party zone. Think an eight-seat soundproof screening room, a brick-walled gym, an infrared sauna, a cold plunge and a game room.
Residents also get a 24-hour doorman, a building gym and a private roof deck. The property, once known as the Wool Exchange Building, was among Tribeca’s earliest luxury condo conversions and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.
Zoia is selling as he looks to downsize, and he’s clear-eyed about who the next owner really answers to.
“Whoever owns this home next isn’t just buying a property that includes the trading floor of the American Wool Association,” he said. “They’re becoming the caretaker of arare work of art.”

hed: Why Gen Z and millennials are choosing rent over ownership at shockingly high rate
subhead: Why wealthy households are choosing to rent
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.


More of America’s highest-income households are choosing not to turn their purchasing power into homeownership in a rental market that offers them more flexibility, mobility, and choice.
The number of U.S. households earning at least $1 million a year while renting the home they live in rose 229% between 2020 and 2024, climbing to about 18,400 households, according to a new RentCafe analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data.
“Standard measures treat renting as a fallback for people who can’t buy. Here, the top of the income distribution may increasingly be renting by choice,” explains Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.
And overwhelmingly, young high-income households are the ones leveraging that choice. Nearly half (49%) of millionaire renters are Millennials, whose numbers surged 392% between 2020 and 2024. While Gen Z accounts for just 2% of the market, its millionaire renter population grew 46-fold over the same period—the fastest of any generation.
Millionaire homeowner households also grew rapidly over the same period, rising 193%. Renters still make up only a small share of $1 million-income households, but their share rose from 8% to just under 9%, according to Jones.
It suggests that the trend isn’t a rejection of homeownership but a generational complication of it. These younger millionaires came of age in a housing market dominated by the ultralow mortgage rate homebuying boom and the steep run-up in home prices and borrowing costs that followed.
And for many, it would seem, that made buying less of an obvious next step—even once they could afford it.
Some of the dramatic growth comes down to math, according to Jones.
“Part of the gap is a base effect, since renters started from far fewer households; it is possible to see more growth,” she explains.
The total number of households earning at least $1 million nearly tripled, from about 70,000 to 208,000, and owners accounted for the overwhelming majority of that increase. In absolute terms, renter households grew by roughly 12,800, compared with about 125,000 additional millionaire homeowners.
Jones also notes that the $1 million threshold is nominal rather than adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the growth reflects more households crossing a fixed income benchmark over time.
Even so, the math still doesn’t explain why high earners might find renting attractive in the first place.

On that front, the occupational makeup of millionaire renters offers some clues. RentCafe’s data says many work as chief executives, technology professionals, and financial managers—high-paying careers that can come with greater geographic mobility.
And renting gives these professionals something ownership doesn’t: the ability to easily move.
About 21.6% of people living in renter-occupied households changed residences in 2024, compared with 6.2% of those living in owner-occupied households, according toU.S. Census Bureau data. Renters were also roughly three times as likely to have moved from another state.
That mobility can carry economic value of its own, particularly early in a career, when changing jobs—and sometimes cities—can open the door to better opportunities. Workers in their first seven years of employment got roughly 36% to 42% of their cumulative earnings growth from moves between employers, according to a2021 study using U.S. Census Bureau employer-employee data.
RentCafe says this dynamic is particularly visible in Houston, where affluent newcomers—including executives, professional athletes, and entertainers—often rent after relocating before deciding whether to buy.
Homeowners, meanwhile, are getting hit with more incentives to stay put.Federal Reserve researchers estimatethat mortgage rate lock-in explained 44% of the decline in mortgage-borrower mobility from 2021 to 2022.
The rate cycle also helps explain why millionaire renting survived a period that initially seemed tailor-made for buying.
“The rate environment worked both for and against these households,” Jones says. Ultralow rates made borrowing cheap early in the period, but inventory was scarce.
“By the time inventory started to recover, both prices and rates were higher, making buying less attractive,” she adds.

hed: Who wins and who gets burned as The Plaza goes dark for four years
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The Plaza Hotel willshut its doorsfor at least four years starting in January 2027 , with operator Fairmont Hotels and Resorts saying the 18-story Fifth Avenue landmark needs a top-to-bottom restoration of its historic facade . City Buildings inspectors found the facade unsafe in their latest review, the reason a sidewalk shed already hugs the building.
The news ricocheted far beyond Manhattan within hours.
“I woke up this morning to many, many messages of, is this true? Is this happening? Did you hear this?” Julie Estes, founder of event production firm SOP House, who has worked events at the Plaza since 2007, told The Post.
“It’s not just the most iconic hotel in New York. It’s the most iconic hotel in the world,” she added.
So who comes out ahead, and who gets stuck holding the bag? The Post breaks it down.
Talk about timing. Park Avenue’s other legendreopened last yearafter a closure dating to 2017 and amakeoverpegged at roughly $2 billion , and it now looks like the default destination for anyone who had their heart set on the Plaza.
Leslie Wilson, senior EVP and managing director at Douglas Elliman Development Marketing, sounded downright bullish.
“With The Plaza preparing to close for an extended period, we expect renewed attention on New York’s historic luxury properties with high levels of hotel services,” Wilson said, calling theWaldorf “a unique combinationof residential living and world-class hospitality that few properties can replicate.”
Couples chasing white-glove, Gilded Age glamour have other places to turn, and Estes rattled off a short list.
“The Pierre is right next to the plaza and it has a wonderful history in the city,” she said. For something sleeker nearby, “the Mandarin’s really close by as well.”
She also pointed to the Rainbow Room, which she described as “another fantastic, iconic ballroom in our city that has gorgeous views,” along with Cipriani’s grand halls on 42nd Street, Wall Street, Broadway and South Street. Some of those rooms are smaller, but they carry the same pedigree, she said.
Pricing shouldn’t scare off Plaza defectors either. Venue minimums plus catering tabs land in roughly the same territory across the top tier, Estes said, because “they’re all of a similar caliber.” A typical wedding at these venues runs $250,000 to $500,000.
And Aman New York, the hushed luxury retreat inside the Crown Building a few blocks down Fifth, sits ready to absorb deep-pocketed guests who would otherwise have checked in across from Central Park.
Douglas Elliman’s Michael Passaro, who has brokered numerous deals inside The Plaza, expects buyers to drift to the supertalls along 57th Street and the towers of Central Park South.
“I don’t think many people are gonna be too thrilled about going to look at The Plaza in the near future,” he said.
Roughly 29 Plaza condos are already on the market, Passaro said, and he suspects a few more owners are quietly shopping theirs.
“I think it is going to be difficult to sell in the building over the next couple years,” he said, predicting that “buyers will be able to find deals from certain sellers.”
“Negotiability, I think it’s just gone up for anybody that’s looking possibly to purchase in the building,” he added.
Patience could pay off. “They’ll have a fully restored facade that protects the building’s values for decades,” Passaro said of long-haul owners, who could cash in big once a polished Plaza reopens.
“It’s a short-term inconvenience for a long-term gain,” he said.
Weddings at venues like this are often locked in six months to a year or more ahead, according to Estes, since the venue is the first thing couples nail down. That leaves plenty of 2027 celebrations suddenly homeless.
“People dream of having a wedding or an event there,” she said.
The silver lining, she said, is that the high-end vendors who work Plaza events tend to rally when a venue falls through. “They band together and they shift and really work as a team to make the change as easy and smooth as possible for the client,” Estes said.
The Hotel and Gaming Trades Council said in a statement that the 378 members working at the hotel will be able to return to their jobs at the same pay when it reopens. Four years is still a long time to wait.
Estes said the fate of longtime employees, including the hotel’s in-house CPS Events team that books every gala and wedding, is the industry’s top talking point. Staff had heard “there were some rumblings,” she said, but “I think the actual announcement of it was rather sudden.”
She offered one bright spot. “I think it’s a really great time to be looking for an opportunity or a position in the industry,” Estes said.
The residents of the Plaza’s 181 condos  aren’t being forced out, according to Passaro, whose clients in the building checked with management and doormen. But they will lose the hotel amenities and services, plus live behind scaffolding for years.
Gone too, Passaro said, is “the vibe and the energy of such an iconic property.”
Selling won’t be easy. Passaro closed a $10.625 million sale in the building in February 2025, and the buyer relisted the apartment about a year later. Many units haven’t been updated since the condos first hit the market two decades ago, and buyers balk at gut jobs.
“It’s been a little bit of a challenge to get people excited about doing a renovation because obviously the costs have gone up drastically,” he said.
Out-of-towners who planned a pilgrimage to the hotel where Macaulay Culkin’s Kevin McCallister famously checked in on his dad’s credit card in “Home Alone 2”  have one last window. Passaro expects the hotel to be mobbed through the holidays as New Yorkers and visitors grab a farewell cocktail at the Palm Court.
As for when the doors reopen, even the brokers are hedging. Four years could easily stretch to five or six, Passaro said, adding that “nobody knows.”

hed: Mortgage rates are soaring, another blow to Mass. housing affordability as buyers face higher monthly payments
content: What Caitlin Fontecchio and her family have been attempting to pull off this year — selling their home in Worcester to buy a bigger, newly built house in nearby Warren — was already a delicate balancing act. Then the global economy tipped the scales against her.After steadily declining for more than a year, mortgage rates have soared in recent months, particularly in September, as the average on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is now at nearly 7.3 percent — the highest since 2023. The surge is adding potentially $1,000 to a monthly payment for a typical home purchase in Greater Boston. It’s a huge financial blow to prospective home buyers. And suddenly, no one is coming to see Fontecchio’s home in Worcester. Two open houses for the place — a cozy, 2,500-square-foot colonial a mile from Union Station — did not draw a single prospective buyer, even after the family cut the price to under $450,000. So in a state with so much pent-up demand for housing, taking on a mortgage has become so expensive that many moderate-income buyers have all but given up.“It’s left me wondering: Is there something wrong with our house?” Fontecchio, 38, said. “We’ve tried to do everything the right way. Not even our agent seems to understand why it won’t sell.”Related: Boston’s housing market is so out of whack that it’s in a class largely by itselfThe market for home sales has been effectively frozen since early 2022, when mortgage rates began to soar after nearly a decade of decline. Rates more than doubled in a nine-month span in 2022 and have, for the most part, remained at those high levels, sidelining both would-be buyers and sellers daunted by the prospect of higher monthly payments on top of the region’s sky-high home prices.There was a brief period of optimism earlier this year when the average for a 30-year fixed-rate loan slid below 6 percent for the first time in four years. Some sellers, including Fontecchio and her husband, dipped their toes back into the market. But any modest progress has been swiftly erased in recent months.Last week, the average on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.28 percent, according to Freddie Mac, after months of steep increases. A combination of worrisome issues, including persistent inflation, volatile fuel prices from the war in Iran, and surging US debt levels, has prompted investors in the bond market to demand higher yields, and that’s flowed through to mortgage loans.Caitlin Fontecchio's son Vincent crawled up the steps to the family's back shed with their dog, Dolcezza.Meleck Eldahshoury for The Boston GlobeFontecchio stands for a portrait at the window by her stairs. She and her husband want to buy a new home in nearby Warren, with a larger, safer yard for their children.Meleck Eldahshoury for The Boston GlobeIt’s a blow to housing affordability, as the higher rates mean higher monthly housing payments for new buyers. For families that had hoped they might have the means to afford a new place, the math has shifted dramatically. “What you are effectively seeing when rates rise by that much, that quickly, is thousands of buyers being priced out of the marketplace,” said Theresa Hatton, CEO of the Massachusetts Association of Realtors. “You have a lot of people who maybe could’ve bought six months ago at 6 percent who are now realizing they’d have to pay $1,000 more a month on the same house.” All that leaves people like Fontecchio and her husband, Anthony Pellechio, in limbo. The couple — who together earn about $150,000 a year — see the problem from both sides as buyers and sellers. They bought their current home for $365,000 in 2020 and have fixed it up, with new windows, appliances, and solar panels. But with two kids and a third on the way, they want a bigger yard, and Fontecchio longs for the quiet outside of the city. They have a house in Warren under agreement — four bedrooms with a big yard that’s supposed to be complete in November, around the time Fontecchio is due to give birth.But with interest rates rising, the couple slashed the asking price on their Worcester home to attract buyers. Any further concessions may mean they won’t have enough for the new house, which they’ve agreed to buy for just over $500,000. The prevailing feeling, said Fontecchio, is disillusionment with the economy. She and her husband entered the job market during the Great Recession and have struggled with student loan debt. Now they’re trying to navigate a turbulent housing market that makes it difficult to take advantage of the equity they’ve built in their current home.“It would be very disappointing to have come this far and lose out on our next home because of fuel prices and geopolitical instability,” she said.Related: Is there anywhere in Mass. that is accessible to middle-income households? See where you can afford to buy a house.Housing costs have long been high in Massachusetts, but grew especially fast over the last decade, driven by population growth, a surge in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic, and decades of underbuilding that made for a huge shortage of homes. Since 2016, home values in the region have grown by over 50 percent, according to one national index.But homeownership was still relatively accessible during that stretch, at least for some middle-income families, because mortgage rates were historically low. During an 18-month period in 2020 and 2021, a 30-year fixed-rate loan averaged around 3 percent, according to Freddie Mac, the lowest point since the company began tracking rates in 1971. If you could afford a down payment, monthly mortgage costs were often lower than rents. But higher mortgage rates have erased any semblance of affordability.In August 2021, the typical monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home of $780,000 in Greater Boston was about $2,554, according to Bankrate’s mortgage calculator. In February of this year, when the median-priced house in the region sold for around $852,500, that monthly payment was more like $4,137. And in September, after interest rates began to soar again, it jumped to $5,168.There’s a mental hurdle that comes with the rise in rates too, said Paul Willen, a senior economist with the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. For buyers who can afford it, “there’s no logical reason why 7 is any different from 6 percent,” he said. “But there may be some sort of psychological difference at 7 that’s just too much.”For sellers, the higher rates feel like a cruel turn: many have much lower rates on their current home, so giving that up for such a significant step up is broadly unappealing, Willen said. “For a lot of people, if they want to move, they’re looking at, ‘Well, how much can I afford?’” Willen said. “And the answer is: something much smaller than the house they’re in.”Some sellers are taking a chance and putting their properties on the market anyway, said Mary Gillach, principal of the Gillach Group at William Raveis in Brookline. But it’s harder to predict if they will sell because so many buyers, especially middle-income families looking for a first home, simply cannot afford them.Related: The Globe’s housing reporter thought he’d have an edge finding an apartment. He had no idea what was coming.Homes that do sell quickly, Gillach said, are in a rare atmosphere: above $3 or $4 million, as their likely buyers have the means. Gillach listed a home in Brookline recently for $5 million that went under agreement within 24 hours, she said. But she can’t find a buyer anywhere for a home on Pond Street in Jamaica Plain priced at $1.7 million. Of course, there is more at play in the state’s housing market slowdown than just interest rates. The general state of the economy and the rising cost of everyday goods and services are weighing heavily on those who may otherwise be ready to purchase their first place. It is a vexing problem, said Melvin Vieira Jr., an agent at Re/Max Real Estate Center in Boston, because there is little anyone in Massachusetts can do about the global instability bringing down the housing market. “Uncertainty can be a powerful force when it comes to the housing market,” he said. “And right now, we have plenty of it.”Fontecchio carries her son downstairs.Meleck Eldahshoury for The Boston GlobeAndrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: Enjoy a healthy dose of Miami at its new luxury wellness condos
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Miami was already on a hardcore health kick. The last dose of luxury new-construction condos almost universally came with concierge medical services, saunas, plunge pools and infrared zap zones massaged in.
Buyers oohed and aahed, but now they want more — lots more. From the beach to Brickell, Miami is about to get a fresh injection of condos that function like more swish Swiss sanatoria than usual luxe residences.
In January, the Well Coconut Grove began manifesting a new eight-story sister to its Bay Harbor abodes.
Its 194 units at 2835 Tigertail Ave. are marketed by Douglas Elliman and range from $1.6 million for a one-bedroom to over $10 million for a four-bedroom.
Spend up a bit for your unit and you can choose from an array of “dens” (Longevity, Mindful or Mobility), or The Well Office.
But if you can’t nab one of those units, focus your third eye on this: a 13,000-square-foot Wellness Club and a 40,000-square-foot rooftop, designed, of course, as “an outdoor wellness oasis.”
The list of healing communal amenities is literally too long to list, but some highlights are a “recovery chair” said to reset the nervous system, a “fitness forest,” a bathhouse, a crystal cave and a hyperbaric chamber.
“People are becoming much more aware of how the choices they make every day can impact how they feel, perform and age. Increasingly, that means having them built into where they live rather than treating wellness as something they have to seek out,” says Kane Sarhan, co-founder of The Well and the Wellness Program Creator for the new 35-story, 229-unit HQ Residences Miami in Edgewater, which also has a wellness focus.
“The Well [Bay Harbor] was the first of its kind in South Florida,” adds Mike Martirena of Compass. “Now, developers are ramping it up. You could say it’s wellness on peptides.”
Martirena and business partner Ivan Chorney are co-listing a penthouse at the new 24-story, 61-unit Rivage Bal Harbour at 10245 Collins Ave. that asks, “What’s the fountain of youth worth?”
The Compass team, along with real estate firm Million Luxury, reckon about $75 million.
That’s the ask for the “longevity penthouse” — penthouse C on the building plan. It promises to blend “the science of longevity,” with “the art of living.”
Part home, part private clinic with three types of pods (hyperbaric, meditation and the multi-modality Ammortal), hospital-grade air filtration, whole-home water purification, full-spectrum cellular light and contrast therapy, it features all the “modalities of human regeneration.”
There are also four beds and four full baths, two elevators, 10,264 square feet of interior space and 9,531 square feet of outdoor terrace.
Over at 152 SW Ninth St. in Brickell, the 34-story, 656-unit House of Wellness is rising.
Prices range from $400,000 for a 335-square-foot studio to $1.1 million for top units (Fortune is handling sales), and for that price, each resident receives a health and wellness assessment, facilitating a custom wellness plan.
These shiny happy people will also get access to a private spa with the requisite sauna and steam rooms, a “wellness bar” for getting juiced up and a rooftop pool deck.
We’re picking up good vibrations.

hed: Scandi Dandies: Towers by Danish and Norwegian designers heighten New York’s skyline
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
New York’s skyline is getting serious Scandi style. Among the handful of significant new-construction residential towers currently coming online is a trio of buildings by a triumphant triumvirate of Danish and Norwegian designers.
One of the most striking newcomers to the Manhattan skyline is Five Points Development’s 26-unit, 52-story 262 Fifth Ave.
The tallest all-residential building on Fifth Avenue, it’s nearing completion now. The developer tapped Copenhagen-based Norm Architects to craft a Nordic “sanctuary in the sky.”
“There’s an appreciation for the minimalism, craftsmanship and exceptional quality of Norm Architects’ Scandinavian design,” says Nikki Field of Sotheby’s International Realty, who is operating the exclusive sales team for the building, where prices range from $7.5 million to $18 million for a duplex.
Norm used natural materials like oak and Grigio Alpi stone, as well as stainless steel in its design of these column-free “vertical villas.”
“At extreme heights, natural materials become grounding elements and tactile finishes counterbalance the panoramic views of Manhattan,” says Norm partner Peter Eland.
Steps from Lincoln Center, and half a block from the park, Oslo-based firm Snøhetta is making its US residential debut at 50 W. 66th St.
The 70-story tower is now the tallest on the Upper West Side after developer Extell completed construction in August.
Snøhetta is known for grand venues, like the Norwegian National Opera and Ballet and the Shanghai Grand Opera House, but here they’ve aimed for intimacy.
Despite its height, the building blends into the existing streetscape with a warm palette of hand-set, textured limestone and bronze-and-glass storefronts.
Meanwhile, the residential entrance welcomes owners with burnished bronze and limestone.
The goal: “an approachable neighborhood character.” Higher up, things become more geometric and sculptural, with the building’s opposing corners sliced away to create balconies and a “zipper of loggias” running the length of the facade. “Fifty West 66th will glow as a warm lantern, a new friend in the New York City skyline,” the firm states. The building’s top listing is asking $85 million with a team of brokers including Extell Marketing Group, Beth Benalloul and Hilary Landis of Corcoran, and Janice Chang of Douglas Elliman.
Finally, in Chelsea, New York’s favorite designing Dane, Thomas Juul-Hansen (sorry Bjarke Ingels), is the architect of 550 W. 21st St. The new 23-story, 83-unit by Legion Investment Group, located on the Hudson, is slated to complete construction next year, with one- to four-bedroom homes currently on the market ranging in price from $2.25 million to over $30 million with Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group.
Juul-Hansen drew on his experience growing up on the waterfront among historic brick warehouses in Denmark in his design. To create calm, he developed a palette of light-toned limestone, alabaster, bronze and natural stone. A reference to the neighborhood’s industrial history, a brick gatehouse fronts the entrance to a private motor court with a grove of birch trees, planted beds and a bubbling fountain.
Need serenity now? Perfect, it’s a Scandi design principle.

hed: Massachusetts home declared ‘Scariest House’ in New England by HGTV
subhead: Host Retta (“Parks and Recreation”) toured four New England houses on “Scariest House in America.” Here’s a peek at all of them.
content:
ByLauren Daley
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
An ancient jail cell. Eerie voices. A haunted closet. Chipmunk and bat infestations.
These are just some reasons given by four sets of New England homeowners making their case for having the“Scariest House in America.”
HGTV’s “Scariest House in America” sees hostRetta(who also hosts “Ugliest House in America”) exploring homes in a new region of the country each week. On Oct. 16, the hour-long episode explored “Nightmarish New England.” The episode is available to stream starting Oct. 17 on HBO MAX.
The episode featured homes in Guildhall, Vermont; Dighton, Massachusetts; Enfield, Connecticut; and Searsport, Maine.
Spoiler alert: Retta declared the Massachusetts home the scariest in the region, and it’s now among the top five regional winners. The house deemed scariest in America by HGTV will win a renovation from HGTV designer Alison Victoria in the season finale airing Oct. 23.
A Vermont home got that same winning treatment earlier this year when it won“Ugliest House in America.”
Here’s a look at each of New England’s scary house candidates.
It’s a large shingled home with peeling trim, circa 1751.
There are six residents, including Dave, Jen, and their family. “We hear stuff, see stuff,” says Jen.
“Lot of footsteps,” Dave adds. “We have rats and bats.”
Retta walks onto a sloping floor, and the show points out gaps in the walls and door as “signs of bad floor pitch.” In the parlor, Retta notices another soft-spot in the floor, which could be explained by trees being used as support beams in the basement.
Upstairs is a very unfinished attic, with rusty nails pointing out of every board, including the low ceiling. The attic had seen a bat infestation, and the camera shows what looks like bat droppings and a dead mouse, blurred out.
The owners take Retta to “the birthing room,” a small room that HGTV explains were common in the 18th century. In the primary bedroom, all the furniture has “shims” underneath to level it so drawers won’t open.
Jen claims the closet was opening by itself “only between 2 and 3 in the morning.”
The unassuming 2,274-square-foot home was built in 1878 and is owned by Cody and Jesse.
“I mean, the French porch could use some work,” Retta quips, adding that the house overall “doesn’t look scary.”
But, Jesse explains, “open up that big iron door in the back and here you are at the former Essex County jail.” HGTV explains the house was built to be the residence of the town jailer; the jail operated until 1969.
We see a hallway with rusted jail bars lining both sides. The ceilings and walls are cast iron. The electricity into the cells has been disconnected, Jesse explains, handing Retta a flashlight.
Cody says they have “not been brave enough to do anything with this part of the house yet,” as the camera peers into the cells themselves with cobwebs, an old mattress, rusty sinks and toilets. The jail is infested with spiders and chipmunks, the show points out. In the women’s cell, we see the footprint of an old shower, a toilet, a rusty bed frame, and a floor covered in dirt.
In the main bedroom, the “focal point is the witch window,” Jesse says. The window is slanted at a 45-degree angle “so witches can’t fly into your house.”
Built in 1874 by a sea captain, the large house looks “so pretty” from the outside with its white with green trim and red door, Retta says.
“It’s very pretty — and haunted,” owner Gillian says.
Gillian and Larry purchased the home in 2014, per HGTV. It was previously an inn and antique shop. Inside, there’s colorful pastel wallpaper and ornate carpeting.
Troops lived in the home during WWII to protect against invasion, HGTV says, and the home was formerly owned by impressionist and pal of Ernest Hemingway,Waldo Peirce.
But the house is not as “pretty” as it seems, the owners claim. Wallpaper will peel off the wall, they say. One light fixture “just started to drip some liquid,” Larry says. The bed often looks slept in, says Gillian.
They bring Retta into a bedroom with a fireplace where bats come down the chimney “fairly regularly.” In another bedroom, the ceiling has a rotting hole, dropping chunks to the ground.
“She definitely has spirits,” says Gillian.
An unassuming duplex built in 1771, painted in faded yellow and olive green “doesn’t seem that scary,” Retta says.
Elke, Jay and their twin daughters live there, and they tell Retta it’s a two-family home — they live on one side and “the ghosts live next door.” No tenant has lasted more than a year, the show explains.
Jay says they bought the house 20 years ago for an offer they couldn’t refuse: $122,000.
A paranormal investigator, Jim, tells the camera, “This place has been a hotspot of activity. We’ve had growls, disembodied voices, footsteps.”
Lauren Daley is a freelance culture writer. She can be reached at[email protected]. She tweets@laurendaley1and Instagrams at@laurendaley1.
