hed: My neighborhood Karen tried to shut down my Halloween display, but I’m fighting back
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
The Craigslist ad was just three words: Free Halloween decorations.
That was all Nate Taylor, 49, a part-time DJ and stay-at-home dad inTraverse City, MI, needed. He met the woman giving away a holiday collection spanning 20 years.
“Really, ma’am? You want us to take this?” he asked. She was downsizing due to a recent divorced, so the answer was a resounding yes.
It took Taylor three trips in his truck to transport the animatronics and other decorations back home. He then set to work making a plan to display as much as possible in front of hisCape Cod-style homewith a 40-foot-wide yard near Kid’s Creek Park.
Most of the decor wasn’t really weatherproof, so Taylor had to construct a makeshift tarp, anchored by a sizable branch of a big tree in the yard.
He was so proud of what he had though, in 2017, he invited passersby and neighbors to enjoy the display—and he had a decent turnout.
Being located close to Munson Medical, the city’s biggest hospital, many visitors who stopped by had family members in the hospital. As the display leaned more toward whimsical, not scary, it was a welcomed respite.
“I’m not into blood and gore or jump scares,” Taylor says.
Inspired, the next year, Taylor created a bigger covered area and put out more decorations, including a big graveyard with headstones. Word had begun to spread, and out-of-town guests were starting to arrive to see his display.
Year after year, Taylor and his wife kept building on the display. By 2021, they started going “all night,” which started to draw anywhere from 30 to 40 visitors are night, by their estimation.
“That doesn’t sound like a lot, but for a seasonal display, it is.”
They wanted to share the joy with even more people, especially neurodivergent and special needs kids and groups. Taylor has two kids on the autism spectrum, and had long been disappointed that during Halloween, there is “nothing for special needs kids to do overall.”
That’s really his goal in doing this–to create a safe, entertaining space that is “easily accessible and free” to the special needs community.
“We have never charged a dime–not one–for any ticket,” he says.
In 2023, Taylor put out a guestbook, and that’s where he saw that several people suggested he put out a donation box.
“We didn’t need it,” he says. “I am grateful my wife has a decent job at the hospital.”
But the build does take him two months, which is time away from family and home responsibilities. In mid October 2023, he followed the suggestion and added a donation box. It brought in $1,200.
Taylor insists that “every penny helps with the build,” and that by “no means” is anyone charged to see his display.
In 2024, his neighbors helped him get hisDead Ends on Sprucedisplay up on Facebook so more families could enjoy it. That year saw the biggest crowds, with Taylor estimating that 18,000 people, including six school groups, visited throughout the month of October.
Then Taylor took 2025 off to care for two ailing family members, including his mother who was fighting colon cancer and has now had a full recovery.
He was ready to come back strong in 2026. As he does every year, he started on August 1 by meeting with fire marshals and the city manager in charge of code enforcement to share his plans. He also requested that his street be shut down to traffic on Halloween night as an additional safety precaution, something he started doing in 2024.
The city had always consented and there had never been a problem–until this year.
According to Taylor, one of his neighbor’s complained to the city, accusing him of running a business from his yard by “selling tickets” for the display.
In response, Taylor said the city sent him a “four-page letter from the city’s lawyers” outlining the rules and regulations that need to be followed for home operations.
“They think I am a business,” Taylor says,” I am not.” (Realtor.com reached out to city officials for comment on this story, but did not immediately hear back.)
In reading the letter over, there was one rule in particular that would be especially hard to enforce: No more than eight car trip ends.
In other words, no more than eight cars at a time can park infront of the display.If a ninth car comes, the city can shut him down.
Taylor contested that all of this was initiated by a complaint that was never thoroughly investigated.
“So I requested a meeting,” he says.
Taylor tried to reason with him. “They had a tip that I had 18,000 people, but if you spread that out over 30 days, it’s not any busier than a big garage sale. Nobody is blocking driveways.”
Taylor insists he’s also careful to limit noise and end at 10 pm, all while ensuring light displays don’t impede on neighbors’ properties.
The real issue, he says, is the money.
When Taylor took 2025 off, he “had a little bit of trouble getting things up and running” for 2026 and because of that, he shared his Venmo online, asking fans if they were willing to donate.
“We got maybe $400,” Taylor admitted. At the same time, he started selling some DJ equipment to help fund the project.
“We have been bare-bonesing hardcore to make this display work,” he says.
He certainly didn’t have the funds to hire a lawyer to help fight the allegations. Luckily, he didn’t need that.
“Three lawyers reached out to me, saying they would love to represent me about this.”
Taylor and his lawyer ultimately sent a letter to the city, asking them to spell out their “true intents” in a response no later than September 18, noting that his Halloween display is a time-sensitive issue as Taylor needs time to build.
“We never heard back,” Taylor says.
And so, Taylor’s display has been open every night this month, with 400 people showing up the first night by his own estimation. He has reservations from 25 special needs groups to come during the day throughtout the season, during which he will make special allowances to open the display.
“We haven’t had one city official come,” Taylor says. “It has been absolutely successful.”
The display is in its full glory this year. It includes about 25 different animatronics that range from 6 to 12 feet tall, each with “their own scene.” There’s the 12-foot headless horseman and a 7-foot werewolf. Forty speakers emit sounds of a rainstorm, with cracks of thunder.
Taylor’s even trenched 400 feet of yard to install his own fog system.
He expects close to 25,000 happy visitors this year.

hed: St. Louis wants to build a $3 billion tech hub — but the data center anchoring it is sparking backlash
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Best known as America’s historic brewing capital,St. Louisis seeking to reinvent itself as a regional tech hub by rolling out the red carpet for a sprawling new technology park anchored by a giantdata center—a project that has drawn public backlash and triggered legal battles.
A city of roughly 280,000 people, St. Louis already hosts more than a dozen operational data centers, with three more currently under construction in the area and up to 10 more in various stages of planning.
The most visible and controversial of the projects in the pipeline is the 120-megawatt, 525,000-square-foot hyperscale facility slated for Midtown St. Louis. The chosen site previously housed a Macy’s and Famous-Barr warehouse adjacent to the historic Armory building.
The data center, co-developed by TeraWatt Infrastructure—aSan Francisco–based company that specializes in commercial electric vehicle-charging networks—is envisioned as the linchpin of the privately funded $3.1 billionArmory Innovation District.
Sitting alongside Interstate Highway 64, the long-vacant Armory building, which previously housed a tennis training center, an entertainment complex, and a sports venue, is poised to be converted into 214,500 square feet of high-tech office and creative space.
According to developer statements, the district project will create more than 1,000 temporary union construction jobs and 200 permanent on-site positions. Prohibited from seeking tax abatements, the Armory center is projected to generate $432 million in tax revenue over its first decade, with nearly half of that amount going to St. Louis public schools.
If development proceeds on schedule, construction will get underway in August 2027 and conclude by late 2029. Supports of the project say it will give the local economy a shot in the arm.
“Data centers allow communities to repopulate the middle class,”Ron Kitchens, CEO ofGreater St. Louis, the metro’s leading economic development organization championing the Armory project and other local data centers, tells Realtor.com®.
According to Kitchens, data centers like the TeraWatt development are a boon to the local housing market because they create well-paying jobs for local residents without consuming land that could have been used for residential construction.
“We have housing demand coming on because we have electricians making $80,000,” argues Kitchens. “Families that could not talk about homeownership now have access to it.”
Both the Armory Innovation District and the adjacent data center have secured key municipal approvals, including a conditional use permit and a community benefits agreement. Under that agreement, developers are required to contribute $15.75 million toward infrastructure, digital access, job retraining for workers affected by artificial intelligence, and environmental justice activities.
However, opposition to bringing a hulking data center to Midtown St. Louis remains fierce, setting the stage for legal action on both sides.
In August, opponent groups filed a lawsuit challenging the project’s use permit, claiming that the decision to grant it was made “contrary to law.”
“These hyperscale data centers are not welcome in St. Louis, and the residents are going to continue to fight tooth and nail at every chance we get to stop them,” plaintiffKerry McCullentoldSt. Louis Public Radio at the time.
Fellow plaintiffDaniel Pateclaimed that potential negative health and environmental risks related to data centers were not thoroughly studied and taken into account before the project was green-lit by the city.
“The city is bending and twisting themselves into pretzels to try to get this thing through,” Pate said.
Just weeks later, TeraWatt, the company behind the Midtown data center, filed its own lawsuit against the city of St. Louis, reportedSt. Louis Public Radio.
In the complaint, TeraWatt partnerDavid Lambiasoalleges that two conditions the Board of Adjustment imposed as prerequisites for the construction are illegal and exceed “the scope of authority” of the board.
According to the lawsuit, forcing the data center to use 2.4 MWs of renewable energy would be “practically impossible” on the 11-acre site.
Lambiaso also took issue with a provision requiring the city’s Board of Aldermen to approve the community benefits agreement.
The rapid expansion of data infrastructure necessary to support AI buildout has been highly controversial, drawing widespread opposition over surging residential electricity rates, grid strain, high water consumption for cooling systems, noise pollution near residential areas, as well as a broader distrust of AI itself.
The technology remains unregulated at the federal level, despite recent high-profile appeals for guardrails and safety controls from industry leaders, including Anthropic’sDario Amodeiand OpenAI’sSam Altman.
In May,Gallup’s first poll on data center constructionfound 71% of Americans oppose AI data centers in their local area.
On the housing front, a recent Realtor.com report revealed that the share of U.S. home sales near large data centers has more than doubled since 2018 as the number of these facilities grew more than sevenfold.
Economists forecast that by the end of next year, more than 2% of all home sales will take place within 5 miles of a large data center.
In good news for homeowners, the analysis found that home prices near newly operational data centers rise in line with comparable neighborhoods that did not welcome a data center.
In response to local protests and following months of heated debates, St. Louis in September enacted a set of rules restricting future data center construction and operation within city limits, reported the stationKSDK.
Signed into law by MayorCara Spencer, the legislation establishes buffer zones between data centers and sensitive areas like residential neighborhoods and schools, imposes caps on noise levels, and requires facilities to transition to renewable energy over time.
AlderwomanAnne Schweitzer, who co-sponsored the bill touted by Spencer as “nation-leading,” acknowledged that while the rules provide important safeguards, they fall short of addressing every concern.
“It doesn’t stop data centers from being allowed in the city of St. Louis,” Schweitzer said. “It doesn’t prevent every single harm that could be caused. It doesn’t protect ratepayers from the increases in their utility bills that we should expect.”
Kitchens, however, believes that AI and data centers have been built up in the public imagination into “a bit of a bogeyman.”
According to the Greater St. Louis CEO, water depletion is no longer an issue in modern facilities due to the use of closed-loop cooling systems and regulations are in place protecting ratepayers from bearing data centers’ energy costs.
“The people that we care about need jobs,” he says. “Data centers are the future.”
While Kitchens acknowledged that people’s anxiety about the impact of AI on their employment is not unfounded, he believes the technology will create new opportunities that never existed before. Consequently, stalling local development is a losing strategy.
“Should there be regulation of AI? Probably, but not building a data center inMissouriand building in Taipei or Chile doesn’t stop AI. It just stops prosperity,” he argues. “We’re going to lose twice.”

hed: Amazon subleasing Seaport building, another blow to office market
content: Technology behemoth Amazon will no longer occupy about half of an office in Boston’s Seaport District, where it once planned to hire 3,000 people.Amazon is subleasing about 375,000 square feet of 1 Boston Wharf Road, a 17-story building the company was slated to fully occupy next year. Amazon’s partial exit from the space comes less than a year after CEO Andy Jassy moved leadership of the company’s Alexa AI development from Boston to Seattle. Rohit Prasad, who’d been running that group in the Seaport, left at the end of last year. (This week, he joined the Waltham robotics firm Boston Dynamics as chief executive.)Amazon’s Seaport “tech hub” was big news back in 2022. An adjacent property at 111 Harbor Way has 480,000 square feet and is occupied by Amazon employees. That first lease was set to receive some $25 million in state and city tax breaks in exchange for creating thousands of jobs, but there was no similar agreement for the 1 Boston Wharf office. An Amazon representative did not respond to requests for comment. The buildings are part of WS Development’s Seaport Square, a mammoth 20-building mixed-use project on 23 acres that includes multiple luxury apartment and condominium buildings and high-end office space. This summer, the Chestnut Hill-based company took out a $660 million mortgage on a portion of the 1 Boston Wharf property from Wells Fargo, Suffolk County property records show. WS Development declined to comment.To Mark Fallon, director of research and strategy at real estate brokerage Hunneman in Boston, such a large sublease is an example of Boston’s uneven office market recovery following the pandemic. Business leaders last month cheered Fidelity Investments reopening Commonwealth Pier, where it now expects workers to report five days a week. But this week, Amazon, a tech giant with a market capitalization of $2.76 trillion, said it no longer needs office space it had long planned to occupy.Recovery “is not going to be perfectly linear,” Fallon said. “There’s going to be fits and starts.” There’s about 2.3 million square feet of office space available for sublease in Boston, Fallon said. Of that, about 900,000 square feet is located in the Seaport District.The smaller office that Amazon already occupies, at 111 Harbor Way, is expected to eventually also house a small-format Whole Foods grocery store. Whole Foods, which Amazon owns, has not said when the store will open.The 1 Boston Wharf space, meanwhile, will have a 500-seat theater and a 100-seat black box theater, which Amazon has previously said “will add significant state-of-the-art capacity for the performing arts in Boston.” WS Development has not said when the theaters are expected to open.Amazon’s offices are close to the headquarters of Foundation Medicine, a subsidiary of Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche, at 400 Summer St. Foundation has subleased offices within its 16-story life-science laboratory to toymaker Hasbro, which intends to relocate 700 employees from Providence to its new Boston headquarters by the end of this year. Aaron Pressman of the Globe Staff contributed reporting.Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

hed: Former Patriots player’s Foxboro home hits the market, and it has a football field in the front yard
subhead: Antonio Gibson, who was released from the Patriots in January, just listed his Foxboro home for $1.2 million.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
There’s being a football fan, and then there’s having a football field in your front yard. For the next owner of former New England Patriots player Antonio Gibson’s house, those two things can co-exist.
Gibson, who was released from the Patriotsin January, just listed his Foxboro home at76 Carroll Drivefor $1.199 million.
“He’s a really good guy,” saidPaul Campanoof Keller Williams Realty, who has thelisting. “I’ve had the opportunity to work with a lot of athletes across almost every sport, and he’s one of the best.”
It’s the white-lined football field dominating the front yard that’s most noticeable upon driving up to the 4,200-square-foot colonial, which was built in 1987. The field may not be regulation size, but it’s perfect for practice.
Tucked behind a white fence at the end of a cul-de-sac in a peaceful neighborhood, the four-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bathroom house welcomes guests through a foyer with stone flooring. The flooring changes to hardwood in the formal dining room, and on the right, a spacious living room with the same hardwood floor features plenty of windows that let in natural light. Continue down the hall to the kitchen, where there’s hardwood floors, stainless steel appliances, green cabinetry, and black granite countertops. A large bay window overlooks the yard.
A great family room in the back of the house has a fireplace and large sliders that open to the hardscape patio and fire pit. On the second floor there are four bedrooms, including the spacious primary wing. The primary bathroom features a glass step-in shower and an oversized soaking tub. The primary bedroom has a walk-in closet and a passageway to a 432-square-foot additional space that could be used as a closet and dressing area. There is an additional full bathroom on this floor.
The finished basement measures around 950 square feet and has luxury vinyl plank floors. It could function as anything from a playroom to a workout space. There’s also a half-bathroom with laundry facilities.
The side driveway, which sits under a mature tree, leads to a two-car garage. The home sits on just over one acre.

hed: What’s it like to live in Salem in October? It’s a real-life ‘Halloweentown’
subhead: Salem residents describe the city as a living museum during high tourism season — and they are sometimes the exhibit.
content:
ByMegan Johnson
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Ryan Strack’s wife was sitting on the couch in theirSalem homepumping milk for their newborn daughter when someone pushed open the mail slot on the front door and peered through.
“My wife’s like, ‘What are you doing?’” Strack recalled. “They’re just tourists who have no common sense.”
For most Massachusetts homeowners, that would be an experience out of the norm. But for people who live in downtownSalem during the high tourism season — Halloween— bizarre run-ins with tourists have become par for the course.
It’s not unusual for Salem to welcomeone million visitorsover October. While the Witch City’s general population is around 45,000, that number balloons during the Halloween season. As the years go on, tourism has only increased.CBS Newsrecently reported that Salem saw 136,500 visitors on an early October Saturday, a 12 percent jump from the same Saturday last year. And for the residents of the downtown area, the growth brings joy, frustration, and a whole lot of traffic, even before the end of summer hits.
“It’s literally like the Disney movie ‘Halloweentown,’” said Gia Buxton, who owns the downtown Salem shopsZitelle, a hat bar, andLil’ Zitelle, a gelato bar, with her family, who all moved up to Salem from Long Island, including her parents. “The second the end of July hits, you see all the little witch hats on the streets and groups of bachelorette parties, and you’re like, ‘Fall is here.”
For residents who live in Salem’s downtown area, unusual characters are everywhere. Buxton is used to everyone from costumed buskers to a nun on stilts popping by for gelato.
“He eats his gelato on the top of our freezers because he’s that tall,” laughed Buxton.
Caitlin Bayer, a fundraising manager at a Salem nonprofit, frequently walks her terrier mix, Captain, on bustling streets like Essex and Washington. The pup is entirely desensitized to spooky sights — like a clown on stilts named Big Top Tiny. But the people in costume trying to make a living in Salem pale in comparison to the hordes of tourists who seem mystified by Salem residents carrying on their day-to-day lives.
“I’ve heard of people literally trying to open people’s doors before. People confuse people’s homes for a museum or a public place. I’ve heard of tourists not knowing that people actually live in Salem,” said Bayer.
In the historic McIntire District, which is known for its 18th and 19th-century architecture, residents are used to endless walking tours wandering the streets. Strack said 40-person tours come down his street three times per hour in October. While he has a fence, city regulations don’t permit him to have one that’s higher than four feet, which means people are constantly walking by staring at him as he sits on his patio.
“You’re a little zoo animal in there,” said Strack, who added that he doesn’t blame the tour attendees.
Ty Hapworth, a Salem City Councilor and a Microsoft commercial executive, has had similar uncomfortable moments, like tourists who beat up his kids’ jack-o’-lanterns and leave bottles on his steps. Last week, a person rang his doorbell and asked if the home he shares with his wife and two children was the Salem Witch Museum.
“We’re a city of [about] 40,000 people,” said Hapworth. “With 120,000 people on a Saturday in like a two-block radius of the downtown, it’s a lot.”
Caitlin Grasso moved to Salem during the pandemic when she was trying to find a place she could afford to buy. The attorney eagerly ditched her 500-square-foot rental in Southie that cost $2,700 in rent to buy a carriage house attached to a condo in Salem, where she now pays a mortgage of $1,500. After moving to Salem, she decided to buy a car; she has two parking spots and a private driveway. That’s a big bonus in a city where the biggest frustrations tend to be the excessive traffic and lack of parking. Residents say navigating the city when you need to get your kids to soccer or gymnastics can be a bit of a mess.
Bayer said she doesn’t even bother to drive into downtown at all on the weekends, and relies on walking instead.
“I get a lot of steps in in October,” she noted.
If Strack wants to go grocery shopping, he gets up extremely early in the morning during the high season.
“We have bad traffic across the board, and so when it’s already bad, it’s exacerbated a hundredfold by the influx of an additional million people in their cars,” he said.
Hapworth notes that one of the city council’s biggest challenges is finding enough residential parking in the fall when so many tourists come in.
“If you get 120,000 people coming in on a Saturday, there’s no possible way to park that many people in any city,” he said.
But it’s also getting out of town in October that gives residents stress. When Bayer and her husband were looking at Salem real estate, one of the issues they considered most was how they could manage to exit town in October.
“That definitely was a decision when trying to find a place. We looked at some places where you kind of could not escape the town center. I was like, ‘Absolutely not. This will just be a nightmare,’” she recalled.
Streets are frequently shut down to welcome foot traffic, and the city has an app to notify residents of the changes. That’s why it’s not unusual for residents to have their phones constantly going off all weekend due to the alerts. The city does its best to discourage tourists from driving in during the high season, and the MBTA adds additional commuter rail trains during October. TheSalem ferryis a particularly helpful lifeline for both tourists coming in and residents who commute into Boston for work. Hapworth noted they even encourage tourists to take an Uber to drop them off on the edge of town to minimize the traffic.
When it comes to reasons for the growing numbers of Salem tourists, residents think social media plays an influential role. Everyone floods the streets of Salem during the Halloween season hoping to get plenty of good content for TikTok and Instagram.
“It’s the start of the season you can tell when all the Instagram influencers start descending and posing on people’s doorsteps,” said Grasso.
When Hapworth first moved to Salem about 12 years ago, it was already “very busy.” About a decade later, the tourism continued to jump.
“They see an idealized version of Salem — and it’s a beautiful city — but they see that on TikTok and Instagram, and they want to come and get either their own content, or they want to come and experience something they saw on their phones,” said Hapworth, who noted six people with witch hats were currently walking by his window, while about another 40 hung out in the street outside.
While tourism benefits the city, the money that comes in isn’t quite as significant as it seems, when you consider the city has to pay out for additional police, security, overtime, porta potties, trash cleanup, and the Department of Public Works, said Hapworth.
“I think that the misconception out there is that this is a major cash cow for Salem. It’s good for the small business owners around here, and a lot of our neighbors that rely on this month,” said Hapworth. “That’s incredible. But as a city, we don’t charge admission to come in. It’s a situation where we just barely break even every year, and I think that’s the frustration residents feel sometimes.”
Despite the frustrations, residents largely say there’s still plenty of fun that comes from living in Salem.
“It’s honestly the people that we’ve met. We feel like we’ve known them for one hundred years, and they kind of take you in. We’ve just met the nicest community,” said Buxton. “It’s a great place to live.”

hed: America’s densest apartment development with 4,000 units and skyscraping heights may rise along NYC’s waterfront
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
This sure puts the “up” in upgrade.
A nine-story city office building at 100 Gold St. inManhattan’s Financial Districtstands to be demolished and replaced with a massive-scale development that could set a towering new benchmark for New York — and the nation.
That’s according tothe City Reporter, which says the city’s Economic Development Corporation is joining forces withGFP Real Estateon a proposal for two towers joined by a podium base, which together will house some 4,000 apartments. While one tower could stand at 78 stories, the other may scrape the sky at 115 stories — roughly the same height as the Empire State Building.
If thesheer number of unitsand potential height of the building raises eyebrows, those factors did just that at a Community Board meeting held on Oct. 5.
“I think it would be fair to say, correct me if I’m wrong, that this is the single most dense — from a dwelling-unit perspective — building in the history of New York City, right? This is density on steroids, isn’t it?” asked board member Patrick Kennell, according to the outlet.
Replied Brian Steinwurtzel, CEO and principal of GFP Development: “There are plenty of buildings in the Financial District and this community board district that are built to that density,” he said. “They just happen to be built as office buildings primarily.”
Not just the city, but also the densest apartment development in the nation. So much so that, if approved in its current state, 100 Gold St.’s new life could make for a population boom in the Lower Manhattan district. It could bring in 8,080 residents, whose move-ins would boost the Financial District’s population by 10%.
However, it’s unclear if this first proposal will become reality. It still must go through the environmental review process, which the team aims to begin in March, before any construction can kick off. If approved, 100 Gold St.’s current building will be demolished in 2030 — and the new development would be slated for a 2037 completion.
As it stands, the existing office building is home to the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development, other city agencies and a senior center. It requires expensive repairs; proceeds from a sale would allow for the relocation of city workers elsewhere.
The mission to redevelop 100 Gold St. began underMayor Eric Adams’ administration, which picked GFP for the work. Now, in a new administration, Mayor Zohran Mamdani aims to maximize the housing on the site to help bring 200,000 affordable units by 2036.
At 100 Gold St., approximately 1,000 units will be designated as permanently affordable, rent-stabilized residences.

hed: Gen Z renters ditch the homeownership dream for the stock market as high costs languish
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
For young renters, the American Dream may come with a stock portfolio instead of a picket fence.
Gen Z renters are more likely to identify investing as a milestone that makes them feel successful than buying a home, according to a new Entrata surveyreported by MarketWatch.
Some 37% chose investing, compared with 25% who selected homeownership — making Gen Z the only generation surveyed to put investing ahead of purchasing a property on that measure.
The findings suggest a shift in how young Americans define financial achievement as thetraditional path to homeownership grows harder to navigate.
“The data shows a clear shift in what success looks like for today’s renters. Instead of focusing on homeownership, many are prioritizing financial freedom and debt-free living,” Chase Harrington, president of Entrata, told MarketWatch.
In a separate measure, 70% of Gen Z renters associated success with financial freedom, compared with 55% who associated it with owning a home. Renters across age groups shared that preference.
The financial hurdles to buying help explain the appeal of building wealth elsewhere.
US housing costs couldtake until 2031 to return to their 2018 levelsrelative to household income — even if mortgage rates fall to 6% and annual home-price growth holds around 2.1%, according to a Redfin analysis. Buyers in New York City and Long Island could face a wait of more than a decade.
And a down payment is only the beginning.Mortgage interest,property taxes, insurance and maintenance all factor into the cost of ownership.
That leaves renters weighing whether buying is the best use of their money, particularly if a job change or growing family could prompt another move before the upfront costs pay off.
“Homeownership can be an important part of long-term financial security, but today’s home prices and mortgage rates mean that renting while investing may make more financial sense for many young people — especially if they do not expect to stay in one home for seven to 10 years,” Brian Walsh, head of advice and planning at SoFi, told MarketWatch.
“Gen Z’s focus on investing may therefore reflect a thoughtfulrent-versus-buy decisionwhile still building wealth for the future.”
The Entrata findings don’t establish that young renters have abandoned homeownership or are redirecting down-payment savings into stocks. But separate research shows younger adults are entering financial markets much earlier.
An August 2025JPMorganChase Institute analysisfound that 37% of 25-year-olds in its sample in 2024 had transferred money from checking accounts into investment accounts since age 22. Among people who turned 25 in 2015, the equivalent figure was just 6%.
Researchers pointed to falling investment minimums and trading costs, pandemic-era savings and stock-market performance as factors behind the broader rise in retail investing.
They also suggested that housing’s strained affordability may be making stocks more accessible or attractive than home equity.
But where does the money to invest come from?
For some young adults, family support helps make room in the budget — including by covering the cost of keeping a roof over their heads.
An August 2026MarketWise surveyof 704 US investors ages 18 to 34 found that 28% had relatives covering rent or housing, while 35% received help with phone bills and 21% with groceries.
Respondents invested an average of $492 monthly and estimated that one-third of their contributions would disappear without family assistance.
Some 11% said they would own no investments without that support, rising to 25% among those whose families entirely covered their housing.
The findings illustrate how parental help can support a portfolio indirectly: Covering everyday bills frees up money young adults can invest themselves.
That assistance wasn’t universal. Some 46% said their families covered none of the expenses listed in the survey.
The MarketWise sample included both Gen Z and millennials and surveyed a different group from Entrata’s renters. Still, it highlights how family resources can shape who has room to invest while renting.

hed: Homebuyers say secret property listings benefit brokers — and many feel cheated
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Homebuyers are growing suspicious of a real estate practice that keeps properties out of public view — and many believe brokers are the biggest winners.
Nearly three-quarters of buyers, or 72%, believe homes sold privately without being publicly marketed benefit real estate agents, while roughly 40% say they would feel cheated if a home matching their needs sold without their knowledge, according to a newZillow reportreleased last week.
The findings come as so-called “pocket listings” — homes marketed through private brokerage networks rather than widely advertised on public real estate platforms — fuel a growing industry battle overwho gets access to properties for sale.
While most buyers believe agents benefit from the practice, just 58% say private listings benefit sellers, and 55% believe they benefit buyers themselves, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.
“I think people have pretty good instincts about what’s fair and what’s not fair and about misalignment of incentives,” Zillow’s chief economist Mischa Fisher told The Post.
Private listings can offer homeowners greater privacy and flexibility, allowing them to test the market discreetly or avoid the disruption of publicly marketing their properties.
But critics argue that keeping homes off widely accessible listing platforms limits competition, potentially leaving buyers in the dark and sellers with fewer offers.
“It’s already a struggle enough, affordability wise, and now people are hiding inventory, making it harder to find something that’s a good match,” Fisher said, describing the challenges facing homebuyers.
The financial stakes can be significant.
A separateZillow analysisreleased in May found that homes sold through private listings typically fetched 1.3% less than comparable publicly listed properties — costing sellers an estimated $4,230 per transaction.
Based on an examination of home sales between 2023 and 2025, Zillow estimated that sellers who used private listings collectively missed out on $1.36 billion over the three-year period.
But brokerages that embrace private listings argue that the practice gives sellers greater control over how their homes are marketed.
Real estate giant Compass, which has championed a three-phase marketing strategy that introduces properties privately before a wider public launch, says the approach allows homeowners to gauge buyer interest, test asking prices and make adjustments before accumulating public days on market or a history of price cuts.
Critics, however, contend that restricting access to properties can limit the pool of potential buyers and undermine the competition that helps sellers secure the best possible price.
The controversy has sparked an increasingly bitter fight among some of the country’s biggest real estate players.
On Friday, Compass filed an antitrust lawsuit against California Regional Multiple Listing Service, accusing the industry group of unlawfully restricting how homeowners can market their properties.
Compass argues that sellers should have the freedom to market their homes outside the shared listing system, while CRMLS maintains that its rules protect an open and transparent marketplace.
The lawsuit came less than two weeks after CRMLS filed its own legal action against Compass, seeking a court declaration that its listing rules are lawful.
The dispute underscores a fundamental disagreement over whether restricting access to listings gives sellers greater control or leaves potential buyers at a disadvantage.
Despite buyers’concerns about private listings, real estate agents remain a central part of the homebuying process.
“Home buying is still very much an emotional journey,” said Fisher, emphasizing that real estate professionals remain essential to the home buying process.
Zillow found that 85% of buyers used an agent during their purchase, while 78% believed their agent’s commission was fair for the services provided.
For buyers navigating high prices and limited inventory, however,the possibility of missing out on homesthey never even knew were for sale adds another layer of frustration.

hed: San Francisco’s doomed mall probed as future data center
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Just months after closing, San Francisco’s Centre mall could be turned into amassive AI data center.
Maryland-based financial advisory firm KG Growth Partners inquired about a permit for a data center at the shuttered mall in June, theSan Francisco Chroniclereports.
The firm told the City of San Francisco that it is working with an unidentified partner who is interested in the 350,000-square-foot portion of the mall that was once home to a Bloomingdale’s.

The news comes just as San Francisco istaking measures against AI data centers. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie signed a moratorium barring the city from approving new data centers for 45 days.
Under the moratorium, he San Francisco Planning Department is tasked with studying the impacts of data centers.
San Francisco Centre Mall closed in January 2026 after suffering a high vacancy rate and the closure of several major businesses, including Nordstrom in 2025 and Bloomingdale’s in 2025.
KG’s CEO Jared Kreiger shared details of the planned project with the Chronicle, saying the ground floors of the building would remain ‘active and open’, while upper floors would be reserved for technical use.
“Downtown San Francisco has a vacancy problem in exactly this building type, and the premise is that reuse with a mixed public and technical program does more for the block than a dark box does,” Kreiger said.
The proposed new owner plans to partner with ‘known AI Lab’ for the development, to create AI-controlled living space,” continued.
“Our client is interested, in partnership with a known AI Lab, in developing the mall property, including Bloomingdale’s, into an AI-controlled living space,” Krieger said, further telling the Chronicle that the planned facility’s “proprietary AI design can utilize resources, such as dedicating water to a rooftop garden. This would then be donated to a nonprofit focusing on food insecurity for use in transient shelters.”
While Kreiger declined to share who KG’s client was, the Chronicle reported last month that commercial real estate firm  B3 Investors was nearing a deal to purchase the Bloomingdale’s section of the mall, and also put in a bid to buy the rest of the mall.
Earlier this year, Presidio Bay Ventures and Prado Group purchased the mall, with plans to convert it into a retail and commercial space. But the developers walked away from the deal in July due to failed talks over the ground lease.
Former mayor London Breed floated the idea of turning the mall into a soccer stadium back in 2023, while a more recent plan from Urban Land Development and TMG Partners suggests the space be transformed into a multi-level sports complex complete with a members-only club and a basketball academy.

hed: Some say this North End building is jarringly modern, an eyesore, and worse. Its owner says wait and see.
subhead: The unfinished project at the gateway to the neighborhood has split residents and tourists
content: For Frank DePasquale, new ventures are old hat. The prominent restaurateur owns more than a half-dozen establishments in the North End, where he is known as the neighborhood’s unofficial mayor. But sipping an espresso at Dolce, his gelato shop, on a brisk autumn morning, DePasquale said he’s been baffled and frustrated by the criticism swirling around his latest, biggest, and possibly last project — a building some critics have panned as jarringly modern, an eyesore, and worse.“Anybody could critique it right now,” he said. ”They look at it and they see an empty building. That’s like you’re putting a T-shirt on, and you still haven’t put on your suit and tie."The project at the entrance to the North End on Cross Street will bring shops, restaurants, and an Italian culinary school to what until recently was a block of blighted and vacant storefronts.North End restauranteur Frank DePasquale opened a sliding doorway inside the new development on Cross Street during a tour of the building on Oct. 7.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffIts look, while still incomplete, has sharply divided residents and tourists over whether the contemporary facade of matte stucco and metal siding fits the character of Boston’s oldest neighborhood.Construction began last year, but the controversy erupted after a local food influencer posted a video on social media with a photo of the half-finished building provocatively titled “Why the North End’s new entrance is so ugly.” The video has earned more than 10,000 likes.Will Watson said his account, @willeatsboston, usually focuses on food-related content. But as a former resident and frequent visitor to the neighborhood, he said he feels the new building, as it stands now, is a “missed opportunity.”“The North End is very warm, inviting — you know, brick but also colorful,” Watson said in an interview. “You walk down Prince Street and you have those really beautiful, old-school, oxidized sides on the houses ... it has a great patina to it.”A new building in the North End has sparked online controversyCritics say the building doesn't match the North End's historic character. Frank DePasquale, the owner and North End restaurateur, says to be patient. (Video by Maria Pemberton/Globe Staff.)“A very modern, strip mall-esque, gray building with neon lights for the signage just doesn’t really match,” he said. Many commenters agreed, heaping scorn on the design and color scheme. Some residents aren’t sold either.“I feel like most of the places in the North End are all old buildings, and the people who live here are fine with living in old buildings because it has that charm,” said Emily Newton, 26, gazing up at the unfinished structure. “And this just doesn’t.”DePasquale has bristled at the uproar over a project that he views as part of his legacy in the neighborhood where he and his family have lived for decades. But he’s confident the critics will come around.“I forgive them,” he said. “Because they haven’t seen the final product, you know. Because when they see the final product, they’re going to say, ‘Wow.’”The new development on Cross Street (left) in the North End in September. Pat Greenhouse/Globe StaffThis stretch of Cross Street has long been described as the unofficial gateway to the North End. When the Big Dig opened the neighborhood to the rest of the city by tearing down the old Central Artery, the project’s backers said that keeping local business on Cross Street was “crucial” to preserving the neighborhood’s character.That has been easier said than done.At various points, this stretch of Cross Street has hosted a liquor store, a juice bar, and a nail salon. Bread & Butter, a bakery-cafe, closed in 2015. A proposed Starbucks stalled in 2018 after fierce community opposition. For years, the property sat vacant. Tom Damigella, president of the North End Historical Society, said anything would be better than such an “eyesore.”“You have to uplift the neighborhood. You’ve got to keep enhancing it, keep improving the infrastructure,” he said. Other locals said they are perfectly happy with the design.“There’s just so much brick down here; to try to replicate that would just look artificial,” longtime resident Vincent Marasa said. “He went in a completely different direction, which I think is really great.”A rendering of a planned boutique hotel on Cross Street in Boston's North End, which would have been next to DePasquale's development. The hotel, like many planned developments on Cross Street, ultimately did not come to fruition.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffDePasquale’s plan, revised after community feedback, was approved by the city in 2024.“Right now, my goal is to make everybody happy,” he said. Last week, painters began replacing the dark grey exterior with a warmer shade of brown, a change DePasquale said was always part of the plan. Builders are installing striped awnings over the windows and marble wainscoting.Once the building is done, DePasquale said, there will be plenty of signs of the neighborhood’s heritage: falling vines, flower boxes, a repaired Freedom Trail sidewalk, and patio seating to rival “any piazza in Italy.”Rooftops of older buildings in the neighborhood hovered above the new development in the North End.  David L. Ryan/Globe StaffRenderings of the new development's exterior and its interior stairwell, along with a photo of the Cross Street plaza as it looked before redevelopment (top).David L. Ryan/Globe StaffRenderings show a building less at odds with its surroundings, and publicizing them might have blunted some of the criticism. But DePasquale said he was reluctant to ”show the whole world what I’m doing before I do it.“ “If you come to one of my restaurants, you’re not going to show the steak uncooked; you wait till the steak is done, and then you taste it and say, ‘Wow.’”If people are looking for a postcard-style image of the past, they will be disappointed, DePasquale said. “But for an entrance coming into the greatest inner-city Italian community in the country, this is what it is.” The work-in-progress interior of DePasquale's Pastry, one of several new businesses that will open in the new development on Cross Street.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffLucy Maulsby, a historian of architecture and urbanism at Northeastern University, said that these kinds of tensions are “almost always present when you insert something new into the historical fabric.”“The ‘new’ is never going to be the ‘old,’ so there is inherently a conflict there,” she said. For Americans who might imagine Italy as somehow insulated from the modern world, it’s not just a matter of what an Italian American neighborhood should look like, it’s also a question of what it means to be Italian American, she said. ”The debate is perhaps less about the building and more about a whole set of other issues that are being projected," Maulsby said. DePasquale, for his part, says he simply wants the new building to be worthy of the neighborhood.“Why should just the Seaport have these beautiful buildings? Why not the North End as well?” he said. “You know, the Back Bay, the South End — why should they be the only ones to say welcome?”A worker walked through the interior of the new development on Cross Street in the North End.David L. Ryan/Globe StaffCamilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.

hed: Neighbors fiercely protested this housing project for formerly homeless people. It opened anyway.
content: For a moment in 2023, it looked like the same powerful force that derails many housing projects might have the traction to stop the redevelopment of an old Comfort Inn on Morrissey Boulevard into homes for formerly homeless people: neighborhood opposition. For all the social good the project promised, neighbors fiercely protested. Some complained it would transform the area into another Mass. and Cass, the intersection in the South End that has become an epicenter of the region’s addiction crisis and the city’s largest homeless encampment.But the two nonprofits heading up the project — The Community Builders and the Pine Street Inn — trudged ahead, and on Wednesday, the revamped hotel officially opened its doors, with 96 of its 99 new single-occupancy units already home to people who used to live on the street. “The way to solve homelessness is to build homes,” Mayor Michelle Wu said at an event Wednesday marking the project’s opening. “The numbers show that this works, but we know that actually this isn’t about numbers at all. It’s about people. It’s about neighbors.”Related: From 2023: Despite neighborhood pushback, BPDA OKs homeless housing in Dorchester hotelIt’s the latest investment in the city in the so-called permanent supportive housing model, which places formerly homeless people in their own apartments, with services like caseworkers and counseling under the same roof. The model is aimed specifically at the city’s chronically homeless population, which includes people living with severe mental or physical health issues, substance use disorders, or developmental disabilities. For many in those groups, the temporary shelter system has historically been ineffective. The new Comfort Inn project, which was developed by The Community Builders and will have on-site services run by Pine Street, is one of only a handful of standalone, permanent, supportive housing projects in New England. (Many of the roughly 4,000 supportive housing units in Massachusetts are leased apartments in private buildings.)“All of the tenants here are over 62,” said Lyndia Downie, executive director of Pine Street Inn. “Six are veterans. More importantly, everyone here is now a tenant with a key. They’re friends. They’re neighbors. They aren’t worried about where they are going to sleep tonight.”From the outside, the new development doesn’t look like much. The boxy, five-story building sits on a concrete island between the six-lane Morrissey Boulevard and Red Line tracks. It still has the same hotel entrance canopy at the front of the building, tan finishes, and the same narrow hallways that stretch between rooms. But the old hotel rooms were all torn out and redone with modern finishes, new appliances, and marble countertops. Residents of the site have access to free laundry services. On the fourth floor, developers knocked down a wall between two rooms and transformed the space into a small library. There are movie nights in a common space on the first floor. For the building’s new residents, living there has already been transformative.Reginald, a new resident of the permanent supportive housing development at 900 Morrissey Boulevard, said living in the new building has transformed his life.John Wilcox, City of Boston/John WilcoxOne new resident, Reginald, who did not want to use his last name, has called a studio apartment on the fourth floor home since December 2025. It is the first permanent home he has had in years. While battling substance abuse, Reginald lived “in a cardboard box” on the street for two years before moving into Pine Street’s temporary shelter. When he found out he would have an apartment to himself in the new Comfort Inn building, “I felt the direction of my life shift,” he said. With the help of caseworkers, he’s been sober for a year now, he said, and is training for a job in the restaurant industry. “Just being able to close my door and get away from the cold, the turmoil outside,” he said. “It has changed my life.”Related: ‘Unimaginably inhumane’: Federal cuts threaten to undo Boston’s progress fighting homelessnessStill, projects like the Comfort Inn development are often controversial. Another permanent supportive housing project by the two nonprofits on Washington Street in Jamaica Plain drew a lawsuit from neighbors in 2020 who claimed the zoning decision to allow it was flawed. That project opened its doors last year.At the Comfort Inn, neighbors and local representatives, including State Senator Nick Collins and former city councilor Frank Baker, protested over concerns that housing nearly 100 formerly homeless people at the site would bring an influx of drugs and crime to the neighborhood. At one point, opponents protested outside the hotel, holding signs with images of people living on the street in the neighborhood.People expressed their concerns during a protest outside a Comfort Inn on Morrissey Boulevard in Boston on Dec. 17, 2022. Craig F. Walker/Globe StaffThe Boston Planning and Development Agency board greenlit the project in May 2023 after developers scaled the project down by 11 units and pledged to allow only residents 62 or older. Lately, the Trump administration has sought to curtail permanent supportive housing, which relies heavily on federal funding. Advocates in the state have said proposed federal cuts aimed at shifting away from the model could put some chronically homeless people back on the street. “No matter what bad faith arguments people put out there, there is a very deep human truth to the need for a roof over your head and the way in which people are able to flourish when they have it,” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “And it is by people seeing that reality and how it’s changed the lives of other people we will continue to make projects like this happen.”Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

hed: Home of the Week: This Hingham Cape dating back to 1687 has been renovated for 2026 living
subhead: The historic Samuel Hobart House is on the market for $1.5 million.
content:
ByJohn R. Ellement
Send this article to your social connections.
Send this article to your social connections.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

217 North St., Hingham

$1.499 million

StyleCape

Year built1687; renovated since

Square feet2,665

Bedrooms4

Baths2 full, 1 half

Sewer/WaterPublic

Taxes$11,000 (2026, estimate)


Like the South Shore town it sits in, this Cape-style home, known as the Samuel Hobart House, has grown. It was built around 1687, about 50 years after the settlement of Bare Cove was renamed Hingham,town historic societyandmunicipal records show.

According to studies of the Samuel Hobart House by the Massachusetts Historical Commission, then is now. The  classic face of a Cape persists with the main entry in the center topped by a four-window transom that is flanked by two bays of double-hung windows. The single massive chimney of brick still rises above the sloped roof broken only by two ridged gables.


Beyond the front door is a horizontal hallway connecting the wings of the home while directly ahead is a historic feature. The narrow, twisting central stairwell is enclosed by “vertical board panels … cut to form a curve,” a historic researcher wrote. There are three closets in the foyer.

Time has expanded this home beyond the traditional Cape. The first floor is 1,501 square feet divided up into a great room, living room, family room, dining area, kitchen, and breakfast room. And the flooring in the majority of this level is wide planked pine — fully refinished — as was used back in the day.


The three spaces at the front of the house (the 256-square-foot great room, 210-square-foot family room, and 415-square-foot living room) are built around the central chimney and each has a brick-framed fireplace with a wooden mantel. However, only the living room’s massive 7-foot wide fireplace is currently functional; the others must be tested. Along with multiple double-hung windows in each room, there is now recessed lighting.


Features in the family room include an embossed tin ceiling with an egg and dart motif and a glass tiered drum chandelier in the center of the room that looks like a waterfall. The walls have white wainscoting with the upper level colored by flat-style rose. The living room, along with the large fireplace, has built-in bookshelves sitting on an exterior wall.



In the right rear of the home, the kitchen has just a touch of the past. There is an island topped by a shiny plank of wood with an overhang with seating for three. The flooring is tile, the countertops are speckled granite, and the appliances are stainless steel, including a high-end six-burner gas stove. The Shaker-style cabinets are white. The white farmhouse-style sink is installed in undermount fashion beneath a bank of three double-hung windows. There is a walk-in pantry.

From the kitchen, a tiled hallway runs along the back of the house hosting a wide stairwell to the second floor, a door to the rear brick patio with a pergola, and to a 125-square-foot mudroom with the home’s half bath.


Reflecting the current era and expansion over the centuries, there are now three separate stairwells to the second floor where the primary suite, three bedrooms, and the two full bathrooms are located. The secondary bedrooms are in the rear of the house and range in size from 194 to 121 square feet. Flooring remains refinished wide planked pine.

The shared 48-square-foot bathroom has a hexagonal tiled shower behind a clear glass door, hexagonal marble tile flooring, and a white cabinet vanity with white farmhouse sink.



The primary suite spreads across roughly half the entire second level and has four closets, 28 square feet of storage, and the laundry room. The 345-square-foot bedroom has its own brick-lined fireplace, wide planked pine flooring, and white painted beams crossing the sloping ceiling that created a visually dramatic frame for the entire space. Natural light is pulled in through sets of windows on three walls.



The 152-square-foot private full bathroom is across a short hallway. It contains a cathedral ceiling rising to a gable peak crossed by hand-hewn exposed wooden beams, a double vanity underneath a large mirror, and wide planked pine flooring. There is a large soaking tub and a separate glass-enclosed shower with a subway tile backsplash. At the peak of the ceiling is a circular window, sometimes called an oculus. There are additional windows on two walls.

There is a full, unfinished basement. Baseboard heat is by gas.

Tara Coveney of Coldwell Bankerin Hingham has the listing.

hed: America’s dismal housing market to get even worse in 2027, grim forecast predicts
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
America’s already frozen housing market could be headed for an even deeper chill next year — with Goldman Sachs warning that stubbornlyhigh mortgage rateswill keep buyers sidelined and homeowners trapped in their properties.
The Wall Street giant predicts just 3.9 million existing homes will change hands in 2027, slightly fewer than this year and a staggering 26% below pre-pandemic levels in 2019, according to aMarketWatch reportpublished Tuesday.
The grim outlook comes as mortgage rates have climbed back above 7%, further squeezing would-be buyers already struggling withsky-high home prices.
“In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker wrote in a note to clients Monday.
At the heart of the problem is a growing divide between homeowners who secured rock-bottom mortgage rates during the pandemic — and even earlier — and prospective buyers now facing dramatically higher borrowing costs.
More than 95% of existing mortgage borrowers have interest rates below current market levels, while 65% have rates at least 2 percentage points lower, according to Goldman Sachs.
That means millions of Americans have little financial incentive to sell their homes, since moving would likely mean trading an affordable mortgage for a significantly more expensive one.
The phenomenon, known as the mortgage-rate lock-in effect, has helped keep the housing market in a deep freeze even as demand from prospective buyers remains constrained by affordability challenges.
Mortgage rates have surged nearly 1.5 percentage points since their February lows, making the prospect of moving even less appealing.
And while the number of homes available for sale has improved, inventory remains historically tight, according to Goldman Sachs.
There are some bright spots, including favorable demographic trends and expectations that wage growth will outpace inflation. But those positives may not be enough to revive the market.
Surveys show Americans’intentions to purchase homes have fallen sharply in recent months, while reduced immigration is expected to weigh on household formation and housing demand.
Goldman Sachs isn’t alone in its gloomy assessment.
TheMortgage Bankers Associationrecently forecast that total single-family mortgage lending will decline 5% in 2027 to just under $2 trillion, down from an estimated $2.1 trillion this year.
The industry group also expects new-home construction to slow, while national home-price growth decelerates next year before gradually picking up again in 2028.
“We expect declining levels of new construction for both single-family and multifamily homes over the forecast period,” MBA deputy chief economist Joel Kan said in a statement.
The bleak outlook is already taking a toll on housing-related investments.
The SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF has fallen roughly 9% this year, while the iShares Mortgage Real Estate ETF has plunged about 24%, according to MarketWatch.
For Americans hoping the housing market would finally thaw in 2027, Wall Street’s latest forecast suggests the wait could stretch even longer.

hed: California mobile home park doubles rent on senior residents after sale
content:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Residents of the Crestview HillsMobile HomePark in Fallbrook, CA, are facing two rent increases this year as the community is under new ownership.
The 55-and-older community was recently purchased by a new owner, which informed the residents of a second rent increase due to aproperty taxreassessment.
“The recent sale of Crestview Hills will result in a substantial and near-term property tax reassessment, including supplementalproperty taxespayable by the new owner. And higher ongoing annual property taxes,” reads the letter, according toKGTV.
The management company provided tenants with information about a subsidized rent program in addition to informing them about the additional increase.
ResidentRita Burn, who provided KGTV with the letter from the company, said that her rent has nearly doubled since she moved into Crestview Hills.
When Burn moved into the park when she retired in 2017, she paid $825 a month for rent. Now, her rent is $1,600 per month and could climb higher if a second increase goes through.
Burn, who is on a fixed income, was shocked to find out a second increase was coming.
“I couldn’t believe it. I mean, I had heard rumors that it was gonna happen and then we got the letter,” she told KGTV.
A spokesperson from the park’s management company, Cabrillo Management Corporation, toldRealtor.com®that the rent increase was calculated based upon two elements: the replacement of the park’s sewer system and the anticipated increase in property taxes following the park’s sale.
“This increase covers the cost of the sewer system and the estimated property tax increase costs moving forward. Please know that this increase is not profitable to ownership this simply covers increased operating cost,” read the company’s emailed statement.
The email noted that Crestview Hills is a “five star community” with a clubhouse, pool and Jacuzzi, dog park, and fitness center, and that “continued investment helps maintain the quality of the community.”
Cabrillo Management Corporation did not provide details on the amount that resident rent went up at either of this year’s increases.
Manufactured homes, widely known as mobile homes, are structures built off-site and assembled on-site without a permanent foundation.
While they were traditionally built on a chassis with wheels, hence the nickname “mobile” home, modern manufactured homes are not generally intended to be moved for more than their initial placement inside a manufactured-home park such as Crestview Hills.
Experts believe that manufactured housing is an alternative way to build cheaper homes. However, as a long stigmatized product, financial ease and modernization are necessary.
Earlier this year, the bipartisan Housing for the 21st Century Act was passed, which, among other things, removes the requirement for all manufactured housing to be built on a permanent chassis.
Being built without a chassis cuts down the cost of a unit by roughly $10,000.
Then, in early October, theU.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development announcedplans to upgrade its energy efficiency standards, update design and construction codes, and scale the industry in order to keep pace with efforts to encourage the building of manufactured housing.
While encouraging the construction of manufactured homes shows progress, another part of the equation needs to be addressed: rental practices for manufactured home spaces.
San Diego County, where Fallbrook is located, does not have specific rental laws for mobile-home parks, and instead defers to California’s statewideMobilehome Residency Law(MRL).
“State law does not regulate the amounts of rent that can be charged to a homeowner for rent in a mobilehome park,” reads the MRL.
While most rentals in California are subject to AB 1482, which states that the maximum annual rent increase is limited to 10% and consists of a local cost-of-living adjustment of no more than 5%, mobile-home parks are exempt from rent-control laws.
The MRL requires that management provides at least a 90-day written notice of any increase in rent, but lays out few other restrictions on mobilehome park rent.
Still, Burn and other residents of Crestview Hills are hoping find a solution to the second increase.
“As a group, I think we wanna come up with a plan. Quite a few of us have written to our congressmen and officials to see if they can help in any way. We’re hoping to get some legal advice,” said Burn.
Cabrillo Management informed Realtor.com that a meeting for all homeowners to “discuss the rent increase, the rent subsidy program, and other questions or concerns” as been scheduled.
